Per Isaiam quoque impio loquitur Deus: Ponam circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum maxillis tuis.
paras.en: [[5:16|And to the needy there shall be hope|Et erit egeno spes]] of escape. For from his experience of God's help and of his providence in the governing of men, he puts his hope in God. And God himself is his hope, that is, the object of his trust, and the more so the less he sees that he is to be helped by men. So let us too always trust in the Lord, obeying his commandments, according to that word: [[Osee 12:6|hope in thy God always|Spera in Deo tuo semper]]. [[5:16|but iniquity shall draw in her mouth|Iniquitas autem contrahet os suum]], that is, the wicked, held down by the power of God, will be curbed from the words of wickedness that they are used to. The Psalmist too declares this: [[Ps 106:41|he helped|Adjuvit]], he says, [[Ps 106:41|the poor out of poverty|pauperem de inopia]]; [[Ps 106:42|and all iniquity shall stop her mouth|et omnis iniquitas oppilabit os suum]]. And again: [[Ps 62:12|the mouth is stopped of them that speak wicked things|Obstructum est os loquentium iniqua]]. Through Isaias too God says to the wicked man: [[Is 37:29|I will put a ring in thy nose, and a bit between thy lips|Ponam circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum maxillis tuis]] [Denis reads *maxillis*, "jaws", where the Vulgate has *in labiis*, "lips"].

paras.t: Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino, id est, qui in præsenti castigatur et emendatur a Deo per suæ paternæ pietatis flagella aut increpatoria verba. Hoc enim est signum paternæ dilectionis, curæ atque clementiæ Dei ad hominem, quum peccata sint animæ vulnera, quæ per adversa tanquam emplastra optimaque remedia jam curantur. Propter quod Dominus protestatur: Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Et alibi inducitur: Etenim multo tempore non sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium. Hinc Jeremias sapienter rogavit: Corripe me, Domine; verumtamen in judicio, et non in furore tuo. Porro non castigari ita a Deo, sed in propriis voluntatibus derelinqui, et cum securitate peccare atque ad libitum prosperari, horribilissimum est, indiciumque maximæ iræ ac odii Dei, et metuendissima ultio ejus, secundum quod ipse de reprobis fatetur in Psalmo: Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum; ibunt in adinventionibus suis. Et per Ezechielem indurato populo ait: Zelus meus recessit a te: non irascar tibi amplius. Cupiamus ergo nunc visitari a Deo; patientiamque postulemus ab eo, qua omnem vitæ hujus adversitatem æquanimiter toleremus, tanquam purgamentum vitiorum nostrorum, et tanquam præparamentum gratiæ amplioris, pensantes illud Apostoli: Quum judicamur autem, a Domino corripimur, ut non cum hoc mundo damnemur. Et illud: Quis filius quem non corripit pater? Quod si extra disciplinam estis, ergo adulteri, et non filii estis.
paras.en: [[5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth|Beatus homo qui corripitur a Domino]], that is, who in this present life is chastised and amended by God through the scourges or the rebuking words of his fatherly love. For this is a sign of God's fatherly love, care and clemency towards man, since sins are wounds of the soul, which are healed even now by adversities as by plasters and the best of remedies. For this reason the Lord declares: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. And elsewhere it is set down: [[2 Mach 6:13|it is a token of great goodness, when sinners are not suffered to go on in their ways for a long time, but are presently punished|Etenim multo tempore non sinere peccatoribus ex sententia agere, sed statim ultiones adhibere, magni beneficii est indicium]]. Hence Jeremias wisely prayed: [[Jer 10:24|Correct me, O Lord, but yet with judgment: and not in thy fury|Corripe me, Domine; verumtamen in judicio, et non in furore tuo]]. But not to be chastised thus by God, and instead to be left to one's own will, to sin without fear and to prosper at one's pleasure, is most horrible: a sign of God's greatest wrath and hatred, and his most fearful vengeance; as he himself declares of the reprobate in the Psalm: [[Ps 80:13|I let them go according to the desires of their heart: they shall walk in their own inventions|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum; ibunt in adinventionibus suis]]. And through Ezechiel he says to the hardened people: [[Ezech 16:42|my jealousy shall depart from thee|Zelus meus recessit a te]]: I will [[Ezech 16:42|be angry no more|non irascar tibi amplius]]. Let us desire, then, to be visited by God now; and let us ask him for patience, by which we may bear every adversity of this life with an even mind, as a purging of our vices and a preparing for fuller grace, weighing that word of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 11:32|But whilst we are judged, we are chastised by the Lord, that we be not condemned with this world|Quum judicamur autem, a Domino corripimur, ut non cum hoc mundo damnemur]]. And that one: [[Heb 12:7|what son is there whom the father doth not correct?|Quis filius quem non corripit pater?]] [[Heb 12:8|But if you be without chastisement|Quod si extra disciplinam estis]], [[Heb 12:8|then are you bastards and not sons|ergo adulteri, et non filii estis]].

paras.t: Ex his Eliphaz convertit se ad exhortationem ipsius Job, quem putavit ex impatientia, desperatione et tædio vitæ, verba capituli tertii protulisse etiam secundum rationem passione devictam, videlicet, Pereat dies in qua natus sum. Increpationem ergo Domini, id est hanc tuam tribulationem et quamcumque adversitatem tibi ex judicio divinæ providentiæ accidentem, ne reprobes, murmurando et maledicendo; quia ipse vulnerat, peccatorem in corpore plagando, et medetur, inflictam plagam tollendo, et consolationem præstando, a vitiisque purgando: imo vulnerando medetur, ita quod ejus vulneratio est peccati medela. Pœnæ etenim vitæ præsentis sunt remedia vitiorum. Sic et medicus vulnerando medetur, dum incidendo expellit materiam morbum causantem. Percutit pœna, et manus ejus sanabunt a culpa, itemque crebro a pœna inflicta, quemadmodum in Deuteronomio testatur: Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam; percutiam, et ego sanabo. Salomon quoque huic alludit doctrinæ, dicens: Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, et ne deficias quum ab eo corriperis. Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit; et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi. Et Apostolus ad Hebræos: Omnis disciplina in præsenti quidem non videtur esse gaudii, sed mœroris; postea autem fructum pacatissimum exercitatis per eam reddet justitiæ. Postremo, ad patientem ac humilem disciplinæ, sive in verbis, sive in pœnis susceptionem, potissime monent nos libri Sapientiales; laudantque eos, qui eam gratanter recipiunt, eam vero spernentes dire vituperant. Hinc nempe scriptum est: Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur. Alibi quoque: Qui projicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis. Similiter in Ecclesiastico legitur: Quam bonum est correptum manifestare pœnitentiam! Sic enim effugies peccatum.
paras.en: From this Eliphaz turns to exhorting Job himself, whom he thought had spoken the words of the third chapter out of impatience, despair and weariness of life, and even with his reason overcome by passion: namely, [[Job 3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]]. Therefore [[5:17|the chastising of the Lord|Increpationem ergo Domini]], that is, this tribulation of yours and whatever adversity befalls you by the judgment of divine providence, [[5:17|refuse not|ne reprobes]] it by murmuring and cursing; [[5:18|For he woundeth|quia ipse vulnerat]], striking the sinner in his body, [[5:18|and cureth|et medetur]], taking away the stroke he has dealt, giving consolation and purging from vices: nay, he heals by wounding, so that his wounding is the remedy of sin. For the pains of the present life are remedies for vices. So too the physician heals by wounding, when by cutting he drives out the matter that causes the disease. [[5:18|he striketh|Percutit]] with punishment, [[5:18|and his hands shall heal|et manus ejus sanabunt]] from guilt, and often also from the punishment inflicted; as he testifies in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live: I will strike, and I will heal|Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam; percutiam, et ego sanabo]]. Solomon too alludes to this teaching, saying: [[Prov 3:11|My son, reject not the correction of the Lord: and do not faint when thou art chastised by him:|Disciplinam Domini, fili mi, ne abjicias, et ne deficias quum ab eo corriperis]] [[Prov 3:12|For whom the Lord loveth, he chastiseth: and as a father in the son he pleaseth himself.|Quem enim diligit Dominus, corripit; et quasi pater in filio complacet sibi]] And the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:11|all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy, but sorrow: but afterwards it will yield to them that are exercised by it the most peaceable fruit of justice|Omnis disciplina in præsenti quidem non videtur esse gaudii, sed mœroris; postea autem fructum pacatissimum exercitatis per eam reddet justitiæ]]. Lastly, the Sapiential books above all urge us to receive correction patiently and humbly, whether in words or in punishments; and they praise those who receive it gladly, but sharply rebuke those who spurn it. For thus it is written: [[Prov 13:18|Poverty and shame to him that refuseth instruction: but he that yieldeth to reproof shall be glorified.|Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur]] And elsewhere: [[Prov 15:32|He that rejecteth instruction, despiseth his own soul: but he that yieldeth to reproof, possesseth understanding.|Qui projicit disciplinam, despicit animam suam; qui autem acquiescit increpationibus, possessor est cordis]] [Denis reads *projicit*, "casteth away", where the Vulgate has *abjicit*] Likewise we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:4|How good is it, when thou art reproved, to shew repentance!|Quam bonum est correptum manifestare pœnitentiam!]] [[Ecclus 20:4|for so thou shalt escape|Sic enim effugies]] sin.

paras.t: Consequenter Eliphaz specificat, a quibus adversitatibus eruendus fuerit Job, si pœnitentiam veram egisset, atque illata flagella de manu Dei æquanimiter suscepisset. In sex tribulationibus liberabit te, et in septima non tanget te malum. Hæc autem liberatio dupliciter potest intelligi. Primo, per anticipationem, ita quod nulla earum eveniet justo, seu peccatori per pœnitentiam et flagella sufficienter purgato et emendato. Secundo, per sublationem, ita quod quum aliqua earum cuique evenerit, auferetur, si ille pœnitentiam fecerit. Quumque per sex fuerit emendatus, in septima adversum nil patietur.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz specifies from what adversities Job would have been delivered if he had done true penance and had borne with an even mind the scourges laid on him by the hand of God. [[5:19|In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh, evil shall not touch thee.|In sex tribulationibus liberabit te, et in septima non tanget te malum.]] Now this deliverance can be understood in two ways. First, by prevention: so that none of them shall befall the just man, or the sinner sufficiently purged and amended by penance and scourges. Secondly, by removal: so that when any of them befalls someone, it will be taken away if he does penance. And when he has been amended through six, in the seventh he will suffer nothing adverse.

paras.t: Deinde nominat tribulationes. In fame eruet te de morte, id est, tempore caristiæ aliis fame labentibus, necessaria vitæ habebis. Vel, In fame, id est, si famem ex naturalium defectu pertuleris, providebitur tibi a Deo ne pereas fame. Et in bello de manu gladii, id est, si in bellum descenderis, non permittet te Deus occidi. Hæc est tribulatio secunda. De tertia subditur: A flagello linguæ absconderis, id est, persecutionem verborum ab aliis non patieris, videlicet detractionem, convitia, diffamiam. Justus enim, vereque pœnitens, digni sunt laudibus, exemplaresque aliis. Ideo eis non debent verborum inferre molestiam. Unde Ecclesiasticus dicit: A laqueo linguæ iniquæ liberasti me. Hæc tria Eliphaz commemoravit, quoniam fames causata est sancto Job ex ablatione substantiæ; bellum, quia Chaldæi contra eum tres turmas fecerunt; flagellum linguæ ex improperio conjugis. Et non timebis calamitatem, id est cladem pestilentialem sive hostilem, quum venerit aliis, certus de protectione divina. Hæc est tribulatio quarta. Alias duas tangens, subjungit: In vastitate, id est fructuum devastatione vel hominum oppressione, et fame inde procedente, ridebis, id est, lætus eris, quia nullum istorum tunc patieris. Sed quum superius posuerit famem pro prima tribulatione, cur nunc eam resumit et ponit pro sexta? Et respondendum, quod ibi sumitur fames pro ea, quæ generatur ex terræ sterilitate; hic pro ea, quæ concomitatur vastitatem terræ ab hostibus. Hæc tria Eliphaz dixit, quoniam filii et filiæ Job erant sibi repente ablati, sicut in pestilentia; et quoniam bona ejus erant a Chaldæis et Sabæis vastata, ex qua re etiam penuria sibi exorta est. Et bestias terræ non formidabis, quia securus eris, quod nec tibi, nec soboli aut familiæ, seu gregibus tuis nocebunt.
paras.en: Then he names the tribulations. [[5:20|In famine he shall deliver thee from death|In fame eruet te de morte]]: that is, in a time of dearth, when others are failing from hunger, thou shalt have the necessities of life. Or, [[5:20|In famine|In fame]]: that is, if thou suffer hunger through a failure of the fruits of nature, God will provide for thee so that thou perish not of hunger. [[5:20|and in battle, from the hand of the sword|Et in bello de manu gladii]]: that is, if thou go down to war, God will not let thee be slain. This is the second tribulation. Of the third he adds: [[5:21|Thou shalt be hidden from the scourge of the tongue|A flagello linguæ absconderis]]: that is, thou shalt not suffer persecution of words from others, namely detraction, abuse, defamation. For the just and the truly penitent are worthy of praise and an example to others; therefore men ought not to trouble them with words. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 51:3|from the snare of an unjust tongue|A laqueo linguæ iniquæ]] thou hast delivered me. Eliphaz mentioned these three because hunger was brought upon holy Job by the taking away of his substance; war, because the Chaldeans made three troops against him; and the scourge of the tongue by the reproaches of his wife. [[5:21|and thou shalt not fear calamity|Et non timebis calamitatem]], that is, slaughter by pestilence or by the enemy, [[5:21|when it cometh|quum venerit]] upon others, being sure of God's protection. This is the fourth tribulation. Touching on the other two, he adds: [[5:22|In destruction|In vastitate]], that is, in the laying waste of the fruits or the oppression of men, [[5:22|and famine|et fame]] that comes of it, [[5:22|thou shalt laugh|ridebis]], that is, thou shalt be glad, because thou shalt then suffer none of these things. But since he set down famine above as the first tribulation, why does he now take it up again and set it down as the sixth? The answer is that there famine is taken for that which is produced by the barrenness of the earth; here, for that which goes with the laying waste of the land by enemies. Eliphaz said these three things because Job's sons and daughters had been suddenly taken from him, as in a pestilence; and because his goods had been laid waste by the Chaldeans and the Sabeans, from which want also arose for him. [[5:22|and thou shalt not be afraid of the beasts of the earth|Et bestias terræ non formidabis]], because thou shalt be sure that they will do no harm to thee, nor to thy offspring or household, nor to thy flocks.

paras.t: Denique, verba hæc Eliphaz ad litteram generaliter stare non possunt. Quamvis interdum contingat justos, seu per pœnitentiam emendatos, ab his erui malis, non autem semper sic fit: imo sæpe virtuosi hæc patiuntur, vitiosi vero ab eis immunes sunt. Nam et Apostolus ait: Esurimus et sitimus. Multique martyrum ac justorum afflicti aut etiam perempti sunt fame. In præliis quoque interdum cadunt qui justam causam habebant, et sceleratissimi prævalent, sicut et filii Benjamin bis prævaluerunt contra filios Israel. Sed et justi detractionibus invidorum quotidie corroduntur, et ceteris adversitatibus jam præfatis electi a reprobis exercentur, juxta quod scriptum est in eorum persona: Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die.
paras.en: However, these words of Eliphaz cannot stand as a general rule in the literal sense. Although it sometimes happens that the just, or those amended by penance, are delivered from these evils, it is not always so: on the contrary, the virtuous often suffer them, while the vicious are free of them. For the Apostle too says: [[1 Cor 4:11|we both hunger and thirst|Esurimus et sitimus]]. And many of the martyrs and of the just have been afflicted or even killed by hunger. In battles too those who had a just cause sometimes fall, and the most wicked prevail, as the children of Benjamin twice prevailed against the children of Israel[[Judg 20:21||]] [the margin gives Judg. xx, 16–25; the two victories of Benjamin are at vv. 21 and 25]. And the just are daily gnawed by the detractions of the envious, and the elect are tried by the reprobate with the other adversities already mentioned, according to what is written in their person: [[Ps 43:22|Because for thy sake we are killed all the day long|Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die]].

paras.t: Deinde Eliphaz spondet beato Job abundantiam bonorum post sublationem malorum. Sed cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum, id est, terræ saxosæ erunt tibi fructiferæ, quasi fœdus amicitiæ tecum inierint. Ita exponit Thomas. Quodque subjungitur, et bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt tibi, exponit de brutis, quod ei nocumentum non inferent. Albertus vero, per lapides terræ, intelligit viros constantes, ob animi soliditatem sic dictos, cum quibus erit ei pactum socialis atque pacificæ conversationis; per bestias autem, intelligit crudeles sive tyrannos. Et scies, per experientiam, quod pacem habeat tabernaculum tuum, id est, domus tua erit quieta, et bene disposita in personis, rebus et fabricis; et visitans speciem tuam, id est proximum tuum seu conjugem ejusdem tecum speciei exsistentem, non peccabis, inordinate te ad eos habendo, sed moderate. Vel, Visitans speciem tuam, id est divitiarum et rerum decorem, non peccabis per superfluum affectum ad talia. Et scies quoniam multiplex erit semen tuum, id est, filii tui multi erunt et plurimos generabunt, et progenies tua erit virens, fecunda et pulchra, sicut herba terræ.
paras.en: Next Eliphaz promises blessed Job an abundance of good things after his evils are taken away. [[5:23|But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands|Sed cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum]]: that is, stony lands will bear fruit for thee, as though they had made a covenant of friendship with thee. So Thomas explains it. And what is added, [[5:23|and the beasts of the earth shall be at peace with thee|et bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt tibi]], he explains of the brute beasts, that they will do him no harm. But Albert understands by the stones of the land men of constancy, so called for the solidity of their minds, with whom he will have a covenant of friendly and peaceable dealing; and by the beasts he understands the cruel, or tyrants. [[5:24|And thou shalt know|Et scies]] by experience [[5:24|that thy tabernacle is in peace|quod pacem habeat tabernaculum tuum]], that is, thy house will be quiet and well ordered in persons, goods and buildings; [[5:24|and visiting thy beauty|et visitans speciem tuam]] [*species*, "beauty", also means "kind" or "species": Denis's first reading turns on this], that is, thy neighbour or thy wife, who are of the same species as thou, [[5:24|thou shalt not sin|non peccabis]], by behaving towards them inordinately, but with moderation. Or, [[5:24|visiting thy beauty|Visitans speciem tuam]], that is, the comeliness of riches and of things, [[5:24|thou shalt not sin|non peccabis]] by an excessive affection for such things. [[5:25|Thou shalt know also that thy seed shall be multiplied|Et scies quoniam multiplex erit semen tuum]], that is, thy sons will be many and will beget very many, [[5:25|and thy offspring|et progenies tua]] will be green, fruitful and fair, [[5:25|like the grass of the earth|sicut herba terræ]].

paras.t: Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum, id est, plenus divitiis morieris ac sepelieris, sicut infertur acervus tritici in tempore suo, id est tempore maturitatis seu messis, ita quod ante decrepitam senectutem non morieris. Circa quod scribit Albertus: Acervus ex multis colligitur, et triticum pretiosius granum est. Et vult dicere, quod merita cumulabit, et in æterna erit refectione pretiosissimorum bonorum. Unde Albertus, quantum ad hoc, subtilius considerasse censetur mentem amicorum Job, quod asserit eos posuisse vitam post hanc vitam, seu animam immortalem, quam alii quidam asserentes oppositum.
paras.en: [[5:26|Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance|Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum]], that is, thou shalt die and be buried full of riches, [[5:26|as a heap of wheat is brought in its season|sicut infertur acervus tritici in tempore suo]], that is, at the time of ripeness or of harvest, so that thou shalt not die before decrepit old age. On which Albert writes: A heap is gathered from many grains, and wheat is the more precious grain. And he means that he will heap up merits, and will be in the eternal refreshment of the most precious goods. Hence Albert is judged on this point to have considered the mind of Job's friends more subtly, in holding that they set down a life after this life, or an immortal soul, than certain others who hold the opposite.

paras.t: Postremo, quoniam Eliphaz rhetorice disputavit, in fine sermonem suum de duobus commendat, videlicet, quod probatus exsistat et verus. Ecce hoc, totum quod nunc introduxi in istis duobus capitulis contra te, ut investigavimus, per diligentem considerationem et orationem ad Deum pro sua illuminatione fusam, ita est, id est, verum est. Quod auditum a me, mente pertracta, id est, mentaliter pensa, ut revertaris ad cor et corrigaris. Et in hoc, secundum Gregorium, Eliphaz animositatem suam ostendit. Sed (ut ante tactum est, et Thomas fatetur), quædam verborum Eliphaz secundum ejus intentionem universaliter vera non sunt, quamvis aliquando impleantur: imo promissio ista prosperitatis jam tacta, in ipso Job postea effectum sortita est.
paras.en: Lastly, since Eliphaz has argued as an orator, at the end he commends his speech on two counts, namely that it is well tested and true. [[5:27|Behold, this|Ecce hoc]], all that I have now brought forward against thee in these two chapters, [[5:27|as we have searched out|ut investigavimus]] by careful consideration and by prayer poured out to God for his light, [[5:27|is even so|ita est]], that is, it is true. [[5:27|which thou having heard|Quod auditum]] from me, [[5:27|consider it thoroughly in thy mind|mente pertracta]], that is, weigh it in thy mind, so that thou mayest return to thy heart and be corrected. And in this, according to Gregory, Eliphaz shows his self-assurance. But (as was touched on before, and as Thomas acknowledges) some of Eliphaz's words, in the sense he meant them, are not true universally, though they are sometimes fulfilled: indeed, this promise of prosperity just mentioned did afterwards come to pass in Job himself.

5.title: Mystica ejusdem capituli explanatio.
5.title_en: Mystical explanation of the same chapter

paras.t: Qualiter exordium præelucidati hujus capituli unicuique fideli queat aptari, ex principio præcedentis claret articuli.
paras.en: How the opening of this chapter, already explained, may be applied to every believer is clear from the beginning of the preceding article.

paras.t: Porro quod dicitur, Ego vidi stultum firma radice, B. Gregorius de perfido populo Judæorum exponit: qui populus firma radice convaluit, multis Dei beneficiis in spiritualibus ac corporalibus radicatus; et tandem collata sibi potestate abutens, Christum et primitivam ejus Ecclesiam persecutus est, atque exstinxit saltem pro parte, videlicet multos credentium. Cui stulto populo Eliphaz maledixit, id est, quicumque Christi amicus periturum prædixit. Longe fient filii ejus a salute. Omnes namque posteri perfidæ plebis illius, qui infidelitatem patrum suorum sequuntur, vera beatitudine sunt privati. De quibus populus ille clamavit: Sanguis ejus, scilicet Christi, super nos et super filios nostros. De quibus ait Apostolus: Pervenit super eos ira Dei usque in finem. Et conterentur in porta. Ad litteram, in portis Jerusalem urbiumque Judææ a Romanis occisi sunt. Contriti sunt quoque in porta, id est in Christo, qui ait, Ego sum ostium ovium: quia in ejus præsentia increduli facti sunt, quem crediderunt venturum. Unde Simeon ait de Christo: Positus est hic in ruinam et resurrectionem multorum in Israel. Et ipsemet Christus: In judicium, inquit, ego in hunc mundum veni, ut qui non vident, videant, et qui vident, cæci fiant. Juxta hunc modum dicitur Christus factus lapis offensionis et petra scandali incredulis.
paras.en: Now what is said, [[5:3|I have seen a fool with a strong root|Ego vidi stultum firma radice]], blessed Gregory expounds of the faithless people of the Jews: a people that grew strong with a firm root, rooted in many benefits of God in things spiritual and bodily; and at last, abusing the power granted to it, it persecuted Christ and his primitive Church, and destroyed it at least in part, that is, many of the believers. This foolish people Eliphaz cursed: that is, every friend of Christ foretold that it would perish. [[5:4|His children shall be far from safety|Longe fient filii ejus a salute]]. For all the descendants of that faithless people who follow the unbelief of their fathers are deprived of true beatitude. Of them that people cried out: [[Matt 27:25|His blood|Sanguis ejus]], that is, Christ's, [[Matt 27:25|be upon us and upon our children|super nos et super filios nostros]]. Of them the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 2:16|the wrath of God is come upon them to the end|Pervenit super eos ira Dei usque in finem]]. [[5:4|And shall be destroyed in the gate|Et conterentur in porta]]. According to the letter, they were slain by the Romans in the gates of Jerusalem and of the cities of Judæa. They were also crushed in the gate, that is, in Christ, who says, [[John 10:7|I am the door of the sheep|Ego sum ostium ovium]]: because in his presence they became unbelievers, though they had believed that he would come. Hence Simeon says of Christ: [[Luke 2:34|this child is set for the fall and for the resurrection of many in Israel|Positus est hic in ruinam et resurrectionem multorum in Israel]]. And Christ himself: [[John 9:39|For judgment|In judicium]], he says, [[John 9:39|I am come into this world: that they who see not may see; and they who see may become blind|ego in hunc mundum veni, ut qui non vident, videant, et qui vident, cæci fiant]]. In this way Christ is said to have become [[1 Pet 2:8|a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal|lapis offensionis et petra scandali]] to unbelievers.

paras.t: Cujus messem famelicus comedet. Messis Judæorum, fuit sacra veteris Testamenti Scriptura animæ refectiva, qua Judæi refecti non sunt, dum eam carnaliter acceperunt, nec spiritualiter intellexerunt. Alienus vero, id est plebs gentilis conversa, eam comedit, quoniam per Apostolicam prædicationem et Sancti Spiritus illustrationem ad veram ipsius intelligentiam est perducta. Fuitque esuriens intellectum sacræ Scripturæ et prædicationem verbi cœlestis, quemadmodum de Thessalonicensibus recitat Lucas, quod cum omni aviditate susceperunt verbum Dei. De fame hujusmodi Dominus ait: Mittam famem in terra: non famem panis, neque sitim aquæ, sed audiendi verbum Dei. De qua loquitur Christus: Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam. Et ipsum populum Judæorum incredulum, rapiet armatus populus Romanus. De quo scribit Daniel: Civitatem et sanctuarium dissipabit populus cum duce venturo. Rapuit etiam eos diabolus suis suggestionibus, eos per infidelitatem necando. De quo in Evangelio dicit Salvator: Quum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum. Armatus est quippe multiplici experientia, naturali industria, acutissima fraude, et grandi potentia contra electos. Et bibent sitientes aquam sapientiæ salutaris, videlicet conversi gentiles, divitias ejus, id est pretiosissima spiritualia pocula Judaicæ plebis, puta sacræ Scripturæ fluenta, gratiarum charismata. Quibus dicit Isaias: Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas. Et alibi: Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris. De tali siti et poculo ait Christus: Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat. Qui credit in me, sicut dicit Scriptura, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ. Hæ fuerunt cœlestes divitiæ, quas Salvator propinavit obtulitque Judæis: quas ipsi spreverunt, gentes vero consecutæ sunt eas. Præterea, sicut ista exposita sunt mystice de perfido populo Judæorum, ita possunt exponi de docto, sed vitioso populo Christianorum, eis præsertim qui alios docent quæ ipsi non faciunt.
paras.en: [[5:5|Whose harvest the hungry shall eat|Cujus messem famelicus comedet]]. The harvest of the Jews was the holy Scripture of the Old Testament, which refreshes the soul; by it the Jews were not refreshed, since they took it carnally and did not understand it spiritually. But the stranger, that is, the Gentile people converted, ate it, since by the preaching of the Apostles and the enlightening of the Holy Ghost it was led to the true understanding of it. And it was hungry for the understanding of holy Scripture and for the preaching of the heavenly word, as Luke relates of the Thessalonians that they [[Acts 17:11|received the word with all eagerness|cum omni aviditate susceperunt verbum Dei]] [Luke in fact says this of the Jews of Berea, as against those of Thessalonica]. Of hunger of this kind the Lord says: [[Amos 8:11|I will send forth a famine into the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord|Mittam famem in terra: non famem panis, neque sitim aquæ, sed audiendi verbum Dei]] [Denis reads “of God” for “of the Lord”]. Of it Christ speaks: [[Matt 5:6|Blessed are they that hunger and thirst after justice|Beati qui esuriunt et sitiunt justitiam]]. And as for him, that is, the unbelieving people of the Jews: [[5:5|the armed man shall take him by violence|rapiet armatus]], namely the Roman people. Of whom Daniel writes: [[Dan 9:26|a people, with their leader, that shall come, shall destroy the city, and the sanctuary|Civitatem et sanctuarium dissipabit populus cum duce venturo]]. The devil too took them by violence with his suggestions, slaying them through unbelief. Of him the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:21|When a strong man armed keepeth his court|Quum fortis armatus custodit atrium suum]]. For he is armed with manifold experience, natural skill, the sharpest cunning, and great power against the elect. [[5:5|And the thirsty shall drink up|Et bibent sitientes]] the water of saving wisdom, namely the converted Gentiles, [[5:5|his riches|divitias ejus]], that is, the most precious spiritual draughts of the Jewish people, to wit, the streams of holy Scripture and the gifts of graces. To these Isaias says: [[Is 55:1|All you that thirst, come to the waters|Omnes sitientes, venite ad aquas]]. And elsewhere: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]]. Of such thirst and such a draught Christ says: [[John 7:37|If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink|Si quis sitit, veniat ad me, et bibat]]. [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me, as the scripture saith: Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.|Qui credit in me, sicut dicit Scriptura, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ.]] These were the heavenly riches which the Saviour poured out and offered to the Jews: they spurned them, but the Gentiles obtained them. Moreover, as these things have been expounded mystically of the faithless people of the Jews, so they can be expounded of the learned but vicious people of Christians, above all of those who teach others what they themselves do not do.

paras.t: Nihil in terra sine causa fit. Circa quod scribit Gregorius: Idcirco sæpe desidiosus ingenium accipit, ut de negligentia justius puniatur. Et ideo nonnunquam studiosus tarditate intelligentiæ premitur, ut eo plus mereatur, quo magis studendo laborat. Denique, judicia Dei sunt prorsus rationabilissima et sapientissima, quamvis occulta. Ideo sine causa nil efficit nec permittit. Propter quod undecimo de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus: Deus nullum aut hominum aut angelorum quem malum futurum providit, creasset, nisi novisset quibus eos bonorum usibus commodaret, atque ita ordinem sæculorum tanquam carmen pulcherrimum honestaret. Præterea, quamvis malum culpæ secundum quod tale, non sit pulchrum, nec ad pulchritudinem conferens: tamen in quantum per sapientiam Creatoris omnia convenientissime ordinantis, ex ipso elicitur bonum, atque ex ejus justa punitione divina æquitas commendatur, bona quoque sibi opposita comparatione evidentius innotescunt, et pulchriora apparent; sic malum culpæ confert ad pulchritudinem universi. Sic namque electorum beatitudo et gloria ex reproborum miseria et tormento amplius decoratur, augetur, ipsosque electos ad pleniorem Dei amorem et gratiarum actionem inflammat, dum mala culpæ et pœnæ in damnatis adspiciunt, quæ ipsi divinæ miserationis auxilio evaserunt. Unde rursus in Enchiridion loquitur Augustinus: Universa simul sunt valde bona, quia ex omnibus consistit universitatis admirabilis pulchritudo: in qua id quod malum dicitur, bene ordinatum et suo loco positum eminentius commendat bona, ut magis complaceant, laudabilioraque sint.
paras.en: [[5:6|Nothing upon earth is done without a cause|Nihil in terra sine causa fit]]. On which Gregory writes: For this reason the slothful man often receives a good mind, that he may be punished the more justly for his negligence; and for this reason the studious man is sometimes weighed down by slowness of understanding, that he may merit the more, the more he labours in study. In short, the judgments of God are wholly most reasonable and most wise, though hidden; therefore he does nothing and permits nothing without a cause. For this reason Augustine says in the eleventh book of the City of God: God would not have created any man or angel whom he foresaw would be evil, had he not known to what uses of the good he would put them, and so would adorn the order of the ages like a most beautiful poem. Moreover, although the evil of guilt [that is, sin itself, as distinct from the evil of punishment], as such, is not beautiful and does not contribute to beauty, yet inasmuch as, by the wisdom of the Creator who orders all things most fittingly, good is drawn out of it, and by its just punishment the divine equity is commended, and the goods opposed to it become known more clearly by comparison and appear more beautiful, in this way the evil of guilt contributes to the beauty of the universe. For thus the beatitude and glory of the elect is further adorned and increased by the misery and torment of the reprobate, and it inflames the elect themselves to a fuller love of God and thanksgiving, when they behold in the damned the evils of guilt and of punishment which they themselves escaped by the help of the divine mercy. Hence again Augustine says in the Enchiridion: All things together are very good, because of them all consists the admirable beauty of the universe; in which what is called evil, well ordered and set in its place, commends the good more eminently, so that they please the more and are more praiseworthy.

paras.t: Et de humo non egredietur dolor. Per humum seu humidam terram, peccator aliquis concupiscentia et fluxu carnalium desideriorum pertransiens, apte signatur: de quo dolor pœnitentiæ non procedit; imo lætatur quum male fecerit, et exsultat in rebus pessimis, sicut et omnis induratus in vitiis. Qui etsi nonnunquam divinitus flagelletur, non tamen de suis veraciter dolet excessibus. De qualibus scriptum est in Jeremia: Percussisti eos, Domine, et non doluerunt; renuerunt accipere disciplinam; induraverunt facies suas supra petram, et noluerunt reverti. Quod etiam in Judæis obstinatis videmus potissime adimpletum. Nam usque in præsens, quantumlibet premantur adversis, nolunt advertere quod propter Christi occisionem hæc patiantur, nec de ejus occisione atque blasphemia dolent, juxta illud in Psalmo: Obscurentur oculi eorum ne videant.
paras.en: [[5:6|and sorrow doth not spring out of the ground|Et de humo non egredietur dolor]] [Denis reads egredietur, “shall come forth”, for the Vulgate’s oritur]. By the ground, or the moist earth, is fitly signified some sinner who passes through life in concupiscence and the flowing of carnal desires: from whom the sorrow of penance does not come forth; rather, like those who [[Prov 2:14|are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in the most wicked things|lætatur quum male fecerit, et exsultat in rebus pessimis]], so too does every man hardened in vices. Even if he is sometimes scourged by God, yet he does not truly grieve for his excesses. Of such it is written in Jeremias: [[Jer 5:3|thou hast struck them|Percussisti eos]], O Lord, [[Jer 5:3|and they have not grieved|et non doluerunt]]; [[Jer 5:3|they have refused to receive correction: they have made their faces harder than the rock, and they have refused to return|renuerunt accipere disciplinam; induraverunt facies suas supra petram, et noluerunt reverti]]. This too we see fulfilled above all in the obstinate Jews. For to this day, however much they are pressed by adversities, they will not consider that they suffer these things for the slaying of Christ, nor do they grieve for his slaying and for their blasphemy, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:24|Let their eyes be darkened that they see not|Obscurentur oculi eorum ne videant]].

paras.t: Homo ad laborem nascitur. Unde et Adæ Dominus dixit: In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo. Sunt autem quidam labores boni, virtuosi, laudabiles, ad quos nascitur homo, ut scilicet per studium et labores scientiis atque virtutibus decoretur, divinis præceptis obtemperet, pro peccatis suis per labores pœnitentiales satisfaciat, omni custodia cor suum custodiat: quo nihil laboriosius invenitur. Itaque, væ eis qui in his hominum laboribus non sunt, nec cum hominibus flagellantur; qui otiositatibus ac vanitatibus vacant, et tempus sibi concessum non infructuose dumtaxat, sed et vitiose expendunt. Et avis ad volatum. Potest per avem mens contemplativa intelligi, quæ ad contemplationis elevationem perducitur, ut carnalibus ac terrenis contemptis, ad Dei amorem totam se erigat, ad contuendam pulchritudinem ejus supersanctissimam totam se acuat, pennas orationis ac devotionis præassumendo, virtutumque plumis se vestiendo. De talibus loquitur Isaias: Sancti qui sperant in Domino, assument pennas ut aquilæ; volabunt, et non deficient. Sicque volare optavit qui dixit: Quis dabit mihi pennas sicut columbæ, et volabo, et requiescam? Itaque temporalia vana et vilia transcendamus, et quo corpore anima exstat nobilior, eo plus delicias atque divitias animæ quam corporis exquiramus. Quod ut implere possimus, dicamus singuli quod adjecit:
paras.en: [[5:7|Man is born to labour|Homo ad laborem nascitur]]. Hence the Lord said to Adam too: [[Gen 3:19|In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread|In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane tuo]]. But there are certain labours that are good, virtuous and praiseworthy, to which man is born: that is, that by study and labours he may be adorned with knowledge and virtues, obey the divine precepts, make satisfaction for his sins by the labours of penance, and keep his heart with all watchfulness[[Prov 4:23||]], than which nothing is found more laborious. Therefore woe to those who [[Ps 72:5|are not in the labour of men|in his hominum laboribus non sunt]], nor are scourged with men; who give themselves to idleness and vanities, and spend the time granted them not only fruitlessly but viciously. [[5:7|And the bird to fly|Et avis ad volatum]]. By the bird can be understood the contemplative mind, which is led up to the height of contemplation, so that, despising carnal and earthly things, it raises itself wholly to the love of God and sharpens itself wholly to behold his most holy beauty, first taking the wings of prayer and devotion and clothing itself with the feathers of the virtues. Of such Isaias speaks: The saints [[Is 40:31|that hope in the Lord|qui sperant in Domino]] [[Is 40:31|shall take wings as eagles|assument pennas ut aquilæ]]; they shall fly, and [[Is 40:31|not faint|non deficient]] [Denis reads “they shall fly” for the Vulgate’s “they shall run … they shall walk”]. And so he longed to fly who said: [[Ps 54:7|Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly and be at rest?|Quis dabit mihi pennas sicut columbæ, et volabo, et requiescam?]] Let us therefore rise above temporal things, vain and base, and the more the soul stands nobler than the body, the more let us seek the delights and riches of the soul rather than of the body. That we may be able to fulfil this, let each of us say what he added:

paras.t: Quamobrem ego deprecabor Dominum, et ad Deum ponam eloquium meum. Non enim sine affectuosis, quotidianis, imo et incessabilibus precibus gratiam adimplendi hoc sortiemur. Qui facit magna et inscrutabilia et mirabilia absque numero. Nam Augustino testante, majus opus est Dei, justificatio impii, quam creatio mundi. Quam magna vero et inscrutabilia ac mirabilia sine numero facit Deus omnipotens et excelsus quotidie in Sacramento altaris, in creatione rationabilium animarum, in Baptismo ac ceteris sacramentis, in immutatione voluntatum mentiumque nostrarum! Verum, in regno beatitudinis sempiternæ, in magno illo supermundano suo palatio, in triumphanti Ecclesia, vere permaxima, inscrutabilissima et mirabilissima facit. Hinc Unigenitus Patris æterni ait: Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor. Præterea, nonne mirabilissimum Dei opus fuit, conversio mundi ad tam incomprehensibilem ac arduissimam Evangelii fidem ac legem, quod sine innumerabilibus miraculis factum non est? Sed et quotidiana ac naturalia Dei opera, nonne tanto majora, inscrutabiliora et mirabiliora probantur, quo diligentius considerantur, quamvis assiduitate non advertantur? Quomodo fetus, qui mox natus, per brevissimum tempus sine aeris attractione seu respiratione vivere nequit, tot diebus in utero matris sine illa vivere valet? Si unus suscitetur defunctus, omnes accurrunt, mirantur, stupescunt, quum quotidie tot homines nasci non admirentur: quamvis utique plus sit, quod non erat, creare, quam quod cecidit et divisum est, reparare et denuo adunare. Postremo, sicut Ecclesiasticus scribit: Multa sunt abscondita, majora his; pauca enim vidimus operum ejus. Nihilominus ex his paucis quæ novimus, supergloriosi Creatoris majestatem jugiter revereri discamus, et omne opus sui obsequii cum diligentia et affectu solvamus.
paras.en: [[5:8|Wherefore I will pray to the Lord, and address my speech to God|Quamobrem ego deprecabor Dominum, et ad Deum ponam eloquium meum]]. For not without affectionate, daily, indeed unceasing prayers shall we obtain the grace to fulfil this. [[5:9|Who doth great things, and unsearchable and wonderful things without number|Qui facit magna et inscrutabilia et mirabilia absque numero]]. For, as Augustine testifies, the justification of the ungodly is a greater work of God than the creation of the world. And how great, unsearchable and wonderful are the things without number that almighty and most high God does daily in the Sacrament of the altar, in the creation of rational souls, in Baptism and the other sacraments, in the changing of our wills and minds! But in the kingdom of everlasting beatitude, in that great palace of his above the world, in the Church triumphant, he does things truly the very greatest, most unsearchable and most wonderful. Hence the Only-begotten of the eternal Father says: [[John 5:17|My Father worketh until now; and I work|Pater meus usque modo operatur, et ego operor]]. Moreover, was it not a most wonderful work of God, the conversion of the world to so incomprehensible and so arduous a faith and law as the Gospel’s, which was not done without countless miracles? And the daily and natural works of God too: are they not proved so much the greater, more unsearchable and more wonderful, the more carefully they are considered, though by their constancy they go unnoticed? How is it that the child, which as soon as it is born cannot live even the shortest time without drawing in the air, that is, without breathing, can live so many days in its mother’s womb without it? If one dead man is raised, all run up, marvel and are astonished, while they do not marvel that so many men are born every day: although it is surely more to create what was not than to repair what fell and was broken up, and to join it together again. Lastly, as Ecclesiasticus writes: [[Ecclus 43:36|There are many things hidden from us that are greater than these: for we have seen but a few of his works|Multa sunt abscondita, majora his; pauca enim vidimus operum ejus]]. Nevertheless, from these few that we know, let us learn to revere continually the majesty of the all-glorious Creator, and let us render every work of his service with diligence and affection.

paras.t: Qui dat pluviam super faciem terræ. Pluvia hæc, est prædicatio cœlestis doctrinæ, procedens de nubibus, id est prædicatoribus atque doctoribus virtuosis. De quibus loquitur Isaias: Qui sunt isti qui ut nubes volant? Facies autem terræ, est intellectus viatorum in terra peregrinantium, qui docetur. De qua pluvia ait Psalmista: Pluviam voluntariam segregabis, Deus, hæreditati tuæ. Et irrigat aquis, id est gratiarum fluminibus, donis et consolationibus, universa fidelium corda. De quibus Christus prædixit: Omnia traham ad me ipsum. Et alibi: Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ. De hac irrigatione insolita tempore gratiæ facta, prædictum fuit ab Isaia: Repleta est terra scientia Domini, sicut aqua maris operientes. Unde Salvator testatur: Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum: sed aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam.
paras.en: [[5:10|Who giveth rain upon the face of the earth|Qui dat pluviam super faciem terræ]]. This rain is the preaching of heavenly doctrine, coming from the clouds, that is, from virtuous preachers and doctors. Of whom Isaias speaks: [[Is 60:8|Who are these, that fly as clouds|Qui sunt isti qui ut nubes volant]]? And the face of the earth is the understanding of wayfarers on pilgrimage on earth, which is taught. Of this rain the Psalmist says: [[Ps 67:10|Thou shalt set aside for thy inheritance a free rain, O God|Pluviam voluntariam segregabis, Deus, hæreditati tuæ]]. [[5:10|And watereth|Et irrigat]] [[5:10|with waters|aquis]], that is, with rivers of graces, gifts and consolations, [[5:10|all things|universa]], the hearts of the faithful. Of whom Christ foretold: [[John 12:32|will draw all things to myself|Omnia traham ad me ipsum]]. And elsewhere: [[Mark 16:15|preach the gospel to every creature|Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]. Of this unwonted watering, done in the time of grace, it was foretold by Isaias: [[Is 11:9|the earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the covering waters of the sea|Repleta est terra scientia Domini, sicut aqua maris operientes]]. Hence the Saviour testifies: [[John 4:13|he that shall drink of the water that I will give him shall not thirst for ever|Qui biberit ex aqua quam ego dabo ei, non sitiet in æternum]]: [[John 4:14|But the water that I will give him shall become in him a fountain of water, springing up into life everlasting|sed aqua quam ego dabo ei, fiet in eo fons aquæ salientis in vitam æternam]].

paras.t: Qui ponit humiles in sublime. Consonat huic Christi sententia, asserentis: Omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Unde et Petrus in prima sua epistola nos hortatur: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, ut vos exaltet in die visitationis. Væ ergo superbis, væ ambitiosis atque inanibus, qui quum indigni sint pane quo vescuntur, vel quod a terra portantur, nihilominus excæcatissima mente inflantur. Ideo consideremus nos per comparationem ad mala quæ fecimus, ad bona debita quæ omisimus, ad nihil ex quo conditi sumus, ad propriam fragilitatem et corporis vilitatem, ac animæ in omne vitium pronitatem, ad pericula quibus expositi sumus, ad Deum a cujus perfectione, sanctitate et gloria infinite deficimus: sicque nobis ipsis intime vilescamus, nos ipsos spernamus, nihil de nostris viribus præsumamus, divinæ pietati omne bonum nostrum sinceriter adscribamus, et Deo superexaltato profundissime substernamur, ei in omnibus cum debita, amorosa atque humillima obedientia subditi, qui cunctis vere in infinitum honorabilior demonstratur, et immensa reverentia dignus exsistit. Isti sunt actus veræ humilitatis, in quibus quanto nos amplius actuamus, tanto plus erigemur in præsenti per gratiam, atque in futuro per gloriam: imo in die judicii judicabunt cum Christo, qui nunc juxta ejus consilia mundum relinquunt et sub obedientia sancta militant Deo, dicente Apostolo: Nescitis quia angelos judicabimus?
paras.en: [[5:11|Who setteth up the humble on high|Qui ponit humiles in sublime]]. With this agrees the saying of Christ, who declares: [[Luke 14:11|every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled|Omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]]. Hence Peter too in his first epistle exhorts us: [[1 Pet 5:6|Be you humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation|Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, ut vos exaltet in die visitationis]] [Denis reads “in the day of visitation”]. Woe then to the proud, woe to the ambitious and the vain, who, though they are unworthy of the bread they eat, or even to be borne by the earth, are nevertheless puffed up with a mind utterly blinded. Let us therefore consider ourselves by comparison with the evils we have done, with the good we owed and have left undone, with the nothing out of which we were made, with our own frailty and the baseness of the body, and the soul’s proneness to every vice, with the dangers to which we are exposed, and with God, from whose perfection, holiness and glory we fall infinitely short: and so let us become inwardly vile to ourselves, despise ourselves, presume nothing of our own strength, sincerely ascribe all our good to the divine goodness, and lay ourselves most deeply beneath God, who is exalted above all, subject to him in all things with due, loving and most humble obedience; for he is shown to be truly infinitely more worthy of honour than all, and is worthy of boundless reverence. These are the acts of true humility: the more we put them into act, the more we shall be raised up, in the present by grace and in the future by glory. Indeed, in the day of judgment they shall judge with Christ who now, following his counsels, leave the world and serve God as soldiers under holy obedience, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 6:3|Know you not that we shall judge angels?|Nescitis quia angelos judicabimus?]]

paras.t: Per diem incurrent tenebras. Sic Judæi in die Christi et tempore prædicationis ac gratiæ miraculorumque ejus, quando in terra visus et cum hominibus conversatus est, incurrerunt tenebras errorum, vitiorum atque perfidiæ, contradicendo, persequendo et tandem occidendo Dei Filium Jesum Christum, quemadmodum Isaias prædixit: Excæca cor populi hujus. Et quasi in nocte sic palpabunt, id est, mente nutabunt, et dubiose inquirent de Christo, in meridie, id est in evidentissima suæ veritatis declaratione, quando per miracula soli Deo possibilia Pater testimonium perhibuit Christo, quemadmodum ait: Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater, quæ facio, testimonium perhibent de me. Et iterum ait Joannes: Quum tanta fecisset coram eis, non crediderunt. Imo quasi palpando sciscitabantur, dicentes ad Christum: Quousque animam nostram tollis? Si tu es Christus, dic nobis palam. Unde ob inexcusabilem eorum cæcitatem dixit Salvator passioni jam proximus: Si opera non fecissem in eis, quæ nullus alius fecit, peccatum non haberent. Denique, In meridie seu claro die quasi in nocte, etiam corporaliter pro Christo inveniendo palpabant, quando quærebant eum præcipitare, lapidare, comprehendere, et exivit de manibus eorum, ita quod subito fecit se invisibilem eis, et elapsus est manus eorum, non percipientibus eis quomodo.
paras.en: [[5:14|They shall meet with darkness in the day|Per diem incurrent tenebras]]. So the Jews, in the day of Christ and the time of his preaching, his grace and his miracles, when [[Bar 3:38|he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|in terra visus et cum hominibus conversatus est]], met with the darkness of errors, vices and faithlessness, by gainsaying, persecuting and at last slaying the Son of God, Jesus Christ, as Isaias foretold: [[Is 6:10|Blind the heart of this people|Excæca cor populi hujus]]. [[5:14|as in the night|Et quasi in nocte]], [[5:14|grope|sic palpabunt]], that is, they shall waver in mind and inquire doubtfully about Christ, [[5:14|at noonday|in meridie]], that is, in the most evident declaration of his truth, when the Father bore witness to Christ by miracles possible to God alone, as he says: [[John 5:36|the works which the Father hath given me|Opera quæ dedit mihi Pater]], [[John 5:36|the works themselves which I do, give testimony of me|quæ facio, testimonium perhibent de me]]. And again John says: [[John 12:37|whereas he had done so many miracles before them, they believed not|Quum tanta fecisset coram eis, non crediderunt]]. Indeed, as if groping, they questioned him, saying to Christ: [[John 10:24|How long dost thou hold our souls in suspense? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly|Quousque animam nostram tollis? Si tu es Christus, dic nobis palam]]. Hence, because of their inexcusable blindness, the Saviour, when his passion was now near, said: [[John 15:24|If I had not done among them the works that no other man hath done, they would not have sin|Si opera non fecissem in eis, quæ nullus alius fecit, peccatum non haberent]]. Lastly, [[5:14|at noonday|In meridie]], or in clear day, [[5:14|as in the night|quasi in nocte]], they groped bodily too in seeking Christ, when they sought to cast him down headlong[[Luke 4:29||]], to stone him, to take him, and [[John 10:39|he escaped out of their hands|exivit de manibus eorum]]: that is, he suddenly made himself invisible to them, and slipped out of their hands, without their perceiving how.

paras.t: Porro salvum faciet egenum de gladio oris eorum. Christum enim propter nos tam pauperem factum, ut diceret, Filius hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet (de quo scriptum est, Ipse pauper et ascendens super asinam), salvum fecit Pater de gladio oris Judæorum clamantium, Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum, tertia die suscitando eum a mortuis, imo in puncto suæ mortis eum ab omni deinceps passibilitate ac passione eripiens, sicut ait Apostolus: Christus resurgens a mortuis, jam non moritur. Imo ipsemet Christus mortem devicit, ut in Osee profitetur: Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne. Et erit egeno, id est pauperi Christo, spes, id est certa exspectatio resurrectionis, ascensionis et glorificationis in corpore, seu præmii accidentalis. Nam et tempore passionis constanter adversariis dixit: Amodo videbitis Filium hominis sedentem a dextris virtutis Dei, et venientem in nubibus cœli. Spem vero quæ est theologica virtus, non habuit, quoniam anima ejus a primo suæ creationis instanti vidit Deum clare per speciem: sicque essentiale præmium non exspectavit. Potest etiam per egenum intelligi pauper ille populus discipulorum Christi, qui in ejus passione spem perdidit, quam post resurrectionem ipsius resumpsit.
paras.en: [[5:15|But he shall save the needy from the sword of their mouth|Porro salvum faciet egenum de gladio oris eorum]]. For Christ, made so poor for our sake that he said, [[Matt 8:20|the Son of man hath not where to lay his head|Filius hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet]] (of whom it is written, [[Zach 9:9|he is poor, and riding upon an ass|Ipse pauper et ascendens super asinam]]), the Father saved from the sword of the mouth of the Jews crying out, [[John 19:15|Away with him: Away with him: Crucify him|Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum]], by raising him from the dead on the third day; or rather, at the very moment of his death, rescuing him from all passibility [that is, capacity to suffer] and suffering thenceforth, as the Apostle says: [[Rom 6:9|Christ, rising again from the dead, dieth now no more|Christus resurgens a mortuis, jam non moritur]]. Indeed Christ himself overcame death, as he professes in Osee: [[Osee 13:14|O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite|Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne]]. [[5:16|And to the needy there shall be|Et erit egeno]], that is, to the poor Christ, [[5:16|hope|spes]], that is, the sure expectation of his resurrection, ascension and glorification in the body, or of the accidental reward [that is, the joys added to the essential reward of the vision of God]. For in the time of his passion too he said steadfastly to his adversaries: [[Matt 26:64|hereafter you shall see the Son of man sitting on the right hand of the power of God and coming in the clouds of heaven|Amodo videbitis Filium hominis sedentem a dextris virtutis Dei, et venientem in nubibus cœli]]. But hope, which is a theological virtue, he did not have, since his soul from the first instant of its creation saw God clearly face to face, and so he did not await the essential reward. By the needy can also be understood that poor people of Christ’s disciples, who lost hope in his passion and took it up again after his resurrection.

paras.t: Iniquitas autem contrahet os suum, quia post Christi ascensionem, misso desuper Spiritu Sancto, atque Apostolis in Jerusalem Christum publice prædicantibus, et in nomine ejus miracula magna agentibus, repressa et confusa est loquacitas Judæorum; quemadmodum recitat Lucas, quod principes sacerdotum et seniores, auditis verbis Petri apostoli, et viso nato claudo quem curavit, nil contradicere potuerunt. Et postea scribit, qualiter Judæi disputantes cum Stephano, non potuerunt resistere sapientiæ et Spiritui qui loquebatur. Hoc equidem Christus in Evangelio ante promisit: Dabo, inquiens, vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri.
paras.en: [[5:16|but iniquity shall draw in her mouth|Iniquitas autem contrahet os suum]]: because after Christ’s ascension, when the Holy Ghost had been sent from above, and the Apostles were preaching Christ publicly in Jerusalem and working great miracles in his name, the talk of the Jews was checked and confounded; as Luke relates that the chief priests and ancients, having heard the words of the apostle Peter and seen the man born lame whom he had healed, [[Acts 4:14|could say nothing against it|nil contradicere potuerunt]] [the margin’s verse number is unclear]. And afterwards he writes how the Jews [[Acts 6:9|disputing with Stephen|disputantes cum Stephano]] [[Acts 6:10|were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit that spoke|non potuerunt resistere sapientiæ et Spiritui qui loquebatur]]. This indeed Christ had promised beforehand in the Gospel: [[Luke 21:15|I will give|Dabo]], he says, [[Luke 21:15|you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]].

paras.t: Præterea, sicut jam dictum est, Judæos per diem incurrisse tenebras, sic generaliter vitiosi ac invidi die incurrunt caliginem, dum aliorum opera bona pervertere student, de aliorum profectu tristantur, bonos diffamant, et indifferentia seu dubia interpretantur in pejus: imo sæpe quæ apertissime bona sunt, offuscare nituntur, asserendo quod ex vanitate aut singularitate procedant, et ob gloriam propriam peragantur. Invidia namque mentem prorsus excæcat: et quo is qui oditur, virtuosius operatur, clariusque famatur ac amplius honoratur; eo qui odit eum, plus in se ipso torquetur, et acutiores nocendi modos excogitare conatur. Sed Deus pauperem spiritu, id est virtuosum seu humilem, salvat de gladio oris eorum, ostendens quod vera virtutum luce ornatus sit; et iniquum ac invidum monstrabit mendacem.
paras.en: Moreover, as it has now been said that the Jews [[5:14|meet with darkness in the day|per diem incurrisse tenebras]], so in general the vicious and the envious meet with gloom by day, when they strive to pervert the good works of others, are saddened at others’ progress, defame the good, and interpret things indifferent or doubtful for the worse; indeed they often try to darken what is most plainly good, by asserting that it comes from vanity or singularity and is done for their own glory. For envy blinds the mind completely: and the more virtuously the one who is hated works, the more brightly he is spoken of and the more he is honoured, the more the one who hates him is tormented within himself, and the sharper the ways of harming him that he tries to devise. But God saves the poor in spirit, that is, the virtuous or humble man, [[5:15|from the sword of their mouth|de gladio oris eorum]], showing that he is adorned with the true light of the virtues; and he will show the wicked and envious man to be a liar.

paras.t: In sex tribulationibus liberabit te, et in septima non tanget te malum. Septenario universitas designatur: nam septem diebus omne tempus hoc volvitur; et in Apocalypsi, per septem spiritus qui in conspectu throni Dei sunt, omnes angeli denotantur. Itaque sensus est, quod omnem electum in vita hac tribulatum Deus cito, saltem in morte et aliquando in vita, a cunctis suis adversitatibus ac ærumnis eripiet, juxta id Psalmistæ: Multæ tribulationes justorum, et de omnibus his liberabit eos Dominus.
paras.en: [[5:19|In six troubles he shall deliver thee, and in the seventh, evil shall not touch thee.|In sex tribulationibus liberabit te, et in septima non tanget te malum.]] By the number seven totality is signified: for all this time rolls round in seven days; and in the Apocalypse all the angels are denoted by the seven spirits that are in the sight of the throne of God[[Apoc 1:4||]]. So the sense is that every elect soul afflicted in this life God will soon rescue from all its adversities and hardships, at least at death and sometimes in life, according to that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just; but out of them all will the Lord deliver them|Multæ tribulationes justorum, et de omnibus his liberabit eos Dominus]].

paras.t: In fame audiendi verbum Dei et acquirendi justitiam, eruet te de morte animi, quod est peccatum mortale: ita quod præ inopia verbi Dei non incurres peccatum; imo actibus justis reficieris, et verbo Dei erudieris, et Deum intra audies te affantem ac informantem. Et in bello animæ contra tres hostes ipsius, videlicet contra dæmonem, mundum et carnem, eruet te de manu gladii, id est acutæ atque pestiferæ suggestionis diaboli, et de pœna quam ipse suis servitoribus pro præmio reddit. De hujusmodi bello scribit Apostolus, quod colluctatio nobis est adversus principes et potestates, contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus. Et in Psalmo: Obumbrasti super caput meum in die belli.
paras.en: [[5:20|In famine|In fame]] of hearing the word of God and of gaining justice [[5:20|he shall deliver thee from death|eruet te de morte]] of the soul, which is mortal sin: so that thou shalt not fall into sin for want of the word of God; rather thou shalt be refreshed with just acts, and taught by the word of God, and shalt hear God within thee, speaking to thee and forming thee. [[5:20|and in battle|Et in bello]] of the soul against its three enemies, namely the devil, the world and the flesh, he shall deliver thee [[5:20|from the hand of the sword|de manu gladii]], that is, of the sharp and pestilent suggestion of the devil, and from the punishment which he pays his servants as their wages. Of this kind of battle the Apostle writes that [[Eph 6:12|our wrestling|colluctatio nobis est]] is [[Eph 6:12|against principalities and powers|adversus principes et potestates]], [[Eph 6:12|against the spirits of wickedness in the high places|contra spiritualia nequitiæ in cœlestibus]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 139:8|thou hast overshadowed my head in the day of battle|Obumbrasti super caput meum in die belli]].

paras.t: A flagello linguæ absconderis, juxta præcedentis articuli expositionem. Porro, quum homo cœperit esse perfectus, eradicato privato amore, irrisiones, detractiones, vituperationes cum gaudio patietur; et male loquentibus condolens, pro ipsis precabitur. Et non timebis calamitatem quum venerit, id est penuriam. Imo perfectorum thesaurus paupertas est, in quo sicut in omnibus divitiis gloriantur, secundum illud Apostoli: Altissima paupertas eorum abundavit in divitias simplicitatis eorum.
paras.en: [[5:21|Thou shalt be hidden from the scourge of the tongue|A flagello linguæ absconderis]], according to the exposition of the preceding article. Further, when a man has begun to be perfect, self-love having been rooted out, he will suffer mockery, detraction and reproaches with joy; and, grieving for those who speak ill, he will pray for them. [[5:21|and thou shalt not fear calamity when it cometh|Et non timebis calamitatem quum venerit]], that is, want. Rather, poverty is the treasure of the perfect, in which they glory as in all riches, according to that of the Apostle: [[2 Cor 8:2|their very deep poverty hath abounded unto the riches of their simplicity|Altissima paupertas eorum abundavit in divitias simplicitatis eorum]].

paras.t: In vastitate et fame ridebis, id est, in die judicii, quando reprobi consummata vastitate prementur, omnique refectione lætitiæ privabuntur, toto corde gaudebis: juxta illud, Ridebit in die novissimo. Et per Malachiam Dominus ait electis: Egrediemini, et salietis sicut vituli de armento, et calcabitis impios in die quo ego facio, scilicet die judicii, de quo loquitur ibi. Quod autem in inferno sit infelicissima fames, insinuatur in Ecclesiastico, quo habetur: Ante obitum tuum operare justitiam, quoniam non est apud inferos invenire cibos. Et bestias terræ, id est dæmones ferocissimos impiorum in terra hominum deceptores ac voratores: de quibus fertur in Psalmo, Ne tradas bestiis animam confitentem tibi; non formidabis. Perfecta etenim caritas excludit servilem timorem quo diabolus et infernus timentur. In morte quoque et in divino judicio, virtuosi, Deo subveniente, a timore dæmonum eruuntur, quos ad patriam pervenientes in æternum securi contemnunt.
paras.en: [[5:22|In destruction and famine|In vastitate et fame]] [[5:22|thou shalt laugh|ridebis]]: that is, in the day of judgment, when the reprobate shall be crushed by utter destruction and deprived of all refreshment of joy, thou shalt rejoice with all thy heart; according to that saying, [[Prov 31:25|she shall laugh in the latter day|Ridebit in die novissimo]]. And by Malachias the Lord says to the elect: [[Mal 4:2|you shall go forth, and shall leap like calves of the herd|Egrediemini, et salietis sicut vituli de armento]], [[Mal 4:3|And you shall tread down the wicked|et calcabitis impios]] [[Mal 4:3|in the day that I do this|in die quo ego facio]], that is, on the day of judgment, of which he speaks there. And that in hell there is a most wretched famine is suggested in Ecclesiasticus, where we read: [[Ecclus 14:17|Before thy death work justice: for in hell there is no finding food|Ante obitum tuum operare justitiam, quoniam non est apud inferos invenire cibos]]. And [[5:22|the beasts of the earth|bestias terræ]], that is, the most savage demons, deceivers and devourers of the ungodly men on earth, of whom it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 73:19|Deliver not up to beasts the souls that confess to thee|Ne tradas bestiis animam confitentem tibi]]: [[5:22|thou shalt not be afraid of|non formidabis]] them. For perfect charity shuts out the servile fear with which the devil and hell are feared [servile fear: fear of punishment, as distinct from the filial fear of offending God]. At death too, and in the divine judgment, the virtuous, with God coming to their aid, are delivered from the fear of the demons, whom, reaching the fatherland, they despise for ever in safety.

paras.t: Sed cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum erit. Lapides regionum, sunt electi fideles particularium Ecclesiarum, quemadmodum per Isaiam Dominus pollicetur Ecclesiæ: Ecce ego sternam per ordinem lapides tuos. Et Petrus fidelibus dicit: Ad quem (puta ad Christum) accedentes, et vos tanquam lapides vivi, superædificamini domus spirituales. Cum his est cuicumque justo fœdus dilectionis et pacis. Et bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt, id est pacem cum Deo facientes, tibi, non ex intentione, sed occasionaliter. Dæmones namque, qui (ut dictum est) per bestias exprimuntur, quo electos plus persequuntur, eo resistentibus fiunt occasio meriti amplioris et incrementi pacis ac caritatis. Possunt quoque per bestias, motus carnales ac bestiales intelligi, quos viri virtutum habent rationi subjectos. Unde nec eos verentur, sed facile vincunt, gratiæ magnitudine id agente.
paras.en: [[5:23|But thou shalt have a covenant with the stones of the lands|Sed cum lapidibus regionum pactum tuum erit]]. The stones of the lands are the elect faithful of the particular Churches, as the Lord promises the Church through Isaias: [[Is 54:11|behold I will lay thy stones in order|Ecce ego sternam per ordinem lapides tuos]]. And Peter says to the faithful: [[1 Pet 2:4|Unto whom|Ad quem]] (that is, to Christ) [[1 Pet 2:4|coming|accedentes]], [[1 Pet 2:5|Be you also as living stones built up, a spiritual house|et vos tanquam lapides vivi, superædificamini domus spirituales]]. With these every just man has a covenant of love and peace. [[5:23|and the beasts of the earth shall be at peace|Et bestiæ terræ pacificæ erunt]], that is, bringing about peace with God, [[5:23|with thee|tibi]]: not by intention, but by occasion. For the demons, who (as has been said) are expressed by the beasts, the more they persecute the elect, the more they become, to those who resist them, the occasion of greater merit and of an increase of peace and charity. By the beasts can also be understood the carnal and bestial movements which men of virtue keep subject to reason. Hence they do not fear them, but overcome them easily, the greatness of grace bringing this about.

paras.t: Et scies quod pacem, id est quietem in Deo, seu subjectionem tranquillam sub ratione, habeat tabernaculum tuum, id est domus conscientiæ tuæ, animique cubile, vel corpus: de quo loquitur Petrus, Scio quia velox est depositio tabernaculi mei. Porro pax corporis, est ejus tranquilla directio, sive subjectio ejus sub rationis imperio. Et visitans speciem tuam, id est, pulchritudinem et ornatum tibi a Deo concessum in naturalibus atque gratuitis considerans, non peccabis, id est, per vanam gloriam aliquid tibi attribuendo, aut in te ipso inaniter gloriando, quasi non acceperis omne bonum a Deo; sed illi omne bonum adscribes, gratias cordialiter ages, tantoque amorosius obtemperabis, et humilius ac formidolosius subditus eris, quo plura tibi bona largitus est, et quo ad reddendam rationem obligatiorem te pensas, metuens ne tam piissimo benefactori fias ingratus. Cui enim plus datum est, plus utique requiretur ab eo. Imo et inde nobis cordialiter est dolendum, quod id ipsum bonitatis, lucis et sapientiæ, quod ex divina pietate nobis gratiose collatum est, nostra pravitate, cæcitate et negligentia tantum et toties offuscamus, Deique dona præinclyta et Deum in suis donis inhonoramus, dum ea non satis reverenter atque sollicite custodimus, imo et nostra peccata eis miscemus. Propter quod valde plangendum est nobis, semperque humiliandum est cor coram judice Deo.
paras.en: [[5:24|And thou shalt know that|Et scies quod]] [[5:24|thy tabernacle is|habeat tabernaculum tuum]] [[5:24|in peace|pacem]]: peace, that is, quiet in God, or tranquil subjection under reason; the tabernacle, that is, the house of thy conscience and the chamber of the soul, or the body, of which Peter speaks: I know that [[2 Pet 1:14|the laying away of this my tabernacle is at hand|velox est depositio tabernaculi mei]]. And the peace of the body is its tranquil ordering, or its subjection under the rule of reason. [[5:24|and visiting thy beauty|Et visitans speciem tuam]], that is, considering the beauty and adornment granted thee by God in the gifts of nature and of grace, [[5:24|thou shalt not sin|non peccabis]]: that is, by attributing anything to thyself through vainglory, or glorying emptily in thyself, as if thou hadst not received every good from God; but thou shalt ascribe every good to him, give him heartfelt thanks, and obey him the more lovingly, and be subject to him the more humbly and fearfully, the more good things he has bestowed on thee, and the more bound thou thinkest thyself to render an account, fearing lest thou be ungrateful to so most loving a benefactor. For [[Luke 12:48|unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required|Cui enim plus datum est, plus utique requiretur ab eo]]. Indeed we must grieve from the heart for this, that through our wickedness, blindness and negligence we so much and so often darken that very goodness, light and wisdom which has been graciously conferred on us by the divine mercy, and dishonour the most glorious gifts of God, and God in his gifts, since we do not guard them reverently and carefully enough, and even mingle our sins with them. For this we must greatly lament, and the heart must ever be humbled before God the judge.

paras.t: Et scies quoniam multiplex erit semen tuum, id est, verbo doctrinæ et bonis operibus a Deo ditaberis: quia per virtuosa virtutum moralium exercitia, scilicet per passionum reformationem, tanquam per viam purgativam, ad supernam illuminationem pertingitur; unaque actio virtuosa disponit ad aliam. Propter quod ait Salvator: Habenti dabitur, et abundabit. Et Ecclesiasticus asserit: Fili, concupiscens sapientiam, conserva justitiam, et Deus præbebit illam tibi. Et progenies tua, id est filii tui spirituales, videlicet operum tuorum imitatores, vel tuæ doctrinæ sectatores, erunt sicut herba terræ, per gratiam reflorentes, et bonis operibus se ac alios fecundantes, ut sint arbores fructuosæ, non steriles.
paras.en: [[5:25|Thou shalt know also that|Et scies quoniam]] [[5:25|thy seed shall be multiplied|multiplex erit semen tuum]]: that is, thou shalt be enriched by God with the word of doctrine and with good works; because by the virtuous exercises of the moral virtues, namely by the reforming of the passions, as by the purgative way [that is, the first stage of the spiritual life, the cleansing of the soul from sin, which leads to the illuminative and unitive ways], one reaches the illumination from above; and one virtuous act disposes to another. For this reason the Saviour says: [[Matt 25:29|that hath shall be given, and he shall abound|Habenti dabitur, et abundabit]]. And Ecclesiasticus declares: [[Ecclus 1:33|Son, if thou desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will give her to thee|Fili, concupiscens sapientiam, conserva justitiam, et Deus præbebit illam tibi]]. [[5:25|and thy offspring|Et progenies tua]], that is, thy spiritual children, namely the imitators of thy works or the followers of thy doctrine, shall be [[5:25|like the grass of the earth|sicut herba terræ]], flourishing again through grace, and making themselves and others fruitful with good works, so that they may be fruitful trees and not barren.

paras.t: Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum, id est, plenus virtutibus morieris, sicut de justis ait Scriptura, quod mortui sunt in senectute bona, pleni dierum. Iterum, Ingredieris in abundantia præcedentium meritorum vitæ activæ seu virtutum moralium, sepulcrum solitudinis, id est locum secretum orationis, meditationis, et potissime secretum contemplationis. Vita etenim contemplativa sepulcrum vocatur, quia a mundi actibus nos abscondit, huicque sæculo mortuos exhibet, prout scribit Apostolus: Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. De contemplativis quoque Psalmista loquitur Deo: Abscondes eos in abscondito faciei tuæ a conturbatione hominum. Qui autem in actibus virtutum moralium se rite exercitavit, et animum habet purgatum, simplificatum, sancta caritate ferventem, ad contemplationis divitias aptus est, instarque vitri tersi, pervii et politi dispositus, ut in mente ipsius splendeat, ferveat ac moretur Sol sapientiæ, Lux æterna, Deus altissimus.
paras.en: [[5:26|Thou shalt enter into the grave in abundance|Ingredieris in abundantia sepulcrum]]: that is, thou shalt die full of virtues, as Scripture says of the just that they died [[Gen 25:8|in a good old age|in senectute bona]], [[1 Par 29:28|full of days|pleni dierum]]. Again: thou shalt enter, in abundance of the preceding merits of the active life, or of the moral virtues, into the grave of solitude, that is, the secret place of prayer and meditation, and above all the secret place of contemplation. For the contemplative life is called a grave because it hides us from the doings of the world and shows us dead to this world, as the Apostle writes: [[Col 3:3|For you are dead: and your life is hid with Christ in God|Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo]]. Of contemplatives too the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 30:21|Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy face, from the disturbance of men|Abscondes eos in abscondito faciei tuæ a conturbatione hominum]]. And he who has rightly exercised himself in the acts of the moral virtues, and has a soul cleansed, made simple and fervent with holy charity, is fit for the riches of contemplation, and like a glass wiped clean, clear and polished is disposed for the Sun of wisdom, the eternal Light, God most high, to shine, burn and dwell in his mind.

paras.t: Ecce hoc ut investigavimus, per studium Scripturarum et considerationem actuum humanorum, ita est: quod auditum mente pertracta.
paras.en: [[5:27|Behold, this|Ecce hoc]] [[5:27|as we have searched out|ut investigavimus]] by the study of the Scriptures and the consideration of human acts, [[5:27|is even so|ita est]]: [[5:27|which thou having heard, consider it thoroughly in thy mind|quod auditum mente pertracta]].

paras.t: Qui alium ex caritate instruit, corrigit seu hortatur, non proprium quærit lucrum aut commodum inordinatum, sed audientis correctionem, illuminationem sive profectum; totaque mente peroptat, ne alter ad suæ damnationis incrementum, audita spernat aut negligat. Ideo de veritate dictorum reddit eum securum, dicendo: Ecce (quod est seriositatis indicium) hoc ut investigavimus, ita est. Deinde hortatur ad vigilantem auditorum memoriam ac operis exhibitionem, subdendo: Quod auditum mente pertracta.
paras.en: He who out of charity instructs, corrects or exhorts another seeks not his own gain or an inordinate advantage, but the correction, enlightenment or progress of the hearer; and he desires with his whole mind that the other may not, to the increase of his own damnation, despise or neglect what he has heard.
