Rightly, then, does the Psalmist pray, and we ought always to pray with him: [[Ps 142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]], O Lord (that is, by judging according to the rigour of strict justice: for we do not pray not to be judged by God at all, since that would derogate from the divine justice, but that he judge us mercifully), [[Ps 142:2|for in thy sight no man living shall be justified|quia non justificabitur in conspectu tuo omnis vivens]]. Further, what Job says, [[9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificetur homo compositus Deo]], Eliphaz also said[[Job 4:17||]]: so Job grants it, because above he made no answer to it.

paras.t: Si voluerit homo contendere cum eo, id est ex æquo litigare aut disceptare cum Deo, hoc est, si voluerit probare justum se esse, absolute loquendo, vel quantum ad Deum, non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille, id est, nec in uno seu minimo poterit se excusare ex mille defectuositatibus seu peccatis saltem venialibus, quæ Deus potest ei objicere. Et ponitur hic numerus determinatus pro indeterminato; loquiturque de homine secundum communem ejus conditionem et statum. Idcirco istis non obstat, quod Virgo beata ex singulari gratia nulli fuit peccato obnoxia.
paras.en: [[9:3|If he will contend with him|Si voluerit homo contendere cum eo]], that is, go to law or dispute with God on equal terms: that is, if he will try to prove himself just, absolutely speaking, or with regard to God, [[9:3|he cannot answer him one for a thousand|non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille]]: that is, he will not be able to clear himself in one, even the least, out of a thousand failings, or sins at least venial, which God can lay to his charge. And a definite number is put here for an indefinite one; and he speaks of man according to his common condition and state. Hence it is no objection to this that the Blessed Virgin, by a singular grace, was subject to no sin.

paras.t: Insuper, Thomas exponit hæc sic: Non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille, id est, nulla determinata numeri specie seu mensura metiri aut exprimi potest, quantum divina justitia excedit humanam. Millenarius namque, quum sit maximus numerus qui apud nos proprium nomen habet (ceteri enim numeri majores per replicationem minorum numerorum promuntur, ut duo millia, decem millia, mille millia); ideo pro quantumcumque magno numero sumitur, quemadmodum et in Psalmo: Memor fuit testamenti sui, verbi quod mandavit in mille generationes. Itemque in Apocalypsi: Regnabunt cum Christo mille annis.
paras.en: Further, Thomas expounds this thus: [[9:3|he cannot answer him one for a thousand|Non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille]]: that is, by no definite kind or measure of number can it be measured or expressed how far the divine justice exceeds the human. For since a thousand is the greatest number that has a name of its own among us (the other, greater numbers being expressed by repeating smaller numbers, as two thousand, ten thousand, a thousand thousand), it is therefore taken for any number however great, as also in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:8|He hath remembered his covenant|Memor fuit testamenti sui]], [[Ps 104:8|the word which he commanded to a thousand generations|verbi quod mandavit in mille generationes]]. And likewise in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 20:4|reigned with Christ a thousand years|Regnabunt cum Christo mille annis]] [Denis reads *regnabunt*, they shall reign].

paras.t: Itaque humiliemur sub omnipotenti manu superjustissimi Dei; et imperfectum nostrum videant oculi nostri; et impleamus quod in Ecclesiastico scriptum est, Non te justifices ante Deum. Hinc ait Apostolus: Qui se putat aliquid esse, quum nihil sit, ipse se seducit. Et iterum: Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis. Metuamus ergo districtionem divini judicii. Etenim, Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus.
paras.en: Let us therefore humble ourselves under the almighty hand[[1 Pet 5:6||]] of the more than most just God; and let our eyes see our imperfect being[[Ps 138:16||]]; and let us fulfil what is written in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 7:5|Justify not thyself before God|Non te justifices ante Deum]]. Hence the Apostle says: [[Gal 6:3|if any man think himself to be some thing, whereas he is nothing, he deceiveth himself|Qui se putat aliquid esse, quum nihil sit, ipse se seducit]]. And again: [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis]]. Let us therefore fear the strictness of the divine judgment. For [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]].

paras.t: Sapiens corde est: imo mens Dei non solum sapiens veraciter appellatur, sed ipsa essentialiter est Sapientia independens, æterna, idealis, exemplaris, immensa, a cujus perfectione, splendore ac puritate omnis creata mens deficit infinite. Propter quod ad Romanos ait Apostolus: Soli sapienti Deo honor et gloria. Et fortis robore. Est namque omnipotens et prima ac infinita potestas: de quo dicitur in Esther, Domine, rex omnipotens, in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita. Denique, ad perfectionem justitiæ requiritur sapientia dirigens et potentia exsequens. Duplex quoque est contentio: una verbalis in disputando, quæ per sapientiam maxime agitur; alia realis in pugnando, quæ per fortitudinem fit. Ad insinuandum ergo, quod justitia Dei est undequaque perfecta, et quod nec disputando neque pugnando possit quis cum Deo contendere, perhibet quod Deus sit sapiens atque robustus.
paras.en: [[9:4|He is wise in heart|Sapiens corde est]]: indeed the mind of God is not only truly called wise, but is itself in its essence Wisdom, independent, eternal, ideal, exemplary [that is, holding in itself the ideas or patterns of all things], immeasurable, from whose perfection, splendour and purity every created mind falls infinitely short. Wherefore the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 16:27|To God, the only wise|Soli sapienti Deo]], [[Rom 16:27|honour and glory|honor et gloria]]. [[9:4|and mighty in strength|Et fortis robore]]. For he is almighty, the first and infinite power: of whom it is said in Esther, O Lord, [[Esth 13:9|almighty king|rex omnipotens]], [[Esth 13:9|all things are in thy power|in ditione tua cuncta sunt posita]]. Further, the perfection of justice requires wisdom to direct and power to carry out. Contention too is of two kinds: one in words, by disputing, which is carried on chiefly by wisdom; the other in deeds, by fighting, which is done by strength. To intimate, then, that the justice of God is perfect on every side, and that no one can contend with God either by disputing or by fighting, he declares that God is wise and mighty.

paras.t: Quis restitit ei tam sapienti, justo ac omnipotenti, et habuit pacem? quasi dicat, Nullus. Sed videtur contrarium. Omnes enim vitiose viventes, Deo rebelles sunt; et juxta Apostolum, Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Et tamen videmus hujusmodi temporaliter prosperari, et carnalem pacem habere: de quibus cantamus, Zelavi super iniquos, pacem peccatorum videns.
paras.en: [[9:4|who hath resisted him|Quis restitit ei]], so wise, just and almighty, [[9:4|and hath had peace?|et habuit pacem?]] As if to say, No one. But the contrary seems true. For all who live viciously are rebels against God; and according to the Apostle, [[Rom 13:2|he that resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God|Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit]]. And yet we see such men prosper in this world and have a fleshly peace: of whom we sing, [[Ps 72:3|I had a zeal on occasion of the wicked, seeing the prosperity of sinners|Zelavi super iniquos, pacem peccatorum videns]] [*pacem peccatorum*, literally the peace of sinners].

paras.t: Et respondendum, quod dupliciter dicitur aliquis Deo resistere. Primo, ei dissentiendo: sicque iniqui, quorum affectiones et operationes sapientis ac justi Dei difformes sunt atque contrariæ, Deo rebelles seu resistentes dicuntur. Secundo, divinæ voluntati seu Deo volenti renitendo, ita quod eam ab effectu impediat: sicque nulla creatura potest Deo resistere. Divina enim voluntas, ut in Deo accipitur pro ipsa ejus volitione ut aliquid fiat, nullatenus impeditur, sed semper infallibiliterque impletur, quemadmodum in Isaia Deus testatur: Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet. Hinc scriptum est alibi: Non est qui possit tuæ resistere voluntati. Et in Jeremia: Quis similis mei? et quis sustinebit me? dicit Dominus. Et quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo? Deus nempe in infinitum fortior est cunctis creatis. Ideo ejus voluntati hoc modo accepti, nullus valet resistere, sed conantem resistere Deus mox impedit et superat: sicque turbatur desiderio suo frustratus, qui resistere nitebatur, ut patuit in Herode volente Christum occidere. Ideo talis pacem non habet. Hinc Salomon loquitur: Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum. Qui vero secundum primum modum Deo resistentes dicuntur, vera, interna, spiritualique pace privantur, quum pax talis sit tranquillitas ordinis, et quies mentis in Deo. Ideo in Isaia fertur: Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus. Insuper contingit hominem acquirere pacem, impotentiori vel æquipotenti resistendo; sed a potentiori non solet quis pacem obtinere resistendo, sed ei cedendo, seque illi humiliter subjiciendo. Unde cum Deo omnipotente ac supersapiente non valet quis pacem habere, nisi se ei subjiciat.
paras.en: The answer is that a man is said to resist God in two ways. First, by disagreeing with him: and in this way the wicked, whose affections and works are unlike and contrary to the wise and just God, are said to be rebels against God, or to resist him. Secondly, by withstanding the divine will, or God as he wills, so as to hinder it from taking effect: and in this way no creature can resist God. For the divine will, taken in God for his very willing that something be done, is in no way hindered, but is always and infallibly fulfilled, as God testifies in Isaias: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]]. Hence it is written elsewhere: [[Esth 13:9|there is none that can resist thy will|Non est qui possit tuæ resistere voluntati]]. And in Jeremias: [[Jer 49:19|who is like to me? and who shall abide me?|Quis similis mei? et quis sustinebit me?]] saith the Lord. [[Jer 49:19|and who is that shepherd that can withstand my countenance?|Et quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo?]] For God is infinitely stronger than all created things. Therefore no one can resist his will taken in this way; but whoever tries to resist, God soon hinders and overcomes: and so he who strove to resist is troubled, frustrated of his desire, as appeared in Herod, who wished to kill Christ[[Matt 2:1||]] [the margin gives only Matth. ii; Herod seeks the child to destroy him at Matt 2:13]. Therefore such a one has no peace. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 21:30|There is no wisdom, there is no prudence, there is no counsel against the Lord.|Non est sapientia, non est prudentia, non est consilium contra Dominum.]] But those who are said to resist God in the first way are deprived of true, inward and spiritual peace, since such peace is the tranquillity of order and the rest of the mind in God. Therefore it is said in Isaias: [[Is 48:22|There is no peace to the wicked, saith the Lord.|Non est pax impiis, dicit Dominus.]] Moreover, it happens that a man gains peace by resisting one less powerful or equally powerful; but from one more powerful a man does not usually obtain peace by resisting, but by yielding to him and humbly submitting himself to him. So no one can have peace with the almighty and all-wise God unless he submits himself to him.

paras.t: Deinde potentiam Dei per ejus effectus declarat. Qui transtulit montes, id est, dejecit, destruxit, vel ad alia loca transposuit, et nescierunt hi quos subvertit in furore suo, id est, tam repente id fecit, quod prævideri non potuit ab his, qui circa vel supra montes morabantur; atque per montium translationem exstincti sunt in rigore divinæ justitiæ; quæ per montium translationem eorum peccata sic ulta est.
paras.en: Next he declares the power of God by its effects. [[9:5|Who hath removed mountains|Qui transtulit montes]], that is, cast them down, destroyed them, or moved them to other places, [[9:5|and they whom he overthrew in his wrath, knew it not|et nescierunt hi quos subvertit in furore suo]]: that is, he did it so suddenly that it could not be foreseen by those who dwelt about or upon the mountains; and through the removal of the mountains they were destroyed in the rigour of the divine justice, which by the removal of the mountains thus avenged their sins.

paras.t: Præterea, juxta Thomam, montium translatio dupliciter fit, scilicet: miraculose ad fidei confirmationem, prout ait Salvator in Evangelio: Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis, dicetis monti, Tolle, et jacta te in mare, et obediet vobis. Secundo fit naturaliter. Omne enim quod naturaliter generatur, tempore determinato corrumpitur. Quum ergo generatio montium sit naturalis, quandoque naturaliter destruuntur. Quorum destructio fertur translatio, quia cum quadam translatione partium ipsorum fit montium: et de hac naturali translatione videtur Thomæ sanctus Job loqui. Potius tamen reor, quod de miraculosa translatione loquatur, quia in illa evidentius divina potestas ostenditur; et quoniam addit, Quos subvertit in furore suo. Miraculosa namque translatio montium, ad peccatorum vindictam magis ordinatur et fit, quam naturalis. Naturalis quoque translatio montium, non videtur tam subitanea, ut nulla præcedant indicia, quibus homines admoveantur ad fugam. Generatio quippe et corruptio fiunt cum dispositionibus præviis.
paras.en: Further, according to Thomas, the removal of mountains happens in two ways: first, miraculously, for the confirmation of the faith, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Matt 17:19|if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed|Si habueritis fidem sicut granum sinapis]], you shall say to the mountain, [[Matt 21:21|Take up and cast thyself into the sea|Tolle, et jacta te in mare]], [[Luke 17:6|And it would obey you|et obediet vobis]] [the margin notes here are unreadable; Denis joins words of Matt 17:19, Matt 21:21 and Luke 17:6]. Secondly, it happens naturally. For everything that is generated naturally is corrupted in a set time. Since, then, the generation of mountains is natural, they are at times destroyed naturally. Their destruction is called a removal, because it comes about with a certain removal of their parts: and it seems to Thomas that holy Job is speaking of this natural removal. Yet I think rather that he speaks of the miraculous removal, because in it the divine power is shown more plainly; and because he adds, [[9:5|whom he overthrew in his wrath|Quos subvertit in furore suo]]. For the miraculous removal of mountains is ordained and done for the punishment of sins more than the natural. Also, the natural removal of mountains does not seem so sudden that no signs go before it, by which men are moved to flee [the margin gives the reading *admoneantur*, are warned]. For generation and corruption come about with dispositions going before them.

paras.t: Qui commovet terram de loco suo: quia in terræ motu tam naturali quam miraculoso, terra secundum aliquas sui partes de loco suo movetur, juxta id Psalmi: Qui respicit terram, et facit eam tremere. Terra autem secundum se totam, de loco suo nunquam movetur, sed manet immobilis, vel tanquam centrum mundi, quemadmodum ab Ecclesiaste inducitur: Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit; terra vero in æternum stat. Et columnæ ejus concutientur. Quod accipi potest de montibus, qui sunt velut columnæ super terram fundatæ; vel de inferioribus terræ partibus, quibus superiores videntur inniti, sicut columnis structura innititur. His consonat illud Ecclesiastici: Ecce cœlum et cœli cœlorum, abyssus et universa terra, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, in conspectu Dei commovebuntur, montes simul et colles et fundamenta terræ; et quum conspexerit illa Deus, tremore concutientur. Naturalis autem terræ motus, causatur ex vaporibus terræ inclusis, egressum petentibus. Deus vero interdum speciali ex causa supernaturaliter movet terram, sicut in Christi passione ac resurrectione.
paras.en: [[9:6|Who shaketh the earth out of her place|Qui commovet terram de loco suo]]: because in an earthquake, natural as well as miraculous, the earth is moved from its place in some of its parts, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 103:32|He looketh upon the earth, and maketh it tremble|Qui respicit terram, et facit eam tremere]]. But the earth as a whole is never moved from its place, but remains unmoved, as being the centre of the world, as is brought forward by Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:4|One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: but the earth standeth for ever|Generatio præterit, et generatio advenit; terra vero in æternum stat]]. [[9:6|and the pillars thereof tremble|Et columnæ ejus concutientur]] [the margin gives the reading *concutiuntur*, as in the Vulgate]. This can be taken of the mountains, which are as pillars founded upon the earth; or of the lower parts of the earth, on which the upper seem to rest, as a building rests on pillars. With this agrees that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 16:18|Behold the heaven, and the heavens of heavens, the deep, and all the earth, and the things that are in them, shall be moved in his sight|Ecce cœlum et cœli cœlorum, abyssus et universa terra, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, in conspectu Dei commovebuntur]], [[Ecclus 16:19|The mountains also, and the hills, and the foundations of the earth: when God shall look upon them, they shall be shaken with trembling|montes simul et colles et fundamenta terræ; et quum conspexerit illa Deus, tremore concutientur]]. Now a natural earthquake is caused by vapours shut up in the earth seeking a way out. But God sometimes moves the earth supernaturally for a special cause, as at the passion[[Matt 27:51||]] and resurrection of Christ[[Matt 28:2||]].

paras.t: Qui præcipit soli, et non oritur, id est, per circulum suum non movetur: quemadmodum tempore Josue factum est, quando sol stetit in medio cœli, spatio unius diei. Luna quoque tunc tanto tempore stetit immota. Ita exponit Albertus. Thomas exponit sic: Non oritur, id est, claritas solis hominibus non apparet, interposito aere nebuloso. Et stellas claudit, id est, visui hominum occultat, quasi sub signaculo aliquam rem tegente. Sic enim per interpositionem nubium stellæ clauduntur. Cui concordat illud in Psalmo: Qui operit cœlum nubibus.
paras.en: [[9:7|Who commandeth the sun, and it riseth not|Qui præcipit soli, et non oritur]], that is, does not move along its circuit: as was done in the time of Josue, when [[Jos 10:13|the sun stood still in the midst of heaven|sol stetit in medio cœli]], for [[Jos 10:13|the space of one day|spatio unius diei]]. The moon too stood unmoved for the same time. So Albertus expounds it. Thomas expounds it thus: [[9:7|it riseth not|Non oritur]], that is, the brightness of the sun does not appear to men, cloudy air coming between. [[9:7|and shutteth up the stars|Et stellas claudit]], that is, hides them from the sight of men, [[9:7|as it were, under a seal|quasi sub signaculo]] covering some thing. For so the stars are shut up when clouds come between. With this agrees that in the Psalm: [[Ps 146:8|Who covereth the heaven with clouds|Qui operit cœlum nubibus]].

paras.t: Est quoque consuetudo, præsertim in libris propheticis, ut luminaria cœli obscurari, et non oriri seu operiri dicantur, non propter mutationem in eis effectam, sed dum homines in aliquam præcipuam labuntur tristitiam, ita quod hominibus ad consolationem non lucent. Sic quippe in Isaia scribitur: Stellæ cœli et splendor earum non expandent lumen suum; obscuratus est sol in ortu suo, et luna non splendebit in lumine suo. Quod totum illic dicitur propter Babylonis destructionem, de qua ibi ad litteram sermo est. Simili modo scriptum est in Joele: Sol et luna obtenebrati sunt, et stellæ retraxerunt splendorem suum. Quod dicitur ibi propter vastitatem Jerusalem a Chaldæis. In Ezechiele quoque Dominus loquitur regi Ægypti: Operiam, quum exstinctus fueris, cœlos, et nigrescere faciam stellas ejus; solem nube tegam, et luna non dabit lumen suum. Omnia luminaria cœli mœrere faciam super te. Denique, in Exodo scriptum est, qualiter tribus diebus fuerunt tenebræ horribiles atque palpabiles in terra Ægypti, itaque tunc sol non oriebatur Ægyptiis. In Actis quoque fertur, quemadmodum nec sol nec sidera apparuerunt multis diebus, his qui cum Paulo erant in navi. Postremo, Deus omni creaturæ, etiam inanimatæ et irrationali præcipere dicitur, et illa obedit: quia potentia quædam obedientialis ei innata asseritur, qua Creatori obedit. Hinc Christus mari et ventis præcepit, loquens ad mare, Tace et obmutesce, ut legitur in Marco.
paras.en: It is also customary, especially in the prophetic books, for the lights of heaven to be said to be darkened, and not to rise, or to be covered, not because of any change brought about in them, but when men fall into some great sorrow, so that the lights do not shine for men's comfort. For so it is written in Isaias: [[Is 13:10|the stars of heaven, and their brightness shall not display their light: the sun shall be darkened in his rising, and the moon shall not shine with her light|Stellæ cœli et splendor earum non expandent lumen suum; obscuratus est sol in ortu suo, et luna non splendebit in lumine suo]]. All this is said there because of the destruction of Babylon, of which the passage speaks literally. In like manner it is written in Joel: [[Joel 2:10|the sun and moon are darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their shining|Sol et luna obtenebrati sunt, et stellæ retraxerunt splendorem suum]]. This is said there because of the wasting of Jerusalem by the Chaldeans. In Ezechiel too the Lord says to the king of Egypt: [[Ezech 32:7|And I will cover the heavens, when thou shalt be put out, and I will make the stars thereof dark: I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give her light|Operiam, quum exstinctus fueris, cœlos, et nigrescere faciam stellas ejus; solem nube tegam, et luna non dabit lumen suum]]. [[Ezech 32:8|I will make all the lights of heaven to mourn over thee|Omnia luminaria cœli mœrere faciam super te]]. Lastly, it is written in Exodus how for three days there was horrible and palpable darkness in the land of Egypt[[Ex 10:22||]] [the margin gives Exod. x, 21, 23], so that the sun did not then rise for the Egyptians. In the Acts too it is told how neither sun nor stars appeared for many days to those who were with Paul in the ship[[Acts 27:20||]]. Finally, God is said to command every creature, even the inanimate and irrational, and it obeys: because a certain obediential power is said to be inborn in it, by which it obeys its Creator. Hence Christ commanded the sea and the winds, saying to the sea, [[Mark 4:39|Peace, be still|Tace et obmutesce]], as we read in Mark.

paras.t: Qui extendit cœlos solus, id est, sine cujusquam adjutorio seu cooperatione dedit cœlestibus orbibus magnitudinem, certamque quantitatis mensuram seu sphæricam quam habent figuram, secundum sapientiæ suæ inscrutabile profundissimumque decretum. Unde ait Psalmista: Extendens cœlos sicut pellem. Et Isaias scribit: Qui extendit velut nihilum cœlos, et expandit illos sicut tabernaculum ad inhabitandum. Ex quibus quorumdam philosophorum ac hæreticorum, dicentium omnia corporalia ab aliqua mente creata esse producta, non immediate a Deo, error confunditur. Nam et Ariani dixerunt Christum puram esse creaturam, et nihilo minus universa creasse. Cujus oppositum hoc loco et infra clarissime edocetur. Et graditur super fluctus maris, id est, instar gradientis atque calcantis subjicit eos suæ sapientiæ dispositioni, suæque voluntatis imperio, ne terminos sibi præfixos egrediantur. Quemadmodum enim ambulans super aliquid, pedibus illud suis substernit; sic Deus sua virtute fluctus maris ad libitum suum reprimit, mitigat et compescit, dicente Psalmista: Tu dominaris potestati maris; motum autem fluctuum ejus tu mitigas. Simili modo scriptum est in Michæa: Dominus calcabit super excelsa terræ.
paras.en: [[9:8|Who alone spreadeth out the heavens|Qui extendit cœlos solus]], that is, without anyone's help or cooperation he gave the heavenly spheres their size, and the fixed measure of their quantity, and the spherical shape they have, according to the unsearchable and most deep decree of his wisdom. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 103:2|Who stretchest out the heaven like a pavilion|Extendens cœlos sicut pellem]] [*pellem*, literally a skin, as of a tent]. And Isaias writes: [[Is 40:22|he that stretcheth out the heavens as nothing, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in|Qui extendit velut nihilum cœlos, et expandit illos sicut tabernaculum ad inhabitandum]]. By these words is refuted the error of certain philosophers and heretics who said that all bodily things were produced by some created mind, not immediately by God. For the Arians too said that Christ was a mere creature, and yet created all things. The opposite of this is taught most clearly in this place and below. [[9:8|and walketh upon the waves of the sea|Et graditur super fluctus maris]], that is, like one who walks and treads, he subjects them to the ordering of his wisdom and the command of his will, so that they do not pass the bounds set for them. For as one walking on something puts it under his feet, so God by his power restrains, calms and checks the waves of the sea at his pleasure, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 88:10|Thou rulest the power of the sea: and appeasest the motion of the waves thereof|Tu dominaris potestati maris; motum autem fluctuum ejus tu mitigas]]. In like manner it is written in Micheas: The Lord [[Mich 1:3|will tread upon the high places of the earth|calcabit super excelsa terræ]].

paras.t: Qui facit Arcturum, et Oriona, et Hyadas. Per Arcturum, Albertus intelligit polum arcticum ac principium frigoris. Thomas vero ait, quod Arcturus sit quædam constellatio in cœlo, quæ dicitur Ursa major, et habet septem stellas claras, quæ nobis nunquam occidunt, sed semper circumeunt polum septentrionalem seu arcticum. Idem asserit Glossa super illud Amos: Facientem Arcturum et Orionem. In Mammotrectu quoque Bibliæ fertur: Arcturus est signum septem stellis in axe lucens, et semper versatur, nunquamque mergitur: quod sæculares Currum appellant. Itaque horum aggregatio siderum, vocatur Arcturus.
paras.en: [[9:9|Who maketh Arcturus, and Orion, and Hyades|Qui facit Arcturum, et Oriona, et Hyadas]]. By Arcturus Albertus understands the arctic pole and the source of cold. But Thomas says that Arcturus is a certain constellation in the heavens called the Great Bear, which has seven bright stars that never set for us, but always go round the northern or arctic pole. The Gloss says the same on that of Amos: [[Amos 5:8|him that maketh Arcturus, and Orion|Facientem Arcturum et Orionem]]. In the Mammotrectus on the Bible [a thirteenth-century handbook explaining the words of the Bible] it is also said: Arcturus is a sign shining with seven stars at the axis, and it always turns and never sinks: what people of the world call the Wain. So the gathering of these stars is called Arcturus.

paras.t: Orion vero seu Oriona, dicitur constellatio quædam nota ac evidens ob magnitudinem suam et claritatem, partim exsistens in Tauro, et partim in Geminis. Quidam vero affirmant, quod sit signum ante Tauri vestigia fulgens. Porro, Hieronymus super Amos dicit, quod Orion hieme oritur, suoque ortu tempestates signat et excitat. Cui concordans Gregorius: Oriones, inquit, in ipso pondere temporis hiemalis oriuntur, et ortu suo tempestates excitant, maria terrasque perturbant. Unde (secundum quosdam) Orion dicitur quasi Urion, ab urina, id est ab inundatione aquarum. Ex quibus patet, cur in libro Meteororum dicat Philosophus, quod Orion sit indiscretus atque difficilis. Postremo, Albertus scribit hoc loco: Orion constellatio est versus meridiem, lucens sub Sagittario, et sole exsistente in Sagittario ortu cosmico sive mundano; estque principium hiemalis tempestatis, dum frigidum movet ad elementorum commixtionem, ut inspissentur elementa ad generationem. Verba hæc intricata, et a prædictis partim discrepantia mihi videntur.
paras.en: Orion, or Oriona, is said to be a certain constellation, well known and conspicuous for its size and brightness, lying partly in Taurus and partly in Gemini. But some say that it is a sign shining before the feet of Taurus. Further, Jerome on Amos says that Orion rises in winter, and by its rising signals and stirs up storms. Gregory agrees with him: The Orions, he says, rise in the very depth of the winter season, and by their rising stir up storms and trouble seas and lands. Hence (according to some) Orion is so called as if Urion, from *urina*, that is, from the flooding of waters [*urina*, properly urine, is taken here for water]. From this it is plain why the Philosopher says in the book of the Meteorology that Orion is uncertain and troublesome. Lastly, Albertus writes on this place: Orion is a constellation toward the south, shining under Sagittarius, and, when the sun is in Sagittarius, rising with a cosmic or worldly rising [that is, rising at the same time as the sun]; and it is the beginning of the winter storms, while it moves the cold toward the mingling of the elements, so that the elements may be thickened for generation. These words seem to me involved, and partly at odds with what was said before.

paras.t: Præterea, secundum Thomam, Hyades, stellæ quædam sunt, in pectore Tauri consistentes, suntque multum notabiles visu. Huic dicto saltem partim concordat, quod alii dicunt, hanc esse constellationem in fronte Tauri, vernali tempore orientem. Gregorius quoque testatur: Juvenescente verno, Hyades ad cœli faciem prodeunt, atque illius signi inhærent initiis, quod sapientes sæculi Taurum appellant. Græco autem nomine hyados pluvia dicitur, et Hyades a pluviis nomen acceperunt, quoniam ortæ, procul dubio imbres ferunt. Hinc ait Albertus: Hyades dicuntur a Græco hydor, quod est aqua, et sunt stellæ quæ dicuntur caput Tauri: oriunturque ortu cosmico in Maio, qui etiam Maius, quasi madidus, dicitur, et movent humidum generationis ad nativitatem et germen.
paras.en: Further, according to Thomas, the Hyades are certain stars standing in the breast of Taurus, and very noticeable to the sight. With this saying what others say agrees at least in part, that this is a constellation on the forehead of Taurus, rising in springtime. Gregory too testifies: As spring grows young, the Hyades come forth on the face of the sky, and cling to the beginning of that sign which the wise of the world call Taurus. Rain is called *hyados* by a Greek name, and the Hyades took their name from rains, since when they have risen they without doubt bring showers. Hence Albertus says: The Hyades are so called from the Greek *hydor*, which is water, and they are the stars called the head of Taurus: they rise with a cosmic rising in May, which is called *Maius* as if *madidus*, wet, and they move the moisture of generation toward birth and sprouting.

paras.t: Et interiora austri, id est abscondita et secreta, quæ sunt circa partem cœli australem seu meridionalem, videlicet stellas quæ ibi sunt circa polum antarcticum, qui simul cum astris sibi propinquis manet nobis (in parte septentrionali locatis) semper invisibilis et occultus, interior et depressus. Circa quod scribit Thomas: Illis qui sub æquinoctiali habitant, si tamen aliqui ibi habitant, uterque polus conspicuus est, quum horizon eorum ad rectos angulos æquinoctialem secet, sicque oportet ut transeat per utrumque polum æquinoctialem. Recedentibus autem ab æquinoctiali, et accedentibus versus polum septentrionalem, elevatur super horizontem polus septentrionalis, et deprimitur polus australis, secundum mensuram elongationis ab æquinoctiali. Hinc nobis non potest esse conspicuus, nec stellæ ei vicinæ. Albertus quoque hic ait: Interiora austri dicuntur, quia sub axe sphæræ in polo antarctico nobis in quarta aquilonaris terræ habitantibus deprimuntur. Unde Lucanus: Hic vertex nobis semper sublimis, at illum Occultum Styx atra tegit. Et stellæ ibi positæ, principium sunt caloris: propter quod infra habetur, Nonne vestimenta tua calida sunt, quum perflatæ fuerint Austro?
paras.en: [[9:9|and the inner parts of the south|Et interiora austri]], that is, the hidden and secret things which are about the southern or meridional part of the sky, namely the stars which are there about the antarctic pole, which, together with the stars near it, remains for us (who are placed in the northern part) always invisible and hidden, inward and sunk down. On this Thomas writes: For those who live under the equinoctial line, if any do live there, both poles are visible, since their horizon cuts the equinoctial at right angles, and so must pass through both poles of the equinoctial. But for those who go away from the equinoctial and draw toward the northern pole, the northern pole is raised above the horizon, and the southern pole is sunk below it, according to the measure of their distance from the equinoctial. Hence it cannot be visible to us, nor the stars near it. Albertus too says here: [[9:9|the inner parts of the south|Interiora austri]] are so called because under the axis of the sphere at the antarctic pole they are sunk down for us who live in the northern quarter of the earth. Hence Lucan: This pole is ever high above us; but that other the black Styx covers, hidden [the lines are Virgil's, Georgics I, 242–243, given here in a different form]. And the stars placed there are a source of heat: for which reason it is said below, [[Job 37:17|Are not thy garments hot, when the south wind blows upon the earth?|Nonne vestimenta tua calida sunt, quum perflatæ fuerint Austro?]] [Denis reads: when they have been blown upon by the south wind].

paras.t: Qui facit magna, et inscrutabilia, et mirabilia, quorum non est numerus. Hoc ipsum supra locutus est Eliphaz: quod ibidem diffuse expositum est, idcirco pertranseundum.
paras.en: [[9:10|Who doth things great and incomprehensible, and wonderful, of which there is no number|Qui facit magna, et inscrutabilia, et mirabilia, quorum non est numerus]] [Denis reads *inscrutabilia*, unsearchable; the margin gives the reading *incomprehensibilia*, as in the Vulgate]. Eliphaz said this very thing above[[Job 5:9||]]; and since it was expounded at length there, it is to be passed over.

paras.t: Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; si abierit, non intelligam. Hoc aliqui sic exponunt: Si venerit ad me per suam gratiam, seu gratiæ infusionem, non videbo eum, hunc adventum percipiendo; si abierit, gratiam subtrahendo, non intelligam hujusmodi subtractionem: quoniam nescit homo an amore vel odio dignus sit, ut in Ecclesiaste habetur. Sed circa hanc expositionem, cui secundum unam interpretationem concordat quod ait Salvator, Spiritus ubi vult spirat, et vocem ejus audis, et nescis unde veniat, aut quo vadat, dubitationes occurrunt. Frequenter etenim homo scit se peccare mortaliter: et tunc utique certus esse potest, quod Deus ab ipso recedat, et gratiam subtrahat. Rursus, dum adultus baptizatur recta intentione, scit se gratiam adipisci, et Deum per gratiæ infusionem ad se venire. Denique aliqui sic rapiuntur ad Deum, sicque inflammantur in eo, et ad mysticam theologiam sic elevantur, quod certissimi sunt se divinitus visitari, supernaturali dulcedine affici, in Deum sincerissime absorberi, quemadmodum sanctissimi viri sibi sæpius contigisse humiliter grataque mente suis in scripturis fatentur. Apostolus quoque affirmat: Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. Itemque: Ipse Spiritus testimonium perhibet spiritui nostro, quod filii Dei sumus.
paras.en: [[9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him: if he depart, I shall not understand|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; si abierit, non intelligam]]. Some expound this thus: [[9:11|If he come to me|Si venerit ad me]] by his grace, or the infusion of grace, [[9:11|I shall not see him|non videbo eum]], by perceiving this coming; [[9:11|if he depart|si abierit]], by withdrawing grace, [[9:11|I shall not understand|non intelligam]] such a withdrawal: because [[Eccles 9:1|man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|nescit homo an amore vel odio dignus sit]], as we have in Ecclesiastes. But about this exposition, with which, in one interpretation, agrees what the Saviour says, [[John 3:8|The Spirit breatheth where he will and thou hearest his voice: but thou knowest not whence he cometh and whither he goeth|Spiritus ubi vult spirat, et vocem ejus audis, et nescis unde veniat, aut quo vadat]], doubts arise. For often a man knows that he is sinning mortally: and then he can surely be certain that God withdraws from him and takes away his grace. Again, when an adult is baptized with a right intention, he knows that he receives grace, and that God comes to him by the infusion of grace. Lastly, some are so rapt to God, and so set on fire in him, and so raised up to mystical theology, that they are most certain that they are visited by God, touched by a supernatural sweetness, and most purely absorbed into God, as most holy men humbly and gratefully confess in their writings to have happened to them quite often. The Apostle too affirms: [[1 Cor 2:12|we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]. And again: [[Rom 8:16|the Spirit himself giveth testimony to our spirit that we are the sons of God|Ipse Spiritus testimonium perhibet spiritui nostro, quod filii Dei sumus]].

paras.t: Ad ista atque similia arbitror respondendum, quod verba inducta, uno modo queunt secundum modum prætactum exponi, ita ut verbis consonent Salomonis. Sed tunc universaliter ita exponi non valent, sicut nec verba Salomonis inducta. Multis quippe infusa est gratia cum certitudine absoluta, ut ipsi Apostoli Spiritum Sanctum ac ejus charismata, multique alii, de quibus in Actibus Apostolorum narratur, cum clarissima certitudine susceperunt. Sic et ipsi ac alii innumerabiles viri perfecti, in vita hac certi fuerunt se esse in caritate et gratia, seu dignos amore. Unde etiam sine hæsitatione cupiebant dissolvi, et esse cum Christo. Et Paulus de se, ceterisque ait Apostolis: Nos ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes. Præterea, vitiosi publicis intenti sceleribus, sciunt dignos se odio. Itaque verba Job ac Salomonis intelligenda sunt secundum communem legem, cursum atque processum, secundum quem nescit homo certitudinaliter an dignus sit amore. Verumtamen, ex singulari munere pietatis divinæ, interdum simul cum visitatione Dei et gratiæ infusione, datur a Deo certitudo de gratiosa Dei præsentia, seu pio ejus adventu, sive per exteriora quædam indicia, vel angelicam apparitionem, vel inspirationem internam, seu revelationem occultam. Itaque, quod ait, Si venerit ad me, etc., non est sic intelligendum, quasi semper sic sit, sed quia frequenter sic accidit tam sancto Job, quam ceteris viris perfectis. Aliquibus tamen imperfectis semper sic potest accidere, atque quamplurimis in tota sua vita ita contingit.
paras.en: To these and the like I think the answer is that the words brought forward can in one way be expounded in the manner touched on, so as to agree with the words of Solomon. But then they cannot be expounded so universally, any more than the words of Solomon brought forward. For to many grace has been given with absolute certainty, as the Apostles themselves, and many others of whom the Acts of the Apostles tell[[Acts 8:17||]] [the margin, hard to read, seems to give Act. viii, 17, 18], received the Holy Ghost and his gifts with the clearest certainty. So too they and countless other perfect men were certain in this life that they were in charity and grace, or worthy of love. Hence too they desired without hesitation [[Phil 1:23|to be dissolved and to be with Christ|dissolvi, et esse cum Christo]]. And Paul says of himself and the other Apostles: [[Rom 8:23|ourselves also, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit|Nos ipsi primitias Spiritus habentes]]. Further, the vicious, bent on open crimes, know that they are worthy of hatred. Therefore the words of Job and of Solomon are to be understood according to the common law, course and process, under which man does not know with certainty whether he is worthy of love. Yet by a singular gift of the divine goodness, sometimes together with the visitation of God and the infusion of grace, certainty is given by God of the gracious presence of God, or of his loving coming, whether by certain outward signs, or by the appearing of an angel, or by inward inspiration, or by a hidden revelation. So what he says, [[9:11|If he come to me|Si venerit ad me]], etc., is not to be understood as though it were always so, but because it often happens so, to holy Job as well as to other perfect men. To some imperfect men, though, it can always happen so, and to very many it so happens all their life.

paras.t: Hinc etiam Thomas istud particulariter exponit, dicendo: Ad rectorem rerum humanarum pertinent tria: primo, suis subjectis præcepta justitiæ ac alia beneficia dispensare; secundo, actus eorum examinare; tertio, culpabiles pœnis subjicere. In his tribus ostendit Job divinæ sapientiæ profunditatem. Primo, quod tam profunde atque subtiliter subditis suis sua beneficia providet, quod etiam recipientibus ea incomprehensibile est: et hoc est quod ait, Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum. Deus namque ad hominem venire asseritur, quum ei beneficia sua largitur; et recedere ab eo, quum beneficia aut protectionem subtrahit ei. Interdum autem contingit, quod Deus tribulationes aliosve spirituales defectus electis provenire permittit ad procurandum eorum salutem: sicque venit ad eos, et tamen ipsi eum non vident, quoniam beneficium ejus non percipiunt, nec attendunt. Quibusdam vero quædam beneficia manifesta non subtrahit, quæ tamen in eorum perniciem vergunt: sicque recedit ab eis, ita quod eum non intelligunt abeuntem. Ista expositio Thomæ fundatur in verbis Gregorii hic scribentis: Homo sæpe iram putat, quod gratiæ donum est; et sæpe quod divinæ districtionis ira est, gratiam æstimat. Et consequenter Gregorius horum declarationem prosequitur clarius multo quam Thomas.
paras.en: Hence Thomas too expounds this in its parts, saying: Three things belong to the ruler of human affairs: first, to dispense to his subjects the precepts of justice and other benefits; secondly, to examine their acts; thirdly, to subject the guilty to punishment. In these three Job shows the depth of the divine wisdom. First, that he provides his benefits for his subjects so deeply and subtly that it is incomprehensible even to those who receive them: and this is what he says, [[9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum]]. For God is said to come to a man when he bestows his benefits on him; and to go away from him when he withdraws his benefits or protection from him. But sometimes it happens that God allows tribulations or other spiritual defects to befall the elect in order to bring about their salvation: and so he comes to them, and yet they do not see him, since they do not perceive or heed his benefit. But from some he does not withdraw certain manifest benefits, which nevertheless turn to their ruin: and so he withdraws from them in such a way that they do not understand that he is going. This exposition of Thomas is founded on the words of Gregory, who writes here: Man often thinks to be wrath what is a gift of grace; and often reckons to be grace what is the wrath of the divine strictness. And Gregory then goes on to explain these things much more clearly than Thomas.

paras.t: Albertus insuper ita exponit: Si venerit ad me, in aliquo effectu gratiæ vel naturæ apparens, non videbo eum, supple, perfecte: quoniam Deus effectum infinite excedit. Si abierit, effectum subducendo, non intelligam ubi sit.
paras.en: Albertus, further, expounds it thus: [[9:11|If he come to me|Si venerit ad me]], appearing in some effect of grace or of nature, [[9:11|I shall not see him|non videbo eum]], understand, perfectly: since God infinitely exceeds the effect. [[9:11|if he depart|Si abierit]], by withdrawing the effect, [[9:11|I shall not understand|non intelligam]] where he is.

paras.t: Deinde ostenditur profunditas sapientiæ Dei examinatione actuum humanorum. Si repente interroget, id est, vitam hominis discutiendo, rationem totius conversationis suæ ab eo requirat, quis respondebit ei? id est, nullus poterit sufficienter respondere de se ipso præsumens, aut suæ æquitati innitens, præsertim si secundum solum rigorem justitiæ judicetur. Signanterque addit, Repente, quia si respondendi spatium detur, potest homo pœnitendo peccata delere. Verumtamen, quidam in hac vita sunt viri heroici seu perfecti, qui etiam dum moriuntur, mox evolant: qui et si repente ad Dei judicium deducantur, respondere idonei sunt, quia et pro venialibus satisfecerunt. Propter quod in Sapientiæ libro habetur: Justus si morte præoccupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit. Unde quod ait, Quis respondebit ei, intelligi potest esse dictum ad insinuandum quam pauci sint tales. Vel generaliter intelligendum est, juxta sensum prætactum, quia et justi misericorditer judicantur ac coronantur.
paras.en: Next the depth of the wisdom of God is shown in the examining of human acts. [[9:12|If he examine on a sudden|Si repente interroget]], that is, sifting a man's life, require of him an account of all his conduct, [[9:12|who shall answer him?|quis respondebit ei?]] that is, no one will be able to answer sufficiently who presumes on himself or leans on his own fairness, especially if he be judged according to the rigour of justice alone. And he adds pointedly, [[9:12|on a sudden|Repente]], because if time to answer be given, a man can blot out his sins by doing penance. Yet there are some heroic or perfect men in this life who, even when they die, fly away at once [that is, straight to heaven, without passing through purgatory]: and these, even if they are brought suddenly to the judgment of God, are fit to answer, because they have made satisfaction even for venial sins. For which reason we have in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 4:7|the just man, if he be prevented with death, shall be in rest|Justus si morte præoccupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit]] [prevented, that is, overtaken]. So what he says, [[9:12|who shall answer him|Quis respondebit ei]], can be understood as said to intimate how few such men are. Or it is to be understood generally, in the sense touched on, because even the just are judged and crowned mercifully.

paras.t: Vel quis dicere ei potest rationabiliter et impune, Cur ita facis? opera Dei dijudicando aut reprobando vel præsumptuose scrutando? Nullus omnino, quum Deus sit judex altissimus, a quo appellare nec licet, neque possibile est, fons virtutum, mensura veritatis, et regula æquitatis. Ideo dicit Apostolus: O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Scriptumque est in Isaia: Væ qui contradicit factori suo. Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?
paras.en: [[9:12|or who can say|Vel quis dicere ei potest]] reasonably and with impunity, [[9:12|Why dost thou so?|Cur ita facis?]] judging or condemning the works of God, or searching them presumptuously? No one at all, since God is the most high judge, from whom it is neither lawful nor possible to appeal, the fount of virtues, the measure of truth and the rule of equity. Therefore the Apostle says: [[Rom 9:20|O man, who art thou that repliest against God?|O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo?]] And it is written in Isaias: [[Is 45:9|Woe to him that gainsayeth his maker|Væ qui contradicit factori suo]]. [[Is 45:9|shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it: What art thou making|Numquid dicit lutum figulo suo, Quid facis?]]?

paras.t: Deus cujus iræ resistere nemo potest. Si iræ Dei nemo resistere potest, quomodo in Exodo Dominus loquitur Moysi, Dimitte me ut irascatur furor meus contra eos? Et postea legitur Deus precibus Moysis esse placatus. In Ezechiele quoque Dominus protestatur: Quæsivi virum qui interponeret sepem, et staret oppositus contra me pro terra, ne dissiparem eam. Denique, in Numeris Dominus loquitur Moysi: Phinees filius Eleazari avertit iram meam a filiis Israel, ut non ipse delerem filios Israel in zelo meo. Cui consonat illud in Psalmo: Et stetit Phinees, et placavit; et cessavit quassatio. Multaque talia possent commemorari.
paras.en: [[9:13|God, whose wrath no man can resist|Deus cujus iræ resistere nemo potest]]. If no one can resist the wrath of God, how is it that in Exodus the Lord says to Moses, [[Ex 32:10|Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them|Dimitte me ut irascatur furor meus contra eos?]]? And afterwards we read that God was appeased by the prayers of Moses. In Ezechiel too the Lord declares: [[Ezech 22:30|I sought among them for a man that might set up a hedge, and stand in the gap before me in favour of the land, that I might not destroy it|Quæsivi virum qui interponeret sepem, et staret oppositus contra me pro terra, ne dissiparem eam]]. Lastly, in Numbers the Lord says to Moses: [[Num 25:11|Phinees the son of Eleazar|Phinees filius Eleazari]] [[Num 25:11|hath turned away my wrath from the children of Israel|avertit iram meam a filiis Israel]], [[Num 25:11|that I myself might not destroy the children of Israel in my zeal|ut non ipse delerem filios Israel in zelo meo]]. With this agrees that in the Psalm: [[Ps 105:30|Then Phinees stood up, and pacified him: and the slaughter ceased|Et stetit Phinees, et placavit; et cessavit quassatio]]. And many such passages could be recounted.

paras.t: Et respondendum, quod ira Dei designat vel divinæ æquitatis rigorem, videlicet ipsam Dei rigorosam justitiam, quam Paulus apostolus severitatem absque trepidatione appellat, vel Dei vindictam. Ira igitur Dei primo modo accepta, inflexibilis est, quum sit ipsemet justus et invariabilis Deus. De quo primo Regum fertur: Porro triumphator in Israel non parcet, et pœnitudine non flectetur. Et in Numerorum libro: Non est Deus quasi homo, ut mentiatur; nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur. Sic igitur iræ Dei in se ipsa et secundum se, nullus valet resistere, quin quidquid decrevit et vult, faciat: est enim omnipotens. Propter quod ait Psalmista: Quo ibo a spiritu tuo etc.? Vel certe ira Dei designat divinæ justitiæ districtam ultionem: cui etiam nemo valet resistere propria potestate, et nisi quantum Deus voluerit atque præstiterit. Auxilio autem gratiæ Dei possumus Deum placare, ejusque iram exstinguere, peccata diluere, et omnem justam vindictam per ejus clementiam et pœnitentiam nostram evadere. Ex quo innotescit concordantia et intelligentia omnium auctoritatum istarum, et verbi beati Job nunc introducti.
paras.en: The answer is that the wrath of God signifies either the rigour of the divine equity, namely the rigorous justice of God itself, which the apostle Paul does not hesitate to call severity[[Rom 11:22||]] [the margin reference is barely legible; Rom 11:22 speaks of the severity of God], or else the vengeance of God. The wrath of God taken in the first way is unbending, since it is the just and unchangeable God himself. Of whom it is said in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 15:29|the triumpher in Israel will not spare, and will not be moved to repentance|Porro triumphator in Israel non parcet, et pœnitudine non flectetur]]. And in the book of Numbers: [[Num 23:19|God is not a man, that he should lie, nor is the son of man, that he should be changed|Non est Deus quasi homo, ut mentiatur; nec ut filius hominis, ut mutetur]]. So, then, no one can resist the wrath of God in itself and as it is in itself, so as to keep him from doing whatever he has decreed and wills: for he is almighty. Wherefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 138:7|Whither shall I go from thy spirit?|Quo ibo a spiritu tuo]] etc. Or else the wrath of God signifies the strict vengeance of the divine justice: which also no one can resist by his own power, except so far as God wills and grants. But by the help of the grace of God we can appease God, quench his wrath, wash away our sins, and escape all just vengeance through his clemency and our penance. From this the agreement and the meaning of all these authorities, and of the word of blessed Job now brought forward, become known.

paras.t: Postremo, quum juxta Senecam ira viri moralis ac probi sit maxime ponderanda ac devitanda, quæ tamen aliquando irrationabilis esse potest atque injusta: quanto magis ira supervirtuosissimi omnipotentis Dei, quæ nec injusta nec irrationabilis esse valet, est metuenda, vitanda, placanda? Ideo orat vir sanctus: Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me.
paras.en: Lastly, since according to Seneca the anger of a moral and upright man is very much to be weighed and avoided, though it can sometimes be unreasonable and unjust, how much more is the wrath of the almighty God, who is beyond all virtue, a wrath that can be neither unjust nor unreasonable, to be feared, avoided and appeased? Therefore the holy man prays: [[Ps 6:2|O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor chastise me in thy wrath|Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me, neque in ira tua corripias me]] [the margin seems to give both Ps. vi, 2 and Ps. xxxvii, 2, where the same words stand].

paras.t: Sub quo curvantur, id est, sub cujus majestate humiliantur, qui portant orbem, id est angelicæ potestates: per quas ecclesiastica hierarchia nunc gubernatur, secundum Dionysium, totaque corporalis creatura administratur, secundum Augustinum, tertio de Trinitate; quæ sapientia providentiali, et virtute deiformi, atque regiminis sui cura orbem portant, sustentant, et suo in cursu seu profectu conservant hunc mundum et homines. De horum spirituum incurvatione scriptum est in Apocalypsi: Omnes angeli stabant in circuitu in conspectu throni, et ceciderunt in facies suas, et adoraverunt Deum. In cœlesti etenim curia, plenissime adimpletur quod ait Scriptura: Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus. Quo namque superni cives ac spiritus altioris sunt ordinis, eo reverentialius parent, atque profundius se Deo subjiciunt, prosternunt, humiliant: præsertim quia quo altioris sunt chori, eo divinæ majestatis incircumscriptibilem dignitatem ac lucem clarius intuentur, hincque profundius se ei inclinant.
paras.en: [[9:13|under whom they stoop|Sub quo curvantur]], that is, beneath whose majesty they are humbled, [[9:13|that bear up the world|qui portant orbem]], that is, the angelic powers: by whom the ecclesiastical hierarchy is now governed, according to Dionysius, and the whole bodily creation is administered, according to Augustine in the third book On the Trinity; who by provident wisdom, godlike power and the care of their rule bear up the world, sustain it, and keep this world and men in their course or progress. Of the bowing down of these spirits it is written in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 7:11|all the angels stood round about the throne|Omnes angeli stabant in circuitu in conspectu throni]], and [[Apoc 7:11|they fell down before the throne upon their faces and adored God|ceciderunt in facies suas, et adoraverunt Deum]]. For in the heavenly court is most fully accomplished what Scripture says: [[Ecclus 3:20|The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things|Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus]]. For the higher the order of the citizens and spirits on high, the more reverently they obey, and the more deeply they submit, prostrate and humble themselves before God: especially since the higher their choir, the more clearly they behold the uncircumscribable dignity and light of the divine majesty, and hence bow themselves the more deeply before him.

paras.t: Denique, orbem portantes, intelligi possunt principes et prælati, in sæculo isto aliis præsidentes, quorum est alios paternaliter ferre, imbecillitates eorum portare, et ipsos in omnibus providentialiter sustentare: propter quod tales vocantur aliorum columnæ. Qui curvantur sub Deo: quemadmodum scriptum est, Adorabunt eum omnes reges. Hinc princeps Græco nomine basileos appellatur, id est a basis, quod est fundamentum, et laos, quod interpretatum est populus, quasi basis populi sibi subjecti. Potest et ita exponi: Sub quo curvantur, id est, dejecti et a propria altitudine fracti humiliantur, qui portant orbem, id est superiores superbe se erigentes, qui alios in sua habent potestate ac manu, et ferunt eos quo volunt: qui primo deficient, juxta id Sapientis, Judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt fiet; et, Potentes potenter tormenta patientur. In Ecclesiastico quoque Sapientia ait: Superborum et sublimium colla propria virtute calcavi.
paras.en: Lastly, by those that bear up the world may be understood princes and prelates presiding over others in this world, whose part it is to bear with others like fathers, to carry their weaknesses, and to sustain them providently in all things: for which reason such men are called the pillars of others. These stoop beneath God: as it is written, [[Ps 71:11|all kings of the earth shall adore him|Adorabunt eum omnes reges]]. Hence a prince is called by the Greek name *basileos*, that is, from *basis*, which is foundation, and *laos*, which is interpreted people, as it were the foundation of the people subject to him. It can also be expounded thus: [[9:13|under whom they stoop|Sub quo curvantur]], that is, are cast down and broken from their own height and humbled, [[9:13|that bear up the world|qui portant orbem]], that is, superiors who proudly lift themselves up, who have others in their power and hand and carry them where they will: who will be the first to fail, according to that of the Wise Man, [[Wis 6:6|a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|Judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt fiet]]; and, [[Wis 6:7|the mighty shall be mightily tormented|Potentes potenter tormenta patientur]]. In Ecclesiasticus too Wisdom says: The necks of the proud and the lofty I have trodden down by my own power[[Ecclus 24:11||]] [the margin gives Eccli. xxiv, 14; the passage is Ecclus 24:11, which in the Clementine text reads: by my power I have trodden under my feet the hearts of all the high and low].

paras.t: Quantus ergo sum ego ut respondeam ei? id est, quum tales ac tanti se Deo sic subdant, et ab ejus excellentia tam immense deficiant, ego nequaquam sufficio ei in districto examine respondere, nec ad omnia rationem proferre secundum rigorem justitiæ. Sic enim universæ justitiæ nostræ essent multipliciter, imo et ineffabiliter defectuosæ, ut pannus utique menstruatæ. Et loquar verbis meis, id est ex proprio sensu formatis, cum eo, quasi ex æquo et contentiose, seu ejus judicia nimis audacter scrutando? Verumtamen, affectuosis precibus, devotisque laudibus, possumus et debemus jugiter alloqui Deum; et in hoc distributa est nobis a Deo dignitas præamanda, quod indesinenter licitum nobis est cum Deo adorando habere colloquium: in quo et divinæ majestatis infinita monstratur dignatio.
paras.en: [[9:14|What am I then, that I should answer him|Quantus ergo sum ego ut respondeam ei]]? That is: since beings of such a kind and so great thus submit themselves to God, and fall so immeasurably short of his excellence, I am in no way able to answer him in a strict examination, nor to give an account of all things according to the rigour of justice. For in that way all our justices would be defective in many ways, nay, beyond all telling, like, indeed, [[Is 64:6|the rag of a menstruous woman|pannus utique menstruatæ]]. [[9:14|and have words|Et loquar verbis meis]], that is, words formed by my own understanding, [[9:14|with him|cum eo]], as it were on equal terms and contentiously, or by searching into his judgments too boldly? Nevertheless with loving prayers and devout praises we can and ought continually to speak to God; and in this a dignity greatly to be loved has been bestowed on us by God, that it is lawful for us without ceasing to hold converse with God in adoring him: in which the infinite condescension of the divine majesty is also shown.

paras.t: Qui, etiamsi habuero quidpiam justum, id est, quamvis fuero justus, non respondebo, id est, ad respondendum secundum rigorem justitiæ me exhibere non audeo Deo, sed misericordiam peto, quia et mea justitia comparatione justitiæ Dei, nullius momenti potest censeri. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Omnis humana justitia, injustitia esse convincitur, si districte judicetur. Ideo subditur, sed meum judicem deprecabor, dicens: Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, Domine; et: Ab occultis meis munda me, quia in tua clementia potius quam in mea spero justitia: juxta id Daniel, Neque in justificationibus nostris prosternimus preces ante faciem tuam, sed in miserationibus tuis multis.
paras.en: [[9:15|I, who although I should have any just thing|Qui, etiamsi habuero quidpiam justum]], that is, although I were just, [[9:15|would not answer|non respondebo]], that is, I dare not present myself before God to answer according to the rigour of justice, but I ask for mercy, because even my justice, compared with the justice of God, can be reckoned of no weight. Hence Gregory says: All human justice is shown to be injustice, if it be strictly judged. Therefore it is added, [[9:15|but would make supplication to my judge|sed meum judicem deprecabor]], saying: [[Ps 142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]], O Lord; and: [[Ps 18:13|from my secret ones cleanse me|Ab occultis meis munda me]], for I hope in thy clemency rather than in my own justice: according to that of Daniel, [[Dan 9:18|it is not for our justifications that we present our prayers before thy face, but for the multitude of thy tender mercies|Neque in justificationibus nostris prosternimus preces ante faciem tuam, sed in miserationibus tuis multis]].

paras.t: Et quum invocantem me exaudierit, non credo quod exaudierit vocem meam. Loquitur sanctus Job in persona sui ipsius, aliorumque justorum graviter afflictorum, qui frequenter tempore suæ angustiæ preces fundunt ad Deum, ut releventur seu alia consequantur, quæ quandoque eorum saluti vel non proficiunt, vel minus proficiunt. Unde in talibus Deus tanquam piissimus pater ac sapientissimus medicus audit eos aliquando ad profectum, non autem ad votum. Id equidem dat, quod scit eis finaliter magis prodesse, quamvis ipsi ita non putent. Sicque salubrius ac paternalius audit eos quam ipsi desiderant; nec tamen exauditos se credunt, quia votum suum non consequuntur. Iterum, sæpe contingit hoc virtuosis, ut post altam cœlestium contemplationem, ferventem in Deo affectionem, præcipuam sanctæ devotionis alacritatem, subito tentationibus agitentur, vanis et frivolis cogitationibus impleantur, vitiosis passionum motibus impugnentur: in tantum, ut ipsi vehementer mirentur, quomodo post tantam in Deo serenitatem tantis repente caliginibus involvantur. Hinc ergo eorum mens ex ipsa sua alternatione et mutabilitate fit trepida, atque per hæc quæ nolens patitur, repulsam se suspicatur, suasque preces abjectas, quibus in præhabita serenitate stabiliri, imo et perfici exoravit.
paras.en: [[9:16|And if he should hear me when I call, I should not believe that he had heard my voice|Et quum invocantem me exaudierit, non credo quod exaudierit vocem meam]]. Holy Job speaks in his own person and in that of other just men grievously afflicted, who often in the time of their distress pour out prayers to God that they may be relieved or obtain other things, which sometimes either do not profit their salvation, or profit it less. So in such cases God, as a most loving father and a most wise physician, sometimes hears them for their profit, but not according to their wish. He gives, indeed, what he knows will in the end profit them more, though they themselves do not think so. And so he hears them more wholesomely and more as a father than they desire; and yet they do not believe they have been heard, because they do not obtain their wish. Again, it often happens to the virtuous that after a lofty contemplation of heavenly things, a fervent affection in God, and a special eagerness of holy devotion, they are suddenly shaken by temptations, filled with vain and frivolous thoughts, assailed by sinful motions of the passions: so much so that they wonder greatly how, after so great a serenity in God, they are suddenly wrapped in such darkness. Hence their mind becomes fearful from this very alternation and changeableness, and through the things it suffers against its will it suspects that it has been repulsed, and its prayers cast off, the prayers by which, in the serenity it had before, it begged to be made steadfast, nay, perfect.

paras.t: Insuper, Deus servos suos frequenter ignorantibus eis exaudit, et gratiam concupitam insensibiliter ipsis infundit; multotiesque largitur, quod vix credebant se sortituros, quoniam ipse supergloriosus Deus, infinite ac naturaliter bonus, abundantia pietatis suæ merita supplicum excedit et vota. Nihilo minus Deus frequenter ita suos exaudit, quod non solum credunt et sciunt, imo et magnifice experiuntur se exauditos, dicentes, gratias referendo cum Psalmista: Benedictus Dominus, quoniam audivit vocem deprecationis meæ; et item: Benedictus Dominus qui non amovit orationem meam, et misericordiam suam a me.
paras.en: Moreover, God often hears his servants without their knowing it, and pours into them the grace they longed for without their feeling it; and many times he bestows what they scarcely believed they would obtain, since the supremely glorious God himself, infinitely and by nature good, in the abundance of his loving-kindness goes beyond both the merits and the wishes of those who pray to him. Nevertheless God often so hears his own that they not only believe and know, but even experience abundantly, that they have been heard, saying, as they give thanks with the Psalmist: [[Ps 27:6|Blessed be the Lord, for he hath heard the voice of my supplication|Benedictus Dominus, quoniam audivit vocem deprecationis meæ]]; and again: [[Ps 65:20|Blessed be God, who hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me|Benedictus Dominus qui non amovit orationem meam, et misericordiam suam a me]].

paras.t: Deinde aperit causam, cur dixit, Non credo quod exaudierit vocem meam. In turbine enim, id est adversitatum inquietudine angustiarumque tenebris, conteret me, id est, dire affliget, et quasi consumet, quum tamen oraverim relevari; et multiplicabit vulnera mea etiam sine causa, id est sine culpa mea, vel sine causa mihi nota, non tamen penitus absque causa. Hoc ait beatus Job, quia semel sibi sic accidit, et ignoravit an adhuc sibi tale quid esset futurum: magisque dixit hoc, quia sic fieri potuit sine derogatione divinæ justitiæ, quam quia ita evenit. Nec enim legitur Job post hanc plagam durius aut iterato percussus.
paras.en: Then he discloses the reason why he said, [[9:16|I should not believe that he had heard my voice|Non credo quod exaudierit vocem meam]]. For [[9:17|in a whirlwind|In turbine]], that is, in the unrest of adversities and the darkness of distresses, [[9:17|he shall crush me|conteret me]], that is, he will afflict me dreadfully and as it were consume me, though I have prayed to be relieved; [[9:17|and multiply my wounds even without cause|et multiplicabit vulnera mea etiam sine causa]], that is, without fault of mine, or without a cause known to me, yet not wholly without cause. Blessed Job says this because it had once happened to him so, and he did not know whether some such thing was yet to befall him: and he said it rather because it could happen so without detracting from the divine justice than because it did so happen. For we do not read that Job was struck more severely, or a second time, after this plague.

paras.t: Non concedit quiescere spiritum meum. Hoc ait, quia hæc sua dolorosa percussio cito sanata non est, sed diu duravit, ita quod anima ejus a doloribus multis diebus non quievit. Et implet me amaritudinibus, id est pœnis animæ et corporis, dum et causam percussionis meæ ignoro, et de relevamine spem certam non habeo, imo et de gravioribus plagis formido. Hæc eadem dixit Job supra: quæ ibi sunt plenius explanata.
paras.en: [[9:18|He alloweth not my spirit to rest|Non concedit quiescere spiritum meum]]. He says this because this painful stroke of his was not quickly healed, but lasted long, so that his soul did not rest from its pains for many days. [[9:18|and he filleth me with bitterness|Et implet me amaritudinibus]], that is, with pains of soul and body, while I both do not know the cause of my stroke, and have no sure hope of relief, nay, I dread even heavier blows. Job said these same things above, and they are explained more fully there [the margin's reference here cannot be read; Job 3:26 or 7:11 may be meant].

paras.t: Si fortitudo quæritur, robustissimus est. Imo in infinitum universis et singulis fortior, tanquam Omnipotens, cujus incircumscripta essentia est sua illimitata potentia: idcirco judici Deo contradicere non præsumo, nec me ei opponere audeo. Si æquitas judicii in judice quæritur, nemo audet pro me testimonium dicere, id est, tunc Deus tam justus mox invenitur, quod ipso me accusante, nullus audet me excusare, quum certum sit, Deum omnibus esse veriorem ac justiorem; qui etiam solus cordium novit secreta, nec alii ea agnoscunt, nisi in quantum ipse eis revelat. Verumtamen, angeli sancti pro animabus virtuosis seu bonis hominibus testimonium perhibent coram Deo, tam in vita eorum quam in judicio; sed hoc contra dæmones accusantes seu adversantes, non contra Deum dijudicantem.
paras.en: [[9:19|If strength be demanded, he is most strong|Si fortitudo quæritur, robustissimus est]]. Nay, he is infinitely stronger than all things together and than each one, as being Almighty, whose uncircumscribed essence is his own unlimited power: therefore I do not presume to contradict God as judge, nor dare I set myself against him. [[9:19|if equity of judgment|Si æquitas judicii]] be sought in the judge, [[9:19|no man dare bear witness for me|nemo audet pro me testimonium dicere]], that is, then God is at once found so just that, when he accuses me, no one dares excuse me, since it is certain that God is truer and juster than all; who also alone knows the secrets of hearts, and others do not know them except in so far as he reveals them to them. Yet the holy angels bear witness before God for virtuous souls, or good men, both in their lifetime and at the judgment; but this is against the demons who accuse or oppose them, not against God who judges.

paras.t: Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me. Nonne sicut et ante præfatum est, sanctus Job in omni hac disputatione contra suos amicos justum se esse affirmat, defendit, et probat? Unde et infra habetur: Omiserunt autem viri isti respondere Job, eo quod sibi justus videretur. Quomodo ergo nunc ait, Si justificare, etc.? Et respondendum, quod verbum istud tripliciter potest exponi. Primo, Si justificare me voluero, id est justum affirmare, Deo judicante oppositum. Ita exponit Albertus, et Thomas. Secundo, Si justificare me voluero, id est, ab omni peccato prorsus immunem me dixero. Tertio, Si justificare me voluero, coram Deo, seu comparatione ipsius, os meum condemnabit me, id est, verba oris mei iniqua me condemnabilem facient tanquam mendacem. Os enim quod mentitur, occidit animam, ut dicit Sapiens. Et alibi scriptum est: Ex verbis tuis justificaberis, et ex verbis tuis condemnaberis. Quod autem Job non fuit a venialibus prorsus immunis, sæpe jam patuit, quum de talibus præsertim Jacobus protestetur: In multis offendimus omnes: et Joannes: Si dixerimus, quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus. Si innocentem ostendero, id est, si probavero quod nulli nocuerim, vel malo exemplo, vel damni illatione, pravum me comprobabit, id est præsumptuosum et mentientem: quod intelligi potest tripliciter, prout in expositione præcedentis particulæ claruit.
paras.en: [[9:20|If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me|Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me]]. Does not holy Job, as was said before, throughout this whole dispute against his friends affirm, defend and prove that he is just? Hence it is also found below: [[Job 32:1|So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he seemed just to himself|Omiserunt autem viri isti respondere Job, eo quod sibi justus videretur]]. How then does he now say, [[9:20|If I would justify|Si justificare]], etc.? And the answer is that this saying can be explained in three ways. First, [[9:20|If I would justify myself|Si justificare me voluero]], that is, affirm that I am just, when God judges the contrary. So Albert and Thomas explain it. Second, [[9:20|If I would justify myself|Si justificare me voluero]], that is, if I should say that I am wholly free from all sin. Third, [[9:20|If I would justify myself|Si justificare me voluero]] before God, or in comparison with him, [[9:20|my own mouth shall condemn me|os meum condemnabit me]], that is, the wicked words of my mouth will make me worthy of condemnation, as a liar. For [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os enim quod mentitur, occidit animam]], as the Wise Man says. And elsewhere it is written: [[Matt 12:37|by thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned|Ex verbis tuis justificaberis, et ex verbis tuis condemnaberis]]. That Job was not wholly free from venial sins [that is, lesser sins, which do not destroy charity in the soul] has often been made plain already, since of such sins especially James declares: [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|In multis offendimus omnes]]; and John: [[1 John 1:8|If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves|Si dixerimus, quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus]]. [[9:20|if I would shew myself innocent|Si innocentem ostendero]], that is, if I should prove that I have harmed no one, either by bad example or by inflicting loss, [[9:20|he shall prove me wicked|pravum me comprobabit]], that is, presumptuous and lying: which can be understood in three ways, as was made clear in the explanation of the preceding clause.

paras.t: Etiamsi simplex fuero, simplicitate virtutis, et exclusione duplicitatis ac dolositatis: sicut diffuse elucidatum est in pertractatione primi capituli; hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea. Hic rursus dubitatio oritur, quomodo verum sit hoc, quum jam supra tam frequenter constanterque dixerit se sine sua culpa percussum. Et respondendum, quod ob varias causas, præsertim ob instabilitatem et varietatem motuum affectionumque animæ, nescit homo an amore an odio dignus sit, juxta sensum præhabitum, nisi in quantum Deo revelante certitudinaliter noverit amore se dignum. Talis autem revelatio seu certificatio non semper actualiter adest viris sanctis. Idcirco, pro tempore quo talis assecuratio eis non datur, absolutam certitudinem non habent de hoc, quod sint digni amore, quamvis hoc conjecturaliter ac probabiliter sciant: et ita nunc loquitur Job. Et tædebit me vitæ meæ, partim ex hac ignorantia, quia inter causas quibus fit justis vita hæc tædiosa, ita quod ad aliam adspirant, una hæc est, quod quamvis virtutibus studeant, atque quotidie contra vitia laboriose compugnent, nihilo minus manent incerti an amore Dei sint digni, nisi (ut dictum est) desuper certificentur. Unde vita hæc anxietatibus plena est. Quomodo autem liceat tædium habere de vita hac, in expositione capituli tertii patuit.
paras.en: [[9:21|Although I should be simple|Etiamsi simplex fuero]], with the simplicity of virtue, and with doubleness and guile shut out, as was explained at length in the treatment of the first chapter[[Job 1:1||]]; [[9:21|even this my soul shall be ignorant of|hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]]. Here again a question arises: how this can be true, since above he has said so often and so steadfastly that he was struck without fault of his own. And the answer is that for various reasons, above all because of the instability and variety of the motions and affections of the soul, [[Eccles 9:1|man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love, or hatred|nescit homo an amore an odio dignus sit]], in the sense given before, except in so far as by God's revelation he knows with certainty that he is worthy of love. But such a revelation or assurance is not always actually present to holy men. Therefore, for the time in which such assurance is not given them, they have no absolute certainty that they are worthy of love, though they know it by conjecture and with probability: and so Job speaks now. [[9:21|and I shall be weary of my life|Et tædebit me vitæ meæ]], partly from this ignorance; for among the causes by which this life becomes wearisome to the just, so that they long for the other, one is this: that though they strive after the virtues and fight laboriously every day against the vices, they nevertheless remain uncertain whether they are worthy of the love of God, unless (as was said) they be assured from above. Hence this life is full of anxieties. But how it is lawful to be weary of this life was shown in the explanation of the third chapter [the margin refers to Art. XI, on chapter 3].

paras.t: Unum, id est præcipue quoddam, est quod locutus sum, supra disputando contra Eliphaz: et quid sit illud, subjungit: et innocentem et impium ipse consumit: quod tripliciter accipi potest. Primo, quia tam justi quam impii communiter mortem patiuntur, quæ a Deo est, habente imperium seu potestatem vitæ et mortis, prout in Sapientia scribitur. Qui in Deuteronomio testatur: Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam. Mors autem est viventis quædam consumptio. Secundo, quia tam justos quam pravos Deus in vita hac adversitatibus, pœnis, et tribulationibus attenuat et fatigat, ita ut et corpore per maciem consumantur, sicut sancto Job contigit. Tertio, quoniam Deus immensitate suæ justitiæ non vitiosos dumtaxat, sed et virtuosos superat infinite, ita ut comparatione Dei etiam innocentes inveniantur defectuosi, nec divinæ æquitatis possint ferre rigorem, nisi misceatur effectus clementiæ, prout clarius dictum est. Unde in Exodo Moyses loquitur Deo: Nullus per se apud te innocens est. Ex quibus Job reprobat opinionem amicorum suorum pro sola culpa pœnam a Deo infligi dicentium: cujus oppositum asserit se dixisse, et adhuc firmiter sustinere.
paras.en: [[9:22|One thing|Unum]], that is, one thing in particular, [[9:22|there is that I have spoken|est quod locutus sum]] above, in disputing against Eliphaz: and what that is, he adds: [[9:22|both the innocent and the wicked he consumeth|et innocentem et impium ipse consumit]]: which can be taken in three ways. First, because the just and the wicked alike suffer death, which is from God, who has dominion, or [[Wis 16:13|power of life and death|potestatem vitæ et mortis]], as is written in Wisdom. He it is who testifies in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live|Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam]]. Now death is a kind of consuming of the living. Second, because God in this life wears down and wearies both the just and the wicked with adversities, pains and tribulations, so that they are consumed even in body by wasting, as befell holy Job.
