Third, because God by the immensity of his justice surpasses infinitely not only the vicious but the virtuous too, so that in comparison with God even the innocent are found wanting, and cannot bear the rigour of the divine equity unless the effect of clemency be mixed with it, as was said more clearly above. Hence in Exodus Moses says to God: [[Ex 34:7|no man of himself is innocent before thee|Nullus per se apud te innocens est]]. By these words Job rejects the opinion of his friends, who said that punishment is inflicted by God for sin alone: the opposite of which he affirms that he has said, and still firmly maintains.

paras.t: Si flagellat, id est, quia Deus per quotidianas tribulationes justos incessanter in hac vita exercet, ita ut fateantur, Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die; occidat semel, id est, justis brevem imponat adversitatis finem, et non tam diuturna eos morte afficiat. Hoc enim (ut superius expositum est) justi aliquando licite orant desiderio futuræ quietis, et ex timore, ne pondere adversitatis ad impatientiam ruant, aut aliquo modo Deum offendant. Necesse est autem ad intelligendum verba beati Job, considerare proprietatem hominis in maximis constituti doloribus, qui cordis sui pandit affectum, tamen sub regula rationis, et sub conditione implicita, dummodo scilicet Deo sic placeat, quoniam afflictus, quantum in se est, ita cupit. Et non de pœnis innocentis rideat, id est, per modum ridentis se habeat, permittendo eos diu sine eorum culpa affligi, ac si Deus in ipsa eorum afflictione secundum se complacentiam quamdam haberet: quod tamen benignissimo Deo non competit, sed tyrannis sævissimis. Deo quippe innocentium pœnæ placent, non secundum se, sed propter fructum ex eis sequentem, et finem a supersapiente Deo intentum, qui diligentibus se electis omnia facit cooperari in bonum. Verumtamen, quamvis Deus de innocentium pœnis non rideat, nihilo minus orat Job, ut nec per modum ridentis se habeat, id est, ut eis finem cito imponat: quod intelligendum est juxta expositionem capituli tertii. Interdum nempe hoc licite postulatur, sicut et Moyses dixit: Obsecro ut interficias me, ne tantis malis afficiar.
paras.en: [[9:23|If he scourge|Si flagellat]], that is, since God unceasingly exercises the just in this life with daily tribulations, so that they confess, [[Ps 43:22|Because for thy sake we are killed all the day long|Quoniam propter te mortificamur tota die]]; [[9:23|let him kill at once|occidat semel]], that is, let him set a short end to the adversity of the just, and not afflict them with so long-drawn a death. For (as was explained above) the just sometimes lawfully pray for this[[Job 6:9||]] [the margin gives Job vi, 9, 10], out of desire for the rest to come, and from fear lest under the weight of adversity they fall into impatience, or offend God in some way. But to understand the words of blessed Job it is necessary to consider the condition of a man set in the greatest pains, who lays open the feeling of his heart, yet under the rule of reason and under an implied condition, namely, provided it so please God; since the afflicted man, as far as in him lies, desires this. [[9:23|and not laugh at the pains of the innocent|Et non de pœnis innocentis rideat]], that is, let him not behave in the manner of one laughing, by allowing them to be afflicted for a long time without their fault, as if God took some pleasure in their affliction for its own sake: which does not befit the most kind God, but most cruel tyrants. For the pains of the innocent please God, not for their own sake, but for the fruit that follows from them, and for the end intended by the all-wise God, who for his elect that love him maketh [[Rom 8:28|all things work together unto good|omnia facit cooperari in bonum]]. Yet although God does not laugh at the pains of the innocent, Job nevertheless prays that he behave not even in the manner of one laughing, that is, that he quickly put an end to them: which is to be understood according to the explanation of the third chapter [the margin seems to refer here to Art. XI, on chapter 3]. For at times this is lawfully asked, as Moses too said: [[Num 11:15|I beseech thee to kill me|Obsecro ut interficias me]], [[Num 11:15|that I be not afflicted with so great evils|ne tantis malis afficiar]].

paras.t: Cur autem hæc dixerit, subdit: Terra data est in manus impii, id est, homines habitantes in terra traduntur diabolo ad tentandum, et impii ejus dominationi subduntur, quemadmodum ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus: Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem. Unde diabolum Christus principem mundi appellat. Apostolus quoque spiritus malignos vocat mundi rectores, id est hominum mundanorum, qui diabolicas suggestiones sequuntur, et non Spiritu Dei, sed spiritu infernali aguntur. Hinc in Apocalypsi scribitur: Væ terræ et mari, quia descendit diabolus ad vos habens iram magnam. Attamen non sic data est terra in manus impii, ut liceat diabolo pro libitu suo homines infestare, sed tantumdem quantum a Deo permittitur.
paras.en: Why he said these things, he adds: [[9:24|The earth is given into the hand of the wicked|Terra data est in manus impii]], that is, the men who dwell on the earth are handed over to the devil to be tempted, and the wicked are made subject to his dominion, as the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:26|they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil by whom they are held captive at his will|Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]]. Hence Christ calls the devil the [[John 12:31|prince of this world|principem mundi]]. The Apostle too calls the evil spirits [[Eph 6:12|rulers of the world|mundi rectores]], that is, of worldly men, who follow the suggestions of the devil, and are not led by the Spirit of God[[Rom 8:14||]], but driven by the spirit of hell. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 12:12|Woe to the earth and to the sea, because the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath|Væ terræ et mari, quia descendit diabolus ad vos habens iram magnam]]. And yet the earth is not so given [[9:24|into the hand of the wicked|in manus impii]] that the devil may molest men at his pleasure, but only so far as God permits.

paras.t: Vultum, id est intellectum, qui est vultus interior hominis, judicum ejus, id est eorum qui judicant habitantes in terra, operit, id est, impius iste diabolus excæcat, ita quod judicando indiscrete et vitiose se habent. Excæcat quippe eos, tam per se ipsum, suis videlicet tentamentis eos a veritate et æquitate multipliciter abducendo, phantasiam perturbans, et varias deceptionis causas ministrans. Insuper, eos excæcat per homines malos, quos instigat ad hoc, ut adulatione, comminatione, donis, dolis aut aliis modis judicum mentes corrumpant. Talibus judicibus dicitur in Sapientia: Audite et discite, judices terræ: quoniam data est vobis a Deo potestas, qui interrogabit opera vestra, et cogitationes vestras scrutabitur; quoniam quum essetis ministri regni illius, non recte judicastis, neque custodistis legem justitiæ, neque secundum voluntatem Dei ambulastis. Horrende et cito apparebit vobis, quoniam judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt fiet. Postremo, his verbis sanctus Job suos notat amicos, quod quum judices essent hominum sibi subjectorum, veritatem tamen a se prolatam atque probatam, dæmone cooperante, non susceperunt, sed reprobaverunt, in suis erroribus pertinaces.
paras.en: [[9:24|the face|Vultum]], that is, the understanding, which is the inner face of man, [[9:24|of the judges thereof|judicum ejus]], that is, of those who judge the dwellers on the earth, [[9:24|he covereth|operit]], that is, this wicked one, the devil, blinds, so that in judging they act without discernment and viciously. For he blinds them both by himself, that is, by leading them away in many ways from truth and equity with his temptations, disturbing the imagination and supplying various occasions of deception; and he also blinds them through evil men, whom he incites to corrupt the minds of judges by flattery, threats, gifts, deceits or other means. To such judges it is said in Wisdom: [[Wis 6:2|Hear|Audite]] and [[Wis 6:2|learn ye that are judges of the ends of the earth|discite, judices terræ]]: [[Wis 6:4|For power is given you by the Lord, and strength by the most High, who will examine your works: and search out your thoughts|quoniam data est vobis a Deo potestas, qui interrogabit opera vestra, et cogitationes vestras scrutabitur]]; [[Wis 6:5|Because being ministers of his kingdom, you have not judged rightly, nor kept the law of justice, nor walked according to the will of God|quoniam quum essetis ministri regni illius, non recte judicastis, neque custodistis legem justitiæ, neque secundum voluntatem Dei ambulastis]]. [[Wis 6:6|Horribly and speedily will he appear to you: for a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|Horrende et cito apparebit vobis, quoniam judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt fiet]]. Lastly, by these words holy Job censures his friends, in that, though they were judges of the men subject to them, yet, with the devil working with them, they did not accept the truth he had put forward and proved, but rejected it, obstinate in their errors.

paras.t: Quod si ille non est, quis ergo est? Hoc dupliciter valet intelligi, secundum quod dictio hæc, Ille, duplicem potest facere demonstrationem seu relationem. Si enim referatur ad impium, cujus manui data est terra, iste est sensus: Si ille, puta diabolus, non est causa prædictorum malorum in judicibus terræ, quis ergo est causa illorum malorum? quasi dicat, Nullus. Non quia homines, dæmone secluso, errare non possent neque peccarent; sed quia ad tantam impietatem non devenirent, ut asserit Origenes. Si vero quod ait, Ille, referatur ad Deum, de quo principalis sermo præcessit, qui et terram diabolo secundum sensum inductum donavit, iste est sensus: Si ille, scilicet Deus, non est gubernator vitæ humanæ et dator terræ in manus iniqui, quis ergo est qui innocentem et impium sic consumit? quasi dicat: Oportet primam horum causam ad Deum reducere, ita quod dæmon justum nequit affligere, nisi Deo sinente.
paras.en: [[9:24|and if it be not he, who is it then|Quod si ille non est, quis ergo est]]? This can be understood in two ways, according as the word *he* can point to, or refer to, two things. For if it be referred to the wicked one, into whose hand the earth is given, this is the sense: If he, namely the devil, is not the cause of the aforesaid evils in the judges of the earth, who then is the cause of those evils? as if to say, No one. Not that men, with the demon set aside, could not err or would not sin; but because they would not come to such great impiety, as Origen asserts. But if what he says, *he*, be referred to God, of whom the principal discourse went before, who also gave the earth to the devil in the sense brought forward, this is the sense: If he, namely God, is not the governor of human life and the giver of the earth into the hand of the wicked one, who then is it that thus consumeth [[9:22|the innocent and the wicked|innocentem et impium]]? as if to say: The first cause of these things must be traced back to God, so that the demon cannot afflict the just man unless God permit it.

paras.t: Sanctus Thomas, libri hujus expositor inclytus et subtilis, quantum ad litteralem pertinet sensum, verba nunc introducta ad sensum alium, isto (ni fallor) difficiliorem trahit et applicat, eo quod dicat amicos Job non posuisse vitam post hanc vitam. Quod quia non reor, ab expositione ipsius in multis declinare compellor, quanquam multa scholastica valde utilia scribat ad prosequendum suum intentum, videlicet ad declarandum, quod liber iste sic litteraliter possit exponi, ut amici Job dicantur non posuisse vitam post hanc vitam. Mihi tamen apparet, quod verius certiusque elucidari queat ad litteram, dato quod posuerunt vitam futuram, seu animam rationalem consistere immortalem. Porro, Lyra in expositione libri hujus in tantum sequitur Thomam, ut expositio ejus videatur quasi quoddam excerptum ex Thoma.
paras.en: Saint Thomas, the renowned and subtle expositor of this book, as far as the literal sense is concerned, draws and applies the words now brought forward to another sense, more difficult (unless I am mistaken) than this one, because he says that Job's friends did not hold that there is a life after this life. Since I do not think so, I am compelled to depart from his exposition in many things, although he writes many scholastic points that are very useful for pursuing his purpose, namely, to show that this book can be so expounded according to the letter that Job's friends are said not to have held a life after this life. To me, however, it seems that it can be explained according to the letter more truly and more surely on the supposition that they held a future life, that is, that the rational soul abides immortal. Lyra, moreover, in his exposition of this book follows Thomas so closely that his exposition seems a kind of extract from Thomas.

paras.t: Consequenter tangit causam quamdam tædii hujus vitæ, ejusque labilitatem, et quod in ea non consistat felicitas. Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore, id est, celerius præterierunt, quam cursor possit percurrere. Dies namque sine interpolatione pertranseunt; cursor autem in cursu pedem figendo, quietibus cursum seu motum intercipit, quoniam inter duos motus semper mediat quies, ut probat Philosophus. Fugerunt, id est, continuo defecerunt: quia in tempore, sicut in ceteris successivis, idem est esse et fieri; et non viderunt, visione perfecta et fruitiva, bonum, id est, id quod vere et per essentiam bonum est, scilicet Deum, cujus comparatione nil aliud bonum, quemadmodum Veritas ait: Nemo bonus nisi Deus. Vel, Non viderunt bonum fixum et stabile in hac vita, in quo fuerit mihi vera felicitas. Porro tempori adscribitur, quod fit in eo, vel accidit his qui in tempore sunt: sicque nunc ait, Non viderunt bonum, id est, ego in eis exsistendo bonum non vidi. De qua visione loquitur Deus ad Moysen: Non videbit me homo, et vivet. Et alibi scriptum est: Deum nemo vidit unquam.
paras.en: Next he touches on one cause of the weariness of this life, and on its fleetingness, and that happiness does not lie in it. [[9:25|My days have been swifter than a post|Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore]] [the Latin *cursor* is a runner; the Douay-Rheims's *post* is a courier], that is, they have passed by more swiftly than a runner can run his course. For days pass without a break; but the runner, by planting his foot as he runs, breaks his course or motion with rests, since between two motions there is always a rest, as the Philosopher proves. [[9:25|they have fled away|Fugerunt]], that is, they have continually failed: because in time, as in other successive things, to be and to come to be are the same; [[9:25|and have not seen|et non viderunt]], with perfect and fruitive vision [that is, the vision that enjoys God, as the blessed do], [[9:25|good|bonum]], that is, that which is truly and by essence good, namely God, in comparison with whom nothing else is good, as the Truth says: [[Mark 10:18|None is good but one, that is God|Nemo bonus nisi Deus]]. Or, they [[9:25|have not seen good|Non viderunt bonum]] that is fixed and stable in this life, in which there might have been true happiness for me. Now to time is ascribed what happens in it, or befalls those who are in time: and so he now says, [[9:25|have not seen good|Non viderunt bonum]], that is, I, living in them, have not seen good. Of which vision God speaks to Moses: [[Ex 33:20|man shall not see me, and live|Non videbit me homo, et vivet]]. And elsewhere it is written: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]].

paras.t: Pertransierunt quasi naves poma portantes, id est multum velociter, quoniam navis poma deferens cum festinantia ducitur, ne et poma lædantur sive putrescant: et sicut hujusmodi navis bono odore ac fructibus plena est, sic utique dies Job fructuosi fuerunt, ut sanctæ famæ odore respersi. Sic in Sapientia inducitur: Transierunt omnia illa tanquam navis quæ pertransit fluctuantem aquam: cujus quum præterierit, non est vestigium invenire, neque semitam carinæ illius in fluctibus. Sicut aquila volans ad escam: quæ cito provolat ad cadaver dum fame urgetur. Cui consonat illud Sapientis: Aut tanquam avis quæ transvolat in aere, nullum invenitur argumentum itineris illius. Et Christus testatur: Ubi fuerit corpus, congregabuntur aquilæ.
paras.en: [[9:26|They have passed by as ships carrying fruits|Pertransierunt quasi naves poma portantes]], that is, very swiftly, since a ship carrying fruit is sailed in haste, lest the fruit be bruised or rot: and as such a ship is full of good scent and of fruits, so the days of Job were fruitful, as though sprinkled with the scent of a holy fame. So it is put in Wisdom: [[Wis 5:9|All those things are passed away|Transierunt omnia illa]] [[Wis 5:10|as a ship, that passeth through the waves: whereof when it is gone by, the trace cannot be found. nor the path of its keel in the waters|tanquam navis quæ pertransit fluctuantem aquam: cujus quum præterierit, non est vestigium invenire, neque semitam carinæ illius in fluctibus]]. [[9:26|as an eagle flying to the prey|Sicut aquila volans ad escam]]: which flies swiftly to the carcass when it is pressed by hunger. With this agrees that saying of the Wise Man: [[Wis 5:11|Or as when a bird flieth through the air, of the passage of which no mark can be found|Aut tanquam avis quæ transvolat in aere, nullum invenitur argumentum itineris illius]]. And Christ testifies: [[Matt 24:28|Wheresoever the body shall be, there shall the eagles also be gathered together|Ubi fuerit corpus, congregabuntur aquilæ]].

paras.t: Quum dixero, Nequaquam ita loquar, id est, quum ex aliquibus causis motus proposuero non taliter loqui de mea calamitate, præsentique vitæ molestia, commuto faciem meam, id est, novam quamdam dispositionem vultus incurro: quia ex variis animæ considerationibus, affectionibus, atque propositis facies diversimode coloratur, disponitur, seu mutatur, nunc pallens, nunc rubens, nuncque albescens: quod in afflictis, contristatis, et plura cogitantibus solet accidere; et dolore torqueor: quia ex hoc quod dolor interior per verba et signa aut gesta non exprimitur, nec erumpit, plus aggravatur, quoniam quasi intra se clausus violenter tenetur; dum vero præfatis modis foris ostenditur, quasi per quamdam evaporationem minoratur.
paras.en: [[9:27|If I say: I will not speak so|Quum dixero, Nequaquam ita loquar]], that is, when, moved by certain causes, I resolve not to speak in this way of my calamity and of the trouble of this present life, [[9:27|I change my face|commuto faciem meam]], that is, I fall into a new cast of countenance: because from the various considerations, affections and resolves of the soul the face is coloured, set, or changed in different ways, now pale, now red, and now white: which commonly happens in the afflicted, the saddened, and those who are thinking of many things; [[9:27|and am tormented with sorrow|et dolore torqueor]]: because, when inward sorrow is not expressed by words and signs or gestures, and does not break out, it grows heavier, since it is held violently shut up, as it were, within itself; but when it is shown outwardly in the ways just named, it is lessened as by a kind of evaporation.

paras.t: Nec immerito torqueor: nam verebar omnia opera mea, id est, in omnibus timorate me habui, et actus meos cum formidine feci, ne in eis te Deum offenderem, et pœnam incurrerem: sciens quod non parceres delinquenti, id est peccanti peccato omissionis sive commissionis, quia culpam non relinquis inultam, nec ignoscis peccanti nisi pœniteat. Pro omni autem peccato quædam pœna infligitur, quia et ipsa pœnitentia est dolor de peccatis interior, et pro peccato fit satisfactio. Hinc secundo Paralipomenon scriptum est: Sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cum diligentia cuncta facite. Et alibi: Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus. Et: Sapiens in omnibus metuit. Quod de filiali ac casto timore potissime verum est. Christus quoque in Evangelio comminatur: Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes simul peribitis. Et in Josue libro habetur: Deus sanctus et fortis, æmulator est, nec ignoscet sceleribus vestris.
paras.en: Nor am I tormented without reason: for [[9:28|I feared all my works|verebar omnia opera mea]], that is, in all things I bore myself with fear, and did my acts with dread, lest in them I should offend thee, God, and incur punishment: [[9:28|knowing that thou didst not spare the offender|sciens quod non parceres delinquenti]], that is, one who sins by a sin of omission or of commission; for thou dost not leave guilt unpunished, nor pardon the sinner unless he repent. For some punishment is inflicted for every sin, since penance itself is an inward sorrow for sins, and satisfaction is made for sin. Hence it is written in the second book of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 19:7|Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do all things with diligence|Sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cum diligentia cuncta facite]]. And elsewhere: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]]. And: [[Ecclus 18:27|A wise man will fear in every thing|Sapiens in omnibus metuit]] [the margin seems to give Ecclus. xvi, 21; the words are Ecclus 18:27]. Which is most of all true of filial and chaste fear [that is, the fear of a son who dreads to offend his father, as against the servile fear of punishment]. Christ too threatens in the Gospel: [[Luke 13:5|except you do penance, you shall all likewise perish|Nisi pœnitentiam egeritis, omnes simul peribitis]]. And in the book of Josue it is found: [[Jos 24:19|a holy God, and mighty and jealous, and will not forgive your wickedness|Deus sanctus et fortis, æmulator est, nec ignoscet sceleribus vestris]].

paras.t: Si autem et sic impius sum, id est tantæ impietatis, ut vos amici mei mihi imponitis, ita quod enormitate vitiorum meorum tantam plagam meruerim; quare frustra laboravi? id est, infructuose atque inaniter, tam sollicite peccare vitavi, adipiscendisque virtutibus studui: quod dici non potest, quia quicumque debitam diligentiam adhibet, faciens quod in se est, ut peccata devitet, gratiamque suscipiat, talis juvatur a Deo, et virtuosus efficitur, et quod petit a Deo, si perseveret in bono incepto, sortitur. Propter quod secundo libro Paralipomenon fertur: Non dissolvantur manus vestræ; erit enim merces operi vestro. Et in libro Sapientiæ: Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus.
paras.en: [[9:29|But if so also I am wicked|Si autem et sic impius sum]], that is, of such great wickedness as you, my friends, lay upon me, so that by the enormity of my vices I deserved so great a plague; [[9:29|why have I laboured in vain|quare frustra laboravi]]? that is, fruitlessly and to no purpose did I so carefully avoid sinning and strive to gain the virtues: which cannot be said, because whoever applies due diligence, doing what is in him to shun sins and to receive grace, is helped by God and made virtuous, and, if he persevere in the good he has begun, obtains what he asks of God. Wherefore it is said in the second book of Paralipomenon: [[2 Par 15:7|let not your hands be weakened: for there shall be a reward for your work|Non dissolvantur manus vestræ; erit enim merces operi vestro]]. And in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:15|the fruit of good labours is glorious|Bonorum laborum gloriosus est fructus]].

paras.t: Sed ne ista jactanter et præsumptuose dicere videatur, seque coram Deo nimium justificare, proinde subdit, alloquens Deum: Si lotus fuero quasi aquis nivis, id est, quamvis valde diligenter me a peccatis meis per contritionem, confessionem, satisfactionem, et lamenta pœnitentiæ purgavero, sicut linteum aqua nivea clarius emundatur, quum aquæ nivis sint subtiles magisque penetrativæ, et bis ablutæ dicuntur; et fulserint velut mundissimæ manus meæ, id est, actiones meæ præcipuo decore virtutum apparuerint splendidæ et ornatæ, ita ut in suo genere sint perfectæ; tamen sordibus intinges me, id est, maculatum ostendes et multis imperfectionibus offuscatum, comparatione tuæ claritatis et æquitatis immensæ: ad quam comparata nostra justitia, velut injustitia reputatur, ut sæpius dictum est. Unde per Isaiam Dominus ait: Ego contaminavi principes sanctos. Venialibus quoque culpis viri perfecti quotidie aliqualiter inquinantur, et ipsis eorum actibus virtuosis multæ imperfectiones atque defectus miscentur. Denique, quantumcumque dilectionis aut cultus Deo impenderint, infinite minus est dilectione, veneratione et cultu, quibus Deus est dignus. Ideo judicium misericordia temperatum, eis est necessarium.
paras.en: But lest he should seem to say these things boastfully and presumptuously, and to justify himself too much before God, he therefore adds, addressing God: [[9:30|If I be washed, as it were, with snow waters|Si lotus fuero quasi aquis nivis]], that is, although I should cleanse myself very diligently from my sins by contrition, confession, satisfaction and the laments of penance, as linen is made cleaner by snow water, since snow waters are fine and more penetrating, and are said to be twice washed; [[9:30|and my hands shall shine ever so clean|et fulserint velut mundissimæ manus meæ]], that is, my actions shall appear splendid and adorned with a special beauty of virtues, so that they are perfect in their kind; [[9:31|Yet thou shalt plunge me in filth|tamen sordibus intinges me]], that is, thou wilt show me stained and darkened with many imperfections, in comparison with thy brightness and immense equity: compared with which our justice is reckoned as injustice, as has been said many times. Hence the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 43:28|I have profaned the holy princes|Ego contaminavi principes sanctos]] [the Latin *contaminavi* is literally 'I have defiled']. Perfect men too are daily defiled in some measure by venial faults, and many imperfections and defects are mingled with their very acts of virtue [the margin's reference here cannot be read]. Lastly, however much love or worship they spend on God, it is infinitely less than the love, veneration and worship of which God is worthy. Therefore a judgment tempered with mercy is necessary for them.

paras.t: Et abominabuntur, id est, abominabilem reddent et demonstrabunt, me vestimenta mea, id est opera: quæ licet hominibus videantur pura, sublimia, et perfecta, tamen coram Deo imperfecta et contemptibilia comprobantur, si secundum immensitatem divinæ justitiæ judicentur, ut ex præhabitis innotescit. Præterea, opera hominis vestimenta ejus dicuntur, quoniam ornamenta sunt animæ opera virtuosa, et instar vestis agentem circumdant et muniunt contra adversarias potestates. Unde in Canticis dicitur: Exui tunicam meam, quomodo induar illam? Et in Apocalypsi loquitur Christus: Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis. Sic et Judas in sua scribit Canonica: Odientes eam quæ carnalis est, maculatam tunicam. Sed et Salvator: Veniunt (inquit) ad vos in vestimentis ovium. Thomas, per vestimenta, intelligit opera exteriora, quæ hominem abominantur quando exteriora opera virtuosa apparent, et tamen interiori puritati non correspondent, dum scilicet cor intus impurum est. Exteriora equidem opera virtutum, sunt velut signa interioris virtutis. Idcirco, si mens intus pura non est, exteriora opera quæ justitiam prætendunt, ei non competunt.
paras.en: [[9:31|and my garments shall abhor me|Et abominabuntur]], that is, shall make me abominable and show me so, [[9:31|my garments|me vestimenta mea]], that is, my works: which, though to men they seem pure, sublime and perfect, are yet proved imperfect and contemptible before God, if they be judged according to the immensity of the divine justice, as is plain from what was said before. Moreover, a man's works are called his garments, since virtuous works are the ornaments of the soul, and like a garment they surround the doer and guard him against the adverse powers. Hence it is said in the Canticles: [[Cant 5:3|I have put off my garment, how shall I put it on|Exui tunicam meam, quomodo induar illam]]? And in the Apocalypse Christ says: [[Apoc 3:4|which have not defiled their garments: and they shall walk with me in white|Qui non inquinaverunt vestimenta sua, ambulabunt mecum in albis]]. So too Jude writes in his canonical epistle: [[Jude 1:23|hating also the spotted garment which is carnal|Odientes eam quæ carnalis est, maculatam tunicam]]. And the Saviour as well: [[Matt 7:15|come|Veniunt]] (he says) [[Matt 7:15|to you in the clothing of sheep|ad vos in vestimentis ovium]]. Thomas understands by *garments* the outward works, which abhor a man when outward works of virtue appear and yet do not answer to inward purity, that is, when the heart within is impure. For the outward works of the virtues are as signs of inward virtue. Therefore, if the mind within is not pure, the outward works that make a show of justice do not belong to it.

paras.t: Neque enim viro qui similis mei est, respondebo: id est, idcirco coram Deo me justum asserere non præsumo, quamvis mihi de mortali non sim conscius culpa, quia in divino judicio habeo respondere non homini mortali, mihi in natura, statu et culpa simili, sed Deo immortali et omnipotenti. Hinc ipso me sordibus intingente, non audeo reclamare, quamvis contra homines arguens, justum me asseram. Nec qui mecum in judicio ex æquo possit audiri, id est, non tali habeo respondere, qui simul mecum coram judice tertio altiore illum et me judicante, possit adsistere, sed Deo, quem judicare nullus valet, quia nec auctoritate, nec sapientia altior illo quis est. Quum ergo a judicio Dei appellare non queam, restat ut me ei prorsus subjiciam.
paras.en: [[9:32|For I shall not answer a man that is like myself|Neque enim viro qui similis mei est, respondebo]]: that is, this is why I do not presume to assert that I am just before God, although I am not conscious to myself of mortal guilt [that is, of mortal sin, which kills the life of grace in the soul], because in the divine judgment I have to answer, not a mortal man, like me in nature, state and guilt, but God, immortal and almighty. Hence, when he plunges me in filth, I dare not protest, although in arguing against men I assert that I am just. [[9:32|nor one that may be heard with me equally in judgment|Nec qui mecum in judicio ex æquo possit audiri]], that is, I have not to answer such a one as could stand together with me before a third and higher judge, who judges both him and me, but God, whom no one can judge, since no one is higher than he, either in authority or in wisdom. Since therefore I cannot appeal from the judgment of God, it remains that I submit myself wholly to him.

paras.t: Ideo sequitur: Non est qui utrimque valeat arguere, scilicet Deum et me: quia licet ego argui possim, Deum tamen nullus potest arguere, quum ipse sit sapientior infinite; et ponere manum suam, id est potestatem, in ambobus, puta in Deo et me: quia nullus tantæ potentiæ est, ut Deum compescere possit, aut vincere seu impedire a prosecutione suæ sententiæ.
paras.en: Therefore there follows: [[9:33|There is none that may be able to reprove both|Non est qui utrimque valeat arguere]], namely God and me: for though I can be reproved, yet no one can reprove God, since he is infinitely wiser; [[9:33|and to put his hand|et ponere manum suam]], that is, his power, [[9:33|between both|in ambobus]], namely on God and on me: for no one is of such power that he could restrain God, or overcome him, or hinder him from carrying out his sentence.

paras.t: Auferat a me virgam suam, id est plagam istam pœnosam: et pavor ejus de futura percussione, vel timor reverentialis conceptus ex consideratione majestatis divinæ, non me terreat terrore dejiciente. Loquar, fiducialiter veritatem positionis meæ tuendo, et non timebo eum timore servili seu immoderato, actum rationis impediente, sed confidenter quod verum est defensabo; nec Deum quasi adversantem seu increpantem formidabo, imo ut patrem amabo. Denique vehemens dolor corporis seu animæ, excessivusque timor, actum rationis impediunt, sicut et ceteræ passiones intensæ. Animam etenim inquietant ac turbant. Ad actus autem rationis interiores, quies et pax potissimum prosunt. Sed et vehemens occupatio mentis circa unum aliquem actum sive objectum, impedit atque diminuit eam circa alios actus. Hinc Job petit ut Deus auferat a se plagam inductam, et terrorem quo timuit Deum temperare dignetur, quatenus libera et tranquilla mente veritatis inquisitioni contemplationique vacet.
paras.en: [[9:34|Let him take his rod away from me|Auferat a me virgam suam]], that is, this painful plague: [[9:34|and let not his fear|et pavor ejus]], the dread of a stroke to come, or the reverential fear conceived from considering the divine majesty, [[9:34|terrify me|non me terreat]] with a terror that casts down. [[9:35|I will speak|Loquar]], confidently defending the truth of my position, [[9:35|and will not fear him|et non timebo eum]] with a servile or immoderate fear that hinders the act of reason, but I will confidently defend what is true; nor will I dread God as an adversary or a rebuker, but rather love him as a father. For vehement pain of body or soul, and excessive fear, hinder the act of reason, as do the other passions when they are intense. For they disquiet and trouble the soul. But for the inward acts of reason rest and peace are of most help. And a vehement occupation of the mind about some one act or object also hinders and lessens it in regard to other acts. Hence Job asks that God take away from him the plague he has brought on him, and deign to temper the terror with which he feared God, so that with a free and tranquil mind he may give himself to the search for truth and to contemplation.

paras.t: Propterea subditur: Neque enim possum metuens respondere, id est, excessive timendo, per ipsum timorem, præsertim ut est passio appetitus sensitivi, a consideratione, et per consequens a rationabili locutione impedior, ita ut nec Deo nec homini respondere valeam expedite atque sagaciter. Nam et timor tremorem facit in corpore, qui cito monstratur in locutione. Imo tremor ex timore, est primo in corde, prout cor est quid corporale, quod dicitur primum vivens in animali et ultimum moriens. Deinde hic tremor maxime apparet in voce, propter vicinitatem cordis ac vocalis arteriæ. At vero corporalis transmutatio, quæ est in passione timoris, est contractiva spirituum et caloris, et retractiva eorum ad interiora. Unde in timentibus propter frigiditatem naturæ ipsi spiritus ingrossantur, calor quoque propter phantasiam debilitatis a corde dispergitur. Ob hæc timentes tremere solent; et si loquuntur, non fortiter, sed cum tremore loquuntur. Similiter est de his, qui in maximis sunt constituti doloribus, quibus multa loqui solet esse molestum. Verumtamen moderatus timor ad actum rationis disponit, et bene consiliativum facit, secundum Philosophum: quoniam parit diligentiam, et animum facit intentum, stultam quoque aufert securitatem et dissolutionem infrenem.
paras.en: Therefore it is added: [[9:35|for I cannot answer while I am in fear|Neque enim possum metuens respondere]], that is, by fearing excessively I am hindered, through the fear itself, above all as it is a passion of the sensitive appetite, from consideration, and consequently from reasonable speech, so that I can answer neither God nor man readily and shrewdly. For fear also causes trembling in the body, which soon shows itself in speech. Indeed the trembling that comes of fear is first in the heart, inasmuch as the heart is something bodily, which is said to be the first thing to live in an animal and the last to die. Then this trembling appears most in the voice, because of the nearness of the heart and the vocal artery [that is, the windpipe]. But the bodily change that takes place in the passion of fear contracts the spirits [the vital spirits of the old physiology] and the heat, and draws them back to the inner parts. Hence in those who are afraid the spirits themselves thicken because of the coldness of nature, and the heat too, because of the imagining of weakness, is scattered from the heart. For these reasons those who are afraid commonly tremble; and if they speak, they speak not strongly but with trembling. It is the same with those who are set in the greatest pains, to whom it is commonly burdensome to speak much. Yet moderate fear disposes to the act of reason, and makes a man take good counsel, according to the Philosopher: since it begets diligence and makes the mind intent, and also takes away foolish security and unbridled laxity.

9.title: De moralitate et mysteriis ejusdem capituli noni.
9.title_en: On the moral and mystical sense of the same ninth chapter

paras.t: Bonæ ac docilis mentis est, veritati auditæ mox consentire. Perversi autem dum aliquid suis verbis contrarium audiunt, aut contra aliquem disputare exorsi sunt, reluctari non cessant; et sive verum sit sive rectum quod eis objicitur, illud reprobare nituntur: quia non ipsam quærunt ac diligunt veritatem et æquitatem, sed propriam potius voluntatem; et dum persona eis contraria per contrarietatem displicet, vera quæ dicit, non acceptant. Talis ergo sanctus Job non fuit; nec sapientes et justi per ipsum expressi, tales consistunt. Ideo in illorum persona sic ait adversario vera dicenti: Vere scio quod ita sit, et quod non justificetur homo compositus Deo. Itaque, ad humiliandum nos ipsos plenissime, consideremus immensitatem sanctitatis, perfectionis atque justitiæ Dei nostri; et cernentes quod infinite deficiamus ab eo, pro nihilo reputemus quæ agimus, nec magni simus in oculis nostris.
paras.en: It belongs to a good and teachable mind to agree at once with the truth when it hears it. But the perverse, when they hear something contrary to what they have said, or when they have begun to dispute against someone, do not cease to struggle against it; and whether what is put to them is true or right, they strive to reject it: for they do not seek and love truth itself and equity, but rather their own will; and since a person opposed to them displeases them by that very opposition, they do not accept the true things he says. Such, then, holy Job was not; nor are the wise and just whom he represents such men. Therefore in their person he speaks thus to his adversary, who was saying what is true: [[9:2|Indeed I know it is so, and that man cannot be justified, compared with God|Vere scio quod ita sit, et quod non justificetur homo compositus Deo]]. Therefore, to humble ourselves most fully, let us consider the immensity of the holiness, perfection and justice of our God; and seeing that we fall infinitely short of him, let us count as nothing what we do, and not be great in our own eyes.

paras.t: Si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille. Audiant et formident verba hæc audaces sibi placentes, seque excusare quam accusare paratiores. Advertant quod innumerabilia habent peccata occulta, quæ nec ipsi determinate valent agnoscere. Qui autem contra prælatos suos contendit, quum contra Dei contendat vicarios, sciat se contra Deum contendere. Ideo Deus tempore suo contendet cum eo, quemadmodum ait per Jeremiam: Ego judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi. Unde restat, ut perpendentes quod non valeamus unum respondere pro mille, reconciliari quæramus, misericordiam postulemus, nosque in omnibus reos, et plus quam comprehendere aut exprimere possumus reos humillime fateamur, dicentes: Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco. Et iterum: Peccavi super numerum arenæ maris. Ideo orat vir justus: Non declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis.
paras.en: [[9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand|Si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit ei respondere unum pro mille]]. Let the bold, who are pleased with themselves and readier to excuse than to accuse themselves, hear these words and tremble. Let them consider that they have countless hidden sins, which not even they themselves can distinctly recognize. And he who contends against his prelates, since he contends against the vicars of God, should know that he is contending against God. Therefore God in his own time will contend with him, as he says through Jeremias: [[Jer 2:35|I will contend with thee in judgment, because thou hast said: I have not sinned|Ego judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi]]. Hence it remains that, weighing how we cannot answer one for a thousand, we should seek to be reconciled, beg for mercy, and most humbly confess ourselves guilty in all things, and guilty beyond what we can grasp or express, saying: [[Ps 50:5|For I know my iniquity|Quoniam iniquitatem meam ego cognosco]]. And again: I have sinned above the number of the sand of the sea [these words are from the Prayer of Manasses, which is not among the books of the Douay-Rheims canon given in this app]. Therefore the just man prays: [[Ps 140:4|Incline not my heart to evil words; to make excuses in sins|Non declines cor meum in verba malitiæ, ad excusandas excusationes in peccatis]].

paras.t: Sapiens corde est: idcirco cordium nostrorum occulta clarissime inspicit; et fortis robore: ideo cognita mala valenter ulciscitur, nec ejus potestati resistitur. Si ergo in nobis est vera atque infusa sapientia, debet ex ea in nobis oriri castus pudor, quo erubescamus in præsentia mentis divinæ omnia lucidissime intuentis, irreverenter et viliter conversari. Ejus quoque omnipotentiam sapienter formidare debemus, quoniam ejus vindictam evadere nunquam valebimus in futuro, nisi jam ei nos humiliter subjiciamus, obediendo omni divino præcepto.
paras.en: [[9:4|He is wise in heart|Sapiens corde est]]: therefore he sees most clearly the hidden things of our hearts; [[9:4|and mighty in strength|et fortis robore]]: therefore he mightily avenges the evils he knows, nor is his power resisted. If, then, there is in us true and infused wisdom, there ought to arise from it in us a chaste shame, by which we blush to behave irreverently and basely in the presence of the divine mind, which beholds all things most clearly. We ought also wisely to fear his omnipotence, since we shall never be able to escape his vengeance in the time to come, unless we now humbly subject ourselves to him[[1 Pet 5:6||]] [the margin reads 1 Petr. x, 6; 1 Pet 5:6, "Be you humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God", is meant], obeying every divine command.

paras.t: Quis restitit ei, et habuit pacem? Palam quod nullus. Etenim, eo ipso quo mens creata suo se Creatori opponit, ejusque dispositioni renititur, ejus voluntati dissentit, et contra divina præcepta erigitur: in se ipsa confunditur, inordinationi peccati subjicitur, omnique vera pace privatur, videlicet pace pectoris et pace æternitatis, quamvis interdum pacem carnalem aut temporalem mundanam sortiatur, per quam ad æternam confusionem perducitur. Vera equidem pax creaturæ, est tranquillitas ordinis consistens in debita habitudine inferioris sub superiori, præsertim sub Deo: quam pacem efficit caritas Dei, juxta quod scriptum est, Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Qui ergo a Deo aversus est, pace caret interna. Porro, qui Deo in cunctis obedit, omnemque suam affectionem, intentionem, actum et delectationem in ipso constabilit, pacem veraciter possidet. De qua ait Apostolus: Pax Christi exsultet semper in cordibus vestris. Et rursus: In pace vocavit nos Deus. Itemque: Solliciti servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis. Sic ergo Deo subdamur, in ipso simplificemur et quietemur, et quidquid occurrerit, aciem mentis in ipso figamus.
paras.en: [[9:4|who hath resisted him, and hath had peace?|Quis restitit ei, et habuit pacem?]] Plainly, no one. For by the very fact that a created mind sets itself against its Creator, resists his ordering, dissents from his will, and rises up against the divine commands, it is thrown into confusion within itself, is made subject to the disorder of sin, and is deprived of all true peace, that is, of peace of heart and the peace of eternity, although it sometimes obtains a carnal or temporal, worldly peace, by which it is led on to eternal confusion. For the true peace of a creature is the tranquillity of order [Augustine's definition of peace, *tranquillitas ordinis*], consisting in the due relation of the lower under the higher, above all under God: and this peace the charity of God brings about, according to what is written: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. He, then, who is turned away from God lacks inward peace. But he who obeys God in all things, and establishes in him all his affection, intention, action and delight, truly possesses peace. Of which the Apostle says: Let [[Col 3:15|the peace of Christ rejoice|Pax Christi exsultet]] always [[Col 3:15|in your hearts|in cordibus vestris]]. And again: [[1 Cor 7:15|God hath called us in peace|In pace vocavit nos Deus]]. And likewise: [[Eph 4:3|Careful to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace|Solliciti servare unitatem spiritus in vinculo pacis]]. Let us therefore be subject to God thus, be made simple and be at rest in him, and whatever may befall, fix the gaze of the mind on him.

paras.t: Qui transtulit montes: superbos namque et sæculi hujus magnates Deus de vita hac transtulit ad infernum; et nescierunt hi quos subvertit in furore suo: id est, montes hi divinam justitiam non attenderunt, nec suam præviderunt ruinam, qui in rigore divinæ æquitatis subversi sunt per mortem et damnationem perpetuam. Insuper, Nescierunt, id est, causam suæ punitionis, videlicet propriam culpam, non adverterunt. Multi enim pro suis a Deo plagantur excessibus, qui tamen nec in ipsa sua percussione sua vitia recognoscunt, sicut per Isaiam de populo Judæorum prædictum est: Facti sunt in ruinam; non est qui eruat. Quis dedit Israel vastantibus eum? nonne Dominus cui peccaverunt? Ipse combussit eum in circuitu, et non cognovit; succendit eum, et non intellexit. De talibus quoque scriptum est in Jeremia: Percussisti eos, Domine, et non doluerunt. Tales autem sunt omnes qui murmurant in adversis, et qui nec in extremis veraciter pœnitent.
paras.en: [[9:5|Who hath removed mountains|Qui transtulit montes]]: for God has removed the proud and the great ones of this world from this life to hell; [[9:5|and they whom he overthrew in his wrath, knew it not|et nescierunt hi quos subvertit in furore suo]]: that is, these mountains did not heed the divine justice, nor foresee their own ruin, who were overthrown in the rigour of the divine equity by death and everlasting damnation. Moreover, [[9:5|knew it not|Nescierunt]], that is, they did not perceive the cause of their punishment, namely their own fault. For many are struck by God for their excesses who yet, even in the very blow that strikes them, do not recognize their vices, as was foretold of the people of the Jews through Isaias: [[Is 42:22|they are made a prey, and there is none to deliver them|Facti sunt in ruinam; non est qui eruat]] [Denis reads *in ruinam*, "into ruin", where the Vulgate has *in rapinam*, "a prey"]. [[Is 42:24|Who hath given|Quis dedit]] [[Is 42:24|Israel to robbers|Israel vastantibus eum?]]? [[Is 42:24|hath not the Lord himself, against whom|nonne Dominus cui]] they have sinned? He himself [[Is 42:25|hath burnt him round about, and he knew not: and set him on fire, and he understood not|combussit eum in circuitu, et non cognovit; succendit eum, et non intellexit]]. Of such men it is also written in Jeremias: [[Jer 5:3|thou hast struck them|Percussisti eos]], O Lord, [[Jer 5:3|and they have not grieved|et non doluerunt]]. And such are all who murmur in adversity, and who do not truly repent even at the last.

paras.t: Qui commovet terram de loco suo, id est, habitatores terræ, prædictorum montium subditos seu ministros, tollit de vita hujus mansionis terrenæ: qui majorum suorum negligentia pereunt, quorum mores sequendo damnantur. Impia namque conversatio prælatorum, maxima causa est damnationis inferiorum, quemadmodum in Jeremia fertur: Quia stulte egerunt pastores, et Dominum non exquisierunt, propterea omnis grex eorum dissipatus est. Et in Osee: Attendite hoc, sacerdotes, quoniam laqueus facti estis speculationi, et sicut rete expansum super montem Thabor. Et columnæ ejus, id est prælati et principes reprobi præfatæ plebis subjectæ ac pereuntis: qui columnæ merito essent, quamvis non sint; concutientur admiratione et pœna gravissima. Quum enim viderint in inferno, quam innumerabiles seu multi suo vitioso exemplo perierint, aut sua negligentia pereant in hoc mundo, admirabuntur de damnatione tantorum per suam ignorantiam, atque pro singulis patientur supplicia, quemadmodum Ezechieli Dominus contestatur: Sanguinem ejus (scilicet pereuntis) de manu tua requiram.
paras.en: [[9:6|Who shaketh the earth out of her place|Qui commovet terram de loco suo]], that is, he takes away the dwellers on the earth, the subjects or servants of the aforesaid mountains, from the life of this earthly abode: who perish through the negligence of their superiors, and are damned by following their ways. For the wicked conduct of prelates is the greatest cause of the damnation of those under them, as is said in Jeremias: [[Jer 10:21|Because the pastors have done foolishly, and have not sought the Lord|Quia stulte egerunt pastores, et Dominum non exquisierunt]]: therefore [[Jer 10:21|all their flock is scattered|omnis grex eorum dissipatus est]]. And in Osee: [[Osee 5:1|Hear ye this, O priests|Attendite hoc, sacerdotes]], [[Osee 5:1|because you have been a snare to them whom you should have watched over and a net spread upon Thabor|quoniam laqueus facti estis speculationi, et sicut rete expansum super montem Thabor]]. [[9:6|and the pillars thereof|Et columnæ ejus]], that is, the reprobate prelates and princes of the aforesaid people, subject to them and perishing: who ought by rights to be pillars, though they are not; shall [[9:6|tremble|concutientur]] with amazement and most grievous punishment. For when they see in hell how countless, or how many, have perished through their vicious example, or are perishing in this world through their negligence, they will be amazed at the damnation of so many through their own ignorance, and will suffer torments for each one of them, as the Lord solemnly declares to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 3:20|I will require his blood|Sanguinem ejus]] (that is, of him that perishes) [[Ezech 3:20|at thy hand|de manu tua requiram]].

paras.t: Qui præcipit soli, et non oritur. Sol intelligentiæ atque justitiæ, Christus est: cui Pater, totaque superbeatissima Trinitas præcipit, secundum quod homo est. Secundum quod etiam in prima sua Canonica ait de Christo Joannes, Advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum justum: qui (Paulo testante) interpellat pro nobis. Christus autem secundum humanitatem assumptam, habet in se gratiam capitis, per quam influit membris suis, puta fidelibus, charismata gratiarum: quia (ut Joannes ait) de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes. Hanc autem gratiæ infusionem Christus, ut homo, secundum superbenedictæ Trinitatis præordinationem æternam præstat et subtrahit. Unde nonnunquam exigentibus hominum culpis, ad Dei præceptum Christus, ut homo, injustis ac intimoratis non oritur, id est, gratiæ dona eis non impertitur, quam electis largitur, juxta id Malachiæ: Orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ, dicit Dominus. Hinc Christus disseruit: Sicut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio. Et stellas claudit quasi sub signaculo, id est, Sanctorum et Beatorum suffragia suspendit ab impiis propter eorum excessus, Sanctis inspirans aut jubens, ne orent pro pessimis, quemadmodum etiam loquitur Jeremias: Ne assumas laudem et orationem pro eis. Quod et Beatis in patria interdum inspirat. De quibus in Daniele legitur: Fulgebunt quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates.
paras.en: [[9:7|Who commandeth the sun, and it riseth not|Qui præcipit soli, et non oritur]]. Christ is the [[Wis 5:6|sun of understanding|Sol intelligentiæ]] and of justice: whom the Father, and the whole most blessed Trinity, commands, according as he is man. According to which John also says of Christ in his first canonical epistle: [[1 John 2:1|we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just|Advocatum habemus apud Patrem, Jesum Christum justum]]: who (as Paul testifies) [[Rom 8:34|maketh intercession for us|interpellat pro nobis]]. Now Christ, according to the humanity he assumed, has in himself the grace of headship [*gratia capitis*: the fullness of grace Christ has as head of the Church, from which grace flows to his members], by which he pours into his members, that is, the faithful, the gifts of graces: for (as John says) [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|de plenitudine ejus accepimus omnes]]. And this infusion of grace Christ, as man, grants and withdraws according to the eternal foreordaining of the supremely blessed Trinity. Hence sometimes, when the faults of men require it, at God's command Christ, as man, [[9:7|riseth not|non oritur]] for the unjust and those without fear of God, that is, he does not impart to them the gifts of the grace which he bestows on the elect, according to that word of Malachias: [[Mal 4:2|unto you that fear my name, the Sun of justice shall arise|Orietur vobis timentibus nomen meum Sol justitiæ]], saith the Lord [the margin reads Malach. iv, 2, 3]. Hence Christ declared: [[John 14:31|as the Father hath given me commandments, so do I|Sicut mandatum dedit mihi Pater, sic facio]] [the margin reads Joann. xi, 31; the words are John 14:31]. [[9:7|and shutteth up the stars, as it were, under a seal|Et stellas claudit quasi sub signaculo]], that is, he withholds the suffrages of the Saints and the Blessed from the wicked because of their excesses, inspiring or bidding the Saints not to pray for the worst of men, as Jeremias also says: [[Jer 7:16|nor take to thee praise and supplication for them|Ne assumas laudem et orationem pro eis]][[Jer 11:14||]]. And this he sometimes inspires in the Blessed in our homeland as well. Of whom we read in Daniel: [[Dan 12:3|shall shine|Fulgebunt]] [[Dan 12:3|as stars for all eternity|quasi stellæ in perpetuas æternitates]].

paras.t: Præterea, nomine solis, donum sapientiæ; per stellas, cetera sex dona inferiora et minus lucentia intelligi possunt. Soli ergo præcipit Dominus, et non oritur: quia et hi qui dono sapientiæ decorantur quantum ad habitum doni, aliquoties actu hujusmodi doni Deo dispensante destituuntur, ita ut non ad divinorum contemplationem atque saporem leventur, sed distractionibus involvantur. Habitus quippe virtutum et donorum, ad eliciendum actus meritorios non sufficiunt, nisi per actualem motionem Spiritus Sancti: quæ aliquando pio moderamine etiam electis […] non oritur, id est, habitus hujus doni in actum suum præcipuum atque splendifluum non procedit. Similiter fit de stellis, id est inferioribus donis, quæ velut sub signeto clauduntur, dum actuum suorum fulgoribus animam non illustrant.
paras.en: Moreover, by the name of the sun the gift of wisdom may be understood, and by the stars the other six gifts, which are lower and less bright. The Lord, then, [[9:7|commandeth the sun, and it riseth not|Soli ergo præcipit Dominus, et non oritur]]: for even those who are adorned with the gift of wisdom as to the habit of the gift are at times, by God's dispensation, deprived of the act of this gift, so that they are not raised to the contemplation and savour of divine things, but are entangled in distractions. For the habits of the virtues and gifts do not suffice to elicit meritorious acts, except through the actual moving of the Holy Ghost: which sometimes, by a loving restraint, even to the elect […] [[9:7|riseth not|non oritur]], that is, the habit of this gift does not go forth into its chief and resplendent act. The same happens with the stars, that is, the lower gifts, which are shut up as under a seal, when they do not light up the soul with the brightness of their acts.

paras.t: Qui extendit cœlos solus, id est, homines spirituales ac cœliformes, quorum conversatio est in cœlis, extendit mentaliter usque ad summum cœlorum, ut ament […] cœlis; atque per omnia climata terræ, ut diligant omnes habitantes in orbe terrarum. Caritate nempe quid latius, quæ et amicos et inimicos complectitur, per quam fit ista extensio? Imo hæc ipsa extensio quid est, nisi actualis dilectio? Quam extensionem non efficit nisi Deus, qui habitum caritatis creando infundit, et ad actus ejus elicitos voluntatem creatam movet, incendit et excitat. Nam et solus Deus dicitur immediate in ipsam agere voluntatem, illam ad nutum immutando et afficiendo. Sic quoque extendit ad se et ad viatores ipsos cœlestes cives, quos incessanter tenet extensos et caritate succensos in se et ad omnes electos, etiam viatores. Porro ob hanc caritativam extensionem cantat Psalmista: Et ambulabam in latitudine; et, Statuisti in loco spatioso pedes meos.
paras.en: [[9:8|Who alone spreadeth out the heavens|Qui extendit cœlos solus]], that is, he spreads out in mind spiritual and heavenly-minded men, whose [[Phil 3:20|conversation is in heaven|conversatio est in cœlis]], even to the highest of the heavens, so that they love […] heaven; and through all the regions of the earth, so that they love all who dwell in the world. For what is wider than charity, which embraces both friends and enemies, and through which this spreading out comes about? Nay, what is this spreading out itself, but actual love? And this spreading out none but God brings about, who pours in the habit of charity by creating it, and moves, kindles and stirs up the created will to the acts it elicits. For God alone is said to act immediately upon the will itself, changing and moving it at his nod. So too he spreads out the citizens of heaven themselves, towards himself and towards wayfarers [that is, those still on their journey in this life], keeping them unceasingly spread out and on fire with charity in himself and towards all the elect, wayfarers too. And on account of this spreading out by charity the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 118:45|And I walked at large|Et ambulabam in latitudine]] [*in latitudine*, literally "in breadth"]; and: [[Ps 30:9|thou hast set my feet in a spacious place|Statuisti in loco spatioso]].

paras.t: Et graditur super fluctus maris. Per mare, corda inquieta vitiis amaricata signantur, juxta illud Isaiæ: Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest. Quorum fluctus sunt, perstrepentes cogitationes carnales, instabiles et turbulentæ affectiones, operaque pomposa. Super quos fluctus graditur Deus dupliciter. Primo, per suam infinitam clementiam eos reformando, sedando, tollendo, dum scilicet gratiose mentem vitiosam reformat, convertens mare amarum ac turbidum in aquam quietam ac dulcem, quemadmodum scriptum est: Dixit Dominus, Ex Basan convertam, convertam in profundum maris. Secundo, per suam justitiam im[…] tumorem frenando, puniendo, damnando. De quibus scriptum est: Hi sunt in epulis suis convivantes, sine timore, arbores infructuosæ, bis mortuæ, fluctus feri maris, despumantes suas confusiones, quibus procella tenebrarum conservata est in æternum.
paras.en: [[9:8|And walketh upon the waves of the sea|Et graditur super fluctus maris]]. By the sea are signified restless hearts made bitter by vices, according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]. Their waves are the clamorous thoughts of the flesh, unstable and turbulent affections, and works of display. Upon these waves God walks in two ways. First, by his infinite clemency, reforming, calming and removing them, that is, when by his grace he reforms a vicious mind, turning the bitter and troubled sea into calm and sweet water, as it is written: [[Ps 67:23|The Lord said: I will turn them from Basan, I will turn them into the depth of the sea|Dixit Dominus, Ex Basan convertam, convertam in profundum maris]]. Secondly, by his justice, curbing, punishing and damning the […] swelling. Of whom it is written: [[Jude 1:12|These are|Hi sunt]] [[Jude 1:12|in their banquets, feasting together without fear|in epulis suis convivantes, sine timore]], trees [[Jude 1:12|unfruitful, twice dead|infructuosæ, bis mortuæ]], [[Jude 1:13|Raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own confusion|fluctus feri maris, despumantes suas confusiones]], [[Jude 1:13|to whom the storm of darkness is reserved for ever|quibus procella tenebrarum conservata est in æternum]].

paras.t: Qui facit Arcturum, et Orionas, et Hyadas. Per Arcturum septem stellis fulgentem, Ecclesia septenario Spiritus Sancti […] semper circa polum movetur, nec mergitur: quoniam indesinenter circa Deum immobilem occupatur, ad ipsumque graditur; et tribulationibus agitatur, nec tamen deficiendo occumbit, sed usque in finem sæculi perseverat. Porro, per Orionas hyeme apparentes, designati sunt martyres, qui ebulliente perfidorum tyrannide, ad fidei constantissimam prædicationem quasi sub frigore adversitatis splendide surrexerunt: quorum constantia signum fuit, quod tyrannorum persecutiva tempestas contra Christianos mox graviter desæviret. Insuper, per Hyadas verni seu Maii tempore orientes, et imbrem secum ferentes, intelliguntur confessores atque doctores, qui pacis redeunte quiete et tempestate persequentium mitigata, pluviam divinæ prædicationis fuderunt; ac tanto liberius aqua sapientiæ salutaris corda rigabant fidelium, quo adversariorum insania magis fuit exstincta. Facit etiam Deus et interiora austri, id est sanctos occultos foris non apparentes ac solitarios, qui austro, id est Spiritus Sancti fervore, clariorique luce perfusi sunt, et in abscondito Domini commorantur, in locis secretis, solitariis et quietis. De quibus ait Psalmista: Abscondes eos in abscondito faciei tuæ a conturbatione hominum; proteges eos in tabernaculo tuo a contradictione linguarum. Qui Deo experimentaliter grata affectuosaque mente proclamant: Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine! Hos universos facit Deus in esse naturæ, in esse gratiæ, quos in patria facit in esse gloriæ.
paras.en: [[9:9|Who maketh Arcturus, and Orion, and Hyades|Qui facit Arcturum, et Orionas, et Hyadas]] [Denis reads *Orionas*, in the plural, and so below; a marginal note here, not legible in the scan, seems to give another reading]. By Arcturus, shining with seven stars, the Church, by the sevenfold number of the Holy Ghost […] always moves about the pole, and never sets: for she is unceasingly busied about God, who is unmoved, and journeys towards him; and she is tossed by tribulations, yet does not fail and go down, but endures to the end of the world. Further, by the Orions, which appear in winter, are signified the martyrs, who, when the tyranny of the faithless was seething, rose up splendidly to the most steadfast preaching of the faith, as it were in the cold of adversity: whose steadfastness was a sign that the persecuting storm of the tyrants would soon rage fiercely against the Christians. Moreover, by the Hyades, which rise in springtime or in May and bring rain with them, are understood the confessors and doctors, who, when the quiet of peace returned and the storm of the persecutors was calmed, poured out the rain of divine preaching; and they watered the hearts of the faithful with the water of saving wisdom all the more freely, the more the madness of the adversaries had been quenched. God also makes [[9:9|the inner parts of the south|interiora austri]], that is, hidden saints, who do not appear outwardly, and solitaries, who are filled with the south wind [*auster*, the south wind], that is, the fervour of the Holy Ghost, and with a clearer light, and dwell in the hiding-place of the Lord, in places secret, solitary and quiet. Of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 30:21|Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy face, from the disturbance of men. Thou shalt protect them in thy tabernacle from the contradiction of tongues|Abscondes eos in abscondito faciei tuæ a conturbatione hominum; proteges eos in tabernaculo tuo a contradictione linguarum]]. And they, with a mind grateful and full of affection, cry out to God from experience: [[Ps 30:20|O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord|Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine!]]! All these God makes in the being of nature and in the being of grace, and in our homeland he makes them in the being of glory.

paras.t: Circa hunc locum scribit Gregorius: Nequaquam Scriptura vanas Hesiodi et Arati atque Callimachi fabulas sequitur, ut Arcturum nominans, extremam septem stellarum caudam Ursæ suspicetur, et quasi Orion gladium teneat, amator insanus. Hæc quippe astrorum nomina, a cultoribus sapientiæ carnalis inventa sunt, quibus Scriptura utitur, ut res quas insinuare appetit, usitatis appellationibus exprimantur.
paras.en: On this place Gregory writes: In no way does Scripture follow the idle fables of Hesiod, Aratus and Callimachus, so that in naming Arcturus it should suppose it to be the last of the seven stars, the tail of the Bear, or that Orion, as a mad lover, holds a sword. For these names of the stars were invented by those who cultivated carnal wisdom, and Scripture uses them so that the things it wishes to convey may be expressed by familiar names.

paras.t: Qui facit magna, et inscrutabilia, et mirabilia, quorum non est numerus. Divinæ potentiæ effectus tunc verius atque completius explicamus, dum nos hos non posse plene exprimere profitemur. Ideo ait Psalmista: Laudate eum secundum multitudinem magnitudinis ejus. Ille quippe Deum secundum multitudinem magnitudinis suæ laudat, qui se succumbere in ejus laudis expletione considerat, ut hic dicit Gregorius.
paras.en: [[9:10|Who doth things great and incomprehensible, and wonderful, of which there is no number|Qui facit magna, et inscrutabilia, et mirabilia, quorum non est numerus]] [Denis reads *inscrutabilia*, "unsearchable", for the Vulgate's *incomprehensibilia*]. We set forth the works of the divine power more truly and more completely when we confess that we cannot fully express them. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 150:2|praise ye him according to the multitude of his greatness|Laudate eum secundum multitudinem magnitudinis ejus]]. For he praises God according to the multitude of his greatness who considers that he falls short in completing his praise, as Gregory says here.

paras.t: Sed in consideratione rerum cur longe extra nos ducimur, qui hoc ipsum quod circa nos et intra nos agitur, sæpius ignoramus? Nam subditur: Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; si abierit, non intelligam. De quibus verbis præcedenti articulo satis dictum opinor. Quibus tamen verbis salubriter admonemur, ne unquam inaniter præsumamus, ne insensata securitate laxemur, ne pusillanimiter desperemus. Multi enim ad tempus in gratiarum eminentia fulgent, et paulo post damnabilius ruunt, quia incustoditi fuerunt. Quibus contigit illud Proverbiorum: Prosperitas stultorum perdet illos. Alii ad tempus tentationum duritia deprimuntur, et cito post hoc cautiores exsurgunt, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Qui non est tentatus, quid scit? Vir in multis expertus, cogitabit multa; qui non est expertus, pauca recognoscit.
paras.en: But why are we led far outside ourselves in considering things, we who more often do not know the very thing that goes on around us and within us? For there follows: [[9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him: if he depart, I shall not understand|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum; si abierit, non intelligam]]. Of these words enough has been said, I think, in the preceding article. Yet by these words we are wholesomely warned never to presume vainly, never to grow slack in a senseless security, never to despair faint-heartedly. For many shine for a time in an eminence of graces, and shortly after fall the more damnably, because they did not keep watch over themselves. To these happens that word of Proverbs: [[Prov 1:32|the prosperity of fools shall destroy them|Prosperitas stultorum perdet illos]]. Others are weighed down for a time by the hardness of temptations, and soon after rise up more cautious, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:9|What doth he know, that hath not been tried? A man that hath much experience, shall think of many things|Qui non est tentatus, quid scit? Vir in multis expertus, cogitabit multa]]; [[Ecclus 34:10|He that hath no experience, knoweth little|qui non est expertus, pauca recognoscit]].

paras.t: Si repente interroget, id est, inopinatos ac improvisos nos ad sui judicii districtionem vocet; quis respondebit ei, id est, ad singula rationem reddere poterit? Denique Deus interrogat hominem, dum eum ad suæ conscientiæ considerationem reducit, vel interius illustrando, vel exterius per flagella aut beneficia provocando, juxta id Psalmi: Dominus interrogat justum et impium. Tunc vero Deo sufficienter respondet homo, dum in eo nil invenitur, quod juste divinitus reprehendatur: quod nemini accidit, secundum illud Proverbiorum: Quis dicere potest, Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato? Itaque, Deus interrogat, dum duris nos percussionibus pulsat, ut dum mens nostra magna de se in tranquillitate æstimat, se ipsam qualis sit veraciter in adversitatibus ac perturbationibus deprehendat. Vel quis ei dicere potest, Cur ita facis? Ideo opera Creatoris inconsulte discutere non debemus, sed humiliter admirari, certi quod injusta esse non possunt, nec mentis humanæ acies imbecillis penetrare aut capere valet secreta Divinitatis. Hinc ait Gregorius: Rationem de occulto Dei judicio quærere, nihil est aliud, quam contra ejus consilium superbire. Unde in Proverbiis habetur: Sicut qui mel comedit multum, non est ei bonum; sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria.
paras.en: [[9:12|If he examine on a sudden|Si repente interroget]], that is, if he call us, unexpecting and unprepared, to the strictness of his judgment; [[9:12|who shall answer him|quis respondebit ei]], that is, who will be able to render an account for each thing? Again, God examines [*interrogat*, literally "questions"] a man when he brings him back to the consideration of his own conscience, either by enlightening him within, or by rousing him without through scourges or benefits, according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 10:6|The Lord trieth the just and the wicked|Dominus interrogat justum et impium]] [here too the Latin has *interrogat*, "questions"]. And then does a man answer God sufficiently, when nothing is found in him that God could justly reprove: which happens to no one, according to that word of Proverbs: [[Prov 20:9|Who can say: My heart is clean, I am pure from sin?|Quis dicere potest, Mundum est cor meum, purus sum a peccato?]] And so God examines us when he strikes us with hard blows, so that our mind, which in tranquillity thinks great things of itself, may in adversities and troubles truly discover what it is. [[9:12|or who can say: Why dost thou so?|Vel quis ei dicere potest, Cur ita facis?]] Therefore we ought not to discuss the works of the Creator rashly, but humbly to wonder at them, certain that they cannot be unjust, and that the feeble gaze of the human mind cannot pierce or grasp the secrets of the Godhead. Hence Gregory says: To seek the reason of God's hidden judgment is nothing else than to swell with pride against his counsel. Whence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 25:27|As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, so he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|Sicut qui mel comedit multum, non est ei bonum; sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria]].

paras.t: Deus cujus iræ resistere nemo potest. Quo major est divina justitia, et post vitam hanc inflexibilior ejus iracundia; quo item graviorem ac diuturniorem infligit vindictam: eo utique amplius formidare debemus Deum sublimem et benedictum, quanquam ob suam puram bonitatem, immensam amabilitatem, atque paternam ad nos caritatem, potissime sit timendus filiali timore, ne a nobis in aliquo offendatur. Et sub quo curvantur qui portant orbem. Si rectores mundi, omnesque angelici spiritus divinæ se majestati inclinant, quanto magis nos subditi et pusilli, Domino majestatis immensæ cum profunda humiliatione subdi debemus?
paras.en: [[9:13|God, whose wrath no man can resist|Deus cujus iræ resistere nemo potest]]. The greater the divine justice, and the more unbending His anger after this life, and the heavier and more lasting the vengeance He inflicts, so much the more surely ought we to dread God, the sublime and blessed; although, by reason of His pure goodness, His boundless lovableness and His fatherly charity toward us, He is above all to be feared with filial fear [that is, the fear of a son who dreads to offend his father, as distinct from servile fear, which dreads only punishment], lest He be offended by us in anything. [[9:13|and under whom they stoop that bear up the world|Et sub quo curvantur qui portant orbem]]. If the rulers of the world and all the angelic spirits bow themselves before the divine majesty, how much more ought we, His subjects and little ones, to submit ourselves with deep humility to the Lord of boundless majesty?

paras.t: Quantus ergo sum ego ut respondeam ei, et loquar verbis meis cum eo? Si sanctus Job homo tantæ perfectionis, hoc dixit, restat ut unusquisque nostrum tanto hoc humilius dicat, quanto se reputat sancto illo inferiorem; et quo peccando viliores sumus effecti, eo ad alloquendum Deum indigniores nos jugiter arbitremur. Nec sine timore et reverentia, attentione ac diligentia, Deo loqui orando sive psallendo ullatenus præsumamus; sed in hujusmodi locutione simul pensemus eminentiam majestatis divinæ ac vilitatem fragilitatis conversationisque propriæ. Imo, quo major est defectuositas nostra et gravior culpa, eo timoratius cum Deo loquamur, quemadmodum publicanus, qui non audebat oculos levare ad cœlum. Hinc Abraham ait: Loquar ad Dominum meum, quum sim pulvis et cinis.
paras.en: [[9:14|What am I then, that I should answer him, and have words with him?|Quantus ergo sum ego ut respondeam ei, et loquar verbis meis cum eo?]] If holy Job, a man of such perfection, said this, it remains that each one of us should say it the more humbly, the further he reckons himself beneath that holy man; and the viler we have become by sinning, the more unworthy let us always judge ourselves to address God. Let us by no means presume to speak to God, in prayer or in psalmody, without fear and reverence, attention and diligence; but in speech of this kind let us weigh together the eminence of the divine majesty and the vileness of our own frailty and manner of life. Nay, the greater our defectiveness and the graver our guilt, the more fearfully let us speak with God, like the publican, who dared not [[Luke 18:13|lift up his eyes towards heaven|oculos levare ad cœlum]]. Hence Abraham says: [[Gen 18:27|I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes|Loquar ad Dominum meum, quum sim pulvis et cinis]].

paras.t: Qui, etiamsi habuero quippiam justum, non respondebo, quasi mea æquitate absque divina clementia quærens salvari; sed ut meum judicem deprecabor, ad solam ipsius confugiens pietatem. Non ergo de propriis meritis præsumamus. Hinc enim ait Salvator: Quum feceritis omnia quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus. Et in Psalmo cantamus: Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ, et sperate in Domino. In Domino (inquit) sperate, non in opere vestræ justitiæ, in quo etsi spes aliquo modo habenda sit, principaliter tamen in Deo ponenda est, quemadmodum Osee scribit: Misericordiam et judicium custodi, et spera in Deo tuo semper.
paras.en: [[9:15|I, who although I should have any just thing|Qui, etiamsi habuero quippiam justum]], [[9:15|would not answer|non respondebo]], as though seeking to be saved by my own equity without the divine mercy; [[9:15|but would make supplication to my judge|sed ut meum judicem deprecabor]], fleeing to His mercy alone. Let us not, then, presume on our own merits. For hence the Saviour says: [[Luke 17:10|when you shall have done all these things that are commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which we ought to do|Quum feceritis omnia quæ præcepta sunt vobis, dicite: Servi inutiles sumus; quod debuimus facere, fecimus]]. And in the Psalm we sing: [[Ps 4:6|Offer up the sacrifice of justice, and trust in the Lord|Sacrificate sacrificium justitiæ, et sperate in Domino]]. In the Lord (he says) trust, not in the work of your own justice; for though hope is in some way to be had in that, it is to be placed chiefly in God, as Osee writes: [[Osee 12:6|keep mercy and judgment, and hope in thy God always|Misericordiam et judicium custodi, et spera in Deo tuo semper]].

paras.t: In turbine enim, id est in tempestate mortis seu extremi judicii: juxta illud, Ignis in conspectu ejus exardescet, et in circuitu ejus tempestas valida; et, Dominus in tempestate et turbine viæ ejus. Conteret me, id est damnabit, nisi jam eum ut judicem fuero deprecatus; et multiplicabit vulnera mea etiam sine causa. Posset hoc ex persona generis humani proferri, in quantum pro originali peccato animæ infantium quatuor vulneribus vulnerantur: quæ sunt, concupiscentia in vi concupiscibili, infirmitas in irascibili, ignorantia in ratione, malitia (id est pronitas ad malum) in voluntate. Gregorius vero exponit hoc ex persona infantium non baptizatorum, ante usum rationis morientium. De quibus ait: Unum vulnus eis est, corruptibiles nasci; aliud, carnaliter mori. Sed quia post mortem æterna quoque mors sequitur, occulto eis justoque judicio etiam sine causa vulnera multiplicantur. Perpetua quippe tormenta percipiunt et qui nihil ex propria voluntate peccaverunt. Si autem Gregorius intelligit hoc, quod et pœnam sensus sustineant, consonat Augustino. Verius tamen, probabilius, atque communius dicunt doctores, quod non habeant nisi pœnam damni, videlicet pro originali peccato, cui in eis non debetur nisi divinæ visionis carentia.
paras.en: For [[9:17|in a whirlwind|In turbine enim]], that is, in the storm of death or of the last judgment; according to that saying: [[Ps 49:3|A fire shall burn before him: and a mighty tempest shall be round about him|Ignis in conspectu ejus exardescet, et in circuitu ejus tempestas valida]]; and: [[Nah 1:3|The Lord's ways are in a tempest, and a whirlwind|Dominus in tempestate et turbine viæ ejus]]. [[9:17|he shall crush me|Conteret me]], that is, shall damn me, unless I have already besought Him as my judge; [[9:17|and multiply my wounds even without cause|et multiplicabit vulnera mea etiam sine causa]]. This could be spoken in the person of the human race, inasmuch as, for original sin, the souls of infants are wounded with four wounds: concupiscence in the concupiscible power, weakness in the irascible [the two powers of the sensitive appetite: the one seeks what is pleasant, the other strives against what is hard], ignorance in the reason, malice (that is, proneness to evil) in the will. Gregory, however, explains it in the person of infants who die unbaptized before the use of reason, of whom he says: One wound they have, to be born corruptible; another, to die in the flesh. But because after death eternal death also follows, by a hidden and just judgment their wounds are multiplied even without cause. For they receive perpetual torments, even they who have sinned in nothing by their own will.
