If Gregory means by this that they also suffer the pain of sense [that is, positive torment, as distinct from the pain of loss, the bare privation of the sight of God], he agrees with Augustine. Yet the doctors say more truly, more probably and more commonly that they have only the pain of loss, namely for original sin, to which in them nothing is due but the lack of the divine vision.

paras.t: Præterea multiplicat Deus quotidie vulnera electorum sine causa, id est absque eorum culpa, dum eos tentari, tribulari, fatigari, infirmari permittit seu facit, ut magis proficiant, in gratia crescant, in felicitate abundent, aliosque sua patientia ac virtute ædificent. Unde et Paulo responsum est: Sufficit tibi gratia mea, nam virtus in infirmitate perficitur.
paras.en: Moreover, God daily multiplies the wounds of the elect without cause, that is, without fault of theirs, when He permits or causes them to be tempted, troubled, wearied and made sick, so that they may make more progress, grow in grace, abound in happiness, and edify others by their patience and virtue. Hence it was answered to Paul too: [[2 Cor 12:9|My grace is sufficient for thee: for power is made perfect in infirmity|Sufficit tibi gratia mea, nam virtus in infirmitate perficitur]].

paras.t: Non concedit quiescere spiritum meum. Quamvis enim interdum justorum mens aliquantulum conquiescat, consoletur et delectetur in Deo, cito tamen occurrent variæ causæ virtuosi doloris: nec a labore divini cultus diu quiescere permittimur; virtutum quoque profectui quotidie digne studere debemus.
paras.en: [[9:18|He alloweth not my spirit to rest|Non concedit quiescere spiritum meum]]. For although the mind of the just sometimes rests a little, and is consoled and delights in God, yet soon various causes of virtuous sorrow will meet it: nor are we allowed to rest long from the labour of divine worship; and we ought also daily to apply ourselves worthily to progress in the virtues.

paras.t: Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me; si innocentem me ostendero, pravum me comprobabit. Timeant hæc vani et excæcati, qui putant se aliquid esse quum nihil sint: qui accusati seu increpati, pertinaciter se excusant; disciplinati autem, injuriam sibi conqueruntur illatam. O quam parum illuminata, imo quam multum obtenebrata est anima horum; quam modice attendunt suos quotidianos defectus et culpas, omissiones et commissiones culpabiles in cogitatione, affectione, verbo et opere, temporisque perditione ac negligentia agendorum! Denique, quis nostrum valeat numerare distractiones, imperfectionesque suas tempore divinorum? Hinc ergo diligentissime ista pensemus, et adhuc imperfecti ac passionati exsistentes, agamus quod scriptum est de viro perfecto: Justus in principio accusator est sui. Nam et Paulus indicibili humilitate fatetur: Venit Jesus Christus peccatores salvos facere, quorum primus ego sum.
paras.en: [[9:20|If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me: if I would shew myself innocent, he shall prove me wicked|Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me; si innocentem me ostendero, pravum me comprobabit]]. Let the vain and the blinded fear these words, who think themselves something when they are nothing; who, when accused or rebuked, stubbornly excuse themselves, and when corrected complain that a wrong has been done them. O how little enlightened, nay how greatly darkened is the soul of these men; how little they heed their daily defects and faults, their culpable omissions and commissions in thought, affection, word and deed, their loss of time and their neglect of what is to be done! Lastly, which of us could number his distractions and imperfections in the time of the divine office? Here, then, let us weigh these things most carefully, and, being still imperfect and subject to the passions, let us do what is written of the perfect man: [[Prov 18:17|The just is first accuser of himself|Justus in principio accusator est sui]]. For Paul too confesses with unspeakable humility: [[1 Tim 1:15|Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the chief|Venit Jesus Christus peccatores salvos facere, quorum primus ego sum]].

paras.t: Etiamsi simplex fuero, id est virtuosus, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea, donec certificetur a Deo. Certitudinaliter enim scire non possumus, an simus in caritate et gratia, nisi revelatione divina. Verumtamen probabiliter seu conjecturaliter id scire valemus per aliqua signa, videlicet: si verbum Dei libenter audimus: qui enim ex Deo est, verba Dei audit; si peccata ratione suæ turpitudinis, et quia offensiva sunt Dei, non solum timore pœnæ, odimus atque vitamus; si ad ea quæ divini sunt cultus, paratos et alacres nos sentimus: quemadmodum enim vita naturæ agnoscitur operatione et motu, sic vita caritatis et gratiæ, præceptorum obeditione, bonorumque exsecutione: postremo si experimur in nobis augeri mundi contemptum, exstirpationem passionum, et cordialem affectum ad Deum, ac zelum honorandi eum in omnibus, trahendique alios ad ejus amorem ac cultum.
paras.en: [[9:21|Although I should be simple|Etiamsi simplex fuero]], that is, virtuous, [[9:21|even this my soul shall be ignorant of|hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]], until it be made certain by God. For we cannot know with certainty whether we are in charity and grace, save by divine revelation. Yet we can know it probably or by conjecture through certain signs: namely, if we gladly hear the word of God, for [[John 8:47|He that is of God heareth the words of God|qui enim ex Deo est, verba Dei audit]]; if we hate and shun sins by reason of their foulness, and because they offend God, not only from fear of punishment; if we feel ourselves ready and eager for the things that belong to divine worship (for as the life of nature is known by operation and movement, so the life of charity and grace is known by obedience to the commandments and the doing of good works); lastly, if we find growing in us contempt of the world, the rooting out of the passions, heartfelt affection toward God, and zeal to honour Him in all things and to draw others to His love and worship.

paras.t: Si flagellat, occidat semel, id est, per flagella propriam voluntatem et passiones et vitia in nobis mortificet; et non de pœnis innocentium rideat, id est, virtuosos non desinat sine ipsorum profectu affligi, ne per modum ridentis videatur in eorum afflictione secundum se complacentiam quamdam habere.
paras.en: [[9:23|If he scourge, let him kill at once|Si flagellat, occidat semel]], that is, by scourges let Him put to death in us our own will, our passions and our vices; [[9:23|and not laugh at the pains of the innocent|et non de pœnis innocentium rideat]], that is, let Him not suffer the virtuous to be afflicted without profit to themselves [the print reads *desinat*, “cease”; the sense seems to call for *sinat*, “suffer”], lest He seem, in the manner of one who laughs, to take a certain pleasure in their affliction for its own sake.

paras.t: Terra data est in manus impii. Videmus impios in bonis terrenis amplius abundare quam justos. Vultum judicum ejus operit impius, puta diabolus, sicut expositum est. Porro judices terræ, amore et odio potissime corrumpuntur; interdum vero, timore seu comminatione potentiorum, seu adulatione aut donis injustorum. Sed qui aliorum est judex, debet esse tanquam lex viva, et quasi animata justitia, ut nequaquam ab æquitate et veritate declinet, sed uniformis et constans, regia semper via incedat. Hinc in Deuteronomio Moyses ait: Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, quorum conversatio sit probata in tribubus vestris, et ponam eos vobis principes. Jethro etiam loquitur Moysi: Provide de omni plebe viros potentes et timentes Deum, in quibus sit veritas, et qui oderint avaritiam, et constitue ex eis qui judicent populum. Sed heu! jam nimis impletur, quod Isaias asserit: Omnes diligunt munera, sequuntur retributionem.
paras.en: [[9:24|The earth is given into the hand of the wicked|Terra data est in manus impii]]. We see the wicked abound in earthly goods more than the just. [[9:24|he covereth the face of the judges thereof|Vultum judicum ejus operit]]: the wicked one, that is, the devil, as has been explained. Further, the judges of the earth are corrupted above all by love and hatred; and sometimes by the fear or threats of the more powerful, or by the flattery or gifts of the unjust. But he who is the judge of others ought to be as it were a living law, and justice made animate, so that he never turn aside from equity and truth, but, uniform and constant, always walk by the king's highway. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 1:13|Let me have from among you wise and understanding men, and such whose conversation is approved among your tribes, that I may appoint them your rulers|Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, quorum conversatio sit probata in tribubus vestris, et ponam eos vobis principes]]. Jethro also says to Moses: [[Ex 18:21|provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, in whom there is truth, and that hate avarice, and appoint of them|Provide de omni plebe viros potentes et timentes Deum, in quibus sit veritas, et qui oderint avaritiam, et constitue ex eis]] [[Ex 18:22|Who may judge the people|qui judicent populum]]. But alas! now is too fully fulfilled what Isaias declares: [[Is 1:23|they all love bribes, they run after rewards|Omnes diligunt munera, sequuntur retributionem]].

paras.t: Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore. Secundum Thomam, tendentibus ad aliquem finem tria sunt necessaria. Primo, ut in nullo alio cor suum figant quo retardari possint a fine, sed in ipsum finem festinent. Secundo, ut ea acquirant, per quæ possint ad finem pertingere: quemadmodum volens sanari, necesse est ut quærat remedia quibus sanetur. Similiter qui vult ad Deum venire, oportet ut adipiscatur virtutes, quibus summum bonum consequi queat. Tertium restat, videlicet consecutio finis. Porro de vanitate, labilitate ac brevitate vitæ præsentis, dicta sunt plurima in expositione capituli septimi.
paras.en: [[9:25|My days have been swifter than a post|Dies mei velociores fuerunt cursore]]. According to Thomas, three things are necessary for those who tend toward some end. First, that they fix their heart on nothing else by which they could be held back from the end, but hasten toward the end itself. Second, that they acquire the things by which they can reach the end: as one who wishes to be healed must seek the remedies by which he may be healed. So too whoever would come to God must obtain the virtues by which he can attain the highest good. The third remains, namely the attainment of the end. As for the vanity, instability and brevity of the present life, a great deal was said in the exposition of the seventh chapter[[Job 7:6||]] [the margin gives only Job vii; v. 6 there speaks of the swiftness of man's days].

paras.t: Verebar omnia opera mea, sciens quod non parceres delinquenti. Verbum hoc exhortationem magis quam explanationem requirit. Si ergo beatus Job opera sua tam virtuosa, quæ in volumine hoc scribuntur, sic verebatur, ne scilicet minus devote ac reverenter, minus amorose ac perseveranter ea exsequeretur: quid agendum est nobis, qui tam infirmi sumus in bonis, tam proni ad mala? Nonne tanto plus formidandum est nobis, quo imperfectiores atque ad casum procliviores et propinquiores nos esse cognoscimus? Denique ad hoc quod actio sit veraciter virtuosa, Deoque placita ac meritoria, non sufficit facere bonum, sed ut bene fiat exigitur, puta cum debitis virtutum circumstantiis, hoc est debito loco, suoque tempore, recta intentione, cum debita reverentia, ex divino amore. Maledictus enim qui facit opus Dei negligenter. Et qui quærunt proprium commodum seu humanum præconium, suam receperunt mercedem. Itaque timeamus actus nostros etiam bonos, ne forte ex nostra imperfectione contemnantur a Deo, ne sine debita alacritate, puritate ac diligentia fiant. Hinc quippe in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Timor Domini corona justitiæ *. Quæ utique corona seu filialis timor, omni actui nostro superponenda est semper; et quo aliquis Deum sincerius atque ardentius diligit, eo in suis actibus eum inhonorare seu offendere plus veretur. Propter quod scriptum est: Timete Dominum, omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum. Hoc est quod in Proverbiis docetur: Omni custodia custodi cor tuum. Et in Michæa: Indicabo tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, et quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam, et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo.
paras.en: [[9:28|I feared all my works, knowing that thou didst not spare the offender|Verebar omnia opera mea, sciens quod non parceres delinquenti]]. This saying calls for exhortation more than explanation. If, then, blessed Job so feared his works, virtuous as they were, which are written in this book, lest, that is, he should perform them less devoutly and reverently, less lovingly and perseveringly: what must we do, who are so weak in good and so prone to evil? Is there not so much the more for us to dread, the more imperfect, and the more inclined and nearer to falling, we know ourselves to be? Lastly, for an act to be truly virtuous, pleasing to God and meritorious, it is not enough to do good: it is required that it be done well, that is, with the due circumstances of the virtues: in the due place, at its own time, with right intention, with due reverence, out of divine love. For [[Jer 48:10|Cursed be he that doth the work of the Lord|Maledictus enim qui facit opus Dei]] negligently [Denis reads *negligenter*, “negligently”, where the Vulgate has *fraudulenter*, “deceitfully”]. And they who seek their own advantage or the praise of men, [[Matt 6:2|they have received their reward|suam receperunt mercedem]][[Matt 6:5||]][[Matt 6:16||]]. Let us therefore fear our acts, even the good ones, lest through our imperfection they be despised by God, lest they be done without due eagerness, purity and diligence. For hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:22|The fear of the Lord is a crown|Timor Domini corona]] of justice [the edition marks *justitiæ*, “of justice”, with an asterisk and gives in the margin *sapientiæ*, “of wisdom”, the Vulgate's reading]. This crown, that is, filial fear, must always be set over every act of ours; and the more sincerely and ardently anyone loves God, the more he fears to dishonour or offend Him in his acts. Wherefore it is written: [[Ps 33:10|Fear the Lord, all ye his saints: for there is no want to them that fear him|Timete Dominum, omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum]]. This is what is taught in Proverbs: [[Prov 4:23|With all watchfulness keep thy heart|Omni custodia custodi cor tuum]]. And in Micheas: [[Mich 6:8|I will shew thee, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requireth of thee: Verily to do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God|Indicabo tibi, o homo, quid sit bonum, et quid Dominus requirat a te: utique facere judicium, et diligere misericordiam, et sollicitum ambulare cum Deo tuo]].

paras.t: Delinquenti autem Deus non parcit, sed pœnitenti ac metuenti; nec culpa relinquitur impunita, quia aut homo pœnitens hanc in se punit, aut hanc Deus cum homine seu alio vindicante vindicans percutit. Hinc David post confessionem audire […] meruit, Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum: et tamen multis postea cruciatibus afflictus, ac fugiens, reatum culpæ quam perpetravit, exsolvit. Nam et Deus piissimus ab electis suis maculas vitiorum temporali solet afflictione detergere. Unde per Malachiam ait: Parcam timentibus me, sicut vir parcit filio suo servienti sibi.
paras.en: But God does not spare [[9:28|the offender|delinquenti]]: He spares the penitent and the one who fears; nor is guilt left unpunished, for either the man, repenting, punishes it in himself, or God, avenging it, strikes it together with the man, or with another as the avenger. Hence David after his confession was found worthy to hear […]: [[2 Kings 12:13|The Lord also hath taken away thy sin|Dominus transtulit peccatum tuum]]; and yet afterwards, afflicted by many torments[[2 Kings 12:14||]] and fleeing[[2 Kings 15:1||]], he paid off the guilt of the sin he had committed [the margin gives II Reg. xii, 13; ibid. 14–16; xv–xix]. For God most loving is wont to wipe away the stains of vices from His elect by temporal affliction. Hence He says by Malachias: [[Mal 3:17|I will spare|Parcam]] them that fear me[[Mal 3:16||]], [[Mal 3:17|as a man spareth his son that serveth him|sicut vir parcit filio suo servienti sibi]].

paras.t: Si autem et sic impius sum, quare frustra laboravi? Frequenter perversi, rancore aut alia passione vel impietate commoti, justos calumniantur, accusant, diffamant; et quantum valent, ad desperationem seu boni cessationem ac animi fractionem inducere moliuntur, gravia eis crimina objiciendo, quemadmodum in Proverbiis legitur: Ambulans recto itinere et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via. Tunc ergo vir justus consolari et confortare in Domino potest se ipsum, vitæ suæ justitias ad memoriam reducendo, ad gloriam Dei et ad repulsionem peccati, ut dicat: Si autem sic impius sum ut mihi imponitur, quare frustra laboravi, custodiendo quæ Deo sunt placita cum labore, ambulans per arctam viam quæ ducit ad vitam, et in actibus pœnitentiæ me exercens, ita ut Deo dicere possim, Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras? Sicque loquitur justus, non quod se frustra æstimet laborasse, sed quia ex verbis calumniantium eum hoc sequitur. Quod quia dici non valet, sequitur illos errare, quia ex vero non nisi verum concluditur.
paras.en: [[9:29|But if so also I am wicked, why have I laboured in vain?|Si autem et sic impius sum, quare frustra laboravi?]] The perverse, moved by rancour or some other passion or impiety, often slander, accuse and defame the just; and as far as they can, they strive to bring them to despair, or to giving up what is good, and to brokenness of spirit, by charging them with grave crimes; as we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:2|He that walketh in the right way, and feareth God, is despised by him that goeth by an infamous way|Ambulans recto itinere et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via]]. Then, therefore, the just man can console and strengthen himself in the Lord by calling to mind the just deeds of his life, for the glory of God and the repelling of sin, so as to say: [[9:29|But if so also I am wicked|Si autem sic impius sum]], as is laid to my charge, [[9:29|why have I laboured in vain|quare frustra laboravi]], keeping with labour the things that are pleasing to God, walking in the strait way, [[Matt 7:14|the way that leadeth to life|viam quæ ducit ad vitam]], and exercising myself in works of penance, so that I can say to God: [[Ps 16:4|for the sake of the words of thy lips, I have kept hard ways|Propter verba labiorum tuorum ego custodivi vias duras?]]? Thus the just man speaks, not because he thinks he has laboured in vain, but because this follows from the words of those who slander him. And since that cannot be said, it follows that they are in error, for from what is true nothing but what is true is concluded.

paras.t: Neque enim viro qui similis mei est, respondebo. Quoniam ergo Deo omnipotenti et supersapienti sumus in judicio responsuri, quemadmodum ait Apostolus, Omnes nos ante Christi tribunal oportet adstare: quid nobis incumbit, nisi ut ad reddendum rationem de omnibus nos quotidie præparemus, vitam et mores incessabiliter emendemus, ad Dei clementiam confugiamus, apostolicum illud pensantes, Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis! Risus ergo et levitas, torpor, præsumptio atque securitas immoderata, penitus abscindantur, et impleamus quod scriptum est: In timore Domini esto tota die, quia habebis spem in novissimo.
paras.en: [[9:32|For I shall not answer a man that is like myself|Neque enim viro qui similis mei est, respondebo]]. Since, then, we are to answer in judgment to God almighty and all-wise (as the Apostle says, [[Rom 14:10|we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ|Omnes nos ante Christi tribunal oportet adstare]][[2 Cor 5:10||]] [Denis's words join Rom 14:10 and 2 Cor 5:10, both given in the margin]), what is incumbent on us but daily to prepare ourselves to render account of all things, unceasingly to amend our life and conduct, and to flee to God's mercy, pondering that saying of the Apostle: [[Heb 10:31|It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God|Horrendum est incidere in manus Dei viventis!]]! Let laughter, then, and levity, sluggishness, presumption and immoderate security be cut off entirely, and let us fulfil what is written: [[Prov 23:17|be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long|In timore Domini esto tota die]], [[Prov 23:18|Because thou shalt have hope in the latter end|quia habebis spem in novissimo]].

paras.t: Auferat a me virgam suam, id est, rigorem æquitatis in dulcorem pietatis convertat, et disciplinam quam pro peccatis aut alia causa sustineo, in me mitigare dignetur, ne sub onere ruam. Hoc in afflictionibus petere aliquando possumus, præsertim dum diu aut graviter fuimus tribulati, ipsaque pœnæ seu adversitatis magnitudine a virtutum actibus impedimur. Nam, ceteris paribus, aptior est homo ad Dei obsequium ac profectum tempore sanitatis et roboris, quam infirmitatis. Verumtamen in hoc exspectanda est manus Domini longanimiter, patienter et confidenter.
paras.en: [[9:34|Let him take his rod away from me|Auferat a me virgam suam]], that is, let Him turn the rigour of equity into the sweetness of mercy, and deign to lighten in me the chastisement which I bear for my sins or for some other cause, lest I fall beneath the burden. This we may sometimes ask in afflictions, especially when we have been long or grievously troubled, and are hindered from acts of virtue by the very greatness of the pain or adversity. For, other things being equal, a man is fitter for the service of God and for progress in time of health and strength than in time of sickness. Yet in this the hand of the Lord is to be awaited with long-suffering, patience and confidence.

paras.t: Et pavor ejus non me terreat. Moderatus timor diligentiam parit; immoderatus vero, anxietatem et scrupulum excessivum, inquietudinem et plurima proficiendi obstacula. Talem ergo pavorem tollat a nobis Deus, ne scilicet nimium insistamus considerationi divinæ justitiæ ac propriæ infirmitatis, sicque pusillanimes efficiamur; sed ad considerandum infinitam Dei bonitatem et pietatem mentem fideliter erigamus, caritatemque ejus ad nos, et quanta pro nobis Unigenitus Dei assumpsit, fecit ac pertulit: ex qua consideratione concipiamus ad Deum filialem fiduciam, caritativum affectum, fortitudinemque constantem. Nam et Deus potius vult a nobis ut clementissimus pater amari, quam ut rigorosus judex ac dominus formidari. Idque præsertim complacet sibi, ut in ipso filialiter confidamus, dicentes: Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea, quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ, a quo trepidabo? Et item: Ego autem mendicus sum et pauper: Dominus sollicitus est mei. Hinc aliqui vituperabiliter scrupulosi, a vero profectu non parum retardant se ipsos, nec sinceram in Deo sortiuntur quietem contemplationisve gratiam.
paras.en: [[9:34|and let not his fear terrify me|Et pavor ejus non me terreat]]. Moderate fear begets diligence; but immoderate fear begets anxiety and excessive scruple, restlessness and very many obstacles to progress. Let God, then, take such dread from us, lest we dwell too much on the consideration of the divine justice and of our own weakness, and so become faint-hearted; but let us faithfully raise our mind to consider the infinite goodness and mercy of God, and His charity toward us, and how much the Only-begotten of God took upon Himself, did and endured for us: and from this consideration let us conceive toward God filial trust, loving affection and steadfast fortitude. For God too would rather be loved by us as a most merciful father than feared as a rigorous judge and lord. And this above all pleases Him, that we trust in Him as sons, saying: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?|Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea, quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ, a quo trepidabo?]] And again: [[Ps 39:18|But I am a beggar and poor: the Lord is careful for me|Ego autem mendicus sum et pauper: Dominus sollicitus est mei]]. Hence some, blameworthily scrupulous, hold themselves back not a little from true progress, and do not obtain sincere rest in God or the grace of contemplation.

paras.t: Loquar ad eum confidenter et amorose, juxta id Psalmi: Sperate in eo omnis congregatio populi, effundite coram illo corda vestra; Deus adjutor noster in æternum. Et non timebo eum servili timore: de quo ait Joannes, Timor non est in caritate, sed perfecta caritas foras mittit timorem. Qui autem timet, non est perfectus in caritate. Hinc scriptum est: Sine timore, de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, serviamus illi in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso. Et Apostolus ait: Non accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis spiritum filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba (Pater).
paras.en: [[9:35|I will speak|Loquar]] to Him confidently and lovingly, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 61:9|Trust in him, all ye congregation of people: pour out your hearts before him. God is our helper for ever|Sperate in eo omnis congregatio populi, effundite coram illo corda vestra; Deus adjutor noster in æternum]]; [[9:35|and will not fear him|Et non timebo eum]] with servile fear [that is, the fear of a slave, who dreads only punishment, as distinct from the filial fear of a son], of which John says: [[1 John 4:18|Fear is not in charity: but perfect charity casteth out fear|Timor non est in caritate, sed perfecta caritas foras mittit timorem]]. [[1 John 4:18|And he that feareth is not perfected in charity|Qui autem timet, non est perfectus in caritate]]. Hence it is written: [[Luke 1:74|being delivered from the hand of our enemies, we may serve him without fear|Sine timore, de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberati, serviamus illi]] [[Luke 1:75|In holiness and justice before him|in sanctitate et justitia coram ipso]]. And the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:15|you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear: but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, whereby we cry: Abba|Non accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis spiritum filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba]] (Father).

paras.t: Neque enim possum metuens respondere: id est, habendo servilem timorem, Deo reddere rationem non valeo, nec ejus beneficiis vicem rependere, aut pietati et caritati ipsius per omnia respondere condigna. Qui enim solum serviliter timet, caritatem non habet; nec aliquid meritorium agit, sed displicet Deo, atque damnatur si taliter moriatur. Quoniam ergo Deus prior dilexit nos, eum reamare tenemur. Nec aliter respondere valebimus in divino judicio, quum amor Dei sit vestis nuptialis, quam non habens, obmutuit, et ejectus, in tenebras corruit infernales.
paras.en: [[9:35|for I cannot answer while I am in fear|Neque enim possum metuens respondere]]: that is, having servile fear, I cannot render account to God, nor repay His benefits, nor answer worthily in all things to His mercy and charity. For he who fears only servilely has not charity; nor does he do anything meritorious, but displeases God, and is damned if he dies so. Since, then, [[1 John 4:19|God first hath loved us|Deus prior dilexit nos]][[1 John 4:10||]], we are bound to love Him in return. Nor shall we be able to answer otherwise in the divine judgment, since the love of God is the wedding garment[[Matt 22:11||]]; not having it, the man was silent[[Matt 22:12||]], and, cast out, fell into the darkness of hell[[Matt 22:13||]].

10.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli decimi: Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ.
10.title_en: Literal explanation of the tenth chapter: My soul is weary of my life

paras.t: Circa præcedentis capituli finem aliqua dixit Job, ex quibus insinuavit causas quasdam, ex quibus inclinabatur ad loquendum de suis doloribus. Nunc ergo sumpta ex divina pietate loquendi fiducia, prosequitur inchoatum de suo dolore sermonem, et dispositionem suam internam, angustiamque declarat.
paras.en: Towards the end of the preceding chapter Job said certain things[[Job 9:27||]][[Job 9:35||]] by which he hinted at certain causes that inclined him to speak of his sorrows. Now therefore, having taken from the divine goodness the confidence to speak, he goes on with the discourse he had begun about his sorrow, and declares his inward state and his anguish.

paras.t: Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ in sæculo isto et corruptibili corpore meo, id est, tædet me vivere in hoc mundo. Non autem optavit anima sancti Job prorsus non esse, nec alicubi vivere, quia hoc impatientiæ et desperationis fuisset; sed ob pœnarum suarum et adversitatum gravitatem ac multiplicitatem, itemque desiderio quietioris vitæ in limbo patrum, et ne ex magnitudine tribulationis tandem a patientia caderet ac Deum offenderet, desideravit separari a corpore et esse in limbo præfato, in exspectatione certa adventus Christi beatitudinisque supernæ. Sic namque tædium habere de vita præsenti, est licitum et aliquando laudabile. Nam et de Christo scriptum est: Cœpit Jesus pavere et tædere. Qui alio loco disseruit: O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero, quamdiu patiar vos? Apostolus quoque: Supra modum (inquit) gravati sumus, ita ut etiam tæderet nos vivere; sed et ipsi intra nos responsum mortis habuimus. Si quis autem propter adversa sic tristaretur, quod absolute et solum ex tristitia desideraret etiam secundum rationem non vivere: hoc impatientiæ esset, quum patientis sit passionem tristitiæ moderari, ne limites exeat rationis, vel hominem vincat. Absolute quippe loquendo, melius et desiderabilius est esse et vivere in tribulationibus vitæ præsentis, secundum quod æquanimiter tolerantur intuitu Dei propter felicitatem futuram, quam prorsus non esse nec vivere, imo et quam esse in purgatorio, saltem eo modo quo aliqui ibi sunt, quorum pœna omnem vitæ hujus pœnam transcendit; nec dubium quin melius, quam in inferno. De hac re dictum est plenius in expositione capituli tertii.
paras.en: [[10:1|My soul is weary of my life|Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ]] in this world and in this corruptible body of mine; that is, I am weary of living in this world. Yet the soul of holy Job did not wish not to be at all, nor to live nowhere, for that would have been a matter of impatience and despair; but because of the weight and the number of his pains and adversities, and likewise from desire of a quieter life in the limbo of the fathers [the abode of the just who died before Christ, where they awaited his coming], and lest through the greatness of his tribulation he should at last fall from patience and offend God, he desired to be separated from the body and to be in that limbo, in sure expectation of the coming of Christ and of heavenly beatitude. For to be weary of the present life in this way is lawful and sometimes praiseworthy. For of Christ too it is written that Jesus [[Mark 14:33|began to fear and to be heavy|Cœpit Jesus pavere et tædere]] [the Latin tædere, 'to be heavy', is the word of Job's 'my soul is weary']. And in another place he said: [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I suffer you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero, quamdiu patiar vos?]] The Apostle too: [[2 Cor 1:8|we were pressed out of measure|Supra modum]], he says, [[2 Cor 1:8|so that we were weary even of life|gravati sumus, ita ut etiam tæderet nos vivere]]; but [[2 Cor 1:9|we had in ourselves the answer of death|ipsi intra nos responsum mortis habuimus]]. But if anyone were so saddened by adversity that, absolutely and from sadness alone, he desired, even with the consent of reason, not to live, this would be impatience, since it belongs to the patient man to moderate the passion of sadness, so that it does not pass the bounds of reason or overcome the man. For, speaking absolutely, it is better and more desirable to be and to live in the tribulations of the present life, in so far as they are borne with an even mind for God's sake and for the sake of the happiness to come, than not to be or live at all; yes, and better than to be in purgatory, at least in the way some are there, whose pain surpasses every pain of this life; and there is no doubt that it is better than to be in hell. Of this matter more has been said in the exposition of the third chapter [the margin refers to Art. XI, near the end].

paras.t: Dimittam adversum me eloquium meum, id est, verba effundam quæ sunt vitæ meæ contraria, quoniam dico me mortem (quæ vitæ contraria est) desiderare. Loquar in amaritudine animæ meæ, id est, amaritudine mea durante, et exsistens in ea, loquar ut loqui solent afflicti. Loquar quoque in amaritudine animæ meæ, id est, secundum quod amaritudo hæc me ad loquendum inclinat, dicamque verba meæ amaritudinis ostensiva, non tamen passionem irrefrenate sequendo, sed sub rationis directione manendo. Hoc est quod septimo dixit capitulo: Loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei, confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ. Sic et primo Regum sancta Anna dicebat: Ex multitudine doloris et mœroris mei locuta sum usque in præsens.
paras.en: [[10:1|I will let go my speech against myself|Dimittam adversum me eloquium meum]]; that is, I will pour out words that are contrary to my life, since I say that I desire death, which is contrary to life. [[10:1|I will speak in the bitterness of my soul|Loquar in amaritudine animæ meæ]]; that is, while my bitterness lasts and I am in it, I will speak as the afflicted are wont to speak. Again, [[10:1|I will speak in the bitterness of my soul|Loquar quoque in amaritudine animæ meæ]]; that is, as this bitterness inclines me to speak, I will say words that show my bitterness, yet not following the passion unbridled, but remaining under the direction of reason. This is what he said in the seventh chapter: [[Job 7:11|I will speak in the affliction of my spirit: I will talk with the bitterness of my soul|Loquar in tribulatione spiritus mei, confabulabor cum amaritudine animæ meæ]]. So too in the first book of Kings holy Anna said: [[1 Kings 1:16|out of the abundance of my sorrow and grief have I spoken till now|Ex multitudine doloris et mœroris mei locuta sum usque in præsens]].

paras.t: Dicam Deo, suppliciter exorando: Noli me condemnare, ne de pœnis his temporalibus deducar ad pœnas graviores æternas. Consequenter causam suæ punitionis inquirit, alloquens Deum. Indica mihi, id est, per revelationem internam seu exteriorem, seu alio modo tibi placente, fac me cognoscere, cur me ita judices, id est, tuo judicio tantis pœnis addicas aut infestari permittas: hoc est, causam hujus pœnæ cupio scire, an scilicet pro culpa purganda, an pro virtute probanda, aut aliis ostendenda percussus sim.
paras.en: [[10:2|I will say to God|Dicam Deo]], humbly beseeching him: [[10:2|Do not condemn me|Noli me condemnare]], lest from these temporal pains I be led on to heavier, eternal pains. Next he asks the cause of his punishment, addressing God: [[10:2|tell me|Indica mihi]], that is, by inward or outward revelation, or in some other way that pleases thee, make me know [[10:2|why thou judgest me so|cur me ita judices]], that is, why by thy judgment thou dost deliver me over to such great pains, or allow me to be assailed by them: that is, I desire to know the cause of this pain, whether I have been struck to purge a fault, or to prove virtue, or to show it to others.

paras.t: Deinde fatetur, quod non ita quærit hanc causam, quasi putet quod Deus injuste hæc egerit. Numquid bonum tibi naturaliter bono ac sapienti, in quo nec malum nec error esse potest, videtur, ut calumnieris per astutiam sive malitiam, et opprimas per potentiam aut violentiam, me opus manuum tuarum, id est creaturam scientiæ tuæ practicæ, potestatisque omnium productivæ? quum causa intellectualis naturaliter diligat suum effectum, conservet et protegat, in quantum est suus effectus: quod etiam in irrationalibus cernitur. Et numquid bonum tibi videtur, ut consilium impiorum adjuves, cooperando talibus in oppressione injuriationeque innocentium? Et per impios intelligi possunt tam invisibiles, quam visibiles justorum persecutores. Itaque, hæc atque sequentia sic quærit, ut neget.
paras.en: Then he professes that he does not ask this cause as though he thought that God had done these things unjustly. [[10:3|Doth it seem good to thee|Numquid bonum tibi]], who art by nature good and wise, in whom there can be neither evil nor error, [[10:3|that thou shouldst calumniate me|ut calumnieris]] by cunning or malice, [[10:3|and oppress me|et opprimas]] by power or violence, me, [[10:3|the work of thy own hands|opus manuum tuarum]], that is, the creature of thy practical knowledge [scientia practica: the knowledge by which a maker brings a thing into being] and of thy power that brings forth all things? For an intelligent cause naturally loves its effect, and preserves and protects it in so far as it is its effect: which is seen even in creatures without reason. And again, [[10:3|Doth it seem good to thee|numquid bonum tibi videtur]] [[10:3|and help the counsel of the wicked|ut consilium impiorum adjuves]], working together with such men in oppressing and wronging the innocent? And by the wicked may be understood the persecutors of the just, the invisible as well as the visible. So he asks this and what follows in such a way as to deny it.

paras.t: Unde consequenter fatetur, quod non sit taliter judicatus, seu absque culpa percussus ex ignorantia Dei. Numquid oculi carnei tibi sunt? id est, non utique oculos habes carnales secundum divinitatis naturam. Aut sicut videt homo, et tu vides? id est, non ita cognoscis et inspicis cuncta quæ fiunt, ut homo, qui quum sensibus utatur corporeis, interiora et secretissima intellectus et voluntatis non intuetur. Ideo judex homo ex defectu cognitionis veritatis aliquando innocentem condemnat, aut per tormenta veritatem ab eo extorquet: quæ Deo simplicissimo nequaquam conveniunt, quum ipse sit supersapientissima mens, in qua universorum rationes, ideæ et species certitudinalissime æternaliterque relucent. Propter quod omnia quantumcumque secreta, in se ipso superclarissime intuetur. Propter quod primo Regum ait: Non juxta intuitum hominis ego judico. Homo enim videt quæ parent; Dominus autem intuetur cor. Homo quoque per visum carnalem non bene discernit vel percipere nequit, quæ plurimum distant, aut in tenebris sita sunt: sed talia Deo certissime innotescunt, secundum quod per Jeremiam loquitur: Numquid Deus e vicino ego sum, et non Deus de longe? Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum?
paras.en: Hence he next professes that it is not through any ignorance in God that he has been so judged, or struck without fault. [[10:4|Hast thou eyes of flesh|Numquid oculi carnei tibi sunt]]? that is, surely thou hast no eyes of flesh, according to the nature of the Godhead. [[10:4|or, shalt thou see as man seeth|Aut sicut videt homo, et tu vides]]? [Denis reads vides, 'seest', for the Vulgate's videbis] that is, thou dost not know and look upon all that is done in the way of man, who, since he uses the bodily senses, does not behold the inmost and most secret things of the intellect and will. Therefore a human judge, through want of knowledge of the truth, sometimes condemns the innocent, or wrings the truth from him by torture: things which in no way befit God, who is most simple, since he is the supremely wise Mind, in which the reasons, ideas and species of all things shine back most certainly and eternally. Wherefore he beholds in himself all things, however secret, with a clearness beyond all clearness. Wherefore he says in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 16:7|nor do I judge according to the look of man|Non juxta intuitum hominis ego judico]]: [[1 Kings 16:7|for man seeth those things that appear, but the Lord beholdeth the heart|Homo enim videt quæ parent; Dominus autem intuetur cor]]. Man too, by bodily sight, does not discern well, or cannot perceive at all, things that are very far off or set in darkness; but such things are most certainly known to God, as he says by Jeremias: [[Jer 23:23|Am I, think ye, a God at hand, saith the Lord, and not a God afar off?|Numquid Deus e vicino ego sum, et non Deus de longe?]] [[Jer 23:24|Shall a man be hid in secret places, and I not see him|Si occultabitur vir in absconditis, et ego non videbo eum?]]?

paras.t: Numquid sicut dies hominis dies tui? Non utique, quum dies hominis, id est, quibus homo subsistit, vivit, cognoscit, sint successivi, temporales et breves; sed dies Dei sunt æternales, imo unus dies æternus et ipsa æternitas, in qua nulla vicissitudo, nulla successio, sed unum nunc, æternum, fixum, non fluens: et omnia ista sunt unum, scilicet ipse Deus æternus, cujus mensura ponitur ipsa æternitas, secundum nostram considerationem, quum in re Deus benedictus sit omnium mensura, efficienter mensurans, non mensurata. Et anni tui sicut humana sunt tempora? id est, anni tui non assimilantur humanis temporibus ratione prædicta. Ponitur autem in Deo dies et annus, seu anni et dies, non quod in ipso consistat pluralitas, prius, posterius, majus aut minus; sed quia æternitas omnem diem omneque tempus complectitur, comprehendit seu continet. Hinc ait Psalmista: Tu autem idem ipse es, et anni tui non deficient.
paras.en: [[10:5|Are thy days as the days of man|Numquid sicut dies hominis dies tui]]? Surely not: for the days of man, that is, those in which man subsists, lives and knows, are successive, temporal and short; but the days of God are eternal, or rather one eternal day and eternity itself, in which there is no change, no succession, but one now, eternal, fixed, not flowing: and all these are one, namely God himself, the Eternal, whose measure is said to be eternity itself, according to our way of considering him, since in reality God, blessed be he, is the measure of all things, measuring them as their efficient cause, not measured. [[10:5|and are thy years as the times of men|Et anni tui sicut humana sunt tempora]]? that is, thy years are not like the times of men, for the reason given. Now day and year, or years and days, are ascribed to God, not because there is in him plurality, before and after, greater or less, but because eternity embraces, comprehends or contains every day and all time. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 101:28|But thou art always the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail|Tu autem idem ipse es, et anni tui non deficient]].

paras.t: Quoniam autem dies et anni hominum sunt successivi, homines quoque successive in eis ad cognoscendum veritatem proficiunt, quod immutabili ac perfecto Deo non congruit; ideo subditur, Ut quæras iniquitatem meam in Deum commissam, per flagella seu testes, et peccatum meum in proximum, scruteris, per discursum et inquisitionem, quasi non omnia uno simplicissimo videres intuitu. Et scias, per hujusmodi vias, quia nihil impium fecerim, id est tam enorme atque mortale, quo tam gravem plagam meruerim; facias quoque ista libera quadam tyrannide, quum sit nemo qui de manu tua possit eruere, id est, qui me de tua potestate queat eripere, quum sis omnipotens et potestatis immensæ. Quasi dicat: Hoc tibi non competit, nec sic in innocentium suppliciis delectaris, præsertim quum sint opera tua tibi naturaliter dilecta: prout in Sapientia scriptum est, Diligis omnia quæ sunt, et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti. Siquidem quantum ad id quod habent a Deo, amantur ab eo.
paras.en: Now since the days and years of men are successive, men also advance in them step by step towards knowing the truth; which does not befit God, who is unchangeable and perfect. Therefore it is added: [[10:6|That thou shouldst inquire after my iniquity|Ut quæras iniquitatem meam]] committed against God, by scourges or witnesses, [[10:6|and search after my sin|et peccatum meum in proximum, scruteris]] against my neighbour, by reasoning and inquiry, as though thou didst not see all things in one most simple glance. [[10:7|And shouldst know|Et scias]], by such ways, [[10:7|that I have done no wicked thing|quia nihil impium fecerim]], that is, nothing so enormous and mortal that by it I should have deserved so heavy a stroke; and that thou shouldst do these things by a kind of free tyranny, [[10:7|whereas there is no man that can deliver out of thy hand|quum sit nemo qui de manu tua possit eruere]], that is, who can snatch me from thy power, since thou art almighty and of boundless power. As if he said: This does not befit thee, nor dost thou thus take delight in the torments of the innocent, especially since thy works are naturally dear to thee: as it is written in Wisdom, [[Wis 11:25|thou lovest all things that are, and hatest none of the things which thou hast made|Diligis omnia quæ sunt, et nihil odisti eorum quæ fecisti]]. For in so far as they have what they have from God, they are loved by him.

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Manus tuæ, id est sapientia et potentia tua: quæ licet sint idem in re atque in te, tamen pluraliter manus dicuntur, quoniam ratione distinguuntur, et propter diversitatem effectuum: vocanturque manus, quoniam sunt principia operationis ad extra: sapientia, tanquam dirigens; potentia, tanquam exsequens. Propter quod scriptum est: Omnia in sapientia fecisti. Et in Jeremia: Domine Deus, ecce tu fecisti cœlum et terram in fortitudine tua magna. Domine, fecerunt me: quia animam meam creaverunt, imo et corpus meum, quantum ad primordialem materiæ ejus productionem. Prima namque materia non nisi per creationem producta est. Et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu, id est, undique in corporis gyro seu superficie formaverunt, membra aptando, corpus organizando, et usque ad debita incrementa ac lineamenta perducendo. Quemadmodum enim res differunt formis specificis, ita et suis figuris, ut asserit Commentator: ideo utrumque Deo adscribitur. Hanc tamen formationem facit Deus per causas secundas naturales et medias. Propter quod ait Philosophus: Homo generat hominem et sol. Corpora namque cælestia materiam ad formæ receptionem suis influentiis motibusque disponunt: quod tamen (ut tactum est) Deo tanquam primo causali principio principaliter debet adscribi. Sic secundo Machabæorum libro, legitur venerabilis illa septem fratrum mater, filiis suis dixisse: Nescio quomodo in utero meo apparuistis. Neque enim ego spiritum et animam donavi vobis et vitam, et singulorum membra non ego compegi; sed est mundi Creator, qui formavit hominem, quique omnium invenit originem. Denique bona dispositio corporis, donum est Dei, et magna præparatio ad virtutes: quia (ut ait Albertus, sequens in hoc Averroem) commensuratio apta membrorum, indicat habilitatem ad justitiam; bona complexio, habilitatem ad temperantiam; robur corporis, habilitatem ad fortitudinem: spiritus vigor et claritas sensuum, habilitatem ad prudentiam.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[10:8|Thy hands|Manus tuæ]], that is, thy wisdom and thy power, which, though they are the same in reality and in thee, are yet called hands in the plural, because they are distinguished in reason and because of the diversity of their effects; and they are called hands because they are the principles of operation outward: wisdom as directing, power as executing. Wherefore it is written: [[Ps 103:24|thou hast made all things in wisdom|Omnia in sapientia fecisti]]. And in Jeremias: [[Jer 32:17|O Lord God, behold thou hast made heaven and earth by thy great power|Domine Deus, ecce tu fecisti cœlum et terram in fortitudine tua magna]]. O Lord, [[10:8|have made me|fecerunt me]]: for they created my soul, and my body too, as regards the first bringing forth of its matter. For prime matter is brought forth only by creation. [[10:8|and fashioned me wholly round about|Et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu]], that is, they formed me on every side, in the round or surface of the body, fitting the members together, organizing the body, and bringing it on to its due growth and features. For as things differ by their specific forms, so also by their shapes, as the Commentator [Averroes] asserts: therefore both are ascribed to God. Yet God brings about this forming through natural secondary and intermediate causes. Wherefore the Philosopher says: Man begets man, and the sun [Aristotle, Physics II]. For the heavenly bodies dispose matter to receive the form by their influences and motions: which nevertheless (as was touched on) must be ascribed principally to God as the first causal principle. So in the second book of Machabees we read that the venerable mother of the seven brothers said to her sons: [[2 Mach 7:22|I know not how you were formed in my womb|Nescio quomodo in utero meo apparuistis]]: [[2 Mach 7:22|for I neither gave you breath, nor soul, nor life, neither did I frame the limbs of every one of you|Neque enim ego spiritum et animam donavi vobis et vitam, et singulorum membra non ego compegi]]; [[2 Mach 7:23|But the Creator of the world, that formed the nativity of man, and that found out the origin of all|sed est mundi Creator, qui formavit hominem, quique omnium invenit originem]]. Finally, a good disposition of the body is a gift of God and a great preparation for the virtues; for (as Albert says, following Averroes in this) a fitting proportion of the members points to an aptness for justice; a good complexion, to an aptness for temperance; strength of body, to an aptness for fortitude; vigour of spirit and clearness of the senses, to an aptness for prudence.

paras.t: Et sic repente præcipitas me? Hoc admirando profatur, tanquam dicat: Quum tam sapienter ac diligenter effeceris me secundum corpus et animam, mirum quod tam improvise et subito a vigore, sanitate et prosperitate, quibus præfulsi, me dejicis, et per pœnas ita consumis. Unde infra ait: Ego ille quondam opulentus, repente contritus sum. Denique ista atque sequentia profert se humiliando, ut Dei ad se clementiam provocet.
paras.en: [[10:8|and dost thou thus cast me down headlong on a sudden?|Et sic repente præcipitas me]] He says this in wonder, as if to say: Since thou hast made me so wisely and carefully in body and soul, it is a wonder that thou dost so unexpectedly and suddenly cast me down from the vigour, health and prosperity in which I shone, and dost so consume me with pains. Hence he says below: [[Job 16:13|I that was formerly so wealthy, am all on a sudden broken to pieces|Ego ille quondam opulentus, repente contritus sum]]. Finally, he says this and what follows humbling himself, to move God's clemency towards him.

paras.t: Memento, quæso, o Domine, qui proprie nunquam oblivisceris, neque de novo reminisceris: sed per modum reminiscentis, precor, te habe, fragili creaturæ misericorditer succurrendo, cujus quasi oblitus videris, quum eam tam dire flagellas; quod sicut lutum feceris me. Lutum enim fit ex terra humori contemperata, dum scilicet aqua terræ miscetur. Sic corpus humanum ex elementis terræ et aquæ consistit, et sua mollitie, immunditia, humiditate non parum luto assimilatur. Rursus, quemadmodum lutum res exstat fragilissima, sic et caro humana. Idcirco Apostolus corpora nostra vocat vasa fictilia, quæ sunt valde fragilia: Habemus, inquit, thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus. His insuper verbis, sanctus Job tangit primam hominis constitutionem, alludens ei quod scriptum est in Genesi: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ. Hinc quoque Isaias ait: Et nunc, Domine, pater noster es tu, nos vero lutum; et fictor noster es tu, et opera manuum tuarum omnes nos. Sed et in Jeremia Dominus loquitur: Sicut lutum in manu figuli, ita et vos in manu mea. Itaque carnis fragilitatem divinæ objicit pietati, dicendo: Memento, etc. Tanquam dicat: Carnis infirmitatem considera, et sic culpam dimitte, pœnamque relaxa.
paras.en: [[10:9|Remember, I beseech thee|Memento, quæso]], O Lord, who properly speaking never forgettest nor rememberest anew; but bear thyself, I pray, after the manner of one who remembers, mercifully succouring a frail creature which thou seemest as it were to have forgotten, since thou scourgest it so cruelly; [[10:9|that thou hast made me as the clay|quod sicut lutum feceris me]]. For clay is made of earth tempered with moisture, when water is mixed with earth. So the human body consists of the elements of earth and water, and in its softness, uncleanness and moistness is not a little like clay. Again, as clay is a most fragile thing, so too is human flesh. Therefore the Apostle calls our bodies earthen vessels, which are very fragile: [[2 Cor 4:7|we have|Habemus]], he says, [[2 Cor 4:7|this treasure in earthen vessels|thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus]]. Moreover, by these words holy Job touches on the first making of man, alluding to what is written in Genesis: God [[Gen 2:7|formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ]]. Hence too Isaias says: [[Is 64:8|And now, O Lord, thou art our father, and we are clay: and thou art our maker, and we all are the works of thy hands|Et nunc, Domine, pater noster es tu, nos vero lutum; et fictor noster es tu, et opera manuum tuarum omnes nos]]. And in Jeremias the Lord says: [[Jer 18:6|as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand|Sicut lutum in manu figuli, ita et vos in manu mea]]. So he sets the frailty of the flesh before the divine goodness, saying: [[10:9|Remember|Memento]], etc. As if he said: Consider the weakness of the flesh, and so forgive the fault and lighten the pain.

paras.t: Et in pulverem reduces me, id est, corpus exanimatum per resolutionem convertes in pulverem. In ea enim fit resolutio, ex quibus est compositio. Ideo corpus sumptum ex terra, in minutissimas terræ partes naturaliter resolubile exstat: quod tamen Deo adscribitur tanquam primæ causæ et institutori totius naturæ, præsertim quum in hominibus mors corporis et resolutio ejus sint pœnæ originalis peccati, dicente Apostolo: Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur. Et alibi: Per unum hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit, et per peccatum mors. Unde primo parenti post transgressionem Dominus dixit: Pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris.
paras.en: [[10:9|and thou wilt bring me into dust|Et in pulverem reduces me]], that is, thou wilt turn my lifeless body into dust by dissolution. For a thing is dissolved into those things of which it is composed. Therefore the body, taken from earth, is by nature dissoluble into the smallest parts of earth: which is nevertheless ascribed to God as the first cause and founder of all nature, especially since in men the death of the body and its dissolution are a penalty of original sin, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:22|as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive|Sicut in Adam omnes moriuntur, ita et in Christo omnes vivificabuntur]]. And elsewhere: [[Rom 5:12|by one man sin entered into this world and by sin death|Per unum hominem peccatum in hunc mundum intravit, et per peccatum mors]]. Hence after the transgression the Lord said to our first parent: [[Gen 3:19|dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return|Pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris]].

paras.t: Consequenter tangit ordinem in naturali hominis generatione. Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me? In hominis enim generatione, primo est resolutio seminis, quod est superfluum alimenti, sicut et lac, estque album instar lactis. Circa quod scribit Albertus: Semen quum sit superfluum quartæ digestionis, primo est sicut lac, et mulgetur per vim generativæ potentiæ de omnibus membris. Itaque operationem naturæ, videlicet generativæ virtutis, attribuit Deo, quemadmodum actio instrumenti adscribitur principali agenti: et quantum ad corporis propagationem in seminis destitutione, dicit quod Deus mulserit eum; quia videlicet ordinatione divina hoc fit quod natura quasi mulgendo eliciat semen ex suis latibulis.
paras.en: Next he touches on the order in the natural generation of man. [[10:10|Hast thou not milked me as milk|Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me]]? For in the generation of man there is first the release of the seed, which is a surplus of nourishment, as milk also is, and is white like milk. On which Albert writes: The seed, since it is the surplus of the fourth digestion [in the physiology of the time, the last stage of nourishment, completed in the members themselves], is at first like milk, and is milked from all the members by the force of the generative power. So he ascribes to God the working of nature, that is, of the generative power, as the action of an instrument is ascribed to the principal agent: and as regards the propagation of the body in the release of the seed, he says that God milked him; because, that is, it comes about by divine ordinance that nature, as it were by milking, draws the seed out of its hiding places.

paras.t: Et sicut caseum me coagulasti? In hominis namque generatione, occurrit secundo ipsa compactio massæ corporeæ in utero mulieris; et ita se habet semen viri ad materiam quam femina administrat in generatione hominis, aliorumque animalium, sicut se habet coagulum ad lac in formatione casei. In semine autem viri ponitur vis activa seu formativa. Hinc ait Albertus: Gutta viri conjuncta guttæ feminæ, vaporabiliter ingreditur eam sicut spiritus in corpus; et virtute formativa comprehendit eam atque coagulat, sicut coagulum vaporabiliter ingreditur in lac et coagulat ipsum, prout sextodecimo de Animalibus ait Philosophus. Unde in Threnis, ubi nostra translatio habet, Nitidiores lacte, Septuaginta transtulerunt, Sicut lac coagulati sunt. Sic ergo, quoad corporis formationem, me, o Deus, per naturæ operationem quasi caseum coagulasti, id est, quasi lac uniri coegisti. Coagulum quippe a cogendo nomen sortitur, quoniam cogit lac coadunari seu coagulari.
paras.en: [[10:10|and curdled me like cheese|Et sicut caseum me coagulasti]]? For in the generation of man there comes, second, the very compacting of the bodily mass in the woman's womb; and the man's seed stands to the matter which the woman supplies in the generation of man and of the other animals as rennet stands to milk in the making of cheese. In the man's seed lies the active or formative power. Hence Albert says: The man's drop, joined to the woman's drop, enters it as a vapour, as spirit enters a body; and by the formative power it lays hold of it and curdles it, as rennet enters milk as a vapour and curdles it, as the Philosopher says in the sixteenth book On Animals. Hence in Lamentations, where our translation has [[Lam 4:7|purer than milk|Nitidiores lacte]], the Septuagint translated: They were curdled as milk. So then, as regards the forming of the body, thou, O God, hast curdled me like cheese by the working of nature, that is, hast made me come together like milk. For rennet [coagulum, from cogere, 'to drive together'] takes its name from driving together, because it drives the milk to unite or curdle.

paras.t: Pelle et carnibus vestisti me. In hominis generatione, tertio occurrit membrorum distinctio, quorum robur et consistentia ex nervis ossibusque dependet. Membra autem vitalia interiora, ut hepar, cor, stomachus, pelle et carnibus velut vestibus operiuntur, ne effluant, aut eorum appareat fœditas: imo et caro ob hanc causam tegitur pelle, secundum Hieronymum super Ezechielem. Propterea dicit Albertus: Tertium opus seminis viri in gutta feminæ, est pellem circumducere, ne spiritus evaporet, sed lustrans universo per circuitum operator spiritus pulset ad vitam. In carne autem quartum opus est, quam vis formativa circumducit, ut sensus diffundatur in ea. Porro, de his in quibus robur corporis est, et per quæ cetera sibi cohærent, subjungit: Ossibus et nervis compegisti me, id est, membra mea pariter conjunxisti. Ossa enim carnem sustentant, ne per suam mollitiem decidat. Nervi vero per totum corpus expansi sunt.
paras.en: [[10:11|Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh|Pelle et carnibus vestisti me]]. In the generation of man there comes, third, the distinction of the members, whose strength and firmness depend on the sinews and bones. But the inner vital members, such as the liver, the heart and the stomach, are covered with skin and flesh as with garments, so that they do not flow out and their foulness does not appear; and the flesh too is covered with skin for this reason, according to Jerome on Ezechiel. Therefore Albert says: The third work of the man's seed in the woman's drop is to draw the skin round about, so that the spirit does not escape as vapour, but the working spirit, ranging round through the whole, may stir it to life. The fourth work is in the flesh, which the formative power draws round about, so that sense may be spread through it. Then, of the things in which the body's strength lies and through which the rest hold together, he adds: [[10:11|thou hast put me together with bones and sinews|Ossibus et nervis compegisti me]], that is, thou hast joined my members together. For the bones hold up the flesh, so that it does not sink down through its softness; and the sinews are spread through the whole body.

paras.t: Vitam, id est formam vitalem, videlicet animam rationalem vitæ meæ conjunctam tanquam formale principium, et misericordiam, id est supernaturalia munera gratiarum seu varia beneficia gratiæ gratis et misericorditer datæ, tribuisti mihi: quoniam corpore sufficienter disposito, Deus animam rationalem creando infundit. Thomas et alii quidam, per misericordiam loco hoc intelligunt naturale seminarium virtutum et scientiarum nobis innatum, de quo in regula sua scribit Basilius: Innatus enim est animæ habitus principiorum tam speculabilium quam operabilium. Et ex seminario tali quidam naturaliter dispositi sunt ad hanc virtutem, quidam ad illam. Job vero ad pietatem eminenter dispositus fuit, prout infra testatur: Ab infantia crevit mecum miseratio, et de utero egressa est mecum. Et visitatio tua, id est beneficiorum tuorum largitio, gratiarum influxio, clemens conservatio, custodivit spiritum meum, id est, animam meam conservavit in vita hucusque et necessaria victui tribuit; me quoque a peccatis retraxit, et in gratia conservavit. Quod etiam Deus partim per angelorum facit custodiam. Quemadmodum autem in Scripturis dicitur Deus a quibusdam recedere, quoniam gratiam abstrahit eis, sic fertur visitare atque accedere dona sua præstando.
paras.en: He goes on: [[10:12|life|Vitam]], that is, the living form, namely the rational soul, joined to my life as its formal principle, [[10:12|and mercy|et misericordiam]], that is, the supernatural gifts of graces, or the various benefits of grace given freely and mercifully, [[10:12|Thou hast granted me|tribuisti mihi]]: for when the body has been sufficiently disposed, God pours in the rational soul by creating it. Thomas and certain others understand by mercy in this place the natural seed-bed of the virtues and sciences that is inborn in us, of which Basil writes in his Rule: For there is inborn in the soul a habit of the principles of speculative as well as of practical things. And from such a seed-bed some are disposed by nature to this virtue, others to that. Job was disposed in an eminent degree to compassion, as he testifies below: [[Job 31:18|from my infancy mercy grew up with me: and it came out with me from my mother's womb|Ab infantia crevit mecum miseratio, et de utero egressa est mecum]]. [[10:12|and thy visitation|Et visitatio tua]], that is, the bestowing of thy benefits, the inflowing of graces, thy merciful keeping, [[10:12|hath preserved my spirit|custodivit spiritum meum]], that is, has kept my soul in life until now and given what is needful for living; it has also drawn me back from sins and kept me in grace. This too God does partly through the guardianship of the angels. Now as in the Scriptures God is said to withdraw from some because he takes his grace away from them, so he is said to visit and draw near when he grants his gifts.

paras.t: Omnia hæc sanctus Job introduxit, ad insinuandum quod omnia quæ in homine sunt, Deo sint nota, et ad impetrandum misericordiam ejus ex propriæ fragilitatis et imperfectionis confessione. Itemque, ad innuendum quod homo tam fragile vas, sustinere non valet regulam indeclinabilis justitiæ; sed, ut quinto Ethicorum docet Philosophus, Hominum rectorem necesse est uti regula ædificationis Lesbiæ: quæ est terra, in qua nullus lapis dolabilis est ad regulam rectam. Incolæ vero illius, ne careant ædificiis, faciunt plumbeam regulam, ut ubi lapis non dolatur ad regulam, regula curvetur ad lapidem; et ubi non fuerit enormis curvitas, sustineatur. Sic inter homines oportet leges regiminis remitti ad infirmitatem humanam, et quod enormiter distortum non est, tolerare.
paras.en: Holy Job brought in all these things to hint that all that is in man is known to God, and to obtain his mercy by confessing his own frailty and imperfection; and likewise to suggest that man, so fragile a vessel, cannot bear the rule of unbending justice; but, as the Philosopher teaches in the fifth book of the Ethics, the ruler of men must use the rule of Lesbian building [Aristotle's image of equity: the builders' rule of lead, which bends to the shape of the stone]: for Lesbos is a land in which no stone can be hewn to a straight rule. So its inhabitants, so as not to be without buildings, make a rule of lead, so that where the stone is not hewn to the rule, the rule is bent to the stone; and where the crookedness is not enormous, it is let stand. So among men the laws of government must be relaxed to suit human weakness, and what is not enormously crooked must be borne with.

paras.t: Deinde fatetur in Deo oblivionem proprie dictam non esse. Licet hæc celes in […] commemoravi, quasi intra te abscondas, dum eam verbis non pandis, nec per opera monstras; sed ita me affligi permittis, quasi creatura tua non essem, aut quasi dire peccassem, vel quasi tantæ fragilitatis naturaliter non consisterem; tamen scio quia universorum memineris, id est, omnium actualem notitiam habes, nec præteritorum immemor usquam efficeris.
paras.en: Next he confesses that there is no forgetting, properly so called, in God. [[10:13|Although thou conceal these things|Licet hæc celes]] in […] I have recalled, as though thou wouldst hide it within thyself, while thou dost not lay it open by words nor show it by deeds; but thou dost let me be so afflicted as if I were not thy creature, or as if I had sinned grievously, or as if I were not by nature of so great frailty; [[10:13|yet I know that thou rememberest all things|tamen scio quia universorum memineris]], that is, thou hast actual knowledge of all things, and art never forgetful of things past.

paras.t: Si peccavi: quod ait, vel ad insinuandum quod enormiter non peccavit, vel ad fatendum quod venialibus non caruit: quoniam tertio Regum Salomon loquitur, Non est homo super terram, qui faciat bonum et non peccet; et ad horam pepercisti mihi, id est, non statim quum peccassem, me punivisti, sed paternaliter distulisti donec correxi; cur ab iniquitate mea olim commissa, cujus dilata fuerat pœna, mundum me esse non pateris? Id est, cur me nunc tanquam justum non desinis impunitum, sed peccata quæ ego deflevi et emendavi, mihi modo imponis, et me quasi maculosum per tantam plagam ostendis? Per hoc probat, quod pro suis peccatis non sit ita percussus.
paras.en: [[10:14|If I have sinned|Si peccavi]]: this he says either to hint that he had not sinned gravely, or to confess that he was not without venial sins; for in the third book of Kings[[3 Kings 8:46||]] Solomon says: There is no man [[Eccles 7:21|upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|super terram, qui faciat bonum et non peccet]] [the margin gives 3 Kings 8:46, There is no man who sinneth not, and Eccles. vii, 21, whose wording Denis follows]; [[10:14|and thou hast spared me for an hour|et ad horam pepercisti mihi]], that is, thou didst not punish me at once when I had sinned, but didst put it off like a father until I amended; [[10:14|why dost thou not suffer me to be clean|mundum me esse non pateris]] [[10:14|from my iniquity|cur ab iniquitate mea]], once committed, whose punishment had been put off? That is, why dost thou not now leave me unpunished as one who is just, but layest on me now the sins which I have bewailed and amended, and showest me as one stained by so great a stroke? By this he proves that he was not struck so for his sins.

paras.t: Quod etiam probat deinceps, quia justis atque injustis communiter adversa vitæ præsentis eveniunt. Et si impius fuero, væ mihi est: quia tunc damnationem promereor, et juste hæc patior; et si justus fuero, non levabo caput, id est, adversitatibus istis non sublevor, et (ut apparet) non relevabor, nisi forte in morte. Vel, Non levabo caput, id est, me contra tuam æquitatem et dispositionem non erigam, me justificando in tuo conspectu, teque reprehendendo. Saturatus afflictione et miseria, id est pœnis et calamitate repletus multiplici, quia despectus ab omnibus, et rebus nudatus ac sobole.
paras.en: This too he proves next, because the adversities of the present life befall the just and the unjust alike. [[10:15|And if I be wicked, woe unto me|Et si impius fuero, væ mihi est]]: for then I deserve damnation, and suffer these things justly; [[10:15|and if just|et si justus]], [[10:15|I shall not lift up my head|non levabo caput]], that is, I am not relieved of these adversities, and (as it appears) shall not be relieved of them, unless perhaps in death. Or, [[10:15|I shall not lift up my head|Non levabo caput]], that is, I will not raise myself against thy equity and ordering, justifying myself in thy sight and finding fault with thee. [[10:15|Being filled with affliction and misery|Saturatus afflictione et miseria]], that is, filled with manifold pains and calamity, because despised by all, and stripped of goods and of offspring.

paras.t: Et propter superbiam meam, si me opposuero tuo judicio, quasi leænam capies me, id est, retiaculis suppliciorum me undique angustabis atque circumdabis, quemadmodum leæna in foveam lapsa, per industrias capitur. Quia (ut narrat Gregorius) in ejus via fit fovea, in qua pecus ponitur: […] foveam projicit. Fovea autem facta est profunda et angusta, ut in eam leæna cadere queat, sed exsilire non valeat. Sicque venatoribus eam desuper ictibus lanceisque vexantibus, ipsa in aream seu caveam prope foveam a venantibus factam seu positam, vectibus fortissimis circumpositam ac ligatam, cogitur fugere et se ipsam comprimere, quia resistere nequit: sicque conclusa, cum vectibus elevatur et capitur. Reversusque, non per tuam mutationem, sed per pœnarum mearum innovationem, mirabiliter me crucias doloribus animæ et corporis, et in somno atque vigilia, diu quoque continuando meas afflictiones.
paras.en: [[10:16|And for pride|Et propter superbiam]] of mine, if I set myself against thy judgment, [[10:16|thou wilt take me as a lioness|quasi leænam capies me]], that is, thou wilt hem me in and surround me on every side with the nets of punishment, as a lioness that has fallen into a pit is taken by skill. For (as Gregory tells) a pit is made in her path, in which a beast is placed: […] into the pit. The pit is made deep and narrow, so that the lioness can fall into it but cannot leap out. And so, while the hunters harass her from above with blows and lances, she is forced to flee into an enclosure or cage which the hunters have made or set beside the pit, surrounded and bound with very strong bars, and to squeeze herself in, because she cannot resist; and so, shut in, she is lifted out with the bars and taken. [[10:16|And returning|Reversusque]], not by any change in thee but by the renewing of my pains, [[10:16|thou tormentest me wonderfully|mirabiliter me crucias]] with pains of soul and body, both in sleep and waking, and also prolonging my afflictions for a long time.

paras.t: Instauras, id est, renovas et confortas, testes tuos contra me, id est amicos meos, qui videntur et esse se jactant testes tuæ veritatis: quoniam contra me tuam defendunt justitiam velut contra blasphemum, et per pœnas meas videris testimonium verbis eorum conferre, eosque in suo contra me exercitio confirmare. Et multiplicas iram tuam, id est punitionem quæ esse videtur ira tua, seu ex rigore tuæ justitiæ emanare. Hanc enim multiplicem facis in me. Et pœnæ militant in me, id est, pœnæ istæ te permittente mihi inflictæ, me impugnant et vulnerant, sicut milites hostes invadunt. Hoc plenius elucidatum recordor in expositione sexti capituli, ubi Job ait: Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum: et terrores Domini militant contra me. In hoc equidem libro, quia rhetorice scriptus est, et disputative procedit, eadem sententia frequenter aliis verbis repetitur, sicut in disputationibus rhetoricisque fieri solet codicibus; et præsertim in sermonibus dolorosis et affectuosis, in quibus amor et dolor renovant spiritum ad resumendum quæ dicta sunt. Tales autem sunt sermones beati Job. Quod etiam ex passu immediate sequenti fit evidens. Nam subditur:
paras.en: [[10:17|Thou renewest|Instauras]], that is, thou dost renew and strengthen, [[10:17|thy witnesses against me|testes tuos contra me]], that is, my friends, who seem to be, and boast that they are, witnesses of thy truth: for they defend thy justice against me as against a blasphemer, and through my pains thou seemest to lend support to their words, and to confirm them in their attack on me. [[10:17|And multipliest thy wrath|Et multiplicas iram tuam]], that is, the punishment which seems to be thy wrath, or to flow from the rigour of thy justice. For this thou makest manifold upon me. [[10:17|And pains war against me|Et pœnæ militant in me]], that is, these pains laid on me by thy permission attack and wound me, as soldiers fall upon their enemies. I remember that this was explained more fully in the exposition of the sixth chapter, where Job says: [[Job 6:4|the arrows of the Lord are in me, the rage whereof drinketh up my spirit, and the terrors of the Lord war against me|Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum: et terrores Domini militant contra me]]. Indeed in this book, because it is written in the manner of rhetoric and proceeds by disputation, the same thought is often repeated in other words, as is usual in disputations and in books of rhetoric; and above all in sorrowful and heartfelt speeches, in which love and grief stir the spirit to take up again what has been said. Such are the speeches of blessed Job. This also becomes evident from the passage that follows straight after. For it goes on:

paras.t: Quare de vulva eduxisti me? Qui utinam consumptus essem, ne oculus me videret. Hoc enim est quod supra ait: Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? egressus ex utero non statim perii? Sic quoque quod subditur, Fuissem quasi non essem, de utero translatus ad tumulum, ibidem aliis verbis ita exprimitur: Sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem, vel qui concepti non viderunt lucem. Quoniam ergo verba hæc tertio capitulo diffuse atque prolixe exposita sunt, et prætacta nunc hujus capituli verba ad intelligendum plenarie difficillima sunt, nec paucis verbis ibi præhabita hic repeti possunt; idcirco prolixitatem devitans, ad expositionem tertii capituli legentem remitto: nam et Gregorius ita facit.
paras.en: [[10:18|Why didst thou bring me forth out of the womb? O that I had been consumed, that eye might not see me!|Quare de vulva eduxisti me? qui utinam consumptus essem, ne oculus me videret.]] For this is what he said above: [[Job 3:11|Why did I not die in the womb? why did I not perish when I came out of the belly?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? egressus ex utero non statim perii?]] So too what follows, [[10:19|I should have been as if I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave|Fuissem quasi non essem, de utero translatus ad tumulum]], is expressed in the same place in other words thus: [[Job 3:16|as a hidden untimely birth, I should not be; or as they that, being conceived, have not seen the light|Sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem, vel qui concepti non viderunt lucem]]. Since, then, these words were explained at length and in detail in the third chapter, and the words of this chapter just quoted are very hard to understand fully, and what was set out there cannot be repeated here in a few words, I avoid lengthiness and send the reader back to the exposition of the third chapter: for Gregory too does so.

paras.t: Verumtamen verbum istud, Fuissem quasi non essem, non tam clare patet ex eo, quod tertio capitulo dicitur, Sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem, sicut quod ait hic, Quare de vulva, etc., ex eo quod scribitur ibi, Quare non in vulva mortuus sum? Idcirco particula ista jam exponenda est breviter. Fuissem quasi non essem: id est, si in utero matris obissem, nec vivus inde fuissem eductus, fuissem quasi non essem, id est, esse meum tam breve et occultum, fuisset pro nihilo reputatum; nec mala hæc sustinerem, imo immunis essem a vitæ hujus miseriis, quasi nunquam fuissem, seu quasi prorsus non essem. Sed quomodo hæc licite ac rationabiliter dici possint, in expositione tertii capituli requiratur.
paras.en: Yet this saying, [[10:19|I should have been as if I had not been|Fuissem quasi non essem]], is not made so clear by what is said in the third chapter, [[Job 3:16|as a hidden untimely birth, I should not be|Sicut abortivum absconditum non subsisterem]], as what he says here, [[10:18|Why didst thou bring me forth out of the womb|Quare de vulva]], etc., is made clear by what is written there, [[Job 3:11|Why did I not die in the womb?|Quare non in vulva mortuus sum?]] So this phrase must now be explained briefly. [[10:19|I should have been as if I had not been|Fuissem quasi non essem]]: that is, if I had died in my mother's womb and had not been brought out of it alive, [[10:19|I should have been as if I had not been|fuissem quasi non essem]], that is, my being, so brief and hidden, would have been reckoned as nothing; nor would I be bearing these evils, but rather I should be free of the miseries of this life, as though I had never been, or as though I were not at all. But how these things may be said lawfully and reasonably is to be sought in the exposition of the third chapter [the margin refers to Art. XI, near the end].

paras.t: Numquid non paucitas dierum meorum finietur brevi? id est, utique dies mei restantes, qui pauci sunt, præsertim comparatione perpetuitatis sequentis, cito finem habebunt, præteribunt seu defluent. Unde septimo capitulo dixit: Parce mihi, Domine, nihil enim sunt dies mei. Et iterum: Dies mei velocius transierunt, quam a texente tela succiditur, et consumpti sunt absque spe. Ad litteram quoque hoc dixit, quoniam propter acerbitatem dolorum suorum putavit se protinus moriturum, nec naturaliter longa sibi vita in sæculo isto restabat.
paras.en: [[10:20|Shall not the fewness of my days be ended shortly?|Numquid non paucitas dierum meorum finietur brevi?]] that is, surely my remaining days, which are few, above all in comparison with the everlasting age that follows, will soon come to an end, will pass and flow away. Hence he said in the seventh chapter: [[Job 7:16|spare me|Parce mihi]], O Lord, [[Job 7:16|for my days are nothing|nihil enim sunt dies mei]]. And again: [[Job 7:6|My days have passed more swiftly than the web is cut by the weaver, and are consumed without any hope|Dies mei velocius transierunt, quam a texente tela succiditur, et consumpti sunt absque spe]].
