He said this according to the letter too, because by reason of the bitterness of his pains he thought he would die at once, and by the course of nature no long life was left him in this world.

paras.t: Dimitte ergo me, id est, paulisper me respirare concede, et ab afflictionis hujus magnitudine modicum cessa, eamve tempera, ut plangam paululum dolorem meum, id est, adversitates et pœnas quæ mihi evenerunt et insunt, aliqualiter seu moderanter deplorem, quum et fletus sit alleviativus interni doloris, ut sæpe expositum est. Quasi dicat: Tanta est plagarum mearum acerbitas, ut præ pœnarum vehementia lacrimas fundere nequeam. Hinc ait Gregorius: Sicut moderata afflictio lacrimas exprimit, ita immoderata subducit: quæ mentem afflicti absorbens, sic ejus considerationem impedit, ut flendo æstimare non possit quid ferat: mentem namque quasi insensibilem reddit ac induratam.
paras.en: [[10:20|Suffer me, therefore|Dimitte ergo me]], that is, let me breathe for a little while, and cease a little from the greatness of this affliction, or temper it, [[10:20|that I may lament my sorrow a little|ut plangam paululum dolorem meum]], that is, that I may bewail somewhat, or in measure, the adversities and pains which have come upon me and are in me; for weeping too lightens inward grief, as has often been explained. As if to say: So great is the bitterness of my wounds that for the violence of the pains I cannot shed tears. Hence Gregory says: As moderate affliction draws out tears, so immoderate affliction takes them away: for it swallows up the mind of the afflicted, and so hinders his reflection that he cannot weigh by weeping what he bears; for it makes the mind as it were insensible and hardened.

paras.t: Antequam vadam per mortem de sæculo et corpore isto, et non revertar ad statum vitæ præsentis corruptibilem ac mortalem: secundum quod septimo dixit capitulo: Non revertetur oculus meus ut videat bona; nec adspiciet me visus hominis. Et infra: Semitam (inquit) per quam non revertar, ambulo. Ad terram tenebrosam et opertam mortis caligine, id est infernum: ad quem ante Christi passionem omnes etiam justi descenderunt, secundum quod infernus late accipitur, prout comprehendit limbum patrum, in quo justi in tenebris, non tamen in sensibilibus pœnis, fuerunt. Unde et Jacob ait in Genesi: Descendam ad filium meum lugens in infernum. Et infra beatus Job: In profundissimum infernum descendent omnia mea.
paras.en: [[10:21|Before I go|Antequam vadam]] by death out of this world and this body, [[10:21|and return no more|et non revertar]] to the corruptible and mortal state of the present life: as he said in the seventh chapter: [[Job 7:7|my eye shall not return to see good things|Non revertetur oculus meus ut videat bona]]; [[Job 7:8|Nor shall the sight of man behold me|nec adspiciet me visus hominis]]. And further on he says: [[Job 16:23|I am walking in a path by which I shall not return|Semitam (inquit) per quam non revertar, ambulo]]. [[10:21|to a land that is dark and covered with the mist of death|Ad terram tenebrosam et opertam mortis caligine]], that is, to hell: to which before the passion of Christ all men, even the just, went down, taking hell in the broad sense, in which it includes the limbo of the fathers, where the just were in darkness, though not in pains of sense. Hence Jacob too says in Genesis: [[Gen 37:35|I will go down to my son into hell, mourning|Descendam ad filium meum lugens in infernum]]. And further on blessed Job: [[Job 17:16|All that I have shall go down into the deepest pit|In profundissimum infernum descendent omnia mea]] [Latin *infernum*, which the Douay-Rheims here renders "pit", elsewhere "hell"].

paras.t: Porro infernus dicitur terra tenebrosa ex utriusque lucis carentia, scilicet spiritualis et corporalis, secundum Albertum; vel ex carentia claritatis visionis beatificæ ac divinæ. Dicitur demum operta mortis caligine, id est ipsa caliginosa morte, puta æterna damnatione, quæ in Apocalypsi dicitur mors secunda. Estque contraria vitæ gloriæ, imo et vitæ gratiæ, quamvis non vitam perimat naturæ. Vel, Mortis caligo, est teterrima illa obscuritas, mortem corporalem secuta, videlicet mœror, desolatio, seu desperatio sempiterna. Thomas autem, per caliginem mortis, intelligit originale peccatum, mortem inducens, quod in damnatis manet, quoad hoc quod damnum patiuntur illius peccati.
paras.en: Further, hell is called [[10:21|a land that is dark|terra tenebrosa]] from the lack of both lights, the spiritual and the bodily, according to Albert; or from the lack of the brightness of the beatific and divine vision. Lastly it is said to be [[10:21|covered with the mist of death|operta mortis caligine]], that is, with death itself full of mist, namely eternal damnation, which in the Apocalypse is called [[Apoc 20:14|the second death|mors secunda]]. And it is contrary to the life of glory, and indeed to the life of grace, though it does not destroy the life of nature. Or, the mist of death is that most foul darkness which follows bodily death, namely everlasting grief, desolation or despair. Thomas, however, understands by the mist of death original sin, which brings in death, and which remains in the damned in so far as they suffer the loss [that is, the pain of loss, the lack of the vision of God] due to that sin.

paras.t: Terram miseriæ, per abundantiam, quia in ea est plenitudo totius calamitatis, et sensibilium pœnarum acerbitas perhorrenda, et tenebrarum horribiliorum ac palpabiliorum quam fuerunt tenebræ Ægypti, de quibus scriptum est in Exodo: Facta sunt tenebræ horribiles atque palpabiles in terra Ægypti. Denique aer qui in inferno est, spissus, teter, inconvenientissimusque consistit; et ignis infernalis (secundum Gregorium) calorem habet et concremat, lucem non habet nec radiat. Nam de reprobo præcipit Christus: Projicite eum in tenebras exteriores. Verumtamen, aliqui satis probabiliter dicunt, et Thomas super quartum Sententiarum hoc tenet, quod ignis inferni modicum luminis habet, lucens tantumdem, ut in miseriis exsistentes possint se mutuo videre corporaliter, scilicet resumptis corporibus: quod non ad pœnæ relevamen, sed ad ingens calamitatis spectat gravamen, quia et corpora reproborum horribilissimi, turpissimi, atque mœstissimi erunt adspectus. Nihilominus, in aliquibus locis inferni potest esse mera obscuritas. Insuper, infernus terra tenebrarum vocatur, propter actualia peccata quibus involvuntur damnati.
paras.en: [[10:22|A land of misery|Terram miseriæ]], by abundance, because in it is the fullness of all calamity, and a most dreadful bitterness of pains of sense, [[10:22|and darkness|et tenebrarum]] more horrible and more palpable than was the darkness of Egypt, of which it is written in Exodus: [[Ex 10:22|there came horrible darkness|Facta sunt tenebræ horribiles]], and palpable[[Ex 10:21||]], [[Ex 10:22|in all the land of Egypt|in terra Ægypti]] [Denis joins the two verses: "palpable" is from v. 21, darkness "so thick that it may be felt"]. Then the air that is in hell is thick, foul and wholly unfit; and the fire of hell (according to Gregory) has heat and burns, but has no light and gives no radiance. For Christ commands concerning the reprobate: [[Matt 22:13|cast him into the exterior darkness|Projicite eum in tenebras exteriores]][[Matt 25:30||]] [the margin gives both Matt. xxii, 13 and xxv, 30; Denis's *eum*, "him", is that of xxii, 13]. Nevertheless some say, with good probability, and Thomas holds it on the fourth book of the Sentences, that the fire of hell has a little light, shining just so much that those who are in misery can see one another bodily, that is, once their bodies are taken up again: which serves not to relieve their pain but to weigh their calamity down enormously, because the bodies of the reprobate will be most horrible, most foul and most dismal to look upon. Nonetheless, in some places of hell there may be utter darkness. Moreover, hell is called a land of darkness because of the actual sins [that is, the sins a person commits himself, as opposed to original sin] in which the damned are wrapped.

paras.t: Ubi umbra mortis, id est mœstissima habitudo mortiformisque vita, quæ similitudo est mortis, quoniam sic affliguntur, ac si jugiter morerentur: propter quod mortem exoptant, et Deum vitæ fontem blasphemant. Vel, Umbra mortis, secundum Albertum, designat imagines timidis occurrentes in pœnis, juxta id Sapientis: Personæ tristes illis apparentes, pavorem illis præbebant.
paras.en: [[10:22|Where the shadow of death|Ubi umbra mortis]], that is, a most mournful condition and a life in the form of death, which is a likeness of death, because they are so afflicted as if they were dying continually: for which reason they long for death, and blaspheme God, the fountain of life. Or, [[10:22|the shadow of death|Umbra mortis]], according to Albert, signifies the images that meet the fearful in their pains, according to that saying of the Wise man: [[Wis 17:4|sad visions appearing to them, affrighted them|Personæ tristes illis apparentes, pavorem illis præbebant]].

paras.t: Et nullus ordo virtutum, sed conturbatio conscientiæ et confusio vitiorum. Nam omne bonum honestum detestantur ac odiunt, suntque prorsus aversi a Deo ordinis auctore fontano, atque totius honestatis fontem supermundissimum indicibiliter odiunt, et ejus beatitudini inæstimabiliter invident. Idcirco, inter eos nullus est ordo laudabilis, sed inordinatio consummata. Verumtamen objici potest, quoniam (teste Apostolo) quæ sunt a Deo ordinata sunt. Damnatorum autem supplicia a Deo infliguntur. Denique quod inordinatum est per culpam, ordinat Deus per pœnam, et dedecus injustitiæ ordinat et reformat decore suæ justitiæ, et juxta mensuram peccati est mensura supplicii, juxta quod scriptum est in libro Sapientiæ: Fortioribus fortior instat cruciatus. Et in Apocalypsi: Quantum glorificavit se et in deliciis fuit, tantum date illi tormentum et luctum. Quanto equidem voluntas creata plus sibi ipsi contra divinam voluntatem indulsit et satisfecit, tanto plus sustinere compellitur contra propriam affectionem. Sed jam ad ista est data responsio. Non enim idcirco in inferno dicitur nullus ordo, quia tormenta eorum ordinata non sint secundum dictamen sapientiæ, exigentiamque justitiæ Dei excelsi; sed quoniam mentibus damnatorum summa inest pravitas, confusio, vitiosa aversio, inordinatissima ac turbulentissima vita. Propter quod divinus Dionysius scribit, quod in dæmonibus sit amens furor, irrationalis concupiscentia et phantasia proterva. Hinc ait Gregorius: Ipsa supplicia per Dei justitiam ordinata, in mentibus damnatorum ordinata non sunt. Dum enim damnatus quisque foris igne succenditur, intus cæcitatis igne voratur, et in dolore positus, interius exteriusque confunditur, ut sua confusione deterius crucietur.
paras.en: [[10:22|And no order|Et nullus ordo]] of virtues, but disturbance of conscience and confusion of vices. For they loathe and hate every honest good, and are wholly turned away from God, the fountainhead and author of order, and they hate beyond words the most pure fountain of all honesty, and envy his blessedness beyond measure. Therefore among them there is no praiseworthy order, but complete disorder. Yet it can be objected that (as the Apostle witnesses) [[Rom 13:1|those that are ordained of God|quæ sunt a Deo ordinata sunt]] [Denis's Latin means "the things that are from God are ordered"; he takes it of order in general]. Now the punishments of the damned are inflicted by God. Further, what is disordered by fault God orders by punishment, and he orders the disgrace of injustice and reshapes it by the beauty of his justice; and the measure of the punishment answers to the measure of the sin, according to what is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 6:9|a greater punishment is ready for the more mighty|Fortioribus fortior instat cruciatus]]. And in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 18:7|As much as she hath glorified herself and lived in delicacies, so much torment and sorrow|Quantum glorificavit se et in deliciis fuit, tantum date illi tormentum et luctum]]. Indeed, the more the created will has indulged and pleased itself against the divine will, the more it is forced to endure against its own liking. But the answer to this has already been given. For it is not said that there is [[10:22|no order|nullus ordo]] in hell because their torments are not ordered according to the bidding of wisdom and the demands of the justice of God most high; but because in the minds of the damned there is the utmost depravity, confusion, vicious aversion, a life most disordered and most turbulent. For this reason the divine Dionysius writes that in the demons there is mindless fury, irrational desire and wanton imagination. Hence Gregory says: The punishments themselves, ordered by the justice of God, are not ordered in the minds of the damned. For while each of the damned is burned outwardly by fire, inwardly he is devoured by the fire of blindness, and set in pain he is confounded within and without, so that he is tormented the worse by his own confusion.

paras.t: Sed sempiternus horror inhabitat: quoniam pœnas quas sciunt se in æternum passuros, dolorose sentiunt ut præsentes, et pœnaliter horrent ut futuras: sed et se ipsos abhorrent, et corporum suorum deformitatem turpitudinemque cernentes, resurrectione peracta, vehementer stupebunt atque horrebunt: turpiora siquidem corpora illa erunt, quam fuerunt quando pro media parte a vermibus erant corrosa. Præterea, dæmonum adspectus horribilissimus erit damnatis, et unus alteri gravis erit ad intuendum. Hinc super Apocalypsim ait Albertus: Damnati non tantum affligentur in corpore ab igne inferni, quantum eorum mens affligetur ex hoc quod damnationem illam mœstissimam perpendet æternaliter duraturam. Gregorius quoque hic ait: In hoc sæculo flamma quæ succendit, illuminat; in inferno autem ignis qui cruciat, obscurat. Hic metus amittitur, quum tolerari cœperit quod timebatur; illic vero dolor dilaniat, et pavor angustat. Horrendo igitur modo erit tunc reprobis dolor cum formidine, flamma cum obscuritate. Quamvis autem Gregorius supra jam dixerit ignem infernalem nequaquam lucere, jam tamen post verba inducta subjungit, et verba præhabita quasi exponit: Illic ignis et ad consolationem non lucet, et tamen ut magis torqueat, ad aliquid lucet. Nam sequaces [suos] secum in tormentis reprobi, flamma illustrante, visuri sunt, ut amplius torqueantur.
paras.en: [[10:22|But everlasting horror dwelleth|Sed sempiternus horror inhabitat]]: for the pains which they know they will suffer for ever, they feel with grief as present, and dread with anguish as to come; and they abhor themselves too, and seeing the deformity and foulness of their bodies once the resurrection is accomplished, they will be greatly stunned and filled with horror: for those bodies will be fouler than they were when they had been half eaten away by worms. Besides, the sight of the demons will be most horrible to the damned, and each will be a burden for the other to look upon. Hence Albert says on the Apocalypse: The damned will not be so much afflicted in body by the fire of hell as their mind will be afflicted by considering that that most mournful damnation will last eternally. Gregory too says here: In this world the flame that burns gives light; but in hell the fire that torments darkens. Here fear is lost when what was feared begins to be borne; but there pain tears and dread oppresses. In a dreadful manner, then, the reprobate will then have pain with fear, flame with darkness. And although Gregory has already said above that the fire of hell gives no light at all, yet after the words quoted he adds, and as it were explains what he said before: There the fire gives no light for consolation, and yet, that it may torment the more, it gives light for something. For the reprobate, by the light of the flame, will see their followers with them in torments, that they may be tormented the more.

paras.t: Postremo, cordibus imprimenda et vehementer timenda sunt ista, sicque vivendum est nobis, ne ad tantam miseriam pertrahamur, ne ad tristissimam illam mansionem perpetuo deputemur, ne intolerabilissima illa tormenta æternaliter tolerare cogamur. Unde ad evadendum illa supplicia, patiamur libenter quidquid molestiæ, quidquid adversitatis in isto sæculo occurrit sive infligitur. Pensemus quam male sit eis, qui ibi jam detinentur; et Deo præcordialissime regratiemur, quod toties atque tam diu nobis pepercit, nec dudum in tartarum nos projecit, quum jam multos damnaverit, qui minus quam nos peccaverunt. Idcirco, quidquid potest manus nostra, instanter ac fervide operemur.
paras.en: Lastly, these things are to be pressed upon our hearts and greatly feared, and we must so live that we are not dragged into such misery, nor assigned for ever to that most mournful dwelling, nor forced to bear eternally those most unbearable torments. So, to escape those punishments, let us gladly suffer whatever trouble, whatever adversity befalls us or is laid on us in this world. Let us weigh how ill it is with those who are already held there; and let us thank God from the very depths of our heart that he has spared us so often and so long, and has not long since cast us into hell, when he has already damned many who sinned less than we. Therefore let us work earnestly and fervently at whatever our hand can do[[Eccles 9:10||]].

10.title: De mystico ejusdem capituli decimi intellectu.
10.title_en: On the mystical sense of the same tenth chapter

paras.t: Cum menti nostræ divinæ dulcedinis sapor gratiosus infunditur, ipsaque mens summæ, puræ, ac immensæ bonitatis amore ignitur, omne mox desiderium vitæ præsentis exstinguitur, delectatio carnalis in tædium vertitur. Vir itaque afflictus et justus, cupiens dissolvi et esse cum Christo, dicat: Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ, in hac corruptibili carne, ubi a divinæ lucis beato ac desideratissimo adspectu impedior. Corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, quoniam centena millia contemplationis obstacula ingerit. Hinc clamavit Apostolus: Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus? Et Psalmista: Educ de custodia animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo. Tot quoque defectus culpabiles omni die illabimur, quibus Deum aliqualiter inhonoramus, ut non immerito de vita hac tanto plus attædiemur, quanto plus in Divinitatis sancto amore fervemus. Et quid mirum, si esse in vita et exsilio attædiemur, atque ad patriæ accendamur ingressum, si tamen veraciter viatores consistimus?
paras.en: When the gracious savour of the divine sweetness is poured into our mind, and the mind itself is set on fire with love of the supreme, pure and boundless Goodness, all desire for the present life is soon quenched, and carnal delight is turned into weariness. Let the man who is afflicted and just, then, desiring [[Phil 1:23|to be dissolved and to be with Christ|dissolvi et esse cum Christo]], say: [[10:1|My soul is weary of my life|Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ]], in this corruptible flesh, where I am kept from the blessed and most longed-for sight of the divine light. [[Wis 9:15|For the corruptible body is a load upon the soul|Corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam]], since it thrusts upon it a hundred thousand hindrances to contemplation. Hence the Apostle cried out: [[Rom 7:24|Unhappy man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?|Infelix ego homo! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?]] And the Psalmist: [[Ps 141:8|Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name|Educ de custodia animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo]]. We slip, too, every day into so many culpable failings, by which we in some way dishonour God, that not without reason we grow the more weary of this life, the more we burn with the holy love of the Godhead. And what wonder if we grow weary of being in this life and exile, and are kindled to enter our fatherland, if indeed we are truly wayfarers?

paras.t: Denique, dum gratia operante cœperit ita præsens vita vilescere, Creatorisque amor menti dulcescere, restat ut quidquid in se reprehensibile perpendere poterit, fortiter arguat et accuset ac corrigat. Ideo sequitur: Dimittam adversum me eloquium meum, id est, in omnibus reprehendam me ipsum. In multis enim offendimus omnes; et justus in principio accusator est sui. Scriptum est: Dixi, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino. Ei autem qui culpam suam excusat, Dominus ait per Jeremiam: Judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi. Prima etenim via post culpam redeundi ad Deum, est propriam iniquitatem cognoscere, quam in confessione debemus præcipue adversum nos manifestare, non sine pudore peccati, et cum interno dolore quod inhonoravimus Deum. Ideo additur: Loquar in amaritudine animæ meæ: id est, in pœnitentiali dolore et ex vera contritione peccata mea fatebor, non nudis verbis me accusando, ut illi qui ex consuetudine quadam mente arida confitentur, et lugenda quasi lætantes aut fabulam recitantes pronuntiant. Quo autem confitens majorem habet de suis peccatis pudorem et cordialiorem dolorem, eo plus dimittitur ei, etiam de pœnis peccati, plusque sortitur de gratia ad vitandum deinceps peccata, et prosequendum opera bona.
paras.en: Next, when by the working of grace the present life has begun thus to grow worthless, and the love of the Creator to grow sweet to the mind, it remains that the man should firmly reprove, accuse and correct whatever he can find in himself worthy of blame. Therefore there follows: [[10:1|I will let go my speech against myself|Dimittam adversum me eloquium meum]], that is, I will reprove myself in all things. [[Jas 3:2|For in many things we all offend|In multis enim offendimus omnes]]; and the [[Prov 18:17|just is first accuser of himself|justus in principio accusator est sui]]. It is written: [[Ps 31:5|I said I will confess against my self my injustice to the Lord|Dixi, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino]]. But to him who excuses his fault the Lord says through Jeremias: [[Jer 2:35|I will contend with thee in judgment, because thou hast said: I have not sinned|Judicio contendam tecum, eo quod dixeris, Non peccavi]]. For the first way of returning to God after sin is to know one's own iniquity, which in confession we ought above all to make known against ourselves, not without shame for the sin, and with inward sorrow that we have dishonoured God. Therefore is added: [[10:1|I will speak in the bitterness of my soul|Loquar in amaritudine animæ meæ]]: that is, in penitential sorrow and out of true contrition I will confess my sins, not accusing myself with bare words, like those who confess out of a kind of habit with a dry mind, and pronounce what should be wept over as if they were rejoicing or reciting a tale. And the more shame for his sins and the more heartfelt sorrow the penitent has, the more is forgiven him, even of the punishments of sin, and the more grace he obtains for avoiding sins thereafter and pursuing good works.

paras.t: Dicam Deo supplici mente: Noli me condemnare, sed peccatis ignosce, gratiam tribue, confer salutem. Si autem quis oret non condemnari ex privato amore, quo sicut amat delicias, sic fugit tristitias, seu solo servili timore pœnarum, non est magnum, imo nec meritorium, quum radix merendi sit caritas Dei infusa, supernaturalis, gratuita, ita quod nullus actus est meritorius, nisi imperetur a caritate, quæ vita est animæ. Si autem quis postulet non damnari desiderio felicitatis æternæ, meritorium quidem est, si ex caritate procedat, ita quod plus quæratur ac intendatur Dei honor et gloria, quam proprium præmium; sed non est perfectum, quia mens reflectitur ad se ipsam, propter quod non est ibi purus et non reciprocus amor, sed partim reflexus. Porro si quis poscat non condemnari, solo sincero amore exsistendi cum Deo et laudandi eum, [cum] filiali timore separandi ab ipso, maxime meritorium est atque perfectum. Tali ergo affectu hoc deprecemur: alias magnum non esset. Siquidem nullus tam vitiosus est, qui non cupiat non damnari.
paras.en: [[10:2|I will say to God|Dicam Deo]] with a suppliant mind: [[10:2|Do not condemn me|Noli me condemnare]], but pardon my sins, grant grace, bestow salvation. But if anyone prays not to be condemned out of private love, by which, as he loves delights, so he flees sorrows, or out of servile fear of punishment alone [servile fear: the fear a slave has of the lash, as against filial fear, a son's fear of offending his father], this is no great thing, nay, it is not even meritorious, since the root of merit is the charity of God, infused, supernatural and freely given, so that no act is meritorious unless it is commanded by charity, which is the life of the soul. If anyone asks not to be damned out of desire for eternal happiness, it is indeed meritorious if it proceeds from charity, so that God's honour and glory are sought and intended more than one's own reward; but it is not perfect, since the mind bends back upon itself, so that the love there is not pure and wholly outgoing, but partly turned back on itself. But if anyone asks not to be condemned solely out of a sincere love of being with God and of praising him, with a filial fear of being separated from him, it is most meritorious and perfect. With such an affection, then, let us pray for this: otherwise it would be no great thing. For no one is so vicious as not to wish not to be damned.

paras.t: Indica mihi, id est, revela mihi, o Deus, omnium judex justissime, cur me ita judices in hac vita, id est, quare me nunc tot adversitatibus imples, tribulationibusque circumdas: an scilicet hoc fiat ad meum profectum, et ut per præsentis vitæ flagella evadam futura supplicia; an forte idcirco mecum occulto sic agis judicio, quatenus hæc mea tribulatio sit futuræ damnationis inchoatio. Nempe (ut ait Gregorius) duobus modis judicat Deus hominem in hac vita: quia aut per mala præsentia irrogare jam tormenta sequentia incipit, aut tormenta sequentia præsentibus flagellis exstinguit. Rursus, quibusdam justis contingit, ut exemplo beati Job, omni se diligentia coram Deo custodiant, et de mortalibus sibi conscii non sint, nihilominus graviter tribulentur. Illi ergo verba hæc dicere queunt eo sensu, quo præcedenti articulo de sancto Job litteraliter fuerunt exposita. Iterum, si quis justus dire afflictus, quamvis aliquando se peccasse testetur, nesciat tamen pro quo excessu specialiter puniatur, Deum potest orare ut sibi indicare dignetur, cur seu pro qua causa culpabili taliter visitetur.
paras.en: [[10:2|tell me|Indica mihi]], that is, reveal to me, O God, most just judge of all, [[10:2|why thou judgest me so|cur me ita judices]] in this life: that is, why dost thou now fill me with so many adversities and surround me with tribulations? Is it that this may be done for my profit, so that through the scourges of the present life I may escape the punishments to come? Or dost thou perhaps deal thus with me by a hidden judgement, so that this tribulation of mine may be the beginning of the damnation to come? For (as Gregory says) God judges man in this life in two ways: either through present evils he already begins to inflict the torments that are to follow, or by present scourges he extinguishes the torments that were to follow. Again, it happens to some just men that, after the example of blessed Job, they guard themselves with all diligence before God and are not conscious of any mortal sins, and nevertheless are grievously afflicted. These, then, can say these words in the sense in which they were expounded literally of holy Job in the preceding article. Again, if a just man who is cruelly afflicted, though he admits that he has sinned at some time, yet does not know for which excess in particular he is being punished, he can pray God to deign to show him why, or for what culpable cause, he is visited in this way.

paras.t: Præterea, si quis nimia pusillanimitate tentetur, aut immoderata scrupulositate laboret, aut desperatione tangatur: quasi periturus sit, etiamsi fecerit quod in se est, et debita sua impleverit; aut quod prædestinatus non sit, ideo salvari non valeat: talis confortet se ipsum, et animetur in Deo, fiducialiterque loquatur ad ipsum: Numquid bonum tibi videtur, si calumnieris me, et opprimas me opus manuum tuarum? quasi dicat, Non utique. Imo spero in tua pietate, o Domine, quod quum sim opus tuum, et ad tuam imaginem similitudinemque creatus, quantum in te est, non velis nec permittas me perire, sed speranti, timenti et invocanti paternaliter subvenire digneris. Sic et Isaias orat: Ecce respice, opera manuum tuarum, et populus tuus omnes nos. Et consilium impiorum adjuves? id est, non utique bonum tibi videtur, ut adversarios meæ salutis, qui sunt præsertim invisibiles hostes, adjuves ad perdendum me; sed gratiam tribues resistendi, per angelum meum mihi succurres, per meritum passionis Christi, per preces Sanctorum, nec ultra vires me tentari permittes. Invisibilium autem hostium incessabile consilium, studium, exercitium est, animarum impedire salutem, et nos suæ damnationis consortes peragere. Quibus tanto ferventius ac robustius reniti debemus, quo noscimus eos contra nos malitiosius, invidiosius, incessabiliusque conari. Hæc vero resistentia quid est, nisi Deum jugiter invocare, se ipsum in omnibus penitus humiliare, et quæ Deus requirit, obedientialiter observare?
paras.en: Moreover, if anyone is tempted by excessive faintheartedness, or labours under immoderate scrupulosity, or is touched by despair, as though he were going to perish even if he has done what is in him and fulfilled his obligations, or as though, not being predestined, he therefore cannot be saved: let such a man strengthen himself and take heart in God, and speak to him with confidence: [[10:3|Doth it seem good to thee that thou shouldst calumniate me, and oppress me, the work of thy own hands|Numquid bonum tibi videtur, si calumnieris me, et opprimas me opus manuum tuarum?]]? As if to say: Surely not. Nay, I hope in thy goodness, O Lord, that since I am thy work, and created to thy image and likeness, so far as lies in thee thou wilt neither will nor permit me to perish, but wilt deign to come like a father to the help of one who hopes, fears and calls upon thee. So too Isaias prays: [[Is 64:9|behold, see|Ecce respice]], [[Is 64:8|the works of thy hands|opera manuum tuarum]], and [[Is 64:9|we are all thy people|populus tuus omnes nos]]. [[10:3|and help the counsel of the wicked|Et consilium impiorum adjuves]]? that is, surely it does not seem good to thee to help the adversaries of my salvation, who are above all the invisible enemies, to destroy me; but thou wilt grant the grace to resist, wilt succour me through my angel, through the merit of Christ's passion, through the prayers of the Saints, and wilt not let me be tempted beyond my strength. Now the unceasing counsel, study and exercise of the invisible enemies is to hinder the salvation of souls and to make us sharers in their damnation. We ought to resist them the more fervently and stoutly, the more we know them to strive against us maliciously, enviously and unceasingly. And what is this resistance but to call upon God continually, to humble oneself utterly in all things, and to keep obediently what God requires?

paras.t: Præterea, si post grandem in spiritualibus profectibus prosperitatem, post præcipuam aliquam devotionem aut anagogicam contemplationem, ferventissimamve affectionem in Deo, contigerit nos subito gratiæ dispensativam suspensionem incurrere, gravem tentationem incidere, magnam animi ariditatem pati, aut forte (quod absit) per culpam graviter labi; redeundo ad cor, dicamus Creatori, quasi pie conquerendo, fiducialiter blandiendo, humiliter exorando, pristinam gratiam implorando, quod sequitur: Manus tuæ, Domine, fecerunt me, et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu, id est, quidquid sum et habeo in corpore ejusque membris, in anima ejusque viribus, tu mihi dedisti; et tamen sic repente præcipitas me ab alto contemplationis ac spiritualis perfectionis in ima vanæ imaginationis, internæ sterilitatis, diabolicæ tentationis? aut labi permittis in vitia propriæ fragilitatis, quasi factura tua non essem, et quasi tibi non esset cura de tuis effectibus? quasi dicat: Istud mirum videtur, non tamen injustum censetur. Sic et Psalmista affirmat: Poculum meum cum fletu miscebam a facie iræ indignationis tuæ, quia elevans allisisti me. Istud etiam dici posset ab eo, qui in magnam corporis infirmitatem rerumque damna, et a statu sublimi ad inopiam deveniret. Ex litterali autem sensu istorum, impiissima impuri Manichæi confutantur figmenta, dicentis, hæc inferiora operaque naturæ in corporum productione ac formatione, nequaquam esse a bono Deo, quem nominat Deum lucis, sed a principio tenebrarum, puta diabolo.
paras.en: Moreover, if after great prosperity in spiritual progress, after some special devotion or anagogical contemplation [that is, contemplation that lifts the mind up to heavenly things], or a most fervent affection in God, it happens that we suddenly incur a suspension of grace by God's dispensation, fall into a grievous temptation, suffer great dryness of soul, or perhaps (God forbid) fall gravely through sin: returning to our heart, let us say to the Creator, as though piously complaining, confidently coaxing, humbly entreating and imploring our former grace, what follows: [[10:8|Thy hands have made me|Manus tuæ, Domine, fecerunt me]], O Lord, [[10:8|and fashioned me wholly round about|et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu]], that is, whatever I am and have in the body and its members, in the soul and its powers, thou hast given me; and yet [[10:8|dost thou thus cast me down headlong on a sudden|sic repente præcipitas me]] from the height of contemplation and spiritual perfection into the depths of vain imagination, inward barrenness and diabolical temptation? Or dost thou let me fall into the vices of my own frailty, as though I were not thy handiwork, and as though thou hadst no care for thy works? As if to say: this seems strange, yet it is not judged unjust. So too the Psalmist affirms: I [[Ps 101:10|mingled my drink with weeping|Poculum meum cum fletu miscebam]] [[Ps 101:11|Because of thy anger and indignation: for having lifted me up thou hast thrown me down|a facie iræ indignationis tuæ, quia elevans allisisti me]]. This could also be said by one who has fallen into great sickness of body and loss of goods, and from a lofty state into want. But by the literal sense of these words the most impious fictions of the impure Manichæus are refuted, who says that these lower things and the works of nature in the producing and forming of bodies are in no way from the good God, whom he calls the God of light, but from the principle of darkness, namely the devil.

paras.t: Deinde videndum quomodo quæ sequuntur, de interiori homine (scilicet anima) possint exponi. Memento, quæso, id est, paternaliter ignoscendo, celeriter succurrendo, ostende te memorem seu immutabiliter cognoscentem, quod sicut lutum feceris me, id est, animam meam luto assimilasti, gratiæ tuæ fluenta in eam fundendo, ut spiritualiter irrigata fructificet, sicut in terram funditur imber de cœlo ut germinet. Anima quoque ad Sancti Spiritus influxionem se habet, quemadmodum terra ad pluviæ perfusionem. Propter quod ait Psalmographus: Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi. Nam sicut terra sine aqua seu pluvia sicca exstat et infructuosa, sic anima sine influentia Spiritus Sancti. Insuper, sicut lutum a Deo facta est anima, quoniam intellectualitas non est pura in ea, sed terrenæ sensualitati permixta, quemadmodum flamma candelæ superius clara est, inferius autem fumosa. Rursus anima, ob ejus ad carnalia concupiscentias ac vitia carnis, non immerito similis fertur luto. Et in pulverem reduces me. In pulverem reducitur anima, non quod substantialiter corrumpatur, aut vitam naturæ amittat; sed quia nonnunquam post divinorum charismatum irrigationem, propriæ infirmitati relinquitur et siccatur, vel peccando spiritualiter moritur vitam gratiæ amittendo. Hoc ergo vir justus loquitur, non simpliciter asserendo, sed caute timendo: quia dum homo in donis gratiæ prosperatur, timere debet de casu, quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Qui stat, videat ne cadat. Ecclesiasticus quoque dicit: In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum, et in die malorum ne immemor sis bonorum.
paras.en: Next we must see how what follows can be expounded of the inner man (that is, of the soul). [[10:9|Remember, I beseech thee|Memento, quæso]], that is, by pardoning like a father and succouring swiftly, show thyself mindful, or unchangeably knowing, [[10:9|that thou hast made me as the clay|quod sicut lutum feceris me]], that is, thou hast made my soul like clay by pouring into it the streams of thy grace, that, watered spiritually, it may bear fruit, as the rain from heaven is poured on the earth that it may spring up. The soul, too, stands to the inflowing of the Holy Spirit as the earth to the pouring of the rain. Wherefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 142:6|my soul is as earth without water unto thee|Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi]]. For as earth without water or rain stands dry and fruitless, so does the soul without the influence of the Holy Spirit. Moreover, the soul was made by God as clay, since its intellectual nature is not pure in it but mingled with earthly sensuality, as the flame of a candle is bright above but smoky below. Again, the soul, because of its desires for carnal things and the vices of the flesh, is not undeservedly said to be like clay. [[10:9|and thou wilt bring me into dust|Et in pulverem reduces me]]. The soul is brought into dust, not because it is corrupted in its substance or loses the life of nature, but because sometimes, after being watered with divine gifts, it is left to its own weakness and dries up, or by sinning dies spiritually, losing the life of grace. This, then, the just man says, not asserting it simply but fearing it with caution: for while a man prospers in the gifts of grace, he ought to fear a fall, as the Apostle says: He that standeth, [[1 Cor 10:12|let him take heed lest he fall|videat ne cadat]]. Ecclesiasticus also says: [[Ecclus 11:27|In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils: and in the day of evils be not unmindful of good things|In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum, et in die malorum ne immemor sis bonorum]].

paras.t: Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me? id est, sicut extrahitur lac de corpore bruti, sic animam meam eduxisti de vanis mundi affectibus ad novam conversationem teneritudinis spiritualis, ut spiritu mentis renovata, vetera vitia deserat, atque in donis Spiritus Sancti quotidie recenter crescat ac floreat: juxta illud ad Corinthios, Licet is qui foris est noster homo, corrumpatur, tamen is qui intus est, renovatur de die in diem. Hinc Petrus hortatur in prima sua Canonica: Deponentes omnem malitiam, et omnem dolum, et simulationes, et invidias, et detractiones, sicut modo geniti infantes rationabiles, lac concupiscite, ut in eo crescatis in salutem. Et sicut caseum me coagulasti: id est, caritatis coagulo menti meæ infuso, animam meam spiritualiter adunasti, constrinxisti, firmasti ut caseum, ne per multa vagetur, et peccando pereffluat, sed tibi summo bono, quod solum necessarium est, simplificata firmiter semper inhæreat, in te suos affectus omnesque actus reducat et figat. Hoc facit Deus electis, qui grata mente ei decantant: Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me. Hinc anima amorosa fatetur in Canticis: Ordinavit in me caritatem. Nam et hæc divinæ pietatis munera gratiosa justus sibi narrat a Deo collata, humiliter, non jactanter, ut gratias referat, custoditus consistat, seque beneficiorum Dei memorem esse declaret. Hoc quippe ad perfectionem requiritur, ut homo dona sibi præstita recognoscat, dicente Apostolo: Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis. Postremo, est et coagulatio mala, quæ est induratio in peccato, quemadmodum ait Scriptura de impiis: Coagulatum est sicut lac cor eorum.
paras.en: [[10:10|Hast thou not milked me as milk|Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me]]? that is, as milk is drawn from the body of a beast, so thou hast drawn my soul out of the vain affections of the world to a new way of life of spiritual tenderness, that, renewed in the spirit of the mind[[Eph 4:23||]], it may forsake its old vices and grow and flourish afresh every day in the gifts of the Holy Spirit: according to that word to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 4:16|though our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day|Licet is qui foris est noster homo, corrumpatur, tamen is qui intus est, renovatur de die in diem]]. Hence Peter exhorts in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 2:1|laying away all malice and all guile and dissimulations and envies and all detractions|Deponentes omnem malitiam, et omnem dolum, et simulationes, et invidias, et detractiones]], [[1 Pet 2:2|As newborn babes|sicut modo geniti infantes]] endowed with reason, desire milk [Denis reads *rationabiles*, agreeing with the babes; the Vulgate has *rationabile*, agreeing with the milk, as in the Douay-Rheims: desire the rational milk], [[1 Pet 2:2|that thereby you may grow unto salvation|ut in eo crescatis in salutem]]. [[10:10|and curdled me like cheese|Et sicut caseum me coagulasti]]: that is, by pouring into my mind the rennet of charity [*coagulum*, rennet, that which makes milk curdle, from the same root as *coagulasti*], thou hast spiritually gathered, bound together and made firm my soul like cheese, so that it may not wander among many things and flow away by sinning, but, made simple, may ever cling firmly to thee, the supreme good, which alone is necessary[[Luke 10:42||]], and may draw back and fix in thee all its affections and all its acts. This God does for the elect, who sing to him with a grateful mind: [[Ps 72:24|Thou hast held me by my right hand; and by thy will thou hast conducted me|Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me]]. Hence the loving soul confesses in the Canticle: [[Cant 2:4|he set in order charity in me|Ordinavit in me caritatem]]. For the just man also recounts to himself these gracious gifts of the divine goodness as bestowed on him by God, humbly, not boastfully, that he may give thanks, remain guarded, and show himself mindful of God's benefits. For this is required for perfection, that a man acknowledge the gifts granted him, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 2:12|we have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is of God: that we may know the things that are given us from God|Non spiritum hujus mundi accepimus, sed Spiritum qui ex Deo est, ut sciamus quæ a Deo donata sunt nobis]]. Lastly, there is also an evil curdling, which is hardening in sin, as Scripture says of the wicked: [[Ps 118:70|Their heart is curdled like milk|Coagulatum est sicut lac cor eorum]].

paras.t: Pelle et carnibus vestisti me: quoniam anima ad cœlestia ac divina suspirans, corruptibili corpore ejusque necessitudinibus ac motibus circumvallatur. Ossibus, id est virtutum firmitatibus, et nervis, id est virtutum et donorum connexionibus, compegisti me: id est, animam meam confortasti, et tibi junxisti, ac mystico Christi corpori cohærere fecisti. Virtutes namque et dona Spiritus Sancti sunt concatenata, ac animam in Deo firmantia, incorporantia quoque corpori electorum.
paras.en: [[10:11|Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh|Pelle et carnibus vestisti me]]: since the soul, sighing for heavenly and divine things, is walled about by the corruptible body and its needs and movements. [[10:11|with bones|Ossibus]], that is, with the firmness of the virtues, [[10:11|and sinews|et nervis]], that is, with the bonds that link the virtues and gifts together, [[10:11|thou hast put me together|compegisti me]]: that is, thou hast strengthened my soul and joined it to thyself, and made it cleave to the mystical body of Christ. For the virtues and the gifts of the Holy Spirit are linked together as in a chain, making the soul firm in God and incorporating it also into the body of the elect.

paras.t: Vitam gratiæ et misericordiam, id est supernaturalia varia dona, tribuisti mihi, in Baptismo, et post lapsum in Pœnitentia, imo quotiescumque post peccatum mortale conversus sum. Quoniam enim ad supernaturalem finem (qui est visio Dei per speciem) creatus est homo, indiget supernaturalibus mediis, quibus finem hunc sortiatur, quum necesse sit fini media proportionari. Hæc autem supernaturalia media sunt, gratia gratum faciens, virtutes infusæ ac dona: quæ rite misericordiæ appellantur, quoniam ex supermunificentissima Dei pietate penitus gratis ac misericordissime dantur, quemadmodum ad Titum ait Apostolus: Non ex operibus justitiæ quæ fecimus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam salvos nos fecit: et ad Ephesios: Gratia estis salvati per fidem, et hoc non ex vobis: Dei enim donum est, non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur.
paras.en: [[10:12|Thou hast granted me|tribuisti mihi]] [[10:12|life|Vitam]] of grace [[10:12|and mercy|et misericordiam]], that is, various supernatural gifts, in Baptism, and after a fall in Penance, nay, as often as I have turned back after mortal sin. For since man was created for a supernatural end (which is the vision of God face to face [literally *per speciem*, by sight, as against by faith]), he needs supernatural means by which to attain this end, since means must be proportioned to the end. Now these supernatural means are sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God], the infused virtues and the gifts: and these are rightly called mercies, since they are given wholly freely and most mercifully out of the surpassingly bountiful goodness of God, as the Apostle says to Titus: [[Tit 3:5|Not by the works of justice which we have done, but according to his mercy, he saved us|Non ex operibus justitiæ quæ fecimus nos, sed secundum suam misericordiam salvos nos fecit]]: and to the Ephesians: [[Eph 2:8|by grace you are saved through faith: and that not of yourselves, for it is the gift of God|Gratia estis salvati per fidem, et hoc non ex vobis: Dei enim donum est]], [[Eph 2:9|Not of works, that no man may glory|non ex operibus, ne quis glorietur]].

paras.t: Et visitatio tua custodivit spiritum meum. Non solum indigemus gratia præveniente, sed etiam subsequente et consummante. A Deo namque est omnis boni inchoatio, conservatio et consummatio. Vitam virtuosam ipse in nobis incipit, prosequitur, terminat. Itaque, Visitatio tua, id est tu ipse clementer me visitans, seu pietatis tuæ subsidium, custodivit spiritum meum: quia quamdiu mansit in esse vitaque gratiæ, hoc fuit, te eum custodiente, tuaque dona in eo conservante ac perficiente. Non enim minus, sed plus dependent omnia gratiæ dona, spiritualiaque charismata Deo, quam dies a sole, seu splendor a luce: et tamen, si ad momentum sol cessaret diem, aut lux fusam claritatem conservare, nonne dies et claritas talis subito esse desinerent? Sic si per momentum Deus conservationem seu custodiam suam abstraheret, quidquid spiritualis fuerit perfectionis, subito disperiret. Hinc orat Psalmista: Custodi me, Domine, ut pupillam oculi; et: Visita nos in salutari tuo. Rursusque asserit: Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, frustra vigilat qui custodit eam. Ex quo clarissime innotescit, quantum nos humiliare, quantum Deo regratiari, quantum inanem et fatuam in nobis ipsis gloriationem aspernari debemus, præsertim quum ipsemet beatissimus Jeremias testetur: Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos.
paras.en: [[10:12|and thy visitation hath preserved my spirit|Et visitatio tua custodivit spiritum meum]]. We need not only prevenient grace but also subsequent and consummating grace [that is, grace that goes before our good acts, grace that follows and sustains them, and grace that brings them to completion]. For from God is every beginning, preserving and completing of good. He begins the virtuous life in us, carries it on and brings it to its end. Therefore [[10:12|thy visitation|Visitatio tua]], that is, thou thyself mercifully visiting me, or the help of thy goodness, [[10:12|hath preserved my spirit|custodivit spiritum meum]]: for as long as it remained in being and in the life of grace, this was because thou didst keep it, and preserve and perfect thy gifts in it. For all the gifts of grace and spiritual charisms depend on God not less but more than the day on the sun, or brightness on light: and yet if for a moment the sun ceased to keep the day, or the light to keep the brightness it sheds, would not such a day and brightness at once cease to be? So, if God for a moment withdrew his preserving or keeping, whatever there is of spiritual perfection would at once perish. Hence the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 16:8|keep me|Custodi me]], O Lord, [[Ps 16:8|as the apple of thy eye|ut pupillam oculi]]; and: [[Ps 105:4|visit us with thy salvation|Visita nos in salutari tuo]]. And again he declares: [[Ps 126:1|Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it|Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, frustra vigilat qui custodit eam]]. From this it is made most clear how much we ought to humble ourselves, how much to give thanks to God, how much to spurn empty and foolish glorying in ourselves, especially since the most blessed Jeremias himself bears witness: [[Jer 10:23|I know, O Lord, that the way of a man is not his: neither is it in a man to walk, and to direct his steps|Scio, Domine, quia non est hominis via ejus, nec viri est ut ambulet et dirigat gressus suos]].

paras.t: Licet hæc celes in corde tuo, tamen scio quia universorum memineris. Quum Deum pro aliqua gratia speciali deposcimus, et diversa quæ eum ad miserendum ac audiendum inclinent, orando commemoramus, videlicet quæ ad propriam pertinent fragilitatem, præcedentia quoque beneficia pietatis divinæ, nec tamen ad libitum exaudimur, imo diu differimur; tunc Deus quasi celat in corde suo quæ dicimus, quoniam instar non advertentis se habet. Sed tunc nequaquam frangamur aut diffidamus, sed perseveranter precemur, dicentes quod subditur: Scio quia universorum memineris, qualiter scilicet sperantibus et constanter orantibus promisisti: Petite, et dabitur vobis. Itaque cuncta advertis, nec minima affectio aut verbi prolatio tuam effugit memoriam: ideo fiducialiter usque in finem te invocabo, præsertim quum in Evangelio Christus locutus sit: Si vos quum sitis mali, nostis bona data dare filiis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester de cœlo dabit spiritum bonum petentibus se? Denique ipse jubet se exorari: et hoc quare, nisi quia paratus est exaudire?
paras.en: [[10:13|Although thou conceal these things in thy heart|Licet hæc celes in corde tuo]], [[10:13|yet I know that thou rememberest all things|tamen scio quia universorum memineris]]. When we beg God for some special grace, and in praying call to mind various things that may incline him to have mercy and to hear, namely those that belong to our own frailty, and also the former benefits of the divine goodness, and yet we are not heard as we wish, but are put off for a long time: then God as it were conceals in his heart what we say, since he behaves like one who does not attend. But then let us by no means be broken or lose confidence, but pray perseveringly, saying what is added: [[10:13|I know that thou rememberest all things|Scio quia universorum memineris]], that is, how thou hast promised to those who hope and pray constantly: [[Matt 7:7|Ask, and it shall be given you|Petite, et dabitur vobis]]. So thou attendest to all things, and not the least affection or uttered word escapes thy memory: therefore I will call upon thee with confidence even to the end, especially since Christ has said in the Gospel: [[Luke 11:13|If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father from heaven give the good Spirit to them that ask him?|Si vos quum sitis mali, nostis bona data dare filiis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester de cœlo dabit spiritum bonum petentibus se?]] Lastly, he himself bids us entreat him: and why so, unless because he is ready to hear?

paras.t: Si, pro quia, peccavi tibi, id est ad tuæ sanctitatis injuriam, ad tuæ majestatis inhonorationem, et contra tuam voluntatem. Siquidem, tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci. Quod utique non sine cordiali dolore fateri et fari debemus, eo quod tam immensæ celsitudinis Dominum, tam superclementissimum Patrem, tam incomparabilem benefactorem, toties et tam dire offendimus. Et ad horam pepercisti mihi, non statim te ulciscendo: juxta illud Joelis, Benignus et misericors est Dominus, et præstabilis super malitia. Et in Psalmo: Non secundum peccata nostra fecit nobis, neque secundum iniquitates nostras retribuit nobis. Cur ab iniquitate mea mundum me esse non pateris? Id est, cur permittis me nunc recidivare? cur gratiam abstinendi a culpis non tribuis? cur me præteritorum vitiorum impuris memoriis aut delectationibus desinis inquinari? Quod totum non divinam pietatem reprehendendo, sed propriam calamitatem deflendo profertur, et eo quod Deus permittit nos a dæmonibus impugnari ac superari. Pati tamen Deo improprie seu metaphorice constat adscribi. In tantum quoque puritas nostra, omnisque virtus ac meritum dependent a Deo, ut quum vitiis sordidamur, nec pœnitemus, dicamur a Deo indurari, et ipsum non pati ut puri simus, dicamus. Sic nempe Isaias scribit: Tu, Domine, quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra, ne timeremus te?
paras.en: [[10:14|If|Si]], put for *since*, [[10:14|I have sinned|peccavi]] against thee, that is, to the injury of thy holiness, to the dishonouring of thy majesty, and against thy will. For [[Ps 50:6|To thee only have I sinned, and have done evil before thee|tibi soli peccavi, et malum coram te feci]]. This indeed we ought to confess and to utter not without heartfelt sorrow, because we have so often and so cruelly offended a Lord of such boundless loftiness, a Father so surpassingly merciful, a benefactor so beyond compare. [[10:14|and thou hast spared me for an hour|Et ad horam pepercisti mihi]], not taking vengeance at once: according to that word of Joel: The Lord [[Joel 2:13|is gracious and merciful|Benignus et misericors est]], and [[Joel 2:13|ready to repent of the evil|præstabilis super malitia]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 102:10|He hath not dealt with us according to our sins: nor rewarded us according to our iniquities|Non secundum peccata nostra fecit nobis, neque secundum iniquitates nostras retribuit nobis]]. [[10:14|why dost thou not suffer me to be clean from my iniquity?|Cur ab iniquitate mea mundum me esse non pateris?]] That is, why dost thou let me now relapse? why dost thou not grant the grace of abstaining from faults? why dost thou let me be defiled [the print has *desinis*, cease; the sense asks for *sinis*, allow] by impure memories or delights of past vices? All this is said not in blame of the divine goodness but in lament for one's own calamity, and because God permits us to be assailed and overcome by the demons. Yet it is clear that *suffering* [that is, permitting, as in *dost thou not suffer*] is ascribed to God improperly, or by a metaphor. And so far do our purity and all our virtue and merit depend on God, that when we are soiled with vices and do not repent, we are said to be hardened by God, and we say that he does not suffer us to be pure. Thus indeed Isaias writes: [[Is 63:17|Why hast thou made us to err, O Lord, from thy ways: why hast thou hardened our heart, that we should not fear thee?|Tu, Domine, quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis, indurasti corda nostra, ne timeremus te?]]

paras.t: Et si impius fuero, væ mihi est: id est, æterna damnatio imminet, nisi pœnitentiam egero, secundum illud Isaiæ: Væ impio in malum; retributio enim fiet ei. Et si justus fuero, non levabo caput, id est, mentem superbiendo, præsumendo, inaniter gloriando, non erigam, sed tibi tanto subjectior ero, quo gratiosius egeris mecum, et tibi gratus esse conabor, Apostolicum illud attendens: Gratia Dei sum id quod sum. Et denuo: Quid habes quod non accepisti? Ideo ait Psalmista: Vanum est vobis ante lucem surgere. Et Baruch: Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva, dat gloriam Domino. Vel, Non levabo caput, quoniam justi variis adversitatibus in hac vita premuntur, dicente Apostolo: Omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur. Hinc in Threnis scriptum est: Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum; et in Psalmo: Veni in altitudinem maris, et tempestas demersit me. Sciens equidem Deus quam fructuosum sit ferre adversa, tribulationibus exerceri, donat hæc suis electis in vita præsenti.
paras.en: [[10:15|And if I be wicked, woe unto me|Et si impius fuero, væ mihi est]]: that is, eternal damnation threatens, unless I do penance, according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 3:11|Woe to the wicked unto evil: for the reward of his hands shall be given him|Væ impio in malum; retributio enim fiet ei]]. [[10:15|and if just|Et si justus]], [[10:15|I shall not lift up my head|non levabo caput]], that is, I will not raise up my mind by pride, presumption or vain glorying, but will be the more subject to thee the more graciously thou hast dealt with me, and will strive to be grateful to thee, heeding that word of the Apostle: [[1 Cor 15:10|by the grace of God, I am what I am|Gratia Dei sum id quod sum]]. And again: [[1 Cor 4:7|what hast thou that thou hast not received|Quid habes quod non accepisti]]? Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 126:2|It is vain for you to rise before light|Vanum est vobis ante lucem surgere]]. And Baruch: [[Bar 2:18|the soul that is sorrowful for the greatness of evil she hath done, and goeth bowed down|Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva]], [[Bar 2:18|giveth glory|dat gloriam]] to the Lord. Or: [[10:15|I shall not lift up my head|Non levabo caput]], since the just are pressed by various adversities in this life, as the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ|Omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo]] [[2 Tim 3:12|shall suffer persecution|persecutionem patientur]]. Hence it is written in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:54|Waters have flowed over my head|Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:3|I am come into the depth of the sea, and a tempest hath overwhelmed me|Veni in altitudinem maris, et tempestas demersit me]]. For God, knowing how fruitful it is to bear adversity and to be exercised by tribulations, gives these things to his elect in the present life.

paras.t: Ideo subditur, Saturatus afflictione, id est dolore interno de propriis ac proximorum peccatis, de exsistentium in purgatorio pœnis, de imperfectione animæ meæ, de gloriæ dilatione. Itemque, Saturatus afflictione, id est adversitatum angustiis. De qua saturatione fertur in Psalmo: Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte. Et iterum: Cibabis nos pane lacrimarum. Itemque tertio Regum libro: Sustentate Michæam pane tribulationis et aqua angustiæ. Et miseria, qua plena est vita ista. Miseria tamen magis proprie competit malis culpæ, quibus plena est vita impiorum, quam malis pœnæ, quibus plena vita est bonorum, quemadmodum in Threnis perhibetur: Sedebit solitarius et tacebit, quia levabit se super se. Dabit percutienti se maxillam, saturabitur opprobriis.
paras.en: Therefore is added: [[10:15|being filled with affliction|Saturatus afflictione]], that is, with inward sorrow for one's own sins and those of one's neighbours, for the pains of those who are in purgatory, for the imperfection of my soul, for the delay of glory. And again: [[10:15|being filled with affliction|Saturatus afflictione]], that is, with the straits of adversity. Of this filling it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 41:4|My tears have been my bread day and night|Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte]]. And again: Thou wilt [[Ps 79:6|feed us with the bread of tears|Cibabis nos pane lacrimarum]]. And in the third book of Kings: [[3 Kings 22:27|feed|Sustentate]] Micheas [[3 Kings 22:27|with bread of affliction, and water of distress|pane tribulationis et aqua angustiæ]]. [[10:15|and misery|Et miseria]], of which this life is full. Yet misery belongs more properly to the evils of guilt, of which the life of the wicked is full, than to the evils of punishment, of which the life of the good is full, as is said in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:28|He shall sit solitary, and hold his peace|Sedebit solitarius et tacebit]], because he will raise himself above himself [Denis reads *levabit se super se*; the Vulgate has *levavit super se*, he hath taken it up upon himself]. [[Lam 3:30|He shall give his cheek to him that striketh him, he shall be filled with reproaches|Dabit percutienti se maxillam, saturabitur opprobriis]].

paras.t: Reversusque ad me per gratiæ confortationem, per caritatis inflammationem, per mentis meæ illuminationem, mirabiliter me crucias desiderio te videndi clare, sicuti es in te ipso, qui in propria lucis puritate pulchritudinis es immensæ, et serenitatis supergratissimæ, dulcedinisque prorsus interminatæ. Ideo, quanto te nunc ardentius amo, clariusque contemplor, eo plus provocor, æstuo, suspiro te videre per speciem, ita ut amore jam langueam: qui languor cruciatum habet mirabilem, et inexpertis frigidisque ignotum. Insuper, quo Deum sincerius contemplamur, et ejus amore plus inflammamur, eo de nostris peccatis, id est de Dei offensa, præcordialius mirabiliusque torquemur: qui dolor omnem pro temporalibus damnis ortum excedit dolorem. Et mirum quod cor nostrum non rumpitur præ dolore, quod Deum creatorem nostrum unquam offendimus, imo et quotidie heu! toties miserrimi inhonoramus. Potissime autem cruciari debemus (si tamen vera caritate ardemus) de malo statu, casu, divisione Ecclesiæ, de prælatorum ejus impia conversatione, de multorum religiosorum, sacerdotum et clericorum detestabili vita scandalis plena: Deumque jugiter affectuosissime ac devotissime implorare pro plenissima reformatione in omnibus, ad gloriam Salvatoris. Adhuc mirabiliter cruciantur electi, Christo mentaliter compatiendo, ejus vestigia cruciformiter imitando, in actibus se pœnitentiæ exercendo, in jejuniis, disciplinis, vigiliis.
paras.en: [[10:16|and returning|Reversusque]] to me by the strengthening of grace, by the kindling of charity, by the enlightening of my mind, [[10:16|thou tormentest me wonderfully|mirabiliter me crucias]] with the desire of seeing thee clearly as thou art in thyself, who in the very purity of thy light art of boundless beauty, of a serenity lovely beyond all, and of a sweetness wholly without end. Therefore the more ardently I now love thee and the more clearly I contemplate thee, the more I am roused, burn and sigh to see thee face to face, so that I now languish with love: and this languor holds a wonderful torment, unknown to the untried and the cold. Moreover, the more sincerely we contemplate God, and the more we are inflamed with his love, the more deeply at heart and the more wonderfully are we tormented over our sins, that is, over the offence given to God: and this sorrow exceeds every sorrow that arises over temporal losses. And it is a wonder that our heart does not burst for sorrow that we have ever offended God our creator, nay, that daily, alas, most wretched as we are, we dishonour him so many times. But most of all we ought to be tormented (if indeed we burn with true charity) over the evil state, the fall and the division of the Church, over the impious conduct of her prelates, over the detestable life, full of scandals, of many religious, priests and clerics: and to implore God continually, most affectionately and devoutly, for the fullest reform in all things, to the glory of the Saviour. Further, the elect are wonderfully tormented by suffering with Christ in their minds, by following his footsteps in the way of the cross, by exercising themselves in acts of penance, in fasts, disciplines [that is, the scourgings undertaken as bodily penance] and vigils.

paras.t: Instauras testes tuos contra me. Quamvis testes Dei sint angeli sancti, et prædicatores electi, doctoresque virtuosi, et omnes qui fide et opere pro Deo, pro fide et æquitate loquuntur, quemadmodum per Isaiam Dominus ait, Vere vos testes mei: et in Actibus Christus Apostolis loquens, Eritis (inquit) mihi testes usque ad ultimum terræ: tamen hoc loco, testes intelligi possunt spiritus maligni, qui contra iniquos testimonium perhibent veritati, et aliquando ad accusandum electos justitiam Dei allegant. Hos testes Deus contra bonos instaurat, dans eis licentiam impugnandi electos: in qua pugna dum vel in toto vel partim triumphant, ad accusandum bonos instaurantur. Imo, quantum Deus nos peccare permittit, tantum illi contra nos instaurantur. Et multiplicas iram tuam, gratiam tuam multis justo judicio subtrahendo: propter quod intime doleo, secundum quod subditur, et pœnæ militant in me, id est invalescunt. Quo enim anima corpore dignior est, eo de ejus periculo amplius quam de corporis qualibet infirmitate contristari debemus.
paras.en: [[10:17|Thou renewest thy witnesses against me|Instauras testes tuos contra me]]. Although the witnesses of God are the holy angels, and chosen preachers, and virtuous doctors, and all who by faith and works speak for God, for the faith and for justice, as the Lord says through Isaias, Truly [[Is 43:10|You are my witnesses|vos testes mei]] [the margin is unreadable here; the words stand in Is 43:10 and 43:12], and Christ in the Acts, speaking to the Apostles, [[Acts 1:8|you shall be|Eritis]] (he says) [[Acts 1:8|witnesses unto me|mihi testes]] [[Acts 1:8|even to the uttermost part of the earth|usque ad ultimum terræ]]: yet in this place the witnesses can be understood as the evil spirits, who bear witness to the truth against the wicked, and sometimes plead the justice of God in order to accuse the elect. These witnesses God renews against the good, giving them leave to attack the elect: and in that fight, when they triumph either wholly or in part, they are renewed for accusing the good. Indeed, as far as God permits us to sin, so far are they renewed against us. And thou [[10:17|multipliest thy wrath|multiplicas iram tuam]], by withdrawing thy grace from many by a just judgment: for which I grieve inwardly, according to what is added, [[10:17|and pains war against me|et pœnæ militant in me]], that is, grow strong. For the more worthy the soul is than the body, the more ought we to be saddened over its peril than over any infirmity of the body.

paras.t: Præterea, quoniam multæ tribulationes justorum, multiplicatio iræ et militatio pœnarum in homine virtuoso intelligi possunt varia ejus afflictio: quanquam talis afflictio in electis non proprie ira Dei dicatur, sed opus clementiæ ejus, aliqualiter tamen ira est, in quantum est in ultionem peccati, et quoniam propter pœnæ acerbitatem ira videtur. Unde et Christus ait in Psalmo ad Patrem: In me transierunt iræ tuæ.
paras.en: Moreover, since [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|multæ tribulationes justorum]] [the margin note here is garbled; the words are Ps 33:20], the multiplying of wrath and the warring of pains in a virtuous man can be understood as his various afflictions: although such affliction in the elect is not properly called the wrath of God, but the work of his clemency, yet it is in some way wrath, in so far as it is in punishment of sin, and because by the bitterness of the pain it seems to be wrath. Hence Christ too says to the Father in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:17|Thy wrath hath come upon me|In me transierunt iræ tuæ]].

paras.t: Denique, principium hujus capituli quidam in persona animæ in purgatorio exsistentis exponunt, præsertim quum lectiones Officii defunctorum ex hoc loco partim sumantur. Verumtamen littera ad hoc proprie applicari non valet, saltem pro magna parte: nec oportet ideo ista de anima tali exponi, quia pro eis leguntur, sicut et psalmi qui pro defunctis leguntur, in illorum persona non proprie exponuntur, et pro maxima parte exponi non possunt. Nihilominus lectiones et psalmi hujusmodi pro defunctis leguntur, quoniam specialiter tractant de animabus, et his quæ earum causam necessitatemque respiciunt, et de fragilitate conditionis humanæ, quæ commemoratur ad impetrandam Dei pietatem ac veniam. Aliqua quoque continentur in eis, quæ in defunctorum persona seu animæ in purgatorii potestate, congrue exponuntur ac proferuntur.
paras.en: Lastly, some expound the beginning of this chapter in the person of a soul that is in purgatory, especially since the lessons of the Office of the Dead are taken in part from this place. Yet the letter cannot properly be applied to this, at least for the greater part: nor need these things be expounded of such a soul because they are read for such souls; just as the psalms that are read for the dead are not properly expounded in their person, and for the most part cannot be so expounded. Nevertheless such lessons and psalms are read for the dead because they treat especially of souls, and of the things that concern their cause and need, and of the frailty of the human condition, which is recalled in order to obtain God's pity and pardon. Some things too are contained in them which are fittingly expounded and uttered in the person of the dead, or of a soul in the power of purgatory [a footnote gives the reading *in purgatorio posita*, 'placed in purgatory'].

paras.t: Præterea, quod in capituli hujus exordio scribitur, Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ, anima in purgatorio non proprie loquitur de se ipsa, nisi forte loqui dicatur in persona defuncti, cujus anima fuit ipsa. Sæpe enim totum pro parte, et econtrario ponitur: ut quum dicimus, Petrus apostolus est in cœlo; vel, Sancte Petre, ora pro nobis. Breviter ergo tangam hujusmodi expositionem, quoniam quosdam delectat: quæ tamen ex præhabitis elucescit.
paras.en: Further, in what is written at the opening of this chapter, [[10:1|My soul is weary of my life|Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ]], a soul in purgatory does not properly speak of itself, unless perhaps it be said to speak in the person of the dead man whose soul it was. For the whole is often put for the part, and the other way round: as when we say, Peter the apostle is in heaven; or, Saint Peter, pray for us. I will therefore touch briefly on this kind of exposition, since it pleases some: though it is clear enough from what has been said already.

paras.t: Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ, id est, animam quæ ego sum, seu me quæ anima sum, tædet in his vivere pœnis, propter earum acerbitatem, et desiderio gloriæ, a qua nihil retardat me nisi reatus culpæ, id est obligatio ad tormenta propter peccata, quia nondum condignas sustinui pœnas. Dimittam adversum me eloquium meum, id est, ea intellectualiter dicam seu cogitabo, quæ me ipsam contristant, affligunt, culpabilemque demonstrant; me quoque accusabo atque deflebo. Pœnitet enim in purgatorio exsistentes, quod peccaverunt, quoniam inavertibiliter manent in caritate. Loquar in amaritudine animæ meæ, id est in propria hac mea afflictione me ad loquendum intellectuali locutione movente. Dolor enim incitat ad loquendum, quia per verba evaporando seu erumpendo, quodammodo minoratur; et tanto minus anima percipit unum, quo plus intendit ad aliud.
paras.en: [[10:1|My soul is weary of my life|Tædet animam meam vitæ meæ]], that is: the soul that I am, or I who am a soul, am weary of living in these pains, because of their bitterness, and from desire of glory, from which nothing holds me back but the guilt of fault [*reatus culpæ*: the liability to punishment that remains from sin], that is, the obligation to torments on account of sins, because I have not yet undergone the pains that are due. [[10:1|I will let go my speech against myself|Dimittam adversum me eloquium meum]], that is, I will say or think, in the manner of the intellect, the things that sadden me, afflict me and show me guilty; I will also accuse and bewail myself. For those who are in purgatory repent of having sinned, since they abide in charity without being able to turn from it. [[10:1|I will speak in the bitterness of my soul|Loquar in amaritudine animæ meæ]], that is, as this affliction of mine moves me to speak with an intellectual speech [that is, a speech of the mind, not of the tongue]. For pain spurs one to speak, because by evaporating or breaking out in words it is in some way lessened; and the soul perceives the one thing the less, the more it attends to the other.

paras.t: Dicam Deo: Noli me condemnare. Hoc videtur animabus in purgatorio non convenire, quum sint certæ de gloria; quædam tamen (ut dicitur) sunt incertæ de hoc, quia sic pœnis addictæ sunt, ut nesciant an finaliter sint salvandæ an condemnandæ: quæ utique optant non condemnari, idque precantur secundum quod oratio est interpres desiderii. Proprie tamen orare eis non competit, prout oratio est meritoria seu impetrativa, quum non sint in statu merendi, sed viam finiverunt, nec valent juvare se ipsas. Verum quod ait, Noli me condemnare, potest sic improprie explanari, id est, noli me in pœnis his tam dire punire, quasi essem damnata. Indica mihi, cur me ita judices, id est, tam graviter punias. Dicunt aliqui, quod animæ purgatorio deputatæ, interdum ex magnitudine suæ pœnæ arbitrantur se ultra condignum et sine admixtione misericordiæ cruciari, quoniam plus attendunt acerbitatem pœnæ quam sentiunt, quam peccati sui enormitatem seu quantitatem. Ideo petunt sibi indicari divinitus, pro qua culpa sic torqueantur. Sed non videtur, quod æstiment Deum esse injustum, vel ejus judicium esse perversum; quod sequeretur, si putarent eum punire ultra condignum. Verumtamen esse potest, quod magnitudo pœnæ impediat aliqualiter in eis rationis judicium, et scientiæ usum diligentemque considerationem, ita ut eis appareat, quod Deus nimis seu plurimum rigorose puniat eas, sic quod admirative dicant verba inducta, quærendo sibi causam apertius insinuari. Tanquam dicant: Mirum videtur, o Domine, quod tam horribiliter nos affligis.
paras.en: [[10:2|I will say to God: Do not condemn me|Dicam Deo: Noli me condemnare]]. This seems not to fit the souls in purgatory, since they are certain of glory; yet some of them (as is said) are uncertain of it, because they are so given over to pains that they do not know whether they are finally to be saved or condemned: these at any rate wish not to be condemned, and pray for this, in the sense in which prayer is the interpreter of desire. Yet to pray does not properly belong to them, taking prayer as meritorious or impetratory [that is, as earning merit or obtaining what it asks], since they are not in the state of meriting, but have finished the way, and cannot help themselves. But what it says, [[10:2|Do not condemn me|Noli me condemnare]], can be explained, improperly, thus: that is, do not punish me so dreadfully in these pains, as if I were damned. [[10:2|tell me why thou judgest me so|Indica mihi, cur me ita judices]], that is, punish me so heavily. Some say that the souls assigned to purgatory sometimes, from the greatness of their pain, think that they are being tormented beyond their due and without any mixture of mercy, because they attend more to the bitterness of the pain they feel than to the enormity or quantity of their sin. Therefore they ask that it be shown them by God for what fault they are so tormented. But it does not seem that they think God unjust, or his judgment perverse; which would follow if they thought he punished beyond what is due. Yet it may be that the greatness of the pain somewhat hinders in them the judgment of reason, and the use of knowledge and careful consideration, so that it appears to them that God punishes them too much, or most rigorously, so that they speak the words quoted in wonder, asking that the cause be made more plainly known to them. As if they said: It seems a marvel, O Lord, that thou afflictest us so horribly.

paras.t: Numquid bonum tibi videtur, si calumnieris et opprimas me opus manuum tuarum, etc.? Quidam exponunt hoc per modum quæstionis et affirmationis, quasi anima in purgatorio sita, ad tantum per pœnas devolvatur errorem, ut putet Deum sui esse calumniatorem et oppressorem: quod nequaquam putandum est. Ideo sciscitatur hæc atque sequentia, ita ut neget sic esse, sicut expositum est. Itaque dicit hæc ad provocandum misericordiam Dei, juxta expositionem inductam. Denique subditur, et consilium impiorum adjuves? id est, numquid tibi bonum videtur, ut dæmonum coopereris consilio, qui me ad hoc tentaverunt, quatenus me ad pœnas istas perducerent, imo et ad infernales, si potuissent et permisisses? Verumtamen, istud aliquo modo affirmative potest exponi. In hoc enim Deus consentit illis tortoribus, ut peccatrix anima puniatur; sed non eo modo consentit id fieri, quo dæmones illud exoptant. Ipsi enim crudeliter perversoque fine hoc exsequuntur seu cupiunt, quod Deus juste et fine laudabili præcipit fieri.
paras.en: [[10:3|Doth it seem good to thee|Numquid bonum tibi videtur]], [[10:3|that thou shouldst calumniate me, and oppress me, the work of thy own hands|si calumnieris et opprimas me opus manuum tuarum]], etc.? Some expound this by way of question and affirmation, as though the soul placed in purgatory were brought by its pains into such error as to think God its calumniator and oppressor: which is by no means to be thought. Therefore it asks this and what follows so as to deny that it is so, as has been expounded. And so it says these things to move God's mercy, according to the exposition given. Then is added, [[10:3|and help the counsel of the wicked|et consilium impiorum adjuves]]? that is: Does it seem good to thee to cooperate with the counsel of the demons, who tempted me to this so as to bring me to these pains, and indeed to those of hell, had they been able and hadst thou permitted? Yet this can in some way be expounded as an affirmation. For in this God consents with those torturers, that the sinful soul be punished; but he does not consent that it be done in the way the demons desire. For they carry out or desire cruelly, and for a perverse end, what God commands to be done justly and for a praiseworthy end.

paras.t: Numquid oculi carnei tibi sunt? Istud usque ad id, quum sit nemo qui de manu tua possit eruere, interrogat ac denegat anima, ut fateatur Deum perfectæ infallibilisque scientiæ, nec posse in judicando errare, secundum intellectum expositum.
paras.en: [[10:4|Hast thou eyes of flesh|Numquid oculi carnei tibi sunt]]? All this, as far as [[10:7|whereas there is no man that can deliver out of thy hand?|quum sit nemo qui de manu tua possit eruere]] the soul asks and denies, so as to confess that God is of perfect and infallible knowledge, and cannot err in judging, according to the sense already expounded.

paras.t: Insuper ait: Manus tuæ, Domine, fecerunt me, et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu. Jam litteralis et mystica expositio lectionis istius præhabita est. Quomodo autem animæ in purgatoriis pœnis detentæ ista conveniant, ex præinductis expositionibus satis reor patere. Sed percurrendo, modicum addam. Itaque anima seu spiritus rationalis, quum sit simplex et incorporeus, non est aliquod totum integrale, nec corporalem habet circuitum; sed est quid totum essentiale in suo ordine, et totum potestativum quantum ad naturales vires, seu potentias quas habet in se permanentes: sicque se totum dicit creatum a Deo, et in circuitu spirituali formatum, quia ejus essentia est finita, atque a Deo determinata seu limitata, qui in numero, pondere et mensura constituit universa.
