Et sic repente præcipitas me? id est, per mortem corporalem a terra in locum purgatorii projicis, et igni alligas ad tempus quoddam, variisque vilitatibus pœnalibus subjicis, quem ad tuam imaginem condidisti. Tanquam dicat: Hoc miserabile est, mirabile, miserationeque dignum.
paras.en: Further it says: [[10:8|Thy hands|Manus tuæ]], O Lord, [[10:8|have made me, and fashioned me wholly round about|fecerunt me, et plasmaverunt me totum in circuitu]]. The literal and mystical exposition of this lesson [of the Office of the Dead, which is Job 10:8–12] has been given already. How these things fit the souls held in the pains of purgatory is, I think, plain enough from the expositions given before. But running through it, I will add a little. The soul, then, or rational spirit, since it is simple and incorporeal, is not an integral whole, nor has it a bodily circuit; but it is an essential whole in its own order, and a potestative whole as to its natural strengths, or the powers it has abiding in it [scholastic terms: an *integral* whole is made of parts lying outside one another, as a body; an *essential* whole is one in its essence; a *potestative* whole contains several powers]: and so it says that it was created whole by God, and formed in a spiritual circuit, because its essence is finite, and determined or limited by God, who has set up all things in number, weight and measure[[Wis 11:21||]]. [[10:8|and dost thou thus cast me down headlong on a sudden?|Et sic repente præcipitas me]] that is, by bodily death thou castest me from the earth into the place of purgatory, and bindest to fire for a time [the Latin here is damaged; read as *ad tempus quoddam*], and subjectest to various penal indignities, me whom thou didst make to thy own image. As if it said: This is pitiable, and wondrous, and worthy of compassion.

paras.t: Memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me. Quomodo totum residuum hujus lectionis de anima exponitur, quantum ad dona gratiæ sibi collata, jam patuit: in qua expositione B. Gregorium pro magna parte secutus sum. Potest quoque totum exponi in persona spiritus seu animæ rationalis in purgatorio constitutæ, quantum ad dona naturæ sibi collata. Itaque anima talis ad provocandum Dei clementiam, propriam allegat declivitatem et fragilitatem, ex qua inerat sibi magna proclivitas ad peccandum, magna demum infirmitas ad resistendum: ex quibus alleviatur culpa et excusatur, etsi non in toto, tamen a tanto. Memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me, id est similem vili materiæ. Ut enim philosophi dicunt, præsertim Averroes, sicut se habet materia prima in ordine entium, ita intellectus animæ rationalis in ordine intellectualium substantiarum. Unde quemadmodum materia prima secundum se est infimum entium et pura potentia, atque principium transmutationis et motus, sic anima rationalis in ordine intellectualium substantiarum est infima, et in principio sui est sicut tabula rasa, in qua nihil est scriptum. Estque naturaliter multum instabilis, vaga et labilis. Propter quod Deus piissimus magnam cum ea patientiam habet in vita ista, atque in purgatorio misericorditer agit cum ea, tam per se ipsum quam per comprehensores ac viatores multipliciter ei subveniens.
paras.en: [[10:9|Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay|Memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me]]. How the whole remainder of this lesson is expounded of the soul, as to the gifts of grace bestowed on it, has already been shown: in which exposition I have for the most part followed blessed Gregory. The whole can also be expounded in the person of a spirit, or rational soul, placed in purgatory, as to the gifts of nature bestowed on it. So such a soul, to move God's clemency, pleads its own downward bent and frailty, from which it had in it a great proneness to sin, and a great weakness in resisting: by which the fault is lightened and excused, if not wholly, yet in part. [[10:9|Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay|Memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me]], that is, like a base matter. For as the philosophers say, especially Averroes, as prime matter stands in the order of beings, so stands the intellect of the rational soul in the order of intellectual substances. Hence, as prime matter in itself is the lowest of beings and pure potency, and the principle of change and motion, so the rational soul is the lowest in the order of intellectual substances, and at its beginning is like a blank tablet on which nothing is written. And it is by nature very unstable, wandering and prone to slip. For which reason the most loving God has great patience with it in this life, and in purgatory deals mercifully with it, coming to its help in many ways both by himself and through comprehensors and wayfarers [that is, through the blessed in heaven and the faithful still on earth].

paras.t: Et in pulverem reduces me, id est, per pœnas has ad nihilum rediges, non ut essentialiter non sim, sed ut pœnis oppressa pro nihilo me reputem, meque profunde humiliem ac tibi prosternam in locis istis terrenis pœnalibus. Juxta quem modum pro parte ait Psalmista: Humiliata est in pulvere anima mea. Et rursus: Ego ad nihilum redactus sum, et nescivi. Præterea, quasi in pulverem reducitur anima talis, quando post consolationem et altam considerationem, quas habet interdum ex visitatione angelica aut Sanctorum, ut pie putatur, mox visitatione tali cessante, ad cogitationes affectionesque varias quasi ad pulverem rapitur: non tamen ab ultimo fine unquam suum avertit affectum, sed cogitando prorsus instabilis est, et varia cupit remedia.
paras.en: [[10:9|and thou wilt bring me into dust|Et in pulverem reduces me]], that is, through these pains thou wilt bring me to nothing: not that I should cease to be in my essence, but that, weighed down by pains, I should count myself as nothing, and humble myself deeply and lie prostrate before thee in these earthly places of pain. In which manner, in part, the Psalmist says: [[Ps 43:25|our soul is humbled down to the dust|Humiliata est in pulvere anima mea]] [Denis has *anima mea*, 'my soul'; the margin's numerals are misread, the words are Ps 43:25]. And again: [[Ps 72:22|I am brought to nothing, and I knew not|Ego ad nihilum redactus sum, et nescivi]]. Moreover, such a soul is brought as it were into dust when, after the consolation and lofty contemplation that it sometimes has from a visit of the angels or of the Saints (as is piously believed), as soon as such a visit ceases it is swept away, as if into dust, to various thoughts and affections: yet it never turns its affection away from its last end, but in its thinking it is wholly unstable, and longs for various remedies.

paras.t: Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me? id est, ad esse novum ac tenerum quasique lacteum, eduxisti de utero simul cum corpore, cui me per creationem infudisti: in quo sub infantilibus annis tam imperfectæ exsistentiæ fui, quod ob corporis indispositionem, fluxibilitatem, mollitiem, ratione uti non potui; et sicut caseum me coagulasti, tempore pueritiæ, dando mihi tunc aliqualem rationis et virtutum corroborationem, quum cœpi inter bonum et malum, inter verum et falsum discernere, sicque instar casei a pristina instabilitate ad cohærentiam boni ac veri attingere.
paras.en: [[10:10|Hast thou not milked me as milk|Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me]]? that is: thou didst bring me forth from the womb to a new and tender being, as it were milky, together with the body into which thou didst pour me by creation: in which, in the years of infancy, I was of so imperfect an existence that, because of the body's unfitness, fluidity and softness, I could not use reason; [[10:10|and curdled me like cheese|et sicut caseum me coagulasti]], in the time of boyhood, giving me then some strengthening of reason and of the virtues, when I began to discern between good and evil, between true and false, and so, like cheese, to come from my former unsteadiness to a firm hold on the good and the true.

paras.t: Pelle et carnibus vestisti me, ita quod fui forma, motor, ac habitator infectæ ac fragilis carnis, ex qua ad multa illicita inclinabar, a spiritualibus sæpius impediebar; ossibus et nervis compegisti me. Ossa ista, intelligi possunt fortiores animæ vires, in quibus superbenedictæ Trinitatis imago relucet, videlicet intellectus, voluntas, memoria; nervi autem, vires organicæ, quæ manent in anima separata tanquam in radice. Istis compingitur anima, id est conjungitur, in quantum est totum potestativum, continens in se vires has, tanquam quasdam partes.
paras.en: [[10:11|Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh|Pelle et carnibus vestisti me]], so that I was the form, the mover and the dweller of an infected and frail flesh, by which I was inclined to many unlawful things, and often hindered from spiritual ones; [[10:11|thou hast put me together with bones and sinews|ossibus et nervis compegisti me]]. These bones can be understood as the stronger powers of the soul, in which the image of the supremely blessed Trinity shines, namely intellect, will and memory; and the sinews as the organic powers [that is, those that work through bodily organs, as the senses], which remain in the separated soul as in their root. By these the soul is put together, that is, joined, in so far as it is a potestative whole, containing these powers in itself as so many parts.

paras.t: Vitam intellectualem, non vegetativam aut sensitivam dumtaxat, et misericordiam tribuisti mihi, id est cetera quibus in naturali vita indigui, de quibus mihi in corpore misericorditer providisti; in purgatorio quoque hoc, quo affligor, mihi clementer multoties subvenisti. Et visitatio tua, id est adsistentia gratiosa, custodivit spiritum meum, id est superiorem animæ portionem, scilicet intellectum et voluntatem: præsertim in hora mortis, quando gravior periculosiorque tentatio solet accidere; quando et anima propriis viribus minime valet resistere, etiam ob corporalem illum dolorem gravissimum, rationis judicium debilitantem non parum, nisi gratiæ adsit auxilium. Unde tunc amplius indiget divinitus adjuvari, ne tentationibus superetur, et in mortali culpa decedat, sed in gratia tunc persistat ac separetur. Hæc autem custodia summe necessaria est, et maxime fructuosa, quia in ea dispositione seu affectione, qua per mortem anima recedit a corpore, permanet in æternum. Hinc si in caritate et gratia separetur, manet inavertibiliter conversa ad Deum; si vero in mortali culpa quis moriatur, manet anima ejus inconvertibiliter a Deo aversa. Propter quod asserit Damascenus: Quod angelis est ruina, hoc hominibus est mors. Angeli namque æternaliter manent in eo affectu, in quo vel ceciderunt, vel Deo in principio adhæserunt. Quod in Ecclesiaste Salomon innuens: Si ceciderit (inquit) lignum ad austrum, aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit. Quotidie igitur Deum devotissime deprecemur, quatenus in illa hora visitatio ejus paterna atque piissima spiritum nostrum custodiat, ne succumbat tempore mortis.
paras.en: [[10:12|Thou hast granted me life|Vitam]] (intellectual life, not vegetative or sensitive only) [[10:12|and mercy|et misericordiam tribuisti mihi]], that is, the other things I needed in natural life, which thou didst mercifully provide for me in the body; in this purgatory too, in which I am afflicted, thou hast many times graciously come to my help. [[10:12|and thy visitation|Et visitatio tua]], that is, thy gracious assistance, [[10:12|hath preserved my spirit|custodivit spiritum meum]], that is, the higher portion of the soul, namely intellect and will: especially in the hour of death, when temptation is wont to come more heavily and more dangerously; when the soul too can hardly resist by its own strength, also because of that most grievous bodily pain which weakens the judgment of reason not a little, unless the help of grace be present. Hence it then needs all the more to be helped by God, lest it be overcome by temptations and depart in mortal sin, and so that it may then persevere in grace and be parted from the body in it. And this keeping is supremely necessary and most fruitful, because the soul remains for ever in the disposition or affection in which it leaves the body by death. Hence, if it is parted in charity and grace, it remains turned towards God without being able to turn away; but if anyone dies in mortal sin, his soul remains turned away from God without being able to be converted. For which reason Damascene says: What the fall is to the angels, death is to men. For the angels remain eternally in the affection in which they either fell or cleaved to God in the beginning. Which Solomon hints at in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:3|If the tree fall|Si ceciderit]] (he says) [[Eccles 11:3|to the south, or to the north, in what place soever it shall fall, there shall it be|lignum ad austrum, aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit]]. Let us therefore pray God most devoutly every day that in that hour his fatherly and most loving visitation may keep our spirit, lest it give way at the time of death.

paras.t: Quare de vulva eduxisti me? Qui utinam consumptus essem, ne oculus me videret. Lectio ista minus proprie, quam præcedentes, videtur de anima purgatorio adjudicata, posse exponi. Animæ enim quæ ibi sunt, quum sint in certa beatitudinis exspectatione, quam indicibiliter cupiunt, non optant non esse, nec eis competit de utero ferri ad tumulum, sicut mox subditur: Fuissem quasi non essem, de utero translatus ad tumulum. Sed et dies vitæ earum perpetui sunt, ut dicere eis non congruat, quæ post pauca sequuntur: Numquid non paucitas dierum meorum finietur brevi? Denique certæ sunt, quod ad infernum nunquam devenient, sicque eis non competit quod postremo adjicitur: Dimitte ergo me, ut plangam paululum dolorem meum antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam, etc. Verumtamen, auxiliante Spiritu Sancto, quantum ipse donaverit, exponenda sunt de hujuscemodi anima.
paras.en: [[10:18|Why didst thou bring me forth out of the womb?|Quare de vulva eduxisti me]] [[10:18|O that I had been consumed, that eye might not see me|Qui utinam consumptus essem, ne oculus me videret]]! This lesson seems less properly than the preceding ones to be capable of being expounded of a soul sentenced to purgatory. For the souls that are there, being in sure expectation of beatitude, which they desire unspeakably, do not wish not to be, nor does it befit them to be carried from the womb to the grave, as is added straight after: [[10:19|I should have been as if I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave|Fuissem quasi non essem, de utero translatus ad tumulum]]. And the days of their life are everlasting, so that it does not befit them to say what follows a little after: [[10:20|Shall not the fewness of my days be ended shortly?|Numquid non paucitas dierum meorum finietur brevi]] Lastly, they are certain that they will never come to hell, and so what is added at the end does not befit them: [[10:20|Suffer me, therefore, that I may lament my sorrow a little|Dimitte ergo me, ut plangam paululum dolorem meum]] [[10:21|Before I go and return no more, to a land that is dark|antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam]], etc. Nevertheless, with the help of the Holy Ghost, and as far as he shall grant, they are to be expounded of such a soul.

paras.t: Itaque, spiritus rationalis in purgatorio constitutus, querula voce ad insinuandum pœnarum suarum acerbitatem, loquitur Creatori: Quare de vulva eduxisti me? Quod ait, non quasi anima sit educta de potentia materiæ, ut dixit Alexander peripateticus, vel quasi sit ex traduce, ut finxit Apollinaris hæreticus; sed quoniam corpori intra maternum uterum clauso per creationem infunditur, et simul cum eo inde educitur. Itaque ait: Quare de vulva eduxisti me? tanquam dicat: Melius mihi esset non esse, quam in pœnis his æternaliter permanere. An vero animæ in gravioribus purgatorii pœnis detentæ, aliquando tormentorum suorum vehementia sic opprimantur, vincantur, obtenebrentur, ut quantum in ipsis est, potius velint prorsus non esse, æternamque beatitudinem nunquam acquirere, quam taliter diu seu absque scitu finis sui supplicii cruciari, affirmare non audeo. Idcirco sequentia textus verba ad hunc sensum non applicabo.
paras.en: So the rational spirit placed in purgatory, in a plaintive voice, to make known the bitterness of its pains, says to its Creator: [[10:18|Why didst thou bring me forth out of the womb?|Quare de vulva eduxisti me]] It says this not as though the soul were drawn out of the potency of matter, as Alexander the Peripatetic said, or as though it came by traduction [that is, handed on from the parents' soul, as a cutting is taken from a plant], as the heretic Apollinaris imagined; but because it is poured by creation into the body enclosed within the mother's womb, and is brought forth from there together with it. So it says: [[10:18|Why didst thou bring me forth out of the womb?|Quare de vulva eduxisti me]] as if it said: It would be better for me not to be than to remain for ever in these pains. But whether the souls held in the heavier pains of purgatory are sometimes so oppressed, overcome and darkened by the vehemence of their torments that, as far as in them lies, they would rather not be at all, and never gain eternal beatitude, than be tormented so long, or without knowing the end of their punishment, I do not dare affirm. Therefore I shall not apply the following words of the text in this sense.

paras.t: Qui utinam consumptus essem: non amittendo esse et vivere naturale, aut vitam caritatis et gratiæ, in qua sum; sed amittendo quod per culpam effectus sum, ut scilicet consumatur et pereat in me id, quo a gloria differor: quod est reatus seu obligatio ad pœnam. Sic namque dicitur aliquis abnegare, relinquere, mortificare se ipsum, non exstinguendo in se esse naturæ, sed malum culpæ, quemadmodum etiam Christus jubet manum, pedem, oculum scandalizantem, eruendum et projiciendum. Atque Apostolus: Mortificate (inquit) membra vestra quæ sunt super terram. Sic in Evangelio ait Salvator: Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, salvam faciet illam. Salomon quoque: Verte impios, et non erunt. Præterea, Apostolus sic consumptus: Vivo, ait, jam non ego, vivit vero in me Christus. Ne oculus me videret, id est, ne quis me in tantis suppliciis cerneret.
paras.en: [[10:18|O that I had been consumed|Qui utinam consumptus essem]]: not by losing my natural being and living, or the life of charity and grace in which I am; but by losing what I have become through fault, namely, that there be consumed and perish in me that by which I am kept back from glory: which is the guilt, or obligation to pain. For thus a man is said to deny, to leave, to mortify himself, not by extinguishing in himself the being of nature, but the evil of fault; as Christ too bids the hand, the foot, the eye that scandalizes be plucked out and cast away[[Mark 9:42||]][[Mark 9:44||]][[Mark 9:46||]]. And the Apostle: [[Col 3:5|Mortify|Mortificate]] (he says) [[Col 3:5|your members which are upon the earth|membra vestra quæ sunt super terram]]. So the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 9:24|he that shall lose his life for my sake shall save it|Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, salvam faciet illam]]. And Solomon: [[Prov 12:7|Turn the wicked, and they shall not be|Verte impios, et non erunt]]. Again, the Apostle, consumed in this way: [[Gal 2:20|And I live|Vivo]], he says, [[Gal 2:20|now not I: but Christ liveth in me|jam non ego, vivit vero in me Christus]]. [[10:18|that eye might not see me|Ne oculus me videret]], that is, that no one might see me in such great torments.

paras.t: Fuissem quasi non essem, id est, si malum culpæ seu debitum sustinendi purgatorii pœnas, fuisset ante mortem consumptum in me, ita quod a culpa et pœna absolutus fuissem ac liber; tunc utique fuissem in gloria statim post egressum a corpore; quasi non essem, id est, sic quod non essem in pœnis: ut Quasi, dicat veritatem, non similitudinem tantum; et quod sequitur, de utero translatus ad tumulum, non separatim, sed conjunctim legatur cum clausula præcedente, qua dicitur, Fuissem, ut sit sensus: Fuissem in gloria, sic quod non essem translatus de utero, id est de terra (secundum quod supra ait Job: Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ, et nudus revertar illuc: sicque Ecclesiasticus dicit: Grave jugum super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium), ad tumulum, id est ad subterraneum seu bassum ac tetrum purgatorii latibulum, quo abscondor, detineor et affligor. Sic quippe Salvator asserit divitem in inferno sepultum. Et in Ezechiele reproborum sepulcra in inferno posita referuntur, quum dicitur: Loquentur potentissimi robustorum de medio inferni. Ibi Assur et omnis multitudo ejus; in circuitu illius sepulcra ejus, cum his qui descenderunt in lacum.
paras.en: [[10:19|I should have been as if I had not been|Fuissem quasi non essem]], that is: if the evil of fault, or the debt of undergoing the pains of purgatory, had been consumed in me before death, so that I had been absolved and free from fault and pain, then surely I should have been in glory straight after going out of the body; [[10:19|as if I had not been|quasi non essem]], that is, so that I should not be in pains: so that *as if* expresses the truth, not a likeness only; and what follows, [[10:19|carried from the womb to the grave|de utero translatus ad tumulum]], is to be read not separately but together with the clause before it, in which is said, [[10:19|I should have been|Fuissem]], so that the sense is: I should have been in glory, so that I should not have been carried from the womb, that is, from the earth (as Job said above: [[Job 1:21|Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither|Nudus egressus sum de utero matris meæ, et nudus revertar illuc]]; and so Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 40:1|a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming out of their mother's womb, until the day of their burial into the mother of all|Grave jugum super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium]]), [[10:19|to the grave|ad tumulum]], that is, to the underground, or low and foul, hiding place of purgatory, where I am hidden, held and afflicted. For so the Saviour says that the rich man was buried in hell[[Luke 16:22||]]. And in Ezechiel the graves of the reprobate are spoken of as placed in hell, where it is said: [[Ezech 32:21|The most mighty among the strong ones shall speak to him from the midst of hell|Loquentur potentissimi robustorum de medio inferni]]. [[Ezech 32:22|Assur is there, and all his multitude: their graves are round about him|Ibi Assur et omnis multitudo ejus; in circuitu illius sepulcra ejus]], with them that went down into the pit[[Ezech 32:24||]] [these last words are joined from the end of Ezech 32:24 and 32:25].

paras.t: Numquid non paucitas dierum meorum finietur brevi? Hoc anima loquitur sciscitando ac desiderando, ut dies quibus in purgatorio erit, qui respectu æternitatis in patria breves sunt, celeriter finiantur, quatenus concupitam beatitudinem sortiatur. Dimitte ergo me, id est, relevamen aliquod mihi pœnæ hujus concede. Aliquoties enim animæ in purgatorio exsistentes, aliquam consolationem suscipiunt ex visione angelica, et per suffragia eis exhibita, seu alio modo. Ut plangam spirituali ploratu paululum dolorem meum, quem habeo, non solum ex pœna sensus qua crucior, sed et ex pœna damni qua a gloria dividor. Porro, ut tactum est, ex vehementia acerbitatis pœnarum purgatorii, animæ consistentes in eo, frequenter a libero usu rationis seu diligenti proprii status consideratione impediri creduntur: ex quo fit, ut ex immoderato dolore, planctum (ut patuit) impediente, se ipsas expedite ac ordinate nequeant deplorare, magnitudine tormentorum quasi absorptæ. Hinc cupiunt, ut pœnis quas patiuntur, clementer per intervallum aliquod relevatis, deflere propriam queant calamitatem. Unde ob defectum usus rationis in condemnatis, Salomon in Ecclesiaste hortatur: Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare; quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia, erunt apud inferos quo tu properas. Hujuscemodi tamen rationis defectus, longe minor est in purgatorio quam inferno. Siquidem in purgatorio positæ animæ, jugiter manent in caritate, et per consequens habent septem dona Spiritus Sancti, omnesque virtutes caritati connexas. Quicumque enim habet caritatem, habet et dona Spiritus Sancti, saltem secundum aliquem gradum, quemadmodum Thomas et Bonaventura ceterique doctores concorditer scribunt. Propterea, in purgatorio sitæ, per donum sapientiæ, in aliqualem divinorum considerationem, et per donum scientiæ, in proprii status attentionem possunt utcumque, pœnis earum moderatis, procedere.
paras.en: [[10:20|Shall not the fewness of my days be ended shortly?|Numquid non paucitas dierum meorum finietur brevi]] The soul says this asking and desiring that the days it will spend in purgatory, which are short compared with the eternity of the fatherland, may quickly be ended, so that it may obtain the beatitude it longs for. [[10:20|Suffer me, therefore|Dimitte ergo me]], that is, grant me some relief from this pain. For at times the souls that are in purgatory receive some consolation from a vision of angels, and through the suffrages offered for them, or in some other way. [[10:20|that I may lament|Ut plangam]] with a spiritual weeping [[10:20|my sorrow a little|paululum dolorem meum]], which I have not only from the pain of sense by which I am tormented, but also from the pain of loss by which I am parted from glory [*pœna sensus*, the pain that is felt, and *pœna damni*, the pain of being deprived of God]. Moreover, as was touched on, from the vehemence of the bitterness of the pains of purgatory, the souls that are in it are believed often to be hindered from the free use of reason, or from careful consideration of their own state: whence it comes that, through an immoderate pain that hinders lament (as was shown), they cannot bewail themselves readily and in order, being as it were swallowed up by the greatness of their torments. Hence they desire that, their pains being mercifully relieved for some interval, they may be able to bewail their own calamity. So, because of the lack of the use of reason in the condemned, Solomon exhorts in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 9:10|Whatsoever thy hand is able to do, do it earnestly: for neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening|Quodcumque potest manus tua, instanter operare; quia nec opus, nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia, erunt apud inferos quo tu properas]]. Yet such a lack of reason is far less in purgatory than in hell. For the souls placed in purgatory abide continually in charity, and consequently have the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, and all the virtues connected with charity. For whoever has charity has also the gifts of the Holy Ghost, at least in some degree, as Thomas and Bonaventure and the other doctors write with one accord. Therefore the souls in purgatory can, in some fashion, when their pains are moderated, go on by the gift of wisdom to some consideration of divine things, and by the gift of knowledge to attention to their own state.

paras.t: Antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam, etc. Hoc anima in purgatorio collocata precatur, non quod post fletum præfatum sit unquam in infernum lapsura, sed quoniam certum est, quod post hujusmodi planctum nunquam in tartarum ruet: sicut a Matthæo narratur, quod Joseph non cognovit beatissimam Christiferamque Mariam, donec peperit Filium suum primogenitum. In Psalmo quoque Pater loquitur Christo: Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum.
paras.en: [[10:21|Before I go and return no more, to a land that is dark|Antequam vadam, et non revertar, ad terram tenebrosam]], etc. The soul placed in purgatory prays this, not because after the weeping just spoken of it will ever fall into hell, but because it is certain that after such lament it will never fall into Tartarus: just as Matthew relates that Joseph knew not the most blessed Mary, the bearer of Christ, [[Matt 1:25|till she brought forth her first born son|donec peperit Filium suum primogenitum]]. In the Psalm too the Father says to Christ: [[Ps 109:1|Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool|Sede a dextris meis, donec ponam inimicos tuos scabellum pedum tuorum]] [as *till* and *until* in these places do not mean that what is said will change afterwards, so *before I go* does not mean that the soul will go].

paras.t: Postremo, verba hæc quibus infernalis locus describitur, diligentissime sunt pensanda ac intime formidanda. Itaque oculis mentis proponamus teterrima illa tartari loca, horridum chaos inferni, profundissimas foveas gehennales; desperationis illius ineffabilem amaritudinem perpendamus, sempiterna tormenta, inexstinguibilem, æstuantissimum ignem. Imaginemur quam intolerabile nobis esset, per unum diem in ardenti fornace jacere: quomodo ergo poterimus gehennale incendium æternaliter tolerare? Væ infelicissimis amatoribus sæculi hujus. Beati vero qui in hoc mundo lugent se ipsos. De his infernalibus pœnis scriptum est in Apocalypsi: Cruciabitur iniquus igne et sulfure, et fumus tormentorum ejus ascendet in sæcula sæculorum. Et, ut loquitur Isaias, ignis damnatorum non exstinguetur, et vermis eorum non morietur. Ibi, ut ait Salvator, erit fletus et stridor dentium. Taliter ergo vivamus, ac si per diem jam in inferno adfuissemus, pœnasque illas experti essemus: imo sic eas frequenter imaginemur, quasi eas præsentialiter intueremur.
paras.en: Lastly, these words with which the place of hell is described are to be weighed most carefully and dreaded inwardly. Let us then set before the eyes of the mind those most foul places of Tartarus, the horrid chaos of hell, the deepest pits of Gehenna; let us ponder the unspeakable bitterness of that despair, the everlasting torments, the unquenchable, most scorching fire. Let us imagine how unbearable it would be for us to lie for one day in a burning furnace: how then shall we be able to bear the fire of Gehenna for ever? Woe to the most unhappy lovers of this world. But [[Matt 5:5|Blessed|Beati]] are they who in this world [[Matt 5:5|mourn|lugent]] for themselves [the margin note is illegible; the words are Matt 5:5]. Of these pains of hell it is written in the Apocalypse: The wicked man [[Apoc 14:10|shall be tormented with fire and brimstone|Cruciabitur iniquus igne et sulfure]], [[Apoc 14:11|And the smoke of their torments, shall ascend up for ever and ever|et fumus tormentorum ejus ascendet in sæcula sæculorum]]. And, as Isaias says, the fire of the damned [[Is 66:24|shall not be quenched|non exstinguetur]], and [[Is 66:24|their worm shall not die|vermis eorum non morietur]]. [[Matt 8:12|There|Ibi]], as the Saviour says, [[Matt 8:12|shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth|erit fletus et stridor dentium]][[Matt 22:13||]][[Matt 25:30||]] [the margin's numerals are partly unreadable; the words stand in Matt 8:12, 13:42, 22:13, 24:51 and 25:30]. Let us therefore live as if we had already been in hell for a day and had felt those pains: indeed let us often picture them to ourselves as if we saw them present before us.

11.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli undecimi: Respondens autem Sophar Naamathites, dixit.
11.title_en: Literal explanation of the eleventh chapter: Then Sophar the Naamathite answered, and said

paras.t: Forti pusillo et victorioso athletæ, contra quem successive plures congrediuntur, eo quod priores dejecerit, sanctus Job comparatur. Unde nunc quum duos contra disputando pugnasset, tertius contra eum procedit, atque ab increpatione et contumelia exorditur. Respondens autem Sophar Naamathites, dixit: Numquid qui multa loquitur, non audiet? id est, decet ut multiloquus verbis suis superfluis finem imponens, curet audire et informari. Aut vir verbosus justificabitur? id est, non decet loquacem reputari justum; imo nec justus, nec sapiens est, quum scriptum sit: Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio. Et iterum Salomon ait: In multiloquio non deerit peccatum. Itemque: Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum. Denique his verbis quasi in communi prolatis, Sophar notat et pungit beatum Job, innuens quod in disputatione hac multiloquus fuerit et verbosus.
paras.en: Holy Job is compared to a brave athlete, small but victorious, against whom several come forward to fight one after another, because he has thrown the ones before. So now, since he had fought in disputation against two, a third comes forward against him, and begins with rebuke and insult. [[11:1|Then Sophar the Naamathite answered, and said|Respondens autem Sophar Naamathites, dixit]]: [[11:2|Shall not he that speaketh much, hear also?|Numquid qui multa loquitur, non audiet?]] that is, it is fitting that a man of many words should put an end to his superfluous words and take care to listen and be instructed. [[11:2|or shall a man full of talk be justified?|Aut vir verbosus justificabitur?]] that is, it is not fitting that a talkative man should be reputed just; nay, he is neither just nor wise, since it is written: [[Prov 29:20|Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment|Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio]]. And again Solomon says: [[Prov 10:19|In the multitude of words there shall not want sin|In multiloquio non deerit peccatum]]. And again: [[Prov 29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind: a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum]]. Lastly, by these words, uttered as if in general, Sophar marks and stings blessed Job, hinting that in this disputation he had been a man of many words and full of talk.

paras.t: Tibi soli tacebunt homines? quasi dicat: Non es tantæ auctoritatis, ut tibi nullus contradicat, aut erroribus tuis resistat. Et quum ceteros irriseris, id est, cum derisu seu aspernatione redargueris, quasi virtuosior ac sapientior eis (disputationes autem rhetoricæ, cujusmodi istæ sunt, cum irrisione adversarii fiunt, secundum Albertum), a nullo confutaberis? tanquam dicat: Nequaquam hoc decet, quum non sis tantæ sapientiæ et virtutis, quin possis confundi, reprobari et vinci: et ego te confutabo. Sophar autem duos amicos et socios suos reputavit derisos a Job, quoniam dixit ante: Considerate semitas Theman, itinera Saba, et exspectate paulisper. Confusi sunt, quia speravi. Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis, quum e vobis nullus sit qui possit arguere me? Ad increpandum tantum eloquia concinnatis, et in ventum verba profertis. Sed talia atque similia dixit non ex elatione aut cum culpabili derisione, sed ex caritate, zeloque veritatis, vel cum justa etiam ironia. Subinde equidem licet errantem ac pertinacem deridere, ut corrigatur, ne ceteri decipiantur, quum rationabiliter informari ac corrigi dedignatur.
paras.en: [[11:3|Shall men hold their peace to thee only?|Tibi soli tacebunt homines?]] as if to say: Thou art not of such authority that no one may contradict thee or resist thy errors. [[11:3|and when thou hast mocked others|Et quum ceteros irriseris]], that is, hast refuted them with derision or contempt, as though more virtuous and wiser than they (for rhetorical disputations, of which kind these are, are carried on with mockery of the opponent, according to Albert), [[11:3|shall no man confute thee?|a nullo confutaberis?]] as if to say: This is in no way fitting, since thou art not of such wisdom and virtue that thou canst not be confounded, refuted and overcome: and I will confute thee. Now Sophar considered that his two friends and companions had been mocked by Job, since he had said before: [[Job 6:19|Consider the paths of Thema, the ways of Saba, and wait a little while|Considerate semitas Theman, itinera Saba, et exspectate paulisper]]. [[Job 6:20|They are confounded, because I have hoped|Confusi sunt, quia speravi]]. [[Job 6:25|Why have you detracted the words of truth, whereas there is none of you that can reprove me?|Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis, quum e vobis nullus sit qui possit arguere me?]] [[Job 6:26|You dress up speeches only to rebuke, and you utter words to the wind|Ad increpandum tantum eloquia concinnatis, et in ventum verba profertis]]. But he said these and like things not out of pride or with blameworthy derision, but out of charity and zeal for the truth, or even with a just irony. For it is sometimes lawful to deride one who errs and is obstinate, so that he may be corrected and others not deceived, when he scorns to be reasonably instructed and corrected.

paras.t: Consequenter proponit, cur debeat confutari: Dixisti enim: Purus est sermo meus, id est a falsitate et iniquitate alienus et mundus. Quamvis Job formaliter hoc non dixit, æquivalenter tamen aliquid tale asseruit supra: Non invenietis, inquiens, in lingua mea iniquitatem, nec in faucibus meis stultitia personabit. Et mundus sum in conspectu tuo, id est immaculatus coram te, Deus. Hoc (secundum Gregorium) Sophar false imponit beato Job: imo Job dixit oppositum. Nam ait in superioribus: Peccavi, quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum? Et: Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me. Verumtamen aliqua protulit Job, ex quibus Sophar interpretabatur eum dixisse verbum textus inductum æquivalenter. Superius namque (sicut jam dictum est) dixit: Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis, quum e vobis nullus sit qui possit arguere me? Et alibi: Verebar, ait, omnia opera mea, sciens quod non parceres delinquenti. Sed videtur Job ita sensisse ut Sophar sibi imponit. Nam infra affirmat: Si in manibus meis adhæsit macula: et capitur ibi si pro non. Et denuo: Neque reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea. Et respondendum, quod Job non se dixit venialibus culpis prorsus immunem, imo in illis se fassus est esse culpabilem; sed a talibus se excusat peccatis, qualia sibi amici sui imposuerunt, putantes eum tam graviter excessisse, quod tantam meruerit adversitatem et plagam.
paras.en: Next he sets out why Job ought to be confuted: [[11:4|For thou hast said: My word is pure|Dixisti enim: Purus est sermo meus]], that is, free and clean of falsehood and iniquity. Although Job did not say this in so many words, he asserted something equivalent above, saying: [[Job 6:30|And you shall not find|Non invenietis]], he says, [[Job 6:30|iniquity in my tongue, neither shall folly sound in my mouth|in lingua mea iniquitatem, nec in faucibus meis stultitia personabit]]. [[11:4|and I am clean in thy sight|Et mundus sum in conspectu tuo]], that is, spotless before thee, O God. This (according to Gregory) Sophar falsely imputes to blessed Job: nay, Job said the opposite. For he says above: [[Job 7:20|I have sinned: what shall I do to thee, O keeper of men?|Peccavi, quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum?]] And: [[Job 9:20|If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me|Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me]]. Nevertheless Job uttered some things from which Sophar took him to have said the equivalent of the words given in the text. For above (as has just been said) he said: [[Job 6:25|Why have you detracted the words of truth, whereas there is none of you that can reprove me?|Quare detraxistis sermonibus veritatis, quum e vobis nullus sit qui possit arguere me?]] And elsewhere: [[Job 9:28|I feared|Verebar]], he says, [[Job 9:28|all my works, knowing that thou didst not spare the offender|omnia opera mea, sciens quod non parceres delinquenti]]. But Job seems to have meant what Sophar imputes to him. For further on he affirms: [[Job 31:7|if a spot hath cleaved to my hands|Si in manibus meis adhæsit macula]]: and *if* is taken there for *not* [that is, it is a form of oath: “if a spot hath cleaved” means that none has]. And again: [[Job 27:6|my heart doth not reprehend me in all my life|Neque reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea]]. And it is to be answered that Job did not say he was wholly free of venial faults; nay, he confessed himself guilty of them; but he excuses himself of such sins as his friends imputed to him, thinking that he had transgressed so grievously that he had deserved so great an adversity and plague.

paras.t: Deinceps Sophar ostendit se ista loqui non ex rancore, sed amore cum desiderio correctionis ipsius Job, ex zelo quoque divini honoris. Atque utinam Deus loqueretur tecum, id est, te intus instrueret: juxta illud, Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus. Et rursus: Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum. Et aperiret labia sua tibi, id est, per se ipsum tibi aperte et clare panderet veritatem: sicut in prima sua epistola scribit Joannes, Unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus. Apostolus quoque ad Timotheum, Dabit tibi Dominus de omnibus intellectum. Labia autem Deo metaphorice adscribuntur, sicut lingua et os: quæ in Deo spiritualiter sunt sumenda, et indivise sive identice, suntque intellectus divinus, seu sapientia ejus. Vel, labia Dei sunt opera ejus, in quibus divina relucet perfectio, sicque per ea revelantur divina hominibus.
paras.en: Then Sophar shows that he says these things not out of rancour, but out of love, with a desire for the correction of Job himself, and also out of zeal for God’s honour. [[11:5|And I wish that God would speak with thee|Atque utinam Deus loqueretur tecum]], that is, would instruct thee inwardly: according to the words, [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]. And again: [[Ps 93:12|Blessed is the man whom thou shalt instruct, O Lord: and shalt teach him out of thy law|Beatus homo quem tu erudieris, Domine, et de lege tua docueris eum]]. [[11:5|and would open his lips to thee|Et aperiret labia sua tibi]], that is, would by himself lay open the truth to thee openly and clearly: as John writes in his first epistle, [[1 John 2:27|his unction teacheth you of all things|Unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus]]. And the Apostle to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:7|the Lord will give thee in all things understanding|Dabit tibi Dominus de omnibus intellectum]]. Now lips are ascribed to God metaphorically, as are tongue and mouth: these are to be taken spiritually in God, and as undivided or identical [that is, not distinct parts in him but one and the same thing], and they are the divine intellect, or his wisdom. Or, the lips of God are his works, in which the divine perfection shines out, and so through them divine things are revealed to men.

paras.t: Ut ostenderet tibi secreta sapientiæ suæ, id est veritates seu notitias sapientiales, quæ naturali ratione investigari et sciri non queunt ab homine. Invisibilia etenim Dei naturaliter cognoscere non valemus nisi per creaturas: quæ quum in infinitum deficiant ab excellentia Creatoris, certum quod plurima nobis incognita manent, quæ in Dei sapientia continentur, et circa Deum consideranda occurrunt: et ita dicuntur secreta sapientiæ Dei, quæ quibusdam ad hoc desuper electis supernaturaliter revelantur. Unde et David Deo humiliter, gratoque animo confitetur: Incerta et occulta sapientiæ tuæ manifestasti mihi. Amos quoque ait: Non faciet Dominus verbum, nisi revelaverit secretum suum ad servos suos Prophetas.
paras.en: [[11:6|That he might shew thee the secrets of wisdom|Ut ostenderet tibi secreta sapientiæ suæ]], his own, that is, truths or wise knowledge which cannot be searched out and known by man through natural reason. For we cannot know the invisible things of God naturally except through creatures[[Rom 1:20||]]: and since these fall infinitely short of the Creator’s excellence, it is certain that very many things remain unknown to us which are contained in God’s wisdom and present themselves to be considered concerning God: and so they are called the secrets of God’s wisdom, which are revealed supernaturally from above to some chosen for this. Hence David too confesses to God with a humble and grateful mind: [[Ps 50:8|the uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me|Incerta et occulta sapientiæ tuæ manifestasti mihi]]. And Amos says: [[Amos 3:7|the Lord God doth nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets|Non faciet Dominus verbum, nisi revelaverit secretum suum ad servos suos Prophetas]].

paras.t: Et quod multiplex sit lex ejus. Lex Dei dupliciter consideratur. Primo exemplariter, prout in Deo accipitur ratio sapientialis, qua disponit, regit et regulat cuncta creata: et hæc lex quamvis sit prima, universalis et simplicissima, scilicet omnium comprehensiva et ordinativa, nihilo minus multiplex, distincta et propria appellatur, quoniam usque ad omnia etiam infima ac minima se extendit, universa ordinans et complectens. Unde quidquid inordinate fit et cum culpa quantumlibet parva, a divina lege sic sumpta recedit, dissentit, seu aliquo modo contrariatur, quamvis homo sæpius non attendat. Secundo accipitur lex Dei pro lege divinitus impressa et data, videlicet pro lege naturali et scripta seu evangelica: quæ et ipsa multiplex dicitur, quantum ad particularia præcepta sub ea contenta, et quoniam virtualiter continet multa. Omne quoque peccatum, quantumcumque parvum, prohibet vel dissuadet et punit. Hæc enim lex primo et maxime est de caritate Dei et proximi, in qua utique caritate omnes virtutes virtualiter ac radicaliter continentur. Quum itaque peccatum sit transgressio legis divinæ, non potest plene cognosci, nisi agnoscatur lex Dei: quam qui cognoscit, scit quam difficile et quam impossibile sit purum esse a culpa, quum omne peccatum quantumlibet modicum, sit recessus a lege Dei, quæ omnem inutilem cogitationem, inordinatam affectionem, otiosam locutionem, illicitam operationem, omnemque omissionem culpabilem reprehendit, [et] quum difficillimum sit in nullo horum deficere seu peccare. Quoniam ergo Job dixit sermonem suum purum et vitam innocentem, conclusit Sophar, quod proprietates legis divinæ non nosceret. Ideo optando disseruit: Utinam Deus loqueretur tecum, ut ostenderet tibi quod multiplex sit lex ejus. Tanquam dicat: Tunc, o Job, cautius loquereris, et non ita te coram Deo justificare præsumeres. Sicque verba Sophar sunt valde subtilia, profunda et vera, quoad hoc quod legem Dei dicit multiplicem; sed male hoc applicat ad Job. Hinc et per Osee Dominus ait: Scribam eis multiplices leges meas, quæ velut alienæ computatæ sunt.
paras.en: [[11:6|and that his law is manifold|Et quod multiplex sit lex ejus]] [the margin gives the reading *esset* for *sit*, as in the Vulgate]. The law of God is considered in two ways. First, as exemplar, inasmuch as there is understood in God the ordering of his wisdom by which he disposes, rules and regulates all created things: and this law, although it is first, universal and most simple, that is, comprehending and ordering all things, is nonetheless called manifold, distinct and particular, since it reaches to all things, even the lowest and least, ordering and embracing them all. Hence whatever is done inordinately and with fault, however small, departs from the divine law so taken, disagrees with it, or is in some way contrary to it, although man very often does not notice it. Secondly, the law of God is taken for the law impressed and given by God, namely the natural law and the written or gospel law: and this too is called manifold, as to the particular precepts contained under it, and because it virtually contains many things. It also forbids or dissuades and punishes every sin, however small. For this law is first and chiefly about the charity of God and of our neighbour, and in that charity all the virtues are virtually and radically contained. Since, then, sin is the transgression of the divine law, it cannot be fully known unless the law of God is known: and he who knows it knows how hard, and how impossible, it is to be pure of fault, since every sin, however slight, is a departure from the law of God, which reproves every useless thought, inordinate affection, idle word, unlawful deed and every blameworthy omission; and since it is most difficult not to fail or sin in any of these. Since, then, Job said that his word was pure and his life innocent, Sophar concluded that he did not know the properties of the divine law. Therefore he spoke in the form of a wish: [[11:5|I wish that God would speak with thee|Utinam Deus loqueretur tecum]], [[11:6|That he might shew thee|ut ostenderet tibi]] [[11:6|that his law is manifold|quod multiplex sit lex ejus]]. As if to say: Then, O Job, thou wouldst speak more warily, and wouldst not presume so to justify thyself before God. And so Sophar’s words are very subtle, deep and true, in that he calls the law of God manifold; but he applies this wrongly to Job. Hence the Lord also says through Osee: [[Osee 8:12|I shall write to him my manifold laws, which have been accounted as foreign|Scribam eis multiplices leges meas, quæ velut alienæ computatæ sunt]].

paras.t: Et intelligeres, id est, ex allocutione instructioneque Dei, et ex intelligentia multiplicis legis ejus cognosceres, quod multa minora supplicia pati exigaris a Deo, quam meretur iniquitas tua, id est, citra condignum a Deo plagatus es, et minora tibi induxit adversa quam meruisti. Et in hoc Sophar apertissime contradicit verbis Job, quibus ante jam dixit: Utinam appenderentur peccata mea, quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera; quasi arena maris hæc gravior appareret. Frequenter quoque se dixit sine suis percussum demeritis.
paras.en: [[11:6|and thou mightest understand|Et intelligeres]], that is, wouldst know from God’s speaking to thee and instructing thee, and from understanding his manifold law, [[11:6|that he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth|quod multa minora supplicia pati exigaris a Deo, quam meretur iniquitas tua]] [Denis’s text reads “that thou art required by God to suffer far lesser punishments than thy iniquity deserveth”; the margin notes the reading *ab eo*, “by him”, for *a Deo*], that is, thou hast been struck by God less than thou deservest, and he has brought lesser adversities on thee than thou hast merited. And in this Sophar most openly contradicts the words of Job which he had already spoken: [[Job 6:2|O that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance|Utinam appenderentur peccata mea, quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera]]; [[Job 6:3|As the sand of the sea, this would appear heavier|quasi arena maris hæc gravior appareret]]. He also often said that he was stricken without his own deserving.

paras.t: Insuper, quod Job secreta sapientiæ Dei perscrutari nequiverit, Sophar deducit: Forsitan vestigia Dei comprehendes? Deridendo atque negando hoc dicit. Quemadmodum autem vestigia appellamus signa euntis per viam, ex quibus transitus transeuntis et species ejus noscuntur; sic vestigia Dei sunt quædam proprietates vel signa, seu naturæ in creaturis inventæ, ad Creatoris notitiam deducentes, juxta illud Sapientis: Vani sunt omnes homines, quibus non subest scientia Dei, et de eis quæ videntur bona, non potuerunt intelligere eum qui est. A magnitudine enim speciei et creaturæ poterit Creator cognoscibiliter videri. Propter quod ad Romanos ait Apostolus: Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, conspiciuntur, sempiternaque virtus ejus et divinitas. Nempe effectus suam causam ostendit, quum sit participata similitudo propriæ causæ, eo quod agens simile sibi producat. Prædicta autem Dei vestigia homo in vita hac comprehendere omnia plene non valet: imo nec de vilissimis rebus potest perfectam habere notitiam, ut cur arboris folium sit taliter figuratum, tantæ quantitatis, talis distinctionis, formationis, virtutis. Ideo scriptum est in Ecclesiaste: Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone. Et in Sapientiæ libro: Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore. Quæ autem in cælo sunt, quis investigabit? Sed et in Ecclesiastico habetur: Quis sufficiet enarrare opera Dei? Non est minuere, neque adjicere, nec est invenire magnalia Dei.
paras.en: Further, Sophar draws the conclusion that Job could not search out the secrets of God’s wisdom: [[11:7|Peradventure thou wilt comprehend the steps of God|Forsitan vestigia Dei comprehendes]]? He says this mocking and denying. Now just as we call footprints [*vestigia*, which the Douay-Rheims renders “steps”] the marks of one who goes along a road, from which the passing of the passer-by and his appearance are known, so the footprints of God are certain properties or marks, or natures, found in creatures, which lead to the knowledge of the Creator, according to the words of the Wise Man: [[Wis 13:1|all men are vain, in whom there is not the knowledge of God: and who by these good things that are seen, could not understand him that is|Vani sunt omnes homines, quibus non subest scientia Dei, et de eis quæ videntur bona, non potuerunt intelligere eum qui est]]. [[Wis 13:5|by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature, the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby|A magnitudine enim speciei et creaturæ poterit Creator cognoscibiliter videri]]. Wherefore the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. His eternal power also and divinity|Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, conspiciuntur, sempiternaque virtus ejus et divinitas]]. For an effect shows its cause, since it is a likeness shared from its own cause, because an agent produces what is like itself. But man in this life cannot fully comprehend all these footprints of God: nay, not even of the meanest things can he have perfect knowledge, as why the leaf of a tree is shaped as it is, of such a size, such a division, form and power. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:8|All things are hard: man cannot explain them by word|Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone]]. And in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 9:16|And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth: and with labour do we find the things that are before us. But the things that are in heaven, who shall search out?|Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore. Quæ autem in cælo sunt, quis investigabit?]] And in Ecclesiasticus too we have: [[Ecclus 18:2|Who is able to declare his works?|Quis sufficiet enarrare opera Dei?]] [[Ecclus 18:5|Nothing may be taken away, nor added, neither is it possible to find out the glorious works of God|Non est minuere, neque adjicere, nec est invenire magnalia Dei]].

paras.t: Et usque ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies, id est, ad plenam et comprehensivam Dei cognitionem perscrutando devenies. Quasi dicat: Impossibile hoc est, quia si etiam cuncta creata perfecte cognosceres, adhuc a plena Creatoris notitia infinite distares. Creaturæ enim in tantum ad Dei perducunt notitiam, quantum de divina perfectione in eis resplendet. Quum ergo a perfecta perfectionis divinæ immensæ repræsentatione deficiant infinite, certum quod ad plenam Dei contemplationem non ducant. Nec Deus in vita hac reperibilis aut cognoscibilis est, quoad quid est, seu comprehensive et per essentiam. Propter quod ait ad Moysen: Faciem meam videre non poteris: non enim videbit me homo, et vivet. Denique, illud perfecte cognoscitur, quod tantum cognoscitur, quantum est cognoscibile. Quum ergo Deus incomparabilis, superessentialis, immensus, sit purus et incircumscriptibilis actus, ipsaque veritas illimitata, et ipsum esse plenum, perfectum, interminatum, constat quod sit infinitæ cognoscibilitatis: ideo non nisi ab intellectu infinitæ capacitatis, perspicacitatis seu intellectivitatis, potest perfecte ac comprehensive cognosci secundum hunc modum.
paras.en: [[11:7|and wilt find out the Almighty perfectly?|Et usque ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies]] that is, wilt come by searching to a full and comprehensive knowledge of God. As if to say: This is impossible, because even if thou knewest all created things perfectly, thou wouldst still be infinitely distant from a full knowledge of the Creator. For creatures lead to the knowledge of God only so far as the divine perfection shines out in them. Since, then, they fall infinitely short of perfectly representing the immense divine perfection, it is certain that they do not lead to the full contemplation of God. Nor can God in this life be found or known as to what he is, that is, comprehensively and in his essence. Wherefore he says to Moses: [[Ex 33:20|Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me, and live|Faciem meam videre non poteris: non enim videbit me homo, et vivet]]. Lastly, that is known perfectly which is known as much as it is knowable. Since, then, God, incomparable, superessential, immense, is pure and uncircumscribable act, truth itself without limit, and being itself, full, perfect and without bounds, it is clear that he is infinitely knowable: and so he cannot be known perfectly and comprehensively in this way except by an intellect of infinite capacity, insight or power of understanding.

paras.t: Excelsior cælo est, et quid facies contra eum, quum cœperit te (nisi pœnitueris) condemnare? Profundior inferno, et unde cognosces? id est, ex qua creatura eum perfecte reperies? Longior terra mensura ejus, et latior mari. His verbis immensitatem majestatis divinæ et incomprehensibilitatem Dei metaphorice sub corporalium rerum nominibus innuit et fatetur. Idcirco ista intelligenda non sunt, quasi in Deo sit aliqua corporalis dimensio aut quantitativa extensio, vel materialis mensura, quum Deus supergloriosus et sanctus sit supersimplicissimus spiritus, mundissima mens, primum et simplicissimum esse. Sed per prædicta insinuatur, quod Deo conveniat incomparabilis celsitudo, omnipotens virtus, spiritualisque magnitudo sine limitante mensura. Propter quod ab homine perfecte cognosci non potest, sed cunctis infinite præeminet, nec mundi hujus circumscribitur aut finitur limitibus. Possent autem per cælum, infernum, terram et mare, contenta in eis intelligi. De infinitate vero Dei et intelligentia verborum istorum, multa superius dicta sunt.
paras.en: [[11:8|He is higher than heaven, and what wilt thou do|Excelsior cælo est, et quid facies]] against him, when he begins (unless thou repent) to condemn thee? [[11:8|he is deeper than hell, and how wilt thou know?|Profundior inferno, et unde cognosces?]] that is, from what creature wilt thou find him out perfectly? [[11:9|The measure of him is longer than the earth, and broader than the sea|Longior terra mensura ejus, et latior mari]]. In these words he hints at and confesses, metaphorically, under the names of bodily things, the immensity of the divine majesty and the incomprehensibility of God. Therefore they are not to be understood as if there were in God any bodily dimension, quantitative extension or material measure, since God, most glorious and holy, is a spirit supremely simple, a mind most pure, the first and simplest being. But by these words it is suggested that to God belong incomparable height, almighty power, and a spiritual greatness without limiting measure. Wherefore he cannot be known perfectly by man, but infinitely surpasses all things, and is not circumscribed or bounded by the limits of this world. But by heaven, hell, earth and sea, the things contained in them might be understood. Of the infinity of God, and of the understanding of these words, much has been said above[[Job 9:9||]][[Job 10:4||]] [the margin reads Job ix, 9 (the chapter numeral half unread) and x, 4 “et passim”: the places where Denis treated this before].

paras.t: Si subverterit omnia, id est, ad nihilum redegerit, sicut ex nihilo ea fecit: quod utique posset secundum absolutam suam potentiam, per solam suæ conservationis subtractionem. Omnia enim incessanter et maxime ab ipso dependent. Propter quod a Sapiente dicitur ei: Quomodo autem posset aliquid permanere, nisi tu voluisses? aut quod a te vocatum non esset, conservaretur? Unde primo Timæi Plato inducit summum Deum, quem patrem opificemque appellat, loquentem: O dii deorum, natura quidem corruptibiles, mea autem voluntate incorruptibiles! Aristoteles quoque: Ab hoc, inquit, ente dependent cælum et terra, et tota natura universi. Vel in unum coarctaverit, id est, ad confusum seu inordinatum chaos ea reduxerit: prout aliqui exponunt principium Genesis de mundi creatione, quod primo omnia corporalia fuerunt indeterminata, postea per intervalla dierum distincta; quis contradicet ei? id est, nullus efficaciter contradicere poterit, quia et contradictorem Deus in instanti annihilare posset. Hinc Sapiens dicit Deo: Quis tibi imputabit, si perierint nationes quas tu fecisti? Vel quis dicere ei potest: Cur ita facis? id est, nullus reprehendere potest opus ipsius. Quum enim Deus sit omnipotens, nullus ei valet resistere; quum sit essentialiter ipsa sapientia, errare non potest, nec emendari, increpari seu corrigi; quum sit substantialiter virtus et sanctitas, ipse est principium et mensura omnis virtutis et sanctitatis. Ideo eo ipso quo ipse quid facit, sequitur quod illud sit bene et irreprehensibiliter factum. Unde Isaias asserit: Væ qui contradicit factori suo.
paras.en: [[11:10|If he shall overturn all things|Si subverterit omnia]], that is, shall bring them to nothing, as he made them out of nothing: which he certainly could do by his absolute power, merely by withdrawing his preservation of them. For all things depend on him unceasingly and in the highest degree. Wherefore the Wise Man says to him: [[Wis 11:26|And how could any thing endure, if thou wouldst not? or be preserved, if not called by thee?|Quomodo autem posset aliquid permanere, nisi tu voluisses? aut quod a te vocatum non esset, conservaretur?]] Hence in the first part of the *Timaeus* Plato brings in the supreme God, whom he calls father and maker, saying: O gods of gods, corruptible indeed by nature, but incorruptible by my will! And Aristotle too: On this being, he says, depend heaven and earth and the whole nature of the universe. [[11:10|or shall press them together|Vel in unum coarctaverit]], that is, shall bring them back to a confused or disordered chaos: as some explain the beginning of Genesis on the creation of the world, that at first all bodily things were undetermined, and afterwards were distinguished through the intervals of the days; [[11:10|who shall contradict him?|quis contradicet ei?]] that is, no one will be able to contradict him effectively, since God could annihilate the gainsayer in an instant. Hence the Wise Man says to God: [[Wis 12:12|who shall accuse thee, if the nations perish, which thou hast made?|Quis tibi imputabit, si perierint nationes quas tu fecisti?]] Or: [[Job 9:12|or who can say: Why dost thou so?|Vel quis dicere ei potest: Cur ita facis?]] [Denis gives this as another wording, in the words of Job 9:12] that is, no one can find fault with his work. For since God is almighty, no one can resist him; since he is in his essence wisdom itself, he cannot err, nor be amended, rebuked or corrected; since he is in his substance virtue and holiness, he is the principle and measure of all virtue and holiness. Therefore, by the very fact that he does something, it follows that it is done well and blamelessly. Hence Isaias declares: [[Is 45:9|Woe to him that gainsayeth his maker|Væ qui contradicit factori suo]].

paras.t: Ipse enim novit hominum vanitatem, id est facta inania, per quæ a vero ac ultimo beatifico fine impediuntur. Vanitas quoque interdum accipitur, non pro culpa, sed pro quadam generali conditione, concomitante creaturam seu esse creatum, in quantum ex nihilo est. Sic enim ex se competit ei quidam defectus a vero, stabili et incommutabili esse, qui vanitas dicitur. Unde in Ecclesiaste habetur: Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes, vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas. Et Psalmista: Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens. Porro, de vanitate culpabili, quæ est inordinatus recessus ab æquitate et veritate, Dominus ait per Jeremiam: Quid invenerunt patres vestri in me iniquitatis, quia ambulaverunt post vanitatem, et vani facti sunt? Et videns iniquitatem, nonne considerat eam ad judicandum et ulciscendum? quasi dicat: Utique, quia sapientia et justitia Dei id exigunt. Ideo per Sophoniam testatur: Disperdam eos qui avertuntur de post tergum Domini, et qui non exquisierunt Dominum.
paras.en: [[11:11|For he knoweth the vanity of men|Ipse enim novit hominum vanitatem]], that is, their empty deeds, by which they are hindered from the true and final end that makes blessed. Vanity is also sometimes taken not for fault, but for a certain general condition that goes with the creature or created being, inasmuch as it is from nothing. For thus there belongs to it of itself a certain falling short of true, stable and unchangeable being, which is called vanity. Hence we have in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:2|Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity|Vanitas vanitatum, dixit Ecclesiastes, vanitas vanitatum, et omnia vanitas]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 38:6|And indeed all things are vanity: every man living|Verumtamen universa vanitas omnis homo vivens]]. But of blameworthy vanity, which is an inordinate departure from equity and truth, the Lord says through Jeremias: [[Jer 2:5|What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?|Quid invenerunt patres vestri in me iniquitatis, quia ambulaverunt post vanitatem, et vani facti sunt?]] [[11:11|and when he seeth iniquity, doth he not consider it|Et videns iniquitatem, nonne considerat]], to judge and avenge it? as if to say: Certainly, because the wisdom and justice of God require it. Therefore he testifies through Sophonias: [[Soph 1:4|I will destroy|Disperdam]] [[Soph 1:6|them that turn away from following after the Lord, and that have not sought the Lord|eos qui avertuntur de post tergum Domini, et qui non exquisierunt Dominum]].

paras.t: Vir vanus, id est mente aversus a summo, vero et invariabili bono, caducis inhærens, virtutibus carens, vitiis deditus, qui omni luto et stercore vilior est, in superbiam erigitur, id est, mente extollit se ipsum ultra proprium gradum atque mensuram, quasi Creatori suo subdi obligatus non esset, oblitus propriæ infirmitatis, et pericula quibus expositus est, non perpendens. Quum enim a Deo aversus est, vitiorum caligine obtenebratur; et ea quæ habet et quod est, sic adspicit quasi ea a Deo non essent, menteque cæcus, sua et se plus reputat quam sit verum: qui si adverteret quantum per solam suam superbiam vilificetur, sciret et fateretur se indignum a terra portari aut inter homines conversari. Et quasi pullum onagri, id est fetum silvestris asini, qui in deserto, silva seu campo genitus, libere discurrit, nec servire compellitur, nec loro compescitur; se liberum natum putat, id est non obligatum subjici Deo, loro disciplinæ frenari, jugo legis divinæ constringi, sed in propria voluntate libere vult vagari, vivere et peccare: qui etsi verbis dicat se Deo subdi debere, aut per scientiam id agnoscat, operibus tamen negat, quia sic conversatur, ac si se instar pulli onagri liberum arbitretur. De talibus Dominus loquitur in Jeremia: A sæculo confregisti jugum, rupisti vincula, et dixisti, Non serviam.
paras.en: [[11:12|A vain man|Vir vanus]], that is, one turned away in mind from the highest, true and unchangeable good, clinging to perishable things, lacking virtues, given to vices, who is viler than any mud and dung, [[11:12|is lifted up into pride|in superbiam erigitur]], that is, exalts himself in mind beyond his own rank and measure, as though he were not bound to be subject to his Creator, forgetful of his own weakness and not weighing the dangers to which he is exposed. For when he is turned away from God, he is darkened by the gloom of vices; and he looks on what he has and what he is as though it were not from God, and, blind in mind, he thinks more of himself and his own than is true: and if he considered how much he is debased by his pride alone, he would know and confess that he is unworthy to be borne by the earth or to live among men. [[11:12|like a wild ass’s colt|Et quasi pullum onagri]], that is, the foal of the wild ass, which, born in the desert, the forest or the open country, runs about freely, and is neither forced to serve nor held by a halter; [[11:12|thinketh himself born free|se liberum natum putat]], that is, not bound to be subject to God, to be reined in by the halter of discipline, or held fast by the yoke of the divine law; but he wishes to wander, live and sin freely in his own will: and though he may say in words that he ought to be subject to God, or know it by learning, yet he denies it by his works, for he lives as though he thought himself free like the wild ass’s colt. Of such men the Lord speaks in Jeremias: [[Jer 2:20|Of old time thou hast broken my yoke, thou hast burst my bands, and thou saidst: I will not serve|A sæculo confregisti jugum, rupisti vincula, et dixisti, Non serviam]].

paras.t: His verbis notat, pungit et reprobat sanctum Job, quia supra jam dixit: Auferat a me Deus virgam suam. Loquar, et non timebo eum. Quod Sophar sic sumpsit, quasi Job de pari vellet cum Deo contendere. Ideo subdit: Tu autem firmasti, id est indurasti, cor tuum in malitia, quoniam pertinaciter manes in tua præsumptione, propriique erroris defensione; et expandisti ad eum manus tuas in oratione, quasi innocens esses. Quasi dicat, Talis expansio sive oratio exstat inutilis: prout per Isaiam Dominus ait: Quum extenderitis manus vestras, avertam oculos meos; manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt. Qui ergo vult exaudiri a Deo, studeat opera verbis conformare, docilis esse, divinæ voluntati se subdere.
paras.en: In these words he marks, stings and condemns holy Job, because he had already said above: [[Job 9:34|Let him take his rod away from me|Auferat a me Deus virgam suam]]. [[Job 9:35|I will speak, and will not fear him|Loquar, et non timebo eum]]. Sophar took this as though Job wished to contend with God as an equal. Therefore he adds: [[11:13|But thou hast hardened|Tu autem firmasti]], that is, made obdurate, [[11:13|thy heart|cor tuum]] in malice, since thou remainest obstinately in thy presumption and in the defence of thine own error; [[11:13|and hast spread thy hands to him|et expandisti ad eum manus tuas]] in prayer, as though thou wert innocent. As if to say: Such a spreading out, or prayer, is useless: as the Lord says through Isaias: [[Is 1:15|when you stretch forth your hands, I will turn away my eyes|Quum extenderitis manus vestras, avertam oculos meos]]; [[Is 1:15|for your hands are full of blood|manus enim vestræ sanguine plenæ sunt]]. Let him, then, who wishes to be heard by God strive to make his works agree with his words, to be teachable, and to submit himself to the divine will.

paras.t: Hinc Sophar subjungit congruum modum orandi, pœnitendi et redeundi ad Deum. Si iniquitatem, quæ est in manu, id est operatione tua, vel in potestate tua, quantum ad hoc quod libere potes eam dimittere, abstuleris a te, pœnitendo atque cessando a malo præterito seu præsenti, et bonum habendo propositum emendandi in posterum; et non manserit in tabernaculo tuo injustitia, id est, bona injuste acquisita restitueris. Non enim dimittitur peccatum, nisi restituatur ablatum. Vel per tabernaculum, designatur familia, quam paterfamilias debet in æquitate servare: nam et pro domesticorum delictis dominus domus quandoque divinitus flagellatur, quoniam negligens est in correctione suorum. Tunc levare poteris faciem tuam corporalem ad cælum in prece, faciem quoque spiritualem, videlicet intellectum, ad Deum, absque macula culpæ: quæ dividit inter Deum et hominem, et precem facit inexaudibilem, juxta illud Threnorum: Nos inique egimus, et te ad iracundiam provocavimus, idcirco tu inexorabilis es; et eris stabilis, mente Deo fortiter adhærendo; nec a medio virtutis tam cito recedes, sed in oratione gratiam te intus corroborantem suscipies: sicut ait Apostolus ad Hebræos, Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor. Peccatum autem menti instabilitatem inducit, et ad illicita pronam facit. Ideo scriptum est: Peccatum peccavit Jerusalem, propterea instabilis facta est. Sophar tamen (ut æstimatur) intellexit istud etiam de stabilitate in bonis terrenis, quæ non putavit cuiquam auferri nisi pro culpa. Et non timebis adversariorum incursus. Vel, Non timebis Deum timore servili. In die quoque judicii eris securus: secundum illud Sophoniæ, Dominus in medio tui est, non timebis malum ultra.
paras.en: Then Sophar adds the fitting way of praying, repenting and returning to God. If [[11:14|the iniquity that is in thy hand|iniquitatem, quæ est in manu]], that is, in thy working, or in thy power, inasmuch as thou canst freely give it up, [[11:14|thou wilt put away from thee|abstuleris a te]], by repenting and ceasing from evil past or present, and having a good purpose of amendment for the future; [[11:14|and let not injustice remain in thy tabernacle|et non manserit in tabernaculo tuo injustitia]], that is, if thou restore goods unjustly acquired. For the sin is not forgiven unless what was taken is restored. Or by the tabernacle is meant the household, which the father of the family is bound to keep in equity: for the master of a house is sometimes scourged by God for the offences of his household, because he is negligent in correcting his own. [[11:15|Then mayst thou lift up thy face|Tunc levare poteris faciem tuam]], thy bodily face to heaven in prayer, and thy spiritual face too, namely the intellect, to God, [[11:15|without spot|absque macula]] of sin: which divides God from man, and makes prayer unheard, according to the words of Lamentations: [[Lam 3:42|We have done wickedly, and provoked thee to wrath: therefore thou art inexorable|Nos inique egimus, et te ad iracundiam provocavimus, idcirco tu inexorabilis es]]; [[11:15|and thou shalt be steadfast|et eris stabilis]], by cleaving strongly to God in mind; nor wilt thou so quickly depart from the mean of virtue, but in prayer thou shalt receive grace strengthening thee within: as the Apostle says to the Hebrews, [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor]]. But sin brings instability to the mind and makes it prone to unlawful things. Therefore it is written: [[Lam 1:8|Jerusalem hath grievously sinned, therefore is she become unstable|Peccatum peccavit Jerusalem, propterea instabilis facta est]]. Sophar, however (as is thought), understood this also of steadfastness in earthly goods, which he thought were taken from no one except for a fault. [[11:15|and shalt not fear|Et non timebis]] the onsets of adversaries. Or, thou shalt not fear God with servile fear [that is, the fear of punishment, as a slave fears, not the filial fear of offending]. Thou shalt also be secure in the day of judgement: according to the words of Sophonias, [[Soph 3:15|the Lord, is in the midst of thee, thou shalt fear evil no more|Dominus in medio tui est, non timebis malum ultra]].

paras.t: Miseriæ quoque, id est prioris calamitatis et plagæ, quam usque nunc sustines, oblivisceris præ abundantia prosperitatis: quemadmodum Joseph testatur, Oblivisci me fecit Deus omnium laborum meorum et domus patris mei. Et hæc oblivio dupliciter intelligi potest. Primo, quod prioris adversitatis non erit memoria in gravamen, sed magis in gaudium: quia jucundum est patientibus sustinuisse adversa, dicente Psalmista: Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala. Secundo, quod memoria talis absorbebitur, ac cessabit per occupationem in abundantia prosperitatis: sicque videtur Sophar jam loqui. Nam subditur: et quasi aquarum quæ præterierunt, non recordaberis, id est, memor non eris prioris adversitatis: sicut homo faciliter obliviscitur pluviæ quæ cecidit, vel fluvii qui cursim transfluxit. Juxta hunc modum loquendi ait Christus: Mulier quum parit, tristitiam habet, quia venit hora ejus; quum autem pepererit puerum, jam non meminit pressuræ propter gaudium.
paras.en: [[11:16|misery|Miseriæ quoque]], that is, the former calamity and plague which thou sufferest until now, [[11:16|Thou shalt also forget|oblivisceris]] for the abundance of prosperity: as Joseph testifies, [[Gen 41:51|God hath made me to forget all my labours, and my father's house|Oblivisci me fecit Deus omnium laborum meorum et domus patris mei]]. And this forgetting can be understood in two ways. First, that the memory of the former adversity will not be a burden, but rather a joy: for it is pleasant to those who have suffered to have borne adversities, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 89:15|We have rejoiced for the days in which thou hast humbled us: for the years in which we have seen evils|Lætati sumus pro diebus quibus nos humiliasti, annis quibus vidimus mala]]. Secondly, that such a memory will be swallowed up and will cease through being taken up with abundance of prosperity: and this seems to be how Sophar speaks here. For it goes on: [[11:16|and remember it only as waters that are passed away|et quasi aquarum quæ præterierunt, non recordaberis]] [Denis’s text reads “and as of waters that are passed away thou shalt not remember”], that is, thou wilt not be mindful of the former adversity: as a man easily forgets rain that has fallen, or a river that has flowed swiftly by. In this manner of speaking Christ says: [[John 16:21|A woman, when she is in labour, hath sorrow, because her hour is come; but when she hath brought forth the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy|Mulier quum parit, tristitiam habet, quia venit hora ejus; quum autem pepererit puerum, jam non meminit pressuræ propter gaudium]].

paras.t: Et quasi meridianus fulgor consurget tibi ad vesperam. Claritas solis in meridie fortissima est, totumque implet hemisphærium. Per hunc ergo fulgorem notatur status floridus, præcipue prosperitatis in bonis animæ et corporis, quem Sophar disseruit Job præfata agenti, in vespera, id est in senectute sua, donandum. Quod consequenter quasi exponit. Et quum consumptum putaveris, id est per infirmitatem et adversitatem jam defecisse, et protinus moriturum, orieris ut lucifer, id est, grandi decore temporalium fulcieris et spiritualiter renovaberis, et quasi de novo splendiflue surges ac reflorebis: juxta illud Proverbiorum, Justorum semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem. Et habebis fiduciam, id est cordis certitudinem, certamque confidentiam de futuro bono seu præmio post mortem, proposita tibi spe hujusmodi boni, seu spe pietatis ac liberalitatis divinæ: prout ad Hebræos dicit Apostolus, Firmissimum habemus solatium, qui confugimus ad tenendam propositam nobis spem.
paras.en: [[11:17|And brightness like that of the noonday, shall arise to thee at evening|Et quasi meridianus fulgor consurget tibi ad vesperam]]. The brightness of the sun at noon is strongest, and fills the whole hemisphere. By this brightness, then, is meant a flourishing state, above all of prosperity in goods of soul and body, which Sophar declared would be given to Job, if he did the things spoken of, in the evening, that is, in his old age. And this he next as it were explains.
