[[11:17|and when thou shalt think thyself consumed|Et quum consumptum putaveris]], that is, to have failed already through sickness and adversity and to be about to die at once, [[11:17|thou shalt rise as the day star|orieris ut lucifer]], that is, thou shalt be upheld by great splendour of temporal things and renewed spiritually, and shalt rise as it were anew in splendour and flourish again: according to the words of Proverbs, [[Prov 4:18|the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|Justorum semita quasi lux splendens, procedit et crescit usque ad perfectam diem]]. [[11:18|And thou shalt have confidence|Et habebis fiduciam]], that is, certainty of heart, and sure trust of a good, or reward, to come after death, [[11:18|hope being set before thee|proposita tibi spe]] of such a good, or hope in the divine goodness and bounty: as the Apostle says to the Hebrews, [[Heb 6:18|we may have the strongest comfort, we who have fled for refuge to hold fast the hope set before us|Firmissimum habemus solatium, qui confugimus ad tenendam propositam nobis spem]].

paras.t: Deinceps subjungit de mercede æquitatis post mortem. Et defossus, id est sepultus, securus ab hostium afflictione dormies requie Sanctorum in limbo patrum, donec per Christum ad patriam Beatorum devenias. Requiesces in spe, donec fruaris et re, et in bonis Dei tandem æternaliter requiesces; et non erit qui te exterreat, quia Beatis et glorificatis nulla potest pœna accidere, suntque perpetuo assecurati de sua felicitate. Et deprecabuntur faciem tuam plurimi, id est, multi tuum patrocinium invocabunt, et te ut intercessorem rogabunt: secundum quod viatores soliti sunt Sanctorum implorare auxilium. Unde et supra Eliphaz dixit ad Job: Ad aliquem Sanctorum convertere.
paras.en: Next he adds the reward of righteousness after death. [[11:18|and being buried|Et defossus]], that is, interred, [[11:18|thou shalt sleep secure|securus ab hostium afflictione dormies]], safe from the affliction of enemies, with the rest of the Saints in the limbo of the fathers, until through Christ thou come to the country of the Blessed. [[11:19|Thou shalt rest|Requiesces]] in hope, until thou enjoy the thing itself also, and at last thou shalt rest eternally in the good things of God; [[11:19|and there shall be none to make thee afraid|et non erit qui te exterreat]], because no punishment can befall the Blessed and glorified, and they are made secure for ever of their happiness. [[11:19|and many shall entreat thy face|Et deprecabuntur faciem tuam plurimi]], that is, many will call on thy patronage and ask thee as an intercessor: as wayfarers [that is, those still on the way in this life] are accustomed to implore the help of the Saints. Hence Eliphaz too said to Job above: [[Job 5:1|turn to some of the saints|Ad aliquem Sanctorum convertere]].

paras.t: Oculi autem impiorum deficient, id est, oculi eorum interiores, bonum optatum post mortem non obtinebunt, quia non pure et vere illud intendebant, sed præsentia præposuerunt futuris; et effugium peribit ab eis, id est, damnationem non valebunt evadere, quemadmodum loquitur Isaias: Quid facietis in die calamitatis de longe venientis? ad cujus fugietis auxilium? Et secundo Machabæorum libro ait vir timoratus: Manum Omnipotentis neque vivus, neque defunctus effugiam. Et spes illorum vana et falsa, qua speraverunt non in Deo, sed in re creata, et bonum caducum finaliter quæsierunt. Hæc spes non est theologica virtus, imo nec virtus, sed fallax fiducia: de qua dicitur in Sapientiæ libro, Spes impii tanquam lanugo est, quæ a vento tollitur, et tanquam spuma. Hæc itaque spes illorum, est abominatio animæ, id est, abominabilem Deo atque damnabilem efficit animam, estque omni animæ bonæ abominanda. Potest quoque exponi de spe quæ est virtus theologica, loquendo de spe informi, secundum quod impii sperant salvari, quum tamen vivant injuste. Definitio autem spei, quæ dicitur, Spes est certa exspectatio futuræ beatitudinis, ex gratia Dei et bonis operibus seu meritis proveniens, datur de spe formata.
paras.en: [[11:20|But the eyes of the wicked shall decay|Oculi autem impiorum deficient]], that is, their inner eyes will not obtain the good they desired after death, because they did not aim at it purely and truly, but preferred present things to those to come; [[11:20|and the way to escape shall fail them|et effugium peribit ab eis]], that is, they will not be able to escape damnation, as Isaias says: [[Is 10:3|What will you do in the day of visitation, and of the calamity which cometh from afar? to whom will ye flee for help?|Quid facietis in die calamitatis de longe venientis? ad cujus fugietis auxilium?]] And in the second book of Machabees a God-fearing man says: [[2 Mach 6:26|should I not escape the hand of the Almighty neither alive nor dead|Manum Omnipotentis neque vivus, neque defunctus effugiam]]. [[11:20|and their hope|Et spes illorum]], vain and false, by which they hoped not in God but in a created thing, and in the end sought a perishable good. This hope is not the theological virtue, nay not a virtue at all, but a deceitful trust: of which it is said in the book of Wisdom, [[Wis 5:15|the hope of the wicked is as dust, which is blown away with the wind|Spes impii tanquam lanugo est, quæ a vento tollitur]], [[Wis 5:15|and as a thin froth|et tanquam spuma]]. This hope of theirs, then, is [[11:20|the abomination of the soul|abominatio animæ]], that is, it makes the soul abominable to God and damnable, and is to be abhorred by every good soul. It can also be explained of the hope which is the theological virtue, speaking of unformed hope [that is, hope without charity], in that the wicked hope to be saved though they live unjustly. But the definition of hope which runs, Hope is the sure expectation of future beatitude, coming from the grace of God and good works or merits, is given of formed hope [that is, hope quickened by charity].

paras.t: Postremo, ex præinductis eloquiis Sophar clarissime patet, quod posuit vitam post hanc vitam. Ei enim qui nec corpore nec anima vivit, non competit secure dormire, nec ei promittitur non terreri, nec competit ei ut alii eum exorent: nec Sophar dixisset ad Job, quod post mortem suam plurimi faciem ejus essent deprecaturi, nisi sensisset animam post corpus subsistere, vivere, coronari. Illi quoque qui asserunt, amicos Job non posuisse vitam futuram, exponunt hanc litteram non parum (ut reor) extorte, quemadmodum provide intuenti scripta eorum constabit. Porro S. Gregorius et Albertus Magnus vir ingeniosus, exponunt ista, ita quod Sophar posuit animam immortalem.
paras.en: Lastly, from the words of Sophar set out above it is most clearly evident that he held there is a life after this life. For to one who lives neither in body nor in soul it does not belong to sleep securely, nor is it promised him that he shall not be afraid, nor does it belong to him that others should entreat him: nor would Sophar have said to Job that after his death many would entreat his face, unless he had held that the soul survives the body, lives and is crowned. Those too who assert that Job’s friends did not hold a life to come explain this text, I think, in no small degree forcedly, as will be plain to anyone who looks carefully at their writings. But St Gregory, and Albert the Great, a man of genius, explain these words so that Sophar held the soul to be immortal.

11.title: De spirituali hujus capituli undecimi intelligentia.
11.title_en: On the spiritual understanding of this eleventh chapter

paras.t: Respondens Sophar Naamathites, dixit: Numquid qui multa loquitur, non audiet? aut vir verbosus justificabitur? Per Sophar signantur sapientes in oculis suis, zelumque Dei habentes, sed non secundum scientiam: qui verba increpatoria, instructoria, et dictis suis obviantia æquanimiter audire non valent; sed pauca verba justorum, quibus ipsi redarguuntur, quasi multa atque superflua criminantur; et prolatores verborum talium reputant vitiosos, atque ut eos juste reprehendere videantur, verba authentica contra eos proponunt. Unde et verba hæc Sophar, in se ipsis vera, notabilia atque moralia sunt, sed indebite applicantur adversus moralem ac sapientem.
paras.en: [[11:1|Then Sophar the Naamathite answered, and said|Respondens Sophar Naamathites, dixit]]: [[11:2|Shall not he that speaketh much, hear also?|Numquid qui multa loquitur, non audiet]] [[11:2|or shall a man full of talk be justified?|aut vir verbosus justificabitur]] By Sophar are signified those who are wise in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]], and who [[Rom 10:2|have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge|zelumque Dei habentes, sed non secundum scientiam]]: who cannot calmly bear to hear words of rebuke, of instruction, and words that run counter to what they themselves say; but the few words of the just by which they are reproved they accuse as many and superfluous; and they hold those who utter such words to be at fault, and, so that they may seem to reprove them justly, they set authoritative sayings against them. Hence these words of Sophar too, true in themselves, are notable and moral, but they are wrongly turned against a man who is moral and wise.

paras.t: Itaque, vir verbosus non justificatur, Psalmista dicente, Vir linguosus non dirigetur in terra: quia dum quisque per verba defluit, perdita gravitate silentii, custodiam mentis amittit, secundum Gregorium. Hinc scriptum est in Proverbiis: Qui custodit os suum et linguam suam, custodit ab angustiis animam suam. Et alibi Salomon ait: Qui inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala. Et denuo: Qui moderatur sermones suos, doctus et prudens est. In Ecclesiastico quoque scriptum est: Odibilis est, qui procax est ad loquendum: et: Qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam. Denique, sicut vas carens operculo, immunditiis deturpatur; sic anima quæ ori suo virtutem silentii non superponit, nec illud tempore congruo clausum tenet, vitiis inquinatur. Porro religiosis et maxime solitariis attendenda sunt ista, quum Jacobus dicat: Si quis putat se religiosum esse, non refrenans linguam suam, sed seducens cor suum, hujus vana est religio. Et Isaias ait: Erit cultus justitiæ, silentium. Præterea, verbo Sophar quo ait, Numquid qui multa loquitur, non audiet? consonat illud Jacobi: Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum.
paras.en: And so [[11:2|a man full of talk|vir verbosus]] is not justified, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 139:12|A man full of tongue shall not be established in the earth|Vir linguosus non dirigetur in terra]]: because, as Gregory says, when anyone runs away in words, he loses the weight of silence and lets go the guard of his mind. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 21:23|He that keepeth his mouth and his tongue, keepeth his soul from distress|Qui custodit os suum et linguam suam, custodit ab angustiis animam suam]]. And elsewhere Solomon says: [[Prov 13:3|he that hath no guard on his speech shall meet with evils|Qui inconsideratus est ad loquendum, sentiet mala]]. And again: [[Prov 17:27|He that setteth bounds to his words, is knowing and wise|Qui moderatur sermones suos, doctus et prudens est]]. In Ecclesiasticus too it is written: [[Ecclus 20:5|there is another that is hateful, that is bold in speech|Odibilis est, qui procax est ad loquendum]]; and: [[Ecclus 20:8|He that useth many words shall hurt his own soul|Qui multis utitur verbis, lædit animam suam]]. Then, just as a vessel without a cover is fouled with uncleanness[[Num 19:15||]], so the soul that does not set the virtue of silence over its mouth, nor keep it closed at the fitting time, is stained with vices. These things, moreover, must be heeded by religious, and most of all by solitaries, since James says: [[Jas 1:26|if any man think himself to be religious, not bridling his tongue but deceiving his own heart, this man's religion is vain|Si quis putat se religiosum esse, non refrenans linguam suam, sed seducens cor suum, hujus vana est religio]]. And Isaias says: [[Is 32:17|the service of justice quietness|Erit cultus justitiæ, silentium]] [Latin *silentium*, silence: the point Denis presses on religious]. Further, with Sophar's saying, [[11:2|Shall not he that speaketh much, hear also?|Numquid qui multa loquitur, non audiet]] there agrees that saying of James: [[Jas 1:19|let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak|Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum]].

paras.t: Denique, impatientes, vitiosi et scioli, eos a quibus reprehenduntur, superbos et sui irrisores frequenter existimant. Idcirco in persona cujuslibet talis, reprehensorem suum impie redarguentis, subjungitur: Tibi soli tacebunt homines? et quum ceteros deriseris, a nullo confutaberis? quasi dicat: Non es talis aut tantus, ut deceat me tacere. Ubi Gregorius ait: Quum vera vox justorum pravorum se auribus admovet, memoriam culpa mordet, et in redargutione vitiorum, quo intus cognitione mens tangitur, foris ad contradictionis studium provocatur. Ferre vocem non valet, quia tacta in vulnere sui reatus dolet; et per hoc quod generaliter contra perversos dicitur, se impeti specialiter suspicatur. Hinc quoque sæpe correptori falsa imponit, sicut et Sophar ait ad Job: Dixisti: Purus est sermo meus, et mundus sum in conspectu tuo. Quod Job non dixit eo modo quo sibi objicitur.
paras.en: Moreover, the impatient, the vicious and the half-learned often think those by whom they are reproved to be proud and to be mocking them. Therefore, in the person of any such man, who impiously rebukes his reprover, there follows: [[11:3|Shall men hold their peace to thee only?|Tibi soli tacebunt homines]] [[11:3|and when thou hast mocked others, shall no man confute thee?|et quum ceteros deriseris, a nullo confutaberis]] As if to say: Thou art not such a one, nor so great, that it should become me to hold my peace. On which Gregory says: When the true voice of the just comes near the ears of the wicked, guilt bites the memory; and in the rebuking of vices, touched within by the knowledge of itself, the mind is roused outwardly to an eagerness to contradict. It cannot bear the voice, because, touched in the wound of its guilt, it smarts; and from what is said in general against the perverse, it suspects that it is itself being attacked in particular. Hence too it often lays false charges on its reprover, as Sophar too says to Job: [[11:4|thou hast said: My word is pure, and I am clean in thy sight|Dixisti: Purus est sermo meus, et mundus sum in conspectu tuo]]. Which Job did not say in the way in which it is laid against him.

paras.t: Insuper, vitiosi ficteque boni, ne ex passione loqui putentur, bona verbo tenus suo correptori aliquando imprecantur, sicut et Sophar ait ad Job: Utinam Deus loqueretur tecum, et aperiret labia sua tibi. Hoc utique nos ex vera caritate optare, orare et dicere his debemus, quos a veritate et æquitate deviare, nobisque improperare videmus. Optare namque debemus, ut eorum corda Deus gratiose illuminet, sanet et salvet. Denique, Deus supersapiens et excelsus, frequenter secretissime et interne loquitur his, qui sinceriter et ardenter diligunt eum; qui toto affectu ei intenti sunt, et ejus amore penitus aspernantur quidquid a Deo impedit mentem; quorum purificata ac stabilita est mens; quorum voluntas in serenum bonitatis affectum conversa est tota; quibus viluit mundus, et quidquid mundanum est; qui in dono sapientiæ fulgent, divinæque lucis radiis perfunduntur, atque ad mysticam theologiam deveniunt, in qua Deus ostendit se menti simplificatæ in ipso, secundum capacitatem illius ad supernaturalem divinitatis contemplationem erigens eam: in qua indicibiliter Deo unitur et fruitur, gustans veraciter quam dulcis sit Deus.
paras.en: Furthermore, the vicious and the falsely good, so that they may not be thought to speak from passion, sometimes wish good things to their reprover, in words only, as Sophar too says to Job: [[11:5|I wish that God would speak with thee, and would open his lips to thee|Utinam Deus loqueretur tecum, et aperiret labia sua tibi]]. This indeed we ought, out of true charity, to wish, to pray for and to say to those whom we see straying from truth and equity and reproaching us. For we ought to wish that God may graciously enlighten, heal and save their hearts. Again, God, who is supremely wise and exalted, often speaks most secretly and inwardly to those who love Him sincerely and ardently; who are intent on Him with all their affection, and for love of Him utterly spurn whatever hinders the mind from God; whose mind is purified and made steadfast; whose will is wholly turned to the serene affection of goodness; to whom the world, and whatever is worldly, has grown worthless; who shine in the gift of wisdom and are steeped in the rays of the divine light, and come to mystical theology [that is, the hidden knowledge of God given in contemplation], in which God shows Himself to the mind made simple in Him, raising it, according to its capacity, to the supernatural contemplation of the Godhead: in which it is unspeakably united to God and enjoys Him, truly tasting how sweet God is[[1 Pet 2:3||]].

paras.t: Hinc subditur, Ut ostenderet tibi secreta sapientiæ. Secreta sapientiæ intelligi possunt, vel occulti et imperscrutabiles effectus sapientiæ Dei, vel ipsa Dei sapientia infinita, incomprehensibilis, supersecretissima, quoad quid est nobis ignota. Quæ licet sit simplex et una, tamen pluraliter designatur, quum dicitur, Secreta sapientiæ, id est sapientiam in qua omnium secretorum secretissimæ ac sapientissimæ rationes idealiter atque fontaliter continentur: sicque ob diversitatem scitorum seu objectorum creatorum, pluraliter nominatur, sicut in Deo dicuntur plures ideæ.
paras.en: Hence there follows: [[11:6|That he might shew thee the secrets of wisdom|Ut ostenderet tibi secreta sapientiæ]]. *The secrets of wisdom* may be understood either as the hidden and unsearchable effects of the wisdom of God, or as the very wisdom of God, infinite, incomprehensible, secret beyond all secrecy, unknown to us as to what it is. Though it is simple and one, it is nevertheless designated in the plural when it is said, [[11:6|the secrets of wisdom|Secreta sapientiæ]], that is, the wisdom in which the most secret and most wise reasons [*rationes*, the exemplars of things in the divine mind] of all secret things are contained ideally and as in their fount: and so, because of the diversity of the things known, or of created objects, it is named in the plural, just as many ideas are said to be in God.

paras.t: Itaque secreta sapientiæ suæ Deus nobis revelat dupliciter. Primo, ad suæ sapientiæ contemplationem nos elevando. Secundo, occultorum suorum effectuum secretas rationes in ipso originaliter consistentes, nostræ menti aperiendo, quemadmodum varias rationes incarnationis Christi et ceterorum mysteriorum ejus, sanctis patribus revelavit. Hinc ait Gregorius: Secreta sapientiæ superna sunt opera: quum Deus quos creavit, deserit; quum bona quæ præveniendo cœperat, nequaquam prosequendo consummat; quum claritate nos suæ illustrationis illustrat, et tamen permissis carnis tentationibus, cæcitatis tenebris pulsat; quum dona quæ contulit, non custodit; quum et mentis nostræ ad se desideria excitat, et tamen occulto judicio difficultate nos nostræ imbecillitatis angustat. Quæ secreta sapientiæ ejus pauci valent inquirere, sed nullus invenire: quia quod super nos de nobis ab immortali Sapientia non injuste disponitur, justum profecto est ut a nobis adhuc mortalibus ignoretur. Hinc Paulus exclamat: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus! Et in Sapientia habetur: Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum tuum de cœlis? Jeremias quoque ait: Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit et audivit sermonem ejus?
paras.en: So God reveals the secrets of His wisdom to us in two ways. First, by raising us to the contemplation of His wisdom. Second, by opening to our mind the secret reasons of His hidden effects, which have their origin in Him: as He revealed to the holy fathers the various reasons of the incarnation of Christ and of His other mysteries. Hence Gregory says: The secrets of wisdom are works from on high: when God forsakes those whom He created; when the good things He had begun by preventing [that is, by going before us with His grace] He by no means brings to completion by following them up; when He enlightens us with the brightness of His illumination, and yet, permitting temptations of the flesh, strikes us with the darkness of blindness; when He does not keep the gifts He bestowed; when He both stirs up the desires of our mind towards Himself, and yet by a hidden judgement straitens us with the difficulty of our weakness. These secrets of His wisdom few are able to search into, but none to find out: because what is disposed concerning us, above us, by the immortal Wisdom, and not unjustly, it is surely just that it should be unknown to us while we are still mortal. Hence Paul exclaims: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus]] And in Wisdom we have: [[Wis 9:17|who shall know thy thought, except thou give wisdom, and send thy holy Spirit from above|Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum tuum de cœlis]]? Jeremias too says: [[Jer 23:18|who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath seen and heard his word?|Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit et audivit sermonem ejus]]

paras.t: Et quod multiplex sit lex ejus. Præter expositionem verbi hujus præcedenti articulo positam, potest hoc ipsum exponi de legis divisione in varias leges. Est enim lex æterna, lex naturalis, lex humana, lex divina seu supernaturalis, quæ dividitur in legem evangelicam atque Mosaicam. Lex quippe æterna, est ratio gubernationis rerum in divina mente consistens. Hoc etenim lex est ratio divinæ sapientiæ, in quantum est directiva actuum ac motuum omnium creaturarum. Unde in libro Sapientiæ scriptum est: Quum sis justus, o Domine, omnia juste disponis. Porro lex naturalis, est quædam participatio legis æternæ, naturis rerum creatarum naturaliter indita, per quam unaquæque tendit in proprium finem naturalem, sibi a divina sapientia præstitutum. Sed quoniam rationalis creatura ad supernaturalem felicitatem creata est, indigemus lege supernaturali, per quam de vera et supernaturali beatitudine instruamur, atque de præceptis et actibus perveniendi ad eam, illuminemur. Hæc ergo lex supernaturalis, dicitur lex divina, quæ est mensura et regula actuum humanorum in ordine ad beatitudinem supernaturalem æternam. De qua lege divina ait Psalmista: Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas. Lex autem humana, est quoddam rationis dictamen, quo diriguntur actus humani in ordine ad finem boni communis. Et hæc lex ex naturali lege progreditur, estque quasi determinatio et explicatio legis naturalis circa particulares hominum status atque negotia, casus et opera. Quemadmodum enim ratio speculativa ex primis et indemonstrabilibus principiis per se notis elicit varias diversarum scientiarum conclusiones, sic ratio practica ex primis principiis operativis, quæ ad jus seu legem naturalem respiciunt, tendit ad particulariora, inquirendo ac discutiendo quid in certis negotiis sit agendum. Hæ vero particulares dispositiones per rationem inventæ, vocantur leges humanæ. Denique, contingit hominem contra quamlibet harum legum peccare, propter quod fragilitati humanæ difficile est omnem culpam vitare. De hac materia loquitur Thomas pulcherrime in prima secundæ: secundum quem præfata distinctio est inducta.
paras.en: [[11:6|and that his law is manifold|Et quod multiplex sit lex ejus]]. Besides the exposition of these words given in the preceding article, the same can be expounded of the division of law into various laws. For there is the eternal law, the natural law, human law, and the divine or supernatural law, which is divided into the law of the Gospel and the law of Moses. The eternal law is the reason [*ratio*, the plan] of the governance of things, existing in the divine mind. For this law is the reason of the divine wisdom, inasmuch as it directs the acts and movements of all creatures. Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 12:15|as thou art just, thou orderest all things justly|Quum sis justus, o Domine, omnia juste disponis]]. The natural law, again, is a certain sharing in the eternal law, put by nature into the natures of created things, by which each of them tends to its own natural end, set for it by the divine wisdom. But since the rational creature was created for supernatural happiness, we need a supernatural law, by which we may be instructed about true and supernatural beatitude, and enlightened about the precepts and acts by which it is reached. This supernatural law, then, is called the divine law, which is the measure and rule of human acts as they are ordered to supernatural and eternal beatitude. Of this divine law the Psalmist says: [[Ps 18:8|The law of the Lord is unspotted, converting souls|Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas]]. Human law, again, is a certain dictate of reason by which human acts are directed as they are ordered to the end of the common good. And this law proceeds from the natural law, and is as it were a determining and unfolding of the natural law with regard to the particular states, affairs, cases and works of men. For just as the speculative reason draws from first and indemonstrable principles, known of themselves, the various conclusions of the different sciences, so the practical reason, from the first principles of action, which concern natural right or law, goes on to more particular things, inquiring and discussing what is to be done in given affairs. These particular dispositions, found by reason, are called human laws. Finally, it happens that man sins against any one of these laws, for which reason it is hard for human frailty to avoid all fault. Thomas speaks most beautifully of this matter in the Prima Secundae [the first part of the second part of his Summa, q. 91], and the distinction set out above has been drawn after him.

paras.t: Et intelligeres, ex consideratione multiplicis legis Dei, quod multo minora exigaris a Deo, quam meretur iniquitas tua. Hoc utique verificatur in nobis. Quo enim legem naturalem, humanam ac evangelicam clarius consideramus atque cognoscimus, eo nos culpabiliores damnabilioresque invenimus. Unde agnoscimus et fatemur, quod minus flagellamur seu quibuslibet adversitatibus exercemur, quam peccando meruimus. Hoc ergo semper pensemus, et in omni tribulatione quantumlibet gravi, constanter et humiliter fateamur, præsertim quum uno peccato mortali æternam meruerimus pœnam inferni. Sicque non murmurabimus in adversis, pensantes illud Judith: Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur; sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini (quasi servi qui corripimur) ad emendationem, et non ad perditionem nostram, evenisse credamus. Hinc infra dicitur, quod quilibet nostrum ex corde jugiter dicere habet, præsertim dum corripitur aut plagatur: Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut eram dignus non recepi.
paras.en: [[11:6|and thou mightest understand|Et intelligeres]], from considering the manifold law of God, [[11:6|that he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth|quod multo minora exigaris a Deo, quam meretur iniquitas tua]]. This is indeed borne out in us. For the more clearly we consider and know the natural, the human and the gospel law, the more guilty and the more deserving of damnation we find ourselves. Hence we acknowledge and confess that we are scourged, or tried by adversities of whatever kind, less than we deserved by sinning. Let us then always weigh this, and in every tribulation, however heavy, confess it steadfastly and humbly, especially since by one mortal sin we have deserved the eternal pain of hell. And so we shall not murmur in adversity, weighing that saying of Judith: [[Jdt 8:26|let us not revenge ourselves for these things which we suffer|Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur]]; [[Jdt 8:27|But esteeming these very punishments to be less than our sins deserve, let us believe that these scourges of the Lord, with which like servants we are chastised, have happened for our amendment, and not for our destruction|sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini (quasi servi qui corripimur) ad emendationem, et non ad perditionem nostram, evenisse credamus]]. Hence it is said further on what each of us ought to say continually from the heart, especially when he is chastised or struck: [[Job 33:27|I have sinned, and indeed I have offended, and I have not received what I have deserved|Peccavi, et vere deliqui, et ut eram dignus non recepi]].

paras.t: Forsitan vestigia Dei comprehendes? Per vestigia Dei, Gregorius intelligit visitationes Dei benignas, quibus ad supernorum contemplationem atque amorem erigimur: quas comprehendere non valemus, quia ubi et quomodo veniant, ignoramus. De hoc dicta sunt plurima super illud, Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum, etc. Unde et Salomon ait: Quis hominum potest intelligere viam suam?
paras.en: [[11:7|Peradventure thou wilt comprehend the steps of God|Forsitan vestigia Dei comprehendes]]? By *the steps of God* [*vestigia*, footprints] Gregory understands the kindly visitations of God, by which we are raised to the contemplation and love of things above: which we cannot comprehend, because we do not know where and how they come. Much has been said of this on the words [[Job 9:11|If he come to me, I shall not see him|Si venerit ad me, non videbo eum]], etc. Hence Solomon too says: [[Prov 20:24|who is the man that can understand his own way?|Quis hominum potest intelligere viam suam]]

paras.t: Et usque ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies. Secundum beatissimum Dionysium (quibusdam Mysticæ theologiæ capitulis et in aliis pluribus locis), dupliciter Deum in hac vita cognoscimus, videlicet per positionem, et per ablationem. Modus autem cognoscendi Deum per positionem, est quidquid perfectionis in creaturis consistit, Deo adscribere tanquam totius perfectionis primo principio. Modus vero cognoscendi per ablationem, est quidquid in creaturis invenitur, negare de Deo, tanquam ab ente omnia in infinitum excedente, et superposito universis per eminentiam infinitam, cui cum creaturis nihil univoce competit. Idcirco, secundum Dionysium, iste cognoscendi modus in divinis est potior primo, ita quod melius veriusque cognoscimus quid Deus non est, quam quid est: imo, quid est, penitus ignoramus. Unde in mysticæ theologiæ theorica visione, quæ est altissima Dei cognitio in hac vita possibilis, mens conjungitur Deo tanquam omnino incomprehensibili et ignoto, ita quod Deum tanto perfectius cognoscimus, quanto clarius cernimus quod ipse sit penitus invisibilis, incomprehensibilis et ignotus.
paras.en: [[11:7|and wilt find out the Almighty perfectly?|Et usque ad perfectum Omnipotentem reperies]] According to the most blessed Dionysius (in certain chapters of the Mystical Theology and in many other places), we know God in this life in two ways, namely by positing and by taking away [that is, by affirming of God and by denying of Him]. The way of knowing God by positing is to ascribe to God whatever perfection exists in creatures, as to the first principle of all perfection. The way of knowing by taking away is to deny of God whatever is found in creatures, as of a being that exceeds all things infinitely and is set above all things by an infinite eminence, to whom nothing belongs univocally with creatures [that is, in the same sense in which it belongs to them]. Therefore, according to Dionysius, this way of knowing is the better of the two in divine things, so that we know better and more truly what God is not than what He is: indeed, what He is we do not know at all. Hence in the theoric vision [that is, the contemplative seeing] of mystical theology, which is the highest knowledge of God possible in this life, the mind is joined to God as to one wholly incomprehensible and unknown, so that we know God the more perfectly, the more clearly we see that He is wholly invisible, incomprehensible and unknown.

paras.t: Hoc quoque elegantiores noverunt philosophi: scilicet, Plato, prout in libris de Civitate Dei recitat Augustinus. Proclus etiam Platonicus in Elementatione sua theologica subtiliter probat hoc. Sed et auctor libri de Causis, affirmat hoc ipsum. Ideo Omnipotentem perfecte invenire non possumus, sed aliqualiter tantum. Unde in primo Timæi: Genitorem opificemque universi tam difficile invenire, inventum autem impossibile digne profari. Et auctor libri de Causis: Causa prima est super omne nomen quo nominatur, et non pertinet ei diminutio neque complementum. Ea quippe quæ Deo adscribimus, conveniunt ei per modum infinite excellentiorem, quam capere seu comprehendere in vita hac possumus.
paras.en: The more refined philosophers also knew this: namely Plato, as Augustine relates in the books of the City of God. Proclus the Platonist, too, proves it subtly in his Elements of Theology. And the author of the book On Causes also affirms this very thing. Therefore we cannot find the Almighty perfectly, but only in some measure. Hence in the first book of the Timaeus: The begetter and maker of the universe is so hard to find, and, once found, it is impossible to speak of him worthily. And the author of the book On Causes: The first cause is above every name by which it is named, and neither diminishing nor completing belongs to it. For the things we ascribe to God belong to Him in a manner infinitely more excellent than we can grasp or comprehend in this life.

paras.t: Excelsior cœlo est: quia incircumscriptus, et angelicis spiritibus incomprehensibilis comprehensione perfecta; profundior inferno: quia hunc subvehit, et malignorum spirituum versutias longe subtilius quam ipsi putaverant, judicans, damnat. Longior terra mensura ejus: quæ est ipsa æternitas, quæ longior est spiritualiter quam terra materialiter; et longanimitatem habitantium in terra, patientia suæ longanimitatis exsuperat; et latior mari: quoniam temporalium rerum fluctus sua potestate coercet, circumdat, et cunctis limitibus claudit.
paras.en: [[11:8|He is higher than heaven|Excelsior cœlo est]]: because He is uncircumscribed, and incomprehensible to the angelic spirits, that is, with a perfect comprehension; [[11:8|he is deeper than hell|profundior inferno]]: because He bears it up from beneath, and, judging the wiles of the evil spirits far more subtly than they themselves had supposed, He condemns them. [[11:9|The measure of him is longer than the earth|Longior terra mensura ejus]]: which is eternity itself, which is longer spiritually than the earth is materially; and by the patience of His long-suffering He surpasses the long-suffering of those who dwell on the earth [*longanimitas*, literally length of soul, taking up *longior*, longer]; [[11:9|and broader than the sea|et latior mari]]: since by His power He restrains and surrounds the waves of temporal things, and shuts them in on every side with bounds.

paras.t: Si subverterit omnia. Interdum, per omnem creaturam, seu per omnia, solus homo seu genus humanum exprimitur, quemadmodum Christus ait: Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ; et: Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum. Itaque sensus est: Si subverterit omnia, id est, homines universos in terra gratia privaverit, ita quod spiritualiter moriantur, et nihil sint quantum ad esse meritorium, eosque perire seu damnari permiserit. Vel in unum coarctaverit, id est, simul collectos, et in unam congeriem adunatos, simul in infernum projecerit, sicut in die judicii projiciendi sunt reprobi; quis contradicet ei? id est, nullus reprehendere posset, quia Deus per suam justitiam nos omnes posset relinquere.
paras.en: [[11:10|If he shall overturn all things|Si subverterit omnia]]. Sometimes by *every creature*, or by *all things*, man alone, or the human race, is meant, as Christ says: [[Mark 16:15|preach the gospel to every creature|Prædicate Evangelium omni creaturæ]]; and: [[John 12:32|if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself|Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum]]. So the sense is: [[11:10|If he shall overturn all things|Si subverterit omnia]], that is, if He deprives all men on the earth of grace, so that they die spiritually and are nothing as regards meritorious being, and lets them perish or be damned; [[11:10|or shall press them together|Vel in unum coarctaverit]], that is, if, having gathered them together and brought them into one heap, He casts them all together into hell, as the reprobate are to be cast at the day of judgement; [[11:10|who shall contradict him|quis contradicet ei]]? that is, no one could reprove Him, because God by His justice could forsake us all.

paras.t: Ipse enim novit hominum vanitatem, id est proclivitatem ad malum, atque multiplicem defectuositatem et impietatem. Propter quod ait Psalmista: Filii hominum usquequo gravi corde? ut quid diligitis vanitatem, et quæritis mendacium? Itemque: Verumtamen vani filii hominum.
paras.en: [[11:11|For he knoweth the vanity of men|Ipse enim novit hominum vanitatem]], that is, their proneness to evil, and their manifold defectiveness and impiety. For which reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 4:3|O ye sons of men, how long will you be dull of heart? why do you love vanity, and seek after lying?|Filii hominum usquequo gravi corde? ut quid diligitis vanitatem, et quæritis mendacium]] And again: [[Ps 61:10|But vain are the sons of men|Verumtamen vani filii hominum]].

paras.t: Tu autem firmasti cor tuum in malitia. Hæc est confirmatio prava et falsa, quia iniquitas non est firmitas, sed defectus atque debilitas. Virtus vero est animi fortitudo. Ideo vera cordis confirmatio, est virtutum possessio, constantiaque mentis in Deo, sicut ait Apostolus: Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor. Et ad Ephesios: Confortamini (inquit) in Domino et in potentia virtutis ejus. Hinc ait Scriptura: Non roboratur homo ex iniquitate. Et Anselmus disseruit: Qui hoc potest quod sibi non expedit, quanto plus hoc potest, tanto infirmior est. Denique, quicumque peccat ex deliberatione, ex certa scientia, ex habitu vitioso, confirmat cor suum in malo, et preces ipsius Deo indignæ sunt, quemadmodum scriptum est in Proverbiis: Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis.
paras.en: [[11:13|But thou hast hardened thy heart|Tu autem firmasti cor tuum]] in malice [*firmasti*, literally thou hast made firm, on which Denis plays below: *firmitas*, firmness; *in malitia* is in his text, not in the Vulgate]. This is a perverse and false strengthening, because iniquity is not firmness but defect and weakness, while virtue is fortitude of soul. Therefore the true strengthening of the heart is the possession of the virtues and the constancy of the mind in God, as the Apostle says: [[Heb 13:9|it is best that the heart be established with grace|Optimum est gratia stabiliri cor]]. And to the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:10|be strengthened|Confortamini]] (he says) [[Eph 6:10|in the Lord and in the might of his power|in Domino et in potentia virtutis ejus]]. Hence Scripture says: [[Prov 12:3|Man shall not be strengthened by wickedness|Non roboratur homo ex iniquitate]]. And Anselm argues: He who can do what is not expedient for him, the more he can do it, the weaker he is. Again, whoever sins deliberately, from sure knowledge, or from a vicious habit, strengthens his heart in evil, and his prayers are unworthy of God, as it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]].

paras.t: Si iniquitatem abstuleris a te, vere pœnitendo, dignosque pœnitentiæ fructus agendo, et non manserit in tabernaculo […] domo, vel in corpore tuo, quod quasi tabernaculum animæ est, injustitia, id est, si ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus te purgaveris; tunc levare poteris faciem tuam absque macula, id est, Deo mente pura, decora ac splendida te præsentabis, et eris acceptus. Deus namque requirit animam sine peccato, quod solum inimicitiam parit inter Creatorem et creaturam.
paras.en: [[11:14|If thou wilt put away from thee|Si iniquitatem abstuleris a te]] the iniquity, by truly repenting and bringing forth worthy fruits of penance[[Matt 3:8||]], [[11:14|and let not|et non]] [[11:14|remain in thy tabernacle|manserit in tabernaculo]] […] house, or in thy body, which is as it were the tabernacle of the soul, [[11:14|injustice|injustitia]]: that is, if thou cleanse thyself [[2 Cor 7:1|from all defilement of the flesh and of the spirit|ab omni inquinamento carnis et spiritus]]; [[11:15|Then mayst thou lift up thy face without spot|tunc levare poteris faciem tuam absque macula]], that is, thou shalt present thyself to God with a pure, comely and shining mind, and shalt be accepted. For God requires a soul without sin, which alone begets enmity between the Creator and the creature.

paras.t: Et eris stabilis, in judicio rationis: quæ vitiis excæcatur, nutat et ruit. Passiones namque et vitia mentem efficiunt vagam. Eris quoque stabilis in bonitatis affectu, in oratione, meditatione, contemplatione: in quibus omnibus tanto stabiliores efficimur, quo amplius, vitiis eradicatis, in caritate et gratia crescimus. Et non timebis timore inordinato, carnali, sæculari, servili: secundum illud Proverbiorum, Justus quasi leo confidens, absque timore erit. Et tamen eodem capitulo scribitur: Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus. Sed hoc de timore ordinato, præsertim casto et filiali, asseritur. Qui enim Deum pure pleneque metuit, nil nisi ipsius offensam et separationem ab ipso veretur, quamvis naturali timore affici possit. Hinc scriptum est: Qui timet Deum, nihil trepidabit.
paras.en: [[11:15|and thou shalt be steadfast|Et eris stabilis]] in the judgement of reason, which, when it is blinded by vices, wavers and falls; for passions and vices make the mind wander. Thou shalt be steadfast also in the affection for goodness, in prayer, meditation and contemplation: in all of which we are made the more steadfast, the more we grow in charity and grace, with the vices rooted out. [[11:15|and shalt not fear|Et non timebis]] with an inordinate fear, carnal, worldly, servile [servile fear: the fear of punishment, as distinct from chaste or filial fear, the fear of offending God]: according to that saying of Proverbs: [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Justus quasi leo confidens, absque timore erit]]. And yet in the same chapter it is written: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]]. But this is said of ordered fear, especially chaste and filial fear. For he who fears God purely and fully dreads nothing but offending Him and being separated from Him, although he may be touched by natural fear. Hence it is written: [[Ecclus 34:16|He that feareth the Lord shall tremble at nothing|Qui timet Deum, nihil trepidabit]].

paras.t: Miseriæ quoque oblivisceris, id est priores animi tui inquietudines, perturbationes, vitiositates trades oblivioni, ita quod eas per complacentiam animo non revolves, nec talia sicut ante admittes. Denique, Sancti in patria dicuntur malorum vitæ præsentis oblivisci, non quod eorum prorsus immemores sint, sed quia non complacent neque molestant. Unde Isaias loquitur: Oblivioni datæ sunt angustiæ priores.
paras.en: [[11:16|Thou shalt also forget misery|Miseriæ quoque oblivisceris]], that is, thou shalt give over to forgetfulness the former disquiets, disturbances and vices of thy soul, so that thou wilt not turn them over in thy mind with complacency, nor admit such things as before. Again, the Saints in the fatherland are said to forget the evils of the present life, not that they are wholly unmindful of them, but because these neither please nor trouble them. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 65:16|the former distresses are forgotten|Oblivioni datæ sunt angustiæ priores]].

paras.t: Et quasi meridianus fulgor, id est doni sapientiæ splendor ceteris donis candidior, sicut sol ceteris astris atque planetis præfulget, consurget tibi ad vesperam, id est hora adversitatis, tribulationis seu tentationis: quoniam his malis occurrentibus, per donum sapientiæ te contra armabis et prævalebis. Per sapientiam nempe, qua homo sapit quam dulcis est […] et suavitatem experiens, repellit peccata, parvipendit adversa, et constans manet in omnibus. Ideo in libro Sapientiæ inducitur: Per sapientiam sanati sunt quicumque placuerunt tibi, Domine, ab initio. Et Ecclesiasticus: Homo (inquit) sanctus in sapientia manet sicut sol; nam stultus mutatur ut luna.
paras.en: [[11:17|And brightness like that of the noonday|Et quasi meridianus fulgor]], that is, the splendour of the gift of wisdom, brighter than the other gifts, as the sun outshines the other stars and the planets, [[11:17|shall arise to thee at evening|consurget tibi ad vesperam]], that is, in the hour of adversity, tribulation or temptation: since, when these evils come upon thee, thou wilt arm thyself against them by the gift of wisdom and prevail. For by wisdom, by which a man savours how sweet is […][[1 Pet 2:3||]] [some words are unreadable in the scan here; the margin note beside them seems to give 1 Pet. ii, 3] and experiencing the sweetness, he drives back sins, makes light of adversities, and remains constant in all things. Therefore it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 9:19|by wisdom they were healed, whosoever have pleased thee, O Lord, from the beginning|Per sapientiam sanati sunt quicumque placuerunt tibi, Domine, ab initio]]. And Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 27:12|A holy man continueth in wisdom as the sun|sanctus in sapientia manet sicut sol]]; [[Ecclus 27:12|but a fool is changed as the moon|nam stultus mutatur ut luna]].

paras.t: Et quum te consumptum putaveris, id est, præ multitudine tentationum et angustiarum animi tui, te quasi jam victum et gratia evacuatum censueris, utpote a pusillanimitate spiritus et tempestate jam pene dejectus; orieris ut lucifer, id est, ingenti divinæ confortationis perfunderis fulgore, et tangente te intus Spiritu Sancto, virtutum indueris decore: ita quod major tibi erit mentis ornatus, morum venustas, ædificationis exemplaritas post tribulationem et tentationem, quam ante, faciente Deo cum tentatione proventum, et post tempestatem faciente tranquillum. Hinc in Isaia promittitur justo: Requiem dabit tibi Dominus, et implebit splendoribus animam tuam.
paras.en: [[11:17|and when thou shalt think thyself consumed|Et quum te consumptum putaveris]], that is, when, through the multitude of the temptations and straits of thy soul, thou judgest thyself as already overcome and emptied of grace, as one already almost cast down [[Ps 54:9|from pusillanimity of spirit, and a storm|a pusillanimitate spiritus et tempestate]]; [[11:17|thou shalt rise as the day star|orieris ut lucifer]], that is, thou shalt be steeped in the great brightness of divine strengthening, and, the Holy Ghost touching thee within, thou shalt be clothed with the beauty of the virtues: so that the adornment of thy mind, the comeliness of thy ways and the example thou givest for edification will be greater after tribulation and temptation than before, God making [[1 Cor 10:13|with temptation issue|cum tentatione proventum]] [that is, a way out], and, [[Tob 3:22|after a storm|post tempestatem]], making [[Tob 3:22|a calm|tranquillum]]. Hence in Isaias it is promised to the just man: [[Is 58:11|the Lord will give thee rest|Requiem dabit tibi Dominus]], [[Is 58:11|and will fill thy soul with brightness|et implebit splendoribus animam tuam]].

paras.t: Et habebis fiduciam, non solum retributionis æternæ, beatitudinisque supernæ, sed et in omni eventu, in omni adversitate et prece cor tuum fiducialius ad Deum confugiet, constantius stabit, et tutius erit, innitendo pietati divinæ, et de providentia dispositionis ejus sperando. Proposita tibi spe hujusmodi boni a te ipso vel ab alio, ita quod non corrues a spe. Quo enim quis virtuosius vixerit, et pro justitia duriora pertulerit, tanto fit ei major fiducia ac solidior spes de Deo: quia et bona conscientia parit fiduciam, spemque robustam, sicut et mala conscientia est gravida. Propterea in Sapientiæ libro legitur: Ingrati spes tanquam hibernalis glacies tabescet, et disperiet tanquam aqua supervacua. Et sequenti ibi capitulo: Quum sit timida nequitia, dat testimonium condemnata. In Proverbiis quoque: Fugit impius nemine persequente: justus ut leo confidit. Hinc Aristoteles ait, quod melioris sunt spei qui bene se habent in divinis. Et Jeremias fatetur: Benedictus qui confidit in Domino, et erit Dominus fiducia ejus.
paras.en: [[11:18|And thou shalt have confidence|Et habebis fiduciam]], not only of the eternal reward and of heavenly beatitude, but also in every event: in every adversity and in prayer thy heart will flee to God more trustfully, will stand more steadfastly and will be safer, leaning on the divine goodness and hoping in the providence of His disposing. [[11:18|hope being set before thee|Proposita tibi spe]]: the hope of such good being set before thee, by thyself or by another, so that thou wilt not fall away from hope. For the more virtuously one has lived, and the harder the things one has borne for justice, the greater is one's confidence and the firmer one's hope in God: because a good conscience begets confidence and a strong hope, just as a bad conscience is heavy-laden. Therefore in the book of Wisdom we read: [[Wis 16:29|the hope of the unthankful shall melt away as the winter's ice, and shall run off as unprofitable water|Ingrati spes tanquam hibernalis glacies tabescet, et disperiet tanquam aqua supervacua]]. And in the next chapter there: [[Wis 17:10|whereas wickedness is fearful, it beareth witness of its condemnation|Quum sit timida nequitia, dat testimonium condemnata]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 28:1|The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth|Fugit impius nemine persequente]]: [[Prov 28:1|the just, bold as a lion|justus ut leo confidit]]. Hence Aristotle says that those who stand well in divine things are of better hope. And Jeremias declares: [[Jer 17:7|Blessed be the man that trusteth in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his confidence|Benedictus qui confidit in Domino, et erit Dominus fiducia ejus]].

paras.t: Et defossus securus dormies obdormitione mentis in Deo per fruitionem beatificam ejus. Hæc dormitio est perfecta et gloriosa mentis in Deo pausatio, contentatio, quietatio. Requiesces quiete beata in patria, quantum ad animam, corpus vero interim requiescet in monumento: quemadmodum breviter et dulciter tangit Psalmista, In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam. Hinc S. Cassianus a beatissimo Germano episcopo ad ipsius sepulcrum progresso interrogatus, Quid agis, o frater Cassiane, respondit: Dulci somno perfruor, et adventum Salvatoris securus exspecto.
paras.en: [[11:18|and being buried thou shalt sleep secure|Et defossus securus dormies]], with the falling asleep of the mind in God through the beatific enjoyment of Him. This sleep is the perfect and glorious resting, contentment and stilling of the mind in God. [[11:19|Thou shalt rest|Requiesces]] with a blessed rest in the fatherland as to the soul, while the body meanwhile will rest in the tomb: as the Psalmist touches on briefly and sweetly: [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam]]. Hence St Cassian [bishop of Autun], asked by the most blessed bishop Germanus, who had come to his tomb, What art thou doing, O brother Cassian? answered: I enjoy a sweet sleep, and securely await the coming of the Saviour.

paras.t: Et deprecabuntur faciem tuam plurimi. Viatores enim communiter Beatorum subsidia flagitant saltem in generali, quia et una est generalis Sanctorum festivitas. Nominatim vero non invocamus defunctos, nisi quos canonizavit Ecclesia: nisi forte Deo revelante, aliunde constet esse beatos et in patria coronatos.
paras.en: [[11:19|and many shall entreat thy face|Et deprecabuntur faciem tuam plurimi]]. For wayfarers [that is, those still on the way, in this life] commonly beg the help of the Blessed, at least in general, since there is also one general feast of the Saints. But by name we do not invoke the departed, except those whom the Church has canonized: unless perhaps, by God's revealing it, it is known from elsewhere that they are blessed and crowned in the fatherland.

paras.t: Oculi autem impiorum deficient ab intuitione gloriæ Dei, quemadmodum scriptum est: Tollatur impius ne videat gloriam Dei. Deficient quoque oculi illorum interiores, quoniam tenebris erroris erunt repleti, ita ut Deum in æternum blasphement, injustumque reputent. Deficient etiam tristia jugiter intuendo, videlicet dæmones in inferno. Oculi autem eorum exteriores, mœstissima habebunt objecta ineffabiliter afflictiva: imo proprii corporis turpitudo erit eis horrenda. Hinc Isaias fatetur: Domine, exaltetur manus tua ut non videant. Ad quod Deus respondet sanctis, zelo justitiæ illud petentibus: Videant, et confundantur zelantes populi. Unde Daniel dicit de injustis: Evigilabunt in opprobrium, ut videant semper, haud dubium quin suas miserias.
paras.en: [[11:20|But the eyes of the wicked shall decay|Oculi autem impiorum deficient]] [*deficient*, shall fail] from beholding the glory of God, as it is written: Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God[[Is 26:10||]] [Denis quotes Isaias 26:10 in an older Latin form; the Vulgate has: he shall not see the glory of the Lord]. Their inner eyes too shall fail, since they will be filled with the darkness of error, so that they blaspheme God for ever and think Him unjust. They shall fail also from gazing continually on sorrowful things, namely the demons in hell. Their outward eyes will have the most grievous objects, unspeakably afflicting: nay, the foulness of their own body will be horrible to them. Hence Isaias declares: [[Is 26:11|Lord, let thy hand be exalted, and let them not see|Domine, exaltetur manus tua ut non videant]]. To which God answers the saints, who ask it out of zeal for justice: [[Is 26:11|let the envious people see, and be confounded|Videant, et confundantur zelantes populi]]. Hence Daniel says of the unjust: [[Dan 12:2|shall awake|Evigilabunt]] [[Dan 12:2|unto reproach, to see it always|in opprobrium, ut videant semper]], no doubt their own miseries.

12.title: Declaratio capituli duodecimi: Respondens autem Job, dixit.
12.title_en: Explanation of the twelfth chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit: Ergo vos soli estis homines? Job sciens tres suos amicos contra se concordare, respondendo in hujus capituli principio ipsi Sophar, omnes tres pariter atque æqualiter reprobat, dicens: Ergo vos soli estis homines? id est, tam sapientes estis in oculis vestris, tamque jactanter loquimini, quasi ceteri homines comparatione vestri bruta consisterent, vobisque tantum veritas esset nota. Et vobiscum morietur sapientia? quia si vos soli estis homines, sequitur quod morientibus vobis, non permanebit sapientia in hoc mundo. Unde hoc verbo Job non intendit asserere, quod homine moriente, ejus sapientia moriatur, sed manet in anima immortali, quamvis forte in damnatis diu non maneat. Nec obstat illud Apostoli, Sive scientia destruetur. Non enim intelligitur hoc de destructione habitus scientialis, aut cujuslibet actus ejus, sed de modo sciendi. Aliqui textus habent, Moratur, vel, Moretur sapientia: et tunc interrogative exponitur, ut sit sensus: An vobiscum manet seu maneat sapientia, quæ est divinorum cognitio? Et intendit quod non. Unde infra testatur, Absit ut sapientes vos reputem: quod intelligendum videtur de sapientia erroribus non permixta. Quamvis enim amici Job fuerint viri plurimum eruditi, et in Dei notitia quadam instructi, nihilo minus in aliquibus erraverunt circa divina, et circa providentiam atque justitiam Dei, videlicet quod Deus non puniret quempiam, nisi pro sua culpa, et quod justis in vita hac temporalis prosperitas semper divinitus donaretur. Ea quoque si in communi vere et sine errore cognoverant, ad sanctum Job erronee applicabant.
paras.en: [[12:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]]: [[12:2|Are you then men alone|Ergo vos soli estis homines]]? Job, knowing that his three friends were agreed against him, in answering Sophar himself at the beginning of this chapter rebukes all three alike and equally, saying: [[12:2|Are you then men alone|Ergo vos soli estis homines]]? that is, are you so wise in your own eyes, and do you speak so boastfully, as though other men were brute beasts in comparison with you, and the truth were known to you alone? [[12:2|and shall wisdom die with you|Et vobiscum morietur sapientia]]? For if you alone are men, it follows that when you die, wisdom will not remain in this world. Hence by this word Job does not mean to assert that when a man dies his wisdom dies; for it remains in the immortal soul, though perhaps in the damned it does not remain long. Nor does that saying of the Apostle stand in the way: [[1 Cor 13:8|or knowledge shall be destroyed|Sive scientia destruetur]]. For this is not understood of the destruction of the habit of knowledge, or of any act of it, but of the manner of knowing. Some texts have *Moratur* or *Moretur sapientia* [that is, “wisdom abides” or “should wisdom abide”, in place of *morietur*, “shall die”]: and then it is explained as a question, so that the sense is: Does wisdom, which is the knowledge of divine things, abide, or should it abide, with you? And he means that it does not. Hence he declares below: God forbid that I should account you wise[[Job 27:5||]] [the margin gives Job xxvi, 5; Denis’s words are closest to Job 27:5, “God forbid that I should judge you to be just”]; which seems to be understood of wisdom unmixed with errors. For although Job’s friends were very learned men, and instructed in a certain knowledge of God, they nevertheless erred in some points about divine things, and about the providence and justice of God: namely, that God would punish no one except for his own fault, and that temporal prosperity in this life was always bestowed by God on the just. And even where they knew these things truly and without error in general, they applied them wrongly to holy Job.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Thomam, sicut ex verbis amicorum Job perpenditur, tota eorum intentio circa tria versatur. Primo enim studebant sublimia loqui de Deo, extollendo ejus sapientiam, potentiam, æquitatem, ut per hoc eorum causa rectior videretur. Secundo, talia dogmata ad quædam falsa applicabant, quod scilicet propter justitiam homines temporaliter prosperarentur, et propter peccata hic tribularentur. Tertio, ex his redarguebant Job quasi iniquum, eo quod fuit tam dire percussus.
paras.en: Further, according to Thomas, as is gathered from the words of Job’s friends, their whole intention turns on three things. First, they were eager to speak lofty things of God, extolling His wisdom, power and equity, so that by this their case might seem the more right. Secondly, they applied such teachings to certain false conclusions: namely, that men prosper in this world because of their justice, and are afflicted here because of their sins. Thirdly, from these they rebuked Job as wicked, because he had been so dreadfully stricken.

paras.t: Et mihi est cor, id est intellectus, sicut vobis: ideo vos soli non estis homines, sed etiam ego. Nec inferior vestri sum in divinorum notitia, in virtute et vita. Non præsumptuose hoc ait, sed zelo veritatis ex caritate, ut amicorum exstirpet errorem, reprimatque jactantiam. Virtuosi enim sua interdum bona commemorant ad glo[…] Paulus ait: Non arbitror me aliquid minus fecisse a magnis Apostolis. Itemque: Plus omnibus laboravi. David quoque absque superbia dixit ad Dominum: Fecisti me spectabilem præ cunctis hominibus super terram. Imo Job verba hæc cum magna protulit discretione, dicente Gregorio: Quis nesciat quantum beati Job vita atque scientia, amicorum ejus vitam scientiamque ex[…] inferiorem esse se negat, et ne humilitatis suæ limitem transeat, superiorem esse se tacet. Quis enim hæc quæ nostis, ignorat? Nonne multa alta ac difficilia sciverunt et protulerunt amici Job, quæ communis homo ignorat? Et respondendum, quod Job non intendit asserere, quod omnia amicis suis cognita essent et aliis omnibus nota, sed principalia ista, quæ jam de excellentia Dei et aliis quibusdam similitudinibus et proprietatibus naturalium fuerunt locuti. Idcirco notanter ait, Quis hæc quæ nostis, etc. Omnibus enim faciliter constare potest, quod Deus sit in omni perfectione altissimus. Vel Job loquitur non de omnibus absolute, sed de omnibus disputationi huic præsentibus.
paras.en: [[12:3|I also have a heart|Et mihi est cor]], that is, understanding, [[12:3|as well as you|sicut vobis]]: therefore you alone are not men, but I am one too. *Nor am I inferior to you* [these words stand in the Vulgate of this verse, but not in the Douay-Rheims] in the knowledge of divine things, in virtue and in life. He does not say this presumptuously, but out of zeal for the truth, from charity, to root out his friends’ error and to check their boasting. For the virtuous sometimes recall their own good things for the glo[…] Paul says: I do not reckon that I have done anything less than the great apostles[[2 Cor 11:5||]] [the margin gives II Cor. xi, 9; the words are those of 2 Cor 11:5]. And again: [[1 Cor 15:10|I have laboured more abundantly than all they|Plus omnibus laboravi]]. David too said to the Lord without pride: Thou [[1 Par 17:17|hast made me remarkable above all men|Fecisti me spectabilem præ cunctis hominibus]] upon the earth [the margin gives I Par. xviii, 17; the verse is 1 Par 17:17]. Indeed Job uttered these words with great discretion, as Gregory says: Who does not know how far the life and knowledge of blessed Job […] the life and knowledge of his friends? […] he denies that he is inferior, and lest he pass the bounds of his humility, he is silent about being superior. [[12:3|for who is ignorant of these things, which you know|Quis enim hæc quæ nostis, ignorat]]? [It may be objected:] Did not Job’s friends know and utter many lofty and difficult things which the common man does not know? And the answer is that Job does not mean to assert that everything known to his friends was also known to all others, but those chief things which they had already said about the excellence of God and about certain other likenesses and properties of natural things. That is why he says pointedly: [[12:3|who is ignorant of these things, which you know|Quis hæc quæ nostis]], etc. For it can easily be plain to all that God is most high in every perfection. Or Job is speaking not of all men absolutely, but of all those present at this disputation.

paras.t: Qui deridetur ab amico suo, sicut ego a vobis tribus meis amicis derideor, quasi ista ignorem quæ omnibus patent, et quasi divinæ justitiæ derogem, invocabit Deum, ut sibi clementer adsistat, et ne per impatientiam cadat. Qui enim se conspicit despici, quasi impellitur ut ad Deum confugiat, qui mœstorum et afflictorum ac pauperum est misericordissimus patrocinator, quemadmodum scriptum est: Tibi derelictus est pauper; orphano tu eris adjutor. Et quod ait, Invocabit Deum, non loquitur asserendo, quasi omnes derisi sic faciant, quum multi tales per impatientiam indignentur et irascantur. Sed dicit hoc exhortando seu consulendo, ut sic faciant. Quo enim videmus nobis plura aut fortiora peccandi incitamenta occurrere, eo seriosius ad Deum debemus recurrere, ipsum deposcere, in ejus protectione qui[…]
paras.en: [[12:4|He that is mocked by his friends as I|Qui deridetur ab amico suo, sicut ego]] am mocked by you, my three friends, as though I were ignorant of things plain to all, and as though I detracted from God’s justice, [[12:4|shall call upon God|invocabit Deum]], that He may mercifully stand by him, and that he may not fall through impatience. For he who sees himself despised is, as it were, driven to flee to God, who is the most merciful patron of the sorrowful and afflicted and of the poor; as it is written: [[Ps 9:35|To thee is the poor man left: thou wilt be a helper to the orphan|Tibi derelictus est pauper; orphano tu eris adjutor]]. And when he says, [[12:4|shall call upon God|Invocabit Deum]], he is not speaking by way of assertion, as though all who are mocked did so, since many such men grow indignant and angry through impatience; but he says it by way of exhortation or counsel, that they should do so. For the more numerous or the stronger the incitements to sin that we see coming upon us, the more earnestly we ought to run back to God, to beg Him, and in His protection to […]

paras.t: Et exaudiet eum: quia tanta est misericordia superbenignissimi Dei, ut quo orator fuerit despectior, infirmior, indigentior, eo plus inclinetur hunc exaudire. Propterea dicit: Invoca me in die tribulationis; eruam te, et honorificabis me. Rursus, quo Deus videt hominem plus contemni, irrideri, opprimi, injurias pati, eo pronior est ei succurrere, secundum quod ait: Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum. Ideo dicit Gregorius: Hos elegit Deus, quos despicit mundus. Imo ipse Apostolus fassus est: Quæ stulta sunt (inquit) mundi, elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes; et infirma mundi et contemptibilia elegit Deus. Denique, ubi deest auxilium hominum, potissime solet adesse divinum, præsertim si fideliter et constanter quæratur, dicente Psalmista: Quoniam pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me: Dominus autem assumpsit me. Amici autem qui vere amici sunt et virtuosi, amicum suum non derident, sed erranti condolent: et si valent, succurrunt. Hoc enim exigit caritas, et sapientia docet hoc; quum dicat Apostolus: Qui stat, videat ne cadat. Et denuo: Debemus nos firmiores, imbecillitates infirmorum portare, et non nobis placere. Alium vero, et præsertim amicum ex contemptu aut superbia deridere, non est parvum peccatum. Sed et qui proprium imperfectum considerat, non faciliter quemquam deridet.
paras.en: [[12:4|and he will hear him|Et exaudiet eum]]: for so great is the mercy of the supremely kind God that the more despised, the weaker, the needier the one who prays, the more He is inclined to hear him. Therefore He says: [[Ps 49:15|call upon me in the day of trouble: I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify me|Invoca me in die tribulationis; eruam te, et honorificabis me]]. Again, the more God sees a man despised, mocked, oppressed and suffering wrongs, the readier He is to help him, according to what He says: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation, I will deliver him, and I will glorify him|Cum ipso sum in tribulatione, eripiam eum, et glorificabo eum]]. Therefore Gregory says: God has chosen those whom the world despises. Indeed the Apostle himself has declared: [[1 Cor 1:27|the foolish things|Quæ stulta sunt]], he says, [[1 Cor 1:27|of the world hath God chosen, that he may confound the wise|mundi, elegit Deus, ut confundat sapientes]]; [[1 Cor 1:27|and the weak things of the world|et infirma mundi]] [[1 Cor 1:28|and the things that are contemptible, hath God chosen|et contemptibilia elegit Deus]]. Lastly, where the help of men is lacking, the help of God is most wont to be present, especially if it is sought faithfully and constantly; as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 26:10|For my father and my mother have left me: but the Lord hath taken me up|Quoniam pater meus et mater mea dereliquerunt me: Dominus autem assumpsit me]]. But friends who are truly friends and virtuous do not mock their friend, but grieve with him when he errs, and help him if they can. For charity requires this, and wisdom teaches it, since the Apostle says: He that standeth, [[1 Cor 10:12|let him take heed lest he fall|videat ne cadat]] [the margin’s reference is misread; the words are 1 Cor 10:12]. And again: [[Rom 15:1|we that are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak and not to please ourselves|Debemus nos firmiores, imbecillitates infirmorum portare, et non nobis placere]]. But to mock another, and especially a friend, out of contempt or pride, is no small sin. And whoever considers his own imperfection does not easily mock anyone.

paras.t: Deridetur enim justi simplicitas, id est simplex et innocens conversatio, a callidis et dolosis præsentia et terrena æternis et futuris bonis præferentibus. Quemadmodum enim sapientia seculi, stultitia a Deo et ejus electis fidelibus reputatur; sic vera sapientia electorum et Dei, ab amatoribus hujus mundi insipientia judicatur. Hinc religiosi a carnalibus contemnuntur, et qui mundo renuntiant, religionemque intrant, vel humili vestitu inter homines gradiuntur, mundanis cordibus delirare videntur. Unde quarto Regum, principes Israel, viso filio prophetarum ab Eliseo ad Jehu directo, dixisse leguntur ad Jehu: Quid venit insanus iste ad te? Idcirco, in Proverbiorum libro scribitur: Ambulans recto itinere, et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via. Sed aliud est judicium Dei, aliud hominum, prout in Proverbiis tangitur: Abominatio est Domino omnis illusor, et cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus. Postremo, sicut justorum simplicitas a dolosis et callidis deridetur, sic ceteræ virtutes ab his qui contraria habent vitia, irridentur, ut a lubricis castitas, a cupidis liberalitas. Unde in Ecclesiastico fertur: Abominatio superbo humilitas, et exsecratio diviti pauper.
paras.en: [[12:4|for the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn|Deridetur enim justi simplicitas]], that is, his simple and innocent way of life, by the crafty and deceitful, who prefer present and earthly goods to eternal and future ones. For as the wisdom of the world is accounted folly by God and by His elect and faithful ones[[1 Cor 3:19||]], so the true wisdom of the elect and of God is judged foolishness by the lovers of this world. Hence religious are despised by carnal men, and those who renounce the world and enter religion, or go about among men in lowly dress, seem to worldly hearts to be out of their minds. Hence in the fourth book of Kings the princes of Israel, on seeing the son of the prophets sent by Eliseus to Jehu, are read to have said to Jehu: [[4 Kings 9:11|why came this madman to thee|Quid venit insanus iste ad te]]? Therefore it is written in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 14:2|He that walketh in the right way, and feareth God, is despised by him that goeth by an infamous way|Ambulans recto itinere, et timens Deum, despicitur ab eo qui infami graditur via]]. But the judgment of God is one thing, and that of men another, as is touched on in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:32|every mocker is an abomination to the Lord, and his communication is with the simple|Abominatio est Domino omnis illusor, et cum simplicibus sermocinatio ejus]]. Lastly, as the simplicity of the just is mocked by the deceitful and crafty, so the other virtues are derided by those who have the contrary vices: chastity by the lustful, liberality by the covetous. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 13:24|humility is an abomination to the proud|Abominatio superbo humilitas]], and [[Ecclus 13:24|the rich man abhorreth the poor|exsecratio diviti pauper]].

paras.t: Hinc subditur: Lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum, id est simplicitas justi: quæ lampas vocatur per claritatem suæ virtuositatis, et quoniam aliis lucet præbendo exemplum, ardet quoque per caritatem accensa, sicut lampas oleo infusa: quæ tamen apud cogitationes divitum spernitur, quia ab his qui in temporalibus finem sibi constituunt, tanquam stulta inutilisque contemnitur. Tales enim non reputant ea, nisi ad quæ ipsi potissime afficiuntur; eos vero qui talia spernunt, abominantur ut insensatos. Unde in Evangelio scriptum est, quod Scribæ et Pharisæi, prædicante contra avaritiam Christo, deridebant eum, dicentes: Insanit; quid eum auditis? Parata ad tempus statutum, id est disposita revelari et coronari a Deo in die judicii particularis seu universalis divinitus præordinato, quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Nolite ante tempus judicare, quoadusque veniat Dominus, qui illuminabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium; et tunc laus erit unicuique a Deo. Hinc in Sapientiæ libro scriptum est: In tempore erit respectus illorum, puta justorum. Nunc enim est tempus meritorum et demeritorum; postea erit tempus præmiorum.
paras.en: Hence it is added: [[12:5|The lamp despised in the thoughts of the rich|Lampas contempta apud cogitationes divitum]], that is, the simplicity of the just man: which is called a lamp because of the brightness of its virtue, and because it gives light to others by offering them an example; it also burns, kindled by charity, as a lamp filled with oil. Yet it is scorned in the thoughts of the rich, because it is despised as foolish and useless by those who set their end in temporal things. For such men esteem nothing but the things to which they themselves are most attached, and those who scorn such things they abhor as senseless. Hence it is written in the Gospel that when Christ preached against avarice, the Scribes and Pharisees derided Him[[Luke 16:14||]] [the deriding after the preaching against avarice is Luke 16:14; the words that follow are from John 10:20, which the margin gives], saying: He [[John 10:20|is mad. Why hear you him?|Insanit; quid eum auditis?]] [[12:5|is ready for the time appointed|Parata ad tempus statutum]], that is, disposed to be revealed and crowned by God on the day of judgment, particular or universal, foreordained by God; as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 4:5|judge not before the time: until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts. And then shall every man have praise from God|Nolite ante tempus judicare, quoadusque veniat Dominus, qui illuminabit abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit consilia cordium; et tunc laus erit unicuique a Deo]]. Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:6|in time there shall be respect had to them|In tempore erit respectus illorum]], that is, to the just. For now is the time of merits and demerits; afterwards will be the time of rewards.

paras.t: Abundant tabernacula prædonum, quoniam domos suas spoliis implent et opibus, et audacter provocant Deum, id est, sine timore et remorsu Deum offendunt, alios opprimendo ac spoliando. Tales enim, quum in profundum venerint peccatorum, contemnunt et indurantur; sicque consuetudine peccandi seu vitiosis habitibus excæcantur, ut malum judicent bonum, et bonum reputent malum. Ideo, Audacter provocant Deum, quia sine conscientiæ suæ remorsu perpetrant mala. Isti potissime sunt, a quibus deridetur justi simplicitas. Quibus dicit Isaias: Væ qui dicitis bonum malum, et malum bonum. Ad quos itidem Dominus increpatorie loquitur: Quare atteritis populum meum, et facies pauperum commolitis? Quum ipse dederit omnia in manibus eorum. Hoc ideo dicit, quia tam potestas qua prædantur, quam opulentia sequens, sunt a Deo. Potestas quippe nocendi non est nisi a Deo; sed mala voluntas et potestatis abusio sunt a se ipso. Propter quod dixit Salvator Pilato: Non haberes potestatem adversus me ullam, nisi tibi esset datum desuper. Vel ideo dicitur Deus omnia dedisse in manus prædonum, quia frequenter Deus per tales ulciscitur peccata prædatorum, ita quod tradit eos et bona eorum prædonibus; sed prædones nihilo minus peccant, quoniam impio fine et ex cupiditate crudeliter agunt. Præterea, verbis his Job aperte reprobat errorem amicorum suorum, dicentium opes dari merito justitiæ, quum sceleratissimi abundent divitiis.
paras.en: [[12:6|The tabernacles of robbers abound|Abundant tabernacula prædonum]], because they fill their houses with spoils and riches, [[12:6|and they provoke God boldly|et audacter provocant Deum]], that is, they offend God without fear or remorse, oppressing and despoiling others. For such men, when they are come into the depth of sins, contemn and are hardened[[Prov 18:3||]]; and so they are blinded by the habit of sinning, or by vicious habits, that they judge evil good and reckon good evil. Therefore [[12:6|they provoke God boldly|Audacter provocant Deum]], because they commit evil without remorse of conscience. These above all are the ones by whom the simplicity of the just man is mocked. To them Isaias says: [[Is 5:20|Woe to you that call evil good, and good evil|Væ qui dicitis bonum malum, et malum bonum]] [Denis has the order “good evil, and evil good”]. To them likewise the Lord speaks in rebuke: [[Is 3:15|Why do you consume my people, and grind the faces of the poor?|Quare atteritis populum meum, et facies pauperum commolitis?]] [[12:6|whereas it is he that hath given all into their hands|Quum ipse dederit omnia in manibus eorum]] [the print has *in manibus*, with a note giving *manus*, the Vulgate reading]. He says this because both the power by which they plunder and the wealth that follows are from God. For the power of doing harm is only from God; but the evil will and the abuse of the power are from the man himself. Wherefore the Saviour said to Pilate: [[John 19:11|Thou shouldst not have any power against me, unless it were given thee from above|Non haberes potestatem adversus me ullam, nisi tibi esset datum desuper]]. Or God is said to have given all things into the hands of robbers because God often punishes through such men the sins of those who are plundered [the print reads *prædatorum*, which the sense takes as those preyed upon], so that He hands them and their goods over to robbers; but the robbers sin none the less, since they act cruelly, for a wicked end and out of greed. Moreover, by these words Job openly rebukes the error of his friends, who said that riches are given as the reward of justice, when the most wicked abound in riches.

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit non esse difficilia, quæ amici pro magno jactabant se scire de Deo, et specialiter alloquitur ipsum Sophar, qui præcedenti capitulo arguit contra Job. Nimirum interroga, id est, diligenter considera, jumenta, et docebunt te, id est, materiam sciendi tibi præbebunt, materialiter inducendo te ad veritatem agnoscendam de Creatore: juxta quem modum irrationalia et inanimata dicuntur Deum benedicere atque laudare. Interroga quoque et volatilia cœli aerei, in quo volant, et indicabunt tibi, materialiter tibi veritatem monstrando, ut dictum est de jumentis. Proprie autem jumenta vocantur domestica bruta, hominum necessitati servientia. Jumenta quippe quasi juvamenta dicuntur. Loquere terræ, eam considerando et de ea disputando, et respondebit tibi, sicut de aliis dictum est. Et narrabunt pisces maris: imo et ipsum mare, omnisque creatura, si fuerit considerata, testabitur quod ipsa sit ens per participationem, ideoque necesse sit ponere ens per essentiam, a quo fluxerint universa: quod Deum vocamus.
paras.en: Next he shows that the things his friends boasted, as something great, of knowing about God are not difficult; and he addresses Sophar in particular, who argued against Job in the preceding chapter.
