[[12:7|But ask now|Nimirum interroga]], that is, consider diligently, [[12:7|the beasts, and they shall teach thee|jumenta, et docebunt te]], that is, they will furnish thee with matter for knowing, leading thee materially to acknowledge the truth about the Creator; in which manner irrational and inanimate things are said to bless and praise God[[Dan 3:57||]][[Ps 148:3||]] [the margin gives Dan. iii, 57 and Ps. cxlviii, 3–5, 7–10]. Ask also [[12:7|the birds of the air|volatilia cœli]], the air in which they fly, [[12:7|and they shall tell thee|et indicabunt tibi]], showing thee the truth materially, as was said of the beasts. Now properly speaking *jumenta* [beasts of burden] are the domestic animals that serve the needs of men; for *jumenta* are so called as being *juvamenta* [helps]. [[12:8|Speak to the earth|Loquere terræ]], by considering it and reasoning about it, [[12:8|and it shall answer thee|et respondebit tibi]], as was said of the others. [[12:8|and the fishes of the sea shall tell|Et narrabunt pisces maris]]: indeed the sea itself, and every creature, if it is considered, will bear witness that it is a being by participation, and that therefore one must posit a being by essence, from which all things have flowed: whom we call God.

paras.t: Propter quod subditur: Quis ignorat, si ordinem universi rerumque naturas ac proprietates, modum, speciem, ordinem, seu numerum, pondus et mensuram consideret, quod hæc omnia manus Domini, id est omnipotentia Dei, fecerit? Omnia nempe confitentur, pandunt, respondent se facta, atque concorditer clamant: Ipse fecit nos, et non ipsi nos. Quid enim est quælibet creatura, nisi radius Creatoris, in qua tanquam in effectu causa et artifex Deus relucet? Propter quod Isaias dicit: Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc. Et in Ecclesiastico: Gloria Domini plenum est opus ejus.
paras.en: Wherefore it is added: [[12:9|Who is ignorant|Quis ignorat]], if he considers the order of the universe, and the natures and properties of things, their measure, form and order, or their number, weight and measure, [[12:9|that the hand of the Lord|quod hæc omnia manus Domini]], that is, the almighty power of God, [[12:9|hath made all these things|fecerit]]? For all things confess, declare and answer that they were made, and cry out with one accord: [[Ps 99:3|he made us, and not we ourselves|Ipse fecit nos, et non ipsi nos]]. For what is any creature but a ray of the Creator, in which God shines forth as the cause and maker in his effect? Wherefore Isaias says: [[Is 40:26|Lift up your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]]. And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 42:16|full of the glory of the Lord is his work|Gloria Domini plenum est opus ejus]].

paras.t: In cujus manu, id est potestate, est anima omnis viventis sub homine. Deus enim omnia in esse conservat, omnibus providet; et dum voluerit, mori seu deficere quævis permittit. Ideo cantat Psalmista: Avertente te faciem tuam, turbabuntur; auferes spiritum eorum, et deficient, et in pulverem suum revertentur. Et spiritus universæ carnis hominis, id est, omnis anima rationalis in manu est Dei, quantum ad esse naturæ, gratiæ et gloriæ. Unde Daniel impio dicit: Deum qui habet flatum tuum in manu sua, non glorificasti. Et Daniel rursus dixit de Deo: Juxta voluntatem suam facit tam in virtutibus cœli, quam in habitatoribus terræ.
paras.en: [[12:10|In whose hand|In cujus manu]], that is, power, [[12:10|is the soul of every living thing|est anima omnis viventis]] below man. For God keeps all things in being and provides for all; and when He wills, He lets any of them die or fail. Therefore the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 103:29|if thou turnest away thy face, they shall be troubled: thou shalt take away their breath, and they shall fail, and shall return to their dust|Avertente te faciem tuam, turbabuntur; auferes spiritum eorum, et deficient, et in pulverem suum revertentur]]. [[12:10|and the spirit of all flesh of man|Et spiritus universæ carnis hominis]], that is, every rational soul, is in the hand of God, as to its being in nature, in grace and in glory. Hence Daniel says to the wicked king: [[Dan 5:23|the God who hath thy breath in his hand|Deum qui habet flatum tuum in manu sua]], [[Dan 5:23|thou hast not glorified|non glorificasti]]. And Daniel said again of God: [[Dan 4:32|he doth according to his will, as well with the powers of heaven, as among the inhabitants of the earth|Juxta voluntatem suam facit tam in virtutibus cœli, quam in habitatoribus terræ]].

paras.t: Deinde ostendit, quod ex sensibilium cognitione, et per experientiam quamdam homines ad Dei cognitionem deveniant. Nonne auris verba dijudicat? id est, aures per vim auditivam in eis plantatam verba audiendo, ea discernunt, voces et sonos distinctim percipiendo. Nam et delectantur in sono convenienti ac dulci, et affliguntur in objecto disconvenienti. Hinc ait Gregorius: Quinque sensus corporis in omne quod sentiunt et discernunt, virtutem discretionis et sensus a cerebro trahunt. Basilius quoque: Concava, inquit, est auris, ut profunde recipiat; sordibus cholericis infecta viscosis, ut teneat; tympano arido perfecta, ut facile sentiat; quieto aere plena, ut nullus tumultus impediat. Et fauces comedentis, in quibus est sensus gustus, saporem dijudicant. Cibum enim contritum et undique tactum, quantum ad saporem, discernunt. Facit autem mentionem de auditu et gustu, quia auditus est sensus disciplinæ, secundum Philosophum. Per auditum enim plura discuntur, quam per alium sensum. Gustus vero est perceptivus alimentorum, quæ ad vitæ conservationem necessaria sunt. Hoc idem Eliu infra dicit: Auris verba dijudicat.
paras.en: Then he shows that men come to the knowledge of God from the knowledge of sensible things and through a kind of experience. [[12:11|Doth not the ear discern words|Nonne auris verba dijudicat]]? that is, the ears, by the power of hearing implanted in them, discern words in hearing them, perceiving voices and sounds distinctly. For they both take delight in a fitting and sweet sound, and are pained by an unfitting object. Hence Gregory says: The five senses of the body draw from the brain the power of discernment and of sensation in all that they perceive and discern. Basil too: The ear, he says, is hollow, that it may receive deeply; coated with sticky bilious wax, that it may hold fast; furnished with a dry drum, that it may perceive easily; filled with still air, that no tumult may hinder it. [[12:11|and the palate of him that eateth|Et fauces comedentis]], in which is the sense of taste, discern [[12:11|the taste|saporem]]: for they discern, as to its savour, food that has been ground and touched on every side. Now he mentions hearing and taste because hearing is the sense of learning, according to the Philosopher: for more is learned through hearing than through any other sense. And taste perceives foods, which are necessary for preserving life. Eliu says the same thing below: [[Job 34:3|the ear trieth words|Auris verba dijudicat]] [the Vulgate there has *probat* for *dijudicat*].

paras.t: In antiquis est sapientia: quod potissime verum est de sapientia acquisita per studium et laborem. Antiqui enim plura audierunt, legerunt, consideraverunt; nec ad sapientiam naturalem et philosophicam addiscendam aptus est homo, nisi prius addiscat scientias naturales inferiores. Sapientia autem ad contemplationem, prudentia vero ad practicam pertinet. Hinc subditur, et in multo tempore prudentia, id est, in his qui longe vixerunt, est prudentia, quæ est recta ratio agibilium, et per experientiam longam addiscitur. Unde et juvenes quum sint passionum sectatores, ad prudentiam minus sunt apti: quia non bene judicant de agendis, passione rationem obnubilante. Hinc in Ecclesiastico habetur: Quam speciosa veteranis sapientia et consilium! Corona senum multa peritia. Et alibi: Qui non est expertus, pauca recognoscit. Hinc quoque insipientia in senibus maxime vituperabilis indecensque consistit, sicut prætacto Ecclesiastici capitulo fertur: Tres species odivit anima mea: pauperem superbum, divitem mendacem, et senem fatuum et insensatum. Porro secundum Albertum, Job tacet de scientia: quia scientia est de rebus necessariis ac demonstrabilibus, ad quas unum est medium; et hoc juvenes facilius vident quam senes.
paras.en: [[12:12|In the ancient is wisdom|In antiquis est sapientia]]: which is most of all true of wisdom acquired by study and labour. For the ancients have heard, read and considered more things; nor is a man fit to learn natural and philosophical wisdom unless he first learns the lower natural sciences. Now wisdom belongs to contemplation, prudence to practice. Hence it is added, [[12:12|and in length of days prudence|et in multo tempore prudentia]], that is, in those who have lived long there is prudence, which is right reason about things to be done [*recta ratio agibilium*, the scholastic definition of prudence: reason rightly applied to action], and is learned by long experience. And so the young, since they are followers of the passions, are less fit for prudence: for they do not judge well of what is to be done, passion clouding their reason. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 25:7|O how comely is wisdom for the aged|Quam speciosa veteranis sapientia]] [[Ecclus 25:7|and counsel|et consilium]]! [[Ecclus 25:8|Much experience is the crown of old men|Corona senum multa peritia]]. And elsewhere: [[Ecclus 34:10|He that hath no experience, knoweth little|Qui non est expertus, pauca recognoscit]] [the margin's reference here is unreadable; the words are Ecclus 34:10]. Hence too folly in the old is most blameworthy and unseemly, as is said in the chapter of Ecclesiasticus just mentioned: [[Ecclus 25:3|Three sorts my soul hateth|Tres species odivit anima mea]]: [[Ecclus 25:4|A poor man that is proud: a rich man that is a liar: an old man that is a fool, and doting|pauperem superbum, divitem mendacem, et senem fatuum et insensatum]]. Further, according to Albert, Job is silent about knowledge [*scientia*: demonstrative science, as distinct from wisdom and prudence]: because knowledge is of things necessary and demonstrable, to which there is one middle term; and this the young see more easily than the old.

paras.t: Insuper tangit Job quid homines ex sensatis atque expertis de Deo addiscant. Apud ipsum est sapientia et fortitudo, id est, in Deo est sapientia, qua se ipsum et cuncta cognoscit, ceteraque disponit ac ordinat, et ipse est sapientia sua. Ipse quoque est sua potestas, qua cuncta creavit, et quæcumque placent, exsequitur. Et ipse habet consilium. Secundum Damascenum, consilium est ignorantis natura, quia consilium proprie sumptum, includit alicujus non sciti inquisitionem: sicque non competit Deo. Sed quum ei adscribitur, secluditur a ratione consilii quidquid est imperfectionis; et quod perfectionis in eo est, Deo superexcellenter adscribitur. Consilium ergo competit Deo, in quantum nil agit præcipitanter et sine idonea ratione, sed cuncta agit cum provida dispositione. Unde secundum Gregorium, consilium Dei est immobilis definitio de agendis: et sic in Scripturis frequenter adscribitur Deo, sicut in Psalmo: Consilium autem Domini in æternum manet. Et in Isaia Deus testatur: Consilium meum stabit. In Actis quoque Petrus affirmat, Christum consilio et præscientia Patris traditum. Et intelligentiam, id est purum simplicemque intuitum universorum. Vel, Intelligentiam, id est cognitionem eorum quæ non fuerunt, nec sunt, nec unquam erunt. Theologi enim ponunt in Deo duplicem notitiam, utpote notitiam simplicis visionis, qua noscit ea quæ fuerunt, sunt, vel erunt; et notitiam simplicis intelligentiæ, qua inspicit infinita quæ facere posset, nec tamen unquam fecit, facit aut faciet.
paras.en: Furthermore, Job touches on what men learn about God from things perceived by the senses and from experience. [[12:13|With him is wisdom and strength|Apud ipsum est sapientia et fortitudo]], that is, in God is the wisdom by which he knows himself and all things, and disposes and orders the rest; and he is his own wisdom. He is also his own power, by which he created all things and carries out whatever he pleases. [[12:13|He hath counsel|Et ipse habet consilium]]. According to Damascene, counsel belongs to the nature of one who does not know, because counsel, properly taken, includes the inquiry into something not known: and so it does not befit God. But when it is ascribed to him, whatever is of imperfection is set apart from the notion of counsel; and what of perfection is in it is ascribed to God in a surpassing way. Counsel, then, befits God in so far as he does nothing hastily and without fitting reason, but does all things with provident disposition. Hence according to Gregory, the counsel of God is his unchangeable determination about what is to be done: and in this sense it is often ascribed to God in the Scriptures, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:11|But the counsel of the Lord standeth for ever|Consilium autem Domini in æternum manet]]. And in Isaias God testifies: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand|Consilium meum stabit]]. In the Acts too Peter affirms that Christ was delivered up by the counsel and foreknowledge of the Father[[Acts 2:23||]]. [[12:13|and understanding|Et intelligentiam]], that is, a pure and simple gaze upon all things. Or, *understanding*, that is, the knowledge of things which have not been, are not, and never will be. For theologians posit in God a twofold knowledge: namely, the knowledge of simple vision, by which he knows the things which have been, are, or will be; and the knowledge of simple understanding, by which he beholds the infinite things he could make and yet never has made, makes or will make [the scholastic distinction between God's knowledge of what is actual at some time and of what is merely possible].

paras.t: Si destruxerit, auferendo ab homine esse naturæ vel gratiæ, aut regna seu alia quælibet dissipando, nemo est qui ædificet, id est, nullus destructa poterit reparare, Deo nolente, aut non cooperante, seu virtutem non dante. Si incluserit hominem carcere captivitatis, seu cujuslibet molestiæ adversitatis: unde superius Job dixit ad Dominum, Circumdedisti me carcere; nullus est qui aperiat contra Dei voluntatem. Si continuerit aquas pluviales aut fluviales, ne terram humectent, omnia siccabuntur, id est, terrarum spatia in superficie sicca fient, et fructus arescent. Aliquæ autem terræ rigantur aqua pluviali, aliquæ aqua fluviali. Propter quod in Deuteronomio Moyses ait ad Israelem: Terra quam ingredieris, non est sicut terra Ægypti, ubi jacto semine aquæ ducuntur irriguæ; sed montuosa est et campestris, de cœlo exspectans pluviam. Si emiserit eas super terram cum impetu et abundantia nimiis, ut in diluvio, subvertent terram, habitatores ejus interimendo, terræ nascentia corrumpendo, et glebas plurimas consumendo, vel etiam ædificia dirimendo. Itaque guttatim quasi per rivulos facit aquam moderanter descendere. In quibus omnibus sapientia et potestas Dei monstrantur. Hinc infra habetur: Qui ligat aquas in nubibus, ut non erumpant pariter deorsum.
paras.en: [[12:14|If he pull down|Si destruxerit]], by taking away from a man the being of nature or of grace, or by scattering kingdoms or any other things, [[12:14|there is no man that can build up|nemo est qui ædificet]], that is, no one will be able to repair what has been destroyed if God is unwilling, or does not cooperate, or does not give the power. [[12:14|if he shut up a man|Si incluserit hominem]] in the prison of captivity, or of any troublesome adversity (whence Job said to the Lord above, thou hast [[Job 7:12|enclosed me in a prison|Circumdedisti me carcere]] [the margin gives Job vi, 12; the words are Job 7:12]), [[12:14|there is none that can open|nullus est qui aperiat]] against the will of God. [[12:15|If he withhold the waters|Si continuerit aquas]] of rain or of rivers, so that they do not moisten the earth, [[12:15|all things shall be dried up|omnia siccabuntur]], that is, the expanses of the lands will become dry on the surface, and the crops will wither. For some lands are watered by rain, others by rivers. Wherefore in Deuteronomy Moses says to Israel: [[Deut 11:10|the land, which thou goest to possess, is not like the land of Egypt|Terra quam ingredieris, non est sicut terra Ægypti]], [[Deut 11:10|where, when the seed is sown, waters are brought in to water it|ubi jacto semine aquæ ducuntur irriguæ]]; [[Deut 11:11|But it is a land of hills and plains, expecting rain from heaven|sed montuosa est et campestris, de cœlo exspectans pluviam]]. [[12:15|and if he send them out|Si emiserit eas]] upon the earth with excessive force and abundance, as in the flood, [[12:15|they shall overturn the earth|subvertent terram]], by killing its inhabitants, spoiling what the earth brings forth, and consuming a great many clods, or even breaking down buildings. And so he makes the water come down in due measure, drop by drop, as through little channels. In all of which the wisdom and power of God are shown. Hence it is said below: [[Job 26:8|He bindeth up the waters in his clouds, so that they break not out and fall down together|Qui ligat aquas in nubibus, ut non erumpant pariter deorsum]].

paras.t: Apud ipsum est fortitudo et sapientia. Hoc sequitur atque concluditur a posteriori ex memoratis effectibus. Hinc Daniel: Sit nomen Domini benedictum a sæculo et usque in sæculum, quia sapientia et fortitudo ejus sunt. Ipse novit et decipientem, et omnem ejus astutiam, pravitatem atque processum, et eum qui decipitur, qua simplicitate vel ignorantia decipiatur. Aliter enim judex hominum justus et perfectus non esset, nisi inter virtuosos ac vitiosos discerneret. Hoc (ut apparet) Job interserit, quoniam vidit amicos suos partim a dæmone, partim a se ipsis deceptos, in tantum ut sic arguerent contra eum.
paras.en: [[12:16|With him is strength and wisdom|Apud ipsum est fortitudo et sapientia]]. This follows, and is concluded *a posteriori* [that is, by reasoning back from effects to their cause], from the effects just mentioned. Hence Daniel: [[Dan 2:20|Blessed be the name of the Lord from eternity and for evermore: for wisdom and fortitude are his|Sit nomen Domini benedictum a sæculo et usque in sæculum, quia sapientia et fortitudo ejus sunt]]. [[12:16|he knoweth both the deceivers|Ipse novit et decipientem]], and all his cunning, wickedness and course of action, [[12:16|and him that is deceived|et eum qui decipitur]], and by what simplicity or ignorance he is deceived. For otherwise he would not be a just and perfect judge of men, unless he distinguished between the virtuous and the vicious. Job puts this in, it seems, because he saw that his friends were deceived partly by the devil and partly by themselves, so far as to argue against him as they did.

paras.t: Adducit consiliarios in stultum finem. Dupliciter facit hoc. Primo, quia nonnunquam acutos consules justo judicio privat industria consiliandi, ita ut fini ab eis intento contraria veniant. Sicque Isaias dicit: Sapientes consiliarii Pharaonis dederunt consilium insipiens. David quoque secundo Regum precatus est: Obsecro, Domine, infatua consilium Achitophel. Secundo, exponitur de consiliariis impiis et obtusis, qui suis vitiis divina directione privantur, prout tertio Regum legitur accidisse filio Salomonis, qui inexpertorum juvenum sequens consilium, finem sortitus est stultum. Et judices in stuporem, ita ut quid agere debeant, non advertant, nec inquirere valeant. Deus enim variis modis considerationem rationis in eis impedire juste sapienterque potest, ita ut ipsi de sua hebetudine obstupescant, et in stuporem versi, ad judicia proferenda inepti sint. Hinc Isaias dicit: Dat scrutatores secretorum quasi non sint; judices terræ velut inane facit.
paras.en: [[12:17|He bringeth counsellors to a foolish end|Adducit consiliarios in stultum finem]]. He does this in two ways. First, because by a just judgment he sometimes deprives shrewd counsellors of skill in counselling, so that things contrary to the end they intended come about. And so Isaias says: [[Is 19:11|the wise counsellors of Pharao have given foolish counsel|Sapientes consiliarii Pharaonis dederunt consilium insipiens]]. David too prayed, in the second book of Kings: [[2 Kings 15:31|Infatuate, O Lord, I beseech thee, the counsel of Achitophel|Obsecro, Domine, infatua consilium Achitophel]]. Second, it is explained of wicked and dull counsellors, who through their own vices are deprived of divine guidance, as we read in the third book of Kings happened to the son of Solomon, who, following the counsel of inexperienced young men, came to a foolish end[[3 Kings 12:8||]] [the margin gives III Kings xii, 8–19]. [[12:17|and judges to insensibility|Et judices in stuporem]], so that they do not perceive what they ought to do, nor are able to inquire into it. For God can, justly and wisely, hinder in various ways the consideration of their reason, so that they are stupefied at their own dullness and, turned to stupor, are unfit to give judgments. Hence Isaias says: [[Is 40:23|He that bringeth the searchers of secrets to nothing, that hath made the judges of the earth as vanity|Dat scrutatores secretorum quasi non sint; judices terræ velut inane facit]].

paras.t: Circa hæc Thomas scholastice scribit, quod sicut Deus scit principia speculativarum scientiarum, et conclusiones ordinemque eorum ad invicem; non tamen ex principiis cognitionem conclusionum accepit, sed omnia puro ac simplici intellectu cognoscit: ita in operativis scit finem, et ea quæ sunt ad finem, et quæ viæ ad diversos fines obtinendos expediant; non tamen vias seu media ex finibus exquirit, sicut nos dum consiliamur. Quemadmodum ergo in Deo dicitur esse ratio, in quantum cognoscit ordinem principiorum ad sequentia, non tamen ei convenit investigare per modum rationis, ut in nobis ratio facit; ita apud Deum dicitur esse consilium, non per modum inquisitionis, sed per modum absolutæ ac simplicis cognitionis. Denique, profunditas consilii ex duobus perpenditur. Primo, dum quis subtilitate sui consilii adversarios suos consiliarios ad hoc deducit, ut ad inconvenientem finem deveniant: et quantum ad hoc, ait de Deo, Adducit consiliarios in stultum finem. Secundo, dum quis subtilitate sui consilii adversarios suos ducit ad hoc, ut ignorent quid agere debeant: sicut efficax disputator respondentem ducit ad hoc, sicque convincit, ut contradicere seu respondere nil queat. Et quoad hoc, ait de Deo: Et judices in stuporem. Quod consequenter quasi exemplariter manifestat.
paras.en: On these things Thomas writes in the scholastic manner that, just as God knows the principles of the speculative sciences, and the conclusions and their order to one another, and yet has not received the knowledge of the conclusions from the principles, but knows all things by a pure and simple understanding: so in practical matters he knows the end, and the things that are for the end, and what ways serve for obtaining various ends; and yet he does not search out the ways or means from the ends, as we do when we take counsel. As, then, reason is said to be in God in so far as he knows the order of principles to what follows from them, though it does not befit him to investigate in the manner of reason, as reason does in us: so counsel is said to be with God, not by way of inquiry, but by way of absolute and simple knowledge. Further, the depth of counsel is weighed in two ways. First, when someone by the subtlety of his counsel leads the counsellors opposed to him to come to an unfitting end: and with regard to this he says of God, [[12:17|He bringeth counsellors to a foolish end|Adducit consiliarios in stultum finem]]. Second, when someone by the subtlety of his counsel leads his adversaries to the point of not knowing what they ought to do: as a skilful disputant leads the respondent to this, and so refutes him that he can make no contradiction or answer. And with regard to this he says of God: [[12:17|and judges to insensibility|Et judices in stuporem]]. And this he next shows, as it were by examples.

paras.t: Balteum regum dissolvit, id est, reges expugnari facit, ita quod regali balteo spoliantur; et præcingit fune renes eorum: quia adversarii qui eos vicerunt, vili cingulo eos præcingunt virtute divina, sicut in Isaia Deus Cyro promisit: Ego, inquiens, ante te ibo, et gloriosos terræ humiliabo.
paras.en: [[12:18|He looseth the belt of kings|Balteum regum dissolvit]], that is, he causes kings to be overcome, so that they are stripped of the royal belt; [[12:18|and girdeth their loins with a cord|et præcingit fune renes eorum]]: for the enemies who have conquered them gird them with a mean girdle, by the power of God, as God promised Cyrus in Isaias, saying: [[Is 45:2|I will go before thee, and will humble the great ones of the earth|Ego, inquiens, ante te ibo, et gloriosos terræ humiliabo]].

paras.t: Ducit sacerdotes inglorios, id est, solita gloria quam habere solent a populo, eos privat, dum et ipsi simul cum regibus seu alias, voluntati hostium exponuntur, quemadmodum scripsit Osee: Attendite hoc, sacerdotes, quia vobiscum judicium est; et: Ruent in iniquitatibus suis. Sic et Amos in libro suo loquitur Amasiæ sacerdoti: Tu in terra polluta morieris. Jeremias quoque: Propheta, inquit, et sacerdos abierunt in terram quam ignoraverunt: quando videlicet in Chaldæam captivi abducti sunt. Et quam irreverenter Chaldæi tractaverunt sacerdotes Judæorum, Jeremias in Threnis deplorat. Et optimates, id est superiores in plebe, melioresque consules, supplantat, ita quod inutilia promunt consilia, et vincuntur, prout Amos de Deo asserit: Qui deridet vastitatem super robustum, et depopulationem super potentem affert. Itemque: Optimates capita populorum, nunc migrabunt in capite transmigrantium.
paras.en: [[12:19|He leadeth away priests without glory|Ducit sacerdotes inglorios]], that is, he deprives them of the glory they are wont to have from the people, when they too, together with kings or in other ways, are exposed to the will of their enemies, as Osee wrote: [[Osee 5:1|Hear ye this, O priests|Attendite hoc, sacerdotes]], [[Osee 5:1|for there is a judgment against you|quia vobiscum judicium est]]; and: [[Osee 5:5|shall fall in their iniquity|Ruent in iniquitatibus suis]]. So too Amos in his book says to Amasias the priest: [[Amos 7:17|thou shalt die in a polluted land|Tu in terra polluta morieris]]. Jeremias also: [[Jer 14:18|The prophet|Propheta]], he says, [[Jer 14:18|and the priest are gone into a land which they knew not|et sacerdos abierunt in terram quam ignoraverunt]]: namely, when they were led away captive into Chaldæa. And how irreverently the Chaldeans treated the priests of the Jews, Jeremias laments in the Lamentations[[Lam 4:16||]] [the margin's reference here is unreadable; Lam 4:16 is the likeliest place]. [[12:19|nobles|Et optimates]], that is, the chief men among the people and the better counsellors, he [[12:19|overthroweth|supplantat]], so that they put forth useless counsels and are overcome, as Amos asserts of God: [[Amos 5:9|He that with a smile bringeth destruction upon the strong, and waste upon the mighty|Qui deridet vastitatem super robustum, et depopulationem super potentem affert]] [Denis reads *deridet*, "mocks", where the Vulgate has *subridet*, "smiles"]. And again: [[Amos 6:1|great men, heads of the people|Optimates capita populorum]], [[Amos 6:7|now they shall go captive at the head of them that go into captivity|nunc migrabunt in capite transmigrantium]].

paras.t: Commutans labium veracium, id est, linguam eorum mutans a veritate ad loquendum mendacia: quod Deus non facit directe et effective, sed permissive, dum eos falli permittit, vel lumen naturale in eis propter eorum culpam obtenebrat, vel gratiam tollit: quemadmodum de philosophis ait Apostolus ad Romanos, quod Deus illis revelavit, videlicet lumen naturalis rationis præstando, per quod ad Dei notitiam ex creaturis perducti sunt; et postea addit, quod dicentes se sapientes esse, stulti facti sunt, quia videlicet propter eorum elationem, vanamque gloriam, naturale lumen in eis Deus offuscari permisit, ita quod innaturalissima docuerunt atque fecerunt, sicut ibidem Apostolus scribit. Denique, in Regum libro ait Michæas propheta, quomodo spiritus dixit: Egrediar, et ero spiritus mendax in ore omnium prophetarum ejus, scilicet regis Israel. Illi tamen non reputantur fuisse veraces. Juxta hunc modum loquens Dominus in Ezechiele: Propheta (inquit) quum erraverit, ego Dominus decepi prophetam illum. Et doctrinam senum auferens, dum senes propter eorum demerita vera sapientia privat, sicut et cor Salomonis tempore senectutis legitur infatuatum. Aliquando etiam propter subditorum peccata, tollit ab eis doctrinam senum, juxta quod ait Ezechieli: Linguam tuam adhærere faciam palato tuo, et eris mutus, nec quasi vir objurgans, quia domus exasperans est.
paras.en: [[12:20|He changeth the speech of the true speakers|Commutans labium veracium]], that is, changing their tongue from the truth to the speaking of lies: which God does not do directly and effectively, but by permission, when he allows them to be deceived, or darkens the natural light in them because of their guilt, or takes away grace: as the Apostle says of the philosophers in the Epistle to the Romans, that [[Rom 1:19|God hath manifested it unto them|Deus illis revelavit]], namely by granting the light of natural reason, by which they were led to the knowledge of God from creatures; and afterwards he adds that, [[Rom 1:22|professing themselves to be wise, they became fools|dicentes se sapientes esse, stulti facti sunt]], because, namely, on account of their pride and vainglory God allowed the natural light in them to be darkened, so that they taught and did the most unnatural things, as the Apostle writes in the same place[[Rom 1:26||]] [the margin gives Rom. i, 23–28]. Lastly, in the book of Kings the prophet Michæas tells how the spirit said: [[3 Kings 22:22|I will go forth, and be a lying spirit, in the mouth of all his prophets|Egrediar, et ero spiritus mendax in ore omnium prophetarum ejus]], that is, of the king of Israel. And yet those prophets are not reckoned to have been truthful. In this manner the Lord speaks in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 14:9|when the prophet shall err|Propheta (inquit) quum erraverit]], [[Ezech 14:9|I the Lord have deceived that prophet|ego Dominus decepi prophetam illum]]. [[12:20|and taketh away the doctrine of the aged|Et doctrinam senum auferens]], when he deprives old men of true wisdom because of their demerits, as we read that the heart of Solomon too was infatuated in the time of his old age[[3 Kings 11:4||]]. Sometimes too, because of the sins of their subjects, he takes away from them the doctrine of the aged, according to what he says to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 3:26|I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth, and thou shalt be dumb, and not as a man that reproveth: because they are a provoking house|Linguam tuam adhærere faciam palato tuo, et eris mutus, nec quasi vir objurgans, quia domus exasperans est]].

paras.t: Effundit despectionem super principes, id est, contemptos efficit eos, et honore præsidentiæ privat sæpe propter eorum excessus, prout in Nabuchodonosor factum legitur. Et in Isaia fertur: Ecce dominator Dominus auferet a Jerusalem judicem et principem. In libro Numerorum quoque Dominus ait ad Moysen: Suspende cunctos principes tribuum Israel in patibulis. Et Ecclesiasticus ait: Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis. Et eos qui oppressi fuerant per violentiam a potentioribus, relevat a sua angustia, juxta id Nahum: Bonus Dominus, et confortans in die tribulationis. Item in Psalmo: Dominus solvit compeditos; Dominus erigit elisos. Quandoque enim Deus hoc facit corporaliter et ante mortem: quemadmodum secundo Paralipomenon legitur, Manassen regem de carcere liberasse. Interdum agit hoc spiritualiter, dando patientiam in adversis, ut cum gaudio patiantur: sicut Apostoli ibant gaudentes a conspectu concilii, quia digni habiti sunt pro nomine Jesu contumeliam pati. Nonnunquam vero permittit electos usque ad mortem adversitatibus opprimi, ut in martyribus constat: sed tanto hos gloriosius relevat et coronat in patria, quo durius permisit flagellari in via, juxta illud libri Sapientiæ: In paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur.
paras.en: [[12:21|He poureth contempt upon princes|Effundit despectionem super principes]], that is, he makes them despised, and often deprives them of the honour of their rule because of their excesses, as we read was done in Nabuchodonosor[[Dan 4:28||]] [the margin gives Dan. iv, 28 and following]. And in Isaias it is said: [[Is 3:1|behold the sovereign Lord of hosts shall take away from Jerusalem|Ecce dominator Dominus auferet a Jerusalem]] [[Is 3:2|the judge|judicem]] and [[Is 3:3|The captain|principem]] [Denis draws together Is 3:1–3, which the margin cites]. In the book of Numbers too the Lord says to Moses: [[Num 25:4|Take all the princes of the people, and hang them up on gibbets|Suspende cunctos principes tribuum Israel in patibulis]] [Denis has "the princes of the tribes of Israel" for "the princes of the people"]. And Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes, and hath set up the meek in their stead|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus, et sedere fecit mites pro eis]]. [[12:21|and relieveth them that were oppressed|Et eos qui oppressi fuerant]], those, that is, who had been oppressed by violence at the hands of the more powerful, he relieves from their distress, according to that of Nahum: [[Nah 1:7|The Lord is good, and giveth strength in the day of trouble|Bonus Dominus, et confortans in die tribulationis]]. Also in the Psalm: [[Ps 145:7|The Lord looseth them that are fettered|Dominus solvit compeditos]]; [[Ps 145:8|The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down|Dominus erigit elisos]]. For sometimes God does this bodily and before death: as we read in the second book of Paralipomenon that he freed King Manasses from prison[[2 Par 33:13||]]. At times he does it spiritually, by giving patience in adversity, so that they suffer with joy: as the Apostles [[Acts 5:41|went from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were accounted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus|ibant gaudentes a conspectu concilii, quia digni habiti sunt pro nomine Jesu contumeliam pati]]. But sometimes he allows the elect to be crushed by adversities even to death, as is plain in the martyrs: but he raises them up and crowns them in the fatherland the more gloriously, the more harshly he allowed them to be scourged on the way, according to that of the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 3:5|Afflicted in few things, in many they shall be well rewarded|In paucis vexati, in multis bene disponentur]].

paras.t: Qui revelat profunda de tenebris, id est, occulta et mystica per revelationem clare facit cognosci: quæ manifestantur de tenebris, id est occulto quo latent. Hinc scriptum est in Daniele: Ipse revelat profunda et abscondita, et novit in tenebris constituta. Et alibi legitur: Est Deus in cœlo revelans mysteria. Sic docuit Salomonem. Et producit in lucem umbram mortis: quia dispositos ad interitum, reducit ad sanitatem; et quæ ita sunt clausa ut mortis umbra, Deo illustrante, fiunt clara et certa. Unde et Christus ait Apostolis: Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni Dei; ceteris autem in parabolis. Et rursus: Quod dico vobis in tenebris, dicite in lumine. Hoc etiam efficit Deus, dum radiante gratia ejus, peccata diu abscondita in confessione lucide aperiuntur, seu infideles ad fidei claritatem ac gratiam convertuntur, quemadmodum per Isaiam Pater loquitur Christo: Dedi te in lucem gentium, ut aperires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de conclusione vinctum, de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris. Unde et Thomas dicit: Umbra mortis, ignorantia vel stultitia esse videtur, quum per cognitionem viventia a non viventibus maxime distinguantur. Producit ergo umbram mortis in lucem, dum ignorantibus sapientiam tribuit, vel sapientes, quorum sapientia fuit ignota, sapientes esse ostendit.
paras.en: [[12:22|He discovereth deep things out of darkness|Qui revelat profunda de tenebris]], that is, he makes hidden and mystical things clearly known by revelation: things which are brought to light out of darkness, that is, out of the hiddenness in which they lie. Hence it is written in Daniel: [[Dan 2:22|He revealeth deep and hidden things, and knoweth what is in darkness|Ipse revelat profunda et abscondita, et novit in tenebris constituta]]. And elsewhere we read: [[Dan 2:28|there is a God in heaven that revealeth mysteries|Est Deus in cœlo revelans mysteria]]. So he taught Solomon. [[12:22|and bringeth up to light the shadow of death|Et producit in lucem umbram mortis]]: for he brings back to health those who were on the way to death; and things so shut up as to be like the shadow of death become clear and certain when God sheds his light on them. Hence Christ too says to the Apostles: [[Luke 8:10|To you it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest in parables|Vobis datum est nosse mysteria regni Dei; ceteris autem in parabolis]] [the margin gives Matt. xiii, 11 and Luke viii, 10; Denis's *mysteria*, "mysteries", is Matthew's word, the rest is Luke's]. And again: [[Matt 10:27|That which I tell you in the dark, speak ye in the light|Quod dico vobis in tenebris, dicite in lumine]]. God brings this about also when, by the shining of his grace, sins long hidden are laid open plainly in confession, or unbelievers are converted to the brightness of faith and to grace, as the Father says to Christ through Isaias: [[Is 42:6|I have given thee|Dedi te]] [[Is 42:6|for a light of the Gentiles|in lucem gentium]], [[Is 42:7|That thou mightest open the eyes of the blind, and bring forth the prisoner out of prison, and them that sit in darkness out of the prison house|ut aperires oculos cæcorum, et educeres de conclusione vinctum, de domo carceris sedentes in tenebris]]. Hence Thomas too says: The shadow of death seems to be ignorance or folly, since living things are distinguished from non-living above all by knowledge. He brings the shadow of death to light, then, when he gives wisdom to the ignorant, or shows to be wise those wise men whose wisdom was unknown.

paras.t: Qui multiplicat gentes, per nativitatem quotidie, juxta illud in Psalmo: Secundum altitudinem tuam multiplicasti filios hominum. Multiplicat quoque gentes per diversitates nationum, terrarum, linguarum, quemadmodum post diluvium in constructione turris Babel, confudit labium universæ carnis, prout in Genesi legitur: Descendit Dominus ut videret civitatem et turrim quam ædificaverant filii Adam, et dixit: Ecce unus est populus et labium unum omnibus. Venite ergo, et confundamus ibi linguam eorum. Et divisit eos Dominus ex illo loco in universas terras. Et perdit eas, per diversa genera mortis, puta per pestilentiam, famem, gladium, et per bestias terræ, seu aliam speciem mortis. De quibus ait in Ezechiele frequenter: Quod si misero in eos quatuor judicia mea pessima, id est quatuor pœnas has judiciales et malas malitia pœnæ, non culpæ, imo et pessimas, quia valde acerbas. Et subversas in integrum restituet, id est, ad priorem statum numerumque reducet, non easdem numero, sed specie. Propter quod ait in Deuteronomio: Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam. Et in Baruch scriptum est: Exterminati sunt, et alii in loco eorum surrexerunt.
paras.en: [[12:23|He multiplieth nations|Qui multiplicat gentes]], by birth every day, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 11:9|according to thy highness, thou hast multiplied the children of men|Secundum altitudinem tuam multiplicasti filios hominum]]. He multiplies nations also by diversities of peoples, lands and tongues, as after the flood, at the building of the tower of Babel, he confounded the speech of all flesh, as we read in Genesis: [[Gen 11:5|the Lord came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of Adam were building|Descendit Dominus ut videret civitatem et turrim quam ædificaverant filii Adam]]. [[Gen 11:6|And he said: Behold, it is one people, and all have one tongue|et dixit: Ecce unus est populus et labium unum omnibus]]. [[Gen 11:7|Come ye, therefore, let us go down, and there confound their tongue|Venite ergo, et confundamus ibi linguam eorum]]. [[Gen 11:8|And so the Lord scattered them from that place into all lands|Et divisit eos Dominus ex illo loco in universas terras]]. [[12:23|and destroyeth them|Et perdit eas]], by various kinds of death, for instance by pestilence, famine, the sword and the beasts of the earth, or some other kind of death. Of these he often says in Ezechiel: if I shall send upon them [[Ezech 14:21|my four grievous judgments|quatuor judicia mea pessima]], that is, these four judicial punishments, evil with the evil of punishment, not of guilt [that is, evil as suffering is evil, not as sin is], and indeed most evil, because very bitter [*pessima*, "most evil", which the Douay-Rheims renders "grievous"]. [[12:23|and restoreth them again after they were overthrown|Et subversas in integrum restituet]] [a note in the margin gives the variant reading *restituit*, "restoreth"], that is, he will bring them back to their former state and number, not the same in number, but in kind. Wherefore he says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:39|I will kill and I will make to live|Ego occidam, et ego vivere faciam]]. And in Baruch it is written: [[Bar 3:19|They are cut off|Exterminati sunt]], [[Bar 3:19|and others are risen up in their place|et alii in loco eorum surrexerunt]].

paras.t: Qui immutat cor principum populi terræ, id est, intellectum et voluntatem dominorum et principum ad libitum suum movet, alterat, afficit et disponit, vertendo et inclinando corda illorum ad omne complacitum sibi, ita ut cogitent et velint quæ Deus inspirat, quidquid antea aliter disposuerint atque decreverint, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Cor regis in manu Dei est; quocumque voluerit, vertet illud. Ex quo innotescit, sapientiam Dei intima cordium intueri. Unde primo Regum de Saule conscribitur: Immutavit ei Deus cor aliud. Et decipit eos, id est, falli permittit, illuminationem suam juste subtrahendo, sicut in Ezechiele scriptum jam retuli; ut frustra incedant, id est, inaniter tendant ad finem intentum, per invium, id est per falsitatis et impietatis opera atque consilia, per quæ ad finem non perducuntur optatum, sicut per Jeremiam dicitur Sedeciæ regi: Seduxerunt te, et prævaluerunt adversus te omnes viri pacifici tui.
paras.en: [[12:24|He changeth the heart of the princes of the people of the earth|Qui immutat cor principum populi terræ]], that is, he moves, alters, affects and disposes as he pleases the understanding and will of lords and princes, turning and bending their hearts to all that pleases him, so that they think and will what God inspires, however they had previously disposed and decreed otherwise, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 21:1|the heart of the king is in the hand of the Lord: whithersoever he will, he shall turn it|Cor regis in manu Dei est; quocumque voluerit, vertet illud]]. From this it is made known that the wisdom of God looks upon the inmost parts of hearts. Hence it is written of Saul in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 10:9|God gave unto him another heart|Immutavit ei Deus cor aliud]] [the Latin has *immutavit*, "changed", the word of Job's *immutat*]. [[12:24|and deceiveth them|Et decipit eos]], that is, allows them to be deceived, justly withdrawing his enlightenment, as I have already quoted from Ezechiel; [[12:24|that they walk in vain|ut frustra incedant]], that is, strive emptily toward the end they intend, [[12:24|where there is no way|per invium]], that is, through works and counsels of falsehood and impiety, by which they are not brought to the end they desire, as is said through Jeremias to King Sedecias: [[Jer 38:22|Thy men of peace have deceived thee, and have prevailed against thee|Seduxerunt te, et prævaluerunt adversus te omnes viri pacifici tui]] [the margin gives Jer. xxxviii, 23; the words are in v. 22].

paras.t: Palpabunt, id est, periculose, timide et dubiose incedent, quasi certum ac sanum consilium non habentes, quasi in tenebris ignorantiæ, in quibus vere sunt, et non in luce veritatis atque justitiæ. Vel, Quasi in tenebris, id est, sicut ambulantes in tenebris solent palpare, ne se lædant aut pedem offendant. Hoc dicitur quantum ad eos, qui ex ignorantia errant et peccant. Quantum vero ad eos, qui errant seu peccant ex passione judicium rationis ligante et contenebrante circa particularia agenda vel omittenda, ne cognitionem universalem quam habebant vel habent, ad talia applicent, sed mala judicent bona, juxta illud Proverbiorum, Omnis via viri recta sibi videtur: quantum (inquam) ad hos, subditur, et errare eos faciet a luce veritatis et rectitudine æquitatis, quasi ebrios, in quibus ratio per ebrietatem et passiones eam sequentes, maxime impeditur. Hoc autem facit Deus, quia permittit, ut loquitur Isaias: Quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis? Itemque Psalmographus: Turbati sunt et moti sunt sicut ebrius, et omnis sapientia eorum devorata est. Unde in Proverbiis inducitur: Via impiorum tenebrosa: nesciunt ubi corruunt.
paras.en: [[12:25|They shall grope|Palpabunt]], that is, they will go forward perilously, timidly and doubtfully, as having no sure and sound counsel, [[12:25|as in the dark|quasi in tenebris]] of ignorance, in which they truly are, [[12:25|and not in the light|et non in luce]] of truth and justice. Or, *as in the dark*, that is, as those who walk in the dark are wont to grope, so as not to hurt themselves or strike their foot. This is said with regard to those who err and sin out of ignorance. But with regard to those who err or sin out of passion, which binds and darkens the judgment of reason about particular things to be done or left undone, so that they do not apply to such things the universal knowledge they had or have, but judge evil things good, according to that of Proverbs, [[Prov 21:2|Every way of a man seemeth right to himself|Omnis via viri recta sibi videtur]]: with regard to these (I say) it is added, [[12:25|and he shall make them stagger|et errare eos faciet]] from the light of truth and the uprightness of equity, [[12:25|like men that are drunk|quasi ebrios]], in whom reason is hindered most of all by drunkenness and the passions that follow it. Now God does this because he permits it, as Isaias says: [[Is 63:17|Why hast thou made us to err, O Lord, from thy ways|Quare nos errare fecisti de viis tuis?]]? And the Psalmist: [[Ps 106:27|They were troubled, and reeled like a drunken man; and all their wisdom was swallowed up|Turbati sunt et moti sunt sicut ebrius, et omnis sapientia eorum devorata est]]. Hence it is brought in in Proverbs: [[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|Via impiorum tenebrosa: nesciunt ubi corruunt]].

paras.t: Ex omnibus istis effectibus probatur profunditas sapientiæ atque subtilitas consilii Dei, qua omnia quæ in rebus humanis reputantur excelsa, perducuntur in stultum finem sive stuporem. Quod ex libris historialibus sacræ Scripturæ, præsertim ex libris Judicum, Regum et Paralipomenon, clarissime potest pensari ex his, quæ ibi de regibus ac principibus, eorumque prœliis recitantur: quæ, nisi quis providentiam Dei attenderet, incredibilia viderentur.
paras.en: From all these effects is proved the depth of the wisdom and the subtlety of the counsel of God, by which all things that are reckoned lofty in human affairs are brought to a foolish end or to stupor. And this can be weighed most clearly from the historical books of sacred Scripture, especially from the books of Judges, Kings and Paralipomenon, from what is related there of kings and princes and their battles: things which, unless one looked to the providence of God, would seem incredible.

12.title: De tropologica ejusdem capituli duodecimi intelligentia.
12.title_en: On the tropological sense of the same twelfth chapter

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dicit: Ergo vos soli estis homines? Job contra veritatis a se prolatæ adversarios disputans, figurat quemlibet justum ac sapientem, vera ac justa disputando seu alio modo tuentem, et culpabiles increpantem: qui si viderit aliquos nimis de suo ingenio confidentes, de sua scientia præsumentes, et ceteros velut indoctos superbe seu aspernanter affantes, zelo Dei increpatorie dicere potest eis: Ergo vos soli estis homines? Quod etiam quilibet devotus abbas, prior, decanus, dicere potest, si in suo conventu viderit aliquos proprio sensui nimium innitentes. Tanquam dicat: Nolite tantum præsumere de vestra industria, ratione, scientia. Nam, ut ait Gregorius, Quisquis præire se ratione omnes existimat, scilicet omnes de suo consortio, vel omnes simpliciter, quid aliud quam solum se esse hominem putat? Per rationem quippe homo a brutis secernitur. Hinc vere sapientes et humiles, alieno magis quam proprio credere solent judicio, et præsertim superiorum suorum judicio contradicere perterrentur. Unde Romanos monet Apostolus: Nolite prudentes esse apud vosmetipsos. Itaque, dociles ac dirigibiles simus, propriæ mentis imbecillitatem pensemus; et quam modica sunt quæ scimus, respectu eorum quæ ignoramus, sagaciter ponderemus. Alioqui formidandum, ne verificetur in nobis illud Isaiæ: Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te.
paras.en: [[12:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dicit]]: [[12:2|Are you then men alone|Ergo vos soli estis homines]]? Job, disputing against the adversaries of the truth he had uttered, figures any just and wise man who defends what is true and just, by disputing or in some other way, and rebukes the guilty: if such a man sees some trusting too much in their own wit, presuming on their own knowledge, and addressing the rest proudly or scornfully as though they were unlearned, he can say to them in rebuke, with the zeal of God: [[12:2|Are you then men alone|Ergo vos soli estis homines]]? Any devout abbot, prior or dean can say this too, if he sees some in his community leaning too much on their own judgment. As if to say: Do not presume so much on your own diligence, reason and knowledge. For, as Gregory says, Whoever thinks that he goes before all in reason (that is, all of his own company, or simply all), what else does he think but that he alone is a man? For it is by reason that man is set apart from the brutes. Hence those who are truly wise and humble are wont to trust another's judgment more than their own, and are greatly afraid above all to contradict the judgment of their superiors. So the Apostle admonishes the Romans: [[Rom 12:16|Be not wise in your own conceits|Nolite prudentes esse apud vosmetipsos]]. Let us therefore be teachable and ready to be guided, let us weigh the weakness of our own mind, and shrewdly ponder how little the things we know are beside those we do not know. Otherwise it is to be feared that that word of Isaias may be made true in us: [[Is 47:10|Thy wisdom, and, thy knowledge, this hath deceived thee|Sapientia tua et scientia tua decepit te]].

paras.t: Insuper, talibus sciolis subsannatorie dici potest ex caritate, ut corrigantur confusi: Et vobiscum morietur sapientia? hoc est, nolite ita de vobis sentire: nolite putare, quod vos solos Deus illuminet, quod intra vos tantum loquatur, quod Sol sapientiæ alibi quoque non splendeat: præsertim quum dicat Apostolus, Quis scit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus hominis? Et denuo: Per humilitatem superiores invicem arbitramini. Postremo, etsi quis doctior sit aliis eruditione humana, nihilominus pie credat, quod alii plus eo abundant sapientia atque scientia, in quantum sunt dona Spiritus Sancti: quæ tanto plus abundant in unoquoque, quanto perfectior exstat in caritate et humilitate.
paras.en: Moreover, such smatterers may be told mockingly, out of charity, so that they may be put to shame and corrected: [[12:2|and shall wisdom die with you?|Et vobiscum morietur sapientia?]] That is, do not think so of yourselves; do not think that God enlightens you alone, that he speaks within you only, that the Sun of wisdom does not shine elsewhere too: especially since the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 2:11|what man knoweth the things of a man, but the spirit of a man|Quis scit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus hominis?]]? [Denis's wording is looser: who knows what goes on in a man, but the spirit of the man?] And again: [[Phil 2:3|in humility, let each esteem others better than themselves|Per humilitatem superiores invicem arbitramini]]. Lastly, even if someone is more learned than others in human learning, let him nevertheless piously believe that others abound more than he in wisdom and knowledge, in so far as these are gifts of the Holy Ghost: which abound the more in each one, the more perfect he is in charity and humility.

paras.t: Et mihi est cor sicut vobis. Hoc præsertim superior dicere potest inferiori superbienti de sua scientia. Nec inferior vestri sum: imo superior tanquam Christi vicarius: idcirco mihi credere et deferre tenemini propter ejus, cujus circa vos gero vices, reverentiam et personam. Contra rebelles quidem potest et debet prælatus suo tempore auctoritatem prætendere, ut refrenetur eorum elatio, et formident.
paras.en: [[12:3|I also have a heart as well as you|Et mihi est cor sicut vobis]]. A superior especially can say this to an inferior who is proud of his knowledge. Nor am I inferior to you [these words of the Vulgate, nec inferior vestri sum, are left out in the Douay-Rheims]: nay, I am your superior, as the vicar of Christ; and therefore you are bound to believe me and defer to me, out of reverence for him whose place I hold over you, and for his person. Against the rebellious, indeed, a prelate can and ought in due time to put forward his authority, so that their pride may be curbed and they may fear.

paras.t: Qui deridetur ab amico suo sicut ego, invocabit Deum, et exaudiet eum. Hujus verbi recordemur, si contigerit nos a confratre et proximo, præsertim ab aliquo specialiter caro, derideri. Tunc itaque non irascamur, non indignemur, non reddamus malum pro malo: sed indulgeamus ex animo, et erranti condoleamus: quod si culpabiles fuerimus, emendemus. Itaque Deum tunc invocemus, orando pro irrisore et pro nobis, ut simul in vera caritate crescamus. Denique, alium deridere non est leve peccatum, quum scriptum sit in libro Proverbiorum: Illusores Deus deludet. Deridetur justi simplicitas. Quo aliquem virtuosiorem et Christo in omni paupertate, persecutione, patientia, abjectione, humilitate et sancta simplicitate conformiorem adspicimus; eo hunc cordialiter plus amemus, reputemus ac veneremur, tanquam Dei electum, et Sancti Spiritus templum. Nec eos qui sæculo sunt abjecti, vilipendamus: imo potius eos qui in mundo hoc prosperantur, deliciantur, et impie conversantur, secundum quod tales sunt, justo zelo spernamus; personam tamen amemus, et pro ipsa affectuose precemur, pensantes nos quoque tales dudum potuisse fuisse, nisi Dei nos prævenisset clementia: qua abstracta, adhuc tales efficeremur. Hoc plane spectat ad virum justum, secundum id Psalmi: Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus; timentes autem Dominum glorificat.
paras.en: [[12:4|He that is mocked by his friends as I, shall call upon God and he will hear him|Qui deridetur ab amico suo sicut ego, invocabit Deum, et exaudiet eum]]. Let us remember this word if it happens that we are mocked by a brother and neighbour, above all by someone especially dear to us. Then let us not be angry, not be indignant, not render evil for evil, but forgive from the heart and have compassion on the one who errs; and if we are at fault, let us amend. And so let us then call upon God, praying for the mocker and for ourselves, that we may grow together in true charity. Further, to mock another is no light sin, since it is written in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 3:34|He shall scorn the scorners|Illusores Deus deludet]]. [[12:4|for the simplicity of the just man is laughed to scorn|Deridetur justi simplicitas]]. The more virtuous we see someone to be, and the more conformed to Christ in all poverty, persecution, patience, abjection, humility and holy simplicity, the more heartily let us love, esteem and venerate him, as one chosen of God and a temple of the Holy Ghost. Nor let us make light of those who are cast off by the world: rather let us scorn with a just zeal, in so far as they are such, those who prosper in this world, live in pleasures and behave impiously; yet let us love the person, and pray for him affectionately, considering that we too could long since have been such, had not the mercy of God gone before us: and were that withdrawn, we should even now become such. This plainly belongs to the just man, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 14:4|In his sight the malignant is brought to nothing: but he glorifieth them that fear the Lord|Ad nihilum deductus est in conspectu ejus malignus; timentes autem Dominum glorificat]].

paras.t: Lampas contempta. Recte justus seu ejus simplicitas lampas vocatur, propter virtutum splendorem. Nam et Apostolis loquitur Christus: Vos estis lux mundi. Et ad Philippenses scribit Apostolus: In medio nationis perversæ lucetis sicut luminaria mundi. De Christo quoque Isaias inducit: Egrediatur ut splendor justus ejus, et salvator ejus ut lampas accendatur. Sic Christi justi justorum simplicitas a Judæis deridebatur, dicentibus: Homo vorax, potator vini, amicus peccatorum. Quem et Herodes illudens, induit veste alba, milites purpura. Sed hi justorum contemptores, in die judicii dicturi sunt illud libri Sapientiæ: Nos insensati, vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam, et finem sine honore: quomodo ergo computati sunt inter filios Dei?
paras.en: [[12:5|The lamp despised|Lampas contempta]]. The just man, or his simplicity, is rightly called a lamp, because of the splendour of his virtues. For Christ too says to the apostles: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]]. And the Apostle writes to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:15|in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation|In medio nationis perversæ]] [[Phil 2:15|you shine as lights in the world|lucetis sicut luminaria mundi]]. Of Christ, too, Isaias brings in the words: [[Is 62:1|her just one come forth as brightness, and her saviour be lighted as a lamp|Egrediatur ut splendor justus ejus, et salvator ejus ut lampas accendatur]] [Denis reads it as a wish: let her just one come forth as brightness, and let her saviour be lighted as a lamp]. So the simplicity of Christ, the Just One of the just, was mocked by the Jews, who said: [[Matt 11:19|a man that is a glutton and a wine drinker|Homo vorax, potator vini]], [[Matt 11:19|a friend of publicans and sinners|amicus peccatorum]] [Denis has only: a friend of sinners]. Herod too, mocking him, put a white garment on him[[Luke 23:11||]], and the soldiers clothed him in purple[[Mark 15:17||]]. But these despisers of the just will say on the day of judgment that word of the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:4|We fools esteemed their life madness, and their end without honour|Nos insensati, vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam, et finem sine honore]]: [[Wis 5:5|how they are numbered among the children of God|quomodo ergo computati sunt inter filios Dei?]]?

paras.t: Abundant tabernacula prædonum, et audacter provocant Deum. Prædo intelligi potest omnis peccator, præsertim superbus, qui gloriam et honorem soli Deo debita ac solvenda, appetit et usurpat. Omnis quoque peccator debitum Deo subtrahit cultum; et quæ Dei sunt, in suum redigit usum ac commodum, quasi a Deo creata sibique data ab illo non essent. Nam, ut ait S. Hilarius, Sicut a Deo est quidquid habemus et sumus, ita in Dei honorem et cultum expendere omne illud debemus. Qui ergo pro libitu proprio utitur membris suis et sensibus, viribus, rebus et opibus, magnam committit fraudem, grande furtum, vitiosam rapinam. Verumtamen tales temporalibus sæpe abundant; sed vitiis magis exuberant, et audacter provocant Deum, sicut et omnes intimorati et vitiosi, divini judicii rigorem non perpendentes: quorum contenebrata est mens, ut immensa pericula, quibus circumdati sunt, non advertant, nec caveant, neque formident. De quibus dicit Ecclesiastes: Quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala. De quorum quolibet fert Psalmista: Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso; non est timor Dei ante oculos ejus. Hi sunt qui quum Deum offenderint, et concupiscentiæ damnandæ satisfecerint, pro eo quod pœnitere et erubescere mox deberent, gaudent, jactant, propalant talia se fecisse: quod est peccatum gravissimum. De quibus scribitur in Proverbiis: Lætantur quum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis. Isaias quoque: Peccatum suum quasi Sodoma prædicaverunt, nec absconderunt.
paras.en: [[12:6|The tabernacles of robbers abound, and they provoke God boldly|Abundant tabernacula prædonum, et audacter provocant Deum]]. By the robber may be understood every sinner, above all the proud man, who covets and usurps the glory and honour that are owed and to be paid to God alone. Every sinner, too, withholds from God the worship owed to him, and turns the things that are God's to his own use and profit, as if they had not been created by God and given to him by God. For, as St. Hilary says, As whatever we have and are is from God, so we ought to spend all of it on the honour and worship of God. He, then, who uses his members and senses, his strength, goods and wealth at his own pleasure, commits a great fraud, a grievous theft, a wicked robbery. Yet such men often abound in temporal things; but they overflow still more with vices, and [[12:6|they provoke God boldly|audacter provocant Deum]], as do all who are without fear and full of vice, not weighing the rigour of the divine judgment: whose mind is so darkened that they neither notice nor guard against nor fear the immense dangers that surround them. Of them Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 8:11|because sentence is not speedily pronounced against the evil, the children of men commit evils without any fear|Quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala]]. Of each one of them the Psalmist says: [[Ps 35:2|The unjust hath said within himself, that he would sin: there is no fear of God before his eyes|Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso; non est timor Dei ante oculos ejus]]. These are they who, when they have offended God and satisfied a damnable concupiscence, instead of repenting and blushing at once, as they ought, rejoice, boast and make it known that they have done such things: which is a most grievous sin. Of them it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 2:14|are glad when they have done evil, and rejoice in the most wicked things|Lætantur quum male fecerint, et exsultant in rebus pessimis]]. And Isaias: [[Is 3:9|they have proclaimed abroad their sin as Sodom, and they have not hid it|Peccatum suum quasi Sodoma prædicaverunt, nec absconderunt]].

paras.t: Hoc ergo faciunt, non obstante quod ipse Deus dederit omnia quæ habent et sunt in manibus eorum, id est in eorum libertate ac potestate, ut de his Creatori suo sponte servirent, propter quod eum merito amarent et honorarent in omnibus; sed ingrati et excæcati sunt prorsus. Quod etiam in divitibus magis contingit, quia superbiores esse consueverunt, et sensualitatem foventes, Deum ac spiritualia non advertunt, secundum illud Deuteronomii: Incrassatus est dilectus, et recalcitravit; dereliquit Deum factorem suum.
paras.en: This, then, they do, although [[12:6|it is he that hath given all|ipse Deus dederit omnia]] that they have and are [[12:6|into their hands|in manibus eorum]], that is, into their freedom and power, so that with these they might serve their Creator freely, and for this might deservedly love and honour him in all things; but they are wholly ungrateful and blinded. This happens more among the rich, because they are wont to be prouder, and, fostering their sensuality, they pay no heed to God and spiritual things, according to that of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:15|The beloved grew fat, and kicked|Incrassatus est dilectus, et recalcitravit]]; [[Deut 32:15|he forsook God who made him|dereliquit Deum factorem suum]].

paras.t: Interroga jumenta, id est ingenio tardiores, et docebunt te; et volatilia cœli, id est contemplativos, doctos, ingeniosos. Loquere terræ, id est carnalibus terrena sapientibus, et respondebit tibi. Et narrabunt pisces maris, id est animo vagi, curiosi, instabiles. Omnes hi concorditer sciunt, dicunt, respondent quod subditur: Quis ignorat, quod hæc omnia manus Domini fecerit? Quod enim unum sit omnium rerum causale principium, omnes jam boni et mali, litterati et simplices, norunt.
paras.en: [[12:7|ask now the beasts|Interroga jumenta]], that is, those slower of wit, [[12:7|and they shall teach thee|et docebunt te]]; [[12:7|and the birds of the air|et volatilia cœli]], that is, the contemplative, the learned, the gifted. [[12:8|Speak to the earth|Loquere terræ]], that is, to the carnal, who savour earthly things, [[12:8|and it shall answer thee|et respondebit tibi]]. [[12:8|and the fishes of the sea shall tell|Et narrabunt pisces maris]], that is, those wandering in mind, curious, unstable. All these with one accord know, say and answer what follows: [[12:9|Who is ignorant that the hand of the Lord hath made all these things?|Quis ignorat, quod hæc omnia manus Domini fecerit?]] For that there is one causal principle of all things, all now know, good and bad, learned and simple.

paras.t: Nonne auris verba dijudicat? Hoc de interioribus auribus accipi potest, quæ verba vocalia, mediante sensu exteriori et sensu communi ac imaginatione, percipiunt, noscunt et judicant. Verba autem mentalia, quæ intellectus intra se profert, immediate advertunt atque discernunt. Verba vero interna, quæ Deus per se ipsum vel per angelos loquitur animæ, per illuminationem supernam audiunt, noscunt, dijudicant, juxta illud Zachariæ: Angelus loquebatur in me. Et in Psalmo: Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus. Sed, proh dolor! multi sunt qui internam Dei et angeli allocutionem advertere nolunt; qui divinæ inspirationi resistunt; qui bonis inclinationibus ac admonitionibus renituntur, diabolicis vero suggestionibus præbent consensum.
paras.en: [[12:11|Doth not the ear discern words|Nonne auris verba dijudicat]]? This can be taken of the inward ears, which perceive, know and judge spoken words by means of the outward sense and of the common sense [that is, the inner sense that gathers and compares what the outward senses report] and the imagination. Mental words, which the intellect utters within itself, they notice and discern immediately. And the inward words which God speaks to the soul, by himself or through the angels, they hear, know and discern by a light from above, according to that of Zacharias: [[Zach 2:3|the angel that spoke in me|Angelus loquebatur in me]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 84:9|I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me|Audiam quid loquatur in me Dominus Deus]]. But, alas! there are many who will not heed the inward speaking of God and of the angel; who resist divine inspiration; who struggle against good inclinations and admonitions, but give their consent to the suggestions of the devil.

paras.t: Et fauces comedentis, saporem. Fauces sunt angusta fistula gutturis, per quas jam gustus signatur. Est autem et gustus interior, qui est ipsemet intellectus, cui omnium exteriorum sensuum nomina adscribuntur et competunt, secundum diversas rationes, ut ex verbis Basilii patuit præcedenti articulo. Hic ergo gustus intellectualis sapit, discernit et masticat spiritualem saporem veritatis atque virtutis; gustat et experitur, quam dulcis est Dominus, secundum quod veritas prima ac bonitas summa se ei ostendit, infundit, conjungit magis aut minus. Ad quam degustationem ac gustus dijudicationem hortatur, qui ait: Gustate, et videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus. Quum vero hic gustus sic sapit et judicat, experimentaliter sciens, quantum spiritalis dulcedo omnem carnalem transcendat, tunc intellectus reficitur, cujus cibus est veritas, virtus, omnisque spiritualis perfectio. De qua comestione et refectione ait Sponsus cœlestis: Comedi favum meum cum melle meo; et rursus: Comedite, amici mei, et bibite, et inebriamini, carissimi.
paras.en: [[12:11|and the palate of him that eateth, the taste|Et fauces comedentis, saporem]]. The palate [fauces, properly the throat] is the narrow pipe of the gullet, by which taste is here signified. But there is also an inward taste, which is the intellect itself, to which the names of all the outward senses are ascribed and fitly belong, under different aspects, as was shown in the preceding article from the words of Basil [a footnote in the edition corrects this to Gregory]. This intellectual taste, then, savours, discerns and chews the spiritual savour of truth and virtue; it tastes and experiences how sweet the Lord is, according as the first truth and highest goodness shows itself to it, pours itself into it and joins itself to it, more or less. To this tasting and this discerning by taste he exhorts us who says: [[Ps 33:9|O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet|Gustate, et videte, quoniam suavis est Dominus]]. And when this taste so savours and judges, knowing by experience how far spiritual sweetness surpasses all carnal sweetness, then the intellect is refreshed, whose food is truth, virtue and every spiritual perfection. Of this eating and refreshment the heavenly Bridegroom says: [[Cant 5:1|I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey|Comedi favum meum cum melle meo]]; and again: [[Cant 5:1|eat, O friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearly beloved|Comedite, amici mei, et bibite, et inebriamini, carissimi]].

paras.t: In antiquis est sapientia. Sapientia vero spiritualis interna, et quæ donum est Spiritus Sancti, dicitur in antiquis: quia eo ipso quo habent hanc cum eminentia seu abundantia quadam, ita ut per eam vitam suam et mores in omnibus ordinent et componant, senes rite vocantur, etiamsi tempore juvenes sint: senes, inquam, probitate atque valore, juxta illud libri Sapientiæ: Senectus venerabilis est, non diuturna, neque annorum numero computata. Cani autem sunt sensus hominis, et ætas senectutis vita immaculata. Unde de S. Agnete scribit Ambrosius: Infantia computabatur in annis, sed erat senectus mentis immensa.
paras.en: [[12:12|In the ancient is wisdom|In antiquis est sapientia]]. Inward spiritual wisdom, the wisdom that is a gift of the Holy Ghost, is said to be [[12:12|in the ancient|in antiquis]]: because, by the very fact that men have it with a certain eminence or abundance, so that by it they order and compose their life and conduct in all things, they are rightly called old, even if they are young in years: old, I say, in uprightness and worth, according to that of the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 4:8|venerable old age is not that of long time, nor counted by the number of years: but the understanding of a man is grey hairs|Senectus venerabilis est, non diuturna, neque annorum numero computata. Cani autem sunt sensus hominis]], [[Wis 4:9|And a spotless life is old age|et ætas senectutis vita immaculata]]. Hence Ambrose writes of St. Agnes: Her infancy was reckoned in years, but the old age of her mind was boundless.

paras.t: Apud ipsum est sapientia et fortitudo. Nam apud Patrem est Verbum et unigenitus Filius ejus, de quo loquitur Paulus, Prædicamus Christum Dei virtutem et Dei sapientiam; de quo ait Joannes, In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum. Ipse habet consilium quo disponit sua, et intelligentiam qua inspicit nostra.
paras.en: [[12:13|With him is wisdom and strength|Apud ipsum est sapientia et fortitudo]]. For with the Father is the Word, his only-begotten Son, of whom Paul says: [[1 Cor 1:23|we preach Christ|Prædicamus Christum]], [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God and the wisdom of God|Dei virtutem et Dei sapientiam]]; of whom John says: [[John 1:1|In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God|In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum]]. [[12:13|he hath counsel|Ipse habet consilium]], by which he disposes his own affairs, [[12:13|and understanding|et intelligentiam]], by which he looks into ours.

paras.t: Si destruxerit, nemo est qui ædificet. Destruit Deus intellectualem creaturam, spiritualiter quidem, non essentialiter, dum vel gratiam non infundit, aut infusam non conservat, sed perdi permittit, sicut de impiis et dolosis ait Psalmista: Destrues illos, et non ædificabis eos. Qui autem ita destructus est, reparari non potest, nisi a Deo, qui solus gratiæ est collator atque creator. Si incluserit hominem, id est, intra cæcitatis impietatisque suæ caliginem angustari permiserit, vel peccati ac dæmonum captivitati tradiderit, seu intra conscientiæ suæ remorsum ac carcerem comprehensum tenuerit, ita ut vitia sua abscondat, et confitendo non exeat; nullus est qui aperiat infelicissimam hanc clausuram, id est, qui mentem de captivitate ista educat ad libertatem virtutum, ac gratiæ lucem, ad latitudinem caritatis, ad patriam felicitatis. Hæc enim non efficit nisi Deus. Unde in Apocalypsi legitur: Hæc dicit Sanctus et Verus, qui habet clavem David: qui claudit, et nemo aperit: aperit, et nemo claudit. Postremo, si incluserit quempiam in inferno, nunquam poterit salvandus educi.
paras.en: [[12:14|If he pull down, there is no man that can build up|Si destruxerit, nemo est qui ædificet]]. God pulls down the intellectual creature (spiritually, that is, not in its being) when he either does not pour in grace, or does not keep it once poured in but lets it be lost, as the Psalmist says of the wicked and deceitful: [[Ps 27:5|thou shalt destroy them, and shalt not build them up|Destrues illos, et non ædificabis eos]]. And one who has been so pulled down cannot be repaired except by God, who alone is the giver and creator of grace. [[12:14|if he shut up a man|Si incluserit hominem]], that is, if he lets him be hemmed in within the darkness of his own blindness and impiety, or hands him over to the captivity of sin and of the demons, or holds him shut up within the remorse and prison of his own conscience, so that he hides his vices and does not come out by confessing them, [[12:14|there is none that can open|nullus est qui aperiat]] this most unhappy enclosure: that is, who can lead the mind out of that captivity to the freedom of the virtues and the light of grace, to the breadth of charity, to the fatherland of happiness. For none but God does this. Hence we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:7|These things saith the Holy One and the true one, he that hath the key of David|Hæc dicit Sanctus et Verus, qui habet clavem David]]: [[Apoc 3:7|he that openeth and no man shutteth, shutteth and no man openeth|qui claudit, et nemo aperit: aperit, et nemo claudit]] [Denis has the two clauses the other way round: who shutteth, and no man openeth; openeth, and no man shutteth]. Lastly, if he shuts anyone up in hell, he can never be brought out to be saved.

paras.t: Si continuerit aquas, id est gratiarum charismata, doctrinæ fluenta, prædicationisque verba. De quibus loquitur Isaias: Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris. Salomon quoque: Torrens inundans, fons sapientiæ. Itemque: Aqua profunda, verba ex ore viri. Omnia siccabuntur, id est, omnium corda spiritualiter arefient, infecundaque erunt. Si enim Deus ista abstraxerit, omnis decor, ubertas et fructus mentis humanæ depereunt. Propter quod ait vir sanctus Deo: Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi.
paras.en: [[12:15|If he withhold the waters|Si continuerit aquas]], that is, the gifts of graces, the streams of doctrine and the words of preaching. Of these Isaias speaks: [[Is 12:3|Thou shall draw waters with joy out of the saviour's fountains|Haurietis aquas in gaudio de fontibus Salvatoris]]. Solomon too: [[Prov 18:4|the fountain of wisdom is an overflowing stream|Torrens inundans, fons sapientiæ]]. And again: [[Prov 18:4|Words from the mouth of a man are as deep water|Aqua profunda, verba ex ore viri]]. [[12:15|all things shall be dried up|Omnia siccabuntur]], that is, the hearts of all will dry up spiritually and be barren. For if God withdraws these, all the beauty, richness and fruit of the human mind perish. For this reason a holy man says to God: [[Ps 142:6|my soul is as earth without water unto thee|Anima mea sicut terra sine aqua tibi]].

paras.t: Si emiserit eas, id est, si dona hæc gratiarum infuderit mentibus, subvertent terram, id est, corda terrena vincent, et quantum ad esse impietatis, destruent, peccata expellent. Hæc est subversio bona et annihilatio desideranda, ut homo desinat esse sui, et incipiat esse Dei, exstirpato amore privato, atque divino amore sibi infuso. Unde ait Salvator: Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, in vitam æternam custodiet illam. Vel sic: Si emiserit eas, id est, cum magna abundantia dona ista infuderit, subvertent terram, id est, facient hominem a se ipso deficere, viribus suis destitui, ut patet in raptu et ecstasi. Propter quod ait Psalmista: Defecit caro mea et cor meum. Et Jeremias: Factus est sermo Domini in corde meo, quasi ignis exæstuans, et defeci, ferre non sustinens. Interdum quoque contingit, ut quis ex nimia copia gratiæ sibi clementer infusæ spiritualiter intumescat, præsumat, incautus reddatur, et alios spernetur: sicque terra subvertitur, quia homo in terra degens, ex subita gratiarum abundanti infusione occasionaliter labitur. Ideo Deus non semper dat statim quod petitur, sciens quid nobis magis expediat; vultque ut paulatim crescamus, ne postea gravius corruamus.
paras.en: [[12:15|and if he send them out|Si emiserit eas]], that is, if he pours these gifts of graces into minds, [[12:15|they shall overturn the earth|subvertent terram]]: that is, they will overcome earthly hearts and destroy them as to their being wicked, and drive out sins. This is a good overturning and an annihilation to be desired: that a man cease to be his own and begin to be God's, private love being rooted out and divine love poured into him. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:39|he that shall lose his life for me|Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me]] [[John 12:25|keepeth it unto life eternal|in vitam æternam custodiet illam]] [Denis joins Matt 10:39 to the end of John 12:25, as the two margin notes show]. Or thus: [[12:15|and if he send them out|Si emiserit eas]], that is, if he pours in these gifts in great abundance, [[12:15|they shall overturn the earth|subvertent terram]]: that is, they will make a man fail from himself and be bereft of his own strength, as is plain in rapture and ecstasy. For this reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 72:26|my flesh and my heart hath fainted away|Defecit caro mea et cor meum]]. And Jeremias: [[Jer 20:9|there came in my heart as a burning fire|Factus est sermo Domini in corde meo, quasi ignis exæstuans]] [Denis reads: the word of the Lord came into my heart as a burning fire], [[Jer 20:9|and I was wearied, not being able to bear it|et defeci, ferre non sustinens]]. Sometimes, too, it happens that someone, from too great an abundance of grace mercifully poured into him, swells up spiritually, presumes, grows careless and despises others: and so the earth is overturned, because a man dwelling on earth falls, by occasion of the sudden and abundant pouring-in of graces. Therefore God does not always give at once what is asked, knowing what is more expedient for us; and he wills that we grow little by little, lest afterwards we fall more grievously.
