paras.t: Ipse novit et decipientem, et eum qui decipitur. Justos atque electos Deus noscit notitia non solum simplicis intuitionis, sed etiam approbationis. Reprobos vero et pravos nescit notitia approbationis, quos noscit notitia intuitionis, prout talibus ait Salvator: Nescio vos; discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis. Præterea, invisibilem hostem nos quotidie decipientem Deus agnoscit, attendens ejus fortitudinem, calliditatem, experientiam, crudelissimam intentionem, infatigabilem importunitatem, et quod videns nos, a nobis videri non possit. Noscit autem et nos, qui ab illo decipimur, pensans quam fragiles, infirmi, ignarique simus: ideo non permittit nos ultra vires tentari. Paratus est suffragari, deceptis pronus est misereri, calamum conquassatum non conterit, linumque fumigans non exstinguit. Si ergo tentatione dejecti fuerimus, non pusillanimes efficiamur, non desperemus; sed ad Dei clementiam protinus cum omni humilitate atque fiducia properemus, imperfectum nostrum pensantes, et in sola Dei clementia jugiter confidentes.
paras.en: [[12:16|he knoweth both the deceivers, and him that is deceived|Ipse novit et decipientem, et eum qui decipitur]]. God knows the just and the elect with a knowledge not only of simple intuition but also of approval. The reprobate and wicked he does not know with the knowledge of approval, though he knows them with the knowledge of intuition [that is, God's plain sight of all that is, as distinct from the knowledge by which he approves and loves], as the Saviour says to such: [[Luke 13:27|I know you not|Nescio vos]]; [[Luke 13:27|Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity|discedite a me, operarii iniquitatis]]. Moreover, God knows the invisible enemy who deceives us daily, marking his strength, his cunning, his experience, his most cruel intention, his tireless importunity, and that he sees us and cannot be seen by us. And he knows us too, who are deceived by him, weighing how frail, weak and ignorant we are: therefore he does not let us be tempted beyond our strength[[1 Cor 10:13||]]. He is ready to help, inclined to have mercy on the deceived: [[Is 42:3|The bruised reed he shall not break, and smoking flax he shall not quench|calamum conquassatum non conterit, linumque fumigans non exstinguit]]. If then we have been cast down by temptation, let us not become faint-hearted, let us not despair; but let us hasten at once to the mercy of God with all humility and confidence, weighing our imperfection and trusting always in the mercy of God alone.

paras.t: Adducit consiliarios in stultum finem. Invisibiles hostes multiformiter inter se consulunt, quomodo hominem, præcipue qualiter justum quemquam decipiant; quorum consilia Deus adducit ad stultum finem, quia sive prævaleant, sive succumbant, totum cooperatur eis in majorem miseriam. Et frequenter per studia quibus conantur justum ad damnationem pertrahere, occasio sunt præclarioris profectus in eo, beatitudinisque majoris. Diligentibus equidem Deum electis omnia cooperantur in bonum. Insuper, consiliarii intelligi possunt prædicatores atque doctores, salutis consilia proponentes: qui, dum exigentibus suis culpis, in tantum divinitus relinquuntur, ut propriis perversitatibus contenebrati, spiritualia, divina, æterna prædicent doceantque propter terrena, temporalia et caduca, in finem utique stultum ducuntur, media fini, vilia optimis præferentes. Et judices in stuporem. Hoc fit, dum Deo juste sinente, principes et prælati alios judicaturi, non rationem, sed passionem sequuntur, vel gratia discernendi inter bonum et malum privantur, aut alio modo a rectitudine justitiæ obliquantur: sicut Micheas dicit de quibusdam, Principes ejus, puta Jerusalem seu Israel, in muneribus judicabant, et sacerdotes ejus in mercede docebant.
paras.en: [[12:17|He bringeth counsellors to a foolish end|Adducit consiliarios in stultum finem]]. The invisible enemies take counsel among themselves in many ways how they may deceive a man, and above all how they may deceive some just man; and God brings their counsels to a foolish end, because whether they prevail or are worsted, the whole works together for their greater misery. And often, through the very efforts by which they try to drag the just man to damnation, they become the occasion of more splendid progress in him, and of greater beatitude. For [[Rom 8:28|to them that love God|Diligentibus equidem Deum]], the elect, [[Rom 8:28|all things work together unto good|omnia cooperantur in bonum]]. Besides, the counsellors may be understood as the preachers and teachers who set forth the counsels of salvation: who, when their faults so require, are so far forsaken by God that, darkened by their own perversity, they preach and teach spiritual, divine and eternal things for the sake of earthly, temporal and perishable ones; and so they are indeed brought to a foolish end, putting the means before the end, the vile before the best. [[12:17|and judges to insensibility|Et judices in stuporem]]. This happens when, God justly permitting it, princes and prelates who are to judge others follow not reason but passion, or are deprived of the grace of discerning between good and evil, or in some other way are bent aside from the rightness of justice: as Micheas says of certain men, [[Mich 3:11|Her princes|Principes ejus]] (that is, of Jerusalem or Israel) [[Mich 3:11|have judged for bribes: and her priests have taught for hire|in muneribus judicabant, et sacerdotes ejus in mercede docebant]].

paras.t: Balteum regum dissolvit. Reges, spiritualiter omnes sunt qui rationis aguntur imperio, et carnem cum sensualitate rationis in cunctis subdunt judicio: quorum balteus est castitas seu continentia. De castitate enim loquitur Christus: Sint lumbi vestri præcincti. Et de Christo vaticinans Isaias: Erit (inquit) justitia cingulum lumborum ejus. Dum ergo continentes seu justi, propter inanem suam gloriam, aut spiritualem superbiam vel aliam causam, e continentia ad vitia carnis vel consensum ad ea, delectationemve de eis in cogitatione conceptam labuntur, vel a justitia ad injustitiam dejiciuntur, balteus regum dissolvitur. Denique, per spiritualem superbiam inanemque gloriam, meretur homo potissime a castitate ad immunditiam carnis, et ab æquitate ad iniquitatem corruere. Hinc humilitas castis præcipue necessaria est atque servanda, dicente Ambrosio: Necesse est ut quanto castior virgo, tanto humilior sit. Et præcingit permissive fune, id est vili carnis delectatione ac fœtido iniquoque opere, renes eorum, id est corporis membra, ita ut interior et occulta ipsorum impuritas, foris per facta obscena omnibus innotescat. Ad quod illud Isaiæ spiritualiter pertinet: Erit pro zona funiculus. Et de impio Salomon ait in Proverbiis: Funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur. Porro S. Thomæ de Aquino, in adolescentia sua angeli sancti locuti sunt: Præcingimus te cingulo castitatis.
paras.en: [[12:18|He looseth the belt of kings|Balteum regum dissolvit]]. Spiritually, kings are all who are ruled by the command of reason, and subject the flesh with its sensuality to the judgment of reason in all things: and their belt is chastity or continence. For Christ speaks of chastity: [[Luke 12:35|Let your loins be girt|Sint lumbi vestri præcincti]]. And Isaias, prophesying of Christ, says: [[Is 11:5|justice shall be the girdle of his loins|Erit (inquit) justitia cingulum lumborum ejus]]. When, then, the continent or the just, through their own vainglory, or spiritual pride, or some other cause, fall from continence into the vices of the flesh, or into consent to them, or into a delight in them conceived in thought, or are cast down from justice into injustice, the belt of kings is loosed. Indeed, it is above all through spiritual pride and vainglory that a man deserves to fall from chastity into uncleanness of the flesh, and from equity into iniquity. Hence humility is especially necessary for the chaste, and must be kept, as Ambrose says: It must be that the more chaste a virgin is, the more humble she is. [[12:18|and girdeth|Et præcingit]], by permission [that is, God allows it rather than does it], [[12:18|with a cord|fune]] (that is, with the vile delight of the flesh and with foul and wicked deeds) [[12:18|their loins|renes eorum]], that is, the members of the body, so that their inward and hidden impurity becomes known to all outwardly through obscene deeds. To this that word of Isaias belongs in a spiritual sense: There shall be [[Is 3:24|instead of a girdle, a cord|Erit pro zona funiculus]]. And Solomon says of the wicked man in Proverbs: [[Prov 5:22|he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins|Funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur]]. Moreover, holy angels said to St. Thomas Aquinas in his youth: We gird thee with the girdle of chastity.

paras.t: Ducit sacerdotes inglorios. Heu! quam dolorose et copiose hoc modo impletur, dum multi sacerdotes et clerici propter vitiosissimam suam ac lubricam vitam ab omnibus contemnuntur, diffamantur, et debita bonis sacerdotibus, imo et ordini sacerdotii gloria privantur ac inhonorantur! Denique, gloria sacerdotum est spiritualis profectus subditorum suorum, quemadmodum discipulis suis Thessalonicensibus scribit Apostolus: Quæ est spes nostra et gaudium aut corona gloriæ? Nonne vos in adventu Domini? Dum igitur sacerdotes subditos suos verbo et opere non informant, nec ad salutem quantum in eis est, pertrahunt, inglorii fiunt, et detestabiles Deo; nec faciem ejus feliciter intuebuntur, quemadmodum Joseph in persona Christi locutus est fratribus suis Patriarchis, pastorum personam gerentibus: Non videbitis faciem meam, nisi adduxeritis fratrem vestrum minimum vobiscum. O quam despectissimi tales coram summo Judice apparebunt! Præterea, bonis sacerdotibus ac prælatis potissima gloria est, subditorum vita salubris, sicut in tertia sua Canonica scribit Joannes: Majorem horum gratiam non habeo, quam ut audiam filios meos in veritate ambulantes. Verumtamen qui veraciter sapiens est, præsertim si de subditorum aut laicorum seu inferiorum sit numero, sacerdotibus honorem et gloriam sacerdotio debita debet impendere intuitu Dei, et pro reverentia sacramentali, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: In tota anima tua time Deum, et sacerdotes illius sanctifica. Nam et Paulus ad Romanos ait: Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit. Et Petrus admonet etiam dyscolis dominis obedire. Postremo, Paulo testante, qui bene præsunt presbyteri, duplici honore digni sunt.
paras.en: [[12:19|He leadeth away priests without glory|Ducit sacerdotes inglorios]]. Alas, how sorrowfully and how abundantly this is fulfilled, when many priests and clerics, because of their most vicious and slippery life, are despised and defamed by all, and are stripped of the glory owed to good priests, nay, to the order of the priesthood itself, and are dishonoured! Further, the glory of priests is the spiritual progress of those in their charge, as the Apostle writes to his disciples the Thessalonians: [[1 Thess 2:19|what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Are not you, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ at his coming?|Quæ est spes nostra et gaudium aut corona gloriæ? Nonne vos in adventu Domini?]] So when priests do not form those in their charge by word and deed, nor draw them to salvation as far as in them lies, they become without glory and hateful to God; nor will they look happily upon his face, as Joseph, in the person of Christ, said to his brothers the patriarchs, who bore the person of the shepherds [that is, of the pastors of souls]: [[Gen 43:3|You shall not see my face, unless you bring your youngest brother with you|Non videbitis faciem meam, nisi adduxeritis fratrem vestrum minimum vobiscum]] [the margin gives Gen. xliv; the words, as Denis gives them, are those reported at Gen 43:3, and again at Gen 44:23]. O how utterly despised will such men appear before the supreme Judge! Moreover, for good priests and prelates the greatest glory is the wholesome life of those in their charge, as John writes in his third canonical epistle: [[3 John 1:4|I have no greater grace than this, to hear that my children walk in truth|Majorem horum gratiam non habeo, quam ut audiam filios meos in veritate ambulantes]]. Yet he who is truly wise, above all if he is among those under authority, or among the laity or those of lower rank, ought to pay priests the honour and glory due to the priesthood, with an eye to God and out of reverence for the sacrament, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:31|With all thy soul fear the Lord, and reverence his priests|In tota anima tua time Deum, et sacerdotes illius sanctifica]]. For Paul too says to the Romans: [[Rom 13:1|Let every soul be subject to higher powers|Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit]]. And Peter admonishes us to obey even froward masters[[1 Pet 2:18||]] [dyscolis, the Greek word kept in the Vulgate: ill-tempered, hard to please]. Lastly, as Paul testifies, [[1 Tim 5:17|the priests that rule well be esteemed worthy of double honour|qui bene præsunt presbyteri, duplici honore digni sunt]].

paras.t: Et optimates supplantat, dum justo judicio desinit eos de primatu seu præsidentia inaniter gloriari, voluptatibus subjici, vitiis superari, atque ob hæc æternæ eos deputat pœnæ, juxta illud Sapientis: Judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet. Exiguo enim conceditur misericordia; potentes autem potenter patientur tormenta. Et Jeremias ait: Adspergite vos cinere, optimates gregis, quia completi sunt dies vestri ut interficiamini, et cadetis quasi vasa pretiosa.
paras.en: [[12:19|and overthroweth nobles|Et optimates supplantat]]: when by a just judgment he lets them glory vainly in their pre-eminence or authority, be made subject to pleasures and be overcome by vices [the text reads desinit, 'ceases'; the sense seems to need sinit, 'lets'], and for these things assigns them to eternal punishment, according to that of the Wise man: [[Wis 6:6|a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|Judicium durissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet]]. [[Wis 6:7|For to him that is little, mercy is granted: but the mighty shall be mightily tormented.|Exiguo enim conceditur misericordia; potentes autem potenter patientur tormenta]] And Jeremias says: [[Jer 25:34|sprinkle yourselves with ashes, ye leaders of the flock|Adspergite vos cinere, optimates gregis]]: [[Jer 25:34|for the days of your slaughter and your dispersion are accomplished|quia completi sunt dies vestri ut interficiamini]] [Denis omits 'and your dispersion'], [[Jer 25:34|and you shall fall like precious vessels|et cadetis quasi vasa pretiosa]].

paras.t: Effundit despectionem super principes, et eos qui oppressi fuerant, relevat. Hoc specialiter exponi potest de populo Judæorum atque gentilibus. Judæi enim ante Christi adventum præ cunctis populis præclariores et principales fuerunt, gentiles vero innumerabilibus vitiis erroribusque oppressi. Unde secundo Regum David loquitur Deo: Quæ est gens in terra ut populus tuus Israel? Et Moyses ait ad plebem Israel: Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis, qui sunt super terram. Super hunc populum, quoniam Christum negavit et crucifixit, effudit Deus despectionem, auferendo eis spiritualia gratiæ bona, ita quod permanent excæcati usque in finem mundi, dicente Apostolo: Pervenit super eos ira Dei usque in finem. Quod et David prænuntians: Furor, inquit, iræ tuæ comprehendat eos. Insuper abstulit eis corporalia bona, videlicet propriam terram, regnum et maximam partem eorum interimens per Romanos, secundum illud Danielis: Non erit ejus (videlicet Christi) populus, qui eum negaturus est; et civitatem et sanctuarium dissipabit populus cum duce venturo, et finis ejus vastitas, et usque in finem perseverabit desolatio. Gentiles autem Deus per evangelicam prædicationem a suis erroribus relevavit, gratia decoravit, et Christo incorporavit, quemadmodum in Isaia Pater ait de Christo: Ecce testem populis dedi eum, ducem ac præceptorem gentibus. Talibus namque scribit Apostolus, loquens Ephesiis: Vos qui aliquando longe fuistis a Deo, nunc prope facti estis in sanguine Christi. Præterea oppressos adversitate, mœrore, angustia, Deus communiter relevat, per internæ consolationis infusionem, per angelicam inspirationem, per piorum hominum allocutionem, per tribulationis terminationem, seu alio modo, sicut in Tobia dicitur: Et post fletum consolationem infundis. Et in Psalmo: Juxta est Dominus his qui tribulato sunt corde.
paras.en: [[12:21|He poureth contempt upon princes|Effundit despectionem super principes]], [[12:21|and relieveth them that were oppressed|et eos qui oppressi fuerant, relevat]]. This can be expounded especially of the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles. For before the coming of Christ the Jews were more illustrious than all peoples and the chief among them, while the Gentiles were oppressed by countless vices and errors. Hence in the second book of Kings David says to God: [[2 Kings 7:23|what nation is there upon earth, as thy people Israel|Quæ est gens in terra ut populus tuus Israel]]? And Moses says to the people of Israel: [[Deut 7:6|The Lord thy God hath chosen thee, to be his peculiar people of all peoples that are upon the earth|Te elegit Dominus, ut sis ei populus peculiaris de cunctis populis, qui sunt super terram]]. Upon this people, because it denied and crucified Christ, God poured out contempt, taking from them the spiritual goods of grace, so that they remain blinded until the end of the world, as the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 2:16|the wrath of God is come upon them to the end|Pervenit super eos ira Dei usque in finem]]. Which David too foretold, saying: [[Ps 68:25|let thy wrathful anger take hold of them|Furor, inquit, iræ tuæ comprehendat eos]]. Moreover he took from them their bodily goods, namely their own land and kingdom, slaying the greater part of them by the Romans, according to that of Daniel: [[Dan 9:26|the people that shall deny him shall not be his|Non erit ejus (videlicet Christi) populus, qui eum negaturus est]] (that is, Christ's); [[Dan 9:26|And a people, with their leader, that shall come, shall destroy the city, and the sanctuary: and the end thereof shall be waste|et civitatem et sanctuarium dissipabit populus cum duce venturo, et finis ejus vastitas]], [[Dan 9:27|the desolation shall continue even to the consummation, and to the end|et usque in finem perseverabit desolatio]]. But the Gentiles God relieved of their errors through the preaching of the Gospel, adorned with grace and incorporated into Christ, as the Father says of Christ in Isaias: [[Is 55:4|Behold I have given him for a witness to the people, for a leader and a master to the Gentiles.|Ecce testem populis dedi eum, ducem ac præceptorem gentibus]] For it is to such that the Apostle writes, speaking to the Ephesians: [[Eph 2:13|you, who some time were afar off, are made nigh by the blood of Christ|Vos qui aliquando longe fuistis a Deo, nunc prope facti estis in sanguine Christi]] [Denis adds: afar off from God]. Further, God commonly relieves those oppressed by adversity, grief and distress, by pouring in inward consolation, by the inspiration of angels, by the words of devout men, by bringing the tribulation to an end, or in some other way, as is said in Tobias: [[Tob 3:22|after tears and weeping thou pourest in joyfulness|Et post fletum consolationem infundis]] [Denis reads: after weeping thou pourest in consolation]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 33:19|The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a contrite heart|Juxta est Dominus his qui tribulato sunt corde]].

paras.t: Qui revelat profunda de tenebris. Occulta namque et difficillima legis ac Prophetarum oracula, Christus per se et per apostolica documenta nobis lucide patefecit, tenebras (id est varias veritatum circumvolutiones) detegens et illustrans: ad quod designandum tempore Passionis scissum est velum templi a summo usque deorsum. Et producit in lucem umbram mortis, id est, rigorem legis, mortem corporalem pro peccato infligi jubentis, in lucem miserationis et mansuetudinis serenitatem convertit. In lege enim sæpissime scribitur: Qui fecerit hoc vel hoc, moriatur seu lapidetur. Christus autem peccatoribus confessionem præcepit, confitentibus remissionem gratiamque promisit.
paras.en: [[12:22|He discovereth deep things out of darkness|Qui revelat profunda de tenebris]]. For the hidden and most difficult oracles of the Law and the Prophets Christ has opened clearly to us, by himself and by the teaching of the apostles, uncovering and lighting up the darkness (that is, the various wrappings of the truths): and to signify this, at the time of the Passion [[Matt 27:51|the veil of the temple was rent|scissum est velum templi]] [[Matt 27:51|from the top even to the bottom|a summo usque deorsum]]. [[12:22|and bringeth up to light the shadow of death|Et producit in lucem umbram mortis]]: that is, the rigour of the Law, which commands bodily death to be inflicted for sin, he turns into the light and serenity of mercy and gentleness. For in the Law it is written very often: He that shall do this or that, let him die, or be stoned [the margin seems to cite Exodus here, but its chapter and verse cannot be read; see for instance Ex 21:12–17]. But Christ commanded sinners to confess, and promised remission and grace to those who confess [a margin reference beside this line cannot be read in the scan].

paras.t: Qui multiplicat gentes, augendo Ecclesiam seu plures convertendo ad fidem vel vitam virtuosam: quod in primitiva Ecclesia maxime implebatur, juxta illud Actuum: Dominus augebat quotidie qui salvi fierent in id ipsum. Unde et Christus ait in Psalmo: Annuntiavi, et locutus sum; multiplicati sunt super numerum. Et perdit eas: quod dupliciter accipi potest. Primo, de optima perditione, qua electos suos variis permisit necari suppliciis. De qua perditione in Isaia legitur: Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, et non est qui intelligat. Secundo, de perditione mala, qua occulto et justo judicio permisit credentes variis vitiis atque erroribus deperire. Et subversas in integrum restituit: quia vel eos qui corruerunt per culpam, reduxit ad gratiam et vitæ integritatem; vel loco pereuntium posuit alios, quos per suam salvavit clementiam, et reparavit ac reformavit Ecclesiam.
paras.en: [[12:23|He multiplieth nations|Qui multiplicat gentes]], by enlarging the Church, or converting more people to the faith or to a virtuous life: which was fulfilled above all in the early Church, according to that of the Acts: [[Acts 2:47|the Lord increased daily together such as should be saved|Dominus augebat quotidie qui salvi fierent in id ipsum]]. Hence Christ too says in the Psalm: [[Ps 39:6|I have declared and I have spoken they are multiplied above number|Annuntiavi, et locutus sum; multiplicati sunt super numerum]]. [[12:23|and destroyeth them|Et perdit eas]]: which can be taken in two ways. First, of the best kind of destruction, by which he let his elect be put to death by various torments. Of this destruction we read in Isaias: [[Is 57:1|The just perisheth, and no man layeth it to heart, and men of mercy are taken away, because there is none that understandeth|Justus perit, et non est qui recogitet; et viri misericordiæ tolluntur, et non est qui intelligat]]. Secondly, of the evil destruction, by which, by a hidden and just judgment, he let believers perish through various vices and errors. [[12:23|and restoreth them again after they were overthrown|Et subversas in integrum restituit]]: because either he has brought back to grace and to integrity of life those who fell through sin; or in place of those who perished he has set others, whom he saved by his mercy, and so has repaired and reformed the Church.

paras.t: Qui immutat cor principum populi terræ: vel effective inclinando illud a malo ad bonum, secundum illud Apostoli: Deus operatur in vobis et velle et perficere. Tertio quoque Regum Salomon orat: Inclinet corda nostra post se, ut ambulemus in omnibus viis ejus. Vel permissive facit hoc Deus, dum cor subverti permittit atque corruere a bono in malum, vel a malo in pejus: quod etiam in ceteris hominibus inferioribus efficit Deus, secundum sapientiæ suæ inscrutabilem profunditatem, unum pie convertens, alterum juste relinquens. Cetera patent ex præcedenti articulo.
paras.en: [[12:24|He changeth the heart of the princes of the people of the earth|Qui immutat cor principum populi terræ]]: either effectively, inclining it from evil to good, according to that of the Apostle: [[Phil 2:13|God who worketh in you, both to will and to accomplish|Deus operatur in vobis et velle et perficere]]. And in the third book of Kings Solomon prays: [[3 Kings 8:58|may he incline our hearts to himself, that we may walk in all his ways|Inclinet corda nostra post se, ut ambulemus in omnibus viis ejus]] [the margin reference here cannot be read; the words are those of 3 Kings 8:58]. Or God does this permissively, when he lets the heart be overturned and fall from good into evil, or from evil into worse: which God also does in other men of lower rank, according to the unsearchable depth of his wisdom, mercifully converting one, justly leaving another. The rest is plain from the preceding article.

13.title: Elucidatio capituli tertiidecimi: Ecce omnia hæc vidit oculus meus, et audivit auris mea.
13.title_en: Explanation of the thirteenth chapter: Behold my eye hath seen all these things, and my ear hath heard
13.note: This article goes on into chapter 14 (vv. 1–4); that part is shown there.

paras.t: Hinc particularius sanctus Job descendit ad reprehensionem et informationem amicorum suorum. Ecce omnia hæc vidit oculus meus, et audivit auris mea: id est, prædictos in præcedenti capitulo divinæ sapientiæ ac omnipotentiæ effectus circa homines, corporalibus oculis vidi in se vel in aliquo signo, vel per visum exteriorem ad eorum cognitionem deveni; auribus quoque ea ex aliquorum relatu, fama vel instructione percepi; et intellexi singula, per diligentem mentis considerationem, imo potius per divinam illuminationem. Secundum scientiam vestram et ego novi, nec inferior vestri sum. Hoc est quod circa præcedentis capituli principium ait, Et mihi est cor sicut vobis, nec inferior vestri sum: quod qualiter non superbe aut præsumptuose, sed humiliter ac discrete sit dictum, ibi expositum est.
paras.en: From here holy Job comes down more particularly to reproving and instructing his friends. [[13:1|Behold my eye hath seen all these things, and my ear hath heard them|Ecce omnia hæc vidit oculus meus, et audivit auris mea]]: that is, the effects of the divine wisdom and almighty power in regard to men, spoken of in the preceding chapter, I have seen with my bodily eyes, in themselves or in some sign, or I have come to know them by outward sight; with my ears too I have perceived them, from the report of others, from common fame or from instruction; [[13:1|and I have understood them all|et intellexi singula]], by diligent consideration of the mind, or rather by divine enlightenment. [[13:2|According to your knowledge I also know: neither am I inferior to you|Secundum scientiam vestram et ego novi, nec inferior vestri sum]]. This is what he said near the beginning of the preceding chapter, [[Job 12:3|I also have a heart as well as you|Et mihi est cor sicut vobis]], neither am I inferior to you: and how this was said not proudly or presumptuously, but humbly and with discretion, has been explained there.

paras.t: Sed tamen ad Omnipotentem loquar, ipsum laudando, orando, causamque meam ei ut judici proponendo, et cor meum coram eo cum debita modestia effundendo: juxta illud Threnorum, Effunde sicut aquam cor tuum ante conspectum Domini Dei tui. Sic et Abraham disseruit: Loquar ad Dominum meum, quum sim pulvis et cinis. Et disputare cum Deo cupio: non ejus gesta seu judicia temerarie dijudicando, sed veritatem humiliter inquirendo, et percussionis meæ causam plenius investigando, de modo quoque providentiæ ejus, et processu regiminis vitæ humanæ loquendo. Sic quippe discipulus disputat cum magistro, non ut reprehendat, sed ut informetur; et rationes se moventes proponit, ut a magistro solvantur. Sic etiam Jeremias ait: Justus quidem tu es, Domine, si disputem tecum.
paras.en: [[13:3|But yet I will speak to the Almighty|Sed tamen ad Omnipotentem loquar]], praising him, praying, setting my case before him as before a judge, and pouring out my heart before him with due restraint, according to that of Lamentations: [[Lam 2:19|pour out thy heart like water, before the face of the Lord|Effunde sicut aquam cor tuum ante conspectum Domini Dei tui]]. So too Abraham reasoned: [[Gen 18:27|I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes|Loquar ad Dominum meum, quum sim pulvis et cinis]]. And [[13:3|I desire to reason with God|disputare cum Deo cupio]]: not by rashly passing judgment on his deeds or judgments, but by humbly seeking the truth, and inquiring more fully into the cause of my stroke, and speaking also of the manner of his providence and of the course of his governance of human life. For so a disciple disputes with his master, not to find fault with him, but to be instructed; and he puts forward the reasons that move him, so that the master may resolve them. So too Jeremias says: [[Jer 12:1|Thou indeed, O Lord, art just, if I plead with thee|Justus quidem tu es, Domine, si disputem tecum]] [the Latin *disputem*, “if I dispute”, is the same verb as Job’s *disputare*, “to reason”].

paras.t: Prius vos ostendens fabricatores, id est artificiosos compositores, mendacii, id est falsi sermonis: quoniam multa mihi crimina imposuistis, ut vestras defendatis erroneas opiniones circa providentiam Dei, putantes nullum puniri a Deo, nisi pro sua culpa. Sic et in Jeremia dicitur de quibusdam: Docuerunt linguam suam loqui mendacium; ut inique agerent, laboraverunt. Et cultores, id est amatores, tractatores, seu veneratores, perversorum dogmatum, quibus asseritis non infligi pœnam, nisi pro culpa, et justis temporalem prosperitatem in vita hac tribui, impiis autem adversa: cujus oppositum sæpe contingit, et supra partim probatum est, infra vero a beato Job clarius efficaciusque probatur.
paras.en: [[13:4|Having first shewn that you are forgers|Prius vos ostendens fabricatores]], that is, cunning makers, [[13:4|of lies|mendacii]], that is, of false speech: since you have laid many crimes to my charge, in order to defend your erroneous opinions about the providence of God, thinking that no one is punished by God except for his own fault. So it is said of certain men in Jeremias too: [[Jer 9:5|they have taught their tongue to speak lies: they have laboured to commit iniquity|Docuerunt linguam suam loqui mendacium; ut inique agerent, laboraverunt]]. And [[13:4|maintainers|cultores]] [the Latin *cultores* is literally “tillers” or “worshippers”], that is, lovers, handlers or venerators, [[13:4|of perverse opinions|perversorum dogmatum]], by which you assert that punishment is inflicted only for fault, and that temporal prosperity is granted to the just in this life, and adversity to the wicked: the contrary of which often happens, as has partly been proved above [the margin refers to Art. XIV and another article, whose number is unread], and is proved below by blessed Job more clearly and more forcefully.

paras.t: Atque utinam taceretis, cessando a defensione errorum vestrorum: quia quo magis loquimini, eo insipientiam majorem ostenditis. Ideo subditur, ut putaremini esse sapientes. Sapientis enim est, docilem, taciturnum, corrigibilem esse, non loquacem aut in sensu proprio pertinacem. Ideo, si taceretis, videremini sapientes, sapientioresque essetis quam nunc; et tamen non essetis simpliciter sapientes, propter vestras erroneas opiniones. Hinc in Proverbiis legitur: Qui moderatur sermones suos, doctus et prudens est. Stultus si tacuerit, sapiens reputabitur.
paras.en: [[13:5|And I wish you would hold your peace|Atque utinam taceretis]], by ceasing to defend your errors: because the more you speak, the greater the folly you show. Therefore it is added, [[13:5|that you might be thought to be wise men|ut putaremini esse sapientes]]. For it belongs to a wise man to be teachable, silent and open to correction, not talkative, nor stubborn in his own opinion. So, if you held your peace, you would seem wise, and you would be wiser than you are now; and yet you would not be wise simply speaking, because of your erroneous opinions. Hence we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 17:27|He that setteth bounds to his words, is knowing and wise|Qui moderatur sermones suos, doctus et prudens est]]. [[Prov 17:28|Even a fool, if he will hold his peace, shall be counted wise|Stultus si tacuerit, sapiens reputabitur]].

paras.t: Audite ergo correptiones meas. Quia ex caritate vos arguo de excessu verborum, de falsitate intellectus, de pravitate affectus. Sic et Sapientia ait in Proverbiis: Convertimini ad correptionem meam; en proferam vobis spiritum meum. Et judicium labiorum meorum, id est, judicium reprobationis, quo per veram prudentiam errare vos judico, idque per labia mea denuntio, attendite, non statim ex indignatione verba mea more impatientium aversando, sed ea sapienter pensando. Porro, secundum Gregorium, bene primo ponit correptionem, deinde judicium: quia nisi per correptiones primus stulti tumor deprimatur, nequaquam per intelligentiam judicium justi cognoscitur.
paras.en: [[13:6|Hear ye therefore my reproof|Audite ergo correptiones meas]]: for it is out of charity that I rebuke you for excess of words, for falsity of understanding, for perversity of affection. So too Wisdom says in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:23|Turn ye at my reproof|Convertimini ad correptionem meam]]; [[Prov 1:23|behold I will utter my spirit to you|en proferam vobis spiritum meum]]. And [[13:6|the judgment of my lips|judicium labiorum meorum]], that is, the judgment of condemnation by which, through true prudence, I judge that you are in error, and which I declare with my lips, [[13:6|attend to|attendite]]: not turning away from my words at once in indignation, after the manner of the impatient, but weighing them wisely. Moreover, according to Gregory, he does well to put reproof first and then judgment: because unless the swelling of the fool is first brought down by reproofs, the judgment of the just man is in no way grasped by the understanding [the printed text has *primus*, with a footnote giving the reading *prius*, “first”].

paras.t: Numquid Deus indiget vestro mendacio? id est, ad defensionem suæ justitiæ non ei necesse est ut vos proferatis mendosa, asserendo nullum a Deo flagellari, nisi pro propria culpa: ex quo ultra proceditis ad falsam innocentium atque justorum accusationem, quum tales adspiciatis affligi; ut pro illo loquamini dolos, id est versutas ac fraudulentas propositiones ad colorandum vestra mendacia. Denique, veritas non eget mendacio, sicut nec virtus peccato; et quod probari non valet nisi per falsas præmissas, verum non est. Quum vero quis aliquam falsitatem probare et defensare conatur, fraudulentis uti mediis solet. Ita amici Job, ut suam assertionem defenderent, ipsumque Job comprobarent injustum, cautelose egerunt, extollendo divinam perfectionem, et ostendendo humanam defectuositatem: ex quibus concluserunt beati Job impietatem, quasi Deus per gratiam præservare hominem non posset a ruina per culpam.
paras.en: [[13:7|Hath God any need of your lie|Numquid Deus indiget vestro mendacio]]? that is, for the defence of his justice he has no need that you should bring forth falsehoods, asserting that no one is scourged by God except for his own fault: from which you go further, to a false accusation of the innocent and the just, when you see such men afflicted; [[13:7|that you should speak deceitfully for him|ut pro illo loquamini dolos]] [the Latin *dolos* is literally “deceits”], that is, crafty and fraudulent propositions, to colour your lies. Lastly, truth has no need of a lie, as neither has virtue need of sin; and what cannot be proved except through false premises is not true. But when someone tries to prove and defend some falsehood, he commonly uses fraudulent means. So the friends of Job, to defend their assertion and to prove Job unjust, acted craftily, extolling the divine perfection and pointing out human defectiveness: from which they concluded blessed Job’s impiety, as if God could not by grace preserve a man from falling through sin.

paras.t: Numquid faciem ejus accipitis? id est, in judicio isto, quo inter Deum et me judicatis, illum laudando, me condemnando, faciem Dei seu Deum ubique præsentem et omnia intuentem, approbatis et justificatis per inordinationem in judicio devitandam, quæ vocatur personarum acceptio, et fit, dum quis manifestam alicujus justitiam negat seu despicit, intuitu magnitudinis alterius partis. Quum ergo amici Job manifestam ejus justitiam negarint, eumque damnarint solo intuitu divinæ justitiæ, quoniam secundum dogmata sua videre non poterant, quomodo salva divina justitia, ipse Job juste a Deo flagellaretur nisi culpæ suæ demerito: videbantur faciem seu personam Dei accipere. Nam et præinducta magnifica de majestate, æquitate et sapientia Dei, quasi blandiendo, propter hoc disserebant, ne Deus videretur injustus innocentes plagando. Hinc subditur: et pro Deo judicare nitimini, id est, judicando conamini Deum justificare per quæcumque media et falsa; quod Deo non placet, quoniam falsitas displicet ei jugiter propter se ipsam, quum sit obliquatio atque recessus a veritate.
paras.en: [[13:8|Do you accept this person|Numquid faciem ejus accipitis]]? [the Latin is literally “do you accept his face”, the scriptural idiom for showing partiality] that is, in this judgment of yours, in which you judge between God and me, praising him and condemning me, you approve and justify the face of God, that is, God who is present everywhere and beholds all things, through a disorder in judgment that ought to be avoided, which is called acceptance of persons, and which comes about when someone denies or disregards the manifest justice of one party out of regard for the greatness of the other. Since, then, Job’s friends denied his manifest justice, and condemned him solely out of regard for the divine justice, because by their doctrines they could not see how, the divine justice being kept safe, Job himself could justly be scourged by God except for the demerit of his own fault, they seemed to accept the face or person of God. For the magnificent things they said earlier of the majesty, equity and wisdom of God they set out, as if flattering him, for this reason: lest God should seem unjust in striking the innocent. Hence it is added: [[13:8|and do you endeavour to judge for God|et pro Deo judicare nitimini]], that is, by judging you try to justify God by any means whatever, even false ones; which does not please God, since falsehood always displeases him for its own sake, being a turning aside and a departure from the truth.

paras.t: Porro Gregorius exponit hæc aliter, dicens: Faciem Dei accipere, est auctoritatem ipsius in judicando assumere, hoc est, quasi divina auctoritate seu in persona Dei, per modum quo judicat Deus, ferre judicium. Deus enim sic judicat, quod ipse nil reprehensibile in se habet, quod ab aliquo judicetur: sicque, secundum Gregorium, amici Job ejus opera reprehenderunt, ac si ipsi reprehensibile nihil haberent. Insuper, pro Deo judicare, est alterius defectus sine compassione discutere et damnare: quod amici Job videntur fecisse, quia dure et invective locuti sunt contra eum. Dicit autem Gregorius: Illius solius est peccata hominum sine compassione discutere, qui ex naturæ suæ omnipotentia nescit peccare. Homines vero justi quum pravorum facta redarguunt, suæ semper infirmitatis conscii, eos etsi exterius sæviendo, tamen interius compatiendo redarguunt.
paras.en: Gregory, however, explains these words otherwise, saying: To accept the face of God is to take on his authority in judging; that is, to pass judgment as if with divine authority, or in the person of God, in the way that God judges. For God judges in such a way that he himself has nothing reprehensible in him to be judged by anyone: and so, according to Gregory, Job’s friends found fault with his works as if they themselves had nothing reprehensible. Further, to judge for God is to examine and condemn another’s faults without compassion: which Job’s friends seem to have done, since they spoke against him harshly and with invective. And Gregory says: It belongs to him alone to examine the sins of men without compassion, who by the almightiness of his nature cannot sin. But just men, when they rebuke the deeds of the wicked, being ever conscious of their own weakness, rebuke them with severity outwardly, yet with compassion within.

paras.t: Aut placebit vester inordinatus processus in judicando, ei quem celare nihil potest, id est Deo omnia infallibiliter cognoscenti? Interdum enim alicui placet causæ suæ defensio, quamvis sit injusta, vel quamvis fiat per media inordinata, quoniam nescit causam suam esse injustam aut media illa quibus defenditur, esse distorta: quod in Deo omnia contuente locum nequit habere. Aut decipietur ut homo, vestris fraudulentiis, id est callidis contra me processibus, ut putet vos ordinate suam causam contra me defensare? sicut interdum aliquis simplex putat suam causam esse injustam, ideoque non cupit eam defendi; sed ab advocatis persuadetur ei quod causa sua sit justa, sicque petit ut defendatur. Sed Deus cujus sapientiæ non est finis aut numerus, sic falli non potest.
paras.en: [[13:9|Or shall it please him|Aut placebit]], your disordered way of proceeding in judgment, [[13:9|from whom nothing can be concealed|ei quem celare nihil potest]], that is, God, who knows all things infallibly? For sometimes the defence of his cause pleases a man, though it is unjust, or though it is carried on by disordered means, because he does not know that his cause is unjust, or that the means by which it is defended are crooked: which cannot happen in God, who beholds all things; [[13:9|or shall he be deceived as a man, with your deceitful dealings?|Aut decipietur ut homo, vestris fraudulentiis]] that is, by your cunning proceedings against me, so as to think that you are rightly defending his cause against me? as sometimes a simple man thinks his cause is unjust, and therefore does not wish it to be defended; but he is persuaded by advocates that his cause is just, and so he asks that it be defended. But God, of whose wisdom there is no end or number[[Ps 146:5||]], cannot be deceived in this way.

paras.t: Ipse vos arguet de vestra inordinata disputatione adversum me: sicut et infra ultimo capitulo patet. Qui enim Deum per falsa commendat, non solum ei non placet, sed insuper displicet, pœnam meretur, et Deo qui veritas est, adversatur: quemadmodum ad Corinthios scribit Apostolus: Invenimur (inquit) et falsi testes Dei (videlicet si resurrectio mortuorum non est), quoniam testimonium diximus adversus Deum, quod suscitavit Christum: quem non suscitavit, si mortui non resurgunt. Nempe quidquid veritati contrariatur, divinitus reprobatur. Quoniam in abscondito, id est cordis occulto, faciem ejus accipitis: secundum sensum præhabitum; ita quod vobis conscii estis, vel saltem essetis, si advertere veritatem velletis, quod judicando inter Deum et me, accipitis faciem ejus: quia justitia mea vobis et omnibus nota fuit, sicque per falsam mei accusationem defenditis Dei justitiam.
paras.en: [[13:10|He shall reprove you|Ipse vos arguet]] for your disordered disputing against me: as is plain below, in the last chapter. For he who commends God by falsehoods not only does not please him, but even displeases him, deserves punishment, and sets himself against God, who is truth; as the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 15:15|we are found false witnesses of God|Invenimur (inquit) et falsi testes Dei]] (that is, if there is no resurrection of the dead), [[1 Cor 15:15|because we have given testimony against God, that he hath raised up Christ, whom he hath not raised up, if the dead rise not again|quoniam testimonium diximus adversus Deum, quod suscitavit Christum: quem non suscitavit, si mortui non resurgunt]]. Indeed, whatever is contrary to the truth is condemned by God. Then: [[13:10|because in secret|Quoniam in abscondito]], that is, in the hidden place of the heart, [[13:10|you accept his person|faciem ejus accipitis]], in the sense given above; so that you are conscious, or at least would be if you were willing to attend to the truth, that in judging between God and me you accept his face: since my justice was known to you and to all, and so by a false accusation of me you defend the justice of God.

paras.t: Statim ut se commoverit, non per suæ naturæ aliquam variationem, sed per potestatis suæ processum in actum exteriorem, id est, mox quum exercere cœperit ultionem. Juxta hunc modum loquendi, Plato dixit primum motorem moveri. Et Aristoteles Platonem super hoc arguens, verba ejus, non mentem, impugnat. Nam et beatissimus Dionysius ait primo de Divinis nominibus capitulo: Omnes Patre moto illuminationes descendunt. Vel humano modo loquitur Job de Deo, quoniam homo vindicaturus, ira seu aliqua affectione intra se movetur, et sic in ultionem progreditur. Turbabit vos, per pœnam infligendam, ita quod pacem et tranquillitatem, in qua nunc esse et contra me disputare videmini, ex levi etiam percussione perdetis, qui reprehenditis me quod propter plagam hanc maximam sum turbatus. Et terror ejus, id est timor quem ex consideratione Dei et suæ vindictæ concipietis, vel terribilis ejus majestas, irruet super vos, id est, corda vestra deprimet ita, quod alia seu graviora tormenta timebitis: et hoc dicitur, nisi pœnituissent, sicut sequentia.
paras.en: [[13:11|As soon as he shall move himself|Statim ut se commoverit]]: not by any change in his nature, but by the going forth of his power into outward act; that is, as soon as he begins to take vengeance. In this manner of speaking Plato said that the first mover is moved; and Aristotle, finding fault with Plato on this point, attacks his words, not his meaning. For the most blessed Dionysius too says, in the first chapter of the Divine Names: All illuminations come down when the Father is moved. Or else Job speaks of God after the manner of men, since a man about to take vengeance is moved within himself by anger or some other affection, and so proceeds to vengeance. Then: [[13:11|he shall trouble you|Turbabit vos]], by the punishment he will inflict, so that you, who blame me for being troubled by this very great stroke, will lose even through a light stroke the peace and calm in which you now seem to be, and to dispute against me; and [[13:11|his dread|terror ejus]], that is, the fear you will conceive from considering God and his vengeance, or his terrible majesty, [[13:11|shall fall upon you|irruet super vos]], that is, shall weigh your hearts down, so that you will fear other and heavier torments. And this is said with the condition, unless they should repent; and so is what follows.

paras.t: Memoria vestra comparabitur cineri, id est, cito cessabit et auferetur, quemadmodum cinis faciliter tollitur, cessat et perit. Sed quomodo verum est hoc, quum usque in præsens per totum mundum tam communis sit virorum istorum memoria, præsertim quum liber hic legitur? Et respondendum, quod loquitur eis tanquam errantibus: sicque eorum memoria cito deperiit, non quasi omnino non manserit, sed quia non mansit ad bonum seu ad laudem eorum, quomodo justorum memoria dicitur permanere, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet. Et in Psalmo: In memoria æterna erit justus. Et de impiis: Periit (inquit) memoria eorum cum sonitu. Et redigentur in lutum, id est vilem materiam, cervices vestræ, anima a corpore separata, quando corpora vestra putrefient et incinerabuntur.
paras.en: [[13:12|Your remembrance shall be compared to ashes|Memoria vestra comparabitur cineri]], that is, it shall soon cease and be taken away, as ashes are easily removed, cease and perish. But how is this true, when to this day the memory of these men is so common throughout the whole world, especially when this book is read? The answer is that he speaks to them as men in error: and so their memory soon perished, not as though it did not remain at all, but because it did not remain to their good or to their praise, in the way that the memory of the just is said to endure, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 10:7|The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot|Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 111:7|The just shall be in everlasting remembrance|In memoria æterna erit justus]]. And of the wicked: [[Ps 9:7|Their memory hath perished with a noise|Periit (inquit) memoria eorum cum sonitu]]. And [[13:12|your necks|cervices vestræ]] [[13:12|shall be brought to clay|Et redigentur in lutum]], that is, to vile matter, when the soul has been separated from the body, when your bodies shall rot and turn to ashes.

paras.t: Consequenter Job contra amicos disputaturus, et eorum falsa dogmata destructurus, audientiam petit. Tacete paulisper: quia diu tacere, impatientiæ vestræ esset molestum; ego quoque non inordinate protraham verba; ut loquar quodcumque mihi mens suggesserit, id est, quod ratio dictaverit esse dicendum, non ad quod inclinaverit passio: et ita succinctus ero in verbis.
paras.en: Next Job, being about to dispute against his friends and to overthrow their false doctrines, asks for a hearing. [[13:13|Hold your peace a little while|Tacete paulisper]]: for to keep silence long would be irksome to your impatience; and I for my part will not draw out my words without measure; [[13:13|that I may speak whatsoever my mind shall suggest to me|ut loquar quodcumque mihi mens suggesserit]], that is, what reason shall dictate ought to be said, not that to which passion shall incline me: and so I shall be brief in words.

paras.t: Quare lacero carnes meas dentibus meis? id est, cur corpus meum dire affligo instar eorum qui præ fame carnem suam manducant? Ut enim præhabitum est in expositione secundi capituli, pœnam plagæ sibi inflictæ Job auxit, saniem testa radendo, quod fuit quædam corporis laceratio, atque in sterquilinio residendo. Juxta hunc modum David concinit: Dum appropiant super me nocentes, ut edant carnes meas. Et in Michea Dominus ait de impiis: Qui comedunt carnem populi mei. Et animam meam porto in manibus meis, id est, morti expono me ipsum, et animam meam separationi a corpore, quemadmodum quod fertur in manibus, exponi videtur raptoribus. Job autem (ut sæpius patuit) mortem optavit. Porro, per hoc quod anima alicujus dicitur esse seu portari in manibus, designat Scriptura aliquod magnum seu manifestum mortis periculum, seu propinquitatem aut dispositionem ad necem. Unde Jephthe reversus de bello: Posui, inquit, animam meam in manibus meis. De David quoque primo Regum, Jonathas dixit: Posuit animam suam in manibus suis, et percussit Philistæum.
paras.en: [[13:14|Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth|Quare lacero carnes meas dentibus meis]]? that is, why do I afflict my body so cruelly, like those who eat their own flesh for hunger? For, as was said in the exposition of the second chapter, Job increased the pain of the stroke inflicted on him by scraping the corrupt matter with a potsherd, which was a kind of tearing of the body, and by sitting on the dunghill[[Job 2:8||]]. After this manner David sings: [[Ps 26:2|Whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh|Dum appropiant super me nocentes, ut edant carnes meas]]. And in Micheas the Lord says of the wicked: [[Mich 3:3|Who have eaten the flesh of my people|Qui comedunt carnem populi mei]]. And [[13:14|carry my soul in my hands|animam meam porto in manibus meis]], that is, I expose myself to death, and my soul to separation from the body, as what is carried in the hands seems to be exposed to robbers. And Job (as has often appeared) wished for death. Moreover, when someone’s soul is said to be, or to be carried, in his hands, Scripture signifies some great or manifest danger of death, or nearness or readiness to die. So Jephte, returning from the war, says: [[Judg 12:3|I put my life in my own hands|Posui, inquit, animam meam in manibus meis]] [the Latin *anima* is both “soul” and “life”: the Douay-Rheims has “soul” in Job and “life” in these two places]. And of David, in the first book of Kings, Jonathan said: [[1 Kings 19:5|he put his life in his hand, and slew the Philistine|Posuit animam suam in manibus suis, et percussit Philistæum]].

paras.t: Ad hanc quæstionem respondet: Etiamsi occiderit me, corporaliter usque ad mortem vexando, in ipso sperabo, quod miserebitur animæ meæ, et per præsentes tribulationes a futuris æternis eripiar atque salvificer. Ac si dicat: Præinducta verba de carnium laceratione non dixi, nec me ita afflixi mortemque petii, ex desperatione, ut mihi imponitis, quum propter nullam adversitatem quantumlibet gravem et magnam, sim desperaturus. Nam, ut ait Apostolus, Spes non confundit. Et Psalmista loquitur Deo: Sperent in te qui noverunt nomen tuum, quoniam non dereliquisti quærentes te, Domine. Vel, Si occiderit me, id est, spiritualiter occidi permiserit me: quod fit, dum Deus sinit hominem mortali obrui culpa; in ipso sperabo, quod pœnitenti indulgeat, gratiamque faciat abundare, ubi abundavit iniquitas: nec ex præsumptione hoc dico, vel sine meritis me vere atque salubriter sperare existimo. Ideo subditur: Veruntamen vias meas, id est cogitationes, affectiones, locutiones et opera, quibus quasi per medium iter tendo ad ultimum finem ac patriam, in conspectu ejus arguam, id est, coram Deo examinabo ac reprehendam, detestando ac emendando quidquid in eis reprehensione dignum conspexero. Imo, etsi sine peccato notabili fuerint viæ hæ, tamen comparatione sanctitatis ac majestatis divinæ, nullius momenti sunt, nihilque satis rectum est, secundum Albertum.
paras.en: To this question he answers: [[13:15|Although he should kill me|Etiamsi occiderit me]], afflicting me in body even unto death, [[13:15|I will trust in him|in ipso sperabo]], that he will have mercy on my soul, and that through present tribulations I shall be rescued from the eternal ones to come, and saved. As if he were saying: I did not say the words above about tearing my flesh, nor did I so afflict myself and ask for death, out of despair, as you charge me; for I shall despair because of no adversity, however heavy and great. For, as the Apostle says, [[Rom 5:5|hope confoundeth not|Spes non confundit]]. And the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 9:11|let them trust in thee who know thy name: for thou hast not forsaken them that seek thee, O Lord|Sperent in te qui noverunt nomen tuum, quoniam non dereliquisti quærentes te, Domine]]. Or, [[13:15|Although he should kill me|Si occiderit me]], that is, though he should allow me to be killed spiritually, which happens when God permits a man to be overwhelmed by mortal sin, [[13:15|I will trust in him|in ipso sperabo]], that he will pardon the penitent, and make grace abound where iniquity abounded[[Rom 5:20||]]: nor do I say this out of presumption, nor do I think that I hope truly and to my salvation without merits. Therefore it is added: [[13:15|but yet I will reprove my ways|Veruntamen vias meas]], that is, my thoughts, affections, words and works, by which, as by a road in between, I make my way to my last end and my fatherland, [[13:15|in his sight|in conspectu ejus arguam]], that is, before God I will examine and reprove them, detesting and amending whatever I see in them worthy of reproof. Nay, even if these ways have been without notable sin, yet compared with the divine holiness and majesty they are of no account, and nothing is right enough, according to Albert.

paras.t: Hujus felicis reprehensionis fructum subjungit: Et ipse erit salvator meus, id est dator veræ salutis, quam non tollit nisi peccatum. Propter quod ait Isaias: Iste omnis fructus, ut auferatur peccatum. Qui enim cordialiter se accusat, pœnitet et emendare proponit, remissionem culpæ, infusionem gratiæ, adeptionem gloriæ promeretur. Hinc ait Psalmista: Dixi, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino; et tu remisisti impietatem peccati mei. Apostolus quoque: Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Hoc itaque vere, non ficte, agam. Non enim veniet in conspectu ejus, id est, Deo per complacentiam non apparebit, non ei placebit, neque ab eo consequetur salutem, veniendo ad clarum Dei conspectum, omnis hypocrita, qui aliud intus est, utpote impius, aliud foris ostendit, quia virtuosum se simulat; id est, nullus talis in conspectu Dei sic veniet, nisi pœniteat. Unde Christus tam sæpe ait in Evangelio: Væ vobis, hypocritæ. Itemque: Nolite fieri sicut hypocritæ. Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam. Et in hoc verbo notat Job suos amicos, qui foris justitiam videbantur defendere ac zelari, quum intus pleni essent erroribus.
paras.en: He adds the fruit of this happy reproof: [[13:16|And he shall be my saviour|Et ipse erit salvator meus]], that is, the giver of true salvation, which nothing takes away but sin. For this reason Isaias says: [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|Iste omnis fructus, ut auferatur peccatum]]. For he who accuses himself from the heart, repents and purposes to amend, merits the remission of guilt, the infusion of grace and the attainment of glory. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 31:5|I said I will confess against my self my injustice to the Lord: and thou hast forgiven the wickedness of my sin|Dixi, Confitebor adversum me injustitiam meam Domino; et tu remisisti impietatem peccati mei]]. And the Apostle: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. This, then, I will do truly, not feignedly. For [[13:16|no hypocrite shall come before his presence|Non enim veniet in conspectu ejus]], that is, shall not appear before God so as to be pleasing to him, shall not please him, nor obtain salvation from him by coming into the clear sight of God, [[13:16|no hypocrite|omnis hypocrita]], who is one thing within, namely wicked, and shows another without, since he feigns himself virtuous; that is, no such man shall come so into God’s sight unless he repents. Hence Christ says so often in the Gospel: [[Matt 23:15|Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites|Væ vobis, hypocritæ]]. And again: [[Matt 6:16|be not as the hypocrites|Nolite fieri sicut hypocritæ]]. [[Matt 6:16|Amen I say to you, they have received their reward|Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam]]. And in this word Job censures his friends, who outwardly seemed to defend justice and to be zealous for it, when within they were full of errors.

paras.t: Audite auribus mentis et corporis sermonem meum, et ænigmata, id est obscuritates seu difficultates in meis latentes sermonibus, percipite auribus vestris: quia diligentissimam considerationem requirunt. Vel, Ænigmata, id est figurativas locutiones vel similitudines, quibus probo quæ dico. Hoc etenim spectat ad sapientem, secundum illud Proverbiorum: Animadvertet parabolam et interpretationem, verba sapientium et ænigmata eorum.
paras.en: [[13:17|Hear ye|Audite]] with the ears of mind and body [[13:17|my speech|sermonem meum]], and [[13:17|hidden truths|ænigmata]], that is, the obscurities or difficulties lying hidden in my words, [[13:17|receive with your ears|percipite auribus vestris]]: for they call for the most diligent consideration. Or, [[13:17|hidden truths|Ænigmata]] [the Latin *ænigmata* is literally “riddles”], that is, figurative expressions or similitudes, by which I prove what I say. For this belongs to the wise man, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 1:6|He shall understand a parable and the interpretation, the words of the wise, and their mysterious sayings|Animadvertet parabolam et interpretationem, verba sapientium et ænigmata eorum]].

paras.t: Si fuero judicatus a Deo vel quocumque judice justo, scio quod justus inveniar. Hoc (secundum Thomam et quosdam) non dicit Job de justitia vitæ, quia jam dixit, Vias meas in conspectu ejus arguam; sed de veritate doctrinæ, de qua judicialiter contendebatur. Deus autem infra ultimo capitulo, dat sententiam pro Job, ipsum laudando, quod recta et recte locutus sit coram se. Verumtamen intelligi potest de justitia vitæ, præsertim quum tantæ justitiæ in conversatione fuerit Job, ut Deo teste non fuerit ei similis in terra, homo simplex et rectus. Ad hoc autem quod homo justificetur a Deo, non oportet quod nunquam peccatum mortale incurrerit, aut nullum habeat veniale: quum et Paulus tam dire peccaverit, et Spiritu Sancto recepto postea, non prorsus ab omni veniali fuit immunis; sicut nec ceteri Apostoli, nec Joannes Baptista, propter quod dixit ad Christum: Ego a te debeo baptizari. Sed sufficit quod sine mortali peccato sit, et de venialibus saltem in communi doluerit. Talis autem fuit beatus Job. Unde et nunc dicit se certum, quod justus invenietur, præsertim ab his peccatis, quæ sibi ab amicis suis imponebantur. Sed quomodo potuit certus esse de isto, quum superius jam dixerit: Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me; etiamsi simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea? Sed hujus solutio ex dictis ibidem est evidens. Deo enim revelante scire hoc potuit; et variis modis dicitur aliquis justus seu justificari, ut patet ex dictis. Denique injustus pœnitendo fit justus.
paras.en: [[13:18|If I shall be judged|Si fuero judicatus]] by God or by any just judge, [[13:18|I know that I shall be found just|scio quod justus inveniar]]. This (according to Thomas and some others) Job does not say of justice of life, since he has already said, [[13:15|I will reprove my ways in his sight|Vias meas in conspectu ejus arguam]]; but of the truth of doctrine, which was the matter in dispute, as in a court. And God, below in the last chapter, gives sentence for Job, praising him because he had spoken right things, and rightly, before him[[Job 42:8||]]. Yet it can be understood of justice of life, especially since Job was of such justice in his conduct that, by God’s own witness, [[Job 1:8|there is none like him in the earth, a simple and upright man|non fuerit ei similis in terra, homo simplex et rectus]] [the same words stand in Job 2:3]. Now for a man to be justified by God it is not necessary that he should never have fallen into mortal sin, or that he should have no venial sin: since Paul too sinned so grievously[[1 Cor 15:9||]] [the margin’s reference here is hard to read; it is probably 1 Cor. xv, 9], and after receiving the Holy Ghost was still not wholly free of every venial sin; nor were the other Apostles, nor John the Baptist, for which reason he said to Christ: [[Matt 3:14|I ought to be baptized by thee|Ego a te debeo baptizari]]. But it is enough that a man be without mortal sin, and have sorrowed for his venial sins, at least in general. And such was blessed Job. So now too he says he is certain that he will be found just, above all as regards the sins laid to his charge by his friends. But how could he be certain of this, when he has already said above: [[Job 9:20|If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me|Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me]]; [[Job 9:21|Although I should be simple, even this my soul shall be ignorant of|etiamsi simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]]? But the answer to this is evident from what was said there. For he could know this by God’s revealing it; and a man is said to be just, or to be justified, in various ways, as is plain from what has been said. Lastly, the unjust man becomes just by repenting.

paras.t: Quis est qui judicetur mecum, id est, contra me disputans, judicetur a Deo an ipse veram justamque teneat partem, an ego? Veniat, id est, me accedat. Sic et in Isaia dicitur: Quis est adversarius meus? accedat ad me. Quis contradicit mihi? stemus simul. Quare tacens, falsitati non contradicendo, consumor, id est, graviter intus affligor, et morti propinquo? Justo quidem zelo contra amicorum errores atque mendacia incitabatur, atque ad defendendum veritatem accendebatur: ita quod dolor intus manens inclusus, amplius augebatur: per verba autem quasi evaporans, alleviabatur. Sic ait et Isaias: Væ mihi, quia tacui. Tempus enim loquendi, et tempus tacendi, ut Salomon protestatur. Defendenda autem est veritas atque justitia, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Pro anima tua non confundaris dicere verum. Pro justitia agonizare pro anima tua, et usque ad mortem certa pro justitia.
paras.en: [[13:19|Who is he that will plead against me|Quis est qui judicetur mecum]], that is, who, disputing against me, will be judged by God as to whether he holds the true and just side, or I? [[13:19|let him come|Veniat]], that is, let him come up to me. So too it is said in Isaias: [[Is 50:8|who is my adversary? let him come near to me|Quis est adversarius meus? accedat ad me]]; [[Is 50:8|who will contend with me? let us stand together|Quis contradicit mihi? stemus simul]]. Why am I, [[13:19|holding my peace|tacens]], and not contradicting falsehood, [[13:19|consumed|consumor]], that is, grievously afflicted within, and brought near to death? For he was stirred by a just zeal against the errors and lies of his friends, and kindled to defend the truth: so that his grief, staying shut up within, grew greater, but was relieved by words, as though it breathed itself out. So too Isaias says: [[Is 6:5|Woe is me, because I have held my peace|Væ mihi, quia tacui]]. For there is [[Eccles 3:7|a time to speak|Tempus enim loquendi]], and [[Eccles 3:7|a time to keep silence|et tempus tacendi]], as Solomon declares. And truth and justice must be defended, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 4:24|For thy soul be not ashamed to say the truth|Pro anima tua non confundaris dicere verum]]. [[Ecclus 4:33|Strive for justice for thy soul, and even unto death fight for justice|Pro justitia agonizare pro anima tua, et usque ad mortem certa pro justitia]].

paras.t: Duo tantum ne facias mihi, id est, duo mala pœnalia et disputationis ac responsionis impeditiva, non mihi, o Deus, infligas; et tunc a facie tua non abscondar, id est, a collatione tecum disputativa non me abscondam, nec abstraham, sed tecum fiducialiter disputabo. Porro, quod ait, Non abscondar, non ita intelligit, quasi aliquis (absolute loquendo) possit se a Deo abscondere, qui æternaliter, invariabiliter et superclarissime omnia intuetur: sed quoniam homo, quantum in se est, se conatur abscondere Deo, dum ei apparere seu loqui refugit et formidat. Unde et Adam loquitur Deo: Vocem tuam audivi, et timui, et abscondi me. Jonas quoque surrexit ut fugeret a facie Domini in Tharsis. Manum tuam longe fac a me, id est, potestatis tuæ hanc quam patior plagam seu pœnam aufer a me, et formido tua, id est timor de te conceptus, timor, inquam, de futuris suppliciis, non me terreat. Siquidem duo hæc, scilicet dolor vehemens de malo præsenti, et formido intensa de malo pœnali futuro, actum impediunt rationis. Hoc est quod supra dixit Job: Auferat a me virgam suam, et pavor ejus non me terreat; neque enim possum metuens respondere. Præterea quod ait, A facie tua non abscondar, consonat ei quod in Joanne scriptum est: Qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem, ut manifestentur opera ejus, quia in Deo sunt facta. Siquidem veritas non quærit angulum, sed falsitas et peccatum. Hinc qui bonæ conscientiæ securitate aut confidentia est armatus, non se subtrahit aut abscondit a Deo ac luce virtutis, sed quem conscientia sua remordet, secundum illud Joannis: Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem et non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera ejus.
paras.en: [[13:20|Two things only do not to me|Duo tantum ne facias mihi]], that is, do not inflict on me, O God, two penal evils that hinder disputing and answering; [[13:20|and then from thy face I shall not be hid|et tunc a facie tua non abscondar]], that is, I will not hide myself from conferring with thee in disputation, nor draw back, but will dispute with thee confidently. Now when he says, [[13:20|I shall not be hid|Non abscondar]], he does not mean it as though anyone (speaking absolutely) could hide himself from God, who beholds all things eternally, unchangeably and with surpassing clearness: but because a man, so far as in him lies, tries to hide himself from God, when he shrinks from appearing before him or speaking to him, and dreads it. So Adam says to God: [[Gen 3:10|I heard thy voice|Vocem tuam audivi]], [[Gen 3:10|and I was afraid|et timui]], [[Gen 3:10|and I hid myself|et abscondi me]]. And [[Jon 1:3|Jonah rose up to flee into Tharsis from the face of the Lord|Jonas quoque surrexit ut fugeret a facie Domini in Tharsis]]. [[13:21|Withdraw thy hand far from me|Manum tuam longe fac a me]], that is, take away from me this stroke or punishment of thy power that I suffer; [[13:21|and let not thy dread|et formido tua]], that is, the fear conceived of thee, the fear, I mean, of torments to come, [[13:21|terrify me|non me terreat]]. For these two things, namely vehement grief at a present evil and intense dread of a penal evil to come, hinder the act of reason. This is what Job said above: [[Job 9:34|Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me|Auferat a me virgam suam, et pavor ejus non me terreat]]; [[Job 9:35|for I cannot answer while I am in fear|neque enim possum metuens respondere]]. Further, his saying, [[13:20|from thy face I shall not be hid|A facie tua non abscondar]], agrees with what is written in John: [[John 3:21|he that doth truth cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest: because they are done in God|Qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem, ut manifestentur opera ejus, quia in Deo sunt facta]]. For truth does not seek a corner, but falsehood and sin do. Hence he who is armed with the security or confidence of a good conscience does not withdraw or hide himself from God and from the light of virtue [a footnote gives the reading *veritatis*, “of truth”, for *virtutis*], but he whose conscience gnaws at him does, according to that of John: [[John 3:20|every one that doth evil hateth the light and cometh not to the light, that his works may not be reproved|Omnis qui male agit, odit lucem et non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera ejus]].

paras.t: Consequenter ostendit se paratum in disputatione cum Deo habenda ad actum opponentis, et insuper ad actum respondentis, quasi indifferens ad utrumque, et Deo quasi dans optionem: non quod velit objicere ad reprehendendum, sed ad veritatis notitiam adipiscendam, ut dictum est plenius. Unde ista sunt verba bonæ fiduciæ et familiaritatis cum Deo, non ex superbia aut præsumptione, quasi velit de pari cum Deo contendere. Voca me, id est, jube me apparere ad respondendum, et ego respondebo tibi pro posse, rationem pro veritate reddendo, et vera quæ dixi defendendo; aut certe loquar, proponendo et inquirendo quæ movent me, et tu responde mihi, me instruendo ac certificando de dubiis.
paras.en: Next he shows that, in the disputation to be held with God, he is ready for the part of the opponent and also for the part of the respondent [in a scholastic disputation the opponent raises objections and the respondent answers them], as though indifferent to either, and as it were giving God the choice: not that he wishes to object in order to find fault, but in order to come to knowledge of the truth, as has been said more fully. So these are words of good confidence and familiarity with God, not of pride or presumption, as though he wished to contend with God as an equal. [[13:22|Call me|Voca me]], that is, bid me appear to answer, [[13:22|and I will answer thee|et ego respondebo tibi]] as far as I can, giving reasons for the truth, and defending the true things I have said; [[13:22|or else I will speak|aut certe loquar]], putting forward and inquiring into what moves me, [[13:22|and do thou answer me|et tu responde mihi]], instructing me and making me certain about my doubts.

paras.t: Responde mihi, quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata; scelera mea atque delicta ostende mihi. Hic sanctus Job, in disputatione quam cum Deo aggreditur ut instruatur ab eo, assumit personam proponentis seu opponentis. Præterea, quoniam amici ejus sibi a principio imposuerunt, quod pro suis peccatis esset percussus, imo pro gravibus excessibus esset tam graviter cæsus, ideo Deum primo deposcit, ut eum de hac re plenius doceat. Responde mihi, id est, mihi te, o Deus, sciscitanti ostende per inspirationem occultam seu angelicam revelationem, quantas, id est quam intensas, graves seu magnas, habeo iniquitates, ut amici mei calumniantur. Quasi dicat: Si, ut illi affirmant, pœna non infligitur nisi pro culpa, ita quod ista supplicia pro meis peccatis sustineo, tunc utique valde graves habeo iniquitates: quia pro majori culpa infligitur major pœna; ego autem gravissime sum plagatus. Hæc ergo humiliter sciscitatur, ad excludendum falsam suæ flagellationis causam, quam amici ejus asserebant esse ipsius iniquitatem; et etiam, ut clarius desuper illustretur.
paras.en: [[13:22|do thou answer me|Responde mihi]]: [[13:23|How many are my iniquities and sins?|quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata]] [[13:23|make me know my crimes and offenses|scelera mea atque delicta ostende mihi]]. Here holy Job, in the disputation which he undertakes with God in order to be instructed by him, takes the part of one who propounds, or objects. Moreover, since his friends had charged him from the beginning with being struck for his sins, nay, with being smitten so heavily for grievous excesses, he therefore first asks God to teach him more fully on this matter. [[13:22|do thou answer me|Responde mihi]], that is, show me, O God, as I question thee, by a hidden inspiration or by the revelation of an angel, [[13:23|How many|quantas]], that is, how intense, grave or great, [[13:23|are my iniquities|habeo iniquitates]], as my friends falsely charge. As if to say: If, as they affirm, punishment is inflicted only for guilt, so that I suffer these torments for my sins, then indeed I have very grave iniquities: for a greater punishment is inflicted for a greater fault; and I have been most grievously stricken. He asks this humbly, then, to rule out the false cause of his scourging which his friends alleged, namely his own iniquity; and also so that he may be more clearly enlightened from above.

paras.t: Et peccata. Quædam peccata fiunt in proximum, quæ hic designantur per iniquitates; quædam in se ipsum, ut vitia gustus et tactus, quæ ipsius peccantis personæ et corpori maxime nocent, quæ jam per peccata notantur; quædam fiunt directe in Deum, quæ sunt contra tria præcepta primæ tabulæ, ut sunt infidelitas, blasphemia, sacrilegium, odium Dei: et ista vocantur scelera, quasi accusatione dignissima. Rursus, præcepta divina duplicia sunt, scilicet affirmativa: et contra hæc sunt peccata omissionis, quæ hic dicuntur delicta, quasi derelicta, quia in eis homo omittit et negligit quod Deus fieri jubet. Alia sunt præcepta negativa: contra quæ sunt peccata commissionis, in quibus homo agit quæ fieri Deus prohibuit, ut quum ait: Non occides. Petit itaque Job, ut si hujusmodi mala habuerit, vel de eis (si qua habuit) non pœnituerit, sibi a Deo pandatur.
paras.en: [[13:23|and sins|Et peccata]]. Some sins are committed against one's neighbour, and these are signified here by *iniquities*; some against oneself, such as the vices of taste and touch, which chiefly harm the sinner's own person and body, and these are here denoted by *sins*; some are committed directly against God, namely those against the three commandments of the first table, such as unbelief, blasphemy, sacrilege, hatred of God: and these are called *crimes* [Latin scelera], as most deserving of accusation. Again, the divine commandments are of two kinds: the affirmative, and against these are the sins of omission, which are here called *offenses* [delicta, as if derelicta, “things left undone”], because in them man omits and neglects what God commands to be done. The others are the negative commandments, against which are the sins of commission, in which man does what God has forbidden to be done, as when he says: [[Ex 20:13|Thou shalt not kill.|Non occides]] Job asks, then, that if he has had evils of this kind, or has not repented of them (if he had any), it may be laid open to him by God.

paras.t: Deinde ex caritatis fiducia querulose interrogat: Cur faciem tuam abscondis? id est, pietatis tuæ respectum, consolationem relevamenque subtrahis, quantum ad hoc quod permittis me gravissimis animæ corporisque doloribus affici, nec me pro relevamine deprecantem exaudis. Hinc infra etiam ait: Sto, et non respicis me; clamo ad te, et non exaudis me: mutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in duritia manus tuæ adversaris mihi. Hinc subdit, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum? id est, ita affligis me, quasi impius essem, et per consequens inimicus tuus, qui odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem: juxta illud Sapientis, Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus. Hoc est quod supra jam dixit: Quare posuisti me contrarium tibi? Verumtamen, absolute loquendo, Deus tempore afflictionis hujus non abscondit faciem suam a Job, nec eum sibi adversarium arbitrabatur: imo gratiosissime eum adspexit ac conservavit in anima, paternaliter castigavit in corpore, illuminavit et spiritu prophetico decoravit in mente. Sic loquitur more afflictorum, qui verba doloris sui expressive solent effari.
paras.en: Then, out of the confidence of charity, he asks plaintively: [[13:24|Why hidest thou thy face|Cur faciem tuam abscondis]]? that is, why dost thou withdraw the regard of thy loving-kindness, thy consolation and relief, inasmuch as thou permittest me to be afflicted with most grievous pains of soul and body, and dost not hear me when I pray for relief? So too he says below: [[Job 30:20|I stand up, and thou dost not regard me|Sto, et non respicis me]]; [[Job 30:20|I cry to thee, and thou hearest me not|clamo ad te, et non exaudis me]]: [[Job 30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me, and in the hardness of thy hand thou art against me|mutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in duritia manus tuæ adversaris mihi]]. Hence he adds, [[13:24|and thinkest me thy enemy?|et arbitraris me inimicum tuum]] that is, thou afflictest me as though I were wicked, and consequently thy enemy, thou who [[Ps 5:7|hatest all the workers of iniquity|odisti omnes qui operantur iniquitatem]]: according to that of the Wise Man, [[Wis 14:9|to God the wicked and his wickedness are hateful alike|Odio sunt Deo impius et impietas ejus]]. This is what he said already above: [[Job 7:20|why hast thou set me opposite to thee|Quare posuisti me contrarium tibi?]]? Yet, speaking absolutely, God did not hide his face from Job in the time of this affliction, nor did he think him his adversary: rather he looked upon him most graciously and preserved him in his soul, chastised him as a father in his body, enlightened him and adorned him with the spirit of prophecy in his mind. He speaks thus after the manner of the afflicted, who are wont to utter the words of their grief vividly.

paras.t: Deinceps ad provocandum clementiam Dei, hoc est ad impetrandum ejus auxilium, inducit verba humanam fragilitatem infirmitatemque signantia.
