Contra folium quod vento rapitur, id est in me et ad meam afflictionem, qui folio quod vento impellitur, similis sum: quia res sum labilis atque infirma; et ut folium vento movetur, sic ego variis cogitationibus, affectionibus, tentationibusque impellor et feror seu moveor; juxta id Isaiæ: Cecidimus quasi folium universi; iniquitates nostræ quasi ventus abstulerunt nos; ostendis potentiam tuam, qua me faciliter dejecisti atque vicisti. Quasi dicat: Potestas tua quum sit immensa, importabilis mihi est: nec decens videtur, ut eam in tam infirma ac fragili creatura ostendas. Ista sunt verba misericordiæ provocativa, non reprobativa operationis seu dispositionis divinæ.
paras.en: Next, to call forth the clemency of God, that is, to obtain his help, he brings in words that signify human frailty and weakness. [[13:25|Against a leaf, that is carried away with the wind|Contra folium quod vento rapitur]], that is, against me and to my affliction, who am like a leaf driven by the wind: for I am a thing unsteady and weak; and as a leaf is moved by the wind, so I am driven and carried or moved by divers thoughts, affections and temptations; according to that of Isaias: [[Is 64:6|we have all fallen as a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, have taken us away|Cecidimus quasi folium universi; iniquitates nostræ quasi ventus abstulerunt nos]]; [[13:25|thou shewest thy power|ostendis potentiam tuam]], by which thou hast easily cast me down and overcome me. As if to say: Since thy power is immense, it is unbearable to me: nor does it seem fitting that thou shouldst show it upon so weak and frail a creature. These are words that call forth mercy, not words that find fault with the working or disposition of God.

paras.t: Et stipulam siccam persequeris, id est me veteranum instar stipulæ per ætatem et infirmitatem siccatum, graviter impetis et invadis, continuando plagas tuas in me. Denique homo in juventute assimilatur herbæ virenti, in senectute autem stipulæ siccæ. Quemadmodum vero Job, ita et alii viri virtutum, præsertim in tribulationibus constituti, infimis ac vilibus rebus se comparant, prout primo Regum David ait ad Saul: Quem persequeris, rex Israel? quem persequeris? Canem mortuum persequeris, et pulicem unum. Sic quoque secundo libro Regum, Miphiboseth loquitur David regi: Quis ego sum servus tuus, quoniam respexisti super canem mortuum similem mei? Certum est autem, quod homines tribulati ea libenter allegant, quæ aliquo modo possint eis pro relevamine cooperari. Ita et Job divinam potentiam atque humanam imbecillitatem commemorat, ut quasi ratiocinando concludat, quod deceat Deum homini misereri: sicut si robustissimus pugil aut gigas projecisset puerulum in terram sub pedibus suis, deceret ut eum pie erigeret.
paras.en: [[13:25|and thou pursuest a dry straw|Et stipulam siccam persequeris]], that is, me, an old man dried up like straw by age and sickness, thou dost heavily assail and attack, continuing thy strokes upon me. For man in youth is likened to green grass, but in old age to dry straw. And as Job does, so other men of virtue too, especially when set in tribulations, compare themselves to the lowest and meanest things; as in the first book of Kings David says to Saul: [[1 Kings 24:14|After whom dost thou come out, O king of Israel?|Quem persequeris, rex Israel?]] [[1 Kings 24:15|After whom dost thou pursue? After a dead dog, after a flea.|quem persequeris? Canem mortuum persequeris, et pulicem unum]] [in the Douay-Rheims the first of these words stand at the end of v. 14; in the Vulgate all are in v. 15]. So also in the second book of Kings Miphiboseth speaks to king David: [[2 Kings 9:8|Who am I thy servant, that thou shouldst look upon such a dead dog as I am?|Quis ego sum servus tuus, quoniam respexisti super canem mortuum similem mei?]] Now it is certain that men in tribulation gladly put forward whatever can in any way help to relieve them. So Job too recalls the divine power and human feebleness, so as to conclude, as it were by reasoning, that it befits God to have mercy on man: just as, if a very strong boxer or a giant had thrown a little boy to the ground under his feet, it would befit him to raise him up kindly.

paras.t: Scribis enim, id est, memoriter tenes, sicut quod scriptum est firmiter manet, contra me, id est ad mei gravamen, amaritudines, id est culpas diu præteritas, quæ ad amaritudinem ultionis perducunt, et suo remorsu quem pariunt, mentem affligunt. Nam et animus inordinatus sibi ipsi solet esse pœnalis. Vel, Amaritudines, id est pœnas amaras, quas mihi (sicut præordinasti) inflixisti; quas in me quoque efficis perdurare, quemadmodum durat verbum scriptum, non dictum. Unde et infra loquitur Deo: Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea. Et dixit supra: Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum.
paras.en: [[13:26|For thou writest|Scribis enim]], that is, thou keepest in memory, as what is written stands firm, [[13:26|against me|contra me]], that is, to my burden, [[13:26|bitter things|amaritudines]], that is, faults long past, which lead on to the bitterness of vengeance, and afflict the mind by the remorse they beget. For a disordered mind is wont to be a punishment to itself [an echo of Augustine, Confessions I, 12]. Or, [[13:26|bitter things|amaritudines]], that is, bitter punishments, which thou hast inflicted on me (as thou didst foreordain); which thou also makest to last on in me, as a written word lasts, not a spoken one. Hence he says to God below too: [[Job 14:17|Thou hast sealed up my offences as it were in a bag|Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea]]. And he said above: [[Job 6:4|the arrows of the Lord are in me, the rage whereof drinketh up my spirit|Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum]].

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod Job loquitur affectu dolentis, qui vocabulis sæpe improprie utitur, magisque loquitur secundum id quod ratione doloris aut foris apparet, quam secundum id quod in occulto veritas habet. Unde flagellatio Job, a Deo pie pro illius profectu permissa, non fuit proprie persecutio, sed exercitatio atque probatio, purgatio, gratiarumque auctio. Similiter Deus non scripsit contra eum ipsius peccata, de quibus pœnituit: quin quoad culpam ea pœnitenti statim indulsit. Sed pœnam interdum reservat in posterum: sicque (ut ante aliqualiter tactum est) una causarum percussionis Job fuit, ut a pristinis culpis, etiam quoad pœnam, eriperetur in sæculo isto. Illa tamen causa non fuit principalis, neque præcipua: quia et ipse Job satisfecisse ante percussionem suam credendus est, quamvis forte non penitus plene. Propter quod subdit: et consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ, id est, per infirmitatem hanc meam vis me (ut videtur) usque ad mortem affligere, propter peccata mea in adolescentia mea commissa, tanto tempore mihi pœnam reservans. Quod nimis rigorosum apparet, eo quod adolescentia fluxibilis sit, instabilis ac lasciva: propter quod in Ecclesiaste habetur, Adolescentia et voluptas vana sunt. Hinc peccatis illius ætatis facilius indulgendum censetur.
paras.en: Moreover it is to be noted that Job speaks with the feeling of one in pain, who often uses words improperly, and speaks rather according to what appears outwardly or by reason of the pain than according to what the truth holds in secret. Hence the scourging of Job, permitted by God in kindness for his advancement, was not properly a persecution [persecutio, a pursuing: the word of v. 25, “thou pursuest”], but an exercise and a trial, a cleansing and an increase of graces. Likewise God did not write against him his sins, of which he had repented: rather, as to the guilt, he forgave them at once to the penitent. But he sometimes reserves the punishment for later: and so (as was touched on somewhat before) one of the causes of Job's being struck was that he might be delivered from his former faults, even as to the punishment, in this world. Yet that cause was not the principal nor the chief one: for Job too must be believed to have made satisfaction before he was struck, though perhaps not altogether fully. Wherefore he adds: [[13:26|and wilt consume me for the sins of my youth|et consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ]], that is, by this sickness of mine thou wilt (as it seems) afflict me even unto death, for the sins committed in my youth, keeping the punishment for me so long a time. Which seems too rigorous, since youth is fickle, unstable and wanton: for which reason it is said in Ecclesiastes, [[Eccles 11:10|youth and pleasure are vain|Adolescentia et voluptas vana sunt]]. Hence it is held that the sins of that age are to be forgiven more readily.

paras.t: Posuisti in nervo pedem meum, id est, spirituales pedes meos, videlicet cordis affectum et intentionem, operumque processum, tua lege frenasti, et sub jugo disciplinæ ligasti, ne huc illucque libere ac injuste vagarer et prævaricarer, sicut pedes incarceratorum ligantur in nervo atque compedibus. Hæc est maxima misericordia Dei, qua suos electos a pravis itineribus retrahit, a peccatis refrenat, et per semitas sibi placentes deducit, juxta illud Sapientis: Justum deduxit Dominus per vias rectas. Et in Psalmo: Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me. O quam beati sunt, qui hoc ex sententia dicere habent, horumque verborum gustant virtutem! qui utique omne bonum quod habent, Deo devotissime gratissimeque adscribunt, dicentes id Psalmi: Deduxit me super semitas justitiæ propter nomen suum, id est ob sui ipsius propriam benignissimamque bonitatem. Verumtamen verbum hoc aliter potest intelligi, eritque sensus: Posuisti, etc., id est, plaga tua gressus meos velut quodam nervo seu cippo arctasti, ita quod præ infirmitate progredi nequeo. Unde superius dixit: Circumdedisti me carcere.
paras.en: [[13:27|Thou hast put my feet in the stocks|Posuisti in nervo pedem meum]] [Latin in nervo, literally “in the cord”, a fetter for the feet], that is, thou hast bridled my spiritual feet, namely the affection and intention of the heart and the course of my works, with thy law, and bound them under the yoke of discipline, lest I should wander and transgress hither and thither freely and unjustly, as the feet of prisoners are bound in the stocks and fetters. This is the greatest mercy of God, by which he draws his elect back from evil ways, reins them in from sins, and leads them along the paths that please him, according to that of the Wise Man: The Lord [[Wis 10:10|conducted the just|Justum deduxit]] [[Wis 10:10|through the right ways|per vias rectas]] [Denis names the Lord; in Wisdom the subject is Wisdom herself]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:24|Thou hast held me by my right hand; and by thy will thou hast conducted me|Tenuisti manum dexteram meam, et in voluntate tua deduxisti me]]. O how blessed are they who can say this from the heart, and taste the power of these words! who indeed ascribe all the good they have to God most devoutly and most gratefully, saying that of the Psalm: [[Ps 22:3|He hath led me on the paths of justice, for his own name's sake|Deduxit me super semitas justitiæ propter nomen suum]], that is, for the sake of his own most kind goodness. But this saying can be understood otherwise, and the sense will be: [[13:27|Thou hast put|Posuisti]], etc., that is, by thy stroke thou hast confined my steps as with a kind of cord or stocks, so that for sickness I cannot walk. Hence he said above: [[Job 7:12|thou hast enclosed me in a prison|Circumdedisti me carcere]].

paras.t: Et observasti, id est, diligenter considerasti ad judicandum ac præmiandum, omnes semitas meas, id est interiores actus animæ meæ in cogitando, appetendo, atque similibus; et vestigia, id est exteriora opera seu processus, pedum meorum, tam corporalium quam spiritualium, scilicet affectionum et intentionum seu consiliorum, ex quibus opera proficiscuntur, considerasti. Quum enim semitæ dicantur strictiora itinera, recte per eas actus interiores signantur, qui subtiliores sunt, efficaciusque atque directius ducunt ad Deum, quam opera exteriora, in quibus non est ratio meriti neque demeriti, nisi ex interioribus actu et habitu. Hinc de Deo ait Psalmista: Qui intelligit omnia opera eorum. Et rursus: Scrutans corda et renes, Deus. In Proverbiis quoque habetur: Respicit Dominus viam hominis, et omnes gressus illius considerat. Imo, tam distincte atque plenissime Deus universos hominum actus perpendit, judicat, numerat, ut et corporalium pedum, cæterorumque membrorum usum, progressum, cunctaque gesta observet, in quantum ex deliberata ratione procedunt. Sic enim sunt vel meritoria, vel demeritoria, præsertim quum secundum probabilem positionem, quam et Thomas defendit, in actibus humanis non sit indifferens, ita quod omnes actus hominis, qui ex rationis deliberatione procedunt, qui proprie actus humani vocantur, sunt vel meritorii vel demeritorii: sicque singuli sub providentia cadunt divina. Propterea Jeremias inducit: Fortissime; magnus consilio et incomprehensibilis cogitatu, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam.
paras.en: [[13:27|and hast observed|Et observasti]], that is, thou hast diligently considered, in order to judge and to reward, [[13:27|all my paths|omnes semitas meas]], that is, the inward acts of my soul in thinking, desiring and the like; and [[13:27|the steps|vestigia]], that is, the outward works or goings, [[13:27|of my feet|pedum meorum]], both bodily and spiritual (namely of the affections and intentions or counsels, from which works proceed), [[13:27|hast considered|considerasti]]. For since paths are the name for narrower ways, the inward acts are rightly signified by them, which are subtler, and lead to God more effectively and more directly than outward works, in which there is no ground of merit or demerit except from the inward act and habit. Hence the Psalmist says of God: [[Ps 32:15|who understandeth all their works|Qui intelligit omnia opera eorum]]. And again: [[Ps 7:10|the searcher of hearts and reins is God|Scrutans corda et renes, Deus]]. In Proverbs too we have: [[Prov 5:21|The Lord beholdeth the ways of man, and considereth all his steps|Respicit Dominus viam hominis, et omnes gressus illius considerat]]. Nay, God weighs, judges and numbers all the acts of men so distinctly and so fully that he observes even the use, the movement and all the doings of the bodily feet and of the other members, in so far as they proceed from deliberate reason. For so they are either meritorious or demeritorious, especially since, according to a probable position which Thomas too defends, no human act is indifferent [that is, neither good nor bad], so that all the acts of man which proceed from the deliberation of reason, which are properly called human acts, are either meritorious or demeritorious: and thus each one of them falls under the providence of God. Therefore Jeremias brings in: [[Jer 32:18|O most mighty|Fortissime]]; [[Jer 32:19|Great in counsel, and incomprehensible in thought: whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the children of Adam|magnus consilio et incomprehensibilis cogitatu, cujus oculi aperti sunt super omnes filios Adam]].

paras.t: Grandis ergo et maxima nobis ratio est bene vivendi, quum ante oculos strictissimi Judicis cuncta cernentis, nilque impræmiatum relinquentis, cuncta agamus, et quæ agenda sunt omittamus. Ideo ait Psalmista: Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo.
paras.en: Great, then, and very great is our reason for living well, since all that we do, and all that we leave undone of what is to be done, we do before the eyes of a most strict Judge, who sees all things and leaves nothing unrequited. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:168|I have kept thy commandments and thy testimonies: because all my ways are in thy sight.|Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo]]

paras.t: Qui quasi putredo consumendus sum, id est instar putredinis redigendus in vermes et in cineres, quantum ad corpus meum: secundum illud Ecclesiastici, Quum morietur homo, hæreditabit serpentes, et bestias, et vermes.
paras.en: [[13:28|Who am to be consumed as rottenness|Qui quasi putredo consumendus sum]], that is, to be brought down like rottenness to worms and ashes, as regards my body: according to that of Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 10:13|For when a man shall die, he shall inherit serpents, and beasts, and worms.|Quum morietur homo, hæreditabit serpentes, et bestias, et vermes]]

paras.t: Et quasi vestimentum quod comeditur a tinea. Quemadmodum enim tineæ de vestimento nascuntur, et illud corrodunt: sic corpus ante mortem consumitur a naturali calore velut a tinea; post mortem vero de ipso corpore vermes gignuntur, a quibus corroditur, juxta quod in Isaia legitur: Subter te sternetur tinea, et operimentum tuum erunt vermes. His verbis denuo suam fragilitatem fatetur, ut tanto sit ei Deus clementior, quanto ipse se fragiliorem veraciter recognoscit. Quasi dicat: Pene mirum videtur, quod creaturam tam fragilem sic indesinenter observas, tam districte judicas ac graviter punis.
paras.en: [[13:28|and as a garment that is motheaten|Et quasi vestimentum quod comeditur a tinea]]. For as moths are born of a garment and gnaw it away: so the body before death is consumed by its natural heat as by a moth; but after death worms are bred from the body itself, and by them it is gnawed away, according to what is read in Isaias: [[Is 14:11|under thee shall the moth be strewed, and worms shall be thy covering|Subter te sternetur tinea, et operimentum tuum erunt vermes]]. With these words he confesses his frailty once more, so that God may be the more merciful to him the more truly he acknowledges himself to be frail. As if to say: It seems almost a wonder that thou watchest so frail a creature so unceasingly, judgest it so strictly and punishest it so heavily.

13.title: De tropologia ejusdem capituli tertiidecimi.
13.title_en: On the tropology of the same thirteenth chapter

paras.t: Licet aliquoties ratio exigat, ut contra veritatem protervientis, garrientis ac disputantis pompam ac præsumptionem sagaciter retundamus, ne veritas patiatur jacturam, non superbe aut impatienter loquamur; sed beati Job sequamur modestiam: qui quum valde sapientior esset disputantibus secum, non passionate se extulit, nec præsumptuose locutus est, Plus scio quam vos; sed modeste effatur: Secundum scientiam vestram et ego novi. Etenim qui minus dicit, majus non negat, sicut et numerus minor non excludit majorem. Aliquando autem necesse seu utile est, ut homo gratiam sibi concessam aperiat ad Dei honorem, ad veritatis atque justitiæ defensionem, ad spei confortationem, ad tentationis repulsionem, ad aliorum ædificationem, quum dicat Salvator: Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est.
paras.en: Although reason sometimes demands that we shrewdly beat back the pomp and presumption of one who wantonly assails the truth, who chatters and disputes against it, lest the truth suffer loss, let us not speak proudly or impatiently, but follow the modesty of blessed Job: who, though he was far wiser than those disputing with him, did not exalt himself out of passion, nor say presumptuously, I know more than you; but modestly declares: [[13:2|According to your knowledge I also know|Secundum scientiam vestram et ego novi]]. For he who says the less does not deny the greater, just as a smaller number does not exclude a larger. Sometimes, however, it is necessary or useful for a man to make known the grace granted him: for the honour of God, for the defence of truth and justice, for the strengthening of hope, for the repelling of temptation, for the edification of others; since the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:16|let your light shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven|Luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra, et glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in cœlis est]].

paras.t: Sed tamen ad Omnipotentem loquar. Non sic propriæ vilitatis, vitiositatis et contemptibilitatis intuitu dejiciamur, pusillanimesve reddamur, ut ad Omnipotentem loqui non audeamus: imo consideratione superinfinitæ bonitatis, caritatis et misericordiæ ejus, consolemur, confidamus, inflammemur et invalescamus, atque cum Omnipotente loquamur, cum filiali timore, grandi reverentia, ferventi amore, ipsum laudando, orando, jugiterque circa ipsum nos mentaliter occupando. Præterea, secundum philosophos, actio dignificatur, nominatur, speciemque sortitur ab objecto seu termino ad quem. Quum ergo Deus superbeatissimus sit prorsus in infinitum universis et singulis melior atque præstantior, nonne dignitatis præclaræ est circa ipsum sic occupari, in ipsum tendere et moveri, in ipso actum finire ac mentem defigere? Itaque deliciosius valde sit nobis, Omnipotentem affari, cum Christo miscere colloquia, in Domino occupari, quam cum hominibus fabulari, et tempus infideliter perdere.
paras.en: [[13:3|But yet I will speak to the Almighty|Sed tamen ad Omnipotentem loquar]]. Let us not be so cast down, or made faint-hearted, by the sight of our own vileness, viciousness and contemptibleness, that we dare not speak to the Almighty: rather, by considering his more than infinite goodness, charity and mercy, let us take comfort, trust, be kindled and grow strong, and speak with the Almighty with filial fear, great reverence and fervent love, praising him, praying, and continually occupying ourselves with him in mind. Moreover, according to the philosophers, an action is ennobled, named, and receives its species from its object, or the term to which it tends. Since, then, God, who is more than most blessed, is altogether and infinitely better and more excellent than each and every thing, is it not a thing of splendid dignity to be so occupied with him, to tend and be moved towards him, to end our act and fix our mind in him? Let it therefore be far more delightful to us to address the Almighty, to converse with Christ, to be occupied in the Lord, than to gossip with men and faithlessly waste our time.

paras.t: Et cum Deo disputare cupio: non divinæ sapientiæ profunditatem præsumptuose scrutando, vel divinæ justitiæ judicia reprobando; sed incomprehensibilium operum ejus aliqualem rationem quærendo, et quidquid ad promerendam misericordiam Dei facere potest, diligentius proponendo. Sic disputavit cum Deo Jeremias, dicendo: Quare quasi colonus futurus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum? Habacuc quoque propheta: Mundi sunt, inquiens, oculi tui, Domine, ne videas malum, et respicere ad iniquitatem non potes. Quare non respicis super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se?
paras.en: [[13:3|and I desire to reason with God|Et cum Deo disputare cupio]]: not by presumptuously searching into the depth of the divine wisdom, or finding fault with the judgments of the divine justice, but by seeking some reason for his incomprehensible works, and setting forth the more diligently whatever can serve to merit God's mercy. So Jeremias reasoned with God, saying: [[Jer 14:8|why wilt thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man turning in to lodge?|Quare quasi colonus futurus es in terra, et quasi viator declinans ad manendum?]] And Habacuc the prophet too: [[Hab 1:13|Thy eyes are too pure|Mundi sunt]], he says, [[Hab 1:13|to behold evil, and thou canst not look on iniquity. Why lookest thou upon them that do unjust things, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more just than himself?|oculi tui, Domine, ne videas malum, et respicere ad iniquitatem non potes. Quare non respicis super inique agentes, et taces devorante impio justiorem se?]]

paras.t: Prius vos ostendens fabricatores mendacii, et cultores perversorum dogmatum. Hoc contra hæreticos, qui de cordibus suis vanissima sibi idola fingunt, mendacia artificiose componunt, et propria documenta tanquam simulacra venerantur, dicere nos oportet. Itemque contra boni communis hostes, contra religiosorum adversarios, contra voluntarie et ex industria mentientes, dicenda sunt hæc ab eo cui incumbit ratione officii seu debito caritatis.
paras.en: [[13:4|Having first shewn that you are forgers of lies, and maintainers of perverse opinions|Prius vos ostendens fabricatores mendacii, et cultores perversorum dogmatum]]. This we must say against heretics, who fashion for themselves out of their own hearts the vainest idols, artfully compose lies, and venerate their own teachings like images. Likewise these words are to be said against the enemies of the common good, against the adversaries of religious, against those who lie willingly and of set purpose, by him on whom it is incumbent by reason of his office or by the debt of charity.

paras.t: Qui etiam loquacibus, quorum ad se spectat correctio, dum ad loquendum sunt immoderati, dicere potest: Atque utinam taceretis, ut putaremini esse sapientes. Sermo enim est cordis ostensor. Et qualis vir, talis oratio, id est locutio, ut Seneca ait. Ideo immoderantia fandi latentem cordis pandit stultitiam, quum dicat Salvator: Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Et in Proverbiis habetur: Os fatuorum ebullit stultitiam. Quum enim refrenatio linguæ sit signum sapientis, juxta illud Proverbiorum, Qui moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est: taciturnitas prætendit prudentiam, facitque hominem reputari prudentem. Loquacitas vero insipientis exstat indicium, quemadmodum Salomon contestatur: Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum. Ecclesiasticus quoque ait: Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabunt tempus.
paras.en: He may also say to the talkative whose correction belongs to him, when they are immoderate in speaking: [[13:5|And I wish you would hold your peace, that you might be thought to be wise men|Atque utinam taceretis, ut putaremini esse sapientes]]. For speech is the revealer of the heart; and as the man is, so is his discourse (that is, his speech), as Seneca says. Therefore immoderate talking lays open the hidden folly of the heart, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur]]. And in Proverbs we have: [[Prov 15:2|the mouth of fools bubbleth out folly|Os fatuorum ebullit stultitiam]]. For since the bridling of the tongue is the sign of a wise man, according to that of Proverbs, [[Prov 10:19|he that refraineth his lips, is most wise|Qui moderatur labia sua, prudentissimus est]], silence holds out a show of prudence and makes a man be reputed prudent. But talkativeness stands as the mark of a fool, as Solomon testifies: [[Prov 29:11|A fool uttereth all his mind: a wise man deferreth, and keepeth it till afterwards.|Totum spiritum suum profert stultus; sapiens differt et reservat in posterum]] Ecclesiasticus also says: [[Ecclus 20:7|A wise man will hold his peace till he see opportunity: but a babbler, and a fool, will regard no time.|Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus et imprudens non servabunt tempus]]

paras.t: Audite ergo correptiones meas. Hoc singuli impleamus, dum a superioribus nostris, vel a quocumque caritative corripimur. Hoc enim est boni ac docilis viri, et sapientiæ ac humilitatis indicium. Superbi equidem correcti, mox indignantur, parvipendi nolentes. Unde in Proverbiis scribitur: Qui odit increpationes, insipiens est. Et alibi: Vir sapiens non murmurabit correptus. Itemque: Qui acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur.
paras.en: [[13:6|Hear ye therefore my reproof|Audite ergo correptiones meas]] [Denis has the plural, *correptiones meas*, ‘my reproofs’]. Let each of us fulfil this when we are corrected in charity by our superiors, or by anyone at all. For this belongs to a good and teachable man, and is a sign of wisdom and humility. The proud, indeed, when corrected, are at once indignant, not wishing to be made little of. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 12:1|he that hateth reproof, is foolish|Qui odit increpationes, insipiens est]]. And elsewhere: [[Ecclus 10:28|a man that is prudent and well instructed will not murmur when he is reproved|Vir sapiens non murmurabit correptus]] [Denis has *vir sapiens*, ‘a wise man’]. And again: [[Prov 13:18|he that yieldeth to reproof shall be glorified|Qui acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur]].

paras.t: Nunquid Deus indiget vestro mendacio, ut pro illo loquamini dolos? Hoc testimonio contra eos utamur, qui hypocrisi pleni sunt; contra simulatores et callidos; contra falsitatis magistros, qui se ipsos justificare et alios reprehensibiles ostendere cupientes, ut veraces et justi putentur, sublimia dicunt de Deo intentione dolosa, et falsa vera esse probare conantur per veritatum assumptiones, seu Scripturarum allegationes, juxta illud Apostoli ad Romanos: Qui commutaverunt veritatem Dei in mendacium. De quibus in Isaia habetur: Posuimus mendacium spem nostram, et mendacio protecti sumus. Porro, qui verax et justus est, non in sui defensionem et opem assumit mendacium; nec veritas, quum sit res firmissima, sicut in apocryphis Esdræ habetur, quod super omnia veritas vincit, eget mendacio, quod infirmissimum judicatur. Unde in secunda ad Corinthios epistola dicit Apostolus: Non possumus aliquid adversus veritatem, sed pro veritate.
paras.en: [[13:7|Hath God any need of your lie, that you should speak deceitfully for him?|Nunquid Deus indiget vestro mendacio, ut pro illo loquamini dolos?]] Let us use this testimony against those who are full of hypocrisy; against dissemblers and the crafty; against the masters of falsehood who, wishing to justify themselves and to show others blameworthy, that they may be thought truthful and just, say lofty things of God with a deceitful intention, and try to prove false things true by taking up truths, or by alleging the Scriptures; according to that of the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 1:25|Who changed the truth of God into a lie|Qui commutaverunt veritatem Dei in mendacium]]. Of whom we have in Isaias: [[Is 28:15|we have placed our hope in lies, and by falsehood we are protected|Posuimus mendacium spem nostram, et mendacio protecti sumus]]. Moreover, he who is truthful and just does not take up a lie for his defence and help; nor does truth, since it is a most firm thing (as we have in the apocryphal books of Esdras, that truth overcomes all things [the margin gives 3 Esdras 3:12, a book printed among the apocrypha of the Vulgate and not in the app]), need a lie, which is judged the weakest of things. Hence the Apostle says in the second epistle to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 13:8|we can do nothing against the truth: but for the truth|possumus aliquid adversus veritatem, sed pro veritate]].

paras.t: Etiamsi occiderit me, in ipso sperabo. Ex hoc verbo discamus immobiliter, firmissime, filialiterque semper in Deo sperare, in omni eventu, adversitate, infirmitate, etiam quando non exaudimur ab eo ad libitum, certi quod ipse sit bonitatis atque clementiæ infinitæ, caritatis ac veritatis immensæ. Idcirco impossibile est, ut in se confidentem relinquat. Imo speranti in se omnia convertit in melius, et firma in ipso spes maxime placet ei; estque meritoria valde. Deus quoque sperantibus in se auxilium suum in Scripturis uberrime pollicetur. Etenim ait: Quoniam in me speravit, liberabo eum; protegam eum, quoniam cognovit nomen meum. Ad Jeremiam quoque: Eruens liberabo te; et erit tibi anima tua in salutem, quia in me habuisti fiduciam. Hinc Ecclesiasticus monet: Respicite, filii, nationes hominum; et scitote quia nullus speravit in Domino, et confusus est. In Proverbiis quoque: Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo, et ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ. Merito ergo ait Psalmista: Domine virtutum, beatus homo qui sperat in te. Hinc jugiter propriam fragilitatem, infirmitatem, insufficientiam, atque ad omne malum deplorandissimam proclivitatem pensantes, et Dei benedicti immensam potentiam, infinitamque pietatem considerantes, non in nobis, sed in Deo speremus, gloriemur et quiescamus. Sicque veraciter erimus fortes, secundum illud Machabæorum: Omnes qui sperant in Domino, non infirmantur. Et Psalmista: In Domino sperans non infirmabor.
paras.en: [[13:15|Although he should kill me, I will trust in him|Etiamsi occiderit me, in ipso sperabo]]. From this word let us learn always to hope in God immovably, most firmly and as sons, in every event, adversity and infirmity, even when we are not heard by him as we would wish, certain that he is of infinite goodness and clemency, of immeasurable charity and truth. It is therefore impossible that he should forsake one who trusts in him. Rather, for one who hopes in him he turns all things to the better; and firm hope in him pleases him greatly, and is very meritorious. God also promises his help most abundantly in the Scriptures to those who hope in him. For he says: [[Ps 90:14|Because he hoped in me I will deliver him: I will protect him because he hath known my name.|Quoniam in me speravit, liberabo eum; protegam eum, quoniam cognovit nomen meum]] And to Jeremias too: [[Jer 39:18|delivering, I will deliver thee|Eruens liberabo te]]; [[Jer 39:18|thy life shall be saved for thee, because thou hast put thy trust in me|et erit tibi anima tua in salutem, quia in me habuisti fiduciam]] [these words are sent through Jeremias to Abdemelech the Ethiopian]. Hence Ecclesiasticus admonishes: [[Ecclus 2:11|My children behold the generations of men: and know ye that no one hath hoped in the Lord, and hath been confounded|Respicite, filii, nationes hominum; et scitote quia nullus speravit in Domino, et confusus est]]. And in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:5|Have confidence in the Lord with all thy heart, and lean not upon thy own prudence.|Habe fiduciam in Domino ex toto corde tuo, et ne innitaris prudentiæ tuæ]] Rightly then does the Psalmist say: [[Ps 83:13|O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man that trusteth in thee|Domine virtutum, beatus homo qui sperat in te]]. Therefore, continually weighing our own frailty, infirmity, insufficiency, and our most lamentable proneness to every evil, and considering the immense power and infinite loving-kindness of the blessed God, let us hope, glory and rest, not in ourselves, but in God. And so we shall truly be strong, according to that of the Machabees: [[1 Mach 2:61|none that trust in him, fail in strength|Omnes qui sperant in Domino, non infirmantur]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 25:1|I have put my trust in the Lord, and shall not be weakened|In Domino sperans non infirmabor]].

paras.t: Circa hæc scribit Gregorius: Nunquam est patientiæ virtus in prosperis. Ille autem vere est patiens, qui quum adversis atteritur, nec tamen a spei suæ rectitudine incurvatur. De reprobo etenim scriptum est: Confitebitur tibi quum benefeceris ei. In hoc itaque mens justa ab injusta discernitur, quod omnipotentis Dei laudem et inter adversa confitetur; quod adversis non frangitur.
paras.en: On this Gregory writes: The virtue of patience is never found in prosperity. He is truly patient who, when he is worn down by adversity, is yet not bent from the uprightness of his hope. For of the reprobate it is written: [[Ps 48:19|he will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him|Confitebitur tibi quum benefeceris ei]]. In this, then, the just mind is distinguished from the unjust: that it confesses the praise of almighty God even amid adversity; that it is not broken by adversity.

paras.t: Postremo, si sapienter perpendimus quanta sit bonitas, caritas, clementia Dei in semetipso, quantam insuper nobis caritatem clementiamque ostendit, præsertim in Verbi incarnatione, passione, et Sancti Spiritus missione, diffidere non valemus. Imo, si occiderit nos, in ipso sperabimus. Nam et Deus tanquam benignissimus pater, potentissimus dominus, fidelissimus quoque adjutor, præcipit et requirit ut in ipso jugiter confidamus: quod cur facit, si desperatio sibi summe non displicet? Sperantem vero in Domino misericordia circumdat.
paras.en: Lastly, if we wisely weigh how great is the goodness, charity and clemency of God in himself, and how great a charity and clemency he has moreover shown to us, above all in the incarnation and passion of the Word and the sending of the Holy Spirit, we cannot lose confidence. Nay, though he should kill us, we will hope in him. For God too, as a most kind father, a most mighty lord, and a most faithful helper, commands and requires that we trust in him continually: why should he do this, if despair did not supremely displease him? [[Ps 31:10|mercy shall encompass him that hopeth in the Lord|Sperantem vero in Domino misericordia circumdat]] [Denis has the present tense, *circumdat*, ‘encompasses’].

paras.t: Verumtamen vias meas in conspectu ejus arguam: id est, non sic in Deo sperabo, ut nuda informique spe me arbitrer posse salvari; sed pœnitentiæ actibus adhærebo, coram Deo me in omnibus accusabo, peccata mea pure mala fatebor. Si boni quid egero, imperfectiones adjunctas mihi adscribam; quidquid autem virtutis exstiterit, Deo attribuam. Præterea, decet et expedit quemlibet Christianum, potissime religiosum, quotidie bis ad minus, scilicet mane et sero, cor suum intra se revocare, colligere atque ad Deum erigere: ut de mane commemoret, Deoque fateatur, ac defleat, quidquid culpæ in nocte incurrerit; similiter sero faciat pro culpis tota die habitis seu commissis: et post talem sui reprehensionem satagat detestata peccata corrigere ac vitare, humiliter de se sentire, omnem elationis motum abjicere.
paras.en: [[13:15|but yet I will reprove my ways in his sight|Verumtamen vias meas in conspectu ejus arguam]]: that is, I will not so hope in God as to think I can be saved by a bare and unformed hope [that is, hope not given its form by charity and good works]; but I will hold fast to acts of penance, accuse myself before God in all things, and confess my sins as simply evil. If I do anything good, I will ascribe to myself the imperfections joined to it; but whatever of virtue there has been, I will attribute to God. Moreover, it is fitting and expedient for every Christian, above all for a religious, at least twice a day, namely morning and evening, to call his heart back within himself, recollect it and raise it to God: so that in the morning he may call to mind, confess to God and bewail whatever fault he has incurred in the night; and in the evening do the same for the faults had or committed in the whole day: and after such self-reproach, strive to correct and avoid the sins he has detested, to think humbly of himself, and to cast off every stirring of pride.

paras.t: Et ipse erit salvator meus. Ideo de sperantibus dicit Psalmographus: Adjuvabit eos Dominus, et liberabit eos, et salvabit eos; quia speraverunt in eo. Itemque: Voluntatem timentium se faciet, et deprecationem eorum exaudiet, et salvos faciet eos. Nempe eo ipso quod nostra piacula reprehendimus, confitemur, deflemus, ipse tanquam misericordissimus mox indulget, gratiamque refundit et gloriam præparat.
paras.en: [[13:16|And he shall be my saviour|Et ipse erit salvator meus]]. Therefore the Psalmist says of those who hope: [[Ps 36:40|the Lord will help them and deliver them|Adjuvabit eos Dominus, et liberabit eos]], [[Ps 36:40|and save them because they have hoped in him|et salvabit eos; quia speraverunt in eo]]. And again: [[Ps 144:19|He will do the will of them that fear him: and he will hear their prayer, and save them.|Voluntatem timentium se faciet, et deprecationem eorum exaudiet, et salvos faciet eos]] For by the very fact that we reprove, confess and bewail our offences, he, as most merciful, at once forgives, pours back grace and prepares glory.

paras.t: Non enim veniet in conspectu ejus omnis hypocrita. Hypocritæ virtuosos se simulant, vel aliud repræsentant quam sunt. Hypocritæ nempe dicuntur fictores, simulatores, repræsentatores aliarum personarum. Isti coram Deo vias suas non arguunt, nec conscientiam suam examinant, non mentem simplificant, nec animam purgant; sed duplices sunt et sophistæ, simplicissimo Deo præcipue difformes ac displicentes. Unde Ecclesiasticus scribit: Qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est. Non est illi data a Domino sapientia. In talibus præsertim impletur illud Proverbiorum: Stultus illudit peccatum. Dum enim alios fallere quærunt, se ipsos gravius infeliciusque decipiunt. Ideo fugiamus, detestemur, odiamus hypocrisim, et mente pura ac simplici Deum semper et ubique in cunctis quæramus.
paras.en: [[13:16|for no hypocrite shall come before his presence|Non enim veniet in conspectu ejus omnis hypocrita]]. Hypocrites feign themselves virtuous, or represent something other than what they are. For hypocrites are called feigners, dissemblers, representers of other persons [the Greek word means a stage actor]. These do not reprove their ways before God, nor examine their conscience; they do not make their mind simple, nor cleanse their soul; but they are double and sophists, and so above all unlike and displeasing to God, who is most simple. Hence Ecclesiasticus writes: [[Ecclus 37:23|He that speaketh sophistically, is hateful|Qui sophistice loquitur, odibilis est]]. [[Ecclus 37:24|Grace is not given him from the Lord|Non est illi data a Domino sapientia]] [Denis has *sapientia*, ‘wisdom’, where the Vulgate has *gratia*, ‘grace’]. In such men above all is fulfilled that of Proverbs: [[Prov 14:9|A fool will laugh at sin|Stultus illudit peccatum]]. For while they seek to deceive others, they deceive themselves more gravely and more unhappily. Therefore let us flee, detest and hate hypocrisy, and with a pure and simple mind seek God always and everywhere in all things.

paras.t: Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar. Hoc dicere possunt, qui ex speciali revelatione sciunt se esse in caritate. In quorum persona ait Apostolus: Quis nos separabit a caritate Dei?
paras.en: [[13:18|If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just.|Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar]] This can be said by those who know by a special revelation that they are in charity. In whose person the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:35|Who then shall separate us from the love of Christ?|Quis nos separabit a caritate Dei?]] [Denis has *a caritate Dei*, ‘from the love of God’, as at Rom 8:39]

paras.t: Manum tuam longe fac a me, et formido tua non me terreat. Hoc juxta expositionem præhabitam orare possumus, quando graviter valde affligimur: optare namque debemus mentem tranquillam, securam, imperturbatam.
paras.en: [[13:21|Withdraw thy hand far from me, and let not thy dread terrify me.|Manum tuam longe fac a me, et formido tua non me terreat]] We can pray this, according to the exposition given before, when we are very grievously afflicted: for we ought to desire a mind tranquil, secure and undisturbed.

paras.t: Responde mihi, quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata; scelera mea atque delicta ostende mihi. Quia in multis offendimus omnes, in tantum, ut pene vel prorsus innumerabilia sint peccata nostra tam omissionis quam commissionis, quæ latent nos ipsos; nec universa et singula ad memoriam revocare valemus sine illuminatione divina: hinc necessario orare habemus, ut Deus sua unctione piissima, illuminatione angelica, prælatorum instructione paterna, lectione aut aliis modis dignetur nobis respondere sive ostendere, quanta habeamus peccata; imo, quæ, quanta et qualia, ut enormitatem eorum noscentes, quælibet ut oportet pœnitentialiter emendemus. Hinc etiam confessurus præmeditari diligentissime debet, in quibus aut quomodo Deum offendit: pro illuminatione quoque compunctionisque gratia exorare, attendentes illud in Psalmo: Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me, et ab alienis parce servo tuo. Denique, dum ab aliquo, potissime a superiore, arguimur, in Domino gratulemur, gratias ei agentes, quia respondet nobis quantas habeamus iniquitates et peccata. Quod si in illis qui nobis objiciuntur, nobis conscii non fuerimus, nihilo minus patienter feramus, attendentes quam innumerabilia sint peccata, quibus latenter obnoxii sumus.
paras.en: [[13:22|do thou answer me|Responde mihi]]: [[13:23|How many are my iniquities and sins? make me know my crimes and offenses.|quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata; scelera mea atque delicta ostende mihi]] Since [[Jas 3:2|in many things we all offend|in multis offendimus omnes]], so much so that our sins, of omission as well as of commission, which are hidden from ourselves, are almost or altogether innumerable; and since we cannot recall them all and each to memory without divine enlightenment: hence we must needs pray that God may deign, by his most loving unction, by the enlightenment of angels, by the fatherly instruction of prelates, by reading or in other ways, to answer us, that is, to show us, how many sins we have; nay, which, how many, and of what kind, so that, knowing their enormity, we may amend each of them by penance as we ought. Hence too one who is about to confess ought to think over beforehand most diligently in what things and how he has offended God, and pray for enlightenment and for the grace of compunction, heeding that in the Psalm: [[Ps 18:13|Who can understand sins? from my secret ones cleanse me|Delicta quis intelligit? ab occultis meis munda me]], [[Ps 18:14|And from those of others spare thy servant|et ab alienis parce servo tuo]]. Lastly, when we are reproved by anyone, especially by a superior, let us rejoice in the Lord, giving him thanks, because he is answering us how many iniquities and sins we have. And if we are not conscious in ourselves of the faults laid to our charge, let us nonetheless bear it patiently, considering how innumerable are the sins to which we are secretly liable.

paras.t: Cur faciem tuam abscondis? Quo quis justior est, Deumque ardentius diligit, eo cordialius illi cupit uniri. A tali autem suo amatore Deus interdum in vita hac consuetam contemplationis gratiam, solitæ consolationis suavitatem, pristinæ gratiositatis experimentalem præsentiam, ad tempus dispensative suspendit propter varias rationes. Verum devotus amator superdilectissimi Dei occultationem perpeti æquanimiter nequiens ex amoris sancti ardore, conqueritur amorosa querela, dicendo: Cur faciem tuam abscondis? id est, noli eam diutius mihi abscondere: juxta illud Canticorum, Ostende mihi faciem tuam, sonet vox tua in auribus meis. Quæ licet sint Sponsi ad Sponsam, tamen ibidem post pauca Sponsa æquivalenter eidem loquitur Sponso: Revertere, inquiens; dilecte mi, similis esto capreæ hinnuloque cervorum super montes Bether.
paras.en: [[13:24|Why hidest thou thy face|Cur faciem tuam abscondis]]? The more just a man is, and the more ardently he loves God, the more heartily he longs to be united to him. But God sometimes in this life, by way of dispensation and for various reasons, withholds for a time from such a lover of his the accustomed grace of contemplation, the sweetness of his wonted consolation, the felt presence of his former favour. But the devout lover of God, who is beloved above all, unable for the ardour of holy love to bear his hiding with an even mind, complains with a loving complaint, saying: [[13:24|Why hidest thou thy face|Cur faciem tuam abscondis]]? that is, hide it from me no longer: according to that of the Canticle, [[Cant 2:14|shew me thy face, let thy voice sound in my ears|Ostende mihi faciem tuam, sonet vox tua in auribus meis]]. And though these are the words of the Bridegroom to the Bride, yet there, a little after, the Bride says the equivalent to the same Bridegroom: [[Cant 2:17|Return|Revertere]], she says, [[Cant 2:17|be like, my beloved, to a roe, or to a young hart upon the mountains of Bether|dilecte mi, similis esto capreæ hinnuloque cervorum super montes Bether]].

paras.t: Et arbitraris me inimicum tuum? Non tam asserendo, quam blandiendo, hoc dicitur in viri justi persona. Quasi dicat: Ita te a me te desiderante, et super omnia diligente, abscondis, quasi tibi displicens et inobediens essem. Verumtamen hæc in persona peccatoris, sed pœnitentis ac incipientis, possunt exponi: qui dum ad libitum non exauditur, nec proficit, videtur ei quod Deus suum ab eo vultum abscondat, et se velut adversarium habeat. Sed in his non cessemus Dei gratiosam implorare præsentiam, splendidam contemplationem, stabilem inhabitationem, pensantes illud Psalmistæ: Lætetur cor quærentium Dominum. Quærite Dominum, et confirmamini; quærite faciem ejus semper. Itemque: Tibi dixit cor meum, exquisivit te facies mea; faciem tuam, Domine, requiram.
paras.en: [[13:24|and thinkest me thy enemy|Et arbitraris me inimicum tuum?]]? This is said in the person of a just man, not so much by way of assertion as of endearment. As if to say: Thou hidest thyself so from me, who desire thee and love thee above all things, as if I were displeasing and disobedient to thee. Yet these words can be expounded in the person of a sinner, but a penitent and a beginner: who, when he is not heard as he would wish and makes no progress, thinks that God hides his face from him and holds him as an adversary. But in these trials let us not cease to implore God's gracious presence, his splendid contemplation, his abiding indwelling, weighing that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 104:3|let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord|Lætetur cor quærentium Dominum]]. [[Ps 104:4|Seek ye the Lord, and be strengthened: seek his face evermore.|Quærite Dominum, et confirmamini; quærite faciem ejus semper]] And again: [[Ps 26:8|My heart hath said to thee: My face hath sought thee: thy face, O Lord, will I still seek.|Tibi dixit cor meum, exquisivit te facies mea; faciem tuam, Domine, requiram]]

paras.t: Insuper, quomodo quæ sequuntur, in persona cujuslibet justi afflicti, pœnitentis, aut aliunde virtuose dolentis, per sanctum Job figurati, queant exponi, nullam habent difficultatem, si præcedentis articuli expositio rite pensetur; sed in omnibus quæ hic scribuntur, nostram defectuositatem, fragilitatem, vilitatem debemus perpendere, humillimi esse, atque ad Deum in cunctis affectuose semper confugere.
paras.en: Further, how the words that follow can be expounded in the person of any just man who is afflicted, or a penitent, or one who grieves virtuously for some other cause, figured by holy Job, presents no difficulty, if the exposition of the preceding article is duly weighed; but in all that is written here we ought to weigh our own defectiveness, frailty and vileness, to be most humble, and always to take refuge lovingly in God in all things.

paras.t: Denique, quoniam in Officio defunctorum ex capitulo isto quædam lectiones sumuntur, breviter reor tangendum, quomodo lectiones hæ in persona animæ defuncti possint interpretari. Itaque anima in purgatorio sita, suppliciorum suorum finem scire et experiri desiderans (talis enim præscientia finis pœnarum, magna est consolatio afflictorum), loquitur Deo: Responde mihi, quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata, ut ex consideratione culparum mearum perpendam mearum durationem pœnarum. Cur faciem tuam abscondis? id est, a conspectu gloriæ tuæ, a beatifica visione sapientiæ atque essentiæ tuæ me differs, et te quasi iratum mihi nunc exhibes. Ideo subdit, Et arbitraris me (spiritum defuncti) inimicum tuum? id est, quasi hostis essem, me punis, quum tamen in caritate sim tua. Quasi dicat: Noli te mihi abscondere, noli me ut hostem habere, sed clementer indulge, succurre et redime. Tali animæ, quum fuerit liberata, dicet Deus illud Isaiæ: In momento indignationis meæ abscondi parumper faciem meam a te, et in misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui.
paras.en: Lastly, since certain lessons in the Office of the Dead are taken from this chapter, I think it should be touched on briefly how these lessons can be interpreted in the person of a departed soul [a heading in the margin here reads: Of the souls detained in purgatory]. A soul, then, placed in purgatory, desiring to know and to experience the end of its torments (for such foreknowledge of the end of their pains is a great consolation to the afflicted), speaks to God: [[13:22|do thou answer me|Responde mihi]], [[13:23|How many are my iniquities and sins|quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata]], so that from considering my faults I may weigh the duration of my pains. [[13:24|Why hidest thou thy face|Cur faciem tuam abscondis]]? that is, why dost thou put me off from the sight of thy glory, from the beatific vision of thy wisdom and essence, and show thyself now as if angry with me? Therefore it adds: [[13:24|and thinkest me|Et arbitraris me]] (the spirit of the departed) [[13:24|thy enemy|inimicum tuum]]? that is, dost thou punish me as if I were an enemy, when yet I am in thy charity? As if to say: Do not hide thyself from me, do not hold me as an enemy, but mercifully forgive, help and redeem. To such a soul, when it has been set free, God will say that of Isaias: [[Is 54:8|In a moment of indignation have I hid my face a little while from thee|In momento indignationis meæ abscondi parumper faciem meam a te]], [[Is 54:8|but with everlasting kindness have I had mercy on thee|et in misericordia sempiterna misertus sum tui]].

paras.t: Contra folium quod vento rapitur, ostendis potentiam tuam, et stipulam siccam persequeris: id est, contra me imperfectam atque instabilem, pœnis exustam, ostendis quanta sit justitiæ tuæ potestas, qua per pœnas me istas infestas. Tanquam dicat: Decet, o Domine, ut ignoscas.
paras.en: [[13:25|Against a leaf, that is carried away with the wind, thou shewest thy power, and thou pursuest a dry straw.|Contra folium quod vento rapitur, ostendis potentiam tuam, et stipulam siccam persequeris]] that is, against me, imperfect and unstable [the Latin is feminine, *imperfectam*: the soul speaks], burnt up by pains, thou shewest how great is the power of thy justice, by which thou dost assail me through these pains. As if to say: It is fitting, O Lord, that thou shouldst pardon.

paras.t: Præterea Christus, sapientia Patris, lignum vitæ est: de qua Salomon ait in libro Proverbiorum: Lignum vitæ est omnibus apprehendentibus eam. Christus enim saluberrimos fructus producit, quibus mentes feliciter reficiuntur. Hujus autem arboris velut folia sunt animæ christianæ, in Christo per caritatem manentes. Unde et ipse ait discipulis: Ego sum vitis, vos palmites. Quemadmodum vero per ventum folium ab arbore abjectatur, sic anima a Christo vento superbiæ, tentationis, vanitatis, et passionum impulsibus separatur: ideo vocat se folium vento raptum. Ob quam a Christo separationem punitur: quia etsi de mortali pœnituit, non tamen plenarie in vita hac satisfecit.
paras.en: Moreover Christ, the wisdom of the Father, is the tree of life: of which wisdom Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 3:18|She is a tree of life to them that lay hold on her|Lignum vitæ est omnibus apprehendentibus eam]] [Denis has *omnibus apprehendentibus eam*, ‘to all that lay hold on her’]. For Christ brings forth most wholesome fruits, by which minds are happily refreshed. And the leaves, as it were, of this tree are Christian souls, abiding in Christ through charity. Hence he himself says to the disciples: [[John 15:5|I am the vine: you the branches|Ego sum vitis, vos palmites]]. And as a leaf is thrown off from the tree by the wind, so the soul is separated from Christ by the wind of pride, of temptation, of vanity, and by the impulses of the passions: therefore it calls itself a leaf carried away by the wind. And for this separation from Christ it is punished: because, though it repented of mortal sin, it did not make full satisfaction in this life.

paras.t: Præterea, Christus comparat se grano frumenti, dicendo: Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram, mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet. Ipse etenim (secundum Augustinum) exstitit granum mortificandum perfidia Judæorum, et vivificandum fide credentium. Unde homo seu anima consistens in caritate et gratia, est velut culmus seu calamus hujus grani, trahens ab eo spiritualis alimenti humorem et gratiæ rorem, quem peccando amittit, et velut stipula sicca efficitur: quoniam stipula dicitur herba a trunco abscisa atque siccata. Et juxta hunc sensum, possunt hæc verba de homine viatore ac peccatore exponi.
paras.en: Moreover, Christ compares himself to a grain of wheat, saying: [[John 12:24|unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die|Nisi granum frumenti cadens in terram, mortuum fuerit]], [[John 12:25|Itself remaineth alone|ipsum solum manet]]. For he (according to Augustine) was the grain to be put to death by the faithlessness of the Jews, and to be brought to life by the faith of believers. Hence a man, or a soul, abiding in charity and grace is like the stalk or stem of this grain, drawing from it the sap of spiritual nourishment and the dew of grace; which it loses by sinning, and becomes like a dry straw: for straw is the name of a plant cut off from its stock and dried. And in this sense these words can be expounded of a man still on the way [that is, a wayfarer, one still in this life] and a sinner.

paras.t: Postremo, quo homo seu anima naturaliter imperfectioris est intellectualitatis, eo naturaliter instabilior est atque mobilior, et minus de sapientiæ habens dulci ac refectivo humore: ideo rite folio ac stipulæ comparatur.
paras.en: Lastly, the more imperfect by nature is the intellectuality of a man, or of a soul, the more unstable and changeable it is by nature, having less of the sweet and refreshing sap of wisdom: therefore it is fitly compared to a leaf and to straw.

paras.t: Scribis enim, id est, tenaciter infers et retines, contra me, id est ad meam desolationem, amaritudines, id est pœnas quas patior præamaras, et consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ, id est, propter peccata mea in illa ætate commissa, tam acerbe me crucias, quasi velles me prorsus consumere. Constituti autem in magnis doloribus, solent cum quadam excedentia loqui, ad insinuandum magnitudinem sui affectus atque doloris.
paras.en: [[13:26|For thou writest|Scribis enim]], that is, thou dost hold fast and keep, and lay upon me, [[13:26|against me|contra me]], that is, to my desolation, [[13:26|bitter things|amaritudines]], that is, the most bitter pains that I suffer, [[13:26|and wilt consume me for the sins of my youth|et consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ]]: that is, for my sins committed in that age thou dost torment me so sharply, as if thou wouldst consume me altogether. Those who are set in great sufferings are wont to speak with a certain excess, to convey the greatness of their feeling and pain.

paras.t: Posuisti in nervo pedem meum, id est, in loco isto pœnali me arctasti et arctas, ut quo cupio, ire non queam, nec manum tuam evadere. Denique omnem animam electam seu ejus pedem, id est affectum, Deus ponit in nervo, id est in legis suæ custodia, caritatisque vinculo, antequam separetur a corpore, ita quod caritatis præceptum adimplet, se ad Deum convertendo, atque in ejus amore suam voluntatem figendo.
paras.en: [[13:27|Thou hast put my feet in the stocks|Posuisti in nervo pedem meum]] [Denis has the singular, *pedem meum*, ‘my foot’], that is, thou hast confined and dost confine me in this place of pains, so that I cannot go where I long to, nor escape thy hand. And indeed God puts every elect soul, or its foot, that is, its affection, in the stocks [*nervus*, the stocks, is properly a cord or bond], that is, in the keeping of his law and the bond of charity, before it is parted from the body: so that it fulfils the precept of charity by turning itself to God and fixing its will in his love.

paras.t: Et observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti. Anima quæ in vita hac negligenter se habet, nec Dei præsentiam providentiamque perpendit ut decet, in purgatorio experitur, quam distinctissime ac diligentissime Deus omnia ejus in via ista pensaverit, quoniam ibi pro minimis cruciatur.
paras.en: [[13:27|and hast observed all my paths, and hast considered the steps of my feet|Et observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti]]. The soul that bears itself negligently in this life, and does not weigh God's presence and providence as it should, learns by experience in purgatory how very exactly and diligently God has weighed all its doings on this way, since there it is tormented for the least things.

paras.t: Qui (spiritus defuncti) quasi putredo consumendus sum: non consumptione essentiæ, sed eo modo, quo dictum est, Consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ.
paras.en: [[13:28|Who|Qui]] (the spirit of the departed) [[13:28|am to be consumed as rottenness|quasi putredo consumendus sum]]: not by a consuming of its essence, but in the way in which it was said, [[13:26|wilt consume me for the sins of my youth|Consumere me vis peccatis adolescentiæ meæ]].

paras.t: Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore, etc. Verba lectionis hujus, in persona animæ exsistentis in purgatorio, congrue exponi non valent. Nec anima talis de se ea pronuntiat; sed a viatore leguntur pro hujuscemodi anima: quæ etiam ea de homine, cujus ipsa forma et spiritus fuit, potest proferre, profitendo humanæ conditionis fragilitatem atque multiplicem defectuositatem, divinam insuper providentiam, quatenus Deus ad propitiandum et redimendum velocius inclinetur, id est, promptum se præbeat. Sic et mendici divitibus suas ostendunt penurias, vulnera et defectus, ut divites ad subveniendum mox moveantur. Quo enim quis imperfectum suum Deo humilius confitetur, eo Deus copiosius miseretur.
paras.en: [[Job 14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time|Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore]], etc. The words of this lesson cannot fittingly be expounded in the person of a soul in purgatory. Nor does such a soul pronounce them of itself; but they are read by one still on the way, on behalf of such a soul: though the soul too can utter them concerning the man whose form and spirit it was, professing the frailty and manifold defectiveness of the human condition, and moreover the divine providence, so that God may be inclined the more swiftly to be propitious and to redeem, that is, may show himself ready. So beggars, too, show the rich their want, their wounds and their defects, that the rich may be moved at once to help them. For the more humbly a man confesses his imperfection to God, the more abundantly God has mercy on him.

14.title: Elucidatio capituli tertiidecimi: Ecce omnia hæc vidit oculus meus, et audivit auris mea.
14.title_en: Explanation of the thirteenth chapter: Behold my eye hath seen all these things, and my ear hath heard
14.note: The last part of Art. XXXI, which treats chapter 13 (see there); Denis carries the exposition on to 14:4 before Art. XXXIII.

paras.t: Qui autem a judice est percussus, appetitque ab eo curari, omnia illa libenter commemorat et ei proponit, ex quibus aliqua videtur posse persuasio elici aut ratio sumi, ad obtinendam judicis propitiationem atque optatam salutem aut sanitatem. Denique, juxta industriam hanc subjungit, pandendo hominis fragilitatem, defectuositatem, miserabilitatem in ejus ingressu, progressu, egressu: ingressu, inquam, in mundum hunc per nativitatem: progressu, per vitæ extensionem seu continuationem; egressu de mundo, per mortem.
paras.en: Now one who has been struck by a judge, and seeks to be healed by him, gladly recalls and lays before him all those things from which, it seems, some persuasion can be drawn or some argument taken for obtaining the judge's favour and the deliverance or health he longs for. And so, with this skill, he goes on, setting forth the frailty, defectiveness and wretchedness of man in his entry, his progress and his exit: in his entry, I say, into this world by birth; in his progress, by the extension or continuance of life; in his exit from the world, by death.

paras.t: Itaque quod de se singulariter dixit, de homine communiter seu ipso genere humano prosequitur atque ostendit, subdendo: Homo, quicumque sit ille, natus de muliere, infirmo et fragili vasculo. Mulier enim a molliendo quasi mollis aer dicitur. Et quod de homine nato asseritur, de feminis quoque, non de viris tantum, accipitur, quamvis adjectiva sequentia masculina, videantur ad masculos homines determinare. Denique, omnis homo de muliere est natus, demptis primis parentibus. Nam et de Christo ait Apostolus ad Galatas: Misit Deus Filium suum, factum sub lege, natum ex muliere. Cui et Christus dixit in passione: Mulier, ecce filius tuus. In quibus sermonibus mulier sexum, non connubium notat. Quum ergo homo de muliere nascatur, mollis et tener est, ad bona virtutum debilis ex se ipso, fortis ad ea ex Deo: cujus electi, quantum ad esse naturæ, nati sunt ex muliere, non autem quantum ad esse gratiæ. Propter quod a Joanne de eis inductum est: Qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt.
paras.en: And so what he said of himself in particular, he goes on to say and show of man in general, that is, of the human race itself, adding: [[14:1|Man|Homo]], whoever he be, [[14:1|born of a woman|natus de muliere]], a weak and frail little vessel. For woman is so named from softening, as if “soft air” [mulier, from mollire, “to soften”, as if mollis aer: a play on the Latin]. And what is said of man who is born is to be taken of women too, not of men only, though the masculine adjectives that follow seem to restrict it to males. Indeed every man is born of woman, our first parents excepted. For of Christ too the Apostle says to the Galatians: [[Gal 4:4|God sent his Son|Misit Deus Filium suum]], [[Gal 4:4|made under the law|factum sub lege]], [[Gal 4:4|made of a woman|natum ex muliere]] [Denis has natum, “born”, for the Vulgate's factum, and puts these words last]. And Christ said to her in his passion: [[John 19:26|Woman, behold thy son|Mulier, ecce filius tuus]]. In these sayings *woman* denotes the sex, not marriage [that is, a woman, not a wife]. Since, then, man is born of woman, he is soft and tender, weak of himself for the goods of the virtues, strong for them from God: whose elect, as regards the being of nature, are born of woman, but not as regards the being of grace. For which reason it is said of them by John: [[John 1:13|Who are born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.|Qui non ex sanguinibus, neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri, sed ex Deo nati sunt]]

paras.t: Brevi vivens tempore. Nam et naturalis periodus vitæ humanæ est brevis, sicut in Psalmo habetur: Dies annorum nostrorum in ipsis septuaginta anni. Multorum autem irrationalium animalium naturalis vivendi periodus, duratio seu mensura, multo diuturnior est periodo vitæ humanæ. Porro quod aliqui ante diluvium vel etiam postea tam diu vixerunt, miraculo magis adscribitur quam naturæ. Quidam vero homines brevissimæ vitæ sunt, qui vel in infantia, vel in adolescentia aut in pueritia moriuntur. Postremo, quantumlibet vitæ hujus duratio protendatur, nihilominus comparatione æternitatis quæ restat, momentanea comprobatur. De brevitate quoque vitæ præsentis tot dicta et allegata sunt, ut ea repetere vel plura adjicere, superfluum judicetur.
paras.en: [[14:1|living for a short time|Brevi vivens tempore]]. For the natural span of human life is short, as we have it in the Psalm: [[Ps 89:10|The days of our years in them are threescore and ten years|Dies annorum nostrorum in ipsis septuaginta anni]]. But the natural span of living, the duration or measure, of many irrational animals is far longer than the span of human life. And that some lived so long before the flood, or even after it, is to be ascribed to miracle rather than to nature. Some men, again, are of very short life, dying in infancy, or in youth or in boyhood. Lastly, however far the duration of this life be stretched, it is nonetheless shown to be but a moment in comparison with the eternity that remains. On the brevity of the present life, too, so much has been said and cited that to repeat it or add more would be judged superfluous.

paras.t: Repletur multis miseriis, id est malis pœnæ et culpæ, defectuositatibus naturalibus, adversitatibus, morbis, angustiis. Maxime autem misera reputanda est vita hæc propter peccata, quæ omni die abundanter innumerabiliterque incidimus, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Miseros facit populos peccatum. Hinc et Christus testatur in Psalmo: Quia repleta est malis (scilicet pœnalibus) anima mea. Et in Ecclesiastico legitur: Jugum grave super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium. Cogitationes eorum, et timores cordis, adinventiones exspectationis, et dies finitionis; a præsidente super sedem gloriosam, usque ad humiliatum in terram et cinerem; ab eo qui utitur hyacintho et portat coronam, usque ad eum qui cooperitur lino crudo. Furor, zelus, tumultus, fluctuatio, timor mortis, fames, flagella et mors. Sic et Salomon: Vidi, inquit, cuncta quæ fiunt sub sole, et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus.
paras.en: [[14:1|is filled with many miseries|Repletur multis miseriis]], that is, with evils of punishment and of guilt, natural defects, adversities, diseases, straits. But this life is to be reckoned wretched above all because of sins, into which we fall every day, abundantly and past numbering, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 14:34|sin maketh nations miserable|Miseros facit populos peccatum]]. Hence Christ too testifies in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:4|For my soul is filled with evils|Quia repleta est malis]] (evils, that is, of punishment). And in Ecclesiasticus we read: [[Ecclus 40:1|a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their coming out of their mother's womb, until the day of their burial into the mother of all|Jugum grave super omnes filios Adam, a die exitus de ventre matris eorum, usque in diem sepulturæ in matrem omnium]]. [[Ecclus 40:2|Their thoughts, and fears of the heart, their imagination of things to come, and the day of their end|Cogitationes eorum, et timores cordis, adinventiones exspectationis, et dies finitionis]]; [[Ecclus 40:3|From him that sitteth on a glorious throne, unto him that is humbled in earth and ashes|a præsidente super sedem gloriosam, usque ad humiliatum in terram et cinerem]]; [[Ecclus 40:4|From him that weareth purple, and beareth the crown, even to him that is covered with rough linen: wrath, envy, trouble, unquietness, and the fear of death|ab eo qui utitur hyacintho et portat coronam, usque ad eum qui cooperitur lino crudo. Furor, zelus, tumultus, fluctuatio, timor mortis]], famine, scourges and death[[Ecclus 40:9||]]. So too Solomon: [[Eccles 1:14|I have seen|Vidi]], he says, [[Eccles 1:14|all things that are done under the sun, and behold all is vanity, and vexation of spirit|cuncta quæ fiunt sub sole, et ecce universa vanitas et afflictio spiritus]].

paras.t: Qui quasi flos egreditur et conteritur: id est, quemadmodum flos exit de terra, et primo viret, deinde cito marcescit; sic homo in infantia de ventre parentis progreditur, et in flore ætatis apparens ad modicum, deinde statim deficit et decrescit, siccatur, arescit: sicut in Psalmo cantamus, Homo sicut fœnum dies ejus, et tanquam flos agri sic efflorebit. Hinc in Isaia fertur: Omnis caro fœnum, et omnis gloria ejus tanquam flos agri.
paras.en: [[14:2|Who cometh forth like a flower, and is destroyed|Qui quasi flos egreditur et conteritur]]: that is, as a flower comes out of the earth, and is green at first, then soon withers; so man in infancy comes forth from the womb of his parent, and, appearing for a little while in the flower of his age, then straightway fails and dwindles, dries up, withers away: as we sing in the Psalm, [[Ps 102:15|Man's days are as grass, as the flower of the field so shall he flourish.|Homo sicut fœnum dies ejus, et tanquam flos agri sic efflorebit]] Hence it is said in Isaias: [[Is 40:6|All flesh is grass, and all the glory thereof as the flower of the field|Omnis caro fœnum, et omnis gloria ejus tanquam flos agri]].

paras.t: Et fugit velut umbra, id est, indesinenter tendit, propinquat, imo et currit ad mortem. Propter quod primo Paralipomenon libro loquitur David: Dies nostri sicut umbra super terram, et nulla est mora. Itemque in Psalmo: Homo vanitati similis factus est; dies ejus sicut umbra prætereunt. Unde in Sapientis libro etiam impii hoc testantur: Umbra transitus est tempus nostrum.
paras.en: [[14:2|and fleeth as a shadow|Et fugit velut umbra]], that is, he ceaselessly tends, draws near, nay, runs towards death. For which reason David says in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:15|Our days upon earth are as a shadow, and there is no stay|Dies nostri sicut umbra super terram, et nulla est mora]]. And likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 143:4|Man is like to vanity: his days pass away like a shadow.|Homo vanitati similis factus est; dies ejus sicut umbra prætereunt]] Hence in the book of the Wise Man even the wicked bear witness to this: [[Wis 2:5|our time is as the passing of a shadow|Umbra transitus est tempus nostrum]] [the margin reads Sap. v, 5; the words are Wis 2:5, where the wicked are speaking].

paras.t: Et nunquam in eodem statu permanet, id est, in una dispositione fixus non manet per tempus notabile, et forte nec per momentum omnifarie. Licet enim secundum mentem ad tempus stabiliter Deo inhæreat et intendat per contemplationem interioresque actus virtutum theologicarum ac donorum et latriæ seu pœnitentiæ; in corpore tamen continua alteratio, variatio seu motio esse cognoscitur. Sed et mens dum sic Deo fixe et amorose intenta est, in pristino statu non manet, sed crescit et proficit: et in actu hujusmodi diu non figitur, sed ad propriam defectuositatem cito relabitur. Quumque debitam diligentiam non adhibuerit ad vitandum Dei offensam, ad complendum ejus voluntatem, ad profectum virtutum, mox a pristino statu cadens, decrescit. Ideo dicit Bernardus: In via Dei non proficere, est deficere; non progredi, est regredi; non crescere, est decrescere. Unde verissimum est illud Ecclesiastici: Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua, id est, conscientia tua lædetur, mensque tua a summo cadet ad infima. Hinc, juxta Micheam prophetam, oportet cum Deo sollicitum ambulare; et juxta Salomonem, omni custodia cor custodire. Quocirca Gregorius pulchre scribit: Hoc ipsum, inquiens, nostrum vivere, quotidie a vita transire est. Nam postquam homo deliquit, in quodam se temporalitatis lubrico posuit: quam mobilitatem etiam interius patitur, dum ad opera surgere meliora conatur. Mens etenim mutabilitatis suæ pondere ad alia semper impellitur; et nisi in statu suo arcta disciplinæ custodia teneatur, semper ad deteriora dilabitur.
paras.en: [[14:2|and never continueth in the same state|Et nunquam in eodem statu permanet]], that is, he does not stay fixed in one disposition for any notable time, and perhaps not wholly even for a moment. For though in mind he may for a time cleave steadfastly to God and be intent on him through contemplation and the inward acts of the theological virtues and of the gifts, and of latria [the worship due to God alone] or of penance; yet in the body there is known to be continual alteration, variation or motion. And the mind too, while it is thus fixedly and lovingly intent on God, does not remain in its former state, but grows and advances: and it is not held long in an act of this kind, but soon slips back to its own defectiveness. And when it has not used due diligence to avoid offending God, to fulfil his will and to advance in virtue, it soon falls from its former state and goes back. Therefore Bernard says: In the way of God not to go forward is to fall away; not to advance is to go back; not to grow is to grow less. Hence most true is that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 27:4|Unless thou hold thyself diligently in the fear of the Lord, thy house shall quickly be overthrown|Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua]], that is, thy conscience will be wounded, and thy mind will fall from the highest to the lowest. Hence, according to the prophet Micheas, one must [[Mich 6:8|walk solicitous with thy God|cum Deo sollicitum ambulare]]; and, according to Solomon, [[Prov 4:23|With all watchfulness keep thy heart|omni custodia cor custodire]]. Whereupon Gregory finely writes: This very living of ours, he says, is to pass away daily from life. For after man sinned, he set himself on a kind of slippery ground of temporality: and this changeableness he suffers inwardly too, while he strives to rise to better works. For the mind is ever driven to other things by the weight of its own mutability; and unless it be held in its state by the close custody of discipline, it is ever slipping down to worse things.

paras.t: Denique, affectiones animarum nostrarum sunt valde mutabiles. Jam enim lætamur, jam contristamur; jam ira nos pulsat, jam mititas afficit; jam tranquillitate fungimur, jam inquietudine agitamur: nunc timor, nunc securitas; nunc dolor, nunc sospitas; jam devotio, jam distractio; nunc mentis ubertas, nunc cordis sterilitas. Ex quibus omnibus patet, quasi immensa imperfectio nostra atque distantia a primo, summo, perfecto et incommutabili ente: in quo non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio.
paras.en: Further, the affections of our souls are very changeable. For now we rejoice, now we are saddened; now anger stirs us, now mildness moves us; now we enjoy tranquillity, now we are tossed by disquiet: now fear, now security; now grief, now well-being; now devotion, now distraction; now fruitfulness of mind, now barrenness of heart. From all of which our well-nigh immense imperfection is plain, and our distance from the first, highest, perfect and unchangeable Being: in whom [[Jas 1:17|there is no change nor shadow of alteration|non est transmutatio, nec vicissitudinis obumbratio]].

paras.t: Itaque, considerata Dei altitudine et hominis vilitate, sanctus Job miratur diligentiam providentiæ Dei ad hominem, quodque Altissimus tantam de re fragili habet curam. Ideo subdit: Et dignum ducis super hujuscemodi creaturam tam imperfectam aperire oculos tuos, id est curam ejus habere, ei de necessariis providere, omnia ejus considerare, legem ac præcepta præbere, ejusque jugiter memorem esse? juxta id Psalmi: De cœlo respexit Dominus; vidit omnes filios hominum. De præparato habitaculo suo respexit super omnes qui habitant terram. Denique in isto apparet immensa dignatio Dei, velut si potentissimus rex, infimos subditorum suorum tam provide curet ac dirigat. Quo enim major est Dei celsitudo et dignitas, et major imperfectio nostra, eo major in istis ostenditur Dei dignatio.
paras.en: And so, having weighed the height of God and the lowliness of man, holy Job marvels at the diligence of God's providence towards man, and that the Most High has such care of so frail a thing. Therefore he adds: [[14:3|And dost thou think it meet|Et dignum ducis]] [[14:3|to open thy eyes|aperire oculos tuos]] [[14:3|upon such an one|super hujuscemodi]], a creature so imperfect, that is, to have care of him, to provide him with what he needs, to consider all that is his, to give him law and commandments, and to be ever mindful of him? according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 32:13|The Lord hath looked from heaven: he hath beheld all the sons of men.|De cœlo respexit Dominus; vidit omnes filios hominum]] [[Ps 32:14|From his habitation which he hath prepared, he hath looked upon all that dwell on the earth.|De præparato habitaculo suo respexit super omnes qui habitant terram]] Indeed in this the immense condescension of God appears, as if a most mighty king were to care for and direct the lowest of his subjects so providently. For the greater the loftiness and dignity of God, and the greater our imperfection, the greater the condescension of God that is shown in these things.
