paras.t: Et adducere eum tecum in judicium, id est eum ad judicandum tibi adsistere, et de universis judicare ac præmiare? Hoc utique exigit sapientia atque justitia Dei. Non enim frustra contulit homini rationem, sed ob debitum finem, ut scilicet ea utatur, et Deo fideliter obsequatur. Unde qui ita se habet, laudem et gloriam promeretur; qui aliter, pœnam. Propterea in Ecclesiaste dicitur: Cuncta quæ fiunt, adducet Deus in judicium pro omni errato, sive bonum sit, sive malum. Per Jeremiam quoque: Ego sum, inquit, judex et testis. Atque in Psalmo: Judicabit orbem terræ in æquitate; judicabit populos in justitia.
paras.en: [[14:3|and to bring him into judgment with thee?|Et adducere eum tecum in judicium]] that is, that he should stand before thee to be judged, and that thou shouldst judge and reward him for all things? This indeed the wisdom and justice of God require. For not in vain did he give man reason, but for a due end, namely that he should use it and serve God faithfully. Hence he who so conducts himself merits praise and glory; he who does otherwise, punishment. Therefore it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 12:14|all things that are done, God will bring into judgment for every error, whether it be good or evil|Cuncta quæ fiunt, adducet Deus in judicium pro omni errato, sive bonum sit, sive malum]]. And by Jeremias too: [[Jer 29:23|I am|Ego sum]], he says, [[Jer 29:23|the judge and the witness|judex et testis]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 9:9|he shall judge the world in equity, he shall judge the people in justice|Judicabit orbem terræ in æquitate; judicabit populos in justitia]].

paras.t: Deinde ostendit qua virtute homo salvetur in Dei judicio. Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? id est, quis potest hominem ex immundo infectoque semine patris conceptum, a peccatis purgare, virtutibus decorare? Nonne tu? qui per essentiam mundus, sanctus, virtuosusque es: qui solus peccata dimittis, gratiam creas, virtutes infundis. Imo, secundum Augustinum, majus miraculum est justificatio impii, quam creatio mundi, quum in justificatione tali sit aliquid quasi resistens, scilicet mala voluntas, in creatione autem nihil resistit. Et quamvis sacramenta et homines dicantur aliquem purgare, gratiis adornare, perficere et salvare, hoc tamen [non] propria potestate, nec auctoritative ac principaliter agunt, sed virtute divinitus data, et dispositive ac instrumentaliter. Porro semen (secundum Augustinum) immundum vocatur propter annexam libidinem, quæ fomes et nutrimentum est improbæ voluntatis ad culpam: quæ libido in semine ante animæ infusionem, dicitur esse quasi in radice.
paras.en: Then he shows by what power man is saved in the judgement of God. [[14:4|Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed?|Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine?]] that is, who can cleanse from sins and adorn with virtues a man conceived of the unclean and infected seed of his father? [[14:4|is it not thou|Nonne tu]]? who art clean, holy and virtuous by thine essence: who alone forgivest sins, createst grace, infusest virtues. Nay, according to Augustine, the justification of the wicked is a greater miracle than the creation of the world, since in such justification there is something that as it were resists, namely the evil will, whereas in creation nothing resists. And though sacraments and men are said to cleanse someone, to adorn him with graces, to perfect and to save him, yet they do this not by their own power, nor with authority and as principal agents, but by a power given them by God, and as disposing causes and as instruments. Moreover the seed (according to Augustine) is called unclean because of the lust joined to it, which is the fomes [the tinder of sin: the inclination to sin left by original sin] and nourishment of the wicked will towards sin: and this lust is said to be in the seed, before the infusion of the soul, as it were in its root.

paras.t: Qui solus es: id est, solus omniformiter ac quomodolibet perfectum esse habes, in quo nihil est de non esse, nihil de imperfecto esse; sed tu es ipsum supersimplicissimum esse, plenum, perfectum, immensum: in quo est omnis beatitudo, perfectio, sanctitas, gloria, pulchritudo, voluptas cum plenitudine penitus infinita, sine omni limite et mensura. Itaque dicitur Deus solus esse, quoniam comparatione sui esse, creatum esse est magis non esse, quam esse, utpote ab illo deficiens infinite, sicut comparatione Dei nemo bonus, nullus sapiens, nullus sanctus. Hinc, esse ponitur nomen Dei, ipsomet Deo sublimi et benedicto, superessentiali et superglorioso, dicente ad Moysen: Ego sum qui sum. Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos. Hinc et Hilarius: Esse non est accidens Deo, sed subsistens veritas, manens causa, et naturalis vel rei generis proprietas.
paras.en: [[14:4|who only art|Qui solus es]]: that is, thou alone hast perfect being in every form and in every way, in whom there is nothing of non-being, nothing of imperfect being; but thou art being itself, simple beyond all simplicity, full, perfect, immense: in whom is all beatitude, perfection, holiness, glory, beauty and delight, in a fulness wholly infinite, without any limit or measure. And so God is said alone to be, since in comparison with his being, created being is rather non-being than being, as falling infinitely short of it; just as in comparison with God none is good[[Mark 10:18||]], none wise, none holy. Hence *being* is set down as the name of God, God himself, sublime and blessed, superessential and superglorious, saying to Moses: [[Ex 3:14|I AM WHO AM|Ego sum qui sum]]. [[Ex 3:14|Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you|Hæc dices filiis Israel: Qui est, misit me ad vos]]. Hence Hilary too: Being is not an accident in God, but subsisting truth, abiding cause, and the natural property of the thing or of its kind.

14.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli quartidecimi: Breves dies hominis sunt.
14.title_en: Literal explanation of the fourteenth chapter: The days of man are short

paras.t: Inchoatam humanæ conditionis descriptionem, quantum ad ejus calamitatem, vanitatem et vilitatem multiplicem, capitulo isto Job sanctus prosequitur. Breves dies hominis sunt. Hoc, quantum ad sensum, supra præhabitum est. Iste equidem liber rhetoricus, instar rhetorice scriptorum voluminum, eamdem sententiam sub aliis verbis frequenter continet repetitam. Unde quod nunc ait, paulo ante sic protulit: Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore.
paras.en: Holy Job continues in this chapter the description of the human condition that he had begun, as to its manifold calamity, vanity and vileness. [[14:5|The days of man are short|Breves dies hominis sunt]]. This, as to its sense, has been given above. For this book, being rhetorical, like volumes written in the manner of rhetoric, often contains the same thought repeated in other words. Hence what he says now he put thus a little before: [[14:1|Man born of a woman, living for a short time|Homo natus de muliere, brevi vivens tempore]].

paras.t: Denique quo aliquis magis a Spiritu Sancto illuminatur, et in dono sapientiæ atque scientiæ abundat, eo non solum certius et clarius, sed insuper saporosius intuetur et noscit, quam breve, imo quam momentaneum sit omne tempus vitæ nostræ in sæculo isto. Hinc viri sancti, vitæ hujus tempus pro nihilo reputaverunt. Siquidem, per donum sapientiæ, rectum et saporosum sortitur homo judicium de divinis, hoc est de Deo ejusque æternitate ac ceteris attributis seu proprietatibus ejus. Porro, per donum scientiæ, recte saporoseque judicat de creatis, puta de tempore ac ceteris creaturis, quomodo in eis non sit finis ultimus constituendus. Qui ergo tam de æternitate quam de tempore taliter judicat, et utrumque ad invicem comparat, clarissime conspicit quam breve sit hominis tempus. Aliquibus tamen dies quibus vivunt, multi ac longi videntur, quia videlicet exercitiis laboriosis intenti sunt, vel doloribus afficiuntur, seu delectationibus in his quæ agunt, non relevantur. Alii cuncta cum delectatione prompte et alacriter peragunt, ideo tempus eis breve videtur. Unde (secundum Albertum in libro de IV Coæquævis) voluptuosis, itemque divinis hominibus tempus est breve. Illi enim carnalibus, isti spiritualibus abundant deliciis.
paras.en: Moreover, the more anyone is enlightened by the Holy Ghost and abounds in the gift of wisdom and of knowledge, the more surely and clearly, and the more savourily besides [*saporosius*: wisdom, *sapientia*, gives a judgement that tastes, *sapit*, what it knows], does he see and know how short, nay how momentary, is the whole time of our life in this world. Hence holy men counted the time of this life as nothing. For by the gift of wisdom man obtains a right and savoury judgement of divine things, that is, of God and his eternity and his other attributes or properties. And by the gift of knowledge he judges rightly and savourily of created things, for instance of time and the other creatures, how the last end is not to be set in them. Whoever, then, judges thus both of eternity and of time, and compares the one with the other, sees most clearly how short the time of man is. Yet to some the days they live seem many and long, because they are taken up with toilsome exercises, or are afflicted with pains, or are not relieved by delight in what they do. Others do everything readily and briskly, with delight, and so the time seems short to them. Hence (according to Albert in the book On the Four Coequals) time is short for the voluptuous, and likewise for godly men: for the former abound in fleshly delights, the latter in spiritual ones.

paras.t: Numerus mensium ejus apud te est, id est tibi certitudinaliter cognitus est, quot scilicet mensibus vivet, quanquam aliqui primo suæ nativitatis mense decedant. Constituisti terminos ejus, id est, ultimum diem suæ vitæ, et ultimam horam, imo ultimum minutum, ultimumque momentum, quo unusquisque vivit in mundo, tu (o Deus) in tua sapientia prævidisti, præordinasti, et præfixisti: quemadmodum in Actis loquitur Paulus, Deus fecit ex uno homine omne humanum genus inhabitare super universam faciem terræ, definiens statuta tempora et terminos habitationis eorum.
paras.en: [[14:5|the number of his months is with thee|Numerus mensium ejus apud te est]], that is, it is known to thee with certainty, namely for how many months he will live, although some die in the first month after their birth. [[14:5|thou hast appointed his bounds|Constituisti terminos ejus]], that is, the last day of his life, and the last hour, nay the last minute and the last moment in which each one lives in the world, thou (O God) hast in thy wisdom foreseen, foreordained and fixed beforehand: as Paul says in the Acts: God [[Acts 17:26|hath made of one, all mankind, to dwell upon the whole face of the earth, determining appointed times and the limits of their habitation|fecit ex uno homine omne humanum genus inhabitare super universam faciem terræ, definiens statuta tempora et terminos habitationis eorum]].

paras.t: Qui præteriri non poterunt, id est variari, minorari, seu prolongari, secundum quod cadunt sub immobili et infallibili providentia Dei, cujus respectu seu comparatione omnia quantumcumque mutabilia, successiva, incerta, invariabiliter et infallibiliter cognoscuntur, imo et certe proveniunt. Divina nempe providentia complectitur universa, estque certus ordo causarum per comparationem ad eam. Nihilo minus res aliquæ, per comparationem ad proprias, naturales et immediatas causas, contingentes variabilesque consistunt et prorsus incertæ. Divina namque providentia non tollit a rebus, quod eis naturaliter competit; sed secundum suæ divinæ eminentiæ infinitæ modum ac perfectionem cognoscit, prævidet ac disponit res modo sublimiori, quam illæ in se ipsis sint. Unde etiam (secundum Boetium) cognitio fit secundum modum cognoscentis, non cogniti. Hinc etiam periodus seu duratio vitæ hominis, si comparetur ad causas naturales ac proprias, videlicet ad complexionem, potest quidem variis modis abbreviari, quamvis non prolongetur, absolute loquendo. Aliquo tamen modo prolongatur, occurrendo causis suæ abbreviationis. Sed et supernaturaliter certum est eam posse ad Dei beneplacitum prolongari.
paras.en: [[14:5|which cannot be passed|Qui præteriri non poterunt]], that is, varied, shortened or lengthened, inasmuch as they fall under the unmoved and unfailing providence of God, in respect of which, or in comparison with which, all things, however changeable, successive and uncertain, are known unchangeably and unfailingly, and indeed come to pass with certainty. For divine providence embraces all things, and there is a sure order of causes by comparison with it. Nevertheless some things, by comparison with their own natural and immediate causes, are contingent and changeable, and wholly uncertain. For divine providence does not take from things what belongs to them by nature; but it knows, foresees and disposes things after the mode and perfection of its own infinite divine eminence, in a more sublime way than they are in themselves. Hence too (according to Boethius) knowledge is after the mode of the knower, not of the known. Hence too the period or duration of man's life, if it is compared with its natural and proper causes, namely with his complexion [that is, the balance of humours in his body], can indeed be shortened in various ways, though it is not lengthened, speaking absolutely. Yet in some way it is lengthened, by meeting the causes of its shortening. And it is certain too that it can be lengthened supernaturally at God's good pleasure.

paras.t: Recede ergo paululum, etc. Hoc dupliciter explanatur. Primo, secundum Gregorium et Albertum. Recede, id est, potentiæ tuæ flagellationem amove, paululum ab eo, id est ab homine tribulato, ut quiescat a doloribus suæ adversitatis, ne supra vires gravetur, vel per impatientiam ruat. Unde non orat ut totaliter sic recedat, sed paululum: quoniam moderata adversitas sive afflictio perutilis est, et a multis malis præservans. Propter quod Jeremias dicit: Corripe me, Domine; verumtamen in judicio, et non in furore tuo, ne forte ad nihilum redigas me. In Apocalypsi quoque Dominus protestatur: Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Hinc supra habetur: Beatus qui corripitur a Domino. Secundo, exponitur juxta Thomam. Recede paululum ab eo, id est, vitæ conversationem abstrahe ei, et mori eum permitte, ut quiescat, id est, per mortem obdormiat, et a vitæ hujus doloribus liber sit. Sicut enim sol est causa diei, sic Deus est auctor vitæ. Ideo, sicut sole recedente dies finitur, sic Deo conversationis influentiam abstrahente, vita hominis terminatur. Sicque Job mortem precatur homini a Deo inferri eo modo, quo supra frequenter oravit se a vita hac tolli, videlicet desiderio majoris quietis, et ne in vita ista Deum amplius inhonoret, aut in peccati pericula incidat; atque ob id ut a præsentibus tribulationibus eripiatur, secundum modum quo id licite affectatur: qui modus sæpe jam tactus est.
paras.en: [[14:6|Depart a little|Recede ergo paululum]], etc. This is explained in two ways. First, according to Gregory and Albert: [[14:6|Depart|Recede]], that is, take away the scourging of thy power, [[14:6|a little from him|paululum ab eo]], that is, from the man in tribulation, [[14:6|that he may rest|ut quiescat]] from the pains of his adversity, lest he be weighed down beyond his strength or fall through impatience. Hence he does not pray that he depart thus altogether, but a little: for moderate adversity or affliction is very profitable, and preserves from many evils. Wherefore Jeremias says: [[Jer 10:24|Correct me, O Lord, but yet with judgment: and not in thy fury, lest thou bring me to nothing.|Corripe me, Domine; verumtamen in judicio, et non in furore tuo, ne forte ad nihilum redigas me]] In the Apocalypse also the Lord declares: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. Hence it is said above: [[Job 5:17|Blessed is the man whom God correcteth|Beatus qui corripitur a Domino]] [Denis has “Blessed is he who is corrected by the Lord”]. Secondly, it is expounded according to Thomas: [[14:6|Depart a little from him|Recede paululum ab eo]], that is, withdraw from him the keeping of his life [the print has *conversationem*, “dealing”, here and below, probably for *conservationem*, “preservation”], and let him die, [[14:6|that he may rest|ut quiescat]], that is, fall asleep through death, and be free of the pains of this life. For as the sun is the cause of the day, so God is the author of life. Therefore, as the day ends when the sun departs, so when God withdraws the influence of preservation, man's life comes to an end. And so Job prays that death be brought upon man by God in the way in which he often prayed above to be taken from this life: namely from desire of a greater rest, and lest in this life he dishonour God further or fall into the dangers of sin; and for that reason, that he may be rescued from present tribulations, in the way in which this may lawfully be desired: a way already touched on often.

paras.t: Donec optata veniat, sicut mercenarii dies ejus, id est, donec adveniat dies suæ retributionis a te: quam diem optavit, cupiens præmium felicitatis æternæ. Quæ dies est sicut dies mercenarii, qui pro mercede laborat, cupitque diem in qua se novit accepturum mercedem. Sic homo justus desiderat diem glorificationis suæ a Deo. Porro, ante Christi adventum, justi optabant aliquando quietem in limbo patrum, sicut et Simeon ait: Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum in pace. Verumtamen illam quietem imperfectam retulerunt finaliter ad perfectam patriæ cœlestis quietem, cujus consolationis respectu, quies in limbo patrum quasi desolatio fuit. Propter quod a Zacharia dicitur Christo: Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu, in quo non est aqua. Ubi per lacum, intelligitur limbus patrum; per aquam, consolatio seu beata refectio.
paras.en: [[14:6|until his wished for day come, as that of the hireling|Donec optata veniat, sicut mercenarii dies ejus]], that is, until the day of his reward from thee come: which day he longed for, desiring the prize of eternal happiness. This day is like the day of a hireling, who labours for wages and longs for the day on which he knows he will receive his wages. So the just man longs for the day of his glorification by God. Moreover, before the coming of Christ the just sometimes longed for rest in the limbo of the fathers, as Simeon too says: [[Luke 2:29|Now thou dost dismiss thy servant, O Lord, according to thy word in peace|Nunc dimittis servum tuum, Domine, secundum verbum tuum in pace]]. Yet in the end they referred that imperfect rest to the perfect rest of the heavenly fatherland, in comparison with whose consolation the rest in the limbo of the fathers was a kind of desolation. Wherefore Zacharias says to Christ: [[Zach 9:11|Thou also by the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, wherein is no water.|Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu, in quo non est aqua]] Where by the pit is understood the limbo of the fathers; by water, consolation or blessed refreshment.

paras.t: Deinde ostendit quod homo post mortem ad statum hujus vitæ non redeat, et quantum ad hoc, sit etiam infimis rebus vilioris proprietatis. Lignum habet spem, id est, arbor naturalem habet aptitudinem seu exspectationem ut reviviscat, si præcidatur aut vetustate deficiat. Itaque, lignum habet spem materialiter sive causaliter, quia in se habet unde spem homo concipiat de ligni renovatione. Hinc subditur: Si præcisum fuerit, rursum virescit, et rami ejus pullulant. Hoc videmus ad oculum, quia si arbor usque ad terram præcidatur, nova exsurgunt virgulta. Ramusculi quoque abscisi, alibi rite plantati, crescunt et germinant. Hoc itaque dicitur de ligno, quantum ad ejus defectum qui per violentiam sibi infertur, sicut et homo interdum violenta deficit morte.
paras.en: Next he shows that man after death does not return to the state of this life, and that in this respect he is of a viler condition even than the lowest things. [[14:7|A tree hath hope|Lignum habet spem]], that is, a tree has a natural aptitude or expectation of reviving, if it is cut down or fails through age. And so a tree *hath hope* materially or causally, because it has in itself that from which man may conceive hope of the tree's renewal. Hence it is added: [[14:7|if it be cut, it growth green again, and the boughs thereof sprout|Si præcisum fuerit, rursum virescit, et rami ejus pullulant]]. This we see with our eyes, for if a tree is cut down to the ground, new shoots spring up. Little branches too, cut off and duly planted elsewhere, grow and sprout. This, then, is said of the tree as to the failing that is brought upon it by violence, as man too sometimes fails by a violent death.

paras.t: Quantum vero ad ligni naturalem defectum, quem incurrit ex hoc, quod ex defectu naturalis suæ virtutis vegetativæ non valet attrahere alimentum, subjungitur: Si senuerit in terra radix ejus, id est, si senectute confecta per pororum obstructionem aruerit, et in pulvere emortuus fuerit truncus illius, vegetativam vitam perdendo, deficiente radice; ad odorem aquæ germinabit: id est, humore aquæ sibi infuso, vim pristinam recuperabit, et fructificabit, juxta illud Jeremiæ: Lignum ad humorem mittit radices suas. Et faciet comam, id est congeriem ramorum et florum seu frondium ad similitudinem capillorum, quasi quum primum plantatum est, id est, sicut in prima sua egit plantatione. Siquidem in putrefacta ligni materia, manet vis seminativa seu ratio seminalis, per quam reparatio ista infuso fomento peragitur. Denique, secundum Albertum, tangitur hic opus rusticanum, quod Aristoteles quoque in libro de Plantis, atque Palladius in libro de Agricultura tangunt, videlicet quod fit in arbore vetusta, in cujus radice cortex induratus, et in poris suis obstructus, humorem ad intima mittere nequit, propter quod arbor aret et infructuosa efficitur. Si autem majores radices nudentur ac securi findantur, lapisque in fissura ponatur, ne rursus valeat claudi, et stercora circumponantur, terra quoque cooperiantur; in fissuris incipit humorem attrahere, et redit ad ipsam juventus, comatur, foliis ornatur, et fructibus fecundatur. Simile quid loquitur Christus, dicens: Ecce tres anni sunt, ex quo venio quærens fructum in ficulnea hac, et non invenio. Succide ergo illam. Dixit autem cultor vineæ: Domine, dimitte eam et hoc anno, usque dum fodiam circa illam, et mittam stercora.
paras.en: But as to the natural failing of the tree, which it incurs because, through the failing of its natural vegetative power, it cannot draw in nourishment, it is added: [[14:8|If its roots be old in the earth|Si senuerit in terra radix ejus]], that is, if, worn out with age, it has dried up through the stopping of its pores, [[14:8|and its stock be dead in the dust|et in pulvere emortuus fuerit truncus illius]], losing its vegetative life as the root fails; [[14:9|At the scent of water, it shall spring|ad odorem aquæ germinabit]]: that is, when the moisture of water is poured into it, it will recover its former strength and bear fruit, according to that of Jeremias: A tree [[Jer 17:8|that spreadeth out its roots towards moisture|ad humorem mittit radices suas]]. [[14:9|and bring forth leaves|Et faciet comam]] [*comam*, literally “hair”], that is, a mass of branches and flowers or leaves after the likeness of hair, [[14:9|as when it was first planted|quasi quum primum plantatum est]], that is, as it did when it was first planted. For in the rotted matter of the wood there remains a seminative power or seminal reason [*ratio seminalis*: the hidden principle of growth set in things at their making], through which this restoring is brought about when nourishment is poured in. Moreover, according to Albert, a husbandman's work is touched on here, which Aristotle too in his book On Plants, and Palladius in his book On Agriculture, touch on: namely what is done with an old tree, at whose root the bark has hardened and become stopped in its pores, so that it cannot send moisture to the inner parts, on account of which the tree dries up and becomes fruitless. But if the larger roots are laid bare and split with an axe, and a stone is put in the cleft so that it cannot close again, and dung is put round them and they are covered over with earth, it begins to draw moisture in the clefts, and its youth comes back to it: it grows its crown again, is adorned with leaves and made fruitful with fruit. Christ says something similar: [[Luke 13:7|Behold, for these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree and I find none. Cut it down therefore|Ecce tres anni sunt, ex quo venio quærens fructum in ficulnea hac, et non invenio. Succide ergo illam]]. And the dresser of the vineyard said: [[Luke 13:8|Lord, let it alone this year also, until I dig about it and dung it|Domine, dimitte eam et hoc anno, usque dum fodiam circa illam, et mittam stercora]].

paras.t: Homo vero, quum mortuus fuerit, et nudatus tegumentis, quibus corpus exanime solet obvolvi ac sepeliri, quæ sub terra putrefiunt, atque consumptus, per corporis resolutionem, ubi, quæso, est? id est, ad oculum seu sensibiliter nihil ipsius manet. Nam anima insensibiliter egreditur ac recedit; nec homo, quomodo lignum, habet spem redeundi ad pristinam juventutem in statu sæculi hujus: quod consequenter per simile aperit. Quomodo si recedant aquæ de mari, ita ut alveus prorsus siccetur, et fluvius vacuefactus arescat, dum scilicet totaliter deficit, sicut in fabula Phaethontis per diluvium ignis factum asserit Plato: sic homo quum dormierit moriendo: de qua dormitione in Scripturis toties dicitur, Dormivit cum patribus suis; non resurget, ita ut revertatur ad statum vitæ præsentis, ut quidam philosophi æstimabant; naturali quoque potentia nunquam resurget a morte.
paras.en: [[14:10|But man when he shall be dead|Homo vero, quum mortuus fuerit]], [[14:10|and stripped|et nudatus]] of the coverings in which a lifeless body is usually wrapped and buried, which rot under the earth, [[14:10|and consumed|atque consumptus]] by the dissolving of the body, [[14:10|I pray you where is he?|ubi, quæso, est?]] that is, to the eye, or to the senses, nothing of him remains. For the soul goes out and departs unseen; nor has man, as a tree has, hope of returning to his former youth in the state of this world: which he next makes plain by a likeness. [[14:11|As if the waters should depart out of the sea|Quomodo si recedant aquæ de mari]], so that the bed is wholly dried, [[14:11|and an emptied river should be dried up|et fluvius vacuefactus arescat]], that is, when it fails altogether, as Plato asserts was done in the fable of Phaethon by a deluge of fire: [[14:12|So man when he is fallen asleep|sic homo quum dormierit]] by dying (of which sleep it is said so often in the Scriptures, He slept with his fathers), [[14:12|shall not rise again|non resurget]], so as to return to the state of the present life, as certain philosophers supposed; and by natural power, too, he will never rise from death.

paras.t: Donec atteratur cœlum, non evigilabit, nec consurget de somno suo. Hoc dupliciter exponitur. Primo, ut superiori consonet verbo, eritque sensus: Donec atteratur, etc., id est, quemadmodum cœlum quod incorruptibile est, nunquam atteretur seu destruetur substantialiter, sic homo mortuus præfato modo nunquam resurget, nec de somno mortis taliter evigilabit. Secundo exponitur sic: Donec atteratur, etc., id est, tunc, puta in fine mundi, per supernaturalem resurget potentiam, quando cœlestia corpora atterentur quantum ad modum essendi accidentalemque dispositionem, et quoad officium quod modo exercent, ad generationem et corruptionem movendo: quia tunc stabunt. Hinc ait Salvator: Cœlum et terra transibunt. Et Psalmista: Opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli: ipsi peribunt. In Apocalypsi quoque ait Joannes: Vidi cœlum novum et terram novam: primum enim cœlum et prima terra abiit. Tunc ergo homo mortuus evigilabit, resuscitatus ad vitam animalem et rationalem, ut vivat, non super terram, ac denuo moriatur, sed in loco sibi debito æternaliter collocetur, vivat et maneat, prout de se ipso Unigenitus Dei Patris fatetur: Veniet hora, in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus. Porro, vigilia (secundum Albertum) est expansio spiritus caloris et virtutis ad organa sensuum.
paras.en: [[14:12|till the heavens be broken, he shall not awake, nor rise up out of his sleep|Donec atteratur cœlum, non evigilabit, nec consurget de somno suo]]. This is expounded in two ways. First, so as to agree with the words before; and the sense will be: [[14:12|till the heavens be broken|Donec atteratur]], etc., that is, as the heaven, which is incorruptible, will never be worn away or destroyed in its substance, so a dead man will never rise in the aforesaid way, nor so wake from the sleep of death. Secondly it is expounded thus: [[14:12|till the heavens be broken|Donec atteratur]], etc., that is, then, namely at the end of the world, he will rise by supernatural power, when the heavenly bodies are worn away [*atterentur*, the verse's word] as to their accidental mode of being and disposition, and as to the office they now perform, of moving things to generation and corruption: for then they will stand still. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 24:35|Heaven and earth shall pass|Cœlum et terra transibunt]] [the margin note is unreadable; the words stand also in Mark 13:31 and Luke 21:33]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 101:26|the heavens are the works of thy hands|Opera manuum tuarum sunt cœli]]: [[Ps 101:27|They shall perish|ipsi peribunt]]. In the Apocalypse also John says: [[Apoc 21:1|I saw a new heaven and a new earth. For the first heaven and the first earth was gone|Vidi cœlum novum et terram novam: primum enim cœlum et prima terra abiit]]. Then therefore the dead man will awake, raised again to animal and rational life [that is, to the life of body and soul together], so as to live, not upon earth and die anew, but to be set for ever in the place due to him, to live and abide, as the Only-begotten of God the Father declares of himself: [[John 5:28|the hour cometh wherein all that are in the graves shall hear the voice|Veniet hora, in qua omnes qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus]] [Denis has “the hour shall come … his voice”]. Moreover, waking (according to Albert) is the spreading of the spirit, of heat and of power to the organs of the senses.

paras.t: Consequenter beatus Job clarissime protestatur, quid ipse de animarum immortalitate, et corporum sentiat resuscitatione. Quis mihi tribuat, id est, vehementer cupio mihi donari, ut in inferno, id est in limbo patrum: qui aliquando infernus vocatur, sicut in Genesi Jacob, Descendam, inquit, ad filium meum lugens in infernum; protegas me a locis pœnalibus damnatorum atque molestia dæmonum, qui mihi in vita hac tam infesti consistunt; et abscondas me a malis vitæ præsentis, ne videam ea ac patiar. Sic enim quarto Regum legitur Deus promisisse Josiæ sanctissimo: Jam colligam te ad patres tuos, ut non videant oculi tui mala Jerusalem, scilicet pœnas ejus. Donec pertranseat furor tuus, id est tempus tuæ districtæ ultionis, quo, propter primi parentis peccatum, omnes electi impediebantur a gloria, et genus humanum innumerabilibus miseriis, vitiis atque erroribus plenum fuit, et quotidie plurimi perierunt. Hoc autem tempus duravit usque ad Christi adventum ac passionem, quando ira Dei in misericordiam versa est, et rigor justitiæ in dulcorem clementiæ, juxta illud ad Ephesios: Christus per crucem dissolvit inimicitias in semetipso. Hinc ad Romanos inducitur: Quum adhuc inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus.
paras.en: Next blessed Job declares most clearly what he himself holds of the immortality of souls and of the raising again of bodies. [[14:13|Who will grant me this|Quis mihi tribuat]], that is, I earnestly long that it be given me, that [[14:13|in hell|in inferno]], that is, in the limbo of the fathers (which is sometimes called hell, as in Genesis Jacob says: [[Gen 37:35|I will go down|Descendam]], he says, [[Gen 37:35|to my son into hell, mourning|ad filium meum lugens in infernum]]), [[14:13|thou mayst protect me|protegas me]] from the places of punishment of the damned and from the harassing of the demons, who are so hostile to me in this life; [[14:13|and hide me|et abscondas me]] from the evils of the present life, that I may not see and suffer them. For so we read in the fourth book of Kings that God promised the most holy Josias: [[4 Kings 22:20|I will gather thee to thy fathers|Jam colligam te ad patres tuos]], [[4 Kings 22:20|that thy eyes may not see|ut non videant oculi tui]] the evils of Jerusalem, that is, its punishments. [[14:13|till thy wrath pass|Donec pertranseat furor tuus]], that is, the time of thy strict vengeance, in which, because of the sin of the first parent, all the elect were kept from glory, and mankind was full of countless miseries, vices and errors, and every day very many perished. This time lasted until the coming and the passion of Christ, when the wrath of God was turned into mercy, and the rigour of justice into the sweetness of clemency, according to that to the Ephesians: Christ, [[Eph 2:16|by the cross, killing the enmities in himself|per crucem dissolvit inimicitias in semetipso]] [Denis has “by the cross dissolved the enmities in himself”, joining Eph 2:14 and 16]. Hence it is brought in to the Romans: [[Rom 5:10|when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son|Quum adhuc inimici essemus, reconciliati sumus Deo per mortem Filii ejus]].

paras.t: Et constituas mihi tempus in quo recorderis mei, id est, tempus glorificationis seu liberationis mihi præfigas, quo per Christum me de limbo educas atque glorifices. Hoc nempe novit Job sanctus futurum, ut omnes electi in limbo patrum detenti, per Christum educerentur. De quo a Zacharia fuit prædictum: Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu, in quo non est aqua. Unde in Osee Christus prædixit: De manu mortis liberabo eos; de morte redimam eos. Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne. De hoc Apostolus verba Psalmistæ allegans, sic ait de Christo: Ascendens in altum, captivam duxit captivitatem. Christus quoque de se ipso: Ego si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum. Quidam autem per tempus, de quo loquitur Job, intelligunt tempus resurrectionis futuræ; sed prior expositio aptior est. Non enim Job petiit in inferno abscondi usque ad illud tempus, nec tam diu Deus electorum in limbo olim exsistentium oblitus visus est; sed tunc ostendit se memorem horum, quando per Christum præfato modo educti sunt: imo eodem momento quo anima Christi venit ad eos in limbum, beatificati sunt, et Deum per speciem beatifice videre cœperunt, secundum doctores. Christus namque in sua morte pro originali peccato, ob cujus reatum illi a gloria differebantur, plenissime satisfecit. Idcirco causa non fuit dilationis a gloria longioris.
paras.en: [[14:13|and appoint me a time when thou wilt remember me?|Et constituas mihi tempus in quo recorderis mei]] that is, fix for me the time of glorification or of deliverance, in which thou mayest lead me out of limbo through Christ and glorify me. For holy Job knew that this would come about, that all the elect held in the limbo of the fathers would be led out through Christ. Of which it was foretold by Zacharias: [[Zach 9:11|Thou also by the blood of thy testament hast sent forth thy prisoners out of the pit, wherein is no water.|Tu quoque in sanguine testamenti tui emisisti vinctos tuos de lacu, in quo non est aqua]] Hence in Osee Christ foretold: [[Osee 13:14|I will deliver them out of the hand of death. I will redeem them from death: O death, I will be thy death; O hell, I will be thy bite|De manu mortis liberabo eos; de morte redimam eos. Ero mors tua, o mors; morsus tuus ero, inferne]]. Of this the Apostle, citing the words of the Psalmist[[Ps 67:19||]], says thus of Christ: [[Eph 4:8|Ascending on high, he led captivity captive|Ascendens in altum, captivam duxit captivitatem]]. Christ too says of himself: [[John 12:32|And I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.|Ego si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum]] Some, however, understand by the time of which Job speaks the time of the resurrection to come; but the former exposition is more fitting. For Job did not ask to be hidden in hell until that time, nor did God seem to have forgotten for so long the elect who were once in limbo; but he showed himself mindful of them when they were led out through Christ in the way described: indeed, at the very moment when the soul of Christ came to them in limbo, they were made blessed and began to see God by sight [*per speciem*: face to face, in the beatific vision], according to the doctors. For Christ in his death made fullest satisfaction for original sin, for whose guilt they were kept back from glory. Therefore there was no cause for a longer delay of glory.

paras.t: Putasne mortuus homo rursus vivat per resuscitationem in die novissimo? quasi dicat: Hoc tu, o Deus, possibile censes. Et hoc futurum esse, tenendum est. Ideo subdit: Cunctis diebus quibus nunc milito, id est omni tempore quo in terra vivo, et contra adversarios meæ salutis pugno. Unde superius dictum est: Militia est vita hominis super terram. Exspecto donec veniat immutatio mea ad immortalitatem, id est resuscitatio ad vitam corporalem meliorem, quam sit vita hæc præsens. Immutatio quippe, mutationem dicit in melius. Hinc ad Corinthios scribit Apostolus: Omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur: quia videlicet electi immutabuntur, non reprobi, dicente Apostolo, Mortui resurgent incorrupti, et nos immutabimur. Denique, quod ait, Exspecto, etc., non est intelligendum, quod tam diu insinuaverit se victurum in corpore, et exspectaturum in eo, quousque immutatio illa veniret; sed quia exspectatio sua in corpore hic incepit, et usque ad mortem duravit. Postea vero mansit et manet in anima, donec adveniat. Verumtamen, per immutationem forte intelligi posset translatio sancti Job seu animæ ejus de sæculo isto ad limbum patrum, in quo melius habuit quam dum verba hæc protulit.
paras.en: [[14:14|Shall man that is dead, thinkest thou, live again|Putasne mortuus homo rursus vivat]] by being raised up on the last day? as if to say: Thou, O God, judgest this possible. And it must be held that it will come about. Therefore he adds: [[14:14|all the days in which I am now in warfare|Cunctis diebus quibus nunc milito]], that is, all the time in which I live on earth and fight against the enemies of my salvation. Hence it was said above: [[Job 7:1|The life of man upon earth is a warfare|Militia est vita hominis super terram]]. [[14:14|I expect until my change come|Exspecto donec veniat immutatio mea]] to immortality, that is, the raising up to a bodily life better than this present life. For *change* means a change for the better. Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 15:51|We shall all indeed rise again: but we shall not all be changed|Omnes quidem resurgemus, sed non omnes immutabimur]]: that is, the elect will be changed, not the reprobate, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 15:52|the dead shall rise again incorruptible. And we shall be changed|Mortui resurgent incorrupti, et nos immutabimur]]. Moreover, when he says, [[14:14|I expect|Exspecto]], etc., it is not to be understood that he implied he would live in the body so long, and wait in it, until that change should come; but that his waiting began here in the body and lasted until death, and afterwards remained, and remains, in the soul, until it come. Yet by *change* might perhaps be understood the passing of holy Job, or of his soul, from this world to the limbo of the fathers, where he was better off than when he spoke these words.

paras.t: Vocabis me, id est, resuscitari jubebis ac resurgere facies, corpus ex cineribus reparando famulatu angelico, et animam meam corpori reuniendo. Hinc ait (quod nunc commemoravi) Salvator: Qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus; et qui audierint, vivent. Paulus quoque: Canet enim tuba, et mortui resurgent. Et ego respondebo tibi, id est, imperio tuo obediam, ad tuum placitum resurgendo. Operi manuum tuarum, id est mihi tuæ creaturæ, ceteris quoque hominibus operibus manuum tuarum, id est tuæ scientiæ practicæ et operativæ potentiæ, porriges dexteram, id est auxilium et virtutem resurgendi: quia non naturali, sed divina virtute resurrectio fiet.
paras.en: [[14:15|Thou shalt call me|Vocabis me]], that is, thou wilt bid me be raised up and make me rise again, restoring the body from its ashes by the service of angels and reuniting my soul to the body. Hence the Saviour says (as I recalled just now): [[John 5:28|all that are in the graves shall hear the voice|Qui in monumentis sunt, audient vocem ejus]]; [[John 5:25|and they that hear shall live|et qui audierint, vivent]]. Paul also: [[1 Cor 15:52|for the trumpet shall sound and the dead shall rise again|Canet enim tuba, et mortui resurgent]]. [[14:15|and I will answer thee|Et ego respondebo tibi]], that is, I will obey thy command, rising at thy pleasure. [[14:15|to the work of thy hands|Operi manuum tuarum]], that is, to me thy creature, and to other men too, the works of thy hands, that is, of thy practical knowledge and working power, [[14:15|thou shalt reach out thy right hand|porriges dexteram]], that is, help and the power of rising again: for the resurrection will take place not by natural but by divine power.

paras.t: Tu quidem gressus, id est omnes actus, meos interiores et exteriores, quibus gradior vel ad miseriam, vel ad beatitudinem, dinumerasti, id est, diligenter attendisti, ut pro quolibet actu dignam rependas mercedem. Dinumeramus autem, quorum diligentiam quamdam habemus. Hinc paulo ante disseruit: Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti. Sed parce peccatis meis, sine quorum pia indulgentia nemo nostrum ad gaudia pertingit æterna. Unde patet, quod Job non intendit se omni a culpa excusare, sed a talibus vitiis, qualia sibi imposuerunt sui amici, puta enormibus, non autem a venialibus. Propterea addit: Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea, id est, in abscondito sapientiæ et scientiæ tuæ diligenter notasti, sicut quæ curantur, in sacco clauduntur ne amittantur. Hinc in Deuteronomio Dominus ait: Nonne hæc condita sunt apud me, et signata in thesauris meis? Sed curasti iniquitatem meam, id est, a vulneribus animæ meæ quibus læsa fuit peccatis, me per gratiam pie sanasti, et per pœnitentiam reformasti. Sic orat et Jeremias: Sana me, Domine, et sanabor; salvum me fac, et salvus ero. Et Psalmista: Sana me, Domine, quoniam conturbata sunt ossa mea. Quamvis ergo Deus peccata nostra diligenter observet, nihilo minus ad ignoscendum, durante hac via, est pronus. Per flagella quoque et pœnas curat cœlestis medicus culpas.
paras.en: [[14:16|Thou indeed|Tu quidem]] [[14:16|my steps|gressus]], that is, all my acts, inner and outer, by which I walk either toward misery or toward beatitude, [[14:16|hast numbered|dinumerasti]], that is, hast diligently attended to them, so that for every act thou mayest repay a fitting reward. Now we number the things of which we take a certain care. Hence a little before he said: [[Job 13:27|hast observed all my paths, and hast considered the steps of my feet|Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti]]. [[14:16|but spare my sins|Sed parce peccatis meis]], without whose loving pardon none of us reaches the joys of eternity. Whence it is plain that Job does not mean to excuse himself from all fault, but from such vices as his friends laid to his charge, namely enormous ones, and not from venial ones. Therefore he adds: [[14:17|Thou hast sealed up my offences as it were in a bag|Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea]], that is, thou hast diligently noted them in the hidden place of thy wisdom and knowledge, as things that are cared for are shut up in a bag lest they be lost. Hence in Deuteronomy the Lord says: [[Deut 32:34|Are not these things stored up with me, and sealed up in my treasures?|Nonne hæc condita sunt apud me, et signata in thesauris meis?]] [[14:17|but hast cured my iniquity|Sed curasti iniquitatem meam]], that is, thou hast lovingly healed me by grace of the wounds of my soul, by which it was hurt through sins, and hast restored me by penance. So too Jeremias prays: [[Jer 17:14|Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed: save me, and I shall be saved|Sana me, Domine, et sanabor; salvum me fac, et salvus ero]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 6:3|heal me, O Lord, for my bones are troubled|Sana me, Domine, quoniam conturbata sunt ossa mea]]. Though God, then, diligently watches our sins, he is none the less inclined to pardon while this way lasts [that is, while we are still wayfarers in this life]. By scourges and punishments too the heavenly physician cures faults.

paras.t: Deinde vitæ humanæ quotidianum monstrat defectum per quædam similia. Mons cadens defluit, id est, cadendo paulatim deficit. Omne enim generabile, corruptibile est. Ideo montes quamvis sint magni, tamen per causam naturalem et violentiam possunt deficere. Et saxum transfertur de loco suo, id est, lapides quamvis sint duri, tamen exciduntur, et ad alia loca portantur. Lapides excavant aquæ. Frequenti enim incidentia stillicidiorum perforantur, juxta illud: Gutta cavat lapidem, non vi, sed sæpe cadendo. Ad quam cavationem præcedentes guttæ disponunt, et quamdam perforationem inducunt, secundum Philosophum. Et alluvione, id est inundatione aquarum et consumptione riparum ex aquis, paulatim terra consumitur: unum enim elementum agit in aliud et ipsum corrumpit, quia contrarias habent inter se qualitates. Et homines ergo similiter perdes, id est, a vita hac abstrahes, et consumptione humidi radicalis a calido naturali deficere facies, quum homo naturaliter sit res mollior saxo, minorque montibus, et instabilior lapide, habens in se qualitates contrarias, in se invicem agentes, atque ab invicem patientes.
paras.en: Next he shows the daily failing of human life by certain likenesses. [[14:18|A mountain falling cometh to nought|Mons cadens defluit]], that is, by falling it gradually fails. For everything that can be generated can be corrupted. Therefore mountains, though they are great, can yet fail through a natural cause and through violence. [[14:18|and a rock is removed out of its place|Et saxum transfertur de loco suo]], that is, stones, though they are hard, are yet cut out and carried to other places. [[14:19|Waters wear away the stones|Lapides excavant aquæ]]. For they are pierced through by the frequent falling of drops, according to the saying [a proverbial verse]: “The drop hollows the stone, not by force, but by often falling.” For this hollowing the drops that go before prepare the way and bring about a certain piercing, according to the Philosopher [that is, Aristotle]. [[14:19|and with inundation|Et alluvione]], that is, by the flooding of waters and the eating away of the banks by the waters, [[14:19|the ground by little and little is washed away|paulatim terra consumitur]]: for one element acts on another and corrupts it, because they have contrary qualities between them. [[14:19|so in like manner thou shalt destroy man|Et homines ergo similiter perdes]], that is, thou wilt take them from this life, and make them fail by the consuming of the radical moisture by the natural heat [terms of medieval physiology: the vital moisture of the body and the innate heat that slowly spends it], since man is by nature a thing softer than a rock, smaller than the mountains and less stable than a stone, having in himself contrary qualities that act on one another and suffer from one another.

paras.t: Roborasti eum paululum, id est, dedisti ei virtutem subsistendi in vita hac ad modicum tempus: sicut jam dictum est, Breves dies hominis sunt. Complexio etenim hominis exigit brevem esse periodum vitæ humanæ. Ut in perpetuum pertransiret, id est, sic de vita ista per mortem abiret, quod nunquam ad hujus vitæ statum revertitur. Sicque ut, tenetur hic consecutive, non causaliter. Unde inferius dicit: Semitam per quam non revertar, ambulo. Præterea S. Thomas exponit hæc aliter, asserens beatum Job per hæc futuram resurrectionem probare ex comparatione hominis ad inferiora, quæ totaliter consumuntur absque spe reparationis, ut montes et lapides. Sicque quod ait, Homines ergo similiter perdes, interrogando et negando legendum est, quasi dicat: Non decet rationalem creaturam sic corrumpi absque spe reparationis seu resurrectionis, ut illa infima corrumpuntur. Sic quoque exponit quod ait, Roborasti eum paululum, ut in perpetuum pertransiret: id est, non decet, ut ita ad modicum tempus confirmaveris eum in tanta excellentia donorum naturæ, ut moriendo omnino desinat esse, nec unquam resuscitetur.
paras.en: [[14:20|Thou hast strengthened him for a little while|Roborasti eum paululum]], that is, thou hast given him the power of continuing in this life for a short time: as was said already, [[14:5|The days of man are short|Breves dies hominis sunt]]. For man's complexion [the balance of the humours in his body] requires that the span of human life be short. [[14:20|that he may pass away for ever|Ut in perpetuum pertransiret]], that is, that he may so depart from this life by death that he never returns to the state of this life. And so *that* is taken here of the consequence, not of the cause [that is, it says what follows, not what God intends]. Hence he says further on: [[Job 16:23|I am walking in a path by which I shall not return|Semitam per quam non revertar, ambulo]]. St Thomas, moreover, expounds these words otherwise, asserting that blessed Job here proves the resurrection to come by comparing man with lower things, which are wholly consumed without hope of restoration, as mountains and stones. And so his saying, [[14:19|so in like manner thou shalt destroy man|Homines ergo similiter perdes]], is to be read as a question expecting the answer no, as if to say: It is not fitting that a rational creature be so corrupted without hope of restoration or resurrection, as those lowest things are corrupted. So too he expounds the saying, [[14:20|Thou hast strengthened him for a little while, that he may pass away for ever|Roborasti eum paululum, ut in perpetuum pertransiret]]: that is, it is not fitting that thou shouldst have so strengthened him for a short time with so great an excellence of the gifts of nature, that by dying he should wholly cease to be and never be raised again.

paras.t: Immutabis faciem ejus: id est, in morte eam alteres et marcescere facies; in vita quoque variis modis alteratur atque disponitur, secundum varietates affectionum atque eventuum animæ, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem. Et iterum ait Scriptura: Cor hominis immutat faciem ejus; et de sermone bono lætificabitur. Et emittes eum, id est, de terra tolles per mortem: quemadmodum Jeremias dixit ad Hananiam, Ecce Dominus emittet te a facie terræ.
paras.en: [[14:20|thou shalt change his face|Immutabis faciem ejus]]: that is, in death thou wilt alter it and make it wither; in life too it is altered and disposed in various ways, according to the varieties of the soul's affections and of what befalls it, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 15:13|A glad heart maketh a cheerful countenance|Cor gaudens exhilarat faciem]]. And again Scripture says: [[Ecclus 13:31|The heart of a man changeth his countenance|Cor hominis immutat faciem ejus]]; and [[Prov 12:25|with a good word he shall be made glad|de sermone bono lætificabitur]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Denis joins Ecclus 13:31 and Prov 12:25]. [[14:20|and shalt send him away|Et emittes eum]], that is, thou wilt take him from the earth by death: as Jeremias said to Hananias: [[Jer 28:16|Behold I will send thee away from off the face of the earth|Ecce Dominus emittet te a facie terræ]] [Denis has “Behold, the Lord will send thee away …”; the margin gives Jer. xxviii].

paras.t: Sive nobiles fuerint filii ejus nobilitate sæculari atque carnali, sive ignobiles, non intelliget pater eorum post mortem. In quo etiam imperfectio hominis declaratur, quod post mortem nescit quid agant, aut quomodo se habeant filii ejus, nisi quantum fuerit ei revelatum, vel per species in anima remanentes, seu ex prævia cognitione in communi scire seu conjicere poterit. Quocirca scribit Gregorius: Sicut viventes ignorant quo loco mortuorum animæ habeantur, ita mortui vitam in carne viventium nesciunt, quomodo disponatur: quod tamen de animabus sanctis sentiendum non est, quæ quoniam intus omnipotentis Dei claritatem conspiciunt, nil foris exsistens ignorant. Denique verbo Job consonat illud Isaiæ, Abraham nescivit nos, et Israel ignoravit nos: quod de Abraham et Jacob accipitur pro tempore quo erant in limbo, et de naturali eorum notitia. Animæ vero mortuorum quæ in purgatorio sunt, per angelicam revelationem, et item per animas de sæculo hoc illuc advenientes aliqua noscunt. De hac re plenius scripsi super Isaiam, et alibi.
paras.en: [[14:21|Whether his children come to honour|Sive nobiles fuerint filii ejus]] by worldly and fleshly nobility, [[14:21|or dishonour|sive ignobiles]], [[14:21|he shall not understand|non intelliget]], that is, their father, after death. In this too man's imperfection is shown, that after death he does not know what his children are doing or how they fare, save so far as it has been revealed to him, or as he can know or guess in general by the species remaining in his soul [that is, the images and ideas kept from his life on earth] or from earlier knowledge. Wherefore Gregory writes: “As the living do not know in what place the souls of the dead are kept, so the dead do not know how the life of those living in the flesh is ordered: which, however, is not to be held of holy souls, for since they behold within the brightness of almighty God, they are ignorant of nothing that exists outside.” Moreover, with Job's word agrees that of Isaias: [[Is 63:16|Abraham hath not known us, and Israel hath been ignorant of us|Abraham nescivit nos, et Israel ignoravit nos]]: which is understood of Abraham and Jacob for the time when they were in limbo, and of their natural knowledge. But the souls of the dead who are in purgatory know some things through the revelation of angels, and also through souls arriving there from this world. I have written of this more fully on Isaias, and elsewhere.

paras.t: Et tamen caro ejus dum vivit, dolebit, id est, quamdiu animata est, variis subjacet corporalibus pœnis, spirituales quoque dolores animæ in corpus redundant; et anima ejus super semetipsam lugebit, id est, propriam calamitatem, angustiam, imperfectionem et culpam in vita hac deplorabit, si tamen sensata sit. Ex quibus omnibus miseria hominis innotescit, quodque beatitudo ipsius, vera et consummata non sit, nisi in Deo post vitam hanc.
paras.en: [[14:22|But yet his flesh, while he shall live, shall have pain|Et tamen caro ejus dum vivit, dolebit]], that is, as long as it is alive it is subject to various bodily pains, and the spiritual sorrows of the soul also overflow into the body; [[14:22|and his soul shall mourn over him|et anima ejus super semetipsam lugebit]] [Denis reads *super semetipsam*, “over itself”], that is, it will lament its own calamity, distress, imperfection and fault in this life, if it has understanding. From all which the misery of man is made known, and that his beatitude, true and consummate, is not to be found save in God after this life.

14.title: De moralitate ejusdem capituli quartidecimi.
14.title_en: On the moral sense of the same fourteenth chapter

paras.t: Lignum habet spem. Teste Gregorio, in Scripturis nomine ligni, aliquando crux designatur, ut quum in Jeremia impii dicunt de Christo: Mittamus lignum in panem ejus. Interdum, per lignum homo justus sive injustus exprimitur, ut quum per Ezechielem Dominus loquitur: Humiliavi lignum sublime, et exaltavi lignum humile: quandoque per lignum, incarnata Patris Sapientia figuratur, Salomone de ea dicente, Lignum vitæ est omnibus apprehendentibus eam. Itaque hoc loco dum lignum homini præfertur, nomine ligni homo justus significatur. Per hominem autem, homo carnalis notatur, eo modo, quo ait Apostolus: Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne homines estis?
paras.en: [[14:7|A tree hath hope|Lignum habet spem]]. As Gregory witnesses, in the Scriptures the cross is sometimes signified by the name of *tree* [*lignum*, which means both “tree” and “wood”], as when in Jeremias the wicked say of Christ: [[Jer 11:19|Let us put wood on his bread|Mittamus lignum in panem ejus]]. At other times the just or the unjust man is expressed by a tree, as when the Lord speaks through Ezechiel: I [[Ezech 17:24|have brought down the high tree, and exalted the low tree|Humiliavi lignum sublime, et exaltavi lignum humile]]: and sometimes the incarnate Wisdom of the Father is figured by a tree, Solomon saying of her: She is [[Prov 3:18|a tree of life to them that lay hold on her|Lignum vitæ est omnibus apprehendentibus eam]]. And so in this place, where the tree is preferred to man, the just man is signified by the name of *tree*. By *man*, on the other hand, the carnal man is denoted, in the way in which the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio]], [[1 Cor 3:4|are you not men?|nonne homines estis?]] [Denis joins the words of 1 Cor 3:4 to 3:3, where the Vulgate has “are you not carnal?”]

paras.t: Itaque Lignum, id est vir justus, habet spem retributionis æternæ felicitatis. Si præcisum fuerit, id est, pro fide seu justitia occiditur, rursum virescit in patria, luce gloriæ immarcescibiliter hilariterque perfusus; et rami ejus, id est imitatores ejus ex ipso spiritualiter prodeuntes, pullulant, id est, virtuosis insistunt operibus, ejus exemplo accensi, juxta Apostolum: In omni opere bono fructificantes.
paras.en: So then the [[14:7|tree|Lignum]], that is, the just man, [[14:7|hath hope|habet spem]] of the reward of eternal happiness: [[14:7|if it be cut|Si præcisum fuerit]], that is, if he is slain for the faith or for justice, [[14:7|it growth green again|rursum virescit]] in the fatherland, suffused unfadingly and joyfully with the light of glory; [[14:7|and the boughs thereof|et rami ejus]], that is, his imitators, who spring from him spiritually, [[14:7|sprout|pullulant]], that is, they apply themselves to virtuous works, kindled by his example, according to the Apostle: [[Col 1:10|being fruitful in every good work|In omni opere bono fructificantes]].

paras.t: Si senuerit in terra radix ejus, id est, virtus qua alios spiritualiter generare consuevit, in hujus peregrinationis exsilio aliquando (Deo permittente) peccati vetustatem incurrerit; et in pulvere, id est terrenis infimisque affectibus, emortuus morte peccati fuerit truncus, id est corpus illius. Quod fit, quando membra exhibentur arma iniquitatis peccato; peccatorum autem carnalium est corpus præcipue instrumentum atque subjectum, saltem quoad materiale hujusmodi vitiorum.
paras.en: [[14:8|If its roots be old in the earth|Si senuerit in terra radix ejus]], that is, if the power by which he was wont to beget others spiritually should at some time, in the exile of this pilgrimage (God permitting it), fall into the oldness of sin; and [[14:8|its stock|truncus]], that is, his body, [[14:8|be dead|emortuus]] with the death of sin [[14:8|in the dust|in pulvere]], that is, in earthly and base affections. This happens when the members are yielded [[Rom 6:13|as instruments of iniquity unto sin|arma iniquitatis peccato]]; for the body is chiefly the instrument and subject of carnal sins, at least as to what is material in vices of this kind.

paras.t: Ad odorem aquæ germinabit, id est, per irrigationem et infusionem donorum Spiritus Sancti, vivificabitur vita gratiæ et virtutum, et æquitati fructuosæ deserviet, et faciet comam, id est ornamentum bonarum cogitationum sanctarumque affectionum in capite animæ, puta in mente. De hujusmodi coma loquitur Sponsa, Sponsum describens: Comæ ejus sicut elatæ palmarum. Quasi quum primum plantatum est, id est, sicut in prima sua conversione ad Deum. Justus enim electus, ut ait Psalmista, quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam. Imo talis frequenter post casum cautior surgit, atque humilius vivit, propriam infirmitatem expertus et magis perpendens, aliis quoque magis compatiens.
paras.en: [[14:9|At the scent of water, it shall spring|Ad odorem aquæ germinabit]], that is, through the watering and infusion of the gifts of the Holy Ghost it shall be quickened with the life of grace and of the virtues, and shall serve fruitful justice; [[14:9|and bring forth leaves|et faciet comam]] [*comam*, literally “hair”, and so the foliage of a tree], that is, the adornment of good thoughts and holy affections on the head of the soul, namely in the mind. Of hair of this kind the Bride speaks, describing the Bridegroom: [[Cant 5:11|his locks as branches of palm trees|Comæ ejus sicut elatæ palmarum]]. It shall flourish [[14:9|as when it was first planted|Quasi quum primum plantatum est]], that is, as at his first conversion to God. For the just and elect man, as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 36:24|When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, for the Lord putteth his hand under him|quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam]]. Nay, such a one often rises more wary after a fall, and lives more humbly, having experienced his own weakness and weighing it the more, and having more compassion on others too.

paras.t: Homo vero carnalis, arbor infructuosa, aridum lignum, quum mortuus fuerit per peccatum mortale: de qua morte loquitur Christus, Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos; et nudatus vestimentis innocentiæ ac virtutum: de quibus ait in Apocalypsi Joannes, Beatus qui vigilat, et custodit vestimenta sua, ne ambulet nudus; atque consumptus pœnalitatibus culpam sequentibus, omnique esse gratiæ gratum facientis privatus, sicque spiritualiter annihilatus, ita ut de eo dicat Apostolus: Qui se putat aliquid esse quum nihil sit. Siquidem peccatum nihil est, et nihil fit homo peccando. Ubi, quæso, est? quasi dicat: Infeliciter fluctuat, miserabiliter evagatur, quia in Creatore suo non quietatur, et ab eo qui vere est, aversus, in regione dissimilitudinis sub jugo peccati et dominatu diaboli, hinc inde jactatur, de iniquitate ad iniquitatem ruendo. Hinc Adæ post culpam divinitus dictum est: Adam, ubi es?
paras.en: [[14:10|But man|Homo vero]] who is carnal, an unfruitful tree, a dry wood, [[14:10|when he shall be dead|quum mortuus fuerit]] through mortal sin (of which death Christ speaks: [[Matt 8:22|let the dead bury their dead|Dimitte mortuos sepelire mortuos suos]]), [[14:10|and stripped|et nudatus]] of the garments of innocence and of the virtues (of which John says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 16:15|Blessed is he that watcheth and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked|Beatus qui vigilat, et custodit vestimenta sua, ne ambulet nudus]]), [[14:10|and consumed|atque consumptus]] by the penalties that follow on guilt, and deprived of all the being of sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God], and so spiritually brought to nothing, so that the Apostle may say of him: [[Gal 6:3|if any man think himself to be some thing, whereas he is nothing|Qui se putat aliquid esse quum nihil sit]]. For sin is nothing, and man becomes nothing by sinning. [[14:10|I pray you where is he?|Ubi, quæso, est?]] as though he said: He drifts unhappily, he strays about wretchedly, because he does not rest in his Creator; and, turned away from him who truly is, he is tossed this way and that in the region of unlikeness [Augustine’s phrase, *Confessions* VII, 10, for the state of the soul far from God], under the yoke of sin and the dominion of the devil, rushing from iniquity to iniquity. Hence after the fault it was said to Adam by God: Adam, [[Gen 3:9|Where art thou?|ubi es?]]

paras.t: Quomodo si recedant aquæ de mari, sic homo quum dormierit somno peccati. De quo loquitur Paulus: Surge qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis. Itemque: Tempus est nos jam de somno surgere. Hæc est dormitio vitiosa, cui pervigil mentis custodia, et actuale virtutum exercitium contrariantur. Quemadmodum enim somnus naturæ est ligatio sensuum et suspensio eorum ab actibus suis; sic somnus culpæ est virtuosæ actionis cessatio in commissione illiciti, vel omissione præcepti.
paras.en: [[14:11|As if the waters should depart out of the sea|Quomodo si recedant aquæ de mari]], [[14:12|So man when he is fallen asleep|sic homo quum dormierit]] with the sleep of sin. Of this Paul speaks: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]. And again: [[Rom 13:11|it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep|Tempus est nos jam de somno surgere]] [Denis has *tempus*, “time”, where the Vulgate has *hora*, “hour”]. This is the sleep of vice, to which the wakeful watch of the mind and the actual exercise of the virtues are opposed. For as the sleep of nature is a binding of the senses and their suspension from their acts, so the sleep of guilt is a ceasing from virtuous action, in committing what is forbidden or in omitting what is commanded.

paras.t: Non resurget per pœnitentiam a peccato: quod de reprobo induratoque homine dicitur. De quo Ecclesiasticus ait: Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum. Unde legitur in Psalmo: Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio: quod de judicio discretionis accipitur, quo homo inter bonum malumque judicans, et pretiosum a vili discernens, detestatur culpam quam incidit, per pœnitentiamque resurgit. De qua resurrectione ad Colossenses scriptum est: Si consurrexistis cum Christo, quæ sursum sunt quærite. Donec atteratur cælum, non evigilabit ad virtutum vigiliam. Quum enim homo in mortali decesserit, nunquam ad gratiam reducetur, sicut et cælum nunquam substantialiter destruetur.
paras.en: He [[14:12|shall not rise again|Non resurget]] by penance from sin: this is said of the reprobate and hardened man, of whom Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 3:29|the sinner will add sin to sin|Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum]]. Hence we read in the Psalm: [[Ps 1:5|Therefore the wicked shall not rise again in judgment|Ideo non resurgunt impii in judicio]] [the margin, as read, gives Ps. ix, 9; the words are Ps 1:5]: which is taken of the judgment of discernment, by which a man, judging between good and evil and discerning the precious from the vile, detests the fault into which he has fallen, and rises again by penance. Of this resurrection it is written to the Colossians: [[Col 3:1|if you be risen with Christ, seek the things that are above|Si consurrexistis cum Christo, quæ sursum sunt quærite]]. And [[14:12|till the heavens be broken, he shall not awake|Donec atteratur cælum, non evigilabit]] to the watch of the virtues. For when a man has died in mortal sin, he will never be brought back to grace, just as the heaven will never be destroyed in its substance.

paras.t: Quis mihi tribuat, ut in inferno protegas me et abscondas me, donec pertranseat furor tuus, et constituas mihi tempus in quo recorderis mei? Istud cum verbis sequentibus in Officio legitur defunctorum: quod prima facie non faciliter videtur posse exponi in persona animæ in purgatorio constitutæ. Quidam enim hæc verba ita intelligunt, quod tantus erit rigor et terror Christi in die judicii, quod animæ defunctorum mallent, durante judicio, in inferno abscondi, quam irati vultum Judicis intueri. Sed non videtur hoc generaliter stare posse. Animæ enim in purgatorio consistentes, sciunt se in die judicii nequaquam damnandas, imo interim vel saltem ante prolationem sententiæ omnino purgandas. Christus autem in die judicii electis non apparebit terribilis, maxime his qui de sua salvatione interim seu tunc certi sunt. Verumtamen, reprobis judex tam metuendus parebit, quod pœna inferni his pro tunc tolerabilior videretur.
paras.en: [[14:13|Who will grant me|Quis mihi tribuat]] [[14:13|that thou mayst protect me in hell, and hide me till thy wrath pass, and appoint me a time when thou wilt remember me?|ut in inferno protegas me et abscondas me, donec pertranseat furor tuus, et constituas mihi tempus in quo recorderis mei?]] This, with the words that follow, is read in the Office of the Dead; and at first sight it does not seem easy to explain it in the person of a soul placed in purgatory. For some understand these words thus: that so great will be the rigour and terror of Christ on the day of judgment that the souls of the dead would rather be hidden in hell while the judgment lasts than look upon the face of an angry Judge. But this does not seem able to stand generally. For the souls that are in purgatory know that on the day of judgment they will by no means be damned; nay, that in the meantime, or at least before the sentence is pronounced, they will be wholly purged. And Christ on the day of judgment will not appear terrible to the elect, above all to those who are certain of their salvation, whether in the meantime or then. To the reprobate, however, the Judge will appear so fearful that the pain of hell would seem to them, for that moment, more bearable.

paras.t: Nihilo minus ista de anima in purgatorio sita queunt intelligi. Infernus quippe quatuor modis accipitur, scilicet pro loco damnatorum: de quo ait Salvator, quod dives epulo sepultus est in inferno; et Psalmista: Eruisti animam meam ex inferno inferiori. Secundo, pro limbo patrum: sicque Christus ad infernum dicitur descendisse. Tertio, pro purgatorio: unde in Missa cantatur, Domine Jesu Christe, libera animas fidelium defunctorum de pœnis inferni. Quarto, pro limbo puerorum. Tanta autem est acerbitas suppliciorum purgatorii, quod animæ ibi detentæ, mallent esse in inferno, secundum quod sumitur pro limbo patrum et puerorum, ubi pœna sensus non fuit nec est, quam in purgatorii sensibilibus pœnis. Imo, in inferno damnatorum mallent esse, et ab ejus sensibilibus pœnis divinitus protegi, atque ibidem a purgatorii tormentis abscondi, donec pertransiret furor Dei, id est, tempus divinæ ultionis, quo in purgatorio affliguntur, seu affligendæ sunt, finiretur, et tunc Deus recordaretur earum, perducendo ipsas ad patriam.
paras.en: Nevertheless these words can be understood of the soul placed in purgatory. For *hell* [*infernus*, literally “the place below”] is taken in four ways: namely, for the place of the damned, of which the Saviour says that the rich glutton [[Luke 16:22|was buried in hell|sepultus est in inferno]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 85:13|thou hast delivered my soul out of the lower hell|Eruisti animam meam ex inferno inferiori]]. Secondly, for the limbo of the fathers: and so Christ is said to have descended into hell. Thirdly, for purgatory: whence it is sung in the Mass, Lord Jesus Christ, deliver the souls of the faithful departed from the pains of hell [from the Offertory of the Mass for the Dead]. Fourthly, for the limbo of children. Now so great is the bitterness of the torments of purgatory that the souls held there would rather be in hell, as it is taken for the limbo of the fathers and of children, where there neither was nor is any pain of sense [that is, torment felt, as distinct from the pain of loss, the lack of the sight of God], than in the pains of sense of purgatory. Nay, they would rather be in the hell of the damned, and be protected by God from its pains of sense, and there be hidden from the torments of purgatory, until the wrath of God should pass, that is, until the time of the divine vengeance, in which they are afflicted or are to be afflicted in purgatory, should be ended, and then God should remember them, bringing them to the fatherland.

paras.t: Itaque juxta hunc sensum loquitur anima purgatorio deputata: Quis mihi tribuat, id est, utinam mihi (o Deus) donetur, ut in inferno protegas me: secundum sensum prætactum. Denique etiam de inferno, id est purgatorio, potest exponi, ut sit sensus: In inferno protegas me, id est, in purgatorio isto quo crucior, mihi clementer obumbres, supplicia releves, a tam intensis doloribus me defendas. Et abscondas me, id est sub tua miseratione a tam districta punitione, donec pertranseat furor tuus, id est, quousque mihi prorsus ignoscas, et a pœnali loco ad felicitatem deducas, et constituas mihi tempus in quo recorderis mei, id est, horam miserendi, redimendi, beatificandique me, mihi ostendas, præfigas, acceleres: quia hoc relevamen est pœnæ, præcognitio termini ejus.
paras.en: So in this sense the soul consigned to purgatory speaks: [[14:13|Who will grant me|Quis mihi tribuat]], that is, O that it may be granted me (O God), [[14:13|that thou mayst protect me in hell|ut in inferno protegas me]], in the sense touched on above. Then again, it can also be explained of hell taken as purgatory, so that the sense is: [[14:13|thou mayst protect me in hell|In inferno protegas me]], that is, in this purgatory in which I am tormented, overshadow me mercifully, lighten my torments, defend me from pains so intense; [[14:13|and hide me|Et abscondas me]], that is, under thy mercy, from so strict a punishment, [[14:13|till thy wrath pass|donec pertranseat furor tuus]], that is, until thou forgive me altogether and lead me from the place of pain to happiness, [[14:13|and appoint me a time when thou wilt remember me?|et constituas mihi tempus in quo recorderis mei]] that is, show me, fix beforehand and hasten the hour of having mercy on me, redeeming me and making me blessed: for this is a relief of pain, to know its end beforehand.

paras.t: Putasne mortuus homo rursus vivat? Hoc anima loquitur, insinuans se optare sui corporis resuscitationem et resumptionem, ut simul cum illo glorificetur. Quasi dicat: Tu (o Deus) nosti, quod defuncti resurgent. Ergo ad beatam resurrectionem celeriter opto pertingere. Hinc subdit: Cunctis diebus quibus nunc milito, id est, contra pœnas quibus affligor, quodammodo pugno, quoniam naturali appetitu eas abhorreo atque refugio, quamvis ratio dictet quod ad satisfaciendum divinæ justitiæ sint patienter ferendæ; exspecto donec veniat immutatio mea, id est translatio a miseria ista pœnali ad gloriam, resurrectio quoque futura, quam vehementer affecto, in quantum erit pro felicitatis augmento.
paras.en: [[14:14|Shall man that is dead, thinkest thou, live again?|Putasne mortuus homo rursus vivat?]] The soul says this, hinting that she desires the raising up and taking back of her body, so as to be glorified together with it. As though she said: Thou (O God) knowest that the dead will rise again; therefore I long to come quickly to the blessed resurrection. Hence she adds: [[14:14|all the days in which I am now in warfare|Cunctis diebus quibus nunc milito]], that is, in a manner I fight against the pains by which I am afflicted, since by natural appetite I shrink from them and flee them, although reason tells me that they are to be borne patiently, to make satisfaction to the divine justice; [[14:14|I expect until my change come|exspecto donec veniat immutatio mea]], that is, the passage from this misery of punishment to glory, and also the resurrection to come, which I vehemently desire inasmuch as it will be for the increase of happiness.

paras.t: Vocabis me tempore a te præordinato a purgatorii pœna ad thronum cælestem, et in fine sæculi me corpori reuniri jubebis; et ego respondebo tibi, tuæ voluntati obediendo. Operi manuum tuarum porriges dexteram: quia tua omnipotenti virtute hæc fient; et nunc in purgatorio mihi (ut spero) manum porriges adjutricem, citra condignum puniendo, et per aliorum suffragia succurrendo, tempus et vehementiam punitionis meæ misericorditer minorando.
paras.en: [[14:15|Thou shalt call me|Vocabis me]], at the time foreordained by thee, from the pain of purgatory to the heavenly throne, and at the end of the world thou wilt bid me be reunited to my body; [[14:15|and I will answer thee|et ego respondebo tibi]], by obeying thy will; [[14:15|to the work of thy hands thou shalt reach out thy right hand|Operi manuum tuarum porriges dexteram]]: for these things will be done by thy almighty power; and now in purgatory thou wilt (as I hope) reach out to me a helping hand, punishing me short of what I deserve and succouring me through the suffrages of others [that is, the prayers, Masses and good works offered for the dead], mercifully lessening the time and the vehemence of my punishment.

paras.t: Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti: quod nunc experimentaliter scio, dum pro omni actu illicito quantumlibet modico, non satisfactorie emendato, pœnam sustineo; sed parce peccatis meis, pœnam nunc mitigando. Nam quantum ad culpam, in vita ista dimissa sunt eorum peccata, qui in purgatorio statuuntur: qui etiam orant pro venia, secundum quod oratio est desiderii nuntius et interpres, non prout est meritoria impetrativaque indulgentiæ, quum se ipsos juvare non queant. Non enim sunt in statu merendi aut demerendi, quoniam status ille finitur in termino viæ præsentisque vitæ, puta in morte.
paras.en: [[14:16|Thou indeed hast numbered my steps|Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti]]: which I now know by experience, while for every unlawful act, however small, not amended by satisfaction, I suffer punishment; [[14:16|but spare my sins|sed parce peccatis meis]], by mitigating the punishment now. For as to the guilt, the sins of those who are placed in purgatory were forgiven in this life; and they also pray for pardon, in so far as prayer is the messenger and interpreter of desire, not as it is meritorious and obtains indulgence, since they cannot help themselves. For they are not in the state of meriting or demeriting, since that state ends at the end of the way and of the present life, that is, at death.

paras.t: Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea. Pensandum ac formidandum hoc nobis est, quod scilicet Deus omnia nostra peccata tam diligenter conservat, signat, atque commemorat, ut tempore suo nobis ea objiciat, nisi jam pœnitentiam veram egerimus. Hinc ait in Psalmo: Existimasti inique, quod ero tui similis? Arguam te, et statuam contra faciem tuam. Porro, pœnitentibus pie indulget. Propter quod additur, sed curasti iniquitatem meam. Varia namque sunt remedia contra peccata, et medicamina quibus curantur, quia et sacramenta novæ legis (secundum Hugonem) sunt vasa medicinalia gratiæ contentiva, vitiorumque curativa. Insuper, per opera satisfactionis, per adversa et lacrimas, vel potius per patientiam in adversis et internum dolorem de Dei offensa, curantur præsertim peccata.
paras.en: [[14:17|Thou hast sealed up my offences as it were in a bag|Signasti quasi in sacculo delicta mea]]. We must weigh and dread this: that God keeps, seals and records all our sins so carefully that in his own time he will lay them before us, unless we have first done true penance. Hence he says in the Psalm: [[Ps 49:21|Thou thoughtest unjustly that I should be like to thee: but I will reprove thee, and set before thy face|Existimasti inique, quod ero tui similis? Arguam te, et statuam contra faciem tuam]]. But to the penitent he mercifully grants pardon. For this reason it is added: [[14:17|but hast cured my iniquity|sed curasti iniquitatem meam]]. For there are various remedies against sins, and medicines by which they are cured; since the sacraments of the new law too (according to Hugh [of St Victor]) are medicinal vessels, containing grace and curing vices.
