Besides, sins are cured above all by works of satisfaction, by adversities and tears, or rather by patience in adversity and inward sorrow for having offended God.

paras.t: Mons cadens defluit, etc. Et hominem ergo similiter perdes? quasi dicat: Quamvis, o Deus, homo (quantum ad corpus corruptibile) inanimatis rebus sit similis, quantum ad corruptibilitatem, non tamen decet ut eum perire permittas per culpam, quem ad tuam imaginem similitudinemque creasti, sicut inanimata destruuntur seu pereunt per naturam.
paras.en: [[14:18|A mountain falling cometh to nought|Mons cadens defluit]], etc. And [[14:19|so in like manner thou shalt destroy man|Et hominem ergo similiter perdes]]? as though he said: Although, O God, man (as to his corruptible body) is like lifeless things in being corruptible, yet it is not fitting that thou shouldst let him perish through guilt, whom thou didst create to thy image and likeness, as lifeless things are destroyed or perish by nature.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Gregorium, Mons cadens defluit, et saxum transfertur de loco suo, dum hominem justum, qui est per sapientiam altus, et virtutibus firmus ac solidus, repentina et improvisa tentatio invadit et concutit et prosternit, ita ut non nisi post ruinam, tentationem suam perpendat. Lapides vero excavant aquæ, et alluvione paulatim terra consumitur, dum justus paulatim tentatione inficitur, et levibus motibus successive dejicitur, non tam nimietate, quam assiduitate tentationis, qua impugnatur. Exemplum primi, in adulterio David cum Bethsabee. Exemplum secundi, in Salomone, quoad incontinentiam ejus.
paras.en: Further, according to Gregory: [[14:18|A mountain falling cometh to nought|Mons cadens defluit]], [[14:18|and a rock is removed out of its place|et saxum transfertur de loco suo]], when a sudden and unforeseen temptation assails the just man, who is high through wisdom and firm and solid in the virtues, and shakes him and lays him low, so that he does not weigh his temptation until after his fall. [[14:19|Waters wear away the stones|Lapides vero excavant aquæ]], [[14:19|and with inundation the ground by little and little is washed away|et alluvione paulatim terra consumitur]], when the just man is tainted little by little by temptation and is cast down step by step by slight movements, not so much by the excess of the temptation that assails him as by its persistence. An example of the first is in the adultery of David with Bethsabee[[2 Kings 11:4||]] [the margin here is hard to read (“li t”); the story is told in 2 Kings 11]; an example of the second, in Solomon, as to his incontinence.

paras.t: Roborasti eum paululum, donis gratiæ in præsenti, ut in perpetuum pertransiret, id est de vita hac ad perpetuam cælestis paradisi mansionem, atque ad dona gloriæ æternaliter perveniret. Parva autem sunt omnia vitæ præsentis, comparatione beatitudinis sempiternæ.
paras.en: [[14:20|Thou hast strengthened him for a little while|Roborasti eum paululum]] with the gifts of grace in the present, [[14:20|that he may pass away for ever|ut in perpetuum pertransiret]] [*transire*, “to pass away”, is also “to pass over”, and so Denis takes it], that is, from this life to the everlasting dwelling of the heavenly paradise, and come for ever to the gifts of glory. Now all the things of the present life are little in comparison with everlasting beatitude.

paras.t: Sive nobiles fuerint filii ejus, sive ignobiles, non intelliget. Hoc valet ad increpationem et informationem parentum carnalium, qui superflue pro filiorum nobilitatione, prosperitate, promotione sollicitantur et occupantur: qui quum venerint ad tormenta, nil sciunt de statu vitæ præsentis et consistentia filiorum suorum, nisi per modum præcedenti articulo scriptum. Imo, frequenter mortuorum parentum augentur supplicia ex vita carnali filiorum, quam adjutorio parentum suorum adepti sunt.
paras.en: [[14:21|Whether his children come to honour or dishonour, he shall not understand|Sive nobiles fuerint filii ejus, sive ignobiles, non intelliget]]. This serves to rebuke and instruct carnal parents, who are needlessly anxious and busy over the ennobling, prosperity and advancement of their children: for when they have come to their torments, they know nothing of the state of the present life and the condition of their children, except in the way described in the preceding article. Nay, the torments of dead parents are often increased by the carnal life of their children, which these obtained by their parents’ help.

15.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli quintidecimi: Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites, dixit.
15.title_en: Literal explanation of the fifteenth chapter: And Eliphaz the Themanite answered, and said

paras.t: Hic jam inchoatur secundus circulus disputationis inter amicos Job et ipsum beatum Job. Et ista eorum disputatio est replicatio quædam contra responsiones, quibus Job respondit primis illorum instantiis. In principio ergo hujus capituli, Eliphaz invective profatur adversum Job, quasi superbe, præsumptuose, jactanter, et iracunde seu impatienter locutus sit. Præterea, secundum quosdam, amici Job non posuerunt homini vitam aliam quam præsentem, ita quod animam rationalem dixerunt mortalem; et secundum eos, Job disputat contra hoc. Sed, ut sæpius jam ostendi, illa non fuit opinio virorum illorum. Quod etiam conjici potest ex hoc, quod nullus eorum arguit contra verba Job, quibus asserit animæ immortalitatem et resurrectionem futuram: quod tamen (ni fallor) diligenter fecissent, si talis fuisset eorum opinio.
paras.en: Here now begins the second round of the disputation between Job's friends and blessed Job himself. And this disputation of theirs is a kind of rejoinder against the answers with which Job replied to their first arguments. At the beginning of this chapter, then, Eliphaz breaks out in invective against Job, as though he had spoken proudly, presumptuously, boastfully, and wrathfully or impatiently. Moreover, according to some, Job's friends allowed man no life other than the present one, so that they said the rational soul is mortal; and according to these, Job is disputing against this. But, as I have often shown already, that was not the opinion of those men. This can also be gathered from the fact that none of them argues against the words of Job in which he asserts the immortality of the soul and the resurrection to come: which (unless I am mistaken) they would have done diligently, had that been their opinion.

paras.t: Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites, dixit: Numquid sapiens respondebit quasi in ventum loquens? quasi dicat: Ad sapientem non pertinet inaniter loqui, et jactanter atque inutiliter respondere aut fari non ad veritatem et rem, sed solum ad aerem, loquacitati superfluæ insistendo, ne victus aut indoctus putetur; imo sapientis est, verba sententiosa humiliter et modeste proferre, ordinateque loqui, et respondere succincte, multiloquia devitando. Hinc scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Verba sapientium statera ponderabuntur. Et rursus: In ore fatuorum cor illorum, et in corde sapientium os illorum. Fatui enim quidquid corde conceperint, mox proferunt ore. Sapientes vero os suum aperiunt secundum rectæ rationis censuram. Hinc quoque Proverbiis dicitur: Qui moderatur sermones suos, doctus et prudens est.
paras.en: [[15:1|And Eliphaz the Themanite, answered, and said|Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites, dixit]]: [[15:2|Will a wise man answer as if he were speaking in the wind|Numquid sapiens respondebit quasi in ventum loquens?]]? As if to say: It does not belong to a wise man to speak idly, and boastfully and uselessly to answer or to talk, not to the truth and the matter, but only to the air, keeping on in superfluous talkativeness lest he be thought beaten or unlearned; rather it is the part of a wise man to utter weighty words humbly and modestly, to speak in order, and to answer briefly, avoiding much speaking. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 21:28|the words of the wise shall be weighed in a balance|Verba sapientium statera ponderabuntur]] [the margin gives only Ecclus. xxi, 29, beside this and the next quotation; Denis has *sapientium*, of the wise, where the Vulgate has *prudentium*]. And again: [[Ecclus 21:29|The heart of fools is in their mouth: and the mouth of wise men is in their heart|In ore fatuorum cor illorum, et in corde sapientium os illorum]]. For fools at once bring forth with the mouth whatever they have conceived in the heart; but the wise open their mouth according to the judgement of right reason. Hence too it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 17:27|He that setteth bounds to his words, is knowing and wise|Qui moderatur sermones suos, doctus et prudens est]].

paras.t: Et implebit ardore, id est fervore et impetu iræ, indignationis seu impatientiæ, stomachum suum, id est animum suum vel mentem? quæ metaphorice stomachus appellatur. Nam sicut in stomacho cibaria digeruntur, sic meditationes quibus anima pascitur, in mente tractantur. Rursus, sicut ex stomacho ardore impleto fœtidus fumus eructatur, ita ex animo passionum ardore succenso, verba prodeunt vitiosa. Verumtamen ardor iræ, seu ira quæ fervor quidam est, subjective est in appetitu sensitivo, non in superiori animæ portione, nisi per consensum et affectum, in quantum mens passioni consentit, et ea obruitur. Ira autem per zelum, est in ratione seu mente, etiam per causam, quoniam ratio illam sponte assumit. Vult itaque dicere, quod sapientis non est, ira aut impatientia inflammari, quum scriptum sit: Ira in sinu stulti requiescit; et: Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere? Mansuetudo nempe et patientia sunt signa sapientis, juxta illud Jacobi: Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos? Ostendat operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ. In Proverbiis quoque scribitur: Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur prudentia; qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam. Et alibi Salomon ait: Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur; et gloria ejus est iniqua prætergredi. Sapientiæ quippe est, ordinare et irrationabiles motus compescere. His vero verbis Eliphaz arguit sanctum Job de elatione, inanique gloria et iracundia, quoniam aliqua dixit ad suam laudem et perfectionem spectantia, amicos quoque suos dure corripuit.
paras.en: [[15:2|and fill|Et implebit]] [[15:2|with burning heat|ardore]], that is, with the fervour and onrush of anger, indignation or impatience, [[15:2|his stomach|stomachum suum]], that is, his soul or mind? which is called the stomach by a metaphor. For as food is digested in the stomach, so the meditations on which the soul feeds are worked over in the mind. Again, as a foul smoke is belched up from a stomach filled with heat, so from a soul set on fire by the heat of the passions vicious words come forth. Yet the heat of anger, or the anger that is a kind of fervour, is in the sensitive appetite as in its subject, not in the higher part of the soul, except by consent and affection, in so far as the mind consents to the passion and is overwhelmed by it. But anger through zeal [that is, anger taken up by reason against evil, as distinct from anger as a passion] is in the reason or mind, and by its cause as well, since reason takes it up of its own will. He means, then, that it is not the part of a wise man to be inflamed with anger or impatience, since it is written: [[Eccles 7:10|anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|Ira in sinu stulti requiescit]]; and: [[Prov 18:14|a spirit that is easily angered, who can bear?|Spiritum ad irascendum facilem quis poterit sustinere?]] For meekness and patience are the signs of a wise man, according to that saying of James: [[Jas 3:13|Who is a wise man and endued with knowledge, among you?|Quis sapiens et disciplinatus inter vos?]] Let him shew [[Jas 3:13|his work in the meekness of wisdom|operationem suam in mansuetudine sapientiæ]]. In Proverbs too it is written: [[Prov 14:29|He that is patient, is governed with much wisdom: but he that is impatient, exalteth his folly|Qui patiens est, multa gubernatur prudentia; qui autem impatiens est, exaltat stultitiam suam]]. And elsewhere Solomon says: [[Prov 19:11|The learning of a man is known by patience: and his glory is to pass over wrongs|Doctrina viri per patientiam noscitur; et gloria ejus est iniqua prætergredi]]. For it belongs to wisdom to set in order and to restrain irrational motions. With these words Eliphaz accuses holy Job of self-exaltation, vainglory and wrath, because he said some things that tended to his own praise and perfection, and also rebuked his friends harshly.

paras.t: Arguis verbis eum, qui non est æqualis tibi, id est, verbis tuis præsumptuosis derogas Deo, ejusque judicium reprehendis, asserendo te absque tua culpa a Deo plagatum, qui major est te infinite. Hoc Eliphaz ait, quia Job superius dixit: Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar. Et multa similia dixit. Sed Eliphaz non recte intellexit sermones Job, nec originem unde processerunt, attendit. Sicut quum Job asseruit, Disputare cum Deo cupio, Eliphaz intellexit, quod vellet quasi discutiendo opera ejus et contentiose disputare cum ipso, quasi ambigeret, an justa essent Dei judicia. Et loqueris quod tibi non expedit. Minus dicit, et magis intendit. Tanquam dicat: Verba tuæ saluti contraria profers.
paras.en: [[15:3|Thou reprovest him by words, who is not equal to thee|Arguis verbis eum, qui non est æqualis tibi]], that is, by thy presumptuous words thou detractest from God and findest fault with his judgement, asserting that thou hast been struck without fault of thine by God, who is infinitely greater than thou. Eliphaz says this because Job said above: [[Job 13:18|If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just|Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar]]. And he said many like things. But Eliphaz did not rightly understand Job's words, nor did he attend to the source from which they came. Thus when Job declared, [[Job 13:3|I desire to reason with God|Disputare cum Deo cupio]], Eliphaz understood that he wished to dispute with him as it were by sifting his works, and contentiously, as though he doubted whether God's judgements were just. [[15:3|and thou speakest that which is not good for thee|Et loqueris quod tibi non expedit]]. He says less, and means more [that is, *not good for thee* understates it: he means that it does thee harm]. As if to say: Thou utterest words contrary to thy salvation.

paras.t: Quantum in te est, evacuasti timorem, id est, a timore Dei reverentiali ostendis te alienum ac nudum. Imo ostendis quantum in te est, Deum a nullo esse curandum, aut formidandum, dum tam irreverenter alloqueris eum, et faris de eo. Hinc superius Eliphaz loquitur ipsi Job: Ubi est timor tuus? Et tulisti, id est abstulisti, preces coram Deo, id est, per impietates tuas fecisti te indignum exaudiri ab eo; secundum illud Proverbiorum, Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis. Docuit enim iniquitas tua os tuum, id est, ex impia conversatione et interioris malitiæ abundantia didicisti tam impie loqui de Deo: prout asserit Christus, Malus homo ex malo thesauro cordis sui profert mala; itemque, Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur. Et imitaris linguas blasphemantium, id est, verba blasphemiam includentia profers, affirmans quod sine tuo demerito te Deus plagaverit. Hoc enim Eliphaz reputavit derogare divinæ justitiæ, et ex consequenti blasphemiam continere, præsertim quia Job dixit de Deo: Si flagellat, occidat semel, et non de pœnis innocentium rideat. Quod Eliphaz sic accepit, quasi Job insinuaret Deum esse crudelem, atque in punitione justorum ac perditione hominum gloriantem.
paras.en: [[15:4|As much as is in thee, thou hast made void fear|Quantum in te est, evacuasti timorem]], that is, thou showest thyself a stranger to the reverential fear of God, and bare of it. Nay, thou showest, as much as is in thee, that God is to be heeded or feared by no one, when thou addressest him and talkest of him so irreverently. Hence above Eliphaz says to Job himself: [[Job 4:6|Where is thy fear|Ubi est timor tuus]]? [[15:4|and hast taken away|Et tulisti]], that is, hast removed, [[15:4|prayers from before God|preces coram Deo]], that is, by thy impieties thou hast made thyself unworthy to be heard by him; according to that saying of Proverbs, [[Prov 28:9|He that turneth away his ears from hearing the law, his prayer shall be an abomination|Qui declinat aurem suam ne audiat legem, oratio ejus erit exsecrabilis]]. [[15:5|For thy iniquity hath taught thy mouth|Docuit enim iniquitas tua os tuum]], that is, from an impious way of life and the abundance of inward malice thou hast learnt to speak so impiously of God: as Christ declares, [[Matt 12:35|an evil man out of an evil treasure bringeth forth evil things|Malus homo ex malo thesauro cordis sui profert mala]] [Denis's *cordis sui*, of his heart, is the wording of Luke 6:45]; and again, [[Matt 12:34|out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh|Ex abundantia cordis os loquitur]]. [[15:5|and thou imitatest the tongue of blasphemers|Et imitaris linguas blasphemantium]] [Denis has *linguas*, tongues, in the plural], that is, thou utterest words that contain blasphemy, affirming that God has struck thee without any desert of thine. For Eliphaz reckoned that this detracted from God's justice and consequently contained blasphemy, especially because Job said of God: [[Job 9:23|If he scourge, let him kill at once, and not laugh at the pains of the innocent.|Si flagellat, occidat semel, et non de pœnis innocentium rideat]] [the margin's reference here is misprinted or misread; the passage is Job 9:23] Eliphaz took this as though Job were hinting that God is cruel, and glories in the punishment of the just and the ruin of men.

paras.t: Condemnabit te os tuum, et non ego: id est, tam vitiosa et impia tua sunt verba, ut ipsa te reprobatione damnationeque dignum monstrent ac statuant, nec opus est ut ego vel alter te condemnet; et labia tua respondebunt tibi, id est, verba labiorum tuorum per modum causæ meritoriæ, vicissitudinem tibi reddent, hoc est, causa erunt, quod pro tanto verborum excessu adhuc debite punieris. Sicque Dominus ait per Joelem: Cito velociter reddam vicissitudinem super caput vestrum. Vel, Labia tua respondebunt tibi, id est, materiam tibi respondendi præstabunt: juxta illud, Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam. Vel, Respondebunt tibi, id est, causam ejus quod quæris, videlicet causam tuæ flagellationis tibi ostendent, eo quod sua pravitate pandant te esse nimis culpabilem, ideoque percussum.
paras.en: [[15:6|Thy own mouth shall condemn thee, and not I|Condemnabit te os tuum, et non ego]]: that is, thy words are so vicious and impious that they themselves show and establish thee worthy of reprobation and damnation, and there is no need for me or anyone else to condemn thee; [[15:6|and thy own lips shall answer thee|et labia tua respondebunt tibi]], that is, the words of thy lips, by way of meritorious cause, will pay thee back in kind [Latin *vicissitudinem reddent*, will render a return, which is the sense he gives *answer*]: that is, they will be the cause why thou wilt yet be duly punished for so great an excess of words. And so the Lord says through Joel: [[Joel 3:4|I will very soon return you a recompense upon your own head|Cito velociter reddam vicissitudinem super caput vestrum]]. Or, [[15:6|thy own lips shall answer thee|Labia tua respondebunt tibi]], that is, they will furnish thee with matter for answering: according to that saying, [[Luke 19:22|Out of thy own mouth I judge thee, thou wicked servant|Ex ore tuo te judico, serve nequam]]. Or, [[15:6|shall answer thee|Respondebunt tibi]], that is, they will show thee the cause of what thou askest, namely the cause of thy scourging, in that by their wickedness they make plain that thou art exceedingly guilty, and therefore stricken.

paras.t: Consequenter per multa ostendit excellentiam Dei super Job, ad probandum quod non decuit ipsum Job tam audenter alloqui Deum, aut fari de eo, ita ut diceret, Disputare cum Deo cupio. Numquid primus homo tu natus es, et ante colles formatus? Numquid consilium Dei audisti, aut inferior te erit ejus sapientia? tanquam dicat: Tam superbe profaris, quasi primus et eminentissimus hominum esses, sicque competeret tibi pro toto genere humano disputare cum Deo, et quasi Dei consilio interfuisses, aut Deo in sapientia esses æqualis; quum tamen non sis hominum primus, nec Dei consilio interfuisti, sed ejus sapientia inferior es infinite. Unde Jeremias dicit: Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit, et audivit sermonem ejus?
paras.en: Next he shows by many things the excellence of God above Job, to prove that it did not become Job to address God, or to talk of him, so boldly as to say, [[Job 13:3|I desire to reason with God|Disputare cum Deo cupio]]. [[15:7|Art thou the first man that was born, or wast thou made before the hills?|Numquid primus homo tu natus es, et ante colles formatus?]] [[15:8|Hast thou heard God's counsel, and shall his wisdom be inferior to thee?|Numquid consilium Dei audisti, aut inferior te erit ejus sapientia?]] As if to say: Thou speakest as proudly as if thou wert the first and most eminent of men, so that it fell to thee to dispute with God on behalf of the whole human race, and as if thou hadst been present at God's counsel, or wert equal to God in wisdom; whereas thou art not the first of men, nor wert thou present at God's counsel, but art infinitely inferior to his wisdom. Hence Jeremias says: [[Jer 23:18|who hath stood in the counsel of the Lord, and hath seen and heard his word?|Quis adfuit in consilio Domini, et vidit, et audivit sermonem ejus?]]

paras.t: Denique consilium Dei, prout in ipso Deo est, nullus perfecte scire aut comprehendere valet: nihilo minus partim et aliqualiter hominibus innotescit dupliciter. Primo, per suos effectus, ut quum in re ipsa completum est, quod Deus suo decrevit se facturum consilio. Sicque per Jeremiam populo Judæorum testatur: In novissimis diebus intelligetis consilium meum. Secundo, per revelationem, qua divinitus revelatum est sanctis quibusdam hominibus, et per illos ceteris. Sic enim Christus secundum formam assumptam vocatur magni consilii Angelus, id est nuntius, qui divinæ sapientiæ secreta ac dispositionem circa hominum salvationem nuntiavit hominibus, sicut ait Apostolis: Quæcumque audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis. Paulus quoque loquens discipulis: Non subterfugi, inquit, quominus annuntiarem vobis omne consilium Dei. Hoc etiam modo beatus Job aliqua divini consilii mysteria per revelationem interiori auditu audivit magis, quam Eliphaz æstimavit. Quomodo autem consilium Deo conveniat, supra expositum est.
paras.en: Now the counsel of God, as it is in God himself, no one can perfectly know or comprehend: nevertheless it becomes known to men in part and in some measure, in two ways. First, by its effects, as when what God decreed by his counsel that he would do has been fulfilled in the event. And so he testifies to the people of the Jews through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:20|in the latter days you shall understand his counsel|In novissimis diebus intelligetis consilium meum]] [Denis has *consilium meum*, my counsel, for the Vulgate's *consilium ejus*]. Secondly, by revelation, by which it has been revealed from God to certain holy men, and through them to the rest. For so Christ, according to the form he assumed, is called the Angel of great counsel[[Is 9:6||]] [the Septuagint reading of Isaias 9:6, sung at the Christmas Mass, where the Vulgate has *Counsellor*; the margin notes here cannot be read], that is, the messenger who announced to men the secrets of the divine wisdom and its ordering for the salvation of men, as he says to the Apostles: [[John 15:15|all things, whatsoever I have heard of my Father, I have made known to you|Quæcumque audivi a Patre meo, nota feci vobis]]. Paul too, speaking to the disciples: [[Acts 20:27|I have not spread|Non subterfugi]] [that is, I have not shrunk], he says, [[Acts 20:27|to declare unto you all, the counsel of God|quominus annuntiarem vobis omne consilium Dei]]. In this way too blessed Job heard, by revelation with the inward hearing, more of the mysteries of the divine counsel than Eliphaz supposed. How counsel befits God has been explained above.

paras.t: Porro, quod ait, Numquid primus homo tu natus es? diligenter oportet advertere. Si enim de prioritate temporis sermo sit, primus homo non est proprie natus, sed Deo agente formatus. Si vero de prioritate dignitatis sit sermo, iste est sensus: Numquid primus, id est excellentissimus, homo tu natus es, ut sic te præferas ceteris?
paras.en: Further, what he says, [[15:7|Art thou the first man that was born|Numquid primus homo tu natus es]]? must be carefully noted. For if he is speaking of priority of time, the first man was not properly born, but formed by God's working. But if he is speaking of priority of dignity, this is the sense: [[15:7|Art thou the first|Numquid primus]], that is, the most excellent, [[15:7|man that was born|homo tu natus es]], that thou shouldst so set thyself before the rest?

paras.t: Quid nosti quod ignoremus? quid intelligis quod nesciamus? In hoc patet superbia Eliphaz. Job enim amicis suis illuminatior ac sapientior fuit, et rectius sensit de providentia Dei, quam illi. Denique, quod ait, Quid nosti? accipi potest de notitia humanorum, vel de notitia ex instructione aliorum, vel de notitia fidei; quod vero subjungit, Quid intelligis? de scientia divinorum, vel ex consideratione propria cognitorum, vel eorum quæ per naturalem rationem noscuntur.
paras.en: [[15:9|What knowest thou that we are ignorant of? what dost thou understand that we know not?|Quid nosti quod ignoremus? quid intelligis quod nesciamus]] In this the pride of Eliphaz is plain. For Job was more enlightened and wiser than his friends, and judged more rightly than they of the providence of God. Further, what he says, [[15:9|What knowest thou|Quid nosti]]? can be taken of the knowledge of human things, or of knowledge gained by the instruction of others, or of the knowledge of faith; and what he adds, [[15:9|what dost thou understand|Quid intelligis]]? of the knowledge of divine things, or of things known by one's own consideration, or of those that are known by natural reason.

paras.t: Et senes, morum probitate, seu mentis canitie, et antiqui, temporum longiturnitate, seu experimentorum acceptione, sunt in nobis, a quibus instructi, vel etiam propagati sumus, multo vetustiores quam patres tui, a quibus doctus et genitus es. Ideo plura quam tu scire valemus. Unde superius dictum est: In antiquis est sapientia, et in multo tempore prudentia. Talibus ergo cedendum, credendum, attendendumque est, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Non te prætereat narratio seniorum; et ipsi enim didicerunt a patribus suis: quoniam ab ipsis disces intellectum. Et alibi: In medio presbyterorum sapientium sta, et ex corde conjungere sapientiæ illorum.
paras.en: And [[15:10|aged|senes]] men, in uprightness of life or the grey hairs of the mind, [[15:10|and ancient men|et antiqui]], in length of years or the gathering of experience, [[15:10|are with us|sunt in nobis]], by whom we have been instructed, or even from whom we are descended, [[15:10|much elder than thy fathers|multo vetustiores quam patres tui]], by whom thou wast taught and begotten. Therefore we can know more than thou. Hence it was said above: [[Job 12:12|In the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days prudence.|In antiquis est sapientia, et in multo tempore prudentia]] Such men, then, are to be yielded to, believed and heeded, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 8:11|Let not the discourse of the ancients escape thee, for they have learned of their fathers|Non te prætereat narratio seniorum; et ipsi enim didicerunt a patribus suis]]: [[Ecclus 8:12|For of them thou shalt learn understanding|quoniam ab ipsis disces intellectum]]. And elsewhere: [[Ecclus 6:35|Stand in the multitude of ancients that are wise, and join thyself from thy heart to their wisdom|In medio presbyterorum sapientium sta, et ex corde conjungere sapientiæ illorum]] [Denis has *In medio*, in the midst, for the Vulgate's *In multitudine*].

paras.t: Numquid grande est, id est, magnum atque insolitum aut arduum Deo est, ut consoletur te Deus in tanta pœna ac desolatione? quasi dicat: Non utique, quum Deo velut consuetudinarium facillimumque consistat, afflictorum angustiam relevare, desolatorum mœstitiam mitigare, omnique pœnitenti et justo consolationem in adversis conferre: sicut ait Apostolus, Benedictus Deus, Pater misericordiarum, et Deus totius consolationis, qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra. Qui per Isaiam ait: Quomodo si cui mater blandiatur, ita et ego consolabor vos. Sed verba tua prava, quibus te exaltando, derogas Deo, hoc prohibent, id est, consolatione divina te indignum efficiunt. Peccata etenim nostra inter Deum et nos inducunt distantiam, impediuntque a nobis Dei consolationem et gratiam, sicut in persona peccatorum in Jeremia habetur: Iniquitates nostræ declinaverunt hæc, et peccata nostra prohibuerunt bonum a nobis.
paras.en: [[15:11|Is it a great matter|Numquid grande est]], that is, is it a great and unusual or hard thing for God, [[15:11|that God should comfort thee|ut consoletur te Deus]] in so great a punishment and desolation? As if to say: Certainly not, since it is for God a customary thing, as it were, and most easy, to relieve the anguish of the afflicted, to soften the sorrow of the desolate, and to bestow comfort in adversity on everyone who is penitent and just: as the Apostle says, [[2 Cor 1:3|Blessed be the God|Benedictus Deus]], [[2 Cor 1:3|the Father of mercies and the God of all comfort|Pater misericordiarum, et Deus totius consolationis]]: [[2 Cor 1:4|Who comforteth us in all our tribulation|qui consolatur nos in omni tribulatione nostra]]. It is he who says through Isaias: [[Is 66:13|As one whom the mother caresseth, so will I comfort you|Quomodo si cui mater blandiatur, ita et ego consolabor vos]]. [[15:11|but thy wicked words|Sed verba tua prava]], with which, by exalting thyself, thou detractest from God, [[15:11|hinder this|hoc prohibent]], that is, make thee unworthy of divine comfort. For our sins put a distance between God and us, and keep from us the comfort and grace of God, as is found in Jeremias in the person of sinners: [[Jer 5:25|Your iniquities have turned these things away, and your sins have withholden good things from you.|Iniquitates nostræ declinaverunt hæc, et peccata nostra prohibuerunt bonum a nobis]] [Denis has *nostræ*, *nostra*, our, where the Vulgate has *vestræ*, *vestra*, your]

paras.t: Quid te elevat cor tuum? id est, cur te supra proprium gradum et humanæ fragilitatis mensuram sic erigis? Superbia enim est velut tumor, atque erectio cordis cæca, inordinata et stulta, juxta illud Abdiæ: Superbia cordis tui extulit te. Et Isaias: Elevatæ sunt filiæ Sion, et ambulaverunt collo extento. Et quasi magna cogitans, id est mirabilia, divina et alta contemplans, attonitos, id est signum interioris superbiæ prætendentes foris in apertione et erectione, habes oculos. Nempe, qui talia sublimia intuetur, in stuporem adducitur, ab exterioribus quoque abstractus, oculos habet quasi pavefactos sive attonitos. Interior enim dispositio animæ, in exterioribus, præsertim in visu, cognoscitur ac relucet, juxta quod legitur in Ecclesiastico: Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus. Itaque Eliphaz intendit, quod Job ex superbia talem assumpsit oculorum qualificationem, qualem solent habere sapientes magnis contemplando intenti, quatenus ipse putaretur sublimia considerare. Et sic etiam notat eum hypocrisis.
paras.en: [[15:12|Why doth thy heart elevate thee|Quid te elevat cor tuum]]? that is, why dost thou so raise thyself above thy own rank and the measure of human frailty? For pride is like a swelling, and a blind, disordered and foolish lifting up of the heart, according to that saying of Abdias: [[Abd 1:3|The pride of thy heart hath lifted thee up|Superbia cordis tui extulit te]]. And Isaias: [[Is 3:16|the daughters of Sion are haughty, and have walked with stretched out necks|Elevatæ sunt filiæ Sion, et ambulaverunt collo extento]] [the Latin *elevatæ sunt*, are lifted up, echoes *elevat* in the verse; the Douay-Rheims has *are haughty*; the margin's reference is partly unreadable]. [[15:12|as if they were thinking great things?|Et quasi magna cogitans]] that is, contemplating wonderful, divine and lofty things, [[15:12|why dost thou stare|attonitos]] [Latin *attonitos*, thunderstruck, astonished], that is, showing outwardly a sign of inward pride in their opening wide and lifting up, [[15:12|with thy eyes|habes oculos]]. For he who gazes on such lofty things is brought into amazement, and, withdrawn also from outward things, has eyes as it were awestruck or staring. For the inward disposition of the soul is known and shines out in outward things, above all in the look, according to what is read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:26|A man is known by his look, and a wise man, when thou meetest him, is known by his countenance|Ex visu cognoscitur vir, et ab occursu faciei cognoscitur sensatus]]. So Eliphaz means that Job, out of pride, took on such a cast of the eyes as wise men are wont to have when intent on contemplating great things, so that he himself might be thought to be considering lofty things. And so he also charges him with hypocrisy.

paras.t: Quid tumet contra Deum, id est ad Dei contumeliam atque injuriam et contra ipsius justitiam, spiritus tuus? quia ita te laudas, ut divinam justitiam neges, et cum Deo quasi cum pari contendere seu disputare usurpas. Ideo addit, ut proferas de ore tuo hujusmodi sermones: quos nefas est mente tractare; concepti autem, sunt reprimendi, ne foris erumpant. Hinc eos sine pavore proferre, intolerandæ est arrogantiæ. Sic Eliphaz æstimavit Job reprehendendum, quia nimis se justificaverit, ut Eliphaz apparebat. Unde adjecit: Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit? id est, homo non est tam excellentis naturæ, ut inculpabiliter conversetur. Et justus appareat homo, qui natus est de muliere? propter quod fragilis est natura, præsertim in adolescentia pronus ad vitia, et debilis ratione, videlicet sapientia et virtutibus nondum perfecte armatus. Propter quod sine peccatis non vivit, sicut et Salomon loquitur: Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet. Sed, ut patet ex dictis, nec Job ista negavit, et Eliphaz cum ceteris condisputantibus, verba magis quam mentem Job multoties reprobarunt.
paras.en: [[15:13|Why doth|Quid]] [[15:13|swell against God|tumet contra Deum]], that is, to the insult and injury of God and against his justice, [[15:13|thy spirit|spiritus tuus]]? because thou praisest thyself so as to deny the divine justice, and presumest to contend or dispute with God as with an equal. Therefore he adds, [[15:13|to utter such words out of thy mouth?|ut proferas de ore tuo hujusmodi sermones]] words which it is wicked to turn over in the mind; and once conceived, they are to be held back, lest they break out. Hence to utter them without dread is a mark of intolerable arrogance. So Eliphaz judged that Job was to be rebuked, because he had justified himself too much, as it seemed to Eliphaz. Hence he added: [[15:14|What is man that he should be without spot|Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit]]? that is, man is not of so excellent a nature as to live without fault. [[15:14|and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just?|Et justus appareat homo, qui natus est de muliere?]] because nature is frail, prone to vices especially in youth, and weak in reason, that is, not yet perfectly armed with wisdom and virtues. For this reason he does not live without sins, as Solomon also says: [[Eccles 7:21|there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet]][[3 Kings 8:46||]] [Denis's wording is that of Eccles 7:21, without its *justus*, just; the margin gives 3 Kings 8:46 as well, from Solomon's prayer]. But, as is plain from what has been said, Job did not deny these things either[[Job 7:21||]][[Job 9:20||]], and Eliphaz with the others disputing with him many times condemned Job's words rather than his meaning.

paras.t: Ecce inter sanctos ejus: sive sint comprehensores, ut cives cœlestes; sive viatores, ut viri heroici, divini, perfecti; nemo, id est nullus, immutabilis. Quod dupliciter verum est. Primo, quoniam omnis creatura aliquam habet variabilitatem, imo et variationem: quia in Beatis etiam post resurrectionem erit successio apprehensionum circa quædam inferiora objecta, secundum Augustinum; corpora quoque hominum glorificata, erunt mobilia loco. Hinc (secundum Apostolum) solus Deus habet immortalitatem, id est omnimodam incommutabilitatem, secundum Augustini interpretationem. Secundo, quoniam omnis intellectualis creatura, etiam angelica, quia ex nihilo est, et distans a suo fine, secundum se accepta ac libera, naturaliter flecti potest sive in bonum, sive in malum. Confirmationem autem in bono sortitur per gratiam; obstinationem in malo per malitiam propriam. Hoc idem Eliphaz dixit supra: Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles, et in angelis suis reperit pravitatem: de quorum intelligentia plenius dictum est ibi. Et cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus, id est, nec cives nec orbes cœlorum mundi sunt comparatione Dei, qui infinitæ est puritatis, sicut comparatione ejus nemo bonus aut sapiens. In omni quoque creatura est aliquid potentialitatis, defectibilitatis ac indigentiæ: propter quod indiget indesinenter conservari a Deo. De hoc dictum sæpe atque diffuse.
paras.en: [[15:15|Behold among his saints|Ecce inter sanctos ejus]], whether they be comprehensors [that is, those who already possess God in glory], as the citizens of heaven, or wayfarers [that is, those still on the way in this life], as heroic, godly and perfect men, [[15:15|none|nemo]], that is, not one, [[15:15|is unchangeable|immutabilis]]. This is true in two ways. First, because every creature has some changeableness, nay even change: for in the Blessed, even after the resurrection, there will be a succession of apprehensions concerning certain lower objects, according to Augustine; and the glorified bodies of men will be movable in place. Hence (according to the Apostle) God [[1 Tim 6:16|only hath immortality|solus Deus habet immortalitatem]], that is, unchangeableness of every kind, according to Augustine's interpretation. Secondly, because every intellectual creature, even the angelic, since it is from nothing and distant from its end, taken in itself and being free, can by nature be bent either to good or to evil. It obtains confirmation in good through grace, and obstinacy in evil through its own malice. Eliphaz said this same thing above: [[Job 4:18|Behold, they that serve him are not steadfast, and in his angels he found wickedness|Ecce qui serviunt ei, non sunt stabiles, et in angelis suis reperit pravitatem]]: of the understanding of which more has been said there. [[15:15|and the heavens are not pure in his sight|Et cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus]], that is, neither the citizens nor the spheres of the heavens are pure in comparison with God, who is of infinite purity, just as in comparison with him no one is good or wise. In every creature too there is something of potentiality, of defectibility and of want: for which reason it needs to be preserved by God without ceasing. Of this much has been said, often and at length.

paras.t: Quanto magis abominabilis, per graviora peccata, et inutilis, per peccata minora, homo, qui bibit quasi aquam iniquitatem? id est, per consensum eam intra se trahit et glutit tam immoderate, abundanter et prompte, ut bibitur aqua: quæ cara non est, propter quod sine difficultate accipitur. Et per hominem hunc, intelligit ipsum Job: quem ex detestatione non exprimit, quemadmodum nec Judæi Jesum Christum coram Pilato, dicentes: Non hunc, sed Barabbam. Et iterum: Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram. Similiter infra Eliu ait: Quis est vir ut Job, qui bibit subsannationem quasi aquam? In his atque similibus considerare et imitari debemus persecutiones, derisiones et patientiam sancti Job, et ex levibus causis non instar canum ad impatientiam agitari.
paras.en: [[15:16|How much more is man abominable|Quanto magis abominabilis]], through graver sins, [[15:16|and unprofitable|et inutilis]], through lesser sins, [[15:16|who drinketh iniquity like water|homo, qui bibit quasi aquam iniquitatem]]? that is, by consent draws it into himself and gulps it down as immoderately, abundantly and readily as water is drunk, which is not dear, and so is taken without difficulty. And by this man he means Job himself, whom out of loathing he does not name, just as the Jews did not name Jesus Christ before Pilate, saying: [[John 18:40|Not this man, but Barabbas|Non hunc, sed Barabbam]]. And again: [[Luke 23:2|We have found this man perverting our nation|Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram]]. In like manner Eliu says below: [[Job 34:7|What man is there like Job, who drinketh up scorning like water?|Quis est vir ut Job, qui bibit subsannationem quasi aquam?]] In these and like things we ought to consider and imitate the persecutions, the mockeries and the patience of holy Job, and not, like dogs, be stirred to impatience for slight causes.

paras.t: Ostendam tibi veritatem et tuum errorem; audi me, ut decet reprehensibilem a correptore audire intente; quod vidi oculis mentis seu corporis, et ex rerum processu consideravi, narrabo tibi. Sapientes confitentur vera esse quæ dico, et veritatem in omnibus ipsi fatentur: juxta illud Proverbiorum, Labia justi erudiunt plurimos. Nam et Ecclesiasticus dicit: Sapientia absconsa et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque? Et non abscondunt patres suos, a quibus generati sive instructi sunt, sed eos allegant, laudant, cognitos faciunt: secundum illud Ecclesiastici, Sapientiam patrum narrant populi, et laudem eorum nuntiat ecclesia.
paras.en: [[15:17|I will shew thee|Ostendam tibi]] the truth and thy error; [[15:17|hear me|audi me]], as it befits one who deserves reproof to listen attentively to the one who corrects him; [[15:17|what I have seen|quod vidi]] with the eyes of the mind or of the body, and have considered from the course of events, [[15:17|I will tell thee|narrabo tibi]]. [[15:18|Wise men confess|Sapientes confitentur]] that what I say is true, and they themselves acknowledge the truth in all things: according to that saying of Proverbs, [[Prov 10:21|The lips of the just teach many|Labia justi erudiunt plurimos]]. For Ecclesiasticus too says: [[Ecclus 20:32|O Wisdom that is hid, and treasure that is not seen: what profit is there in them both?|Sapientia absconsa et thesaurus invisus, quæ utilitas in utrisque?]] [[15:18|and hide not their fathers|Et non abscondunt patres suos]], by whom they were begotten or instructed, but cite them, praise them and make them known: according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 44:15|Let the people shew forth their wisdom, and the church declare their praise|Sapientiam patrum narrant populi, et laudem eorum nuntiat ecclesia]] [Denis has *patrum*, of the fathers, for the Vulgate's *ipsorum*, their].

paras.t: Quibus solis data est terra, id est, terrenorum dominativa possessio solis sapientibus est collata: quoniam sic possident terram, quod non possidentur ab ea; utunturque sensibilibus rebus salubriter, referendo eas ad debitum finem. Porro insipientes ac impii possidentur a terra, et abutuntur terrenis, victi illorum inordinato amore, secundum quod in Sapientiæ libro fertur: Creaturæ factæ sunt in odium, et in tentationem animæ hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium. Hinc mitibus possessio terræ promittitur.
paras.en: [[15:19|To whom alone the earth was given|Quibus solis data est terra]], that is, the lordly possession of earthly things has been conferred on the wise alone: for they so possess the earth that they are not possessed by it; and they use the things of sense to their salvation, referring them to their due end. But the foolish and the wicked are possessed by the earth, and abuse earthly things, overcome by an inordinate love of them, according to what is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 14:11|the creatures of God are turned to an abomination, and a temptation to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the unwise|Creaturæ factæ sunt in odium, et in tentationem animæ hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium]]. Hence to the meek is promised the possession of the land[[Matt 5:4||]] [Latin *terra*, both the earth of this verse and the land of the Beatitude].

paras.t: Et non transibit alienus per eos, id est, insipientes et impii cum sapientibus sortem et societatem non obtinebunt, sicut inter electos reprobi non annumerabuntur. Alienus quoque a sapientia non transit per sapientes, id est per viam illorum, videlicet per divinorum observantiam præceptorum, juxta illud in Isaia: Via sancta vocabitur, et non transibit per eam alienus. Hinc in Ecclesiaste habetur: Vidi quod tantum præcederet sapientia stultitiam, quantum differt lux a tenebris. Quibus consonat illud ad Corinthios: Quæ societas luci ad tenebras? Quæ autem conventio Christi ad Belial? aut quæ pars fideli cum infideli?
paras.en: [[15:19|and no stranger hath passed among them|Et non transibit alienus per eos]], that is, the foolish and the wicked shall not obtain a lot and fellowship with the wise, just as the reprobate shall not be numbered among the elect. Again, the stranger to wisdom does not pass through the wise, that is, by their way, namely by the keeping of the divine commandments, according to that in Isaias: [[Is 35:8|it shall be called the holy way: the unclean shall not pass over it|Via sancta vocabitur, et non transibit per eam alienus]] [Denis reads *alienus*, "the stranger", where the Vulgate has *pollutus*, "the unclean"; the margin's reference is unreadable]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 2:13|I saw that wisdom excelled folly, as much as light differeth from darkness|Vidi quod tantum præcederet sapientia stultitiam, quantum differt lux a tenebris]]. With these agrees that to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 6:14|what fellowship hath light with darkness?|Quæ societas luci ad tenebras?]] [[2 Cor 6:15|And what concord hath Christ with Belial? Or what part hath the faithful with the unbeliever?|Quæ autem conventio Christi ad Belial? aut quæ pars fideli cum infideli?]]

paras.t: Cunctis diebus suis impius superbit, non omnibus diebus suæ vitæ, quia non ante usum rationis; sed cunctis diebus suæ impietatis. Quicumque in mortali peccato est, superbus censetur: quia divinis præceptis rebellis, et Deo non subditus. Sic fertur in Psalmo ad Deum: Superbia eorum qui te oderunt, ascendit semper. Præterea, electi aliquoties ad tempus errant atque superbiunt: imo interdum de speciali sibi data gratia seu bonis operibus extolluntur. Sed quia electi sunt, ante vitæ terminum ad humilitatem per pœnitentiam revertuntur. Et numerus annorum incertus est tyrannidis ejus, id est, quamdiu in vita manebit, et tyrannidem exercere sinetur, ignorat. Potestatem enim qua abutitur, habet a Deo, et nescit quando tolletur ab eo. Tyrannus autem (ut dicit Boetius, quem ad hoc allegat Albertus) est, qui regimen rei publicæ in nocumentum populi et utilitatem sui malitiose convertit. Unde ait Gregorius: Tyrannus proprie dicitur, qui in communi re publica non jure principatur. Verumtamen, tyrannus in Scripturis aliquando aliter sumitur, sicut in Daniele et Esther.
paras.en: [[15:20|The wicked man is proud all his days|Cunctis diebus suis impius superbit]]: not all the days of his life, since not before the use of reason, but all the days of his wickedness. Whoever is in mortal sin is reckoned proud, because he is rebellious against the divine commandments and not subject to God. So it is said to God in the Psalm: [[Ps 73:23|the pride of them that hate thee ascendeth continually|Superbia eorum qui te oderunt, ascendit semper]]. Moreover, the elect sometimes go astray for a time and are proud; indeed they are now and then puffed up over a special grace given them, or over their good works. But because they are elect, they return to humility through penance before the end of their life. [[15:20|and the number of the years of his tyranny|Et numerus annorum incertus est tyrannidis ejus]], that is, he does not know how long he will remain alive and be suffered to exercise tyranny. For the power that he abuses he has from God, and he does not know when it will be taken from him. Now a tyrant (as Boethius says, whom Albert cites on this point) is one who maliciously turns the government of the commonwealth to the harm of the people and to his own advantage. Hence Gregory says: He is properly called a tyrant who rules in the common commonwealth not by right. Nevertheless, *tyrant* is sometimes taken otherwise in the Scriptures, as in Daniel[[Dan 1:3||]] and Esther [there it means a prince or great man of the realm, as at Dan 3:2 and Esth 6:9; the margin's reading, "Dan. 13", is probably Dan. i, 3].

paras.t: Ex his generaliter dictis, descendit ad increpationem beati Job, qui supra frequenter asseruit se in angustiis et timore doloreque positum: in dolore, propter mala præsentia; in timore futurorum. Sonitus terroris semper in auribus illius, id est, ad quemlibet strepitum improvisum metuit sibi aliquid mali jam imminere: quia de nullo confidit, metuitque sic sibi ab aliis fieri, quomodo ipse eis fecit; et quum pax sit, id est, nemo sibi adversetur, ille insidias suspicatur. Quidquid enim contra proximos cogitat, hoc contra se a proximis excogitari formidat; et conscius sibi propriæ crudelitatis, veretur semper sibi instare quod meruit, sciens se dignum odio, non amore ex se, quamvis propter Deum amandus sit. Hinc in libro Sapientiæ dicitur: Quum sit timida nequitia, dat testimonium condemnata; semper enim præsumit sæva, perturbata conscientia. Et in Proverbiis: Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit. Siquidem conversatio virtuosa parit fiduciam, et fortitudinem tribuit cordi. Ideo Salomon protestatur: In timore Domini fiducia fortitudinis. Et de justo loquens Psalmista: Ab auditione, inquit, mala non timebit. Paratum cor ejus sperare in Domino. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Nil simplici corde felicius: quia quo innocentiam erga alios exhibet, nihil est quod ab aliis pati formidet. At contra mens prava semper in laboribus est: quia aut molitur mala quæ inferat, aut metuit ne hæc sibi ab aliis inferantur; et quia semper agit dolose, contra se agi metuit insidiose.
paras.en: From these things said in general, he comes down to rebuking blessed Job, who above often declared that he was set in straits, in fear and in sorrow: in sorrow because of present evils, in fear of those to come. [[15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus illius]], that is, at any sudden noise he fears that some evil is already hanging over him, because he trusts no one, and fears that others will do to him as he himself has done to them; [[15:21|and when there is peace|et quum pax sit]], that is, when no one opposes him, [[15:21|he|ille]] [[15:21|suspecteth treason|insidias suspicatur]]. For whatever he plots against his neighbours he dreads that his neighbours are plotting against him; and conscious of his own cruelty, he is ever afraid that what he has deserved is at hand, knowing that of himself he is worthy of hatred, not of love, though for God's sake he is to be loved. Hence it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 17:10|whereas wickedness is fearful, it beareth witness of its condemnation: for a troubled conscience always forecasteth grievous things|Quum sit timida nequitia, dat testimonium condemnata; semper enim præsumit sæva, perturbata conscientia]] [Denis reads *condemnata*, "being condemned", for the Vulgate's *condemnationis*]. And in Proverbs: [[Prov 28:1|The wicked man fleeth, when no man pursueth: but the just, bold as a lion, shall be without dread|Fugit impius nemine persequente; justus autem quasi leo confidens, absque terrore erit]]. For a virtuous way of life begets confidence and gives strength to the heart. Therefore Solomon declares: [[Prov 14:26|In the fear of the Lord is confidence of strength|In timore Domini fiducia fortitudinis]]. And the Psalmist, speaking of the just man, says: [[Ps 111:7|the evil hearing|Ab auditione]], he says, [[Ps 111:7|he shall not fear|mala non timebit]]. [[Ps 111:7|His heart is ready to hope in the Lord|Paratum cor ejus sperare in Domino]]. Hence Gregory says: Nothing is happier than a simple heart, for since it shows innocence towards others, there is nothing it fears to suffer from others. But on the contrary a depraved mind is always in toil, for either it is contriving evils to inflict, or it fears that these will be inflicted on it by others; and because it always acts deceitfully, it fears that others are acting treacherously against it.

paras.t: Non credit quod reverti possit de tenebris ad lucem, id est de adversitatibus atque periculis ad securitatem et pacem, quia de nullius ope et fidelitate confidit, circumspectans undique gladium, id est ex omni parte suspicans sibi gladium imminere hostilem: intelligendo per gladium, omne prælii instrumentum, sicut per panem intelligitur quilibet cibus. Unde subjungitur: Quum se moverit ad quærendum panem, id est, cibum sumere voluerit, novit quod paratus sit in manu ejus tenebrarum dies, id est hora mortis, quia et tunc metuit infici et veneno aut aliquo modo perire, secundum quod novit se meruisse: unde nec in domesticis suis confidit. Terrebit eum tribulatio, quam apprehendit sibi instare; et angustia, id est timor comprimens, vallabit eum, id est, circumdabit intus, sicut regem qui præparatur ad prælium vallat exercitus vel premit angustia. Nam metuit plurimum ne vincatur, aut a suis derelinquatur, seu proditus occidatur ab hostibus.
paras.en: [[15:22|He believeth not that he may return from darkness to light|Non credit quod reverti possit de tenebris ad lucem]], that is, from adversities and dangers to safety and peace, because he trusts in no one's help and faithfulness, [[15:22|looking round about for the sword on every side|circumspectans undique gladium]], that is, suspecting on every side that a hostile sword hangs over him: understanding by *sword* every instrument of battle, just as by *bread* any food is understood. Hence there follows: [[15:23|When he moveth himself to seek bread|Quum se moverit ad quærendum panem]], that is, when he would take food, [[15:23|he knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand|novit quod paratus sit in manu ejus tenebrarum dies]], that is, the hour of death, because then too he fears being poisoned or perishing in some other way, as he knows he has deserved: hence he does not trust even those of his own household. [[15:24|Tribulation shall terrify him|Terrebit eum tribulatio]], which he perceives to be hanging over him; [[15:24|and distress|et angustia]], that is, a crushing fear, [[15:24|shall surround him|vallabit eum]], that is, shall hem him in within, [[15:24|as a king that is prepared for the battle|sicut regem qui præparatur ad prælium]] is surrounded by an army or pressed by distress. For he greatly fears that he will be beaten, or forsaken by his own men, or betrayed and slain by his enemies.

paras.t: In omnibus his atque sequentibus Eliphaz notat, tangit et pungit beatum Job, quod scilicet ita pavidus fuit ex mala conscientia et præcedente superbia atque sævitia, ideoque desperaverit de cura suæ percussionis, et angustiatus sit undique.
paras.en: In all these words and those that follow, Eliphaz censures, touches and stings blessed Job: namely, that he was so fearful from an evil conscience and from the pride and cruelty that went before, and that therefore he despaired of the healing of his stroke and was in straits on every side.

paras.t: Tetendit enim adversus Deum manum suam, id est, actus suos exhibuit divinæ legi et voluntati contrarios: juxta illud Osee, Extendit manum suam cum illusoribus. Et contra Omnipotentem roboratus est, id est, potentia sibi data abusus est, ad illicita utens ea, atque ad operandum iniqua se variis modis armavit, fraude, ferro, insidiis, auxiliariis, consiliariis.
paras.en: [[15:25|For he hath stretched out his hand against God|Tetendit enim adversus Deum manum suam]], that is, he has shown forth acts contrary to the divine law and will: according to that of Osee, [[Osee 7:5|he stretched out his hand with scorners|Extendit manum suam cum illusoribus]]. [[15:25|and hath strengthened himself against the Almighty|Et contra Omnipotentem roboratus est]], that is, he has abused the power given him, using it for unlawful things, and has armed himself in various ways to work iniquity: with fraud, with the sword, with ambushes, with auxiliaries and with counsellors.

paras.t: Cucurrit, id est, ad impietates processit cum fervore peccandi, et sine obstaculo, adversus eum, id est contra Dei prohibitionem, erecto collo ex interiori pompa inflato, et pingui cervice armatus est, id est, crapulose se habuit, et carnalitate contra justitiam se munivit. Pinguedo autem ex abundantia humorum causatur. Tales quidam fuisse in Scripturis leguntur, ut Pharao, qui ait in Exodo: Quis est Dominus, ut dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam. Sennacherib quoque rex Assyriorum, qui (ut in quarto Regum libro et in Isaia legitur) scripsit ad Ezechiam: Non te decipiat Deus tuus, quia non poterit te liberare de manu hac. Denique Daniel loquitur Balthasar regi: Adversus Dominatorem cæli elevatus es, et Deum qui habet flatum tuum in manu sua, non glorificasti. Sed et secundo Machabæorum fertur: Nicanor extendens manum ad templum, juravit: Nisi Judam vinctum mihi tradideritis, istud Dei fanum in planitiem deducam. Et sequenti ibi capitulo interrogavit, si est potens in cælo, qui jussit agi diem sabbatorum. Et respondentibus Judæis, Est, ille ait: Et ego potens sum super terram, qui impero sumi arma. Ecce quomodo mentem excæcat superbia.
paras.en: [[15:26|He hath run|Cucurrit]], that is, he has gone forward into impieties with the heat of sinning, and without hindrance, [[15:26|against him|adversus eum]], that is, against God's prohibition, [[15:26|with his neck raised up|erecto collo]], puffed up with inward pomp, [[15:26|and is armed with a fat neck|et pingui cervice armatus est]], that is, he has behaved with surfeiting [*crapulose*, as one gorged with food and drink], and has fortified himself with carnality against justice. Fatness is caused by an abundance of humours. Some such men are read of in the Scriptures, like Pharao, who says in Exodus: [[Ex 5:2|Who is the Lord|Quis est Dominus]], that I should [[Ex 5:2|let Israel go? I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go|dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam]]. Sennacherib too, king of the Assyrians, who (as is read in the fourth book of Kings and in Isaias[[Is 37:10||]]) wrote to Ezechias: [[4 Kings 19:10|Let not thy God deceive thee|Non te decipiat Deus tuus]], for he will not be able to deliver thee from this hand [the margin gives 4 Kings 19:10; Denis's *decipiat* is the wording of Is 37:10, and the second half is a loose rendering of 4 Kings 18:29]. And then Daniel says to King Balthasar: Thou [[Dan 5:23|hast lifted thyself up against the Lord of heaven|Adversus Dominatorem cæli elevatus es]], and [[Dan 5:23|the God who hath thy breath in his hand|Deum qui habet flatum tuum in manu sua]] [[Dan 5:23|thou hast not glorified|non glorificasti]]. And in the second of Machabees it is told that Nicanor, stretching out [[2 Mach 14:32|his hand to the temple|manum ad templum]], [[2 Mach 14:33|swore, saying: Unless you deliver Judas prisoner to me, I will lay this temple of God even with the ground|juravit: Nisi Judam vinctum mihi tradideritis, istud Dei fanum in planitiem deducam]]. And in the next chapter there he [[2 Mach 15:3|asked, if there were a mighty One in heaven, that had commanded the sabbath day to be kept|interrogavit, si est potens in cælo, qui jussit agi diem sabbatorum]]. And when the Jews answered, There is,[[2 Mach 15:4||]] he said: [[2 Mach 15:5|And I am mighty upon the earth, and I command to take arms|Et ego potens sum super terram, qui impero sumi arma]]. See how pride blinds the mind.

paras.t: Operuit, id est, vitiosa caligine texit, faciem ejus, id est oculum mentis seu intellectualem notitiam, pinguedo, id est carnalitas et opulentia rerum: quæ considerationem mentis obnubilant, et divinam illuminationem impediunt, juxta illud Isaiæ: Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere. Et a lateribus ejus arvina dependet, id est, collateralibus ejus similis carnalitas ex ipso adhæret. Frequenter etiam corporaliter sic contingit, quod facies principis superbi taliter impinguetur, et latera ejus arvina abundent: quemadmodum in Judicum libro legitur, Erat autem Eglon rex Moab crassus nimis. Et Agag rex Amalec, fertur fuisse pinguissimus.
paras.en: [[15:27|hath covered|Operuit]], that is, has veiled with a vicious darkness, [[15:27|his face|faciem ejus]], that is, the eye of the mind or its intellectual knowledge, [[15:27|Fatness|pinguedo]] [Denis reads *pinguedo* for the Vulgate's *crassitudo*; both mean fatness], that is, carnality and abundance of goods, which cloud the mind's consideration and hinder the divine illumination: according to that of Isaias: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge?|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam?]] [[Is 28:9|and whom shall he make to understand the hearing? them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]] [Denis adds *Dominus*, "the Lord", to the first question]. [[15:27|and the fat hangeth down on his sides|Et a lateribus ejus arvina dependet]], that is, a like carnality clings, from him, to those at his side. It often happens bodily too, that the face of a proud prince grows fat in this way and his sides abound with fat: as is read in the book of Judges, [[Judg 3:17|Now Eglon was exceeding fat|Erat autem Eglon rex Moab crassus nimis]]. And Agag king of Amalec is said to have been very fat[[1 Kings 15:32||]].

paras.t: Consequenter tangit adversa, quæ crudeli, superbo et opulento solent accidere. Interdum enim de loco suo expellitur: unde adjungit, Habitavit, postquam factus est fugitivus, in civitatibus desolatis et in domibus desertis, quæ pro parte in tumulos, id est acervos, sunt redactæ. Talia enim latibula secreta collapsa consueverunt quærere fugitivi, expulsi, inveniri timentes. Non ditabitur; quia aliorum bona amplius tollere non audebit, nec poterit: nec perseverabit substantia ejus, id est, opes suæ ab eo tollentur, ut sicut alios spoliavit, spolietur et ipse: juxta illud Isaiæ, Mittet Dominus in pinguibus tenuitatem. Nec mittet in terram radicem suam, id est, de cetero fecundus et fructuosus non erit, nec ad pristinam prosperitatem redibit: quomodo arbor extracta et iterum implantata, si in terram miserit radicem, denuo convalescit; quod si non fecerit, prorsus arescit. Hinc in Sapientis libro habetur: Adulterinæ plantationes non dabunt radices altas. Atque in Psalmo dicitur impio: Deus destruet te in finem; evellet te, et emigrabit te de tabernaculo tuo, et radicem tuam de terra viventium.
paras.en: Next he touches on the adversities that are wont to befall the cruel, the proud and the rich. For sometimes such a man is driven from his place: hence he adds, [[15:28|He hath dwelt|Habitavit]], after he became a fugitive, [[15:28|in desolate cities, and in desert houses|in civitatibus desolatis et in domibus desertis]], which in part [[15:28|are reduced|sunt redactæ]] [[15:28|into heaps|in tumulos]], that is, into piles of rubble. For fugitives and exiles who fear to be found are wont to seek out such hidden, ruined lurking-places. [[15:29|He shall not be enriched|Non ditabitur]], because he will not dare, nor be able, to take away the goods of others any more: [[15:29|neither shall his substance continue|nec perseverabit substantia ejus]], that is, his wealth shall be taken from him, so that as he despoiled others, he too may be despoiled: according to that of Isaias, The Lord [[Is 10:16|shall send leanness among his fat ones|Mittet Dominus in pinguibus tenuitatem]]. [[15:29|neither shall he push his root in the earth|Nec mittet in terram radicem suam]], that is, he shall no longer be fruitful and productive, nor return to his former prosperity: just as a tree pulled up and planted again revives if it puts its root into the ground, but if it does not, withers altogether. Hence it is said in the book of the Wise Man: [[Wis 4:3|bastard slips shall not take deep root|Adulterinæ plantationes non dabunt radices altas]] [Denis reads *adulterinæ plantationes*, "adulterous plantings", for the Vulgate's *spuria vitulamina*]. And in the Psalm it is said to the wicked man: [[Ps 51:7|God destroy thee for ever: he will pluck thee out, and remove thee from thy dwelling place: and thy root out of the land of the living|Deus destruet te in finem; evellet te, et emigrabit te de tabernaculo tuo, et radicem tuam de terra viventium]].

paras.t: Non recedet de tenebris adversitatis et pravitatis, sed in miseriis erit culpæ et pœnæ. Ramos ejus, id est sobolem, arefaciet flamma, id est gravis adversitas, seu rigorosum et consumens judicium Dei; et auferetur de vita, spiritu oris sui ab eo, id est per ablationem spiritus sui a corpore: juxta illud Psalmi, Exibit spiritus ejus, et revertetur in terram suam. Vel, Spiritu oris sui, id est propter animositatem sui cordis, quæ in verbis ore prolatis ostenditur. Non credet frustra, id est inaniter errore vanæ spei deceptus, quod aliquo pretio redimendus sit, id est alicujus subsidio de manu summi Judicis eruendus vel a præsenti miseria sublevandus; sed tanquam pravissimus et a suis spernetur. Sic ait Psalmista: Frater non redimit, redimet homo? Non dabit Deo placationem suam, et pretium redemptionis animæ suæ. In libro quoque Paralipomenon dicitur: Non est apud Dominum Deum nostrum iniquitas, nec personarum acceptio, nec acceptio munerum.
paras.en: [[15:30|He shall not depart out of darkness|Non recedet de tenebris]] of adversity and wickedness, but shall be in the miseries of guilt and of punishment. [[15:30|his branches|Ramos ejus]], that is, his offspring, [[15:30|the flame shall dry up|arefaciet flamma]], that is, grievous adversity, or the rigorous and consuming judgement of God; [[15:30|and he shall be taken away|et auferetur]] from life, [[15:30|by the breath of his own mouth|spiritu oris sui]] [being taken] from him, that is, by the taking away of his spirit from the body: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 145:4|His spirit shall go forth, and he shall return into his earth|Exibit spiritus ejus, et revertetur in terram suam]]. Or, *by the breath of his own mouth*, that is, because of the vehemence of his heart, which shows itself in the words uttered by his mouth. [[15:31|He shall not believe|Non credet]] [[15:31|vainly|frustra]], that is, idly, [[15:31|deceived|deceptus]] by the [[15:31|error|errore]] of a vain hope, [[15:31|that he may be redeemed with any price|quod aliquo pretio redimendus sit]], that is, that he is to be rescued by anyone's help from the hand of the supreme Judge, or relieved of his present misery; but as one most depraved he shall be despised even by his own. So says the Psalmist: [[Ps 48:8|No brother can redeem, nor shall man redeem|Frater non redimit, redimet homo?]] [[Ps 48:8|he shall not give to God his ransom|Non dabit Deo placationem suam]], [[Ps 48:9|Nor the price of the redemption of his soul|et pretium redemptionis animæ suæ]]. In the book of Paralipomenon too it is said: [[2 Par 19:7|there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, nor respect of persons, nor desire of gifts|Non est apud Dominum Deum nostrum iniquitas, nec personarum acceptio, nec acceptio munerum]] [Denis reads *acceptio munerum*, "taking of gifts", for the Vulgate's *cupido munerum*].

paras.t: Antequam impleantur dies ejus, peribit, id est, antequam naturalis periodus suæ ætatis compleatur, decedet seu morietur; et manus ejus arescent, id est, vis operativa et opera ejus cessabunt. Sic et in Proverbiis legitur: Quasi tempestas transiens, impius non erit. Ecclesiastes quoque: Non sit, inquit, bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus; sed quasi umbra transeant, qui non timent faciem Domini. Et in Psalmo: Viri sanguinum et dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos. Lædetur quasi vinea in primo flore suo, id est, sicut vinea læditur in primo suo flore, quando levi pruina excoquitur, et parvo ardore incenditur, ita lædetur botrus ejus, id est fructus seu opus iniqui, ita quod opera viva vita gratiæ non habebit, nec diu subsistet; et quasi oliva projiciens florem suum, id est cujus flos decidit, et in oleastrum degenerat, infructuosaque fit, ita et iste perit ac defluit.
paras.en: [[15:32|Before his days be full he shall perish|Antequam impleantur dies ejus, peribit]], that is, before the natural course of his age is completed he shall depart, or die; [[15:32|and his hands shall wither away|et manus ejus arescent]], that is, his power of working and his works shall cease. So too it is read in Proverbs: [[Prov 10:25|As a tempest that passeth, so the wicked shall be no more|Quasi tempestas transiens, impius non erit]]. Ecclesiastes too: [[Eccles 8:13|But let it not|Non sit]], he says, [[Eccles 8:13|be well with the wicked, neither let his days be prolonged, but as a shadow let them pass away that fear not the face of the Lord|bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus; sed quasi umbra transeant, qui non timent faciem Domini]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 54:24|Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days|Viri sanguinum et dolosi non dimidiabunt dies suos]]. [[15:33|He shall be blasted as a vine|Lædetur quasi vinea]] [[15:33|in the first flower|in primo flore suo]], that is, as a vine is blasted in its first flower, when it is scorched by a light frost and burnt by a little heat, so [[15:33|its grapes|botrus ejus]] [[15:33|shall be blasted|lædetur]], that is, the fruit or work of the wicked man, so that he will have no works living with the life of grace, nor will he last long; [[15:33|and as an olive tree that casteth its flower|et quasi oliva projiciens florem suum]], that is, whose flower falls, and which degenerates into a wild olive and becomes unfruitful, so he too perishes and wastes away.

paras.t: Congregatio enim hypocritæ sterilis, id est, res ab hypocrita collecta, fit infructuosa, quia habenti nociva, et aliquando ei aufertur. Ipsi quoque hypocritæ pariter congregati, a bonis sunt actibus steriles, et infructuosis arboribus similes; nec apud Deum sortiuntur mercedem, qui humanam cupiunt laudem, et simulatione se palliant. Et ignis devorabit tabernacula eorum, qui munera libenter accipiunt, id est avarorum qui amore donorum pervertunt judicium. Aliquando namque contingit, ut injuste adepta, per graves adversitatum molestias auferantur, et talium domus incendantur.
paras.en: [[15:34|For the congregation of the hypocrite is barren|Congregatio enim hypocritæ sterilis]], that is, what the hypocrite has gathered becomes unfruitful, because it is harmful to him who has it, and sometimes it is taken from him. The hypocrites themselves too, gathered together, are barren of good acts and like unfruitful trees; nor do they obtain a reward with God, since they desire the praise of men and cloak themselves with pretence. [[15:34|and fire shall devour their tabernacles, who love to take bribes|Et ignis devorabit tabernacula eorum, qui munera libenter accipiunt]], that is, of the avaricious, who for love of gifts pervert judgement. For it sometimes happens that things unjustly gained are taken away through the grievous troubles of adversity, and that the houses of such men are burnt.

paras.t: Sed nec istud, nec alia jam prædicta, universaliter accidunt secundum superficiem litteralem, quum impii sæpe usque ad ultimam perlingant ætatem, et usque ad mortem prosperitatibus jugiter potiantur, neque ab homine aliquo devastentur. Unde in istis spiritualis expositio subtilior, verior, generaliorque consistit. Verumtamen loquitur ista quasi ad litteram, quia in omnibus notat et pungit Job, quod scilicet ob suam avaritiam substantia ejus igne consumpta sit, et ipse adhuc satis recens usque ad mortem ob suam impietatem percussus sit, nec putet se aliquo pretio redimendum.
paras.en: But neither this nor the other things already foretold happen universally according to the surface of the letter, since the wicked often reach extreme old age and enjoy prosperity continually until death, and are not laid waste by any man. Hence in these things the spiritual exposition is the subtler, the truer and the more general. Yet he says these things as it were according to the letter, because in all of them he censures and stings Job: namely, that because of his avarice his substance was consumed by fire, and that he himself, while still fairly young, was struck even unto death because of his wickedness, and should not think that he can be redeemed with any price.

paras.t: Concepit dolorem, id est tristitiam de aliquorum prosperitate, et præcogitavit qualiter aliis noceat, doloremque inferat; et peperit iniquitatem, id est, impiam conceptionem opere adimplevit. Et uterus ejus, id est mens sua: quæ in Scripturis sæpe venter vocatur, ut quum ait Salvator, Flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ. Et in Psalmo: Ex utero ante luciferum genui te. Quemadmodum enim corporales conceptus fiunt in utero, sic spirituales in mente. Præparat dolos, id est, artes fallendi excogitat, atque inferre disponit: quod de hypocrita dicitur. Hypocritarum nempe est, non aperte, sed latenter ac fraudulenter aliis nocumentum inferre.
paras.en: [[15:35|He hath conceived sorrow|Concepit dolorem]], that is, sadness at the prosperity of others, and has thought out beforehand how he may harm others and bring sorrow on them; [[15:35|and hath brought forth iniquity|et peperit iniquitatem]], that is, he has fulfilled in deed his wicked conception. [[15:35|and his womb|Et uterus ejus]], that is, his mind, which in the Scriptures is often called the belly [*venter*], as when the Saviour says, [[John 7:38|Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|Flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 109:3|from the womb before the day star I begot thee|Ex utero ante luciferum genui te]]. For as bodily conceptions take place in the womb, so spiritual ones take place in the mind. [[15:35|prepareth deceits|Præparat dolos]], that is, he devises arts of deceiving and makes ready to bring them upon others: which is said of the hypocrite. For it belongs to hypocrites to bring harm on others not openly, but secretly and by fraud.

paras.t: Similiter ait Psalmista: Ecce parturivit injustitiam; concepit dolorem, et peperit iniquitatem. Lacum aperuit, et effodit eum. Et Jeremias: Habitatio tua in medio doli. In dolo renuerunt me scire, dicit Dominus. Postremo (secundum Gregorium) tanto semper majorem malitiam contra proximos in mente hypocrita concipit, quanto præ aliis videri innocentior quærit. Quod quam impium sit, Isaias sic aperit: Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt; ipse enim cogitationes concinnabit ad perdendos mites in sermone mendacii. Itemque in Psalmo: Linguis suis dolose agebant. Ubi mox subditur: Judica illos, Deus. Decidant a cogitationibus suis; secundum multitudinem impietatum eorum expelle eos, quoniam irritaverunt te, Domine. Hæc autem de hypocrita Eliphaz introduxit, ad insinuandum quod Job hypocrita fuit: ideoque congregata ab eo perierunt, et ipse plagatus hinc fuerit.
paras.en: Likewise the Psalmist says: [[Ps 7:15|Behold he hath been in labour with injustice: he hath conceived sorrow, and brought forth iniquity|Ecce parturivit injustitiam; concepit dolorem, et peperit iniquitatem]]. [[Ps 7:16|He hath opened a pit and dug it|Lacum aperuit, et effodit eum]]. And Jeremias: [[Jer 9:6|Thy habitation is in the midst of deceit: through deceit they have refused to know me, saith the Lord|Habitatio tua in medio doli. In dolo renuerunt me scire, dicit Dominus]]. Lastly (according to Gregory), the more the hypocrite seeks to appear more innocent than others, the greater the malice he always conceives in his mind against his neighbours. How wicked this is, Isaias shows thus: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful are most wicked: for he hath framed devices to destroy the meek, with lying words|Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt; ipse enim cogitationes concinnabit ad perdendos mites in sermone mendacii]]. And again in the Psalm: [[Ps 5:11|they dealt deceitfully with their tongues|Linguis suis dolose agebant]]. Where straightway there follows: [[Ps 5:11|judge them, O God. Let them fall from their devices: according to the multitude of their wickednesses cast them out: for they have provoked thee, O Lord|Judica illos, Deus. Decidant a cogitationibus suis; secundum multitudinem impietatum eorum expelle eos, quoniam irritaverunt te, Domine]]. Now Eliphaz brought in these things about the hypocrite to hint that Job was a hypocrite, and that therefore what he had gathered perished, and he himself was stricken for this reason.

15.title: De moralitate ejusdem capituli quintidecimi.
15.title_en: On the moral sense of the same fifteenth chapter

paras.t: Respondens autem Eliphaz, dixit: Numquid sapiens respondebit quasi in ventum loquens, et implebit ardore stomachum suum? Per Eliphaz designatur quispiam errans, proprio judicio sapiens, sed a veraciter sapiente diligenter correptus, et caritative instructus. Per Job autem intelligitur quicumque vir justus et sapiens, erroribus impiorum resistens, veraque docens. Quemadmodum ergo Eliphaz a Job digne correptus, reprobatus, instructus, non gratanter accepit, nec acquievit, sed invective locutus est, et duriora respondit; ita animosi et scioli, audaces et sibi placentes, a superioribus, melioribus aut sapientioribus amorose correpti, intumescunt, indignantur atque redarguunt, et correptoribus graviora imponunt: et quod ex caritate, æquitate, sapientia vel ira per zelum prolatum est, ex aversione, præsumptione, ira seu impatientia dictum causantur; indeque deteriorantur, unde debuerunt emendari. Tantam ergo abusionem, perversitatem, ingratitudinemque vitemus, et correpti ac informati cum patientia et gratiarum actione acquiescamus.
paras.en: [[15:1|And Eliphaz the Themanite, answered, and said|Respondens autem Eliphaz, dixit]]: [[15:2|Will a wise man answer as if he were speaking in the wind, and fill his stomach with burning heat?|Numquid sapiens respondebit quasi in ventum loquens, et implebit ardore stomachum suum?]] By Eliphaz is signified someone who errs, wise in his own judgment, but carefully reproved and charitably instructed by one who is truly wise. By Job is understood any just and wise man who resists the errors of the wicked and teaches what is true.
