As Eliphaz, then, when rightly reproved, rebuked and instructed by Job, did not take it gratefully nor acquiesce, but spoke in invective and answered more harshly; so the headstrong and the half-learned, the bold and the self-pleasing, when they are lovingly reproved by their superiors, their betters or those wiser than they, swell up, take offence and reprove in their turn, and lay heavier charges on those who correct them; and what was said out of charity, equity, wisdom, or anger moved by zeal [that is, the anger that serves zeal for what is right, not the sinful passion], they make out to have been said out of aversion, presumption, anger or impatience; and so they are made worse by the very thing by which they ought to have been amended. Let us therefore shun such abuse, perversity and ingratitude, and when we are reproved and taught, let us acquiesce with patience and thanksgiving.

paras.t: Denique verba amicorum Job, quamvis ab eis ad malum finem, videlicet ad reprobationem accusationemque Job ordinentur, et ei impie applicentur, nihilo minus in se frequenter sententiosa et profunda sunt. Sic quoque ea secundum se considerare debemus, et ex eis proficere. Unde et nunc ex verbis Eliphaz discamus non loqui in ventum et aerem, nec iracunde aut turbulenter. Scriptum est enim: Sapiens in verbis se ipsum amabilem facit. Et rursum: Responsio mollis frangit iram; sermo durus suscitat furorem. Itemque Ecclesiastes: Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus. Idcirco non decet sapientem cum turbulentia loqui. Propter quod Isaias de Christo prædixit: Non erit tristis neque turbulentus. Itaque verba ventosa et garrula devitemus, quum Ecclesiasticus dicat: Qui odit loquacitatem, exstinguit malitiam.
paras.en: Further, the words of Job's friends, although they direct them to an evil end, namely to the rebuke and accusation of Job, and apply them to him impiously, are nonetheless often weighty and profound in themselves. So we too ought to consider them in themselves, and profit by them. Hence let us learn now from the words of Eliphaz not to speak [[15:2|in the wind|in ventum]] and the air, nor wrathfully or turbulently. For it is written: [[Ecclus 20:13|A man wise in words shall make himself beloved|Sapiens in verbis se ipsum amabilem facit]]. And again: [[Prov 15:1|A mild answer breaketh wrath: but a harsh word stirreth up fury|Responsio mollis frangit iram; sermo durus suscitat furorem]] And Ecclesiastes likewise: [[Eccles 8:1|The wisdom of a man shineth in his countenance|Sapientia hominis lucet in vultu ejus]]. Therefore it does not become a wise man to speak with turbulence. For which reason Isaias foretold of Christ: [[Is 42:4|He shall not be sad, nor troublesome|Non erit tristis neque turbulentus]]. So let us shun windy and garrulous words, since Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 19:5|he that hateth babbling, extinguisheth evil|Qui odit loquacitatem, exstinguit malitiam]].

paras.t: Arguis verbis eum qui non est æqualis tibi. Hoc objiciendum est his, qui superiores suos irreverenter corripiunt, quum et seniores, quamvis non præsint, reverenter alloquendi sint, dicente Apostolo: Seniorem ne increpaveris, sed obsecra ut patrem. Et loqueris quod tibi non expedit. Quicumque alteri verba injuriosa, inordinata aut vindicatoria loquitur, sibi ipsi magis quam alteri nocet directe: imo se graviter lædit; et alter nisi propria impatientia aut simili culpa vincatur, nullum inde sustinet detrimentum, sed magis sortitur profectum. Denique, ad hoc ut homo non loquatur quod sibi non expedit, præcipua indiget gratia. Propter quod orat Psalmista: Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis meis. Ecclesiasticus quoque sic habet: Quis dabit ori meo custodiam, et super labia mea signaculum certum, ut non cadam ab ipsis, et lingua mea me perdat?
paras.en: [[15:3|Thou reprovest him by words, who is not equal to thee|Arguis verbis eum qui non est æqualis tibi]]. This is to be laid against those who irreverently reprove their superiors, since even elders, though they are not set over us, are to be addressed with reverence, as the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 5:1|An ancient man rebuke not, but entreat him as a father|Seniorem ne increpaveris, sed obsecra ut patrem]]. [[15:3|and thou speakest that which is not good for thee|Et loqueris quod tibi non expedit]]. Whoever speaks injurious, disordered or vindictive words to another does more direct harm to himself than to the other: indeed he wounds himself grievously; while the other, unless he is overcome by his own impatience or some like fault, suffers no loss from it, but rather gains profit. Further, for a man not to speak what is not good for him, he needs special grace. For which reason the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 140:3|Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth: and a door round about my lips|Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiæ labiis meis]] Ecclesiasticus too has this: [[Ecclus 22:33|Who will set a guard before my mouth, and a sure seal upon my lips, that I fall not by them, and that my tongue destroy me not?|Quis dabit ori meo custodiam, et super labia mea signaculum certum, ut non cadam ab ipsis, et lingua mea me perdat?]]

paras.t: Quantum in te est, evacuasti timorem. Quicumque audacter et absque timore libere peccat, et alios scandalizare non metuit, se ipsum a divino vacuum facit timore; alios quoque, quantum in ipso est, præbens eis peccandi audaciam: quod vehementer enorme est atque damnabile. Et tulisti preces coram Deo. Quicumque Deum verbis precatur, et impiis actibus eum offendere non veretur, indignum se facit exauditione divina. Qui ergo appetit exaudiri, studeat obedire, vitamque verbis conformare conetur, ut ei Deus per gratiam suffragetur. Maxime autem aufert preces coram Deo, seque inexaudibilem reddit, qui alicui odium tenet, seu alteri non ignoscit. Propter quod ait Salvator: Quum stabitis ad orandum, dimittite si quid habetis adversus aliquem: quod si non dimiseritis, nec Pater vester qui in cœlis est, dimittet vobis peccata vestra. In Ecclesiastico quoque consone scriptum est: Relinque proximo tuo nocenti te, et tunc deprecanti tibi peccata solventur. Homo homini servat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam? Quis exorabit pro delictis illius?
paras.en: [[15:4|As much as is in thee, thou hast made void fear|Quantum in te est, evacuasti timorem]]. Whoever sins boldly and freely without fear, and is not afraid to scandalize others, makes himself empty of the fear of God; and, as far as in him lies, he gives others too the boldness to sin: which is exceedingly monstrous and damnable. [[15:4|and hast taken away prayers from before God|Et tulisti preces coram Deo]]. Whoever prays to God in words and does not fear to offend him by impious deeds makes himself unworthy to be heard by God. Let him, then, who desires to be heard be zealous to obey, and strive to make his life agree with his words, that God may favour him by grace. But he above all takes away prayers from before God, and makes himself one who cannot be heard, who holds hatred against anyone or does not forgive another. For which reason the Saviour says: [[Mark 11:25|when you shall stand to pray, forgive, if you have aught against any man|Quum stabitis ad orandum, dimittite si quid habetis adversus aliquem]]: [[Mark 11:26|But if you will not forgive, neither will your father that is in heaven forgive you your sins|quod si non dimiseritis, nec Pater vester qui in cœlis est, dimittet vobis peccata vestra]]. In Ecclesiasticus too it is written in harmony with this: [[Ecclus 28:2|Forgive thy neighbour if he hath hurt thee: and then shall thy sins be forgiven to thee when thou prayest|Relinque proximo tuo nocenti te, et tunc deprecanti tibi peccata solventur]] [[Ecclus 28:3|Man to man reserveth anger, and doth he seek remedy of God?|Homo homini servat iram, et a Deo quærit medelam?]] [[Ecclus 28:5|who shall obtain pardon for his sins?|Quis exorabit pro delictis illius?]]

paras.t: Docuit enim iniquitas tua os tuum. Hoc competit his, qui ex industria et cum proposito mentiuntur, aut ex vitiosa vita absque formidine perversa loquuntur, quemadmodum de quibusdam asseritur: Acuerunt linguas suas sicut serpentes. Et imitaris linguas blasphemantium. Qui falsa sive sacrilega aut derogatoria manifeste de Deo profatur, evidenter blasphemat; qui vero talia profert, quæ implicite tale quid continent seu includunt, imitatur blasphemantium linguas. Condemnabit te os tuum, et non ego; et labia tua respondebunt tibi. Hoc dicendum est his, qui multum excessive loquuntur, quia et scriptum est: Ex verbis tuis damnaberis. Et Isaias inducit: Peccata nostra responderunt nobis. Quia videlicet peccando meremur ut detur nobis a divina justitia reale responsum, per hoc quod pro culpa infligitur proportionata ac persolutoria pœna.
paras.en: [[15:5|For thy iniquity hath taught thy mouth|Docuit enim iniquitas tua os tuum]]. This fits those who lie on purpose and by design, or who, out of a vicious life, speak perverse things without fear, as is said of certain men: [[Ps 139:4|They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent|Acuerunt linguas suas sicut serpentes]]. [[15:5|and thou imitatest the tongue of blasphemers|Et imitaris linguas blasphemantium]]. He who openly utters false, sacrilegious or disparaging things about God plainly blasphemes; but he who utters such things as implicitly contain or include something of the kind imitates the tongues of blasphemers. [[15:6|Thy own mouth shall condemn thee, and not I: and thy own lips shall answer thee|Condemnabit te os tuum, et non ego; et labia tua respondebunt tibi]]. This is to be said to those who speak very excessively, since it is also written: [[Matt 12:37|by thy words thou shalt be condemned|Ex verbis tuis damnaberis]]. And Isaias brings in: [[Is 59:12|our sins have testified against us|Peccata nostra responderunt nobis]] [the Latin is literally *our sins have answered us*, the word of this verse of Job: *thy own lips shall answer thee*]. That is to say, by sinning we deserve that a real answer be given us by divine justice, in that a punishment proportioned to the fault, and paying its debt, is inflicted for it.

paras.t: Insuper, si audierimus aliquem nimis præsumptuose loquentem, et de sua sapientia inanissime præsumentem, cum justa ironia ei dicere possumus quæ sequuntur. Numquid primus homo tu natus es, et ante colles formatus? Numquid consilium Dei audisti? Numquid grande est ut consoletur te Deus? Sed verba tua prava hoc prohibent. Itaque, si in adversis divinitus consolari optamus, omne illicitum verbum penitus devitemus, non murmuremus, sed Deo gratias referamus, ab ipso consolari petamus. Quod si fiducialiter atque constanter egerimus, abundanter exaudiemur, juxta quod legitur in Isaia: Ecce non est abbreviata manus Domini, ut salvare nequeat: neque aggravata est auris ejus, ut non exaudiat. Sed iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum et vos, et peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus a vobis.
paras.en: Moreover, if we hear someone speaking too presumptuously, and presuming most vainly on his own wisdom, we may with just irony say to him the words that follow: [[15:7|Art thou the first man that was born, or wast thou made before the hills?|Numquid primus homo tu natus es, et ante colles formatus?]] [[15:8|Hast thou heard God's counsel|Numquid consilium Dei audisti]]? [[15:11|Is it a great matter that God should comfort thee?|Numquid grande est ut consoletur te Deus?]] [[15:11|but thy wicked words hinder this|Sed verba tua prava hoc prohibent]]. So then, if we wish to be comforted by God in adversity, let us shun every unlawful word altogether; let us not murmur, but give thanks to God and ask to be comforted by him. If we do this trustfully and steadfastly, we shall be heard abundantly, according to what is read in Isaias: [[Is 59:1|Behold the hand of the Lord is not shortened that it cannot save, neither is his ear heavy that it cannot hear|Ecce non est abbreviata manus Domini, ut salvare nequeat: neque aggravata est auris ejus, ut non exaudiat]] [[Is 59:2|But your iniquities have divided between you and your God, and your sins have hid his face from you|Sed iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum et vos, et peccata vestra absconderunt faciem ejus a vobis]].

paras.t: Quid te elevat cor tuum? id est, ad quid et cur superbis, o homo, res fragilis utique, ad tui ipsius perditionem? Et quoniam propriam imperfectionem, periculositatem, culpam, innumerasque ærumnas non pensas (quæ omnia si rite perpenderes, te vilissimum et humana communione censeres indignum); ideo clamat Scriptura: Quid superbit terra et cinis? Et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos? Quidam tam superbi et vani sunt, ut si forte egerint quid boni, illud pandant, jactent, scirique cupiant: imo sæpe virtutes quibus non decorantur, sibi attribuunt, aut optant attribui, vel simulant. Insuper, ut contemplativi aut magnis intenti putentur, visum confingunt attonitum, qualem habent supernis intenti: quorum vultus et visus interdum sic variantur, ut a talium inexpertis, insensati sive amentes dicantur. Nam et Christus altissima prædicans, a suis discipulis furere putabatur, juxta illud Marci: Exierunt sui tenere eum. Dicebant enim: Quoniam in furorem versus est. Circa hæc scribit Gregorius: Sæpe justorum mens ita ad altiora contemplanda suspenditur, ut exterius eorum facies obstupuisse videatur. Sed quia contemplationis vim in occulto agere pravi ignorant, hoc a justis et sapientibus fieri magis per hypocrisim, quam per veritatem, existimant: quia quod ipsi habere nequeunt, inesse veraciter aliis non suspicantur.
paras.en: [[15:12|Why doth thy heart elevate thee|Quid te elevat cor tuum]]? that is, to what end and why art thou proud, O man, a frail thing indeed, to thy own ruin? And since thou dost not weigh thy own imperfection, thy peril, thy guilt and thy countless miseries (if thou didst weigh all these duly, thou wouldst judge thyself most vile and unworthy of the company of men), therefore Scripture cries out: [[Ecclus 10:9|Why is earth, and ashes proud?|Quid superbit terra et cinis?]] [[15:12|and why dost thou stare with thy eyes, as if they were thinking great things?|Et quasi magna cogitans, attonitos habes oculos?]] Some are so proud and vain that if perhaps they have done something good they make it known, boast of it and want it to be known: indeed they often attribute to themselves virtues with which they are not adorned, or wish them to be attributed to them, or feign them. Moreover, so as to be thought contemplatives or men intent on great things, they put on a rapt look such as those have who are intent on heavenly things; whose countenance and gaze sometimes so change that those who have no experience of such things call them senseless or out of their minds. For Christ too, when he preached the loftiest things, was thought by his own disciples to be mad, according to that passage of Mark: [[Mark 3:21|they went out to lay hold on him|Exierunt sui tenere eum]]. [[Mark 3:21|For they said: He is become mad|Dicebant enim: Quoniam in furorem versus est]]. On this Gregory writes: Often the mind of the just is so suspended in contemplating higher things that outwardly their face seems to be struck with amazement. But because the wicked do not know that the power of contemplation works in secret, they think that this is done by the just and wise through hypocrisy rather than in truth: for what they themselves cannot have, they do not suspect to be truly present in others.

paras.t: Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus, o superbe stultissime? quum Deus sit te in infinitum sublimior, perfectior atque potentior: a quo, quidquid habes et es, suscepisti; qui te cum corpore et anima potest projicere in infernum; qui tanta tibi bona impendit: cui profundissime subjici et vigilanter parere teneris. Itaque resipisce et imple illud principis Apostolorum: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei. Alioqui implebitur in te illud Isaiæ: Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum.
paras.en: [[15:13|Why doth thy spirit swell against God|Quid tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus]], O most foolish proud man? since God is infinitely higher, more perfect and more powerful than thou: from whom thou hast received whatever thou hast and art; who can cast thee body and soul into hell; who bestows so many good things on thee; to whom thou art bound to be most deeply subject and vigilantly obedient. Therefore come to thy senses and fulfil that saying of the prince of the Apostles: [[1 Pet 5:6|Be you humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God|Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei]]. Otherwise that saying of Isaias will be fulfilled in thee: [[Is 2:17|And the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be humbled|Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum]].

paras.t: Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere? Multis modis dicitur homo immaculatus in divinis Scripturis. Uno modo, quia nulli unquam peccato subjacuit, nec mortali, nec veniali, nec actuali, nec originali: quod competit homini Christo. Secundo, quoniam nunquam peccavit, nec venialiter, neque mortaliter, etiam habendo tempora discretionis: quod competit Virgini gloriosæ. Tertio, quoniam ab omni peccato purgatus est: quod tribuitur in Baptismo. Quarto, quoniam sine mortali peccato est, et de venialibus quotidie se custodit, pœnitet et emendat: quales esse debent potissime religiosi. Sicque ait Psalmista: Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini. Proportionabiliter dicitur homo variis modis justus. Sed verba ista prætendunt, quod homo purus, secundum communem legem, non vivat sine peccato, nec penitus justus sit, sed quotidie in multis deficiat ex infectione et fragilitate naturæ, et propter occupationes suas multiplices circa diversa, ita ut nec ipse universas et singulas suas culpas queat determinate advertere.
paras.en: [[15:14|What is man that he should be without spot, and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just?|Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere?]] Man is called *without spot* in many ways in the divine Scriptures. In one way, because he was never subject to any sin, neither mortal nor venial, neither actual nor original: which belongs to the man Christ. Secondly, because he never sinned, neither venially nor mortally, even when he had come to the years of discretion: which belongs to the glorious Virgin. Thirdly, because he has been cleansed of all sin: which is granted in Baptism. Fourthly, because he is without mortal sin, and daily guards himself against venial sins, repents of them and amends them: such as religious above all ought to be. And so the Psalmist says: [[Ps 118:1|Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord|Beati immaculati in via, qui ambulant in lege Domini]] [the Latin word is the same, *immaculati*, the undefiled or spotless]. In proportion, man is called *just* in various ways. But these words put forward that a mere man [*homo purus*, that is, one who is man only, as distinct from Christ], by the common law, does not live without sin, nor is wholly just, but daily fails in many things through the infection and frailty of nature, and on account of his many occupations about diverse things, so that he cannot even advert distinctly to each and every one of his faults.

paras.t: Ecce inter sanctos ejus nemo immutabilis, et cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus. Si angelicæ mentes et cœlestes substantiæ immutabiles non sunt, nec mundæ comparatione puritatis ac invariabilitatis divinæ naturæ: nos, qui sumus, qui reputemus nos mundos ac stabiles coram Deo? Præterea, solus Deus incomparabilis et immensus, sic mundus et sanctus est, ut nec privative, nec contrarie, nec contradictorie aliquid habeat non sanctitatis aut immunditiæ. Cetera omnia aliquo vel aliquibus horum modorum quidpiam non sanctitatis seu immunditiæ habent admixtum. Abominabilis homo. Ratione peccati fit creatura intellectualis (ad Dei imaginem nobiliter condita) penitus abomina[…] […] et melior Deus est, eo peccatum, quod est recessus a Deo, detestabilius viliusque […] consistit. Idcirco per ipsum fit creatura Creatori suo odibilis: nec aliquis in hac vita perfecte capere valet, quanta sit peccati enormitas; sed ex ejus effectu id scimus, pensando quod uno mortali peccato intellectualis creatura (naturaliter Deo amabilis) justo ejus judicio æternaliter relinquitur, oditur, damnatur, punitur, punitione utique ineffabiliter dira. Merito ergo deberemus amore superpræstantissimi Dei omnem culpam cum omni diligentia abhorrere, vitare, deflere; potiusque omnem perpeti pœnam, quam supergloriosissimum Deum per minimam inhonorare atque offendere culpam.
paras.en: [[15:15|Behold among his saints none is unchangeable, and the heavens are not pure in his sight|Ecce inter sanctos ejus nemo immutabilis, et cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus]]. If the angelic minds and the heavenly substances are not unchangeable, nor clean, in comparison with the purity and invariability of the divine nature, we, who are we, that we should reckon ourselves clean and stable before God? Moreover, God alone, incomparable and immense, is so clean and holy that he has nothing of unholiness or uncleanness, whether privatively, contrarily or contradictorily [that is, in none of the three ways in which a thing can be opposed to holiness: as its lack, as its contrary, or as its simple denial]. All other things have something of unholiness or uncleanness mixed in, in one or more of these ways. [[15:16|man abominable|Abominabilis homo]]. By reason of sin an intellectual creature (nobly made to the image of God) becomes utterly abomina[…] […] and better God is, so much the more detestable and vile is sin, which is a turning away from God, […] consists. Therefore through sin the creature becomes hateful to its Creator: nor can anyone in this life fully grasp how great is the enormity of sin; but we know it from its effect, considering that for one mortal sin an intellectual creature (by nature lovable to God) is by his just judgment eternally abandoned, hated, damned and punished, and with a punishment unspeakably dire. Rightly, then, should we, for love of the most surpassingly excellent God, abhor, shun and bewail every fault with all diligence, and rather suffer every pain than dishonour and offend the most supremely glorious God by the least fault.

paras.t: Sapientes confitentur. Si sapientes sapientiam suam et veritatem fatentur, cur in libro Proverbiorum scribitur, Sapientes abscondunt sapientiam? Et respondendum, quia (ut Salomon ait) tempus loquendi, et tempus tacendi. Congruo ergo tempore eam abscondunt, et apta eam hora aperiunt: abscondunt ex humilitate, ne se jactent aut propalent inaniter; confitentur ex caritate, ut loquantur salubriter. Tunc autem scientiam occultare, quando esset communicanda, vituperatur. Ideo in Proverbiis legitur: Homo versutus celat scientiam. Hinc in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus autem et imprudens non servabunt tempus. Et non abscondunt patres suos. Quidam adeo vani sunt, ut in suis dictis aut scriptis majores suos ideo non allegent, quamvis ex eis didicerint quæ dicunt aut scribunt, quatenus quasi ex proprio talia scisse putentur, et ipsi tanquam principales doctores in admiratione habeantur, allegentur, laudentur. Isti patres suos abscondunt: quod et illi magis vituperabiliusque facere judicantur, qui catholicorum et magnorum doctorum dicta irreverenter, faciliter, aut irrationabiliter negant. Nos ergo patres nostros famemus et veneremur, amemus atque sectemur. In opina[…] […] approbemus. Hinc equidem scriptum in Ecclesiastico: Laudemus viros gloriosos et patres nostros in generatione sua.
paras.en: [[15:18|Wise men confess|Sapientes confitentur]]. If wise men confess their wisdom and the truth, why is it written in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 10:14|Wise men lay up knowledge|Sapientes abscondunt sapientiam]] [Denis reads *wisdom*, *sapientiam*, where the Vulgate has *scientiam*, knowledge]? The answer is that (as Solomon says) there is a time to speak and a time to keep silence[[Eccles 3:7||]]. At a fitting time, then, they hide it, and at a suitable hour they disclose it: they hide it out of humility, lest they boast or make a vain show of themselves; they confess it out of charity, so as to speak wholesomely. But to hide knowledge at a time when it ought to be shared is blameworthy. Therefore it is read in Proverbs: [[Prov 12:23|A cautious man concealeth knowledge|Homo versutus celat scientiam]] [Denis reads *versutus*, crafty, where the Vulgate has *versatus*, practised, which the Douay renders *cautious*; so he takes the saying as a reproach]. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 20:7|A wise man will hold his peace till he see opportunity: but a babbler, and a fool, will regard no time|Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus; lascivus autem et imprudens non servabunt tempus]]. [[15:18|and hide not their fathers|Et non abscondunt patres suos]]. Some are so vain that in their sayings or writings they do not cite their elders, though they have learned from them what they say or write, precisely so that they may be thought to have known such things of their own, and may themselves be admired, cited and praised as principal doctors. These hide their fathers: and those are judged to do so still more blameworthily who deny the sayings of catholic and great doctors irreverently, lightly or unreasonably. Let us, then, make our fathers renowned [*famemus*] and venerate them, love and follow them. In opin[…] […] let us approve. Hence indeed it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 44:1|Let us now praise men of renown and our fathers in their generation|Laudemus viros gloriosos et patres nostros in generatione sua]].

paras.t: Non credit quod reverti possit de tenebris, circumspectans undique gladium. Quemadmodum in Proverbiis asseritur, Impius quum in profundum peccatorum venerit, contemnit. Impius ergo et induratus de Dei pietate diffidens, atque in hoc Deum naturaliter bonum, pium et dulcem maxime inhonorans, quum peccata sua attendit, non credit quod per pœnitentiam possit de tenebris impietatum ad lucem divinæ miserationis redire, atque salvari; sed undique gladium ultionis divinæ circumspectando, desperat. Quum se moverit ad quærendum panem, id est, ad aliqua bona agenda se verterit, quorum actione mens pascitur, novit quod paratus sit in manu ejus tenebrarum dies, id est tempus damnationis. Talis enim homo interdum incipit aliquid pœnitentiæ exercere. Sed frequenter contingit eum deficere, quia dum peccatorum suorum multitudinem magnitudinemque perpendit, et Deum immensæ justitiæ pensat, ad desperationem relabitur, reputans damnationem sibi paratam.
paras.en: [[15:22|He believeth not that he may return from darkness|Non credit quod reverti possit de tenebris]], [[15:22|looking round about for the sword on every side|circumspectans undique gladium]]. As is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 18:3|The wicked man, when he is come into the depths of sins, contemneth|Impius quum in profundum peccatorum venerit, contemnit]]. The wicked and hardened man, then, distrusting the goodness of God, and in this most greatly dishonouring God, who is by nature good, kind and sweet, when he considers his sins does not believe that through penance he can return from the darkness of his impieties to the light of divine mercy and be saved; but looking round on every side for the sword of divine vengeance, he despairs. [[15:23|When he moveth himself to seek bread|Quum se moverit ad quærendum panem]], that is, when he turns to doing some good things, by the doing of which the mind is fed, [[15:23|he knoweth that the day of darkness is ready at his hand|novit quod paratus sit in manu ejus tenebrarum dies]], that is, the time of damnation. For such a man sometimes begins to practise some penance. But it often happens that he fails, because while he weighs the multitude and greatness of his sins and considers God of immense justice, he falls back into despair, reckoning that damnation is prepared for him.

paras.t: Terrebit eum tribulatio: quia æternas metuit pœnas, dum eas mente revolvit. Et nihilo minus pondus impietatum suarum, quibus pœna illa augetur, quotidie aggravat, quemadmodum scriptum est: Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum. Et angustia vallabit eum; quia remorsus conscientiæ eum aliquando angit; et tempore mortis, deinde in divino judicio, ac postremo in loco damnationis æternæ vallatur angustia, juxta illud Jeremiæ: Ecce turbo dominicæ indignationis egredietur, et tempestas erumpens super caput impiorum veniet. Tetendit enim adversus Deum manum suam, et contra Omnipotentem roboratus est. Non opponamus nos Deo: cui et ille se opponit, qui superioribus suis inobediens exstat; et juxta Apostolum ad Romanos, Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit. Similiter qui se inordinate intromittit de his, quorum dispositio committenda est Deo, tendit manum suam adversus eum: sicut qui alios per vias iniquas ad officia promovere nituntur, aut certe impedire improbe moliuntur, aut se ipsos ingerunt vel intrudunt, quum juxta Apostolum ad Hebræos, Nemo assumit sibi honorem, nisi qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron.
paras.en: [[15:24|Tribulation shall terrify him|Terrebit eum tribulatio]]: because he fears eternal pains while he turns them over in his mind. And none the less he daily makes heavier the weight of his impieties, by which that pain is increased, as it is written: [[Ecclus 3:29|the sinner will add sin to sin|Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum]]. [[15:24|and distress shall surround him|Et angustia vallabit eum]]: because remorse of conscience sometimes distresses him; and at the time of death, then at the divine judgment, and lastly in the place of eternal damnation, he is surrounded by distress, according to that saying of Jeremias: [[Jer 23:19|Behold the whirlwind of the Lord's indignation shall come forth, and a tempest shall break out and come upon the head of the wicked|Ecce turbo dominicæ indignationis egredietur, et tempestas erumpens super caput impiorum veniet]] [[15:25|For he hath stretched out his hand against God, and hath strengthened himself against the Almighty|Tetendit enim adversus Deum manum suam, et contra Omnipotentem roboratus est]] Let us not set ourselves against God: and he too sets himself against him who is disobedient to his superiors; for according to the Apostle to the Romans, [[Rom 13:2|he that resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God|Qui potestati resistit, Dei ordinationi resistit]]. Likewise he who meddles inordinately in things whose disposal is to be left to God stretches out his hand against him: like those who strive to promote others to offices by wicked ways, or wickedly labour to hinder them, or thrust or intrude themselves, since according to the Apostle to the Hebrews, [[Heb 5:4|Neither doth any man take the honour to himself, but he that is called by God, as Aaron was|Nemo assumit sibi honorem, nisi qui vocatur a Deo tanquam Aaron]].

paras.t: Habitavit in civitatibus desolatis, id est inter cives spiritualibus gratiis atque virtutibus destitutos. Nam qualis ipse, tales et ejus subjecti atque ministri. Ideo additur, et in domibus desertis, id est in familiis ob sua peccata a Deo relictis; quæ in tumulos, id est vitiorum subversiones et lapsus, sunt redactæ. Hinc in Ecclesiastico legitur: Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus; et qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea. In Proverbiis quoque: Regnantibus impiis, ruinæ hominum. Rursus quoque Salomon ait: Rex impius omnes ministros habet iniquos. Non ditabitur charismatibus gratiarum, quæ sunt veræ divitiæ animarum; nec perseverabit substantia ejus: quia exteriora ei celeriter auferentur saltem in morte; et si ad tempus aliquid spiritualis opulentiæ in donis gratiæ ac virtutum habuerit, non perseverat usque in finem, sed peccando illa amittit. Nec mittet in terram radicem […] […] affectum stabili fundamento non infiget, nec ad terram viventium, regionem Beatorum hanc diriget; sed rebus caducis atque inanibus inhærebit, omnique vento vitiorum et impetu passionum impelletur, flectetur, et ruet.
paras.en: [[15:28|He hath dwelt in desolate cities|Habitavit in civitatibus desolatis]], that is, among citizens bereft of spiritual graces and virtues. For as he is, such are his subjects and ministers too. Therefore it is added, [[15:28|and in desert houses|et in domibus desertis]], that is, in households forsaken by God because of their sins; [[15:28|that are reduced into heaps|quæ in tumulos]], that is, into the overthrow and fall of vices. Hence it is read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:2|As the judge of the people is himself, so also are his ministers: and what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein|Secundum judicem populi, sic et ministri ejus; et qualis est rector civitatis, tales et habitantes in ea]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 28:12|when the wicked reign, men are ruined|Regnantibus impiis, ruinæ hominum]]. And again Solomon says: A wicked king hath all his ministers wicked[[Prov 29:12||]] [Denis gives the sense; the verse reads: A prince that gladly heareth lying words, hath all his servants wicked]. [[15:29|He shall not be enriched|Non ditabitur]] with the gifts of graces, which are the true riches of souls; [[15:29|neither shall his substance continue|nec perseverabit substantia ejus]]: because outward things will quickly be taken from him, at death at least; and if for a time he has had some spiritual wealth in the gifts of grace and of the virtues, it does not last to the end, but he loses them by sinning. [[15:29|neither shall he push his root in the earth|Nec mittet in terram radicem]] […] […] he will not fix his affection on a stable foundation, nor direct it to the land of the living, the region of the Blessed; but he will cleave to perishing and empty things, and will be driven, bent and thrown down by every wind of vices and every onset of the passions.

paras.t: Ramos ejus, id est familiares domesticos, sobolem, imitatores, quibus stipatur, ornatur et cingitur sicut arbor propriis ramis; arefaciet flamma, id est ardor vitiorum in præsenti ab humore gratiæ, deinde ignis inferni ab exuberantia gloriæ, dum scilicet dominum suum in vitiis assequuntur. Juxta hunc modum Dominus loquitur per Ezechielem de rege Assyriorum: Ecce Assur quasi cedrus in Libano, frondibus nemorosus: quoniam speciosum feci eum multis condensisque frondibus. Et sequenti ibi capitulo scribitur, quemadmodum Assur et Pharao regesque ceteri descenderint cum suis satellitibus in infernum. Lædetur quasi vinea in primo flore. Hoc fit, dum peccator pœnitere exorsus est, sed tentatione eum invadente, a divino amore frigescit, et peccati torpore constringitur, atque ad pristinas vanitates revertitur.
paras.en: [[15:30|his branches|Ramos ejus]], that is, his intimates and household, his offspring and imitators, by whom he is thronged, adorned and girt about as a tree by its own branches, [[15:30|the flame shall dry up|arefaciet flamma]]: that is, the heat of the vices dries them of the moisture of grace in the present life, and afterwards the fire of hell dries them of the overflowing of glory, when, namely, they follow their lord in his vices. In this manner the Lord speaks through Ezechiel of the king of the Assyrians: [[Ezech 31:3|Behold, the Assyrian like a cedar in Libanus|Ecce Assur quasi cedrus in Libano]], [[Ezech 31:3|full of leaves|frondibus nemorosus]]: [[Ezech 31:9|For I made him beautiful and thick set with many branches|quoniam speciosum feci eum multis condensisque frondibus]]. And in the following chapter there it is written how Assur and Pharao and the other kings went down with their followers into hell[[Ezech 32:18||]]. [[15:33|He shall be blasted as a vine when its grapes are in the first flower|Lædetur quasi vinea in primo flore]]. This happens when a sinner has begun to repent, but, when temptation assails him, grows cold in divine love, is bound fast by the torpor of sin, and returns to his former vanities.

paras.t: Ignis devorabit tabernacula eorum, qui munera libenter accipiunt. Si tabernacula cupidorum, domus conscientiæ et mentis cubile appellentur, illa nunc æstu avaritiæ spiritualiter consumuntur; postea autem avari cum corporibus, quæ animarum velut tabernacula sunt, in ignem tartareum projicientur. Grave ergo est avaritiæ vitium, munerumque acceptio ad subvertendum justitiam. Hinc in Ecclesiastico fertur: Vindicta carnis impii, ignis et vermis. Judith quoque ait: Dominus omnipotens vindicabit in eis. Dabit ignem et vermes in carnem eorum, ut urantur et sentiant […] […] cupiditatis scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Nihil iniquius quam amare pecuniam. Hic enim animam suam habet venalem. Apostolus vero avaritiam, servitutem nominat idolorum. Postremo, in Exodo scriptum est: Non accipies munera, quæ excæcant etiam prudentes, et subvertunt verba justorum.
paras.en: [[15:34|and fire shall devour their tabernacles, who love to take bribes|Ignis devorabit tabernacula eorum, qui munera libenter accipiunt]]. If the tabernacles of the covetous are taken to be the house of the conscience and the chamber of the mind, these are now consumed spiritually by the heat of avarice; and afterwards the avaricious, together with their bodies, which are as it were the tabernacles of their souls, will be cast into the fire of hell. Grievous, then, is the vice of avarice, and the taking of gifts to overthrow justice. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:19|the vengeance on the flesh of the ungodly is fire and worms|Vindicta carnis impii, ignis et vermis]]. Judith too says: [[Jdt 16:20|the Lord almighty will take revenge on them|Dominus omnipotens vindicabit in eis]]. [[Jdt 16:21|he will give fire, and worms into their flesh, that they may burn, and may feel|Dabit ignem et vermes in carnem eorum, ut urantur et sentiant]] […] […] of cupidity it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:10|There is not a more wicked thing than to love money|Nihil iniquius quam amare pecuniam]]: [[Ecclus 10:10|for such a one setteth even his own soul to sale|Hic enim animam suam habet venalem]]. And the Apostle calls avarice a serving of idols[[Eph 5:5||]][[Col 3:5||]]. Lastly, it is written in Exodus: [[Ex 23:8|Neither shalt thou take bribes, which even blind the wise, and pervert the words of the just|Non accipies munera, quæ excæcant etiam prudentes, et subvertunt verba justorum]].

16.title: Expositio litteralis capituli sextidecimi: Respondens autem Job, dixit.
16.title_en: Literal exposition of the sixteenth chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Sanctus Job tanquam insuperabilis pugil, non cessat veritatem justitiamque defendere usque ad mortem: sed et durissime reprobatus et increpatus, non terretur, nec justas atque acerrimas invectiones contra veritatis adversarios inducere mente veretur. Insuper, quamvis Salomone testante, duo prævaleant contra unum, ipse tamen prævalet contra tres, et nunc secundo refellit instantias Eliphaz.
paras.en: Holy Job, like an unconquerable champion, does not cease to defend truth and justice even to death: though most harshly rebuked and chidden, he is not frightened, nor is he afraid in mind to bring just and most sharp invectives against the adversaries of truth. Moreover, although, as Solomon witnesses, two prevail against one, he nonetheless prevails against three, and now for the second time refutes the objections of Eliphaz.

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit: Audivi frequenter talia, scilicet verba injuriosa, reprehensiva et pungitiva, qualia contra me profertis. In disputationibus quoque rhetoricis, qualis exstitit ista, solent contentiosa verba intermisceri. Consolatores onerosi omnes vos estis, videlicet vos tres amici mei, et qui vobis consentiunt sive applaudunt. Multi namque (ut habitum est) disputationi huic interfuerunt, quorum unus Eliu fuit. Dicuntur autem consolatores onerosi, quia ad consolandum venerunt; sed loqui exorsi, ad increpationes acutissimas versi sunt, et onus tribulationis beati Job non parum auxerunt, eum coram multis durissime increpando, quum tamen afflicto non sit addenda afflictio. Quod si necesse fuerit afflictum corripere, blande et molliter fiat hoc, nisi forte ex speciali causa ratio dictet quid rigoris addendum.
paras.en: [[16:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]]: [[16:2|I have often heard such things as these|Audivi frequenter talia]], that is, injurious, reproving and stinging words such as you bring against me. In rhetorical disputations too, such as this one was, contentious words are commonly mixed in. [[16:2|you are all troublesome comforters|Consolatores onerosi omnes vos estis]], namely you three friends of mine, and those who agree with you or applaud you. For many (as has been said) were present at this disputation, one of whom was Eliu. They are called *troublesome comforters* [*onerosi*, literally burdensome] because they came to comfort; but once they began to speak they turned to the sharpest rebukes, and added not a little to the burden of blessed Job's tribulation, rebuking him most harshly before many, although affliction is not to be added to the afflicted. And if it is necessary to reprove one who is afflicted, let it be done gently and softly, unless perhaps for some special cause reason dictates that some severity be added.

paras.t: Numquid habebunt finem verba ventosa? id est, garrulis superfluisque sermonibus tu, Eliphaz, et tui amici tam prolixe insistitis contra me, quasi nunquam velletis terminare sermones hujusmodi. Eadem quoque sæpe repetitis, quantum ad sensum. Aut aliquid tibi molestum est, si loquaris? id est, tibi, o Eliphaz, quum sis sanus et prosperitate vallatus, adjutoresque habens, non est molestum plura proferre, præsertim quia ex hoc quod loqueris contra me, nulla tibi infertur a me molestia aut vindicta, quia patienter sustineo, nec pro convitio convitium reddo. Poteram et ego similia vestri loqui, id est, talia et ea vitia, quæ mihi false imponitis, scilicet iram, impatientiam, divinorum ignorantiam, etc., possem vobis vere imponere, et verbis vos pungere, sicut me pungitis, nisi disciplina frenarer, adversitatibusque gravarer, et si spes profectus esset ex hoc.
paras.en: [[16:3|Shall windy words have no end?|Numquid habebunt finem verba ventosa?]] that is, thou, Eliphaz, and thy friends press so lengthily against me with garrulous and superfluous talk, as though you would never wish to bring such discourses to an end. You also often repeat the same things, as far as the sense goes. [[16:3|or is it any trouble to thee to speak?|Aut aliquid tibi molestum est, si loquaris?]] that is, for thee, O Eliphaz, being in health and hedged about with prosperity, and having helpers, it is no trouble to say a great deal; especially since, for speaking against me, no trouble or revenge is brought upon thee by me, for I bear it patiently and do not render railing for railing. [[16:4|I also could speak like you|Poteram et ego similia vestri loqui]], that is, such things, the very vices which you falsely lay upon me, namely anger, impatience, ignorance of divine things, etc., I could truly lay upon you, and sting you with words as you sting me, were I not reined in by discipline and weighed down by adversities, and if there were any hope of profit from it.

paras.t: Atque utinam esset anima vestra pro anima mea, id est, utinam talia pateretur, qualia mea patitur anima. Quod non ex ira vel odio, sed ex caritate et zelo justitiæ ait, ut per temporalem afflictionem inducerentur ad veritatis cognitionem, qui in prosperitate nolebant informari et corrigi, quatenus, juxta Isaiam, vexatio eis tribueret intellectum. Consolarer et vos ego sermonibus: non eo modo ut vos me, sed verba bona, verba consolatoria vobis vere proponerem. Hoc enim ad vere caritativum sapientemque pertinet, cujus est ordinatum et amorosum proferre sermonem: qui sermo medicamen est animæ desolatæ, quemadmodum in Proverbiis legitur, Favus mellis verba composita. Et iterum Salomon protestatur: Lingua placabilis lignum vitæ. In Ecclesiastico quoque habetur: Nonne ardorem refrigerabit ros? sic et verbum melius quam datum. Et moverem caput meum super vos ex compassione. Denique motio capitis designat mentis inflexionem ad aliquam conceptionem, atque interdum derisionem significat. Sic in Psalmo ait Salvator: Omnes videntes me, deriserunt me; locuti sunt labiis, et moverunt caput. In Threnis quoque loquitur Jeremias: Sibilaverunt, et moverunt capita sua super filiam Jerusalem. Interdum vero denotat admirationem vel congratulationem seu exsultationem: sicut in Isaia de rege Assyriorum narratur, Caput movit super te, filia Jerusalem: quia videlicet certissime æstimavit se eam victurum. Infra etiam capitulo ultimo dicitur, quod fratres et sorores Job venerunt ad eum, et caput super eum moverunt. Aliquando autem compassionem importat, sicut hoc loco.
paras.en: [[16:4|and would God your soul were for my soul|Atque utinam esset anima vestra pro anima mea]], that is, would that your soul suffered such things as my soul suffers. He says this not out of anger or hatred, but out of charity and zeal for justice: that those who would not be taught and corrected in prosperity might be led by temporal affliction to the knowledge of the truth, so that, as Isaias says, vexation might give them understanding[[Is 28:19||]]. [[16:5|I would comfort you also with words|Consolarer et vos ego sermonibus]]: not in the way you comfort me, but I would truly set before you good words, words of comfort. For this belongs to one who is truly charitable and wise, whose part it is to utter ordered and loving speech: and such speech is a medicine for the desolate soul, as is read in Proverbs: [[Prov 16:24|Well ordered words are as a honeycomb|Favus mellis verba composita]]. And again Solomon declares: [[Prov 15:4|A peaceable tongue is a tree of life|Lingua placabilis lignum vitæ]]. In Ecclesiasticus too we have: [[Ecclus 18:16|Shall not the dew assuage the heat? so also the good word is better than the gift|Nonne ardorem refrigerabit ros? sic et verbum melius quam datum]] [[16:5|and would wag my head over you|Et moverem caput meum super vos]] out of compassion. Now the moving of the head signifies an inclining of the mind towards some thought, and sometimes it signifies derision. So in the Psalm the Saviour says: [[Ps 21:8|All they that saw me have laughed me to scorn: they have spoken with the lips, and wagged the head|Omnes videntes me, deriserunt me; locuti sunt labiis, et moverunt caput]]. In Lamentations too Jeremias says: [[Lam 2:15|they have hissed, and wagged their heads at the daughter of Jerusalem|Sibilaverunt, et moverunt capita sua super filiam Jerusalem]]. But sometimes it denotes wonder, or rejoicing at another's lot, or exultation: as is related in Isaias of the king of the Assyrians: [[Is 37:22|the daughter of Jerusalem hath wagged the head after thee|Caput movit super te, filia Jerusalem]] [in Isaias it is the daughter of Jerusalem who wags her head after the king; Denis takes the king as the one who moves his head]: because, namely, he reckoned most surely that he would conquer her. Below too, in the last chapter, it is said that Job's brothers and sisters came to him and moved their heads over him[[Job 42:11||]]. And sometimes it implies compassion, as in this place.

paras.t: Roborarem vos ore meo, id est, bonis oris mei sermonibus corda vestra ad patientiæ robur, ad constantiam et animi fortitudinem exhortarer: quemadmodum secundo Machabæorum de Juda legitur Machabæo, Singulos armavit, non hasta et clypeo, sed sermonibus optimis et exhortationibus. Denique, virtus et sapientia ita confortant perficiuntque habentem, ut de plenitudine sua alios quoque valeat confortare. Hinc scriptum est in Proverbiis: Vir sapiens fortis est, et vir doctus, robustus et validus. Ecclesiastes quoque ait: Sapientia confortavit sapientem super decem principes civitatis. Denique, ad amicum, imo ad quemlibet proximum pertinet, afflictis compassionem et consolationem impendere, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Non desis plorantibus in consolatione. Quasi parcens vobis, id est, non tam districte vos corripiens, sicut culpa vestra meretur, sed reprehendenda in vobis moderate redarguens, doloresque vestros minuere satagens.
paras.en: [[16:6|I would strengthen you with my mouth|Roborarem vos ore meo]], that is, with the good words of my mouth I would exhort your hearts to the strength of patience, to constancy and fortitude of mind: as is read in the second book of Machabees of Judas Machabeus: [[2 Mach 15:11|he armed every one of them, not with defence of shield and spear, but with very good speeches, and exhortations|Singulos armavit, non hasta et clypeo, sed sermonibus optimis et exhortationibus]]. Further, virtue and wisdom so strengthen and perfect the one who has them that out of his fullness he is able to strengthen others too. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 24:5|A wise man is strong: and a knowing man, stout and valiant|Vir sapiens fortis est, et vir doctus, robustus et validus]]. Ecclesiastes too says: [[Eccles 7:20|Wisdom hath strengthened the wise more than ten princes of the city|Sapientia confortavit sapientem super decem principes civitatis]]. Further, it belongs to a friend, nay to any neighbour, to bestow compassion and comfort on the afflicted, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:38|Be not wanting in comforting them that weep|Non desis plorantibus in consolatione]]. [[16:6|as sparing you|Quasi parcens vobis]], that is, not reproving you as strictly as your fault deserves, but rebuking moderately what is to be blamed in you, and taking pains to lessen your sorrows.

paras.t: Sed quid agam? id est, ita negotia mea se habent, ut non faciliter videam quid potius agere debeam. Nam quidquid egero, non per hoc dolorem effugio. Hinc subditur: Si locutus fuero, contra vestros disputando errores, non quiescit dolor meus, imo interior dolor meus ex vestris culpis atque erroribus magis augetur; et si tacuero, vobis et falsitati cedendo, non recedit a me. Nunc autem oppressit me dolor meus, id est, ab omni temporali prosperitate, et corporis sanitate ac firmitate dejecit; usum quoque rationis, seu considerationem et locutionem aliqualiter impedivit. Quum enim dolor est vehemens, intentio revocatur seu impeditur ab intellectualium consideratione. Et in nihilum redacti, id est pro magna parte consumpti, sunt omnes artus mei, ita ut quod remanet in me de corpulentia et forma membrorum, pro nihilo reputetur. Est autem consuetudo afflictis per excessum seu hyperbolice loqui, ad clarius exprimendum magnitudinem rei ac proprii cordis dispositionem. Sic et Psalmista fatetur: Ego ad nihilum redactus sum.
paras.en: [[16:7|But what shall I do?|Sed quid agam?]] that is, my affairs stand so that I do not easily see what I had better do. For whatever I do, I do not escape pain by it. Hence it is added: [[16:7|If I speak|Si locutus fuero]], disputing against your errors, [[16:7|my pain will not rest|non quiescit dolor meus]]; rather my inward pain is increased the more by your faults and errors; [[16:7|and if I hold my peace|et si tacuero]], yielding to you and to falsehood, [[16:7|it will not depart from me|non recedit a me]]. [[16:8|But now my sorrow hath oppressed me|Nunc autem oppressit me dolor meus]], that is, it has cast me down from all temporal prosperity, and from health and strength of body; it has also in some measure hindered the use of reason, that is, reflection and speech. For when pain is violent, the attention is called away or hindered from the consideration of intellectual things. And [[16:8|are brought to nothing|in nihilum redacti]] (that is, for the most part consumed) [[16:8|all my limbs|sunt omnes artus mei]], so that what remains in me of the bulk and shape of my members is counted as nothing. Now it is the custom of the afflicted to speak with excess, or hyperbolically, so as to express more clearly the greatness of the matter and the state of their own heart. So the Psalmist too confesses: [[Ps 72:22|I am brought to nothing|Ego ad nihilum redactus sum]].

paras.t: Rugæ meæ, id est pellis seu cutis meæ contractiones vel plicationes, testimonium dicunt contra me, id est, amicis meis contra me disputantibus præbent materiam, faciuntque apparentiam reprehendendi me de culpa: ex quo enim tam graviter cæsus sum, apparentiam habet, quod merui pœnam hanc. Porro, ex interiori hujusmodi consumptione corpus corrugatur, sicut in senibus et graviter infirmantibus. Et suscitatur falsiloquus adversus faciem meam, id est, Eliphaz mendaciter me accusans, ex inspectu rugarum mearum provocatur ad contradicendum mihi aperte. Potest quoque de diabolo accipi, qui amicos Job incitavit adversus eum. Contradicens mihi, dicenti me absque meo percussum demerito.
paras.en: [[16:9|My wrinkles|Rugæ meæ]], that is, the contractions or folds of my skin and hide, [[16:9|bear witness against me|testimonium dicunt contra me]], that is, they give my friends who dispute against me matter, and make it appear that I may be reproved for guilt: for since I have been so grievously smitten, it has the look of my having deserved this punishment. Moreover, the body is wrinkled by such inward wasting, as in the old and the gravely ill. [[16:9|and a false speaker riseth up against my face|Et suscitatur falsiloquus adversus faciem meam]], that is, Eliphaz, accusing me falsely, is provoked by the sight of my wrinkles to contradict me openly. It can also be taken of the devil, who stirred up Job's friends against him. [[16:9|contradicting me|Contradicens mihi]], when I say that I have been struck without any desert of mine.

paras.t: Collegit furorem suum in me, et comminans mihi, infremuit contra me dentibus suis; hostis meus terribilibus oculis me intuitus est. Totum hoc quidam exponunt de dæmone, qui principalis fuit beati Job tribulator, furoremque suum contra Job collegit, tanto vehementius cupiens eum devincere, quo amplius se hoc facturum præsumpsit, et quo Job justior fuit. Ut autem divinus Dionysius docet, in dæmonibus est amens furor, phantasia proterva, et irrationabilis concupiscentia. Satan insuper comminabatur ipsi Job per ejus amicos, qui asseruerunt sancto Job usque ad mortem mala instare. Forte etiam diabolus per se ipsum comminabatur ipsi Job de futuris adversis, in somno, seu alias apparendo, seu inde tentando. Unde superius Job dixit ad Deum: Terrebis me per somnia, et per visiones horrore concuties. Loquitur autem de adversario suo per modum feræ, quæ dentibus comminatur, illos parans ad lacerandum. Sic et Petrus in prima sua ait epistola: Diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret. Constat præterea, quod amici Job erant contra eum maxime inflammati, quia videbatur eis loqui sicut sacrilegus et blasphemus. Unde et contra eum quasi furebant, et terribiliter adspexerunt, ardentibus oculis furorem pectoris demonstrantes. Satan vero videns patientiam atque constantiam sancti Job, furiosissimis ac terribilissimis eum interioribus oculis intuebatur. Porro (secundum Thomam) placidis oculis hominem intuetur, qui facta ejus in melius interpretatur; terribilibus, qui in pejus: et sic fuit de amicis Job.
paras.en: [[16:10|He hath gathered together his fury against me, and threatening me he hath gnashed with his teeth upon me: my enemy hath beheld me with terrible eyes|Collegit furorem suum in me, et comminans mihi, infremuit contra me dentibus suis; hostis meus terribilibus oculis me intuitus est]]. Some expound all this of the demon, who was the chief afflicter of blessed Job, and gathered his fury against Job, desiring to overcome him all the more vehemently as he presumed the more that he would do it, and as Job was the more just. And, as the divine Dionysius teaches, in demons there is senseless fury, wanton fancy, and irrational desire. Satan, moreover, threatened Job through his friends, who asserted that evils awaited holy Job even to death[[Job 15:21||]] [the margin reads Job xv, 2 (?); Eliphaz says this in 15:20–24]. Perhaps the devil also threatened Job himself with adversities to come, in sleep, or by appearing to him otherwise, or by tempting him in this way. Hence Job said to God above: [[Job 7:14|Thou wilt frighten me with dreams, and terrify me with visions|Terrebis me per somnia, et per visiones horrore concuties]] He speaks of his adversary after the manner of a wild beast, which threatens with its teeth, making them ready to tear. So too Peter says in his first epistle: [[1 Pet 5:8|the devil, as a roaring lion, goeth about seeking whom he may devour|Diabolus tanquam leo rugiens circuit, quærens quem devoret]]. It is clear besides that Job's friends were greatly inflamed against him, because he seemed to them to speak like a sacrilegious man and a blasphemer. Hence they as it were raged against him, and looked at him terribly, showing the fury of their breast with burning eyes. But Satan, seeing the patience and constancy of holy Job, beheld him with most furious and terrible inward eyes. Further (according to Thomas), he looks on a man with gentle eyes who interprets his deeds for the better; with terrible eyes, he who interprets them for the worse: and so it was with Job's friends.

paras.t: Aperuerunt super me ora sua exprobrantes, id est convitia mihi dicentes: quod amici Job multipliciter peregerunt: percusserunt maxillam meam. Hoc Thomas exponit sic: Ille aliquem in maxillam percutit, qui ei improperium in faciem dicit: amici autem Job multa contra eum improperia sunt locuti. Quocirca dicit Albertus: Non legitur, quod ad litteram alapas dederint sancto Job: sed quia maxilla est ad continendum ea quæ sub dentibus masticantur, et quodam spirituali modo masticantur quæ frequenti mentis iteratione discernuntur utrum vera vel falsa sint: memoria talia continens ut bene per mentem discernantur, maxilla vocatur: quæ cæditur, dum bene meditatis per contradictionem obviatur. Satiati, id est mente refecti, atque lætati, sunt pœnis meis. Hoc de amicis Job in tantum accipi potest. Nam quamvis ei in principio condoluerunt, audiendo tamen verba ipsius, cœperunt pessime sentire de ipso, et arbitrari quod justissime pro suis affligeretur excessibus. Idcirco, divinæ justitiæ quasi congratulando, de ejus punitione gaudebant ac replebantur, dum ad eorum libitum torquebatur. Unde et Eliu infra ait: Pater mi, probetur Job usque in finem: ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis, qui addit super peccata sua blasphemiam. Inter nos interim constringatur, et tunc ad judicium provocet sermonibus suis Deum.
paras.en: [[16:11|They have opened their mouths upon me|Aperuerunt super me ora sua]], [[16:11|reproaching me|exprobrantes]], that is, speaking railing words to me: which Job's friends did in many ways: [[16:11|they have struck me on the cheek|percusserunt maxillam meam]]. Thomas expounds this thus: He strikes someone on the cheek who says a reproach to his face: and Job's friends spoke many reproaches against him. Accordingly Albert says: It is not read that they literally gave holy Job blows on the face; but because the jaw [*maxilla*, the word rendered *cheek*] serves to hold what is chewed under the teeth, and in a certain spiritual way those things are chewed which are sifted by frequent turning over in the mind, whether they be true or false, the memory, holding such things so that they may be well sifted by the mind, is called the jaw: and it is struck when what has been well meditated is met with contradiction. [[16:11|they are filled|Satiati]], that is, refreshed in mind and gladdened, [[16:11|with my pains|sunt pœnis meis]]. This can be taken of Job's friends to this extent. For although they grieved with him at the beginning, yet on hearing his words they began to think very ill of him, and to judge that he was most justly afflicted for his excesses. Therefore, as though rejoicing with the divine justice, they were glad and were filled with his punishment, while he was tormented as they pleased. Hence Eliu too says below: [[Job 34:36|My father, let Job be tried even to the end: cease not from the man of iniquity|Pater mi, probetur Job usque in finem: ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis]], [[Job 34:37|Because he addeth blasphemy upon his sins, let him be tied fast in the mean time amongst us: and then let him provoke God to judgment with his speeches|qui addit super peccata sua blasphemiam. Inter nos interim constringatur, et tunc ad judicium provocet sermonibus suis Deum]].

paras.t: Conclusit me Deus apud iniquum, id est, potestati et voluntati Satan me subjecit, quantum ad hoc, quod Deo permittente ille me corporaliter sic afflixit. Nam et superius Job loquitur Deo: Circumdedisti me carcere. Et rursus: Posuisti in nervo pedem meum. Et manibus impiorum me tradidit, id est Chaldæorum et Sabæorum, qui mea mihi abstulerunt. Itemque amicorum reprobationi et subsannationi me subdidit permissive: qui impii appellantur, in quantum veritati et æquitati restiterant.
paras.en: [[16:12|God hath shut me up with the unjust man|Conclusit me Deus apud iniquum]], that is, he has made me subject to the power and will of Satan, in that by God's permission Satan has so afflicted me in body. For above, too, Job says to God: [[Job 7:12|thou hast enclosed me in a prison|Circumdedisti me carcere]]. And again: [[Job 13:27|Thou hast put my feet in the stocks|Posuisti in nervo pedem meum]]. [[16:12|and hath delivered me into the hands of the wicked|Et manibus impiorum me tradidit]], that is, of the Chaldeans and Sabeans[[Job 1:15||]][[Job 1:17||]], who took away from me what was mine. And likewise he has by permission subjected me to the rebuke and derision of my friends: who are called *wicked* inasmuch as they resisted truth and equity.

paras.t: Ego ille quondam opulentus: dicendo, Ille, notat suæ famæ claritatem, quia fama et opibus inclytus fuit; repente contritus sum, id est, subito a maxima prosperitate ad gravissimam calamitatem dejectus: pro[…] ut superius recitatur. In quibus verbis gravamen miseriæ sancti Job multipliciter denotatur. Primo, quia tam improvise ac subito est dejectus: quod gravius fuit, quam si paulatim fuisset dejectus. Secundo, quia post maximam opulentiam devenit ad summam penuriam. Tertio, quia inopia atque calamitas illum magis affligunt, qui in deliciis et abundantia vivere consuevit. Nam et opposita juxta se posita, magis percipiuntur. Teste quoque Boetio, extremum infelicitatis genus est, aliquando fuisse felicem: sicut et primo Machabæorum libro quidam testatur, In quantam tribulationem deveni, et in quos fluctus tristitiæ, qui jucundus eram et dilectus in potestate mea!
paras.en: [[16:13|I that was formerly so wealthy|Ego ille quondam opulentus]]: in saying *that* [*ille*, that man, the one everyone knew], he notes the brightness of his fame, for he was renowned for fame and riches; [[16:13|am all on a sudden broken to pieces|repente contritus sum]], that is, suddenly cast down from the greatest prosperity to the gravest calamity: pro[…] as is related above[[Job 1:14||]][[Job 2:7||]]. In these words the weight of holy Job's misery is shown in several ways. First, because he was cast down so unexpectedly and suddenly: which was heavier than if he had been cast down little by little. Secondly, because after the greatest wealth he came to the utmost want. Thirdly, because want and calamity afflict him the more who has been used to live in delights and abundance. For opposites set beside each other are the more perceived. As Boethius also witnesses, the worst kind of misfortune is to have once been happy: as one also testifies in the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 6:11|Into how much tribulation am I come, and into what floods of sorrow wherein now I am: I that was pleasant and beloved in my power!|In quantam tribulationem deveni, et in quos fluctus tristitiæ, qui jucundus eram et dilectus in potestate mea!]]

paras.t: Tenuit cervicem meam. Istud atque sequentia adscribuntur Deo permissive, diabolo effective, qui tenuit, id est strinxit, cervicem Job: quod et litteraliter et invisibiliter forsitan fecit dum eum percussit. Vel sensus est, quod sicut quis robustissimus alicujus debilioris apprehendit cervicem, ut durissime eum impingat, aut quasi immobilem reddat, sic Satan invasit et impulit sanctum Job. Denique, secundum Albertum, a posteriori parte capitis, nervi in totum corpus descendunt juxta cervicem: cujus signum est, quia si aliquis fortiter in collo stringatur posterius, mox redditur corpore toto immobilis. Unde intendit, quod Satan sic strinxerat eum pœnis, quod se movere nequivit. Confregit me, id est, corpus ulceribus laceravit; et posuit me sibi quasi in signum, id est, sic varia mihi inflixit supplicia, quemadmodum multæ sagittæ diriguntur in signum. Hinc dixit ipse Job supra: Sagittæ Domini in me sunt. Similiter fertur in Threnis: Misit in renibus meis filias pharetræ suæ.
paras.en: [[16:13|he hath taken me by my neck|Tenuit cervicem meam]]. This and what follows are ascribed to God by way of permission, and to the devil as the one who did it: he took, that is, gripped, Job's neck; which perhaps he did both literally and invisibly when he struck him. Or the sense is that, as a very strong man seizes the neck of someone weaker, to dash him down most harshly or to make him as it were unable to move, so Satan assailed and thrust at holy Job. Further, according to Albert, the nerves come down from the back of the head into the whole body by way of the neck: a sign of which is that if anyone is gripped hard at the back of the neck, he is at once made unable to move his whole body. Hence he means that Satan had so gripped him with pains that he could not move. [[16:13|he hath broken me|Confregit me]], that is, he has torn my body with ulcers; [[16:13|and hath set me up to be his mark|et posuit me sibi quasi in signum]], that is, he has inflicted various torments on me, as many arrows are aimed at a mark. Hence Job himself said above: [[Job 6:4|For the arrows of the Lord are in me|Sagittæ Domini in me sunt]]. Likewise it is said in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:13|He hath shot into my reins the daughters of his quiver|Misit in renibus meis filias pharetræ suæ]] [*the daughters of his quiver*, that is, its arrows].

paras.t: Circumdedit me lanceis suis, id est penetrativis doloribus. Vel refertur hoc ad impugnationem hostilem eorum qui beato Job suam abstulerunt substantiam, ejusque pueros occiderunt. Convulneravit lumbos meos, quia a capite usque ad calcaneum me replevit ulceribus pessimis. Non pepercit: dæmon enim atrocissimus est afflictor; et effudit in terram viscera mea, id est, omnem sobolem meam, ut propria viscera mihi dilectam, projecit in mortem. Vel de se ipso hoc ait hyperbolica locutione, ad designandum, quod pœna sua pertingebat usque ad intima, quemadmodum in Threnis habetur: Effusum est in terra jecur meum. Insuper, ad litteram fieri potuit, ut carne Job undique lacerata ac sanie defluente, aliquid viscerum seu vitalium ejus effluxerit. Concidit me vulnere super vulnus, id est, multiplicibus ulcerum vulneribus corpus meum dilaniavit. Irruit in me quasi gigas, id est cum impetu forti. Diabolus etiam naturali potestate tam fortis est, ut de eo infra dicatur: Non est potestas super terram quæ comparetur ei.
paras.en: [[16:14|He hath compassed me round about with his lances|Circumdedit me lanceis suis]], that is, with piercing pains. Or this refers to the hostile assault of those who took away blessed Job's substance and slew his servants[[Job 1:15||]][[Job 1:17||]]. [[16:14|he hath wounded my loins|Convulneravit lumbos meos]], for from head to heel he has filled me with very grievous ulcers. [[16:14|he hath not spared|Non pepercit]]: for the demon is a most cruel afflicter; [[16:14|and hath poured out my bowels on the earth|et effudit in terram viscera mea]], that is, he has cast into death all my offspring, dear to me as my own bowels. Or he says this of himself in a hyperbolic expression, to signify that his pain reached to his inmost parts, as we have in Lamentations: [[Lam 2:11|my liver is poured out upon the earth|Effusum est in terra jecur meum]]. Moreover, it could literally have happened that, Job's flesh being torn everywhere and running with matter, something of his inward or vital parts flowed out. [[16:15|He hath torn me with wound upon wound|Concidit me vulnere super vulnus]], that is, he has rent my body with the many wounds of ulcers. [[16:15|he hath rushed in upon me like a giant|Irruit in me quasi gigas]], that is, with strong onset. For the devil, by his natural power, is so strong that it is said of him below: [[Job 41:24|There is no power upon earth that can be compared with him|Non est potestas super terram quæ comparetur ei]].

paras.t: Saccum consui super cutem meam, id est, tali veste me texi, et eam cuti meæ paravi in signum humiliationis, et ut misericordiam impetrarem. Itemque, ut manum percutientis juvarem, asperitati asperitatem jungendo. Et operui cinere carnem meam, id est, cinerem super me sparsi in signum doloris et humilitatis, in memoriam quoque meæ mortalitatis. Consueverunt autem homines sacco, cinere, pulvere atque cilicio taliter uti, sicut et in Jona fertur: Rex Ninive indutus est sacco, et sedit in cinere, et clamavit: Homines et jumenta operiantur saccis. In Threnis quoque: Sederunt in terra, conticuerunt senes filiæ Sion, consperserunt cinere capita sua; filiæ Jerusalem accinctæ sunt ciliciis. Itemque in Psalmo: Quoniam humiliata est in pulvere anima nostra. His verbis repellit Job falsam accusationem, qua præcedenti capitulo eum Eliphaz de superbia multipliciter accusavit: Quid, inquiens, tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus? Quid te elevat cor tuum?
paras.en: [[16:16|I have sowed sackcloth upon my skin|Saccum consui super cutem meam]], that is, I have covered myself with such a garment, and fitted it to my skin as a sign of humiliation, and to obtain mercy; and also to help the hand of him who strikes me, joining harshness to harshness. [[16:16|and have covered my flesh with ashes|Et operui cinere carnem meam]], that is, I have sprinkled ashes over myself as a sign of grief and humility, and also in remembrance of my mortality. Men were accustomed to use sackcloth, ashes, dust and haircloth in this way, as is told also in Jonas: the king of Ninive [[Jon 3:6|was clothed in sackcloth, and sat in ashes|indutus est sacco, et sedit in cinere]], and cried[[Jon 3:7||]]: [[Jon 3:8|let men and beasts be covered with sackcloth|Homines et jumenta operiantur saccis]]. In Lamentations too: [[Lam 2:10|The ancients of the daughter of Sion sit upon the ground, they have held their peace: they have sprinkled their heads with dust, they are girded with haircloth|Sederunt in terra, conticuerunt senes filiæ Sion, consperserunt cinere capita sua; filiæ Jerusalem accinctæ sunt ciliciis]]. And likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 43:25|For our soul is humbled down to the dust|Quoniam humiliata est in pulvere anima nostra]]. With these words Job repels the false accusation by which Eliphaz, in the preceding chapter, accused him in many ways of pride, saying: [[Job 15:13|Why|Quid,]] [[Job 15:13|doth thy spirit swell against God|tumet contra Deum spiritus tuus]]? [[Job 15:12|Why doth thy heart elevate thee|Quid te elevat cor tuum]]?

paras.t: Facies mea intumuit a fletu, id est, tam abundanter ploravi, quod facies mea inflata est. Ascendente quippe copiosa lacrimarum materia ad caput, facies flentium intumescit. Sed et in magno planctu multa humiditas resolvitur, a cerebro descendens ad vultum et oculos: ideo facit ibi inflationem. Sic et in Threnis habetur: Defecerunt oculi mei præ lacrimis. Primo quoque Regum David et viri ejus fleverunt, donec deficerent in eis lacrimæ. Et palpebræ meæ caligaverunt. Ex ingenti etenim decursu et fluxu humorum, visus debilitatur: et ponitur hic continens pro contento, videlicet palpebræ pro visu sub eis contento. Dicit namque Basilius, quod nigredine palpebrarum circumponitur visus, ut radius visualis dirigatur ad certum.
paras.en: [[16:17|My face is swollen with weeping|Facies mea intumuit a fletu]], that is, I have wept so abundantly that my face is puffed up. For when an abundant matter of tears rises to the head, the face of those who weep swells. And also in great lamentation much moisture is set loose, coming down from the brain to the face and eyes: so it causes a swelling there. So too we have in Lamentations: [[Lam 2:11|My eyes have failed with weeping|Defecerunt oculi mei præ lacrimis]]. In the first book of Kings too, David and his men wept [[1 Kings 30:4|till they had no more tears|donec deficerent in eis lacrimæ]]. [[16:17|and my eyelids are dim|Et palpebræ meæ caligaverunt]]. For by the great running down and flow of humours the sight is weakened: and here the container is put for what is contained, namely the eyelids for the sight contained beneath them. For Basil says that the sight is surrounded by the darkness of the eyelids so that the visual ray may be directed to a fixed point.

paras.t: Hæc passus sum absque iniquitate manus meæ, id est, tam gravem afflictionem non merui. Et quomodo verum sit hoc, diffuse expositum est atque tractatum in expositione superiorum. Per manum autem, operationem seu conversationem intelligit. Quum haberem mundas ad Deum preces, id est, puris orationibus Deum exorarem et colerem.
paras.en: [[16:18|These things have I suffered without the iniquity of my hand|Hæc passus sum absque iniquitate manus meæ]], that is, I have not deserved so grievous an affliction. And how this is true has been expounded and treated at length in the exposition of the earlier chapters. By *hand* he means his works or way of life. [[16:18|when I offered pure prayers to God|Quum haberem mundas ad Deum preces]], that is, when I besought and worshipped God with pure prayers.

paras.t: Terra, ne operias sanguinem meum, neque inveniat in te locum latendi clamor meus. Verbum hoc aliqualiter intricatum videtur, et a diversis diversimode explanatur. Sed apparet, quod vere ac plane sic possit exponi: Terra, ne operias sanguinem meum: id est, pœna quam passus sum in sanguinis mei per ulcera effluentis effusione, non abscondatur, nec occultetur in terra, hoc est, absconsa et injudicata non perseveret; sed ad judicium Dei perveniat et omnibus declaretur quare et qualiter passus sum, ut veritas innotescat, nec propter inanes amicorum meorum argumentationes æstimer pro culpa mea plagatus: sicque sanguis meus terra operiatur, id est, causa mea suppeditetur, et afflictio quam patior, retributione gloriæ digna non reputetur. Simili sensu subjungit, Neque inveniat locum in te latendi clamor meus: id est, universa verba quæ loquor, et pia querela qua me absque culpa mea cæsum jam conqueror, ad lucem perveniant, et judicentur a Deo ad ejus honorem et hominum ædificationem.
paras.en: [[16:19|O earth, cover not thou my blood, neither let my cry find a hiding place in thee|Terra, ne operias sanguinem meum, neque inveniat in te locum latendi clamor meus]]. This saying seems somewhat intricate, and is explained by different men in different ways. But it appears that it can be expounded truly and plainly thus: [[16:19|O earth, cover not thou my blood|Terra, ne operias sanguinem meum]]: that is, let not the pain I have suffered in the shedding of my blood as it flows out through the ulcers be hidden or concealed in the earth, that is, let it not remain hidden and unjudged; but let it come to the judgment of God, and let it be made plain to all why and how I have suffered, that the truth may be known, and that I may not, because of the empty arguments of my friends, be thought to have been stricken for my guilt; nor my blood thus be covered with earth, that is, my cause be trodden under, and the affliction I suffer be reckoned unworthy of the reward of glory. In a like sense he adds: [[16:19|neither let my cry find a hiding place in thee|Neque inveniat locum in te latendi clamor meus]]: that is, let all the words I speak, and the devout complaint in which I now lament that I have been struck without fault of mine, come to the light, and be judged by God, to his honour and the edification of men.

paras.t: Porro Albertus, per terram, intelligit phantasiam terrenam, id est falsam opinionem amicorum Job circa providentiam Dei: qua Job petit sanguinem suum non operiri, quin attestetur veræ sententiæ de providentia Dei. Similiter petit ne clamor suus in terra lateat, quin testetur pro veritate. Thomas, per terram, intelligit terrenam fragilitatem, ob quam Eliphaz conclusit Job sine peccatis non esse, et pro eis esse percussum. Petit ergo Job, ne ob hanc communem fragilitatem afflictio sua operiatur, id est, pro culpis suis sibi inflicta putetur, aut clamor suus in terra sit latens, ita quod sua conquestio videatur injusta. Insuper, per terram, intelligi possent habitantes in terra, a quibus postulat sanguinem suum non operiri, id est sanguinis sui præfatam effluxionem pro suis peccatis inflictam non æstimari, nec clamorem suum in hominibus terræ latere, ut injustus putetur.
paras.en: Albert, further, understands by *earth* an earthly fancy, that is, the false opinion of Job's friends about the providence of God: by which Job asks that his blood be not covered, but that it bear witness to the true view of the providence of God. Likewise he asks that his cry lie not hidden in the earth, but that it testify for the truth. Thomas understands by *earth* earthly frailty, on account of which Eliphaz concluded that Job was not without sins, and had been struck for them. Job asks, then, that because of this common frailty his affliction be not covered, that is, be not thought to have been inflicted on him for his faults, nor his cry lie hidden in the earth, so that his complaint should seem unjust. Moreover, by *earth* those who dwell on the earth could be understood, of whom he asks that his blood be not covered, that is, that the said flowing of his blood be not reckoned to have been inflicted for his sins, nor his cry lie hidden among the men of the earth, so that he be thought unjust.

paras.t: Sed quia sententia Job, qua se tam innocentem dixit, et absque sua culpa cæsum perhibuit, multis incredibilis apparebat, et res mira atque insolita fuit; consequenter testem sibi adhibet infallibilem judicem Deum verum. Ecce enim in cœlo testis meus, id est Deus incircumscriptibilis et immensus: qui licet secundum se sit penitus illocalis, tamen in cœlo specialiter esse asseritur, in quantum ibi evidentius ac magnificentius videtur et operatur. Ipse est testis eorum quæ dico, quod vera sint. Sic et Apostolus ait: Deus mihi testis est; atque Psalmista: Testis in cœlo fidelis. Et conscius meus, id est secretorum conscientiæ meæ cognitor, in excelsis est, puta in cœlo empyreo et civibus ejus. De quo quotidie dicimus: Pater noster, qui es in cœlis: et iterum: Gloria in excelsis Deo.
paras.en: But because Job's statement, in which he called himself so innocent and declared that he had been struck without fault of his own, seemed incredible to many, and was a wonderful and unusual thing, he next calls as his witness the infallible judge, the true God. [[16:20|For behold my witness is in heaven|Ecce enim in cœlo testis meus]], that is, God, who cannot be circumscribed and is immense: who, though in himself he is altogether without place, is yet said to be in heaven in a special way, inasmuch as there he is seen and works more evidently and more magnificently. He is the witness that what I say is true. So too the Apostle says: [[Rom 1:9|God is my witness|Deus mihi testis est]][[Phil 1:8||]]; and the Psalmist: [[Ps 88:38|a faithful witness in heaven|Testis in cœlo fidelis]].
