[[16:20|and he that knoweth my conscience|Et conscius meus]], that is, he who knows the secrets of my conscience, [[16:20|is on high|in excelsis est]], namely in the empyrean heaven and among its citizens. Of whom we say daily: [[Matt 6:9|Our Father who art in heaven|Pater noster, qui es in cœlis]]; and again: [[Luke 2:14|Glory to God in the highest|Gloria in excelsis Deo]].

paras.t: Verbosi amici mei, scilicet Eliphaz, Baldad et Sophar, id est verba insipienter multiplicantes, juxta quod in Ecclesiaste legitur: Stultus verba multiplicat. Insipientium vero est, quando incipiunt a veritate deficere, in multitudine verborum confidere. Propter quod mente egeni sunt destitutione sapientiæ, quæ est opulentia animæ. Hinc in Proverbiis dicitur: Ubi plurima sunt verba, ibi frequenter egestas in opere est. Ad Deum stillat, id est, lacrimose dirigitur, oculus meus interior, consolationem et beatitudinem desuper præstolando. Ex ardenti namque ad Deum affectu oculos etiam corporales cum lacrimis elevavit ad cœlos, dirigendo mentalem oculum ad Regem cœlorum, juxta illud Psalmi: Ad te levavi oculos meos, qui habitas in cœlis. Et denuo: Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte.
paras.en: [[16:21|My friends are full of words|Verbosi amici mei]], namely Eliphaz, Baldad and Sophar, that is, multiplying words foolishly, according to what is read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:14|A fool multiplieth words|Stultus verba multiplicat]]. For it is the way of the foolish, when they begin to fall short of the truth, to trust in a multitude of words. For this reason they are needy in mind through lack of wisdom, which is the wealth of the soul. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:23|where there are many words, there is oftentimes want|Ubi plurima sunt verba, ibi frequenter egestas]] in work. [[16:21|my eye poureth out tears to God|Ad Deum stillat]], that is, my inward eye is directed tearfully to God, awaiting consolation and beatitude from above. For with burning affection towards God he raised even his bodily eyes with tears to the heavens, directing the eye of the mind to the King of heaven, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 122:1|To thee have I lifted up my eyes, who dwellest in heaven|Ad te levavi oculos meos, qui habitas in cœlis]] And again: [[Ps 41:4|My tears have been my bread day and night|Fuerunt mihi lacrimæ meæ panes die ac nocte]].

paras.t: Atque utinam sic judicaretur vir cum Deo: id est, quis det ut homo tam evidenter judicetur modo a Deo? quomodo judicatur filius hominis cum collega suo, id est coram suo consocio et ab eo. Hoc Job dicit de se ipso et in persona perfectorum, qui nunc humano judicio reprobantur, sed a Deo justum proferri optant judicium, ne veritas patiatur dispendium, et ut ipsi salventur. Vel sic: Utinam sic, etc., id est, cupio ut vir justus sic judicetur coram Deo et ab eo, sicut homo coram suo collega, ut scilicet justus secundum merita sua a Deo recipiat etiam in præsenti, quemadmodum homo judicat hominem secundum opera sua.
paras.en: [[16:22|And O that a man might so be judged with God|Atque utinam sic judicaretur vir cum Deo]]: that is, who will grant that a man be judged now by God as evidently [[16:22|as the son of man is judged with his companion|quomodo judicatur filius hominis cum collega suo]], that is, before his fellow and by him? Job says this of himself and in the person of the perfect, who are now condemned by human judgment, but desire that a just judgment be pronounced by God, lest the truth suffer loss, and that they themselves may be saved. Or thus: [[16:22|O that a man might so|Utinam sic]], etc., that is, I desire that a just man be judged before God and by him as a man is before his fellow and by him; that is, that the just man receive from God according to his merits even in the present, as man judges man according to his works.

paras.t: Ecce enim breves anni transeunt, id est, anni vitæ humanæ in sæculo isto perpauci, velociter fluunt ac finiuntur. Idcirco non temporalem, sed æternam a Deo quæro mercedem, et divinum opto præstolorque judicium. Et semitam, id est vitæ hujus curriculum seu peregrinationis atque exsilii præsentis viam, per quam non revertar post mortem, ambulo, id est, ad futuram vitam progredior. Hoc dicit, ad insinuandum quod post mortem, non sit reditus ad statum vitæ præsentis: cujus oppositum quidam philosophi putaverunt. Et de hoc superius multa dixit, ut quum ait: Non revertetur oculus meus, ut videat bona; nec adspiciet me visus hominis.
paras.en: [[16:23|For behold short years pass away|Ecce enim breves anni transeunt]], that is, the very few years of human life in this world flow swiftly and come to an end. Therefore I seek from God not a temporal but an eternal reward, and I desire and wait for the divine judgment. And [[16:23|in a path|Et semitam]], that is, the course of this life, or the way of the present pilgrimage and exile, [[16:23|by which I shall not return|per quam non revertar]] after death, [[16:23|I am walking|ambulo]], that is, I go forward to the life to come. He says this to suggest that after death there is no return to the state of the present life: the opposite of which certain philosophers held. And he said much of this above, as when he says: [[Job 7:7|my eye shall not return to see good things|Non revertetur oculus meus, ut videat bona]]; [[Job 7:8|Nor shall the sight of man behold me|nec adspiciet me visus hominis]].

16.title: De mystica ejusdem capituli sextidecimi intelligentia
16.title_en: On the mystical understanding of the same sixteenth chapter

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit: Audivi frequenter talia. Vir justus verborum injuriis impetitus, non per impatientiam vincitur, nec improborum imperita verba multum ponderat, eisve læditur: imo ut levia æquanimiter patitur, et tanquam adversis assuetus, respondet: Audivi frequenter talia, scilicet injuriosa imperitaque verba; nec de mea injuria, sed de vestra culpa, læsione, ruina contristor. Denique quidam, quorum sermo sale conditus non est, et quibus Dominus linguam eruditam non dedit, alios gratia consolationis impendendæ accedunt; sed incaute loquendo, afflictos magis affligunt, eis inania promittendo, inutilia recitando, increpatoria absque discretione loquendo, aut aliis detrahendo. Quibus afflictus dicere potest: Consolatores onerosi omnes vos estis. Numquid habebunt finem verba ventosa? aut aliquid tibi molestum est, o inordinate locutor ac justi injuriator, si loquaris? id est, facile tibi est multa profari, quoniam tibi non resisto me ulciscendo. Denique teste Gregorio, Quum mali malis convitia dicunt, eo citius tacent, quo de se mox talia audiunt qualia dicunt. Quum autem justos criminantur, eo liberius fabulantur, quo minus redarguuntur: quia justi convitia non reddunt, etiam dum audiunt quod non sunt. Hinc justus injustis talibus dicere valet: Poteram et ego similia vestri loqui. Præsertim vero, dum quis caritative arguitur, redarguere non debet, ne ex impatientia loqui putetur.
paras.en: [[16:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]]: [[16:2|I have often heard such things as these|Audivi frequenter talia]]. The just man, assailed with wrongs in words, is not overcome through impatience, nor does he weigh much the ignorant words of the wicked, nor is he hurt by them: rather he bears them with an even mind as light things, and, as one accustomed to adversity, he answers: [[16:2|I have often heard such things as these|Audivi frequenter talia]], that is, injurious and ignorant words; and I am saddened not at the wrong done to me, but at your fault, your hurt, your ruin. Again, some whose speech is not seasoned with salt[[Col 4:6||]], and to whom the Lord has not given a learned tongue[[Is 50:4||]], come to others for the sake of offering consolation; but by speaking incautiously they afflict the afflicted all the more, promising them vain things, recounting useless things, speaking reproaches without discretion, or disparaging others. To these the afflicted man can say: [[16:2|you are all troublesome comforters|Consolatores onerosi omnes vos estis]]. [[16:3|Shall windy words have no end?|Numquid habebunt finem verba ventosa?]] [[16:3|or is it any trouble to thee|aut aliquid tibi molestum est]], O disorderly speaker and wronger of the just, [[16:3|to speak?|si loquaris?]] that is, it is easy for thee to utter many things, since I do not resist thee by avenging myself. Again, as Gregory witnesses, When the wicked speak insults to the wicked, they fall silent the sooner, as they soon hear about themselves such things as they say. But when they accuse the just, they talk the more freely the less they are refuted: for the just do not return insults, even when they hear what they are not. Hence the just man can say to such unjust men: [[16:4|I also could speak like you|Poteram et ego similia vestri loqui]]. Above all, when someone is reproved in charity, he ought not to reprove in return, lest he be thought to speak from impatience.

paras.t: Atque utinam esset anima vestra pro anima mea: consolarer vos sermonibus. Interdum pravis hominibus, quia humana informatione et increpatione corrigi aspernantur, divina flagella optanda sunt: quod discrete caritativeque agitur, quia errantis non pœna, sed emendatio desideratur. Nam et Apostolus fornicatorem Satanæ tradidit in interitum carnis, ut spiritus ejus fieret salvus, sicut Corinthiis scribit.
paras.en: [[16:4|and would God your soul were for my soul|Atque utinam esset anima vestra pro anima mea]]: [[16:5|I would comfort you also with words|consolarer vos sermonibus]]. Sometimes divine scourges are to be wished for wicked men, since they scorn to be corrected by human instruction and rebuke: and this is done with discretion and charity, since what is desired is not the punishment of the one who errs, but his amendment. For the Apostle too delivered the fornicator to Satan [[1 Cor 5:5|for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved|in interitum carnis, ut spiritus ejus fieret salvus]], as he writes to the Corinthians.

paras.t: Sed quid agas? Si locutus fuero, non quiescit dolor meus; et si tacuero, non recedit. Hoc dicere habet prælatus, seu alius, qui subjectum seu proximum incorrigibilem cernit: quem sive increpaverit, sive irreprehensum reliquerit, de ejus perversitate tristatur. Unde in Proverbiis inducitur: Vir sapiens, si cum stulto contenderit, sive irascatur, sive rideat, non inveniet requiem sibi. Verumtamen, quia interdum secundum veram discretionis censuram tali loquendum est, et interdum silendum (si enim ex taciturnitate communitas læderetur, non esset silendum): ideo in Proverbiis sapientissimus Salomon scribit: Ne respondeas stulto secundum stultitiam suam, ne efficiaris ei similis. Responde stulto secundum stultitiam suam, ne sibi sapiens videatur. In quibus verbis tangitur una causa loquendi, et una tacendi.
paras.en: But what is one to do? [[16:7|If I speak, my pain will not rest: and if I hold my peace, it will not depart|Si locutus fuero, non quiescit dolor meus; et si tacuero, non recedit]]. A prelate, or anyone else, who sees a subject or a neighbour to be incorrigible, can say this: whether he rebukes him or leaves him unrebuked, he is saddened at his perversity. Hence it is put in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:9|If a wise man contend with a fool, whether he be angry, or laugh, he shall find no rest|Vir sapiens, si cum stulto contenderit, sive irascatur, sive rideat, non inveniet requiem sibi]]. Yet since, by the true judgement of discretion, one must sometimes speak to such a man and sometimes keep silent (for if the community were harmed by silence, one ought not to keep silent), therefore the most wise Solomon writes in Proverbs: [[Prov 26:4|Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest thou be made like him|Ne respondeas stulto secundum stultitiam suam, ne efficiaris ei similis]]. [[Prov 26:5|Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he imagine himself to be wise|Responde stulto secundum stultitiam suam, ne sibi sapiens videatur]]. In these words one reason for speaking is touched on, and one for keeping silent.

paras.t: Nunc autem oppressit me dolor meus. Dolor de peccato proprio et confratrum, omni dolore vitæ hujus quodammodo major est, secundum quod malum culpæ pejus est omni malo pœnæ. Quo dolore homo tanto magis afficitur, quanto in vera Dei ac proximi caritate perfectior fuerit: quo enim Deum plus diligit, eo de ipsius inhonoratione atque offensa cordialius contristatur. Et in nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei. Quemadmodum homo peccando nihil fieri dicitur, sic membra ipsius in nihilum rediguntur, dum arma iniquitatis peccato exhibentur, id est, instrumenta fiunt peccati. Hinc Christus membra scandalizantia docet abscindenda et abjicienda, non utique quantum ad eorum substantiam, sed quoad usum illicitum. Quoniam ergo frequenter omnia aut pene omnia membra nostra fecimus instrumenta peccandi, per quæ Deo tanquam Creatori servire debuimus, dicamus hæc verba cum mentali dolore et emendandi integrali proposito.
paras.en: [[16:8|But now my sorrow hath oppressed me|Nunc autem oppressit me dolor meus]]. Sorrow for one's own sin and that of one's brethren is in a manner greater than every sorrow of this life, inasmuch as the evil of fault is worse than every evil of punishment. And a man is the more affected by this sorrow, the more perfect he is in the true charity of God and of his neighbour: for the more he loves God, the more heartily is he saddened at the dishonour and offence done to Him. [[16:8|and all my limbs are brought to nothing|Et in nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei]]. As a man is said to become nothing by sinning, so his members are brought to nothing when they are yielded as instruments of iniquity unto sin [the words echo Rom 6:13], that is, when they become instruments of sin. Hence Christ teaches that members which scandalize are to be cut off and cast away, not indeed as to their substance, but as to their unlawful use. Since, then, we have often made all or nearly all our members, through which we ought to have served God as our Creator, instruments of sinning, let us say these words with sorrow of mind and a whole purpose of amendment.

paras.t: Rugæ meæ testimonium dicunt contra me. Rugæ nostræ, sunt actionum nostrarum obliquitates, culparum contractiones, ex defectu fluentorum gratiæ orientes, quibus opera nostra bona miscentur et inquinantur, ita ut panno menstruatæ feminæ comparentur. Nempe, ut in Ecclesiaste legitur, Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet. Hæ itaque rugæ in judicio Dei contra nos testimonium perhibent, quod defectuosi et pauperes, omni misericordia sumus jugiter indigentes. Interdum quoque, dum alios corripere inchoamus, testimonium perhibent contra nos, quod inidonei vel minus idonei sumus corripere proximos: objiciturque nobis, et dicitur: Medice, cura te ipsum.
paras.en: [[16:9|My wrinkles bear witness against me|Rugæ meæ testimonium dicunt contra me]]. Our wrinkles are the crookednesses of our actions, the contractions of faults, arising from a failing of the streams of grace, by which our good works are mingled and defiled, so that they are compared to the rag of a menstruous woman. For indeed, as we read in Ecclesiastes, [[Eccles 7:21|there is no just man upon earth, that doth good, and sinneth not|Non est homo super terram qui faciat bonum, et non peccet]]. These wrinkles, then, bear witness against us in the judgement of God that we are defective and poor, continually in need of every mercy. Sometimes too, when we begin to correct others, they bear witness against us that we are unfit, or less fit, to correct our neighbours: and it is cast up to us and said: [[Luke 4:23|Physician, heal thyself|Medice, cura te ipsum]].

paras.t: Porro sequentia, quamvis moraliter de quolibet justo per Job figurato queant exponi, tamen de Christo, cujus Job apertissima fuit figura in lege naturæ, placet nunc ea exponere. Ex qua etiam expositione, et ea quæ præcedenti articulo habita est, facillime innotescit, quomodo de ceteris justis, Christique membris possint intelligi. Quam demum expositionem B. Gregorius plene prosecutus est; sed ea de Christo non explanavit, nisi paululum circa finem.
paras.en: Now what follows, although it could be expounded morally of any just man figured by Job, it pleases me now to expound of Christ, of whom Job was a most manifest figure in the law of nature. And from this exposition, and from the one given in the preceding article, it is very easily seen how these words can be understood of the other just men and members of Christ. That exposition [that is, the moral one] Blessed Gregory followed out in full; but he did not explain them of Christ, except a little towards the end.

paras.t: Itaque Unigenitus Dei, rex Messias, omnium sæculorum salvator, testatur: Suscitatur falsiloquus adversus faciem meam, contradicens mihi, videlicet populus Judæorum, qui coram Pilato clamavit, illo dicente, Regem vestrum crucifigam? Non habemus regem nisi Cæsarem. Et rursus: Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem debet mori, quia Filium Dei se fecit. Hinc in Jeremia habetur: Prævaricatione prævaricata est in me domus Israel, et domus Juda. Negaverunt Dominum, et dixerunt: Non est ipse. De quibus in Daniele prædictum est: Non erit ejus populus, qui eum negaturus est. Quibus illud Osee competit: Prævaricati sunt in me, et ego redemi eos; et ipsi locuti sunt contra me mendacia.
paras.en: So the Only-begotten of God, the King Messias, the Saviour of all ages, testifies: [[16:9|a false speaker riseth up against my face, contradicting me|Suscitatur falsiloquus adversus faciem meam, contradicens mihi]], namely the people of the Jews, who cried out before Pilate when he said, [[John 19:15|shall I crucify your king?|Regem vestrum crucifigam?]] [[John 19:15|We have no king but Caesar|Non habemus regem nisi Cæsarem]]. And again: [[John 19:7|We have a law; and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God|Nos legem habemus, et secundum legem debet mori, quia Filium Dei se fecit]]. Hence we have in Jeremias: [[Jer 5:11|the house of Israel, and the house of Juda have greatly transgressed against me|Prævaricatione prævaricata est in me domus Israel, et domus Juda]]. [[Jer 5:12|They have denied the Lord, and said, It is not he|Negaverunt Dominum, et dixerunt: Non est ipse]]. Of whom it was foretold in Daniel: [[Dan 9:26|the people that shall deny him shall not be his|Non erit ejus populus, qui eum negaturus est]]. To whom that word of Osee applies: [[Osee 7:13|they have transgressed against me: and I redeemed them: and they have spoken lies against me|Prævaricati sunt in me, et ego redemi eos; et ipsi locuti sunt contra me mendacia]].

paras.t: Collegit furorem suum in me. Populus enim Judæorum cum omni impetu iræ, rancoris et impatientiæ Christum invasit, cepit, ligavit, multipliciterque afflixit, atque interfici procuravit, dicens illud Sapientiæ: Contumeliis et tormento interrogemus eum. Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum. Morte turpissima condemnemus eum: promittit enim scientiam Dei se habere, et Filium Dei se nominat. Hinc in die sancto Parasceves furentes clamabant ad præsidem: Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum. Et comminans mihi, infremuit contra me dentibus suis. Quum enim Christus a pontifice adjuratus, dixisset se esse Christum Filium Dei, omnes dixerunt: Reus est mortis. Tunc itaque mortem ei minati sunt, et tanquam atrocissimæ feræ eum nocte illa tractabant, secundum illud Lucæ: Viri qui tenebant illum, illudebant ei, cædentes; et velaverunt eum, et percusserunt faciem ejus.
paras.en: [[16:10|He hath gathered together his fury against me|Collegit furorem suum in me]]. For the people of the Jews, with all the onset of anger, rancour and impatience, fell upon Christ, took Him, bound Him, afflicted Him in many ways, and procured His death, saying that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 2:19|Let us examine him by outrages and tortures|Contumeliis et tormento interrogemus eum]]. [[Wis 2:15|He is grievous unto us, even to behold|Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum]]. [[Wis 2:20|Let us condemn him to a most shameful death|Morte turpissima condemnemus eum]]: for [[Wis 2:13|He boasteth that he hath the knowledge of God, and calleth himself the son of God|promittit enim scientiam Dei se habere, et Filium Dei se nominat]]. Hence on the holy day of the Parasceve [that is, Good Friday] they cried out in fury to the governor: [[John 19:15|Away with him: Away with him: Crucify him|Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum]]. [[16:10|and threatening me he hath gnashed with his teeth upon me|Et comminans mihi, infremuit contra me dentibus suis]]. For when Christ, adjured by the high priest[[Matt 26:63||]], had said that He was the Christ, the Son of God[[Matt 26:64||]], they all said: [[Matt 26:66|He is guilty of death|Reus est mortis]]. Then, therefore, they threatened Him with death, and like the most savage beasts they handled Him that night, according to that of Luke: [[Luke 22:63|the men that held him mocked him and struck him|Viri qui tenebant illum, illudebant ei, cædentes]]; [[Luke 22:64|And they blindfolded him and smote his face|et velaverunt eum, et percusserunt faciem ejus]].

paras.t: Hostis meus terribilibus oculis me intuitus est. Quod licet de toto populo Christum in die Parasceves persequente accipi posset, de Caipha tamen, qui principalis fuit in hoc, potissime sumitur: qui (ut Matthæus refert) indignatione repletus, surrexit de throno, dixitque Christo: Adjuro te per Deum vivum, ut dicas nobis si tu es Christus Filius Dei benedicti. Insuper in Joanne legitur: Exiit Jesus portans spineam coronam et purpureum vestimentum. Et dixit Pilatus Judæis: Ecce homo. Quum ergo vidissent eum pontifices et ministri, clamabant: Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum. Tunc ergo eum horribiliter inspexerunt.
paras.en: [[16:10|my enemy hath beheld me with terrible eyes|Hostis meus terribilibus oculis me intuitus est]]. Though this could be taken of the whole people that persecuted Christ on the day of the Parasceve, it is taken above all of Caiphas, who was the chief in this: who (as Matthew relates), filled with indignation, rose from his throne[[Matt 26:62||]] and said to Christ: [[Matt 26:63|I adjure thee by the living God, that thou tell us if thou be the Christ|Adjuro te per Deum vivum, ut dicas nobis si tu es Christus]] [[Mark 14:61|the Son of the Blessed God|Filius Dei benedicti]]. Moreover we read in John: [[John 19:5|Jesus therefore came forth, bearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment|Exiit Jesus portans spineam coronam et purpureum vestimentum]]. And Pilate said to the Jews: [[John 19:5|Behold the Man|Ecce homo]]. [[John 19:6|When the chief priests, therefore, and the servants had seen him, they cried out|Quum ergo vidissent eum pontifices et ministri, clamabant]]: [[John 19:15|Away with him: Away with him: Crucify him|Tolle, tolle, crucifige eum]]. Then, therefore, they looked on Him with terrible eyes.

paras.t: Aperuerunt super me ora sua exprobrantes: quia, ut in Luca legitur, quum Jesum vinctum præsentassent Pilato, cœperunt accusare illum, dicentes: Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram, et prohibentem tributa dari Cæsari, et dicentem se Christum regem esse. Propter quod ait Salvator in Psalmo: Circumdederunt me vituli multi: tauri pingues obsederunt me; aperuerunt super me os suum, sicut leo rapiens et rugiens. Denique, Christo in cruce pendente, prætereuntes blasphemabant eum, moventes capita sua, et dicentes: Vah! qui destruis templum Dei, et in triduo illud reædificas, salva temetipsum. Si Filius Dei es, descende de cruce. Similiter et principes sacerdotum illudentes eum cum Scribis et senioribus, dixerunt: Alios salvos fecit, se ipsum non potest salvum facere. Si rex Israel est, descendat de cruce. Confidit in Deo; liberet eum nunc, si vult: dixit enim, Quia Filius Dei sum.
paras.en: [[16:11|They have opened their mouths upon me, and reproaching me|Aperuerunt super me ora sua exprobrantes]]: for, as we read in Luke, when they had presented Jesus bound to Pilate, [[Luke 23:2|they began to accuse him, saying: We have found this man perverting our nation and forbidding to give tribute to Caesar and saying that he is Christ the king|cœperunt accusare illum, dicentes: Hunc invenimus subvertentem gentem nostram, et prohibentem tributa dari Cæsari, et dicentem se Christum regem esse]]. Wherefore the Saviour says in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:13|Many calves have surrounded me: fat bulls have besieged me|Circumdederunt me vituli multi: tauri pingues obsederunt me]]; [[Ps 21:14|They have opened their mouths against me, as a lion ravening and roaring|aperuerunt super me os suum, sicut leo rapiens et rugiens]]. Then, as Christ hung on the cross, [[Matt 27:39|they that passed by blasphemed him, wagging their heads|prætereuntes blasphemabant eum, moventes capita sua]], [[Matt 27:40|And saying: Vah, thou that destroyest the temple of God and in three days dost rebuild it: save thy own self. If thou be the Son of God, come down from the cross|et dicentes: Vah! qui destruis templum Dei, et in triduo illud reædificas, salva temetipsum. Si Filius Dei es, descende de cruce]]. [[Matt 27:41|In like manner also the chief priests, with the scribes and ancients, mocking said|Similiter et principes sacerdotum illudentes eum cum Scribis et senioribus, dixerunt]]: [[Matt 27:42|He saved others: himself he cannot save. If he be the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross|Alios salvos fecit, se ipsum non potest salvum facere. Si rex Israel est, descendat de cruce]]. [[Matt 27:43|He trusted in God: let him now deliver him if he will have him. For he said: I am the Son of God|Confidit in Deo; liberet eum nunc, si vult: dixit enim, Quia Filius Dei sum]].

paras.t: Percusserunt maxillam meam. De hoc Marcus scribit: Cœperunt quidam conspuere eum, et velare faciem ejus, et colaphis eum cædere; et ministri alapis eum cædebant. Joannes quoque: Unus ministrorum dedit ei alapam, dicens: Sic respondes pontifici? Insuper ministri Pilati hoc ipsum crudelissime peregerunt, quemadmodum Joannes recitat: Milites plectentes coronam de spinis, imposuerunt capiti ejus; et vestem purpuream circumdederunt ei. Et veniebant ad eum, et dicebant: Ave rex Judæorum. Et dabant ei alapas. De hoc et Sibylla prædixit: Dabunt Domino alapas manibus incestis. Cujus versus ac vaticinia Augustinus in libro de Civitate Dei prosequitur. Satiati sunt pœnis meis: quia tam crudelissimam mortem Christo intulerunt, sicut optaverunt et excogitare quiverunt. Videntesque eum in suppliciis positum, tanto plus gloriabantur, quo eum plus oderant.
paras.en: [[16:11|they have struck me on the cheek|Percusserunt maxillam meam]]. Of this Mark writes: [[Mark 14:65|some began to spit on him and to cover his face and to buffet him|Cœperunt quidam conspuere eum, et velare faciem ejus, et colaphis eum cædere]]; [[Mark 14:65|And the servants struck him with the palms their hands|et ministri alapis eum cædebant]]. John too: [[John 18:22|one of the servants standing by gave Jesus a blow, saying: Answerest thou the high priest so?|Unus ministrorum dedit ei alapam, dicens: Sic respondes pontifici?]] Moreover Pilate's servants did this very thing most cruelly, as John recounts: [[John 19:2|the soldiers platting a crown of thorns, put it upon his head: and they put on him a purple garment|Milites plectentes coronam de spinis, imposuerunt capiti ejus; et vestem purpuream circumdederunt ei]]. [[John 19:3|And they came to him and said: Hail, king of the Jews. And they gave him blows|Et veniebant ad eum, et dicebant: Ave rex Judæorum. Et dabant ei alapas]]. Of this the Sibyl also foretold: They will give blows to the Lord with unclean hands. Augustine goes through her verses and prophecies in the book of the City of God [Book XVIII, ch. 23]. [[16:11|they are filled with my pains|Satiati sunt pœnis meis]]: for they brought upon Christ a death as utterly cruel as they wished and could devise. And seeing Him set in torments, they gloried the more, the more they hated Him.

paras.t: Conclusit me Deus apud iniquum, id est, a scelerato Judæorum Pilatique populo capi ac ligari permisit, juxta illud Joannis: Cohors ergo, et tribunus, et ministri Judæorum comprehenderunt Jesum et ligaverunt. Unde in Threnis habetur: Spiritus oris nostri Christus Dominus captus est in peccatis nostris. Et manibus impiorum me tradidit. Proprio enim Filio non pepercit Pater, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, juxta Apostolum. Et passione jam imminente, Christus dixit Apostolis illud: Ecce appropinquabit hora, et Filius hominis tradetur in manus peccatorum. De quibus ait in Psalmo: Circumdederunt me canes multi; concilium malignantium obsedit me. Et Petrus ait Judæis: Jesum Nazarenum, virum approbatum a Deo in vobis virtutibus, et prodigiis, et signis, quæ fecit per illum Deus in medio vestri: hunc definito consilio et præscientia Dei traditum, per manus iniquorum interemistis.
paras.en: [[16:12|God hath shut me up with the unjust man|Conclusit me Deus apud iniquum]], that is, He permitted me to be taken and bound by the wicked people of the Jews and of Pilate, according to that of John: [[John 18:12|Then the band and the tribune and the servants of the Jews took Jesus and bound him|Cohors ergo, et tribunus, et ministri Judæorum comprehenderunt Jesum et ligaverunt]]. Hence we have in Threni: [[Lam 4:20|The breath of our mouth, Christ the Lord, is taken in our sins|Spiritus oris nostri Christus Dominus captus est in peccatis nostris]]. [[16:12|and hath delivered me into the hands of the wicked|Et manibus impiorum me tradidit]]. For [[Rom 8:32|He that spared not even his own Son, but delivered him up for us all|Proprio enim Filio non pepercit Pater, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum]], according to the Apostle. And when the Passion was now at hand, Christ said that word to the Apostles: [[Matt 26:45|Behold the hour is at hand: and the Son of man shall be betrayed into the hands of sinners|Ecce appropinquabit hora, et Filius hominis tradetur in manus peccatorum]]. Of whom He says in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:17|many dogs have encompassed me: the council of the malignant hath besieged me|Circumdederunt me canes multi; concilium malignantium obsedit me]]. And Peter says to the Jews: [[Acts 2:22|Jesus of Nazareth, a man approved of God among you by miracles and wonders and signs, which God did by him, in the midst of you|Jesum Nazarenum, virum approbatum a Deo in vobis virtutibus, et prodigiis, et signis, quæ fecit per illum Deus in medio vestri]]: [[Acts 2:23|This same being delivered up, by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, you by the hands of wicked men have crucified and slain|hunc definito consilio et præscientia Dei traditum, per manus iniquorum interemistis]].

paras.t: Ego ille quondam opulentus, repente contritus sum. Christus, secundum suam divinitatem, dives est in se ipso divitiis infinitis, quæ sunt simplicissima omnis boni omnisque pulchri superplena simpliciterque perfecta possessio. Porro, secundum assumptam humanitatem, divitior est toto utique universo, imo omni creaturæ prælatus ac dominans. Fuitque plenus in anima omni virtute nullam imperfectionem includente, omni sanctitate, gratia, sapientia, perfectione et gloria ab incarnationis exordio, quantum creatura capere quivit. Sed et gratiis gratis datis fuit repletus, et de plenitudine ejus omnes accipimus. Verumtamen, quantum ad corporalium divitiarum substantiam, pauperrimus fuit, quemadmodum protestatur: Filius hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet. De quo in Zacharia asseritur: Ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam. Ipse autem repente contritus est: quia post maximum honorem sibi in die Palmarum et ante aliquoties exhibitum a plebe Judæorum atque gentilium (juxta illud Lucæ: Quum appropinquaret Jesus ad descensum montis Oliveti, cœperunt omnes turbæ descendentium gaudentes laudare Deum voce magna super omnibus quas viderant virtutibus, voce magna dicentes: Benedictus qui venit rex in nomine Domini; pax in cœlo et gloria in excelsis): post hunc, inquam, honorem, repente in die Parasceves omnes ab eo aversi sunt, ita ut simul omnes clamarent: Sanguis ejus super nos et super filios nostros. Deinde acerbissima morte hunc contriverunt, secundum illud Isaiæ: Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra. Itemque: Dominus voluit eum conterere in infirmitate.
paras.en: [[16:13|I that was formerly so wealthy, am all on a sudden broken to pieces|Ego ille quondam opulentus, repente contritus sum]]. Christ, according to His divinity, is rich in Himself with infinite riches, which are the most simple, overflowing and simply perfect possession of all good and all beauty. Moreover, according to the humanity He assumed, He is richer than the whole universe, indeed set over every creature and ruling it. And from the beginning of the Incarnation He was full in His soul, as far as a creature could receive, of every virtue that includes no imperfection, of all holiness, grace, wisdom, perfection and glory. He was also filled with the graces freely given [that is, gifts such as prophecy or the working of miracles, given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who has them], and [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|de plenitudine ejus omnes accipimus]]. Yet as to the substance of bodily riches He was most poor, as He declares: [[Matt 8:20|the Son of man hath not where to lay his head|Filius hominis non habet ubi caput reclinet]]. Of whom it is said in Zacharias: [[Zach 9:9|he is poor, and riding upon an ass|Ipse pauper, et ascendens super asinam]]. And He was suddenly broken to pieces: for after the very great honour shown Him by the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles on Palm Sunday, and at times before (according to that of Luke: [[Luke 19:37|when he was now coming near the descent of Mount Olivet, the whole multitude of his disciples began with joy to praise God with a loud voice, for all the mighty works they had seen|Quum appropinquaret Jesus ad descensum montis Oliveti, cœperunt omnes turbæ descendentium gaudentes laudare Deum voce magna super omnibus quas viderant virtutibus]], with a loud voice [[Luke 19:38|Saying: Blessed be the king who cometh in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory on high!|dicentes: Benedictus qui venit rex in nomine Domini; pax in cœlo et gloria in excelsis]]): after this honour, I say, on the day of the Parasceve they all suddenly turned away from Him, so that all together cried out: [[Matt 27:25|His blood be upon us and upon our children|Sanguis ejus super nos et super filios nostros]]. Then they broke Him to pieces by a most bitter death, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 53:5|But he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins|Ipse autem vulneratus est propter iniquitates nostras, attritus est propter scelera nostra]]. And again: [[Is 53:10|the Lord was pleased to bruise him in infirmity|Dominus voluit eum conterere in infirmitate]].

paras.t: Tenuit cervicem meam. Hoc plebs Christum capiens, ligans atque in collo percutiens, corporaliter et amaritudinaliter fecit, eum furibunde impellens. Confregit me, totum corpus flagellis dilacerando, violentissime distendendo, ita ut corporis dissolveretur compago, rumperenturque venæ, quemadmodum ait Christus in Psalmo: Dispersa sunt omnia ossa mea; et rursus: Dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea. Et posuit me sibi quasi in signum: quia ad Christi vulnerationem omnes concorditer intenderunt, sicut sagittarii ad signi contactum. Ideo ait in Psalmo: Circumdederunt me sicut aqua tota die; circumdederunt me simul.
paras.en: [[16:13|he hath taken me by my neck|Tenuit cervicem meam]]. This the people did to Christ in body and in bitterness, seizing Him, binding Him and striking Him on the neck, driving Him on in fury [the margin notes beside these lines cannot be read in the scan]. [[16:13|he hath broken me|Confregit me]], tearing His whole body with scourges and stretching it most violently, so that the frame of His body was loosened and the veins burst, as Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:15|all my bones are scattered|Dispersa sunt omnia ossa mea]]; and again: [[Ps 21:18|They have numbered all my bones|Dinumeraverunt omnia ossa mea]]. [[16:13|and hath set me up to be his mark|Et posuit me sibi quasi in signum]]: for all with one accord aimed at the wounding of Christ, as archers at hitting the mark. Therefore He says in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:18|They have come round about me like water all the day: they have compassed me about together|Circumdederunt me sicut aqua tota die; circumdederunt me simul]].

paras.t: Circumdedit me lanceis suis: quia, ut Evangelistæ testantur, plebs illa iniqua venit cum armis, facibus, gladiis et fustibus comprehendere Jesum. Propter quod dixit eis illud Matthæi: Tanquam ad latronem existis cum gladiis et fustibus comprehendere me. Quod et circa crucem fecisse creduntur, quando (ut alibi fertur) unus militum lancea latus ejus aperuit. Convulneravit lumbos meos. A capite namque usque ad pedes eum vulneraverunt flagellis; et sicut beatissima Brigitta in Revelationibus suis conscribit, usque ad costas carnem ejus tenerrimam laceraverunt. Sicque sanguis ejus pretiosissimus undique copiosissime emanavit, juxta id Psalmi: Sicut aqua effusus sum. Non pepercit: imo atrocissime desævit; et effudit in terram viscera mea. Hoc de Christo exponitur hyperbolice, sicut præcedenti articulo de Job fuit expositum.
paras.en: [[16:14|He hath compassed me round about with his lances|Circumdedit me lanceis suis]]: for, as the Evangelists testify, that wicked people came with weapons, torches, swords and clubs to take Jesus[[Matt 26:47||]][[John 18:3||]]. Wherefore He said to them that word of Matthew: [[Matt 26:55|You are come out, as it were to a robber, with swords and clubs to apprehend me|Tanquam ad latronem existis cum gladiis et fustibus comprehendere me]]. And they are believed to have done this at the cross too, when (as is told elsewhere) [[John 19:34|one of the soldiers with a spear opened his side|unus militum lancea latus ejus aperuit]]. [[16:14|he hath wounded my loins|Convulneravit lumbos meos]]. For from the head to the feet they wounded Him with scourges[[Is 1:6||]]; and, as the most blessed Bridget writes in her Revelations, they tore His most tender flesh to the ribs. And so His most precious blood flowed out most abundantly on every side, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 21:15|I am poured out like water|Sicut aqua effusus sum]]. [[16:14|he hath not spared|Non pepercit]]: nay, he raged most cruelly; [[16:14|and hath poured out my bowels on the earth|et effudit in terram viscera mea]]. This is expounded of Christ hyperbolically, as it was expounded of Job in the preceding article.

paras.t: Concidit me vulnere super vulnus. Vulneraverunt enim Christum primo flagellis, deinde spinis, tertio clavis, sicut in Psalmo fatetur: Foderunt manus meas et pedes meos. Et rursus: Super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt. Propter quod ab Isaia de Christo prædictum est: Non est ei species neque decor; et reputavimus eum quasi leprosum. Irruit in me quasi gigas, quando et funibus me ligabant. Hinc loquitur Christus ad Patrem: Super me confirmatus est furor tuus, et omnes fluctus tuos induxisti super me.
paras.en: [[16:15|He hath torn me with wound upon wound|Concidit me vulnere super vulnus]]. For they wounded Christ first with scourges[[Matt 27:26||]], then with thorns[[Matt 27:29||]], thirdly with nails, as He confesses in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:17|They have dug my hands and feet|Foderunt manus meas et pedes meos]]. And again: [[Ps 68:27|they have added to the grief of my wounds|Super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt]]. Wherefore it was foretold of Christ by Isaias: [[Is 53:2|there is no beauty in him, nor comeliness|Non est ei species neque decor]]; [[Is 53:4|and we have thought him as it were a leper|et reputavimus eum quasi leprosum]]. [[16:15|he hath rushed in upon me like a giant|Irruit in me quasi gigas]], when they also bound me with cords[[John 18:12||]]. Hence Christ speaks to the Father: [[Ps 87:8|Thy wrath is strong over me: and all thy waves thou hast brought in upon me|Super me confirmatus est furor tuus, et omnes fluctus tuos induxisti super me]].

paras.t: Saccum consui super cutem meam. Per hoc intelligitur asperitas et paupertas vestium Christi. Propter quod ait in Psalmo: Posui vestimentum meum cilicium. Et denuo: Ego autem quum mihi molesti essent, induebar cilicio. Sic et Isaiæ Dominus dixit: Tolle saccum qui est super lumbos tuos. Et operui cinere carnem meam, id est, usque ad terram prostratus sum, et sedi in pulvere ejus. Nam et in monte Calvariæ mortuorum cineribus non carente, Christus sedisse sic creditur, quousque cruce parata eam ascenderet.
paras.en: [[16:16|I have sowed sackcloth upon my skin|Saccum consui super cutem meam]]. By this is understood the roughness and poverty of Christ's garments. Wherefore He says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:12|I made haircloth my garment|Posui vestimentum meum cilicium]]. And again: [[Ps 34:13|But as for me, when they were troublesome to me, I was clothed with haircloth|Ego autem quum mihi molesti essent, induebar cilicio]]. So too the Lord said to Isaias: [[Is 20:2|loose the sackcloth from off thy loins|Tolle saccum qui est super lumbos tuos]] [Denis's wording is: take away the sackcloth that is upon thy loins]. [[16:16|and have covered my flesh with ashes|Et operui cinere carnem meam]], that is, I was laid low to the ground and sat in its dust. For on Mount Calvary, which was not without the ashes of the dead, Christ is believed to have sat thus until the cross was made ready and He mounted it.

paras.t: Facies mea intumuit a fletu. Certum quod Christus tempore passionis, præ corporali dolore et matris suæ compassione, mentali quoque mœrore de Judæorum excæcatione, et innumerabilium hominum ingratitudine ac perditione, uberrime flevit. Propterea ait in Psalmo: Oculi mei languerunt præ inopia. Et iterum: Quasi lugens et contristatus, sic humiliabar. Apostolus etiam ad Hebræos testatur, quod cum lacrimis preces fudit ad Patrem passione instante. Et palpebræ meæ caligaverunt. Paulatim quippe corporalis visus Christi in cruce defecit, quousque præ doloris angustia eversi sunt oculi ejus clarissimi: sed et guttis sanguinis benedicti a capite in oculos Christi fluentibus, præsertim quum spinis coronaretur, visus ejus caligare incepit.
paras.en: [[16:17|My face is swollen with weeping|Facies mea intumuit a fletu]]. It is certain that Christ, at the time of His Passion, wept most abundantly, for bodily pain and for compassion with His Mother, and also for grief of mind at the blinding of the Jews and at the ingratitude and perdition of countless men. Therefore He says in the Psalm: [[Ps 87:10|My eyes languished through poverty|Oculi mei languerunt præ inopia]]. And again: [[Ps 34:14|as one mourning and sorrowful so was I humbled|Quasi lugens et contristatus, sic humiliabar]]. The Apostle too testifies to the Hebrews that He poured out prayers to the Father with tears when the Passion was at hand[[Heb 5:7||]]. [[16:17|and my eyelids are dim|Et palpebræ meæ caligaverunt]]. For the bodily sight of Christ failed little by little on the cross, until for the anguish of pain His most clear eyes were turned up: and also, as drops of His blessed blood ran from His head into His eyes, above all when He was crowned with thorns, His sight began to grow dim.

paras.t: Hæc passus sum absque iniquitate manus meæ: quia, ut in Isaia legitur, Ipse iniquitatem non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus; et Dominus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum. Vere languores nostros tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit. Qui ait in Psalmo: Quæ non rapui, tunc exsolvebam. Unde in prima sua Canonica loquitur Petrus: Peccata nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum. Quum haberem mundas ad Deum preces, id est Deo acceptissimas atque gratissimas, nulla vel minima culpa permixtas: quibus etiam pro inimicis oravi, præcipue tempore passionis, dicendo illud Lucæ: Pater, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt. Quod ab Isaia erat ita prædictum: Ipse peccata multorum tulit, et pro transgressoribus rogavit. Præterea, de hac precum suarum gratissima Deo munditia ait Salvator: Gratias ago tibi, Pater, quoniam audisti me. Ego autem sciebam quoniam semper me audis.
paras.en: [[16:18|These things have I suffered without the iniquity of my hand|Hæc passus sum absque iniquitate manus meæ]]: for, as we read in Isaias, [[Is 53:9|he hath done no iniquity, neither was there deceit in his mouth|Ipse iniquitatem non fecit, nec inventus est dolus in ore ejus]] [Denis's words here, nec inventus est dolus, are those of 1 Pet 2:22]; and [[Is 53:6|the Lord hath laid on him the iniquity of us all|Dominus posuit in eo iniquitatem omnium nostrum]]. [[Is 53:4|Surely he hath borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows|Vere languores nostros tulit, et dolores nostros ipse portavit]]. He it is who says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:5|then did I pay that which I took not away|Quæ non rapui, tunc exsolvebam]]. Hence Peter says in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 2:24|bore our sins in his body upon the tree|Peccata nostra pertulit in corpore suo super lignum]]. [[16:18|when I offered pure prayers to God|Quum haberem mundas ad Deum preces]], that is, most acceptable and pleasing to God, mixed with no fault, not even the least: with which I prayed even for my enemies, especially at the time of the Passion, saying that word of Luke: [[Luke 23:34|Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do|Pater, ignosce illis, quia nesciunt quid faciunt]]. This had been foretold thus by Isaias: [[Is 53:12|he hath borne the sins of many, and hath prayed for the transgressors|Ipse peccata multorum tulit, et pro transgressoribus rogavit]]. Moreover, of this purity of His prayers, most pleasing to God, the Saviour says: [[John 11:41|Father, I give thee thanks that thou hast heard me|Gratias ago tibi, Pater, quoniam audisti me]]. [[John 11:42|And I knew that thou hearest me always|Ego autem sciebam quoniam semper me audis]].

paras.t: Terra, ne operias sanguinem meum, neque inveniat in te locum latendi clamor meus. Sicut expositum est hoc præinducto articulo de Job, quoad eos qui ipsum pro sua culpa putabant percussum; similiter prorsus exponi potest de Christo, quantum ad infideles, qui ipsum pro suis peccatis asserebant occisum. Contra quos Christus precatur sanguinis sui effusionem non occultari, sed desuper indicari, et omnibus publicari, quare et quomodo passus sit. Similiter clamorem suum, quo voce magna clamavit in cruce ad Patrem, Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me? petit omnibus manifestari, ut sciant cur Pater Christum sic pati reliquit. Insuper, secundum Gregorium, terra Christi sanguinem non abscondit, quoniam peccatores ejus sanguine se redemptos fatentur, et laudant. Ecclesia quoque militans Redemptoris sui passionem, ceteraque mysteria publice prædicat, ejus quoque clamorem et verba omnibus evangelizat: quod in suis epistolis Paulus potissime facit.
paras.en: [[16:19|O earth, cover not thou my blood, neither let my cry find a hiding place in thee|Terra, ne operias sanguinem meum, neque inveniat in te locum latendi clamor meus]]. As this was expounded of Job in the preceding article, with regard to those who thought he had been struck for his own fault, so it can be expounded in just the same way of Christ, with regard to the unbelievers who asserted that He was slain for His own sins. Against them Christ prays that the shedding of His blood be not hidden, but shown from on high and made known to all, why and how He suffered. Likewise He asks that His cry, with which He cried with a loud voice on the cross to the Father, [[Matt 27:46|My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me?|Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me?]] be made manifest to all, that they may know why the Father left Christ to suffer thus. Moreover, according to Gregory, the earth does not hide the blood of Christ, since sinners confess and praise Him for redeeming them by His blood. The Church militant too preaches publicly the Passion of her Redeemer and His other mysteries, and proclaims His cry and His words to all: which Paul does above all in his epistles.

paras.t: Ecce enim in cælo testis meus, scilicet Deus Pater, de quo loquitur Christus in Evangelio: Et qui misit me Pater, testimonium perhibet de me. Hinc in prima Joannis epistola dicitur: Qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Deum, quoniam non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo. Denique Spiritus Sanctus perhibuit testimonium Christo, secundum quod ait in Joanne: Quum autem venerit Paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis a Patre, Spiritum veritatis, qui a Patre procedit, ille testimonium perhibebit de me. Tale enim testimonium perhibuit per Apostolos Spiritus Sanctus de Christo in die Pentecostes ac postea, quod Judæi, qui Christum paulo ante ut seductorem crucifixerunt, pro parte magna converterentur ad ipsum, sicut in Actibus Apostolorum docetur. Et conscius meus in excelsis. Tres enim superbenedictæ et superessentiales Personæ, sibi invicem perfecte et comprehensive sunt cognitæ. Imo trium est una scientia, sicut et una essentia. Ideo in Matthæo fertur: Nemo novit Filium nisi Pater, neque Patrem quis novit nisi Filius. Porro (juxta Apostolum) quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus ejus; et Spiritus est qui scrutatur etiam profunda Dei.
paras.en: [[16:20|For behold my witness is in heaven|Ecce enim in cælo testis meus]], namely God the Father, of whom Christ speaks in the Gospel: [[John 5:37|And the Father himself who hath sent me hath given testimony of me|Et qui misit me Pater, testimonium perhibet de me]] [the margin is illegible here; Denis's words open as John 5:37 does, with the present tense of John 8:18]. Hence it is said in the first epistle of John: [[1 John 5:10|He that believeth not the Son maketh him a liar: because he believeth not in the testimony which God hath testified of his Son|Qui non credit in Filium, mendacem facit Deum, quoniam non credit in testimonium quod testificatus est Deus de Filio suo]]. Then the Holy Ghost bore witness to Christ, according to what He says in John: [[John 15:26|But when the Paraclete cometh, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceedeth from the Father, he shall give testimony of me|Quum autem venerit Paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis a Patre, Spiritum veritatis, qui a Patre procedit, ille testimonium perhibebit de me]]. For the Holy Ghost bore such witness of Christ through the Apostles on the day of Pentecost and afterwards, that the Jews, who a little before had crucified Christ as a seducer, were in great part converted to Him, as is taught in the Acts of the Apostles. [[16:20|and he that knoweth my conscience is on high|Et conscius meus in excelsis]]. For the three superblessed and superessential Persons are known to one another perfectly and comprehensively. Indeed the three have one knowledge, as they have one essence. Therefore it is said in Matthew: [[Matt 11:27|no one knoweth the Son but the Father: neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son|Nemo novit Filium nisi Pater, neque Patrem quis novit nisi Filius]]. Further (according to the Apostle), [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit nisi Spiritus ejus]]; and [[1 Cor 2:10|the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God|Spiritus est qui scrutatur etiam profunda Dei]].

paras.t: Verbosi amici mei. Multi se asserunt veraciter Christianos et Christi amicos, quum tamen ei per impiam vitam rebelles sint atque contrarii, animarumque corruptores, pro quarum salute ille sanguinem fudit. Quibus ait: Verbosi amici mei. Et iterum: Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum cœlorum; sed qui facit voluntatem Patris. Præterea, Apostoli veri Salvatoris amici, tempore Cœnæ multipliciter asserebant se Christum nocte illa non relicturos; nihilo minus paulo post omnes ab ipso fugerunt, et primus eorum ter ipsum negavit. Quantum ergo ad hoc, verbum istud eis utcumque competeret.
paras.en: [[16:21|My friends are full of words|Verbosi amici mei]]. Many assert that they are truly Christians and friends of Christ, while yet by an ungodly life they are rebels against Him and opposed to Him, and corrupters of the souls for whose salvation He shed His blood. To them He says: [[16:21|My friends are full of words|Verbosi amici mei]]. And again: [[Matt 7:21|Not every one that saith to me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven: but he that doth the will of my Father|Non omnis qui dicit mihi, Domine, Domine, intrabit in regnum cœlorum; sed qui facit voluntatem Patris]]. Moreover the Apostles, true friends of the Saviour, declared in many ways at the time of the Supper that they would not forsake Christ that night[[Matt 26:35||]]; nevertheless a little after they all fled from Him[[Matt 26:56||]], and the first of them denied Him three times. As to this, then, that word would in some way fit them.

paras.t: Ad Deum stillat oculus meus. Interiori mentis oculo Christus ut homo, seu anima ejus, Deum Patrem, imo totam superadorandam Trinitatem indesinenter adspexit, et tempore passionis lacrimantibus oculis corporis, se sursum erexit.
paras.en: [[16:21|my eye poureth out tears to God|Ad Deum stillat oculus meus]]. With the inner eye of the mind Christ as man, that is, His soul, looked unceasingly upon God the Father, nay upon the whole Trinity, to be adored above all, and at the time of the Passion, with the eyes of His body weeping, He lifted Himself up on high.

paras.t: Atque utinam sic judicaretur vir cum Deo, id est a Deo, ut scilicet secundum merita sua a Deo susciperet, quomodo judicatur filius hominis cum collega suo in humano judicio: quod non est nisi secundum opera judicari. Hoc de se ipso Christus dicere potuit, æquivalenterque dixit, in quantum naturali timore mortem crucis abhorruit, deprecans Patrem: Mi Pater, si possibile est, transeat a me calix iste. Si enim Pater Christum hominem secundum sua merita judicasset, pœnam ei non permisisset inferri, nec voluntatem ei inspirasset spontanee patiendi, quum ipse Christus omni prorsus caruerit culpa.
paras.en: [[16:22|And O that a man might so be judged with God|Atque utinam sic judicaretur vir cum Deo]], that is, by God, so that he might receive from God according to his merits, [[16:22|as the son of man is judged with his companion|quomodo judicatur filius hominis cum collega suo]] in a human judgement: which is nothing else than to be judged according to one's works. Christ could say this of Himself, and in effect did say it, inasmuch as with natural fear He shrank from the death of the cross, beseeching the Father: [[Matt 26:39|My Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me|Mi Pater, si possibile est, transeat a me calix iste]]. For if the Father had judged Christ the man according to His merits, He would not have allowed punishment to be inflicted on Him, nor inspired in Him the will to suffer of His own accord, since Christ Himself was altogether without any fault.

17.title: Expositio litteralis capituli septimidecimi: Spiritus meus attenuabitur.
17.title_en: Literal exposition of the seventeenth chapter: My spirit shall be wasted

paras.t: Circa finem præcedentis capituli dixit Job: Utinam sic judicaretur vir cum Deo, etc. In quibus verbis insinuavit, quod desiderabile sibi fuisset judicari a Deo secundum propria merita, sicut homo ab homine judicatur. Sed quoniam noverat alia esse judicia Dei, alia hominum: ideo in præsenti capitulo prosequitur, quid sibi immineat pœnæ absque suæ demerito culpæ.
paras.en: Towards the end of the preceding chapter Job said: [[16:22|And O that a man might so be judged with God|Utinam sic judicaretur vir cum Deo]], etc. In these words he suggested that it would have been desirable for him to be judged by God according to his own merits, as man is judged by man. But since he knew that the judgments of God are one thing and those of men another, in the present chapter he goes on to say what punishment hangs over him without the desert of any fault of his.

paras.t: Spiritus meus attenuabitur. Hoc dupliciter accipi potest. Primo, de anima, quæ est spiritus simplex: quæ attenuatur, id est, spiritualiter subtiliatur, propriam imperfectionem, vilitatem, modum et dispositionem ac statum industriose considerando, Dei quoque majestatem, perfectionem et excellentiam sagaciter contemplando: quod senibus potissime competit. Et sic spiritus Job, quando hæc dixit, fuit attenuandus: quia post pauca fuit magnifice illustratus, et in prædictorum consideratione exercitatus. Secundo, accipitur de spiritu, qui est quid corporeum, puta de spiritu vitali, qui a corde egreditur, et ad cuncta membra diffunditur: quo durante, vivit corpus. Quum vero virtus caloris naturalis incipit debilitari in corde, spiritus vitalis attenuatur, id est, minoratur et debilitatur, ut jam vector virtutis et vitæ per corpus diu esse non possit. Hoc ergo Job sibi futurum de proximo suspicabatur. Denique, de spiritu primo modo accepto, in Ecclesiaste scribitur: Revertatur pulvis in terram suam, et spiritus redeat ad Deum qui dedit illum. De spiritu autem secundo modo sumpto, in Sapientiæ libro habetur: Spiritus diffundetur tanquam mollis aer.
paras.en: [[17:1|My spirit shall be wasted|Spiritus meus attenuabitur]] [*attenuabitur*, literally shall be made thin or fine]. This can be taken in two ways. First, of the soul, which is a simple spirit: which is *made fine*, that is, spiritually refined, by diligently considering its own imperfection, vileness, measure, disposition and state, and by shrewdly contemplating the majesty, perfection and excellence of God: which belongs above all to the old. And so the spirit of Job, when he said this, was to be refined: for shortly afterwards he was magnificently enlightened, and exercised in the consideration of these things. Secondly, it is taken of the spirit which is something bodily, namely the vital spirit, which goes out from the heart and is spread to all the members: while it lasts, the body lives. But when the power of the natural heat begins to weaken in the heart, the vital spirit is *thinned*, that is, lessened and weakened, so that it can no longer for long be the carrier of power and life through the body. This, then, Job suspected was soon to befall him. Further, of the spirit taken in the first way it is written in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 12:7|the dust return into its earth|Revertatur pulvis in terram suam]], [[Eccles 12:7|and the spirit return to God, who gave it|et spiritus redeat ad Deum qui dedit illum]]. And of the spirit taken in the second way we have in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 2:3|our spirit shall be poured abroad as soft air|Spiritus diffundetur tanquam mollis aer]].

paras.t: Dies mei breviabuntur: quia incessanter tendunt ad mortem et finem; et quo spiritus vitalis plus deficit, dies vitæ humanæ amplius breviantur; et solum mihi superest sepulcrum, id est, de proximo moriturus sum, nec in hac vita habeo prospera præstolari: quia (ut tactum jam sæpe est) tantis fuit repletus vulneribus, languoribus atque doloribus, quod putavit se protinus obiturum: et naturaliter diu victurus non erat; sed Deus supernaturaliter prolongavit vitam ipsius.
paras.en: [[17:1|my days shall be shortened|Dies mei breviabuntur]]: for they tend unceasingly to death and the end; and the more the vital spirit fails, the more the days of human life are shortened; [[17:1|and only the grave remaineth for me|et solum mihi superest sepulcrum]], that is, I am soon to die, nor have I any prosperity to wait for in this life: for (as has often been touched on already) he was filled with so many wounds, sicknesses and pains that he thought he would die forthwith: and by nature he was not going to live long; but God prolonged his life above nature.

paras.t: Non peccavi. Superius dixit, Peccavi: et, Parce peccatis meis, multaque talia: quomodo ergo nunc ait, Non peccavi? præsertim quum Joannes in sua prima scribit Canonica: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus. Sed hujus solutio frequenter inducta est. Non enim se negat quotidianis venialibus subjacuisse peccatis; verumtamen asserit se non tam graviter mortaliterque peccasse, quod tantam meruerit pœnam, præsertim quum de venialibus suis quotidie pœnitentiam dignam peregerit. Quod qualiter intelligi habeat, in expositione sexti capituli clarius dictum est. Et in amaritudinibus, id est variis amarisque pœnis, moratur oculus meus exterior. De cujus fletu præcedenti capitulo dictum est: Facies mea intumuit a fletu; et iterum: Palpebræ meæ caligaverunt. Vel, oculus interior, in quo est spiritualis mœstitia ex consideratione incommodorum et ex inconvenienti objecto. Sicque Job considerando oculo interiori universa quæ sibi acciderant, corde dolebat, sed moderate; in quo dolore, quia diuturnus fuit, suus oculus morabatur. Itaque ait, Non peccavi, etc., quasi dicat: Quamvis peccando pœnam istam non merui, nihilo minus in ea permaneo. Quo testatur, quod pœna non semper pro culpa infligitur, imo boni interdum puniuntur a Deo effective seu permissive, propter probationem, aut propter exemplum, vel propter gloriam Dei manifestandam; vel ut nunc crescant in gratia, deinceps in gloria; vel ut mali cernentes bonos puniri, perpendant quibus pœnis ipsi sint digni nisi pœniteant.
paras.en: [[17:2|I have not sinned|Non peccavi]]. Above he said: [[Job 7:20|I have sinned|Peccavi]]; and: [[Job 14:16|but spare my sins|Parce peccatis meis]], and many such things: how then does he now say, *I have not sinned*? especially since John writes in his first canonical epistle: [[1 John 1:8|If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves|Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus]]. But the answer to this has often been given. For he does not deny that he has been subject to daily venial sins; but he asserts that he has not sinned so gravely and mortally as to have deserved so great a punishment, especially since he did worthy penance daily for his venial sins. How this is to be understood was said more clearly in the exposition of the sixth chapter[[Job 6:3||]]. [[17:2|and my eye abideth in bitterness|et in amaritudinibus moratur oculus meus]], that is, in various bitter pains, abides my outward eye. Of its weeping it was said in the preceding chapter: [[Job 16:17|My face is swollen with weeping|Facies mea intumuit a fletu]]; and again: [[Job 16:17|and my eyelids are dim|Palpebræ meæ caligaverunt]]. Or it is the inward eye, in which there is spiritual sadness from the consideration of troubles and from an unfitting object. And so Job, considering with his inward eye all that had befallen him, grieved in heart, but with moderation; and in that grief, because it was long, his eye abode. So he says, *I have not sinned*, etc., as if to say: Although I have not deserved this punishment by sinning, I nonetheless remain in it. By this he bears witness that punishment is not always inflicted for guilt; rather the good are sometimes punished by God, by his doing or by his permission, for their testing, or for an example, or to show forth the glory of God; or that they may grow now in grace and afterwards in glory; or that the wicked, seeing the good punished, may consider what punishments they themselves deserve unless they repent.

paras.t: Libera me ab impugnationibus invisibilium et visibilium adversariorum meorum, et a corporis mei doloribus, saltem tam vehementer intensis; et pone me juxta te, id est in participatione aliquali tuæ felicitatis et jucunditatis, ut in te cor meum refloreat, mens mea tibi per contemplationem et dilectionem propinquet, tandem ad cœlestem beatitudinem perducatur, et interim in limbo patrum constituatur. Et cujusvis manus, id est potestas seu actio, pugnet contra me: quia te me protegente, nullus mihi poterit prævalere; et si in tuæ felicitatis participatione me posueris atque servaveris, nullus me ad miserias retrahet. Sic et Psalmista decantat: Dominus protector vitæ meæ, a quo trepidabo? Apostolus quoque ad Romanos: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos?
paras.en: [[17:3|Deliver me|Libera me]] from the assaults of my invisible and visible adversaries, and from the pains of my body, at least when they are so violently intense; [[17:3|and set me beside thee|et pone me juxta te]], that is, in some share of thy happiness and joy, that my heart may flourish again in thee, my mind draw near to thee by contemplation and love, and at length be brought to heavenly beatitude, and meanwhile be placed in the limbo of the fathers. [[17:3|and let any man's hand|Et cujusvis manus]], that is, his power or action, [[17:3|fight against me|pugnet contra me]]: for with thee protecting me, no one will be able to prevail against me; and if thou set me and keep me in a share of thy happiness, no one will drag me back to miseries. So too the Psalmist sings: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?|Dominus protector vitæ meæ, a quo trepidabo?]] And the Apostle to the Romans: [[Rom 8:31|If God be for us, who is against us?|Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos?]]

paras.t: Cor eorum, id est intellectum amicorum meorum contra me disputantium, longe fecisti a disciplina, id est a veritatis notitia, quam quis discit a doctiore, præsertim a te. Qua amici Job caruerunt, errando circa providentiam Dei: quam Deus longe fecit ab eis, quomodo dicitur aliquem indurare, videlicet indirecte, in quantum corda illorum propter eorum peccata non illustravit. Sicque Isaias loquitur: Excæca cor populi hujus. Propterea non exaltabuntur ad veram contemplationem divinorum, ad charismata gratiarum, ad patriam Beatorum, nisi pœnitentiam egerint, conversique fuerint. Cui consonat illud Isaiæ: Non est populus sapiens; propterea non miserebitur ejus qui fecit illum. In Proverbiis quoque habetur: Non invenient me, dicit Dominus, eo quod exosam habuerint disciplinam. Sed et Apostolus protestatur: Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur.
paras.en: Thou hast set [[17:4|their heart|Cor eorum]], that is, the understanding of my friends who dispute against me, [[17:4|far from understanding|longe fecisti a disciplina]] [*disciplina*, teaching or instruction, which the Douay renders *understanding*], that is, from the knowledge of the truth which one learns from someone more learned, above all from thee. This Job's friends lacked, erring about the providence of God: and God set it far from them in the way in which he is said to harden someone, namely indirectly, inasmuch as he did not enlighten their hearts because of their sins. And so Isaias says: [[Is 6:10|Blind the heart of this people|Excæca cor populi hujus]]. [[17:4|therefore they shall not be exalted|Propterea non exaltabuntur]] to the true contemplation of divine things, to the gifts of graces, to the fatherland of the Blessed, unless they do penance and are converted. With this agrees that saying of Isaias: [[Is 27:11|it is not a wise people, therefore he that made it, shall not have mercy on it|Non est populus sapiens; propterea non miserebitur ejus qui fecit illum]]. In Proverbs too we have: [[Prov 1:28|shall not find me|Non invenient me]], says the Lord, [[Prov 1:29|Because they have hated instruction|eo quod exosam habuerint disciplinam]]. And the Apostle too declares: [[1 Cor 14:38|if any man know not, he shall not be known|Si quis ignorat, ignorabitur]].

paras.t: Prædam pollicetur sociis, id est, Eliphaz aliis duobus secum contra me disputantibus, promittit certam de me victoriam; et quod me in suam redigant voluntatem, sicut redigitur spolium in potestatem prædantis; et oculi filiorum ejus, id est, qui ejus sequuntur errorem, deficient, id est, interiores illorum oculi a veritatis notitia, vereque beatitudinis adeptione deficient: quia, ut ait Salvator, Cæcus si cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt. Posuit me quasi in proverbium vulgi, et exemplum sum coram eis: id est, Eliphaz asserendo quod temporales adversitates non infliguntur nisi pro culpa, nec maxima nisi pro maxima culpa, et ex consequenti, quod ego qui maximis adversitatibus plenus sum, gravissimis peccatis subjaceo: hæc, inquam, asserendo, posuit me in proverbium vulgi, ita ut vulgares ex me forment proverbium, dicendo: Sicut Job fecit, ita recepit; vel aliquid simile. Sicque factus sum exemplum et forma maledicendi alicui, ita ut dicant: Accidat tibi sicut accidit Job. Sic autem justum ponere in proverbium et exemplum, est grande peccatum, nec fieri debet nisi peccatoribus maximis. Unde, per Jeremiam Dominus comminatur frequenter obstinatis Judæis: Dabo eos in maledictionem et in proverbium, et in exemplum et in stuporem omnibus regnis terræ.
paras.en: [[17:5|He promiseth a prey to his companions|Prædam pollicetur sociis]], that is, Eliphaz promises the other two who dispute with him against me a sure victory over me, and that they will bring me round to their will, as a spoil is brought into the power of the plunderer; [[17:5|and the eyes of his children|et oculi filiorum ejus]], that is, of those who follow his error, [[17:5|shall fail|deficient]]: that is, their inward eyes shall fall short of the knowledge of the truth and of the attaining of true beatitude: for, as the Saviour says, [[Matt 15:14|if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit|Cæcus si cæco ducatum præbeat, ambo in foveam cadunt]] [[17:6|He hath made me as it were a byword of the people, and I am an example before them|Posuit me quasi in proverbium vulgi, et exemplum sum coram eis]]: that is, Eliphaz, by asserting that temporal adversities are inflicted only for guilt, and the greatest only for the greatest guilt, and consequently that I, who am full of the greatest adversities, am under the most grievous sins: by asserting this, I say, he has made me a byword of the people, so that common folk make a proverb of me, saying: As Job did, so he received; or something like it. And so I am made an example and a pattern for cursing someone, so that they say: May it befall thee as it befell Job. To make a just man a byword and an example in this way is a great sin, and should not be done except to the greatest sinners. Hence the Lord often threatens the obstinate Jews through Jeremias: I will give them up to be a curse and a byword, an example and an astonishment to all the kingdoms of the earth[[Jer 24:9||]][[Jer 29:18||]] [Denis gives the sense of these threats; no margin reference was read here].

paras.t: Caligavit ad indignationem oculus meus, id est, ex pœna mihi inflicta, quæ quasi indignatio Dei contra me reputatur, oculus meus sic flevit, quod caligavit. Hoc est quod præcedenti dixit capitulo: Palpebræ meæ caligaverunt. Sic quoque superius ait Job: Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum. Et membra mea quasi in nihilum redacta sunt. Hoc est quod præcedenti capitulo dixit: In nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei. Quod ibi satis reor expositum. Thomas exponit hæc aliter, dicens: Ad zelum justorum pertinet, contra falsitatem et injustitiam indignari. Ideo Job contra errores amicorum suorum indignans, disseruit: Caligavit, id est, turbatus est ad indignationem præfatam, oculus meus interior, id est ratio videns veritatem suppeditari. Ira quippe per vitium, rationem excæcat; sed ira per zelum, hanc turbat, lumen rationis aliqualiter obnubilando, ita quod quasi caligat. Et membra mea quasi in nihilum redacta sunt. Vehementes enim animæ passiones, ut ira et indignatio, valde redundant in corpus, et si corpus sit debile, illud quasi deficere faciunt. Unde primo Machabæorum libro describitur, quod Mathathias cernens Judæum idolis sacrificantem, doluit, et contremuerunt renes ejus.
paras.en: [[17:7|My eye is dim through indignation|Caligavit ad indignationem oculus meus]], that is, from the punishment inflicted on me, which is reckoned as it were God's indignation against me, my eye has so wept that it has grown dim. This is what he said in the preceding chapter: [[Job 16:17|and my eyelids are dim|Palpebræ meæ caligaverunt]]. So too Job said above: [[Job 6:4|For the arrows of the Lord are in me, the rage whereof drinketh up my spirit|Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum]]. [[17:7|and my limbs are brought as it were to nothing|Et membra mea quasi in nihilum redacta sunt]]. This is what he said in the preceding chapter: [[Job 16:8|and all my limbs are brought to nothing|In nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei]]. Which I think was sufficiently expounded there. Thomas expounds these words otherwise, saying: It belongs to the zeal of the just to be indignant against falsehood and injustice. So Job, indignant at the errors of his friends, declared: *is dim*, that is, is troubled to the said indignation, *my eye* within, that is, reason, seeing the truth trodden under. For anger moved by vice blinds the reason; but anger moved by zeal troubles it, somewhat clouding the light of reason, so that it is as it were dim. *And my limbs are brought as it were to nothing.* For the vehement passions of the soul, such as anger and indignation, overflow greatly into the body, and if the body is weak they make it as it were faint. Hence it is described in the first book of Machabees that Mathathias, seeing a Jew sacrificing to idols, [[1 Mach 2:24|was grieved, and his reins trembled|doluit, et contremuerunt renes ejus]].

paras.t: Stupebunt justi super hoc, id est, vehementer admirabuntur de supplantatione veritatis et æquitatis, et amicorum meorum erroribus; et innocens, id est simplex et purus veri et æqui amator, contra hypocritam suscitabitur, id est, animo inflammabitur contra hominem fictum et fraudulentum, qui sub specie veritatis atque justitiæ, ita veritatem et æquitatem subvertit. Ideo dicit Psalmista: Innocentes et recti adhæserunt mihi, quia sustinui te. Sic tertio Regum, Micheas propheta contra pseudo succensus, dicit ad Achab: Dominus dedit spiritum mendacii in ore omnium prophetarum tuorum. Similitudo enim et amor complacentiam gignunt; dissimilitudo vero et odium displicentiam introducunt. Idcirco purus veritatis et æquitatis amator, contra hypocritam ejusque falsitates displicentiam concipit, et resistit.
paras.en: [[17:8|The just shall be astonished at this|Stupebunt justi super hoc]], that is, they will wonder greatly at the overthrow of truth and equity, and at the errors of my friends; [[17:8|and the innocent|et innocens]], that is, the simple and pure lover of what is true and right, [[17:8|shall be raised up against the hypocrite|contra hypocritam suscitabitur]], that is, will be inflamed in mind against the feigning and deceitful man who, under the appearance of truth and justice, thus overthrows truth and equity. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 24:21|The innocent and the upright have adhered to me: because I have waited on thee|Innocentes et recti adhæserunt mihi, quia sustinui te]] So in the third book of Kings the prophet Micheas, kindled against the false prophets, says to Achab: [[3 Kings 22:23|the Lord hath given a lying spirit in the mouth of all thy prophets|Dominus dedit spiritum mendacii in ore omnium prophetarum tuorum]]. For likeness and love beget pleasure; but unlikeness and hatred bring in displeasure. Therefore the pure lover of truth and equity conceives displeasure against the hypocrite and his falsehoods, and resists them.

paras.t: Et tenebit justus viam suam, id est, a rectitudine æquitatis et veritatis defensione justaque conversatione non declinabit amore aut odio vel simili passione, in quantum justus: quamvis ex humana fragilitate possit deficere, justitiamque amittere, et se veritati opponere. Justi namque est regia via incedere, bono tenaciter adhærere, et neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram divertere, quia de ratione justitiæ est rectitudo. Propterea Isaias inducit: Semita justi recta est, rectus callis justi ad ambulandum. De qua via loquitur alibi: Hæc via; ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram. Justitia ergo figit mentem in bono. Ideoque in Proverbiis dicitur: Justus quasi fundamentum æternum.
paras.en: [[17:9|And the just man shall hold on his way|Et tenebit justus viam suam]], that is, he will not turn aside from the rightness of equity, from the defence of truth and from just living, through love or hatred or any like passion, inasmuch as he is just: although through human frailty he may fail, lose justice, and set himself against the truth. For it belongs to the just man to go by the king's highway[[Num 21:22||]], to cleave tenaciously to the good, and to turn aside neither to the right hand nor to the left, for rightness is of the very notion of justice. Therefore Isaias brings in: [[Is 26:7|The way of the just is right, the path of the just is right to walk in.|Semita justi recta est, rectus callis justi ad ambulandum.]] Of which way he speaks elsewhere: [[Is 30:21|This is the way, walk ye in it: and go not aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left|Hæc via; ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dexteram neque ad sinistram]]. Justice, then, fixes the mind in the good. And so it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 10:25|the just is as an everlasting foundation|Justus quasi fundamentum æternum]].

paras.t: Et mundis manibus addet fortitudinem. Si quod ait, Mundis manibus, sit dativi casus, sensus est, quod justus augebit fortitudinem eorum, qui mundarum sunt manuum, id est conversationis sinceræ. Tales etenim diligit et confortat adsistendo pro viribus, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Omnis homo simili sibi sociabitur. Similitudo quippe causat amorem, et amor communionem ac unionem. Porro, si quod ait, Mundis manibus, sit ablativi casus, sensus est, quod justus sibi ipsi addet fortitudinem, in virtute justitiæ proficiendo, mundis manibus, id est virtuosis operibus. Virtutes namque per exercitium actuum suorum conservantur, foventur et perficiuntur, sicut communiter habitus per opera. Unde in Apocalypsi habetur: Justus justificetur adhuc, et sanctus sanctificetur adhuc. In hoc itaque consistit noster profectus, ut a quotidianis impuritatibus nostris quotidie emundemur, atque in bonis quæ agimus perficiamur, eadem quotidie perfectius exhibendo, et bonis operibus bona addendo. Hinc ait Salvator: Omnem qui fert fructum, purgabit eum Pater, ut fructum plus afferat.
paras.en: [[17:9|and he that hath clean hands shall be stronger and stronger|Et mundis manibus addet fortitudinem]] [the Latin is literally *and he shall add strength to clean hands*, or *by clean hands*: Denis weighs both readings]. If *to clean hands* is in the dative case, the sense is that the just man will increase the strength of those who are of clean hands, that is, of sincere life. For he loves such men and strengthens them by standing by them as far as he can, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 13:20|every man shall associate himself to his like|Omnis homo simili sibi sociabitur]]. For likeness causes love, and love communion and union. But if *with clean hands* is in the ablative case, the sense is that the just man will add strength to himself, advancing in the virtue of justice *with clean hands*, that is, with virtuous works. For the virtues are preserved, fostered and perfected by the exercise of their acts, as habits in general are by works. Hence we have in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:11|he that is just, let him be justified still: and he that is holy, let him be sanctified still|Justus justificetur adhuc, et sanctus sanctificetur adhuc]]. In this, then, consists our progress: that we be cleansed daily from our daily impurities, and be perfected in the good things we do, showing them forth daily more perfectly, and adding good to good works.
