Hence the Saviour says: [[John 15:2|every one that beareth fruit, he will purge it, that it may bring forth more fruit|Omnem qui fert fructum, purgabit eum Pater, ut fructum plus afferat]].

paras.t: Igitur, vos omnes tres amici mei, qui hic estis, et præsentes qui vobis consentiunt, convertimini, a falsitate ad veritatem, ab injustitia ad virtutem; et venite mentali accessu, id est, diligenter attendite. De quo adventu ait Psalmista: Venite, filii, audite me. Et non inveniam in vobis ullum sapientem. Superius Eliphaz dixit ad Job: Quid nosti quod ignoremus? Cujus præsumptio his verbis reprimitur. Sed quum sapientia sit divinorum cognitio, quomodo amici Job sapientes non erant, qui jam tot vera et alta de Deo locuti sunt? Et respondendum, quod aliquo modo sapientes fuerunt, sicut et magni philosophi; sed quia eorum sapientiæ periculosi errores circa providentiam Dei et alia quædam fuerunt permixti, hoc loco sapientes esse negantur. Diversi enim sunt gradus sapientiæ, et variis modis sapiens quis vocatur.
paras.en: [[17:10|Wherefore be you all|Igitur, vos omnes]], my three friends who are here, and those present who agree with you, [[17:10|converted|convertimini]] from falsehood to truth, from injustice to virtue; [[17:10|and come|et venite]] by the approach of the mind, that is, attend diligently. Of this coming the Psalmist says: [[Ps 33:12|Come, children, hearken to me|Venite, filii, audite me]]. [[17:10|and I shall not find among you any wise man|Et non inveniam in vobis ullum sapientem]]. Above, Eliphaz said to Job: [[Job 15:9|What knowest thou that we are ignorant of?|Quid nosti quod ignoremus?]] His presumption is checked by these words. But since wisdom is the knowledge of divine things, how were Job's friends not wise, who had already said so many true and lofty things about God? The answer is that in some way they were wise, as the great philosophers also were; but because dangerous errors about the providence of God and certain other things were mixed in with their wisdom, in this place they are denied to be wise. For there are different degrees of wisdom, and one is called wise in various ways.

paras.t: Consequenter documenta attentione digna proponit, ad quorum advertentiam illos jam excitavit. Dies mei transierunt, id est, pro magna parte elapsi sunt: imo omnes dies quibus vixi usque in præsens, esse jam desierunt, quum in successivis idem sit esse et fieri; cogitationes meæ dissipatæ sunt, id est ab unione earum in Deum fractæ, et in diversa partitæ, hinc inde vagantes, meque a stabili divinorum contemplatione impedientes, ex sollicitudinibus, doloribus atque angustiis quibus premor, quæ mentis quietem et libertatem in Deo impediunt. Nam pluribus intentus, minor est ad singula sensus. Unde, quo anima circa plura distrahitur, eo ad contemplandum debilior redditur. Propter quod Christus loquitur Marthæ: Martha, Martha, sollicita es, et turbaris erga plurima. Torquentes cor meum. Tales enim cogitationes dispertitæ, anxiæ atque sollicitæ, mentem affligunt: per eas namque apprehenduntur nociva, adversa, amara, quorum apprehensio est pœnalis. Unde et Christus divitias nominat spinas, propter sollicitudines eis adjunctas.
paras.en: Next he sets forth teachings worthy of attention, to the heeding of which he has just roused them. [[17:11|My days have passed away|Dies mei transierunt]], that is, for the most part they have slipped away: nay, all the days I have lived until now have already ceased to be, since in successive things to be and to come to be are the same [that is, a thing that exists by succession, like time, exists only in its passing]; [[17:11|my thoughts are dissipated|cogitationes meæ dissipatæ sunt]], that is, broken off from their union in God and divided among diverse things, wandering this way and that, and hindering me from the steady contemplation of divine things, because of the cares, pains and anguish by which I am pressed, which hinder the quiet and freedom of the mind in God. For one intent on many things has less sense for each. Hence the more the soul is distracted about many things, the weaker it is made for contemplation. For which reason Christ says to Martha: [[Luke 10:41|Martha, Martha, thou art careful and art troubled about many things|Martha, Martha, sollicita es, et turbaris erga plurima]]. [[17:11|tormenting my heart|Torquentes cor meum]]. For such thoughts, divided, anxious and full of care, afflict the mind: for through them harmful, adverse and bitter things are apprehended, and the apprehension of these is painful. Hence Christ too calls riches thorns, because of the cares joined to them[[Matt 13:22||]][[Luke 8:14||]].

paras.t: Noctem verterunt in diem, id est, solitam noctis quietem, videlicet dormitionem, mihi abstulerunt, eamque mihi in laborem diei et inquietudinem vigiliarum verterunt. Tales enim cogitationes fecerunt ipsum Job insomnes ducere noctes, quæ sibi laboriosæ seu molestæ fuerunt. Hinc ait supra: Noctes laboriosas enumeravi mihi. Si dormiero, dicam: Quando consurgam? Et rursum exspectabo vesperam. Unde subjungitur, et rursum post tenebras spero lucem: id est, quoniam tempus noctis mihi molestum est non valenti dormire, spero et cupio cito fieri diem, in quo cor relevatur ex lucis adspectu, corporis motu, et hominum societate ac varia occupatione.
paras.en: [[17:12|They have turned night into day|Noctem verterunt in diem]], that is, they have taken from me the usual rest of the night, namely sleep, and have turned it for me into the labour of the day and the restlessness of watching. For such thoughts made Job himself pass sleepless nights, which were toilsome and grievous to him. Hence he said above: [[Job 7:3|and have numbered to myself wearisome nights|Noctes laboriosas enumeravi mihi]]. [[Job 7:4|If I lie down to sleep, I shall say: When shall I rise? and again, I shall look for the evening|Si dormiero, dicam: Quando consurgam? Et rursum exspectabo vesperam]]. Hence it is added: [[17:12|and after darkness I hope for light again|et rursum post tenebras spero lucem]]: that is, since the time of night is grievous to me, who cannot sleep, I hope and long for the day to come soon, in which the heart is relieved by the sight of the light, the movement of the body, the company of men and various occupations.

paras.t: Si sustinuero, id est, quamvis hæc omnia patienter pertulero, nihilo minus infernus domus mea est, id est, ad limbum patrum descendam, quantum ad animam. Quod autem limbus appelletur infernus, dictum est sæpe. De quo in Genesi Jacob patriarcha: Descendam, inquit, ad filium meum lugens in infernum. Siquidem, pretio redemptionis humanæ nondum soluto, et janua regni necdum aperta, patres descenderunt in limbum. In tenebris, id est magnis adversitatibus atque suppliciis, stravi lectulum meum, id est locum quo ad dormiendum me pono. Vel istud refertur ad limbum patrum, in quo lectulus fuit, id est quies a pœna sensus, certaque spes felicitatis æternæ. Erant tamen tenebræ ibi, id est carentia lucis beatæ. Job ergo adhuc vivens, in limbo lectulum suum stravit, id est, bene vivendo mansionem sibi ibi promeruit.
paras.en: [[17:13|If I wait|Si sustinuero]], that is, although I bear all these things patiently, none the less [[17:13|hell is my house|infernus domus mea est]], that is, I shall go down to the limbo of the fathers as to my soul. That limbo is called hell has often been said. Of it the patriarch Jacob says in Genesis: [[Gen 37:35|I will go down to my son into hell|Descendam, inquit, ad filium meum lugens in infernum]]. For since the price of human redemption was not yet paid, and the gate of the kingdom not yet opened, the fathers went down into limbo. [[17:13|in darkness|In tenebris]], that is, in great adversities and torments, [[17:13|I have made my bed|stravi lectulum meum]], that is, the place where I lay myself down to sleep. Or this refers to the limbo of the fathers, in which there was a bed, that is, rest from the pain of sense [that is, from positive torment, as distinct from the loss of the vision of God], and a sure hope of eternal happiness. Yet there was darkness there, that is, the lack of the blessed light. Job, then, while still living, made his bed in limbo, that is, by living well he merited a dwelling for himself there.

paras.t: Putredini, id est immundo, infecto, putrescentique semini, dixi, per recognitionem mentalem: Pater meus es, quia ex tali sum semine natus. Denique, in generatione semen patris se habet per modum agentis, quum in ipso vis formativa ponatur: propter quod a Platone dicitur, parvus pater. Unde superius ait Job: Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? Mater mea, id est, putredinem etiam dixi matrem meam. Mater enim ministrat semen quod est generationis materia, et per modum passivi se habet. Quod item instar seminis patris impurum atque infectum est, putredinem habens, secundum Albertum: juxta illud Sapientiæ, Coagulatus sum in sanguine ex semine hominis, et delectamento somni conveniente. Et soror mea, vermibus, id est, vermes vocavi sorores, quia de eadem putredine mecum nati aut nascituri sunt, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico legitur: Quum morietur homo, hæreditabit serpentes, et bestias, et vermes. Insuper, Thomas istud exponens, sic ait: Sicut homo a parentibus originem trahit, ex qua cum eis affinitatem habet; ita in sepulcro in putredinem et vermes resolvitur, qui ex ejus corpore generantur; propter quod affinitatem et propinquitatem habet ad eos. Verumtamen expositio ista non exprimit, cur distincte prolatum est, pater, mater, soror. Ex hoc enim quod vermes oriuntur ex corpore hominis, ejus pater et mater non appellantur.
paras.en: [[17:14|I have said to rottenness|Putredini dixi]], that is, to the unclean, infected and rotting seed, I have said by the mind's acknowledgment: [[17:14|Thou art my father|Pater meus es]], because I was born of such seed. Further, in generation the seed of the father acts in the manner of an agent, since the formative power is placed in it: for which reason Plato calls it a little father. Hence Job said above: [[Job 14:4|Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed?|Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine?]] [[17:14|my mother|Mater mea]], that is, I have also called rottenness my mother. For the mother supplies the seed which is the matter of generation, and acts in the manner of something passive. And this too, like the father's seed, is impure and infected, having rottenness in it, according to Albert: according to that saying of Wisdom: [[Wis 7:2|I was compacted in blood, of the seed of man, and the pleasure of sleep concurring|Coagulatus sum in sanguine ex semine hominis, et delectamento somni conveniente]] [[17:14|and my sister|Et soror mea]], [[17:14|to worms|vermibus]], that is, I have called worms my sisters, because they are born, or will be born, of the same rottenness as I, as is read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:13|For when a man shall die, he shall inherit serpents, and beasts, and worms|Quum morietur homo, hæreditabit serpentes, et bestias, et vermes]] Moreover, Thomas, expounding this, says: As a man draws his origin from his parents, and thereby has kinship with them, so in the grave he is resolved into rottenness and worms, which are generated from his body; and for this reason he has kinship and nearness to them. Yet this exposition does not express why *father*, *mother*, *sister* are said distinctly. For from the fact that worms arise from a man's body, they are not called his father and mother.

paras.t: Ubi est ergo nunc præstolatio mea, id est bonum quod finaliter spero seu præstolor? tanquam dicat: Quum tanta sit vilitas mei corporis et brevitas mei temporis, bonum a me finaliter desideratum, non est temporale aut corporale, sed spirituale et æternale, videlicet Deus sublimis et benedictus. Et patientiam meam, qua tanta adversa æquanimiter tolero, quis considerat? quasi dicat: Nullus amicorum meorum, vel cum eis præsentium, eam perpendit, nec ejus præmium pensat: sed Deus omnia bene disponit. Ideo subditur: In profundissimum infernum, id est in locum inferni valde profundum respectu habitationis præsentis, puta in limbum: qui etiam profundissimus appellatur non absolute, sed respective. Nam respectu cœli terra profunda est, sepulcrum profundius, limbus autem profundissimus: sic tamen, ut superlativus iste non denotet excessum comparationis in locis inferni, ut se dicat ad locum damnatorum iturum. Descendent omnia mea, id est anima cum universis meritis suis ac viribus: quia in anima separata etiam inferiores potentiæ radicaliter ac virtualiter manent. Quidam, per profundissimum infernum, intelligunt sepulcrum: quod ineptum videtur, quia et expositio illa ex inepto censetur fundamento prodire. Putasne saltem ibi erit requies mihi? quasi dicat: Imo utique ibi a vitæ hujus doloribus adversitatibusque quiescam, et in certa spe repausabo. Verumtamen ait, Putasne? sobrie loquens: quia secundum communem legem, de felicitate nemo viator securus est, nisi ex revelatione divina, seu certificatione superna, vel inspiratione occulta.
paras.en: [[17:15|Where is now then my expectation|Ubi est ergo nunc præstolatio mea]], that is, the good that I finally hope for or await? as if to say: Since the vileness of my body is so great and the shortness of my time, the good I finally desire is not temporal or bodily, but spiritual and eternal, namely God, most high and blessed. [[17:15|my patience|Et patientiam meam]], by which I bear such great adversities with equanimity, [[17:15|who considereth|quis considerat?]] as if to say: None of my friends, or of those present with them, weighs it, nor thinks of its reward: but God disposes all things well. Therefore it is added: [[17:16|into the deepest pit|In profundissimum infernum]] [literally *into the deepest hell*], that is, into a place of hell very deep in respect of our present dwelling, namely into limbo: which is called *deepest* not absolutely but relatively. For in respect of heaven the earth is deep, the grave deeper, and limbo deepest: yet in such a way that this superlative does not denote the highest degree of comparison among the places of hell, as though he said he would go to the place of the damned. [[17:16|All that I have shall go down|Descendent omnia mea]], that is, the soul with all its merits and powers: for in the separated soul the lower powers too remain in their root and virtually. Some understand the grave by *the deepest hell*: which seems unfitting, for that exposition too is judged to proceed from an unfitting foundation. [[17:16|thinkest thou that there at least I shall have rest?|Putasne saltem ibi erit requies mihi?]] as if to say: Yes, surely there I shall rest from the pains and adversities of this life, and repose in sure hope. Yet he says *thinkest thou?*, speaking soberly: for by the common law no wayfarer is sure of his happiness, except by divine revelation, or assurance from above, or hidden inspiration.

17.title: De moralitate ejusdem capituli septimidecimi.
17.title_en: On the moral sense of the same seventeenth chapter

paras.t: Spiritus meus attenuabitur. Hoc cuilibet homini viatori justo ac sapienti, tribulationibus exposito, competit: qui quanto se morti amplius appropinquare perpendit, eo se ipsum subtilius discutit, a grossis et terrenis affectibus se magis extenuat, gloriam Beatorum profundius speculari, et superaltissimi Dei proprietates sincerius contemplari conatur. Dies mei breviabuntur. Quo quis futuræ vitæ æternitatem sapientialius pensat, eo tempus quo vivit hic, brevius arbitratur. Nunquam ergo in Dei obsequio attædiemur, nec quasi de temporis longiturnitate gravemur; sed et eo minus afficiamur ad ea quæ mundi sunt, quo majorem temporis nostri partem fluxisse conspicimus. Quod si universa ista caduca atque carnalia Dei amore ut stercora aspernamur, nosque de proximo morituros sagaciter opinamur, nihil nobis in sæculo isto superesse dicemus, quam tumulum, sicut subjungitur, et solum mihi superest sepulcrum.
paras.en: [[17:1|My spirit shall be wasted|Spiritus meus attenuabitur]]. This fits any just and wise man who is a wayfarer and exposed to tribulations: the nearer he considers himself to be drawing to death, the more finely he examines himself, the more he thins himself away from gross and earthly affections, and the more he strives to gaze deeply on the glory of the Blessed and to contemplate more purely the attributes of the most high God. [[17:1|my days shall be shortened|Dies mei breviabuntur]]. The more wisely one weighs the eternity of the life to come, the shorter he judges the time he lives here. Let us never, then, grow weary in God's service, nor be burdened as it were by the length of time; but let us be the less affected towards the things of the world, the greater the part of our time we see has flowed away. And if for the love of God we scorn all these perishing and carnal things as dung, and shrewdly reckon that we shall soon die, we shall say that nothing remains to us in this world but a tomb, as is added: [[17:1|and only the grave remaineth for me|et solum mihi superest sepulcrum]].

paras.t: Denique, si quis Deo revelante aut aliquo modo cognoverit se non pro suis affligi peccatis, sed aut pro sua exercitatione, aut aliorum ædificatione, vel ut in gratia plus abundet et gloriosius coronetur, dicere potest: Non peccavi, tam graviter, ut tantam afflictionem meruerim, eo modo quo hoc de beato Job fuit expositum; et in amaritudinibus moratur oculus meus. Multæ enim tribulationes justorum: qui et quotidianos suos veniales defectus velut magna peccata amaritudinaliter plangunt seu dolent tanto plus, quo Creatorem suum ardentiori ac puriori complectuntur amore, quo item copiosius desuper illustrantur. Siquidem, quo mens radiosius illuminatur a Spiritu Sancto, eo gravitatem peccati profundius conspicit, et cordialius deflet. Præterea, quædam est amaritudo vitiosa, quæ est passio animi immoderata, virtuosæ dulcedini mentis contraria. De qua Ecclesiasticus habet: Non est sensus ubi abundat amaritudo. Et Paulus ad Ephesios: Omnis amaritudo, ira, et indignatio, et clamor tollatur a vobis. Nunc autem de bona et pœnitentiali amaritudine est mentio, et de omni dolore virtuose assumpto, quo quis caritative affligitur de sua aliorumque culpa, de malis Ecclesiæ, dilationeque gloriæ: quibus amaritudinibus electi quotidie afficiuntur. De hujuscemodi amaritudine cui divina consolatio præparatur, Salomon loquitur: Cor quod novit animæ suæ amaritudinem, in gaudio ejus non miscebitur extraneus.
paras.en: Further, if anyone has come to know, by God's revelation or in some other way, that he is afflicted not for his own sins, but either for his exercise, or for the edification of others, or that he may abound more in grace and be crowned more gloriously, he can say: [[17:2|I have not sinned|Non peccavi]] so gravely as to have deserved so great an affliction, in the way this was expounded of blessed Job; [[17:2|and my eye abideth in bitterness|et in amaritudinibus moratur oculus meus]]. For [[Ps 33:20|Many are the afflictions of the just|Multæ enim tribulationes justorum]]: who bewail and grieve bitterly over their daily venial failings as though they were great sins, the more so the more ardent and pure the love with which they embrace their Creator, and the more abundantly they are enlightened from above. For the more brightly the mind is illumined by the Holy Spirit, the more deeply it sees the gravity of sin, and the more heartily it bewails it. There is, moreover, a vicious bitterness, which is an immoderate passion of the soul, contrary to the virtuous sweetness of the mind. Of this Ecclesiasticus has: [[Ecclus 21:15|there is no understanding where there is bitterness|Non est sensus ubi abundat amaritudo]]. And Paul to the Ephesians: [[Eph 4:31|Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamour and blasphemy be put away from you|Omnis amaritudo, ira, et indignatio, et clamor tollatur a vobis]]. But here the mention is of good and penitential bitterness, and of every sorrow virtuously taken up, by which one is afflicted in charity for his own and others' guilt, for the evils of the Church, and for the delay of glory: with which bitternesses the elect are touched daily. Of such bitterness, for which divine consolation is prepared, Solomon speaks: [[Prov 14:10|The heart that knoweth the bitterness of his own soul, in his joy the stranger shall not intermeddle|Cor quod novit animæ suæ amaritudinem, in gaudio ejus non miscebitur extraneus]].

paras.t: Libera me. Hoc oramus indesinenter, in Oratione dominica deprecando: Libera nos a malo, videlicet a malo culpæ et pœnæ, ab omni impugnatione atque periculo. Et pone me juxta te. Juxta Deum immensum, ubique vere præsentem, omnia penetrantem, qui solus rerum essentiis illabitur, omnique homini propinquior est quam essentialia ejus principia, tanto plus ponimur, quo ejus sancto amore magis accendimur, et dono sapientiæ clarius ad ipsum contemplandum perfundimur. Etenim incremento gratiæ ac virtutum Deo incircumscriptibili propinquamus. Sed quoniam durante vitæ hujus curriculo, peregrinamur a Domino, per fidem, non per speciem gradientes, ideo in hac vita non perfecte ponimur apud Deum, sed in patria. Idque precamur, ut ibi juxta eum locemur, id est, per speciem ejus supersanctam essentiam contemplemur. Nihilo minus, boni nunc apud Deum poni dicuntur modo præfato. Unde in Numeris Moyses ait: Mane notum faciet Dominus qui ad se pertineant, et sanctos applicabit sibi; et quos elegerit, appropinquabunt ei. Itemque Psalmista: Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo semper, quoniam a dextris est mihi, ne commovear. Et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me, id est, te mihi adsistente et auxiliante per omnia, nullum timebo, nullum curabo, cum Psalmista decantans: Super inimicos meos despexit oculus meus. Hoc est quod Jeremias ait: Dominus mecum est quasi bellator fortis. Propterea qui me persequuntur, cadent et infirmi erunt.
paras.en: [[17:3|Deliver me|Libera me]]. This we pray unceasingly when we beseech in the Lord's Prayer: [[Matt 6:13|deliver us from evil|Libera nos a malo]], namely from the evil of guilt and of punishment, from every assault and danger. [[17:3|and set me beside thee|Et pone me juxta te]]. Beside God, who is immense, truly present everywhere, penetrating all things, who alone enters into the essences of things, and is nearer to every man than his own essential principles, we are set the more, the more we are kindled with his holy love and the more clearly we are flooded with the gift of wisdom for contemplating him. For by increase of grace and virtues we draw near to God, who cannot be circumscribed. But since, while the course of this life lasts, [[2 Cor 5:6|we are absent from the Lord|peregrinamur a Domino]], [[2 Cor 5:7|For we walk by faith and not by sight|per fidem, non per speciem gradientes]], in this life we are not set perfectly beside God, but in the fatherland. And this we pray for: that there we may be placed beside him, that is, may contemplate his most holy essence by sight. Nonetheless the good are said even now to be set beside God in the way described. Hence Moses says in Numbers: [[Num 16:5|In the morning the Lord will make known who belong to him, and the holy he will join to himself: and whom he shall choose, they shall approach to him|Mane notum faciet Dominus qui ad se pertineant, et sanctos applicabit sibi; et quos elegerit, appropinquabunt ei]] And likewise the Psalmist: [[Ps 15:8|I set the Lord always in my sight: for he is at my right hand, that I be not moved|Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo semper, quoniam a dextris est mihi, ne commovear]] [[17:3|and let any man's hand fight against me|Et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me]], that is, with thee standing by me and helping me in all things, I shall fear no one, I shall care for no one, singing with the Psalmist: [[Ps 53:9|my eye hath looked down upon my enemies|Super inimicos meos despexit oculus meus]]. This is what Jeremias says: [[Jer 20:11|the Lord is with me as a strong warrior: therefore they that persecute me shall fall, and shall be weak|Dominus mecum est quasi bellator fortis. Propterea qui me persequuntur, cadent et infirmi erunt]].

paras.t: Cor eorum longe fecisti a disciplina. Omnium superborum et in propriis oculis sapientium, omnium incorrigibilium, rebellium atque carnalium corda Deus permissive longe fecit a disciplina: id est ab instructione divina, de qua ait Joannes: Unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus; itemque, a sapientia et scientia, secundum quod dona sunt Spiritus Sancti, qui a nullo habentur nisi in quo habitat Spiritus Sanctus per caritatem et gratiam gratificantem; insuper, a disciplina, id est correctione et morum compositione, hoc est a patienti susceptione informativæ correptionis, ac satisfactoriæ et justæ punitionis. Tales enim correpti seu debite castigati, indignantur, remurmurant, deterioresque fiunt, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit. Quibus pensandum ac formidandum est, quod ait Scriptura: Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur. Itaque, disciplinam verborum, imo et verberum seu cujuscumque debitæ correctionis, patienter atque hilariter suscipiamus, quia per hoc ad omnem Dei illuminationem et gratiam potissime disponemur. Ideo Ecclesiasticus dicit: Quam bonum est correptum manifestare pœnitentiam! sic enim effugiet peccatum.
paras.en: [[17:4|Thou hast set their heart far from understanding|Cor eorum longe fecisti a disciplina]] [*disciplina*: teaching, and also correction or chastisement, the senses Denis goes on to give]. The hearts of all the proud and of those wise in their own eyes, of all the incorrigible, the rebellious and the carnal, God by permission has set far from *disciplina*: that is, from divine instruction, of which John says: [[1 John 2:27|his unction teacheth you of all things|Unctio ejus docet vos de omnibus]]; and likewise from wisdom and knowledge, as they are gifts of the Holy Spirit, which no one has except one in whom the Holy Spirit dwells by charity and sanctifying grace [*gratia gratificans*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God]; moreover, from *disciplina*, that is, from correction and the ordering of conduct, that is, from the patient acceptance of reproof that forms us, and of punishment that is just and makes satisfaction. For such men, when reproved or duly chastised, take offence, murmur, and become worse, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 15:12|A corrupt man loveth not one that reproveth him|Non amat pestilens eum qui se corripit]]. Let them weigh and fear what Scripture says: [[Prov 13:18|Poverty and shame to him that refuseth instruction: but he that yieldeth to reproof shall be glorified|Egestas et ignominia ei qui deserit disciplinam; qui autem acquiescit arguenti, glorificabitur]]. So let us receive patiently and cheerfully the discipline of words, nay, of blows too, or of any due correction, for by this we shall be disposed above all to every enlightenment and grace of God. Therefore Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 20:4|How good is it, when thou art reproved, to shew repentance! for so thou shalt escape wilful sin|Quam bonum est correptum manifestare pœnitentiam! sic enim effugiet peccatum]]

paras.t: Qui vero præfatam abjicit disciplinam, coram Deo vilis et ignobilis erit, peccatis oppressus, dæmonibus subditus, proprii sensus perversitate seductus. Ideo subditur: Propterea non exaltabuntur ad cœlestia atque æterna a carnalibus et caducis, sed paulo post in ima trudentur inferni. Ideo scriptum est: Sapientiam et disciplinam qui abjicit, infelix est. Denique reprobos longe facit Deus a disciplina, dum eos in præsenti sæculo non flagellat, sed impune ac libere permittit peccare: quod summe pavendum est, et maxima Dei ira. Electos vero in vita hac disciplinat, ut super hoc Deo gratias referant, atque in futuræ beatitudinis spe firmentur. Unde in Sapientia legitur: Disciplinam nobis das, ut bonitatem tuam cogitemus, et speremus misericordiam tuam. Qui ergo cupit veraciter exaltari, proficere, perfici, docilis disciplinabilisque consistat.
paras.en: But he who casts away this discipline will be vile and ignoble before God, weighed down by sins, subject to demons, led astray by the perversity of his own mind. Therefore it is added: [[17:4|therefore they shall not be exalted|Propterea non exaltabuntur]] from carnal and perishing things to heavenly and eternal ones, but shortly afterwards they will be thrust down into the depths of hell. Therefore it is written: [[Wis 3:11|For he that rejecteth wisdom, and discipline, is unhappy|Sapientiam et disciplinam qui abjicit, infelix est]]. Further, God sets the reprobate far from discipline when he does not scourge them in this present world, but lets them sin freely and with impunity: which is to be dreaded above all, and is the greatest wrath of God. But the elect he disciplines in this life, that they may give thanks to God for it, and be strengthened in the hope of future beatitude. Hence it is read in Wisdom: [[Wis 12:22|whereas thou chastisest us|Disciplinam nobis das]], [[Wis 12:22|we may think on thy goodness|ut bonitatem tuam cogitemus]], and [[Wis 12:22|we may hope for thy mercy|speremus misericordiam tuam]]. Let him, then, who desires truly to be exalted, to advance and to be perfected, remain teachable and open to discipline.

paras.t: Prædam pollicetur sociis. Omnis iniquus qui alios cohortatur ad mala, ad proximorum devastationem, ad impugnationem quorumque, sociis suis præstat prævalendi fiduciam, prædam eis promittens. Quod et superiores dæmones tentatores sociis suis dæmonibus faciunt, dum eos ad hominum impugnationem hortantur et dirigunt, illud Isaiæ dicentes: Cito prædare, velociter spolia detrahe. Posuit me quasi in proverbium vulgi. Impius enim justum irridet, diffamat, et quasi aliorum ludum ac fabulam facit. Propter quod Dominus ait in Ezechiele: Factus es eis quasi carmen musicum, quod suavi dulcique sono canitur. Hinc Christus ait in Psalmo: In me psallebant qui bibebant vinum. In Threnis quoque dicitur: Factus sum in derisum omni populo, canticum eorum tota die. Ego sum psalmus eorum.
paras.en: [[17:5|He promiseth a prey to his companions|Prædam pollicetur sociis]]. Every wicked man who urges others on to evil, to the laying waste of their neighbours, to the assailing of anyone at all, gives his companions confidence that they will prevail, promising them a prey. And this the higher demons, the tempters, do to their fellow demons, when they urge and direct them to assail men, saying those words of Isaias: [[Is 8:1|quickly take the prey|Cito prædare]], [[Is 8:1|Take away the spoils with speed|velociter spolia detrahe]]. [[17:6|He hath made me as it were a byword of the people|Posuit me quasi in proverbium vulgi]]. For the wicked man mocks the just, defames him, and makes him as it were the sport and tale of others. For which reason the Lord says in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 33:32|thou art to them as a musical song which is sung with a sweet and agreeable voice|Factus es eis quasi carmen musicum, quod suavi dulcique sono canitur]]. Hence Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:13|they that drank wine made me their song|In me psallebant qui bibebant vinum]]. In Lamentations too it is said: [[Lam 3:14|I am made a derision to all my people, their song all the day long|Factus sum in derisum omni populo, canticum eorum tota die]] [[Lam 3:63|I am their song|Ego sum psalmus eorum]].

paras.t: Caligavit ad indignationem oculus meus. Hoc (secundum Gregorium) fit, dum viri illuminati se a pravis diutius sperni ac indignationi haberi conspiciunt, atque ex hoc de occulti judicii Dei admiratione turbantur, et secretum Dei nequeunt penetrare cur prævalere perversi contra bonorum innocentiam permittuntur. Quis enim non obstupescat, quum Herodias adultera apud temulentum regem saltatu petulantis filiæ obtinet caput Joannis amici Sponsi, prophetæ et plusquam prophetæ, amputari, et ante convivantium ora in disco deferri? Hinc subditur: Stupebunt justi super hoc, illud in Apocalypsi scriptum exclamantes: Magna et mirabilia sunt opera et judicia tua, Domine Deus omnipotens; justæ et veri sunt viæ tuæ, Rex sæculorum. Quis non timebit te, et magnificabit nomen tuum?
paras.en: [[17:7|My eye is dim through indignation|Caligavit ad indignationem oculus meus]]. This (according to Gregory) happens when enlightened men see themselves long despised by the wicked and held in indignation, and are troubled by this through wonder at the hidden judgment of God, and cannot penetrate God's secret, why the perverse are allowed to prevail against the innocence of the good. For who would not be astounded when Herodias the adulteress, before a drunken king, by the dancing of her wanton daughter, obtains that the head of John, the friend of the Bridegroom[[John 3:29||]], a prophet and more than a prophet[[Matt 11:9||]], be cut off and carried in a dish before the faces of the banqueters[[Matt 14:6||]]? Hence it is added: [[17:8|The just shall be astonished at this|Stupebunt justi super hoc]], crying out those words written in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 15:3|Great and wonderful are thy works, O Lord God Almighty. Just and true are thy ways, O King of ages|Magna et mirabilia sunt opera et judicia tua, Domine Deus omnipotens; justæ et veri sunt viæ tuæ, Rex sæculorum]] [[Apoc 15:4|Who shall not fear thee, O Lord, and magnify thy name?|Quis non timebit te, et magnificabit nomen tuum?]]

paras.t: Et tenebit justus viam suam. Viri justi atque perfecti, desuper copiose sapientiali luce perfusi, eo tenacius cohærent justitiæ, mundana contemnunt, ad cœlestia inflammantur, quo impios in hoc mundo amplius prosperari, lætari et promoveri considerant; intuentes occultum Dei judicium, quo perversos dimittit secundum desideria cordis eorum: sicque pensantes quam contemnenda sunt ea quæ reprobis pessimisque ita præstantur, quam item periculosum sit temporaliter prosperari, carnaliter delectari, nec tamen divinitus castigari. Ex his enim certissime atque clarissime constat, quod in vita præsenti non sit finalis remuneratio operum humanorum. Propterea in Ecclesiaste habetur: Peccator ex eo quod centies facit malum, et tamen per patientiam sustentatur, ego cognovi, quod erit bonum timentibus Deum, qui quærunt faciem ejus.
paras.en: [[17:9|And the just man shall hold on his way|Et tenebit justus viam suam]]. Just and perfect men, abundantly flooded from above with the light of wisdom, cleave the more tenaciously to justice, despise worldly things and are kindled towards heavenly things, the more they see the wicked in this world prosper, rejoice and rise; beholding the hidden judgment of God, by which he lets the perverse go [[Ps 80:13|according to the desires of their heart|secundum desideria cordis eorum]]: and so weighing how contemptible are the things thus granted to the reprobate and the worst of men, and also how dangerous it is to prosper in temporal things and delight in carnal things and yet not be chastised by God. For from this it is most certainly and clearly established that the final reward of human works is not in the present life. Therefore we have in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:12|though a sinner do evil a hundred times, and by patience be borne withal, I know from thence that it shall be well with them that fear God, who dread his face|Peccator ex eo quod centies facit malum, et tamen per patientiam sustentatur, ego cognovi, quod erit bonum timentibus Deum, qui quærunt faciem ejus]] [Denis's wording, *who seek his face*, where the Douay has *who dread his face*].

paras.t: Dies mei transierunt. Quilibet nostrum perpendens quam infructuose tempus suum expenderit, atque proponens se fortiter emendare, et perdita recuperare, dicere debet verbum inductum. Insuper, pensans quanta sit suæ instabilitas mentis, quam vagus sit ipse in cogitando, quam dispersus in appetendo, quam circa multa occupatus, distractus, divisus, querulosa dolorosaque voce loquatur: Cogitationes meæ dissipatæ sunt, quum tamen perfectio nostra sit, Deo stabili mente infigi, cogitationes in ipso colligere, affectiones in ipso adunare, sicque mente collecta ac integra eum laudare, amare et honorare in omnibus, quemadmodum scriptum est: Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo, videlicet intellectu atque affectu. Ad quod Deus piissimus nos clementer hortari dignatur per Joelem: Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro. Sed quoniam hoc implere, non est volentis neque currentis, nisi adsistat gratia Dei miserentis, ipsum fideliter jugiterque precemur, ut det gratiam adimplendi quod monet: sed et satagamus ad hoc cooperando gratiæ Dei, et potissime tempore orationis divinique cultus, mente collecti ac stabiles simus, illud Ecclesiastici servantes: Non impediaris semper orare; et: Ante orationem præpara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo qui tentat Deum.
paras.en: [[17:11|My days have passed away|Dies mei transierunt]]. Any one of us, considering how fruitlessly he has spent his time, and resolving to amend himself strongly and to recover what was lost, ought to say the words brought in here. Moreover, weighing how great is the instability of his mind, how wandering he is in thinking, how scattered in desiring, how occupied, distracted and divided about many things, let him say in a complaining and sorrowful voice: [[17:11|my thoughts are dissipated|Cogitationes meæ dissipatæ sunt]]; whereas our perfection is to be fixed on God with a stable mind, to gather our thoughts in him, to unite our affections in him, and so with a collected and whole mind to praise, love and honour him in all things, as it is written: [[Ps 110:1|I will praise thee, O Lord, with my whole heart|Confitebor tibi, Domine, in toto corde meo]], namely with understanding and affection. To this the most loving God deigns mercifully to exhort us through Joel: [[Joel 2:12|Be converted to me with all your heart|Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro]]. But since to fulfil this [[Rom 9:16|is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth|non est volentis neque currentis]], unless the grace of God who shows mercy assists, let us pray to him faithfully and constantly to give the grace to fulfil what he urges: and let us also take pains to co-operate in this with the grace of God, and above all at the time of prayer and of divine worship let us be collected and stable in mind, keeping that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 18:22|Let nothing hinder thee from praying always|Non impediaris semper orare]]; and: [[Ecclus 18:23|Before prayer prepare thy soul: and be not as a man that tempteth God|Ante orationem præpara animam tuam, et noli esse quasi homo qui tentat Deum]]

paras.t: Torquentes cor meum. Homini enim vere devoto tales distractiones tanto plus displicent, pœnalioresque sunt, quanto ex puro Dei amore plus appetit Deo intendere, opus ejus reverenter persolvere, in ejus caritate et gratia semper proficere: sed et animus inordinatus sibi ipsi pœnalis est, sicut ordinata tranquillaque mente nil dulcius. Porro vitiosi et vani in cogitationibus suis perstrepentibus, fluctuantibus quoque desideriis vilissime gloriantur. Quod si boni interdum ex infirmitate aut inadvertentia in aliquo tali culpabiles fuerint, mox ut distractionem et vanitatem suam adverterint, corde tristantur, pœnitent et emendant, quemadmodum in Proverbiorum libro asseritur: Septies cadet justus, et resurget. Unde in Ecclesiastico docetur: Fili, peccasti? ne adjicias iterum; sed et de præteritis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur. Et: Quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata.
paras.en: [[17:11|tormenting my heart|Torquentes cor meum]]. For to a truly devout man such distractions are the more displeasing and painful, the more, out of pure love of God, he desires to attend to God, to perform his work reverently, and always to advance in his charity and grace: and indeed a disordered mind is a punishment to itself, just as nothing is sweeter than an ordered and tranquil mind. But the vicious and vain glory most vilely in their clamorous thoughts and wavering desires. And if the good are sometimes at fault in some such thing through weakness or inadvertence, as soon as they notice their distraction and vanity they are sad at heart, repent and amend, as is asserted in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 24:16|a just man shall fall seven times, and shall rise again|Septies cadet justus, et resurget]]. Hence Ecclesiasticus teaches: [[Ecclus 21:1|My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more: but for thy former sins also pray that they may be forgiven thee|Fili, peccasti? ne adjicias iterum; sed et de præteritis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur]] And: [[Ecclus 21:2|Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent|Quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata]].

paras.t: Noctem verterunt in diem. Quia frequenter per vitiosas et vagas cogitationes anima sic excæcatur, ut vitiorum caliginem judicet esse lucem virtutum, dum mala sub specie boni sibi proposita approbat et acceptat. Talibus dicit Amos: Convertistis in amaritudinem judicium, et fructum justitiæ in absinthium. Et Isaias: Væ qui dicitis bonum malum, et malum bonum; ponentes tenebras lucem, et lucem tenebras. Denique tales ambulant per viam fallacem, de qua in Proverbiis legitur: Est via quæ videtur homini justa, et novissima ejus deducunt ad mortem. Non ergo securum est proprio stare judicio, sed superiorum obtemperare sententiis, nec cordis secreta eis abscondere, qui discretione ornantur. Et rursum post tenebras spero lucem, id est, quum errasse atque peccasse, sicque tenebras erroris et peccati incidisse me video, pœnitere propono, lucem gratiæ recurrere confido, et post adversa ac tristia consolationem beatitudinemque exspecto, orans illud Ecclesiastici: Miserere nostri, Deus omnium, et respice nos, et ostende nobis lucem miserationum tuarum. Hinc scriptum est in Threnis: Non repellet in sempiternum Dominus, quia si abjecit, et miserebitur secundum multitudinem miserationum suarum.
paras.en: [[17:12|They have turned night into day|Noctem verterunt in diem]]. For often through vicious and wandering thoughts the soul is so blinded that it judges the darkness of vices to be the light of virtues, approving and accepting evils set before it under the appearance of good. To such Amos says: [[Amos 6:13|you have turned judgment into bitterness, and the fruit of justice into wormwood|Convertistis in amaritudinem judicium, et fructum justitiæ in absinthium]]. And Isaias: [[Is 5:20|Woe to you that call evil good, and good evil: that put darkness for light, and light for darkness|Væ qui dicitis bonum malum, et malum bonum; ponentes tenebras lucem, et lucem tenebras]]. Further, such men walk by a deceitful way, of which it is read in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:12|There is a way which seemeth just to a man: but the ends thereof lead to death|Est via quæ videtur homini justa, et novissima ejus deducunt ad mortem]] It is not safe, then, to stand by one's own judgment, but to obey the counsels of superiors, and not to hide the secrets of the heart from those who are adorned with discretion. [[17:12|and after darkness I hope for light again|Et rursum post tenebras spero lucem]], that is, when I see that I have erred and sinned, and so fallen into the darkness of error and sin, I resolve to repent, I trust that the light of grace will return, and after adversities and sorrows I await consolation and beatitude, praying that prayer of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 36:1|Have mercy upon us, O God of all, and behold us, and shew us the light of thy mercies|Miserere nostri, Deus omnium, et respice nos, et ostende nobis lucem miserationum tuarum]]. Hence it is written in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:31|For the Lord will not cast off for ever|Non repellet in sempiternum Dominus]]: [[Lam 3:32|For if he hath cast off, he will also have mercy, according to the multitude of his mercies|quia si abjecit, et miserebitur secundum multitudinem miserationum suarum]]

paras.t: Si sustinuero, id est, a peccatis me vinci permisero, si locum diabolo dedero, nisi culpis restitero; infernus domus mea est, id est, in inferno locabor. Est itaque sustinentia vitiosa, qua quis patitur prævalere peccatum. Unde angelo, id est episcopo, Ephesi Ecclesiæ scribit Joannes: Non potes sustinere malos. In tenebris stravi lectulum meum. Lectulus noster, est contemplatio divinorum, seu pax mentis in Deo. Sed et pœnitentia est lectus doloris. Hinc in Canticis dicitur: Lectulus noster floridus; et: In lectulo meo per noctes quæsivi quem diligit anima mea. Hic lectulus nunc in tenebris sternitur ac paratur: quia contemplatio vitæ hujus, ænigmatica est atque obscura, multis quoque adversitatibus ac defectibus mixta, dicente Apostolo: Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate.
paras.en: [[17:13|If I wait|Si sustinuero]] [*sustinere*, to wait, and also to bear or put up with], that is, if I let myself be overcome by sins, if I give place to the devil, if I do not resist faults, [[17:13|hell is my house|infernus domus mea est]], that is, I shall be placed in hell. There is, then, a vicious bearing, by which one allows sin to prevail. Hence John writes to the angel, that is the bishop, of the Church of Ephesus: [[Apoc 2:2|thou canst not bear them that are evil|Non potes sustinere malos]]. [[17:13|and I have made my bed in darkness|In tenebris stravi lectulum meum]]. Our bed is the contemplation of divine things, or the peace of the mind in God. But penance too is a bed of sorrow. Hence it is said in the Canticle: [[Cant 1:15|Our bed is flourishing|Lectulus noster floridus]]; and: [[Cant 3:1|In my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loveth|In lectulo meo per noctes quæsivi quem diligit anima mea]]. This bed is now made and prepared in darkness: for the contemplation of this life is enigmatic and obscure, and mixed with many adversities and failings, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner|Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate]].

paras.t: Putredini, id est carnali concupiscentiæ, dixi: Pater meus es, mater mea. Concupiscentia enim parentum, conceptioni nostræ non defuit, quamvis per bona sacramenti commixtio conjugalis honestetur, atque a culpa aliquando præservetur. Et soror mea, vermibus, id est peccatis carnalibus, immundis ac putridis, quæ ex concupiscentia oriuntur. Istud tamen secundum præcedentis articuli expositionem quilibet nostrum dicere potest et debet, humiliando se ipsum ex consideratione propriæ originis ac finitionis. Si enim pensemus ex quam immunda materia in utero matris sumus concepti, formati, nutriti, et demum in qualem putredinem, vermiumque congeriem resolvemur; habemus maximam causam humiliandi ac vilipendendi nos ipsos, præsertimque spernendi carnem nostram, ne eam aut alterius carnaliter diligamus.
paras.en: [[17:14|to rottenness|Putredini]], that is, to carnal concupiscence, [[17:14|I have said|dixi]]: [[17:14|Thou art my father|Pater meus es]], [[17:14|my mother|mater mea]]. For the concupiscence of our parents was not absent from our conception, although the marriage union is made honourable by the goods of the sacrament, and is sometimes kept from fault. [[17:14|and my sister|Et soror mea]], [[17:14|to worms|vermibus]], that is, to carnal sins, unclean and rotten, which arise from concupiscence. Yet this, according to the exposition of the preceding article, any one of us can and should say, humbling himself by considering his own origin and end. For if we weigh from what unclean matter we were conceived, formed and nourished in our mother's womb, and into what rottenness and heap of worms we shall at last be resolved, we have the greatest cause to humble and despise ourselves, and above all to spurn our flesh, so as not to love it, or another's, carnally.

paras.t: Ubi est ergo nunc præstolatio mea? id est, non aliud summe aut finaliter præstolor, nisi te, o Deus, summum et incommutabile bonum. Quid enim mihi est in cœlo, et a te quid volui super terram, nisi tu ipse et te ipsum, o Deus cordis mei, et pars mea Deus in æternum? De quo ait fervens amator: Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea; propterea exspectabo eum. Itemque Psalmista: Et nunc quæ est exspectatio mea? nonne Dominus? Et patientiam meam quis considerat? O si attenderemus, quam plenissime Deus omnia bona nostra considerat, quam libenter patientes nos videt, quam paratus est nostram patientiam æternaliter coronare! vigilantius insisteremus virtutibus, et patientiores essemus. In profundissimum infernum descendent omnia mea. Nunc quotidie anima nostra cum omnibus suis superioribus viribus et actibus in infernum descendat, per considerationem, detestationem, et frequentem memoriam infernalium tormentorum, ne postea cum corpore et anima omnibusque nostris peccatis corruamus in eum.
paras.en: [[17:15|Where is now then my expectation?|Ubi est ergo nunc præstolatio mea?]] that is, I await nothing else supremely or finally but thee, O God, the supreme and unchangeable good. [[Ps 72:25|For what have I in heaven? and besides thee what do I desire upon earth?|Quid enim mihi est in cœlo, et a te quid volui super terram]] but thou thyself, and thee thyself, O [[Ps 72:26|God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever|Deus cordis mei, et pars mea Deus in æternum?]]? Of whom a fervent lover says: [[Lam 3:24|The Lord is my portion, said my soul: therefore will I wait for him|Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea; propterea exspectabo eum]] And likewise the Psalmist: [[Ps 38:8|And now what is my hope? is it not the Lord?|Et nunc quæ est exspectatio mea? nonne Dominus?]] [[17:15|and who considereth my patience?|Et patientiam meam quis considerat?]] O if we would attend to how fully God considers all our good things, how gladly he sees us patient, how ready he is to crown our patience eternally! we should apply ourselves to the virtues more watchfully, and be more patient. [[17:16|All that I have shall go down into the deepest pit|In profundissimum infernum descendent omnia mea]]. Let our soul now go down daily into hell, with all its higher powers and acts, by the consideration, detestation and frequent remembrance of the torments of hell, lest afterwards we fall into it with body and soul and all our sins.

paras.t: Postremo, ex verbis hujus capituli sumpta est lectio pro defunctis, quæ incipit: Spiritus meus attenuabitur. Itaque anima in purgatorio constituta fatetur: Spiritus meus, id est intellectus seu mens, attenuabitur, subtilius considerando divina, quum fuero a pœnis istis erepta, seu aliquo earum relevamine mihi concesso. Magnitudo quippe pœnarum, considerationis et contemplationis impedit subtilitatem. Dies mei, quibus hic puniar, breviabuntur. Certa est enim, quod tandem eripietur a pœnis atque salvabitur. Et solum mihi superest sepulcrum, id est, interim non alium habeo locum sive latibulum, nisi hoc pœnale receptaculum quo affligor, nec aliquid rerum terrenarum possideo. Quomodo autem tali loco purgatorii et inferni, conveniat nomen ratioque sepulcri, dictum est supra. Nam et dives epulo fertur sepultus in inferno.
paras.en: Lastly, from the words of this chapter is taken the lesson for the dead which begins: *My spirit shall be wasted.* So the soul placed in purgatory confesses: [[17:1|My spirit|Spiritus meus]], that is, my understanding or mind, [[17:1|shall be wasted|attenuabitur]], considering divine things more finely, when I shall have been snatched from these pains, or some relief from them has been granted me. For the greatness of the pains hinders the fineness of consideration and contemplation. [[17:1|my days|Dies mei]], in which I am punished here, [[17:1|shall be shortened|breviabuntur]]. For it is certain that it will at last be snatched from its pains and saved. [[17:1|and only the grave remaineth for me|Et solum mihi superest sepulcrum]], that is, meanwhile I have no other place or hiding place but this receptacle of punishment in which I am afflicted, nor do I possess anything of earthly things. How the name and notion of a grave fit such a place of purgatory and of hell was said above[[Job 11:1||]] [the margin gives only Job xi]. For the rich feaster too is said to have been [[Luke 16:22|buried in hell|sepultus in inferno]].

paras.t: Non peccavi, id est, in peccato finaliter non permansi, imo pœnitui. Juxta quem sensum accipi potest illud primæ Joannis, tertio capite: Qui natus est ex Deo, non peccat. Et in amaritudinibus purgatoriarum pœnarum moratur oculus meus interior, quousque pro universis et singulis meis peccatis seu debitis fuerit satisfactum. Libera me de pœnis his, et pone me juxta te, in regno jucunditatis ac securitatis æternæ: quod anima talis vehementissime cupit, ut sæpius tactum est; et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me, id est, tunc nullius impugnationem timebo. Non enim hoc dicitur quasi Beati impugnentur ab aliquo, qui omnino impassibiles atque securi sunt; sed quia lædi nullatenus possunt. Verumtamen, inter angelos bonos et malos ponitur pugna in Apocalypsi ac Daniele: quæ tamen angelis sanctis nullam unquam molestiam infert.
paras.en: [[17:2|I have not sinned|Non peccavi]], that is, I did not remain in sin to the end, but repented. In this sense can be taken that saying of the first epistle of John, in the third chapter: [[1 John 3:9|Whosoever is born of God committeth not sin|Qui natus est ex Deo, non peccat]]. [[17:2|in bitterness|Et in amaritudinibus]] of the pains of purgatory [[17:2|my eye abideth|moratur oculus meus]] within, until satisfaction has been made for each and every one of my sins or debts. [[17:3|Deliver me|Libera me]] from these pains, [[17:3|and set me beside thee|et pone me juxta te]], in the kingdom of eternal joy and security: which such a soul most vehemently desires, as has often been touched on; [[17:3|and let any man's hand fight against me|et cujusvis manus pugnet contra me]], that is, then I shall fear no one's assault. For this is not said as though the Blessed were assailed by anyone, who are altogether beyond suffering and secure; but because they can in no way be harmed. Yet a battle between the good and the wicked angels is set down in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 12:7||]] and in Daniel[[Dan 10:13||]]: which nevertheless never brings any trouble to the holy angels.

paras.t: Dies mei transierunt, id est, tempus quo potui me juvare ac promereri, finitum est. Ideo aliorum precor suffragia. Cogitationes meæ dissipatæ sunt. Licet enim anima in purgatorio maneat Deo habitualiter incessanter unita per caritatem quam nunquam amittit, nihilo minus, impellente pœnarum acerbitate, cogitationes habet multiformiter discurrentes. Torquentes cor meum, id est voluntatem, quæ ex talibus cogitationibus et apprehensis per eas non parum affligitur. Noctem verterunt in diem: quia, juxta sensum prætactum, cogitationes illæ propter amaritudines sibi annexas animam sæpe sic obruunt et quasi obscurant, veritatis contemplationem impediendo, ut ipsa anima inter noctem et diem, id est inter verum et falsum, seu bonum et malum, vix queat discernere, imo unam horam judicet multos annos. Et rursum post tenebras, id est pœnas purgatorii, in quo est carentia lucis gloriæ, seu etiam luminis exterioris, quantum ad consolationem et copiam, caligo quoque in judicando et cognoscendo, præsertim respectu cognitionis in patria; spero lucem gloriæ seu visionis beatæ, imo Deum lucem æternam, immensam, fontalem, in cujus certissima exspectatione et spe anima est talis.
paras.en: [[17:11|My days have passed away|Dies mei transierunt]], that is, the time in which I could help myself and merit is ended. Therefore I beg the suffrages of others. [[17:11|my thoughts are dissipated|Cogitationes meæ dissipatæ sunt]]. For although the soul in purgatory remains habitually and unceasingly united to God by the charity which it never loses, nonetheless, driven by the sharpness of its pains, it has thoughts running about in many ways. [[17:11|tormenting my heart|Torquentes cor meum]], that is, the will, which is not a little afflicted by such thoughts and by what is apprehended through them. [[17:12|They have turned night into day|Noctem verterunt in diem]]: because, in the sense touched on before, those thoughts, because of the bitterness joined to them, often so overwhelm the soul and as it were darken it, hindering the contemplation of truth, that the soul can scarcely discern between night and day, that is, between true and false, or good and evil; indeed it judges one hour to be many years. [[17:12|and after darkness|Et rursum post tenebras]], that is, the pains of purgatory, in which there is lack of the light of glory, and also of outward light as to consolation and abundance, and dimness too in judging and knowing, above all compared with knowledge in the fatherland, [[17:12|I hope for light|spero lucem]] of glory or of the blessed vision, nay, God, the eternal, immense light, the fountain of light, in most certain expectation and hope of whom such a soul is.

paras.t: Si sustinuero pœnas has, quas me ferre oportet, id est, quamvis eas pertulero, tamen infernus domus mea est, id est, purgatorium interim manet habitaculum meum, quousque plene fuero emundata. Quod autem infernus quandoque pro purgatorio accipiatur, præhabitum est. Nam et in Missa oramus: Libera animas fidelium defunctorum de pœnis inferni, id est purgatorii. In tenebris stravi lectulum meum: id est, in mundo et corpore vivens, peccando præparavi mihi hunc locum doloris, in quo velut in lectulo teneor et pœnose quiesco. Putredini dixi: Pater meus es, mater mea; et soror mea, vermibus. Hoc anima in persona defuncti seu ex parte compositi dicere potest, juxta expositiones inductas. Vel ideo dicit hoc, quia in vili et putrido loco sic coarctatur, ut quasi affinitatem cum eo contrahere videatur. Vermes quoque, remorsus conscientiæ intelligi possunt, juxta illud Isaiæ: Vermis eorum non morietur. Ubi est ergo nunc præstolatio mea? Utique in cœlo empyreo. Lectio autem sic terminatur: Et patientia mea? Tu es, Domine, Deus meus. Deus nempe patientia animæ est, quia patientiæ dator et causa est, finis ac ratio. Vel, Patientia, id est bonum propter quod omnia longanimiter sustinet, seu præmium objective, patienter exspectatum. Unde ait Psalmista: Quoniam tu es patientia mea, Domine; Domine, spes mea. Et alibi: Deo subjecta esto, anima mea, quoniam ab ipso patientia mea. Patientia autem proprie virtus est, tristitiam moderans, ne inordinata seu excessiva consistat.
paras.en: [[17:13|If I wait|Si sustinuero]] [here *if I bear*] these pains which I must bear, that is, although I bear them through, yet [[17:13|hell is my house|infernus domus mea est]], that is, purgatory meanwhile remains my dwelling, until I am fully cleansed. That *hell* is sometimes taken for purgatory has been treated before. For in the Mass too we pray: Deliver the souls of the faithful departed from the pains of hell, that is, of purgatory. [[17:13|and I have made my bed in darkness|In tenebris stravi lectulum meum]]: that is, while living in the world and in the body, I prepared for myself by sinning this place of sorrow, in which I am held as in a bed and rest in pain. [[17:14|I have said to rottenness: Thou art my father|Putredini dixi: Pater meus es]]; [[17:14|my mother and my sister|mater mea; et soror mea]], [[17:14|to worms|vermibus]]. The soul can say this in the person of the dead man, or on the part of the whole composed of soul and body, according to the expositions given. Or it says this because it is so confined in a vile and rotten place that it seems as it were to contract kinship with it. The worms too can be understood as the remorse of conscience, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 66:24|their worm shall not die|Vermis eorum non morietur]]. [[17:15|Where is now then my expectation?|Ubi est ergo nunc præstolatio mea?]] Surely in the empyrean heaven. But the lesson ends thus: *And my patience? Thou art, O Lord, my God.* For God is the soul's patience, since he is the giver and cause, the end and reason of patience. Or *patience*, that is, the good for the sake of which it bears all things long-sufferingly, or the reward, as the object, patiently awaited. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 70:5|For thou art my patience, O Lord: my hope, O Lord|Quoniam tu es patientia mea, Domine; Domine, spes mea]]. And elsewhere: [[Ps 61:6|But be thou, O my soul, subject to God: for from him is my patience|Deo subjecta esto, anima mea, quoniam ab ipso patientia mea]] Patience, properly, is a virtue that moderates sadness, lest it be disordered or excessive.

18.title: Elucidatio capituli octavidecimi: Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit.
18.title_en: Explanation of the eighteenth chapter: Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said

paras.t: Sapientes et magni in oculis propriis, despectum sui non ferunt: et increpanti veraciter duriora respondent mendaciter. Hinc Baldad secundo objiciens, primoque replicans contra Job, eum de multis redarguit. Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit: Usque ad quem finem verba jactabis? id est, quamdiu vana et frivola jactanter atque procaciter loqueris? quousque sermonem inutilem et pomposum non finis? Hoc est quod in Actis Epicurei et Stoici philosophi dixisse leguntur ad Paulum: Quid vult seminiverbius hic dicere? Id quoque supra protulit Baldad, dicendo: Usquequo loqueris talia, et spiritus multiplex sermonis oris tui? Intellige prius, id est, propriorum verborum insuperque nostrorum sensum attende, et sic loquamur, conferendo et disputando ad invicem. In quo notat beatum Job de magna insipientia, et quod tam passionate loquatur, quod nec se ipsum nec condisputantes intelligat: sicut de quibusdam philosophis Aristoteles scribit, quod propriam vocem non intelligebant.
paras.en: Those who are wise and great in their own eyes cannot bear to be despised: and to one who rebukes them truly they answer more harshly and falsely. Hence Baldad, objecting a second time and replying first against Job, reproves him on many counts. [[18:1|Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said|Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit]]: [[18:2|How long will you throw out words?|Usque ad quem finem verba jactabis?]] that is, how long wilt thou say vain and frivolous things boastfully and insolently? how long wilt thou not end thy useless and pompous talk? This is what the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers are read in the Acts to have said to Paul: [[Acts 17:18|What is it that this word sower would say?|Quid vult seminiverbius hic dicere?]] Baldad also said this above, saying: [[Job 8:2|How long wilt thou speak these things, and how long shall the words of thy mouth be like a strong wind?|Usquequo loqueris talia, et spiritus multiplex sermonis oris tui?]] [[18:2|understand first|Intellige prius]], that is, attend to the sense of thy own words and of ours besides, [[18:2|and so let us speak|et sic loquamur]], conferring and disputing with one another. In this he charges blessed Job with great folly, and with speaking so passionately that he understands neither himself nor those disputing with him: as Aristotle writes of certain philosophers, that they did not understand their own words.

paras.t: Quare reputati sumus ut jumenta? id est, cur reputas et contemnis nos, ac si bruta essemus? quia dixisti (præcedenti capitulo): Non inveniam in vobis ullum sapientem. Et sorduimus coram te? id est, viles nos æstimas tanquam insipientes atque injustos. Per sapientiam etenim et virtutem homo præcipue nobilitatur, ornatur, atque a brutis distinguitur. Propter quod de non intelligente beneficia Dei fertur in Psalmo: Homo, quum in honore esset, non intellexit; comparatus est jumentis insipientibus. Quid perdis animam tuam in furore tuo? id est, insipienter periculoseque agis, quod animam tuam ita damnationi exponis, ex furore passionum falsa atque sacrilega contra Deum et nos proferendo. Nam supra dixisti: Non parcam ori meo; et rursus: Caligavit ad indignationem oculus meus.
paras.en: [[18:3|Why are we reputed as beasts?|Quare reputati sumus ut jumenta?]] that is, why dost thou reckon and despise us as though we were brute animals? for thou saidst (in the preceding chapter): [[Job 17:10|and I shall not find among you any wise man|Non inveniam in vobis ullum sapientem]]. [[18:3|and counted vile before you?|Et sorduimus coram te?]] that is, thou esteemest us vile, as foolish and unjust. For it is above all by wisdom and virtue that man is ennobled and adorned, and distinguished from the brutes. For which reason it is said in the Psalm of one who does not understand the benefits of God: [[Ps 48:13|And man when he was in honour did not understand; he is compared to senseless beasts|Homo, quum in honore esset, non intellexit; comparatus est jumentis insipientibus]]. [[18:4|Thou that destroyest thy soul in thy fury|Quid perdis animam tuam in furore tuo?]] [the Latin reads *Why dost thou destroy thy soul in thy fury?*] that is, thou actest foolishly and dangerously in thus exposing thy soul to damnation, uttering false and sacrilegious things against God and us out of the fury of thy passions. For above thou saidst: [[Job 7:11|I will not spare my mouth|Non parcam ori meo]]; and again: [[Job 17:7|My eye is dim through indignation|Caligavit ad indignationem oculus meus]].

paras.t: Porro in verbis his Baldad reprehendit beatum Job in quinque circa verba quæ dixit. Primo, quod valde fuerit promptulus ad loquendum. Contra quod in Proverbiis dicitur: Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio. Et Jacobus: Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum. Secundo, quod prius responderit quam complete colloquentem audiret. Contra quod ait Scriptura: Qui prius respondet quam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat et confusione dignum. Tertio, quod colloquentem spernat et exprobret: juxta illud Ecclesiastæ, In multa sapientia multa indignatio. Nam qui sapientes se reputant, contradicentibus indignantur, et dura profantur, secundum illud Proverbiorum: Ubi fuerit superbia, ibi erit et contumelia. Quarto, quod ex impetu passionis locutus sit: quod insipientiæ est, prout in Proverbiorum libro scribitur: Fatuus statim indicat iram suam. Quinto, quod verba sua inefficacia sint ad persuadendum intentum, ideoque infructuose verba jactet seu spargat, quemadmodum Ecclesiastes dicit: Stultus verba multiplicat. Quocontra Salomon protestatur: Pretiosi spiritus, vir eruditus: quia videlicet eruditi viri est, sententiosa verba proferre, quæ auro pretiosiora censentur.
paras.en: Further, in these words Baldad blames blessed Job on five counts concerning the words he spoke. First, that he was very quick to speak. Against which it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:20|Hast thou seen a man hasty to speak? folly is rather to be looked for, than his amendment|Vidisti aliquem velocem ad loquendum? Stultitia magis speranda est, quam illius correctio]] And James: [[Jas 1:19|let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak|Sit omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum]]. Secondly, that he answered before he had fully heard the one speaking with him. Against which Scripture says: [[Prov 18:13|He that answereth before he heareth, sheweth himself to be a fool, and worthy of confusion|Qui prius respondet quam audiat, stultum se esse demonstrat et confusione dignum]]. Thirdly, that he despises and reproaches the one speaking with him: according to that of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 1:18|in much wisdom there is much indignation|In multa sapientia multa indignatio]]. For those who think themselves wise are indignant with those who contradict them, and utter hard things, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 11:2|Where pride is, there also shall be reproach|Ubi fuerit superbia, ibi erit et contumelia]]. Fourthly, that he spoke from the onset of passion: which belongs to folly, as is written in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 12:16|A fool immediately sheweth his anger|Fatuus statim indicat iram suam]]. Fifthly, that his words are ineffective for persuading what he intends, and so he throws or scatters words fruitlessly, as Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 10:14|A fool multiplieth words|Stultus verba multiplicat]]. Against which Solomon declares: [[Prov 17:27|the man of understanding is of a precious spirit|Pretiosi spiritus, vir eruditus]]: because, namely, it belongs to a learned man to utter weighty words, which are reckoned more precious than gold.

paras.t: Præterea, quod dicitur, Usque ad quem finem verba jactabis? de duplici potest fine exponi, secundum Albertum. Primo, de fine durationis. Sicque sensus est, quod sine mensura effundit loquelam: quemadmodum scriptum est, Stultus in loquendo non potest cohibere spiritum suum. Secundo, de fine intentionis. Eritque sensus, quod infructuose loquatur, eo quod per verba sua nihil concludat aut consequatur. Jactator equidem sapientiam quam non habet, usurpat seu monstrat.
paras.en: Moreover, what is said, [[18:2|How long will you throw out words?|Usque ad quem finem verba jactabis?]] [literally *To what end wilt thou throw out words?*] can be expounded, according to Albert, of a twofold end. First, of the end of duration. And so the sense is that he pours out speech without measure: as it is written: [[Prov 25:28|a man that cannot refrain his own spirit in speaking|Stultus in loquendo non potest cohibere spiritum suum]] [Denis's wording: *the fool in speaking cannot restrain his spirit*]. Secondly, of the end of intention. And the sense will be that he speaks fruitlessly, in that by his words he concludes or attains nothing. For a boaster lays claim to or displays a wisdom he does not have.

paras.t: Numquid propter te derelinquetur terra, et transferentur rupes de loco suo? Hoc ad litteram sic exponendum opinor: Tam superbe et magnifice loqueris, ita te erigis et alios deprimis, ac si te pereunte aut redarguto, tota terra et habitantes in ea, essent mox perituri, rupes quoque transferendæ essent de propriis locis. Juxta hunc modum solemus dicere his, quos ad vitam hortamur claustralem, qui dicunt: Numquid omnes possunt fieri religiosi seu monachi? quis negotia mundi tractaret? quis de necessariis provideret? quis generationem continuaret? Horum, inquam, cuilibet dicimus: Numquid propter te mundus peribit, aut generatio desinet? Ita ait jam Baldad: Numquid propter te, etc.? hoc est, nimis extollis reputasque te ipsum: quemadmodum in Numeris Moyses ait quibusdam, Nimis erigimini, filii Levi. Porro Thomas et Albertus, per terram et rupes, intelligunt certas, firmas ac solidas veritates sive sententias. Quasi dicat Baldad: Numquid, o Job, ob te et vigorem disputationis tuæ, derelinquentur a suis tentoribus solidæ antiquorum sententiæ de providentia Dei, quod scilicet nullus affligitur pœna a Deo, nisi pro propria culpa? Quod consequenter pro viribus probat.
paras.en: [[18:4|shall the earth be forsaken for thee, and shall rocks be removed out of their place?|Numquid propter te derelinquetur terra, et transferentur rupes de loco suo?]] This, I think, is to be expounded literally thus: Thou speakest so proudly and grandly, thou liftest thyself up so and puttest others down, as if, were thou to perish or be refuted, the whole earth and those who dwell in it would soon perish, and the rocks too would have to be moved from their places. In this way we are wont to speak to those whom we urge to the cloistered life, who say: Can everyone become religious or monks? who would deal with the business of the world? who would provide necessities? who would carry on the generations? To any one of these, I say, we answer: Will the world perish, or the generations cease, for thy sake? So Baldad now says: *Shall the earth be forsaken for thee*, etc.? that is, thou extollest and esteemest thyself too much: as in Numbers Moses says to certain men: [[Num 16:7|you take too much upon you, ye sons of Levi|Nimis erigimini, filii Levi]]. But Thomas and Albert understand by the earth and the rocks certain, firm and solid truths or opinions. As if Baldad said: Will the solid opinions of the ancients about the providence of God, namely that no one is afflicted with punishment by God except for his own guilt, be forsaken by those who hold them, O Job, for thy sake and the vigour of thy disputing? Which he goes on to prove as best he can.

paras.t: Nonne lux, id est prosperitas seu opulentia atque jucunditas, impii exstinguetur, id est peribit, nec splendebit flamma ignis ejus? Per ignem, amor exprimitur, cujus flamma est desiderium æstuans. Ignis vero pravorum, est improbus amor sui, qui est amor privatus ad se reflexus, omnium vitiorum origo; ejusque flamma est intensa affectio proprii boni, delectabilis, utilis aut honesti vere vel apparenter. Baldad ergo vult dicere, quod impiorum, quibus debetur adversitas, cito transibit prosperitas; desiderium quoque eorum non splendebit sive florebit sortiendo effectum, sed evanescet. Quod quamvis sit verum, referendo hoc ad celerem finem vitæ præsentis, in quo cito peribit omnis vitiosorum prosperitas; tamen, secundum intentionem ipsius Baldad non semper verificatur, quum videamus impios in vita hac prosperari, deliciari, et aliquando diutius vivere justis, quibus et multa contingunt adversa. Interdum tamen accidit sicut Baldad intendit. Hinc in Proverbiis dicitur: Lux justorum lætificat; lucerna autem impiorum exstinguetur. Albertus quoque hic ait: Flamma (secundum Aristotelem) est fumus succensus, et significat prosperitatem, quæ ex avaritia et libidine congregatur.
paras.en: [[18:5|Shall not the light|Nonne lux]], that is, the prosperity, wealth and pleasure, [[18:5|of the wicked be extinguished|impii exstinguetur]], that is, perish, [[18:5|and the flame of his fire not shine?|nec splendebit flamma ignis ejus?]] By fire love is expressed, whose flame is burning desire. The fire of the wicked is the wicked love of self, which is a private love bent back upon itself, the origin of all vices; and its flame is an intense affection for one's own good, the pleasant, the useful or the honourable, truly or apparently so. Baldad, then, means that the prosperity of the wicked, to whom adversity is due, will quickly pass; and their desire too will not shine or flourish by obtaining its effect, but will vanish. Though this is true if it is referred to the swift end of the present life, in which all the prosperity of the vicious will quickly perish, yet in the sense Baldad intends it is not always verified, since we see the wicked prosper and live in delights in this life, and sometimes live longer than the just, to whom many adversities also befall. Sometimes, however, it happens as Baldad means. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 13:9|The light of the just giveth joy: but the lamp of the wicked shall be put out|Lux justorum lætificat; lucerna autem impiorum exstinguetur]] Albert too says here: Flame (according to Aristotle) is kindled smoke, and signifies prosperity, which is gathered from avarice and lust.

paras.t: Lux obtenebrescet in tabernaculo illius, id est, prosperitas domesticorum et habitaculi sui, simul cum ipso deficiet, et in adversitatem mutabitur; et lucerna quæ super eum est, id est claritas suæ famæ, exstinguetur, ita quod vilis et miser dicetur, qui paulo ante erat famosus et inclitus. Juxta quem sensum Salomon in Proverbiis loquitur: Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet. Et David regi promiserat Deus, quod daret ei lucernam in Jerusalem, sicut in libris Regum frequenter habetur. E contra demum, de forti muliere in Proverbiis dicitur: Non exstinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus.
paras.en: [[18:6|The light shall be dark in his tabernacle|Lux obtenebrescet in tabernaculo illius]], that is, the prosperity of his household and his dwelling will fail together with him, and be changed into adversity; [[18:6|and the lamp that is over him|et lucerna quæ super eum est]], that is, the brightness of his fame, [[18:6|shall be put out|exstinguetur]], so that he who a little before was famous and renowned will be called vile and wretched. In this sense Solomon speaks in Proverbs: [[Prov 10:7|The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot|Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet]] And God had promised King David that he would give him a lamp in Jerusalem, as is often found in the books of Kings[[3 Kings 11:36||]][[3 Kings 15:4||]][[4 Kings 8:19||]]. And on the contrary, it is said in Proverbs of the valiant woman: [[Prov 31:18|her lamp shall not be put out in the night|Non exstinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus]].

paras.t: Arctabuntur gressus virtutis ejus, id est, processus et opera suæ potentiæ restringentur per adversitatem, infirmitatem, obstacula. Hoc dicit contra Job, quia superius dixit Deo: Posuisti in nervo pedem meum. Sic Deus arctavit gressus Pharaonis, filios Israel persequentis. Et præcipitabit eum consilium suum, id est, erranti consilio credet, falletur, et a fine impedietur intento. Deus enim frequenter infatuat consilia impiorum, sicut ipsius Achitophel. Et de injustis in Proverbiis inducitur: Comedent fructus viæ suæ, suisque consiliis saturabuntur. Talibus loquitur Deus per Isaiam: Væ, filii desertores, ut faceretis consilium, et non ex me: ut adderetis peccatum super peccatum, et os meum non interrogastis. Istud superius dictum pleniusque expositum est, ubi habetur: Deus apprehendit sapientes in astutia eorum, et consilium pravorum dissipat.
paras.en: [[18:7|The step of his strength shall be straitened|Arctabuntur gressus virtutis ejus]], that is, the advances and works of his power will be restrained by adversity, sickness and obstacles. He says this against Job, because above he said to God: [[Job 13:27|Thou hast put my feet in the stocks|Posuisti in nervo pedem meum]]. So God straitened the steps of Pharao as he pursued the children of Israel[[Ex 14:23||]]. [[18:7|and his own counsel shall cast him down headlong|Et præcipitabit eum consilium suum]], that is, he will trust an erring counsel, be deceived, and be hindered from the end he intends. For God often makes the counsels of the wicked foolish, as that of Achitophel[[2 Kings 17:14||]]. And of the unjust it is brought in in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:31|they shall eat the fruit of their own way, and shall be filled with their own devices|Comedent fructus viæ suæ, suisque consiliis saturabuntur]]. To such God speaks through Isaias: [[Is 30:1|Woe to you, apostate children|Væ, filii desertores]], [[Is 30:1|that you would take counsel, and not of me|ut faceretis consilium, et non ex me]]: [[Is 30:1|that you might add sin upon sin|ut adderetis peccatum super peccatum]], [[Is 30:2|and have not asked at my mouth|et os meum non interrogastis]]. This was said and expounded more fully above, where we have: [[Job 5:13|Who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and disappointeth the counsel of the wicked|Deus apprehendit sapientes in astutia eorum, et consilium pravorum dissipat]].

paras.t: Immisit enim in rete, id est captivitatem diaboli, scilicet in peccatum, pedes suos, id est affectus et vitæ processus, implicando se vitiis. Propter quod ad veram prosperitatem tendere impeditur, secundum illud Proverbiorum: Iniquitates suæ capient impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur. Sic de divitibus et avaris ait Apostolus: Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli, et desideria multa inutilia et nociva quæ mergunt homines in interitum et perditionem. Sed tale rete non incidunt oculati, veraciter sapientes, qui norunt astutias Satanæ, jugiterque ad Deum confugiunt. Unde in Proverbiis asseritur: Frustra jacitur rete ante oculos pennatorum. Et in maculis ejus, id est peccati immunditiis, ambulat, perseverando in malis, et de uno peccato in aliud corruendo; quemadmodum Timotheo scribit Apostolus, Mali homines proficient in pejus, errantes, et in errorem mittentes. Nam et unum peccatum, nisi per pœnitentiam deleatur, pondere suo mox trahit ad aliud, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum.
