De talibus Dominus per Sophoniam testatur: Visitabo super viros defixos in fæcibus suis.
paras.en: [[18:8|For he hath thrust|Immisit enim]] [[18:8|into a net|in rete]], that is, into the captivity of the devil, namely into sin, [[18:8|his feet|pedes suos]], that is, his affections and the course of his life, entangling himself in vices. For which reason he is hindered from tending to true prosperity, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 5:22|His own iniquities catch the wicked, and he is fast bound with the ropes of his own sins|Iniquitates suæ capient impium, et funibus peccatorum suorum constringetur]]. So the Apostle says of the rich and avaricious: [[1 Tim 6:9|they that will become rich fall into temptation and into the snare of the devil and into many unprofitable and hurtful desires, which drown men into destruction and perdition|Qui volunt divites fieri, incidunt in tentationem et laqueum diaboli, et desideria multa inutilia et nociva quæ mergunt homines in interitum et perditionem]]. But such a net is not fallen into by the clear-sighted, the truly wise, who know the wiles of Satan and constantly take refuge in God. Hence it is asserted in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:17|a net is spread in vain before the eyes of them that have wings|Frustra jacitur rete ante oculos pennatorum]]. [[18:8|and walketh in its meshes|et in maculis ejus ambulat]] [*maculæ*, meshes, and also stains], that is, in the uncleannesses of sin, persevering in evil and falling from one sin into another; as the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[2 Tim 3:13|evil men and seducers shall grow worse and worse: erring, and driving into error|Mali homines proficient in pejus, errantes, et in errorem mittentes]]. For one sin, unless it is blotted out by penance, soon drags by its weight to another, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:29|the sinner will add sin to sin|Peccator adjiciet ad peccandum]]. Of such the Lord testifies through Sophonias: [[Soph 1:12|will visit upon the men that are settled on their lees|Visitabo super viros defixos in fæcibus suis]].

paras.t: Tenebitur planta illius laqueo. Per plantam, quæ est infimum pedis, intelligitur terrenus affectus, quo homo infimis carnalibus adhæret: qui laqueo tenetur, id est, fraude diaboli retrahit mentem a Deo, et figit in vitio. Laqueus quoque est consuetudo peccandi, tentatio inimici, et quidquid a Deo mentem directe elongat. De quo habetur in Psalmo: Anima nostra sicut passer erepta est de laqueo venantium. Et: Ipse liberabit me de laqueo venantium. Denique, secundum Augustinum, in medio laqueorum ambulamus, quibus si planta seu actio nostra innectatur, a progressu ad beatitudinem detinetur seu impeditur. Et exardescet contra eum, id est, contra ipsius salutem fervebit in eo, sitis, id est ardens peccandi affectus. Quanto enim quis diutius peccatis se ingerit, tanto plus delectat eum peccare, quantum in se est. Propter quod Habacuc de impio ait: Dilatat quasi infernus animam suam, et non implebitur.
paras.en: [[18:9|The sole of his foot shall be held in a snare|Tenebitur planta illius laqueo]]. By the sole, which is the lowest part of the foot, is understood earthly affection, by which man cleaves to the lowest carnal things: and this is held in a snare, that is, by the fraud of the devil it draws the mind back from God and fixes it in vice. The snare too is the habit of sinning, the temptation of the enemy, and whatever directly draws the mind away from God. Of this we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 123:7|Our soul hath been delivered as a sparrow out of the snare of the fowlers|Anima nostra sicut passer erepta est de laqueo venantium]] And: [[Ps 90:3|For he hath delivered me from the snare of the hunters|Ipse liberabit me de laqueo venantium]]. Further, according to Augustine, we walk in the midst of snares, and if our sole, that is our action, is caught in them, it is held back or hindered from progress towards beatitude. [[18:9|and thirst shall burn against him|Et exardescet contra eum]], that is, against his salvation there will burn in him [[18:9|thirst|sitis]], that is, a burning desire to sin. For the longer one thrusts himself into sins, the more it delights him to sin, as far as lies in him. For which reason Habacuc says of the wicked man: [[Hab 2:5|who hath enlarged his desire like hell: and is himself like death, and he is never satisfied|Dilatat quasi infernus animam suam, et non implebitur]].

paras.t: Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus. Pedica est instrumentum capiendi per pedes animalia sub terra absconditum. Dicitur quoque catena seu vinculum pedum. Itaque, Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus, id est, in terrenis et rebus carnalibus latet causa seu laqueus decipiens impium, dum bono in rebus caducis invento afficitur et lætatur, atque a Deo avertitur. Hi sunt quos avaritia decipit, et libido sive elatio. Unde subjungitur, et decipula illius super semitam. Decipula est instrumentum decipiendi vel capiendi, per quam causa alliciens ad peccatum exprimitur; quæ super semitam absconditur, id est, in rebus quibus homo quotidie utitur, et per quas velut per semitam graditur, occultatur. In rebus enim creatis aliquid bonitatis, desiderabilitatis, deliciositatisque est. Sed virtuosi talibus bene utuntur, referendo hæc ad gloriam Creatoris, utendo eis secundum voluntatem ipsius, tanquam mediis ad finem. Vitiosi vero talibus quasi ultimo fini inhærent, et plus afficiuntur ac delectantur in eis, quam in vero, perfecto, immenso, superessentialique bono: ideo decipiuntur. Hoc est quod Sapiens scribit: Creaturæ Dei in odium factæ sunt, et in tentationem hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium. De talibus conqueritur Dominus in Jeremia: Quid invenerunt patres vestri in me iniquitatis, quia elongaverunt a me, et ambulaverunt post vanitatem, et vani facti sunt? Itemque: Duo, inquit, mala fecit populus meus: me dereliquerunt fontem aquæ vivæ, et foderunt sibi cisternas dissipatas, quæ continere non valent aquas.
paras.en: [[18:10|A gin is hidden for him in the earth|Abscondita est in terra pedica ejus]]. A gin is an instrument hidden under the ground for catching animals by the feet. It is also called a chain or fetter of the feet. So, *a gin is hidden for him in the earth*, that is, in earthly and carnal things lies hidden the cause or snare that deceives the wicked man, when he is attached to and delights in the good found in perishing things, and is turned away from God. These are they whom avarice deceives, and lust or pride. Hence it is added: [[18:10|and his trap upon the path|et decipula illius super semitam]]. A trap is an instrument for deceiving or catching, by which is expressed the cause that entices to sin; which is hidden upon the path, that is, it lies concealed in the things man uses daily and through which he walks as along a path. For in created things there is something of goodness, desirability and delight. But the virtuous use such things well, referring them to the glory of the Creator, using them according to his will as means to the end. The vicious cleave to them as to their last end, and are more attached to them and delight in them more than in the true, perfect, immense and superessential good: therefore they are deceived. This is what the Wise man writes: [[Wis 14:11|the creatures of God are turned to an abomination, and a temptation to the souls of men, and a snare to the feet of the unwise|Creaturæ Dei in odium factæ sunt, et in tentationem hominum, et in muscipulam pedibus insipientium]]. Of such the Lord complains in Jeremias: [[Jer 2:5|What iniquity have your fathers found in me, that they are gone far from me, and have walked after vanity, and are become vain?|Quid invenerunt patres vestri in me iniquitatis, quia elongaverunt a me, et ambulaverunt post vanitatem, et vani facti sunt?]] And again: [[Jer 2:13|For my people have done two evils. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have digged to themselves cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water|Duo, inquit, mala fecit populus meus: me dereliquerunt fontem aquæ vivæ, et foderunt sibi cisternas dissipatas, quæ continere non valent aquas]].

paras.t: Creaturæ itaque fallunt peccantem objectaliter, materialiter, seu occasionaliter, movendo ipsius rationem seu appetitum. Peccans vero fallit se ipsum quasi efficienter, dum ratio ejus consentit illicito. Peccatum autem decipit eum formaliter, mentem excæcando, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Stultis illudit peccatum.
paras.en: Creatures, then, deceive the sinner as objects, materially or as occasions, by moving his reason or appetite. But the sinner deceives himself as it were as the efficient cause, when his reason consents to what is unlawful. And sin deceives him formally, by blinding the mind, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 14:9|A fool will laugh at sin|Stultis illudit peccatum]] [Denis reads *sin mocks fools*].

paras.t: Undique terrebunt eum formidines: quia timebit sibi accidere quod meruit; et quod aliis intulit, sibi inferri pavidus suspicatur. Hoc supra jam dictum est plenius atque expositum, ubi habetur: Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur. Contra quod in Proverbiis dicitur: Ne paveas repentino terrore. Hinc habitanti in adjutorio Altissimi fertur in Psalmo: Non timebis a timore nocturno, a sagitta volante in die, etc. Et involvent pedes ejus. Quum enim quis plurimum metuit, non audet ad quælibet loca accedere; atque ab actibus diversis retrahitur, suspicans sibi undique imminere periculum: sicque tam corporales quam spirituales ipsius pedes formidinibus involvuntur, quia a liberis progressibus impediuntur, quemadmodum in libro Judicum filii Benjamin sedisse leguntur in petra Remmon. Denique passio timoris, si sit multum intensa, impedit hominem a cursu et motu, et nonnunquam quasi immobilem reddit.
paras.en: [[18:11|Fears shall terrify him on every side|Undique terrebunt eum formidines]]: for he will fear that what he has deserved will befall him; and he fearfully suspects that what he has inflicted on others will be inflicted on himself. This was said and expounded more fully above, where we have: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears: and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii; et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur]]. Against which it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:25|Be not afraid of sudden fear|Ne paveas repentino terrore]]. Hence it is said in the Psalm to him who dwells in the aid of the Most High[[Ps 90:1||]]: [[Ps 90:5|thou shalt not be afraid of the terror of the night|Non timebis a timore nocturno]], [[Ps 90:6|Of the arrow that flieth in the day|a sagitta volante in die]], etc. [[18:11|and shall entangle his feet|Et involvent pedes ejus]]. For when someone is very much afraid, he does not dare to go to every place; and he is held back from various actions, suspecting that danger threatens him on every side: and so both his bodily and his spiritual feet are entangled by fears, because they are hindered from free going, as in the book of Judges the sons of Benjamin are read to have stayed in the rock Remmon[[Judg 20:47||]]. Further, the passion of fear, if it is very intense, hinders a man from running and moving, and sometimes makes him as it were unable to move.

paras.t: Attenuetur fame robur ejus, id est, fortitudo impii per esuriem debilitetur; et inedia invadat costas illius, id est, paupertas eum sic maceret, quod costæ ejus appareant. Devoret pulchritudinem cutis ejus, id est, ad deformitatem eum perducat. Fames enim pallorem maciemque inducit. Et consumat brachia illius primogenita mors, id est intempestiva sive anticipans, qua quis ante naturalem terminum moritur. Vel, primogenita mors vocatur, quæ ex peccato secuta est, juxta illud Sapientiæ: Deus mortem non fecit; injustitiæ autem mortis est acquisitio. Impii vero manibus et verbis accersierunt illam. Avellatur de tabernaculo suo fiducia ejus, id est, spes quam habuit in rebus atque domesticis, pereat: similiter spes domesticorum ejus. In omnibus his tangit beatum Job, cui ista pro magna parte jam acciderunt. Et calcet super eum, quasi rex, interitus, id est, languor et mors eum omnino potenter opprimant sive dejiciant, sicut rex pauperem calcat.
paras.en: [[18:12|Let his strength be wasted with famine|Attenuetur fame robur ejus]], that is, let the strength of the wicked man be weakened by hunger; [[18:12|and let hunger invade his ribs|et inedia invadat costas illius]], that is, let poverty so waste him that his ribs show. [[18:13|Let it devour the beauty of his skin|Devoret pulchritudinem cutis ejus]], that is, let it bring him to ugliness. For hunger brings on pallor and leanness. [[18:13|let the firstborn death consume his arms|Et consumat brachia illius primogenita mors]], that is, untimely or premature death, by which one dies before the natural term. Or that death is called firstborn which followed from sin, according to that of Wisdom: [[Wis 1:13|For God made not death|Deus mortem non fecit]]; but injustice is the getting of death [Denis's own words, from the sense of Wis 1:12–16]. [[Wis 1:16|But the wicked with works and words have called it to them|Impii vero manibus et verbis accersierunt illam]]. [[18:14|Let his confidence be rooted out of his tabernacle|Avellatur de tabernaculo suo fiducia ejus]], that is, let the hope he had in his goods and household perish: and likewise the hope of his household. In all these things he touches blessed Job, to whom these things have already for the most part befallen. [[18:14|and let destruction tread upon him like a king|Et calcet super eum, quasi rex, interitus]], that is, let sickness and death altogether and mightily overwhelm or cast him down, as a king tramples on a poor man.

paras.t: Habitent in tabernaculo ejus socii ejus qui non est, id est, socii ejus qui obiit, occupent domum ejus, eo jam mortuo. Adspergatur in tabernaculo ejus sulfur, id est fœtidus odor, qui in domibus mortuorum spargi solebat in signum mœroris, ut dicitur. Et hæc duo ad adversitatem pertinent, in quantum consequuntur ad mortem, et privationes sunt bonorum quæ aliquando habebat qui obiit. Unde quidam expositionem Thomæ hic reprobans, deficit.
paras.en: [[18:15|Let the companions of him that is not, dwell in his tabernacle|Habitent in tabernaculo ejus socii ejus qui non est]], that is, let the companions of him who has died occupy his house, now that he is dead. [[18:15|let brimstone be sprinkled in his tent|Adspergatur in tabernaculo ejus sulfur]], that is, a foul smell, which used to be sprinkled in the houses of the dead as a sign of mourning, as is said. And these two things belong to adversity, inasmuch as they follow upon death, and are privations of the goods which he who died once had. Hence a certain writer who here rejects the exposition of Thomas falls short.

paras.t: Deorsum radices ejus siccentur, id est, quæ plantavit, radicitus arescant. Quidam tamen, per radices, filios et nepotes intelligunt. Sursum autem atteratur messis ejus, id est fructus, qui jam ad maturitatem venerunt. Talia filiis Israel propter eorum contigisse peccata, in Joele, Aggæo, et alibi legitur. Memoria illius pereat de terra, id est, nec in hominum recordatione permaneat, saltem quoad præconium aliquod; et non celebretur nomen ejus in plateis, id est, fama ejus non sit in hominum communitate solennis. Quum enim in plateis homines confluant, addidit, In plateis. Quocirca scribit Albertus: Platea dicitur a Græco platon, quod Latine dicitur latum. Unde vult dicere, quod in latitudinibus populi memoriale impii non celebretur: sicut in gestis Romanorum describitur, quod quum Domitianus imperator a senatu occideretur, præceptum est ut nomen infaustum e lignis atque lapidibus eraderetur. Huic consonat illud Proverbiorum, quod allegatum interdum est: Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet, videlicet quoad famæ claritatem: alioqui sicut optimi, ita et pessimi manent in memoriis hominum.
paras.en: [[18:16|Let his roots be dried up beneath|Deorsum radices ejus siccentur]], that is, let what he has planted wither from the root. Some, however, understand by the roots his sons and grandsons. [[18:16|and his harvest destroyed above|Sursum autem atteratur messis ejus]], that is, the fruits that have already come to ripeness. That such things befell the children of Israel for their sins is read in Joel[[Joel 1:4||]], Aggeus[[Agg 1:6||]] and elsewhere. [[18:17|Let the memory of him perish from the earth|Memoria illius pereat de terra]], that is, let it not remain in the recollection of men, at least as regards any praise; [[18:17|and let not his name be renowned in the streets|et non celebretur nomen ejus in plateis]], that is, let his fame not be held in honour in the community of men. For since men flock together in the streets, he added *in the streets*. On this Albert writes: *Platea* [street] is said from the Greek *platon*, which in Latin is *latum*, broad. Hence he means that the memorial of the wicked man is not to be celebrated in the broad places of the people: as is related in the deeds of the Romans that when the emperor Domitian was killed by the senate, it was ordered that his ill-omened name be scraped from wood and stone. With this agrees that saying of Proverbs which has been cited before: [[Prov 10:7|The memory of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot|Memoria justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet]], namely as regards the brightness of fame: otherwise, the worst as well as the best remain in men's memories.

paras.t: Expellet eum Deus de luce vitæ ac prosperitatis, ad tenebras adversitatis ac mortis et damnationis: secundum illud in Evangelio, Servum inutilem projicite in tenebras exteriores. Et de orbe transferet eum, id est, de sæculo isto tollet eum, omnino projiciens ipsum in tristissimum orbem inferni: juxta quod Isaias dicit impio, In infernum detraheris ad fundamenta laci. Hinc Isaac Judæus philosophus, in libro Definitionum secundum Stoicos loquens: Impius, inquit, deprimetur sub orbe tristi, et ardebit ibi in igne magno. Non erit semen ejus, neque progenies in populo suo, id est, filii et posteri ejus peribunt; nec ullæ reliquiæ in regionibus ejus, id est, nulli de ejus semine superstites permanebunt. Hoc interdum corporaliter ita fit, sicut et in libris Regum leguntur quidam decem tribuum reges cum tota sua progenie, quantum ad eos qui masculini fuerant sexus, ob sua peccata Deo jubente, occisi. Spiritualiter autem verius est, quod omnes qui ejus sequuntur malitiam, spiritualiter pereunt et damnantur. Sic et in Psalmo habetur: Semen impiorum peribit. Item in Isaia: Non consurget in æternum semen pessimorum. In die ejus, id est die suæ punitionis a Deo, stupebunt novissimi, id est inferiores sive vulgares, de tanta impii plagatione mirantes; et primos, id est superiores, invadet horror: quia timebunt ne simile quid accidat eis; et quoniam naturale est homini, visis seu cognitis rebus magnis, miris atque insolitis, expavescere.
paras.en: [[18:18|He shall drive him out of light|Expellet eum Deus de luce]] of life and prosperity [*Deus*, God, is Denis's gloss; the OCR of this line is damaged] [[18:18|into darkness|ad tenebras]] of adversity, death and damnation: according to that in the Gospel: [[Matt 25:30|the unprofitable servant, cast ye out into the exterior darkness|Servum inutilem projicite in tenebras exteriores]]. [[18:18|and shall remove him out of the world|Et de orbe transferet eum]], that is, he will take him out of this world, casting him altogether into the most sorrowful world of hell: according to what Isaias says to the wicked man: [[Is 14:15|thou shalt be brought down to hell, into the depth of the pit|In infernum detraheris ad fundamenta laci]]. Hence Isaac the Jew, the philosopher, speaking in the book of Definitions according to the Stoics, says: The wicked man will be pressed down under the sorrowful sphere, and will burn there in a great fire. [[18:19|His seed shall not subsist, nor his offspring among his people|Non erit semen ejus, neque progenies in populo suo]], that is, his sons and descendants will perish; [[18:19|nor any remnants in his country|nec ullæ reliquiæ in regionibus ejus]], that is, none of his seed will remain as survivors. This sometimes happens so in the body, as in the books of Kings we read that certain kings of the ten tribes were slain at God's command for their sins, together with all their offspring, as to those of the male sex[[3 Kings 15:29||]]. But spiritually it is more truly so, that all who follow his malice perish spiritually and are damned. So we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 36:28|the seed of the wicked shall perish|Semen impiorum peribit]]. Likewise in Isaias: [[Is 14:20|the seed of the wicked shall not be named for ever|Non consurget in æternum semen pessimorum]] [Denis's wording: *the seed of the worst shall not rise for ever*]. [[18:20|at his day|In die ejus]], that is, on the day of his punishment by God, [[18:20|They that come after him shall be astonished|stupebunt novissimi]], that is, the lower or common people, wondering at so great a smiting of the wicked man; [[18:20|and horror shall fall upon them that went before|et primos invadet horror]], that is, the higher, because they will fear lest something like it befall them; and because it is natural to man to be terrified on seeing or knowing great, wonderful and unusual things.

paras.t: Postremo, Baldad quasi epilogans, subdit: Hæc sunt ergo tabernacula iniqui, id est, ita contingit injustis, ut dixi, et tabernacula præfato modo pereuntia pertinent ad iniquos; et iste locus ejus, id est, ad prædictum locum terminumque pœnalem ac miserum ducitur, qui ignorat Deum, ignorantia opposita scientiæ Dei formatæ ac practicæ, qua quis noscit Deum non nuda notitia aut fide informi, sed cognitione ornata per actus bonos et caritatem. De qua notitia scriptum est: In hoc scimus quoniam cognovimus Deum, si mandata ejus observamus. Qui dicit se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non servat, mendax est. Hinc omnis malus dicitur ignorans, id est hac practica ac formata scientia carens, et etiam quoniam peccando judicat false.
paras.en: Lastly Baldad, as if summing up, adds: [[18:21|These then are the tabernacles of the wicked|Hæc sunt ergo tabernacula iniqui]], that is, so it befalls the unjust, as I have said, and tabernacles perishing in this way belong to the wicked; [[18:21|and this the place of him|et iste locus ejus]], that is, to the said place and end of punishment and misery is he led [[18:21|that knoweth not God|qui ignorat Deum]], with an ignorance opposed to the formed and practical knowledge of God [*formata*, that is, given its form by charity], by which one knows God not by bare knowledge or unformed faith, but by a knowledge adorned with good acts and charity. Of this knowledge it is written: [[1 John 2:3|by this we know that we have known him, if we keep his commandments|In hoc scimus quoniam cognovimus Deum, si mandata ejus observamus]]. [[1 John 2:4|He who saith that he knoweth him and keepeth not his commandments is a liar|Qui dicit se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non servat, mendax est]]. Hence every wicked man is called ignorant, that is, lacking this practical and formed knowledge, and also because by sinning he judges falsely.

paras.t: Elucescit autem ex præinductis, quod argumentatio Baldad sit prorsus invalida ad probandum propositum, utpote quod adversitates non accidant homini, nisi propter ejus peccata: quum præfatæ adversitates non injustis dumtaxat, sed et justis frequenter eveniant. Imo, martyres sancti in vita et morte durissime passi sunt, et corpora quorumdam prohibebantur sepeliri ac honorari.
paras.en: It is clear from what has been brought in that Baldad's argument is altogether invalid for proving his proposition, namely that adversities befall a man only because of his sins: since these adversities often befall not only the unjust but the just too. Indeed, the holy martyrs suffered most harshly in life and in death, and the bodies of some were forbidden to be buried and honoured.

18.title: De tropologico ejusdem capituli octavidecimi intellectu
18.title_en: On the tropological sense of the same eighteenth chapter

paras.t: Per amicos beati Job, fallaciter justos atque in propriis oculis sapientes intelligi, dictum est sæpe. Qui, quum spiritali superbia pleni sunt, increpationes justas et caritativas non sustinent; sed increpati, duriora respondent, calumniantur, increpantemque criminantur, dicentes ad illum, quod Baldad dixit ad Job: Usque ad quem finem verba jactabis? Quum enim tales sibi ipsis in se ipsis complaceant, tanquam sapientes et justi, quidquid contra eos profertur, inane, ventosum, jactatorium ac frivolum opinantur; eloquentem quoque, inconsiderate et ruditer loquentem affirmant, juxta quod subditur: Intellige prius verba mea et meæ dignitatem personæ, et sic loquamur. Nempe quum suo ingenio nimis confidant, contradictores suos eorum quæ dicuntur intelligentiam non habere testantur. Præterea quidam sunt garruli, qui ipsa loquacitate pascuntur; et conferentes seu disputantes cum aliquo, ita suis intenti sunt verbis et phantasiis, quod colloquentis non advertunt intelliguntque sermones, sed semper ad verba propria reflectuntur. Quibus dicendum est: Intelligite prius, et sic loquamur. Nisi enim colloquentes se mutuo intelligant, inutiliter confabulantur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico habetur: Ubi non est auditus, non effundas sermonem. Et item: Audi tacens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi gratia bona.
paras.en: It has often been said that by the friends of blessed Job are understood those who are falsely just and wise in their own eyes[[Is 5:21||]] [the margin note here is hard to read; it seems to give Is. v, 21]. Since they are full of spiritual pride, they do not bear just and charitable rebukes; but when rebuked they answer more harshly, slander, and accuse the one who rebukes them, saying to him what Baldad said to Job: [[18:2|How long will you throw out words?|Usque ad quem finem verba jactabis?]] For since such men are pleased with themselves in themselves, as being wise and just, whatever is brought forward against them they judge to be empty, windy, boastful and frivolous; and even one who speaks eloquently they declare to be speaking thoughtlessly and crudely, according to what follows: [[18:2|understand first|Intellige prius]] my words and the dignity of my person, [[18:2|and so let us speak|et sic loquamur]]. For since they trust too much in their own wit, they declare that those who contradict them have no understanding of the things that are said. Moreover, there are some chatterers who feed on talkativeness itself; and when they confer or dispute with someone, they are so intent on their own words and fancies that they neither attend to nor understand the words of the one speaking with them, but always turn back to their own words. To these it must be said: [[18:2|understand first, and so let us speak|Intelligite prius, et sic loquamur]]. For unless those who speak together understand one another, they converse to no purpose. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 32:6|Where there is no hearing, pour not out words|Ubi non est auditus, non effundas sermonem]]. And again: [[Ecclus 32:9|Hear in silence, and for thy reverence good grace shall come to thee|Audi tacens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi gratia bona]].

paras.t: Insuper tales, quoniam apud se magni sunt, ab aliis quoque sapientes et magni cupiunt reputari. Quod si quis humiliaverit eos, conqueruntur se despici, dicentes quod sequitur: Quare reputati sumus ut jumenta, et sorduimus coram te? Porro qui vere est humilis, qui in suo lætatur despectu, quantumlibet deprimatur, majori humiliatione dignum se arbitratur, seu propter illata adversa non indignatur. Præterea, magni in proprio corde, dum corripiuntur, corripientem ex impetu impatientiæ, non ex caritatis fervore loqui existimant, dicentes subjuncta: Qui perdis animam tuam in furore tuo? Itaque furor hominis perditio est ipsius. Ideo mansuete agamus, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris. Furor quoque reddit hominem aliis intolerabilem et inclementem, secundum quod in Proverbiis fertur: Ira non habet misericordiam, nec erumpens furor; et impetum concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit?
paras.en: Furthermore, such men, since they are great in their own sight, desire to be reputed wise and great by others too. And if anyone humbles them, they complain that they are despised, saying what follows: [[18:3|Why are we reputed as beasts, and counted vile before you?|Quare reputati sumus ut jumenta, et sorduimus coram te?]] But he who is truly humble, who rejoices in being despised, however much he is put down, judges himself worthy of greater humiliation, or at least is not indignant at the adversities brought upon him. Moreover, those who are great in their own heart, when they are corrected, think that the one correcting them speaks from a rush of impatience, not from the fervour of charity, saying the words that follow: [[18:4|Thou that destroyest thy soul in thy fury|Qui perdis animam tuam in furore tuo?]]? So a man's fury is his own perdition. Therefore let us act meekly, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 3:19|My son, do thy works in meekness, and thou shalt be beloved above the glory of men|Fili, in mansuetudine opera tua perfice, et super hominum gloriam diligeris]]. Fury also makes a man unbearable and unmerciful to others, as is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 27:4|Anger hath no mercy: nor fury, when it breaketh forth: and who can bear the violence of one provoked?|Ira non habet misericordiam, nec erumpens furor; et impetum concitati spiritus ferre quis poterit?]]

paras.t: Nonne lux impii exstinguetur? Naturale enim lumen rationis per peccatum excæcatur, quamvis non prorsus tollatur. Teste siquidem beatissimo ac divino Dionysio, peccatum naturalia non aufert, sed inficit. Potissime autem in inferno lux ista obruitur, quum Ecclesiastes dicat: Nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas. Denique, Lux impii exstinguetur, id est, omnis honor, fama, prosperitas, gloria ejus peribit, sicut in Psalmo de impiis scriptum est: Tanquam fœnum velociter arescent; et tanquam olera herbarum cito decident. Nec splendebit flamma ignis ejus? Flamma ignis impii, id est fervor sui carnalis ac vitiosi amoris, coram Deo non solum non splendet, sed tetra ac fœtida est atque damnanda. Propter quod ad Timotheum ait Apostolus: In novissimis temporibus instabunt tempora periculosa; et erunt homines se ipsos amantes, cupidi, elati, voluptatum amatores magis quam Dei. Hanc igitur per aquam sapientiæ salutaris penitus exstinguamus: quod, agente Spiritu Sancto, completur, juxta quod Isaias inducit, Protectio erit in umbraculum diei ab æstu, et in absconsionem a turbine et a pluvia.
paras.en: [[18:5|Shall not the light of the wicked be extinguished|Nonne lux impii exstinguetur?]]? For the natural light of reason is blinded by sin, though it is not wholly taken away. For, as the most blessed and divine Dionysius witnesses, sin does not take away natural gifts, but infects them [Dionysius the Areopagite, On the Divine Names, ch. 4, where he teaches that even in the demons the natural gifts remain whole]. But this light is overwhelmed most of all in hell, since Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 9:10|nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge shall be in hell, whither thou art hastening|Nec ratio, nec sapientia, nec scientia erunt apud inferos, quo tu properas]]. Lastly, [[18:5|the light of the wicked be extinguished|Lux impii exstinguetur]]: that is, all his honour, fame, prosperity and glory shall perish, as is written in the Psalm of the wicked: [[Ps 36:2|shall shortly wither away as grass, and as the green herbs shall quickly fall|Tanquam fœnum velociter arescent; et tanquam olera herbarum cito decident]]. [[18:5|and the flame of his fire not shine?|Nec splendebit flamma ignis ejus?]] The flame of the fire of the wicked man, that is, the heat of his carnal and vicious love, not only does not shine before God, but is foul and stinking and worthy of damnation. For this reason the Apostle says to Timothy: [[2 Tim 3:1|in the last days shall come dangerous times|In novissimis temporibus instabunt tempora periculosa]]; and [[2 Tim 3:2|Men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, haughty|erunt homines se ipsos amantes, cupidi, elati]], [[2 Tim 3:4|lovers of pleasure more than of God|voluptatum amatores magis quam Dei]]. Let us therefore wholly quench this flame with [[Ecclus 15:3|the water of wholesome wisdom|aquam sapientiæ salutaris]]: which is accomplished by the working of the Holy Ghost, according to what Isaias brings in: There shall be a protection [[Is 4:6|for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a security and covert from the whirlwind, and from rain|in umbraculum diei ab æstu, et in absconsionem a turbine et a pluvia]] [Denis joins the last word of Is 4:5, *protectio*, “a protection”, to v. 6, where the Vulgate has *tabernaculum*].

paras.t: Lux obtenebrescet in tabernaculo illius: quia quanto plus peccat, tanto lux animæ ejus in suo corpore infelicius offuscatur. Arctabuntur gressus virtutis ejus. Quamvis via salutis sit arcta, id est ardua sive difficilis, caritas tamen spiritualiter exstat latissima: quoniam ad omnes et usque inimicos protenditur, omnesque complectitur. Hinc, quanto quis in caritate et gratia amplius crescit, eo gressus animæ ejus plus extenduntur. Propter quod scriptum est: Ambulabam in latitudine, quia mandata tua exquisivi. Itemque: Statuisti in loco spatioso pedes meos. Et: Latum mandatum tuum nimis. Impius ergo, quoniam expers est caritatis infusæ, nec quærit quæ Christi sunt, sed se ipsum, hinc gressus ejus arctantur, dum ad ipsum jugiter reflectuntur. Postremo, in inferno claudetur, et gressus ejus pœnalissime arctabuntur, ita ut nunquam egredi queat. Immisit enim in rete pedes suos. Non implicemus nos laqueo inimici, vinculo peccati, sagenæ diaboli, ut agunt iniqui. De quibus ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus: Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem.
paras.en: [[18:6|The light shall be dark in his tabernacle|Lux obtenebrescet in tabernaculo illius]]: because the more he sins, the more unhappily the light of his soul is darkened in his body. [[18:7|The step of his strength shall be straitened|Arctabuntur gressus virtutis ejus]]. Although the way of salvation is strait[[Matt 7:14||]], that is, steep or difficult, yet charity, spiritually, is very broad: for it reaches out to all, even to enemies, and embraces all [Denis sets the breadth of charity against *arcta*, “strait”, the word of the lemma *Arctabuntur*, “shall be straitened”]. Hence the more anyone grows in charity and grace, the more the steps of his soul are widened. For this reason it is written: [[Ps 118:45|I walked at large: because I have sought after thy commandments|Ambulabam in latitudine, quia mandata tua exquisivi]]. And again: [[Ps 30:9|thou hast set my feet in a spacious place|Statuisti in loco spatioso pedes meos]]. And: [[Ps 118:96|thy commandment is exceeding broad|Latum mandatum tuum nimis]]. The wicked man, then, since he is without infused charity, and seeks not the things that are Christ's but himself[[Phil 2:21||]] [the margin seems to read Phil. ii, 21], hence his steps are straitened, as they are continually bent back upon himself. Lastly, he will be shut up in hell, and his steps will be straitened most painfully, so that he can never go out. [[18:8|For he hath thrust his feet into a net|Immisit enim in rete pedes suos]]. Let us not entangle ourselves in the snare of the enemy, the bond of sin, the net of the devil, as the wicked do. Of these the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[2 Tim 2:26|they may recover themselves from the snares of the devil by whom they are held captive at his will|Resipiscant a laqueis diaboli, a quo captivi tenentur ad ipsius voluntatem]].

paras.t: Attenuetur fame robur ejus. Ista atque sequentia non imprecando malum seu maledicendo, sed prædicendo; seu zelo justitiæ, non livore vindictæ, promuntur. Robur autem hominis, est ratio ejus: quæ fame attenuatur, dum spiritualiter non cibatur pane vitæ et intellectus, actione virtutum, divinorum infusione charismatum. Et inedia, id est gratiarum carentia, quæ est spiritualis et maxima vitæ hujus paupertas, invadat costas illius, id est interiores sensus ipsius, dum spiritualiter non foventur nec roborantur. Quemadmodum autem costæ viscera constringunt, ut earum soliditate muniantur, quæ intrinsecus latent; sic sensus interni interius latentes, contegunt cogitatus: qui nisi per gratiam gubernentur, præfata consumuntur inedia, quia deficiunt.
paras.en: [[18:12|Let his strength be wasted with famine|Attenuetur fame robur ejus]]. These words and those that follow are uttered not by way of calling down evil or cursing, but by way of foretelling; or out of zeal for justice, not from the spite of revenge. Now the strength of a man is his reason: which is wasted with famine when it is not fed spiritually with [[Ecclus 15:3|the bread of life and understanding|pane vitæ et intellectus]], with the exercise of the virtues, with the infusion of divine gifts. [[18:12|and let hunger|Et inedia]], that is, the lack of graces, which is the spiritual and greatest poverty of this life, [[18:12|invade his ribs|invadat costas illius]], that is, his inner senses, when they are not spiritually cherished and strengthened. And as the ribs enclose the bowels, so that the things hidden within are protected by their firmness, so the inward senses, hidden within, cover the thoughts: and these, unless they are governed by grace, are consumed by the aforesaid hunger, because they fail.

paras.t: Devoret inedia ista pulchritudinem cutis ejus, id est exterioris conversationis decorem, qua quis exemplaris efficitur: qui si gratiam perdat, inexemplaris jam redditur. Et consumat brachia, id est opera illius, primogenita mors, id est superbia, omnium vitiorum origo. Unde verissime dicitur: Sola superbia destruit omnia, si comitetur. In ipsa enim initium sumpsit omnis perditio. Idcirco opera hominis ipsa consumit, id est, coram Deo mortua seu immeritoria facit. Præterea, quum peccatum animæ mors vocetur, rite primogenita mors superbia appellatur, quæ in cælo sumpsit exordium ante aliud omne peccatum.
paras.en: [[18:13|Let it devour|Devoret]], namely this hunger, [[18:13|the beauty of his skin|pulchritudinem cutis ejus]], that is, the comeliness of his outward conduct, by which one is made an example to others: and if he loses grace, he is at once made no example. And [[18:13|let the firstborn death|primogenita mors]], that is, pride, the origin of all vices[[Ecclus 10:15||]] [the margin gives Ibid. x, 15, that is, Ecclus 10:15: “pride is the beginning of all sin”], [[18:13|consume his arms|consumat brachia]], that is, his works. Hence it is most truly said: Pride alone destroys all things, if it goes along with them. For [[Tob 4:14|from it all perdition took its beginning|In ipsa enim initium sumpsit omnis perditio]]. Therefore it consumes a man's works, that is, it makes them dead or unmeritorious [that is, of no merit for eternal life] before God. Moreover, since sin is called the death of the soul, pride is rightly called the firstborn death, for it had its beginning in heaven before every other sin.

paras.t: Calcet super eum, quasi rex, interitus, id est diabolus, seu consuetudo iniqua: cui vitiosus prorsus subjicitur, quia (ut ait in secunda sua epistola Petrus) iniqui, servi sunt corruptionis: a quo enim quis victus est, hujus et servus est. Habitent in tabernaculo ejus, id est in domo conscientiæ suæ, socii ejus qui non est, id est spiritus maligni, spiritus elationis, spiritus cupiditatis, spiritus carnalitatis, qui sunt socii principis tenebrarum: qui spiritualiter non est, atque a Christo ad nihilum redactus asseritur, quia convictus et perditus est, et a summo esse, summe aversus est. Hinc Christus in Evangelio ait: Quum immundus spiritus exierit ab homine, ambulat per loca inaquosa, et non inveniens requiem, dicit: Revertar ad locum unde exivi. Tunc vadit, et assumit septem alios spiritus nequiores se, et ingressi habitant ibi. Adspergatur in tabernaculo, id est corpore ejus sulfur, id est fœtor carnalium vitiorum, quibus subjiciuntur et inquinantur reprobi atque perversi. Deorsum radices ejus siccentur, id est, cogitationes affectionesque ejus in fundo suæ mentis humore careant gratiarum, infructuosæque fiant; sursum autem atteratur messis ejus, id est congeries operum, ita ut inutilis Deoque inaccepta sit vita ipsius. Cetera patent.
paras.en: [[18:14|let destruction tread upon him like a king|Calcet super eum, quasi rex, interitus]]: that is, the devil, or wicked habit, to which the vicious man is wholly subject; because (as Peter says in his second epistle) the wicked [[2 Pet 2:19|are the slaves of corruption|servi sunt corruptionis]]. [[2 Pet 2:19|For by whom a man is overcome, of the same also he is the slave|a quo enim quis victus est, hujus et servus est]]. Let there [[18:15|dwell in his tabernacle|Habitent in tabernaculo ejus]], that is, in the house of his conscience, [[18:15|the companions of him that is not|socii ejus qui non est]], that is, the evil spirits, the spirit of pride, the spirit of covetousness, the spirit of carnality, who are the companions of the prince of darkness: who spiritually is not, and is declared to have been brought to nothing by Christ, because he has been convicted and lost, and is turned away in the highest degree from the highest being. Hence Christ says in the Gospel[[Matt 12:43||]] [the margin gives Matt. xii, 43–45, and xi, 24, 26, that is, Luke 11:24, 26, whose wording Denis follows more closely]: [[Luke 11:24|When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through places without water, seeking rest: and not finding, he saith: I will return into my house whence I came out|Quum immundus spiritus exierit ab homine, ambulat per loca inaquosa, et non inveniens requiem, dicit: Revertar ad locum unde exivi]]. [[Luke 11:26|Then he goeth and taketh with him seven other spirits more wicked than himself: and entering in they dwell there|Tunc vadit, et assumit septem alios spiritus nequiores se, et ingressi habitant ibi]]. [[18:15|let brimstone be sprinkled in his tent|Adspergatur in tabernaculo]], that is, in his body; the [[18:15|brimstone|sulfur]], that is, the stench of the carnal vices to which the reprobate and perverse are subject and by which they are defiled. [[18:16|Let his roots be dried up beneath|Deorsum radices ejus siccentur]], that is, let his thoughts and affections at the bottom of his mind lack the moisture of graces and become fruitless; [[18:16|and his harvest destroyed above|sursum autem atteratur messis ejus]], that is, the heap of his works, so that his life is useless and unacceptable to God. The rest is plain.

19.title: Explanatio litteralis capituli nonidecimi: Respondens autem Job, dixit.
19.title_en: Literal explanation of the nineteenth chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit, non ipsi Baldad dumtaxat, qui capitulo loquebatur jam habito, sed omnibus tribus, qui in impugnatione sua fuerunt concordes. Usquequo affligitis animam meam, mendacia proferendo, errores vestros pertinaciter defendendo, inordinate loquendo, mihi blasphemias et maxima crimina imponendo? Quo autem quis veritatis et æquitatis purior ardentiorque amator exstiterit, eo gravius sibi est videre injusta, audire mendosa, præsertim quæ fidei derogant, et Deo directe repugnant. Hinc Christus intuens incredulorum errorem, dicebat: O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? quamdiu patiar vos? Hinc subditur: et atteritis, id est molestatis, me sermonibus vitiosis atque superfluis? ita ut illud Psalmi vobis conveniat: Acuerunt linguam suam sicut serpentes. Sapiens autem inutilium verborum multitudine attæditur, sciens quod scriptum est: In multis verbis invenitur stultitia.
paras.en: [[19:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]], not only to Baldad, who spoke in the chapter just treated, but to all three, who were of one mind in their attack on him. [[19:2|How long do you afflict my soul|Usquequo affligitis animam meam]], by uttering lies, by stubbornly defending your errors, by speaking in a disordered way, by laying blasphemies and the greatest crimes upon me? The purer and more ardent a lover of truth and equity one is, the more grievous it is for him to see unjust things and hear false ones, above all those that detract from the faith and directly oppose God. Hence Christ, beholding the error of the unbelieving, said: [[Mark 9:18|O incredulous generation, how long shall I be with you? How long shall I suffer you?|O generatio incredula, quamdiu apud vos ero? quamdiu patiar vos?]] Hence it is added: [[19:2|and break me in pieces with words?|et atteritis me sermonibus?]] that is, do you trouble me with faulty and superfluous talk? so that that saying of the Psalm fits you: [[Ps 139:4|They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent|Acuerunt linguam suam sicut serpentes]]. But the wise man is wearied by a multitude of useless words, knowing that it is written: [[Eccles 5:2|in many words shall be found folly|In multis verbis invenitur stultitia]].

paras.t: En decies confunditis me: nam quinquies respondistis mihi indignanter et confusive, et verba a me quinquepartita distinctione prolata negastis ac irrisistis. Job enim ante hanc responsionem quinquies est locutus, inchoando a loco quo ait, Pereat dies in qua natus sum, ut intuenti patescit. Eliphaz vero jam bis arguit contra Job, similiter Baldad, Sophar autem semel. Aliqui tamen putant hic numerum determinatum pro indeterminato poni, quum ait, En decies: sicut in Psalmo, Memor fuit in sæculum testamenti sui; verbi quod mandavit in mille generationes. Et non erubescitis opprimentes me, non ratione, sed multitudine et importunitate verborum aut injuriarum, quum tamen verecundum inhonestumque sit, tres simul contra unum afflictum, vulneratum et semimortuum, ita confligere. Sed impatientia ac ceteræ passiones mentem excæcant, ut erubescenda non erubescat. Nempe, id est certe, si ignoravi, id est, tantæ ignorantiæ sum ut mihi imponitis, mecum erit ignorantia mea, id est, ego eam portabo, nec vobis nocebit. Vel, Mecum erit, id est, eam humiliter considerabo atque fatebor, nec me sapientem jactabo ut vos. At vos contra me erigimini, id est, contra me extollitis vos, et pompose loquimini mihi; et arguitis me opprobriis meis, id est verbis opprobriosis adversum me a vobis prolatis. Vel, Opprobriis meis, id est, opprobria quæ passus sum a Satana, et a Chaldæis atque Sabæis, mihi subsannative objicitis, quasi propter meos excessus ea perpessus sim.
paras.en: [[19:3|Behold, these ten times you confound me|En decies confunditis me]]: for five times you have answered me indignantly and confusingly, and have denied and mocked the words I uttered in five several speeches. For Job before this answer had spoken five times, beginning from the place where he says: [[Job 3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]], as is plain to anyone who looks. And Eliphaz has now argued against Job twice, Baldad likewise, and Sophar once. Some, however, think that here a definite number is put for an indefinite one when he says, *Behold, ten times*: as in the Psalm: [[Ps 104:8|He hath remembered his covenant for ever: the word which he commanded to a thousand generations|Memor fuit in sæculum testamenti sui; verbi quod mandavit in mille generationes]] [[19:3|and are not ashamed to oppress me|Et non erubescitis opprimentes me]], not by reason, but by the multitude and importunity of words or injuries, although it is shameful and unseemly for three together to contend in this way against one man, afflicted, wounded and half dead. But impatience and the other passions so blind the mind that it does not blush at what should make it blush. [[19:4|For|Nempe]], that is, surely, [[19:4|if I have been ignorant|si ignoravi]], that is, if I am of such great ignorance as you lay upon me, [[19:4|my ignorance shall be with me|mecum erit ignorantia mea]], that is, I shall bear it, and it will not harm you. Or, *shall be with me*, that is, I shall humbly consider and confess it, and not boast myself wise as you do. [[19:5|But you set yourselves up against me|At vos contra me erigimini]], that is, you extol yourselves against me and speak to me pompously; [[19:5|and reprove me with my reproaches|et arguitis me opprobriis meis]], that is, with reproachful words uttered by you against me. Or, *with my reproaches*, that is, you mockingly throw in my face the reproaches I have suffered from Satan[[Job 2:7||]] and from the Chaldeans and Sabeans[[Job 1:17||]][[Job 1:15||]], as though I had suffered them for my excesses.

paras.t: Saltem nunc intelligite, quia Deus non æquo judicio afflixerit me, et flagellis suis me cinxerit. Verbum hoc prima facie satis horribiliter sonare videtur, præsertim quum teste B. Augustino, judicia Dei esse non possint injusta, quamvis sint frequenter occulta. Sed mentem beati Job pensare debemus, non solum formam superficiemque verborum. Judicium etenim Dei, dupliciter æquum dicitur seu justum. Primo, ex parte Dei: et sic semper est æquum et justum, quia secundum ordinem sapientiæ ejus procedit. Nec ratione caret legitima, etiamsi innocens flagelletur: quia et justum est coram Deo, ut quis pro incremento gratiæ augmentoque gloriæ affligatur. Imo misericors judicium Dei, justum est hoc modo: quia tam bonus est Deus, ut justum sit, ipsum misericorditer judicare, gratiam dare, clementer salvare. Secundo, judicium Dei dicitur justum ex parte judicati, dum quis judicatur, recipitque a Deo secundum quod meruit, scilicet secundum opera sua. Et sic asserit sanctus Job se judicatum a Deo non æquo judicio, non tamen iniquo: quia judicium istud uno modo fuit æquum, alio modo non æquum. Iniquum vero utramque æquitatem excludit. Job ergo considerans quam virtuose et irreprehensibiliter vixit, fiducialiter novit, quod vita sua tam dira non merebatur adversa, nec meruit taliter cingi, id est undique impleri, flagellis, ut superius ait: Si fuero judicatus, scio quia justus inveniar.
paras.en: [[19:6|At least now understand, that God hath not afflicted me with an equal judgment|Saltem nunc intelligite, quia Deus non æquo judicio afflixerit me]], [[19:6|and compassed me with his scourges|et flagellis suis me cinxerit]]. This saying at first sight seems to sound rather horrible, especially since, as blessed Augustine witnesses, the judgments of God cannot be unjust, though they are often hidden. But we must weigh the mind of blessed Job, not only the form and surface of his words. For the judgment of God is called equal or just in two ways. First, on the part of God: and in this way it is always equal and just, for it proceeds according to the order of his wisdom. Nor does it lack a lawful reason even if an innocent man is scourged: for it is just before God that someone be afflicted for the increase of grace and the augmenting of glory. Indeed, the merciful judgment of God is just in this way: for God is so good that it is just for him to judge mercifully, to give grace, to save with clemency. Secondly, the judgment of God is called just on the part of the one judged, when someone is judged and receives from God according to what he has deserved, namely according to his works. And in this sense holy Job asserts that he has been judged by God with a judgment not *equal*, yet not unjust: for that judgment was equal in one way, and not equal in another. But *unjust* excludes both kinds of equity. Job, then, considering how virtuously and blamelessly he had lived, knew with confidence that his life did not deserve such dire adversities, nor deserve to be so *compassed*, that is, filled on every side, with scourges, as he said above: [[Job 13:18|If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just|Si fuero judicatus, scio quia justus inveniar]]

paras.t: Ecce clamabo vim patiens, id est, si pro ope et liberatione clamavero ego violentiam passus ab hostibus, et nemo audiet, id est, nullus homo auxiliabitur mihi. Vociferabor pro adeptione judicii, quo quis recipit secundum merita sua; et non est qui judicet me hoc modo jam, sed tribulari permittor præter mea demerita. Nihilo minus, scivit se tempore mortis a Deo justissime judicandum secundum opera sua. Semitam meam circumsepsit, id est, vitæ meæ processum adversitatibus Deus circumvallavit, et transire non possum, id est, libere progredi seu evadere nequeo; et in calle meo, id est operationum processu, tenebras tribulationum posuit. Ista, quantum ad sensum, frequenter præhabita sunt. Idcirco pertranseo, quia et difficillima restant. Spoliavit me gloria mea, id est inclyta fama, honore et pristina reverentia, qua tanquam justus et sapiens ab hominibus honorabar; et abstulit coronam de capite meo, id est judicialem potestatem ac dignitatem. Unde infra profatur: Quum sederem quasi rex, circumstante exercitu. Destruxit me undique, id est, toto corpore vulnerari permisit, et omnem substantiam quam habui, permisit mihi auferri. Et pereo, id est, morti jam proximus fio, et destruor corpore. Quod secundum inferiorum et naturalium considerationem causarum sic fuit, quemadmodum Ezechiæ Dominus dixit per Isaiam: Dispone domui tuæ, quia morieris tu, et non vives. Hinc subdit: et quasi avulsæ arbori abstulit spem meam, id est, non reliquit mihi fiduciam recuperandi sanitatem et cetera mihi ablata, quemadmodum arbori amputatæ non remanet spes, via seu possibilitas refloritionis ac fructificationis. Supernaturaliter tamen Job omnia recuperavit.
paras.en: [[19:7|Behold I shall cry suffering violence|Ecce clamabo vim patiens]], that is, if I, who have suffered violence from enemies, cry out for help and deliverance, [[19:7|and no one will hear|et nemo audiet]], that is, no man will help me. [[19:7|I shall cry aloud|Vociferabor]] for the obtaining of judgment, by which one receives according to his merits; [[19:7|and there is none to judge|et non est qui judicet]] me in this way now, but I am allowed to be afflicted beyond my deserts. Nonetheless he knew that at the time of death he would be judged most justly by God according to his works. [[19:8|He hath hedged in my path round about|Semitam meam circumsepsit]], that is, God has walled about the course of my life with adversities, [[19:8|and I cannot pass|et transire non possum]], that is, I cannot go forward freely or escape; [[19:8|and in my way|et in calle meo]], that is, in the course of my works, [[19:8|he hath set darkness|tenebras tribulationum posuit]] of tribulations. These things, as to their sense, have often been treated before. Therefore I pass over them, since very difficult things remain. [[19:9|He hath stripped me of my glory|Spoliavit me gloria mea]], that is, of the renowned fame, honour and former reverence with which I was honoured by men as just and wise; [[19:9|and hath taken the crown from my head|et abstulit coronam de capite meo]], that is, the power and dignity of a judge. Hence he says below: [[Job 29:25|when I sat as a king, with his army standing about him|Quum sederem quasi rex, circumstante exercitu]]. [[19:10|He hath destroyed me on every side|Destruxit me undique]], that is, he has let me be wounded in my whole body, and let all the substance I had be taken from me. [[19:10|and I am lost|Et pereo]], that is, I am now becoming very near to death, and am destroyed in body. Which was so, considering the lower and natural causes, as the Lord said to Ezechias through Isaias: [[Is 38:1|Take order with thy house, for thou shalt die, and not live|Dispone domui tuæ, quia morieris tu, et non vives]]. Hence he adds: [[19:10|and he hath taken away my hope, as from a tree that is plucked up|et quasi avulsæ arbori abstulit spem meam]], that is, he has left me no confidence of recovering health and the other things taken from me, as for a tree cut down there remains no hope, no way or possibility of flowering again and bearing fruit. Yet above nature Job recovered all things.

paras.t: Iratus est contra me furor ejus, id est, rigor divinæ justitiæ mihi iratus videtur, quantum ad exteriorem apparentiam, tam dure plagando me; et sic me habuit quasi hostem suum, id est, taliter me tractavit, habendo respectum ad pœnas quibus affligor secundum se ipsas, sicut impios solet tractare. Hinc dixit superius: Cur faciem tuam abscondis, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum? et alibi: Mirabiliter me crucias, et multiplicas iram tuam adversum me. Verumtamen, secundum veritatem non fuit in his ira aut furor Dei adversum Job, sed dilectio et gratia magna, ut dictum est plenius. Simul venerunt latrones ejus, id est Chaldæi et Sabæi: qui dicuntur latrones Dei, quia ab eo creati, et potestatem sortiti ac venire permissi. Dæmones quoque latrones fuerunt in percussione beati Job, et eorum qui pertinebant ad ipsum: quia et Chaldæi et Sabæi a dæmonibus fuerant incitati. Et fecerunt sibi viam per me, id est, me ipsum et mea ad libitum conculcaverunt; obsederunt in gyro tabernaculum meum, id est domesticos meos et bona domus meæ, seu habitaculum ipsum, in quo filii et filiæ opprimebantur illo ruente.
paras.en: [[19:11|His wrath is kindled against me|Iratus est contra me furor ejus]], that is, the rigour of divine justice seems angry with me, as to outward appearance, in smiting me so harshly; [[19:11|and he hath counted me as his enemy|et sic me habuit quasi hostem suum]], that is, he has treated me so, considering the punishments with which I am afflicted in themselves, as he is wont to treat the wicked. Hence he said above: [[Job 13:24|Why hidest thou thy face, and thinkest me thy enemy?|Cur faciem tuam abscondis, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum?]] and elsewhere: [[Job 10:16|thou tormentest me wonderfully|Mirabiliter me crucias]], [[Job 10:17|and multipliest thy wrath upon me|et multiplicas iram tuam adversum me]]. Yet in truth there was in these things no anger or fury of God against Job, but love and great grace, as has been said more fully. [[19:12|His troops have come together|Simul venerunt latrones ejus]] [*latrones*, robbers], that is, the Chaldeans and Sabeans: who are called God's robbers because they were created by him, received their power, and were permitted to come. The demons too were robbers in the smiting of blessed Job and of those who belonged to him[[Job 2:7||]]: for the Chaldeans and Sabeans also had been stirred up by demons. [[19:12|and have made themselves a way by me|Et fecerunt sibi viam per me]], that is, they have trampled me and mine as they pleased; [[19:12|and have besieged my tabernacle round about|obsederunt in gyro tabernaculum meum]], that is, my household and the goods of my house, or the dwelling itself, in which my sons and daughters were crushed when it fell[[Job 1:19||]].

paras.t: Fratres meos, id est cognatos, vel fratres proprie dictos, si habuit eos, longe fecit a me permissive, seu concomitanter: quia per hoc quod Deus ita permisit Job percuti, factus est ipse Job abominabilis suis; et noti mei, scilicet familiares et cari, quasi alieni recesserunt a me, non succurrendo, condolendo, adstando. Dereliquerunt me propinqui mei; et qui me noverunt tempore prosperitatis, obliti sunt mei tempore adversitatis, non impendendo subsidium neque solatium. Ista quoque superius dixit. Inquilini domus meæ, id est advenæ in meis ædibus incolentes, et ancillæ meæ, sicut alienum habuerunt me, non curantes de me, velut si nihil auctoritatis super eos haberem. Ideo additur: et quasi peregrinus fui in oculis eorum, ita quod oblivioni me dabant, vel quasi pertranseundo adspiciebant. Servum meum vocavi, et non respondit; ore proprio deprecabar illum. Puto hic singulare positum pro plurali, ita quod a pluribus famulis suis se dicat contemptum, quia nec jubenti, nec oranti acquieverunt tempore adversitatis istius. Halitum meum exhorruit uxor mea: quia corruptus et fœtidus fuit ex interiorum maxima discrasia. Et orabam filios uteri mei, id est de semine meo progenitos, ut mihi quid deservirent: quibus tamen de lege naturali et scripta potui præcipere. Huic autem verbo videtur obviare quod superius scriptum est, filios ejus et filias simul oppressos in domo per ejus ruinam. Ad quod Thomas respondet: Dici potest, quod vel aliqui parvuli remanserunt, qui non interfuerunt illi convivio; vel aliqui filii eorum, qui mortem propriorum parentum imputantes peccatis Job, ipsum spernebant. Et hoc secundum probabilius reor. Primo enim capitulo dictum est, quod nati sunt ei septem filii et tres filiæ: ubi proles ejus taxari videntur. Infra quoque legitur, quod Dominus reddidit sancto Job omnia duplicia, scilicet post hujus plagæ sanationem: et tamen tunc non sunt ei nati nisi septem filii et tres filiæ. Porro, quod non solum filii immediati dicuntur filii uteri lumborumve patris, constat ex eo quod dicitur Ezechiæ: De filiis tuis qui egredientur ex te, quos generabis, erunt eunuchi in palatio regis Babylonis. Certumque est, Ezechiam non nisi Manassen immediate genuisse.
paras.en: [[19:13|He hath put my brethren far from me|Fratres meos longe fecit a me]], that is, my kinsmen, or brothers in the proper sense, if he had any; he did so by permission, or as a consequence: for through God's permitting Job to be struck in this way, Job himself was made abominable to his own; [[19:13|and my acquaintance like strangers have departed from me|et noti mei quasi alieni recesserunt a me]], namely my intimates and dear ones, by not helping, not grieving with me, not standing by me. [[19:14|My kinsmen have forsaken me|Dereliquerunt me propinqui mei]]; [[19:14|and they that knew me, have forgotten me|et qui me noverunt tempore prosperitatis, obliti sunt mei]], those who knew me in the time of prosperity forgot me in the time of adversity, giving neither help nor comfort. These things too he said above[[Job 6:13||]]. [[19:15|They that dwell in my house|Inquilini domus meæ]], that is, strangers living in my house, [[19:15|and my maidservants have counted me as a stranger|et ancillæ meæ, sicut alienum habuerunt me]], not caring about me, as if I had no authority over them. Therefore it is added: [[19:15|and I have been like an alien in their eyes|et quasi peregrinus fui in oculis eorum]], so that they forgot me, or looked at me as though passing by. [[19:16|I called my servant, and he gave me no answer, I entreated him with my own mouth|Servum meum vocavi, et non respondit; ore proprio deprecabar illum]]. I think the singular is put here for the plural, so that he says he was despised by many of his servants, because they obeyed neither his command nor his entreaty in the time of this adversity. [[19:17|My wife hath abhorred my breath|Halitum meum exhorruit uxor mea]]: because it was corrupt and foul from the very great disorder of his inward parts. [[19:17|and I entreated the children of my womb|Et orabam filios uteri mei]], that is, those begotten of my seed, to do me some service: whom nevertheless I could have commanded by the natural and the written law. But what was written above seems to stand against this saying, that his sons and daughters were crushed together in the house when it fell[[Job 1:19||]]. To this Thomas answers: It can be said either that some little ones remained who were not at that feast; or some of their sons, who, imputing the death of their own parents to Job's sins, despised him. And the second I think more probable. For in the first chapter it was said that [[Job 1:2|there were born to him seven sons and three daughters|nati sunt ei septem filii et tres filiæ]]: where his offspring seem to be counted. Below too it is read that the Lord gave back to holy Job all things double[[Job 42:10||]], namely after the healing of this plague: and yet then there were born to him only seven sons and three daughters[[Job 42:13||]]. Further, that not only immediate sons are called sons of the womb or loins of the father is clear from what is said to Ezechias: [[4 Kings 20:18|of thy sons also that shall issue from thee, whom thou shalt beget, they shall take away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon|De filiis tuis qui egredientur ex te, quos generabis, erunt eunuchi in palatio regis Babylonis]]. And it is certain that Ezechias begot immediately only Manasses[[1 Par 3:13||]][[Matt 1:10||]].

paras.t: Stulti quoque despiciebant me. Stulti quippe, quum non nisi præsentia et terrena adspiciant, in miseriis positos aspernantur. Per stultos autem non intelliguntur dumtaxat, qui usu rationis prorsus privantur; sed et omnes iniqui, qui dono sapientiæ destituti, stoliditate dono illi contraria sunt repleti: qui instar puerorum poma et pira auro et gemmis præferentium, carnalia et caduca spiritualibus præferunt et æternis. De quibus Salomon ait: Stultorum infinitus est numerus. Specialiter tamen stulti hoc loco vocantur, qui vanitatibus se omnino exponunt, vel partim in usu rationis deficiunt, utpote debilis phantasiæ et capitis: qui interiora non penetrantes, alios facile spernunt, quamvis sint justi et sapientes. Hinc Salomon protestatur: Stultus omnes æstimat stultos. Rursusque loquitur: Expedit magis occurrere ursæ raptis fœtibus, quam fatuo confidenti sibi in stultitia sua. Et quum ab eis recessissem, detrahebant mihi, dicentes in secreto, quod dicere verebantur in publico, et implentes quod in Proverbiis legitur: Os stultorum ebullit stultitiam. Et Ecclesiasticus ait: Temerarius in verbo suo odibilis erit. Abominati sunt me quondam consiliarii mei: qui aliquando consiliarii mei tanquam viri prudentes fuerunt; et quem maxime diligebam, aversatus est me, id est, se mihi opposuit. Hoc, secundum Thomam, forsitan dicit propter aliquem eorum qui tunc aderant, qui ei gravius adversabatur. Albertus vero, per hunc maxime dilectum, intelligit Eliphaz Themanitem.
paras.en: [[19:18|Even fools despised me|Stulti quoque despiciebant me]]. For fools, since they look only at present and earthly things, scorn those who are in misery. By fools are understood not only those who are wholly deprived of the use of reason, but also all the wicked, who, lacking the gift of wisdom, are filled with the dullness contrary to that gift: who, like children preferring apples and pears to gold and jewels, prefer carnal and perishing things to spiritual and eternal ones. Of these Solomon says: [[Eccles 1:15|the number of fools is infinite|Stultorum infinitus est numerus]]. In this place, however, those are especially called fools who give themselves over wholly to vanities, or who partly fail in the use of reason, as having a weak imagination and head: who, not penetrating to inward things, easily despise others, though they are just and wise. Hence Solomon declares: [[Eccles 10:3|the fool when he walketh in the way, whereas he himself is a fool, esteemeth all men fools|Stultus omnes æstimat stultos]]. And again he says: [[Prov 17:12|It is better to meet a bear robbed of her whelps, than a fool trusting in his own folly|Expedit magis occurrere ursæ raptis fœtibus, quam fatuo confidenti sibi in stultitia sua]] [[19:18|and when I was gone from them, they spoke against me|Et quum ab eis recessissem, detrahebant mihi]], saying in secret what they feared to say in public, and fulfilling what is read in Proverbs: [[Prov 15:2|the mouth of fools bubbleth out folly|Os stultorum ebullit stultitiam]]. And Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 9:25|he that is rash in his word shall be hateful|Temerarius in verbo suo odibilis erit]]. [[19:19|They that were sometime my counsellors, have abhorred me|Abominati sunt me quondam consiliarii mei]]: who were once my counsellors as prudent men; [[19:19|and he whom I loved most is turned against me|et quem maxime diligebam, aversatus est me]], that is, has set himself against me. According to Thomas he perhaps says this because of one of those then present who opposed him more grievously. But Albert understands by this one most loved Eliphaz the Themanite.

paras.t: Pelli meæ, videlicet cuti siccæ et aridæ, consumptis carnibus meis in magnitudine infirmitatis, adhæsit os meum, id est, ossa mea pelli adhæserunt, carnibus quæ inter pellem et os mediant, consumptis. Hinc supra dixit: Induta est caro mea putredine et sordibus pulveris; cutis mea aruit, et contracta est. Et derelicta sunt tantummodo labia nihil pinguedinis habentia, circa dentes meos: juxta illud Threnorum, Adhæsit cutis eorum ossibus eorum, et facta est quasi lignum. Per quod, secundum Thomam, insinuare videtur quod ceteris membris suo officio destitutis, solum loquendi officium sibi remanserit. Et quia miseriæ debetur seu necessaria est misericordia, cum ingeminatione vocis ex magnitudine desiderii miserationem implorat.
paras.en: [[19:20|to my skin|Pelli meæ]], namely to my dry and withered skin, [[19:20|The flesh being consumed|consumptis carnibus meis]] in the greatness of my sickness, [[19:20|my bone hath cleaved|adhæsit os meum]]: that is, my bones have cleaved to my skin, the flesh that lies between skin and bone being consumed. Hence he said above: [[Job 7:5|My flesh is clothed with rottenness and the filth of dust; my skin is withered and drawn together|Induta est caro mea putredine et sordibus pulveris; cutis mea aruit, et contracta est]] [[19:20|and nothing but lips are left about my teeth|Et derelicta sunt tantummodo labia nihil pinguedinis habentia, circa dentes meos]], lips having no fat: according to that of Lamentations: [[Lam 4:8|their skin hath stuck to their bones, it is withered, and is become like wood|Adhæsit cutis eorum ossibus eorum, et facta est quasi lignum]]. By which, according to Thomas, he seems to suggest that, the other members being deprived of their office, only the office of speaking remained to him. And because mercy is due to misery, or is needed by it, he implores pity with a doubling of the voice from the greatness of his desire.

paras.t: Miseremini mei, miseremini mei, saltem vos, amici mei: quum amicorum sit, sua sibi invicem communicare, et onera invicem supportare, imo dilecti calamitatem quasi propriam reputare, atque pro viribus relevare. Est enim eorum, eadem velle et nolle, secundum Philosophum. Unde Ecclesiasticus inducit: Amicus fidelis, medicamentum vitæ et immortalitatis. Itaque, quum ab aliis sim relictus, ab hostibusque vastatus, saltem vos, amici mei, miseremini mei, quia a fortissimo, cui nemo valet resistere, sum percussus. Quia manus Domini tetigit me, id est, potestas Dei me sic lædi permisit. Nam et supra, Satan loquitur Deo: Mitte manum tuam, et tange os ejus et carnem.
paras.en: [[19:21|Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you my friends|Miseremini mei, miseremini mei, saltem vos, amici mei]]: since it belongs to friends to share their own things with one another, and [[Gal 6:2|Bear ye one another's burdens|onera invicem supportare]], nay, to reckon the calamity of the one they love as their own, and relieve it as far as they can. For it belongs to them to will and not will the same things, according to the Philosopher. Hence Ecclesiasticus brings in: [[Ecclus 6:16|A faithful friend is the medicine of life and immortality|Amicus fidelis, medicamentum vitæ et immortalitatis]]. So, since I am forsaken by others and laid waste by enemies, at least you, my friends, have pity on me, for I have been struck by the strongest, whom no one can resist. [[19:21|because the hand of the Lord hath touched me|Quia manus Domini tetigit me]], that is, the power of God has allowed me to be so harmed. For above, too, Satan says to God: [[Job 2:5|put forth thy hand, and touch his bone and his flesh|Mitte manum tuam, et tange os ejus et carnem]].

paras.t: Quare persequimini me sicut Deus? Non solum non condoletis, neque succurritis, sed afflicto afflictionem adjicitis, tribulando me dure, sicut et Deus dure afflixit me. Vel sic: Quare persequimini me sicut Deus? id est, ita me pro meis increpatis excessibus, quos mihi imponitis, ac si vos ipsi fragiles et ad peccata labiles non essetis, quemadmodum Deus sic increpat quod ipse peccare non valet. Quum homo hominem punit, quum arguit, compassive et pie debet hoc agere, pensans quam infirmus et defectuosus sit ipse, secundum illud Apostoli ad Galatas: Fratres, et si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujuscemodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis, considerans te ipsum, ne et tu tenteris. Vel sic: Quare persequimini me sicut Deus? id est, non est vestrum me persequi, sicut me Deus persequitur. Deus quippe persequitur innocentem, ut probet, vel ad gloriæ suæ manifestationem, aut propter meritorum beatitudinisque augmentum. Vos autem talem causam persequendi me innocentem non habetis. Circa hæc scribit Gregorius: Si sint qui aspera correptione indigeant, tunc eis dura a nobis correptio admovenda est, quum Dei manus cessat a verbere. Quum vero superna insunt flagella, a nobis non jam correptio, sed consolatio debetur, ne, dum dolori increpationem jungimus, percussionem percussioni sociemus.
paras.en: [[19:22|Why do you persecute me as God|Quare persequimini me sicut Deus]]? Not only do you not grieve with me or help me, but you add affliction to the afflicted, troubling me harshly as God too has harshly afflicted me. Or thus: *Why do you persecute me as God?* that is, you rebuke me so for my excesses, which you lay upon me, as though you yourselves were not frail and prone to sin, just as God rebukes so because he himself cannot sin. When man punishes man, when he reproves him, he ought to do it with compassion and kindness, weighing how weak and faulty he himself is, according to that saying of the Apostle to the Galatians: [[Gal 6:1|Brethren, and if a man be overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness, considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted|Fratres, et si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujuscemodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis, considerans te ipsum, ne et tu tenteris]] Or thus: *Why do you persecute me as God?* that is, it is not for you to persecute me as God persecutes me. For God persecutes the innocent to try him, or to show forth his glory, or for the increase of merits and beatitude. But you have no such cause for persecuting me, an innocent man. On this Gregory writes: If there are those who need sharp correction, harsh correction is to be applied to them by us when the hand of God ceases from the scourge. But when scourges from above are upon them, not correction but consolation is owed by us, lest, while we join rebuke to sorrow, we add stroke to stroke.

paras.t: Et carnibus meis saturamini, id est, corporis mei doloribus delectamini, et quasi reficimini? quia putantes me pro peccatis meis percussum, nec tamen pœnitentem, sed induratum atque blasphemum, gaudetis de meis pœnis, velut divinæ congratulantes justitiæ. Insuper, juxta Gregorium, qui proximorum pœnas esuriunt, aut alienæ vitæ detractione pascuntur, alienis procul dubio carnibus satiantur. Sic et David effatur: Dum appropiant super me nocentes, ut edant carnes meas. De talibus Dominus ait in Michæa: Carnem populi mei comederunt, et pellem desuper excoriaverunt. Thomas quoque affirmat, quod detractores carnibus humanis proprie vesci dicuntur. Atque Albertus: Qui pœnam, inquit, auget afflicto, saturatur ac reficitur pœnis ejus. Itaque compassivi simus et ignoscentes, nec aliorum afflictionem optemus, seu approbemus ut pœna est, sed in quantum est effectus justitiæ, remedium culpæ, occasio gratiæ, cumulus gloriæ.
paras.en: [[19:22|and glut yourselves with my flesh?|Et carnibus meis saturamini]] that is, you delight in the pains of my body and are as it were refreshed by them? for thinking that I have been struck for my sins, and yet do not repent but am hardened and a blasphemer, you rejoice at my pains, as though rejoicing with the divine justice. Moreover, according to Gregory, those who hunger for the pains of their neighbours, or feed on disparaging the lives of others, are without doubt glutted with others' flesh. So too David speaks: [[Ps 26:2|Whilst the wicked draw near against me, to eat my flesh|Dum appropiant super me nocentes, ut edant carnes meas]]. Of such the Lord says in Micheas: [[Mich 3:3|Who have eaten the flesh of my people, and have flayed their skin off them|Carnem populi mei comederunt, et pellem desuper excoriaverunt]]. Thomas too affirms that detractors are properly said to feed on human flesh. And Albert: He who adds pain to the afflicted, he says, is glutted and refreshed by his pains. Let us then be compassionate and forgiving, and not desire or approve the affliction of others as it is a punishment, but inasmuch as it is an effect of justice, a remedy for guilt, an occasion of grace, a heaping up of glory.

paras.t: Præterea, quia beatus Job mox utilissima, alta, totique mundo saluberrime innotescenda fuit dicturus, adjecit: Quis mihi tribuat ut scribantur sermones mei? quos dicam ad aliorum instructionem, ut futuris generationibus innotescant. Quis mihi det ut exarentur, id est scribantur, in libro? Verba autem sequentia a diversis diversimode habentur, punctuantur et exponuntur. Quidam enim (ut Albertus et Thomas) sic punctuant: In libro stilo ferreo. Sed non videtur id aptum, quum ferreus stilus aptus non sit ad scribendum in libro. Ad quod solvendum Albertus sic ait: In libro, id est in dura materia sicut in libro. Aliqui autem sic punctuant: Quis mihi det ut exarentur in libro? Deinde subjungunt, stilo ferreo et plumbi lamina, id est, si parum fuerit scribi eos in libro, cupio ut scribantur ferreo stilo in lamina plumbi. Talis etenim plumbea massa apices sibi inscriptos diu conservat. Aliqui legunt et punctuant sic: Quis mihi det ut exarentur in libro stilo ferreo aut plumbi lamina? Quod rursus dupliciter explanatur. Primo, Exarentur in libro stilo ferreo aut plumbi lamina, id est vel in tali materia. Secundo, Aut plumbi lamina, id est, scribantur in libro cum ferreo stilo, aut cum plumbea lamina. Vel certe sculpantur in silice. Silex enim sicut difficillime recipit inscriptionem, ita diutissime tenet eam. Aliqui legunt: Vel celte sculpantur. Asseritque Albertus, quod celte sit nomen indeclinabile, designans instrumentum cæmentarii, quo lapides sculpuntur durissimi. Porro in Mammotractu Bibliæ legitur, quod celte sit ablativus, et declinetur, celtis, celtis, celti; significetque ferreum instrumentum conveniens ad sculpendum. Juxta hunc modum præcipit Dominus Habacuc prophetæ: Scribe visum, et explana eum super tabulam, ut percurrat qui legerit eum. Isaiæ quoque jubetur: Sume tibi librum grandem, et scribe in eo.
paras.en: Moreover, because blessed Job was about to say things most useful and lofty, which it would be most wholesome for the whole world to know, he added: [[19:23|Who will grant me that my words may be written?|Quis mihi tribuat ut scribantur sermones mei?]] the words I shall say for the instruction of others, that they may be known to future generations. [[19:23|who will grant me that they may be marked down|Quis mihi det ut exarentur]], that is, be written, [[19:23|in a book?|in libro?]] The words that follow are read, punctuated and expounded by different men in different ways. For some (as Albert and Thomas) punctuate thus: *in a book with an iron pen.* But this does not seem fitting, since an iron pen is not suited to writing in a book. To resolve this Albert says: *In a book*, that is, in hard material as in a book.
