Paulatim siquidem dejicit nos tentator in primis. Dejectos vero frequenter ad nutum, ad gravissima trahit facinora.
paras.en: [[20:16|He shall suck the head of asps|Caput aspidum surget]] [Denis reads *surget*, *the head of asps shall rise*, where the Vulgate has *suget*, *he shall suck*], [[20:16|and the viper's tongue shall kill him|et occidet eum lingua viperæ]]. On this Gregory writes: The asp is a small serpent; but the viper is longer. Asps lay eggs, from which their young are hatched. But when vipers have conceived, their young rage within their mothers' bellies, and are born by bursting their mothers' sides. Hence it is called *vipera*, because it brings forth by force [*vi parit*]: its offspring is brought forth with the death of the mother. By asps, then, the hidden suggestions of demons are signified; by the viper's tongue, the violent temptation of the devil. So the head of asps rises against the hypocrite, because first he is infected by a hidden and small suggestion. Then the viper's tongue kills him, because a little later he is laid low by a strong and violent temptation. For the tempter casts us down little by little at first; but those cast down he often drags at his will to the gravest crimes.

paras.t: Non videat, id est, non sortiatur nec experiatur, rivulos fluminis, id est charismata Spiritus Sancti. De quibus Joannis septimo adstruit Christus: Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ: ubi mox subditur, Hoc autem dicebat de Spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Torrentis, id est inundationis donorum Spiritus Sancti. Unde in Psalmo habetur: Torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos. Primo quippe, donis Spiritus Sancti perfundimur. Quibus si grati bene utamur, in eisdem crescimus ac replemur, ita ut inundemus, illudque Jeremiæ humiliter fateamur: Factus sum quasi vir ebrius, et quasi homo madidus vino a facie Domini, et a facie verborum sanctorum ejus. Mellis, id est dulcedinis, quæ in actibus divinarum seu theologicarum consistit virtutum; et butyri, id est delectationis, quæ in moralibus habetur virtutibus. Mel etenim desuper et ex floribus venit. Idcirco per ipsum suavitas virtutum, quæ circa Deum versantur, exprimitur. Butyrum autem ex animalium lacte suscipitur. Idcirco per ipsum delectatio virtutum, circa passionum ordinationem versantium, explicatur. Omnibus igitur istis divinis donis ac dulcedinibus seu consolationibus sanctis atque cœlestibus hypocrita et injustus privatur, qui in se ipso et carnalibus impie delectatur, nec Deo rite infigitur.
paras.en: [[20:17|Let him not see|Non videat]], that is, let him not obtain or experience, [[20:17|the streams of the river|rivulos fluminis]], that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Of which Christ affirms in the seventh chapter of John: [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me, as the scripture saith: Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]: where it is added immediately: [[John 7:39|Now this he said of the Spirit which they should receive who believed in him|Hoc autem dicebat de Spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum]]. [[20:17|the brooks|Torrentis]] [literally *of the torrent*], that is, of the flood of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Hence we have in the Psalm: [[Ps 35:9|thou shalt make them drink of the torrent of thy pleasure|Torrente voluptatis tuæ potabis eos]]. For first we are bathed in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. If we use them well and gratefully, we grow and are filled in them, so that we overflow, and humbly confess that saying of Jeremias: [[Jer 23:9|I am become as a drunken man, and as a man full of wine, at the presence of the Lord, and at the presence of his holy words|Factus sum quasi vir ebrius, et quasi homo madidus vino a facie Domini, et a facie verborum sanctorum ejus]] [[20:17|of honey|Mellis]], that is, of the sweetness which lies in the acts of the divine or theological virtues; [[20:17|and of butter|et butyri]], that is, of the delight which is found in the moral virtues. For honey comes from above and from flowers. Therefore by it is expressed the sweetness of the virtues that are concerned with God. But butter is got from the milk of animals. Therefore by it is set forth the delight of the virtues concerned with the ordering of the passions. Of all these divine gifts and sweetnesses, or holy and heavenly consolations, then, the hypocrite and the unjust man is deprived, who takes impious delight in himself and in carnal things, and is not duly fixed on God.

paras.t: Quoniam confringens nudavit pauperis domum. Domus pauperis, est congregatio prælati boni ac humilis, seu corpus vel conscientia ejus: quam frangendo impius seu hypocrita nudat, dum eam ad vitia pravo exemplo, verbis perversis, terrore seu adulatione inducit, sicut de reprobis scribit Apostolus, quia proficient in pejus, errantes et in errorem mittentes. Rapuit, id est, spiritualibus bonis eam præfatis modis privavit; et non ædificavit eam bonis exemplis, juxta illud: Unusquisque proximo suo placeat in bonum ad ædificationem. In Ecclesiastico quoque scriptum est: Unicuique mandavit Deus de proximo suo, ut scilicet eum ædificet loco et tempore opportunis. Nec est satiatus venter ejus, id est peccandi affectus: quo enim quis gravius atque diutius peccat, ac plures scandalizat, tanto plus eum peccare delectat, nisi adspirante Spiritu Sancto pœnitentialiter convertatur. Quemadmodum enim una actio virtuosa disponit et trahit ad aliam, sic unum peccatum, nisi pœnitentia deleatur, suo mox pondere inducit ad aliud. Hoc tamen specialiter aptatur avaro, qui quanto plura acquirit, tanto amplius inflammatur ad ampliora. Hinc Habacuc dicit de cupido: Usquequo aggravat contra se lutum densum? Et in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Qui diligit aurum, non justificabitur.
paras.en: [[20:19|Because he broke in and stripped|Quoniam confringens nudavit]] [[20:19|the poor|pauperis domum]] [Denis reads *the house of the poor*]. The house of the poor is the congregation of a good and humble prelate, or his body or conscience: which the wicked man or hypocrite breaks and strips when he leads it into vices by bad example, perverse words, terror or flattery; as the Apostle writes of the reprobate, that they [[2 Tim 3:13|shall grow worse and worse: erring, and driving into error|proficient in pejus, errantes et in errorem mittentes]]. [[20:19|he hath violently taken away a house|Rapuit]], that is, he has deprived it of spiritual goods in the ways described; [[20:19|which he did not build|et non ædificavit eam]] by good examples, according to that saying: [[Rom 15:2|Let every one of you Please his neighbour unto good, to edification|Unusquisque proximo suo placeat in bonum ad ædificationem]] In Ecclesiasticus too it is written: [[Ecclus 17:12|he gave to every one of them commandment concerning his neighbour|Unicuique mandavit Deus de proximo suo]], namely that he should edify him at a fitting place and time. [[20:20|And yet his belly was not filled|Nec est satiatus venter ejus]], that is, his desire for sinning: for the more gravely and longer one sins, and the more people he scandalizes, the more it delights him to sin, unless by the breathing of the Holy Spirit he is converted in penance. For as one virtuous action disposes and draws to another, so one sin, unless it is blotted out by penance, soon leads by its weight to another. This, however, fits the avaricious man especially, who the more he acquires, the more he is inflamed for more. Hence Habacuc says of the covetous man: [[Hab 2:6|how long also doth he load himself with thick clay?|Usquequo aggravat contra se lutum densum?]] And in Ecclesiasticus it is written: [[Ecclus 31:5|He that loveth gold, shall not be justified|Qui diligit aurum, non justificabitur]].

paras.t: Æstuabit, et omnis dolor irruet super eum. Impius atque hypocrita æstuat nunc infelici fervore iræ, concupiscentiæ, privati amoris, tabescentis rancoris, curis quoque vitæ præsentis, et timore ne alius eum præcedat, excedat, convincat. Sicque partim in vita hac omnis dolor irruit super eum, quoniam (Augustino testante) animus inordinatus sibi ipsi pœnalis est. Nil autem suavius, nil quietius delectabiliusque in sæculo occurrit, quam universis caducis et vanis contemptis, supergloriosissimo Deo pura mente intendere, simplici corde vacare et inhærere. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Mira suavitas cordis, aliena non quærere, sed uniuscujusque diei victu contentum manere: ex qua securitate perennis requies nascitur, quoniam a bona et tranquilla cogitatione ad gaudia æterna transitur. Propterea quoque in Ecclesiaste habetur: Homini bono dedit Deus sapientiam, et scientiam, et lætitiam; peccatori autem afflictionem, et curam superfluam.
paras.en: [[20:22|he shall burn, and every sorrow shall fall upon him|Æstuabit, et omnis dolor irruet super eum]]. The wicked man and the hypocrite burns now with the unhappy heat of anger, of concupiscence, of private love, of wasting rancour, and also with the cares of the present life, and with fear lest another get before him, surpass him or defeat him. And so in part, in this life, *every sorrow falls upon him*, since (as Augustine witnesses) a disordered mind is a punishment to itself. But nothing sweeter, nothing quieter or more delightful is found in the world than, all perishing and vain things being despised, to attend with a pure mind to the most supremely glorious God, to be free for him and cleave to him with a simple heart. Hence Gregory says: It is a wonderful sweetness of heart not to seek what is another's, but to remain content with each day's food: from this security a lasting rest is born, since one passes from good and tranquil thought to eternal joys. Therefore too we have in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 2:26|God hath given to a man that is good in his sight, wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he hath given vexation, and superfluous care|Homini bono dedit Deus sapientiam, et scientiam, et lætitiam; peccatori autem afflictionem, et curam superfluam]].

paras.t: Fugiet arma ferrea, et irruet in arcum æreum. Hoc præcedenti articulo satis expositum est. Porro quod subditur, Eductus et egrediens de vagina sua, et fulgurans in amaritudine sua, ibi exponebatur de æreo arcu. Gregorius vero exponit, et bene, de impio sive hypocrita, de quo immediate sermo præcessit sub eisdem casu et numero. Impius ergo dum mala, mente tractat et nondum prosequitur, quasi in vagina sua persistit: de qua educitur, dum dæmone suggerente, mala forinsecus operatur; egreditur vero, quoniam sponte consentit et efficit quod dæmon suggessit. Fulgurans, id est aliis terribiliter minans, aut subito vano temporali honore clarescens, in amaritudine sua, qua contra alios vitiose ac dure afficitur, per quam et ad infernalem acerbitatem perducitur.
paras.en: [[20:24|He shall flee from weapons of iron, and shall fall upon a bow of brass.|Fugiet arma ferrea, et irruet in arcum æreum.]] This was sufficiently expounded in the preceding article. But what is added, [[20:25|The sword is drawn out, and cometh forth from its scabbard, and glittereth in his bitterness|Eductus et egrediens de vagina sua, et fulgurans in amaritudine sua]] [the Latin has no word for *sword*: literally *drawn out and coming forth from its scabbard*], was there expounded of the bow of brass. Gregory, however, expounds it, and well, of the wicked man or hypocrite, of whom the discourse went immediately before, in the same case and number. The wicked man, then, while he turns over evil in his mind and does not yet carry it out, stays as it were in his scabbard: from which he is *drawn out* when, at the demon's suggestion, he does evil outwardly; and he *comes forth* because he freely consents to and does what the demon suggested. [[20:25|and glittereth|Fulgurans]], that is, threatening others terribly, or suddenly shining with vain temporal honour, [[20:25|in his bitterness|in amaritudine sua]], by which he is viciously and harshly disposed against others, and by which he is also brought to the bitterness of hell.

paras.t: Vadent et venient super eum horribiles, id est, diaboli in hac vita vadent super eum vitia suggerendo, postea venient super eum supplicia inferendo: imo in hoc vitæ curriculo vadunt et veniunt super eum, quia ad libitum eum in peccatis conculcant, spiritualiter vincunt, et suæ dominationi subjiciunt. Diabolus enim pater et rex impiorum vocatur. De quo loquitur Christus: Venit ad me princeps mundi hujus. Quid est, Mundi hujus, nisi hominum mundanorum? Quocontra de electis testatur, loquens ad Patrem: De mundo non sunt, sicut et ego non sum de mundo, id est de societate et numero sæcularium hominum, ea quæ mundi sunt, præferentium Deo. Rursus, dæmones super impium vadunt et redeunt, quia ad culpam eum inducunt: quod si ad tempus pœnitendo eos expulerit, cito ad pristina revertitur vitia; eorumque suggestionibus acquiescens, locum dat eis. Quocontra ait apostolus Paulus: Nolite locum dare diabolo. Et Jacobus: Resistite, inquit, diabolo, et fugiet a vobis. Cetera patent.
paras.en: [[20:25|the terrible ones shall go and come upon him|Vadent et venient super eum horribiles]], that is, the devils will go upon him in this life by suggesting vices, and afterwards will come upon him by inflicting punishments: nay, in the course of this life they go and come upon him, because they trample him in sins as they please, conquer him spiritually and subject him to their dominion. For the devil is called the father and king of the wicked. Of him Christ says: [[John 14:30|the prince of this world: cometh|Venit ad me princeps mundi hujus]] [literally *the prince of this world cometh to me*]. What is *of this world* but *of worldly men*? Against which he testifies of the elect, speaking to the Father: [[John 17:16|They are not of the world, as I also am not of the world|De mundo non sunt, sicut et ego non sum de mundo]], that is, of the society and number of worldly men, who prefer the things of the world to God. Again, the demons go and return upon the wicked man, because they lead him into guilt: and if for a time he drives them out by penance, he soon returns to his former vices; and consenting to their suggestions, he gives place to them. Against which the apostle Paul says: [[Eph 4:27|Give not place to the devil.|Nolite locum dare diabolo.]] And James: [[Jas 4:7|But resist the devil: and he will fly from you|Resistite, inquit, diabolo, et fugiet a vobis]] The rest is plain.

21.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli vicesimi primi: Respondens autem Job, dixit.
21.title_en: Literal declaration of the twenty-first chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit. Sapientis est ad proposita respondere, errantes ac ignorantes instruere, veritatem defendere, arroganter contradicentes ratione compescere. Ita Job agit. Audite, quæso, sermones meos. In eo quod ait, Quæso, humilitatem ostendit. Et agetis pœnitentiam de vestro errore circa providentiam Dei, et quia tam injuriose mihi locuti estis. Sustinete me, ut et ego loquar, id est, me patienter audite; et post mea, si videbitur, verba ridete, id est, si digna fuerint verba mea derisu, zelo veritatis ea contemnite: sicut in libro de Trinitate asserit Augustinus, ridendam esse argumentationem Eunomii. Et in Isaia habetur: Opera eorum inutilia et risu digna. Sic et Deus in Proverbiis loquitur impiis: Ego in interitu vestro ridebo. Simon quoque et Judas apostoli deriserunt verba deorum, vel potius dæmoniorum per idola loquentium.
paras.en: [[21:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]]. It belongs to a wise man to answer what is put forward, to instruct those who err and are ignorant, to defend the truth, and to restrain by reason those who arrogantly contradict. So Job does. [[21:2|Hear, I beseech you, my words|Audite, quæso, sermones meos]]. In saying *I beseech you*, he shows humility. [[21:2|and do penance|Et agetis pœnitentiam]] for your error about the providence of God, and because you have spoken so injuriously to me. [[21:3|Suffer me, and I will speak|Sustinete me, ut et ego loquar]], that is, hear me patiently; [[21:3|and after, if you please, laugh at my words|et post mea, si videbitur, verba ridete]], that is, if my words are worthy of derision, despise them out of zeal for the truth: as Augustine asserts in his book On the Trinity that the argument of Eunomius is to be laughed at. And in Isaias we have: [[Is 59:6|their works are unprofitable works|Opera eorum inutilia]], and [[Jer 51:18|worthy to be laughed at|risu digna]] [the margin gives Is. lix, 6 and Jer. li, 18: Denis joins words from the two places]. So too God says to the wicked in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:26|I also will laugh in your destruction|Ego in interitu vestro ridebo]]. The apostles Simon and Jude also laughed at the words of the gods, or rather of the demons speaking through the idols.

paras.t: Numquid contra hominem disputatio mea est? quasi dicat: Disputatio mea non est principaliter de aliquo facto mihi ab homine illato; nec conqueror me ab hominibus absque demeritis meis percussum, sed a Deo: ita quod disputatio mea principaliter versatur circa hoc, quomodo salva justitia Dei, ego vir justus et innocens tam dire percussus sim. Hinc subditur: Ut merito non debeam contristari, id est, quoniam disputatio mea est non de adversitate mihi ab homine, sed a Deo illata, ideo merito tristor: quoniam causam percussionis meæ nondum plene intelligo, timereque habeo ne forte qui tam pœnose plagatus sum, Deo aliquo modo displiceam. Porro, si ab homine tantum esset mea afflictio, tristitia esset pellenda: quia nec timere habeo ne hominibus displiceam, nisi in quantum hoc esset contra Deum atque justitiam, quoniam scriptum est: Qui timet hominem, cito corruet; et: Qui timet Deum, nihil trepidabit.
paras.en: [[21:4|Is my debate against man|Numquid contra hominem disputatio mea est]]? As if to say: My debate is not chiefly about some deed done to me by a man; nor do I complain that I have been struck by men without any deserving of mine, but by God: so that my debate turns chiefly on this, how, with the justice of God kept whole, I, a just and innocent man, have been struck so dreadfully. Hence he adds: [[21:4|that I should not have just reason to be troubled|Ut merito non debeam contristari]], that is, since my debate is not about an adversity brought upon me by a man but by God, I am therefore rightly sad: for I do not yet fully understand the cause of my being struck, and I have reason to fear lest perhaps, smitten so grievously, I displease God in some way. But if my affliction were from man only, the sadness would have to be driven away: for I have no reason to fear displeasing men, except so far as this would be against God and justice, since it is written: [[Prov 29:25|He that feareth man shall quickly fall|Qui timet hominem, cito corruet]]; and: [[Ecclus 34:16|He that feareth the Lord shall tremble at nothing|Qui timet Deum, nihil trepidabit]].

paras.t: Attendite me, verba mea diligentissime advertendo, et vitam meam pensando, quod item hæc patior qui taliter vixi; et obstupescite, id est, vehementer admiramini, de imperscrutabili profunditate judiciorum Altissimi, de futuro quoque ejus judicio de quo loquor; et superponite digitum ori vestro, id est, cum silentio me audite, prout decet sapientem audiri. Unde in libro Sapientiæ vir sapiens sapientiam inter cetera sic commendat: Audient me reges horrendi, et sermocinante me plura, digitum ori superponent.
paras.en: [[21:5|Hearken to me|Attendite me]], by marking my words most diligently and weighing my life, and how I suffer these things though I have lived in such a way; [[21:5|and be astonished|et obstupescite]], that is, wonder exceedingly at the unsearchable depth of the judgments of the Most High, and also at his judgment to come, of which I speak; [[21:5|and lay your finger on your mouth|et superponite digitum ori vestro]], that is, hear me in silence, as it befits a wise man to be heard. Hence in the book of Wisdom the wise man, among other things, commends wisdom thus: [[Wis 8:15|Terrible kings hearing, shall be afraid of me|Audient me reges horrendi]] [Denis's wording is 'terrible kings shall hear me'], and [[Wis 8:12|if I talk much, they shall lay their hands on their mouth|sermocinante me plura, digitum ori superponent]] [Denis has 'finger' where the Vulgate has 'hands', as in Job's words; the margin gives Wis. viii, 15, 12].

paras.t: Et ego quando recordatus fuero divinorum judiciorum, pertimesco filiali timore: quia altitudinem sapientiæ atque justitiæ Dei, quam penetrare non valeo, nec plus quam decet scrutari præsumo, vereor et honoro; et concutit carnem meam tremor, id est, tantus est animæ meæ timor, quod redundat vehementer in corpus: juxta illud Psalmi, Timor et tremor venerunt super me. Sic et Habacuc ait: Domine, audivi auditum tuum, et timui; consideravi opera tua, et expavi. Sic habet translatio Septuaginta interpretum. Hoc affectu dixit Apostolus: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus! etc.
paras.en: [[21:6|As for me, when I remember|Et ego quando recordatus fuero]] the divine judgments, [[21:6|I am afraid|pertimesco]] with filial fear: for the height of God's wisdom and justice, which I cannot pierce, nor presume to search into more than is fitting, I revere and honour; [[21:6|and trembling taketh hold on my flesh|et concutit carnem meam tremor]], that is, so great is the fear of my soul that it overflows vehemently into the body: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 54:6|Fear and trembling are come upon me|Timor et tremor venerunt super me]]. So also Habacuc says: [[Hab 3:2|O Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid|Domine, audivi auditum tuum, et timui]]; I considered thy works, and was dismayed. So the translation of the Seventy Interpreters has it [the margin's numerals are unclear; the passage is Hab 3:2, where the Vulgate has only the first clause; 'I considered thy works, and was dismayed' is the Septuagint's]. In this frame of mind the Apostle said: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus!]]! etc.

paras.t: Præterea, jam in isto capitulo sanctus Job contra amicos suos evidentius et efficacius disputat, quam fecit hucusque, et errorem eorum clarissime reprobat. Concorditer enim dicebant, virtuosis hominibus in vita hac prospera evenire, et vitiosis adversa; quod item adversitates non nisi pro peccatis infligerentur a Deo. Contra quod ait beatus Job: Quare ergo impii vivunt vita naturæ, quum morte sint digni? Idcirco, si divina justitia non permittit prospera inesse indignis, injusti mox morerentur. Constat itaque quod Deus longanimiter tolerat malos. Sublevati sunt dignitatibus, honore, fama et gloria; confortatique divitiis, ita quod diu et frequenter usque decrepitam senectutem manent in prosperitatibus istis: cujus contrarium sequebatur ex verbis amicorum Job.
paras.en: Moreover, in this chapter holy Job now disputes against his friends more plainly and more forcefully than he has done so far, and most clearly refutes their error. For they said with one accord that in this life prosperity befalls virtuous men, and adversity the vicious; and likewise that adversities are inflicted by God only for sins. Against this blessed Job says: [[21:7|Why then do the wicked live|Quare ergo impii vivunt]] the life of nature, when they are worthy of death? For if divine justice does not allow prosperity to be found in the unworthy, the unjust would die at once. It is clear, then, that God bears with the wicked long-sufferingly. [[21:7|are they advanced|Sublevati sunt]] with dignities, honour, fame and glory, [[21:7|and strengthened with riches|confortatique divitiis]], so that they remain in this prosperity long and often even to decrepit old age: the contrary of which followed from the words of Job's friends.

paras.t: Semen eorum permanet coram eis, id est, in eorum conspectu diu subsistunt ac vivunt nati filiæque ipsorum, juxta illud Psalmistæ: Quorum filii sicut novellæ plantationes in juventute sua. Filiæ eorum compositæ, circumornatæ ut similitudo templi. Hinc Jeremias scribit: Quare via impiorum prosperatur, et bene est omnibus qui prævaricantur et inique agunt? Plantasti eos, Domine, et radicem miserunt; proficiunt, et faciunt fructum. Propinquorum turba et nepotum in conspectu eorum, id est, consanguineorum multitudine gaudent.
paras.en: [[21:8|Their seed continueth before them|Semen eorum permanet coram eis]], that is, their sons and daughters long survive and live in their sight, according to that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 143:12|Whose sons are as new plants in their youth: Their daughters decked out, adorned round about after the similitude of a temple|Quorum filii sicut novellæ plantationes in juventute sua. Filiæ eorum compositæ, circumornatæ ut similitudo templi]]. Hence Jeremias writes: [[Jer 12:1|Why doth the way of the wicked prosper: why is it well with all them that transgress, and do wickedly?|Quare via impiorum prosperatur, et bene est omnibus qui prævaricantur et inique agunt?]] [[Jer 12:2|Thou hast planted them|Plantasti eos]], O Lord, [[Jer 12:2|and they have taken root: they prosper and bring forth fruit|et radicem miserunt; proficiunt, et faciunt fructum]]. [[21:8|a multitude of kinsmen, and of children's children in their sight|Propinquorum turba et nepotum in conspectu eorum]], that is, they rejoice in a multitude of blood relations.

paras.t: Domus eorum securæ sunt et pacatæ, id est, familiæ, habitacula, opes eorum a nemine impugnantur aut destruuntur, sed et pace temporali fruuntur. Ex quibus ostenditur, quod præsentis vitæ adversa non solis injustis eveniant: imo frequenter justis contingunt, juxta illud Ecclesiastæ, Sunt justi, quibus mala proveniunt, quasi opera egerint impiorum; et sunt impii, qui ita securi sunt, quasi justorum facta habeant. Et non est virga, id est correctio, Dei super illos: quia in vita hac pro suis peccatis divinitus non puniuntur; nec adversitatibus exercentur quidam eorum, de quibus Deus in Psalmo testatur: Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum; ibunt in adinventionibus suis. Unde per Ezechielem ad reprobum populum loquitur: Zelus meus recessit a te: non irascar tibi amplius. Quocontra ait electus: Virga tua et baculus tuus, ipsa me consolata sunt. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Virga eos supernæ disciplinæ non perculit; et tanto amplius in culpa proficiunt, quo minus pro ea feriuntur.
paras.en: [[21:9|Their houses are secure and peaceable|Domus eorum securæ sunt et pacatæ]], that is, their households, dwellings and wealth are attacked or destroyed by no one, but they enjoy temporal peace as well. From which it is shown that the adversities of the present life do not befall the unjust alone: nay, they often happen to the just, according to that of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:14|There are just men to whom evils happen, as though they had done the works of the wicked: and there are wicked men, who are as secure as though they had the deeds of the just|Sunt justi, quibus mala proveniunt, quasi opera egerint impiorum; et sunt impii, qui ita securi sunt, quasi justorum facta habeant]]. [[21:9|and the rod|Et non est virga]], that is, the correction, [[21:9|of God is not upon them|Dei super illos]]: because in this life they are not punished by God for their sins; nor are some of them exercised by adversities, those of whom God testifies in the Psalm: [[Ps 80:13|I let them go according to the desires of their heart: they shall walk in their own inventions|Dimisi eos secundum desideria cordis eorum; ibunt in adinventionibus suis]]. Hence he says through Ezechiel to the reprobate people: [[Ezech 16:42|my jealousy shall depart from thee|Zelus meus recessit a te]]: I will [[Ezech 16:42|be angry no more|non irascar tibi amplius]] with thee [Denis's wording is 'my jealousy has departed from thee: I will be angry with thee no more']. Against which the elect says: [[Ps 22:4|Thy rod and thy staff, they have comforted me|Virga tua et baculus tuus, ipsa me consolata sunt]] [the margin gives Ps. xxii, 5]. Hence Gregory says: The rod of heavenly discipline has not struck them; and they advance in guilt all the more, the less they are smitten for it.

paras.t: Bos eorum concepit. Secundum Gregorium, consuetudo vulgaris locutionis est, ut bovem, masculum; vaccam, feminam nominemus. Sed litteratura bovem communis generis vocat: hic ergo pro vacca accipitur. Boves quoque apud antiquos acceptissimi erant propter agriculturam. Et non abortivit, id est, ante tempus aptum non peperit patiendo abortum. Vacca peperit: ejusdem equidem est concipere et parere; et non est privata fœtu suo. Per bovem autem et vaccam, multitudo animalium horum exprimitur.
paras.en: [[21:10|Their cattle have conceived|Bos eorum concepit]] [the Latin has *bos*, 'ox', which the Douay-Rheims renders 'cattle']. According to Gregory, it is the custom of common speech to call the male *bos* (ox) and the female *vacca* (cow). But learned usage treats *bos* as of common gender: here, then, it is taken for the cow. Oxen, too, were most highly prized among the ancients because of agriculture. [[21:10|and failed not|Et non abortivit]], that is, did not bring forth before the fitting time by suffering a miscarriage. [[21:10|their cow has calved|Vacca peperit]]: for it belongs to the same animal to conceive and to bring forth; [[21:10|and is not deprived of her fruit|et non est privata fœtu suo]]. By the ox and the cow the multitude of these animals is expressed.

paras.t: Egrediuntur quasi greges parvuli eorum, id est, in multitudine copiosa procedunt ad spatiandum, sicut greges egrediuntur ad pascua; et infantes eorum exsultant lusibus, ut moris est puerorum, pariter ludendo lætari. Tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi. Quod intelligi potest tam de parentibus, quam de filiis, quod his musicis instrumentis pro solatio utebantur. Dicitque Thomas, quod apud antiquos liberi primo instruebantur in musicis.
paras.en: [[21:11|Their little ones go out like a flock|Egrediuntur quasi greges parvuli eorum]], that is, they go forth in a plentiful multitude to roam about, as flocks go out to pasture; [[21:11|and their children dance and play|et infantes eorum exsultant lusibus]], as is the way of children, to rejoice together in play. [[21:12|They take the timbrel, and the harp, and rejoice at the sound of the organ|Tenent tympanum et citharam, et gaudent ad sonitum organi]]. This can be understood both of the parents and of the children, that they used these musical instruments for their solace. And Thomas says that among the ancients children were first instructed in music.

paras.t: Ducunt in bonis dies suos: id est, tempus suum, sibi ad bene agendum pœnitentialiterque vivendum concessum, expendunt delicate vivendo, et in bonis delectabilibus, falsis et apparentibus conversando, non bonis, honestis, veris ac salutaribus inhærendo. Unde in Sapientiæ libro dixisse scribuntur: Venite, fruamur bonis quæ sunt, et utamur creatura tanquam in juventute celeriter; vino pretioso et unguento nos impleamus; ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ.
paras.en: [[21:13|They spend their days in wealth|Ducunt in bonis dies suos]]: that is, the time granted them for doing well and living in penance they spend in living delicately and in busying themselves among delightful goods, false and only apparent ones, not in cleaving to goods that are honest, true and wholesome [*in bonis*, which the Douay-Rheims renders 'in wealth', is literally 'in good things', and Denis takes it so]. Hence in the book of Wisdom they are written to have said: [[Wis 2:6|Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that are present, and let us speedily use the creatures as in youth|Venite, fruamur bonis quæ sunt, et utamur creatura tanquam in juventute celeriter]]; [[Wis 2:7|Let us fill ourselves with costly wine, and ointments|vino pretioso et unguento nos impleamus]]; [[Wis 2:9|let us every where leave tokens of joy|ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ]].

paras.t: Et in puncto, id est repente hora mortis, ad inferna descendunt, id est ad lacum damnationis æternæ: quoniam non est possibile nunc gaudere cum mundo, et post regnare cum Deo. Hinc fertur in Psalmo: Convertantur peccatores in infernum, omnes gentes quæ obliviscuntur Deum. Rursusque: Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitates suas. Isaias quoque: Congregabuntur, inquit, congregatione unius fascis in lacum, et claudentur ibi in carcere. Ecce quam vana, fallax, falsa, brevis et impia est mundi prosperitas ac voluptas! ad quantum ducit mœrorem, ac quem æternum dolorem! Hanc ergo cordialiter aspernemur, pœnitentialiter conversemur, ne delectatione brevissima, nunquam finienda incidamus tormenta; sed perbrevi dolore, virtuoso labore, puro amore gaudia sortiamur non terminanda.
paras.en: [[21:13|and in a moment|Et in puncto]], that is, suddenly at the hour of death, [[21:13|they go down to hell|ad inferna descendunt]], that is, to the pit of eternal damnation: for it is not possible to rejoice with the world now and to reign with God afterwards. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 9:18|The wicked shall be turned into hell, all the nations that forget God|Convertantur peccatores in infernum, omnes gentes quæ obliviscuntur Deum]]. And again: [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation? they have suddenly ceased to be: they have perished by reason of their iniquity|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitates suas]]. Isaias too: [[Is 24:22|And they shall be gathered together|Congregabuntur]], he says, [[Is 24:22|as in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and they shall be shut up there in prison|congregatione unius fascis in lacum, et claudentur ibi in carcere]]. Behold how vain, deceitful, false, brief and impious is the prosperity and pleasure of the world! To what great grief it leads, and to what eternal sorrow! Let us therefore despise it from the heart and live in penance, lest through the briefest delight we fall into torments that will never end; but by a very short pain, by virtuous labour and pure love, let us win joys that will have no end.

paras.t: Qui dixerunt Deo, si non verbis, tamen proposito mentis, aut factis et reprobis moribus: Recede a nobis, id est, ad relinquendum peccata et nobis placentia non nos horteris; scientiam viarum tuarum, id est præceptorum, consiliorum, testimoniorum, judiciorum, nolumus. Quod pertinet ad ignorantiam affectatam, quæ non excusat, sed contemptum includit. Tales sunt omnes, qui a viris devotis nolunt reprehendi et instrui; qui non acquiescunt divino instinctui, angelicæ inspirationi, fraternæ admonitioni. De quibus in Isaia aptissime scribitur: Populus ad iracundiam provocans est; filii mendaces, filii nolentes audire legem Dei. Qui dicunt videntibus, Nolite videre; et adspicientibus, Nolite adspicere nobis ea quæ recta sunt. Loquimini nobis placentia, videte nobis errores; auferte a me viam, declinate a me semitam; cesset a facie nostra Sanctus Israel. De talibus ad Timotheum inducitur: Erit tempus quum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, sed ad sua desideria coacervabunt sibi magistros prurientes auribus; et a veritate quidem auditum avertent, ad fabulas autem convertentur. Præterea, teste Gregorio, quidam, eo quod Christus dicit, Servus qui non cognovit voluntatem domini sui, et facit digna plagis, vapulabit paucis; sciens autem voluntatem domini sui, et non faciens, vapulabit multis: nolunt scire quid agant, quasi propter ignorantiam minus torquendi sint. Sed aliud est nescire, aliud scire noluisse. Nescit namque, qui apprehendere vult, nec valet. Qui autem ut nesciat, aurem a voce veritatis avertit, iste non nesciens, sed contemptor addicitur.
paras.en: [[21:14|Who have said to God|Qui dixerunt Deo]], if not in words, yet in the purpose of their mind, or by their deeds and reprobate conduct: [[21:14|Depart from us|Recede a nobis]], that is, do not urge us to give up our sins and the things that please us; [[21:14|the knowledge of thy ways|scientiam viarum tuarum]], that is, of thy precepts, counsels, testimonies and judgments, [[21:14|we desire not|nolumus]]. This belongs to affected ignorance [that is, ignorance chosen on purpose so as not to know one's duty], which does not excuse but includes contempt. Such are all who will not be reproved and instructed by devout men; who do not yield to the divine prompting, the angel's inspiration, a brother's admonition. Of them it is most aptly written in Isaias: [[Is 30:9|For it is a people that provoketh to wrath, and lying children that will not hear the law of God|Populus ad iracundiam provocans est; filii mendaces, filii nolentes audire legem Dei]]. [[Is 30:10|Who say to the seers: See not: and to them that behold: Behold not for us those things that are right: speak unto us pleasant things, see errors for us|Qui dicunt videntibus, Nolite videre; et adspicientibus, Nolite adspicere nobis ea quæ recta sunt. Loquimini nobis placentia, videte nobis errores]]; [[Is 30:11|Take away from me the way, turn away the path from me, let the Holy One of Israel cease from before us|auferte a me viam, declinate a me semitam; cesset a facie nostra Sanctus Israel]]. Of such it is set down in the Epistle to Timothy: [[2 Tim 4:3|there shall be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine but, according to their own desires, they will heap to themselves teachers having itching ears|Erit tempus quum sanam doctrinam non sustinebunt, sed ad sua desideria coacervabunt sibi magistros prurientes auribus]]; [[2 Tim 4:4|And will indeed turn away their hearing from the truth, but will be turned unto fables|et a veritate quidem auditum avertent, ad fabulas autem convertentur]]. Moreover, as Gregory witnesses, some people, because Christ says: The servant [[Luke 12:48|that knew not|qui non cognovit]] the will of his lord, [[Luke 12:48|and did things worthy of stripes shall be beaten with few stripes|et facit digna plagis, vapulabit paucis]]; but he that [[Luke 12:47|knew the will of his lord|sciens autem voluntatem domini sui]] and does not do it [[Luke 12:47|shall be beaten with many stripes|vapulabit multis]]: will not know what they ought to do, as though they were to be tormented less because of their ignorance. But it is one thing not to know, another to have refused to know. For he does not know who wishes to grasp it and cannot. But he who turns his ear from the voice of truth so as not to know is judged not ignorant but a despiser.

paras.t: Quis est Omnipotens, ut serviamus ei? et quid nobis prodest, si oraverimus eum? Hoc dicere, videtur proprie esse eorum qui arbitrantur Deum providentiam non habere actuum humanorum, vel unius summi Dei non habent notitiam, prout Pharao ait: Quis est Dominus, ut dimittam Israel? Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam. Et Sennacherib rex Assyriorum: Quis est Dominus, ut eruat Jerusalem de manu mea? De dubitantibus vero circa providentiam Dei, simile huic scriptum est in Malachia: Invaluerunt super me verba vestra, dicit Dominus. Et dixistis: Vanus est qui servit Domino; et quod emolumentum quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et quia ambulavimus tristes coram Domino? Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes: siquidem ædificati sunt facientes impietatem. Denique, quidam ita carnales sunt, sicque extra se ad sola sensibilia fusi, ut velut inutile reputent adorare et colere Deum, a quo, ut eis apparet, exteriora non sortiuntur; vel quantum ad ea quæ appetunt, non exaudiuntur. Verumtamen omnes iniqui Deo non obedientes, æquivalenter dicunt verba inducta, videlicet: Quis est Omnipotens, etc.? Teste enim Apostolo, quamvis fateantur se nosse Deum, factis tamen negant: et ita se habent, quasi Deus non esset, aut frustra invocaretur. De talibus tam perversis in Sapientia conscriptum est: Ignoraverunt sacramenta Dei, nec speraverunt mercedem justitiæ, nec judicaverunt honorem animarum sanctarum.
paras.en: [[21:15|Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him|Quis est Omnipotens, ut serviamus ei]]? [[21:15|and what doth it profit us if we pray to him|et quid nobis prodest, si oraverimus eum]]? To say this seems properly to belong to those who think that God has no providence over human acts, or who have no knowledge of the one supreme God, as Pharao says: [[Ex 5:2|Who is the Lord, that I should|Quis est Dominus, ut]] [[Ex 5:2|let Israel go|dimittam Israel]]? [[Ex 5:2|I know not the Lord, neither will I let Israel go|Nescio Dominum, et Israel non dimittam]]. And Sennacherib king of the Assyrians: Who is the Lord, that he [[4 Kings 18:35|may deliver Jerusalem out of my hand|eruat Jerusalem de manu mea]]?[[2 Par 32:14||]] [the margin here is partly unreadable and seems to give 4 Kings xviii, 35 and 2 Par. xxxii, 14; the words are closest to Is 36:20 and 4 Kings 18:35]. Of those who doubt about the providence of God, something like this is written in Malachias: [[Mal 3:13|Your words have been unsufferable to me, saith the Lord|Invaluerunt super me verba vestra, dicit Dominus]]. And you have said: [[Mal 3:14|He laboureth in vain that serveth God, and what profit is it that we have kept his ordinances, and that we have walked sorrowful before the Lord|Vanus est qui servit Domino; et quod emolumentum quia custodivimus præcepta ejus, et quia ambulavimus tristes coram Domino?]]? [[Mal 3:15|Wherefore now we call the proud people happy, for they that work wickedness are built up|Ergo nunc beatos dicimus arrogantes: siquidem ædificati sunt facientes impietatem]]. Lastly, some are so carnal, and so poured out of themselves upon the things of sense alone, that they count it as useless to adore and worship God, from whom, as it seems to them, they do not obtain outward things, or by whom they are not heard in the things they desire. Yet all the wicked who do not obey God say in effect the words cited, namely: [[21:15|Who is the Almighty|Quis est Omnipotens]], etc.? For as the Apostle witnesses, though they [[Tit 1:16|profess that they know God|fateantur se nosse Deum]], [[Tit 1:16|in their works they deny him|factis tamen negant]]: and they behave as though God did not exist, or were called upon in vain. Of men so perverse it is written in Wisdom: [[Wis 2:22|And they knew not the secrets of God, nor hoped for the wages of justice, nor esteemed the honour of holy souls|Ignoraverunt sacramenta Dei, nec speraverunt mercedem justitiæ, nec judicaverunt honorem animarum sanctarum]].

paras.t: Verumtamen, quia non sunt in manu eorum bona sua, id est, bona temporalia et terrena, quæ impii maxime diligunt, non sunt in potestate eorum: quoniam per violentiam possunt eis auferri, et in morte tolluntur, nec eos sequuntur. Bona autem spiritualia, ut opera virtuosa, quorum homo est dominus, per liberum arbitrium gratia Dei adjutum, sunt in hominis potestate, et morientem non deserunt, nec per violentiam queunt auferri. Hinc in Ecclesiaste habetur: Vir cui dedit Deus divitias, et substantiam, et honorem, et nihil deest animæ ejus ex omnibus quæ desiderat; nec tribuit ei potestatem Deus ut comedat ex eo, sed homo extraneus vorabit illud. Itaque, quoniam bona ista caduca carnalia, non sunt in potestate pravorum, consilium eorum, quo temporalem prosperitatem, carnalem delectationem, humanum honorem Deo præponunt, finaliter quærunt, potissime amant, et aliis quærenda amandaque consulunt, longe sit a me, per displicentiam, quia consilium illud iniquum et fallax est, ipsique impii bonis suis cito privati, experientur se deceptos, quum in infernum senserint se projectos. Itaque et nos tale carnalium hominum, sola quæ mundi et carnis sunt, sapientium, penitus contemnamus consilium, quoniam scriptum est: Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum. Potiusque sequamur sapientissimum atque salvificum Salvatoris consilium, exhortantis ad omnium terrenorum contemptum, ad purissimam mentis in Deo fiduciam, ad perfectionis apprehensionem.
paras.en: [[21:16|Yet because their good things are not in their hand|Verumtamen, quia non sunt in manu eorum bona sua]], that is, their temporal and earthly goods, which the wicked love most, are not in their power: for they can be taken from them by violence, and are taken away at death, and do not follow them. But spiritual goods, such as virtuous works, of which a man is master through free will helped by the grace of God, are in a man's power, and do not desert him when he dies, nor can they be taken away by violence. Hence we have in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 6:2|A man to whom God hath given riches, and substance, and honour, and his soul wanteth nothing of all that he desireth: yet God doth not give him power to eat thereof, but a stranger shall eat it up|Vir cui dedit Deus divitias, et substantiam, et honorem, et nihil deest animæ ejus ex omnibus quæ desiderat; nec tribuit ei potestatem Deus ut comedat ex eo, sed homo extraneus vorabit illud]]. Therefore, since these perishable carnal goods are not in the power of the wicked, may their counsel, by which they set temporal prosperity, carnal delight and human honour before God, seek them as their end, love them above all, and counsel others to seek and love them, [[21:16|be far from me|longe sit a me]], in that it displeases me: for that counsel is wicked and deceitful, and the wicked themselves, soon robbed of their goods, will find that they have been deceived when they feel themselves cast into hell. Let us too, then, utterly despise such counsel of carnal men, who savour only what belongs to the world and the flesh, since it is written: [[Ps 1:1|Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly|Beatus vir qui non abiit in consilio impiorum]]. And let us rather follow the most wise and saving counsel of the Saviour, who exhorts us to contempt of all earthly things, to the purest trust of the mind in God, and to the attaining of perfection.

paras.t: Deinceps ostendit, quod impiis quoque frequenter occurrant adversa. Quoties lucerna impiorum, id est prosperitas, et omne quod instar illuminativi lætificat eos, exstinguetur? quasi dicat: Sæpe hoc accidit, ut quum prole aut contorali, opibus, honoribus aut deliciis destituuntur. Et superveniet eis inundatio, id est grandis adversitatis copia seu tempestas, juxta illud Isaiæ: Flagellum inundans quum transierit, eritis ei in conculcationem. In Threnis quoque: Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum. Dixi: Perii. Et dolores dividet furoris sui: id est, Deus impiis partim in sæculo isto, partim in futuro, infligit dolores seu afflictiones a rigore suæ justitiæ procedentes, dum pœna eorum hic inchoatur, et ibi perpetuatur. Multa siquidem flagella peccatoris.
paras.en: Next he shows that adversities also often befall the wicked. [[21:17|How often shall the lamp of the wicked|Quoties lucerna impiorum]], that is, their prosperity, and everything that gladdens them like a thing that gives light, [[21:17|be put out|exstinguetur]]? As if to say: This often happens, as when they are bereft of offspring or of wife, of wealth, honours or delights. [[21:17|and a deluge come upon them|Et superveniet eis inundatio]], that is, a great flood or storm of adversity, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 28:18|when the overflowing scourge shall pass, you shall be trodden down by it|Flagellum inundans quum transierit, eritis ei in conculcationem]]. In Lamentations too: [[Lam 3:54|Waters have flowed over my head: I said: I am cut off|Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum. Dixi: Perii]]. [[21:17|and he shall distribute the sorrows of his wrath|Et dolores dividet furoris sui]]: that is, God inflicts on the wicked, partly in this world and partly in the next, sorrows or afflictions that proceed from the rigour of his justice, while their punishment is begun here and made everlasting there. For [[Ps 31:10|Many are the scourges of the sinner|Multa siquidem flagella peccatoris]].

paras.t: Erunt sicut paleæ ante faciem venti, id est, impulsu divini judicii et impetu summæ justitiæ, celerrime atque facillime in damnationem, mortem seu quamlibet adversitatem a sua prosperitate dejicientur, juxta illud in Psalmo: Deus meus, pone illos ut rotam, et sicut stipulam ante faciem venti; sicut ignis qui comburit silvam, et sicut flamma comburens montes. Et sicut favilla quam turbo dispergit, id est, impotentes, leves et arefacti erunt coram Deo eos dejiciente. Quibus Isaias prædicit: Erit fortitudo vestra ut favilla stuppæ, et opus vestrum quasi scintilla, et succendetur utrumque simul. Hinc demum per Jeremiam dicitur: Ecce turbo dominicæ indignationis egredietur, et tempestas erumpens super caput impiorum veniet. Non revertetur furor Domini usque dum faciat, et usque dum compleat cogitationes cordis sui. Præterea impii etiam prosperitatibus fulti, paleis et favillis rite assimilantur: quia instabiles animo, leves corde, qui omni tentationis impulsu, omni flatu favoris humani, omni impetu passionum mox prosternuntur atque vincuntur. Idcirco de eis in primo psalmo inducitur: Impii tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ. Agamus ergo quod Ecclesiasticus docet: Non ventiles te in omnem ventum. Esto firmus in via Domini, et in veritate sensus tui.
paras.en: [[21:18|They shall be as chaff before the face of the wind|Erunt sicut paleæ ante faciem venti]], that is, by the thrust of the divine judgment and the onset of the highest justice they shall be cast down from their prosperity most swiftly and most easily into damnation, death or any adversity whatever, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 82:14|O my God, make them like a wheel; and as stubble before the wind|Deus meus, pone illos ut rotam, et sicut stipulam ante faciem venti]]; [[Ps 82:15|As fire which burneth the wood: and as a flame burning mountains|sicut ignis qui comburit silvam, et sicut flamma comburens montes]]. [[21:18|and as ashes which the whirlwind scattereth|Et sicut favilla quam turbo dispergit]], that is, they shall be powerless, light and withered before God as he casts them down. To them Isaias foretells: [[Is 1:31|And your strength shall be as the ashes of tow, and your work as a spark: and both shall burn together|Erit fortitudo vestra ut favilla stuppæ, et opus vestrum quasi scintilla, et succendetur utrumque simul]]. Hence, finally, it is said through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:19|Behold the whirlwind of the Lord's indignation shall come forth, and a tempest shall break out and come upon the head of the wicked|Ecce turbo dominicæ indignationis egredietur, et tempestas erumpens super caput impiorum veniet]]. [[Jer 23:20|The wrath of the Lord shall not return till he execute it, and till he accomplish the thought of his heart|Non revertetur furor Domini usque dum faciat, et usque dum compleat cogitationes cordis sui]]. Moreover, the wicked, even when propped up by prosperity, are fitly likened to chaff and ashes: because, unstable in mind and light of heart, at every thrust of temptation, every breath of human favour, every onset of the passions they are at once laid low and overcome. Therefore it is said of them in the first psalm: [[Ps 1:4|the wicked|Impii]] are [[Ps 1:4|like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth|tanquam pulvis quem projicit ventus a facie terræ]]. Let us therefore do what Ecclesiasticus teaches: [[Ecclus 5:11|Winnow not with every wind|Non ventiles te in omnem ventum]]. [[Ecclus 5:12|Be steadfast in the way of the Lord, and in the truth of thy judgment|Esto firmus in via Domini, et in veritate sensus tui]].

paras.t: Deus servabit filiis illius dolorem patris. Dum filii paternæ fuerint imitatores malitiæ, pœna debita patri, eis quoque infligitur. Interdum etiam filii innocentes patrum luunt peccata, quantum ad aliqua corporalia nocumenta, læsiva seu tristia; non autem quantum ad spiritualia bona, videlicet dona gratiæ ac virtutum, quibus propter parentum peccata non destituuntur. Nam quantum ad corpus, a parentibus sunt; quantum vero ad animam, immediate a Deo. Nam et secundum leges civiles, pro crimine læsæ majestatis commisso a patre, filii ejus puniuntur. Pleniorem vero hujus determinationem prosequerer, nisi super Jeremiam, Ezechielem et alibi hoc fecissem. Porro Scripturæ dicentes filium non puniri pro patris peccato, potissime intelliguntur de spirituali punitione. Præinducto autem verbo Job consonat, quod in Exodo scribitur: Ego sum Dominus Deus, fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem. Rursusque Moyses loquitur: Dominator Domine, qui reddis iniquitatem patrum filiis ac nepotibus, in tertiam et quartam generationem. Quod et in Jeremia habetur. Circa hæc scribit Gregorius: In carne nonnunquam filii etiam ex patris peccato puniuntur. Quid enim est quod parvuli filii plerumque a dæmonibus arripiuntur, nisi quod caro filii ex patris culpa mulctatur? In semetipso enim percutitur pater iniquus, et percussionis vim sentire contemnit; plerumque percutitur in filiis, ut acrius uratur.
paras.en: [[21:19|God shall lay up the sorrow of the father for his children|Deus servabit filiis illius dolorem patris]]. When the sons have imitated their father's wickedness, the punishment due to the father is inflicted on them too. Sometimes, indeed, innocent sons also pay for their fathers' sins as regards certain bodily harms, hurtful or grievous; but not as regards spiritual goods, namely the gifts of grace and of the virtues, of which they are not deprived because of their parents' sins. For as to the body they come from their parents, but as to the soul immediately from God. And even under the civil laws, for the crime of high treason committed by a father, his sons are punished. I would go into this question more fully, had I not done so on Jeremias, Ezechiel and elsewhere. Further, the Scriptures that say the son is not punished for the father's sin[[Deut 24:16||]][[Jer 31:29||]][[Jer 31:30||]][[Ezech 18:20||]] [the margin gives Deut. xxiv; Jer. xxxi, 29, 30; Ezech. xviii, 20] are chiefly to be understood of spiritual punishment. With the word of Job just quoted agrees what is written in Exodus: [[Ex 20:5|I am the Lord thy God, mighty, jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation|Ego sum Dominus Deus, fortis, zelotes, visitans iniquitatem patrum in filios, in tertiam et quartam generationem]]. And again Moses says: [[Ex 34:6|O the Lord, the Lord|Dominator Domine]], [[Ex 34:7|Who renderest the iniquity of the fathers to the children, and to the grandchildren unto the third and fourth generation|qui reddis iniquitatem patrum filiis ac nepotibus, in tertiam et quartam generationem]]. This is also found in Jeremias[[Jer 32:18||]]. On these things Gregory writes: “In the flesh sons are sometimes punished even for their father's sin. For why is it that little children are often seized by demons, unless it is that the son's flesh is punished for the father's fault? For the wicked father is struck in himself and scorns to feel the force of the blow; often he is struck in his sons, that he may smart more keenly.”

paras.t: Et quum reddiderit, id est, quum Deus dolorem patris iniqui inflixerit filiis ejus vel ei, tunc sciet, id est, tunc pater per dolorem ita inflictum filiis suis vel sibi, se peccasse advertet: quemadmodum loquitur Isaias, Sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui. Siquidem culpa mentis oculum claudit, quem pœna post aperit: sicut Antiochus letaliter vulneratus, revertens ad cor, Justum, inquit, est subditum esse Deo, et mortalem non paria Deo sentire. Unde in Prophetis, præsertim in Ezechiele, Dominus iniquorum punitione prædicta, multoties subdit: Et scient quia ego Dominus. Itemque in Psalmo: Erubescant, et conturbentur in sæculum sæculi; et confundantur, et pereant; et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus.
paras.en: [[21:19|and when he shall repay|Et quum reddiderit]], that is, when God has inflicted the sorrow of the wicked father on his sons or on himself, [[21:19|then shall he know|tunc sciet]]: that is, then the father, through the sorrow so inflicted on his sons or on himself, will perceive that he has sinned; as Isaias says, [[Is 28:19|vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear|Sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui]]. For guilt shuts the eye of the mind, which punishment afterwards opens: as Antiochus, mortally wounded[[2 Mach 9:7||]], coming back to his heart, said: [[2 Mach 9:12|It is just|Justum]], [[2 Mach 9:12|to be subject to God, and that a mortal man should not equal himself to God|est subditum esse Deo, et mortalem non paria Deo sentire]]. Hence in the Prophets, especially in Ezechiel, the Lord, having foretold the punishment of the wicked, many times adds: [[Ezech 5:13|and they shall know that I the Lord|Et scient quia ego Dominus]][[Ezech 6:7||]][[Ezech 6:10||]][[Ezech 6:13||]][[Ezech 6:14||]] [that is, that I am the Lord]. And likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 82:18|Let them be ashamed and troubled for ever and ever: and let them be confounded and perish|Erubescant, et conturbentur in sæculum sæculi; et confundantur, et pereant]]: [[Ps 82:19|And let them know that the Lord is thy name|et cognoscant quia nomen tibi Dominus]].

paras.t: Videbunt oculi ejus interfectionem suam, id est filiorum suorum, ut quidam exponunt: quemadmodum quarto Regum leguntur filii Sedeciæ interfecti in oculis ejus. Aptius autem videtur sic exponendum, juxta Gregorium: Videbunt oculi ejus interfectionem suam, id est, propriam dejectionem, pœnam et mortem, pro culpa sua sibi inferendam, experietur. Vel, Interfectionem suam, id est, causam suæ percussionis seu damnationis cognoscet in pœnis, prout in libro Sapientiæ impii dicunt: Erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis. Et de furore Omnipotentis bibet, id est, pœnis divinæ justitiæ velut potu abundanter implebitur, sicut quibusdam Jeremias ait: Bibite, et cadite, et nolite consurgere.
paras.en: [[21:20|His eyes shall see his own destruction|Videbunt oculi ejus interfectionem suam]], that is, that of his sons, as some expound it: just as in the fourth book of Kings we read that the sons of Sedecias were slain before his eyes[[4 Kings 25:7||]] [the margin gives IV Reg. xxv, 1; the slaying is in v. 7]. But it seems more fitting to expound it thus, following Gregory: [[21:20|His eyes shall see his own destruction|Videbunt oculi ejus interfectionem suam]], that is, he will experience his own overthrow, punishment and death, to be brought upon him for his fault. Or: [[21:20|his own destruction|Interfectionem suam]], that is, he will know in his punishments the cause of his being struck down or damned, as the wicked say in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 5:6|we have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice hath not shined unto us|Erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis]]. [[21:20|and he shall drink of the wrath of the Almighty|Et de furore Omnipotentis bibet]], that is, he will be filled abundantly with the punishments of divine justice as with a drink, as Jeremias says to some: [[Jer 25:27|Drink ye|Bibite]], [[Jer 25:27|and fall, and rise no more|et cadite, et nolite consurgere]] [the margin's numeral is misread; the words are Jer. xxv, 27, where Denis leaves out ‘and be drunken, and vomit’].

paras.t: Quid enim ad eum pertinet de domo sua post se? Hoc dupliciter elucidatur. Primo sic: Quid enim, etc.? id est, tantum in vitiis delectatur, et tanto ad peccandum impetu fertur, quod non curat neque perpendit quidquid adversitatis domus, id est proles, familia, possessio sua, ex suo peccato incurrat, dummodo ipse quod concepit et appetit, opere prosequatur: imo vicissim desiderio delectationis vel optati effectus, se ipsum exponit periculis mortis, ut patet in pugnatoribus et immundis. Secundo sic: Quid enim, etc.? id est, ideo filii patris impii, eo vivente et vidente, punientur modo præfato, quia si post mortem ejus hoc fieret, nil pertineret ad eum: quia non inde affligeretur, maxime quum peccator post mortem id nesciat, juxta quod supra jam dictum est: Sive nobiles sive ignobiles fuerint filii ejus, non intelliget. Sic Thomas exponit. Insuper, Quid pertinet ad eum, et si numerus mensium ejus dimidietur? id est, tanta sibi inest peccandi libido, quod nec amore vitæ longioris, nec timore damnorum periculorumque mortis omittit peccare, secundum illud Psalmi: Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso. Vel sensus est, quod non spectat ad eum, si vita ejus pro medietate brevietur, quoniam inde ante non dolet, quum nescierit hoc futurum: ideo et in aliis a Deo punitur. Nihilo minus abbreviatio vitæ multis pro pœna peccati infligitur; sed non est cunctis sufficiens culpæ suæ punitio.
paras.en: [[21:21|For what is it to him what befalleth his house after him|Quid enim ad eum pertinet de domo sua post se]]? This is explained in two ways. First thus: [[21:21|For what is it to him|Quid enim]], etc.? that is, he takes such delight in vices and is carried to sin with such force that he does not care about or weigh whatever adversity his house, that is, his offspring, household and possessions, may incur through his sin, so long as he himself carries out in deed what he has conceived and desires; nay rather, from desire of the pleasure or of the effect he longs for, he in turn exposes himself to the perils of death, as is plain in fighters and in the unchaste. Secondly thus: [[21:21|For what is it to him|Quid enim]], etc.? that is, the sons of the wicked father will be punished in the way described while he is alive and sees it, because if it happened after his death it would be nothing to him: for he would not be grieved by it, especially since the sinner after death does not know of it, according to what was said above: [[Job 14:21|Whether his children come to honour or dishonour, he shall not understand|Sive nobiles sive ignobiles fuerint filii ejus, non intelliget]]. So Thomas expounds it. Further: [[21:21|what is it to him|Quid pertinet ad eum]], [[21:21|and if the number of his months be diminished by one half|et si numerus mensium ejus dimidietur]]? that is, so great a lust for sinning is in him that neither for love of a longer life nor for fear of losses and of the perils of death does he leave off sinning, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 35:2|The unjust hath said within himself, that he would sin|Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso]]. Or the sense is that it does not concern him if his life be shortened by half, since he does not grieve over it beforehand, not knowing that it will happen: therefore he is punished by God in other things too. Nevertheless the shortening of life is inflicted on many as the punishment of sin; but it is not for all a sufficient punishment of their guilt.

paras.t: Præterea, quod ista diversitas eventuum humanorum divinæ sapientiæ non repugnet, pandit subdendo: Numquid Deum quispiam docebit scientiam? Non utique, quum ipse sit substantialiter sapientia et scientia infallibilis et immensa, omnium optime dispositiva ac judicativa. Ideo in Isaia legitur: Cum quo iniit consilium, et instruxit eum, et docuit eum semitam justitiæ, et erudivit eum scientiam, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi? Qui excelsos judicat, utpote judices aliorum, videlicet principes terræ, prælatos Ecclesiæ, sed et angelicos spiritus, quorum in principio partem grandem damnavit, et alios beatificavit.
paras.en: Moreover, he shows that this diversity of human events is not contrary to the divine wisdom, by adding: [[21:22|Shall any one teach God knowledge|Numquid Deum quispiam docebit scientiam]]? Surely not, since he is in his very substance wisdom and knowledge infallible and boundless, who orders and judges all things in the best way. Therefore we read in Isaias: [[Is 40:14|With whom hath he consulted, and who hath instructed him, and taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and shewed him the way of understanding?|Cum quo iniit consilium, et instruxit eum, et docuit eum semitam justitiæ, et erudivit eum scientiam, et viam prudentiæ ostendit illi?]] [[21:22|who judgeth those that are high|Qui excelsos judicat]], namely those who judge others, that is, the princes of the earth, the prelates of the Church, and the angelic spirits too, of whom in the beginning he condemned a great part and made the others blessed.

paras.t: Consequenter subdit de hominum diversa patientium seu recipientium diversitate, ad comprobandum quod adversitates vitæ præsentis non sint generaliter punitiones culparum, nec prosperitates præmia sint virtutum in vita hac. Iste moritur robustus et sanus, dives et felix: id est, unus iniquus usque ad tempus morti suæ vicinum, vivit et permanet in robore sanitateque corporis, in divitiis quoque et felicitate mundana, secundum opinionem humanam erroneam taliter appellata: qua aliquis dicitur felix, quia ad nutum sibi in terrenis carnalibusque succedit. Viscera ejus plena sunt adipe, qui ex abundantia alimenti producitur: quo nomine abundantia opulentiæ designatur. Et medullis ossa illius irrigantur: ita quod lautissimis abundat cibariis, intusque pinguedine, quemadmodum in Jeremia habetur: Fertilis fuit Moab ab adolescentia sua, et requievit in fæcibus suis. Alius vero moritur in amaritudine animæ suæ absque ullis opibus: ita quod etiam totam vitam suam quasi expendit in afflictione atque inopia. Horum exemplum in Evangelio legitur de paupere Lazaro et divite epulone. Tamen quod ait, Alius vero moritur, potest exponi de alio impio. Unus etenim impius tota sua vita abundat et prosperatur, alio impio jugiter quoadusque hic vivit, adversitates et penurias, ac postremo diram mortem ferente.
paras.en: Next he speaks of the diversity of men who suffer or receive different things, to prove that the adversities of the present life are not in general punishments of faults, nor its prosperities the rewards of virtues in this life. [[21:23|One man dieth strong, and hale, rich and happy|Iste moritur robustus et sanus, dives et felix]]: that is, one wicked man, up to the time close to his death, lives and remains in strength and health of body, and also in riches and worldly happiness, so called according to the mistaken opinion of men, by which someone is called happy because things go as he wishes for him in earthly and fleshly matters. [[21:24|His bowels are full of fat|Viscera ejus plena sunt adipe]], which is produced by abundance of food; and by this word abundance of wealth is meant. [[21:24|and his bones are moistened with marrow|Et medullis ossa illius irrigantur]]: so that he abounds in the most sumptuous food, and within in fatness, as is found in Jeremias: [[Jer 48:11|Moab hath been fruitful from his youth, and hath rested upon his lees|Fertilis fuit Moab ab adolescentia sua, et requievit in fæcibus suis]]. [[21:25|But another dieth in bitterness of soul without any riches|Alius vero moritur in amaritudine animæ suæ absque ullis opibus]]: so that he spends, as it were, his whole life in affliction and want. An example of these is read in the Gospel, of poor Lazarus and the rich glutton[[Luke 16:19||]]. Yet what he says, [[21:25|But another dieth|Alius vero moritur]], can be expounded of another wicked man. For one wicked man abounds and prospers all his life, while another wicked man bears adversities and want continually as long as he lives here, and at last a dreadful death.

paras.t: Et tamen simul in pulvere dormient, id est, pariformiter in sepulcro quantum ad corpus quiescent; et vermes operient eos, id est corpora eorum, quum cœperint putrefieri et resolvi: juxta illud Isaiæ, Operimentum tuum erunt vermes. Nascuntur enim ex putrescente cadavere. Ideo Ecclesiasticus ait: Quum morietur homo, hæreditabit serpentes et vermes. Unde supra jam dixit Job: Putredini dixi: Pater meus es, mater mea; et soror mea, vermibus.
paras.en: [[21:26|And yet they shall sleep together in the dust|Et tamen simul in pulvere dormient]], that is, they will rest alike in the grave as to the body; [[21:26|and worms shall cover them|et vermes operient eos]], that is, their bodies, when they begin to rot and decay: according to that of Isaias, [[Is 14:11|worms shall be thy covering|Operimentum tuum erunt vermes]]. For they are born from the rotting corpse. Therefore Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 10:13|when a man shall die, he shall inherit serpents|Quum morietur homo, hæreditabit serpentes]] [[Ecclus 10:13|and worms|et vermes]]. Hence Job has already said above: [[Job 17:14|I have said to rottenness: Thou art my father; to worms, my mother and my sister|Putredini dixi: Pater meus es, mater mea; et soror mea, vermibus]].

paras.t: Ex præhabitis beatus Job contra amicos suos invicta loquitur invectione. Certe novi cogitationes vestras, quibus me in cordibus vestris contemnitis et damnatis, ut ex vestris elicio verbis, et sententias contra me iniquas, id est erroneas opiniones quibus contradicitis mihi. Dicitis enim: Ubi est domus principis? et ubi tabernacula impiorum? quasi dicatis: Deus principes iniquos non diu regnare permittit, et impiorum mansionem, prolem, familiam, opes subvertit; per hoc insinuantes, quod ego cum sobole atque familia mea, propter peccata mea et eorum, simus percussi. Hoc enim amici Job jam sæpe locuti sunt, ad adstruendum quod bonis proveniant prospera, et vitiosis adversa: cujus dicti falsitatem ostendit ex concordi generalique omnium sapientium testimonio.
paras.en: From what has gone before, blessed Job speaks against his friends with an unanswerable invective. [[21:27|Surely I know your thoughts|Certe novi cogitationes vestras]], by which you despise and condemn me in your hearts, as I gather from your words, [[21:27|and your unjust judgments against me|et sententias contra me iniquas]], that is, the mistaken opinions by which you contradict me. [[21:28|For you say: Where is the house of the prince? and where are the dwelling places of the wicked?|Dicitis enim: Ubi est domus principis? et ubi tabernacula impiorum?]] As if you said: God does not let wicked princes reign long, and overthrows the dwelling, offspring, household and wealth of the wicked; hinting by this that I with my children and household have been struck for my sins and theirs. For Job's friends have already said this often, to establish that prosperity comes to the good and adversity to the vicious; and the falsehood of this saying he shows from the agreeing and general testimony of all the wise.

paras.t: Interrogate quemlibet de viatoribus: qui diversa perambulando, audiendo, videndo, in multis experti et docti sunt, multaque pensant, prout Ecclesiasticus asserit: Vir in multis expertus, cogitabit multa. Vel, De viatoribus, id est virtuosis hominibus, qui hoc mundo velut exsilio, et hac vita quasi via utuntur ad patriam: qui peregrini in sæculo isto sunt, sicut ad Hebræos de Sanctis veteris Testamenti scribit Apostolus, Confitentes quia peregrini et advenæ sunt super terram. Atque Psalmista: Ne sileas, quoniam advena ego sum apud te et peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei. Primo quoque Paralipomenon libro David loquitur Deo: Peregrini sumus apud te et advenæ, sicut omnes patres nostri. Et hæc eadem quæ contra vos dixi, et dicam, eum intelligere cognoscetis, utpote quod in hoc sæculo non fiat finalis retributio pro meritis atque demeritis, quodque adversitates non impiis tantum, sed justis quoque contingant, eo quod finalis et plena præmiatio fiet in posterum, sicut subjungitur.
paras.en: [[21:29|Ask any one of them that go by the way|Interrogate quemlibet de viatoribus]]: who, by travelling through various places, hearing and seeing, are experienced and learned in many things and weigh many things, as Ecclesiasticus declares: [[Ecclus 34:9|A man that hath much experience, shall think of many things|Vir in multis expertus, cogitabit multa]]. Or: [[21:29|of them that go by the way|De viatoribus]], that is, of virtuous men, who use this world as an exile and this life as a way to the fatherland; who are pilgrims in this world, as the Apostle writes to the Hebrews of the Saints of the Old Testament, [[Heb 11:13|confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth|Confitentes quia peregrini et advenæ sunt super terram]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 38:13|Be no silent: for I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner as all my fathers were|Ne sileas, quoniam advena ego sum apud te et peregrinus, sicut omnes patres mei]]. In the first book of Paralipomenon, too, David says to God: [[1 Par 29:15|we are sojourners before thee, and strangers, as were all our fathers|Peregrini sumus apud te et advenæ, sicut omnes patres nostri]]. And [[21:29|these same things|hæc eadem]] which I have said and shall say against you, [[21:29|you shall perceive that he knoweth|eum intelligere cognoscetis]]: namely, that in this world the final retribution for merits and demerits is not made, and that adversities befall not the wicked only but the just also, because the final and full rewarding will take place hereafter, as is added.

paras.t: Quia in diem perditionis servatur malus: id est, propterea modo non statim a Deo punitur, sed durante vitæ hujus curriculo, suæ libertati dimittitur, ne se juste valeat excusare, sed prorsus inexcusabilis fiat, quod tam clementer et longanimiter a Deo portatus, vitam non corrigit. Idcirco differtur ejus plenum et finale judicium usque ad diem novissimum, qui erit perditionis totalis omnium reproborum. Hinc in Proverbiis scribitur: Universa propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus; impium quoque ad diem malum. Pravi quippe et reprobi vasa sunt iræ, ut in eis divina ostendatur reluceatque justitia, ut ad Romanos plenius docet Apostolus. Verumtamen culpa et damnatio reproborum Deo nequeunt imputari, quoniam voluntate antecedente vult omnes salvari, nec quempiam, quantum in se est, permittit perire: sed et prima ac directa intentione condidit intellectualem creaturam quamcumque, ut salvaretur. Sed quoniam reproborum perversitatem prævidit, de malo illorum bonum elicere sibi complacuit, ut scilicet in eis suam demonstraret justitiam, ordinando in eis per pœnam, quod inordinatum exstat in ipsis per culpam. Et ad diem furoris ducetur, id est ad extremi judicii discussionem et retributionem. Unde secundo Machabæorum libro habetur: In nationibus Dominus patienter exspectat, ut eas, quum dies judicii advenerit, in plenitudine peccatorum puniat. Hinc Christus prædixit, qualiter in die judicii omnes gentes congregabuntur ante eum. Tantus vero erit illius rigor judicii, ut furor dicatur.
paras.en: [[21:30|Because the wicked man is reserved to the day of destruction|Quia in diem perditionis servatur malus]]: that is, for this reason he is not now punished by God at once, but for the course of this life he is left to his own freedom, so that he may not be able to excuse himself justly, but may become wholly inexcusable, in that, borne by God so mercifully and so patiently, he does not amend his life. Therefore his full and final judgment is put off until the last day, which will be the day of the total destruction of all the reprobate. Hence it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself: the wicked also for the evil day|Universa propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus; impium quoque ad diem malum]]. For the depraved and reprobate are vessels of wrath, that in them the divine justice may be shown forth and shine, as the Apostle teaches more fully to the Romans[[Rom 9:22||]][[Rom 9:23||]]. Yet the guilt and damnation of the reprobate cannot be imputed to God, since by his antecedent will he wills all to be saved[[1 Tim 2:4||]] [that is, his will considered in itself, before he takes account of a man's free refusal], and, as far as lies in him, lets no one perish; nay, by his first and direct intention he created every intellectual creature to be saved. But since he foresaw the perversity of the reprobate, it pleased him to draw good out of their evil, namely to show his justice in them, setting in order in them by punishment what is disordered in them by guilt. [[21:30|and he shall be brought to the day of wrath|Et ad diem furoris ducetur]], that is, to the examination and retribution of the last judgment. Hence it is found in the second book of Machabees: among the nations [[2 Mach 6:14|the Lord patiently expecteth, that when the day of judgment shall come, he may punish them in the fulness of their sins|Dominus patienter exspectat, ut eas, quum dies judicii advenerit, in plenitudine peccatorum puniat]]. Hence Christ foretold how on the day of judgment[[Matt 25:31||]] [[Matt 25:32|all nations shall be gathered together before him|omnes gentes congregabuntur ante eum]]. And so great will be the severity of that judgment that it is called wrath.

paras.t: Quis arguet coram eo viam ejus? et quæ fecit, quis reddet illi? Hoc dupliciter explanatur. Primo, de impio, quasi dicat: Tantæ indocilitatis impietatisque fuit, quod nullus viam, id est opera ejus, potuit coram eo arguere, idcirco omnipotentis Judicis incidit manum: juxta illud Ecclesiastici, Si pœnitentiam non egerimus, incidemus in manus Dei, et non in manus hominum. Secundo, de Deo exponitur, eritque sensus: Quis arguet, etc.? id est, nullus poterit coram Deo reprehendere judicium ejus, aut ei aliquid pro eo quod judicavit et fecit, reprehendere: juxta illud Apostoli ad Romanos, O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo? Sapiens quoque: Quis dicet tibi: Quid fecisti? aut quis stabit contra judicium tuum?
paras.en: [[21:31|Who shall reprove his way to his face?|Quis arguet coram eo viam ejus?]] [[21:31|and who shall repay him what he hath done?|et quæ fecit, quis reddet illi?]] This is explained in two ways. First, of the wicked man, as if he said: he was so unteachable and so wicked that no one could reprove his way, that is, his works, to his face; therefore he fell into the hand of the almighty Judge, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 2:22|If we do not penance, we shall fall into the hands of the Lord, and not into the hands of men|Si pœnitentiam non egerimus, incidemus in manus Dei, et non in manus hominum]]. Secondly, it is expounded of God, and the sense will be: [[21:31|Who shall reprove|Quis arguet]], etc.? that is, no one will be able to find fault with God's judgment before him, or find fault with him in anything for what he has judged and done: according to that of the Apostle to the Romans, [[Rom 9:20|O man, who art thou that repliest against God?|O homo, tu quis es qui respondeas Deo?]] And the Wise Man: [[Wis 12:12|who shall say to thee: What hast thou done? or who shall withstand thy judgment?|Quis dicet tibi: Quid fecisti? aut quis stabit contra judicium tuum?]]

paras.t: Ipse impius ad sepulcra ducetur: quia corpus in terra, anima in inferis sepelitur; et in congerie, id est congregatione, mortuorum vigilabit: quia in die novissimo inter eos atque cum eis est suscitandus a morte. Anima quoque impii jugiter vigilat post mortem vita naturæ, et ut sentiat pœnam inferni.
paras.en: [[21:32|He|Ipse]], the wicked man, [[21:32|shall be brought to the graves|ad sepulcra ducetur]]: for his body is buried in the earth, his soul in hell; and [[21:32|in the heap|in congerie]], that is, in the gathering, [[21:32|of the dead|mortuorum]] he [[21:32|shall watch|vigilabit]]: for on the last day he is to be raised from death among them and with them. The soul of the wicked man, too, keeps watch continually after death, with the life of its nature, and so as to feel the pain of hell.

paras.t: Dulcis fuit impius, id est amicabilis, similis et acceptus, glareis, id est lapillis, puta perversis hominibus per lapillos signatis, Cocyti, id est fluvii infernalis, videlicet gehennalis supplicii. Quemadmodum autem Apostolus nonnunquam inducit verba poetarum (sicut in epistola ad Titum, dicendo: Dixit quidam proprius eorum, scilicet Cretensium, propheta: Cretenses semper mendaces, malæ bestiæ, ventres pigri.
