Atque in Actibus Apostolorum: In ipso vivimus, movemur et sumus); ita et Job hic verba poetarum inducit, eisque ad pium utitur intellectum. Cocytus itaque a poetis fluvius infernalis ponebatur, interpretaturque luctus: qui impiorum animas sibi attraheret ad tormentum, sicut alii fluvii attrahunt lapides. Ideo, per glareas, qui dicuntur lapides parvi, animæ vitiosæ signantur: quibus peccator consentit in vitiis; hincque sociatur eis in infernalibus pœnis. Et post se omnem hominem trahit, id est, pœna infernalis de omni hominum statu, gradu et genere, plurimos acquirit atque involvit: imo tam multos, ut alii comparative sint pauci, et illi, præ multitudine omnes dicantur, sicut Apostolus loquitur: Omnes quæ sua sunt, quærunt. Itemque: Deus in præteritis generationibus dimisit omnes gentes ingredi vias suas. Et ante se innumerabiles, id est, impetu suo plures quasi ante se impellit, instar fortissimi fluminis quidam suo impetu rapientis. Infernus quoque, id est dæmones infernales, fervore concupiscentiarum et impetu passionum innumerabiles vincunt, et ante se quasi impellunt, sicut victor victos ante se minat.
paras.en: [[21:33|He hath been acceptable|Dulcis fuit]] [*dulcis*, literally ‘sweet’], the wicked man, that is, friendly, like and welcome, [[21:33|to the gravel|glareis]], that is, to the pebbles, meaning perverse men signified by the pebbles, [[21:33|of Cocytus|Cocyti]], that is, of the river of hell, namely of the torment of Gehenna. Now as the Apostle sometimes brings in the words of the poets (as in the epistle to Titus, saying: [[Tit 1:12|One of them a prophet of their own, said|Dixit quidam proprius eorum]] (namely of the Cretans): [[Tit 1:12|The Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, slothful bellies|propheta: Cretenses semper mendaces, malæ bestiæ, ventres pigri]]. And in the Acts of the Apostles: [[Acts 17:28|in him we live and move and are|In ipso vivimus, movemur et sumus]]), so Job too here brings in the words of the poets and uses them in a holy sense. So Cocytus was held by the poets to be a river of hell, and the name is interpreted *mourning*; it was said to draw the souls of the wicked to itself for torment, as other rivers draw stones along. Therefore by the gravel, which means small stones, are signified vicious souls, with whom the sinner consents in vices, and hence is joined with them in the pains of hell. [[21:33|and he shall draw every man after him|Et post se omnem hominem trahit]]: that is, the pain of hell gains and entangles very many from every state, rank and kind of men; nay, so many that the others are few by comparison, and these, because of their multitude, are called all, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 2:21|all seek the things that are their own|Omnes quæ sua sunt, quærunt]] [the margin's reading is unclear; the words are Phil. ii, 21]. And again: God, [[Acts 14:15|in times past, suffered all nations to walk in their own ways|in præteritis generationibus dimisit omnes gentes ingredi vias suas]]. [[21:33|and there are innumerable before him|Et ante se innumerabiles]], that is, by its force it drives very many before it, as it were, like a mighty river sweeping things away by its force. Hell too, that is, the demons of hell, overcome innumerable men by the heat of their lusts and the force of their passions, and drive them before them, as it were, as a victor drives the vanquished before him.

paras.t: Quomodo ergo consolamini me frustra, temporalem prosperitatem, si pœnituero, promittendo, quum responsio vestra, qua mihi respondistis vobis contradicenti, repugnare ostensa sit veritati? qua jam evidenter probavi, quod temporalis prosperitas non sit merces justorum finalis aut plena, nec omnibus justis conceditur: nec omnis pœna (ut erronee affirmatis) est præcedentis culpæ purgatio seu vindicta; sed interdum est meriti incrementum et proficiendi augmentum.
paras.en: [[21:34|How then do ye comfort me in vain|Quomodo ergo consolamini me frustra]], promising me temporal prosperity if I repent, [[21:34|whereas your answer|quum responsio vestra]], with which you answered me when I contradicted you, [[21:34|is shewn to be repugnant to truth?|repugnare ostensa sit veritati?]] For I have now plainly proved by the truth that temporal prosperity is not the final or full reward of the just, nor is it granted to all the just; nor is every punishment [the OCR of the print reads *bona*, "good"; *pœna*, "punishment", is what the sense requires] (as you wrongly assert) the cleansing or the avenging of a previous fault, but sometimes it is an increase of merit and a furthering of progress.

22.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli vicesimi secundi: Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites, dixit.
22.title_en: Literal explanation of the twenty-second chapter: Then Eliphaz the Themanite answered, and said.

paras.t: Nunc tertio arguit, secundoque replicat Eliphaz contra Job, sicut docet Scriptura. Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites, dixit: Numquid Deo comparari potest homo, etiam quum perfectæ fuerit scientiæ? Hoc ait in reprehensionem beati Job, quasi dicat: Tam præsumptuose loqueris (dicendo te velle disputare cum Deo; et rursus, Numquid contra hominem disputatio mea est? etc.), quasi in scientia esses Deo æqualis. Qui enim audet disputare cum alio, putat se comparabilem illi. Palam est autem, quod omnis mens creata, distet in infinitum a scientia Dei, cujus illimitata essentia, est sua infinita scientia.
paras.en: Now for the third time Eliphaz argues, and for the second time replies, against Job, as Scripture shows. [[22:1|Then Eliphaz the Themanite answered, and said|Respondens autem Eliphaz Themanites, dixit]]: [[22:2|Can man be compared with God, even though he were of perfect knowledge?|Numquid Deo comparari potest homo, etiam quum perfectæ fuerit scientiæ?]] He says this in rebuke of blessed Job, as if to say: Thou speakest so presumptuously (saying that thou wouldst dispute with God[[Job 13:3||]]; and again, [[Job 21:4|Is my debate against man|Numquid contra hominem disputatio mea est]]? etc.), as though thou wert equal to God in knowledge. For he who dares to dispute with another thinks himself comparable to him. But it is plain that every created mind is infinitely distant from the knowledge of God, whose unlimited essence is his own infinite knowledge.

paras.t: Denique, sumendo perfectum absolute, pro eo scilicet cui nil deest perfectionis, solus Deus est perfectæ scientiæ. Homo autem vel angelus dicitur perfectæ scientiæ, secundum certum gradum, modum seu ordinem. Albertus quoque hic ait, quod aliquis dicitur perfectæ scientiæ in divinis, uno modo perfectione scientis, alio modo perfectione scibilis. Primo modo dicitur homo perfectæ scientiæ in divinis, quando secundum modum humanum perfecte sapit, prout ait Salvator: Non est discipulus super magistrum; perfectus autem omnis erit, si sit sicut magister ejus. Perfectione vero scibilis non est perfectæ scientiæ in divinis, nisi Deus qui solus comprehensive et plene simpliciterque perfecte cognoscit se ipsum. Imo a tali ejus cognitione omnis creatura deficit infinite.
paras.en: Further, taking *perfect* absolutely, that is, for that which lacks nothing of perfection, God alone is of perfect knowledge. But a man or an angel is said to be of perfect knowledge according to a certain degree, measure or order. Albert too says here that someone is said to be of perfect knowledge in divine things in one way by the perfection of the knower, in another by the perfection of the knowable [that is, of the thing known]. In the first way a man is said to be of perfect knowledge in divine things when he is perfectly wise after the human manner, as the Saviour says: [[Luke 6:40|The disciple is not above his master: but every one shall be perfect, if he be as his master|Non est discipulus super magistrum; perfectus autem omnis erit, si sit sicut magister ejus]]. But by the perfection of the knowable none is of perfect knowledge in divine things save God, who alone knows himself comprehensively [that is, exhaustively, as much as he is knowable] and fully and simply and perfectly. Indeed every creature falls infinitely short of such knowledge of him.

paras.t: Quid prodest Deo, si justus fueris? aut quid ei confers, si immaculata fuerit vita tua? id est, ex tuis virtuosis operibus nil perfectionis Deo accrescere potest, qui in se ipso infinite quomodolibetque perfectus est. Ideo ait Psalmista: Dixi Domino: Deus meus es tu, quoniam bonorum meorum non eges. Hoc et Eliu infra sic inducit: Si peccaveris, quid ei nocebis? Porro si juste egeris, quid donabis ei? Homini qui similis est tui, nocebit iniquitas tua, et filium hominis adjuvabit justitia tua. Et hoc ambo hi dicunt adversus Job, tanquam dicant: Tanti te æstimas, et ita te erigis, quasi Deus te indigeret.
paras.en: [[22:3|What doth it profit God if thou be just?|Quid prodest Deo, si justus fueris?]] [[22:3|or what dost thou give him|aut quid ei confers]], [[22:3|if thy way be unspotted|si immaculata fuerit vita tua]]? [Denis reads *vita*, life, for *via*, way.] That is, no perfection can accrue to God from thy virtuous works, for he is infinitely and in every way perfect in himself. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 15:2|I have said to the Lord, thou art my God, for thou hast no need of my goods|Dixi Domino: Deus meus es tu, quoniam bonorum meorum non eges]]. Eliu too brings this in below, thus: [[Job 35:6|If thou sin, what shalt thou hurt him?|Si peccaveris, quid ei nocebis?]] [[Job 35:7|And if thou do justly, what shalt thou give him|Porro si juste egeris, quid donabis ei]]? [[Job 35:8|Thy wickedness may hurt a man that is like thee: and thy justice may help the son of man|Homini qui similis est tui, nocebit iniquitas tua, et filium hominis adjuvabit justitia tua]]. And both of these say this against Job, as if to say: Thou thinkest so much of thyself, and liftest thyself up so, as though God had need of thee.

paras.t: Numquid timens te arguet? id est, non utique judicabit te, timendo te aut aliquem judicem alium: ideo non deberes tam audacter loqui de Deo, sed ejus omnipotentiam revereri, excellentiam quoque ejus immensam vereri. Et veniet tecum ad judicium? id est, non veniet tecum ad judicium alicujus judicis superioris et tertii, qui judicet an Deus te juste judicaverit atque arguerit.
paras.en: [[22:4|Shall he reprove thee for fear|Numquid timens te arguet]]? that is, he will surely not judge thee out of fear of thee or of any other judge: therefore thou oughtest not to speak so boldly of God, but to revere his omnipotence and to stand in awe of his immense excellence also. [[22:4|and come with thee into judgment|Et veniet tecum ad judicium]]? that is, he will not come with thee to the judgment of some higher and third judge, to judge whether God has judged and reproved thee justly.

paras.t: Et non propter, id est imo propter, malitiam tuam plurimam et infinitas iniquitates tuas te arguet? quasi dicat: Nil habes justæ querelæ contra Deum, sed ipse innumerabilia contra te habet, in quibus redargui meruisti. Malitiæ autem proprie dicuntur peccata quæ non fiunt ex ignorantia vel infirmitate, sed ex certa industria vel deliberatione. Dicit Thomas, quod malitia potest referri ad peccata, quibus alios læsit; iniquitas vero ad peccata, quibus justa opera prætermisit: unde malitiam dicit plurimam, sed iniquitates infinitas, quia in pluribus peccat homo omittendo, quam committendo. Hoc ultimum verbum B. Thomæ, mirationem pariter et timorem generat mihi.
paras.en: [[22:5|And not for|Et non propter]], that is, nay rather for, [[22:5|thy manifold wickedness and thy infinite iniquities?|malitiam tuam plurimam et infinitas iniquitates tuas]] will he reprove thee? as if to say: Thou hast no just complaint against God, but he has countless things against thee, in which thou hast deserved to be reproved. Now those sins are properly called *wickedness* [Latin *malitia*, malice] which are done not out of ignorance or weakness but of set purpose or deliberation. Thomas says that *wickedness* can refer to the sins by which he harmed others, but *iniquity* to the sins by which he left just works undone: and so he speaks of *manifold* wickedness but *infinite* iniquities, because a man sins in more things by omitting than by committing. This last word of blessed Thomas stirs in me wonder and fear alike.

paras.t: Deinde peccata quæ imponit beato Job, in speciali prosequitur. Abstulisti enim pignus fratrum, id est proximorum tuorum sine causa justa et opportuna, pignus ab eis irrationabiliter accipiendo, ut agunt tyranni, exactiones pauperibus imponentes, et pignora accipientes, non obstante quod Dominus in Exodo effatur: Si pignus a proximo tuo acceperis vestimentum, ante solis occasum reddes ei; ipsum enim solum est quo operitur, nec habet aliud in quo dormiat. Amos quoque de filiis Israel increpatorie dicit: Super vestimentis pignoratis accubuerunt. Nudos spoliasti vestibus, vel eos qui parum erant vestiti, vestibus suis privando, quod crudelissimum esset: vel his qui nudi sunt, auferendo vestimenta eorum quum essent satis vestiti, quum tamen per Isaiam Dominus dicat: Quum videris nudum, operi eum, et carnem tuam ne despexeris. Et Joannes Baptista ait: Qui habet duas tunicas, det non habenti. Denique, teste Ambrosio, non solum spoliant nudos seu pauperes, qui eis auferunt vestes quas habent, sed et qui quum abundent, illis necessaria non ministrant seu tribuunt.
paras.en: Next he sets out in particular the sins he lays on blessed Job. [[22:6|For thou hast taken away the pledge of thy brethren|Abstulisti enim pignus fratrum]], that is, of thy neighbours, [[22:6|without cause|sine causa]] just and fitting, taking a pledge from them unreasonably, as tyrants do, laying exactions on the poor and taking pledges, notwithstanding that the Lord declares in Exodus: [[Ex 22:26|If thou take of thy neighbour a garment in pledge, thou shalt give it him again before sunset|Si pignus a proximo tuo acceperis vestimentum, ante solis occasum reddes ei]] [[Ex 22:27|For that same is the only thing, wherewith he is covered|ipsum enim solum est quo operitur]], [[Ex 22:27|neither hath he any other to sleep in|nec habet aliud in quo dormiat]]. Amos too says reprovingly of the children of Israel: [[Amos 2:8|they sat down upon garments laid to pledge|Super vestimentis pignoratis accubuerunt]]. [[22:6|and stripped them naked of their clothing|Nudos spoliasti vestibus]]: either by depriving of their clothes those who were scantily clothed, which would be most cruel; or by taking away the clothing of those who are now naked, when they were sufficiently clothed; although the Lord says by Isaias: [[Is 58:7|when thou shalt see one naked, cover him, and despise not thy own flesh|Quum videris nudum, operi eum, et carnem tuam ne despexeris]]. And John the Baptist says: [[Luke 3:11|He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none|Qui habet duas tunicas, det non habenti]]. Further, as Ambrose witnesses, not only do those strip the naked or the poor who take from them the clothes they have, but also those who, having plenty, do not supply or give them what they need.

paras.t: Aquam lasso, id est fatigato ex itinere vel labore, non dedisti, et esurienti subtraxisti panem, vel non dando carenti, vel tollendo habenti: quorum utrumque inclementissimum esset, et directe contra caritatem Dei ac proximi, quum in prima Joannis epistola scriptum sit: Qui habuerit substantiam hujus mundi, et viderit fratrem suum necesse habere, et clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo caritas Dei manet in eo? Nomine autem panis, omnis cibus, et nomine aquæ, omnis potus in Scripturis exprimitur. Hinc et Baptista hortatur: Qui habet escas, similiter faciat, scilicet ut dictum fuit de dando unam tunicam indigenti, quum duæ haberentur.
paras.en: [[22:7|water to the weary|Aquam lasso]], that is, to one tired from a journey or from labour, [[22:7|Thou hast not given|non dedisti]], [[22:7|thou hast withdrawn bread from the hungry|et esurienti subtraxisti panem]], either by not giving to one who lacked it or by taking it from one who had it: either of which would be most merciless, and directly against the charity of God and of our neighbour, since it is written in the first epistle of John: [[1 John 3:17|He that hath the substance of this world and shall see his brother in need and shall shut up his bowels from him: how doth the charity of God abide in him?|Qui habuerit substantiam hujus mundi, et viderit fratrem suum necesse habere, et clauserit viscera sua ab eo, quomodo caritas Dei manet in eo?]] Now in the Scriptures every food is expressed by the name of bread, and every drink by the name of water. Hence the Baptist also exhorts: [[Luke 3:11|he that hath meat, let him do in like manner|Qui habet escas, similiter faciat]], that is, as was said of giving one coat to the needy when one had two.

paras.t: In fortitudine brachii tui, id est per potestatem et violentiam, possidebas terram, id est opes, agros, dominium; et potentissimus obtinebas eam, id est, per eminentiam tuæ potestatis tyrannice eam invasisti et acquisisti, dicens illud Sapientiæ: Sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ.
paras.en: [[22:8|In the strength of thy arm|In fortitudine brachii tui]], that is, by power and violence, [[22:8|thou didst possess the land|possidebas terram]], that is, riches, fields, lordship; [[22:8|and being the most mighty thou holdest it|et potentissimus obtinebas eam]], that is, by the eminence of thy power thou didst tyrannically seize and acquire it, saying that word of Wisdom: [[Wis 2:11|But let our strength be the law of justice|Sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ]].

paras.t: Viduas dimisisti vacuas, earum causam non prosequendo, eis non succurrendo, nec postulata donando: secundum illud Isaiæ, Causa viduæ non ingreditur ad eos. Et lacertos, id est brachia, pupillorum comminuisti, eos non solum non roborando, sed et debilitando. Contra quod Dominus ait in Psalmo: Judicate egeno et pupillo. Quo autem istæ personæ magis humano destituuntur solatio, eo major misericordia impendenda est eis, magisque inhumanum et impium est, ipsis non misereri. Injuriam vero eis inferre, prorsus sævum censetur; et tale peccatum Deus specialiter ulcisci asseritur, prout in Deuteronomio fertur: Dominus facit judicium pupillo et viduæ, amatque peregrinum. Hinc subditur:
paras.en: [[22:9|Thou hast sent widows away empty|Viduas dimisisti vacuas]], by not pursuing their cause, not helping them, nor granting what they asked: according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 1:23|the widow's cause cometh not in to them|Causa viduæ non ingreditur ad eos]]. [[22:9|and the arms|Et lacertos]], that is, the limbs [Latin *lacertos*, the upper arms, glossed by *brachia*], [[22:9|of the fatherless thou hast broken in pieces|pupillorum comminuisti]], not only not strengthening them but even weakening them. Against which the Lord says in the Psalm: [[Ps 81:3|Judge for the needy and fatherless|Judicate egeno et pupillo]]. Now the more these persons are bereft of human comfort, the greater the mercy that must be shown them, and the more inhuman and impious it is not to pity them. But to do them injury is held to be utterly savage; and God is said to avenge such a sin in a special way, as is said in Deuteronomy: the Lord [[Deut 10:18|doth judgment to the fatherless and the widow, loveth the stranger|facit judicium pupillo et viduæ, amatque peregrinum]]. Hence it is added:

paras.t: Propterea, scilicet ob tanta peccata, circumdatus es laqueis, id est, adversitatibus undique adimpleris, et conturbat te formido subita, id est timor improvise superveniens tibi: quia majori culpæ major debetur atque infligitur pœna. Unde in Threnis dicitur: Formido et laqueus factus est nobis.
paras.en: [[22:10|Therefore|Propterea]], that is, for such great sins, [[22:10|art thou surrounded with snares|circumdatus es laqueis]], that is, thou art filled with adversities on every side, [[22:10|and sudden fear troubleth thee|et conturbat te formido subita]], that is, a fear coming upon thee unforeseen: because a greater punishment is due to, and is inflicted on, a greater fault. Hence it is said in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:47|is become to us a fear, and a snare|Formido et laqueus factus est nobis]] [Denis leaves out *vaticinatio*, prophecy, so that his words run: Fear and a snare is become to us].

paras.t: Aut putabas te tenebras adversitatum ac dubiosarum fluctuationum mentis, in quibus nunc es, ita ut quid agere debeas, nescias, non visurum, id est non experturum sive passurum: sicut in Psalmo, Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Et de justo Simeone dicit Lucas: Responsum accepit a Spiritu Sancto non visurum se mortem. Et impetu aquarum inundantium, id est copiosarum tribulationum, non oppressum iri, id est opprimendum non esse: ita quod non suspicabaris talia super te transitura. Impii enim mente cæcati, imminentia sibi pericula non prævident, nec cavent, aut pensant. Qui autem putat se impune peccare, videtur de divina providentia dubitare. Ideo Eliphaz invehitur contra Job:
paras.en: Or [[22:11|didst thou think that thou|Aut putabas te]] [Denis reads *Aut*, Or, for *Et*, And] [[22:11|darkness|tenebras]] of adversities and of the doubtful wavering of the mind in which thou now art, so that thou knowest not what thou oughtest to do, [[22:11|shouldst not see|non visurum]], that is, shouldst not experience or suffer: as in the Psalm, [[Ps 15:10|nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption|Non dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem]]. And Luke says of the just Simeon: [[Luke 2:26|he had received an answer from the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death|Responsum accepit a Spiritu Sancto non visurum se mortem]]. And [[22:11|with the violence of overflowing waters|Et impetu aquarum inundantium]], that is, of abundant tribulations, [[22:11|shouldst not be covered|non oppressum iri]], that is, shouldst not be overwhelmed: so that thou didst not suspect that such things would pass over thee. For the wicked, blinded in mind, do not foresee the dangers hanging over them, nor guard against them, nor weigh them. And he who thinks he sins with impunity seems to doubt of divine providence. Therefore Eliphaz inveighs against Job:

paras.t: An cogitas quod Deus excelsior cœlo sit, et super stellæ verticem sublimetur? id est, an illorum perfidiam incidis et errorem, qui dixerunt Deum sic terrenis et inferioribus præeminere, seu ita ab humanis distare, quod inferiorum et actuum humanorum providentiam determinatam non habeat, nec distinctam, certam claramque scientiam? Hoc quippe quidam philosophi opinabantur, dicentes sola cœlestia divinæ providentiæ ordine gubernari.
paras.en: [[22:12|Dost not thou think that God is higher than heaven, and is elevated above the height of the stars?|An cogitas quod Deus excelsior cœlo sit, et super stellæ verticem sublimetur?]] that is, art thou falling into the faithlessness and error of those who said that God is so far above earthly and lower things, or so distant from human things, that he has no determinate providence of lower things and of human acts, nor distinct, certain and clear knowledge of them? For certain philosophers held this, saying that only heavenly things are governed by the order of divine providence.

paras.t: Et dicis, ut apparet: Quid enim novit Deus de inferioribus actibusque humanis? Et quasi per caliginem judicat, id est, non nisi confusam seu indistinctam habet istorum notitiam, cognoscendo ea in generali, sciendo videlicet genera et species, seu ordinem universi et universalia entia universalesque causas.
paras.en: [[22:13|And thou sayst: What doth God know|Et dicis, ut apparet: Quid enim novit Deus]] [Denis adds *ut apparet*, as it appears] of lower things and of human acts? [[22:13|and he judgeth as it were through a mist|Et quasi per caliginem judicat]], that is, he has only a confused or indistinct knowledge of them, knowing them in general, that is, knowing genera and species, or the order of the universe and universal beings and universal causes.

paras.t: An etiam dicis quæ sequuntur? videlicet, Nubes latibulum ejus, id est, sub nubibus nihil videt, nec providentia ejus infra nubes extenditur, sed usque ad eas exclusive, ita quod nubes sunt quasi quid occultans Deo inferiorum notitiam. Nec nostra opera considerat, et circa cardines cœli perambulat, id est, circa extrema cœli versatur, operatur, seu est, providendo et gubernando superiora, quæ uno modo se habent. Cardo autem quandoque pro extremitate accipitur, interdum pro eo in quo volvitur ostium.
paras.en: Dost thou also say what follows? namely, [[22:14|The clouds are his covert|Nubes latibulum ejus]], that is, he sees nothing below the clouds, nor does his providence reach beneath the clouds, but only as far as them and not including them, so that the clouds are as it were something hiding from God the knowledge of lower things. [[22:14|and he doth not consider our things|Nec nostra opera considerat]] [Denis reads *nostra opera*, our works], [[22:14|and he walketh about the poles of heaven|et circa cardines cœli perambulat]], that is, he moves, works or is about the outer bounds of heaven, providing for and governing the higher things, which are always in one state. Now *cardo* [here poles] is sometimes taken for an extremity, sometimes for that on which a door turns [a hinge].

paras.t: Denique, secundum Albertum, de humanis per caliginem judicare, est ad voluntaria et casualia atque fortuita non immediata consideratione se habere, sed ea quæ fiunt frequenter, per necessaria utcumque perpendere, et per necessaria ac frequentia aliquid de voluntariis et casualibus utcumque judicare. Secundum eumdem, fuit quorumdam opinio, quod Providentia ultra motum cœlorum non extenderetur, nec ad inferiora pertingeret, nisi per aliud atque per accidens: per aliud, ut per partes periodi; per accidens quoque, quia per impressiones accidentales in inferioribus factas: et videntur in hunc errorem consentire Alexander et Averroes, et alii quidam Peripateticorum.
paras.en: Further, according to Albert, to judge of human things *through a mist* is not to regard voluntary, chance and fortuitous things with immediate attention, but to weigh in some fashion the things that happen often through the necessary things, and through the necessary and frequent things to judge somewhat in some fashion of voluntary and chance things. According to the same, it was the opinion of some that Providence did not extend beyond the motion of the heavens, nor reach to lower things except through something else and by accident: through something else, as through the parts of a period [that is, of a cycle of the heavens]; and by accident, because through accidental impressions made on lower things: and Alexander and Averroes, and certain other Peripatetics, seem to agree in this error.

paras.t: Præterea, non gentiles quidam dumtaxat, sed et Judæorum plurimi in veteri Testamento de providentia Dei præfato modo senserunt. De quibus in Ezechiele habetur: Dicunt: Non videt Dominus nos; dereliquit Dominus terram. Et Sophonias ait: Dicunt: Non faciet Dominus bene, et non faciet male. Quorum stultitiam Isaias aperit quum scribit: Quasi si lutum contra figulum cogitet, et dicat opus factori suo, Non fecisti me; et figmentum dicat fictori suo, Non intelligis: sic omnes quorum sunt in tenebris opera, et dicunt: Quis videt nos? et quis novit nos? Itemque in Psalmo: Dixerunt: Non videbit Dominus, nec intelliget Deus Jacob. Quibus mox dicitur: Intelligite, insipientes in populo; et stulti, aliquando sapite. Qui plantavit aurem, non audiet? aut qui finxit oculum, non considerat? Qui corripit gentes, non arguet? aut qui docet hominem scientiam?
paras.en: Moreover, not only certain Gentiles but also very many of the Jews under the Old Testament thought of the providence of God in the aforesaid way. Of whom it is said in Ezechiel: [[Ezech 8:12|they say: The Lord seeth us not, the Lord hath forsaken the earth|Dicunt: Non videt Dominus nos; dereliquit Dominus terram]]. And Sophonias says: They say: [[Soph 1:12|The Lord will not do good, nor will he do evil|Non faciet Dominus bene, et non faciet male]]. Their folly Isaias lays bare when he writes: [[Is 29:16|as if the clay should think against the potter, and the work should say to the maker thereof: Thou madest me not: or the thing framed should say to him that fashioned it: Thou understandest not|Quasi si lutum contra figulum cogitet, et dicat opus factori suo, Non fecisti me; et figmentum dicat fictori suo, Non intelligis]]: so it is with all those of whom it is said: [[Is 29:15|their works are in the dark, and they say: Who seeth us, and who knoweth us?|quorum sunt in tenebris opera, et dicunt: Quis videt nos? et quis novit nos?]] And likewise in the Psalm: [[Ps 93:7|And they have said: The Lord shall not see: neither shall the God of Jacob|Dixerunt: Non videbit Dominus, nec intelliget Deus Jacob]]. To whom it is said soon after: [[Ps 93:8|Understand, ye senseless among the people: and, you fools, be wise at last|Intelligite, insipientes in populo; et stulti, aliquando sapite]] [[Ps 93:9|He that planted the ear, shall he not hear? or he that formed the eye, doth he not consider?|Qui plantavit aurem, non audiet? aut qui finxit oculum, non considerat?]] [[Ps 93:10|He that chastiseth nations, shall he not rebuke: he that teacheth man knowledge?|Qui corripit gentes, non arguet? aut qui docet hominem scientiam?]]

paras.t: Numquid semitam sæculorum custodire cupis, id est latam perditionis viam incedere et servare, per quam sæculares homines gradiuntur? de qua Christus in Evangelio ait: Lata est via quæ ducit ad mortem, et multi ambulant per eam. Qui autem divinam providentiam negant, secure ac libere peccant, omni freno rationis relicto. Quam calcaverunt viri iniqui, passiones sensualitatis et propriam voluntatem in cunctis sequentes: quorum via est conversatio vitiosa, quæ est iter ad damnationem æternam. De quibus Isaias dicit: Semitæ eorum incurvatæ sunt; omnis qui calcat in eis, ignorat pacem. Hinc ait Scriptura: Ne delecteris in semitis impiorum. Et rursus: Via impiorum tenebrosa; nesciunt ubi corruunt. De tam impiis in Sapientiæ libro legitur: Æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram, et conversationem vitæ ad lucra compositam, et oportere undecumque acquirere.
paras.en: [[22:15|Dost thou desire to keep the path of ages|Numquid semitam sæculorum custodire cupis]], that is, to walk and keep the broad way of perdition, by which worldly men go? of which Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 7:13|broad is the way that leadeth to|Lata est via quæ ducit ad]] death, and many walk by it. For those who deny divine providence sin securely and freely, every curb of reason cast off. [[22:15|which wicked men have spurned|Quam calcaverunt viri iniqui]] [Latin *calcaverunt*, have trodden], following in all things the passions of sensuality and their own will: whose way is a vicious manner of life, which is the road to eternal damnation. Of whom Isaias says: [[Is 59:8|their paths are become crooked to them, every one that treadeth in them knoweth no peace|Semitæ eorum incurvatæ sunt; omnis qui calcat in eis, ignorat pacem]]. Hence Scripture says: [[Prov 4:14|Be not delighted in the paths of the wicked|Ne delecteris in semitis impiorum]]. And again: [[Prov 4:19|The way of the wicked is darksome: they know not where they fall|Via impiorum tenebrosa; nesciunt ubi corruunt]]. Of such impious men we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 15:12|they have counted our life a pastime|Æstimaverunt lusum esse vitam nostram]], [[Wis 15:12|and the business of life to be gain|et conversationem vitæ ad lucra compositam]], [[Wis 15:12|and that we must be getting every way|et oportere undecumque acquirere]].

paras.t: Qui sublati sunt ante tempus suum, id est, justo Dei judicio ob hæc sua peccata, per mortem deleti sunt, nondum impleto naturali spatio vitæ suæ, secundum illud Ecclesiastæ: Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus: sed quasi umbra prætereant, qui non timent faciem Domini; et illud Sapientis: Effugere manum tuam, Domine, impossibile est; negantes enim te nosse impii, per fortitudinem brachii tui flagellati sunt. Et fluvius, id est abundantia ac impetus tribulationum seu divinæ ultionis, subvertit fundamentum eorum, id est, funditus eos dejecit, corpus eorum occidit, fiduciam fregit, potestatem et opes his abstulit, prout dicit Salvator: Venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti, et irruerunt in domum illam, et facta est ruina ejus magna.
paras.en: [[22:16|Who were taken away before their time|Qui sublati sunt ante tempus suum]], that is, by the just judgment of God, for these their sins, they were wiped out by death before the natural span of their life was fulfilled, according to that word of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:13|But let it not be well with the wicked, neither let his days be prolonged, but as a shadow let them pass away that fear not the face of the Lord|Non sit bonum impio, nec prolongentur dies ejus: sed quasi umbra prætereant, qui non timent faciem Domini]]; and that of the Wise Man: [[Wis 16:15|to escape thy hand|Effugere manum tuam]], O Lord, [[Wis 16:15|it is impossible|impossibile est]]; [[Wis 16:16|For the wicked that denied to know thee, were scourged by the strength of thy arm|negantes enim te nosse impii, per fortitudinem brachii tui flagellati sunt]]. [[22:16|and a flood|Et fluvius]], that is, the abundance and onrush of tribulations or of divine vengeance, [[22:16|hath overthrown their foundation|subvertit fundamentum eorum]], that is, has cast them down utterly, slain their body, broken their confidence, taken from them power and wealth, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:27|the floods came, and the winds blew, and they beat upon that house, and it fell, and great was the fall thereof|Venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti, et irruerunt in domum illam, et facta est ruina ejus magna]].

paras.t: Qui dicebant Deo: Recede a nobis. Hoc præcedenti articulo in verbis Job dictum atque expositum est. Et quasi nihil posset facere Omnipotens, æstimabant eum. Hoc quoque est quod Job dixit ibidem: Quis est Omnipotens, ut serviamus ei? Tales quippe Deum penitus inhonorant, et velut judex non sit hominum, parvipendunt, vel quasi in inferioribus immediate agere nihil queat.
paras.en: [[22:17|Who said to God: Depart from us|Qui dicebant Deo: Recede a nobis]]. This was said in the words of Job, and explained, in the preceding article[[Job 21:14||]]. [[22:17|and looked upon the Almighty as if he could do nothing|Et quasi nihil posset facere Omnipotens, æstimabant eum]]. This too is what Job said in the same place: [[Job 21:15|Who is the Almighty, that we should serve him?|Quis est Omnipotens, ut serviamus ei?]] For such men dishonour God utterly, and make light of him as though he were not the judge of men, or as though he could do nothing directly among lower things.

paras.t: Quum ille implesset domos eorum bonis. Nam quidquid habent, a Deo sortiti sunt: in quo ingratitudo eorum circa Deum monstratur, qui ex infinita sua bonitate ac munificentia etiam ingratis et pessimis beneficia multa largitur, prout unigenitus Dei Filius protestatur: Solem suum, inquiens, facit oriri super bonos et malos; et pluit super justos et injustos. Quorum sententia longe sit a me. Hoc præcedenti capitulo protulit Job, dicendo: Consilium eorum longe sit a me. Falsitas enim et peccatum sunt infinitæ fugibilitatis, quum sint recessus, aversio et offensa, quibus mens a prima veritate summaque bonitate, quæ infinitæ est dignitatis, avertitur.
paras.en: [[22:18|Whereas he had filled their houses with good things|Quum ille implesset domos eorum bonis]]. For whatever they have they received from God: in which their ingratitude towards God is shown, who out of his infinite goodness and munificence bestows many benefits even on the ungrateful and the most wicked, as the only-begotten Son of God declares: [[Matt 5:45|who maketh his sun|Solem suum]], he says, [[Matt 5:45|to rise upon the good, and bad, and raineth upon the just and the unjust|facit oriri super bonos et malos; et pluit super justos et injustos]]. [[22:18|whose way of thinking be far from me|Quorum sententia longe sit a me]]. Job uttered this in the preceding chapter, saying: [[Job 21:16|may the counsel of the wicked be far from me|Consilium eorum longe sit a me]]. For falsehood and sin are infinitely to be fled from [Latin *infinitæ fugibilitatis*], since they are the withdrawal, turning away and offence by which the mind is turned away from the first truth and the highest goodness, which is of infinite dignity.

paras.t: Videbunt justi dejectionem et pœnam pravorum, et lætabuntur de illorum debita plaga, non ex invidia, sed zelo justitiæ, congratulantes æquitati divinæ; et innocens subsannabit eos. Hoc est quod fertur in Psalmis: Lætabitur justus quum viderit vindictam; manus suas lavabit in sanguine peccatoris. Itemque: Videbunt recti, et lætabuntur; et omnis iniquitas oppilabit os suum. In Isaia quoque justi Deum affantur simili zelo: Domine, exaltetur manus tua, ut non videant impii; et ignis hostes tuos devoret. Rursusque dicitur de electis: Egredientur, et videbunt cadavera virorum, qui prævaricati sunt in me; et erunt usque ad satietatem visionis omni carni.
paras.en: [[22:19|The just shall see|Videbunt justi]] the downfall and punishment of the wicked, [[22:19|and shall rejoice|et lætabuntur]] at their deserved stroke, not out of envy but out of zeal for justice, rejoicing with the divine equity; [[22:19|and the innocent shall laugh them to scorn|et innocens subsannabit eos]]. This is what is said in the Psalms: [[Ps 57:11|The just shall rejoice when he shall see the revenge: he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner|Lætabitur justus quum viderit vindictam; manus suas lavabit in sanguine peccatoris]]. And likewise: [[Ps 106:42|The just shall see, and shall rejoice, and all iniquity shall stop her mouth|Videbunt recti, et lætabuntur; et omnis iniquitas oppilabit os suum]]. In Isaias too the just address God with like zeal: [[Is 26:11|Lord, let thy hand be exalted, and let them not see|Domine, exaltetur manus tua, ut non videant]], the wicked; [[Is 26:11|and let fire devour thy enemies|et ignis hostes tuos devoret]]. And again it is said of the elect: [[Is 66:24|And they shall go out, and see the carcasses of the men that have transgressed against me|Egredientur, et videbunt cadavera virorum, qui prævaricati sunt in me]]; [[Is 66:24|and they shall be a loathsome sight to all flesh|et erunt usque ad satietatem visionis omni carni]].

paras.t: Nonne succisa est erectio eorum? id est, impiorum elatio, prosperitas, sublimatio, a Deo dejecta est, sicut succiditur arbor excrescens, juxta illud Psalmi: Dejecisti eos dum allevarentur. Et reliquias, id est posteros eorum, pravitatem paternam sequentes, devorabit ignis, id est gravis adversitas vitæ præsentis, vel ardor supplicii infernalis? dicente Psalmista: Dominus in ira sua conturbabit eos, et devorabit eos ignis. Fructum eorum de terra perdes, et semen eorum a filiis hominum. Hinc dicit Jacobus: Exortus est sol cum ardore, et arefecit fœnum, et flos ejus decidit. Sic dives in itineribus suis marcescet.
paras.en: [[22:20|Is not their exaltation cut down?|Nonne succisa est erectio eorum?]] that is, the pride, prosperity and loftiness of the wicked has been cast down by God, as a tree that grows too great is cut down, according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 72:18|when they were lifted up thou hast cast them down|Dejecisti eos dum allevarentur]]. And [[22:20|the remnants of them|Et reliquias]], that is, their descendants, who follow their fathers' wickedness, [[22:20|hath not fire devoured|devorabit ignis]] [Denis reads *devorabit*, shall devour], that is, the heavy adversity of the present life, or the burning of the punishment of hell? as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 20:10|the Lord shall trouble them in his wrath, and fire shall devour them|Dominus in ira sua conturbabit eos, et devorabit eos ignis]]. [[Ps 20:11|Their fruit shalt thou destroy from the earth: and their seed from among the children of men|Fructum eorum de terra perdes, et semen eorum a filiis hominum]]. Hence James says: [[Jas 1:11|the sun rose with a burning heat and parched the grass: and the flower thereof fell off|Exortus est sol cum ardore, et arefecit fœnum, et flos ejus decidit]]. [[Jas 1:11|So also shall the rich man fade away in his ways|Sic dives in itineribus suis marcescet]].

paras.t: Consequenter invitat ipsum Job ad pœnitentiam et salutem. Acquiesce igitur ei, id est, voluntati divinæ tuam conforma, et ejus dispositioni circa te consenti, dicendo: Fiat voluntas tua. Et habeto pacem pectoris: quæ est tranquillitas mentis in Deo, oriturque ex hoc, quod homo conformat voluntatem suam divinæ, servando divina præcepta, secundum quod dicitur: Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Et per hoc, quod Deo sic acquiescis, habebis fructus optimos, id est præclarissima incrementa virtutum, charismata gratiarum, consolationes internas: qui etiam per æquanimem adversitatum tolerantiam disciplinamque Dei gignuntur, dicente Apostolo ad Hebræos: Omnis disciplina in præsenti videtur non gaudii esse, sed mœroris: postea autem fructum pacatissimum exercitatis per eam reddet justitiæ. Hi sunt fructus spiritus, de quibus ad Galatas habetur: Fructus spiritus est, caritas, gaudium, pax, patientia, longanimitas, etc.
paras.en: Next he invites Job himself to penance and salvation. [[22:21|Submit thyself then to him|Acquiesce igitur ei]], that is, conform thy will to the divine will, and consent to his disposing of thee, saying: Thy will be done. [[22:21|and be at peace|Et habeto pacem]] of heart: which is the tranquillity of the mind in God, and arises from this, that a man conforms his will to the divine will by keeping the divine precepts, according to the saying: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. [[22:21|and thereby|Et per hoc]], that is, by thus submitting to God, [[22:21|thou shalt have the best fruits|habebis fructus optimos]], that is, the most excellent increase of virtues, the gifts of graces, inward consolations: which are also brought forth by the even-minded bearing of adversities and by the discipline of God, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:11|Now all chastisement for the present indeed seemeth not to bring with it joy, but sorrow: but afterwards it will yield to them that are exercised by it the most peaceable fruit of justice|Omnis disciplina in præsenti videtur non gaudii esse, sed mœroris: postea autem fructum pacatissimum exercitatis per eam reddet justitiæ]] [Latin *disciplina*, discipline, here rendered chastisement.] These are the fruits of the spirit of which it is said to the Galatians: [[Gal 5:22|the fruit of the Spirit is, charity, joy, peace, patience|Fructus spiritus est, caritas, gaudium, pax, patientia]], [[Gal 5:22|longanimity|longanimitas]], etc.

paras.t: Suscipe ex ore illius legem, id est, legem ab intellectu divino procedentem amplectere, præceptis divinæ legis obtemperando, seu quamlibet jussionem Dei implendo, quam ipse sive per internam inspirationem, sive per alium modum proponit. Unde ait Psalmographus: Dulcis et rectus Dominus: propter hoc legem dabit delinquentibus in via. Lex autem pro præcepto accipi solet. Et pone sermones ejus in corde tuo, id est, verba Dei memoriter retine, efficaciter imple, frequenter considera, ut vites peccata: juxta quod scriptum est, In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi. In Proverbiis quoque dicitur: Serva mandata et legem quasi pupillam oculi tui; liga eam in digitis tuis, et in tabulis cordis tui scribe eam. De justo quoque dicitur in Psalmo: In lege Domini voluntas ejus, et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte.
paras.en: [[22:22|Receive the law of his mouth|Suscipe ex ore illius legem]], that is, embrace the law proceeding from the divine understanding, obeying the precepts of the divine law, or fulfilling any command of God, which he puts before thee whether by inward inspiration or in some other way. Hence the Psalmographer says: [[Ps 24:8|The Lord is sweet and righteous: therefore he will give a law to sinners in the way|Dulcis et rectus Dominus: propter hoc legem dabit delinquentibus in via]]. Now *law* is commonly taken for a precept. [[22:22|and lay up his words in thy heart|Et pone sermones ejus in corde tuo]], that is, keep the words of God in memory, fulfil them effectually, consider them often, so as to shun sins: according to what is written: [[Ps 118:11|Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee|In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi]]. In Proverbs too it is said: [[Prov 7:2|Keep my commandments|Serva mandata]], [[Prov 7:2|and my law as the apple of thy eye|et legem quasi pupillam oculi tui]]; [[Prov 7:3|Bind it upon thy fingers|liga eam in digitis tuis]], [[Prov 7:3|write it upon the tables of thy heart|et in tabulis cordis tui scribe eam]]. And of the just man it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 1:2|his will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law he shall meditate day and night|In lege Domini voluntas ejus, et in lege ejus meditabitur die ac nocte]]

paras.t: Si reversus fueris ad Omnipotentem, per conversionem mentalem, pœnitentiamque salubrem et humilem confessionem. De qua reversione hortatur nos Deus, ubique præsens et omnia penetrans, per Joelem: Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro.
paras.en: [[22:23|If thou wilt return to the Almighty|Si reversus fueris ad Omnipotentem]], by a conversion of mind, and wholesome penance and humble confession. To which return God, present everywhere and pervading all things, exhorts us by Joel: [[Joel 2:12|Be converted to me with all your heart|Convertimini ad me in toto corde vestro]].

paras.t: Ædificaberis, id est, in spiritualibus ac temporalibus bonis stabilieris: prout per Zachariam Dominus ait, Convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos. Et longe facies iniquitatem a tabernaculo tuo, id est a te ipso atque domesticis tuis, de præteritis pœnitendo, et futura cavendo, ad similia quoque tuos hortando. Qui enim ad Deum vere convertitur, ita se habet. Nam et pœnitere est præterita mala deplangere, et deplangenda iterum non committere. Unde et justus profatur: Non habitabit in medio domus meæ qui facit superbiam. Pertinet ergo ad virtuosum, imo ad patremfamilias quemlibet, se ipsum exemplarem præbere, suosque domesticos a vitiis refrenare, hortando, corripiendo, disciplinando.
paras.en: [[22:23|thou shalt be built up|Ædificaberis]], that is, thou shalt be established in spiritual and temporal goods: as the Lord says by Zacharias: [[Zach 1:3|Turn ye to me|Convertimini ad me]], [[Zach 1:3|and I will turn to you|et convertar ad vos]]. [[22:23|and shalt put away iniquity far from thy tabernacle|Et longe facies iniquitatem a tabernaculo tuo]], that is, from thyself and thy household, by repenting of past things and guarding against future ones, and exhorting thine own to do likewise. For he who is truly converted to God behaves thus. For to repent is both to bewail past evils and not to commit again things to be bewailed. Hence the just man also declares: [[Ps 100:7|He that worketh pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house|Non habitabit in medio domus meæ qui facit superbiam]]. It belongs therefore to the virtuous man, nay to every father of a family, to show himself an example and to restrain his household from vices, by exhorting, rebuking, chastising.

paras.t: Dabit pro terra silicem, id est, pro vilibus dabit tibi pretiosa, quemadmodum silex prævalet glebæ; et pro silice torrentes aureos, id est, pro pretiosis tribuet pretiosiora, secundum quod aurum præponitur silici. In spiritualibus quoque adjiciet charismata meliora, ut ubi abundavit peccatum, abundet et gratia: tribuetque pro terra, id est pro actione incipientium, silicem, id est exercitium proficientium; et pro silice, id est tali exercitio, torrentes aureos, id est actus perfectorum, contemplationes atque fervores heroicorum. Multi equidem post casum cautiores resurgunt, et firmius stant, salubriusque concrescunt: et hæc est superinfinita misericordia Dei naturaliter boni, qui ita vitiorum nostrorum oblivisci dignatur, et pro malis bona largitur.
paras.en: [[22:24|He shall give for earth flint|Dabit pro terra silicem]], that is, for worthless things he will give thee precious ones, as flint is worth more than a clod; [[22:24|and for flint torrents of gold|et pro silice torrentes aureos]], that is, for precious things he will bestow more precious, as gold is preferred to flint. In spiritual things too he will add better gifts, so that [[Rom 5:20|where sin abounded, grace did more abound|ubi abundavit peccatum, abundet et gratia]]: and he will give for *earth*, that is, for the activity of beginners, *flint*, that is, the exercise of the proficient; and for *flint*, that is, such exercise, *torrents of gold*, that is, the acts of the perfect, the contemplations and fervours of heroic souls [these are the three classic stages of the spiritual life: beginners, the proficient, the perfect]. Indeed many after a fall rise more cautious, stand more firmly and grow together more soundly: and this is the more than infinite mercy of God, good by nature, who so deigns to forget our vices and bestows good things for evil.

paras.t: Eritque Omnipotens contra hostes tuos, id est, ab impugnatione visibilium ac invisibilium hostium te defendet: quia protector est omnium sperantium in se, juxta illud Psalmi, In Domino sperans non infirmabor. Et in Proverbiis habetur: Turris fortissima nomen Domini: ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur. Apostolus quoque ad Romanos ait: Deus conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris velociter. Unde protestatur Psalmista: Super inimicos meos despexit oculus meus. Et argentum, id est temporales divitiæ, coacervabitur, id est congregabitur, tibi. Spiritualiter vero, nomine argenti, sacræ Scripturæ designatur scientia, dicente Psalmista: Eloquia Domini eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum. Ille autem illustratur scientia, cujus vita est virtuosa, dicente Apostolo: Dabit tibi Dominus de omnibus intellectum. Et in prima S. Joannis Canonica legitur: Non necesse habetis ut aliquis doceat vos, sed unctio ejus (scilicet Dei) docet vos de omnibus. Ideo in Ecclesiastico scribitur: Fili, concupiscens sapientiam, serva justitiam, et Deus præbebit illam tibi. Quum enim Deus sit sol sapientiæ, mentem a vitiis mundam radiose perlustrat.
paras.en: [[22:25|And the Almighty shall be against thy enemies|Eritque Omnipotens contra hostes tuos]], that is, he will defend thee from the assault of visible and invisible enemies: because he [[Ps 17:31|is the protector of all that trust in him|protector est omnium sperantium in se]], according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 25:1|I have put my trust in the Lord, and shall not be weakened|In Domino sperans non infirmabor]]. And in Proverbs we have: [[Prov 18:10|The name of the Lord is a strong tower: the just runneth to it, and shall be exalted|Turris fortissima nomen Domini: ad ipsum currit justus, et exaltabitur]]. The Apostle too says to the Romans: [[Rom 16:20|the God of peace crush Satan under your feet speedily|Deus conteret Satanam sub pedibus vestris velociter]]. Hence the Psalmist declares: [[Ps 53:9|my eye hath looked down upon my enemies|Super inimicos meos despexit oculus meus]]. [[22:25|and silver|Et argentum]], that is, temporal riches, [[22:25|shall be heaped together|coacervabitur]], that is, shall be gathered, for thee. But spiritually, by the name of silver is signified the knowledge of Holy Scripture, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 11:7|The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried by the fire|Eloquia Domini eloquia casta, argentum igne examinatum]]. And he is enlightened with knowledge whose life is virtuous, as the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:7|the Lord will give thee in all things understanding|Dabit tibi Dominus de omnibus intellectum]]. And in the first canonical epistle of St John we read: [[1 John 2:27|you have no need that any man teach you|Non necesse habetis ut aliquis doceat vos]]: [[1 John 2:27|but as his unction|sed unctio ejus]] (that is, God's) [[1 John 2:27|teacheth you of all things|docet vos de omnibus]]. Therefore it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:33|Son, if thou desire wisdom, keep justice, and God will give her to thee|Fili, concupiscens sapientiam, serva justitiam, et Deus præbebit illam tibi]]. For since God is the sun of wisdom, he shines brightly through a mind clean of vices.

paras.t: Tunc super Omnipotentem deliciis afflues, id est, in contemplatione Dei gaudebis, ejus consolationes internas experieris, ipsius amore dulciter accenderis, ejus immensæ beatitudini, opulentiæ, perfectioni toto congratulaberis corde, ita ut ex sententia dicere possis: Memor fui Dei, et delectatus sum; itemque: Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine! et rursus: Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam. His puris mentalibusque deliciis tanto plus affluere promeremur, quo ex puro Dei amore omnem carnalem delectationem, vilem consolationem, sæcularem lætitiam plenius aspernamur, juxta illud Psalmi: Renuit consolari anima mea. Denique delectatio ex unione potentiæ cum objecto convenienti procedit. Quum ergo Deus sublimis, incomparabilis et immensus, sit prorsus illimitatæ perfectionis, amœnitatis pulchritudinisque objectum, constat quod in unione mentis cum illo sit summa deliciatio: si tamen mens capax effecta sit, si Dei inardescat amore, si sapientiæ dono perfusa sit, si virtutibus stabilita sit, a privato illo pernicioso amore purgata. Unde de Sponsa in Canticis admirative inquiritur: Quæ est ista quæ ascendit de deserto, deliciis affluens, innixa super dilectum suum?
paras.en: [[22:26|Then shalt thou abound in delights in the Almighty|Tunc super Omnipotentem deliciis afflues]], that is, thou shalt rejoice in the contemplation of God, shalt experience his inward consolations, shalt be sweetly kindled with his love, shalt rejoice with thy whole heart at his immense beatitude, riches and perfection, so that thou canst say from the heart: [[Ps 76:4|I remembered God, and was delighted|Memor fui Dei, et delectatus sum]]; and likewise: [[Ps 30:20|O how great is the multitude of thy sweetness, O Lord|Quam magna multitudo dulcedinis tuæ, Domine!]]! and again: [[Ps 93:19|According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, thy comforts have given joy to my soul|Secundum multitudinem dolorum meorum in corde meo, consolationes tuæ lætificaverunt animam meam]]. We merit to abound the more in these pure delights of the mind the more fully, out of pure love of God, we spurn every carnal delight, every base consolation, all worldly gladness, according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 76:3|My soul refused to be comforted|Renuit consolari anima mea]]. Further, delight proceeds from the union of a power [that is, a faculty of the soul] with a fitting object. Since therefore God, sublime, incomparable and immense, is an object of altogether unlimited perfection, loveliness and beauty, it is plain that in the mind's union with him is the highest delight: provided the mind has been made capable, is aflame with the love of God, is filled with the gift of wisdom, is established in the virtues, and is cleansed of that pernicious private love [that is, self-love]. Hence of the Bride in the Canticles it is asked in wonder: [[Cant 8:5|Who is this that cometh up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved?|Quæ est ista quæ ascendit de deserto, deliciis affluens, innixa super dilectum suum?]]

paras.t: Et elevabis ad Deum faciem tuam intellectualem, scilicet mentem; vel etiam corporalem vultum dirigendo ad cœlum, in quo Deus specialiter esse et habitare asseritur, in quantum ibidem eminentius operatur, clariusque videtur. Itaque, Ad Deum faciem elevabis, tanquam ad bonum finaliter desideratum, ad ens summe dilectum, ad unicum tuum refugium atque solatium. Etenim ubi amor, ibi et oculus; et ubi thesaurus tuus, ibi et cor tuum. Hinc in Threnis admonetur: Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Deum in cœlum. Tobias quoque dicit: Ad te, Domine, faciem meam converto; ad te oculos meos erigo. Postremo quilibet libenter respicit suæ dilectionis et delectationis objectum: ideo qui in Omnipotente solitus est amando fervere, et contemplando gaudere, quid mirum si faciem mentis frequenter levet ad eum in omni loco, occupatione et tempore?
paras.en: [[22:26|and shalt lift up thy face to God|Et elevabis ad Deum faciem tuam]]: the face of the understanding, that is, the mind; or also the bodily countenance, by directing it to heaven, where God is said to be and to dwell in a special way, inasmuch as he works there more eminently and is seen more clearly. So then, thou shalt [[22:26|lift up thy face to God|Ad Deum faciem elevabis]] as to the good desired as the last end, to the being loved above all, to thy one refuge and comfort. For where love is, there is the eye; and [[Matt 6:21|where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also|ubi thesaurus tuus, ibi et cor tuum]]. Hence we are admonished in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:41|Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens|Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Deum in cœlum]]. Tobias too says: [[Tob 3:14|To thee, O Lord, I turn my face, to thee I direct my eyes|Ad te, Domine, faciem meam converto; ad te oculos meos erigo]]. Lastly, everyone gladly looks upon the object of his love and delight: therefore if one who is wont to burn with love and rejoice in contemplation in the Almighty often lifts the face of his mind to him in every place, occupation and time, what wonder?

paras.t: Rogabis eum cum grandi fiducia atque frequentia: quia et in oratione est elevatio mentis ad eum. Unus quoque orationis effectus, est quædam mentalis suavitas, quam devotus experitur orando. Idcirco amator contemplatorque Dei, et dulcedinis ejus gustator, tanto fiducialius et frequentius, tanto libentius ac delectabilius eum precatur, quo ardentiori ipsum intra se amore complectitur. Talemque Deus tanquam filium et amicum paterne exaudit. Ideo subditur, et exaudiet te. In talibus quippe potissime verum est quod ait Salvator: Omnis qui petit, accipit. Unde in Joanne habetur: Si quis cultor est Dei, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc Deus exaudit. Bona enim et irreprehensibilis vita exauditionem a Deo meretur, juxta illud Joannis: Carissimi, si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum; et quidquid petierimus accipiemus. Quod totum intelligendum est, si perseveranter salubriterque oremus.
paras.en: [[22:27|Thou shalt pray to him|Rogabis eum]] with great confidence and often: for in prayer too there is a lifting up of the mind to him. And one effect of prayer is a certain sweetness of mind which the devout man experiences in praying. Therefore the lover and contemplative of God, who tastes his sweetness, prays to him the more confidently and often, the more gladly and delightedly, the more ardent the love with which he embraces him within himself. And God hears such a one in a fatherly way, as a son and friend. Therefore it is added: [[22:27|and he will hear thee|et exaudiet te]]. For in such men above all is that true which the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:8|every one that asketh, receiveth|Omnis qui petit, accipit]]. Hence we have in John: [[John 9:31|if a man be a server of God and doth his, will, him he heareth|Si quis cultor est Dei, et voluntatem ejus facit, hunc Deus exaudit]]. For a good and blameless life merits a hearing from God, according to that word of John: [[1 John 3:21|Dearly beloved, if our heart do not reprehend us, we have confidence towards God|Carissimi, si cor nostrum non reprehenderit nos, fiduciam habemus ad Deum]]; [[1 John 3:22|And whatsoever we shall ask, we shall receive|et quidquid petierimus accipiemus]]. All of which is to be understood if we pray perseveringly and in a way that leads to salvation.

paras.t: Et vota tua reddes, id est, promissa implebis: juxta illud Psalmi, Reddam tibi vota mea quæ distinxerunt labia mea. Porro vovere quid Deo, actus est latriæ, quæ est dignissima virtus moralis. Ideo, sicut vota persolvere, excellenter virtuosum meritoriumque consistit; sic vota non solvere, vehementer vitiosum est atque damnabile. Propterea Ecclesiastes præcipit: Si quid vovisti Deo, ne moreris reddere; displicet enim ei stulta et infidelis promissio. Et in Deuteronomio fertur: Quod semel egressum est de labiis tuis, observabis, et facies sicut promisisti Domino Deo tuo. Unde et Augustinus: Vovere, inquit, voluntatis est: reddere, necessitatis.
paras.en: [[22:27|and thou shalt pay vows|Et vota tua reddes]], that is, thou shalt fulfil thy promises: according to that word of the Psalm: [[Ps 65:13|I will pay thee my vows|Reddam tibi vota mea]], [[Ps 65:14|Which my lips have uttered|quæ distinxerunt labia mea]]. Now to vow something to God is an act of latria [the worship due to God alone], which is the most worthy moral virtue. Therefore, as paying vows is excellently virtuous and meritorious, so not paying vows is gravely vicious and damnable. For this reason Ecclesiastes commands: [[Eccles 5:3|If thou hast vowed any thing to God, defer not to pay it: for an unfaithful and foolish promise displeaseth him|Si quid vovisti Deo, ne moreris reddere; displicet enim ei stulta et infidelis promissio]]. And in Deuteronomy it is said: [[Deut 23:23|that which is once gone out of thy lips, thou shalt observe, and shalt do as thou hast promised to the Lord thy God|Quod semel egressum est de labiis tuis, observabis, et facies sicut promisisti Domino Deo tuo]]. Hence Augustine too: To vow, he says, is of the will; to pay, of necessity.

paras.t: Decernes rem, id est, propones, judicabis seu ordinabis aliquod factum, et qualiter negotium tuum eveniat; et veniet tibi, id est, prosperum habebit successum, Deo dispositioni tuæ cooperante et effectum præstante: secundum quod in Proverbiis legitur, Cor hominis disponit viam suam, sed Dei est dirigere gressus ejus. Et in viis tuis, id est vitæ tuæ processibus seu operibus, splendebit lumen gratiæ et virtutum, prosperitatisque fulgor, id est, Deus te intus illustrabit et diriget, virtuoseque ages, ac lucide vives, atque in sapientia ambulabis: juxta illud Isaiæ, Erumpet quasi mane lumen tuum, et anteibit faciem tuam justitia tua. In Proverbiis quoque: Justorum semita quasi lux splendens procedit, et crescit usque ad perfectam diem.
paras.en: [[22:28|Thou shalt decree a thing|Decernes rem]], that is, thou shalt propose, judge or order some deed, and how thy business is to turn out; [[22:28|and it shall come to thee|et veniet tibi]], that is, it will have a prosperous outcome, God working with thy disposing and granting the effect: according to what we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 16:9|The heart of man disposeth his way: but the Lord must direct his steps|Cor hominis disponit viam suam, sed Dei est dirigere gressus ejus]]. And [[22:28|in thy ways|in viis tuis]], that is, in the courses or works of thy life, [[22:28|light shall shine|splendebit lumen]] of grace and of the virtues, and the brightness of prosperity, that is, God will enlighten thee within and direct thee, and thou shalt act virtuously and live in the light and walk in wisdom: according to that word of Isaias: [[Is 58:8|thy light break forth as the morning|Erumpet quasi mane lumen tuum]], [[Is 58:8|and thy justice shall go before thy face|et anteibit faciem tuam justitia tua]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 4:18|the path of the just, as a shining light, goeth forwards, and increaseth even to perfect day|Justorum semita quasi lux splendens procedit, et crescit usque ad perfectam diem]]

paras.t: Qui enim humiliatus fuerit, se ipsum humiliter condemnando, pœnitentialiter affligendo, adversa patienter ferendo, alios sibi cordialiter præferendo, erit in gloria, id est, a Deo sublimabitur in præsenti per gratiam, et in futuro per felicitatem completam, sicut ait Salvator: Qui se humiliaverit, exaltabitur; et qui se exaltat, humiliabitur. Cui consonat illud Proverbiorum: Humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria, et superbum sequetur humilitas. Ideo Petrus jubet: Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, ut vos exaltet in tempore visitationis. In Matthæo quoque determinat Judex: Quicumque humiliaverit se sicut parvulus iste, hic major erit in regno cœlorum. Et qui inclinaverit oculos suos interiores ad propriæ defectuositatis, fragilitatis, vel impietatis considerationem condignam, ipse salvabitur. Hinc dicit Baruch: Oculi deficientes dant gloriam tibi Domino; et Ecclesiasticus: Humilia valde spiritum tuum. Non ergo extollamus nos ipsos, non magnos et sapientes aut perfectos nos æstimemus; sed innumerabiles nostras pensemus ærumnas, et quod nihil boni a nobis ipsis habemus; quod item celeriter evacuaremur ac periremus, nisi indesinenter pietate et gratia Spiritus Sancti in omni via hac custodiremur. Hinc scriptum est: Oculi sublimis hominis humiliati sunt. Et Sapiens ait: Generatio cujus erecti sunt oculi, et palpebræ ejus in altum surrectæ.
paras.en: [[22:29|For he that hath been humbled|Qui enim humiliatus fuerit]], by humbly condemning himself, afflicting himself in penance, bearing adversity patiently, heartily preferring others to himself, [[22:29|shall be in glory|erit in gloria]], that is, he will be raised up by God in the present by grace, and in the future by complete happiness, as the Saviour says: [[Matt 23:12|he that shall humble himself shall be exalted|Qui se humiliaverit, exaltabitur]]; and he [[Luke 14:11|that exalteth himself shall be humbled|qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]]. With which agrees that word of Proverbs: [[Prov 29:23|glory shall uphold the humble of spirit|Humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria]], and [[Prov 29:23|Humiliation followeth the proud|superbum sequetur humilitas]]. Therefore Peter bids: [[1 Pet 5:6|Be you humbled therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation|Humiliamini sub potenti manu Dei, ut vos exaltet in tempore visitationis]]. In Matthew too the Judge lays down: [[Matt 18:4|Whosoever therefore shall humble himself as this little child, he is the greater in the kingdom of heaven|Quicumque humiliaverit se sicut parvulus iste, hic major erit in regno cœlorum]]. [[22:29|and he that shall bow down his eyes|Et qui inclinaverit oculos]], his inward eyes, to a fitting consideration of his own defectiveness, frailty or impiety, [[22:29|he shall be saved|ipse salvabitur]]. Hence Baruch says: [[Bar 2:18|the eyes that fail|Oculi deficientes]] [[Bar 2:18|giveth glory|dant gloriam]] [[Bar 2:18|to thee the Lord|tibi Domino]]; and Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:19|Humble thy spirit very much|Humilia valde spiritum tuum]]. Let us not therefore extol ourselves, nor think ourselves great and wise or perfect; but let us weigh our countless miseries, and that we have nothing good of ourselves; and that we should quickly be emptied and perish, unless we were kept unceasingly in every way by the goodness and grace of the Holy Ghost. Hence it is written: [[Is 2:11|The lofty eyes of man are humbled|Oculi sublimis hominis humiliati sunt]]. And the Wise Man says: [[Prov 30:13|A generation, whose eyes are lofty, and their eyelids lifted up on high|Generatio cujus erecti sunt oculi, et palpebræ ejus in altum surrectæ]]

paras.t: Salvabitur innocens: quoniam Deus reddet unicuique quod meretur. Innocens autem qui alteri non nocuit, meruit sibi nocumentum non ingeri; et quoniam in Dei caritate et gratia vixit, meruit beatificari. Ideo subditur: salvabitur autem, id est, beatitudinem sortietur, in munditia manuum suarum, id est puritate seu merito vitæ suæ, non utique sine auxilio gratiæ, quum propriis nemo viribus justus aut innocens sit, prout Moyses protestatur: Dominator Domine, clemens, verus, et patiens, nullus apud te per se innocens est.
paras.en: [[22:30|The innocent shall be saved|Salvabitur innocens]]: because God will render to each what he deserves. Now the innocent man, who has not harmed another, has deserved that no harm be done to him; and because he lived in the charity and grace of God, he has deserved to be made blessed. Therefore it is added: [[22:30|and he shall be saved|salvabitur autem]], that is, he will obtain beatitude, [[22:30|by the cleanness of his hands|in munditia manuum suarum]], that is, by the purity or merit of his life, yet surely not without the help of grace, since no one is just or innocent by his own strength, as Moses declares: [[Ex 34:6|O the Lord, the Lord God|Dominator Domine]], gracious, true and patient, [[Ex 34:7|no man of himself is innocent before thee|nullus apud te per se innocens est]] [Denis gives the attributes of Ex 34:6 in his own order].

paras.t: Postremo, istud capitulum alia ac moraliori expositione non eget, quemadmodum nec præcedens.
paras.en: Lastly, this chapter needs no other or more moral exposition, any more than the preceding one did.

23.title: Declaratio litteralis capituli vicesimi tertii: Respondens autem Job, ait.
23.title_en: Literal declaration of the twenty-third chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, ait. Sapientis enim et intelligentis est, arguendo, inquirendo, et respondendo veritatem tueri ac demonstrare. Qui vero indoctus est, non se ad respondendum ingerere debet, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Si est tibi intellectus, responde proximo tuo; sin autem, sit manus tua super os tuum. Quo utique verbo redarguuntur præsumptuosi, vani et scioli, paratiores docere quam discere: quibus convenit illud Apostoli, Non intelligentes neque quæ dicunt, neque de quibus affirmant. Itaque illud Jacobi observemus: Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum.
paras.en: [[23:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, ait]]. For it belongs to the wise and understanding man to defend and show forth the truth by arguing, inquiring and answering. But one who is unlearned ought not to thrust himself forward to answer, according to that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 5:14|If thou have understanding, answer thy neighbour: but if not, let thy hand be upon thy mouth|Si est tibi intellectus, responde proximo tuo; sin autem, sit manus tua super os tuum]]. By this word are rebuked the presumptuous, the vain and the smatterers, readier to teach than to learn, to whom that saying of the Apostle applies: [[1 Tim 1:7|understanding neither the things they say, nor whereof they affirm|Non intelligentes neque quæ dicunt, neque de quibus affirmant]]. Let us therefore observe that saying of James: [[Jas 1:19|And let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak|Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum]].

paras.t: Nunc quoque in amaritudine est sermo meus, id est, cum magna afflictione profertur, quia ab amicis meis dolor meus augetur magis quam relevatur; et manus plagæ meæ, id est fortitudo percussionis, seu potestas adversitatis meæ, aggravata est super gemitum meum, quem habui ante, ita quod recens afflictio priori gemitui meo est addita. Nam vulneribus Job a Satana ei illatis, amici sui adjecerunt contumelias, improperia, irrisiones, accusationesque falsas, ex quibus Job contristabatur atque dolebat: non ex defectu patientiæ, sed zelo justitiæ; imo ex caritate, quia amicis condolebat errantibus, et de proximorum scandalo urebatur, præsertim eorum qui huic intererant disceptationi. Sicque Job fuit Christi figura, in Psalmo dicentis ad Patrem: Quoniam quem tu percussisti, persecuti sunt; et super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt.
paras.en: [[23:2|Now also my words are in bitterness|Nunc quoque in amaritudine est sermo meus]], that is, they are uttered with great affliction, because my grief is increased by my friends rather than relieved; [[23:2|and the hand of my scourge|et manus plagæ meæ]], that is, the force of the blow, or the power of my adversity, [[23:2|is more grievous than my mourning|aggravata est super gemitum meum]] which I had before, so that a fresh affliction has been added to my former mourning. For to the wounds dealt Job by Satan his friends added insults, reproaches, mockeries and false accusations, at which Job was saddened and grieved: not from any want of patience, but from zeal for justice; nay, from charity, because he suffered with his friends in their error, and burned at the scandal of his neighbours[[2 Cor 11:29||]], especially of those who were present at this dispute. And so Job was a figure of Christ, who says to the Father in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:27|Because they have persecuted him whom thou hast smitten; and they have added to the grief of my wounds|Quoniam quem tu percussisti, persecuti sunt; et super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt]].

paras.t: Præterea, quia amici Job imposuerunt ei, quod pro suis esset cæsus excessibus, præsertim quia præcedenti capitulo dixerat Eliphaz, quod propter malitiam suam plurimam, et iniquitates suas infinitas Deus arguerit eum; ideo sanctus Job nunc ostendit hujus oppositum, ad divinum se judicium conferens, quoniam bonæ conscientiæ fuit, ipseque Spiritus testimonium perhibuit conscientiæ suæ, quod filius Dei esset. Quis mihi tribuat, id est, vehementer cupio mihi conferri, ut cognoscam, et inveniam illum, id est, Deum perfectiori modo cognoscam, et inveniam qualiter diversimode disponit homines et gubernat, et diversis de causis eos flagellat? Itaque, Inveniam illum, id est, id de eo agnoscam, quod de ipsius quæro notitia. Ut enim frequenter præhabitum est, Job clarius concupivit suæ percussionis causas agnoscere. Denique ipse sicut et quilibet electorum, desideravit de cognitione viæ per fidem, ad cognitionem patriæ per speciem pervenire. Imo hoc sanctorum finale est desiderium, dicente Apostolo: Sequor autem, si quo modo, etc. Et Psalmista: Ostende faciem tuam.
paras.en: Moreover, because Job’s friends laid it to his charge that he had been struck for his own excesses (especially since in the preceding chapter Eliphaz had said that God reproved him for his manifold wickedness and his infinite iniquities[[Job 22:5||]]), holy Job now shows the contrary, betaking himself to the divine judgment, since he was of a good conscience, and the Spirit himself bore witness to his conscience that he was a son of God[[Rom 8:16||]]. [[23:3|Who will grant me|Quis mihi tribuat]], that is, I vehemently desire that it be granted me, [[23:3|that I might know and find him|ut cognoscam, et inveniam illum]], that is, that I might know God in a more perfect manner, and find how he disposes and governs men in divers ways, and for divers causes scourges them? So then, [[23:3|find him|Inveniam illum]], that is, that I may learn about him what I seek to know of him. For, as has often been said before, Job longed to know more clearly the causes of his being struck. Moreover he, like any of the elect, desired to come from the knowledge of the way, by faith, to the knowledge of the homeland, by sight [that is, from the knowledge proper to the wayfarer in this life to that of the blessed in heaven]. Nay, this is the final desire of the saints, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 3:12|but I follow after, if I may by any means|Sequor autem, si quo modo]], etc. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 79:4|shew us thy face|Ostende faciem tuam]] [the margin’s numeral cannot be read; the words stand in Ps 79:4, 8 and 20].

paras.t: Et veniam usque ad solium ejus, id est ad thronum divini judicii, ut secundum merita mea judicer, et divinorum judiciorum rationem et modos plenius discam. Unde superius dixit: Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar; et item: Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera. Itaque, ad tribunal Dei optavit deduci, non ut corpore mox elevaretur in cœlos, sed ad Dei judicium erigeretur. Thronus autem Dei, uno modo vocatur judiciaria ejus potestas, eminentia sive auctoritas, ejus ubique est sicut et Deus, quum sit ipsemet incircumscriptibilis Deus judex.
paras.en: [[23:3|and come even to his throne|Et veniam usque ad solium ejus]], that is, to the throne of the divine judgment, that I may be judged according to my merits, and learn more fully the reason and manner of the divine judgments. Hence he said above: [[Job 13:18|If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just|Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar]]; and again: [[Job 6:2|O that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance|Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera]]. So he wished to be brought to the tribunal of God, not that he might be raised up forthwith in the body to heaven, but that he might be lifted up to God’s judgment. Now the throne of God, in one sense, is the name given to his judicial power, eminence or authority, and this is everywhere, as God is, since the judge is God himself, who cannot be circumscribed.

paras.t: Ponam coram eo judicium, id est, bona conscientia justum judicium secundum merita exigam, ut donet mihi sicut promerui. Sic et David dixit ad Saul: Judicet Dominus inter me et te. Unde in Psalmo inducitur: Judica me, Deus, et discerne causam meam de gente non sancta. Et iterum: Judica me, Domine, quoniam in innocentia mea ingressus sum. In Threnis quoque: Vidisti, Domine, iniquitatem illorum adversum me; judica judicium meum.
paras.en: [[23:4|I would set judgment before him|Ponam coram eo judicium]], that is, with a good conscience I would demand a just judgment according to my merits, that he may give to me as I have deserved. So too David said to Saul: [[1 Kings 24:13|The Lord judge between me and thee|Judicet Dominus inter me et te]]. Hence it is put in the Psalm: [[Ps 42:1|Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from the nation that is not holy|Judica me, Deus, et discerne causam meam de gente non sancta]]. And again: [[Ps 25:1|Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence|Judica me, Domine, quoniam in innocentia mea ingressus sum]]. In the Lamentations too: [[Lam 3:59|Thou hast seen, O Lord, their iniquity against me: judge thou my judgment|Vidisti, Domine, iniquitatem illorum adversum me; judica judicium meum]].

paras.t: Et os meum replebo increpationibus, id est reprehensionibus contradicentium veritati; vel, increpationibus, id est piis querelis, cur ego justus et innocens tam graviter cæsus sum, quatenus ex divina responsione veritatem clarius noscam, non ut Deum redarguam, aut injuste judicasse prætendam. Sic Thomas exponit. Unde, ut Lyra affirmat, in Hebræo habetur: Os meum replebo argumentationibus, utpote sicut discipulus coram magistro interdum multiplicat argumenta, non ad contentionem, sed ad veritatis inquisitionem, quam a magistro audire desiderat. Potius autem reor nomen Hebræum ad utrumque istorum esse æquivocum. Porro Albertus exponit sic: Os meum replebo increpationibus, increpando me in quibus accusabilis inveniar: juxta illud Proverbiorum, Justus prior accusator est sui. Justum enim est ut homo increpet se in quibus Deus eum accusat, secundum quod dicit Jeremias: Postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum; confusus sum, et erubui, quoniam sustinui opprobrium adolescentiæ meæ. Sed expositio ista videtur non tam litteralis, quam mystica. Job quippe hæc loquitur ad insinuandum suam æquitatem, non culpam, sicut verba clarius pandunt sequentia.
paras.en: [[23:4|and would fill my mouth with complaints|Et os meum replebo increpationibus]] [*increpationes*, properly “rebukes” or “reproofs”], that is, with reproofs of those who gainsay the truth; or, [[23:4|complaints|increpationibus]], that is, with devout complaints, asking why I, just and innocent, have been struck so grievously, so that from the divine answer I may know the truth more clearly; not so as to rebuke God, or to claim that he has judged unjustly. So Thomas explains it.
