Hence, as Lyra affirms, the Hebrew has: I will fill my mouth with arguments; as a disciple before his master sometimes multiplies arguments, not for contention but to search out the truth, which he desires to hear from his master. But I rather think the Hebrew word is equivocal between the two [that is, it can bear either sense, “complaints” or “arguments”]. Albert, again, explains it thus: [[23:4|would fill my mouth with complaints|Os meum replebo increpationibus]], by rebuking myself in the things in which I may be found blameworthy: according to that saying of Proverbs, [[Prov 18:17|The just is first accuser of himself|Justus prior accusator est sui]]. For it is just that a man should rebuke himself in the things in which God accuses him, according to what Jeremias says: [[Jer 31:19|after thou didst shew unto me, I struck my thigh: I am confounded and ashamed, because I have borne the reproach of my youth|Postquam ostendisti mihi, percussi femur meum; confusus sum, et erubui, quoniam sustinui opprobrium adolescentiæ meæ]]. But this exposition seems not so much literal as mystical. For Job says these things to suggest his equity, not his fault, as the words that follow show more clearly.

paras.t: Ut sciam verba quæ mihi respondeat ad quæstionem qua causam meæ percussionis inquiro, seu ad querelam qua me conqueror sine meo plagatum demerito; et intelligam quid loquatur mihi, causam meam determinando. Primo enim audienda et cognoscenda sunt verba, deinde intelligenda et intuenda.
paras.en: [[23:5|That I might know the words that he would answer me|Ut sciam verba quæ mihi respondeat]] to the question in which I ask the cause of my being struck, or to the complaint in which I lament that I have been smitten without my deserving it; [[23:5|and understand what he would say to me|et intelligam quid loquatur mihi]], by deciding my cause. For words must first be heard and known, then understood and pondered.

paras.t: Nolo multa fortitudine contendat mecum, id est, non sic peto judicium Dei, ut velim eum procedere mecum secundum omnipotentiam suam, aut secundum justitiam suam fortissimam, qua in se ipsa justus est infinite, ut scilicet secundum justitiæ suæ rigorem me judicet, non habendo pium respectum ad humanam fragilitatem. Sic enim omnis humana justitia insufficiens est, et comparatione divinæ justitiæ, injustitia quædam, Isaia dicente: Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ. Propter quod ait vir sanctus: Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo, Domine. Et supra dictum est: Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo; et: Si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit respondere unum pro mille. Nec magnitudinis suæ mole [me] premat, id est, majestatis suæ immensitate, atque justitiæ suæ excellentia non mihi prævaleat, quoniam comparatione ipsius scio me infinite deficere, nec aliquid habere condignum.
paras.en: [[23:6|I would not that he should contend with me with much strength|Nolo multa fortitudine contendat mecum]], that is: I do not so ask for God’s judgment as to wish him to proceed with me according to his omnipotence, or according to his most mighty justice, by which in himself he is infinitely just; that is, that he should judge me according to the rigour of his justice, without having a kindly regard to human frailty. For in that way all human justice is insufficient, and, compared with the divine justice, a kind of injustice, as Isaias says: [[Is 64:6|all our justices as the rag of a menstruous woman|Quasi pannus menstruatæ universæ justitiæ nostræ]]. For this reason the holy man [that is, David] says: [[Ps 142:2|enter not into judgment with thy servant|Non intres in judicium cum servo tuo]], O Lord. And it was said above: [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificabitur homo compositus Deo]]; and: [[Job 9:3|If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one for a thousand|Si voluerit contendere cum eo, non poterit respondere unum pro mille]]. [[23:6|nor overwhelm me with the weight of his greatness|Nec magnitudinis suæ mole [me] premat]], that is, let him not prevail over me by the immensity of his majesty and the excellence of his justice, since I know that in comparison with him I fall infinitely short, and have nothing worthy of him.

paras.t: Proponat æquitatem contra me, id est justitiam pietati admixtam, non solum ad suam perfectionem, sed ad meam quoque fragilitatem naturalem ac inevitabilem imperfectionem respiciendo in judicando me secundum opera mea: quæ licet respectu divinæ perfectionis justa non sint, tamen habendo respectum ad meæ naturæ conditionem, modum, gradum et ordinem, in suo genere justa sunt. Unde Albertus hic ait: Æquitas, secundum Chrysostomum, est justitia dulcore misericordiæ temperata: ut sit sensus, Proponat æquitatem contra me, id est, ad æquum infirmitatis humanæ me judicet. Et perveniet ad victoriam judicium meum, id est, judicium quod Deus proferet de me, ostendet me justum et amicorum meorum victorem, veritatisque defensorem. Quomodo autem his verbis non obviet, quod nono capitulo ait Job, Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me; etiamsi simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea: patet ex dictis ibidem.
paras.en: [[23:7|Let him propose equity against me|Proponat æquitatem contra me]], that is, justice mingled with kindness, having regard, in judging me according to my works, not only to his own perfection but also to my natural frailty and unavoidable imperfection: for my works, though they are not just with respect to the divine perfection, are yet just in their own kind, having regard to the condition, measure, degree and order of my nature. Hence Albert says here: Equity, according to Chrysostom, is justice tempered with the sweetness of mercy; so that the sense is: [[23:7|Let him propose equity against me|Proponat æquitatem contra me]], that is, let him judge me according to what is fair to human weakness. [[23:7|and let my judgment come to victory|Et perveniet ad victoriam judicium meum]] [Denis reads *perveniet*, “shall come”], that is, the judgment which God shall pronounce on me shall show me just, the victor over my friends and the defender of the truth. But how these words do not conflict with what Job says in the ninth chapter, [[Job 9:20|If I would justify myself, my own mouth shall condemn me|Si justificare me voluero, os meum condemnabit me]]; [[Job 9:21|Although I should be simple, even this my soul shall be ignorant of|etiamsi simplex fuero, hoc ipsum ignorabit anima mea]], is clear from what was said there.

paras.t: Si ad orientem iero, non apparet; et si ad occidentem, non intelligam eum: id est, sive orientalem cœli partem, sive occidentalem considerem seu accedam, et omnia quæ ibidem geruntur et sunt, pensem, Deum tamen omnium horum conditorem perfecte, plene, et sicut in se ipso est, cognoscere ex illis non queo. In tantum equidem Creator ex creaturis cognoscitur, in quantum ejus perfectio in illis relucet. Creatura autem omnis deficit infinite a plena repræsentatione perfectionis proprii Creatoris.
paras.en: [[23:8|if I go to the east, he appeareth not; if to the west, I shall not understand him|Si ad orientem iero, non apparet; et si ad occidentem, non intelligam eum]]: that is, whether I consider or approach the eastern part of the heavens or the western, and weigh all that is done and exists there, yet from them I cannot know God, the maker of all these things, perfectly, fully, and as he is in himself. For the Creator is known from creatures only so far as his perfection shines out in them; but every creature falls infinitely short of fully representing the perfection of its own Creator.

paras.t: Et si ad sinistram, id est aquilonem, transiero, quid agam? Ad quod respondet: Non apprehendam eum cognitione prædicta. Si me vertam, per considerationem internam, seu corporis gressum, aut vultus directionem, ad dexteram, id est plagam meridianam, non videbo illum, per speciem ex creatis quæ ibi sunt. De qua visione Dominus loquitur Moysi: Non videbit me homo, et vivet. Unde et in Joanne habetur: Deum nemo vidit unquam. In Proverbiis quoque: Quod nomen ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti? Hinc philosophi tam Peripatetici quam Platonici fassi sunt, quod Deus sit penitus innominabilis, insensibilis, inimaginabilis, inopinabilis, inenarrabilis, incomprehensibilis, superessentialis, ignotus et infinitus. Verumtamen, ex creaturis aliquo modo cognoscitur, prout causa supertranscendens ex suo valet effectu cognosci. Propter quod ad Romanos ait Apostolus: Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, a creatura mundi, id est homine, intellecta conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas. In Sapientiæ demum libro scriptum est: A magnitudine speciei et creaturæ poterit cognoscibiliter creator horum videri.
paras.en: [[23:9|If to the left hand|Et si ad sinistram]], that is, to the north, I pass, [[23:9|what shall I do?|quid agam]] To which he answers: [[23:9|I shall not take hold on him|Non apprehendam eum]] by the knowledge just spoken of. [[23:9|if I turn myself|Si me vertam]], by inward consideration, or by the steps of the body, or by the turning of the face, [[23:9|to the right hand|ad dexteram]], that is, to the southern quarter, [[23:9|I shall not see him|non videbo illum]] by an image [*speciem*] drawn from the created things that are there. Of this sight the Lord speaks to Moses: [[Ex 33:20|man shall not see me, and live|Non videbit me homo, et vivet]]. Hence it is said in John as well: [[John 1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 30:4|what is his name, and what is the name of his son, if thou knowest?|Quod nomen ejus, et quod nomen filii ejus, si nosti?]] Hence the philosophers, Peripatetics and Platonists alike, have confessed that God is utterly unnameable, beyond sense, beyond imagination, beyond opinion, unutterable, incomprehensible, superessential, unknown and infinite. Yet he is known in some way from creatures, as a cause that transcends all things can be known from its effect. For this reason the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 1:20|For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world|Invisibilia Dei per ea quæ facta sunt, a creatura mundi]], that is, from man, [[Rom 1:20|are clearly seen, being understood|intellecta conspiciuntur]]; [[Rom 1:20|His eternal power also and divinity|sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas]]. Lastly it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 13:5|by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature, the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby|A magnitudine speciei et creaturæ poterit cognoscibiliter creator horum videri]].

paras.t: Ista inducit Job ad declarandum quam rationabiliter dixit: Quis mihi tribuat ut cognoscam et inveniam illum? quasi dicat: Ad plenam Dei seu claram visionem non propriis viribus naturalive lumine valeo pervenire, ideo gratiæ opem et supernaturalem illuminationem deposco. Item ad innuendum, quod Deus omnipotens et superexcelsus sit penitus incomparabilis, incircumscriptibilis, illocalis, immensus.
paras.en: Job brings in these things to declare how reasonably he said: [[23:3|Who will grant me that I might know and find him|Quis mihi tribuat ut cognoscam et inveniam illum?]]? as if to say: I cannot come to the full or clear vision of God by my own powers or by natural light; therefore I ask for the help of grace and for supernatural enlightenment. Also to hint that God, almighty and exalted above all, is wholly beyond compare, uncircumscribed, in no place, and without measure.

paras.t: Ipse vero scit viam meam, id est omnem vitæ meæ consistentiam et processum. Unde supra locutus est Deo: Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti; itemque: Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti. Et probavit me sicut aurum quod per ignem transit, id est, tribulationibus me exercitavit, atque adversis probatum seu virtuosum ostendit, quemadmodum per ignem probatur aurum an verum sit aurum: hoc enim innotescit, si ignem valeat sustinere. In quibus verbis, divinitus illustratus, unam suæ percussionis aperit causam, ut scilicet ad aliorum ædificationem sua perfectio per tot adversa pateret hominibus, ac toti innotesceret mundo: de qua causa superius dictum est plenius. Unde Sapiens scribit: Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus. Ecclesiasticus quoque: In igne probatur argentum et aurum, homines vero receptibiles in camino humiliationis. Hinc orat Psalmista: Proba me, Domine, et tenta me.
paras.en: [[23:10|But he knoweth my way|Ipse vero scit viam meam]], that is, the whole state and course of my life. Hence he spoke to God above: [[Job 13:27|hast observed all my paths, and hast considered the steps of my feet|Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti]]; and again: [[Job 14:16|Thou indeed hast numbered my steps|Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti]]. [[23:10|and has tried me as gold that passeth through the fire|Et probavit me sicut aurum quod per ignem transit]], that is, he has exercised me with tribulations, and by adversities shown me proved, or virtuous, as gold is tried by fire whether it be true gold: for this becomes known if it can bear the fire. In these words, divinely enlightened, he discloses one cause of his being struck, namely that for the edification of others his perfection should be made plain to men through so many adversities, and become known to the whole world: of which cause more was said above. Hence the Wise Man writes: [[Wis 3:6|As gold in the furnace, he hath proved them|Tanquam aurum in fornace probavit electos Dominus]] [Denis reads: “the Lord hath proved the elect”]. Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 2:5|gold and silver are tried in the fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation|In igne probatur argentum et aurum, homines vero receptibiles in camino humiliationis]]. Hence the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 25:2|Prove me, O Lord, and try me|Proba me, Domine, et tenta me]].

paras.t: Vestigia ejus secutus est pes meus. Vestigia Dei, hoc loco intelligi possunt processus et modi seu varii incessus Dei in suis effectibus, præsertim in suis operibus circa homines, in quibus diversimode operatur, omnibus tamen multiplicem in hoc sæculo exhibet pietatem, et cuncta sapienter dispensat ac regit, recteque judicat. Itaque, Dei vestigia sequi, est ejus perfectionem et opera agendique modum juxta modulum creaturæ agentis imitari, indigentibus succurrendo, offendentibus ignoscendo, ignorantes docendo, sapienter ac ordinate in omnibus se habendo, juste, pie et sancte vivendo. Ad quod hortatur nos Christus: Diligite (inquiens) inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos; ut sitis filii Patris vestri qui in cœlis est, qui solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos. Pro quo Lucas habet: Et eritis filii Altissimi, quia ipse benignus est super ingratos et malos. Rursusque ait: Estote ergo et vos perfecti, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis perfectus est. Hinc ad Ephesios monet Apostolus: Estote imitatores Dei sicut filii carissimi. In Levitico quoque Dominus loquitur: Nolite contaminare animas vestras. Ego enim sum Dominus Deus vester; sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum. Quum enim rationalis creatura sit ad Dei imaginem similitudinemque producta, debet suo Creatori sicut in natura et viribus, ita in vita et actionibus assimilari.
paras.en: [[23:11|My foot hath followed his steps|Vestigia ejus secutus est pes meus]]. The steps of God may be understood in this place as the proceedings and ways, or the various goings, of God in his effects, especially in his works concerning men, in which he works in divers ways, yet to all of them shows manifold kindness in this world, and disposes and rules all things wisely, and judges rightly. So to follow the steps of God is to imitate his perfection and works and manner of acting, according to the measure of a creature that acts: by succouring the needy, forgiving those who offend, teaching the ignorant, behaving wisely and in order in all things, living justly, devoutly and holily. To this Christ exhorts us: [[Matt 5:44|Love|Diligite]] (he says) [[Matt 5:44|your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you|inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos, et orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos]]; [[Matt 5:45|That you may be the children of your Father who is in heaven, who maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad|ut sitis filii Patris vestri qui in cœlis est, qui solem suum oriri facit super bonos et malos]]. In place of this Luke has: [[Luke 6:35|and you shall be the sons of the Highest. For he is kind to the unthankful and to the evil|Et eritis filii Altissimi, quia ipse benignus est super ingratos et malos]]. And again he says: [[Matt 5:48|Be you therefore perfect, as also your heavenly Father is perfect|Estote ergo et vos perfecti, sicut et Pater vester cœlestis perfectus est]]. Hence the Apostle admonishes the Ephesians: [[Eph 5:1|Be ye therefore followers of God, as most dear children|Estote imitatores Dei sicut filii carissimi]]. In Leviticus too the Lord says: [[Lev 11:43|Do not defile your souls|Nolite contaminare animas vestras]]. [[Lev 11:44|For I am the Lord your God. Be holy because I am holy|Ego enim sum Dominus Deus vester; sancti estote, quoniam ego sanctus sum]]. For since the rational creature has been brought forth after the image and likeness of God, it ought to be made like its Creator in life and actions, as it is in nature and powers.

paras.t: Postremo, per pedem, intelligi potest affectus vel quælibet vis activa, per quam homo in opus progreditur. De hujusmodi pede oramus in Psalmo: Non veniat mihi pes superbiæ. Et in Canticis habetur: Lavi pedes meos, id est, affectus et vires operativas a peccatis purgavi.
paras.en: Lastly, by the foot may be understood the affection, or any active power by which a man goes forward into action. Of a foot of this kind we pray in the Psalm: [[Ps 35:12|Let not the foot of pride come to me|Non veniat mihi pes superbiæ]] [the margin’s numeral reads Ps. xxiv, 12; the words are Ps 35:12]. And it is said in the Canticles: [[Cant 5:3|I have washed my feet|Lavi pedes meos]], that is, I have cleansed my affections and working powers from sins.

paras.t: Albertus ait hoc loco: Vestigia hic dicuntur signa voluntatis divinæ, quæ quinque ponuntur, videlicet præceptum, prohibitio, permissio, consilium, opera: quæ secutus est pes Job, quia quod Deus præcepit ei, fecit; quod prohibuit, dimisit; quod permisit, patienter sustinuit; quod consuluit, implevit; quod operatus est, pro exemplo habuit.
paras.en: Albert says on this place: The steps here are the signs of the divine will, of which five are set down, namely precept, prohibition, permission, counsel and works [that is, what God himself does]: these Job’s foot followed, since what God commanded him, he did; what he forbade, he left alone; what he permitted, he bore patiently; what he counselled, he fulfilled; what he wrought, Job took as an example.

paras.t: Viam ejus, id est legem ab eo datam, divinam seu naturalem, custodivi in memoria et effectu: sicut ait Psalmista, Custodiam legem tuam semper. Denique viæ Dei, sunt ejus testimonia et præcepta atque consilia, per quæ velut per iter lucis ad beatificum tendimus finem. De quibus in Proverbiis fertur: Viæ ejus viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ. Via quoque Dei, est ejus doctrina, juxta illud: Facta est illa die turbatio non modica de via Domini. Et non declinavi ex ea, sed perseverans fui in bonis, nec ad aliquod vitiosum extremum diverti, imo regia via incessi; juxta illud Isaiæ: Hæc est via; ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram.
paras.en: [[23:11|his way|Viam ejus]], that is, the law given by him, whether divine or natural, [[23:11|I have kept|custodivi]] in memory and in deed: as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 118:44|So shall I always keep thy law|Custodiam legem tuam semper]]. Moreover the ways of God are his testimonies, precepts and counsels, by which, as by a road of light, we make our way to our beatific end. Of these it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 3:17|Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceable|Viæ ejus viæ pulchræ, et omnes semitæ ejus pacificæ]]. The way of God is also his teaching, according to that saying: [[Acts 19:23|there arose no small disturbance about the way of the Lord|Facta est illa die turbatio non modica de via Domini]] [Denis has “on that day” for “at that time”; the margin’s reference cannot be read, the words are Acts 19:23]. [[23:11|and have not declined from it|Et non declinavi ex ea]], but have persevered in good things, and have not turned aside to any vicious extreme, but have walked in the royal road; according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 30:21|This is the way, walk ye in it: and go not aside neither to the right hand, nor to the left|Hæc est via; ambulate in ea, et non declinetis neque ad dexteram, neque ad sinistram]].

paras.t: A mandatis labiorum ejus non recessi, per mentis aversionem seu rebellionem. De quo recessu scriptum est in Malachia: Vos autem recessistis de via, et scandalizastis plurimos in lege. Præterea, in simplicissimo Deo corporalia membra spiritualiter sunt sumenda. In Deo ergo os et labia, sunt intellectus divinus, proferens verbum, et instruens homines, loquensque eis. Unde per Isaiam Dominus ait: Os meum non interrogastis. Quo rursus inducitur: Labia ejus repleta sunt indignatione. Labia quoque et os Dei, intelligi possunt Scripturæ ac revelationes divinæ, per quas Deus loquitur nobis. Insuper, os et labia Dei, intelliguntur homines sancti, per quorum os et labia loquitur Deus. Propter quod Jeremiæ dicitur: Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris. Mandata autem Decalogi, sunt de dictamine rationis et juris seu legis naturalis: ultra quæ fuerunt ipsi Noe et quibusdam aliis Patriarchis ac Sanctis tempore legis naturalis, quædam præcepta divinitus data de cultu Dei, ut patet de Noe in Genesi. Talibus quoque Deum colentibus, ejusque illuminationem quærentibus, revelabantur inspiratione divina, seu per angelos, aut per quosdam præcipuos homines sanctos, necessaria ad salutem: ut patet de Job, cui quam eminens et præclara facta fuerit revelatio de futura resurrectione, et judicio Dei, ac dispositione inferni, superius patuit.
paras.en: [[23:12|I have not departed from the commandments of his lips|A mandatis labiorum ejus non recessi]], by turning away or rebelling in mind. Of such departing it is written in Malachias: [[Mal 2:8|But you have departed out of the way, and have caused many to stumble at the law|Vos autem recessistis de via, et scandalizastis plurimos in lege]]. Further, in God, who is utterly simple, bodily members are to be taken spiritually. In God, then, the mouth and lips are the divine intellect, uttering the word, instructing men and speaking to them. Hence the Lord says by Isaias: [[Is 30:2|have not asked at my mouth|Os meum non interrogastis]]. In the same place it is also said: [[Is 30:27|his lips are filled with indignation|Labia ejus repleta sunt indignatione]]. The lips and mouth of God may also be understood as the Scriptures and the divine revelations, by which God speaks to us. Moreover, by the mouth and lips of God are understood holy men, through whose mouth and lips God speaks. For this reason it is said to Jeremias: [[Jer 15:19|thou wilt separate the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth|Si separaveris pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris]]. Now the commandments of the Decalogue belong to the dictate of reason and of natural right or law; beyond these, certain precepts concerning the worship of God were given by God to Noe himself and to certain other Patriarchs and Saints in the time of the law of nature, as is plain of Noe in Genesis[[Gen 9:4||]]. To such men, too, who worshipped God and sought his enlightenment, the things necessary for salvation were revealed by divine inspiration, either through angels or through certain eminent holy men: as is plain of Job, to whom, as was shown above, so eminent and glorious a revelation was made of the future resurrection[[Job 19:25||]], of the judgment of God[[Job 9:2||]][[Job 12:13||]], and of the condition of hell[[Job 10:21||]] [the margin gives Job xix, 25, 26; ix, 2–21; xii, 13–25; x, 21, 22].

paras.t: Et in sinu meo, id est cordis arcano seu fundo: juxta illud Joannis, Unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit; abscondi, id est, invisibiliter ac diligenter reposui, verba oris ejus, ut juxta illa me habeam: sicut ait Psalmista, In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi.
paras.en: And [[23:12|in my bosom|in sinu meo]], that is, in the secret place or depth of the heart: according to that saying of John, [[John 1:18|the only begotten Son who is in the Bosom of the Father, he hath declared him|Unigenitus Filius, qui est in sinu Patris, ipse enarravit]]; [[23:12|I have hid|abscondi]], that is, I have laid up invisibly and carefully, [[23:12|the words of his mouth|verba oris ejus]], so as to conduct myself according to them: as the Psalmist says, [[Ps 118:11|Thy words have I hidden in my heart, that I may not sin against thee|In corde meo abscondi eloquia tua, ut non peccem tibi]].

paras.t: Consequenter causam assignat, cur tam timorate atque perfecte servierit Deo. Ipse enim solus est, id est, solus habet esse absolute perfectum, simpliciter plenum, ideo infinitæ est majestatis, incomparabilis dignitatis, interminabilis perfectionis ac sanctitatis: unde cum summa diligentia est colendus. Quomodo autem solus Deus dicitur esse, et qualiter Esse sit proprium nomen ejus, supra diffuse induxi super illud: Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? Nonne tu qui solus es? Et nemo avertere, id est impedire, potest, seu immutare, cogitationes, id est propositum, decretum seu consilium ejus. Deus enim est immutabilis, et ipse est cogitatio sua, et cogitatio sua est omnipotentia sua, cui nulla valet resistere creatura. Ideo fertur in Psalmo: Consilium Domini in æternum manet; cogitationes cordis ejus in generatione et generationem. Per Isaiam quoque protestatur: Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet. Ita exponunt Gregorius et Albertus. Thomas autem et quidam alii legunt sic: Nemo advertere, id est comprehendere, potest, aut certitudinaliter cognoscere, cogitationes ejus, id est dispositiones judiciorum ipsius: juxta illud Apostoli, Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus! Et in Sapientia habetur: Quis hominum poterit scire consilium Dei? aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus? Hæc itaque nequeunt sciri a nobis, nisi in quantum Deus ostenderit, quum David testetur: Incerta et occulta sapientiæ tuæ manifestasti mihi. Et sapiens quidam inducit: Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum tuum de cœlis?
paras.en: Next he gives the reason why he served God with such godly fear and so perfectly. [[23:13|For he is alone|Ipse enim solus est]], that is, he alone has being that is absolutely perfect and simply full; therefore he is of infinite majesty, of incomparable dignity, of boundless perfection and holiness: hence he is to be worshipped with the utmost diligence. How God alone is said to be, and how *Being* is his proper name, I set out at length above on the words: [[Job 14:4|Who can make him clean that is conceived of unclean seed? is it not thou who only art?|Quis potest facere mundum de immundo conceptum semine? Nonne tu qui solus es?]] [[23:13|and no man can turn away|Et nemo avertere]], that is, hinder or change, [[23:13|his thought|cogitationes]] [Denis has the plural, “thoughts”], that is, his purpose, decree or counsel. For God is unchangeable, and he is his own thought, and his thought is his omnipotence, which no creature can resist. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:11|the counsel of the Lord standeth for ever: the thoughts of his heart to all generations|Consilium Domini in æternum manet; cogitationes cordis ejus in generatione et generationem]]. By Isaias too he declares: [[Is 46:10|My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done|Consilium meum stabit, et omnis voluntas mea fiet]]. So Gregory and Albert explain it. But Thomas and some others read thus: No man can *advertere* [that is, “perceive”, a reading in place of *avertere*, “turn away”], that is, comprehend or know with certainty, his thoughts, that is, the dispositions of his judgments: according to that saying of the Apostle, [[Rom 11:33|How incomprehensible are his judgments|Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus!]]! And in Wisdom it is said: [[Wis 9:13|who among men is he that can know the counsel of God? or who can think what the will of God is?|Quis hominum poterit scire consilium Dei? aut quis poterit cogitare quid velit Deus?]] These things, then, cannot be known by us except so far as God shows them, since David testifies: [[Ps 50:8|the uncertain and hidden things of thy wisdom thou hast made manifest to me|Incerta et occulta sapientiæ tuæ manifestasti mihi]]. And a certain wise man says: [[Wis 9:17|And who shall know thy thought, except thou give wisdom, and send thy holy Spirit from above|Sensum tuum, Domine, quis sciet, nisi tu dederis sapientiam, et miseris Spiritum tuum de cœlis?]]?

paras.t: Et anima ejus quodcumque voluit, hoc fecit. Anima in Deo, est ejus voluntas seu mens, quæ quum omnipotens sit, facit quidquid voluerit: cui (ut Sapiens dicit) subest, quum voluerit, posse. Unde et Psalmista decantat: Omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit in cœlo et in terra. Præterea, in Scripturis anima Deo frequenter adscribitur, ut quum ait in Jeremia: Numquid super his non visitabo, et in gente tali non ulciscetur anima mea? Rursusque in eodem Propheta: Non est anima mea ad populum istum. Et Amos: Juravit Dominus in anima sua: Detestor ego superbiam Jacob.
paras.en: [[23:13|and whatsoever his soul hath desired, that hath he done|Et anima ejus quodcumque voluit, hoc fecit]]. The soul in God is his will or mind, which, being almighty, does whatever it will; for, as the Wise Man says, [[Wis 12:18|thy power is at hand when thou wilt|subest, quum voluerit, posse]] [literally “to it, power is at hand whenever it will”]. Hence the Psalmist also sings: [[Ps 134:6|Whatsoever the Lord pleased he hath done, in heaven, in earth|Omnia quæcumque voluit Dominus, fecit in cœlo et in terra]]. Moreover in the Scriptures a soul is often ascribed to God, as when he says in Jeremias: [[Jer 5:9|Shall I not visit for these things|Numquid super his non visitabo]], [[Jer 5:9|and shall not my soul take revenge on such a nation?|et in gente tali non ulciscetur anima mea?]] And again in the same Prophet: [[Jer 15:1|my soul is not towards this people|Non est anima mea ad populum istum]]. And Amos: [[Amos 6:8|The Lord God hath sworn by his own soul|Juravit Dominus in anima sua]]: [[Amos 6:8|I detest the pride of Jacob|Detestor ego superbiam Jacob]].

paras.t: Quumque expleverit in me voluntatem suam, me pro suo libito percutiendo, seu aliter quovis modo tractando, et alia multa similia, quibus me possit ferire, ad libitumque tractare, præsto, id est in præsentia, sunt ei, id est in potestate sua: qui quum omnipotens infinipotensque consistat, non potest in tot aut tanta, quin possit in infinities plura atque majora, quantum in se est.
paras.en: [[23:14|And when he shall have fulfilled his will in me|Quumque expleverit in me voluntatem suam]], by striking me at his pleasure, or dealing with me in any other way whatever, [[23:14|many other like things|et alia multa similia]] with which he could strike me and deal with me at his pleasure [[23:14|are also at hand|præsto]], that is, present, [[23:14|with him|sunt ei]], that is, in his power: for since he is almighty and of infinite power, he cannot do so many or such great things that he could not, as far as lies in him, do infinitely more and greater.

paras.t: Et idcirco a facie ejus, id est consideratione suæ majestatis ubique præsentis, et omnia intuentis. Vel, A facie ejus, id est præsente hac plaga mihi ab eo illata, turbatus sum turbatione ordinata, videlicet reverentiæ seu timoris, expavescendo ac admirando immensitatem excellentiæ Dei; et considerans eum, quam terribilis sit in consiliis suis super filios hominum, quam admiranda ejus judicia, quam horrenda ejus contra iniquos sententia, timore sollicitor, ne eum in aliquo inhonorem, ne rursus aut gravius ab eo percutiar, ne ab eo ullatenus separer.
paras.en: [[23:15|And therefore|Et idcirco]] [[23:15|at his presence|a facie ejus]], that is, at the consideration of his majesty, which is present everywhere and beholds all things. Or, [[23:15|at his presence|A facie ejus]], that is, now that this stroke has been dealt me by him, [[23:15|I am troubled|turbatus sum]] with an ordered trouble, namely of reverence or fear, dreading and wondering at the immensity of God’s excellence; [[23:15|and when I consider him|et considerans eum]], how [[Ps 65:5|terrible in his counsels over the sons of men|terribilis sit in consiliis suis super filios hominum]], how wonderful his judgments, how dreadful his sentence against the wicked, [[23:15|I am made pensive with fear|timore sollicitor]], lest I dishonour him in anything, lest I be struck by him again or more grievously, lest I be in any way separated from him.

paras.t: Deus mollivit cor meum, id est, suo amore seu bono timore liquefecit, et quasi resolvit, compunctionem infudit, atque ad omne bonum promptam capacitatem donavit, qua et cito in lacrimas pias resolvor. Sic quoque per adversa et inspirationem clementem mollivit cor Nabuchodonosor regis, ut Daniel describit; itemque cor Petri apostoli, quum Christum negasset. Omnium quoque peccatorum quos ad pœnitentiam veram convertit, cor mollit. Quibus per Ezechielem locutus est: Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, et dabo vobis cor carneum. Molle etenim dicimus, quod facile cedit tangenti, neque resistit, sed mox recipit impressionem. Talia autem sunt corda bonorum, quæ a Spiritu Sancto dirigibilia sunt atque docilia, et facile acquiescunt in bonis. Unde secundo Regum habetur, quod sedens in cathedra, scilicet David rex, fuit quasi tenerrimus ligni vermiculus. Et Omnipotens conturbavit me, id est, valde alteravit, movit, et terruit me, sicut jam dictum est.
paras.en: [[23:16|God hath softened my heart|Deus mollivit cor meum]], that is, he has melted it with his love or with good fear, and as it were dissolved it, poured compunction into it, and given it a ready capacity for every good, by which I am quickly dissolved into devout tears. So too, through adversity and merciful inspiration, he softened the heart of king Nabuchodonosor, as Daniel relates[[Dan 4:31||]] [the margin reads roughly Dan. iv, 30, 31, 34]; and likewise the heart of Peter the apostle when he had denied Christ[[Luke 22:62||]] [the margin gives Luke xxii, 57, 58, 60–62]. He softens the heart, too, of all the sinners whom he converts to true penance. To them he has spoken by Ezechiel: [[Ezech 36:26|I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and will give you a heart of flesh|Auferam cor lapideum de carne vestra, et dabo vobis cor carneum]]. For we call soft that which yields easily to the touch and does not resist, but at once receives an impression. Such are the hearts of the good, which can be directed by the Holy Ghost and are docile, and readily give their assent to good things. Hence it is said in the second book of Kings that [[2 Kings 23:8|sitting in the chair|sedens in cathedra]], namely king David, was [[2 Kings 23:8|like the most tender little worm of the wood|quasi tenerrimus ligni vermiculus]] [Denis takes the words of David himself; in the Douay-Rheims the one sitting in the chair is Jesbaham, one of David’s valiant men]. [[23:16|and the Almighty hath troubled me|Et Omnipotens conturbavit me]], that is, he has greatly altered, moved and terrified me, as has just been said.

paras.t: Non enim perii, id est, non ita dejectus et cæsus sum, propter imminentes tenebras, id est propter peccata inexsistentia mihi, vel ad quæ proclivis sim. Vel sic: Non perii propter imminentes tenebras, id est, propter tribulationes mihi illatas et imminentes, non cecidi a statu mentis vitæque gratiæ per desperationem aut aliam culpam mortalem. Nec faciem meam, id est aciem rationis, seu mentem, quæ est facies intellectualis, operuit caligo, id est, peccatum impatientiæ aut simile vitium non obtenebravit, sed manet in lumine gratiæ fixa: juxta illud Michææ, Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est. Atque in Psalmo: Si ambulavero in medio umbræ mortis, non timebo mala, quoniam tu mecum es. Itemque: Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea; quem timebo?
paras.en: [[23:17|For I have not perished|Non enim perii]], that is, I have not been so cast down and struck, [[23:17|because of the darkness that hangs over me|propter imminentes tenebras]], that is, because of sins dwelling in me, or to which I may be prone. Or thus: [[23:17|I have not perished because of the darkness that hangs over me|Non perii propter imminentes tenebras]], that is, because of the tribulations dealt me and hanging over me, I have not fallen from the state of mind and from the life of grace through despair or any other mortal fault. Nor [[23:17|my face|faciem meam]], that is, the eye of reason, or the mind, which is the face of the intellect, [[23:17|hath the mist covered|operuit caligo]], that is, the sin of impatience or any like vice has not darkened it, but it remains fixed in the light of grace: according to that saying of Micheas, [[Mich 7:8|when I sit in darkness, the Lord is my light|Quum sedero in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 22:4|though I should walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for thou art with me|Si ambulavero in medio umbræ mortis, non timebo mala, quoniam tu mecum es]]. And again: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?|Dominus illuminatio mea, et salus mea; quem timebo?]]

paras.t: Postremo, hic aliam moralitatem non necesse est introducere, sed sequi curemus virtutes beati Job, et vestigia Dei sequatur pes noster, a testimoniis et præceptis legis divinæ nullatenus declinemus, verba ejus memoriter teneamus, consideremus omnipotentiam, sapientiam, justitiam Dei penitus infinitam, et filiali impleamur timore, sancta sollicitudine concutiamur, cor durum atque impœnitens recedat prorsus a nobis, et ad omne bonum mollificetur cor nostrum, nec tamen a firmitate recedat justitiæ.
paras.en: Lastly, there is no need here to bring in another moral sense; rather let us take care to follow the virtues of blessed Job: let our foot follow the steps of God, let us in no way decline from the testimonies and precepts of the divine law, let us keep his words in memory, let us consider the omnipotence, wisdom and justice of God, wholly infinite, and be filled with filial fear and shaken with holy solicitude; let the hard and impenitent heart depart utterly from us, and let our heart be softened to every good, yet without departing from the firmness of justice.

24.title: Elucidatio litteralis, partimque mystica capituli vicesimi quarti: Ab Omnipotente non sunt abscondita tempora.
24.title_en: Literal, and in part mystical, explanation of the twenty-fourth chapter: Times are not hid from the Almighty

paras.t: Quia vicesimo secundo capitulo Eliphaz dixit ad Job, an providentiam Dei putaret ad inferiora et ad actus hominum non extendi, hinc Job præsenti capitulo ostendit se sane sentire de providentia Dei. Ab Omnipotente non sunt abscondita tempora, id est, omne tempus et quidquid tempori subjacet, a Deo cognoscitur, æternaliter utique et invariabiliter, distincte atque clarissime. Ipse enim unicuique rei inferiori, corruptibili, mixtæ, certam præfixit periodum. Unde superius dixit: Numerus mensium ejus (videlicet hominis) apud te est; constituisti terminos ejus.
paras.en: Since in the twenty-second chapter Eliphaz said to Job, as if he thought that the providence of God does not reach to things below and to the acts of men[[Job 22:13||]] [the margin reference here is unreadable in the scan; Eliphaz's words are at Job 22:13–14], Job in the present chapter shows that he thinks soundly of the providence of God. [[24:1|Times are not hid from the Almighty|Ab Omnipotente non sunt abscondita tempora]]: that is, all time, and whatever is subject to time, is known by God, eternally indeed and unchangeably, distinctly and most clearly. For He has fixed beforehand a certain period for each thing here below, corruptible and compounded [that is, made up of the elements]. Hence he said above: [[Job 14:5|the number of his months|Numerus mensium ejus]] (namely, of man) [[Job 14:5|is with thee: thou hast appointed his bounds|apud te est; constituisti terminos ejus]].

paras.t: Qui autem noverunt eum, ignorant dies illius. Dies Dei, sunt ejus æternitas: quæ interdum singulariter dies vocatur, ob suam simplicissimam et immultiplicabilem unitatem, sicut in Psalmo: Tecum principium in die virtutis tuæ: in splendoribus Sanctorum. Interdum pluraliter dies seu anni exprimitur, quoniam omne tempus includit, continet, comprehendit, ut in Michæa legitur: Egressus illius (scilicet Christi) ab initio, a diebus æternitatis; atque in Psalmo: Tu autem idem ipse es, et anni tui non deficient. Quum ergo Deus æternus, omnipotens, adorandus, sit sua æternitas, quomodo qui eum noverunt, dies ipsius ignorant? Et respondendum, quod noscentes Deum clare per speciem, æternitatem quoque ipsius proportionaliter sciunt, quamvis nec Deum, nec æternitatem aliqua pura creatura plene comprehendere possit. Porro viatores, quamvis Deum quodammodo noscant, quoad quia est, et per naturalem rationem ac fidem, seu per sapientiæ contemplationem fidei innitentem, non tamen comprehendunt, nec clare (sicut Beati) cognoscunt æternitatem Dei sublimis; aliqualiter tamen eam cognoscunt, sicut Boetius in libro de Consolatione philosophiæ, de ea tractat subtiliter.
paras.en: [[24:1|But they that know him, know not his days|Qui autem noverunt eum, ignorant dies illius]]. The days of God are His eternity, which is sometimes called in the singular a day, because of its most simple unity that admits no multiplying, as in the Psalm: [[Ps 109:3|With thee is the principality in the day of thy strength: in the brightness of the saints|Tecum principium in die virtutis tuæ: in splendoribus Sanctorum]]. Sometimes it is expressed in the plural as days or years, since it includes, contains and comprehends all time, as we read in Micheas: [[Mich 5:2|his going forth|Egressus illius]] (that is, of Christ) [[Mich 5:2|is from the beginning, from the days of eternity|ab initio, a diebus æternitatis]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 101:28|But thou art always the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail|Tu autem idem ipse es, et anni tui non deficient]]. Since, then, God, eternal, almighty and to be adored, is His own eternity, how is it that they who know Him do not know His days? The answer is that those who know God clearly by sight [that is, the blessed, who see God face to face] also know His eternity in proportion, although no mere creature can fully comprehend either God or eternity. Wayfarers [that is, men still on the road of this life, not yet in their homeland], on the other hand, though they know God in some manner, as to the fact that He is, both by natural reason and by faith, or by a contemplation of wisdom that rests on faith, yet do not comprehend Him, nor know clearly (as the Blessed do) the eternity of the sublime God; still they know it in some measure, as Boethius treats of it subtly in his book On the Consolation of Philosophy.

paras.t: Consequenter inducit varia hominum scelera, ex quorum justa ultione demonstratur divina providentia ad omnia etiam humana pertingere. Alii terminos transtulerunt, id est, possessionum suarum confinia extenderunt: sicque alienas possessiones usurpaverunt, secundum illud Osee, Facti sunt principes Juda quasi assumentes terminos. Talibus Dominus comminatur per Isaiam: Væ, qui conjungitis domum ad domum, et agrum agro copulatis usque ad terminum loci. Nunc autem de violenta et furtiva hujusmodi translatione potissime sermo est. Hinc quoque in Proverbiis habetur: Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui. Ad quod etiam pertinet illud Deuteronomii: Non transferes terminos, quos fixerunt priores in possessione tua. Diripuerunt greges, et paverunt eos, id est, aliorum animalia rapuerunt, et ad proprium ea usum nutrierunt, sicut Sabæi atque Chaldæi primo hujus libri capitulo fecisse leguntur beato Job.
paras.en: Next he brings forward various crimes of men, from whose just punishment it is shown that divine providence reaches to all things, human ones too. [[24:2|Some have removed landmarks|Alii terminos transtulerunt]], that is, they have extended the bounds of their own possessions, and so have usurped the possessions of others, according to that saying of Osee: [[Osee 5:10|The princes of Juda are become as they that take up the bound|Facti sunt principes Juda quasi assumentes terminos]]. Such men the Lord threatens through Isaias: [[Is 5:8|Woe to you that join house to house and lay field to field, even to the end of the place|Væ, qui conjungitis domum ad domum, et agrum agro copulatis usque ad terminum loci]]. But here the talk is chiefly of a violent and stealthy removing of this kind. Hence too we have in Proverbs: [[Prov 22:28|Pass not beyond the ancient bounds which thy fathers have set|Ne transgrediaris terminos antiquos, quos posuerunt patres tui]]. To this also belongs that saying of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 19:14|Thou shalt not take nor remove thy neighbour's landmark, which thy predecessors have set in thy possession|Non transferes terminos, quos fixerunt priores in possessione tua]]. [[24:2|Have taken away flocks by force, and fed them|Diripuerunt greges, et paverunt eos]]: that is, they have carried off other men's animals and reared them for their own use, as the Sabeans and the Chaldeans are read, in the first chapter of this book, to have done to blessed Job[[Job 1:15||]][[Job 1:17||]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, terminos transferunt, qui leges justitiæ et regulas seu statuta vitæ monasticæ sibi a patribus sanctis præfixas transgrediuntur, parvi pendunt, et negligunt, remissius conversantes, et sine causa idonea dispensatione utentes: quod impium est vehementer, præsertim si contra substantialia religionis quid fiat, videlicet contra castitatem, paupertatem, aut obedientiam. Hoc namque esset directe contra professionem, quæ est solennissimum votum; talisque voti fractio, magis censetur peccatum, quam fractio juramenti, secundum positionem magnorum doctorum, asserentium votum plus obligare quam juramentum. Insuper, greges diripiunt, qui Christifideles verbis aut pravis exemplis ad vitia trahunt, dæmonique incorporant. Unde, secundum Apostolum, luxuriantes, vel alios ad luxuriam inducentes, tollunt membra Christi, et membra efficiunt meretricis. Isti sunt animarum strangulatores, et scandalizatores, pretium sanguinis Christi quantum in ipsis est, evacuantes. Quibus timendum est quod ait Salvator: Qui scandalizaverit unum ex his pusillis, expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus, et demergatur in profundum maris. Væ homini illi per quem scandalum venit. Tales demum greges a se direptos pascunt, id est, vanis documentis informant, vitiis imbuunt, in malis confortant. Tales sunt negligentes, carnales, et vitiosi pastores, doctores, et prædicatores. Unde in Jeremia legitur: Quia stulte egerunt pastores, et Dominum non exquisierunt; propterea omnis grex eorum dissipatus est.
paras.en: Spiritually, they remove landmarks who transgress, make light of and neglect the laws of justice and the rules or statutes of the monastic life fixed for them by the holy fathers, living more slackly and using dispensations without fitting cause. This is exceedingly wicked, above all if something is done against the substantials of religious life [that is, the three vows that make up its substance], namely against chastity, poverty or obedience. For this would be directly against the profession, which is a most solemn vow; and the breaking of such a vow is reckoned a greater sin than the breaking of an oath, according to the position of great doctors, who assert that a vow binds more than an oath. Moreover, they take away flocks by force who draw the faithful of Christ to vice by their words or bad examples, and incorporate them into the devil. Hence, according to the Apostle, those who live in lust, or lead others to lust, [[1 Cor 6:15|take the members of Christ|tollunt membra Christi]] and [[1 Cor 6:15|make them the members of an harlot|membra efficiunt meretricis]]. These are the stranglers of souls and the scandalizers, who make void, as far as in them lies, the price of the blood of Christ. Let them fear what the Saviour says: [[Matt 18:6|he that shall scandalize one of these little ones|Qui scandalizaverit unum ex his pusillis]], [[Matt 18:6|it were better for him that a millstone should be hanged about his neck, and that he should be drowned in the depth of the sea|expedit ei ut suspendatur mola asinaria in collo ejus, et demergatur in profundum maris]]. [[Matt 18:7|woe to that man by whom the scandal cometh|Væ homini illi per quem scandalum venit]]. Such men, finally, feed the flocks they have carried off, that is, they instruct them with vain teachings, steep them in vices, and strengthen them in evil. Such are negligent, carnal and vicious pastors, doctors and preachers. Hence we read in Jeremias: [[Jer 10:21|Because the pastors have done foolishly, and have not sought the Lord|Quia stulte egerunt pastores, et Dominum non exquisierunt]]; therefore [[Jer 10:21|all their flock is scattered|omnis grex eorum dissipatus est]].

paras.t: Asinum pupillorum abegerunt, id est, via divertere fecerunt, ut eum commodius raperent; et abstulerunt pro pignore bovem viduæ pauperis: in quo eorum patet crudelitas, quod personis istis miserabilibus non pepercerunt. Contra quod Dominus in Deuteronomio ait: Quum repetes a proximo tuo rem aliquam, non ingredieris domum ejus ut pignus auferas; sed stabis foris, et ille tibi proferet quod habuerit. Si autem pauper est, non pernoctabit apud te pignus.
paras.en: [[24:3|They have driven away the ass of the fatherless|Asinum pupillorum abegerunt]], that is, they made it turn aside from the road, so as to seize it more easily; [[24:3|and have taken away the widow's ox for a pledge|et abstulerunt pro pignore bovem viduæ]], the poor widow's. In this their cruelty is plain, that they did not spare these pitiable persons. Against this the Lord says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 24:10|When thou shalt demand of thy neighbour any thing|Quum repetes a proximo tuo rem aliquam]], [[Deut 24:10|thou shalt not go into his house to take away a pledge|non ingredieris domum ejus ut pignus auferas]]: [[Deut 24:11|But thou shalt stand without, and he shall bring out to thee what he hath|sed stabis foris, et ille tibi proferet quod habuerit]]. [[Deut 24:12|But if he be poor, the pledge shall not lodge with thee that night|Si autem pauper est, non pernoctabit apud te pignus]].

paras.t: Subverterunt pauperum viam, id est, opera eorum ab expedito et prospero impedierunt successu, ita quod necessaria procurare vix poterant. Quod quam impium sit, constat ex eo quod legitur in Ecclesiastico: Panis egentium, pauperum vita est; qui defraudat illum, homo sanguinis est. Et oppresserunt pariter mansuetos terræ: quibus tanto plus esset parcendum, quo ipsi aliis minus molesti, et magis suaves sunt. Denique (secundum Augustinum) mansuetus est, qui alium injuria sua non provocat, nec provocatur ab aliena. Talium injuriam Deus specialiter ulciscetur, quemadmodum Isaias ait de Christo: Arguet in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ.
paras.en: [[24:4|They have overturned the way of the poor|Subverterunt pauperum viam]], that is, they have hindered their works from a ready and prosperous success, so that they could scarcely provide themselves with necessities. How wicked this is appears from what we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:25|The bread of the needy, is the life of the poor: he that defraudeth them thereof, is a man of blood|Panis egentium, pauperum vita est; qui defraudat illum, homo sanguinis est]]. [[24:4|And have oppressed together the meek of the earth|Et oppresserunt pariter mansuetos terræ]], who ought to be spared all the more, the less troublesome they are to others and the gentler. For (according to Augustine) the meek man is he who does not provoke another by wronging him, nor is provoked by another's wrong. God will avenge in a special way the wrong done to such men, as Isaias says of Christ: [[Is 11:4|shall reprove with equity the meek of the earth|Arguet in æquitate pro mansuetis terræ]] [Latin *pro mansuetis*, that is, on behalf of the meek].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, pauperum viam subvertunt, qui eorum qui nondum in virtutibus roborati sunt, aut gratiæ donis ditati, ut incipientes, conversationem inficiunt, aut pauperes spiritu (scilicet humiles), per laudes aut alio modo, ad inanem pertrahunt gloriam sive superbiam.
paras.en: Spiritually, they overturn the way of the poor who infect the manner of life of those who are not yet strengthened in the virtues or enriched with the gifts of grace, such as beginners; or who draw the poor in spirit (that is, the humble), by praise or in some other way, into vainglory or pride.

paras.t: Alii quasi onagri in deserto, id est sicut asini silvestres, indomiti, in desertis vagantes, egrediuntur ad opus suum, id est, sine freno rationis ac legis, cum crudeli audacia ad nefaria exeunt perpetranda; vigilantesque ad prædam, id est intenti quomodo spolient occurrentes, præparant panem liberis, id est, filiis suis ex prædis procurant cibaria. Quod spiritualiter potissime faciunt schismatici atque hæretici, conantes ecclesiasticos et Catholicos ad suas impietates allicere, sicque alios sibi consentientes ac subditos in suis erroribus confovere. In horum violentorum ac prædantium persona in Proverbiis habetur: Insidiemur sanguini, abscondamus tendiculas contra insontem frustra; omnem substantiam pretiosam reperiemus, implebimus domos nostras spoliis.
paras.en: [[24:5|Others like wild asses in the desert|Alii quasi onagri in deserto]], that is, like untamed forest asses wandering in desert places, [[24:5|go forth to their work|egrediuntur ad opus suum]], that is, without the bridle of reason and law they go out with cruel boldness to commit wicked deeds; [[24:5|by watching for a prey|vigilantesque ad prædam]], that is, intent on how to rob those they meet, [[24:5|they get bread for their children|præparant panem liberis]], that is, they procure food for their sons from their plunder. This, spiritually, schismatics and heretics above all do, trying to entice churchmen and Catholics into their impieties, and so to cherish others who agree with them and are subject to them in their errors. In the person of these violent men and plunderers we have in Proverbs: [[Prov 1:11|let us lie in wait for blood, let us hide snares for the innocent without cause|Insidiemur sanguini, abscondamus tendiculas contra insontem frustra]]; [[Prov 1:13|We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoils|omnem substantiam pretiosam reperiemus, implebimus domos nostras spoliis]].

paras.t: Agrum non suum demetunt, id est, valde metunt, nihil de terræ nascentibus aliorum relinquentes in agro: in quo violentorum istorum avaritia ferociaque monstrantur; et vineam ejus quem vi oppresserunt, vindemiant: prout Achab et Jezabel fecisse leguntur Naboth Jezraelitæ. Istud quoque spiritualiter agunt, qui congregationes devotas sibi non commissas introeunt, et corrumpunt, spirituali earum patre oppresso.
paras.en: [[24:6|They reap the field that is not their own|Agrum non suum demetunt]] [Latin *demetunt*, which Denis takes as reap thoroughly], that is, they reap it utterly, leaving in the field nothing of what others' land brings forth: in this the avarice and ferocity of these violent men are shown; [[24:6|and gather the vintage of his vineyard whom by violence they have oppressed|et vineam ejus quem vi oppresserunt, vindemiant]], as Achab and Jezabel are read to have done to Naboth the Jezrahelite[[3 Kings 21:16||]] [the margin reference is partly unreadable; the story is 3 Kings 21:1–16]. This too is done spiritually by those who enter devout communities not committed to them and corrupt them, having oppressed their spiritual father.

paras.t: Nudos dimittunt homines, indumenta tollentes: juxta illud Michææ, Desuper tunicam pallium sustulistis: quibus non est operimentum in frigore. Quod spiritualiter implent, qui alios virtutibus (quæ animarum vestes sunt) privant, dum eos ad mortale trahunt peccatum: quibus ita nudatis non est operimentum in frigore sæculi hujus, ubi caritate Dei refrigescente, torpor et ignavia, vitiorum constrictio atque duritia, animas lædunt virtutum vestibus spoliatas. Quocontra in Proverbiis de sapiente et forti dicitur muliere: Non timebit domui suæ a frigoribus nivis: omnes enim domestici ejus vestiti sunt duplicibus.
paras.en: [[24:7|They send men away naked, taking away their clothes|Nudos dimittunt homines, indumenta tollentes]], according to that saying of Micheas: [[Mich 2:8|you have taken away the cloak off from the coat|Desuper tunicam pallium sustulistis]]; [[24:7|who have no covering in the cold|quibus non est operimentum in frigore]]. This they fulfil spiritually who strip others of the virtues (which are the garments of souls) by drawing them into mortal sin: for those so stripped there is no covering in the cold of this world, where, as the charity of God grows cold, sloth and idleness, the tightening grip and hardness of vices, hurt the souls stripped of the garments of the virtues. Against this it is said in Proverbs of the wise and valiant woman: [[Prov 31:21|She shall not fear for her house in the cold of snow: for all her domestics are clothed with double garments|Non timebit domui suæ a frigoribus nivis: omnes enim domestici ejus vestiti sunt duplicibus]].

paras.t: Quos imbres montium rigant: quia sic spoliati, ad montana confugiunt loca sive latibula, quasi ad tutiora, ubi ob aeris frigiditatem frequentiores et graviores sunt pluviæ, quibus tunc perfunduntur. Et non habentes velamen, id est aliquod nuditatis ac verecundiæ operimentum, amplexantur lapides, id est, sub lapidibus seu locis petrosis vel cavernis abscondunt se.
paras.en: [[24:8|Who are wet, with the showers of the mountains|Quos imbres montium rigant]]: because, being stripped in this way, they flee to mountain places or hiding places, as to safer ones, where because of the cold of the air the rains are more frequent and heavier, and then they are drenched by them. [[24:8|And having no covering|Et non habentes velamen]], that is, any covering for their nakedness and shame, [[24:8|embrace the stones|amplexantur lapides]], that is, they hide themselves under stones, or in rocky places or caves.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, imbres montium, sunt doctrinæ virtuosorum, quibus spoliati virtutibus mente rigantur, ut reviviscant atque fructificent: qui non habentes velamen, id est animæ ornamentum contra vitiorum fœditatem, amplexantur lapides, id est, ad perfectorum festinant suffragia, ut orent pro se. De quibus viris perfectis loquitur in prima sua Canonica Petrus: Vos tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini.
paras.en: Spiritually, the showers of the mountains are the teachings of virtuous men, by which those stripped of the virtues are watered in mind [Latin *rigare*, to wet, also means to water, as a field], so that they may come to life again and bear fruit. These, having no covering, that is, no adornment of the soul against the foulness of vices, embrace the stones, that is, they hasten to the prayers of the perfect, that they may pray for them. Of these perfect men Peter speaks in his first Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 2:5|Be you also as living stones built up|Vos tanquam lapides vivi superædificamini]].

paras.t: Vim fecerunt deprædantes pupillos, id est, violenter deprædati sunt eos; et vulgum pauperem exspoliaverunt: quum tamen pupillis et pauperibus amplius sit parcendum. Nudis omnino seu parum vestitis, et incedentibus absque vestitu, ita quod præ inopia etiam inter homines nudi ambulaverunt, et esurientibus spicas tulerunt, id est abstulerunt, quas esurientes laboriose collegerunt. Talisque spoliatio ineffabiliter impia est atque crudelis, præsertim quum Dominus jubeat, ut nec dominus agri decidentes aut remanentes colligat spicas, sed pauperibus relinquat legendas.
paras.en: [[24:9|They have violently robbed the fatherless|Vim fecerunt deprædantes pupillos]], that is, they have plundered them by force; [[24:9|and stripped the poor common people|et vulgum pauperem exspoliaverunt]], though the fatherless and the poor ought to be spared the more. [[24:10|From the naked|Nudis]], wholly or scantily clothed, [[24:10|and them that go without clothing|et incedentibus absque vestitu]], so that for want they walked naked even among men, [[24:10|and from the hungry they have taken away the ears of corn|et esurientibus spicas tulerunt]], that is, they took away the ears that the hungry had gathered with toil. Such robbery is unspeakably wicked and cruel, above all since the Lord commands that not even the owner of the field should gather the ears that fall or are left, but leave them for the poor to glean[[Lev 19:9||]][[Lev 19:10||]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter nudus est, meritis et virtutibus destitutus, etiamsi mali nil actualiter operetur. Porro, qui agit inique, nudus incedit. Contingit autem quod talis se cupiat emendare, esuriatque refectionem virtutum, et colligat spicas, id est, perfectorum virtutes incipiat aliqualiter sibi haurire ac sequi: quod videntes animarum corruptores, tristantur, et satagunt eum pristinis vanitatibus implicare, collectasque spicas ei subtrahere, ut anima ejus nullo reficiatur spirituali edulio. Quibus ait Apostolus: Sic autem peccantes in fratres, et percutientes conscientiam eorum infirmam, in Christum peccatis. Unde in Michæa scriptum est: Vir fratrem suum venatur ad mortem. Quod is periculosissime agit, qui aliquem bonæ voluntatis, aut religionem intrare volentem retrahere nititur.
paras.en: Spiritually, he is naked who is bereft of merits and virtues, even if he does no evil in act. But he who acts wickedly goes about naked. Now it happens that such a man desires to amend himself, and hungers for the refreshment of the virtues, and gathers ears of corn, that is, begins in some measure to draw in for himself and to follow the virtues of the perfect. Seeing this, the corrupters of souls are saddened, and strive to entangle him in his former vanities and to take from him the ears he has gathered, so that his soul may be refreshed by no spiritual food. To these the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 8:12|Now when you sin thus against the brethren and wound their weak conscience, you sin against Christ|Sic autem peccantes in fratres, et percutientes conscientiam eorum infirmam, in Christum peccatis]]. Hence it is written in Micheas: [[Mich 7:2|every one hunteth his brother to death|Vir fratrem suum venatur ad mortem]]. This he does most perilously who tries to hold back someone of good will, or someone wishing to enter religion.

paras.t: Inter acervos eorum, id est inter manipulos frugum pauperum esurientium, meridiati sunt, id est, meridie quieverunt seu pransi sunt, de illorum paupertatula deliciantes. Naturale est autem, secundum Albertum, in meridie prandere, dum sol ad summum accedens, alimentum præcedentis comestionis a loco digestionis evocavit ad membra. Qui pauperes calcatis torcularibus sitiunt, id est, uvis calcatis tam parum habent de vino, ut non aut vix necessitati sufficiat.
paras.en: [[24:11|among the stores of them|Inter acervos eorum]], that is, among the sheaves of grain of the hungry poor, they [[24:11|have taken their rest at noon|meridiati sunt]], that is, they rested or dined at midday, feasting on the little that those poor men had. Now it is natural, according to Albert, to dine at noon, when the sun, coming to its height, has drawn the nourishment of the previous meal from the place of digestion to the limbs. [[24:11|who after having trodden the winepresses suffer thirst|Qui pauperes calcatis torcularibus sitiunt]]: that is, the poor, when the grapes have been trodden, have so little wine that it does not suffice, or scarcely suffices, for their need.

paras.t: De civitatibus fecerunt viros gemere, id est, cives urbium ad gemitum atque tristitiam induxerunt, bona eorum in agris vastando, vel concives capiendo sive lædendo. Quod spiritualiter faciunt, qui catholicos viros contristant, quosdam fidelium decipiendo, damnationique exponendo: quod virtuosis caritate ferventibus gravissimum est videre. Unde per Ezechielem Dominus impiis ait: Mœrere fecistis cor justi, quem ego non contristavi.
paras.en: [[24:12|Out of the cities they have made men to groan|De civitatibus fecerunt viros gemere]], that is, they have brought the citizens of the towns to groaning and sorrow, by laying waste their goods in the fields, or by seizing or harming their fellow citizens. This they do spiritually who sadden Catholic men by deceiving some of the faithful and exposing them to damnation: which for virtuous men fervent in charity is a most grievous thing to see. Hence the Lord says to the wicked through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 13:22|you have made the heart of the just to mourn|Mœrere fecistis cor justi]], [[Ezech 13:22|whom I have not made sorrowful|quem ego non contristavi]].

paras.t: Et anima vulneratorum clamabunt, præ dolore vulnerum corporis sui. Vulnerati quoque in anima, quum ad cor per pœnitentiam convertuntur, clamant ad Deum in prece et pœnitudine planctibusque propter peccata. Aliquando etiam clamant zelo justitiæ pro vindicta ad Dominum, sicut in Evangelio loquitur Christus: Deus non faciet vindictam servorum suorum clamantium ad se die ac nocte? In Apocalypsi quoque habetur: Animæ interfectorum clamabant voce magna: Usquequo, Domine, sanctus et verus, non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui habitant in terra? Et Deus inultum abire non patitur, id est, peccata hæc non permittit inulta: qui in Deuteronomio testatur, Reddam ultionem hostibus meis, et his qui oderunt me, retribuam. Hoc enim sapientia Dei dictat agendum, et justitia ejus illud exigit, quia et inordinatio culpæ, ordinanda est per ordinem pœnæ.
paras.en: [[24:12|and the soul of the wounded hath cried out|Et anima vulneratorum clamabunt]] [Denis reads *clamabunt*, shall cry out, for the Vulgate's *clamavit*], for the pain of the wounds of their body. Those wounded in soul, too, when they turn back to the heart by penance, cry out to God in prayer and repentance and with lamentations for their sins. Sometimes also they cry out to the Lord for vengeance, out of zeal for justice, as Christ says in the Gospel: [[Luke 18:7|And will not God revenge his elect who cry to him day and night?|Deus non faciet vindictam servorum suorum clamantium ad se die ac nocte?]] [Denis reads *servorum*, servants, for the Vulgate's *electorum*, elect] In the Apocalypse also we have: [[Apoc 6:9|the souls of them that were slain|Animæ interfectorum]] [[Apoc 6:10|cried with a loud voice|clamabant voce magna]]: [[Apoc 6:10|How long, O Lord (Holy and True), dost thou not judge and revenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?|Usquequo, Domine, sanctus et verus, non vindicas sanguinem nostrum de his qui habitant in terra?]] [[24:12|And God doth not suffer it to pass unrevenged|Et Deus inultum abire non patitur]], that is, He does not let these sins go unpunished; He who testifies in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:41|I will render vengeance to my enemies, and repay them that hate me|Reddam ultionem hostibus meis, et his qui oderunt me, retribuam]]. For the wisdom of God dictates that this be done, and His justice demands it, since the disorder of guilt must be set in order by the order of punishment.

paras.t: Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini, id est inobedientes primæ increatæque luci, cujus transgrediuntur præcepta; angelicæ quoque lucidæ inspirationi non consentientes, nec naturali rationi obtemperantes, neque Scripturarum et hominum virtuosorum seu prælatorum verbis claris ac sanctis acquiescentes. Hinc Joannes dixit: Lux venit in mundum, et dilexerunt homines tenebras magis quam lucem. Talibus Moyses ait in Numeris: Audite, rebelles et increduli. Nescierunt vias ejus, id est mandata justitiæ atque notitiam veritatis, vel ea penitus nesciendo, vel per approbationem non agnoscendo: quomodo omnis malus est ignorans, et via stulti recta in oculis ejus. Nec reversi sunt per semitas illius, id est, ab iniquitate et falsitate non sunt ad lucis itinera per pœnitentiam et satisfactionem correctionemque morum conversi, juxta illud Psalmi: Nescierunt, neque intellexerunt; in tenebris ambulant. De quibus Baruch ait: Quia non habuerunt sapientiam, interierunt propter suam insipientiam. Et rursus: Viam disciplinæ ignoraverunt, neque intellexerunt semitas ejus. Tales sunt omnes impœnitentes et indurati: quibus dicitur a Jeremia: Quare aversus est populus iste aversione contentiosa? Et alibi Dominus ait de talibus: Non dabunt cor suum, ut revertantur ad me.
paras.en: [[24:13|They have been rebellious to the light|Ipsi fuerunt rebelles lumini]], that is, disobedient to the first and uncreated Light, whose precepts they transgress; not consenting either to the bright inspiration of the angels, nor obeying natural reason, nor acquiescing in the clear and holy words of the Scriptures and of virtuous men or prelates. Hence John said: [[John 3:19|the light is come into the world and men loved darkness rather than the light|Lux venit in mundum, et dilexerunt homines tenebras magis quam lucem]]. To such Moses says in Numbers: [[Num 20:10|Hear, ye rebellious and incredulous|Audite, rebelles et increduli]]. [[24:13|they have not known his ways|Nescierunt vias ejus]], that is, the commandments of justice and the knowledge of the truth, either by not knowing them at all, or by not acknowledging them with approval: in the way that every wicked man is ignorant[[Prov 29:7||]] [the margin gives Prov. xxix, 17, which does not fit; xxix, 7, “the wicked is void of knowledge”, is the nearest], and [[Prov 12:15|The way of a fool is right in his own eyes|via stulti recta in oculis ejus]]. [[24:13|neither have they returned by his paths|Nec reversi sunt per semitas illius]], that is, they have not been turned from iniquity and falsehood to the ways of light by penance and satisfaction and the amendment of their lives; according to that saying of the Psalm: [[Ps 81:5|They have not known nor understood: they walk on in darkness|Nescierunt, neque intellexerunt; in tenebris ambulant]]. Of whom Baruch says: [[Bar 3:28|because they had not wisdom, they perished through their folly|Quia non habuerunt sapientiam, interierunt propter suam insipientiam]]. And again: [[Bar 3:20|the way of knowledge they have not known|Viam disciplinæ ignoraverunt]], [[Bar 3:21|Nor have they understood the paths thereof|neque intellexerunt semitas ejus]] [Denis's *disciplinæ*, “of discipline”, is rendered “of knowledge” in the Douay-Rheims]. Such are all the impenitent and hardened, to whom it is said by Jeremias: [[Jer 8:5|Why then is this people in Jerusalem turned away with a stubborn revolting?|Quare aversus est populus iste aversione contentiosa?]] And elsewhere the Lord says of such: [[Osee 5:4|They will not set their thoughts to return to their God|Non dabunt cor suum, ut revertantur ad me]] [Denis reads “they will not give their heart, that they may return to me”].

paras.t: Mane primo, id est valde mane, dum semitenebrosum est tempus, consurgit homicida, interficit egenum et pauperem: quoniam inopes mane consurgunt ad panem suum lucrandum seu procurandum, et illa hora eos homicida observat. Per noctem vero erit quasi fur, id est, aliorum bona furtive tollet, sicque Quasi denotat veritatem, non similitudinem tantum.
paras.en: [[24:14|at the very break of day|Mane primo]], that is, very early, while the time is half dark, [[24:14|The murderer riseth|consurgit homicida]], [[24:14|he killeth the needy, and the poor man|interficit egenum et pauperem]]: for the needy rise early to earn or procure their bread, and at that hour the murderer watches for them. [[24:14|but in the night he will be as a thief|Per noctem vero erit quasi fur]], that is, he will steal the goods of others by stealth; and so *as* here denotes the reality, not only a likeness.

paras.t: Oculus, id est mens, adulteri observat caliginem, id est tempus nocturnum, dicens: Non me videbit oculus. Tunc enim tanto audacius se ingerit ad peccandum, quanto plus putat se non adspiciendum. Et operiet vultum suum, ne agnoscatur, etiam si quis deprehenderit eum. De isto peccato et allegationibus Scripturarum ad verba hæc pertinentium, dictum est supra.
paras.en: [[24:15|The eye|Oculus]], that is, the mind, [[24:15|of the adulterer observeth darkness|adulteri observat caliginem]], that is, the night time, [[24:15|saying: No eye shall see me|dicens: Non me videbit oculus]]. For then he thrusts himself forward to sin the more boldly, the more he thinks he will not be seen. [[24:15|and he will cover his face|Et operiet vultum suum]], so as not to be recognized, even if someone should catch him. Of this sin, and of the passages of Scripture that bear on these words, we have spoken above.

paras.t: Spiritualiter adulter est spiritus rationalis a Deo avertens se, et Scripturis abutens ad proprium quæstum et gloriam vanam. Qui si juste se gubernaret, sponsam haberet sapientiam, juxta quod dicitur in libro Sapientiæ: Hanc amavi, et exquisivi a juventute mea, et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere. Cujus adultera est vanitas et insipientia diabolica. Qui observat caliginem, quoniam quærit latere quantum ad suam perversitatem, cupiens bonus et sapiens reputari. Omnis enim qui male agit, odit lucem. Operit quoque vultum suum, quia et mentem propria excæcat malitia, et foris virtuosum se simulat: sicut de hypocritis ait Salvator, quia exterminant facies suas, ut appareant hominibus jejunantes.
paras.en: Spiritually, the adulterer is the rational spirit that turns itself away from God and abuses the Scriptures for its own gain and vain glory. If it governed itself justly, it would have wisdom for its spouse, according to what is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 8:2|Her have I loved, and have sought her out from my youth, and have desired to take for my spouse|Hanc amavi, et exquisivi a juventute mea, et quæsivi sponsam eam mihi assumere]]. Its adulteress is vanity and devilish folly. It [[24:15|observeth darkness|observat caliginem]], because it seeks to hide its perversity, wishing to be thought good and wise. [[John 3:20|For every one that doth evil hateth the light|Omnis enim qui male agit, odit lucem]]. It also [[24:15|will cover his face|Operit quoque vultum suum]], because it both blinds the mind by its own malice and outwardly feigns itself virtuous: as the Saviour says of the hypocrites, that [[Matt 6:16|they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast|exterminant facies suas, ut appareant hominibus jejunantes]].

paras.t: Perfodit in tenebris domos, id est, adulter, si aliunde ingressum aptum habere nequiverit, perfodiendo aliquam partem, parat sibi ingressum; sicut in die condixerant sibi adulter et adultera. Si subito apparuerit aurora, arbitrantur umbram mortis, id est, lucem habent odiosam, in quantum ea apparente metuunt deprehendi, compelluntur que dividi, et a voluptatibus sequestrari. Sic spiritualiter adulterantes, et dæmonum impietatibus atque erroribus se miscentes, odiunt lucem veritatis et æquitatis, suamque pravitatem aperiri verentur. Et sic in tenebris quasi in luce ambulant: id est, sicut boni tendunt ad bona in die, sic ipsi vadunt ad prava in nocte. In vitiosis quoque operibus ita versantur et delectantur, ut justi in actibus virtuosis. Sed et ita se exhibent, quasi nil impium perpetrassent: quemadmodum in Proverbiis de adultera Salomon loquitur, quod tergens os suum, dicit, Non peccavi. Ecclesiastes quoque asserit: Sunt impii qui ita securi sunt quasi justorum facta habeant. Et ignoraverunt lucem, id est, splendorem virtutum, et veræ sapientiæ claritatem assecuti non sunt, sed contempserunt.
paras.en: [[24:16|He diggeth through houses in the dark|Perfodit in tenebris domos]], that is, the adulterer, if he cannot find a suitable way in elsewhere, makes himself a way in by digging through some part; [[24:16|as in the day they had appointed for themselves|sicut in die condixerant sibi]], the adulterer and the adulteress. [[24:17|If the morning suddenly appear, it is to them the shadow of death|Si subito apparuerit aurora, arbitrantur umbram mortis]], that is, they hate the light, inasmuch as when it appears they fear being caught, and are forced to part and be separated from their pleasures. So those who commit adultery spiritually, mixing themselves with the impieties and errors of the demons, hate the light of truth and justice, and fear that their depravity be laid open. [[24:17|and they walk in darkness as if it were in light|Et sic in tenebris quasi in luce ambulant]]: that is, as the good go towards good things in the day, so they go after evil things in the night. In vicious works too they busy themselves and take delight as the just do in virtuous acts. And they also show themselves as though they had done nothing wicked: as Solomon speaks in Proverbs of the adulteress, that she [[Prov 30:20|wipeth her mouth, and saith|tergens os suum, dicit]]: I have not sinned [Denis reads *Non peccavi*; the Vulgate has *Non sum operata malum*, “I have done no evil”]. Ecclesiastes too asserts: [[Eccles 8:14|there are wicked men, who are as secure as though they had the deeds of the just|Sunt impii qui ita securi sunt quasi justorum facta habeant]]. [[24:16|and they have not known the light|Et ignoraverunt lucem]], that is, the splendour of the virtues; and they have not attained the brightness of true wisdom, but have despised it.

paras.t: Levis est adulter, id est mente vagus, levis, instabilis, super faciem aquæ, id est magis quam superficies aquæ, quæ modico vento movetur. Mens namque adulteri variis concupiscentiis agitatur, omni tentatione concutitur, innumerabilibus passionibus vitiisque movetur, ac vincitur. Passiones quippe et vitia hanc mentis pariunt instabilitatem, debilitatem et levitatem, sicut superius de hoc multa inducta sunt. Maledicta sit pars ejus, id est portio seu hæreditas terrena, videlicet bonum temporale et vanum, in quo sibi finem constituit: quam partem habet in terra, quæ a Deo maledicitur, dum possidenti in perniciem vertitur, maledictionisque causa materialis seu occasio ei efficitur, aut sterilis fit, juxta illud Genesis, Maledicta terra in opere tuo. Quomodo autem liceat alteri maledicere, in expositione capituli tertii patuit. Nec ambulet per viam vinearum, id est, itinera refrigerativa ac læta non habeat. Vinea quippe amœnitatem ac refrigerium parit, et fructu suo exhilarat, bonæque spei efficit hominem. Ideoque in Judicum libro vitis dixisse inducitur: Numquid possum deserere vinum meum, quod lætificat Deum et homines? Itaque metaphorice via vinearum, est via gaudiorum. Denique vinea locum temperatum requirit: siquidem in locis valde frigidis destruitur glacie; in locis nimis calidis destruitur excessivo calore. Impius ergo per viam vinearum non graditur, quoniam rebus mundi hujus moderate non utitur, sed nunc ad unum vitiosum extremum, nunc ad aliud se divertit.
