paras.en: [[24:18|He is light|Levis est]], the adulterer, that is, wandering, light and unstable in mind, [[24:18|upon the face of the water|super faciem aquæ]], that is, more than the surface of the water, which is moved by a little wind. For the adulterer's mind is driven by divers lusts, shaken by every temptation, moved and overcome by innumerable passions and vices. For passions and vices beget this instability, weakness and lightness of mind, as much has been brought forward on this above. [[24:18|cursed be his portion|Maledicta sit pars ejus]], that is, his earthly portion or inheritance, namely the temporal and vain good in which he has set his end: which portion he has [[24:18|on the earth|in terra]] that is cursed by God, when it turns to the ruin of its owner and becomes for him the material cause or occasion of a curse, or becomes barren, according to that saying of Genesis: [[Gen 3:17|cursed is the earth in thy work|Maledicta terra in opere tuo]]. How it is lawful to curse another was shown in the exposition of the third chapter. [[24:18|let him not walk by the way of the vineyards|Nec ambulet per viam vinearum]], that is, let him not have refreshing and joyful ways. For the vineyard brings delight and refreshment, gladdens with its fruit, and makes a man of good hope. And so in the book of Judges the vine is made to say: [[Judg 9:13|Can I forsake my wine, that cheereth God and men|Numquid possum deserere vinum meum, quod lætificat Deum et homines?]]? So, metaphorically, the way of the vineyards is the way of joys. Further, the vine needs a temperate place: for in very cold places it is destroyed by ice, in places too hot it is destroyed by excessive heat. The wicked man therefore does not walk by the way of the vineyards, because he does not use the things of this world with moderation, but turns now to one vicious extreme, now to the other.

paras.t: Ad nimium calorem transeat ab aquis nivium. Hoc communiter de pœna infernali exponitur, quod ibi sit vicissitudo commutatioque pœnarum de maximo frigore ad summum calorem, ad afflictionem majorem. Unde Albertus: Ad nimium calorem æstuantis gehennæ, propter fervorem libidinis transeat successione pœnarum ab aquis nivium: quibus infunditur, gelu mortificante, eo quod per cupiditatem terrenorum refriguit in eo ignis caritatis. Estque miserabile, quia in hac vita non transitur de frigidissimo in calidissimum, nisi per medium quod est temperatum. In inferno autem, de excellentia frigoris mortificantis, transitur ad æstum ignis urentis, ita quod nunquam erunt in medio: quia in hac vita per vitia transierunt a frigore cupiditatis ad æstum libidinis, non attingendo medium virtutis. Propter has duas pœnas dicitur in Matthæo: Ibi (scilicet in inferno) erit fletus et stridor dentium: fletus, propter ignem; stridor dentium, propter gelicidium. Itaque præcogitanda, metuenda, atque cavenda est pœna hæc. An vero per omnipotentiam Dei sit in inferno aqua frigidissima ad reproborum supplicium, vel aliquid proportionale, quod aqua nivis vocatur, quia hæc aqua præfrigida est: quis nisi Deo revelante poterit certitudinaliter scire?
paras.en: [[24:19|Let him pass from the snow waters to excessive heat|Ad nimium calorem transeat ab aquis nivium]]. This is commonly expounded of the pain of hell: that there is there an alternation and exchange of pains, from the greatest cold to the highest heat, for the greater affliction. Hence Albert: “To the excessive heat of seething Gehenna, for the fever of his lust, let him pass, by a succession of pains, from the snow waters, into which he is plunged, the frost putting him to death, because through the desire of earthly things the fire of charity has grown cold in him.” And it is pitiable, for in this life one does not pass from the coldest to the hottest except through the mean, which is temperate; but in hell one passes from the extremity of deadly cold to the heat of burning fire, so that they will never be in the mean: because in this life they passed through their vices from the cold of avarice to the heat of lust, never reaching the mean of virtue. Because of these two pains it is said in Matthew: [[Matt 8:12|there|Ibi]] (namely in hell) [[Matt 8:12|shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth|erit fletus et stridor dentium]][[Matt 13:42||]][[Matt 13:50||]][[Matt 22:13||]][[Matt 24:51||]][[Matt 25:30||]]: weeping, because of the fire; gnashing of teeth, because of the frost. This pain, then, is to be thought on beforehand, feared and guarded against. But whether by the omnipotence of God there is in hell a most cold water for the punishment of the reprobate, or something answering to it which is called the water of snow, because this water is very cold: who, unless God reveals it, can know for certain?

paras.t: Et usque ad inferos peccatum illius, id est, in infernum culpa ejus ipsum sequetur ac ducet. Sic et Joannes in prima sua scribit epistola: Est peccatum ad mortem; non dico ut pro illo quis oret. Peccatum quippe ad mortem, secundum Gregorium, est peccatum usque ad mortem pertractum: quia peccatum quod hic non corrigitur, ejus venia frustra postulatur. Hinc Isaias inducit: Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, et quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum.
paras.en: [[24:19|and his sin even to hell|Et usque ad inferos peccatum illius]], that is, his guilt will follow him and lead him into hell. So John too writes in his first epistle: [[1 John 5:16|There is a sin unto death|Est peccatum ad mortem]]; [[1 John 5:16|For that I say not that any man ask|non dico ut pro illo quis oret]]. For the sin unto death, according to Gregory, is sin drawn out until death: because for sin that is not corrected here, pardon is asked in vain. Hence Isaias brings in: [[Is 5:18|Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as the rope of a cart|Væ qui trahitis iniquitatem in funiculis vanitatis, et quasi vinculum plaustri peccatum]].

paras.t: Obliviscatur ejus misericordia, id est, Deus eum a pœnis per suam misericordiam nunquam eripiat: quo verbo confunditur hæresis confingentium pœnas inferni aliquando terminandas. Ubi Gregorius ait: Omnipotentis Dei misericordia obliviscitur ejus, qui oblitus fuerit justitiam Dei. Nam qui Deum nunc justum non timet, postea invenire eum misericordem non valet. Verumtamen hæc ita intelligenda non sunt, quasi nihil misericordiæ Deus impendat damnatis, quum in omni ejus effectu circa intellectuales creaturas misericordia atque justitia sint commixtæ; sed ideo hæc dicuntur, quoniam in inferno justitia magis relucet, et misericordia vel non, vel minus seu parum apparet. Attamen citra condignum torquentur. Juxta quem modum loquendi Jacobus ait: Judicium sine misericordia ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam. Damnatorum quoque obliviscitur misericordia suffragiorum, quia eis non prosunt. Dulcedo illius vermis, id est, delectatio sua perversa, quam habuit in hac vita, vertatur ei in vermem, id est pœnam amaram, conscientiæ quoque remorsum. Vel, Dulcedo illius, per antiphrasim, id est amaritudo, sit vermis conscientiæ corrodentis: de quo Isaias dicit, Vermis eorum non morietur.
paras.en: [[24:20|Let mercy forget him|Obliviscatur ejus misericordia]], that is, may God never rescue him from his pains by His mercy: by which word is confounded the heresy of those who invent the notion that the pains of hell will some day end. Here Gregory says: “The mercy of almighty God forgets him who has forgotten the justice of God. For he who does not now fear God as just cannot afterwards find Him merciful.” Yet these things are not to be understood as though God bestowed no mercy at all on the damned, since in every work of His towards intellectual creatures mercy and justice are mingled; but they are said because in hell justice shines out the more, and mercy either does not appear, or appears less, or little. For all that, they are punished less than they deserve. After this manner of speaking James says: [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy to him that hath not done mercy|Judicium sine misericordia ei, qui non fecerit misericordiam]]. The mercy of suffrages also forgets the damned [that is, the prayers and good works offered for the dead], because these do not avail them. [[24:20|may worms be his sweetness|Dulcedo illius vermis]] [Denis reads *vermis*, “a worm”, where the Vulgate has *vermes*], that is, may the perverse delight he had in this life be turned for him into a worm, that is, into a bitter pain, and the remorse of conscience as well. Or, [[24:20|his sweetness|Dulcedo illius]], by antiphrasis [that is, a word used for its opposite], that is, his bitterness, be the worm of a gnawing conscience: of which Isaias says, [[Is 66:24|their worm shall not die|Vermis eorum non morietur]].

paras.t: Non sit in recordatione, id est, oblivioni tradatur a Deo, ita quod per misericordiam suam non ostendat se memorem ejus. Ubi rursus damnationis interminabilitas aperitur. Econtrario de electo fertur in Psalmo: In memoria æterna erit justus. Et Salomon: Memoria (inquit) justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet. Sed conteratur quasi lignum infructuosum, id est, variis pœnis teratur, in ignem mittatur; et quantum ad esse gratiæ ac virtutum, in nihilum redigatur, sicut comburitur sterile lignum, juxta illud in Matthæo: Omnis arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur. Et loquitur Christus: Si quis in me non manserit, mittetur foras sicut palmes, et arescet; et colligent eum, et in ignem mittent.
paras.en: [[24:20|let him be remembered no more|Non sit in recordatione]], that is, let him be given over to oblivion by God, so that by His mercy He show no remembrance of him. Here again the endlessness of damnation is laid open. On the contrary it is said of the elect in the Psalm: [[Ps 111:7|The just shall be in everlasting remembrance|In memoria æterna erit justus]]. And Solomon: [[Prov 10:7|The memory|Memoria]] (he says) [[Prov 10:7|of the just is with praises: and the name of the wicked shall rot|justi cum laudibus; nomen impiorum putrescet]]. [[24:20|but be broken in pieces as an unfruitful tree|Sed conteratur quasi lignum infructuosum]], that is, let him be worn down by divers pains and cast into the fire; and, as regards the being of grace and the virtues, be brought to nothing, as a barren tree is burnt, according to that saying in Matthew: [[Matt 3:10|Every tree therefore that doth not yield good fruit, shall be cut down, and cast into the fire|Omnis arbor quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur]]. And Christ says: [[John 15:6|If any one abide not in me, he shall be cast forth as a branch and shall wither: and they shall gather him up and cast him into the fire|Si quis in me non manserit, mittetur foras sicut palmes, et arescet; et colligent eum, et in ignem mittent]].

paras.t: Pavit enim sterilem et quæ non parit, id est, bona sua infructuose consumpsit, instar illius qui infecundam feminam inutiliter nutrit. Vel, quia de adultero loquitur, per sterilem designat adulteram, quæ non parit hæredem ex proprio viro, nec ei cum quo miscetur. Vel, Pavit sterilem, id est infructuosam animam suam, vel carnem immundam, fructum virtutum non parientem. Et viduæ non benefecit: quæ, quum careat viri solatio, magis eget subsidio. Sicque iniquius est ei, quum loco et tempore opportunis non subvenerit. Vel vidua dicitur propria ejus conjux, quam a toro repellit atque infestat.
paras.en: [[24:21|For he hath fed the barren that beareth not|Pavit enim sterilem et quæ non parit]], that is, he has spent his goods without fruit, like one who to no purpose feeds a barren woman. Or, since he is speaking of the adulterer, by *the barren* he means the adulteress, who bears no heir either to her own husband or to the man with whom she lies. Or, [[24:21|he hath fed the barren|Pavit sterilem]], that is, his own unfruitful soul, or his unclean flesh, which bears no fruit of virtues. [[24:21|and to the widow he hath done no good|Et viduæ non benefecit]]: who, since she lacks the comfort of a husband, needs help the more. And so it is the more wicked towards her when he has not come to her aid at a fitting place and time. Or *the widow* is his own wife, whom he drives from his bed and harasses.

paras.t: Detraxit fortes, quibus prævalere potuit, in fortitudine sua; abutens potestate sibi concessa, ad aliorum oppressionem. Vel, Fortes, id est virtuosos vere fortes in Deo per gratiam, persecutus est, juxta illud Jacobi: Nonne divites per potentiam opprimunt vos? Talibus violentis dicit et Amos: Væ qui dicitis: Numquid non in fortitudine nostra assumpsimus nobis cornua? Et quum steterit in sanitate, prosperitate ac robore, non credet vitæ suæ, id est, de aliorum contra se machinatione erit suspectus; nec erit securus, sed pavidus. De hoc et causa hujus, dicta sunt plurima supra, ubi inter cetera dicitur: Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii, et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur. Et angustia vallabit impium.
paras.en: [[24:22|He hath pulled down the strong|Detraxit fortes]], those over whom he could prevail, [[24:22|by his might|in fortitudine sua]], abusing the power granted him to oppress others. Or, [[24:22|the strong|Fortes]], that is, the virtuous, who are truly strong in God by grace, he has persecuted; according to that saying of James: [[Jas 2:6|Do not the rich oppress you by might?|Nonne divites per potentiam opprimunt vos]] To such men of violence Amos also says: Woe to [[Amos 6:14|you that say: Have we not taken unto us horns by our own strength?|qui dicitis: Numquid non in fortitudine nostra assumpsimus nobis cornua?]] [the “woe” is from Amos 6:1] [[24:22|And when he standeth up|Et quum steterit]] in health, prosperity and strength, [[24:22|he shall not trust to his life|non credet vitæ suæ]], that is, he will suspect the plots of others against him, and will not be secure but fearful. Of this and its cause much was said above, where among other things it is said: [[Job 15:21|The sound of dread is always in his ears: and when there is peace, he always suspecteth treason|Sonitus terroris semper in auribus impii, et quum pax sit, ille insidias suspicatur]] [Denis reads “in the ears of the wicked man”]. And [[Job 15:24|distress shall surround|angustia vallabit]] the wicked man [the margin's reference reads “… 24”; the passage is Job 15:21, 24].

paras.t: Dedit ei Deus locum pœnitentiæ, id est, post peccatum ejus non statim eum damnavit, sed misericorditer distulit, dans locum, tempus, et opportunitatem pœnitendi. Ideo equidem Deus differt vindictam, ut peccator se corrigat. Propter quod in Ecclesiastico legitur: Nemini dedit Deus spatium peccandi. Et in Sapientiæ libro: Misereris omnium, Domine, quoniam omnia potes; et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam. Et ille abutitur eo in superbiam, id est, loco et tempore pœnitendi abutitur, augendo contemptum in Deum, hincque securius peccans, quia diu portatur, secundum illud Ecclesiastæ: Etenim, quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala. Hinc ad Romanos ait Apostolus: An divitias bonitatis Dei, et patientiæ, et longanimitatis contemnis? Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit? Secundum duritiam autem tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram in die justi judicii Dei. Itaque indulta pœnitentiæ tempora non perdamus, nullam horulam inutiliter expendamus, divinæ pietati non simus ingrati. Pensemus quod sicut incomprehensibilis est misericordia Dei super peccatores in vita præsenti, sic incomprehensibilis est super eos ipsius justitia in vita futura.
paras.en: [[24:23|God hath given him place for penance|Dedit ei Deus locum pœnitentiæ]], that is, after his sin He did not condemn him at once, but mercifully put it off, giving him place, time and opportunity for penance. For God puts off vengeance so that the sinner may amend himself. Wherefore we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 15:21|he hath given no man license to sin|Nemini dedit Deus spatium peccandi]]. And in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 11:24|thou hast mercy upon all, because thou canst do all things, and overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|Misereris omnium, Domine, quoniam omnia potes; et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]] [Denis adds “O Lord”]. [[24:23|and he abuseth it unto pride|Et ille abutitur eo in superbiam]], that is, he abuses the place and time of penance, increasing his contempt of God, and hence sinning more securely because he is long borne with, according to that saying of Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 8:11|For because sentence is not speedily pronounced against the evil, the children of men commit evils without any fear|Etenim, quia non cito profertur contra malos judicium, absque ullo timore filii hominum perpetrant mala]]. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 2:4|despisest thou the riches of his goodness and patience and longsuffering? Knowest thou not that the benignity of God leadeth thee to penance?|An divitias bonitatis Dei, et patientiæ, et longanimitatis contemnis? Ignoras quoniam benignitas Dei ad pœnitentiam te adducit?]] [[Rom 2:5|But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart, thou treasurest up to thyself wrath|Secundum duritiam autem tuam et impœnitens cor tuum, thesaurizas tibi iram]] in the day [[Rom 2:5|of the just judgment of God|justi judicii Dei]]. Let us not, then, lose the times of penance granted us; let us spend no little hour uselessly; let us not be ungrateful to the divine goodness. Let us consider that, as the mercy of God towards sinners in the present life is beyond comprehension, so His justice towards them in the life to come is beyond comprehension.

paras.t: Oculi enim ejus sunt in viis illius. Hoc dupliciter explanatur. Primo: Oculi ejus (scilicet Dei) sunt in viis illius, id est in operibus peccatorum, ad judicandum puniendumque ea, quemadmodum in Proverbiis legitur: In omni loco oculi Domini contemplantur bonos et malos. Atque in Psalmo: Vultus autem Domini super facientes mala, ut perdat de terra memoriam eorum. Secundo sic: Oculi ejus (id est peccatoris) sunt in viis illius, id est, in propriis suis operibus intenti sunt oculi ejus interiores per approbationem mali, et complacentiam culpæ, considerando quoque qualiter propositum exsequatur ac prosperetur, sicut de filiis hujus sæculi per Jeremiam asseritur: Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt. Secunda quoque Petri epistola: Audaces, sibi placentes; quibus caligo tenebrarum reservatur. Tales modo sunt multi, qui gloriantur in vitiis, astutiasque implendi quod impie cupiunt, machinantur, sequentes pravitatem illorum, qui ante diluvium fuerunt. De quibus legitur in Genesi: Videns Deus quia multa malitia hominum esset in terra, et cuncta cogitatio cordis humani intenta esset ad malum omni tempore. Quocontra vir justus testatur: Iniquitatem si adspexi in corde meo, id est, peccatum per consensum et complacentiam non sum mente intuitus.
paras.en: [[24:23|but his eyes are upon his ways|Oculi enim ejus sunt in viis illius]] [Denis reads *enim*, “for”, where the Vulgate has *autem*]. This is explained in two ways. First: [[24:23|his eyes|Oculi ejus]] (namely God's) [[24:23|are upon his ways|sunt in viis illius]], that is, upon the works of sinners, to judge and punish them; as we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 15:3|The eyes of the Lord in every place behold the good and the evil|In omni loco oculi Domini contemplantur bonos et malos]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 33:17|But the countenance of the Lord is against them that do evil things: to cut off the remembrance of them from the earth|Vultus autem Domini super facientes mala, ut perdat de terra memoriam eorum]]. Secondly thus: [[24:23|his eyes|Oculi ejus]] (that is, the sinner's) [[24:23|are upon his ways|sunt in viis illius]], that is, his inner eyes are intent upon his own works, by approving the evil and taking pleasure in the fault, and by considering too how he may carry out his purpose and prosper in it; as is said through Jeremias of the children of this world: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge|Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt]]. And the second epistle of Peter: [[2 Pet 2:10|audacious, self willed|Audaces, sibi placentes]]; [[2 Pet 2:17|to whom the mist of darkness is reserved|quibus caligo tenebrarum reservatur]]. Such now are many, who glory in their vices and contrive cunning ways to fulfil what they wickedly desire, following the depravity of those who lived before the flood; of whom we read in Genesis: [[Gen 6:5|God seeing that the wickedness of men was great on the earth, and that all the thought of their heart was bent upon evil at all times|Videns Deus quia multa malitia hominum esset in terra, et cuncta cogitatio cordis humani intenta esset ad malum omni tempore]]. Against which the just man testifies: [[Ps 65:18|If I have looked at iniquity in my heart|Iniquitatem si adspexi in corde meo]], that is, I have not looked upon sin in my mind with consent and pleasure.

paras.t: Elevati sunt ad modicum, id est, impii ad breve tempus prosperati sunt, prælati et intumuerunt; et non subsistent, id est, diu non perdurabunt in statu hujuscemodi, juxta illud Psalmi: Dejecisti eos dum allevarentur. Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitatem suam. De hoc dicta sunt multa supra, idcirco pertranseo. Gregorius quoque hic ait: Iniquorum gloria, quum plerumque in annorum multitudinem tenditur, ab infirmorum mentibus esse quasi longa et stabilis æstimatur; sed quum repentinus hanc finis intercipit, brevem fuisse ostendit. Et humiliabuntur, id est, per divinam justitiam deprimentur, sicut et Christus fatetur: Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur; sicut omnia ista corruptibilia et terrena, quibus præfixus est certus terminus durationis, ut dictum est plenius super illud, Constituisti terminos ejus. Et auferentur de vita hac et de consortio electorum: juxta quod scriptum est, Tollatur impius ne videat gloriam Dei. Et sicut summitates spicarum, puta aristæ, conterentur, id est, cito atque faciliter tempore divinitus præordinato peribunt, quum mensuram pravitatis suæ impleverint; sicut fruges quum ad maturitatem devenerint, mox tolluntur, ut grana excutiantur. Unde in Genesi Dominus loquitur: Nondum completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum.
paras.en: [[24:24|They are lifted up for a little while|Elevati sunt ad modicum]], that is, the wicked have prospered for a short time, have been set over others and have swelled with pride; [[24:24|and shall not stand|et non subsistent]], that is, they will not long endure in such a state; according to that saying of the Psalm: [[Ps 72:18|when they were lifted up thou hast cast them down|Dejecisti eos dum allevarentur]]. [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation? they have suddenly ceased to be: they have perished by reason of their iniquity|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitatem suam]]. Much has been said of this above[[Job 20:5||]], and so I pass over it. Gregory too says here: “The glory of the wicked, when it is drawn out, as often happens, over a great number of years, is thought by weak minds to be as it were long and stable; but when a sudden end cuts it off, it shows that it was brief.” [[24:24|and shall be brought down|Et humiliabuntur]], that is, they will be cast down by the divine justice, as Christ too declares: [[Luke 14:11|every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled|Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]][[Luke 18:14||]]; [[24:24|as all things|sicut omnia]], these corruptible and earthly things for which a fixed bound of duration is set, as was said more fully on the words: [[Job 14:5|thou hast appointed his bounds|Constituisti terminos ejus]]. [[24:24|and shall be taken away|Et auferentur]] from this life and from the company of the elect: according to what is written: Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God[[Is 26:10||]] [Denis quotes the older reading of Is. xxvi, 10; the Vulgate has “he shall not see the glory of the Lord”]. [[24:24|and as the tops of the ears of corn|Et sicut summitates spicarum]], say the beards, [[24:24|they shall be broken|conterentur]], that is, they will perish quickly and easily at the time divinely foreordained, when they have filled up the measure of their wickedness; as the crops, when they have come to ripeness, are soon taken away so that the grain may be threshed out. Hence the Lord says in Genesis: [[Gen 15:16|as yet the iniquities of the Amorrhites are not at the full|Nondum completæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum]] [the margin prints Gen. xv, 16].

paras.t: Quod si non est ita, quis me potest arguere esse mentitum? Verbum hoc intricatum videtur. Quid enim est quod ait, Quod si non est ita, nisi, Si quæ dixi falsa sunt, quis me potest arguere esse mentitum? Si enim protulit falsa, nonne fuerat tanquam mentiens arguendus? Gregorius itaque et Albertus exponunt hanc litteram, prout verba prima facie sonant, ita quod Job mystica ratione sic loquitur ad reprimendam amicorum suorum superbiam: quasi dicat, Etiam si mentitus sum, tamen indigni estis me reprobare, quia errori et vitiis subditi estis, quæ mihi falso imponitis. Hinc ait Albertus: Istud in disputationibus rhetoricis verum est, quæ coram judice fiunt, ubi adversarius rite repellitur, quia in simili culpa est. Propter quod ait Salvator: Hypocrita, ejice primo trabem de oculo tuo, et tunc videbis ut ejicias festucam de oculo fratris tui. Verumtamen istud aliter potest exponi: Quod si non est ita? quod interrogative negativeque profert, quasi dicat, Imo sic est, sicut in isto affirmavi capitulo de culpa et pœna malorum. Quis me potest arguere esse mentitum? nullus utique; et ponere ante Deum verba mea, id est Deo judici ea proponere judicanda, tanquam reprehensibiliter dicta?
paras.en: [[24:25|And if it be not so, who can convince me that I have lied|Quod si non est ita, quis me potest arguere esse mentitum]]? This saying seems intricate. For what does he mean by [[24:25|if it be not so|si non est ita]], unless: If what I have said is false, who can convince me that I have lied? For if he spoke falsehoods, ought he not to have been convicted as a liar? So Gregory and Albert expound this text as the words sound at first sight, in such a way that Job speaks thus on a mystical ground [that is, with a hidden purpose] to check the pride of his friends: as if to say, Even if I have lied, yet you are unworthy to reprove me, because you are subject to the error and the vices that you falsely lay upon me. Hence Albert says: “This holds in rhetorical disputations held before a judge, where an opponent is rightly rejected because he is in a like fault.” Wherefore the Saviour says: [[Matt 7:5|Thou hypocrite, cast out first the beam out of thy own eye, and then shalt thou see to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye|Hypocrita, ejice primo trabem de oculo tuo, et tunc videbis ut ejicias festucam de oculo fratris tui]]. Yet this can be expounded otherwise: [[24:25|And if it be not so|Quod si non est ita]]? which he says as a question, in the negative, as if to say: Nay, it is so, as I have affirmed in this chapter of the guilt and punishment of the wicked. [[24:25|who can convince me that I have lied|Quis me potest arguere esse mentitum]]? No one, surely; [[24:25|and set my words before God|et ponere ante Deum verba mea]], that is, put them before God the judge to be judged, as things said blameworthily?

25.title: Explanatio capituli vicesimi quinti: Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit.
25.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-fifth chapter: Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said

paras.t: Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit. Amici Job, contra veritatem verborum Job disputando, paulatim lentescunt. Nam post tertiam argumentationem ipsius Eliphaz, ipse Baldad tertio arguens, admodum brevis est. Sophar autem tertio non argumentatur. Et quamvis præcedenti capitulo multa locutus sit Job, tamen de hoc solo Baldad contra eum objicit, quod adhuc affirmat se justum et sine demeritis suis percussum: ad quod improbandum proponit excellentiam Dei in se ipso ac suis effectibus, cujus comparatione homo non justificatur. Unde quæ in isto capitulo Baldad ait, frequenter præhabita sunt, demptis perpaucis.
paras.en: [[25:1|Then Baldad the Suhite answered, and said|Respondens autem Baldad Suhites, dixit]]. The friends of Job, disputing against the truth of Job's words, slacken little by little. For after the third argument of Eliphaz, Baldad, arguing for the third time, is very brief; and Sophar does not argue a third time at all. And although Job said many things in the preceding chapter, Baldad objects against him on this one point only: that he still affirms that he is just and has been struck without any demerits of his own. To disprove this he sets forth the excellence of God, in Himself and in His effects, in comparison with whom man is not justified. Hence what Baldad says in this chapter has, with very few exceptions, often been said before.

paras.t: Potestas et terror apud eum est, id est omnipotentia est in Deo et terribilitas vel tremenda majestas, quæ sunt ipsemet Deus, et ita apud eum esse dicuntur, sicut misericordia, juxta illud Psalmi, Quia apud Dominum misericordia. Terror quoque est apud Deum, id est, in his qui Deo conjuncti sunt, est timor reverentialis ad Deum, præsertim prout timor est donum: sic enim inest Beatis, et manet in patria, quantum ad habitum et aliquem suum actum, potissime illum, qui est revereri et Deo reverenter substerni.
paras.en: [[25:2|Power and terror are with him|Potestas et terror apud eum est]]: that is, in God there is omnipotence, and terribleness or awful majesty; these are God Himself, and they are said to be with Him in the way that mercy is, according to that saying of the Psalm, [[Ps 129:7|Because with the Lord there is mercy|Quia apud Dominum misericordia]]. Terror is also with God in this sense: in those who are joined to God there is a reverential fear towards God, above all fear as it is a gift [that is, the gift of the Holy Ghost called fear of the Lord, as distinct from servile fear]. For in this way it is in the Blessed and abides in the fatherland, as to the habit and as to some act of its own, chiefly the act of revering God and of being reverently subject to Him.

paras.t: Qui facit concordiam in sublimibus suis, id est in cœlestibus corporibus, in quibus nulla est contrarietas, resistentia naturæ nociva, aut corruptio aliqua. In angelicis quoque spiritibus summam et indissolubilem facit concordiam, implendo eos tanta suæ beatitudinis communione, quod nec a Deo, nec a se invicem discordare ullatenus queunt, sed omnes cives cœlestis Jerusalem, divinæ voluntati inavertibiliter conformantur. Nec obstat quod in Daniele quædam leguntur de angelorum præliis inter se: quæ qualiter intelligi debeant, Gregorius hic exponit, et ego prosequerer, nisi hoc super Danielem scripsissem. Itaque confundantur, qui in cœlesti Beatorum palatio dissensiones et prælia vitiosa esse mentiti sunt. Insuper, Deus facit concordiam in sublimibus suis, id est, considerantes sublimia Dei, videlicet omnipotentiam, sapientiam, beatitudinem ejus, facit in considerando et sentiendo concordes, sicut ait Apostolus: Id ipsum dicatis omnes, et non sint in vobis schismata.
paras.en: [[25:2|who maketh peace in his high places|Qui facit concordiam in sublimibus suis]] [the Latin *concordia* is “concord” or “harmony” rather than “peace”, and Denis's gloss turns on that sense]: that is, in the heavenly bodies, in which there is no contrariety, no harmful resistance of nature, and no corruption of any kind. In the angelic spirits too He makes the highest and an indissoluble concord, filling them with so great a share in His own beatitude that they can in no way be at discord either with God or with one another; but all the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem are conformed to the divine will without any turning away. Nor does it stand in the way that certain things are read in Daniel about battles of the angels among themselves[[Dan 10:13||]] [the margin cites Daniel; its numerals are only partly legible and seem to give ch. x, vv. 13, 20, 21, where the angel tells of his fight with the prince of the Persians]: how these are to be understood, Gregory explains here, and I would go through it, had I not written on this in my commentary on Daniel. Let those, then, be put to shame who have falsely said that there are dissensions and sinful battles in the heavenly palace of the Blessed. Moreover, God [[25:2|maketh peace in his high places|facit concordiam in sublimibus suis]]: that is, those who consider the high things of God, namely His omnipotence, wisdom and beatitude, He makes to be of one accord in considering and in feeling, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 1:10|that you all speak the same thing and that there be no schisms among you|Id ipsum dicatis omnes, et non sint in vobis schismata]].

paras.t: Numquid est numerus militum ejus? id est, innumerabilis nobis est multitudo angelorum sanctorum: qui milites Dei vocantur, quoniam ei ad nutum deserviunt, ejusque adversariis reluctantur ac prævalent. De quibus fertur in Psalmo: Benedicite Domino, angeli ejus, potentes virtute, facientes verbum illius, ad audiendam vocem sermonum ejus. Benedicite Domino, omnes virtutes ejus, ministri ejus, qui facitis voluntatem ejus. Quorum numerus Deo est certus, juxta illud Isaiæ: Qui educit in numero militiam eorum, et omnes ex nomine vocat præ multitudine fortitudinis ejus. De quorum innumerabili nobis multitudine Daniel ait: Millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei. Ubi numerus determinatus pro indeterminato ponitur, sicut in Apocalypsi legitur: Et erat numerus eorum millia millium. Ad Hebræos quoque: Accessistis ad Jerusalem cœlestem, et multorum millium angelorum frequentiam.
paras.en: [[25:3|Is there any numbering of his soldiers?|Numquid est numerus militum ejus?]] that is, the multitude of the holy angels is beyond our numbering. They are called God's soldiers because they serve Him at His nod, and resist His adversaries and prevail over them. Of them it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 102:20|Bless the Lord, all ye his angels: you that are mighty in strength, and execute his word, hearkening to the voice of his orders|Benedicite Domino, angeli ejus, potentes virtute, facientes verbum illius, ad audiendam vocem sermonum ejus]]. [[Ps 102:21|Bless the Lord, all ye his hosts: you ministers of his that do his will|Benedicite Domino, omnes virtutes ejus, ministri ejus, qui facitis voluntatem ejus]]. Their number is certain to God, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 40:26|who bringeth out their host by number, and calleth them all by their names: by the greatness of his might|Qui educit in numero militiam eorum, et omnes ex nomine vocat præ multitudine fortitudinis ejus]]. Of their multitude, which to us is countless, Daniel says: [[Dan 7:10|thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him|Millia millium ministrabant ei, et decies millies centena millia adsistebant ei]]. Here a determinate number is put for an indeterminate one, as we read in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 5:11|and the number of them was thousands of thousands|Et erat numerus eorum millia millium]]. And to the Hebrews also: [[Heb 12:22|you are come|Accessistis]] to [[Heb 12:22|the heavenly Jerusalem, and to the company of many thousands of angels|Jerusalem cœlestem, et multorum millium angelorum frequentiam]].

paras.t: Et super quem non surgit lumen illius? id est, numerus horum militum, super quem lumen Dei non splendeat, certus non est modo præfato. Beati enim in patria omnes immediate sortiuntur a Deo lumen gloriæ, beatificamque divinæ essentiæ clarissimam visionem et illuminationem, ad ea noscenda quæ ad beatitudinem directe ac proprie pertinent, ut est cognitio ordinis universi, omniumque civium supernorum. Illuminationes vero Dei, quantum ad ea noscenda quorum notitia ad beatitudinem accidentaliter se habet, ut sunt quidam effectus divinæ virtutis, primo deveniunt a Deo ad angelos superiores, et per illos ad angelos inferiores, juxta documenta principis theologorum, in libro de Cœlesti hierarchia.
paras.en: [[25:3|and upon whom shall not his light arise?|Et super quem non surgit lumen illius?]] that is, the number of these soldiers upon whom the light of God does not shine is not fixed, in the way said above [that is, there is none of them on whom it does not shine]. For all the Blessed in the fatherland receive immediately from God the light of glory and the beatifying, most clear vision and illumination of the divine essence, for knowing those things that belong directly and properly to beatitude, such as the knowledge of the order of the universe and of all the heavenly citizens. But the illuminations of God for knowing those things whose knowledge stands to beatitude only accidentally, such as certain effects of the divine power, come first from God to the higher angels, and through them to the lower angels, according to the teaching of the prince of theologians [that is, Dionysius the Areopagite] in the book On the Celestial Hierarchy.

paras.t: Numquid justificari potest homo comparatus Deo? Hoc supra Job ait: Non justificatur homo compositus Deo. Quod ibi et aliis locis in hoc opere satis reor expositum. Aut apparere mundus natus de muliere? Hoc est quod supra Eliphaz dixit: Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere? Unde ex dictis ibidem hujus verbi intelligentia patet. Patet quoque in his error Baldad. Non enim beatus Job ita se justum perhibuit, ut comparatione Dei se justum assereret, aut nullam unquam incurrisse maculam ex carnis propagine, fragilitate et infectione; sed qualiter se justum esse testatus sit, frequenter jam dictum est. Ad verbum tamen Baldad applicari potest illud Genesis: Sensus et cogitatio cordis humani prona sunt in malum ab adolescentia sua. Nihilo minus Deus per gratiam supplere faciliter potest naturæ defectum.
paras.en: [[25:4|Can man be justified compared with God|Numquid justificari potest homo comparatus Deo]]? Job said this above: [[Job 9:2|man cannot be justified, compared with God|Non justificatur homo compositus Deo]]; and I think it has been sufficiently explained there and in other places in this work. [[25:4|or he that is born of a woman appear clean?|Aut apparere mundus natus de muliere?]] This is what Eliphaz said above: [[Job 15:14|What is man that he should be without spot, and he that is born of a woman that he should appear just?|Quid est homo ut immaculatus sit, et justus appareat natus de muliere?]] Hence the meaning of this saying is plain from what was said there. Plain too in these words is the error of Baldad. For blessed Job did not declare himself just in such a way as to assert that he was just in comparison with God, or that he had never contracted any stain from the propagation, frailty and infection of the flesh; how he did testify that he was just has already been said often. Yet to Baldad's saying there can be applied that saying of Genesis: [[Gen 8:21|the imagination and thought of man's heart are prone to evil from his youth|Sensus et cogitatio cordis humani prona sunt in malum ab adolescentia sua]]. Nevertheless God by grace can easily make good the defect of nature.

paras.t: Ecce etiam luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus: id est, tanta est claritas atque munditia Dei, quod comparatione ipsius luna non splendet, nec sidera munda sunt: quoniam omnis creatura a divinitatis sanctitate, luce ac puritate distat, occumbit ac deficit infinite. Ideo, sicut quod modice pulchrum est, comparatione ejus quod multum pulchrum est, non dicitur pulchrum; sic luna et stellæ, quoad Deum, non fulgent. Nec facit mentionem de sole, sicut de luna et stellis: quoniam non videmus solem majori lumine offuscari, quemadmodum luna et stellæ luce solis fuscantur. Denique, istud est quod Eliphaz supra ait: Cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus.
paras.en: [[25:5|Behold even the moon doth not shine, and the stars are not pure in his sight|Ecce etiam luna non splendet, et stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus]]: that is, so great is the brightness and the cleanness of God that in comparison with Him the moon does not shine, nor are the stars clean; for every creature stands apart from the holiness, light and purity of the Godhead, falls short of it and fails infinitely. Therefore, just as what is a little beautiful is not called beautiful in comparison with what is very beautiful, so the moon and the stars, with respect to God, do not shine. He makes no mention of the sun as he does of the moon and the stars, because we do not see the sun darkened by a greater light, as the moon and the stars are darkened by the light of the sun. Finally, this is what Eliphaz said above: [[Job 15:15|the heavens are not pure in his sight|Cœli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus]].

paras.t: Mystice per lunam Ecclesia, per stellas viri virtuosi, præsertim aliquorum doctores idonei designantur: qui respectu sapientiæ sanctitatisque Dei non fulgent, nec alicujus momenti sunt.
paras.en: In the mystical sense, the moon signifies the Church, and the stars virtuous men, above all those fit to be teachers of others; and in respect of the wisdom and holiness of God these do not shine and are of no account.

paras.t: Propterea subditur: Quanto magis homo putredo? id est homo, qui vocatur putredo, quia ex materia putredini proxima, et sordibus, immunditiis, fœtoribusque repleta consistit; et filius hominis vermis? id est filius hominis, qui dicitur vermis, quoniam sicut vermis ex putredine nascitur, sic filius hominis ex homine paulo post putrescente, immundoque semine, supple, mundus, justus ac fulgens coram Deo seu comparatione ipsius esse non valet. Argumentatio ista multoties tacta est atque soluta, ideo immorari non decet.
paras.en: Therefore it is added: [[25:6|How much more is man than rottenness|Quanto magis homo putredo?]] [the Latin reads simply “man rottenness”, and Denis takes it as “man, who is rottenness”]: that is, man, who is called rottenness because he consists of matter close to rottenness, and filled with filth, uncleanness and stench; [[25:6|and the son of man than a worm?|et filius hominis vermis?]] that is, the son of man, who is called a worm because, as the worm is born of rottenness, so the son of man is born of man, who shortly after rots, and of unclean seed: supply: he cannot be clean, just and shining before God, or in comparison with Him. This argument has been touched on and answered many times, and so it is not fitting to dwell on it.

26.title: Expositio capituli vicesimi sexti: Respondens autem Job, dixit.
26.title_en: Exposition of the twenty-sixth chapter: Then Job answered, and said

paras.t: Albertus circa principium expositionis hujus capituli ait: Deficientibus adversariis, Job hic suam confirmat sententiam: et quia in duobus consistit, videlicet, quod gubernatio Dei dissimilis sit humano regimini, tanquam ea quæ est secundum excellentiam et scientiam Dei, et quod non sit secundum ordinem humanæ justitiæ; ideo pars ista usque ad verba Eliu, dividitur in duo. In prima, excellentiam Dei ostendit; in secunda, se ipsum in exemplum proponens, confirmat quod ordine justitiæ humanæ Deus humana non regit.
paras.en: Albert, near the beginning of his exposition of this chapter, says: Now that his adversaries are failing, Job here confirms his own opinion. And since it consists in two things, namely that God's governance is unlike human rule, as being according to the excellence and knowledge of God, and that it is not according to the order of human justice, this part, up to the words of Eliu, is divided in two. In the first he shows the excellence of God; in the second, putting himself forward as an example, he confirms that God does not rule human affairs by the order of human justice.

paras.t: Respondens autem Job, dixit ad Baldad: Cujus adjutor es? id est, quem laude extollis, quasi in meam reprobationem ac tuæ positionis confirmationem? Siquidem præcedenti capitulo, Baldad conatus est reprobare beatum Job, ex consideratione infinitæ excellentiæ Dei super hominem, in potestate, sanctitate ac sapientia. Sicque videbatur partem Dei fovere adversus Job, cooperarique Deo, in defensione veritatis et æquitatis divinæ, cui (ut huic Baldad apparuit) Job blasphematorie derogavit: quemadmodum aliquis adstans, dum judicem laudat, cui judicatus derogare videtur. Numquid imbecillis, id est infirmus? quasi diceret, Non. Deus enim quem Baldad sic commendavit, omnipotens est, nec humano eget auxilio. Loquitur autem Job contra Baldad ironice zelo justitiæ, eo quod Baldad laudibus extulit Deum ad sui confirmationem erroris, atque ad reprobationem veritatis prolatæ a Job. Qui autem contra aliquem condemnatum non ratione utuntur, sed judicis sapientiam potentiamque allegant, in judicis favorem facere hoc videntur.
paras.en: [[26:1|Then Job answered, and said|Respondens autem Job, dixit]] to Baldad: [[26:2|Whose helper art thou?|Cujus adjutor es?]] that is, whom dost thou extol with praise, as if to disprove me and to confirm thy own position? For in the preceding chapter Baldad tried to disprove blessed Job from a consideration of the infinite excellence of God above man, in power, holiness and wisdom. And so he seemed to take God's part against Job, and to work together with God in defence of the divine truth and equity, which (as it seemed to this Baldad) Job had blasphemously disparaged: just as someone standing by, when he praises the judge, seems to take the part of the judge whom the man under judgement seems to disparage. [[26:2|is it of him that is weak?|Numquid imbecillis]] that is, infirm? [a printed footnote gives the reading *infirmi*, that is, of one infirm, which matches the genitive *imbecillis*] As if to say: No. For God, whom Baldad has so commended, is almighty, and needs no human help. Now Job speaks against Baldad ironically, out of zeal for justice, because Baldad extolled God with praises to confirm his own error and to disprove the truth put forward by Job. And those who use no reasoning against someone condemned, but plead the wisdom and power of the judge, seem by this to be acting in the judge's favour.

paras.t: Et sustentas brachium ejus qui non est fortis? Interrogative et negative legendum est: quasi dicat, Numquid Deus cujus brachium, id est virtutem seu operationem, fulcire et roborare velle videris, quasi cooperans sibi in veritatis et æquitatis defensione, infirmus est, ut tua sustentatione indigeat? Loquitur autem de Deo more humano, hoc est quasi de homine, cujus brachia præ lassitudine et impotentia indigent sustentari, si elevari, aut elevata debeant diu teneri, quemadmodum in Exodo legitur: Quum elevaret Moyses manus, vincebat Israel; si autem paululum remisisset, vincebat Amalec. Manus autem Moysis erant graves. Sumentes ergo lapidem, posuerunt subter eum. Aaron autem et Hur sustentabant manus ejus. Præterea advertendum quod humiles et electi vicissim Deum juvare dicuntur, non quasi illum roborantes, aut velut insufficienti seu indigenti subvenientes; sed quoniam ejus voluntati ac dispositioni, quantum ad effectuum divinorum exsecutionem cooperantur: et hoc ipsum est ineffabilis dignatio Dei, quod servos suos sibi efficit cooperatores, qui etiam quidquid boni habent aut exhibent, a Deo sortiti sunt. Unde Paulus: Dei, inquit, adjutores sumus. Quod quasi exponens: Ego, ait, plantavi, Apollo rigavit: Deus autem incrementum dedit. Sed neque qui plantat, est aliquid, neque qui rigat: quia videlicet propria virtute non operantur.
paras.en: [[26:2|and dost thou hold up the arm of him that has no strength?|Et sustentas brachium ejus qui non est fortis?]] This is to be read as a question expecting the answer no: as if he said, Is God, whose arm (that is, whose power or working) thou seemest to wish to prop up and strengthen, as though working together with him in defence of truth and equity, so infirm that he needs thy support? He speaks of God in human fashion, that is, as of a man whose arms, for weariness and weakness, need to be held up if they are to be raised, or to be kept raised for long; as we read in Exodus: [[Ex 17:11|when Moses lifted up his hands, Israel overcame; but if he let them down a little, Amalec overcame|Quum elevaret Moyses manus, vincebat Israel; si autem paululum remisisset, vincebat Amalec]]. [[Ex 17:12|Moses's hands were heavy: so they took a stone, and put under him|Manus autem Moysis erant graves. Sumentes ergo lapidem, posuerunt subter eum]]. [[Ex 17:12|Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands|Aaron autem et Hur sustentabant manus ejus]]. It is to be noted besides that the humble and the elect are said in their turn to help God: not as if strengthening him, or coming to the aid of one insufficient or in need, but because they cooperate with his will and disposition as regards the carrying out of the divine works. And this very thing is the unspeakable condescension of God, that he makes his servants his fellow workers, who also have received from God whatever good they have or show. Hence Paul says: [[1 Cor 3:9|we are God's coadjutors|Dei, inquit, adjutores sumus]]. And as if explaining this, he says: [[1 Cor 3:6|I have planted, Apollo watered: but God gave the increase|Ego, ait, plantavi, Apollo rigavit: Deus autem incrementum dedit]]. [[1 Cor 3:7|neither he that planteth is any thing, nor he that watereth|Sed neque qui plantat, est aliquid, neque qui rigat]]: that is, because they do not work by their own power.

paras.t: Cui dedisti consilium? Forsitan illi qui non habet sapientiam. Non est autem putandum quod Baldad tam asininæ fuerit simplicitatis, quod æstimaverit Deum impotentem aut insipientem, vel quod intenderit eum firmare aut informare. Job tamen sic increpat eum, quasi hoc ipsum fecisset, quia taliter loquebatur hic Baldad, et ita se habuit, quasi hoc intendisset, sicut jam declaratum est. Itaque quum Deus sit sapiens et sapientia superessentialis ac infinita, non eget alicujus consilio. Et prudentiam tuam ostendisti plurimam, id est, verba alta loquendo de Deo monstrasti te magnæ esse scientiæ: quod et ostentationis culpa videtur. Nam et Apostolus ad Romanos scribit: Non plus sapere quam oportet, sed sapere ad sobrietatem. Denique, sicut qui comedit mel multum non est ei bonum; sic scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria. Ptolemæus quoque in principio Almagesti disseruit: Qui scientiam suam extendit ultra industriam quæ in ipso est, est sicut pastor debilis cum ovibus multis.
paras.en: [[26:3|To whom hast thou given counsel? perhaps to him that hath no wisdom|Cui dedisti consilium? Forsitan illi qui non habet sapientiam]]. It is not to be thought, however, that Baldad was of so asinine a simplicity as to reckon God powerless or unwise, or that he meant to strengthen or instruct him. Yet Job rebukes him as though he had done this very thing, because this Baldad spoke in such a way and so behaved as if he meant it, as has already been explained. So, since God is wise, and wisdom superessential [that is, beyond all being] and infinite, he needs no one's counsel. [[26:3|and thou hast shewn thy very great prudence|Et prudentiam tuam ostendisti plurimam]]: that is, by speaking lofty words about God thou hast shown thyself to be of great knowledge; which seems also to carry the fault of ostentation. For the Apostle too writes to the Romans: [[Rom 12:3|not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise, but to be wise unto sobriety|Non plus sapere quam oportet, sed sapere ad sobrietatem]]. Finally: [[Prov 25:27|As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, so he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|sicut qui comedit mel multum non est ei bonum; sic scrutator majestatis opprimetur a gloria]]. Ptolemy too declared at the beginning of the Almagest: He who stretches his knowledge beyond the skill that is in him is like a weak shepherd with many sheep.

paras.t: Quem docere voluisti? nonne eum qui fecit spiramentum, id est Deum qui condidit animam rationalem, sapientiæ receptaculum, spirationisque causam? juxta illud Genesis: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ, et inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitæ. Eo autem modo intelligendum est, quod Baldad voluit Deum docere, quo jam dictum est, quod voluit ei consulere.
paras.en: [[26:4|Whom hast thou desired to teach? was it not him that made life?|Quem docere voluisti? nonne eum qui fecit spiramentum]] [*spiramentum*, literally breath], that is, God, who created the rational soul, the receptacle of wisdom and the cause of breathing? According to that of Genesis: [[Gen 2:7|formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life|Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ, et inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitæ]]. Now that Baldad wished to teach God is to be understood in the same way in which, as has just been said, he wished to counsel him.

paras.t: Moraliter autem verba ista dicenda sunt justa derisione, caritativaque increpatione, vanis, præsumptuosis et sciolis; qui sapientiores se instruere, expertioribus consulere verbis aut scriptis præsumunt; qui aliis sapientiores reputari desiderant; qui dum sobrie habere se nesciunt, frequenter stulta loquuntur aut scribunt, suamque fatuitatem ac vanitatem demonstrant.
paras.en: Morally, these words are to be said, with just derision and charitable rebuke, to the vain, the presumptuous and the smatterers: who presume to instruct those wiser than themselves, and to counsel the more experienced by word or writing; who desire to be reputed wiser than others; who, not knowing how to bear themselves soberly, often say or write foolish things, and show their own folly and vanity.

paras.t: Consequenter beatus Job Deum per suos effectus diffusius laudat, quam Baldad superius fecit, ne divinæ videretur excellentiæ derogare. Ecce gigantes gemunt sub aquis, et qui habitant cum eis. Hoc Thomas et alii quidam referunt ad gigantes, qui (ut in Genesi habetur) tempore Noe erant in terra, et diluvio perierunt cum cohabitatoribus suis, qui tam loco quam vitiis cohabitaverant eis: qui omnes simul nunc gemunt in pœnis inferni, qui sub aquis est, quia in medio terræ.
paras.en: Next, blessed Job praises God through his works more fully than Baldad did above, so as not to seem to detract from the divine excellence. [[26:5|Behold the giants groan under the waters, and they that dwell with them.|Ecce gigantes gemunt sub aquis, et qui habitant cum eis]] Thomas and some others refer this to the giants who (as is said in Genesis) were on the earth in the time of Noe[[Gen 6:4||]], and perished in the flood with those who dwelt with them, who had dwelt with them as much in their vices as in place: all of whom now groan together in the pains of hell, which is under the waters, since it is in the middle of the earth.

paras.t: Alii (ut Gregorius et Albertus) per gigantes, intelligunt superbos, Deo rebelles, in suis viribus confidentes, qui in propriis oculis velut in giganteam magnitudinem excreverunt: quales præcipue esse solent principes et potentes ac divites sæculi hujus, sed et prælati nonnulli, inde superbientes, unde se maxime humiliare ac formidare deberent. De quibus omnibus illud in Isaia accipi potest: Mortui non vivant, gigantes non resurgant. Ubi per mortuos, intelliguntur iniqui morte culpæ perempti in anima: qui dum indurantur in vitiis, non vivunt per gratiam. Gigantes quoque præfati, quia non pœnitent, ad vitam gratia non resurgunt. Hi ergo cum cohabitatoribus, id est imitatoribus suis vel commansoribus, sibi in peccato similibus (nam et frequenter quales ipsi, tales et cohabitatores eorum, juxta illud Ecclesiastici, Qualis est rector civitatis, tales habitantes in ea): itaque hi simul gemunt sub aquis, id est abundantia tribulationum ac onerum inquietudinumque suarum. Varii enim sunt tumultus et curæ, timores, terrores, rancores, iræ et impatientiæ talium, quorum inordinatus vitiosusque animus sibi ipsi pœnalis est. Frequenter quoque justo Dei judicio, gravissimæ adversitates et infirmitates eis occurrunt, ita quod gemunt sub aquis tribulationum: in quo divina declaratur potentia. De quibus aquis fertur in Psalmo: Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam. In Threnis quoque: Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum. Unde primo libro Machabæorum Antiochus: In quos, inquit, tristitiæ fluctus deveni!
paras.en: Others (such as Gregory and Albert) understand by the giants the proud, rebels against God, trusting in their own strength, who in their own eyes have grown as it were to a giant's stature: such as are wont to be above all the princes, the powerful and the rich of this world, and some prelates too, who grow proud of the very thing for which they ought most to humble themselves and to fear. Of all of these that saying in Isaias may be taken: [[Is 26:14|Let not the dead live, let not the giants rise again|Mortui non vivant, gigantes non resurgant]]. Here by the dead are understood the wicked, slain in the soul by the death of guilt, who, while they are hardened in vice, do not live by grace. And the giants mentioned, because they do not repent, do not rise again by grace to life. These, then, with those who dwell with them, that is, their imitators or housemates, like them in sin (for often such as they are, such too are those who dwell with them, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:2|what manner of man the ruler of a city is, such also are they that dwell therein|Qualis est rector civitatis, tales habitantes in ea]]): these, I say, [[26:5|groan under the waters|simul gemunt sub aquis]], that is, under the abundance of their tribulations, burdens and disquiets. For manifold are the tumults and cares, the fears, terrors, rancours, angers and impatiences of such men, whose disordered and vicious mind is a punishment to itself. Often, too, by the just judgement of God, the gravest adversities and sicknesses befall them, so that they groan under the waters of tribulation: and in this the divine power is shown. Of these waters it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 68:2|Save me, O God: for the waters are come in even unto my soul|Salvum me fac, Deus, quoniam intraverunt aquæ usque ad animam meam]]. In the Lamentations also: [[Lam 3:54|Waters have flowed over my head|Inundaverunt aquæ super caput meum]]. Hence in the first book of Machabees Antiochus says: [[1 Mach 6:11|Into what floods of sorrow|In quos]], he says, [[1 Mach 6:11|am I come|tristitiæ fluctus deveni]]!

paras.t: Nudus est infernus coram illo, id est, infernus et omnia quæ in eo sunt, Deo conspicua sunt atque clarissime nota; et nullum est operimentum perditioni, id est filiis perditionis seu reprobis, quo abscondantur conspectui Dei, sed certissime cognoscuntur ab ipso, juxta illud Apostoli ad Hebræos: Non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus. Omnia autem nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus. Per Jeremiam quoque Dominus loquitur: Si occultabitur vir in absconditis suis, et ego non videbo eum?
paras.en: [[26:6|Hell is naked before him|Nudus est infernus coram illo]]: that is, hell and all that is in it are visible to God and most clearly known to him; [[26:6|and there is no covering for destruction|et nullum est operimentum perditioni]], that is, for the sons of perdition or the reprobate, by which they might be hidden from the sight of God; but they are most certainly known by him, according to that of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 4:13|Neither is there any creature invisible in his sight: but all things are naked and open to his eyes|Non est ulla creatura invisibilis in conspectu ejus. Omnia autem nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus]]. And through Jeremias the Lord says: [[Jer 23:24|Shall a man be hid in secret places, and I not see him|Si occultabitur vir in absconditis suis, et ego non videbo eum?]]?

paras.t: Qui extendit aquilonem super vacuum. Per aquilonem, Thomas intelligit hemisphærium superius, quantum ad nos, in quo est polus aquilonaris, qui super nostrum horizontem jugiter elevatur. Polus vero australis nobis deprimitur. Hoc ergo hemisphærium super vacuum fertur expansum, quia inter ipsum et terram nihil sensibile nobis apparet; et medium quod ibi est, quamvis sit igne elementari et aere plenum, tamen a vulgo reputatur ut vacuum: sicut lagena dicitur vacua, quamvis aere sit repleta. Loquitur autem Job secundum vulgarium æstimationem, ut consuetudinis est sacræ Scripturæ. Huicque expositioni videtur consonare Albertus, dicendo: Qui extendit aquilonem, id est cœlum ab aquilone. Dicit enim Aristoteles in secundo de Cœlo et mundo, quod longitudo cœli est ab aquilone in meridiem; et si imaginaremur hominem dextera cœlum volventem ab oriente in occidentem, caput ejus esset in aquilone, et pedes in meridie, sicut finxerunt poetæ esse Atlantem: de quo in libro de Civitate Dei recitat Augustinus, quod fuit maximus temporis sui astronomus; ideo ferebatur cœlum movere et sustentare. Porro, per vacuum, intelligit Albertus capacitatem mundi, in qua adhuc nil fuerat factum in rerum exordio, super quod tunc cœlum extendebatur.
paras.en: [[26:7|He stretched out the north over the empty space|Qui extendit aquilonem super vacuum]]. By the north Thomas understands the upper hemisphere, as regards us, in which is the northern pole, which is always raised above our horizon, while the southern pole is depressed below us. This hemisphere, then, is said to be spread out over the empty space, because between it and the earth nothing perceptible appears to us; and the medium that is there, though it is full of elemental fire and of air, is yet reckoned by common people as empty: as a flask is called empty, though it is full of air. For Job speaks according to the common estimation, as is the custom of Holy Scripture. And Albert seems to agree with this exposition, saying: [[26:7|He stretched out the north|Qui extendit aquilonem]], that is, the heaven from the north. For Aristotle says in the second book On the Heaven and the World that the length of the heaven runs from north to south; and if we imagined a man turning the heaven with his right hand from east to west, his head would be in the north and his feet in the south, as the poets feigned Atlas to be: of whom Augustine relates in the book of the City of God that he was the greatest astronomer of his time, and that is why he was said to move and hold up the heaven. Further, by the empty space Albert understands the room of the world, in which nothing had yet been made at the beginning of things, over which the heaven was then stretched out.

paras.t: Et appendit terram super nihilum, id est super inane seu vacuum. Quod ideo dicitur, quia nil solidum est sub terra eam sustentans, sed Deo sic ordinante, manet in medio universi tanquam centrum. Quibus verbis docetur, ipsas naturales proprietates seu virtutes, quibus corpora in propriis locis continentur, ex virtute processisse divina. Quidam præterea dicunt: Terra videtur fulcimentum aquæ, et aqua aeris; sub terra vero nihil est, quum sit infima pars mundi. Hoc sanum exigit intellectum. Elementa enim se mutuo orbiculariter ambiunt: quia superius ambit quod sub ipso est, ut ignis aerem, aer aquam, aqua terram, nisi quod Deo sic disponente, una pars terræ discooperta est aquis, propter hominum et animantium congruam in terra habitationem. Sed et cœlum omnia ista ambit, claudit et continet. Unde tanta pars cœli est sub terra, quanta et super eam. Insuper reor idcirco aquilonem super vacuum dici extentum, et terram super inane et nihilum, quoniam licet realiter aliquid sit infra cœlum et terram, aliquid quoque sub terra modo jam dicto, illa tamen nil conferunt ad cœli terræque sustentationem.
paras.en: [[26:7|and hangeth the earth upon nothing|Et appendit terram super nihilum]], that is, upon the void or empty space. This is said because there is nothing solid under the earth holding it up, but by God's ordering it stays in the middle of the universe as its centre. By these words we are taught that the very natural properties or powers by which bodies are held in their proper places have proceeded from the divine power. Some say besides: The earth seems to be the support of the water, and the water of the air; but under the earth there is nothing, since it is the lowest part of the world. This needs a sound interpretation. For the elements surround one another in spheres: the higher surrounds what is beneath it, as fire the air, air the water, water the earth; except that, by God's disposing, one part of the earth is uncovered by the waters, so that men and animals may have a fitting dwelling on the earth. And the heaven surrounds, encloses and contains all these. Hence as great a part of the heaven is under the earth as is above it. Moreover, I think the north is said to be stretched out over the empty space, and the earth over the void and nothing, for this reason: that although there really is something beneath the heaven and the earth, and something also under the earth in the manner just described, yet these things contribute nothing to holding up the heaven and the earth.

paras.t: Mystice, per aquilonem, designatur diabolus, qui in Isaia loquitur: Sedebo in monte testamenti, in lateribus aquilonis. Qui super vacuum extenditur, quia illorum possidet corda, qui spiritualiter nihil et mortui sunt, id est, esse gratiæ carent. Terram vero, id est Ecclesiam, præcipue primitivam, virtutibus solidam appendit [Deus] super nihilum, id est, super gentilitatem adduxit, ut eam gratia prædicationis impleret, atque ad esse virtutum deduceret, dicente Christo Apostolis: Euntes, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eas. De quibus ab Isaia fuit prædictum: Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram illo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatæ sunt ei.
paras.en: Mystically, by the north is signified the devil, who says in Isaias: [[Is 14:13|I will sit in the mountain of the covenant, in the sides of the north|Sedebo in monte testamenti, in lateribus aquilonis]]. He is stretched out over the empty space, because he possesses the hearts of those who spiritually are nothing and dead, that is, lack the being of grace. But the earth, that is, the Church, above all the primitive Church, made solid by the virtues, God hangs upon nothing: that is, he brought it over the Gentile world, so that it might fill that world with the grace of preaching and lead it to the being of the virtues, as Christ said to the Apostles: [[Matt 28:19|Going therefore, teach ye all nations: baptizing them|Euntes, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eas]]. Of whom it was foretold by Isaias: [[Is 40:17|All nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity|Omnes gentes quasi non sint, sic sunt coram illo, et quasi nihilum et inane reputatæ sunt ei]].

paras.t: Qui ligat aquas in nubibus suis, ut non erumpant pariter deorsum. Divina enim virtute aqua vaporabiliter elevata a terra, in aere suspenditur, atque in nubes convertitur seu densatur: in quibus aquæ quasi ligatæ tenentur, priusquam descendant; nec pariter cadunt, sed paulatim per guttas, ne simul impetuose descendendo terram subvertant. Hinc ait Albertus: Aquas in nubibus ligare, est eas vaporabiliter in nubes convertere, et virtute cœli continere, donec cœlestes induant virtutes, per quas terram fecundent ad germinandum. Guttatim etenim resolutæ, proportionabiliter terram infundunt: quæ pariter erumpentes, terram subverterent, et vim tollerent germinativam. Qualitates quippe elementares ad species generatorum seu formas generabilium non moverent, nisi virtutes cœlestes induerent. Calidum namque ignis consumeret, et frigidum inferiorum elementorum motum abscinderet et mortificaret. Humidum vero diffluere faceret, et siccum non continuaretur ad quantitatem atque figuram. Unde non per se, sed virtutibus cœli, movent ad species generatorum: et hoc declarat, subjungens:
paras.en: [[26:8|He bindeth up the waters in his clouds|Qui ligat aquas in nubibus suis]], [[26:8|so that they break not out and fall down together|ut non erumpant pariter deorsum]]. For by the divine power water, raised from the earth as vapour, hangs in the air and is turned into clouds, or thickened: in these the waters are held as though bound before they come down; nor do they fall all together, but little by little, in drops, lest by coming down all at once with violence they should overturn the earth. Hence Albert says: To bind the waters in the clouds is to turn them as vapour into clouds and to hold them by the power of heaven, until they put on heavenly powers by which they may make the earth fruitful for bringing forth. For let loose drop by drop, they soak the earth in due measure; whereas, breaking out all together, they would overturn the earth and take away its power of bringing forth. For the elemental qualities would not move towards the species of things generated, or the forms of things that can be generated, unless they put on heavenly powers. The heat of fire would consume, and the cold of the lower elements would cut off and deaden motion; the moist would make things flow apart, and the dry would not hold together into quantity and shape. Hence they move towards the species of things generated not of themselves but by the powers of heaven: and this he declares, adding:

paras.t: Qui tenet vultum solii sui. Solium Dei, cœlum est, in quo velut in throno sedet, juxta illud Isaiæ: Cœlum mihi sedes. Vultus autem solii hujus, est superficies cœli ad inferius versa. Estque superficies stellata. Per virtutem namque stellarum, influit elementis omnem potestatem generationis et corruptionis. Hancque superficiem, vultum seu faciem solii sui, Deus tenet, quamdiu virtutes generativas corruptivasque influit, hoc est, quamdiu stat mundus. Et expandit super illud nebulam suam, id est, nebulam sua virtute generatam ponit inter cœlum et visum nostrum, ita quod secundum apparentiam cœlum nebula operitur, et illa super illud seu super faciem ejus conversam ad nos quasi expanditur, juxta illud in Psalmo: Qui operit cœlum nubibus. Et iterum: Nebulam sicut cinerem spargit. Porro, dum nubes resolvuntur in pluviam, remanent quidam vapores, ex quibus nebula generatur, nostro adspectui tegens cœlum. Albertus demum hic ait: Nebula vapor est, quia quum virtus cœli inferioribus infunditur, necesse est, ut inferiora ad receptionem aperiantur ac eleventur: quod fit per evaporationem faciem cœli nobis tegentem.
paras.en: [[26:9|He withholdeth the face of his throne|Qui tenet vultum solii sui]]. The throne of God is heaven, in which he sits as on a throne, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 66:1|Heaven is my throne|Cœlum mihi sedes]] [the margin reading is unclear (it seems to give Is. lv, 3); the words are Is 66:1]. And the face of this throne is the surface of heaven turned downwards; and it is the starry surface. For through the power of the stars heaven pours into the elements all the power of generation and corruption. And this surface, the countenance or face of his throne, God holds [Latin tenet, which the Douay-Rheims renders withholdeth] for as long as he pours in the powers of generation and corruption, that is, for as long as the world stands. [[26:9|and spreadeth his cloud over it|Et expandit super illud nebulam suam]], that is, he sets the mist [Latin nebula, which the Douay-Rheims renders cloud] that his power has generated between heaven and our sight, so that to appearance heaven is covered by the mist, and the mist is as it were spread over it, or over its face turned towards us; according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 146:8|Who covereth the heaven with clouds|Qui operit cœlum nubibus]]. And again: [[Ps 147:5|scattereth mists like ashes|Nebulam sicut cinerem spargit]]. Moreover, when the clouds are resolved into rain, certain vapours remain, from which mist is generated, covering heaven from our sight. Lastly Albert says here: Mist is a vapour, because when the power of heaven is poured into lower things, the lower things must be opened and raised up to receive it: and this comes about through evaporation, which covers the face of heaven from us.

paras.t: Mystice, Deus aquas sapientiæ salutaris in nubibus, id est Apostolis ac prædicatoribus sanctis, ligavit, id est, in corde eorum firmiter statuit, ac moderanter ab effusione et communicatione continuit, ut non erumperent pariter deorsum, id est, ne in tanta plenitudine ac sublimitate a prædicatoribus sanctis præfatis sapientia proponeretur audientium cordibus, sicut eis fuit infusa, quia capacitatem auditorum transcenderet. Paulatim vero effundenda communicandaque fuit, juxta audientium capacitatem, profectum et ordinem, quemadmodum ait Corinthiis Paulus: Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus. Qui denuo profitetur: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. Qui tenet vultum solii sui. Per vultum, cognitio designatur. Vultum itaque solii sui, id est contemplationem cœlestis patriæ, Deus tenet, id est, viatoribus non impendit, sed detinet: nec qualis et quanta sit visio illa beata, clare in hac via scire valemus, dicente Apostolo, Per fidem ambulamus, non per speciem. Ideo additur: et expandit super illud nebulam suam, id est, inter cœleste regnum et nos posuit obscuritatem, videlicet corruptibile corpus nostrum et animæ defectuositatem, peregrinationisque statum. Propter quod videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate, quale sit regnum cœleste: quoniam quidem corpus quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitantem. Idcirco dicit Apostolus: Quia dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur à Domino.
paras.en: Mystically, God has bound the waters of saving wisdom in the clouds, that is, in the Apostles and holy preachers: that is, he has set it firmly in their hearts, and has held it back with measure from being poured out and shared, [[26:8|so that they break not out and fall down together|ut non erumperent pariter deorsum]]: that is, lest wisdom should be set before the hearts of the hearers by the said holy preachers in such fullness and loftiness as it had been poured into them, since it would surpass the capacity of the hearers. Rather, it was to be poured out and shared little by little, according to the capacity, progress and order of the hearers, as Paul says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 3:1|could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal|Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus]]. And again he declares: [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect|Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos]]. [[26:9|He withholdeth the face of his throne|Qui tenet vultum solii sui]]. By the face, knowledge is signified. So the face of his throne, that is, the contemplation of the heavenly fatherland, God withholds: that is, he does not grant it to wayfarers but keeps it back; nor can we know clearly on this way what and how great that blessed vision is, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:7|we walk by faith and not by sight|Per fidem ambulamus, non per speciem]]. Therefore it is added: [[26:9|and spreadeth his cloud over it|et expandit super illud nebulam suam]], that is, he has set darkness between the heavenly kingdom and us: namely our corruptible body, the defectiveness of the soul, and the state of pilgrimage. For this reason [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner|videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate]] what the heavenly kingdom is like: since indeed [[Wis 9:15|the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|corpus quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitantem]]. Therefore the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:6|while we are in the body we are absent from the Lord|dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur à Domino]].

paras.t: Terminum circumdedit aquis, id est, infra certos terminos aquas conclusit, congregans eas intra receptacula apta, præsertim infra ripas Oceani, ne totam terram cooperirent, juxta illud Genesis: Dixit Deus: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Dicit hoc loco Thomas: Aquæ, secundum naturalem ordinem elementorum, undique terram operire deberent; sed quod aliqua pars terræ manet discooperta ab aquis, factum est divina virtute, quæ usque ad certum terminum fecit terram ab aquis cooperiri. Usque dum finiantur lux et tenebræ, id est, tamdiu hoc ita manebit, quousque successio diei et noctis, videlicet status hujus sæculi, finiatur. Lux nempe, id est dies, nobis finitur, dum sol occumbit; tuncque tenebræ oriuntur nocturnæ, rursusque dies succedit, et vicissitudo usque ad finem mundi durabit. Non tamen hæc ita dicuntur, quasi in fine sæculi aqua opertura sit totam terram, quia et postea pars terræ erit nudata et sicca.
paras.en: [[26:10|He hath set bounds about the waters|Terminum circumdedit aquis]], that is, he has shut the waters in within fixed bounds, gathering them into fitting receptacles, above all within the shores of the Ocean, lest they should cover the whole earth; according to that of Genesis: God said: [[Gen 1:9|Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. Thomas says at this place: The waters, according to the natural order of the elements, ought to cover the earth on every side; but that some part of the earth remains uncovered by the waters was done by the divine power, which made the earth to be covered by the waters only up to a fixed bound. [[26:10|till light and darkness come to an end|Usque dum finiantur lux et tenebræ]], that is, this will remain so until the succession of day and night, namely the state of this world, comes to an end. For the light, that is the day, ends for us when the sun sets; and then the darkness of night arises, and the day follows again, and this alternation will last until the end of the world. Yet this is not said as though at the end of the world the water were going to cover the whole earth, for even after that part of the earth will be bare and dry.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, Deus terminum circumdedit aquis, id est populis, qui frequenter aquarum nomine exprimuntur, sicut in Apocalypsi: Aquæ multæ, populi multi sunt. Et Ecclesiastes: Mitte panem tuum super transeuntes aquas. Populis ergo circumdedit terminum, id est, modum et gradum seu mensuram cognoscendi præfixit in vita hac, in qua ad patriæ visionem non eriguntur, usque dum finiantur lux et tenebræ, id est dies et noctes peregrinationis eorum in vita præsenti; vel, Lux, id est profectus in gratia, et tenebræ ignorantiæ vitæ hujus, terminum sortiantur. Durante namque hac vita, durat status merendi ac demerendi, seu proficiendi et decrescendi.
paras.en: Spiritually, God [[26:10|hath set bounds about the waters|terminum circumdedit aquis]], that is, about the peoples, who are often expressed by the name of waters, as in the Apocalypse: Many waters are many peoples[[Apoc 17:15||]] [Denis gives the sense of the verse, not its words]. And Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:1|Cast thy bread upon the running waters|Mitte panem tuum super transeuntes aquas]]. So he has set a bound about the peoples: that is, he has fixed beforehand the manner and degree, or measure, of knowing in this life, in which they are not raised to the vision of the fatherland, [[26:10|till light and darkness come to an end|usque dum finiantur lux et tenebræ]], that is, the days and nights of their pilgrimage in the present life; or, until light, that is, progress in grace, and the darkness of the ignorance of this life, reach their end. For while this life lasts, there lasts the state of meriting and demeriting, or of advancing and falling back.
