paras.t: Columnæ cœli contremiscunt, et pavent ad nutum ejus. Columnæ dicuntur quædam firmiora aliorum sustentativa seu perfectiva. Itaque columnæ cœli intelligi possunt, vel superiores angelici spiritus, qui inferiores purgant, illustrant, perficiunt: vel angelici spiritus illi, qui cœlestium orbium sunt motores, cœlosque quantum ad suam influentiam in hunc mundum actuant, et quasi fulcire dicuntur. Hi ad nutum, id est beneplacitum, vel ad signum voluntatis Dei, contremiscunt timore non pœnali, sed timore admirationis, pavoreque reverentiæ filialis ac humilis, Deo promptissime servientes. Juxta hunc modum in Ecclesiastico fertur: Ecce cœlum et cœli cœlorum in conspectu Dei commovebuntur, et quum conspexerit illa Deus, tremore concutientur. Insuper, Columnæ cœli, id est militantis Ecclesiæ, quam Christus ubertim in Evangelio regnum cœlorum appellat, cujus columnæ sunt sapientiores et fortiores, qui aliorum ignorantiam edocere imbecillitatemque æquanimiter ferre noverunt (quemadmodum Paulus Petrum, Joannem et Jacobum vocat columnas: unde in Apocalypsi Dominus asserit, Qui vicerit, faciam illum columnam in templo meo), pavent ad nutum Dei.
paras.en: [[26:11|The pillars of heaven tremble|Columnæ cœli contremiscunt]], [[26:11|and dread at his beck|et pavent ad nutum ejus]]. Those things are called pillars which are firmer and sustain or perfect others. So the pillars of heaven may be understood either as the higher angelic spirits, which purge, enlighten and perfect the lower; or as those angelic spirits which are the movers of the heavenly spheres, and set the heavens to work as regards their influence on this world, and are said, as it were, to prop them up. These tremble at his beck, that is, at the good pleasure, or at the sign, of the will of God, not with penal fear but with the fear of wonder, and with the awe of a filial and humble reverence, serving God most promptly. In this manner it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 16:18|Behold the heaven, and the heavens of heavens|Ecce cœlum et cœli cœlorum]] [[Ecclus 16:18|shall be moved in his sight|in conspectu Dei commovebuntur]], and [[Ecclus 16:19|when God shall look upon them, they shall be shaken with trembling|quum conspexerit illa Deus, tremore concutientur]]. Moreover, [[26:11|The pillars of heaven|Columnæ cœli]], that is, of the Church militant, which Christ in the Gospel abundantly calls the kingdom of heaven[[Matt 13:1||]] [the margin gives Matth. xiii, the chapter of the parables of the kingdom of heaven], whose pillars are the wiser and stronger, who know how to teach others in their ignorance and to bear their weakness with an even mind (as Paul calls Peter, John and James pillars[[Gal 2:9||]]; whence in the Apocalypse the Lord declares: [[Apoc 3:12|He that shall overcome, I will make him a pillar|Qui vicerit, faciam illum columnam]] in my temple [the Vulgate has in the temple of my God]), [[26:11|dread at his beck|pavent ad nutum Dei]].

paras.t: In fortitudine illius, id est omnipotente Dei virtute, repente maria congregata sunt, id est, aquæ marinæ ad certa loca redactæ. Aitque pluraliter, Maria, propter particularia maria, vel propter magnitudinem aquarum abyssi Oceani. Hinc fertur in Psalmo: Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris, ponens in thesauris abyssos. Spiritualiter quoque maria, id est corda sæcularia, multa et tumida, instar maris inquieta, turbulenta, amara (juxta illud Isaiæ, Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest) per omnipotentiam Dei repente congregata, id est in Christo collecta sunt per fidem et caritatem, prædicantibus ubique Apostolis atque eorum discipulis. Et prudentia ejus percussit superbum, id est, primum illum apostatam angelum, qui dixit, Similis ero Altissimo, dejecit et condemnavit, secundum illud Psalmistæ: Tu humiliasti sicut vulneratum, superbum. Et Isaias: Numquid non tu percussisti superbum, vulnerasti draconem? Hoc tamen de omni superbo impœnitente accipi potest. Deus enim superbis resistit; et, Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur.
paras.en: [[26:12|By his power|In fortitudine illius]], that is, by the almighty power of God, [[26:12|the seas are suddenly gathered together|repente maria congregata sunt]], that is, the waters of the sea were brought into fixed places. And he says in the plural, Seas, because of the particular seas, or because of the greatness of the waters of the abyss of the Ocean. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:7|Gathering together the waters of the sea, as in a vessel; laying up the depths in storehouses|Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris, ponens in thesauris abyssos]]. Spiritually also the seas, that is, worldly hearts, many and swollen, restless like the sea, turbulent and bitter (according to that of Isaias: [[Is 57:20|the wicked are like the raging sea, which cannot rest|Impii quasi mare fervens, quod quiescere non potest]]), were by the almighty power of God [[26:12|suddenly gathered together|repente congregata]], that is, gathered in Christ through faith and charity, as the Apostles and their disciples preached everywhere. [[26:12|and his wisdom has struck the proud one|Et prudentia ejus percussit superbum]], that is, that first apostate angel, who said, [[Is 14:14|I will be like the most High|Similis ero Altissimo]], he cast down and condemned; according to that of the Psalmist: [[Ps 88:11|Thou hast humbled the proud one, as one that is slain|Tu humiliasti sicut vulneratum, superbum]]. And Isaias: [[Is 51:9|Hast not thou struck the proud one, and wounded the dragon?|Numquid non tu percussisti superbum, vulnerasti draconem?]] Yet this may be taken of every impenitent proud man. For [[Jas 4:6|God resisteth the proud|Deus superbis resistit]]; and, [[Luke 14:11|every one that exalteth himself shall be humbled|Qui se exaltat, humiliabitur]] [no margin reference is given for these two sayings; the first also stands in 1 Pet 5:5, the second also in Luke 18:14 and Matt 23:12].

paras.t: Spiritus ejus ornavit cœlos. Per spiritum Dei, intelligi potest Spiritus Sanctus, persona a Patre Filioque distincta; vel mens seu voluntas Dei: qui cœlos, id est angelos sanctos, ornavit, quia ruentibus apostatis, ipsi donis gloriæ confirmabantur, tuncque cœperunt Deum videre per speciem. Insuper, Cœlos, id est orbes cœlestes, stellis, planetis, virtutibus, luce, causalitate ornavit, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Species cœli gloria stellarum, mundum illuminans in excelsis Dominus.
paras.en: [[26:13|His spirit hath adorned the heavens|Spiritus ejus ornavit cœlos]]. By the spirit of God may be understood the Holy Ghost, a Person distinct from the Father and the Son; or the mind or will of God: who adorned the heavens, that is, the holy angels, since, when the apostates fell, they were confirmed with the gifts of glory, and then began to see God by sight [Latin per speciem: face to face, not by faith]. Moreover, the heavens, that is, the heavenly spheres, he adorned with stars, planets, powers, light and causality; according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:10|The glory of the stars is the beauty of heaven; the Lord enlighteneth the world on high|Species cœli gloria stellarum, mundum illuminans in excelsis Dominus]].

paras.t: Rursus, Spiritus ejus ornavit cœlos, id est beatos Apostolos, præsertim in die Pentecostes, quando tot gratiarum charismatibus sunt repleti: quia (ut Paulus testatur) primitias Spiritus acceperunt. De quibus ait Psalmista: Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei. Sed et omnes qui in terra cœliformiter conversantur, et dicere possunt, Nostra conversatio in cœlis est, unde hoc habent, nisi à Spiritu Sancto, per ornamenta gratiæ ac virtutum, quæ illis largitur?
paras.en: Again, [[26:13|His spirit hath adorned the heavens|Spiritus ejus ornavit cœlos]], that is, the blessed Apostles, above all on the day of Pentecost, when they were filled with so many gifts of grace: for (as Paul testifies) they received [[Rom 8:23|the firstfruits of the Spirit|primitias Spiritus]]. Of them the Psalmist says: [[Ps 18:2|The heavens shew forth the glory of God|Cœli enarrant gloriam Dei]]. And indeed all who on earth live a heavenly life and can say, [[Phil 3:20|our conversation is in heaven|Nostra conversatio in cœlis est]]: whence have they this, if not from the Holy Ghost, through the adornments of grace and of the virtues which he bestows on them?

paras.t: Et obstetricante, id est per modum obstetricis leviter educente, manu, id est potentia et sapientia, ejus, scilicet Dei, eductus est coluber tortuosus, id est, diabolus a societate stantium angelorum, et ex corde credentium, est ejectus, quemadmodum ait Salvator: Nunc princeps hujus mundi ejicietur foras; itemque: Videbam Satanam quasi fulgur de cœlo cadentem. Denique diabolus coluber dicitur, propter malitiæ suæ venena pestifera; tortuosus quoque, ob suam obliquitatem et calliditatem. De quo Isaias loquitur: Visitabit Dominus super Leviathan serpentem tortuosum. Quemadmodum etiam obstetrix leviter educit de matris utero fetum periclitantem seu mortuum, ne mater lædatur: sic Deus eduxit diabolum de societate stantium angelorum cordibusque credentium, ne quid læsionis aut indecentis ex eo ipsis adesset.
paras.en: [[26:13|and his obstetric|Et obstetricante]], that is, drawing forth gently after the manner of a midwife, [[26:13|hand|manu]], that is, by the power and wisdom of him, namely of God, [[26:13|brought forth the winding serpent|eductus est coluber tortuosus]]: that is, the devil was cast out of the company of the angels who stood firm, and out of the heart of believers, as the Saviour says: [[John 12:31|now shall the prince of this world be cast out|Nunc princeps hujus mundi ejicietur foras]]; and again: [[Luke 10:18|I saw Satan like lightning falling from heaven|Videbam Satanam quasi fulgur de cœlo cadentem]]. Now the devil is called a serpent because of the pestilent poisons of his malice; and winding, because of his crookedness and cunning. Of him Isaias speaks: The Lord [[Is 27:1|shall visit leviathan the bar serpent, and leviathan the crooked serpent|Visitabit Dominus super Leviathan serpentem tortuosum]] [Denis gives the verse shortened]. And just as a midwife gently draws from the mother's womb a child in danger or dead, lest the mother be harmed: so God drew the devil out of the company of the angels who stood firm and out of the hearts of believers, lest any harm or unseemliness should come to them from him.

paras.t: Ecce hæc ex parte, id est imperfecte seu partim, dicta sunt viarum ejus, id est de operibus Dei, quæ sunt viæ seu media, quibus in hac vita perducimur ad Creatoris notitiam. Quasi dicat: Ea quæ dixi, licet magna videantur et multa, modica tamen sunt comparatione divinorum effectuum quos non dixi, et qui hominibus sunt ignoti. Ideo addit, et quum vix parvam stillam sermonum ejus audierimus, id est, quum ea quæ protuli, vel ab aliis sunt prolata de magnalibus Dei, tam modica sint respectu operum atque magnalium ejus quæ ignorantur, neque audita sunt, neque ab homine pronuntiata quum nesciantur, ut vix stillam parvam, id est minimum quid, audierimus inde; quis poterit tonitruum, id est grandem et excellentem sermonem, magnitudinis ejus, id est de divina majestate, prout in se ipsa est, intueri, id est cognoscere sive concipere? Sic enim de Deo loqui non possumus, quia nec sic eum cognoscere in hac vita valemus. Ideo dicit Albertus: Tonitruum sine concussione capitis non auditur: significatque excellentiam sermonis de Deo in se ipso, qui tam eminens est, quod omnem evertit cogitatum, et concutit intellectum ac superat mentem. Unde Apostolus, qui in raptu Deum per essentiam vidit, asserit se arcana verba audisse, quæ non licet homini loqui.
paras.en: [[26:14|Lo, these things are said in part|Ecce hæc ex parte]], that is, imperfectly or partially, [[26:14|of his ways|dicta sunt viarum ejus]], that is, of the works of God, which are the ways or means by which in this life we are led to the knowledge of the Creator. As if he said: The things I have said, though they seem great and many, are yet small in comparison with the divine effects which I have not told, and which are unknown to men. Therefore he adds, [[26:14|and seeing we have heard scarce a little drop of his word|et quum vix parvam stillam sermonum ejus audierimus]] [Denis reads sermonum, of his words], that is, since what I have uttered, or what others have uttered of the great works of God, is so small with respect to his works and great deeds which are unknown, and are neither heard nor uttered by man since they are not known, that we have heard scarcely a little drop of them, that is, the least thing: [[26:14|who shall be able|quis poterit]] [[26:14|to behold|intueri]], that is, to know or conceive, [[26:14|the thunder|tonitruum]], that is, the great and excellent discourse, [[26:14|of his greatness|magnitudinis ejus]], that is, about the divine majesty as it is in itself? For we cannot speak of God in that way, since neither can we know him in that way in this life. Therefore Albert says: Thunder is not heard without a shaking of the head: and it signifies the excellence of the discourse about God as he is in himself, which is so eminent that it overturns every thought, and shakes the understanding and surpasses the mind. Hence the Apostle, who in his rapture saw God in his essence, declares that he heard [[2 Cor 12:4|secret words which it is not granted to man to utter|arcana verba audisse, quæ non licet homini loqui]].

paras.t: Denique verbis his consonat illud Ecclesiastici: Quis vidit eum et enarrabit? et quis magnificabit eum sicut est a principio? Multa enim absconsa sunt majora his: pauca enim vidimus operum ejus. Hinc etiam scripsit Sapiens: Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore: quæ autem in cœlo sunt, quis investigabit? Itaque quæ scimus, minima et pene nulla sunt respectu eorum quæ ignoramus. Quis enim novit ordinem universi, genera et species piscium, avium et brutorum, herbarum, gemmarum atque similium proprietates, virtutes, conditiones et actus omnium horum? Quod si ista nescimus, quanta nobis ignorantia est de his, quæ ad cœlestia pertinent corpora, angelorumque agmina, et supermundani illius Beatorum palatii consistentiam, proprietatem, naturam? Nemo ergo se jactet, nullus inaniter glorietur, nullus præsumat; sed imperfectum nostrum videant oculi nostri, quia pauperrimi sumus.
paras.en: Lastly, with these words agrees that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:35|Who shall see him, and declare him? and who shall magnify him as he is from the beginning?|Quis vidit eum et enarrabit? et quis magnificabit eum sicut est a principio?]] [[Ecclus 43:36|There are many things hidden from us that are greater than these: for we have seen but a few of his works|Multa enim absconsa sunt majora his: pauca enim vidimus operum ejus]] [the margin seems to read Eccli. xviii, 35, 36; the words are Ecclus 43:35–36]. Hence too the Wise Man wrote: [[Wis 9:16|hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth: and with labour do we find the things that are before us. But the things that are in heaven, who shall search out?|Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore: quæ autem in cœlo sunt, quis investigabit?]] [Denis reads invenimus, we find, where the Vulgate has æstimamus, we guess]. So the things we know are least, and almost nothing, compared with those we do not know. For who knows the order of the universe, the kinds and species of fishes, birds and beasts, the properties, powers, conditions and acts of herbs, gems and the like, of all these? And if we do not know these things, how great is our ignorance of what belongs to the heavenly bodies and the hosts of the angels, and of the constitution, property and nature of that palace of the Blessed above the world? Let no one then boast, let no one glory in vain, let no one presume; but let our eyes see our imperfection[[Ps 138:16||]], for we are very poor.

28.title: Expositio litteralis capituli vicesimi octavi: Habet argentum venarum suarum principia.
28.title_en: Literal exposition of the twenty-eighth chapter: Silver hath beginnings of its veins

paras.t: Capitulum istud non parum difficile est, ideo expositioni ejus est diligentius intendendum. Dicit autem Albertus: In isto capitulo ostendit beatus Job excellentiam sapientiæ Dei in vestigio creaturarum, id est in creaturis, in quibus perfectio Creatoris apparet per modum vestigii; suntque tria alia Scripturæ capitula concordantia super istud, videlicet octavum Proverbiorum, vicesimum quartum Ecclesiastici, et maxime tertium capitulum Baruch.
paras.en: This chapter is not a little difficult, and so its exposition calls for the more careful attention. Albert says: In this chapter blessed Job shows the excellence of the wisdom of God in the trace of creatures, that is, in creatures, in which the perfection of the Creator appears by way of a trace [vestigium: a footprint, the mark a cause leaves in its effect without showing its likeness]; and there are three other chapters of Scripture that agree with this one, namely the eighth of Proverbs, the twenty-fourth of Ecclesiasticus, and above all the third chapter of Baruch.

paras.t: Thomas quoque hic ait: In hoc capitulo ostendit Job spiritualis boni dignitatem, quod justi a Deo recipiunt etiam in hoc mundo: quod bonum sub sapientia comprehendit. Idcirco intendit præferre sapientiam cunctis corporalibus rebus, et quantum ad originem, et quantum ad pretiositatem. Hinc primo ostendit, quod quæ in corporalibus rebus pretiosa videntur, habent in certis locis originem. His consonat quod aliqui dicunt, quia postquam ostendit Job non indecens esse providentiæ divinæ, sed decens, quod aliquando impii temporaliter in hoc sæculo prosperantur, ratione accepta ex parvitate boni, puta temporalis, sensibilis et caduci, quod a Deo sortiuntur; nunc idem ostendit ex magnitudine boni, quod justi etiam in hac vita a Domino consequuntur; quod est bonum spirituale, sic temporalia transcendens, quomodo centenarius parvulum numerum, secundum Hieronymum. Ideo, licet justi temporalibus bonis privati, judicentur miseri ab iniquis temporalia sola quærentibus, tamen revera feliciores sunt illis, utpote majora bona habentes. Ideo mirum non est, quod Deus interdum permittit reprobos et injustos temporaliter abundare, quibus non intendit spiritualia bona, quæ præstantiora sunt, communicare: sicut et pater carnalis ac sapiens, bonis filiis bona meliora concedit, malis filiis dimittens bona minora, quia sunt filii ejus. Sic Deus electis et bonis tribuit bona gratiæ et virtutum, tanquam filiis adoptivis; reprobis vero dat terrena, quia sunt filii ejus per creationem, et ad ejus facti imaginem.
paras.en: Thomas too says here: In this chapter Job shows the dignity of the spiritual good which the just receive from God even in this world, a good which he includes under wisdom. He therefore means to set wisdom above all bodily things, both as to its origin and as to its preciousness. So he first shows that the things which seem precious among bodily things have their origin in certain places. With this agrees what some say: that after Job has shown that it is not unbecoming but becoming to divine providence that the wicked sometimes prosper in temporal things in this world, taking his argument from the smallness of the good, namely temporal, sensible and perishable, which they receive from God, he now shows the same from the greatness of the good which the just obtain from the Lord even in this life; and this is the spiritual good, which surpasses temporal things as the number a hundred surpasses a little number, according to Jerome. Therefore, although the just, deprived of temporal goods, are judged wretched by the wicked who seek temporal things alone, yet in truth they are happier than they, since they have greater goods. So it is no wonder that God sometimes allows the reprobate and the unjust to abound in temporal things, when he does not mean to give them the spiritual goods, which are more excellent: just as a wise father according to the flesh grants the better goods to his good sons, and leaves the lesser goods to his bad sons, because they are his sons. So God gives the goods of grace and of the virtues to the elect and the good, as to adopted sons; but to the reprobate he gives earthly things, because they are his sons by creation, and made to his image.

paras.t: Incipiens itaque a metallis, quæ hominibus pretiosa et necessaria sunt, ait: Habet argentum venarum suarum principia. Circa quod Thomas affirmat: Metalla ex humidis generantur vaporibus ex terra resolutis per virtutem solis atque stellarum, unde metalla ductilia liquabiliaque consistunt: quemadmodum econverso lapides et hujusmodi, quæ non malleantur neque funduntur, ex sicca exhalatione gignuntur intra terram retenta. Diversificantur autem species metallorum, secundum majorem et minorem puritatem resoluti vaporis, et secundum diversitatem digerentis caloris: inter quæ aurum videtur purissimum, deinde argentum, postea æs et ferrum. Insuper, secundum majorem minoremve puritatem, metalla ut plurimum habent diversam originem. Unde argentum communiter invenitur in quibusdam terræ aut lapidum venis seu meatibus, qui per laborem studiumque reperiuntur humanum, quamvis difficulter. Itaque ait: Habet argentum venarum suarum principia, id est origines seu exordia, scilicet in aliquibus locis determinatis, ex quibus resolvuntur vapores apti ad generationem argenti, qui dum immiscentur terræ vel lapidi, efficiuntur ibi venæ argenti. Quidam autem, per principia venarum argenti, intelligunt materiale ejus principium, puta minerias, ex quibus argentum naturaliter generatur: quæ in determinatis terræ venis esse dicuntur.
paras.en: Beginning, then, with the metals, which are precious and necessary to men, he says: [[28:1|Silver hath beginnings of its veins|Habet argentum venarum suarum principia]]. On this Thomas states: Metals are generated from moist vapours released from the earth by the power of the sun and the stars, which is why metals are ductile and fusible: just as, conversely, stones and the like, which are neither hammered nor cast, are produced from a dry exhalation held within the earth. The species of metals differ according to the greater or lesser purity of the vapour released, and according to the difference of the heat that digests it [that is, that works it to ripeness, the concoction of the old natural philosophy]: among them gold seems the purest, then silver, then brass and iron. Moreover, according to their greater or lesser purity, metals for the most part have different origins. So silver is commonly found in certain veins or passages of earth or of stone, which are found by human labour and pains, though with difficulty. And so he says: [[28:1|Silver hath beginnings of its veins|Habet argentum venarum suarum principia]], that is, origins or starting-points, namely in certain fixed places from which vapours fit for the generation of silver are released; and when these are mixed with earth or stone, veins of silver are formed there. Some, however, understand by the beginnings of the veins of silver its material principle, namely the ores from which silver is naturally generated, which are said to be in certain fixed veins of the earth.

paras.t: Et auro locus est in quo conflatur. Secundum Thomam, quia aurum purissimum est, invenitur ut plurimum generatum in sua puritate inter arenas fluminum, propter multitudinem evaporationis et caliditatis arenæ. Ideo ait, Auro locus est in quo conflatur, quia ex multis arenis colliguntur granula auri, quæ in unum liquantur: quod non in omni agitur loco, sed in aliquibus determinatis, ubi concurrit debita virtutis activi proportio ad materiam tali speciei determinatam. Quidam exponunt sic: Auro locus est in quo conflatur, id est generatur: cujus generatio vocatur conflatio, quia materia auri magis digesta est virtute caloris, quam aliorum metallorum; propter quod purius est atque ductilius. Aliqui quoque ita exponunt: Conflatur, id est, in fornace purgatur ab alieni mixtura metalli.
paras.en: [[28:1|and gold hath a place wherein it is melted|Et auro locus est in quo conflatur]]. According to Thomas, because gold is the purest, it is found for the most part already formed in its purity among the sands of rivers, because of the abundance of evaporation and the heat of the sand. Therefore he says, [[28:1|gold hath a place wherein it is melted|Auro locus est in quo conflatur]], because grains of gold are gathered from much sand and melted into one: which is not done in every place, but in certain fixed places, where the due proportion of the active power to a matter determined to such a species is found together. Some explain it thus: [[28:1|gold hath a place wherein it is melted|auro locus est in quo conflatur]], that is, is generated: its generation is called melting [conflatio: smelting or casting], because the matter of gold is more digested by the power of heat than that of the other metals; for which reason it is purer and more ductile. Others again explain it so: [[28:1|melted|Conflatur]], that is, purged in the furnace of any admixture of a foreign metal.

paras.t: Ferrum de terra tollitur: quod scilicet in terra quasi indigesta invenitur, hoc est in terra fæculenta, et nondum perfectam habet ferrum digestionem: cujus videlicet ferri mineria seu materia de terra accipitur, id est ex vapore humido resoluto ex terra, ut patuit. Et lapis solutus calore, in æs vertitur. Lapis enim proportionatus naturæ æris cui permiscetur, solutus calore ignis vehementis, in æs vertitur, dum id quod est de natura æris, per calorem eliquatur, ut asserit Thomas, secundum quem æs invenitur aliis incorporatum. Et ut aliqui dicunt, mineria æris, quæ lapis vocatur, quia ob sui duritiam similitudinem cum lapide quamdam sortitur, in æs vertitur. Porro Albertus hic scribit: Ferrum juxta argentum proportionaliter sumitur, et æs juxta aurum. Itaque ait: Ferrum de terra tollitur. Ferrum enim nascitur de argento fæculento et vivo, scabrosoque sulfure: a quibus si fæculentia scabrositasque tollantur, et maneat minerialis vis frigiditate congelans humidum, valde depuratum efficitur argentum, et lapis calore solutus in æs vertitur. Lapis (ut asserit Hermes) dicitur omne quod non evaporat in igne, eo quod sola coagulatione, quæ generatio lapidis est, generatur. Estque regulariter verum, ut in libro Meteororum habetur, quia omne quod coagulatur ex humido frigido, solvitur calido sicco, sicut argentum, aurum, ferrum, omniaque metalla quæ in profundo terræ gignuntur. In prima enim generatione, in lapide mixtum est æs, quod igne solvente liquescit ac depuratur.
paras.en: [[28:2|Iron is taken out of the earth|Ferrum de terra tollitur]]: that is, because it is found in earth that is as it were undigested, that is, in dreggy earth, and the iron has not yet a perfect digestion; the ore or matter of this iron, namely, is taken from the earth, that is, from the moist vapour released from the earth, as was shown. [[28:2|and stone melted with heat is turned into brass|Et lapis solutus calore, in æs vertitur]]. For a stone proportioned to the nature of the brass with which it is mixed, melted by the heat of a fierce fire, is turned into brass, while what is of the nature of brass is drawn out by the heat, as Thomas asserts, according to whom brass is found incorporated in other things. And, as some say, the ore of brass, which is called a stone because by its hardness it has a certain likeness to stone, is turned into brass. Albert, for his part, writes here: Iron is taken as answering to silver, and brass as answering to gold. And so he says: [[28:2|Iron is taken out of the earth|Ferrum de terra tollitur]]. For iron is born of dreggy quicksilver and rough sulphur [argentum vivum, literally living silver, is quicksilver; with sulphur it was held to be the principle of all metals]: and if the dregs and the roughness are taken from these, and the mineral power remains which congeals the moist by cold, there is produced silver, highly refined; [[28:2|and stone melted with heat is turned into brass|et lapis calore solutus in æs vertitur]]. Stone (as Hermes asserts) is the name for everything that does not evaporate in fire, because it is generated by coagulation alone, which is the generation of stone. And it is true as a rule, as is held in the book of the Meteors, that everything that is coagulated by the moist and cold is dissolved by the hot and dry, as silver, gold, iron, and all the metals that are produced in the depth of the earth. For in its first generation brass is mixed in the stone, and when fire dissolves it, it melts and is refined.

paras.t: Intenditque sanctus Job, quod in occultis terræ hoc principaliter non format nisi sapientia Dei, ad litteram insinuans, quod etiam in infimis terræ, vestigia sapientiæ Dei monstrantur. Unde summum et primum quod in naturæ effectibus investigatur, est sapientia Dei, qui est primum principium vitæ et esse ac luminis, virtutis quoque et pacis, in qua totus animus conquiescit. Ideo Baruch scripsit: Disce ubi sit prudentia, ubi virtus, ubi intellectus, ut scias simul ubi sit longiturnitas vitæ, ubi sit lumen oculorum et pax.
paras.en: And holy Job means that in the hidden places of the earth it is chiefly none other than the wisdom of God that forms this, suggesting according to the letter that even in the lowest parts of the earth traces of the wisdom of God are shown. Hence the highest and first thing that is searched out in the effects of nature is the wisdom of God, who is the first principle of life and of being and of light, of strength also and of peace, in which the whole mind comes to rest. Therefore Baruch wrote: [[Bar 3:14|Learn where is wisdom, where is strength, where is understanding: that thou mayst know also where is length of days and life, where is the light of the eyes, and peace|Disce ubi sit prudentia, ubi virtus, ubi intellectus, ut scias simul ubi sit longiturnitas vitæ, ubi sit lumen oculorum et pax]].

paras.t: Tempus posuit tenebris, id est, Deus præordinavit quando debeat esse nox, et quamdiu debeat perdurare. Successionem enim diei et noctis instituit, juxta illud Genesis: Dixitque Deus, Fiat lux. Et facta est lux. Et divisit lucem a tenebris; appellavitque lucem Diem, et tenebras Noctem. Albertus exponit sic: Tempus posuit tenebris, id est tempus generationis prædictorum posuit in tenebris, hoc est in tenebrosis terræ visceribus, ubi undique circumposita terra et mons, evaporationem fieri non permittunt, imo vaporem ad ima, ut inspissetur, reflectunt. Porro, omnia quæ in superficie terræ nascuntur et luce, aliquid vitæ participant, ut plantæ, animalia, homines.
paras.en: [[28:3|He hath set a time for darkness|Tempus posuit tenebris]], that is, God ordained beforehand when it should be night, and how long it should last. For he established the succession of day and night, according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 1:3|And God said: Be light made. And light was made.|Dixitque Deus, Fiat lux. Et facta est lux]] [[Gen 1:4|and he divided the light from the darkness|Et divisit lucem a tenebris]]; [[Gen 1:5|And he called the light Day, and the darkness Night|appellavitque lucem Diem, et tenebras Noctem]]. Albert explains it thus: [[28:3|He hath set a time for darkness|Tempus posuit tenebris]], that is, he set the time of the generation of the things mentioned in darkness, that is, in the dark bowels of the earth, where the earth and the mountain set round on every side do not allow evaporation to take place, but rather turn the vapour back to the depths, so that it may thicken. Whereas all things that are born on the surface of the earth and in the light share in some measure of life, as plants, animals, men.

paras.t: Et universorum finem, ipse considerat, id est causam eorum finalem, propter quam ea produxit. Nil enim frustra aut casualiter fecit, sed unumquodque ad debitum, convenientem seu naturalem finem præordinavit et condidit, prout spectat ad sapientem auctorem. Ideo Psalmista loquitur Deo: Numquid vane constituisti omnes filios hominum? Philosophus quoque: Natura, inquit, et Deus nil faciunt frustra. Thomas autem exponit sic: Universorum finem considerat, id est terminum resolutionis rerum.
paras.en: [[28:3|and the end of all things he considereth|Et universorum finem, ipse considerat]], that is, their final cause, for the sake of which he produced them. For he made nothing in vain or by chance, but ordained beforehand and made each thing for its due, fitting or natural end, as befits a wise maker. Therefore the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 88:48|hast thou made all the children of men in vain?|Numquid vane constituisti omnes filios hominum?]] And the Philosopher: Nature, he says, and God do nothing in vain. Thomas, however, explains it thus: [[28:3|the end of all things he considereth|Universorum finem considerat]], that is, the term of the dissolution of things.

paras.t: Lapidem quoque caliginis, id est rupem petrosam excelsam, solis ardore nigratam, et umbram mortis, id est profundissimam vallem sub monte jacentem, umbrosam, ad quam vitalis calor et lux solis raro et parum vel nunquam pertingit; dividit torrens, qui scilicet ex monte descendit, in quo nives resolvuntur, qui defluunt, a populo peregrinante, id est hinc inde pro necessariis vagante seu mendicante: qui circa unam torrentis ripam viam habet et graditur, sed ad aliam ripæ partem non patet ei accessus, quoniam torrens ob suam magnitudinem transmeari non valet. Solent etenim in quorumdam radicibus montium defluere immeabiles torrentes. Eos quos oblitus est pes egentis hominis, et invios, id est, torrens dividit a populo peregrinante quosdam habitantes ex alia parte torrentis. Interdum equidem in talibus inaccessibilibus locis pauci aliqui habitant, ad quos mendicantes, impediente in medio torrente, pertingere nequeunt: ideo illos habitatores dicitur pes egentis hominis esse oblitus, quia non vadit ad eos pro pane. Et quoniam habitatores illi manent in loco inaccessibili, additur, Et invios, quia via ad eos non patet de facili. Ita exponit Thomas.
paras.en: [[28:3|the stone also that is in the dark|Lapidem quoque caliginis]], that is, a high rocky crag blackened by the heat of the sun, [[28:3|and the shadow of death|et umbram mortis]], that is, a very deep valley lying beneath a mountain, full of shade, which the vital heat and the light of the sun reach seldom and little, or never: [[28:4|The flood divideth|dividit torrens]], that is, the one that comes down from the mountain on which the snows melt and flow down, [[28:4|from the people that are on their journey|a populo peregrinante]], that is, wandering hither and thither for their needs, or begging: they have a way along one bank of the torrent and walk there, but there is no access for them to the other side, because the torrent is too great to be crossed. For impassable torrents are wont to flow down at the roots of certain mountains. [[28:4|those whom the food of the needy man hath forgotten, and who cannot be come at|Eos quos oblitus est pes egentis hominis, et invios]]: that is, the torrent divides from the wayfaring people certain who live on the other side of it. For sometimes a few people live in such inaccessible places, whom the beggars cannot reach, because the torrent stands in the way between: and so the foot of the needy man is said to have forgotten those inhabitants, because it does not go to them for bread. And because those inhabitants live in an inaccessible place, it is added, [[28:4|and who cannot be come at|Et invios]], because the way to them is not easily open. So Thomas explains it.

paras.t: Albertus vero aliter, dicens: Lapidem, inquit, caliginis, id est in caligine (puta sub terra) natum, et umbram mortis, videlicet locum, vel locatum sub terra, ubi nil vitæ est, dividit torrens de monte cum impetu veniens, secumque trahens lapides, ligna et terram multam, per quæ obruit et occultat generata in imis, a populo peregrinante, id est variis hospitiis demorante in terra, quales præcipue sunt qui metallorum minerias quærunt; quos lapides caliginis oblitus est pes egentis hominis, quia eos ignorat, invenireque nescit, quum tamen ob indigentiam quærat thesauros; et invios, scilicet lapides, qui et caliginis lapides dicuntur, et etiam invii: quia in profundissimis terræ generantur, propter quod a paucissimis inveniuntur.
paras.en: Albert, however, explains it otherwise, saying: [[28:3|the stone|Lapidem]], he says, [[28:3|that is in the dark|caliginis]], that is, born in darkness (namely under the earth), [[28:3|and the shadow of death|et umbram mortis]], namely a place, or a thing placed, under the earth, where there is nothing of life, [[28:4|The flood divideth|dividit torrens]], coming from the mountain with force and dragging with it stones, wood and much earth, with which it overwhelms and hides the things generated in the depths, [[28:4|from the people that are on their journey|a populo peregrinante]], that is, staying in the land in various lodgings, such as are above all those who seek the ores of metals; [[28:4|those whom|quos]], the stones of darkness, [[28:4|the food of the needy man hath forgotten|oblitus est pes egentis hominis]], because he does not know them and cannot find them, though from his need he seeks treasures; [[28:4|and who cannot be come at|et invios]], namely the stones, which are called both stones of darkness and also inaccessible: because they are generated in the deepest parts of the earth, for which reason they are found by very few.

paras.t: Terra de qua oriebatur panis, id est sustentaculum vitæ, seu fructus de quo fit panis, in loco suo, igni subversa est; sicut in Genesi de subversione Pentapolis legitur, quæ igne et sulfure est subversa. Unde in libro Sapientiæ scribitur: Descendente igne in Pentapolim, quibus in testimonium nequitiæ fumigabunda constat terra deserta. Insuper sæpe contingit, ut sub terra habitabili atque arabili lateant venæ sulfureæ, ex quibus aliquando accenditur ignis per modum vaporis infra terram inclusi: fitque terræ motus, terram illam subvertens et inhabitabilem agens. Sic et de igneis vel sulfureis locis seu montibus Siciliæ fertur, quomodo terram vicinam infertilem faciant.
paras.en: [[28:5|The land, out of which bread grew|Terra de qua oriebatur panis]], that is, the support of life, or the fruit from which bread is made, [[28:5|in its place, hath been overturned with fire|in loco suo, igni subversa est]]; as is read in Genesis of the overthrow of Pentapolis, which was overthrown with fire and brimstone[[Gen 19:24||]][[Gen 19:25||]]. Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 10:6|when the fire came down upon Pentapolis|Descendente igne in Pentapolim]]: [[Wis 10:7|Whose land, for a testimony of their wickedness, is desolate, and smoketh|quibus in testimonium nequitiæ fumigabunda constat terra deserta]]. Moreover it often happens that beneath habitable and arable land there lie veins of sulphur, from which fire is sometimes kindled in the manner of a vapour shut in beneath the earth: and an earthquake comes about, which overturns that land and makes it uninhabitable. So too it is told of the fiery or sulphurous places or mountains of Sicily, how they make the land around them barren.

paras.t: Quid autem utilitatis, ordinante Dei sapientia, inde proveniat, subdit. Locus sapphiri lapides ejus, id est, locus generationis sapphiri, est inter lapillos hujusmodi terræ. Ibi enim gignuntur sapphiri. Siquidem, superabundante calore, resolutiones tam siccæ quam humidæ ad magnam digestionem perveniunt, ut ex eis aliqua pretiosa, ut lapides et metalla gignantur. Hinc ait Albertus: Dum igne liquefaciente mineriam, humidum eliquatur, quasi in vitri puritatem convertitur: in quod dum fumosum vaporis penetrat, sapphiri colorem sortitur. In talibus autem locis sapphiri multoties reperiuntur. Et gleba illius, videlicet terræ subversæ, aurum, id est, mineria auri est, quod generatur ex vaporatione humida, resoluta ex hujuscemodi terra. Dicitque Albertus: Generatio auri est ex humido multum claro argenti vivi, et ex terrestri sulfure multum depurato atque digesto, quod præcipue in talibus terræ glebis apparet.
paras.en: What profit comes of this, by the ordering of the wisdom of God, he adds: [[28:6|The stones of it are the place of sapphires|Locus sapphiri lapides ejus]], that is, the place where the sapphire is generated is among the little stones of such land. For sapphires are produced there. For when the heat is overabundant, both the dry and the moist exhalations come to a great digestion, so that some precious things, such as stones and metals, are generated from them. Hence Albert says: When the moist is drawn out by fire melting the ore, it is turned as it were into the purity of glass; and when the smoky part of the vapour penetrates it, it takes on the colour of sapphire. And in such places sapphires are often found. [[28:6|and the clods of it|Et gleba illius]], namely of the overturned land, [[28:6|are gold|aurum]], that is, it is the ore of gold, which is generated from a moist vapour released from such earth. And Albert says: Gold is generated from the very clear moisture of quicksilver and from earthy sulphur well refined and digested, which appears especially in such clods of earth.

paras.t: Semitam terræ talis ignoravit avis: quoniam aves terram hujusmodi vitant propter aeris corruptionem et sulfuris abundantiam, propter quæ in ea non inveniunt locum alimenti aut congruæ nidificationis. Nec intuitus est eam oculus vulturis, quia vitat eamdem: qui tamen a remotis intuetur. Allegat namque Albertus Avicennam, dicentem sexto de Naturalibus, quod (secundum opinionem quorumdam) oculus vulturis ad quingentas leucas cadavera videt. Aliqui textus habent, Oculos: et ita legit Gregorius, qui etiam accipit, Avis, ut est genitivi casus. Sicque sensus est: Semitam ignoravit avis, id est, terra ita subversa, experta non est semitas avium, quia non volant per eam; nec intuitus est, id est, nullus in ea vidit, oculos vulturis. Non calcaverunt eam filii institorum, id est, negotiatores filii negotiatorum talem terram devitant: nec pertransivit per eam leæna, quamvis per diversa decurrat prædam quærendo.
paras.en: [[28:7|the path|Semitam]] of such land the [[28:7|bird hath not known|ignoravit avis]]: because birds avoid such land on account of the corruption of the air and the abundance of sulphur, by reason of which they find in it no place for food or for fit nesting. [[28:7|neither hath the eye of the vulture beheld it|Nec intuitus est eam oculus vulturis]], because it avoids it, though it looks from far off. For Albert cites Avicenna, who says in the sixth book On Natural Things that (according to the opinion of some) the eye of the vulture sees carcasses five hundred leagues away. Some texts have Eyes [oculos, the accusative, so that the eyes are what is not seen]; and so Gregory reads it, who also takes Bird as being in the genitive case [avis can be nominative or genitive: the path of the bird]. And so the sense is: [[28:7|The bird hath not known the path|Semitam ignoravit avis]], that is, the land thus overturned has not known the paths of birds, because they do not fly over it; [[28:7|neither hath the eye of the vulture beheld it|nec intuitus est]], that is, no one in it has seen the eyes of the vulture. [[28:8|The children of the merchants have not trodden it|Non calcaverunt eam filii institorum]], that is, traders, the sons of traders, shun such land: [[28:8|neither hath the lioness passed by it|nec pertransivit per eam leæna]], though she runs about in many places seeking prey.

paras.t: Ad silicem, id est ad loca saxosa, lapidososque montes, extendit Deus manum, id est potestatem, suam, operando ibi magnifica, sicut subjungitur. Subvertit a radicibus montes, id est, funditus eos evertit atque destruxit: quod plenius superiori recordor loco expositum, quo habetur, Qui transtulit montes, et nescierunt hi quos subvertit.
paras.en: [[28:9|to the flint|Ad silicem]], that is, to stony places and rocky mountains, God [[28:9|hath stretched forth his hand|extendit Deus manum]], that is, his power, working mighty things there, as is added. [[28:9|he hath overturned mountains from the roots|Subvertit a radicibus montes]], that is, he overthrew them utterly and destroyed them: which I remember was explained more fully in an earlier place, where we have: [[Job 9:5|Who hath removed mountains, and they whom he overthrew in his wrath, knew it not|Qui transtulit montes, et nescierunt hi quos subvertit]].

paras.t: In petris rivos excidit. Hoc supernaturaliter fecit Deus bis per Moysen in deserto, ut legitur in Exodo et in Numeris. Unde fertur in Psalmo: Qui convertit petram in stagna aquarum, et rupes in fontes aquarum. Naturaliter quoque interdum per terræ motum erumpit rivus defluens inter lapides, qui prius latebat. Similiter interdum medium montium pertranseunt aquæ, quasi divina virtute essent excisi de petris. Sicque, In petris rivos, id est meatus rivorum, excidit, secundum illud Psalmi: Qui emittis fontes in convallibus; inter medium montium pertransibunt aquæ. Et omne pretiosum vidit oculus ejus. Quidquid enim in universo præclarum et carum est in corporalibus aut spiritualibus rebus, mens divina clarissime intuetur.
paras.en: [[28:10|In the rocks he hath cut out rivers|In petris rivos excidit]]. This God did supernaturally twice through Moses in the desert, as is read in Exodus[[Ex 17:6||]] and in Numbers[[Num 20:11||]]. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 113:8|Who turned the rock into pools of water, and the stony hill into fountains of waters.|Qui convertit petram in stagna aquarum, et rupes in fontes aquarum]] Naturally too a stream sometimes breaks out through an earthquake, flowing down among the stones, which before lay hidden. Likewise waters sometimes pass through the midst of mountains, as though by divine power they had been cut out of the rocks. And so [[28:10|In the rocks|In petris]] [[28:10|rivers|rivos]], that is, the channels of rivers, [[28:10|he hath cut out|excidit]], according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 103:10|Thou sendest forth springs in the vales: between the midst of the hills the waters shall pass.|Qui emittis fontes in convallibus; inter medium montium pertransibunt aquæ]] [[28:10|and his eye hath seen every precious thing|Et omne pretiosum vidit oculus ejus]]. For whatever is excellent and dear in the universe, in bodily or in spiritual things, the divine mind beholds most clearly.

paras.t: Profunda quoque fluviorum scrutatus est, id est, certe cognoscit, non per inquisitionem, sed per infallibilem inspectionem, quomodo dicitur scrutari corda et renes; et abscondita produxit in lucem, id est ad hominum cognitionem apertam, quia veritates difficiles, supernaturales, occultas manifeste revelat; ea quoque quæ latent sub terra seu alibi, facit inveniri et sciri. Hoc plenius dictum est atque expositum supra, ubi inter cetera dicitur: Qui revelat profunda de tenebris, et producit in lucem umbram mortis.
paras.en: [[28:11|The depths also of rivers he hath searched|Profunda quoque fluviorum scrutatus est]], that is, he knows them surely, not by inquiry but by an infallible beholding, in the way in which he is called [[Ps 7:10|the searcher of hearts and reins|scrutari corda et renes]] [Denis: he is said to search the hearts and reins; the margin's reference cannot be read, and the words are those of Ps 7:10, compare Jer 11:20 and Apoc 2:23]; [[28:11|and hidden things he hath brought forth to light|et abscondita produxit in lucem]], that is, to the open knowledge of men, because he plainly reveals truths that are difficult, supernatural and hidden; the things too that lie hidden under the earth or elsewhere he causes to be found and known. This was said and explained more fully above, where among other things it is said: [[Job 12:22|He discovereth deep things out of darkness, and bringeth up to light the shadow of death.|Qui revelat profunda de tenebris, et producit in lucem umbram mortis.]]

paras.t: Consequenter beatus Job declarat spiritualis boni dignitatem, quod electis et justis etiam partim in vita confertur præsenti. Sapientia vero ubi invenitur? tanquam dicat: Quum præfata corporalia bona, quæ hominibus pretiosa videntur, et frequenter injustis divinitus conceduntur, in determinatis sint locis, et situales origines habeant, sapientia tamen, quum incorporeum donum sit, spirituale et simplex, loco circumscriptive non continetur.
paras.en: Next blessed Job declares the dignity of the spiritual good which is conferred on the elect and the just, in part, even in the present life. [[28:12|But where is wisdom to be found|Sapientia vero ubi invenitur?]]? As if to say: Since the bodily goods mentioned, which seem precious to men and are often granted by God to the unjust, are in fixed places and have origins tied to a place, yet wisdom, since it is an incorporeal gift, spiritual and simple, is not contained in a place circumscriptively [that is, in the way a body is in a place, bounded by it].

paras.t: Loquitur autem de sapientia, non utique naturali et philosophica, neque de sapientia originaliter supernaturali, scilicet per revelationem primo accepta, quæ est sacræ Scripturæ notitia, prout sapientia illa ponitur donum gratiæ gratis datæ: de qua dicit Apostolus, Alii per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ. Talis quippe sapientia bonis et malis hominibus est communis, sicut et cetera dona gratiæ gratis datæ. Loquitur itaque de sapientia, quæ vere et proprie sapientia appellatur, videlicet de sapientia supernaturali infusa, quæ est unum et primum inter septem dona Spiritus Sancti, quæ solis et omnibus caritatem habentibus inest; per quam mens rectum sortitur judicium de divinis, de Deo et pertinentibus ad ipsum, bene judicans per saporem seu gustum internum et connaturalitatem affectus ad ipsum: quæ sapientia dicitur, quasi sapida scientia, id est caritate formata, et bonis actibus decorata, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Sapientia, secundum nomen est ejus. Ideo Dei dilectionem notitiamque includit, et per consequens gratiam gratum facientem, ceterasque virtutes infusas, quæ sine caritate non insunt, saltem quoad esse formatum atque completum. De hac sapientia dicitur: In malevolam animam non introibit sapientia, nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis. Quod autem sic nunc accipiatur sapientia, in processu hujus patebit capituli.
paras.en: He speaks, however, of wisdom: not indeed of natural and philosophical wisdom, nor of wisdom supernatural in its origin, that is, first received by revelation, which is the knowledge of Sacred Scripture, inasmuch as that wisdom is counted a gift of grace freely given [gratia gratis data: a grace given for the good of others, as prophecy or the word of wisdom, which does not of itself make its bearer holy]: of which the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|Alii per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]]. Such wisdom, indeed, is common to good and bad men alike, as are the other gifts of grace freely given. He speaks therefore of the wisdom that is truly and properly called wisdom, namely the supernatural infused wisdom which is the first of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]], and which is in all those who have charity, and in them alone; by it the mind obtains a right judgment of divine things, of God and of what belongs to him, judging well by an inward savour or taste and by a connaturality of affection towards him: and it is called wisdom as though savoury knowledge [sapientia, as if sapida scientia], that is, knowledge formed by charity and adorned with good acts, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 6:23|the wisdom of doctrine is according to her name|Sapientia, secundum nomen est ejus]]. Therefore it includes the love and the knowledge of God, and in consequence sanctifying grace [gratia gratum faciens: the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God], and the other infused virtues, which are not present without charity, at least as to their formed and complete being. Of this wisdom it is said: [[Wis 1:4|wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins|In malevolam animam non introibit sapientia, nec habitabit in corpore subdito peccatis]]. That wisdom is here taken in this way will appear in the course of this chapter.

paras.t: Et quis est locus intelligentiæ? Per intelligentiam, quidam hoc loco intelligunt intellectum: et sic accipit Thomas. Sed non videtur insinuare quomodo accipiat intellectum, qui valde multis modis accipitur, utpote pro substantia intellectuali, quemadmodum S. Dionysius angelos nominat intellectus supermundanos; pro potentia intellectiva, sicque dividitur in intellectum agentem et possibilem; pro habitu primorum principiorum, et ita Philosophus ponit eum inter quinque habitus intellectuales; pro habitu supernaturali infuso, quo ea quæ fidei sunt, intelliguntur et quodammodo penetrantur, rationes credendorum intuendo, et sic est unum de septem donis Spiritus Sancti; item pro actione intellectiva, scilicet cognitione mentali, quemadmodum ait Apostolus: Dabit tibi Dominus de omnibus intellectum. Videtur tamen Thomas innuere, quod capiat intellectum prout est habitus seu notitia principiorum, quæ in sacra doctrina ponuntur articuli fidei. Dicit etenim, quod intellectus seu intelligentia sit principium sapientiæ et scientiæ, scilicet quoad actum earum, secundum quod sunt habitus supernaturales infusi et dona. Sic quoque intelligentiam sumit Albertus. Juxta quod ultra rationabiliter diceretur, quod intellectus vel intelligentia sumitur jam prout est secundum inter septem dona Spiritus Sancti. Jam enim est sermo de intelligentia, quæ vitiosis non inest, sed virtuosis dumtaxat. Quemadmodum autem sapientia locum circumscribentem seu corporalem non habet, ita nec intelligentia: sed sicut Aristoteles ait, quod intellectus vel memoria est locus intelligibilium specierum, et juxta Scripturas, anima justi sedes est sapientiæ; sic intellectiva vis seu mens, locus est sapientiæ et intelligentiæ. Quod etiam Alphorabius peripateticus, in libro suo de Intellectu et intelligibili, ait.
paras.en: [[28:12|and where is the place of understanding?|Et quis est locus intelligentiæ?]] By understanding some here take the intellect; and so Thomas takes it. But he does not seem to indicate in what sense he takes intellect, which is taken in a great many ways: for an intellectual substance, as St. Dionysius calls the angels supermundane intellects; for the intellective power, and so it is divided into the agent intellect and the possible intellect; for the habit of first principles, and so the Philosopher places it among the five intellectual habits; for a supernatural infused habit by which the things of faith are understood and in a manner penetrated, by beholding the reasons of what is to be believed, and so it is one of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost; and again for the intellective act, that is, the knowing of the mind, as the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:7|the Lord will give thee in all things understanding|Dabit tibi Dominus de omnibus intellectum]]. Yet Thomas seems to hint that he takes intellect as the habit or knowledge of principles, which in sacred doctrine are the articles of faith. For he says that intellect or understanding is the principle of wisdom and of knowledge, namely as to their act, inasmuch as they are supernatural infused habits and gifts. Albert, too, takes understanding in this way. In keeping with which it might further be said with reason that intellect or understanding is here taken as the second of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost[[Is 11:2||]]. For the discourse now is of the understanding which is not in the vicious but only in the virtuous. And as wisdom has no circumscribing or bodily place, so neither has understanding: but as Aristotle says that the intellect, or the memory, is the place of intelligible species, and as according to the Scriptures the soul of the just is the seat of wisdom[[Wis 7:27||]][[Wis 7:28||]] [the margin reads Sap. vii, 7, 28; the thought is that of Wis 7:27–28, wisdom passing into holy souls and dwelling with them], so the intellective power, or mind, is the place of wisdom and understanding. And Alphorabius the Peripatetic says the same in his book On the Intellect and the Intelligible.

paras.t: Deinde ponit sapientiæ dignitatem. Nescit homo pretium ejus, quia impretiabilis est, nec æstimari potest aliquo bono corporali aut temporali, nec est commutabilis seu emptibilis pretio tali. Propter quod in Actis dictum est a principe Apostolorum Simoni mago: Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem, quoniam donum Dei existimasti pecunia possideri. Denique sapientia non amatur ut pretium, quoniam pretium propter aliud diligitur, ut dicitur sexto Ethicorum, quum sit quasi fidejussor futuræ necessitatis. Sapientia vero propter se ipsam diligitur, ad quam corporalia bona sunt ordinanda. Propter quod in Proverbiis scriptum est: Quid prodest divitias habere stulto, quum sapientiam emere non possit? In actu insuper sapientiæ omnes meliores philosophi, Aristoteles, Plato et eorum sequaces, Augustinus quoque cum præclaris theologis, felicitatem constituunt, præsertim quum Unigenitus Dei Patris dicat ad Patrem: Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum. Hinc in Proverbiis fertur: Melior est sapientia cunctis opibus, et omnia quæ desiderantur, huic non valent comparari.
paras.en: Next he sets out the dignity of wisdom. [[28:13|Man knoweth not the price thereof|Nescit homo pretium ejus]], because it is beyond price, and cannot be valued by any bodily or temporal good, nor exchanged or bought for any such price. This is why, in the Acts, the prince of the Apostles said to Simon Magus: [[Acts 8:20|Keep thy money to thyself, to perish with thee: because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money.|Pecunia tua tecum sit in perditionem, quoniam donum Dei existimasti pecunia possideri]] Further, wisdom is not loved as a price is, since a price is loved for the sake of something else, as is said in the sixth book of the Ethics, being as it were a surety for future need [the passage on money as a surety for future need is in book V, ch. 5, of Aristotle's Ethics as now divided]. Wisdom, however, is loved for its own sake, and bodily goods are to be ordered to it. This is why it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 17:16|What doth it avail a fool to have riches, seeing he cannot buy wisdom?|Quid prodest divitias habere stulto, quum sapientiam emere non possit?]] Moreover, all the better philosophers, Aristotle, Plato and their followers, and Augustine too with the eminent theologians, place happiness in the act of wisdom; above all since the only-begotten Son of God the Father says to the Father: [[John 17:3|this is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God|Hæc est vita æterna, ut cognoscant te verum Deum]]. Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:11|wisdom is better than all|Melior est sapientia cunctis]] riches, [[Prov 3:15|and all the things that are desired, are not to be compared to her|et omnia quæ desiderantur, huic non valent comparari]] [the margin gives Prov. viii, 11, which has the first words; the rest of Denis's wording is Prov 3:15].

paras.t: Deinde ponit loca in quibus sapientia non invenitur. Nec invenitur in terra suaviter viventium, id est in carnalibus et voluptuosis hominibus, qui vitam brutalem præeligunt, delectationes gustus et tactus Deo ac spiritualibus bonis vilissime præferentes: qui divina illuminatione, inflammatione caritativa, consolatione interna prorsus indigni sunt, tanquam inepti et incapaces ad talia, sicut vas stercoribus plenum, non est purissimi balsami susceptivum. Idcirco ad Corinthios ait Apostolus: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos; et: Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei. Isaias quoque inducit: Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? et quem intelligere faciet auditum? Ad quod respondet: Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere. Hinc Salomon loquitur: Qui amat vinum et pinguia, non erit sapiens. Et: Cogitavi a vino abstrahere carnem meam, ut animum meum transferrem ad sapientiam, devitaremque stultitiam.
paras.en: Next he sets out the places in which wisdom is not found: [[28:13|neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights|Nec invenitur in terra suaviter viventium]], that is, among carnal and pleasure-loving men, who choose the life of brutes, most basely preferring the delights of taste and touch to God and to spiritual goods; who are wholly unworthy of divine illumination, of the kindling of charity and of inward consolation, being as it were unfit for such things and incapable of them, just as a vessel full of dung cannot receive the purest balsam. Therefore the Apostle says to the Corinthians: [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect|Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos]]; and: [[1 Cor 2:14|the sensual man perceiveth not these things that are of the Spirit of God|Animalis homo non percipit ea quæ sunt Spiritus Dei]]. Isaias too brings in: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge? and whom shall he make to understand the hearing?|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? et quem intelligere faciet auditum?]] To which he answers: [[Is 28:9|them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|Ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]]. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 21:17|he that loveth wine, and fat things|Qui amat vinum et pinguia]] shall not be wise [the Vulgate has non ditabitur, shall not be rich; Denis reads non erit sapiens]. And: [[Eccles 2:3|I thought|Cogitavi]] [[Eccles 2:3|to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might turn my mind to wisdom, and might avoid folly|a vino abstrahere carnem meam, ut animum meum transferrem ad sapientiam, devitaremque stultitiam]].

paras.t: Abyssus dicit: Non est in me; et mare loquitur: Non est mecum. Per abyssum, intelligi potest Oceanus; per mare, quæcumque alia magna aquarum collectio. Hæc ergo facto seu materialiter dicunt, id est, consideranti ostendunt, seu cognoscendi occasionem ministrant, quod in eis non sit sapientia: quæ est spirituale bonum atque dignissima qualitas, cujus subjectum et locus non est nisi vitalis ac intellectualis essentia.
paras.en: [[28:14|The depth saith: It is not in me: and the sea saith: It is not with me|Abyssus dicit: Non est in me; et mare loquitur: Non est mecum]]. By the depth the Ocean can be understood; by the sea, any other great gathering of waters. These, then, say in fact or materially, that is, they show one who considers them, or give him occasion to know, that wisdom is not in them: for wisdom is a spiritual good and a most noble quality, whose subject and place can only be a living and intellectual being.

paras.t: Non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea, tanquam condignum pretium ejus, aut quod pro tali auro valeat emi. Aurum autem obrizum, inter differentias auri pretiosissimum est atque purissimum, optimique coloris. Unde obrizum dicitur, quasi obradians. Vel (secundum Albertum) aurum obrizum dicitur, quasi obrude, quia in sua manens natura, nulli alienæ naturæ permixtum est, nec ad usus aliquos fabricatum: quod in metallis pretiosissimum perhibetur. Hinc in Sapientis libro legitur: Omne aurum in comparatione illius arena est exigua. In Proverbiis quoque: Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam. Melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione auri et argenti. Unde subjungitur: Nec appendetur argentum in commutatione ejus, ut pro argento quasi pro pretio valeat comparari.
paras.en: [[28:15|The finest gold shall not purchase it|Non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea]], as a worthy price for it, nor such that it could be bought for such gold. Now obrizum gold [the Douay-Rheims's 'finest gold'] is, among the kinds of gold, the most precious and purest, and of the best colour. Hence it is called obrizum, as if obradians [shining forth]. Or (according to Albert) gold is called obrizum as if obrude [so printed], because, remaining in its own nature, it is mixed with no other nature, nor worked for any use: and this is held the most precious among metals. Hence we read in the book of the Wise Man: [[Wis 7:9|all gold, in comparison of her, is as a little sand|Omne aurum in comparatione illius arena est exigua]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 3:13|Blessed is the man that findeth wisdom|Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam]]. [[Prov 3:14|The purchasing thereof is better than the merchandise|Melior est acquisitio ejus negotiatione]] of gold and silver [Proverbs has 'of silver' only]. Hence it is added: [[28:15|neither shall silver be weighed in exchange for it|Nec appendetur argentum in commutatione ejus]], so that it could be had for silver, as for a price.

paras.t: Non conferetur, id est, non comparabitur sapientia, tinctis Indiæ coloribus, quia pulchrior est coloribus illis. Circa quod ait Albertus: Colores tincturarum eo pulchriores sunt, quo terra in qua fiunt, calidior est, et ad æquinoctialem, sub quo summum est temperamentum, vicinior. Et quoniam India sub æquinoctiali est, æqualiter distans a polis in quibus locus frigoris est, et æqualiter a tropicis in quibus locus summi caloris est, bis habens æstatem in anno, videlicet in Ariete et in Libra: ibi tincturæ pulcherrimæ sunt. Quos colores pulchritudine superat sapientia, quia omne corporale superat spiritualis pulchritudo. Propterea de sapientia legitur: Hæc est speciosior sole, et super omnem dispositionem stellarum, luci comparata invenitur prior. Thomas, per tinctos Indiæ colores, intelligit lapides pretiosos, diversis coloribus naturaliter tinctos, qui maxime reperiuntur in India.
paras.en: [[28:16|It shall not be compared|Non conferetur]], that is, wisdom shall not be likened, [[28:16|with the dyed colours of India|tinctis Indiæ coloribus]], because it is more beautiful than those colours. On which Albert says: The colours of dyes are the more beautiful the hotter the land in which they are made, and the nearer it is to the equinoctial line, under which is the most perfect balance of temperature. And since India lies under the equinoctial line, equally distant from the poles, where the region of cold is, and equally from the tropics, where the region of greatest heat is, and has summer twice in the year, namely in Aries and in Libra, the dyes there are most beautiful. These colours wisdom surpasses in beauty, because spiritual beauty surpasses everything bodily. Therefore we read of wisdom: [[Wis 7:29|she is more beautiful than the sun, and above all the order of the stars: being compared with the light, she is found before it|Hæc est speciosior sole, et super omnem dispositionem stellarum, luci comparata invenitur prior]]. Thomas understands by the dyed colours of India precious stones, naturally tinted with various colours, which are found chiefly in India.

paras.t: Insuper, sapientia non conferetur, nec lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo, vel sapphiro. Sardonychus seu sardonyx, lapis est similis rubicundissimæ terræ, et splendoris videtur purpurei: cujus lapidis decorem ac dignitatem sapientia vincit. Lapis iste (secundum Thomam) accendit mentem ad gaudium, acuitque ingenium, atque (ut dicitur) luxuriam pellit, hominem pudicum reddens et castum. Ideo pretiosissimus appellatur. Nam et tristitiam ac timorem a lapide onychino excitatos refrenat. Sardonychus quippe (secundum Thomam) ex lapidibus duobus componitur, puta ex sardio, prædictas proprietates efficientiasque habente, quæ et ob id attribuuntur sardonycho; [et onychino]. Denique super Apocalypsim de sardonycho scripsi ex dictis doctorum. Lapis iste candidus perhibetur, in rubeum colorem parumper declinans. Ejus tamen multa sunt genera. Nam alius rubeus fertur; alius bicolor, ut dictum est; alius triformiter coloratur, primum habens nigrum, medium candidum, superiorem rubeum: et iste est pretiosior. Sardonyx etiam humilem facit. Porro sapphirus, cœlestis et aerei est coloris. Qui corpus humanum vegetat, et membra consolidat, tactusque radiis solis, ardentem ex se mittit fulgorem. Ideo pretiosus asseritur.
paras.en: Further, wisdom shall not be compared [[28:16|with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire|lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo, vel sapphiro]]. Sardonychus, or sardonyx, is a stone like the reddest earth, and seems of a purple splendour: the beauty and worth of this stone wisdom surpasses. This stone (according to Thomas) kindles the mind to joy and sharpens the wit, and (so it is said) drives away lust, making a man modest and chaste. Therefore it is called most precious. For it also checks the sadness and fear stirred up by the onyx stone. For the sardonyx (according to Thomas) is made up of two stones, namely of the sardius, which has the properties and effects just named, and these are for that reason attributed to the sardonyx; and of the onyx [these last words stand in brackets in the edition]. I have also written of the sardonyx, from the sayings of the doctors, on the Apocalypse[[Apoc 21:20||]] [the margin gives Apoc. xxi; the sardonyx is named at v. 20]. This stone is said to be white, inclining a little towards red. But there are many kinds of it. For one is said to be red; another two-coloured, as has been said; another is coloured in three ways, having the first layer black, the middle white, the upper red: and this is the more precious. The sardonyx also makes a man humble. The sapphire, again, is of a heavenly and airy colour. It gives vigour to the human body and makes the limbs firm, and when struck by the rays of the sun it sends out a burning brightness. Therefore it is declared precious.

paras.t: Verumtamen S. Gregorius ait hic sardonychum et sapphirum pretiosos non esse, imo aliarum comparatione gemmarum vilissimos: quod ideo dicit, ut persuadeat sensum litteralem relinquendum, præsertim quoniam lapides istis pretiosiores hic reticentur. Potius tamen videtur cum littera standum, et affirmandum, quod sardonychus (sicut hic dicitur) pretiosissimus, id est valde pretiosus fuit, saltem in terra Job et tempore suo. Siquidem pretia lapidum non sunt eadem in omnibus locis, neque in cunctis temporibus, sicut et Thomas hic tangit. Verba B. Gregorii arctari queunt ad loca, in quibus hi lapides magis abundant, ita ut minus curentur. Nihilominus, absolute loquendo, sardonychus et sapphirus pretiosæ sunt gemmæ: quod ex canonica probatur Scriptura. Scriptum est enim Apocalypsis vicesimo primo: Fundamenta muri civitatis omni lapide pretioso ornata. Et ibi consequenter inter lapides pretiosos sapphirus sardonychusque ponuntur.
paras.en: Yet St. Gregory says here that the sardonyx and the sapphire are not precious, but rather the meanest of gems compared with others: and he says this to persuade us that the literal sense is to be left aside, especially since stones more precious than these are not mentioned here. It seems better, however, to stand by the letter, and to affirm that the sardonyx (as is said here) was most precious, that is, very precious, at least in Job's land and in his time. For the prices of stones are not the same in all places, nor at all times, as Thomas too touches on here. The words of blessed Gregory can be restricted to the places where these stones are more plentiful, so that they are less prized. Nevertheless, speaking absolutely, the sardonyx and the sapphire are precious gems: and this is proved from canonical Scripture. For it is written in the twenty-first chapter of the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:19|the foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with all manner of precious stones|Fundamenta muri civitatis omni lapide pretioso ornata]]. And there, next, the sapphire and the sardonyx are set among the precious stones[[Apoc 21:20||]].

paras.t: Non adæquabitur ei aurum, in pretiositate, vel splendore, seu pulchritudine, vel vitrum, in perspicuitate seu claritate. Horum enim decorem et luciditatem sapientia vincit. Unde constat istud ad litteram posse exponi, non obstante verbo dicentis oppositum. Ad diversa enim fit comparatio, non ad idem secundum incrementum, ut ille sentire se innuit. Nec commutabuntur pro ea, juxta æqualitatem valoris, vasa auri excelsa et eminentia, id est aurea vasa quantumcumque prævalida, et quantitate ac qualitate præclara. Artificialia namque sapientiæ nequeunt comparari: imo nullius pene sunt reputationis respectu ipsius. Ideo additur: Non commemorabuntur, id est, commemoratione indigna erunt, comparatione ejus: juxta illud Sapientiæ, Præposui illam regnis et sedibus, et divitias nihil esse duxi in comparatione illius.
paras.en: [[28:17|Gold|Non adæquabitur ei aurum]] (in preciousness, or splendour, or beauty) [[28:17|or crystal cannot equal it|vel vitrum]] (in transparency or clearness) [vitrum is glass; the Douay-Rheims has 'crystal']. For wisdom surpasses their beauty and brightness. Hence it is clear that this verse can be expounded according to the letter, notwithstanding the word of one who says the opposite [Gregory, above]. For the comparison is made with different things, not with the same thing in a rising scale, as he gives us to understand he thinks. [[28:17|neither shall any vessels of gold|vasa auri]] [[28:18|High and eminent things|excelsa et eminentia]] [[28:17|be changed for it|Nec commutabuntur pro ea]] in equal value; that is, golden vessels however massive, and outstanding in size and quality. For works of art cannot be compared with wisdom: indeed they are of almost no account beside it. Therefore it is added: [[28:18|shall not be mentioned|Non commemorabuntur]], that is, they will be unworthy of mention, [[28:18|in comparison of it|comparatione ejus]]: according to that of Wisdom: [[Wis 7:8|I preferred her before kingdoms and thrones, and esteemed riches nothing in comparison of her|Præposui illam regnis et sedibus, et divitias nihil esse duxi in comparatione illius]].

paras.t: Trahitur autem sapientia de occultis, id est, a supernaturali et secretissima omnium causa Deo suscipitur, impetratur et hauritur sapientia ista, videlicet ab incomprehensibili bonitate, caritate et pietate ejus, et ex abysso ineffabili judiciorum Dei. Unde contingit, ut uni hanc sapientiam magis quam alteri præstet. Per occultam quoque pœnitentiam ac præparationem homo ad eam pertingit, atque tam occulte conceditur, ut lateat recipientes eo modo, quo de caritatis inexsistentia exstant ambigui. Præterea sapientia acquisita, ex secretis rerum creatarum proprietatibus, naturis, operibus atque ordinibus trahitur, id est, considerando talia invenitur.
paras.en: [[28:18|but wisdom is drawn out of secret places|Trahitur autem sapientia de occultis]]: that is, this wisdom is received, obtained and drawn from God, the supernatural and most secret cause of all things, namely from his incomprehensible goodness, charity and loving-kindness, and out of the unspeakable abyss of God's judgments. Hence it comes about that he grants this wisdom to one more than to another. By hidden penance and preparation, too, a man attains to it; and it is granted so secretly that it lies hidden from those who receive it, in the same way as they remain uncertain whether charity is in them. Acquired wisdom, moreover, is drawn from the secret properties, natures, workings and orders of created things, that is, it is found by considering such things.

paras.t: […] Juxta Gregorium, πᾶν Græce, Latine dicitur omne. Unde topazion, quoniam omni colore resplendet, quasi topandion appellatur. Itaque gemma hæc pretiosissima omni fulget colore, quamvis color aureus et aereus in ipsa abundent. Quæ dum solis luce perfunditur, jubar suum undique fundit, omniumque gemmarum superat claritatem, in suum adspectum maxime trahens adstantes. Hæc gemmarum amplissima, regibus est tam cara, ut ea nil carius inter divitias suas habere se reputent. Valetque contra iram atque lunaticam passionem. Quæ ab Æthiopia venit. Nec tincturæ mundissimæ componentur, id est, tincturæ quantumlibet puræ pretiosissimarum vestium, poni non poterunt pro condigno sapientiæ pretio.
paras.en: […] [about two lines are unreadable in the scan here; they probably began with the lemma: The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it] According to Gregory, pan in Greek is omne [all] in Latin. Hence it is called topazion, as if topandion, because it shines with every colour. And so this most precious gem glitters with every colour, though the golden and the airy colour abound in it. When it is bathed in the light of the sun, it pours out its radiance on every side, and surpasses the brightness of all gems, drawing the eyes of those standing by to itself above all. This, the most splendid of gems, is so dear to kings that they reckon they have nothing dearer among their riches. It avails, too, against anger and the lunatic affliction. It comes from Ethiopia. [[28:19|neither shall it be compared to the cleanest dyeing|Nec tincturæ mundissimæ componentur]], that is, dyes of the most precious garments, however pure, cannot be set down as a worthy price for wisdom.

paras.t: Unde ergo sapientia venit? id est, quis est dator ipsius? et quæ origo unde emanat? Et quis est locus intelligentiæ? Hoc jam supra interrogavit, sicut expositum est: quærit enim in quo originaliter sit, et cui infundatur.
paras.en: [[28:20|Whence then cometh wisdom?|Unde ergo sapientia venit?]] that is, who is its giver, and what is the source from which it flows? [[28:20|and where is the place of understanding?|Et quis est locus intelligentiæ?]] He has asked this already above, as has been explained: for he asks in what it is at its source, and into whom it is poured.

paras.t: Abscondita est ab oculis omnium viventium. Hoc quidam de increata Sapientia interpretantur, quam nullus in hac vita per speciem contemplatur, vita vivens mortali atque humana. Sed quia de sapientia quæ donum est, sermo fuit hucusque, de illa continuanda est expositio. Ista ergo abscondita est ab oculis omnium viventium: vel quia corporalibus oculis non videtur, quum sit spirituale intellectualeque bonum: vel quoniam latet viventes omnes qui vivunt solum vita naturæ, secundum se ipsos, non secundum caritatem et gratiam Dei (quomodo ait Apostolus: Vivo autem, jam non ego; vivit vero in me Christus); vel quoniam viatores certitudinaliter scire non valent se sapientiam hanc habere, nisi per revelationem, sicut nec caritatem, quæ huic dono inseparabiliter est conjuncta. Unde habentibus sapientiam istam, scripsit Apostolus: Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo.
paras.en: [[28:21|It is hid from the eyes of all living|Abscondita est ab oculis omnium viventium]]. Some interpret this of the uncreated Wisdom, which no one living a mortal and human life contemplates in this life by sight [per speciem: face to face, as opposed to by faith]. But since the discourse so far has been about the wisdom that is a gift, the exposition must go on about that. This, then, is hid from the eyes of all living: either because it is not seen with bodily eyes, being a spiritual and intellectual good; or because it is hidden from all the living who live only the life of nature, according to themselves, not according to the charity and grace of God (as the Apostle says: [[Gal 2:20|And I live, now not I: but Christ liveth in me|Vivo autem, jam non ego; vivit vero in me Christus]]); or because wayfarers [those still on the way, in this life] cannot know with certainty that they have this wisdom, except by revelation, as neither can they know that they have charity, which is inseparably joined to this gift. Hence the Apostle wrote to those who have this wisdom: [[Col 3:3|For you are dead: and your life is hid with Christ in God.|Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo]]

paras.t: Volucres quoque cœli latet.
