Hoc dicitur contra […] avibus ponebant sapientiæ participationem tam altam, quod homo ex illis volucribus perduceretur ad futurorum notitiam: quamvis per volucres cœli, homines ingeniosi, seu leves et animosi possint intelligi, qui superbiæ suæ demerito hac sapientia destituuntur.
paras.en: [[28:21|and the fowls of the air know it not|Volucres quoque cœli latet]]. This is said against […] [about two lines are unreadable in the scan here] attributed to birds a share in wisdom so high that man could be brought by those birds to the knowledge of things to come: although by the fowls of the air may be understood clever men, or flighty and proud ones, who for the demerit of their pride are deprived of this wisdom.

paras.t: Perditio et mors, id est dæmones et reprobi mortui, dixerunt: Auribus nostris interioribus vel exterioribus, audivimus famam ejus, id est præconia sapientiæ hujus, sed ipsam non possedimus permanenter; juxta illud Sapientis, Justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis.
paras.en: [[28:22|Destruction and death|Perditio et mors]], that is, the demons and the reprobate dead, [[28:22|have said: With our ears|dixerunt: Auribus nostris]], inward or outward, [[28:22|we have heard the fame thereof|audivimus famam ejus]], that is, the praises of this wisdom, but we have not possessed it lastingly; according to that of the Wise Man: [[Wis 5:6|the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis]].

paras.t: Denique, præinductis verbis consonant quæ in Baruch scripta sunt: Quis invenit locum sapientiæ? aut quis introivit in thesauros ejus? Quis ascendit in cœlum, et accepit eam, et eduxit eam de nubibus? Quis transfretavit mare, et invenit eam, et attulit illam super aurum electum? Non est qui possit scire viam ejus, neque qui excogitet semitas ejus; sed qui scit universa, novit et adinvenit eam prudentia sua. Hoc est quod subditur.
paras.en: Further, with the words set down above agree those written in Baruch: [[Bar 3:15|Who hath found out her place? and who hath gone in to her treasures?|Quis invenit locum sapientiæ? aut quis introivit in thesauros ejus?]] [[Bar 3:29|Who hath gone up into heaven, and taken her, and brought her down from the clouds?|Quis ascendit in cœlum, et accepit eam, et eduxit eam de nubibus?]] [[Bar 3:30|Who hath passed over the sea, and found her, and brought her preferably to chosen gold?|Quis transfretavit mare, et invenit eam, et attulit illam super aurum electum?]] [[Bar 3:31|There is none that is able to know her ways, nor that can search out her paths|Non est qui possit scire viam ejus, neque qui excogitet semitas ejus]]; [[Bar 3:32|But he that knoweth all things, knoweth her, and hath found her out with his understanding|sed qui scit universa, novit et adinvenit eam prudentia sua]]. This is what follows.

paras.t: Deus intelligit viam ejus, id est modum et proprietatem sapientiæ hujus, et qualiter acquiratur ac infundatur, omnemque ejus processum: et ipse novit locum illius, id est mentes eorum quibus infunditur: quas noscit per approbationem, sicut ad Moysen ait: Te ipsum novi ex nomine. Et Apostolus dicit: Novit Dominus qui sunt ejus. Sapiens quoque: Neminem diligit Deus, nisi qui cum sapientia inhabitat. Denique ipsemet Deus est primus summusque sapientiæ locus: in quo solo plenitudo sapientiæ continetur, a quo omnis sapientia derivatur, qui solus comprehensive et plene noscit se ipsum.
paras.en: [[28:23|God understandeth the way of it|Deus intelligit viam ejus]], that is, the manner and property of this wisdom, and how it is acquired and infused, and its whole course: [[28:23|and he knoweth the place thereof|et ipse novit locum illius]], that is, the minds of those into whom it is poured, which he knows by approving them [that is, with the knowledge by which he owns them as his], as he says to Moses: [[Ex 33:17|thee I have known by name|Te ipsum novi ex nomine]]. And the Apostle says: [[2 Tim 2:19|the Lord knoweth who are his|Novit Dominus qui sunt ejus]]. The Wise Man too: [[Wis 7:28|God loveth none but him that dwelleth with wisdom|Neminem diligit Deus, nisi qui cum sapientia inhabitat]]. Lastly, God himself is the first and highest place of wisdom: in him alone the fulness of wisdom is contained, from him all wisdom is derived, and he alone knows himself comprehensively and fully.

paras.t: Ipse enim fines mundi intuetur, id est finem cujuslibet creaturæ, ad quem ipsa spiritualiter creata et ordinata ab ipso est. Fines etiam mundi, id est extrema universi vel suprema in creaturis et terminos omnium, intuetur, juxta illud Sapientiæ: Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter. Quoniam ergo scit finem rationalis creaturæ, sapientiam ei infundit, per quam ultimo fini qui Deus est, conjungatur. Et omnia quæ sub cœlo sunt, respicit. Idcirco novit sapientiæ locum. Omnia enim (juxta Apostolum) nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus. In Ecclesiastico quoque scriptum est: Domino Deo antequam crearentur, omnia sunt cognita. Omnia enim in divina essentia tanquam in superclarissimo exemplari et speculo fontali atque causali principio, universorum rationibus idealiter pleno, æternaliter certissimeque resplendent. Ideo cognoscendo se ipsum, omnia contemplatur.
paras.en: [[28:24|For he beholdeth the ends of the world|Ipse enim fines mundi intuetur]], that is, the end of every creature, to which it has been spiritually created and ordered by him. He beholds the ends of the world also in this sense: the extremes of the universe, or the highest among creatures, and the bounds of all things; according to that of Wisdom: [[Wis 8:1|She reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily, and ordereth all things sweetly|Attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit omnia suaviter]]. Since, then, he knows the end of the rational creature, he pours wisdom into it, through which it may be joined to its last end, which is God. [[28:24|and looketh on all things that are under heaven|Et omnia quæ sub cœlo sunt, respicit]]. Therefore he knows the place of wisdom. For [[Heb 4:13|all things|Omnia enim]] (according to the Apostle) [[Heb 4:13|are naked and open to his eyes|nuda et aperta sunt oculis ejus]]. In Ecclesiasticus too it is written: [[Ecclus 23:29|all things were known to the Lord God, before they were created|Domino Deo antequam crearentur, omnia sunt cognita]]. For all things shine forth in the divine essence, eternally and most certainly, as in an exemplar and mirror of surpassing clearness, a fountain and causal principle, full, in the manner of ideas, of the reasons of all things [rationes: the eternal patterns of things in the mind of God]. Therefore, in knowing himself, he contemplates all things.

paras.t: Qui fecit ventis pondus, id est, inclinationem eis impressit, qua huc illucque moventur. Unde (secundum Augustinum) amor et inclinatio rei, est quasi pondus ipsius, quoniam instar ponderis trahit eam ad locum aptum, vel ad amatum, aut ad quoddam conveniens. Albertus allegat Avicennam, dicentem: Ventus est vapor terrenus aerem fortiter impellens, cui pondus datur, dum exsufflationi ascensionique ejus terminus certus præfigitur. Unde in apocryphis Esdræ angelus Uriel loquitur Esdræ: Pondera mihi ventum. Et aquas appendit in mensura, id est, vaporabiliter elevat eas, atque in nubibus servat in certa mensura secundum ordinem sapientiæ suæ, prout novit terræ nascentibus expedire, vel prout complacet sibi. In mensura enim magnitudinis ac temporis eas suspendit, determinans quantum concrescant, et quando descendant. Imo, omnia in numero, mensura et pondere fecit, ut Sapiens scribit.
paras.en: [[28:25|Who made a weight for the winds|Qui fecit ventis pondus]], that is, he impressed on them an inclination by which they are moved hither and thither. Hence (according to Augustine) the love and inclination of a thing is as it were its weight, since like a weight it draws it to its fitting place, or to what it loves, or to something suited to it. Albert cites Avicenna, who says: Wind is an earthy vapour driving the air strongly; it is given weight when a fixed limit is set to its blowing out and its rising. Hence in the apocryphal book of Esdras the angel Uriel says to Esdras: Weigh me the wind [the margin gives IV Esdr. iv, a book not in the Douay-Rheims canon; at 4 Esdras 4:5 the angel says: Weigh me the weight of fire, or measure me the blast of the wind]. [[28:25|and weighed the waters by measure|Et aquas appendit in mensura]], that is, he raises them as vapour and keeps them in the clouds in a fixed measure, according to the order of his wisdom, as he knows to be good for what grows from the earth, or as pleases him. For he holds them suspended in a measure of size and of time, determining how much they gather and when they come down. Indeed, he made all things in number, measure and weight, as the Wise Man writes[[Wis 11:21||]].

paras.t: Quando ponebat pluviis legem, id est, naturalem cursum, modum et ordinem eis impressit, quomodo et ubi ac quando descenderent, et viam procellis, id est ventis seu tempestatibus ac undis marinis, sonantibus, quia cum sono et impetu tendunt: quibus viam, id est certum motus et actionis iter ac modum, præstitit.
paras.en: [[28:26|When he gave a law for the rain|Quando ponebat pluviis legem]], that is, he impressed on them a natural course, manner and order, how and where and when they should come down, [[28:26|and a way for the sounding storms|et viam procellis]], that is, for the winds or tempests and the waves of the sea, sounding because they move with noise and violence: to these he gave a way, that is, a fixed path and manner of motion and action.

paras.t: Tunc, scilicet in principio, dum ista creavit et ordinavit, vidit illam, id est, sapientiam in se ipso cognovit, non aliunde accepit; et enarravit, id est, aliis eam communicavit et inspiravit, videlicet angelis, vel in eorum creatione, vel confirmatione; et præparavit, id est, hominibus eam dare disposuit, eorumque corda ad illam aptavit; et investigavit, id est, in aliis eam discussit, inquisivit et consideravit an veraciter eam haberent; et quos invenit ea privatos, abjecit. Vel, Investigavit, id est, ab hominibus eam investigari fecit, corda eorum movens ad adeptionem profectumque ejus.
paras.en: [[28:27|Then|Tunc]], namely in the beginning, when he created and ordered these things, [[28:27|he saw it|vidit illam]], that is, he knew wisdom in himself, and did not receive it from elsewhere; [[28:27|and declared|et enarravit]], that is, he communicated it to others and breathed it into them, namely the angels, either in their creation or in their confirmation; [[28:27|and prepared|et præparavit]], that is, he determined to give it to men, and fitted their hearts for it; [[28:27|and searched it|et investigavit]], that is, he examined, inquired and considered it in others, whether they truly had it; and those whom he found without it he cast off. Or, [[28:27|searched|Investigavit]], that is, he made it be searched for by men, moving their hearts to gain it and to make progress in it.

paras.t: Et dixit homini, scilicet primo parenti, et ceteris ad hoc electis, allocutione interna seu inspiratione angelica. Uni quoque homini hoc per alium insinuavit. Ecce timor Domini ipsa est sapientia. Timor Domini non est sapientia per identitatem, quia realiter differunt, et distinguuntur subjecto, quum timor sit in appetitu seu voluntate.
paras.en: [[28:28|And he said to man|Et dixit homini]], namely to our first parent, and to the others chosen for this, by inward speech or by the inspiration of an angel. To one man, too, he made this known through another. [[28:28|Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom|Ecce timor Domini ipsa est sapientia]]. The fear of the Lord is not wisdom by identity, for they really differ, and are distinguished by their subject, since fear is in the appetite or will [and wisdom in the intellect].

paras.t: Porro timor est triplex: puta, servilis, qui non est sapientia nisi a remoto, disponendo ad eam. Facit enim vitare peccata timore pœnarum, non Dei amore, nec zelo justitiæ: ideo nudus et informis est, seu absque caritate. Secundus, est timor initialis, quo vitatur peccatum partim amore Dei æquitatisque zelo, et partim pœnarum formidine. Hic itaque timor est sapientia non per essentiam, sed per causam: sicut notitia dicitur amor, et dies dicitur latio solis super nostrum horizontem. Timor autem initialis realiter idem est cum timore filiali: ideo simul tempore cum sapientia quæ donum est, datur, inest, atque infunditur, sicut et caritas ac cetera dona caritati inseparabiliter juncta. Si ergo hic timor initialis est causa sapientiæ hujus, et de ipso exponitur illud in Psalmo, Initium sapientiæ timor Domini: hoc sumi oportet, quantum ad profectum et actum sapientiæ hujus, non quantum ad habitum seu essentiam ejus, quia per creationem infunditur. Quo enim quis peccata plenius atque sincerius vitat, eo in dono sapientiæ amplius crescit. Porro tertius, est timor filialis, qui ex caritate procedit: quo vitatur peccatum, ne Deus inhonoretur aut offendatur, seu deseratur vel deserat. Hic timor potest sapientia nominari, per quamdam inclusionem et propinquitatem ad eam: siquidem caritatem magnam sapientiamque includit. De quo scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Plenitudo sapientiæ timere Deum.
paras.en: Now fear is threefold. First, servile fear, which is wisdom only remotely, by disposing to it. For it makes one avoid sins through fear of punishment, not through the love of God nor zeal for justice: therefore it is bare and unformed [informis: not given its form by charity], that is, without charity. The second is initial fear [the fear of beginners, partly servile and partly filial], by which sin is avoided partly from the love of God and zeal for equity, and partly from dread of punishment. This fear, then, is wisdom not by essence but by cause [that is, it is called wisdom because it brings wisdom about]: as knowledge is called love, and day is called the course of the sun over our horizon. Initial fear, however, is really the same as filial fear: therefore it is given, is present and is infused at the same time as the wisdom that is a gift, as are charity and the other gifts inseparably joined to charity. If, then, this initial fear is the cause of this wisdom, and that saying in the Psalm, [[Ps 110:10|The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom|Initium sapientiæ timor Domini]], is expounded of it, this must be taken of the progress and act of this wisdom, not of its habit or essence, for that is infused by creation. For the more fully and sincerely a man avoids sins, the more he grows in the gift of wisdom. The third, again, is filial fear, which proceeds from charity: by it sin is avoided lest God be dishonoured or offended, or be forsaken, or forsake. This fear may be called wisdom by a certain inclusion of it and nearness to it, since it includes great charity and wisdom. Of it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:20|To fear God is the fulness of wisdom|Plenitudo sapientiæ timere Deum]].

paras.t: Et recedere a malo, id est a peccato se elongare, est intelligentia: loquendo de prædicatione per causam, quemadmodum de sapientia dictum est. In hoc enim intelligentia consistit, perficitur et monstratur, quod omnis culpa abjicitur, discernendo inter bonum et malum, verum et falsum: per quod mens in dono intellectus perficitur, ut ea quæ fidei sunt, lucide contempletur.
paras.en: [[28:28|and to depart from evil|Et recedere a malo]], that is, to withdraw oneself from sin, [[28:28|is understanding|est intelligentia]]: speaking of predication by cause [one thing called the other because it causes it], as was said of wisdom. For in this understanding consists, is perfected and is shown, that every fault is cast off, by discerning between good and evil, true and false: by which the mind is perfected in the gift of understanding, so as to contemplate clearly the things that are of faith.

paras.t: Ex quibus omnibus Job intendit, quod præsentis vitæ prosperitas summa non in temporalibus, exterioribus et caducis rebus consistat, sed in actu sapientiæ et intelligentiæ: quod in sæculo isto non fit, nisi timendo Deum vitandoque malum.
paras.en: From all of this Job means that the highest prosperity of the present life does not consist in temporal, outward and perishable things, but in the act of wisdom and understanding: and in this world that comes about only by fearing God and avoiding evil.

28.title: Expositio mystica ejusdem capituli vicesimi octavi.
28.title_en: Mystical exposition of the same twenty-eighth chapter

paras.t: Habet argentum venarum suarum principia, et auro locus est in quo conflatur. Frequenter jam patuit, argento, nitorem eloquentiæ, seu splendida verba sacræ Scripturæ, auro autem, claritatem sapientiæ, seu caritatis fervorem signari. Venæ itaque hujus spiritualis argenti, sunt libri Scripturæ canonicæ, ex quibus velut ex venis, rivuli sanctorum ducuntur profluuntque verborum. Principia autem venarum, exordia sunt librorum. Insuper, locus in quo conflatur, sunt corda fidelium, in quibus sapientiæ donum locatur, et adversis probatur, caritas quoque accenditur: imo et per creationem infunditur, et crescendo quasi conflatur.
paras.en: [[28:1|Silver hath beginnings of its veins|Habet argentum venarum suarum principia]], [[28:1|and gold hath a place wherein it is melted|et auro locus est in quo conflatur]]. It has often been shown already that by silver is signified the brightness of eloquence, or the splendid words of Holy Scripture, and by gold the clearness of wisdom, or the fervour of charity. The veins, then, of this spiritual silver are the books of canonical Scripture, from which, as from veins, the rivulets of the words of the saints are drawn and flow forth. And the beginnings of the veins are the openings of the books. Further, [[28:1|a place wherein it is melted|locus in quo conflatur]] are the hearts of the faithful, in which the gift of wisdom is placed and is proved by adversities, and charity too is kindled: nay, it is even infused by creation, and by growing is, as it were, melted [conflatur: fused and refined, as metal in the furnace].

paras.t: Ferrum de terra tollitur: id est, homo justus ac solidus, veri æquique tenax, de terrena conversatione frequenter ad perfectionem hanc gratiæ, Deo miserante ac operante, provehitur. Cujus etiam origo terrena est, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Omnes homines terra et cinis. Et in Genesi: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ. Lapis, id est peccator lapidei cordis, ad divinorum susceptionem eloquiorum durus, solutus calore, id est divini amoris fervore ab hac duritia resolutus, et pius beneque mollis effectus, in æs vertitur, id est, fortis et constans efficitur, amando splendens, et docendo instar æris sonorus.
paras.en: [[28:2|Iron is taken out of the earth|Ferrum de terra tollitur]]: that is, a just and solid man, holding fast to truth and equity, is often brought forward from an earthly conversation [that is, manner of life] to this perfection of grace, God having mercy and working. His origin, too, is earthly, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 17:31|all men are earth and ashes|Omnes homines terra et cinis]]. And in Genesis: God [[Gen 2:7|formed man of the slime of the earth|Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ]]. [[28:2|stone|Lapis]], that is, the sinner of stony heart, hard to receive the divine words, [[28:2|melted with heat|solutus calore]], that is, released from this hardness by the fervour of divine love, and made devout and well softened, [[28:2|is turned into brass|in æs vertitur]], that is, is made strong and constant, shining by loving, and by teaching resounding like brass.

paras.t: Tempus posuit tenebris. Tenebræ, sunt homines vitiosi, juxta illud Joannis: Lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt. Conversis quoque ad lucem justitiæ loquitur Paulus: Fuistis aliquando tenebræ. His tenebris posuit Deus tempus pœnitendi, ut emendati salventur, juxta illud Isaiæ: Propterea exspectat Dominus ut misereatur vestri. Et Petrus ait: Patienter agit Dominus propter vos, nolens aliquos perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reverti. Insuper, posuit Deus tempus his tenebris, quia præfixit quamdiu eos impœnitentes in suis perversitatibus sustinebit: et pondere ac tempore impietatis eorum completis, mox aufert damnatque eos. Propter quod in Genesi ait: Nondum impletæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum. Et Christus in Evangelio loquens Judæis incredulis: Implete, inquit, mensuram patrum vestrorum. Et universorum, videlicet tam electorum quam reproborum, finem considerat, id est qualiter quisque viam suam hic terminet, quomodo moriatur, in qua affectione et dispositione suæ mentis a corpore separetur; et secundum hoc judicat eum. Quod enim angelis est ruina, hoc hominibus est mors, secundum Damascenum. Ideo, sicut angeli mali inconvertibiliter manent in ea affectione et dispositione, in qua ceciderunt; sic animæ in ea permanent dispositione et affectione, in qua a corpore separantur. Quod in Ecclesiaste Salomon innuens, ait: Si ceciderit lignum ad austrum, aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit.
paras.en: [[28:3|He hath set a time for darkness|Tempus posuit tenebris]]. The darkness is vicious men, according to that of John: [[John 1:5|the light shineth in darkness: and the darkness did not comprehend it|Lux in tenebris lucet, et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt]]. And Paul says to those converted to the light of justice: [[Eph 5:8|you were heretofore darkness|Fuistis aliquando tenebræ]]. For this darkness God hath set a time of repentance, that being amended they may be saved, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 30:18|Therefore the Lord waiteth that he may have mercy on you|Propterea exspectat Dominus ut misereatur vestri]]. And Peter says: The Lord [[2 Pet 3:9|dealeth patiently for your sake, not willing that any should perish, but that all should return to penance|Patienter agit Dominus propter vos, nolens aliquos perire, sed omnes ad pœnitentiam reverti]]. Moreover, God hath set a time for this darkness because he has fixed beforehand how long he will bear with them while they remain unrepentant in their perversities: and when the weight and the time of their impiety are complete, he soon takes them away and condemns them. For this reason he says in Genesis: [[Gen 15:16|as yet the iniquities of the Amorrhites are not at the full|Nondum impletæ sunt iniquitates Amorrhæorum]]. And Christ in the Gospel, speaking to the unbelieving Jews: [[Matt 23:32|Fill ye up|Implete]], he says, [[Matt 23:32|the measure of your fathers|mensuram patrum vestrorum]]. And [[28:3|the end of all things|universorum]], namely of the elect as well as of the reprobate, [[28:3|he considereth|finem considerat]]: that is, how each man ends his way here, how he dies, in what affection and disposition of his mind he is separated from the body; and according to this he judges him. For what the fall is to the angels, death is to men, according to Damascene. Therefore, as the wicked angels remain unchangeably in the affection and disposition in which they fell, so souls remain in the disposition and affection in which they are separated from the body. Hinting at this, Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:3|If the tree fall to the south, or to the north, in what place soever it shall fall, there shall it be|Si ceciderit lignum ad austrum, aut ad aquilonem, in quocumque loco ceciderit, ibi erit]].

paras.t: Lapidem quoque caliginis, id est tenebrosum, induratum, perfidumque populum Judæorum: de quo Dominus loquitur Ezechieli, Filii indomabili corde sunt; et umbram mortis, id est gentiles incredulos, morte peccati fuscatos, dividit torrens, id est inundatio divinæ ultionis: de qua illud Danielis accipi potest, Fluvius igneus rapidusque egrediebatur a facie ejus, videlicet Dei; a populo peregrinante, id est ab electis, qui in vita hac vere sunt viatores, peregrini et hospites, præsentia contemnendo atque cœlestia ferventer ac jugiter appetendo. De quibus ad Hebræos scribit Apostolus: Confitentes quia peregrini et hospites sunt super terram. Prædicta itaque pœna et ultio Dei, in die judicii istos ab invicem dividet, quando reprobi ibunt in ignem æternum, electi vero in vitam æternam. Unde in Isaia legitur: Spiritus Domini velut torrens inundans ad perdendas gentes in nihilum. De quibus subjungitur: eos quos oblitus est pes egentis hominis, id est reprobos, crudeles et immisericordes, ad quos pauperes pro subsidio propter illorum ferocitatem non accesserunt: imo pauperes discipuli Christi, de quo et ejus discipulis scriptum est in Isaia, Conculcabit eam (scilicet civitatem sublimem) pes, pes pauperis, gressus egenorum; a præfatis Judæis propter eorum duritiam recesserunt, sicut in Actibus patet. Et invios: hi enim iniqui, quia errorum viis repleti sunt, et per diversa itinera properant ad infernum, invii nuncupantur.
paras.en: As for [[28:3|the stone also that is in the dark|Lapidem quoque caliginis]], that is, the darksome, hardened and faithless people of the Jews, of whom the Lord says to Ezechiel: They are [[Ezech 2:4|children of a hard face, and of an obstinate heart|Filii indomabili corde sunt]]; [[28:3|and the shadow of death|et umbram mortis]], that is, the unbelieving Gentiles, darkened by the death of sin: [[28:4|The flood divideth|dividit torrens]] these, that is, the inundation of divine vengeance, of which that saying of Daniel may be taken: [[Dan 7:10|A swift stream of fire issued forth from before him|Fluvius igneus rapidusque egrediebatur a facie ejus]], namely, of God; [[28:4|from the people that are on their journey|a populo peregrinante]], that is, from the elect, who in this life are truly wayfarers, pilgrims and strangers, by despising present things and desiring heavenly things fervently and continually. Of whom the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: [[Heb 11:13|confessing that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth|Confitentes quia peregrini et hospites sunt super terram]]. The aforesaid punishment and vengeance of God, then, will divide these from each other on the day of judgement, when the reprobate shall go into everlasting fire, and the elect [[Matt 25:46|into life everlasting|in vitam æternam]]. Hence we read in Isaias: The Spirit of the Lord, [[Is 30:28|as a torrent overflowing|velut torrens inundans]], [[Is 30:28|to destroy the nations unto nothing|ad perdendas gentes in nihilum]]. Of whom it is added: [[28:4|those whom the food of the needy man hath forgotten|eos quos oblitus est pes egentis hominis]], that is, the reprobate, cruel and merciless, to whom the poor did not go for help because of their fierceness: nay, the poor disciples of Christ, of whom and of whose disciples it is written in Isaias, [[Is 26:6|The foot shall tread it down|Conculcabit eam]] (namely, the high city[[Is 26:5||]]), [[Is 26:6|the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy|pes, pes pauperis, gressus egenorum]], withdrew from the aforesaid Jews because of their hardness, as is plain in the Acts[[Acts 13:46||]][[Acts 13:51||]]. And [[28:4|who cannot be come at|Et invios]]: for these wicked men, because they are filled with the ways of errors and hasten by divers roads to hell, are called invii [that is, pathless, not to be come at].

paras.t: Terra de qua oriebatur panis, id est Synagoga vel Ecclesia, de qua, tempore quo in ea viguit fervor caritatis et gratia devotionis, processit panis vitæ et intellectus, refectio bonæ operationis, panis lacrimarum, confortatio internæ consolationis. Talibus enim spiritualibus alimentis fideles communiter abundabant, unusque alium pavit, præsertim prælati subjectos. In loco suo, igni subversa est, id est spiritualiter destructa, virtutibus destituta, mente corrupta igne libidinis, flamma cupiditatis, fervore iræ, impatientiæ atque similium vitiorum. Quanta enim fuerit corruptio Synagogæ in primo Christi adventu, Evangelistæ testantur: cujus, tempore David et Salomonis, fuit magna devotio. Ideo scriptum est: Quomodo facta est meretrix urbs fidelis? Porro, quam ineffabilis fuerit sæpe Ecclesiæ virtus, sanctitas, fervor, atque perfectio, chronicæ narrant. Cujus quam deplangenda, infelix, et maxima sit modo ruina, desolatio, carnalitas, proprius amor, abusio, experientia docet, ita ut illud Apostoli ad Timotheum videatur impleri: Scito, quod in novissimis temporibus instabunt tempora periculosa; et erunt homines se ipsos amantes, cupidi, elati, sine affectione, sine pace, criminatores, voluptatis amatores magis quam Dei.
paras.en: [[28:5|The land, out of which bread grew|Terra de qua oriebatur panis]], that is, the Synagogue or the Church, out of which, at the time when the fervour of charity and the grace of devotion flourished in it, came forth the bread of life and understanding[[Ecclus 15:3||]], the refreshment of good works, and the bread of tears[[Ps 79:6||]], the strengthening of inward consolation. For the faithful commonly abounded in such spiritual food, and one fed another, especially prelates their subjects. [[28:5|in its place, hath been overturned with fire|In loco suo, igni subversa est]], that is, spiritually destroyed, stripped of virtues, corrupted in mind by the fire of lust, the flame of covetousness, the heat of anger, of impatience and of like vices. For how great the corruption of the Synagogue was at Christ's first coming, the Evangelists bear witness: yet in the time of David and Solomon there was great devotion in it. Therefore it is written: [[Is 1:21|How is the faithful city, that was full of judgment, become a harlot?|Quomodo facta est meretrix urbs fidelis?]] Further, how unspeakable the virtue, holiness, fervour and perfection of the Church often was, the chronicles relate. And how lamentable, unhappy and very great its ruin, desolation, carnality, self-love and abuse are now, experience teaches; so that that saying of the Apostle to Timothy seems to be fulfilled: [[2 Tim 3:1|Know also this, that in the last days shall come dangerous times|Scito, quod in novissimis temporibus instabunt tempora periculosa]]; [[2 Tim 3:2|Men shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, haughty|et erunt homines se ipsos amantes, cupidi, elati]], [[2 Tim 3:3|Without affection, without peace, slanderers|sine affectione, sine pace, criminatores]], [[2 Tim 3:4|lovers of pleasure more than of God|voluptatis amatores magis quam Dei]].

paras.t: Locus sapphiri lapides ejus. Lapides Synagogæ seu Ecclesiæ, sunt viri virtutibus stabiles. De quibus in Isaia Dominus promittit Ecclesiæ: Ecce ego sternam per ordinem lapides tuos, et fundabo te in sapphiris, et ponam jaspidem propugnacula tua. Isti fuerunt locus sapphiri, id est subjecta seu congregatio cœlestis conversationis, quæ per sapphirum cœlestis coloris, exprimitur: qui dicere potuerunt, Nostra conversatio in cœlis est. Et gleba illius aurum. Gleba est frustum terræ. Glebæ ergo Ecclesiæ sunt fideles, lutea vasa seu terrena corpora circumferentes: qui olim aurum fuerunt, id est præcipuæ perfectionis in fervore dilectionis, et in sapientiæ claritate. Nunc autem fideles tales non sunt, sed carnales, terreni, insensibiles ad divina et duri, juxta illud Threnorum: Quomodo obscuratum est aurum, mutatus est color optimus? In Isaia quoque: Argentum tuum versum est in scoriam. De præfatis autem glebis cœliformiter decoratis, scribit Apostolus ad Corinthios: Habemus thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus, ut sublimitas virtutis sit ex Deo, et non ex nobis.
paras.en: [[28:6|The stones of it are the place of sapphires|Locus sapphiri lapides ejus]]. The stones of the Synagogue or of the Church are men steadfast in virtues. Of whom the Lord promises the Church in Isaias: [[Is 54:11|behold I will lay thy stones in order, and will lay thy foundations with sapphires|Ecce ego sternam per ordinem lapides tuos, et fundabo te in sapphiris]], [[Is 54:12|And I will make thy bulwarks of jasper|et ponam jaspidem propugnacula tua]]. These were the place of sapphires, that is, the bearers, or the gathering, of a heavenly conversation, which is expressed by the sapphire, of heavenly colour: men who could say, [[Phil 3:20|our conversation is in heaven|Nostra conversatio in cœlis est]]. And [[28:6|the clods of it are gold|Et gleba illius aurum]]. A clod is a lump of earth. The clods of the Church, then, are the faithful, carrying about vessels of clay, that is, earthly bodies: who once were gold, that is, of eminent perfection in the fervour of love and in the clearness of wisdom. But now the faithful are not such, but carnal, earthly, insensible to divine things and hard, according to that of Lamentations: [[Lam 4:1|How is the gold become dim, the finest colour is changed|Quomodo obscuratum est aurum, mutatus est color optimus?]]? In Isaias too: [[Is 1:22|Thy silver is turned into dross|Argentum tuum versum est in scoriam]]. And of the aforesaid clods, adorned after the fashion of heaven, the Apostle writes to the Corinthians: [[2 Cor 4:7|we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency may be of the power of God and not of us|Habemus thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus, ut sublimitas virtutis sit ex Deo, et non ex nobis]].

paras.t: Semitam ignoravit avis: id est, Synagoga viam Christi nescivit per approbationem; imo illam contempsit, abjecit et reprobavit. Christus autem avis vocatur ratione suæ altissimæ contemplationis et ascensionis: qui plumis et alis virtutum atque donorum summe fuit ornatus. Semitam etiam Christi, id est ejus ascensionem, Synagoga credere noluit. Præterea omnes impii Christiani semitam Christi hoc modo ignorant: qui arctam viam salutis, quæ est conversatio virtuosa, ac pœnitentiæ iter relinquunt, latissimamque æternæ perditionis perambulant viam. De Christo quoque ad litteram illud Isaiæ, Vocans ab oriente avem, exponit Hieronymus, per avem ibi intelligens Christum. Nec intuitus est oculos vulturis. Per vulturem Gregorius intelligit Christum, sicut per avem. Qui vultur vocatur, quia ad nostræ fragilitatis morticinium descendit: cujus oculos, id est sapientiam et intentionem qua genus humanum venit proposuitque salvare, Synagoga non novit; imo hunc seductorem et impium exclamavit.
paras.en: [[28:7|The bird hath not known the path|Semitam ignoravit avis]] [Denis reads it as 'hath not known the path of the bird']: that is, the Synagogue did not know the way of Christ so as to approve it; nay, it despised, rejected and reprobated it. Now Christ is called a bird by reason of his most high contemplation and of his ascension: he who was supremely adorned with the feathers and wings of virtues and gifts. The path of Christ, that is, his ascension, the Synagogue also would not believe. Moreover, all wicked Christians are ignorant of the path of Christ in this way: they forsake the strait way of salvation[[Matt 7:14||]], which is a virtuous conversation, and the road of penance, and walk the broadest way of eternal perdition[[Matt 7:13||]]. That saying of Isaias too, [[Is 46:11|Who call a bird from the east|Vocans ab oriente avem]], Jerome expounds literally of Christ, understanding Christ there by the bird. [[28:7|neither hath the eye of the vulture beheld it|Nec intuitus est oculos vulturis]] [Denis reads oculos vulturis as the object: 'nor hath it looked upon the eyes of the vulture']. By the vulture Gregory understands Christ, as he does by the bird. He is called a vulture because he came down to the carrion of our frailty [morticinium: dead flesh, that is, our mortality]: whose eyes, that is, the wisdom and intention with which he came and purposed to save mankind, the Synagogue did not know; nay, it cried out that he was a seducer and wicked[[John 7:12||]].

paras.t: Non calcaverunt eam filii institorum, id est Apostoli filii Prophetarum, qui spirituales institores fuerunt, institutioni morum populi sui jugiter insistentes. Hi, inquam, Apostoli, videntes Synagogæ obstinationem durissimam, amplius eam non calcaverunt, ad eam prædicationis gratia gradiendo; sed ea relicta, ad gentes convertendas profecti sunt, prout Paulus et Barnabas dicunt Judæis: Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei; sed quoniam repulistis illud, et indignos vos judicastis vitæ æternæ, ecce convertimur ad gentes. Nec pertransivit per eam leæna, id est Ecclesia, quæ ratione virtutis seu potestatis, et propter bellum ejus contra invisibiles hostes, nominatur leæna, sicut et Christus dicitur leo. Hæc ergo Ecclesia, cernens Apostolos reliquisse Judæam, eam dimisit et ipsa, nec Christi Evangelium ei prædicare adjecit, de ipsius conversione diffidens.
paras.en: [[28:8|The children of the merchants have not trodden it|Non calcaverunt eam filii institorum]], that is, the Apostles, sons of the Prophets, who were spiritual merchants [institores: Denis links the word with institutio, 'instruction'], continually applying themselves to the instruction of their people in morals. These Apostles, I say, seeing the most hard obstinacy of the Synagogue, trod it no more by going to it for the sake of preaching; but leaving it, they set out to convert the Gentiles, as Paul and Barnabas say to the Jews: [[Acts 13:46|To you it behoved us first to speak the word of God: but because you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold we turn to the Gentiles|Vobis oportebat primum loqui verbum Dei; sed quoniam repulistis illud, et indignos vos judicastis vitæ æternæ, ecce convertimur ad gentes]]. [[28:8|neither hath the lioness passed by it|Nec pertransivit per eam leæna]], that is, the Church, which is named a lioness by reason of its virtue or power, and because of its war against invisible enemies, as Christ also is called a lion[[Gen 49:9||]][[Apoc 5:5||]] [the margin gives Gen. xlix, 9 and a second reference that cannot be read in the scan, probably Apoc. v, 5]. This Church, then, seeing that the Apostles had left Judea, itself also let it go, and did not continue to preach the Gospel of Christ to it, despairing of its conversion.

paras.t: Ad silicem, id est ad duram gentilitatem convertendam, extendit Deus manum suam: quia per Apostolorum prædicationem eam instruxit ac potenter convertit, juxta illud Isaiæ: Ecce levabo ad gentes manum meam. Subvertit a radicibus montes, id est, sæculi principes et tyrannos, ac superbos Judæorum pontifices ac prælatos prorsus dejecit et condemnavit, juxta illud Psalmi: Conturbati sunt montes in fortitudine ejus. De quibus per Isaiam loquitur Christus: Calcavi eos in furore meo, et conculcavi eos in ira mea.
paras.en: [[28:9|to the flint|Ad silicem]], that is, to convert the hard Gentile world, God [[28:9|hath stretched forth his hand|extendit Deus manum suam]]: because through the preaching of the Apostles he instructed it and mightily converted it, according to that of Isaias: [[Is 49:22|Behold I will lift up my hand to the Gentiles|Ecce levabo ad gentes manum meam]]. [[28:9|he hath overturned mountains from the roots|Subvertit a radicibus montes]], that is, he utterly cast down and condemned the princes and tyrants of the world, and the proud high priests and prelates of the Jews, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 45:4|the mountains were troubled with his strength|Conturbati sunt montes in fortitudine ejus]]. Of whom Christ speaks through Isaias: [[Is 63:3|I have trampled on them in my indignation, and have trodden them down in my wrath|Calcavi eos in furore meo, et conculcavi eos in ira mea]].

paras.t: In petris rivos excidit, id est, convertendo gentiles, in cordibus eorum sapientiæ et gratiæ suæ fluenta fundavit, quemadmodum in Joanne legitur: Clamavit Jesus: Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ. Omne pretiosum vidit oculus ejus. Pretiosiora in creaturis, sunt rationales seu intellectuales Dei facturæ, præsertim si donis gratiæ perornatæ, Creatori suo tota mente inhæreant. Omne itaque pretiosum sub sole, id est omnem hominem virtuosum, Deus oculo approbationis conspectat: tantoque homo pretiosior est in oculis Dei, quanto vilior in oculis suis; tanto quoque fit vilior Deo, quanto pretiosior sibi, id est, quanto magis se erigit. Hinc loquitur Christus: Quod hominibus altum est, abominatio est ante Deum.
paras.en: [[28:10|In the rocks he hath cut out rivers|In petris rivos excidit]], that is, by converting the Gentiles he founded in their hearts the streams of his wisdom and grace, as we read in John: [[John 7:37|Jesus stood and cried|Clamavit Jesus]]: [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me|Qui credit in me]], [[John 7:38|Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]. [[28:10|and his eye hath seen every precious thing|Omne pretiosum vidit oculus ejus]]. The more precious among creatures are the rational or intellectual works of God, especially if, richly adorned with the gifts of grace, they cleave to their Creator with their whole mind. Every precious thing under the sun, then, that is, every virtuous man, God beholds with the eye of approval: and a man is the more precious in the eyes of God the viler he is in his own eyes; and he becomes the viler to God the more precious he is to himself, that is, the more he exalts himself. Hence Christ says: [[Luke 16:15|that which is high to men is an abomination before God|Quod hominibus altum est, abominatio est ante Deum]].

paras.t: Profunda quoque fluviorum scrutatus est, id est occulta et intima cordium humanorum. Per aquam enim et flumina, homines designantur, ut patuit, propter abundantiam utriusque, et quoniam cor humanum instar aquæ et fluvii instabile fluidumque consistit. Unde in Psalmo cantatur: Elevaverunt flumina vocem suam. Omnium autem corda Deus scrutatur, juxta illud Jeremiæ: Ego Dominus scrutans cor, et probans renes. Et abscondita produxit in lucem, id est, mysteria legis ac Prophetarum, atque velamina Scripturarum, per evangelicam doctrinam exposuit Christus, et per Apostolorum prædicationem manifestavit. Unde de Christo scriptum est: Aperuit illis sensum, ut intelligerent Scripturas. Et Apostolus ait: Deus qui dixit de tenebris lumen splendescere, illuxit in cordibus nostris ad illuminationem scientiæ veritatis.
paras.en: [[28:11|The depths also of rivers he hath searched|Profunda quoque fluviorum scrutatus est]], that is, the hidden and inmost things of human hearts. For by water and rivers men are signified, as has been shown, because of the abundance of both, and because the human heart, like water and a river, is unstable and fluid. Hence it is sung in the Psalm: [[Ps 92:3|the floods have lifted up their voice|Elevaverunt flumina vocem suam]]. And God searches the hearts of all, according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 17:10|I am the Lord who search the heart, and prove the reins|Ego Dominus scrutans cor, et probans renes]]. [[28:11|and hidden things he hath brought forth to light|Et abscondita produxit in lucem]], that is, Christ expounded the mysteries of the law and of the Prophets, and the veils of the Scriptures, by the teaching of the Gospel, and made them manifest by the preaching of the Apostles. Hence it is written of Christ: [[Luke 24:45|he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures|Aperuit illis sensum, ut intelligerent Scripturas]]. And the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 4:6|God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge|Deus qui dixit de tenebris lumen splendescere, illuxit in cordibus nostris ad illuminationem scientiæ]] of truth [Denis reads scientiæ veritatis, 'of the knowledge of truth', where the Vulgate has 'of the knowledge of the glory of God'].

paras.t: Sapientia vero ubi invenitur? et quis est locus intelligentiæ? Hæc Gregorius de increata Sapientia, id est Unigenito Dei Christo, exponit. De quo loquitur Paulus: Prædicamus Christum Dei virtutem et Dei sapientiam. Ipse quoque est intelligentia increata: de quo reprobi dicunt, Sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis. Siquidem in Deo sunt idem, intelligens et intelligentia, sicut sapiens et sapientia. Hæc ergo Sapientia, secundum suam divinitatem infinita et incircumscriptibilis manens, a nullo perfecte cognoscitur, nullibi circumscriptive continetur aut clauditur.
paras.en: [[28:12|But where is wisdom to be found, and where is the place of understanding?|Sapientia vero ubi invenitur? et quis est locus intelligentiæ?]] Gregory expounds these words of the uncreated Wisdom, that is, of Christ the Only-begotten of God. Of whom Paul says: [[1 Cor 1:23|we preach Christ|Prædicamus Christum]] [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God and the wisdom of God|Dei virtutem et Dei sapientiam]]. He too is the uncreated understanding: of whom the reprobate say, [[Wis 5:6|the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us|Sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis]]. For in God he who understands and understanding are the same, as are he who is wise and wisdom. This Wisdom, then, remaining infinite and uncircumscribable according to its divinity, is known perfectly by none, and is nowhere contained or enclosed circumscriptively.

paras.t: Nescit homo pretium ejus: quia omnia infinite excedit, nec eam quis de condigno propriis potest viribus promereri. Nec invenitur in terra suaviter viventium: quia voluptuosorum delicate viventium corda Christus per gratiam non inhabitat. Propter quod ait: Væ vobis divitibus, qui habetis consolationem vestram; væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esurietis; væ vobis qui ridetis, quia lugebitis et flebitis. In cordibus ergo pœnitentialem vitam ducentium, sua et proximorum peccata deflentium, Christo cordialiter condolentium, propriam calamitatem et exsulationem, ac patriæ dilationem lugentium, habitat Christus, qui ait: Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur. Ideo ait Psalmista: Renuit consolari anima mea. Verumtamen est quædam spiritualis suavitas interna, bona, prædulcis, quæ Christi inhabitationem non excludit, sed præsupponit, aut concomitatur.
paras.en: [[28:13|Man knoweth not the price thereof|Nescit homo pretium ejus]]: because it infinitely exceeds all things, nor can anyone merit it condignly [de condigno: by merit in strict justice] by his own powers. [[28:13|neither is it found in the land of them that live in delights|Nec invenitur in terra suaviter viventium]]: because Christ does not dwell by grace in the hearts of the voluptuous who live delicately. For this reason he says: [[Luke 6:24|woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation|Væ vobis divitibus, qui habetis consolationem vestram]]; [[Luke 6:25|Woe to you that are filled: for you shall hunger. Woe to you that now laugh: for you shall mourn and weep|væ vobis qui saturati estis, quia esurietis; væ vobis qui ridetis, quia lugebitis et flebitis]]. In the hearts, then, of those who lead a penitential life, who bewail their own sins and their neighbours', who suffer with Christ from the heart, who mourn their own wretchedness and exile and the delaying of the homeland, Christ dwells, who says: [[Matt 5:5|Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted|Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur]]. Therefore the Psalmist says: [[Ps 76:3|My soul refused to be comforted|Renuit consolari anima mea]]. Yet there is a certain spiritual sweetness within, good and very sweet, which does not exclude the indwelling of Christ, but presupposes it or accompanies it.

paras.t: Abyssus dicit: Non est in me. Per abyssum, homines sæculares, duplices corde et callidi designantur: qui instar maris, vanitate et peccatis sunt fluidi et duplicitate obscuri, juxta illud Jeremiæ, Pravum est cor hominis et inscrutabile. In talibus autem Christus gratiose non immoratur. Propter quod sapiens quidam monet: Sentite de Domino in bonitate, et in simplicitate cordis quærite illum. Et rursus: Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum. Et mare loquitur: Non est mecum. Per mare, quod orbem sequitur lunæ, et inquietum atque amarum est, mentes vitiis agitatæ et amaricatæ signantur: quæ facto testantur, quod in ipsis non sit Sapientia ista æterna gratiose quiescens, quæ ait, Super quem requiescet Spiritus meus, nisi super quietum et humilem? Unde Ecclesiasticus: Homo sanctus in sapientia manet ut sol; nam stultus mutatur ut luna. Sapientia igitur facit hominem ordinatum et stabilem.
paras.en: [[28:14|The depth saith: It is not in me|Abyssus dicit: Non est in me]]. By the depth are signified worldly men, double of heart and crafty: who like the sea are fluid with vanity and sins, and dark with duplicity, according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 17:9|The heart is perverse above all things, and unsearchable|Pravum est cor hominis et inscrutabile]] [Denis reads cor hominis, 'the heart of man']. In such men Christ does not abide by grace. For this reason a certain wise man warns: [[Wis 1:1|Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart|Sentite de Domino in bonitate, et in simplicitate cordis quærite illum]]. And again: [[Wis 1:5|the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful|Spiritus sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum]]. [[28:14|and the sea saith: It is not with me|Et mare loquitur: Non est mecum]]. By the sea, which follows the circuit of the moon and is restless and bitter, are signified minds tossed and embittered by vices: which testify by their deeds that this eternal Wisdom does not rest by grace in them, the Wisdom which says: Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, but upon him that is quiet and humble?[[Is 66:2||]] [the margin gives 'Cf. Is. lxvi, 2': Denis quotes an old form of the verse, which the Vulgate reads 'to whom shall I have respect, but to him that is poor and little, and of a contrite spirit']. Hence Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 27:12|A holy man continueth in wisdom as the sun: but a fool is changed as the moon|Homo sanctus in sapientia manet ut sol; nam stultus mutatur ut luna]]. Wisdom, therefore, makes a man ordered and steadfast.

paras.t: Non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea. Per aurum obrizum, quod purissimum pretiosissimumque consistit, angeli sancti in sua puritate manentes, et supernaturalibus donis ornati, intelliguntur: qui pro Sapientia increata quasi pretium ejus condignum non dantur, quia incomprehensibiliter inferiores sunt ea, sicut ad Hebræos docet Apostolus: Cui angelorum dixit aliquando Deus: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te? Nec appendetur argentum in commutatione ejus. Sicut per aurum obrizum angeli, ita argento homines exprimuntur: qui quantumlibet venustate eloquentiæ et splendore scientiæ perornentur, Sapientiæ increatæ nequeunt comparari, quum et Joannes Baptista testatus sit indignum se esse solvere corrigiam calceamenti illius.
paras.en: [[28:15|The finest gold shall not purchase it|Non dabitur aurum obrizum pro ea]] [literally 'refined gold (aurum obrizum) shall not be given for it']. By refined gold, which is the purest and most precious, are understood the holy angels, abiding in their purity and adorned with supernatural gifts: who are not given for the uncreated Wisdom as a price worthy of it, because they are incomprehensibly below it, as the Apostle teaches to the Hebrews: [[Heb 1:5|to which of the angels hath he said at any time: Thou art my Son, to-day have I begotten thee?|Cui angelorum dixit aliquando Deus: Filius meus es tu, ego hodie genui te?]][[Ps 2:7||]] [[28:15|neither shall silver be weighed in exchange for it|Nec appendetur argentum in commutatione ejus]]. As the angels are expressed by refined gold, so are men by silver: who, however richly they are adorned with the grace of eloquence and the splendour of knowledge, cannot be compared with the uncreated Wisdom, since even John the Baptist testified that he was unworthy to loose the latchet of his shoe[[John 1:27||]].

paras.t: Non conferetur tinctis Indiæ coloribus. Per Indiam Æthiopes proferentem, mundus hic vitiis tenebrosus notatur: cujus tincti colores, sunt hujus sæculi sapientes, quorum sapientiam (juxta Apostolum ad Corinthios) stultam efficit Deus. Qui licet intus coram Deo immundi sint, coram hominibus tamen se ornant, et velut sapientes virtuososque exhibent, sicut de Scribis et Pharisæis locutus est Christus: Væ vobis qui similes estis sepulcris dealbatis, quæ a foris parent hominibus speciosa, intus vero plena sunt ossibus mortuorum et omni spurcitia: sic et vos quidem a foris paretis hominibus justi, intus vero pleni estis hypocrisi et iniquitate. Itaque horum nullus comparabilis est Sapientiæ increatæ. Nec lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo, vel sapphiro. Per lapidem sardonychum rubeæ terræ colorem habentem, quicumque incola mundi; per sapphirum, cujus color cœlestis est apparentiæ, quicumque supernæ patriæ civis exprimitur. Quum ergo nec terræ, nec cœli habitator comparetur Sapientiæ huic, rite prolatum est verbum inductum.
paras.en: [[28:16|It shall not be compared with the dyed colours of India|Non conferetur tinctis Indiæ coloribus]]. By India, which brings forth Ethiopians, is denoted this world, darkened by vices: whose dyed colours are the wise men of this world, whose wisdom (according to the Apostle to the Corinthians) God makes foolish[[1 Cor 1:20||]]. These, though within they are unclean before God, yet adorn themselves before men and display themselves as wise and virtuous, as Christ spoke of the Scribes and Pharisees: [[Matt 23:27|Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites; because you are like to whited sepulchres, which outwardly appear to men beautiful but within are full of dead men's bones and of all filthiness|Væ vobis qui similes estis sepulcris dealbatis, quæ a foris parent hominibus speciosa, intus vero plena sunt ossibus mortuorum et omni spurcitia]]: [[Matt 23:28|So you also outwardly indeed appear to men just: but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity|sic et vos quidem a foris paretis hominibus justi, intus vero pleni estis hypocrisi et iniquitate]]. None of these, therefore, is comparable with the uncreated Wisdom. [[28:16|or with the most precious stone sardonyx, or the sapphire|Nec lapidi sardonycho pretiosissimo, vel sapphiro]]. By the sardonyx stone, which has the colour of red earth, is expressed every dweller in the world; by the sapphire, whose colour is of heavenly appearance, every citizen of the homeland above. Since, then, neither the dweller on earth nor the dweller in heaven is compared with this Wisdom, the word brought in here is rightly spoken.

paras.t: Non adæquabitur ei aurum vel vitrum. Aurum cunctis metallis præfulget, et tamen quæ continet in se, abscondit. Vitrum vero extra est clarum et intus perspicuum, et qualis sit liquor in ipso contentus, foris apparet. Per aurum ergo et vitrum, superna patria, supernorumque societas civium designatur: quorum corda sibi invicem claritate fulgent, et puritate translucent. De qua in Apocalypsi ait Joannes: Et erat structura muri ejus ex lapide jaspide; ipsa vero ex auro mundo simili vitro mundo. Ibi quippe uniuscujusque mentem ab alterius oculis, membrorum corpulentia non abscondet; sed patebit animus, patebit corporalibus oculis ipsa etiam corporis harmonia. Sicque unusquisque tunc erit conspicabilis alteri, sicut nunc esse non potest conspicabilis sibi; et dum uniuscujusque vultus attenditur, simul et conscientia penetratur.
paras.en: [[28:17|Gold or crystal cannot equal it|Non adæquabitur ei aurum vel vitrum]] [vitrum is glass, where the Douay-Rheims has crystal]. Gold outshines all metals, and yet hides what it contains within it. But glass is clear without and transparent within, and what kind of liquid is contained in it appears outside. By gold and glass, then, is designated the homeland above and the fellowship of its citizens: whose hearts shine to one another with clearness and are seen through by their purity. Of which John says in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:18|And the building of the wall thereof was of jasper stone|Et erat structura muri ejus ex lapide jaspide]]; [[Apoc 21:18|but the city itself pure gold like to clear glass|ipsa vero ex auro mundo simili vitro mundo]]. For there the bulk of the members will not hide the mind of each from the eyes of another; but the soul will lie open, and the very harmony of the body too will lie open to bodily eyes. And so each will then be visible to another as he cannot now be visible to himself; and while each one's face is looked upon, his conscience too is seen through at the same time.

paras.t: Omnia ista sunt verba B. Gregorii. Quibus concordat quod vicesimo secundo de Civitate Dei, de hac materia loquitur Augustinus, insinuans ibi, quod omnis interiorum compago et habitudo, prædicto modo patebit. Quod etiam Thomas super quartum Sententiarum affirmat, asserens hoc dicendum, quia per hoc magis salvatur dignitas corporis glorificati, quam si dicatur, quod perspicua, transparentia, seu translucentia non erunt corpora glorificata, sed solum forinsecus clara et lucida sicut aurum: quod tamen aliqui adstruunt. Sed præfatis sanctis Doctoribus magis credendum est. Quos etiam in hoc sequitur vir magnæ illuminationis, Joannes Ruysbroeck in libro de Regno electorum. Verum nullus in superna hac patria, nec tota illa societas increatæ valet Sapientiæ adæquari.
paras.en: All these are the words of blessed Gregory. With them agrees what Augustine says on this matter in the twenty-second book of the City of God, suggesting there that the whole frame and disposition of the inward parts will lie open in the manner described. Thomas also affirms this on the fourth book of the Sentences, asserting that it is to be held, because by this the dignity of the glorified body is better preserved than if it be said that glorified bodies will not be clear, transparent or translucent, but only bright and shining on the outside, like gold: which some, however, maintain. But the aforesaid holy Doctors are rather to be believed. In this they are followed also by a man of great illumination, John Ruysbroeck, in his book On the Kingdom of the Elect [the work known as The Kingdom of Lovers]. Yet no one in this homeland above, nor that whole fellowship, can be made equal to the uncreated Wisdom.

paras.t: Nec commutabuntur pro ea vasa auri excelsa et eminentia, id est homines præclarissimi, divinorum vasa charismatum exsistentes, sicut de Paulo perhibuit Christus: Quia vas electionis mihi est iste. Non commemorabuntur comparatione ejus. Infinite enim ab ejus majestate deficiunt: ideo comparatione ejus pro nihilo reputantur. Circa quod ait Gregorius: Electi supernæ patriæ, sancti et justi sunt, sed participatione Sapientiæ, non comparatione. Sola enim Sapientia increata cum Patre et Spiritu Sancto veraciter est: cujus essentiæ comparatum esse nostrum, est non esse. Huic si conjungimur, sumus, vivimus, sapimus: ei si comparamur, nec sapimus, nec vivimus omnino, nec sumus. Hinc sancti omnes, quando in visione Dei proficiunt, quanto magis Divinitatis interna conspiciunt, tanto magis se nihil esse cognoscunt.
paras.en: [[28:17|neither shall any vessels of gold be changed for it|Nec commutabuntur pro ea vasa auri]], [[28:18|High and eminent things|excelsa et eminentia]], that is, most illustrious men, who are vessels of divine charisms, as Christ testified of Paul: [[Acts 9:15|this man is to me a vessel of election|Quia vas electionis mihi est iste]]. [[28:18|shall not be mentioned in comparison of it|Non commemorabuntur comparatione ejus]]. For they fall infinitely short of its majesty: therefore in comparison with it they are reckoned as nothing. On this Gregory says: The elect of the homeland above are holy and just, but by participation in Wisdom, not by comparison with it. For only the uncreated Wisdom, with the Father and the Holy Ghost, truly is: and compared with its essence our being is not being. If we are joined to it, we are, we live, we are wise: if we are compared with it, we are neither wise, nor do we live at all, nor are we. Hence all the saints, when they advance in the vision of God, the more they behold the inward things of the Godhead, the more they know themselves to be nothing.

paras.t: Trahitur autem sapientia de occultis: quia invisibilis exsistens, invisibiliter invenitur atque percipitur; et incomprehensibili quoque Dei pietate ac censura infunditur, et interdum pro occultissimis meritis ipsa per gratiæ suæ communicationem se præstat. Ad ejus insuper aliqualem cognitionem, ex occultis rerum proprietatibus, naturis et actibus subtiliter consideratis promovemur: in suis quippe relucet effectibus.
paras.en: [[28:18|but wisdom is drawn out of secret places|Trahitur autem sapientia de occultis]]: because, being invisible, it is found and perceived invisibly; and it is infused also by the incomprehensible mercy and judgement of God, and sometimes, for most hidden merits, it gives itself by the communication of its grace. Moreover, we are brought to some knowledge of it from the hidden properties, natures and acts of things, subtly considered: for it shines back in its effects.

paras.t: Non adæquabitur ei topazius de Æthiopia. Per topazium, lapidem pretiosissimum omni colore ornatum ac splendidum, quicumque vir perfectus ex gentilitate (per Æthiopiam designata) conversus, diversis virtutum atque donorum charismatibus micans, significatur: qui quantumlibet commendetur, Sapientiæ quæ Christus est, non æquatur. Nec tincturæ mundissimæ, id est quibuslibet virtutibus eminenter ornati, seu virtutes creatæ, quamvis clarissimæ in suo ordine, componentur, id est, sapientiæ hujus comparabuntur, quæ est virtus et sanctitas per essentiam, omnemque perfectionem habet per eminentiam infinitam.
paras.en: [[28:19|The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equal to it|Non adæquabitur ei topazius de Æthiopia]]. By the topaz, a most precious stone, adorned with every colour and shining, is signified every perfect man converted from the Gentile world (which is designated by Ethiopia), gleaming with the charisms of divers virtues and gifts: who, however much he be commended, is not equal to the Wisdom which is Christ. Nor shall [[28:19|the cleanest dyeing|Nec tincturæ mundissimæ]], that is, those eminently adorned with any virtues whatever, or created virtues, however bright in their own order, be compared, that is, be likened, to this Wisdom [Denis takes tincturæ mundissimæ, 'the cleanest dyes', as the subject: 'nor shall the cleanest dyes be compared'], which is virtue and holiness by essence, and has all perfection by infinite eminence.

paras.t: Unde ergo sapientia venit? Sapientia ista increata, sicut a Patre æterno procedit, ita ab eo venit ac mittitur, prout protestatur: Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum. Sapiens quoque quidam petit: Mitte illam a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit, et mecum laboret. Et quis est locus intelligentiæ? Intelligentia hæc et Sapientia increata, est in sinu Patris, ut in Joanne habetur: imo quælibet divina et increata Persona est in alia circumincessibiliter vere et inconfusibiliter. Nihilo minus, omnis mens creata, divinæ Sapientiæ contemplativa amatrix, locus, templum et thronus, receptaculumque ipsius vocatur.
paras.en: [[28:20|Whence then cometh wisdom?|Unde ergo sapientia venit?]] This uncreated Wisdom, as it proceeds from the eternal Father, so comes and is sent from him, as it declares: [[John 16:28|I came forth from the Father and am come into the world|Exivi a Patre, et veni in mundum]]. A certain wise man too asks: [[Wis 9:10|Send her|Mitte illam]] [[Wis 9:10|from the throne of thy majesty, that she may be with me, and may labour with me|a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit, et mecum laboret]]. [[28:20|and where is the place of understanding?|Et quis est locus intelligentiæ?]] This uncreated Understanding and Wisdom is [[John 1:18|in the Bosom of the Father|in sinu Patris]], as we have it in John: nay, each divine and uncreated Person is in the other by circumincession [that is, the mutual indwelling of the divine Persons], truly and without confusion. Nevertheless, every created mind that contemplates and loves the divine Wisdom is called its place, temple and throne, and its dwelling.

paras.t: Abscondita est ab oculis omnium viventium, id est, a nullo mortalium in hac vita clare per speciem cernitur. Quod si aliquibus in hac vita datum est Deum videre per speciem, sicut præcipue de Moyse et Paulo asserit Augustinus: tamen pro tunc non vivebant vita sensitiva humana, sed in maxima erant abstractione et ecstasi. Hinc ait Gregorius: Quamdiu hic mortaliter vivitur, videri per quasdam imagines et figuras Deus potest, sed per ipsam naturæ suæ speciem non potest. Refert quoque Gregorius quosdam fuisse, qui Deum dixerunt in patria, non in natura sua, sed in claritate sua videri: cujus oppositum probat Gregorius per certissimas Scripturæ auctoritates, et ratione, quoniam Deo idem est sua natura, suaque claritas. Verumtamen istis obviare videtur quod Sapiens inducit: Sapientia facile videtur ab his qui diligunt illam, et invenitur ab his qui quærunt illam; præoccupat eos qui se concupiscunt. Et respondendum, quod hoc atque similia, de cognitione clara per speciem non profertur, sed de imperfecta quadam notitia, qua etiam Deus facillime a cunctis cognoscitur, quantum ad quia est, et quoad aliquas suas proprietates, quæ ex creaturis de facili perpenduntur.
paras.en: [[28:21|It is hid from the eyes of all living|Abscondita est ab oculis omnium viventium]], that is, it is seen clearly by sight [per speciem: by direct vision of God's own essence] by no mortal in this life. And if it has been given to some in this life to see God by sight, as Augustine asserts especially of Moses and Paul, yet at that time they were not living the human life of the senses, but were in the greatest abstraction and ecstasy. Hence Gregory says: As long as one lives here in mortality, God can be seen through certain images and figures, but through the very sight of his nature he cannot. Gregory also relates that there were some who said that in the homeland God is seen, not in his nature, but in his brightness: the opposite of which Gregory proves by most certain authorities of Scripture, and by reason, since in God his nature and his brightness are the same. Yet what the Wise Man brings in seems to oppose these things: [[Wis 6:13|Wisdom|Sapientia]] [[Wis 6:13|is easily seen by them that love her, and is found by them that seek her|facile videtur ab his qui diligunt illam, et invenitur ab his qui quærunt illam]]; [[Wis 6:14|She preventeth them that covet her|præoccupat eos qui se concupiscunt]]. And the answer is that this and the like is not said of clear knowledge by sight, but of a certain imperfect knowledge, by which God is very easily known by all as to the fact that he is, and as to some of his properties, which are readily inferred from creatures.

paras.t: Volucres quoque cæli latet, id est animas contemplativas seu angelos sanctos, [qui] illam increatam Sapientiam comprehensive non sciunt, nec vident, id est tam perfecte et clare, sicut ipsa ex se cognoscibilis exstat. Sicut enim infinitæ est actualitatis, ita est et infinitæ cognoscibilitatis: idcirco a nullo intellectu comprehensive conspicitur, nisi qui infinitæ est perspicacitatis et perfectionis. Unde solus Deus comprehendit se ipsum. Et de tali cognitione accipi potest illud Apostoli: Beatus et solus potens Rex regum, qui solus habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem: quem nullus hominum vidit, sed nec videre potest. Divinus quoque Dionysius ait sexto Cœlestis hierarchiæ capitulo, quod angeli divinos ornatus perfecte non sciunt, sed sola divina virtus princeps totius illuminationis.
paras.en: [[28:21|and the fowls of the air know it not|Volucres quoque cæli latet]] [literally 'it is hidden from the birds of heaven too'], that is, from contemplative souls or the holy angels, who do not know or see that uncreated Wisdom comprehensively, that is, as perfectly and clearly as it is knowable of itself. For as it is of infinite actuality, so it is of infinite knowability: therefore it is seen comprehensively by no intellect except one of infinite penetration and perfection. Hence God alone comprehends himself. And of such knowledge that saying of the Apostle may be taken: [[1 Tim 6:15|the Blessed and only Mighty, the King of kings|Beatus et solus potens Rex regum]], [[1 Tim 6:16|Who only hath immortality and inhabiteth light inaccessible: whom no man hath seen, nor can see|qui solus habet immortalitatem, et lucem habitat inaccessibilem: quem nullus hominum vidit, sed nec videre potest]]. The divine Dionysius too says in the sixth chapter of the Celestial Hierarchy that the angels do not know the divine adornments perfectly, but only the divine power, the principle of all illumination.

paras.t: Perditio et mors dixerunt: Auribus nostris audivimus famam ejus. Dæmones nempe et condemnati, increatam Sapientiam in se ipsa non vident, sed in suis eam effectibus noscunt, et multa de ea audierunt. In ipsa demum proportione pœnarum ad culpas eam cognoscunt.
paras.en: [[28:22|Destruction and death have said: With our ears we have heard the fame thereof|Perditio et mors dixerunt: Auribus nostris audivimus famam ejus]]. For the demons and the damned do not see the uncreated Wisdom in itself, but know it in its effects, and have heard much of it. Finally, they know it in the very proportion of their punishments to their faults.

paras.t: Deus Pater, imo et Spiritus Sanctus, intelligit viam ejus, id est increatæ Sapientiæ operationem, et iter seu modum quo venit ad mentes creatas per Incarnationis mysterium, seu invisibilem missionem. Et ipse novit locum illius: de quo loco jam dictum est. Nam et Pater, secundum Gregorium, locus est Sapientiæ hujus, quemadmodum ipsa ait: Ego in Patre, et Pater in me est. Pater etiam et Trinitas superbenedicta novit et approbat mentes, quas Sapientia ista inhabitat, quæ loquitur: Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus. Apostolus quoque testatur: Templum Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos.
paras.en: [[28:23|God|Deus]] the Father, nay and the Holy Ghost too, [[28:23|understandeth the way of it|intelligit viam ejus]], that is, the working of the uncreated Wisdom, and the road or manner by which it comes to created minds through the mystery of the Incarnation, or by invisible mission [that is, the sending of a divine Person into the soul by grace]. [[28:23|and he knoweth the place thereof|Et ipse novit locum illius]]: of which place we have spoken already. For the Father too, according to Gregory, is the place of this Wisdom, as it says itself: [[John 14:10|I am in the Father and the Father in me|Ego in Patre, et Pater in me est]][[John 14:11||]]. The Father also, and the superblessed Trinity, knows and approves the minds which this Wisdom indwells, which says: [[John 14:23|If any one love me, he will keep my word. And my Father will love him and we will come to him and will make our abode with him|Si quis diligit me, sermonem meum servabit, et Pater meus diliget eum, et ad eum veniemus, et mansionem apud eum faciemus]]. And the Apostle testifies: [[1 Cor 3:17|the temple of God is holy, which you are|Templum Dei sanctum est, quod estis vos]].

paras.t: Qui fecit ventis pondus. Per ventos, propter eorum velocitatem ac subtilitatem, intellectuales essentiæ, scilicet animæ, angelique signantur: quibus Deus fecit pondus, id est, amorem eis impressit et naturalem inclinationem ad felicitatem; pondus quoque virtuosæ gravitatis ac maturitatis. Et aquas, id est charismata gratiarum, appendit in mensura, hoc est, creatis mentibus indidit secundum ordinem sapientiæ suæ, decenti ac varia diversitate, sicut ait Apostolus: quia alii per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ, alii gratia sanitatum, alii operatio virtutum, alii genera linguarum, alii discretio spirituum. Salvator quoque (ut parabolice ait) uni servorum dedit quinque talenta, alii duo, alii unum. Hinc rursus testatur Apostolus: Unicuique nostrum data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi. Unicuique etiam electorum Deus gratiam præstat juxta mensuram prædestinationis suæ et capacitatis illius. Unus vero solus est, scilicet Christus ut homo, de quo scriptum est: Non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum.
paras.en: [[28:25|Who made a weight for the winds|Qui fecit ventis pondus]]. By the winds, because of their swiftness and subtlety, are signified the intellectual essences, namely souls and angels: for whom God made a weight, that is, he impressed on them love and a natural inclination to happiness; and also the weight of virtuous gravity and maturity. [[28:25|and weighed the waters|Et aquas]], that is, the charisms of graces, [[28:25|by measure|appendit in mensura]], that is, he put them into created minds according to the order of his wisdom, with a fitting and varied diversity, as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|alii per Spiritum datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]], [[1 Cor 12:9|to another, the grace of healing|alii gratia sanitatum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|To another the working of miracles|alii operatio virtutum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, diverse kinds of tongues|alii genera linguarum]], [[1 Cor 12:10|to another, the discerning of spirits|alii discretio spirituum]]. The Saviour too (as he says in a parable): [[Matt 25:15|to one|uni]] of his servants [[Matt 25:15|he gave five talents, and to another two, and to another one|dedit quinque talenta, alii duo, alii unum]]. Hence again the Apostle testifies: [[Eph 4:7|to every one of us is given grace, according to the measure of the giving of Christ|Unicuique nostrum data est gratia secundum mensuram donationis Christi]]. To each of the elect, too, God gives grace according to the measure of his predestination and of that one's capacity. But there is one alone, namely Christ as man, of whom it is written: [[John 3:34|God doth not give the Spirit by measure|Non ad mensuram dat Deus Spiritum]].

paras.t: Quando ponebat pluviis, hoc est doctrinis et sermonibus doctorum ac prædicatorum. Unde in Deuteronomio Moyses ait: Concrescat ut pluvia doctrina mea. Quemadmodum autem prædicatores dicuntur nubes, sic doctrina eorum dicitur pluvia. Legem, id est præceptum, qualiter et quibus debeant impertiri, ac observari primo a docentibus, deinde ab audientibus; et viam procellis sonantibus, id est processum sive effectum terribilibus Scripturarum comminationibus de futuris suppliciis; vel, Viam, id est aditum atque introitum ad mentes audientium.
paras.en: [[28:26|When he gave|Quando ponebat]] [[28:26|for the rain|pluviis]], that is, for the doctrines and discourses of doctors and preachers. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:2|Let my doctrine gather as the rain|Concrescat ut pluvia doctrina mea]]. And as preachers are called clouds, so their doctrine is called rain. [[28:26|a law|Legem]], that is, a precept, how and to whom they ought to be imparted, and that they be observed first by the teachers, then by the hearers; [[28:26|and a way for the sounding storms|et viam procellis sonantibus]], that is, a course or effect for the terrible threatenings of the Scriptures concerning the punishments to come; or, [[28:26|a way|Viam]], that is, an access and entrance into the minds of the hearers.

paras.t: Tunc vidit illam. Pater enim æternaliter noscit, intuetur et comprehendit Unigenitum suum, videlicet Sapientiam hanc increatam ac genitam, sicut et ipse Filius protestatur: Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius, nec Filium quis novit nisi Pater. Vel, Tunc vidit, id est, se videre monstravit, aliosque videre fecit hanc Sapientiam, sicut in Genesi ait ad Abraham: Nunc cognovi quod timeas Deum. Et enarravit, hoc est, aliis eam per lumen fidei declaravit, videlicet prædicatoribus, ceterisque divinitus illustratis; et præparavit, id est, audientium cordibus per prædicatorum sermones infundere seu revelare disposuit: quod tempore apostolicæ prædicationis præsertim fiebat, quando per Apostolorum prædicationem Deus corda illustravit gentilium. Et investigavit, id est, ab aliis investigari fecit, quorum intellectum excitavit ad considerandum et perscrutandum quæ de Sapientia Patris Christo prædicabantur, scriptaque erant: quemadmodum in Actis de Thessalonicensibus legitur, Nobiliores ex eis susceperunt verbum cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas. Et in Sapientiæ libro ait auctor libri hujus: Quid sit sapientia, referam; et non abscondam sacramenta Dei, sed ab initio nativitatis investigabo. Juxta hunc modum loquendi ait Apostolus: Ipse Spiritus postulat pro nobis, id est, postulare nos facit. In Exodo quoque populo Israel loquitur Dominus: Jam nunc depone ornatum tuum, ut sciam quid faciam tibi; id est, scire me monstrem et alios scire hoc faciam.
paras.en: [[28:27|Then he saw it|Tunc vidit illam]]. For the Father eternally knows, beholds and comprehends his Only-begotten, namely this uncreated and begotten Wisdom, as the Son himself declares: [[Matt 11:27|neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son|Nemo novit Patrem nisi Filius]], [[Matt 11:27|no one knoweth the Son but the Father|nec Filium quis novit nisi Pater]]. Or, [[28:27|Then he saw|Tunc vidit]], that is, he showed that he saw this Wisdom, and made others see it, as in Genesis he says to Abraham: [[Gen 22:12|now I know that thou fearest God|Nunc cognovi quod timeas Deum]]. [[28:27|and declared|Et enarravit]], that is, he made it known to others by the light of faith, namely to preachers and to the others divinely enlightened; [[28:27|and prepared|et præparavit]], that is, he disposed to pour it into the hearts of the hearers, or to reveal it to them, through the discourses of preachers: which was done above all in the time of the apostolic preaching, when through the preaching of the Apostles God enlightened the hearts of the Gentiles. [[28:27|and searched it|Et investigavit]], that is, he caused it to be searched out by others, whose understanding he stirred up to consider and scrutinize what was preached and written of Christ, the Wisdom of the Father: as we read in the Acts of the Thessalonians [the verse speaks of the Jews of Berea, more noble than those of Thessalonica], [[Acts 17:11|these were more noble than those in Thessalonica, who received the word with all eagerness, daily searching the scriptures|Nobiliores ex eis susceperunt verbum cum omni aviditate, quotidie scrutantes Scripturas]]. And in the book of Wisdom the author of that book says: [[Wis 6:24|what wisdom is, and what was her origin, I will declare: and I will not hide from you the mysteries of God, but will seek her out from the beginning of her birth|Quid sit sapientia, referam; et non abscondam sacramenta Dei, sed ab initio nativitatis investigabo]]. In keeping with this manner of speaking the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:26|the Spirit himself asketh for us|Ipse Spiritus postulat pro nobis]], that is, makes us ask. In Exodus too the Lord says to the people of Israel: [[Ex 33:5|Now presently lay aside thy ornaments, that I may know what to do to thee|Jam nunc depone ornatum tuum, ut sciam quid faciam tibi]]; that is, that I may show that I know, and make others know it.

paras.t: Denique, juxta Gregorium, notanda sunt hæc quatuor, quæ de Sapientia dicta sunt, scilicet vidit, enarravit, præparavit, investigavit. Vidit namque Pater Sapientiam hanc, quia species est; enarravit, quia verbum; præparavit, quia remedium; investigavit, quia occultum. Quæ quia communitas non capit, fecit quod subditur.
paras.en: Finally, according to Gregory, these four things that are said of Wisdom are to be noted, namely: he saw, he declared, he prepared, he searched. For the Father saw this Wisdom, because it is the Form [species: form or beauty]; he declared it, because it is the Word; he prepared it, because it is the remedy; he searched it, because it is hidden. And since men in common do not grasp these things, he did what follows.
