paras.t: Et dixit homini: Ecce timor Domini, ipsa est sapientia; et recedere a malo, intelligentia: id est, quamvis Sapientia ista tanquam incomprehensibilis et immensa sit omnium oculis viventium, quoad plenam ejus comprehensionem, abscondita: nihilo minus, per timorem Dei castum ac filialem, peccatorumque devitationem, ad eam pertingitur et ipsa acquiritur, ita ut nunc adsit per gratiam, et cognoscatur per fidem ac sapientiæ donum, postea vero adsit per beatificam fruitionem. Hujus namque sapientiæ increatæ gratiosam præsentiam atque internam inhabitationem non impedit nisi peccatum. Propter quod loquitur Isaias: Peccata vestra diviserunt inter Deum et vos. Itemque: Iste est omnis fructus, ut auferatur peccatum. Timor autem aufert, cavet et vitat peccata, quemadmodum scriptum est: Timor Domini expellit peccatum. Et alibi: Per timorem declinat unusquisque a malo. Unde hortatur Psalmographus: Timete Dominum, omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum. Hinc (secundum Gregorium) ille veraciter vim divini timoris intelligit, qui se a cunctis operibus pravis custodit.
paras.en: [[28:28|And he said to man: Behold the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom: and to depart from evil, is understanding|Et dixit homini: Ecce timor Domini, ipsa est sapientia; et recedere a malo, intelligentia]]: that is, although this Wisdom, being incomprehensible and immense, is hidden from the eyes of all living as to the full comprehension of it, nevertheless by the chaste and filial fear of God [the fear of offending God that springs from love, as against servile fear of punishment], and by the avoiding of sins, it is reached and acquired, so that now it is present by grace and is known by faith and the gift of wisdom, and afterwards it is present by beatific fruition. For nothing hinders the gracious presence and inward indwelling of this uncreated Wisdom but sin. For this reason Isaias says: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|Peccata vestra diviserunt inter Deum et vos]] [Denis has peccata, 'sins']. And again: [[Is 27:9|this is all the fruit, that the sin thereof should be taken away|Iste est omnis fructus, ut auferatur peccatum]]. And fear takes away, guards against and shuns sins, as it is written: [[Ecclus 1:27|The fear of the Lord driveth out sin|Timor Domini expellit peccatum]]. And elsewhere: [[Prov 15:27|by the fear of the Lord every one declineth from evil|Per timorem declinat unusquisque a malo]]. Hence the Psalmist exhorts: [[Ps 33:10|Fear the Lord, all ye his saints: for there is no want to them that fear him|Timete Dominum, omnes sancti ejus, quoniam nihil deest timentibus eum]]. Hence (according to Gregory) he truly understands the force of divine fear who guards himself from all evil works.

29.title: Explanatio capituli vicesimi noni: Addidit quoque Job, assumens parabolam suam, et dixit: Quis mihi tribuat, etc.
29.title_en: Explanation of the twenty-ninth chapter: Job also added, taking up his parable, and said: Who will grant me, etc.

paras.t: Addidit quoque Job, assumens parabolam suam. Sicut prehabitum est, ideo dicitur assumpsisse parabolam, quia per similitudines et metaphorice loquitur. Denique (juxta Thomam) verbis ejus jam supra descriptis finitis, præstolabatur ut aliquis amicorum suorum loqueretur: quibus tacentibus, ipse præinductis ista adjecit, in quibus propositum suum diffusius declaravit.
paras.en: [[29:1|Job also added, taking up his parable|Addidit quoque Job, assumens parabolam suam]]. As was said before, he is said to have taken up his parable because he speaks through likenesses and metaphorically. Further (according to Thomas), when his words set down above were finished, he waited for one of his friends to speak; and as they held their peace, he added these words to what he had already brought forward, and in them set out his purpose more fully.

paras.t: Et dixit: Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos, hoc est in tali incolumitate ac prosperitate honestateque famæ? Unde se ipsum declarans, subjungit: Secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me, conservando in bonis, et præservando ab adversis. Et hoc ait, non quasi Deus eum quando hæc dixit, non custodiret: imo virtute et gratia Dei sciebat se in tantis adversitatibus ab impatientia, desperatione, et ceteris vitiis præservari. Sed hoc ideo ait, quia nunc ab invisibilibus ac visibilibus adversariis Deus eum gravissime affligi permisit. Sicque quodammodo a Deo fuit relictus, sicut et Christus tempore passionis clamavit: Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me? Insuper, corporis sospitatem temporalemque prosperitatem optavit, non absolute secundum se, sed ut sunt instrumenta virtutis, et quoniam naturaliter talia appetuntur, præsertim ab ægris et depauperatis.
paras.en: [[29:1|and said|Et dixit]]: [[29:2|Who will grant me, that I might be according to the months past|Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos]], that is, in such soundness and prosperity and good name? Then, explaining himself, he adds: [[29:2|according to the days in which God kept me?|Secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me]] by keeping me in good things and preserving me from adversities. And he says this, not as though God were not keeping him when he said these things; on the contrary, he knew that by the power and grace of God he was being preserved, in such great adversities, from impatience, despair and the other vices. But he says it because God had now permitted him to be most grievously afflicted by invisible and visible adversaries. And so in a manner he was forsaken by God, as Christ too cried out at the time of his passion: [[Matt 27:46|My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me?|Deus meus, Deus meus, ut quid dereliquisti me?]] Moreover, he wished for bodily health and temporal prosperity, not absolutely, for their own sake, but as they are instruments of virtue, and because such things are desired by nature, above all by the sick and the impoverished.

paras.t: Quando splendebat lucerna ejus super caput meum, id est, provisiva, protectiva, et directiva illustratio Dei menti meæ infulsit, seu læta prosperitas a Deo concessa mihi arrisit, et ad lumen ejus, id est secundum instructionem directionemque gratiosæ illustrationis Dei, ambulabam in tenebris, id est, in incertis ac dubiis me habui ac processi, non propriæ prudentiæ innitendo. Sic et Michæas propheta: Quum sedero (inquit) in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est. Et Psalmista: Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea: quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ: a quo trepidabo?
paras.en: [[29:3|When his lamp shined over my head|Quando splendebat lucerna ejus super caput meum]], that is, when God's provident, protecting and directing illumination shone upon my mind, or when glad prosperity granted by God smiled upon me, and [[29:3|by his light|ad lumen ejus]], that is, according to the instruction and direction of God's gracious illumination, [[29:3|I walked|ambulabam]] [[29:3|in darkness|in tenebris]], that is, I conducted myself and went forward in things uncertain and doubtful, not leaning on my own prudence. So too the prophet Micheas: [[Mich 7:8|when I sit|Quum sedero]] (he says) [[Mich 7:8|in darkness, the Lord is my light|in tenebris, Dominus lux mea est]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life: of whom shall I be afraid?|Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea: quem timebo? Dominus protector vitæ meæ: a quo trepidabo?]]

paras.t: Sicut fui in diebus adolescentiæ meæ, ita quod gratia mane prævenit me. Unde non ait, Infantiæ, aut, Pueritiæ: quoniam illa ætas illustrationis divinæ ad regimen vitæ humanæ communiter non est capax, sed adolescentia, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Detur adolescenti scientia et intellectus. Quando secreto Deus erat in tabernaculo meo, id est, domui meæ in omnibus benedixit. Vel, Secreto erat in tabernaculo meo, id est, intus in abdito mentis mihi adfuit per multiplicem pietatis et gratiæ suæ effectum, dum in domo mea orationi et contemplationi instabam: quemadmodum in Actis Cornelius ait, Orans eram in domo mea.
paras.en: [[29:4|As I was in the days of my youth|Sicut fui in diebus adolescentiæ meæ]], so that grace went before me early in the morning. Hence he does not say *of infancy* or *of childhood*, since that age is not commonly capable of the divine illumination for the governing of human life; but youth is, according to that of the Proverbs: Let there be given [[Prov 1:4|to the young man knowledge and understanding|adolescenti scientia et intellectus]]. [[29:4|when God was secretly in my tabernacle?|Quando secreto Deus erat in tabernaculo meo]] that is, he blessed my house in all things. Or, [[29:4|was secretly in my tabernacle?|Secreto erat in tabernaculo meo]] that is, he was present to me within, in the hidden place of my mind, through the manifold working of his goodness and grace, while I was intent on prayer and contemplation in my house: as Cornelius says in the Acts, [[Acts 10:30|I was praying in my house|Orans eram in domo mea]].

paras.t: Quando erat Omnipotens mecum, per varia beneficia corporalia ac spiritualia. Sicut et Satan loquitur Deo de Job: Nonne tu vallasti eum, ac domum ejus universamque substantiam per circuitum? Operibus manuum ejus benedixisti. Et in circuitu meo pueri mei, quos spiritualiter ac corporaliter educavi. Et hoc delectabile est, videre pueros ex se natos, quoniam causa diligit proprium germen, et si cognitiva sit, delectatur in eo. Unde timorato promittitur: Filii tui sicut novellæ olivarum in circuitu mensæ tuæ.
paras.en: [[29:5|When the Almighty was with me|Quando erat Omnipotens mecum]], through various bodily and spiritual benefits. As Satan too says to God of Job: [[Job 1:10|Hast thou not made a fence for him, and his house, and all his substance round about, blessed the works of his hands|Nonne tu vallasti eum, ac domum ejus universamque substantiam per circuitum? Operibus manuum ejus benedixisti]]. [[29:5|and my servants round about me|Et in circuitu meo pueri mei]] [*pueri* means both servants and children; Denis takes it of children], whom I brought up spiritually and bodily. And this is a delight, to see children born of oneself, since a cause loves its own offspring [that is, whatever brings a thing forth loves what it brings forth], and if it has knowledge, it takes delight in it. Hence it is promised to the man who fears God: [[Ps 127:3|Thy children as olive plants, round about thy table|Filii tui sicut novellæ olivarum in circuitu mensæ tuæ]].

paras.t: Quando lavabam pedes meos butyro, id est, in tantum abundabam butyro, ac ceteris animalium pinguedinibus, ut usque ad pedum lotionem […] consuetudinem patriæ. Antiquorum autem divitiæ præcipuæ pecora erant, secundum Augustinum. Hinc a nomine isto, Pecus, pecunia nomen accepit, secundum eumdem. Et petra fundebat mihi rivos olei. Secundum Albertum, oleum de amurca in concavis petræ exprimitur. Sicque depuratum, a petra funditur. Per quod omnis abundantia terræ nascentium designatur. Thomas per petram intelligit terram saxosam: quia (ut asserit) olivæ optimum oleum producentes, in locis lapidosis ac arenosis solent consistere. Itaque sensus est, quod ex talibus locis, rivos, id est copiam, olei sumpsit.
paras.en: [[29:6|When I washed my feet with butter|Quando lavabam pedes meos butyro]], that is, I had such abundance of butter and of the other fats of animals that even for the washing of the feet […] the custom of the country. Now the chief riches of the ancients were their flocks and herds, according to Augustine. Hence *pecunia*, money, took its name from this word *pecus*, cattle, according to the same. [[29:6|and the rock poured me out rivers of oil?|Et petra fundebat mihi rivos olei]] According to Albert, oil is pressed out of the lees [Latin *amurca*, the watery residue of pressed olives] in the hollows of the rock, and so, purified, it is poured out from the rock. By this is signified every abundance of the fruits of the earth. Thomas understands by the rock stony ground: because (as he asserts) olives that yield the best oil usually grow in stony and sandy places. And so the sense is that from such places he took rivers, that is, plenty, of oil.

paras.t: Quando procedebam ad portam civitatis, ad judicandum ibidem. Antiquitus enim judicia proferebantur in urbium portis, ubi judices ab introeuntibus seu aliis promptius inveniebantur, et ne civitas inquietaretur per tumultum causarum. Unde in Deuteronomio scribitur: Judices constitues in omnibus portis tuis. Et in platea, videlicet juxta portam, parabant cathedram mihi, id est solium solenne, quo residerem, ad docendum ac judicandum.
paras.en: [[29:7|When I went out to the gate of the city|Quando procedebam ad portam civitatis]], to judge there. For of old judgments were given in the gates of cities, where the judges could be found more readily by those coming in and by others, and so that the city would not be disturbed by the tumult of lawsuits. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 16:18|Thou shalt appoint judges|Judices constitues]] [[Deut 16:18|in all thy gates|in omnibus portis tuis]]. [[29:7|and in the street|Et in platea]], that is, beside the gate, [[29:7|they prepared me a chair|parabant cathedram mihi]], that is, a solemn seat on which I might sit to teach and to judge.

paras.t: Videbant me juvenes, scilicet vanitatibus dediti, et abscondebantur, id est, coram me apparere, et vanum quid agere erubuerunt timore maturitatis atque justitiæ meæ. Et senes assurgentes mihi accedenti, stabant, mihi in hoc reverentiam impendentes. Principes cessabant loqui, quum ego loqui ordirer, et digitum superponebant ori suo, hoc est, diligentissime tacuerunt, et mea eloquia attenderunt, et forte tali exteriori silendi indicio se ad taciturnitatem cohortabantur. Vocem suam cohibebant duces, et lingua eorum gutturi suo adhærebat, id est, ad loquendum non movebatur, sed tam attonite et attente me auscultabant, quasi lingua eorum ad loquendum laxari non potuisset.
paras.en: [[29:8|The young men saw me|Videbant me juvenes]], that is, those given to vanities, [[29:8|and hid themselves|et abscondebantur]], that is, they were ashamed to appear before me and to do anything vain, for fear of my gravity and justice. And [[29:8|the old men rose up|senes assurgentes]] as I came near, [[29:8|and stood|stabant]], showing me reverence in this. [[29:9|The princes ceased to speak|Principes cessabant loqui]] when I began to speak, [[29:9|and laid the finger on their mouth|et digitum superponebant ori suo]], that is, they kept the strictest silence and attended to my words; and perhaps by such an outward sign of silence they urged one another to keep quiet. [[29:10|The rulers held their peace|Vocem suam cohibebant duces]], [[29:10|and their tongue cleaved to their throat|et lingua eorum gutturi suo adhærebat]], that is, it was not moved to speak, but they listened to me so astonished and so attentive, as though their tongue could not have been loosed to speak.

paras.t: Auris audiens verba mea vel famam meam, beatificabat me, id est, felicem me reputavit; et oculus videns, testimonium reddebat mihi, id est, conspiciendo opera […] vere justus consisterem: quod de interioribus aure et oculo congruentius verificatur. Vel, si de exterioribus sensibus accipiatur, auris et oculus hæc egisse dicuntur, in quantum homines per sensus hos sumpserunt occasionem seu materiam hæc agendi. Eo quod liberassem pauperem de manu potentioris et oppressoris, vociferantem, id est conquerentem, vel ad me pro ope clamantem: et pupillum similiter liberassem, cui non esset adjutor, quia nec patrem nec amicos habuit se juvantes. Benedictio perituri super me veniebat, hoc est, qui periturus seu occidendus vel opprimendus fuerat, nisi ego ei subvenissem, benedixit mihi, optando imprecandoque mihi bona, et gratias referendo. Ad hoc Salomon hortans: Erue, inquit, eos qui ducuntur ad mortem; et eos qui trahuntur ad interitum, liberare ne cesses. Et cor viduæ consolatus sum: quæ ob viri carentiam magis eget solatio. His verbis confutat Job verba amicorum suorum, qui eum superius de crudelitate atque tyrannide accusabant.
paras.en: [[29:11|The ear that heard|Auris audiens]] my words or my fame [[29:11|blessed me|beatificabat me]], that is, accounted me happy; [[29:11|and the eye that saw me gave witness to me|et oculus videns, testimonium reddebat mihi]], that is, by beholding my works […] that I was truly just: which is more fittingly verified of the inner ear and eye. Or, if it is taken of the outward senses, the ear and the eye are said to have done these things inasmuch as men took from these senses the occasion or matter of doing them. [[29:12|Because I had delivered the poor man|Eo quod liberassem pauperem]] from the hand of one more powerful, of the oppressor, [[29:12|that cried out|vociferantem]], that is, who complained, or cried out to me for help; [[29:12|and the fatherless|et pupillum]] I had likewise delivered, [[29:12|that had no helper|cui non esset adjutor]], since he had neither father nor friends to help him. [[29:13|The blessing of him that was ready to perish came upon me|Benedictio perituri super me veniebat]], that is, he who would have perished, or been slain or oppressed, had I not come to his aid, blessed me, wishing and praying good things for me and giving thanks. Solomon exhorts to this: [[Prov 24:11|Deliver|Erue]], he says, [[Prov 24:11|them that are led to death: and those that are drawn to death, forbear not to deliver|eos qui ducuntur ad mortem; et eos qui trahuntur ad interitum, liberare ne cesses]]. [[29:13|and I comforted the heart of the widow|Et cor viduæ consolatus sum]], who for want of a husband has the more need of comfort. By these words Job refutes the words of his friends, who above accused him of cruelty and tyranny[[Job 22:9||]] [the margin reference here is unreadable; Eliphaz makes this charge at Job 22:5–9].

paras.t: Justitia indutus sum, et vestivi me ea sicut vestimento, id est, animam meam justitia decoravi, et in omnibus juste habere studui, ut sicut corpus circumdatur veste, sic ego undique justitiæ actibus perornarer; juxta illud Isaiæ, Induit me Dominus vestimento salutis, et indumento justitiæ circumdedit me. Et diademate judicio meo, id est, justo judicio, quod in omnibus pronuntiavi et feci, ornatus sum in ratione, sicut caput diademate adornatur. Diadema namque est signum recti judicii rationis.
paras.en: [[29:14|I was clad with justice|Justitia indutus sum]], [[29:14|and I clothed myself|et vestivi me]] with it [[29:14|as with a robe|sicut vestimento]], that is, I adorned my soul with justice, and strove to act justly in all things, so that, as the body is surrounded by a garment, so I might be adorned on every side with acts of justice; according to that of Isaias, [[Is 61:10|he hath clothed me with the garments of salvation: and with the robe of justice he hath covered me|Induit me Dominus vestimento salutis, et indumento justitiæ circumdedit me]]. [[29:14|and a diadem|Et diademate]], [[29:14|with my judgment|judicio meo]], that is, with just judgment, which I pronounced and carried out in all things, I was adorned in my reason, as the head is adorned with a diadem. For the diadem is the sign of the right judgment of reason.

paras.t: Oculus, id est director, illuminator, instructor, fui cæco, id est ignoranti, vel etiam corporaliter cæcum, opportunitate se offerente, ducendo. Ignorantem autem instruere, ad spiritualia misericordiæ pertinet opera. Et pes claudo, id est adjutor infirmo: quod et corporaliter facere potuit, talem necessitate ingruente portando. Sic et Apostolus ait: Sumus singuli alter alterius membra. Itemque: Debemus nos firmiores, imbecillitates infirmorum portare. Et Christus Apostolis loquitur: Vos estis lux mundi. Quid enim est lux mundi, nisi oculus hominum mundanorum?
paras.en: [[29:15|I was an eye|Oculus]], that is, a director, enlightener and instructor, [[29:15|to the blind|fui cæco]], that is, to the ignorant, or even bodily to the blind man, by leading him when the occasion offered. Now to instruct the ignorant belongs to the spiritual works of mercy. [[29:15|and a foot to the lame|Et pes claudo]], that is, a helper to the weak: which he could also do bodily, by carrying such a one when need pressed. So too the Apostle says: We are [[Rom 12:5|every one members one of another|singuli alter alterius membra]]. And again: [[Rom 15:1|we that are stronger ought to bear the infirmities of the weak|Debemus nos firmiores, imbecillitates infirmorum portare]]. And Christ says to the Apostles: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]]. For what is the light of the world but the eye of the men of the world?

paras.t: Pater eram pauperum: pater, inquam, per curam et caritatem, opem et consolationem quas eis impendi: secundum illud in Ecclesiastico, Congregationi pauperum te affabilem facito. Tobias quoque: Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere: ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini. Et causam quam nesciebam, hoc est negotium in judicio propositum, mihi ignotum, diligentissime investigabam, inquirendo veritatem facti, processum, originem et circumstantias ejus, ne quid doli lateret, aut aliquid de ordine juris omitterem. Bonum enim bene agendum est, juxta illud Deuteronomii: Juste quod justum est exsequeris. Istud præcipue ad judices spectat, prout rex Josaphat ait judicibus suis: Sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cum diligentia cuncta facite.
paras.en: [[29:16|I was the father of the poor|Pater eram pauperum]]: a father, I say, by the care and charity, the help and comfort that I gave them; according to that in Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 4:7|Make thyself affable to the congregation of the poor|Congregationi pauperum te affabilem facito]]. Tobias also: [[Tob 4:7|turn not away thy face from any poor person: for so it shall come to pass that the face of the Lord shall not be turned from thee|Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere: ita enim fiet, ut nec a te avertatur facies Domini]]. [[29:16|and the cause which I knew not|Et causam quam nesciebam]], that is, the business laid before me in judgment and unknown to me, [[29:16|I searched out most diligently|diligentissime investigabam]], inquiring into the truth of the fact, its course, origin and circumstances, so that no fraud might lie hidden and I might leave out nothing of the order of law. For a good thing is to be done well, according to that of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 16:20|Thou shalt follow justly after that which is just|Juste quod justum est exsequeris]]. This belongs especially to judges, as king Josaphat says to his judges: [[2 Par 19:7|Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do all things with diligence|Sit timor Domini vobiscum, et cum diligentia cuncta facite]] [the margin, as read, gives 1 Par. xix; the words are at 2 Par 19:7].

paras.t: Conterebam molas iniqui, id est, mandibulas ejus destruxi, hoc est, ejus crudelitatem violentiamque repressi, et de dentibus illius auferebam prædam, id est, bona quæ aliis injuste abstulit, excussi ab eo, et quibus pertinebant, restitui. In quo secutus est Deum, de quo in Psalmo cantamus: Deus conteret dentes eorum in ore ipsorum; molas leonum confringet Dominus.
paras.en: [[29:17|I broke the jaws of the wicked man|Conterebam molas iniqui]] [*molas*, literally the grinders or back teeth, which Denis glosses *mandibulas*, jaws], that is, I destroyed his jaws, that is, I held down his cruelty and violence, [[29:17|and out of his teeth I took away the prey|et de dentibus illius auferebam prædam]], that is, the goods he had unjustly taken from others I wrested from him and restored to those to whom they belonged. In this he followed God, of whom we sing in the Psalm: [[Ps 57:7|God shall break in pieces their teeth in their mouth: the Lord shall break the grinders of the lions|Deus conteret dentes eorum in ore ipsorum; molas leonum confringet Dominus]].

paras.t: Dicebamque, id est, propter hæc opera mea pia ac virtuosa fiducialiter cogitavi: In nidulo meo moriar, hoc est, in propria domo manebo quietus, et ibi in pace ac prosperitate stabili vivam, nec alibi velut exsul et pauper decedam. Quia enim tam clementissimus fuit egenis, putavit se in prosperitate mansurum: sicut Berzellai dixit ad David, Obsecro ut revertar in civitatem meam, et moriar ibi, sepeliarque juxta sepulcrum patris mei et matris meæ. Et sicut palma multiplicabo dies, id est, diu victurus sum, sicut palma valde diu vegetabiliter vivit: quia et scriptum est, Justus ut palma florebit.
paras.en: [[29:18|And I said|Dicebamque]], that is, on account of these pious and virtuous works of mine I thought with confidence: [[29:18|I shall die in my nest|In nidulo meo moriar]], that is, I shall remain at rest in my own house, and there live in peace and settled prosperity, and shall not die elsewhere as an exile and a poor man. For because he was so very merciful to the needy, he thought he would remain in prosperity: as Berzellai said to David, [[2 Kings 19:37|I beseech thee let thy servant return, and die in my own city, and be buried by the sepulchre of my father, and of my mother|Obsecro ut revertar in civitatem meam, et moriar ibi, sepeliarque juxta sepulcrum patris mei et matris meæ]] [the margin, as read, gives 2 Kings 19:31; Berzellai's words are at 2 Kings 19:37]. [[29:18|and as a palm tree shall multiply my days|Et sicut palma multiplicabo dies]], that is, I shall live long, as the palm lives and grows for a very long time: for it is also written, [[Ps 91:13|The just shall flourish like the palm tree|Justus ut palma florebit]].

paras.t: Radix mea aperta est juxta aquas: id est, ratio vitæ et prosperitatis meæ plurima habet fomenta diu manendi in vita et prosperitate, quemadmodum arbor juxta aquas plantata, diutius manet, floret, fructificat. Prædicta autem fomenta intelligit sua opera virtuosa, quæ vitam suam interiorem et prosperitatem fovebant ac fulciebant, sicut aqua arborem juxta se sitam. Vel radix ista fuit fundamentum vitæ spiritualis, plantatum juxta charismata gratiarum, qui per aquas signantur: sicque radix potest intelligi fides, seu gratia gratum faciens, vel cordis intentio, quibus ceteræ virtutes ac dona junguntur. Unde Jeremias dicit: Benedictus vir qui confidit in Domino: et erit tanquam lignum quod transplantatum est super aquas, quod ad humorem mittit radices suas.
paras.en: [[29:19|My root is opened beside the waters|Radix mea aperta est juxta aquas]] [the margin gives the Vulgate's reading *secus*, beside, for Denis's *juxta*; the sense is the same]: that is, the root of my life and prosperity has very many nourishments for remaining long in life and prosperity, as a tree planted by the waters lasts longer, flowers and bears fruit. By these nourishments he means his virtuous works, which fostered and upheld his inner life and his prosperity, as water does a tree set beside it. Or this root was the foundation of the spiritual life, planted beside the charisms of graces, which are signified by the waters: and so the root can be understood as faith, or sanctifying grace [Latin *gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God], or the intention of the heart, to which the other virtues and gifts are joined. Hence Jeremias says: [[Jer 17:7|Blessed be the man that trusteth in the Lord|Benedictus vir qui confidit in Domino]]: [[Jer 17:8|And he shall be as a tree that is planted by the waters, that spreadeth out its roots towards moisture|et erit tanquam lignum quod transplantatum est super aquas, quod ad humorem mittit radices suas]].

paras.t: Insuper dixi: Et ros morabitur in messione mea: hoc est, terræ nascentia mea tempore messis solis ardore non comburentur, sed rore erunt humecta. Ros etiam (secundum Albertum) auget, mollificat, et ad digestionem cooperatur, ut fructus fiat boni saporis. Hinc in Genesi dicitur: In pinguedine terræ et in rore cœli desuper erit benedictio tua.
paras.en: Moreover I said: [[29:19|and dew shall continue in my harvest|Et ros morabitur in messione mea]], that is, the fruits of my land will not be burnt up by the heat of the sun at harvest time, but will be moist with dew. Dew also (according to Albert) makes them grow, softens them, and helps their ripening [*digestio*, the ripening or 'cooking' of fruit], so that the fruit may be of a good flavour. Hence it is said in Genesis: [[Gen 27:39|In the fat of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above|In pinguedine terræ et in rore cœli desuper]] [[Gen 27:40|shall thy blessing be|erit benedictio tua]].

paras.t: Dixi quoque: Gloria mea semper innovabitur, hoc est, gaudium conscientiæ meæ, vel claritas famæ, seu delectatio in prosperitate quotidie crescet, perseverante me in bonis inceptis. Unde Apostolus ait: Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ. Et iterum: Licet is qui foris est, noster homo corrumpatur, tamen is qui intus est, renovatur de die in diem. Et arcus meus, id est virtus animi mei, qua hostibus meæ salutis resisto, et jacula virtutum contra eos projicio, in manu mea, hoc est operatione mea, instaurabitur, ita quod de die in diem in virtute proficiam, atque in bonis actibus amplius abundabo.
paras.en: I said also: [[29:20|My glory shall always be renewed|Gloria mea semper innovabitur]], that is, the joy of my conscience, or the brightness of my fame, or my delight in prosperity, will grow daily, as I persevere in the good things begun. Hence the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 1:12|our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience|Gloria nostra hæc est, testimonium conscientiæ nostræ]]. And again: [[2 Cor 4:16|though our outward man is corrupted, yet the inward man is renewed day by day|Licet is qui foris est, noster homo corrumpatur, tamen is qui intus est, renovatur de die in diem]]. [[29:20|and my bow|Et arcus meus]], that is, the strength of my mind, by which I resist the enemies of my salvation and hurl the darts of the virtues against them, [[29:20|in my hand|in manu mea]], that is, in my working, [[29:20|shall be repaired|instaurabitur]], so that from day to day I shall advance in virtue and abound more and more in good deeds.

paras.t: Qui me audiebant, exspectabant sententiam, id est, sollicite præstolabantur quid determinative dictarem, scientes quod verbis meis standum esset, et quod non nisi verba sensibus veritateque plena proferrem; et intenti tacebant ad consilium meum, parati acquiescere definitioni meæ. Verbis meis nihil addere audebant, quia tantæ me prudentiæ reputabant, quod suis verbis verba mea perficere non valerent; et super illos stillabat, hoc est, ordinate et congruenter venit, eloquium meum, quemadmodum guttæ cadunt in terram; juxta illud Deuteronomii, Fluat ut ros eloquium meum, quasi imber super herbam, et quasi stilla super gramina.
paras.en: [[29:21|They that heard me, waited for my sentence|Qui me audiebant, exspectabant sententiam]], that is, they waited anxiously for what I would lay down as settled, knowing that my words were to be abided by, and that I would bring forth only words full of meaning and truth; [[29:21|and being attentive held their peace at my counsel|et intenti tacebant ad consilium meum]], ready to rest in my decision. [[29:22|To my words they durst add nothing|Verbis meis nihil addere audebant]], because they reckoned me of such prudence that they could not perfect my words with words of their own; and [[29:22|dropped upon them|super illos stillabat]], that is, came in due order and fittingly, [[29:22|my speech|eloquium meum]], as drops fall upon the earth; according to that of Deuteronomy, [[Deut 32:2|let my speech distil as the dew, as a shower upon the herb, and as drops upon the grass|Fluat ut ros eloquium meum, quasi imber super herbam, et quasi stilla super gramina]].

paras.t: Exspectabant me sicut pluviam, id est cum grandi affectu, sperantes consolationem et fructum ex verbis meis percipere; et os suum aperiebant quasi ad imbrem serotinum, qui in fructibus debitam complet digestionem, ne amari permaneant. In quo notatur, quod avidissime cupiebant eum audire: nam per os, intellectus vel desiderium cordis exprimitur.
paras.en: [[29:23|They waited for me as for rain|Exspectabant me sicut pluviam]], that is, with great longing, hoping to receive comfort and fruit from my words; [[29:23|and they opened their mouth as for a latter shower|et os suum aperiebant quasi ad imbrem serotinum]], which completes the due ripening in the fruits, so that they do not stay bitter. In this it is noted that they most eagerly desired to hear him: for by the mouth the understanding or the desire of the heart is expressed.

paras.t: Si quando ridebam ad eos, gratiosum et hilarem me eis præbendo: quod aliquando agendum est, ne maturitas sit austera, et homo velut agrestis, sit aliis onerosus, vel etiam immoderato rigore lædat se ipsum. Unde a Philosopho atque moralibus ponitur virtus moralis, quæ eutrapelia vocatur, per quam homo in ludis et recreativis solatiis moderanter se habet. Hinc Seneca docet: Ita te habeas, ut nemo te quasi levem despiciat, aut quasi silvestrem graviter ferat. Porro risus non semper peccatum est; quando autem sit et quomodo, et quando et quomodo non, articulo vicesimo secundo fuit ostensum. Non credebant, quod riderem ex animo et simplici causa, sed potius mystica ratione et ex virtute. Unde et tunc me verebantur.
paras.en: [[29:24|If at any time I laughed on them|Si quando ridebam ad eos]], showing myself gracious and cheerful to them: which must be done at times, lest gravity be austere, and a man, like a rustic, be burdensome to others, or even harm himself by immoderate rigour. Hence the Philosopher and the moralists set down a moral virtue called eutrapelia [that is, pleasantness in play and conversation, the virtue that keeps recreation within measure], by which a man behaves with moderation in games and recreative amusements. Hence Seneca teaches: So bear thyself that no one may despise thee as frivolous, nor find thee hard to bear as uncouth. Laughter, moreover, is not always a sin; but when and how it is, and when and how it is not, was shown in the twenty-second article. [[29:24|they believed not|Non credebant]] that I laughed from the heart and for a simple cause, but rather for a mystical reason [that is, a hidden one] and out of virtue. Hence even then they held me in awe.

paras.t: Et lux vultus mei non cadebat in terram. Si de corporali vultu accipitur, lux vultus est visus vel faciei hilaritas. Per hoc ergo quod ait, Lux, etc., insinuat quod non fuit mœrore depressus, ut hi qui tristitia victi visum in terram defigunt. Sicque per lucem vultus intelligitur oculus: et ita exponit Thomas. Si autem per lucem hanc intelligatur interioris faciei hilaritas, sensus est, quod non fuit inani lætitia dissolutus: ita quod lætitia sua non ruit in terram, id est in vitii conculcationem tanquam confusibilis et inhonesta. Sic exponit Albertus. Potest et ita exponi, quod lux vultus sui, id est visus exterior, non cadebat in terram, id est, ad terrenorum immoderatum adspectum non ferebatur: ut visus illorum qui terrena cælestibus præferunt, ideoque instar porcorum ad carnalia intuenda jugiter flectunt visum; vel vagi sunt oculis, sicut et Salomon loquitur: Oculi stultorum in finibus terræ. Porro, si de interiori spiritualique vultu effatur, lux vultus hujus est ratio vel sapientia ejus: qui in beato Job non cadebat in terram, quia ad divina quotidie erigebatur, nec imprimebatur carnalibus. Jugiter ergo interiori visu et frequenter exteriori ad cælestia se levavit.
paras.en: [[29:24|and the light of my countenance fell not on earth|Et lux vultus mei non cadebat in terram]]. If it is taken of the bodily countenance, the light of the countenance is the sight, or the cheerfulness of the face. By saying, then, [[29:24|the light|Lux]], etc., he implies that he was not cast down by grief, like those who, overcome by sadness, fix their gaze on the ground. And so by the light of the countenance the eye is understood: and so Thomas expounds it. But if by this light is understood the cheerfulness of the inner face, the sense is that he was not dissolved in empty mirth, so that his gladness did not rush down to the earth, that is, into being trampled under by vice, as something shameful and unseemly. So Albert expounds it. It can also be expounded thus: the light of his countenance, that is, his outward sight, did not fall to the earth, that is, was not carried to an immoderate gazing on earthly things, like the sight of those who prefer earthly things to heavenly, and therefore, like swine, keep bending their gaze to look upon carnal things; or they have wandering eyes, as Solomon too says: [[Prov 17:24|the eyes of fools are in the ends of the earth|Oculi stultorum in finibus terræ]]. Further, if it is said of the inner and spiritual countenance, the light of this countenance is its reason or wisdom: which in blessed Job did not fall to the earth, because it was lifted up daily to divine things and did not take the stamp of carnal things. Continually, then, with his inner sight, and often with his outward sight, he lifted himself up to heavenly things.

paras.t: Si voluissem ire ad eos: quod sine idonea causa non fecit; sed propter instructionem, consolationem, judicationem, aut simile aliquid aliquando præfatos accessit; sedebam primus, id est in loco supremo et tempore ante alios, tanquam omnium principalis. Cumque sederem quasi rex circumstante exercitu. Quod ait, Circumstante exercitu, referri potest vel ad ipsius Job sessionem, ut sit sensus, quod sedit circumstantibus multis; vel ad regem, eritque sensus, quod sedit sicut rex sedet circumstante regem exercitu: ex quo patet, quod maximam impendebant reverentiam sancto Job. Eram tamen mœrentium, id est afflictorum et desolatorum seu tristium, consolator, in prosperis me humilians, non extollens, nec illos despiciens. Sicque beatus Job implevit illud Ecclesiastici, Non desis plorantibus in consolatione; et quod rursum eodem in libro præcipitur, In die honoris tui ne extollaris. Hæc quoque præcipue ad reges, prælatos, ac principes spectant, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Misericordia et veritas custodiunt regem, et roboratur clementia thronus ejus.
paras.en: [[29:25|If I had a mind to go to them|Si voluissem ire ad eos]]: which he did not do without fitting cause; but at times he went to the aforesaid for instruction, comfort, judgment or something of the kind; [[29:25|I sat first|sedebam primus]], that is, in the highest place and before the others in time, as the chief of all. [[29:25|and when I sat as a king, with his army standing about him|Cumque sederem quasi rex circumstante exercitu]]. When he says, [[29:25|with his army standing about him|Circumstante exercitu]], it can be referred either to the sitting of Job himself, so that the sense is that he sat with many standing around him; or to the king, and then the sense will be that he sat as a king sits with his army standing around the king: from which it is plain that they paid the greatest reverence to holy Job. [[29:25|yet I was|Eram tamen]] [[29:25|of them that mourned|mœrentium]], that is, of the afflicted and desolate or sorrowful, [[29:25|a comforter|consolator]], humbling myself in prosperity, not exalting myself, nor despising them. And thus blessed Job fulfilled that of Ecclesiasticus, [[Ecclus 7:38|Be not wanting in comforting them that weep|Non desis plorantibus in consolatione]]; and what is enjoined again in the same book, [[Ecclus 11:4|be not exalted in the day of thy honour|In die honoris tui ne extollaris]]. These things also belong especially to kings, prelates and princes, according to that of the Proverbs: [[Prov 20:28|Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency|Misericordia et veritas custodiunt regem, et roboratur clementia thronus ejus]].

29.title: Pertractatio moralis ejusdem capituli vicesimi noni.
29.title_en: Moral treatment of the same twenty-ninth chapter

paras.t: Addidit quoque Job, assumens parabolam suam. Juxta Gregorium, quia parabola similitudo dicitur, constat quod per exteriorum verborum formam mysteria loquitur, qui ad loquendum parabolam assumpsisse memoratur. Denique secundum doctores, sanctus Job nunc Christi, nunc Ecclesiæ, nunc cujuscumque justi seu pœnitentis speciem tenet, figuramque exprimit et personam præsentat. Unde principium hujus capituli exponit Gregorius de Ecclesia pro statu ac tempore ejus in persecutionibus Antichristi, quando (secundum Gregorium) tanta erit Ecclesiæ persecutio atque angustia, ut hæc tempora cum magno suspirio optet, quæ nos cum magno toleramus dolore. Propter quod ait: Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos, secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me? Verum, expositionem hanc, quoniam a B. Gregorio plenissime est digesta, prætereo: aliamque tropologiam inducam.
paras.en: [[29:1|Job also added, taking up his parable|Addidit quoque Job, assumens parabolam suam]]. According to Gregory, since a parable is called a likeness, it is plain that he who is recorded to have taken up a parable in order to speak speaks mysteries under the outward form of words. Further, according to the doctors, holy Job bears the likeness now of Christ, now of the Church, now of any just man or penitent, expresses his figure and represents his person. Hence Gregory expounds the beginning of this chapter of the Church, in her state and time during the persecutions of Antichrist, when (according to Gregory) the persecution and distress of the Church will be so great that she will long with deep sighing for these times which we now endure with great sorrow. Wherefore she says: [[29:2|Who will grant me, that I might be according to the months past, according to the days in which God kept me?|Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos, secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me?]] But since this exposition has been set out most fully by blessed Gregory, I pass it over, and shall bring in another tropology [that is, another moral reading of the text].

paras.t: Quemadmodum ergo Job a temporali prosperitate dejectus, et corporaliter gravissime læsus, verba hæc protulit; sic quilibet veraciter pœnitens, qui aliquando præclaræ exstitit æquitatis, qualis fuit David quum adulterium homicidiumque inexcusabiliter incurrisset, verba hæc dicere potest, tanquam ad pristinum gradum virtutum cupiens reformari: quamvis etiam de homine justo, corporaliter vulnerato aut tribulato et mente afflicto, elucidari hæc possint: quod quomodo fieri possit, ex præinducta explanatione facillime consideratur. Præfata ergo spiritualis moralitas est tractanda.
paras.en: As therefore Job, cast down from temporal prosperity and most grievously stricken in body, uttered these words, so any truly penitent man who was once of outstanding uprightness (such as David was, when he had inexcusably fallen into adultery and murder[[2 Kings 11:4||]][[2 Kings 11:15||]][[2 Kings 11:17||]]) can say these words, as one longing to be restored to his former degree of virtue; although these things can also be explained of a just man wounded or afflicted in body and troubled in mind: how this can be done is very easily seen from the exposition given above. It is the spiritual moral sense, then, that is now to be treated.

paras.t: Pœnitens igitur ait: Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos, id est in tali opulentia spirituali, in tali devotionis compunctionisque gratia, in tali perfectione virtutum, quales aliquando habui? Quo enim spiritualia dona bonis terrenis sunt digniora, et munera gratiæ bonis fortunæ, eo de illarum amissione amplius est dolendum, cordialiusque optandum et efficacius satagendum, ut lapsus ad pristinam revertatur mensuram gratiæ ac virtutum. Si ergo nos in caritate tepuisse, in Dei obsequio pigros factos conspicimus, aut grave incidisse peccatum invenimus, intime doleamus, fortiter emendemus, et verba hæc affectuosissime proferamus, attendentes quod in Apocalypsi Deus ait cuidam: Habeo adversus te, quia caritatem tuam primam reliquisti. Memor esto itaque unde excideris, et pœnitentiam age. Alioqui venio tibi cito. Secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me, id est, in bonis gratiæ conservabat. Sicut enim diei lux incessanter conservatur a sole, sine quo nec ad momentum valet durare; sic nec in ictu oculi in donis gratiæ permanere valemus, nisi indesinenter in eis divinitus conservemur. Non ergo stultissime gloriemur, neque vanissime præsumamus; sed cum Psalmista quilibet nostrum humiliter deprecetur: Custodi me ut pupillam oculi; sub umbra alarum tuarum protege me. Atque ex animo fateatur: Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, frustra vigilat qui custodit eam.
paras.en: The penitent therefore says: [[29:2|Who will grant me, that I might be according to the months past|Quis mihi tribuat, ut sim juxta menses pristinos]], that is, in such spiritual wealth, in such grace of devotion and compunction, in such perfection of virtues as I once had? For as much as spiritual gifts are worthier than earthly goods, and the gifts of grace than the goods of fortune, so much the more is their loss to be grieved over, and the more heartily is it to be desired and the more effectually laboured for, that the fallen man may return to his former measure of grace and virtue. If, then, we see that we have grown lukewarm in charity and slothful in the service of God, or find that we have fallen into grievous sin, let us grieve inwardly, amend stoutly, and utter these words with the deepest feeling, minding what God says to someone in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 2:4|I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first charity|Habeo adversus te, quia caritatem tuam primam reliquisti]]. [[Apoc 2:5|Be mindful therefore from whence thou art fallen: and do penance|Memor esto itaque unde excideris, et pœnitentiam age]]. [[Apoc 2:5|Or else I come to thee|Alioqui venio tibi]] quickly [*cito*, “quickly”, comes from the like warning of Apoc 2:16]. [[29:2|according to the days in which God kept me?|Secundum dies quibus Deus custodiebat me]] That is, he preserved me in the goods of grace. For as the light of day is ceaselessly preserved by the sun, without which it cannot last a moment, so neither can we abide in the gifts of grace for the twinkling of an eye unless we are unceasingly preserved in them by God. Let us not then glory most foolishly, nor presume most vainly; but let each of us humbly pray with the Psalmist: [[Ps 16:8|keep me, as the apple of thy eye. Protect me under the shadow of thy wings|Custodi me ut pupillam oculi; sub umbra alarum tuarum protege me]]. And let him confess from his heart: [[Ps 126:1|Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it|Nisi Dominus custodierit civitatem, frustra vigilat qui custodit eam]].

paras.t: Quando splendebat lucerna ejus, id est lumen gratiæ, vel doctrina sacræ Scripturæ, super caput meum, id est in mente mea, quæ est principium et principale in anima, sicut caput in corpore; et ad lumen ejus, id est secundum directionem illustrationis divinæ, ambulabam in tenebris, id est, inter mundanos ac impios conversabar virtuose ac sapienter, non illorum sequendo peccata: quamvis dicat Scriptura, Cum perverso perverteris. Pro hac directione orat Psalmista: Dirige me Domine, in veritate tua, et doce me. Itemque: Deduc me, Domine, in via tua, et ingrediar in veritate tua. Porro, quod peccatores tenebræ nuncupentur, constat ex eo quod conversis ait Apostolus: Fuistis aliquando tenebræ. Joannes quoque: Tenebræ eam (videlicet lucem, quæ Christus est) non comprehenderunt.
paras.en: [[29:3|When his lamp shined|Quando splendebat lucerna ejus]], that is, the light of grace, or the teaching of sacred Scripture, [[29:3|over my head|super caput meum]], that is, in my mind, which is the beginning and the chief part in the soul, as the head is in the body; and [[29:3|by his light|ad lumen ejus]], that is, according to the guidance of the divine enlightening, [[29:3|I walked|ambulabam]] [[29:3|in darkness|in tenebris]], that is, I lived virtuously and wisely among worldly and ungodly men, not following their sins: although Scripture says, [[Ps 17:27|with the perverse thou wilt be perverted|Cum perverso perverteris]]. For this guidance the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 24:5|Direct me in thy truth, and teach me|Dirige me Domine, in veritate tua, et doce me]]. And again: [[Ps 85:11|Conduct me, O Lord, in thy way, and I will walk in thy truth|Deduc me, Domine, in via tua, et ingrediar in veritate tua]]. Further, that sinners are called darkness is plain from what the Apostle says to the converted: [[Eph 5:8|you were heretofore darkness|Fuistis aliquando tenebræ]]. And John: [[John 1:5|the darkness|Tenebræ]] [[John 1:5|did not comprehend it|non comprehenderunt]] (that is, the light, which is Christ).

paras.t: Sicut fui in diebus adolescentiæ meæ. Spiritualis adolescentia dici potest initium conversionis, dum homo spiritualiter sapere inchoat, sicut in adolescentia corporali, ratione incipit uti. Quidam autem in conversionis suæ exordio sunt ferventes, et postea tepent ac pigri sunt, carnalesque fiunt. Quod quam detestandum sit, ex verbo claret Apostoli ad Galatas: Sic stulti estis, ut quum spiritu cœperitis, nunc carne consummemini? Talibus ergo incumbit dolere, emendare, præinductaque verba proferre, ut scilicet cupiant et conentur esse in tali fervore et gratia, in qualibus in conversionis suæ fuere primordiis. Unde in Apocalypsi hujuscemodi homini dicitur: In mente habe qualiter acceperis, et audieris: et pœnitentiam age, et esto vigilans. Quando secreto Deus erat in tabernaculo meo, id est in conscientiæ thalamo seu cordis mei cubiculo, animam meam familiariter visitando, dulciter consolando, inflammando, regendo: ita quod illud Isaiæ, Secretum meum mihi, dicere potui.
paras.en: [[29:4|As I was in the days of my youth|Sicut fui in diebus adolescentiæ meæ]]. The beginning of conversion may be called spiritual youth, when a man begins to be spiritually wise, as in bodily youth he begins to use reason. Now some are fervent at the outset of their conversion, and afterwards grow lukewarm and slothful, and become carnal. How detestable this is, is clear from the Apostle's word to the Galatians: [[Gal 3:3|Are you so foolish that, whereas you began in the Spirit, you would now be made perfect by the flesh?|Sic stulti estis, ut quum spiritu cœperitis, nunc carne consummemini?]] It falls to such men, then, to grieve, to amend, and to utter the words set down above: that is, to desire and strive to be in such fervour and grace as they were in at the first beginnings of their conversion. Hence it is said in the Apocalypse to a man of this kind: [[Apoc 3:3|Have in mind therefore in what manner thou hast received and heard|In mente habe qualiter acceperis, et audieris]]: [[Apoc 3:3|and do penance|et pœnitentiam age]], and [[Apoc 3:2|Be watchful|esto vigilans]] [Denis joins to these words of Apoc 3:3 the first words of the verse before]. [[29:4|when God was secretly in my tabernacle|Quando secreto Deus erat in tabernaculo meo]], that is, in the bridal chamber of the conscience or the inner room of my heart, visiting my soul familiarly, consoling it sweetly, kindling it, ruling it: so that I could say that word of Isaias, [[Is 24:16|My secret to myself|Secretum meum mihi]].

paras.t: Quando erat Omnipotens mecum: ita quod dicere potui, Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat; et rursum, Deus cordis mei, et pars mea Deus in æternum. Et in circuitu meo pueri mei, id est spirituales filii sive discipuli, vel cogitatus, affectus, actusque virtuosi, quibus undique fecundabar et adornabar.
paras.en: [[29:5|When the Almighty was with me|Quando erat Omnipotens mecum]]: so that I could say, [[Phil 4:13|I can do all things in him who strengtheneth me|Omnia possum in eo qui me confortat]]; and again, [[Ps 72:26|the God of my heart, and the God that is my portion for ever|Deus cordis mei, et pars mea Deus in æternum]]. [[29:5|and my servants round about me|Et in circuitu meo pueri mei]], that is, spiritual sons or disciples, or virtuous thoughts, affections and acts, with which I was made fruitful and adorned on every side [the Latin *pueri* means “boys” or “children” as well as “servants”].

paras.t: Quando lavabam pedes meos butyro. Pedes sunt mentis affectus operumque processus. De quibus in Canticis legitur: Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo eos? Qui pedes butyro lavantur, dum fervidæ caritatis exuberanti affectu, vel internæ devotionis pinguedine, seu bonæ conversationis abundantia, a præteritis malis ac quotidianis defectibus expurgantur. Caritas enim operit multitudinem peccatorum. Et Salvator ait: Qui lotus est, non indiget nisi ut pedes lavet. Hinc orat Psalmista: Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea.
paras.en: [[29:6|When I washed my feet with butter|Quando lavabam pedes meos butyro]]. The feet are the affections of the mind and the course of its works. Of these we read in the Canticles: [[Cant 5:3|I have washed my feet, how shall I defile them?|Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo eos?]] These feet are washed with butter when they are cleansed of past evils and daily failings by the overflowing affection of fervent charity, or by the richness of inward devotion, or by the abundance of good living. For [[1 Pet 4:8|charity covereth a multitude of sins|Caritas enim operit multitudinem peccatorum]]. And the Saviour says: [[John 13:10|He that is washed needeth not but to wash his feet|Qui lotus est, non indiget nisi ut pedes lavet]]. Hence the Psalmist prays: [[Ps 62:6|Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness|Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea]].

paras.t: Quando procedebam ad portam civitatis. Civitas est regnum cœleste, de qua in Apocalypsi habetur: Civitas non eget sole neque luna: nam claritas Dei illuminabit eam. Cui Isaias dicit: Non erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem, sed erit tibi Dominus in lucem sempiternam. Hujus civitatis porta est actio virtuosa, de qua in Evangelio loquitur Christus: Quam angusta porta quæ ducit ad vitam. Ad hanc ergo portam procedere, est ad opera virtutum se ipsum extendere. Et in platea, id est populi latitudine, parabant cathedram, id est auctoritatem et locum docendi.
paras.en: [[29:7|When I went out to the gate of the city|Quando procedebam ad portam civitatis]]. The city is the kingdom of heaven, of which it is said in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 21:23|the city hath no need of the sun, nor of the moon|Civitas non eget sole neque luna]]: [[Apoc 21:23|For the glory of God hath enlightened it|nam claritas Dei illuminabit eam]]. And Isaias says to it: [[Is 60:19|Thou shalt no more have the sun for thy light by day|Non erit tibi sol amplius ad lucendum per diem]], [[Is 60:19|but the Lord shall be unto thee for an everlasting light|sed erit tibi Dominus in lucem sempiternam]]. The gate of this city is virtuous action, of which Christ speaks in the Gospel: [[Matt 7:14|How narrow is the gate|Quam angusta porta]] [[Matt 7:14|that leadeth to life|quæ ducit ad vitam]]. To go out to this gate, then, is to stretch oneself out to the works of the virtues. [[29:7|and in the street|Et in platea]], that is, in the broad place of the people, [[29:7|they prepared me a chair|parabant cathedram]], that is, authority and a place of teaching.

paras.t: Videbant me juvenes, et abscondebantur; et senes assurgentes, stabant. Potest hoc cum verbis sequentibus clausulæ hujus, de ipsis diversæ conditionis personis exponi; et de homine qui aliquando tantæ exstitit auctoritatis, perfectionis ac sapientiæ, ut talia sibi exhiberentur ab illis, qualia sancto Job leguntur exhibita. Spiritualiter vero, per juvenes intelligi possunt affectus et motus indisciplinati ac pueriles, qui ab homine virtuoso ad bona agenda tendente pelluntur. Senes vero, sunt affectus et motus maturi ac sapientiales, qui in virtuoso oriuntur ac stant, ad rationis imperium præparati. Principes cessabant loqui, id est, principales conceptus ipsius intellectus, ratione jubente, intus quieverunt, nec in verba exteriora proruperunt, exigentibus id causa et loco et tempore: quia aliquando vicissim etiam a bonis verbis cessandum est, juxta illud Psalmi: Obmutui, et humiliatus sum, et silui a bonis. Vocem suam cohibebant duces, id est conceptus interiores, directivi operum externorum: qui interdum pro rationabili causa non jubent exteriora opera fieri, dum contemplationi vacandum est, aut aliud quid occurrit.
paras.en: [[29:8|The young men saw me, and hid themselves: and the old men rose up and stood|Videbant me juvenes, et abscondebantur; et senes assurgentes, stabant]]. This, together with the words that follow in this passage, can be expounded of those very persons of differing condition, and of a man who was once of such authority, perfection and wisdom that such things were shown him by them as we read were shown to holy Job. But spiritually, by the young men can be understood the undisciplined and childish affections and movements, which are driven off by the virtuous man as he strives to do good; and the old men are the mature and wise affections and movements, which arise and stand firm in the virtuous man, ready at the command of reason. [[29:9|The princes ceased to speak|Principes cessabant loqui]], that is, the chief conceptions of the intellect itself, at the bidding of reason, were still within and did not break out into outward words, as cause, place and time required: for sometimes one must in turn cease even from good words, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 38:3|I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silence from good things|Obmutui, et humiliatus sum, et silui a bonis]]. [[29:10|The rulers held their peace|Vocem suam cohibebant duces]] [literally “the leaders held back their voice”], that is, the inward conceptions that direct outward works, which sometimes, for a reasonable cause, do not bid outward works be done, when one must be free for contemplation, or something else comes up.

paras.t: Auris audiens beatificabat me, et oculus videns testimonium reddebat mihi. Quicumque irreprehensibiliter conversatur, implens illud Apostoli, Nemini demus ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum, præinducta hæc verba dicere potest: quemadmodum in Actis de Christianis primitivæ Ecclesiæ sub Apostolis in Jerusalem legitur, quod habebant gratiam ad omnem plebem, et ceterorum nemo audebat se jungere eis, sed beatificabat eos populus. Ad quod hortatur nos princeps Apostolorum: Conversationem (inquiens) vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis tanquam malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, glorificent Deum.
paras.en: [[29:11|The ear that heard me blessed me|Auris audiens beatificabat me]], [[29:11|and the eye that saw me gave witness to me|et oculus videns testimonium reddebat mihi]]. Whoever lives blamelessly, fulfilling that word of the Apostle, [[2 Cor 6:3|Giving no offence to any man, that our ministry be not blamed|Nemini demus ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum]] [Denis reads *demus*, “let us give”], can say the words set down above: as we read in the Acts of the Christians of the early Church under the Apostles in Jerusalem, that they had [[Acts 2:47|favour with all the people|gratiam ad omnem plebem]], and [[Acts 5:13|of the rest no man durst join himself unto them|ceterorum nemo audebat se jungere eis]]: [[Acts 5:13|but the people magnified them|sed beatificabat eos populus]] [Denis reads *beatificabat*, “called them blessed”, the word of v. 11, where the Vulgate has *magnificabat*, “magnified”]. To this the prince of the Apostles exhorts us: [[1 Pet 2:12|Having your conversation|Conversationem]] (he says) [[1 Pet 2:12|good among the Gentiles: that whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may, by the good works which they shall behold in you, glorify God|vestram inter gentes habentes bonam, ut in eo quod detrectant de vobis tanquam malefactoribus, ex bonis operibus vos considerantes, glorificent Deum]].

paras.t: Eo quod liberassem pauperem vociferantem, id est hominem spiritualiter indigentem virtute et gratia, invisibilium hostium impugnationibus victum, et pro adjutorio proclamantem: quem vir caritativus ac virtuosus orando, instruendo, consulendoque liberat, sicut monet ad Galatas Apostolus: Fratres, et si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis. Unde, ut a Jacobo scriptum est: Qui converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ, salvabit animam ejus a morte. Et pupillum, id est eum qui spirituali patre, prælato et instructore carebat, cui non esset adjutor contra hostes suæ salutis, quemadmodum Ecclesiastes inducit: Væ soli, quia quum ceciderit, non habet sublevantem se.
paras.en: [[29:12|Because I had delivered the poor man that cried out|Eo quod liberassem pauperem vociferantem]], that is, the man spiritually in need of virtue and grace, overcome by the assaults of invisible enemies and crying out for help: whom the charitable and virtuous man delivers by praying, instructing and counselling, as the Apostle admonishes the Galatians: [[Gal 6:1|Brethren, and if a man be overtaken in any fault, you, who are spiritual, instruct such a one in the spirit of meekness|Fratres, et si præoccupatus fuerit homo in aliquo delicto, vos qui spirituales estis, hujusmodi instruite in spiritu lenitatis]]. Hence, as James has written: [[Jas 5:20|he who causeth a sinner to be converted from the error of his way shall save his soul from death|Qui converti fecerit peccatorem ab errore viæ suæ, salvabit animam ejus a morte]]. [[29:12|and the fatherless|Et pupillum]], that is, him who lacked a spiritual father, prelate and instructor, [[29:12|that had no helper|cui non esset adjutor]] against the enemies of his salvation, as Ecclesiastes brings in: [[Eccles 4:10|woe to him that is alone, for when he falleth, he hath none to lift him up|Væ soli, quia quum ceciderit, non habet sublevantem se]].

paras.t: Et cor viduæ consolatus sum. Vidua est anima, quæ peccando cœlestem Sponsum amisit: quæ consolanda est, ne desperet. Nisi enim hac causa anima vidua diceretur, Jeremias non diceret: Quia non fuit Israel viduatus a Deo suo. Benedictio perituri, id est peccatoris æternaliter condemnandi, nisi Deus ei per meam informationem et subventionem auxiliatus fuisset, super me veniebat. Talis quippe jam conversus et desuper illustratus, intelligens in quantis fuit periculis, et quanta sibi Deus per me beneficia gratiæ præstitisset, benedixit mihi et maximas egit grates. Quo enim vita gratiæ vitaque gloriæ meliores sunt vita naturæ; quo insuper mors æternæ damnationis fugibilior est morte corporali ac temporali, imo brevissima: eo pro ereptione a morte peccati, amplius gloriandum regratiandumque est, quam pro ereptione ab interitu corporali.
paras.en: [[29:13|and I comforted the heart of the widow|Et cor viduæ consolatus sum]]. The widow is the soul that by sinning has lost her heavenly Bridegroom: she is to be comforted, lest she despair. For unless the soul were called a widow for this reason, Jeremias would not say: [[Jer 51:5|For Israel and Juda have not been forsaken by their God|Quia non fuit Israel viduatus a Deo suo]] [where the Douay-Rheims has “forsaken” the Latin has *viduatus*, “widowed”; Denis leaves out “and Juda”]. [[29:13|The blessing of him that was ready to perish|Benedictio perituri]], that is, of the sinner who would have been condemned eternally had not God helped him through my instruction and aid, [[29:13|came upon me|super me veniebat]]. For such a man, now converted and enlightened from above, understanding in what great perils he had been, and what great benefits of grace God had bestowed on him through me, blessed me and gave the greatest thanks. For as much as the life of grace and the life of glory are better than the life of nature, and as much as the death of eternal damnation is more to be fled than bodily and temporal death, which is indeed very short, so much the more is one to glory and give thanks for rescue from the death of sin than for rescue from bodily destruction.

paras.t: Justitia indutus sum, et vestivi me sicut vestimento. Vestis ad duo proficit corpori, scilicet ad ornatum, atque ad protectionem contra nociva, ut sunt frigus et cauma. Sic virtus ad duo animæ prodest. Nam eam coram Deo pulchre perornat, et contra hostes suæ salutis defendit, confortat, seu armat. Denique vestis vestitum ex omni parte circumdat: ille ergo quasi vestimento induit se ipsum justitia, qui in omni quod agit, justus est, nullumque præceptum transgreditur, sed regia semper graditur via, nec ad dexteram nec ad sinistram declinans. Et (ut ait Gregorius) qui in aliis actionibus justus est, in aliis injustus, quasi unum latus operuit, aliudque nudavit. Imo nec jam bona sunt opera, quæ subortis aliis pravis operibus inquinantur. Verba quoque inducta, accipi possunt tam de justitia quæ est virtus communis seu omnis virtus (omnis siquidem virtus est quædam justitia, quia per eam fit quod decens seu debitum est), quemadmodum ea quæ est virtus specialis, moralis et cardinalis, unicuique quod suum est reddens. Et diademate judicio meo. Qui in omnibus rationis judicium sequitur, non passionis impulsum, et recte judicat, discutit, increpat et castigat se ipsum, judicio suo quasi diademate decoratur; et tam sapienter regendo se, rite rex appellatur, impletque quod ait Salvator: Justum judicium judicate. Cujus judicii fructum pandit Apostolus, dicens: Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur.
paras.en: [[29:14|I was clad with justice|Justitia indutus sum]], [[29:14|and I clothed myself|et vestivi me]] [[29:14|as with a robe|sicut vestimento]]. A garment serves the body for two things, namely for adornment, and for protection against harmful things, such as cold and heat. So virtue profits the soul for two things: for it adorns her beautifully before God, and defends, strengthens or arms her against the enemies of her salvation. Further, a garment surrounds its wearer on every side: he therefore clothes himself with justice as with a garment who is just in everything he does, and transgresses no commandment, but walks always on the king's highway, turning aside neither to the right hand nor to the left. And (as Gregory says) he who is just in some actions and unjust in others has, as it were, covered one side and left the other bare. Indeed, works are no longer even good which are defiled by other wicked works springing up beside them. The words set down can also be taken both of justice that is a general virtue, or all virtue (for every virtue is a kind of justice, since by it is done what is fitting or due), and of that which is a special, moral and cardinal virtue, rendering to each what is his. [[29:14|and a diadem|Et diademate]], [[29:14|with my judgment|judicio meo]]. He who in all things follows the judgment of reason, not the impulse of passion, and rightly judges, examines, rebukes and chastises himself, is adorned with his judgment as with a diadem; and ruling himself so wisely, he is rightly called a king, and fulfils what the Saviour says: [[John 7:24|judge just judgment|Justum judicium judicate]]. The fruit of this judgment the Apostle sets out, saying: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]].

paras.t: Oculus fui cæco, et pes claudo. Hoc ad prælatos ac præsidentes potissime pertinet, quorum est inferiores illuminare et sustentare, ne vel per ignorantiam errent, vel per infirmitatem vincantur et peccent. Ideo Apostolis ceterisque prælatis loquitur Christus: Vos estis lux mundi. Vos estis sal terræ. Unde ad Timotheum scribit Apostolus: Attende lectioni, exhortationi, doctrinæ. Hoc enim faciens, te ipsum salvum facies, et eos qui te audiunt. Per Ezechielem quoque reprobis pastoribus Dominus improperatorie loquitur: Quod infirmum fuit, non consolidastis. Præterea, spiritualiter cæcus est, ignorans, et omnis qui in mortali jacet, putet ac putrefit culpa; claudus vero, qui nutat in actibus bonis, et faciliter ruit in eis, aut omnino deficit ab eisdem. Unde monet Apostolus: Rectos facite gressus pedibus vestris, ut non claudicans quis erret, magis autem sanetur. Et in Psalmo scribitur: Claudicaverunt a semitis suis. Postremo, quilibet nostrum pro modulo suo, cæcorum atque claudorum oculus et pes debet consistere, illos pro posse instruendo et roborando, hoc est sapientiam et fortitudinem seu virtutem sibi collatas illis communicando, prout Petrus inducit: Unusquisque, sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei.
paras.en: [[29:15|I was an eye to the blind, and a foot to the lame|Oculus fui cæco, et pes claudo]]. This belongs chiefly to prelates and those set over others, whose part it is to enlighten and support those beneath them, lest they either go astray through ignorance or be overcome through weakness and sin. Therefore Christ says to the Apostles and the other prelates: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]]. [[Matt 5:13|You are the salt of the earth|Vos estis sal terræ]]. Hence the Apostle writes to Timothy: [[1 Tim 4:13|attend unto reading, to exhortation and to doctrine|Attende lectioni, exhortationi, doctrinæ]]. [[1 Tim 4:16|For in doing this thou shalt both save thyself and them that hear thee|Hoc enim faciens, te ipsum salvum facies, et eos qui te audiunt]]. Through Ezechiel too the Lord speaks reproachfully to the reprobate shepherds: [[Ezech 34:4|The weak you have not strengthened|Quod infirmum fuit, non consolidastis]]. Moreover, spiritually, the blind man is the ignorant, and everyone who lies in mortal sin, and stinks and rots in his guilt; and the lame is he who totters in good acts, and easily falls in them, or fails in them altogether. Hence the Apostle admonishes: [[Heb 12:13|make straight steps with your feet: that no one, halting, may go out of the way; but rather be healed|Rectos facite gressus pedibus vestris, ut non claudicans quis erret, magis autem sanetur]]. And in the Psalm it is written: [[Ps 17:46|have halted from their paths|Claudicaverunt a semitis suis]]. Lastly, each of us, according to his small measure, ought to be an eye and a foot to the blind and the lame, instructing and strengthening them as far as he can, that is, sharing with them the wisdom and strength or virtue conferred on him, as Peter says: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another: as good stewards of the manifold grace of God|Unusquisque, sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei]].

paras.t: Pater eram pauperum. Ita et nos omnem pauperem in caritatis visceribus amplectamur, eique cordialiter compatiamur, et efficaciter suffragemur. Et causam quam nesciebam, diligentissime investigabam. Hoc ad prælatos, principes ac judices potissime spectat, ne ex suspicione, aut passione, aut facili creditione ad judicandum procedant: sed cum maturitate et utriusque partis auditione, ac ceteris observandis, omnia agant. Hinc in Deuteronomio Moyses filiis Israel ait: Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, quorum conversatio probata sit in tribubus vestris, et ponam illos vobis principes.
paras.en: [[29:16|I was the father of the poor|Pater eram pauperum]]. So let us too embrace every poor man in the bowels of charity, and have heartfelt compassion on him, and help him effectually. [[29:16|and the cause which I knew not, I searched out most diligently|Et causam quam nesciebam, diligentissime investigabam]]. This concerns above all prelates, princes and judges, that they should not proceed to judgment out of suspicion, or passion, or easy belief, but should do all things with ripe deliberation, hearing both parties and observing everything else that must be observed. Hence in Deuteronomy Moses says to the children of Israel: [[Deut 1:13|Let me have from among you wise and understanding men, and such whose conversation is approved among your tribes, that I may appoint them your rulers|Date ex vobis viros sapientes et gnaros, quorum conversatio probata sit in tribubus vestris, et ponam illos vobis principes]].

paras.t: Dicebamque proposito mentis: In nidulo meo moriar, id est in loco mansionis meæ usque ad mortem stabilis permanebo: quia (ut ait S. Antonius) qui corpus suum in loco uno figere nequit, animum suum in Deum non figet. Hinc sancti Patres loci facilem seu non necessariam mutationem vehementer vituperant, quoniam in Proverbiis legitur: Sicut avis transmigrans de loco suo, sic vir qui relinquit locum suum. Hinc ad Hebræos hortatur Apostolus: Consideremus invicem in provocatione caritatis et bonorum operum, non deserentes collectionem nostram, sicut est consuetudinis quibusdam, sed consolantes. Verumtamen vitiosa ac periculosa societas est vitanda. Spiritualis vero nidulus, in quo manendum et moriendum est, ponitur ipsa tranquillitas internæ pacis mentis humanæ in Deo, seu quies caritatis fideique in eo, juxta illud: In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam. In quo nido etiam quotidie mori debemus propriæ voluntati ac mundo, et sepeliri in luce vultus divini per contemplationem illius. Unde, super illud, Pretiosa in conspectu Domini mors Sanctorum ejus, Maximus ait: Pretiosissimus transitus in lucem conspectus Domini, quo ab omnibus exterioribus absconduntur et moriuntur sibi et mundo, mors Sanctorum est, digna beatitudinis pretio. Talibus dicitur ad Colossenses: Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo. Qui autem propriam voluntatem, et sensualitatem in omnibus frangit, et mundi vanitates contemnit, vivitque secundum legem Dei in cunctis, moritur sibi ipsi ac mundo, et vivit Deo, dignus dicere cum Apostolo: Christo confixus sum cruci; vivo autem, jam non ego.
paras.en: [[29:18|And I said|Dicebamque]] in the purpose of my mind: [[29:18|I shall die in my nest|In nidulo meo moriar]], that is, I shall remain steadfast in the place of my dwelling until death: for (as St. Antony says) he who cannot fix his body in one place will not fix his mind on God. Hence the holy Fathers sharply blame an easy or needless change of place, since we read in Proverbs: [[Prov 27:8|As a bird that wandereth|Sicut avis transmigrans]] from its place, [[Prov 27:8|so is a man that leaveth his place|sic vir qui relinquit locum suum]] [Denis reads *de loco suo*, “from its place”, where the Vulgate has *de nido suo*, “from her nest”]. Hence the Apostle exhorts the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:24|let us consider one another, to provoke unto charity and to good works|Consideremus invicem in provocatione caritatis et bonorum operum]], [[Heb 10:25|Not forsaking our assembly, as some are accustomed: but comforting|non deserentes collectionem nostram, sicut est consuetudinis quibusdam, sed consolantes]]. Yet vicious and dangerous company is to be avoided. But the spiritual nest in which one must abide and die is taken to be the very tranquillity of the inward peace of the human mind in God, or the rest of charity and faith in him, according to that word: [[Ps 4:9|In peace in the self same I will sleep, and I will rest|In pace in id ipsum dormiam et requiescam]]. In this nest we ought also to die daily to our own will and to the world, and to be buried in the light of the divine countenance by contemplating it. Hence, on that verse, [[Ps 115:6|Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints|Pretiosa in conspectu Domini mors Sanctorum ejus]], Maximus says: “Most precious is the passing into the light of the Lord's sight, by which they are hidden from all outward things and die to themselves and to the world: this is the death of the Saints, worthy of the reward of beatitude.” To such it is said in Colossians: [[Col 3:3|For you are dead: and your life is hid with Christ in God|Mortui enim estis, et vita vestra abscondita est cum Christo in Deo]]. And he who breaks his own will and sensuality in all things, and despises the vanities of the world, and lives according to the law of God in everything, dies to himself and to the world and lives to God, worthy to say with the Apostle: [[Gal 2:19|with Christ I am nailed to the cross|Christo confixus sum cruci]]; [[Gal 2:20|And I live, now not I|vivo autem, jam non ego]].

paras.t: Et sicut palma multiplicabo dies, id est, in vita gratiæ floribusque virtutum cunctis diebus manebo. Dies quoque illuminationum, hoc est gratias illustrationum, in aliorum cordibus procreabo, ut illud Psalmi dicere queam, Ego autem quasi oliva fructifera in domo Dei: conveniatque mihi illud Osee, Israel germinabit quasi lilium; et quod Ecclesiasticus habet, Quasi palma exaltata sum in Cades.
paras.en: [[29:18|and as a palm tree shall multiply my days|Et sicut palma multiplicabo dies]], that is, in the life of grace and the flowers of the virtues I shall abide all my days. Days of enlightenment too, that is, graces of illumination, I shall bring forth in the hearts of others, so that I may say that word of the Psalm, [[Ps 51:10|But I, as a fruitful olive tree in the house of God|Ego autem quasi oliva fructifera in domo Dei]]; and that word of Osee may befit me, [[Osee 14:6|Israel shall spring as the lily|Israel germinabit quasi lilium]]; and what Ecclesiasticus has, [[Ecclus 24:18|I was exalted like a palm tree in Cades|Quasi palma exaltata sum in Cades]].

paras.t: Radix mea, id est intima cordis mei affectio, aperta est juxta aquas, id est, ad susceptionem charismatum Spiritus Sancti ardenter desiderando, patula et capax effecta est: quia divinorum charismatum tanto efficimur capaciores, quanto ferventiores: quoniam caritatis affectio aperit cor amantis ad dilecti ingressum. Et ros, id est gratia et consolatio Spiritus Sancti: de quo loquitur Isaias ad Deum, Ros tuus ros lucis: morabitur in messione mea, id est, stabiliter conquiescet in meis operibus bonis ac fructibus tempore suo metendis, atque in horreum Domini colligendis, ut meritorie ac delectabiliter quæ bona sunt agam, et intra cœleste congreger regnum, juxta illud quod dictum est de Christo: Congregabit triticum in horreum suum: paleas autem comburet igne inexstinguibili.
paras.en: [[29:19|My root|Radix mea]], that is, the inmost affection of my heart, [[29:19|is opened beside the waters|aperta est juxta aquas]], that is, by its ardent longing to receive the gifts of the Holy Ghost, it has been made wide open and roomy: for we are made the more capable of the divine gifts the more fervent we are, since the affection of charity opens the lover's heart to the entry of the beloved. [[29:19|and dew|Et ros]], that is, the grace and consolation of the Holy Ghost, of which Isaias speaks to God, [[Is 26:19|thy dew is the dew of the light|Ros tuus ros lucis]], [[29:19|shall continue in my harvest|morabitur in messione mea]], that is, will rest steadily in my good works and fruits that are to be reaped in their season and gathered into the Lord's barn, so that I may do what is good meritoriously and with delight, and be gathered into the heavenly kingdom, according to what is said of Christ: He will [[Matt 3:12|gather his wheat into the barn; but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire|Congregabit triticum in horreum suum: paleas autem comburet igne inexstinguibili]] [Denis's wording here is closer to Luke 3:17].

paras.t: Gloria mea semper innovabitur. Studeamus et nos quotidie in Deo copiosius atque sincerius gloriari, interius renovari, mentaliter reformari. Et arcus meus in manu mea instaurabitur. Hoc juxta expositionem præhabitam completur in eo, qui illud ad Ephesios adimplet: Confortamini in Domino et in potentia virtutis ejus. Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo.
paras.en: [[29:20|My glory shall always be renewed|Gloria mea semper innovabitur]].
