Let us too strive daily to glory in God more abundantly and more sincerely, to be renewed inwardly, to be reformed in mind. [[29:20|and my bow in my hand shall be repaired|Et arcus meus in manu mea instaurabitur]]. This, according to the exposition given before, is fulfilled in him who fulfils that word to the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:10|be strengthened in the Lord and in the might of his power|Confortamini in Domino et in potentia virtutis ejus]]. [[Eph 6:13|take unto you the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day|Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo]].

paras.t: Qui me audiebant, exspectabant sententiam, et intenti tacebant ad consilium meum, etc. Quilibet prædicator, prælatus et doctor ac judex, non ad propriam laudem, sed ad Dei gloriam inferiorumque ædificationem, tam ordinate, virtuose ac sapienter habere se debet, seu habere se studeat in verbis et factis, ut hæc atque sequentia sibi conveniant, ut scilicet a subditis reverentialiter ac avide audiatur, fructuose suscipiatur; sicque in ipso rigor justitiæ et dulcor clementiæ per discretionem debent contemperari, ut simul timeatur ac diligatur, neque ut levis et mobilis, ab aliquo, etiam dum pium se exhibet ac jucundum, spernatur, credatur vel judicetur, competatque ei quod subditur: Si quando ridebam ad eos, non credebant. Itaque, hilares simus absque dissolutione, tristes sine dejectione, maturi sine austeritate, sociales absque levitate, custoditi in visu: et quidquid prosperitatis aut promotionis nobis acciderit, nullatenus extollamur; nec honores mutent mores in pejus, sed pauperum memores simus, verbis et ope eos pro viribus consolantes, quemadmodum scriptum est: In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum.
paras.en: [[29:21|They that heard me, waited for my sentence, and being attentive held their peace at my counsel|Qui me audiebant, exspectabant sententiam, et intenti tacebant ad consilium meum]], etc. Every preacher, prelate, doctor and judge, not for his own praise but for the glory of God and the edification of those beneath him, ought to conduct himself, or should strive to conduct himself, in words and deeds so orderly, virtuously and wisely that these words and those that follow may fit him: that is, that he be heard by his subjects with reverence and eagerness, and received with fruit; and so in him the rigour of justice and the sweetness of clemency ought to be tempered together by discretion, that he may be at once feared and loved, and that no one, even when he shows himself kind and pleasant, may scorn him, or believe or judge him to be light and fickle; and that what follows may befit him: [[29:24|If at any time I laughed on them, they believed not|Si quando ridebam ad eos, non credebant]]. Let us then be cheerful without dissipation, sad without dejection, grave without severity, sociable without levity, guarded in our looks; and whatever prosperity or advancement befalls us, let us in no way be lifted up; nor let honours change our manners for the worse, but let us be mindful of the poor, comforting them with words and help as far as we can, as it is written: [[Ecclus 11:27|In the day of good things be not unmindful of evils|In die bonorum ne immemor sis malorum]].

30.title: Expositio capituli tricesimi: Nunc autem derident me juniores tempore.
30.title_en: Exposition of the thirtieth chapter: But now the younger in time scorn me

paras.t: Opposita juxta se posita clarius innotescunt. Ideo sanctus Job præcedenti capitulo sua præterita prosperitate descripta, nunc suam adversitatem commemorat, ut ejus magnitudo evidentius innotescat; pateatque, quod non pro suis peccatis hæc passus sit, quum tantam fuisse suam perfectionem jam supra ostenderit, et infra ostendet.
paras.en: Opposites set side by side are the more clearly known. Therefore holy Job, having described his past prosperity in the preceding chapter, now recalls his adversity, so that its greatness may be more evidently known; and so that it may be plain that he did not suffer these things for his sins, since he has already shown above, and will show below, how great his perfection was.

paras.t: Nunc autem derident me juniores tempore, propter adversa quibus affligor, reputantes quod ea meruerim, quem olim seniores honorabant. Sic et pueri leguntur derisisse Eliseum prophetam. Quorum non dignabar patres ponere cum canibus gregis mei, id est assumere ut simul cum canibus animalia mea custodirent. Pastores enim Job habuerunt canes gregum custoditores, et protectores a lupis aut similibus feris. Aliqui etiam viles personæ pastoribus illis subjectæ fuerunt, et simul cum canibus a feris animalia tuebantur. Quod autem Job sic tales parvi pendit, non fuit superbiæ, sed potius æquitatis: quoniam illi vitiis suis se contemptibiles exhibebant.
paras.en: [[30:1|But now the younger in time scorn me|Nunc autem derident me juniores tempore]], because of the adversities with which I am afflicted, thinking that I deserved them, I whom once the elders honoured. So too the boys are read to have mocked the prophet Eliseus[[4 Kings 2:23||]]. [[30:1|whose fathers I would not have set with the dogs of my flock|Quorum non dignabar patres ponere cum canibus gregis mei]], that is, to take them on to guard my animals together with the dogs. For Job's shepherds had dogs to guard the flocks and protect them from wolves or like wild beasts. And some base persons were also put under those shepherds, and together with the dogs kept the animals safe from wild beasts. That Job thought so little of such men was not from pride but rather from justice, since by their vices they showed themselves contemptible.

paras.t: Quorum virtus manuum, id est ars vel potestas eorum, erat mihi pro nihilo, id est nullius reputationis; et vita ipsa putabantur indigni, propter eorum excessus.
paras.en: [[30:2|The strength of whose hands|Quorum virtus manuum]], that is, their skill or power, [[30:2|was to me as nothing|erat mihi pro nihilo]], that is, of no account; [[30:2|and they were thought unworthy of life itself|et vita ipsa putabantur indigni]], because of their excesses.

paras.t: Egestate et fame steriles, id est præ inopia atque esurie fructum non producentes, qui rodebant in solitudine, id est, grossa ibi alimenta instar brutorum carpebant, squalentes calamitate interiori et miseria exteriori. Sic in Luca de filio prodigo legitur: Cupiebat implere ventrem suum de siliquis, quas porci manducabant. Porro squalentes, deturpati dicuntur. Proprie autem squalens vocatur, qui laxata cute consumptaque carne, pallore coloratur cinereo, juxta illud Threnorum: Virgines ejus squalidæ.
paras.en: [[30:3|Barren with want and hunger|Egestate et fame steriles]], that is, bearing no fruit for want and hunger, [[30:3|who gnawed in the wilderness|qui rodebant in solitudine]], that is, they cropped coarse food there like brute beasts, [[30:3|disfigured with calamity|squalentes calamitate]] within and with [[30:3|misery|miseria]] without. So in Luke it is read of the prodigal son: [[Luke 15:16|he would fain have filled his belly with the husks the swine did eat|Cupiebat implere ventrem suum de siliquis, quas porci manducabant]]. Further, the *squalentes* ["squalid", Douay "disfigured"] are those who are disfigured. Properly, one is called *squalens* who, his skin slack and his flesh wasted, is coloured with an ashen pallor, according to that of Lamentations: [[Lam 1:4|her virgins are in affliction|Virgines ejus squalidæ]] [Latin "her virgins are squalid"].

paras.t: Et manducabant herbas silvestres et crudas: quæ, secundum Albertum, sunt inconveniens hominis nutrimentum. Allegatque Avicennam, dicentem quod natura nullum nutrimentum sufficienter parat homini, nisi lac; cetera oportet elixari sive assari. Et arborum cortices; quia, secundum Albertum, cortices sunt farinabiles, quod non est lignum. Et radix juniperorum, id est talium arborum. Unde et legitur Elias se projecisse subter unam juniperum. Erat cibus illorum.
paras.en: [[30:4|And they ate grass|Et manducabant herbas]], wild and raw, which according to Albert are unfit food for man. And he cites Avicenna, who says that nature prepares no food sufficiently for man except milk; everything else must be boiled or roasted. [[30:4|and barks of trees|Et arborum cortices]]: because, according to Albert, barks can be ground into meal, which wood cannot. [[30:4|and the root of junipers|Et radix juniperorum]], that is, of such trees. Hence too we read that Elias cast himself down under a juniper tree[[3 Kings 19:4||]]. [[30:4|was their food|Erat cibus illorum]].

paras.t: Qui de convallibus ista rapientes, id est avide capientes, et sibi mutuo præripere cupientes, quum singula jam præfata reperissent, ad ea cum clamore currebant, se invicem prævenire conantes, et de istorum inventione gaudentes. In convallibus quoque humidiora ac esibiliora, in montibus vero duriora nascuntur.
paras.en: [[30:5|Who snatched up these things out of the valleys|Qui de convallibus ista rapientes]], that is, taking them greedily, and each eager to snatch them from the other, [[30:5|and when they had found any of them|quum singula jam præfata reperissent]] (the things already named), [[30:5|they ran to them with a cry|ad ea cum clamore currebant]], trying to get ahead of one another, and rejoicing at finding them. For in the valleys moister and more eatable things grow, but on the mountains harder ones.

paras.t: In desertis habitabant torrentium, id est, ubi torrentes fuerunt, vel in locis torrentium desiccatis, se a caumate protegebant; et in cavernis terræ, propter umbram, vel super glaream, propter refrigerium aquæ vicinæ mollitiemque arenæ. Glarea namque est terra mollis et arenosa. Gregorius tamen dicit: Glaream dicimus minutissimos lapides, quos aqua fluvialis trahit. Secundum Albertum vero, glarea dicitur mobilis arena, significatque loca in paludibus solida, ubi latrones propter tutelam morantur, eo quod loca talia inaccessibilia sint. Dicuntur autem aliqui habitare supra aliquem locum, quia habitant juxta eum: quemadmodum quidam dicuntur habitare super Rhenum: super quem et Colonia dicitur sita, quia juxta eum constructa est.
paras.en: [[30:6|They dwelt in the desert places of torrents|In desertis habitabant torrentium]], that is, where there were torrents, or in the dried-up places of torrents, they sheltered themselves from the heat; [[30:6|and in caves of earth|et in cavernis terræ]], for the shade, [[30:6|or upon the gravel|vel super glaream]], for the coolness of the water nearby and the softness of the sand. For *glarea* [gravel] is soft and sandy earth. Gregory, however, says: We call *glarea* the tiniest stones, which river water carries along. But according to Albert, *glarea* means shifting sand, and signifies firm places in marshes, where robbers stay for safety, because such places are inaccessible. Now some are said to dwell upon a place because they dwell beside it: as some are said to dwell upon the Rhine, and Cologne too is said to be situated upon it, because it is built beside it.

paras.t: Qui inter hujuscemodi lætabantur: quia tantæ fuerunt penuriæ, quod præfata vilissima erant eis pretiosa atque jucunda: juxta illud Proverbiorum: Anima saturata calcabit favum; anima esuriens, etiam amarum pro dulci sumet. Et esse sub sentibus delicias computabant. Sentes sunt spinæ. Itaque sensus est, quod sub locis spinosis, hoc est sub umbra parvarum arborum spinosarum, esse fuit eis amœnum, quoniam commodius refrigerium non habebant.
paras.en: [[30:7|They pleased themselves among these kind of things|Qui inter hujuscemodi lætabantur]]: because they were in such want that these vilest things named above were precious and pleasant to them, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 27:7|A soul that is full shall tread upon the honeycomb: and a soul that is hungry shall take even bitter for sweet|Anima saturata calcabit favum; anima esuriens, etiam amarum pro dulci sumet]]. [[30:7|and counted it delightful to be under the briers|Et esse sub sentibus delicias computabant]]. *Sentes* [briers] are thorns. So the sense is that to be under thorny places, that is, in the shade of small thorny trees, was pleasant to them, since they had no more comfortable coolness.

paras.t: Filii, carnis propagatione vitiorumque imitatione, stultorum in anima, et ignobilium corpore, et in terra penitus non parentes, id est in nullo spectabiles, seu nulla dignitate conspicui. Vel hoc ideo dicit, quia inter homines communiter non manebant, sicut jam dixit. Ex his omnibus magnitudo adversitatis beati Job declaratur: quia quo viliores sunt irrisores, eo illorum derisio solet esse molestior, ignominiosiorque censetur.
paras.en: [[30:8|The children|Filii]], by descent in the flesh and by imitation of their vices, [[30:8|of foolish|stultorum]] men in soul, [[30:8|and base men|et ignobilium]] in body, [[30:8|and not appearing at all upon the earth|et in terra penitus non parentes]], that is, notable in nothing, or distinguished by no rank. Or he says this because they did not live among men in common, as he has just said. From all this the greatness of blessed Job's adversity is made plain: for the baser the mockers are, the more grievous their mockery usually is, and the more shameful it is held to be.

paras.t: Nunc in eorum canticum versus sum, id est, de mea adversitate faciunt decantationes vel cantilenas; et factus sum eis proverbium, id est materia proverbii maledictorii: quia proverbium maledictionis de Job composuerunt, dicendo: Accidat tibi et pereas sicut Job. Hinc supra sanctus Job dixit: Posuit me quasi in proverbium vulgi, et exemplum sum coram eis. Et ibi hæc magis exposita sunt.
paras.en: [[30:9|Now I am turned into their song|Nunc in eorum canticum versus sum]], that is, they make chants or ditties about my adversity; [[30:9|and am become their byword|et factus sum eis proverbium]], that is, the matter of a cursing proverb: for they made up a proverb of cursing about Job, saying: May it befall thee, and mayest thou perish, like Job. Hence holy Job said above: [[Job 17:6|He hath made me as it were a byword of the people, and I am an example before them|Posuit me quasi in proverbium vulgi, et exemplum sum coram eis]]. And these things are explained more fully there.

paras.t: Abominantur me, tanquam miserrimum, et longe fiunt a me, tanquam ab homine penitus detestando; et faciem meam conspuere non verentur, reputantes me tam indignum, ut sine peccato quilibet possit me persequi: quod instigante diabolo fecisse creduntur.
paras.en: [[30:10|They abhor me|Abominantur me]], as a most wretched man, [[30:10|and flee far from me|et longe fiunt a me]], as from a man utterly to be loathed; [[30:10|and are not afraid to spit in my face|et faciem meam conspuere non verentur]], thinking me so unworthy that anyone could persecute me without sin: which they are believed to have done at the devil's prompting.

paras.t: Pharetram enim suam aperuit, id est, Deus ex sua præordinatione quasi ex arcu quodam sagittas adversitatis mihi immisit, sicut ex pharetra mittuntur sagittæ; et afflixit me: quia licentiante vel permittente Deo, hæc omnia acciderunt. Hinc supra dixit: Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum. Et frenum posuit in os meum: id est, tam dire me affligendo, abstulit mihi quodammodo apparentiam me excusandi ac respondendi. Hinc superius dixit: Rugæ meæ testimonium dicunt contra me, et suscitatur falsiloquus contradicens mihi. Denique, Deus interdum justo judicio pravorum malignitatem per adversa compescit: quod per freni impositionem aliquando designatur, quemadmodum in Isaia loquitur regi Assyriorum: Ponam circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum in maxillis tuis.
paras.en: [[30:11|For he hath opened his quiver|Pharetram enim suam aperuit]], that is, God, by his foreordaining, as from a kind of bow, has sent the arrows of adversity into me, as arrows are sent from a quiver; [[30:11|and hath afflicted me|et afflixit me]]: for all these things happened by God's leave or permission. Hence he said above: [[Job 6:4|the arrows of the Lord are in me, the rage whereof drinketh up my spirit|Sagittæ Domini in me sunt, quarum indignatio ebibit spiritum meum]]. [[30:11|and hath put a bridle into my mouth|Et frenum posuit in os meum]]: that is, by afflicting me so dreadfully he has in a manner taken from me any show of excusing myself or answering. Hence he said earlier: [[Job 16:9|My wrinkles bear witness against me|Rugæ meæ testimonium dicunt contra me]], [[Job 16:9|and a false speaker riseth up|et suscitatur falsiloquus]] [[Job 16:9|contradicting me|contradicens mihi]]. Moreover, God sometimes by just judgment curbs the malice of the wicked through adversities: and this is sometimes signified by putting on a bridle, as in Isaias he says to the king of the Assyrians: [[Is 37:29|I will put a ring in thy nose, and a bit between thy lips|Ponam circulum in naribus tuis, et frenum in maxillis tuis]] [Denis has *in maxillis tuis*, "in thy jaws", where the Vulgate has *in labiis tuis*, "between thy lips"].

paras.t: Vel sic: Et frenum posuit in os meum, id est, per gratiam suam os meum a verbis impatientiæ refrenavit in omnibus his adversis, prout supra legitur: In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis.
paras.en: Or thus: [[30:11|and hath put a bridle into my mouth|Et frenum posuit in os meum]], that is, by his grace he has reined in my mouth from words of impatience in all these adversities, as we read above: [[Job 2:10|In all these things Job did not sin with his lips|In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis]] [the margin gives Job i, 22 and ii, 10; the words are those of 2:10].

paras.t: Ad dexteram orientis calamitates meæ illico surrexerunt. Hoc dicit, quia a plaga meridiana (quæ est ad dexteram respectu orientis, in quo Job habitavit, ut supra patuit: nam si quis ad orientem se vertat, meridies apparet ad dexteram): itaque, a parte meridiana cœperunt contra Job suæ adversitates et calamitates insurgere: quia (ut dicitur) ex illa parte venerunt contra eum Sabæi, qui primo boves et asinos sancti Job rapuerunt, ejusque pueros, id est pastores, interfecerunt. Pedes meos subverterunt, id est, a solitis viis impediverunt, et oppresserunt quasi fluctibus, id est, gressus meos impetuose impediverunt, semitis suis, id est violentis suis accessibus contra me, ita quod præ adversitatibus non habeo quo me vertam.
paras.en: [[30:12|At the right hand of my rising, my calamities forthwith arose|Ad dexteram orientis calamitates meæ illico surrexerunt]]. He says this because from the southern quarter (which is on the right with respect to the east, where Job lived, as was shown above[[Job 1:3||]]: for if one turns to the east, the south is on his right): from the southern side, then, his adversities and calamities began to rise up against Job; for (as is said) from that side came the Sabeans against him, who first carried off holy Job's oxen and asses, and slew his servants, that is, the herdsmen[[Job 1:14||]][[Job 1:15||]]. [[30:12|they have overthrown my feet|Pedes meos subverterunt]], that is, they have hindered them from their accustomed ways, [[30:12|and have overwhelmed me|et oppresserunt]] [[30:12|as with waves|quasi fluctibus]], that is, they have violently hindered my steps, [[30:12|with their paths|semitis suis]], that is, with their violent onsets against me, so that for adversities I have nowhere to turn.

paras.t: Dissipaverunt itinera mea, id est operum meorum processus et commoda; vel etiam ipsa corporalia terræ itinera, per quæ pertinentia ad me, duci seu ire solebant. Insidiati sunt mihi, dolose molientes qualiter mihi nocerent, et prævaluerunt, id est, desideriorum suorum effectum sortiti sunt in me; et non fuit qui ferret auxilium mihi adversus eos.
paras.en: [[30:13|They have destroyed my ways|Dissipaverunt itinera mea]], that is, the course and profit of my works; or even the bodily roads themselves on the earth, by which the things belonging to me used to be led or to go. [[30:13|they have lain in wait against me|Insidiati sunt mihi]], craftily contriving how they might harm me, [[30:13|and they have prevailed|et prævaluerunt]], that is, they have obtained against me the effect of their desires; [[30:13|and there was none to help|et non fuit qui ferret auxilium]] me against them.

paras.t: Quasi rupto muro, id est sine resistentia, et aperta janua, id est prompte et absque obstaculo, irruerunt super me Chaldæi, Sabæi et Satan; et ad meas miserias, id est adversitates pœnales, devoluti sunt, id est convenerunt, ut me per illas opprimerent.
paras.en: [[30:14|as when a wall is broken|Quasi rupto muro]], that is, without resistance, [[30:14|and a gate opened|et aperta janua]], that is, readily and without hindrance, there [[30:14|have rushed in upon me|irruerunt super me]] the Chaldeans[[Job 1:17||]], the Sabeans[[Job 1:15||]] and Satan[[Job 2:7||]] [the margin gives Job i, 15–19 and ii, 7]; and [[30:14|to my miseries|et ad meas miserias]], that is, to penal adversities, [[30:14|have rolled themselves down|devoluti sunt]], that is, they came together, to crush me by them.

paras.t: Redactus sum in nihilum, id est, jam pene consumptus sum, mortique proximus. Sic superius dixit: In nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei. Vehementer autem afflicti, hyperbolicis locutionibus, utpote verbis per excessum prolatis, uti consueverunt, ut affectionis suæ magnitudinem clarius promant. Abstulit quasi ventus desiderium meum: id est, quemadmodum ventus repente cum impetu pulverem propellit et agitat, sic Deus subito omne desiderabile in exterioribus bonis abstulit mihi, videlicet substantiam ac sobolem omnem atque familiam. Et velut nubes pertransiit, id est, cito finita est et recessit a me, salus mea, id est corporis sanitas et terrena prosperitas.
paras.en: [[30:15|I am brought to nothing|Redactus sum in nihilum]], that is, I am now almost consumed, and next to death. So he said earlier: [[Job 16:8|all my limbs are brought to nothing|In nihilum redacti sunt omnes artus mei]]. Now those who are vehemently afflicted are wont to use hyperbolical speech, that is, words uttered beyond measure, so as to bring out more clearly the greatness of what they feel. [[30:15|as a wind thou hast taken away my desire|Abstulit quasi ventus desiderium meum]] [Denis reads *abstulit*, "he hath taken away"]: that is, as the wind suddenly drives and tosses the dust with force, so God has suddenly taken from me everything desirable in outward goods, namely my substance and all my offspring and household. [[30:15|hath passed away like a cloud|Et velut nubes pertransiit]], that is, it has quickly come to an end and gone from me, [[30:15|and my prosperity|salus mea]], that is, the health of the body and earthly prosperity.

paras.t: Nunc autem in memetipso marcescit anima mea, id est, variis doloribus premitur, quum naturale sit, rebus liberisque amissis, et corpore vulnerato, tristari. Sed tristitia ista fuit moderata in Job, ut dictum est sæpe. Et possident me dies afflictionis, id est universæ hujus adversitatis meæ pœnosæ.
paras.en: [[30:16|And now my soul fadeth within myself|Nunc autem in memetipso marcescit anima mea]], that is, it is weighed down by various sorrows, since it is natural to be sad when goods and children are lost and the body is wounded. But this sadness was moderate in Job, as has often been said. [[30:16|and the days of affliction possess me|Et possident me dies afflictionis]], that is, of the whole of this painful adversity of mine.

paras.t: Nocte os meum perforatur doloribus, id est, nocturnis temporibus, quibus languores atque dolores aggravantur, puncturæ dolorum meorum usque ad ossa mea pertingunt; et qui me comedunt, id est vermes ex meis putridis ulceribus nascentes, meamque carnem mordentes et consumentes, non dormiunt; sed die et nocte me rodunt, saltem quidam ex eis.
paras.en: [[30:17|In the night my bone is pierced with sorrows|Nocte os meum perforatur doloribus]], that is, at night-time, when sicknesses and pains grow heavier, the stabs of my pains reach even to my bones; [[30:17|and they that feed upon me|et qui me comedunt]], that is, the worms breeding from my putrid ulcers, biting and consuming my flesh, [[30:17|do not sleep|non dormiunt]], but gnaw me day and night, at least some of them.

paras.t: In multitudine eorum, id est a vermibus istis multis, consumitur vestimentum meum: quia tam multi erant, quod et vestes Job corroserunt. Et quasi capitio tunicæ cinxerunt me. Capitium est pars vestis circa collum, per quam caput ingreditur. Itaque sensus est, quod vermium tanta exstitit multitudo, quod undique corpus suum occupaverunt, sicut capitium ambit collum; nec continebantur sub vestibus, sed eruperunt in publicum, et collum circumdabant: quod miserabile ac pœnalissimum fuit.
paras.en: [[30:18|With the multitude of them|In multitudine eorum]], that is, by these many worms, [[30:18|my garment is consumed|consumitur vestimentum meum]]: for they were so many that they gnawed through Job's clothes as well. [[30:18|and they have girded me about, as with the collar of my coat|Et quasi capitio tunicæ cinxerunt me]] [the margin gives the variant *succinxerunt*]. The *capitium* [collar] is the part of the garment round the neck, through which the head goes in. So the sense is that the multitude of worms was so great that they covered his body on every side, as the collar goes round the neck; nor were they kept under his clothes, but they broke out into the open and encircled his neck: which was most wretched and most painful.

paras.t: Comparatus sum luto, id est, vilis reputatus sum, fragilis et putrescens apparui; et assimilatus sum favillæ et cineri, id est, impulsione tentationum et impetu adversitatum diversimode agitatus, sicut favilla et cinis ventis impelluntur; item, pro nihilo habitus, et tanquam levissimus reputatus.
paras.en: [[30:19|I am compared to dirt|Comparatus sum luto]], that is, I am held base, I have appeared frail and rotting; [[30:19|and am likened to embers and ashes|et assimilatus sum favillæ et cineri]], that is, tossed this way and that by the thrust of temptations and the onset of adversities, as embers and ashes are driven by the winds; and also, held as nothing, and counted as the lightest of things.

paras.t: Deinde dirigit verbum ad Deum: Clamabo ad te, id est, affectuose orabo. Apud Deum etenim plus sonat intensa affectio, quam clamor vocalis. Et non exaudies me ad votum, id est tam cito ut cupio. Sto orationi intentus, et non respicis me oculo pietatis, quantum ad corporalis meæ afflictionis amotionem.
paras.en: Then he turns his words to God: [[30:20|I cry to thee|Clamabo ad te]] [Denis reads *clamabo*, "I will cry", and *orabo*, *exaudies*; the margin gives *clamo*, *oro* and, it seems, *exaudis*], that is, I will pray with affection. For with God intense affection sounds louder than a cry of the voice. [[30:20|and thou hearest me not|Et non exaudies me]] as I wish, that is, as quickly as I desire. [[30:20|I stand up|Sto]] intent on prayer, [[30:20|and thou dost not regard me|et non respicis me]] with the eye of pity, as regards the removal of my bodily affliction.

paras.t: Mutatus es mihi in crudelem: id est, tu qui invariabiliter bonus, pius ac dulcis es in te ipso, quantum ad tuum effectum, circa me habes te per modum crudelis, me tam dire ac diu affligendo, nec exaudiendo. Sic et Habacuc ait: Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies? vociferabor ad te vim patiens, et non salvabis? Denique, quid mirum si Deo adscribatur crudelitas, cui furor et severitas attribuuntur? Scriptum est enim: Ulciscens Dominus, et habens furorem. Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me. Ad Romanos quoque Paulus: Vide bonitatem et severitatem Dei. Nonne Deus metuendissimus judex velut crudelis videtur, qui de impiis loquitur per Osee, Occurram eis quasi ursa raptis catulis, dirumpam interiora eorum, et consumam eos ut leo? Et in duritia manus tuæ, id est in pœnali effectu tuæ potentiæ, vel in rigore tuo, secundum quod foris apparet, adversaris mihi, id est, affligis me contra naturalem meam inclinationem, et contra prosperitatem incolumitatemque pristinam. Hinc superius locutus est Deo: Cur faciem tuam abscondis, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum?
paras.en: [[30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me|Mutatus es mihi in crudelem]]: that is, thou who art in thyself unchangeably good, kind and sweet, as to thy effect bearest thyself toward me after the manner of one cruel, afflicting me so dreadfully and so long, and not hearing me. So too Habacuc says: [[Hab 1:2|How long, O Lord, shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear? shall I cry out to thee suffering violence, and thou wilt not save?|Usquequo, Domine, clamabo, et non exaudies? vociferabor ad te vim patiens, et non salvabis?]] And indeed, what wonder if cruelty is ascribed to God, to whom wrath and severity are attributed? For it is written: [[Nah 1:2|the Lord is a revenger, and hath wrath|Ulciscens Dominus, et habens furorem]]. [[Ps 6:2|O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation|Domine, ne in furore tuo arguas me]]. And Paul to the Romans: [[Rom 11:22|See then the goodness and the severity of God|Vide bonitatem et severitatem Dei]]. Does not God, a most dreadful judge, seem as it were cruel, who says of the wicked through Osee: [[Osee 13:8|I will meet them as a bear that is robbed of her whelps|Occurram eis quasi ursa raptis catulis]], [[Osee 13:8|and I will rend the inner parts|dirumpam interiora eorum]], [[Osee 13:8|and I will devour them there as a lion|et consumam eos ut leo]]? [[30:21|and in the hardness of thy hand|Et in duritia manus tuæ]], that is, in the penal effect of thy power, or in thy rigour, as it appears outwardly, [[30:21|thou art against me|adversaris mihi]], that is, thou afflictest me against my natural inclination, and against my former prosperity and well-being. Hence he spoke earlier to God: [[Job 13:24|Why hidest thou thy face, and thinkest me thy enemy?|Cur faciem tuam abscondis, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum?]]

paras.t: Elevasti me temporali prosperitate, honore, fama et gloria, prout præcedenti capitulo patuit; et quasi super ventum ponens, id est alte me promovens, et in statu sublimi instabili instar venti me statuens, elisisti me valide, id est, fortiter dejecisti atque læsisti: juxta illud Psalmi, Quia elevans allisisti me. Unde supra testatus est: Ego ille quondam opulentus, repente contritus sum.
paras.en: [[30:22|Thou hast lifted me up|Elevasti me]] by temporal prosperity, honour, fame and glory, as appeared in the preceding chapter; [[30:22|and set me as it were upon the wind|et quasi super ventum ponens]], that is, raising me on high, and setting me in a lofty state as unstable as the wind, [[30:22|and thou hast mightily dashed me|elisisti me valide]], that is, thou hast thrown me down and hurt me hard: according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 101:11|for having lifted me up thou hast thrown me down|Quia elevans allisisti me]]. Hence he bore witness above: [[Job 16:13|I that was formerly so wealthy, am all on a sudden broken to pieces|Ego ille quondam opulentus, repente contritus sum]].

paras.t: Scio quia morti trades me, id est, non hac tantum tribulatione affliges me, sed tandem per mortem finem hujus vitæ mihi impones. Vel dicit hoc, desperando de vita diuturniori in sæculo isto, eo modo quo supra dixit: Desperavi, nequaquam ultra jam vivam. Et hoc scire se perhibet secundum ordinem inferiorum naturaliumque causarum: quia (ut dictum est sæpe) letaliter fuit percussus, supernaturaliter vero sanatus. Ubi constituta est domus, id est quies a tumultu vitæ præsentis, finalisque mansio a cursu et motu peregrinationis istius; vel monumentum, quod concomitanter se habet ad mortem: omni viventi in carne mortali: juxta illud Psalmi, Sepulcra eorum domus illorum in æternum. Et rursus: Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem?
paras.en: [[30:23|I know that thou wilt deliver me to death|Scio quia morti trades me]], that is, thou wilt not only afflict me with this tribulation, but at last wilt put an end to this life of mine by death. Or he says this despairing of a longer life in this world, in the way he said above: [[Job 7:16|I have done with hope, I shall now live no longer|Desperavi, nequaquam ultra jam vivam]]. And he declares that he knows this according to the order of lower and natural causes: for (as has often been said) he was struck mortally, but healed supernaturally. [[30:23|where a house is appointed|Ubi constituta est domus]], that is, rest from the tumult of the present life, and a final dwelling after the course and movement of this pilgrimage; or the tomb, which goes along with death: [[30:23|for every one that liveth|omni viventi]] in mortal flesh: according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 48:12|And their sepulchres shall be their houses for ever|Sepulcra eorum domus illorum in æternum]]. And again: [[Ps 88:49|Who is the man that shall live, and not see death|Quis est homo qui vivet, et non videbit mortem?]]?

paras.t: Verumtamen, non ad consumptionem eorum emittis manum tuam, id est, potestatem tuam extendis. Tanquam dicat: Quamvis omnem viventem in sæculo morti tradas, non tamen potestate tua eos omnino consumis; nam anima permanet immortalis, nec omnes consumptioni, id est æternæ damnationi, immittis. Vel sensus est, quod licet eos in vita hac puniat per adversa, hoc tamen frequenter facit ad emendationem, non ad destructionem eorum, sicut in Apocalypsi protestatur: Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo. Hinc subditur: Et si corruerint, peccando, moriendo seu adversa ferendo, ipse salvabis animas eorum, per gratiam in præsenti, vel per gloriam in futuro: quemadmodum de justo ait Psalmista, Quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam.
paras.en: [[30:24|But yet thou stretchest not forth thy hand to their consumption|Verumtamen, non ad consumptionem eorum emittis manum tuam]], that is, thou extendest thy power. As if to say: Though thou deliverest everyone living in the world to death, yet thou dost not wholly consume them with thy power; for the soul remains immortal, nor dost thou send all to consumption, that is, to eternal damnation. Or the sense is that, though he punishes them in this life with adversities, yet he often does it for their amendment, not for their destruction, as he declares in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 3:19|Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise|Ego quos amo, arguo et castigo]]. Hence it is added: [[30:24|and if they shall fall down|Et si corruerint]], by sinning, by dying or by bearing adversities, [[30:24|thou wilt save|ipse salvabis]] their souls, by grace in the present, or by glory in the future: as the Psalmist says of the just man: [[Ps 36:24|When he shall fall he shall not be bruised, for the Lord putteth his hand under him|Quum ceciderit, non collidetur, quia Dominus supponit manum suam]].

paras.t: Flebam quondam super eo qui afflictus erat, id est, afflictis usque ad lacrimas tempore prosperitatis meæ condolebam: juxta illud Apostoli, Flere cum flentibus. Et Ecclesiasticus ait: Non desis plorantibus in consolatione. Et compatiebatur anima mea pauperi, id est egenis, apprehendendo eorum inopiam quasi propriam propter communionem naturæ: sicque eis pro posse subveni. Non enim vere compatitur alteri, qui ejus miseriam pro posse non relevat. Hanc pietatem sectemur. Beatus enim qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus.
paras.en: [[30:25|I wept heretofore for him that was afflicted|Flebam quondam super eo qui afflictus erat]], that is, in the time of my prosperity I grieved with the afflicted even to tears: according to that of the Apostle: [[Rom 12:15|weep with them that weep|Flere cum flentibus]]. And Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 7:38|Be not wanting in comforting them that weep|Non desis plorantibus in consolatione]]. [[30:25|and my soul had compassion on the poor|Et compatiebatur anima mea pauperi]], that is, on the needy, taking their want as my own because of our common nature: and so I helped them as far as I could. For he does not truly have compassion on another who does not relieve his misery as far as he can. Let us follow after this kindness. For [[Ps 40:2|Blessed is he that understandeth concerning the needy and the poor: the Lord will deliver him in the evil day|Beatus enim qui intelligit super egenum et pauperem; in die mala liberabit eum Dominus]].

paras.t: Exspectabam bona, id est prosperitatem et consolationem a Deo propter merita mea: quod scilicet faceret mihi sicut ego feci proximis meis inopibus. Communiter enim in lege naturali et scripta, virtuosi etiam in hac vita sortiebantur prospera mundi a Deo, quamvis non semper sic accidit. Unde nec Job talia exspectavit, tanquam principale, sufficiens et finale præmium suorum operum meritoriorum, sed tanquam minus principale, prout de prædicatore evangelicæ veritatis loquitur Christus: Dignus est operarius mercede sua: per mercedem intelligens ibi corporis refectionem. Et venerunt mihi mala pœnæ, id est adversa: de quibus Amos ait, Si erit malum in civitate quod Dominus non fecit? Præstolabar lucem, id est jucunditatem: secundum illud Proverbiorum, Exspectatio justorum lætitia. Et eruperunt tenebræ, id est, desolatio et amaritudo mihi jam evenerunt: quemadmodum Jeremias ait: Exspectavimus pacem, et non est bonum; et tempus curationis, et ecce turbatio.
paras.en: [[30:26|I expected good things|Exspectabam bona]], that is, prosperity and consolation from God for my merits: namely, that he would do to me as I had done to my needy neighbours. For commonly, under the natural and the written law, the virtuous obtained the prosperity of the world from God even in this life, though it did not always so happen. Hence Job did not expect such things as the principal, sufficient and final reward of his meritorious works, but as a less principal one, as Christ says of the preacher of gospel truth: [[Luke 10:7|the labourer is worthy of his hire|Dignus est operarius mercede sua]]: meaning there by *hire* the refreshment of the body. [[30:26|and evils are come upon me|Et venerunt mihi mala]] of penalty [*mala pœnæ*: evils of punishment, as distinct from evils of fault], that is, adversities: of which Amos says: [[Amos 3:6|Shall there be evil in a city, which the Lord hath not done?|Si erit malum in civitate quod Dominus non fecit?]] [[30:26|I waited for light|Præstolabar lucem]], that is, for gladness: according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 10:28|The expectation of the just is joy|Exspectatio justorum lætitia]]. [[30:26|and darkness broke out|Et eruperunt tenebræ]], that is, desolation and bitterness have now come upon me: as Jeremias says: [[Jer 14:19|we have looked for peace, and there is no good: and for the time of healing, and behold trouble|Exspectavimus pacem, et non est bonum; et tempus curationis, et ecce turbatio]].

paras.t: Interiora mea, puta viscera atque vitalia, efferbuerunt, id est, extra ferbuerunt ex calore febris et ulcerum. Ubi Albertus allegat Hippocratem, dicentem: Febris est in generatione saniei magis quam generata jam sanie. Absque ulla requie, id est incessanter ad tempus. Prævenerunt me dies afflictionis, id est, tempore juventutis meæ afflictiones incidi, quæ tempore senectutis naturalius evenirent. Tunc enim homo naturaliter propter invaletudinem suam affligitur, juxta illud in Psalmo: Si autem in potentatibus, octoginta anni; et amplius eorum, labor et dolor.
paras.en: [[30:27|My inner parts|Interiora mea]], namely the bowels and vital parts, [[30:27|have boiled|efferbuerunt]], that is, have boiled over [*extra ferbuerunt*] with the heat of fever and ulcers. Here Albert cites Hippocrates, who says: Fever is more in the forming of pus than when the pus is already formed. [[30:27|without any rest|Absque ulla requie]], that is, unceasingly for a time. [[30:27|the days of affliction have prevented me|Prævenerunt me dies afflictionis]], that is, in the time of my youth I fell into afflictions which would more naturally come in the time of old age. For then a man is naturally afflicted because of his infirmity, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 89:10|But if in the strong they be fourscore years: and what is more of them is labour and sorrow|Si autem in potentatibus, octoginta anni; et amplius eorum, labor et dolor]].

paras.t: Mœrens incedebam, id est, etiam tempore prosperitatis cum mediocri seu ordinato mœrore processi, propter aliorum peccata seu adversa dolendo: juxta illud in Psalmo, Tabescere me fecit zelus meus, quia obliti sunt verba tua inimici mei. Itemque: Zelus domus tuæ comedit me. Unde, secundum Bedam, zelus est indignatio et tristitia de malo culpæ: quæ mala quæ videt, corrigit, si potest; si non potest, tolerat et gemit. Absque furore hoc feci: quoniam mœror et zelus hujusmodi debet esse sine ira fervente. Consurgens, id est vitiis me opponens, in turba clamabam, ejus peccata redarguendo, atque ad bona mansuete hortando.
paras.en: [[30:28|I went mourning|Mœrens incedebam]], that is, even in the time of prosperity I went about with a moderate or ordered sorrow, grieving for the sins or adversities of others: according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 118:139|My zeal hath made me pine away: because my enemies forgot thy words|Tabescere me fecit zelus meus, quia obliti sunt verba tua inimici mei]]. And again: [[Ps 68:10|the zeal of thy house hath eaten me up|Zelus domus tuæ comedit me]]. Hence, according to Bede, zeal is indignation and sorrow over the evil of fault, which corrects the evils it sees if it can; if it cannot, it bears them and groans. [[30:28|without indignation|Absque furore]] [the margin gives the Vulgate's *sine*] I did this: because sorrow and zeal of this kind must be without burning anger. [[30:28|I rose up|Consurgens]], that is, setting myself against vices, [[30:28|and cried in the crowd|in turba clamabam]], reproving its sins, and gently urging it to good.

paras.t: Frater fui draconum, id est, homines venenatos, qui alios verbis et exemplis vitiosis inficiunt, fraternaliter dilexi: qui tamen mihi nunc quasi dracones fuerunt, me infestando; et socius struthionum, id est crudelium. Struthio enim proprii obliviscitur fetus. Unde loquitur Jeremias: Filia populi mei crudelis sicut struthio in deserto. Vel nomine struthionis, quæ pennas habet, nec volat, simulatores atque hypocritæ designantur: inter quos Job sociali caritate se habuit.
paras.en: [[30:29|I was the brother of dragons|Frater fui draconum]], that is, I loved as a brother venomous men, who infect others with vicious words and examples: who yet have now been as dragons to me, in harassing me; [[30:29|and companion of ostriches|et socius struthionum]], that is, of cruel men. For the ostrich forgets its own young. Hence Jeremias says: [[Lam 4:3|the daughter of my people is cruel, like the ostrich in the desert|Filia populi mei crudelis sicut struthio in deserto]]. Or by the name of the ostrich, which has wings and does not fly, pretenders and hypocrites are signified: among whom Job bore himself with companionable charity.

paras.t: Cutis mea denigrata est super me, id est, propter interiorem corruptionem humorum, quasi exusta est, juxta illud in Threnis: Pellis nostra quasi clibanus exusta est a facie tempestatum famis. Unde supra ait: Cutis mea aruit et contracta est. Et ossa mea aruerunt, id est, viribus et medullis destituta sunt atque siccata, præ caumate, id est ex grandi incendio caloris febrilis seu apostematis.
paras.en: [[30:30|My skin is become black upon me|Cutis mea denigrata est super me]], that is, because of the inward corruption of the humours, it is as it were burnt: according to that in Lamentations: [[Lam 5:10|Our skin was burnt as an oven, by reason of the violence of the famine|Pellis nostra quasi clibanus exusta est a facie tempestatum famis]]. Hence he said above: [[Job 7:5|my skin is withered and drawn together|Cutis mea aruit et contracta est]]. [[30:30|and my bones are dried up|Et ossa mea aruerunt]], that is, they are left without strength and marrow and are dried out, [[30:30|with heat|præ caumate]], that is, from the great burning of the heat of fever or of an abscess.

paras.t: Versa est in luctum cithara mea, id est, loco jucunditatis, quam habui ex citharæ usu et melodia, successit mihi hic planctus. Forte enim aliquando musicis instrumentis usus est ordinate, sicut et David lusit in cithara. Et organum meum versum est in vocem flentium: sive per organum intelligatur musicum instrumentum, quod fistulis sonat; sive vox propria, vel membrum corporis ad cantandum sive loquendum, ita quod pro gaudio quod ex organo habui, vox lugubris mihi successit.
paras.en: [[30:31|My harp is turned to mourning|Versa est in luctum cithara mea]], that is, in place of the gladness I had from the use and melody of the harp, this lament has come upon me. For perhaps he sometimes used musical instruments in an ordered way, as David too played on the harp[[1 Kings 16:23||]]. [[30:31|and my organ into the voice of those that weep|Et organum meum versum est in vocem flentium]]: whether by *organ* is understood the musical instrument that sounds by pipes; or his own voice, or the bodily member for singing or speaking; so that in place of the joy I had from the organ, a mournful voice has come upon me.

paras.t: Per organum quoque, quod fistulis sonat, vera prædicatio seu instructio designatur; per citharam, quæ chordis sonat, recta operatio denotatur: quæ in mœrorem vertuntur, dum alii inde non emendantur, aut scandalizantur. Sic et in Threnis inducitur: Versus est in luctum chorus noster.
paras.en: By the organ, too, which sounds by pipes, true preaching or instruction is signified; by the harp, which sounds by strings, right action is denoted: and these are turned to sorrow when others are not amended by them, or are scandalized. So too it is brought in in Lamentations: [[Lam 5:15|our dancing is turned into mourning|Versus est in luctum chorus noster]].

31.title: Elucidatio capituli trigesimi primi: Pepigi fœdus cum oculis meis, ut ne cogitarem quidem de virgine.
31.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-first chapter: I made a covenant with my eyes, that I would not so much as think upon a virgin

paras.t: Quoniam tres amici Job concorditer nisi sunt demonstrare ipsum propter sua peccata plagatum, et non nisi pro magnis excessibus tam dire percussum, cujus oppositum ipse defendit; hinc virtutes suas et merita diligentissime ac distincte prosequitur, ostendens se in virtutibus consummatum fuisse. Et primo se ab inquinamento peccati carnalis excusat: quod peccatum plures commaculat, involvit et damnat: atque, ut Thomas disseruit, peccatum hoc in lubrico positum est, ut nisi quis occasiones et præambula seu principia ejus devitet, a posterioribus vix possit pedem extrahere. Denique, primum in libidine est oculorum adspectus, quo mulier pulchra inspicitur, et præcipue virgo: secundum, est cogitatio: tertium, delectatio in cogitatione: quartum, consensus: quintum, opus. Voluit ergo Job originem hujus peccati excludere, sicut fatetur.
paras.en: Since Job's three friends had striven with one accord to show that he was stricken for his sins, and smitten so dreadfully only for great excesses, the opposite of which he maintains, he now goes through his virtues and merits with the greatest care and point by point, showing that he had been perfect in the virtues. And first he clears himself of the defilement of carnal sin: a sin that stains, entangles and damns a great many; and, as Thomas has explained, this sin is set on slippery ground, so that unless a man shuns its occasions and preliminaries, that is, its beginnings, he can scarcely draw his foot back from what follows. Indeed, the first thing in lust is the sight of the eyes, by which a beautiful woman is looked upon, and above all a virgin; the second is the thought; the third, delight in the thought; the fourth, consent; the fifth, the deed. Job therefore wished to shut out the origin of this sin, as he declares.

paras.t: Pepigi fœdus cum oculis meis, id est, firmiter decrevi oculos meos ab incauto mulierum intuitu custodire. Oculi quippe annuntiant seu ostendunt delectabile venereum, et ex adspectu cogitatio manat, ex qua concupiscentia surgit. Ut ne cogitarem quidem de virgine, id est, ne ab incauto adspectu ad periculosam cogitationem devolverer. Cogitare autem de virgine, secundum Albertum, est decorem et formam ejus cum colore et compositione ac ceteris delectantibus intus tractare: quæ cogitatio frequenter polluit mentem etiam ejus qui impotens est corpore. Nec solum beatus Job oculos custodivit, ne sic cogitaret de virgine, sed etiam ne de aliqua muliere non sua. Verumtamen ideo ait, De virgine, quoniam hæc amplius movet ad concupiscentiam: et magis appetitur, quia intacta est; adhuc quoque majoris decoris est, idcirco facilius decipit. Itaque, quilibet nostrum hanc beati Job cautelam sectari non negligat, præsertim qui imperfectus et juvenis atque ad mala proclivis est. Quam enim periculosa sit incustodia oculorum, constat ex eo quod ait Salvator: Qui viderit mulierem ad concupiscendum eam, jam mœchatus est eam in corde suo. Hinc scriptum est in Ecclesiastico: Virginem ne conspicias, ne scandalizeris in decore ejus. Noli circumspicere in vicis civitatis. Averte faciem tuam a muliere compta. Propter speciem mulieris multi perierunt. Itemque: In specie mulieris, ira et irreverentia, et confusio magna. Quoniam ergo intuitus oculorum tot occasio est malorum, iterum in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Oculo quid nequius creatum est?
paras.en: [[31:1|I made a covenant with my eyes|Pepigi fœdus cum oculis meis]], that is, I firmly resolved to guard my eyes from unwary gazing at women. For the eyes announce, or show, what is pleasing to lust, and from the sight a thought flows, from which concupiscence arises. [[31:1|that I would not so much as think upon a virgin|Ut ne cogitarem quidem de virgine]], that is, lest from an unwary sight I should slide into a dangerous thought. Now to think upon a virgin, according to Albert, is to turn over inwardly her comeliness and form, with her colouring and the shape of her body and the other things that delight: a thought which often defiles the mind even of one who is impotent in body. And blessed Job guarded his eyes not only lest he should so think upon a virgin, but also upon any woman not his own. Yet he says *upon a virgin* because she moves more strongly to concupiscence: she is more desired because she is untouched, and she is besides of greater comeliness, and therefore deceives the more easily. Let each of us, then, not neglect to follow this caution of blessed Job, above all one who is imperfect and young and prone to evil. For how dangerous the unguarded eye is, is plain from what the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:28|whosoever shall look on a woman to lust after her, hath already committed adultery with her in his heart|Qui viderit mulierem ad concupiscendum eam, jam mœchatus est eam in corde suo]]. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 9:5|Gaze not upon a maiden, lest her beauty be a stumblingblock to thee|Virginem ne conspicias, ne scandalizeris in decore ejus]]. [[Ecclus 9:7|Look not round about thee in the ways of the city|Noli circumspicere in vicis civitatis]]. [[Ecclus 9:8|Turn away thy face from a woman dressed up|Averte faciem tuam a muliere compta]]. [[Ecclus 9:9|For many have perished by the beauty of a woman|Propter speciem mulieris multi perierunt]]. And again: In the beauty of a woman, [[Ecclus 25:29|anger, and impudence, and confusion is great|ira et irreverentia, et confusio magna]] [the margin's reference cannot be read; the words are Ecclus 25:29, where the Vulgate begins *Mulieris ira*, a woman's anger; Denis's *In specie mulieris* recalls the verse before]. Since, then, the gaze of the eyes is the occasion of so many evils, it is written again in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:15|What is created more wicked than an eye?|Oculo quid nequius creatum est?]]

paras.t: Porro, secundum Gregorium, exteriores sensus sunt velut foramina et fenestræ, per quas anima exteriora percipit seu respicit, et respiciens concupiscit, quemadmodum loquitur Jeremias: Ascendit mors per fenestras nostras, ingressa est domos nostras. Mors enim per fenestras ascendit, et domum ingreditur, dum per sensus corporis concupiscentia veniens intrat mentem. Hinc (secundum Gregorium) intueri non debet, quod concupisci non licet. Itaque cum Psalmista devote oremus: Averte oculos meos ne videant vanitatem.
paras.en: Further, according to Gregory, the outward senses are like openings and windows through which the soul perceives, or looks upon, outward things, and looking, desires them; as Jeremias says: [[Jer 9:21|death is come up through our windows, it is entered into our houses|Ascendit mors per fenestras nostras, ingressa est domos nostras]]. For death comes up through the windows and enters the house when concupiscence, coming through the senses of the body, enters the mind. Hence (according to Gregory) one ought not to look upon what it is not lawful to desire. Let us therefore pray devoutly with the Psalmist: [[Ps 118:37|Turn away my eyes that they may not behold vanity|Averte oculos meos ne videant vanitatem]].

paras.t: Insuper sanctus Job causam hujus custodiæ et castitatis assignat. Quam enim partem haberet in me Deus desuper? id est, si vitio carnis deditus essem, nihil in me esset quod ad Deum pertineret per caritatem ejus et gratiam: unde non essem pars aut possessio Dei, imo totus essem diaboli. Illi vero sunt pars Dei, in quibus ipse per gratiam habitat, juxta illud Deuteronomii: Pars autem Domini populus ejus. Non autem habitat in inquinatis luxuria. Ideo ait Gregorius: Nulla sunt bona cetera, si Dei oculis testimonio castitatis non approbantur. Thomas quoque hic scribit: Homo per peccatum luxuriæ videtur a Deo recedere. Accedit enim ad Deum per actus spirituales, qui maxime impediuntur per delectationem veneream. Et hereditatem, id est, quam hereditariam possessionem haberet in me, Omnipotens de excelsis? id est Deus altissimus, habitans in supernis ac cœlestibus civibus, juxta illud Deuteronomii: Ascensor cœli Deus rectissimus: habitaculum ejus sursum, et subter brachia sempiterna.
paras.en: Moreover holy Job gives the reason for this guard and this chastity. [[31:2|For what part should God from above have in me|Quam enim partem haberet in me Deus desuper]]? that is, if I had been given over to the vice of the flesh, there would be nothing in me that belonged to God through His charity and grace; and so I should not be God's part or possession, but should belong wholly to the devil. Those, indeed, are God's part in whom He dwells by grace, according to that word of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 32:9|But the Lord's portion is his people|Pars autem Domini populus ejus]]. But He does not dwell in those defiled by lust. Therefore Gregory says: All other goods are nothing if they are not approved in the eyes of God by the witness of chastity. Thomas also writes here: By the sin of lust man is seen to withdraw from God. For he draws near to God by spiritual acts, and these are hindered most of all by venereal pleasure. [[31:2|and what inheritance|Et hereditatem]], that is, what possession by inheritance, should [[31:2|the Almighty from on high|Omnipotens de excelsis]] have in me? that is, the most high God, dwelling on high and among the citizens of heaven, according to that word of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 33:26|he that is mounted upon the heaven|Ascensor cœli]], [[Deut 33:26|God of the rightest|Deus rectissimus]] [Denis reads *Deus rectissimus*, God most righteous, where the Vulgate has *Deus rectissimi*, the God of the rightest]: [[Deut 33:27|His dwelling is above, and underneath are the everlasting arms|habitaculum ejus sursum, et subter brachia sempiterna]].

paras.t: Præterea, juxta Thomam, quandoque contingit quod luxuriosi ad horam de Deo spiritualiter cogitant, sed mox per delectationis concupiscentiam revocantur ad ima. Ideo Deus in eis hereditatem, id est firmam ac stabilem possessionem, non habet. Unde oportet ut hereditas Dei sit in his qui sublimia et spiritualia appetunt, non in his qui ad carnalia corruunt ac descendunt. Itaque electi et virtuosi sunt proprie hereditas Dei, qui per Isaiam testatur: Hereditas mea Israel. In Deuteronomio quoque asseritur: Jacob funiculus hereditatis ejus. Et in Esther libro: Miserere, Domine, sorti tuæ et funiculo hereditatis tuæ. Denique non solum virtuosi sunt pars et hereditas Dei, sed etiam ipse est pars hereditasque illorum. Illi namque dicuntur pars et hereditas ejus, quia præ ceteris eos elegit, assumpsit, ac possidet per dona gratiarum, quæ contulit eis. Ipse vero est pars et hereditas ipsorum, quia per dona gratiæ ab ipso suscepta, præ cunctis quærunt, amant et possident eum. Unde in Threnis dicitur: Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea; propterea exspectabo eum. Et in Psalmo: Dominus pars hereditatis meæ.
paras.en: Again, according to Thomas, it sometimes happens that the lustful think spiritually of God for a while, but are soon called back to the depths by the concupiscence of pleasure. Therefore God has no *inheritance* in them, that is, no firm and settled possession. And so the inheritance of God must be in those who desire high and spiritual things, not in those who rush down and descend to carnal things. Thus the elect and virtuous are properly the inheritance of God, who testifies through Isaias: [[Is 19:25|Israel is my inheritance|Hereditas mea Israel]]. In Deuteronomy too it is declared: [[Deut 32:9|Jacob the lot of his inheritance|Jacob funiculus hereditatis ejus]]. And in the book of Esther: [[Esth 13:17|be merciful to thy lot and inheritance|Miserere, Domine, sorti tuæ et funiculo hereditatis tuæ]] [Denis's wording, Have mercy, O Lord, on thy lot and on the portion of thy inheritance, is freer than the Vulgate here, *propitius esto sorti et funiculo tuo*]. Finally, not only are the virtuous the part and inheritance of God, but He also is their part and inheritance. For they are called His part and inheritance because He chose them before others, took them to Himself, and possesses them by the gifts of graces that He has bestowed on them. But He is their part and inheritance because, through the gifts of grace received from Him, they seek, love and possess Him above all things. Hence it is said in Lamentations: [[Lam 3:24|The Lord is my portion, said my soul: therefore will I wait for him|Pars mea Dominus, dixit anima mea; propterea exspectabo eum]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 15:5|The Lord is the portion of my inheritance|Dominus pars hereditatis meæ]].

paras.t: Postremo, hæc est dignissima atque purissima ratio cavendi peccata, ex sincera caritate procedens, ne scilicet per peccatum Deus amittatur, et ab eo mens separetur. Ideo Job tanquam vir perfectus, hac de causa perhibet se vitasse corporis inquinamenta. Quæ quam vitanda sint, innotescit ex verbis Apostoli, protestantis: Qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat. Et rursus: Neque fornicatores, neque adulteri regnum Dei possidebunt. Itemque: Tollens membrum Christi, faciam membrum meretricis? Siquidem virtuosus et castus, membrum est Christi; vitiosus vero et luxuriosus, membrum est meretricis, imo et dæmonis, qui caput est universorum malorum, secundum Gregorium. Unde et consequenter Job ostendit damna, quæ homo per præfatum incurrit peccatum.
paras.en: Lastly, this is the worthiest and purest reason for shunning sins, proceeding from sincere charity: namely, lest God be lost through sin, and the mind be separated from Him. Therefore Job, as a perfect man, declares that he avoided the defilements of the body for this cause. How much these are to be avoided is made known by the words of the Apostle, who protests: [[1 Cor 6:18|he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body|Qui fornicatur, in proprium corpus peccat]]. And again: [[1 Cor 6:9|Neither fornicators|Neque fornicatores]], [[1 Cor 6:9|nor adulterers|neque adulteri]] [[1 Cor 6:10|shall possess the kingdom of God|regnum Dei possidebunt]]. And again: [[1 Cor 6:15|Shall I then take the members of Christ and make them the members of an harlot?|Tollens membrum Christi, faciam membrum meretricis?]] For the virtuous and chaste man is a member of Christ; but the vicious and lustful man is a member of a harlot, nay, of the devil too, who is the head of all the wicked, according to Gregory. And so Job next shows the losses that a man incurs through the aforesaid sin.

paras.t: Numquid non perditio est iniquo? quasi dicat: Utique luxurioso debetur et inest perditio. Multiplicem enim per luxuriam incurrit perditionem: quia nunc perdit charismata gratiarum, deinde felicitatem æternam: insuper, in præsenti incurrit periculum personæ et rerum, deinceps æternam acquirit damnationem. Etenim impura hujus peccati voluptas, quo major ac turpior est, eo plus mentem excæcat, inconsideratamque efficit, ita ut pro affectu delectationis istius tot se periculis ingerat. Propter quod in Proverbiis Salomon de incontinente juvene scribit: Sequitur eam (scilicet fornicariam) quasi bos ductus ad victimam; et nescit quia de periculo animæ ejus agitur. Hinc in Ecclesiastico habetur: Vinum et mulieres apostatare faciunt etiam sapientes. Et ibidem: Qui se jungit fornicariis, erit nequam. Et Osee ait: Fornicatio, et vinum, et ebrietas auferunt cor. Talibus ait et Amos: Væ qui lascivitis in stratis vestris. Et alienatio operantibus iniquitatem? id est, injustis et fornicatoribus inest aversio mentis a Deo, et recessus a bonis operibus: quoniam delectatio vitiosa incensa, animum fortiter trahit ad mala, retrahitque a bonis. Inest etiam eis alienatio ab usu rationis, quæ in actu hujus peccati totaliter absorbetur: imo et peccatum hoc ad quamdam insaniam amoremque erotos pertrahit cor stultorum, ita ut instar phreneticorum alienationem quamdam videantur incurrere. Quibus competit illud Osee: Spiritus fornicationis decepit eos.
paras.en: [[31:3|Is not destruction to the wicked|Numquid non perditio est iniquo]]? as if to say: Truly, destruction is due to the lustful man and is within him. For through lust he incurs destruction in many ways: now he loses the gifts of the graces, and afterwards eternal happiness; besides, in the present he brings danger upon his person and his goods, and afterwards he earns eternal damnation. For the impure pleasure of this sin, the greater and fouler it is, the more it blinds the mind and makes it heedless, so that for love of this delight a man thrusts himself into so many dangers. Wherefore Solomon writes in Proverbs of the incontinent young man: [[Prov 7:22|he followeth her|Sequitur eam]] (that is, the harlot) [[Prov 7:22|as an ox led to be a victim|quasi bos ductus ad victimam]]; [[Prov 7:23|and knoweth not that his life is in danger|et nescit quia de periculo animæ ejus agitur]]. Hence it is said in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 19:2|Wine and women make wise men fall off|Vinum et mulieres apostatare faciunt etiam sapientes]]. And in the same place: [[Ecclus 19:3|he that joineth himself to harlots, will be wicked|Qui se jungit fornicariis, erit nequam]]. And Osee says: [[Osee 4:11|Fornication, and wine, and drunkenness, take away the understanding|Fornicatio, et vinum, et ebrietas auferunt cor]]. And to such Amos also says: [[Amos 6:1|Woe to you|Væ]] that [[Amos 6:4|are wanton on your couches|lascivitis in stratis vestris]] [*Woe* is from Amos 6:1, the head of the passage; the margin's verse cannot be read]. [[31:3|and aversion to them that work iniquity|Et alienatio operantibus iniquitatem]]? [Denis's text has *iniquitatem*; the margin gives the reading *injustitiam*, as in the Vulgate. *Alienatio* is estrangement, and also derangement of mind; Denis takes it both ways] that is, in the unjust and in fornicators there is a turning away of the mind from God, and a withdrawal from good works; for vicious delight, once kindled, drags the mind powerfully to evil and draws it back from good. There is in them also an estrangement from the use of reason, which in the act of this sin is wholly swallowed up: nay, this sin draws the heart of fools into a kind of madness, the love called *erotos* [the lovesickness of the physicians, reckoned a kind of madness], so that like the frenzied they seem to fall into a kind of derangement. To them applies that word of Osee: [[Osee 4:12|the spirit of fornication hath deceived them|Spiritus fornicationis decepit eos]].

paras.t: Circa hunc locum multa utilia scribit S. Gregorius, inter cetera dicens: Festina consolatio bonorum, est consideratus finis malorum. Dum enim boni ex interitu pravorum mala conspiciunt quæ evadunt, leve existimant quidquid adversi in vita hac patiantur. In suis voluptatibus relaxatur injustus, quoniam tanto plus ei temporalia bona suppetunt, quanto amplius ei denegantur æterna.
paras.en: On this place St. Gregory writes many useful things, saying among others: A swift consolation of the good is the end of the wicked, well considered. For when the good see, in the ruin of the wicked, the evils which they themselves escape, they think light whatever adversity they suffer in this life. The unjust man is given free rein in his pleasures, since the more temporal goods are at his disposal, the more are eternal ones denied him.

paras.t: Insuper causam, cur peccatum istud et alia vitaverit, aliam introducit: quia videlicet Deus judex omnia intuetur et pensat. Nonne ipse considerat vias meas, id est operum meorum processus, et omnes gressus meos dinumerat? id est, etiam minimas meas actiones in cogitando, operando, loquendo, distinctissime perpendit ad judicandum ac remunerandum. Hinc supra ait: Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti. Et rursus superius dixit: Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti. Unde magna nobis indicta est ratio bene agendi, quoniam ante oculos Judicis omnipotentis cuncta cernentis omnia operamur. Ideo fatetur Psalmista: Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo. Divinæ igitur majestatis præsentiam, æternæ Sapientiæ intuitum jugiter consideremus et veneremur; nec humanum intuitum amplius quam divinum revereamur: alioqui Deum dignitatis immensæ parvipendimus nimis, et stulti atque vilissimi comprobamur.
paras.en: Besides this he brings in another reason why he shunned this sin and others: namely, that God the judge beholds and weighs all things. [[31:4|Doth not he consider my ways|Nonne ipse considerat vias meas]], that is, the course of my works, [[31:4|and number all my steps|et omnes gressus meos dinumerat]]? that is, He weighs most exactly even my least actions, in thinking, doing and speaking, to judge and to reward them. Hence he said above: Thou [[Job 13:27|hast observed all my paths, and hast considered the steps of my feet|Observasti omnes semitas meas, et vestigia pedum meorum considerasti]]. And again he said earlier: [[Job 14:16|Thou indeed hast numbered my steps|Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti]]. Hence a great reason for doing well is laid upon us, since we do all that we do before the eyes of the almighty Judge who sees all things. Therefore the Psalmist confesses: [[Ps 118:168|I have kept thy commandments and thy testimonies: because all my ways are in thy sight|Servavi mandata tua et testimonia tua, quia omnes viæ meæ in conspectu tuo]]. Let us therefore continually consider and venerate the presence of the divine majesty, the gaze of the eternal Wisdom; and let us not reverence the gaze of men more than the divine: otherwise we make far too little of God, whose dignity is boundless, and are proved foolish and most vile.

paras.t: Si ambulavi in vanitate, id est, si levitatibus, falsitatibus, jocis, ludis seu risibus fui intentus. Hæc enim ad vanitatem pertinent, tanquam soliditate virtutis ac veritatis carentia. Et festinavit in dolo pes meus corporalis, seu spiritualis, puta affectus, id est, si aliquid per fraudem exsequi properavi. Et mala hæc in luxuriosis præcipue vigent, qui per prætactas vanitates quærunt ad desideratam pertingere voluptatem, atque ad hoc fraudulentiis multis utuntur. Appendat me in statera justa, id est in æquitate sui judicii, per quam omnia recte mensurat ac ponderat, justeque judicat. Unde dixit Job: Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera. Ubi de significatione hujus stateræ dictum est plenius. Porro, in his atque sequentibus hujus capituli verbis, utitur Job juramento exsecrationis, quo jurans obligat se ad pœnam, si quod dicit, verum non est: quo et Apostolus utens, Ego, inquit, Deum testem invoco in animam meam. Et sciet Deus, id est, se scire monstrabit, et alios scire faciet, per approbationemque sciet, simplicitatem meam (quæ duplicitati calliditatis ac simulationis seu fraudis opponitur), et quod sibi soli intentus sum. De simplicitate autem Job, in expositione primi capituli diffuse tractatum est. His verbis beatus Job de vanitate et fraude excusat se, præsertim prout inter peccata mortalia computantur. Cujus gravitatem, sinceritatem ac simplicitatem imitari debemus, illud Tobiæ intuentes: Nunquam cum ludentibus miscui me, neque cum his qui in vanitate ambulant, participem me præbui; et quod Isaias asserit: Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt. Itemque in Psalmo: Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus. Et Sapiens: Sentite de Domino in bonitate, et in simplicitate cordis quærite illum. Spiritus enim sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu.
paras.en: [[31:5|If I have walked in vanity|Si ambulavi in vanitate]], that is, if I have given myself to levities, falsehoods, jests, games or laughter. For these belong to vanity, as lacking the solidity of virtue and truth. [[31:5|and my foot hath made haste to deceit|Et festinavit in dolo pes meus]], bodily or spiritual, that is, my affection; that is, if I have hastened to carry anything out by fraud. And these evils flourish above all in the lustful, who by the vanities just touched on seek to reach the pleasure they desire, and to this end use many frauds. [[31:6|Let him weigh me in a just balance|Appendat me in statera justa]], that is, in the equity of His judgment, by which He measures and weighs all things rightly and judges justly. Hence Job said: [[Job 6:2|O that my sins, whereby I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in a balance|Utinam appenderentur peccata mea quibus iram merui, et calamitas quam patior, in statera]]; where the meaning of this balance was treated more fully. Further, in these and the following words of this chapter Job uses an oath of imprecation, by which the one who swears binds himself to a penalty if what he says is not true [that is, he calls a curse down on himself if he lies]; which the Apostle also uses: [[2 Cor 1:23|But I|Ego]], he says, [[2 Cor 1:23|call God to witness upon my soul|Deum testem invoco in animam meam]]. [[31:6|and let God know|Et sciet Deus]] [Denis's text has *sciet*, God will know; the margin gives the reading *sciat*, let God know, as in the Vulgate], that is, He will show that He knows, and will make others know, and will know by approving, [[31:6|my simplicity|simplicitatem meam]] (which is opposed to the doubleness of craft and pretence or fraud), and that I am intent on Him alone. Of Job's simplicity, moreover, we treated at length in the exposition of the first chapter[[Job 1:1||]]. With these words blessed Job clears himself of vanity and fraud, above all in so far as they are reckoned among mortal sins. His gravity, sincerity and simplicity we ought to imitate, looking to that word in Tobias: [[Tob 3:17|Never have I joined myself with them that play: neither have I made myself partaker with them that walk in lightness|Nunquam cum ludentibus miscui me, neque cum his qui in vanitate ambulant, participem me præbui]] [Denis reads *in vanitate*, in vanity, for the Vulgate's *in levitate*]; and to what Isaias declares: [[Is 32:7|The vessels of the deceitful are most wicked|Fraudulenti vasa pessima sunt]]. And again in the Psalm: [[Ps 5:7|The bloody and the deceitful man the Lord will abhor|Virum sanguinum et dolosum abominabitur Dominus]]. And the Wise Man: [[Wis 1:1|Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart|Sentite de Domino in bonitate, et in simplicitate cordis quærite illum]]. [[Wis 1:5|For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the deceitful, and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding|Spiritus enim sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu]].

paras.t: Si declinavit gressus meus, id est operatio mea, de via, id est de jussione legis divinæ, et de regia via quæ ducit ad vitam: hoc est, opera mea direxi secundum legis divinæ præcepta: juxta illud Jeremiæ, Interrogate quæ sit via bona, et ambulate in ea, et invenietis requiem animabus vestris. Et si secutus est oculus meus cor meum, id est, si oculo exteriori incaute concupiscibiliterque adspexi, quod corde concepi seu cogitavi. Interdum enim oriuntur in mente cogitationes illicitæ per subreptionem: quod etiam homo vitare non valet. Sed tunc cohibendus est oculus corporalis, ne illud inordinate aut appetenter adspiciat, quod menti se ingerit. Hinc ait Gregorius: Quemadmodum sæpe tentatio per oculos trahitur, sic nonnunquam concepta interius, facit sibi extrinsecus oculos deservire. Hoc ergo et nos cum sancto Job vitare curemus, nec exhibeamus membra nostra arma iniquitatis peccato. Et si in manibus meis adhæsit macula, id est, si ad opus iniquum manum extendi, vel impudice aliquam tetigi, aut aliena diripui. Seram, et alius metat, id est, fructus meos alii rapiant, ut sicut feci aliis, fiat mihi; et progenies mea eradicetur, id est, soboles mea seu propinquitas destruatur. Solent enim aliqui aliorum bona auferre, ut filios suos ditent, juxta illud Nahum: Leo cepit prædam sufficienter catulis suis.
paras.en: [[31:7|If my step hath turned|Si declinavit gressus meus]], that is, my working, [[31:7|out of the way|de via]], that is, from the command of the divine law, and from the royal [[Matt 7:14|way that leadeth to life|via quæ ducit ad vitam]]: that is, I directed my works according to the precepts of the divine law [the oath *if my step hath turned* amounts to a denial that it turned]; according to that word of Jeremias: Ask [[Jer 6:16|which is the good way, and walk ye in it: and you shall find refreshment for your souls|Interrogate quæ sit via bona, et ambulate in ea, et invenietis requiem animabus vestris]] [Denis has *requiem*, rest, where the Vulgate has *refrigerium*, refreshment]. [[31:7|and if my heart hath followed my eyes|Et si secutus est oculus meus cor meum]] [Denis reads *secutus est oculus meus cor meum*, if my eye hath followed my heart, and expounds it so; the Vulgate has *secutum est oculos meos cor meum*], that is, if with the outward eye I have looked, heedlessly and with desire, upon what I had conceived or thought in my heart. For unlawful thoughts sometimes rise in the mind by stealth, which a man cannot avoid. But then the bodily eye must be restrained, lest it look in a disordered way or with desire upon what thrusts itself on the mind. Hence Gregory says: As temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes, conceived within, it makes the eyes serve it outwardly. Let us too, then, with holy Job, take care to avoid this, and, in the Apostle's words, [[Rom 6:13|Neither yield ye your members as instruments of iniquity unto sin|nec exhibeamus membra nostra arma iniquitatis peccato]]. [[31:7|and if a spot hath cleaved to my hands|Et si in manibus meis adhæsit macula]], that is, if I have stretched out my hand to a wicked deed, or touched any woman immodestly, or seized what belongs to others. [[31:8|Then let me sow and let another reap|Seram, et alius metat]], that is, let others carry off my fruits, so that as I have done to others it may be done to me; [[31:8|and let my offspring be rooted out|et progenies mea eradicetur]], that is, let my children or my kindred be destroyed. For some are wont to take away the goods of others to enrich their own sons, according to that word of Nahum: [[Nah 2:12|The lion caught enough for his whelps|Leo cepit prædam sufficienter catulis suis]].

paras.t: Si deceptum est cor meum super muliere, id est, si ratio mea concupiscentiæ succubuit et consensit, sicque passione decepta, alterius conjugem concupivit. Contra quod in Proverbiis inducitur: Quare seduceris, fili mi, ab aliena, et foveris in sinu alterius? Et si ad ostium amici mei insidiatus sum, fraudulenter et callide intendendo, quomodo uxorem ejus cognoscerem. Scortum sit alteri uxor mea, id est, publice prostituatur, et super illam incurventur alii, eam per adulterium cognoscendo, ut pœna correspondeat culpæ, et illud compleatur in me: Per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur. Unde David regi, quum uxorem Uriæ cognovisset, locutus est Deus: Ecce ego tollam uxores tuas, et dabo eas proximo tuo, et dormiet cum eis. Sed quum adulterium et prostitutio feminæ maritatæ sit tam grande peccatum, quomodo licuit sancto Job id optare ab aliis fieri, si ipse hoc faceret? Est respondendum, quod desideravit hoc in tali casu, non in quantum prostitutio talis habet rationem culpæ, sed pœnæ.
paras.en: [[31:9|If my heart hath been deceived upon a woman|Si deceptum est cor meum super muliere]], that is, if my reason has given way to concupiscence and consented, and, thus deceived by passion, has lusted after another man's wife. Against which it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 5:20|Why art thou seduced, my son, by a strange woman, and art cherished in the bosom of another?|Quare seduceris, fili mi, ab aliena, et foveris in sinu alterius?]] [[31:9|and if I have laid wait at my friend's door|Et si ad ostium amici mei insidiatus sum]], scheming with fraud and cunning how I might know his wife. [[31:10|Let my wife be the harlot of another|Scortum sit alteri uxor mea]], that is, let her be publicly prostituted, [[31:10|and let other men lie with her|et super illam incurventur alii]], knowing her in adultery, so that the punishment may answer to the fault, and that word be fulfilled in me: [[Wis 11:17|by what things a man sinneth, by the same also he is tormented|Per quæ quis peccat, per hæc et punitur]] [Denis has *punitur*, punished, where the Vulgate has *torquetur*, tormented]. So God spoke to king David when he had known the wife of Urias: Behold, [[2 Kings 12:11|I will take thy wives|ego tollam uxores tuas]] [[2 Kings 12:11|and give them to thy neighbour|et dabo eas proximo tuo]], [[2 Kings 12:11|and he shall lie with thy wives|et dormiet cum eis]]. But since adultery and the prostitution of a married woman is so great a sin, how was it lawful for holy Job to wish it to be done by others if he himself did this? The answer is that he desired it in such a case not in so far as such prostitution has the character of guilt, but in so far as it has the character of punishment.

paras.t: Hoc enim, scilicet adulterium, nefas est, impium et prorsus illicitum, quia contra divinum præceptum, et iniquitas maxima, quia inter peccata quæ fiunt in proximum, est unum de maximis; imo post homicidium ab aliquibus gravissimum dicitur. Unde et Thomas ait: Quanto majus bonum alicui per peccatum aufertur, seu majus nocumentum infertur, tanto peccatum illud est gravius: qui autem alterius conjugem violat, maximum quid et carissimum bonum ejus subtrahit ei, videlicet conjugem, quæ est una caro cum viro: aufert quoque certitudinem prolis, et frequenter totam patrimonii viri successionem, quæ per adulterium ad extraneum venit. Denique, conjugati sibi invicem fidem seu perpetuam fidelitatem promittunt, quod scilicet altero vivente, non erit cum alia quadam persona commixtio. Idcirco in adulterio est fractio voti, quæ a multis doctoribus ponitur majus peccatum quam perjurium.
