In adulterio quoque est furtum, quia possessori res sua, id est marito conjux sua, occulte aufertur, quantum ad usum et tempus. Iterum, adulterium maxime est contra caritatem fraternam seu proximi. Adulter namque invitissime haberet, quod quis suam conjugem violaret, quam vel habet, vel si haberet. Tantum ergo scelus prorsus cavendum est, et ei gravissima debetur damnatio. Quidam quoque pravissimi atque stultissimi sunt, qui tam faciliter et frequenter virorum conjuges appetunt. Interdum etiam in loco sacro et in divino Officio, soloque cogitatu ac desiderio, in tantam se impietatem præcipitant: in quibus nihil divini timoris est, nilque reverentiæ ad Deum immensum.
paras.en: [[31:11|For this|Hoc enim]], namely adultery, [[31:11|is a heinous crime|nefas est]], impious and wholly unlawful, because it is against the divine commandment[[Deut 5:18||]] [the margin's numerals are misread; Deut 5:18, Neither shalt thou commit adultery, fits], [[31:11|and a most grievous iniquity|et iniquitas maxima]], because among the sins committed against one's neighbour it is one of the greatest; nay, by some it is called the gravest after murder. Hence Thomas too says: The greater the good taken from anyone by a sin, or the greater the harm done him, the graver that sin is; but he who violates another man's wife takes from him a very great and very dear good, namely his wife, who is one flesh with her husband[[Gen 2:24||]]; he takes away too the certainty of offspring, and often the whole succession to the husband's patrimony, which through adultery passes to a stranger. Further, the married promise each other faith, that is, lasting fidelity: namely that while the other lives there will be no union with any other person. Therefore in adultery there is the breaking of a vow, which many doctors reckon a greater sin than perjury. In adultery there is theft too, for the owner's own possession, that is, the husband's wife, is secretly taken from him, as to her use and his time. Again, adultery is most of all against fraternal charity, or love of neighbour; for the adulterer would take it very ill that anyone should violate his own wife, whether the one he has or one he might have. So great a crime, then, is to be utterly shunned, and the gravest damnation is due to it. Some too are so very wicked and foolish that they desire men's wives so readily and so often. Sometimes even in a holy place and during the divine Office, by thought and desire alone, they cast themselves headlong into such impiety: there is in them no fear of God, and no reverence for the boundless God.

paras.t: Ignis est adulterium, propter æstum libidinis et per similitudinem operis, sicut subjungitur, usque ad consumptionem devorans, id est adulterantem spiritualiter destruens, ita quod omnem virtutem et gratiam perdit, damnationem incurrit, sæpe etiam facultates suas consumit: et ut dictum est, per adulterium patrimonium alterius ad impertinentem heredem devolvitur, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Omnis mulier relinquens virum suum, peccat, statuens heredem vel hereditatem ex alieno matrimonio. De igne quoque adulterii Osee dicit: Omnes adulterantes quasi clibanus succensus a coquente. Et omnia eradicans genimina, id est germina auferens universa, quia (ut dictum est) certitudinem prolis tollit, et successionem facit incertam: fructum quoque virtutis et gratiæ prorsus exstirpat, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Numquid potest homo abscondere ignem in sinu suo, ut vestimenta illius non ardeant? Sic qui ingreditur ad uxorem proximi sui, non erit mundus quum tetigerit eam.
paras.en: [[31:12|It is a fire|Ignis est]], that is, adultery is, because of the heat of lust and by the likeness of its working, as is added: [[31:12|that devoureth even to destruction|usque ad consumptionem devorans]] [Denis reads *consumptionem*, consuming, for the Vulgate's *perditionem*], that is, destroying the adulterer spiritually, so that he loses all virtue and grace and incurs damnation, and often consumes his wealth as well; and, as has been said, through adultery another man's patrimony passes to an heir who has no right to it, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 23:32|every woman also that leaveth her husband|Omnis mulier relinquens virum suum]] sins, [[Ecclus 23:32|and bringeth in an heir by another|statuens heredem vel hereditatem ex alieno matrimonio]] [literally, setting up an heir or an inheritance from another's marriage]. Of the fire of adultery Osee also says: [[Osee 7:4|They are all adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker|Omnes adulterantes quasi clibanus succensus a coquente]]. [[31:12|and rooteth up all things that spring|Et omnia eradicans genimina]], that is, taking away all offspring, since (as has been said) it takes away the certainty of offspring and makes the succession uncertain; and it utterly roots out the fruit of virtue and grace, according to that word of Proverbs: [[Prov 6:27|Can a man hide fire in his bosom, and his garments not burn?|Numquid potest homo abscondere ignem in sinu suo, ut vestimenta illius non ardeant?]] [[Prov 6:29|So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife, shall not be clean when he shall touch her|Sic qui ingreditur ad uxorem proximi sui, non erit mundus quum tetigerit eam]].

paras.t: Si, pro non, contempsi judicium subire, id est juri et judici me subdere, cum servo meo et ancilla mea, quum disceptarent, id est, in judicio contenderent, adversum me, de subtractione mercedis vel oppressione laboris: quemadmodum in Genesi Jacob ait ad Laban, Mutasti mercedem meam decem vicibus. Ex his patet magna humilitas sancti Job, et quod nulli injuriam fecit, nec avaritiæ deditus fuit. Et hoc fecit intuitu divini judicii. Propter quod subdit: Quid enim facerem, nisi prædicto modo me habuissem, quum surrexerit ad judicandum Deus, id est, potestatem et æquitatem suam exhibuerit circa me, ad judicandum me et ad retribuendum mihi quod merui? quasi diceret: Tunc effugere non valerem, nec ab eo salvarer. Et quum quæsierit, id est, rationem a me exegerit, quid respondebo illi? id est, respondere non potero, si prædicta bona omisero, sed damnabilis invenirer. Gravissimum etenim scelus est, mercenarios et famulos atque ancillas opprimere, aut debita mercede privare. Propter quod in Deuteronomii libro habetur: Non negabis mercedem pauperi, ne clamet contra te ad Dominum, et reputetur tibi in peccatum. Et Ecclesiasticus: Qui effundit sanguinem, et qui fraudem facit mercenario, fratres sunt. Itemque: Panis egentium vita pauperum est: qui defraudat illum, homo sanguinis est. Et Jacobus: Ecce merces operariorum vestrorum quæ fraudata est a vobis, clamat; et clamor eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit.
paras.en: [[31:13|If|Si]], put for *not* [that is, the oath amounts to a denial: I did not despise], [[31:13|I have despised to abide judgment|contempsi judicium subire]], that is, to submit myself to the law and the judge, [[31:13|with my manservant, or my maidservant|cum servo meo et ancilla mea]], [[31:13|when they had any controversy|quum disceptarent]], that is, contended at law, [[31:13|against me|adversum me]] over wages withheld or labour oppressively laid on them: as in Genesis Jacob says to Laban: [[Gen 31:41|thou hast changed also my wages ten times|Mutasti mercedem meam decem vicibus]] [no margin reference is legible here; Jacob says these words to Laban at Gen 31:41, and of him at 31:7]. From this is seen the great humility of holy Job, and that he did no one wrong and was not given to avarice. And he did this out of regard for God's judgment. Wherefore he adds: [[31:14|For what shall I do|Quid enim facerem]], had I not behaved in the aforesaid way, [[31:14|when God shall rise to judge|quum surrexerit ad judicandum Deus]], that is, shall show His power and His justice towards me, to judge me and to repay me what I have deserved? as if he said: Then I should not be able to escape, nor be saved from Him. [[31:14|and when he shall examine|Et quum quæsierit]], that is, shall demand an account of me, [[31:14|what shall I answer him|quid respondebo illi]]? that is, I shall not be able to answer, if I have left undone the good things named, but should be found worthy of damnation. For it is a most grievous crime to oppress hirelings and servants and handmaids, or to deprive them of the wages due. Wherefore it is said in the book of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 24:14|Thou shalt not refuse the hire|Non negabis mercedem]] of the poor, [[Deut 24:15|lest he cry against thee to the Lord, and it be reputed to thee for a sin|ne clamet contra te ad Dominum, et reputetur tibi in peccatum]]. And Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 34:27|He that sheddeth blood, and he that defraudeth the laborer of his hire, are brothers|Qui effundit sanguinem, et qui fraudem facit mercenario, fratres sunt]]. And again: [[Ecclus 34:25|The bread of the needy, is the life of the poor: he that defraudeth them thereof, is a man of blood|Panis egentium vita pauperum est: qui defraudat illum, homo sanguinis est]]. And James: [[Jas 5:4|Behold the hire of the labourers|Ecce merces operariorum vestrorum]] [[Jas 5:4|which by fraud has been kept back by you, crieth: and the cry of them hath entered into the ears of the Lord of Sabaoth|quæ fraudata est a vobis, clamat; et clamor eorum in aures Domini Sabaoth introivit]].

paras.t: Denique, quod ita habere se debuit, ostendit ex parilitate conditionis. Numquid non in utero fecit me, qui et illum operatus est? quasi dicat: Idem Deus meam et servi mei animam creavit, et corpori adhuc in utero exsistenti infudit, atque ibidem nostra corpora organizavit. Et formavit me in vulva unus? id est, per vulvæ conceptum ab eodem Deo sumus formati: sicut superius ait ad Deum, Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me? Ideo similes sumus et æquales in natura specifica. Unde unus super alium extolli non debet, quemadmodum Malachias inducit: Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo despicit unusquisque fratrem suum, violans pactum patrum nostrorum? Hinc scriptum est libro Sapientiæ: Pusillum et magnum Deus fecit, et æqualiter ei cura est de omnibus. Ad hanc considerationem humilitatis inductivam, hortatur Apostolus præsidentes, dicens: Et vos, domini, eadem facite illis, videlicet servis, remittentes minas, scientes quia et illorum et vester Dominus est in cœlis. Cur igitur quidam propriæ conditionis et fragilitatis obliti, alios aspernantur, ita ut eos alloqui aut adspicere vix dignentur, non attendentes quod sola propria sua superbia faciat eos cunctis bestiis coram Deo contemptibiliores? Imo, quanto majora et plura a Deo beneficia sunt sortiti, tanto plus humiliari Deoque regratiari ac subjici, atque ipsius districtum judicium formidare deberent.
paras.en: Then he shows from the equality of their condition that he ought so to have behaved. [[31:15|Did not he that made me in the womb make him also|Numquid non in utero fecit me, qui et illum operatus est?]]? as if to say: The same God created my soul and my servant's, and infused it into the body while it was still in the womb, and there fashioned our bodies. [[31:15|and did not one and the same form me in the womb?|Et formavit me in vulva unus]] that is, conceived in the womb, we were formed by the same God; as he said above to God: [[Job 10:10|Hast thou not milked me as milk|Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me]]? Therefore we are alike and equal in our specific nature [that is, in the nature of our species, human nature]. Hence one ought not to exalt himself over another, as Malachias puts it: [[Mal 2:10|Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us? why then doth every one of us despise his brother, violating the covenant of our fathers?|Numquid non pater unus omnium nostrum? numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Quare ergo despicit unusquisque fratrem suum, violans pactum patrum nostrorum?]] Hence it is written in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 6:8|he made the little and the great, and he hath equally care of all|Pusillum et magnum Deus fecit, et æqualiter ei cura est de omnibus]]. To this consideration, which leads to humility, the Apostle exhorts those set over others, saying: [[Eph 6:9|And you, masters, do the same things to them|Et vos, domini, eadem facite illis]], namely to servants, [[Eph 6:9|forbearing threatenings: knowing that the Lord both of them and you is in heaven|remittentes minas, scientes quia et illorum et vester Dominus est in cœlis]]. Why then do some, forgetful of their own condition and frailty, so despise others that they scarcely deign to speak to them or look at them, not considering that their own pride alone makes them more contemptible before God than all the beasts? Nay, the greater and the more the benefits they have received from God, the more they ought to humble themselves, to give thanks to God and be subject to Him, and to fear His strict judgment.

paras.t: Si, pro non, negavi quod volebant voluntate rationabili, pauperibus: id est, quidquid rationabiliter a me petierunt, eis donavi. De qua voluntate rationabili, intelligendum est quod in Evangelio loquitur Christus: Quæcumque vultis ut faciant vobis homines, facite eis. Hinc Ecclesiasticus docet: Fili, eleemosynam pauperis ne defraudes, et oculos tuos ne transvertas a paupere. Tobiasque dixit: Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere; quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors. Et oculos viduæ exspectare feci: id est, viduis a me consilium, auxilium, eleemosynamve petentibus, mox subvenire non distuli, ne tristarentur, aut me differente verecundatæ abirent. Ideo Proverbiorum liber habet: Non dicas amico tuo, Vade, et revertere, cras dabo tibi, quum statim dare possis. Et Ecclesiasticus: Cor inopis ne afflixeris, et ne protrahas donum angustianti. Unde recte ait Apostolus: Hilarem datorem diligit Deus.
paras.en: [[31:16|If|Si]], put for *not*, [[31:16|I have denied|negavi]] [[31:16|what they desired|quod volebant]] with a reasonable will, [[31:16|to the poor|pauperibus]]: that is, whatever they reasonably asked of me, I gave them. Of this reasonable will we are to understand what Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 7:12|whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do you also to them|Quæcumque vultis ut faciant vobis homines, facite eis]]. Hence Ecclesiasticus teaches: [[Ecclus 4:1|Son, defraud not the poor of alms, and turn not away thy eyes from the poor|Fili, eleemosynam pauperis ne defraudes, et oculos tuos ne transvertas a paupere]]. And Tobias said: [[Tob 4:7|turn not away thy face from any poor person|Noli avertere faciem tuam ab ullo paupere]]; [[Tob 4:8|According to thy ability be merciful|quomodo potueris, ita esto misericors]]. [[31:16|and have made the eyes of the widow wait|Et oculos viduæ exspectare feci]]: that is, when widows asked me for counsel, help or alms, I did not put off helping them at once, lest they should be saddened, or go away ashamed at my delay. Therefore the book of Proverbs has: [[Prov 3:28|Say not to thy friend: Go, and come again: and to morrow I will give to thee: when thou canst give at present|Non dicas amico tuo, Vade, et revertere, cras dabo tibi, quum statim dare possis]]. And Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 4:3|Afflict not the heart of the needy, and defer not to gibe to him that is in distress|Cor inopis ne afflixeris, et ne protrahas donum angustianti]]. Hence the Apostle rightly says: [[2 Cor 9:7|God loveth a cheerful giver|Hilarem datorem diligit Deus]].

paras.t: Si comedi buccellam meam solus, et non comedit pupillus ex ea: id est, pupillos ac indigentes habui commensales, vel de propriis meis cibariis manducantes, quia quæ mihi paravi, eis communicavi. Porro buccella dicitur, quia intra cellam buccæ continetur: per quam hic omne alimentum exprimitur. Hinc Isaias monet: Egenos, inquit, vagosque induc in domum tuam.
paras.en: [[31:17|If I have eaten my morsel alone|Si comedi buccellam meam solus]], [[31:17|and the fatherless hath not eaten thereof|et non comedit pupillus ex ea]]: that is, I had the fatherless and the needy as companions at my table, or eating of my own food, for what I prepared for myself I shared with them. Now it is called *buccella*, a morsel, because it is held within the cell of the mouth [*intra cellam buccæ*: Denis derives *buccella* from *bucca*, mouth, and *cella*, a small room]; and by it all nourishment is here meant. Hence Isaias admonishes: [[Is 58:7|bring the needy|Egenos]], he says, [[Is 58:7|and the harbourless into thy house|vagosque induc in domum tuam]].

paras.t: Quæ ab infantia mea crevit mecum miseratio: id est, quantum ætate et corporis quantitate, tantum in misericordiæ actibus interioribus exterioribusque profeci, me in illis quotidie exercitando. In bonis nempe, ut ætas corporis, ita et ætas crescit virtutis: in malis, crescente ætate, innocentia decrescit, secundum Gregorium. Et de utero matris meæ egressa est mecum, per aptitudinem quamdam, ita quod ex speciali dono auctoris naturæ, naturalique complexione et inclinatione, pronus fui ad opera pietatis: secundum quod aliqui sunt naturaliter bonæ indolis, et secundum diversitatem complexionum dispositionisque naturalis sive ingenitæ, quidam inclinantur ad hanc virtutem, aliique ad aliam. Aliqui quoque ex naturali dispositione proni sunt ad aliqua vitia: ad quod illud in Psalmo potest aptari, Alienati sunt peccatores a vulva, erraverunt ab utero. His demum verbis Deo, non sibi ipsi, Job misericordiam suam adscribit. Juvenes itaque naturalem inclinationem sibi ad virtutes insitam, per vitia non corrumpant: sed ea bene utantur, et laudabilibus studiis eam perficiant, actuent et perornent. Imo, quo aliquis melioris est indolis, eo, ceteris paribus, ad vitam virtuosam plus obligatur, graviusque damnatur, nisi donis Dei bene utatur. Etenim, Christo testante, Cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo.
paras.en: [[31:18|For from my infancy mercy grew up with me|Quæ ab infantia mea crevit mecum miseratio]]: that is, as much as I advanced in age and in bodily size, so much did I advance in the acts of mercy, inward and outward, exercising myself in them daily. For in the good, as the age of the body grows, so too grows the age of virtue; in the wicked, as age grows, innocence diminishes, according to Gregory. [[31:18|and it came out with me from my mother's womb|Et de utero matris meæ egressa est mecum]], by a certain aptitude: so that by a special gift of the Author of nature, and by natural complexion [that is, the bodily temperament, held to dispose a man to certain habits] and inclination, I was prone to works of piety. For some are naturally of a good disposition, and according to the diversity of complexions and of natural or inborn disposition, some are inclined to this virtue, others to that. Some too are prone by natural disposition to certain vices: to which that verse in the Psalm can be applied, [[Ps 57:4|The wicked are alienated from the womb; they have gone astray from the womb|Alienati sunt peccatores a vulva, erraverunt ab utero]]. Lastly, by these words Job ascribes his mercy to God, not to himself. Let the young, then, not corrupt by vices the natural inclination to virtue planted in them, but use it well, and by praiseworthy pursuits perfect it, bring it into act and adorn it. Indeed, the better a man's disposition, the more, other things being equal, is he bound to a virtuous life, and the more heavily is he condemned unless he uses God's gifts well. For, as Christ testifies, [[Luke 12:48|unto whomsoever much is given, of him much shall be required|Cui plus datum est, plus requiretur ab eo]].

paras.t: Si, pro non, despexi prætereuntem, id est quemlibet viatorem, seu peregrinantem, aut mendicantem, eo quod non habuerit indumentum, et absque operimento pauperem: id est, pauperem nudum non sprevi: juxta illud Isaiæ, Quum videris nudum, operi eum, et carnem tuam ne despexeris. Si non benedixerunt mihi latera ejus: id est, ipse mihi gratias egit et bona imprecatus est, eo quod latera ejus vestivi; et de velleribus ovium mearum calefactus est: id est, tunicas pelliceas talibus dedi, quibus calefacta est caro eorum. His verbis redarguuntur qui pannosos despiciunt, quum tamen Deus sit honorandus in paupere. Contra quos terribiliter loquitur Jacobus in sua Canonica: Si introierit, inquiens, vir in veste candida, et pauper in sordido habitu; et intendatis in eum qui indutus est veste præclara, ita ut dicatis ei, Tu sede hic bene; pauperi autem dicatis, Tu sta illic, aut sede sub scabello pedum meorum: nonne facti estis judices cogitationum iniquarum? Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo? Vos autem inhonorastis pauperes. Hinc in Proverbiorum libro scriptum est: Qui despicit pauperem, exprobrat factori ejus. Quocontra de compatiente Salomon ait: Fœneratur Domino qui miseretur pauperis, et vicissitudinem reddet ei. Itaque vestiendi sunt nudi. Nam et Christus dicturum se perhibet in die judicii: Nudus fui, et non cooperuistis me. In Luca ait quoque Joannes Baptista: Qui habet duas tunicas, det non habenti.
paras.en: [[31:19|If|Si]] (put for *not*) [[31:19|I have despised|despexi]] him that was passing by [Denis reads *prætereuntem*, "passing by", where the Vulgate has *pereuntem*, "perishing"], that is, any wayfarer, whether pilgrim or beggar, [[31:19|for want of clothing|eo quod non habuerit indumentum]], [[31:19|and the poor man that had no covering|et absque operimento pauperem]]: that is, I did not spurn the naked poor man, according to that saying of Isaias: [[Is 58:7|when thou shalt see one naked, cover him, and despise not thy own flesh|Quum videris nudum, operi eum, et carnem tuam ne despexeris]]. [[31:20|If his sides have not blessed me|Si non benedixerunt mihi latera ejus]]: that is, he thanked me and wished me well, because I clothed his sides; [[31:20|and if he were not warmed with the fleece of my sheep|et de velleribus ovium mearum calefactus est]]: that is, I gave such men tunics of skins, by which their flesh was warmed. These words rebuke those who despise men in rags, though God is to be honoured in the poor. Against them James speaks terribly in his Canonical Epistle: [[Jas 2:2|if there shall come|Si introierit]], he says, a man [[Jas 2:2|in fine apparel|vir in veste candida]], and [[Jas 2:2|a poor man in mean attire|et pauper in sordido habitu]]; [[Jas 2:3|And you have respect to him that is clothed with the fine apparel and shall say to him: Sit thou here well: but say to the poor man: Stand thou there, or: Sit under my footstool|et intendatis in eum qui indutus est veste præclara, ita ut dicatis ei, Tu sede hic bene; pauperi autem dicatis, Tu sta illic, aut sede sub scabello pedum meorum]]: are you not [[Jas 2:4|become judges of unjust thoughts?|facti estis judices cogitationum iniquarum]] [[Jas 2:5|Hath not God chosen the poor in this world|Nonne Deus elegit pauperes in hoc mundo]]? [[Jas 2:6|But you have dishonoured the poor man|Vos autem inhonorastis pauperes]]. Hence it is written in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 17:5|He that despiseth the poor, reproacheth his maker|Qui despicit pauperem, exprobrat factori ejus]]. On the other hand, of him who has compassion Solomon says: [[Prov 19:17|He that hath mercy on the poor, lendeth to the Lord: and he will repay him|Fœneratur Domino qui miseretur pauperis, et vicissitudinem reddet ei]]. The naked, therefore, are to be clothed. For Christ too declares that he will say on the day of judgement: I was [[Matt 25:43|naked and you covered me not|Nudus fui, et non cooperuistis me]]. And in Luke, John the Baptist says: [[Luke 3:11|He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none|Qui habet duas tunicas, det non habenti]].

paras.t: Si levavi super pupillum manum meam: id est, pupillos seu alios inferiores et impotentiores, quos impune lædere potui, nequaquam per potentiam oppressi, nec molestavi; etiam quum viderem me in porta, id est in loco judicii, quod solebat dari in urbium portis, ut dictum est, superiorem, id est potentiorem. Vel sensus est: Quum in causa justitiæ prior essem, justamque haberem contra inferiores querelam, non dure aut totaliter ab illis exegi, quod juste exigere potui, sed clementer peperci. Humerus meus a junctura sua cadat, et brachium meum cum suis ossibus conteratur, id est, membra hæc mea quibus abusus sum, dissipentur. Siquidem justum est ut homo membris privetur, quibus ad injustitiam utitur.
paras.en: [[31:21|If I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless|Si levavi super pupillum manum meam]]: that is, I never oppressed by my power, nor troubled, the fatherless or others lower and weaker than I, whom I could have harmed with impunity; [[31:21|even when I saw myself|etiam quum viderem me]] [[31:21|in the gate|in porta]], that is, in the place of judgement, which used to be held in the gates of cities, as was said, [[31:21|superior|superiorem]], that is, more powerful. Or the sense is: when I had the better of the case in justice, and had a just complaint against those beneath me, I did not exact from them harshly or in full what I could justly have exacted, but mercifully spared them. [[31:22|Let my shoulder fall from its joint|Humerus meus a junctura sua cadat]], [[31:22|and let my arm with its bones be broken|et brachium meum cum suis ossibus conteratur]] [the margin gives the reading *confringatur*, as in the Vulgate; the sense is the same]: that is, let these members of mine which I have misused be torn apart. For it is just that a man be deprived of the members which he uses for injustice.

paras.t: Semper enim quasi tumentes super me fluctus Deum timui: id est, indesinenter Deum vehementissime formidavi, timore utique filiali, velut si vidissem undas maris in altum crescentes, mihique imminentes, super me cadere; et ut metuunt navigantes, dum fluctus marini super navem elevati, imminent eis. Tunc enim vehementissime timent, nil carnale eos delectat, nil de temporalibus curant, sed vitam solam cupiunt conservare. Taliter sanctus Job timuit Deum et ejus inhonorationem atque judicium. Cujus timorem saltem aliqualiter sequi nitamur, pensantes quantum in Scripturis timor iste laudetur. Salomon itaque in Proverbiis ait: Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus. Et rursus: In timore Domini esto tota die, quia habebis spem in novissimo. Itemque: Per timorem Domini declinat unusquisque a malo. De hoc timore in Ecclesiastico multa scribuntur, videlicet: Timenti Deum bene erit in extremis, et in die defunctionis benedicetur. Et: Qui sine timore est, non potest justificari. Nihil melius quam timere Deum. Timor Domini sicut paradisus benedictionis. Et: Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua. Timor Domini, corona justitiæ est. Sapiens in omnibus metuit. Porro qui ita ut Job Deum formidat, sapit quod scriptum est: Qui timet Deum, nihil trepidabit. Ideo loquitur Christus: Eum timete qui potestatem habet corpus et animam perdere in gehennam.
paras.en: [[31:23|For I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper enim quasi tumentes super me fluctus Deum timui]]: that is, I unceasingly dreaded God most vehemently, with a filial fear, to be sure, as if I had seen the waves of the sea rising on high and hanging over me, about to fall upon me; and as seafarers fear when the waves of the sea, lifted above the ship, hang over them. For then they fear most vehemently: nothing of the flesh delights them, they care nothing for temporal things, but desire only to save their lives. So did holy Job fear God, and fear to dishonour him, and fear his judgement. Let us strive to follow his fear at least in some measure, weighing how greatly this fear is praised in the Scriptures. Thus Solomon says in Proverbs: [[Prov 28:14|Blessed is the man that is always fearful|Beatus homo qui semper est pavidus]]. And again: [[Prov 23:17|be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long|In timore Domini esto tota die]], [[Prov 23:18|Because thou shalt have hope in the latter end|quia habebis spem in novissimo]]. And likewise: [[Prov 15:27|by the fear of the Lord every one declineth from evil|Per timorem Domini declinat unusquisque a malo]]. Of this fear much is written in Ecclesiasticus, namely: [[Ecclus 1:13|With him that feareth the Lord, it shall go well in the latter end, and in the day of his death he shall be blessed|Timenti Deum bene erit in extremis, et in die defunctionis benedicetur]]. And: [[Ecclus 1:28|he that is without fear, cannot be justified|Qui sine timore est, non potest justificari]]. [[Ecclus 23:37|there is nothing better than the fear of God|Nihil melius quam timere Deum]]. [[Ecclus 40:28|The fear of the Lord is like a paradise of blessing|Timor Domini sicut paradisus benedictionis]]. And: [[Ecclus 27:4|Unless thou hold thyself diligently in the fear of the Lord, thy house shall quickly be overthrown|Si non in timore Domini tenueris te instanter, cito subvertetur domus tua]]. [[Ecclus 1:22|The fear of the Lord is a crown|Timor Domini, corona]] of justice [Ecclus 1:22 has "a crown of wisdom"; the margin note here cannot be read]. [[Ecclus 18:27|A wise man will fear in every thing|Sapiens in omnibus metuit]]. Further, he who dreads God as Job did knows by experience what is written: [[Ecclus 34:16|He that feareth the Lord shall tremble at nothing|Qui timet Deum, nihil trepidabit]]. Therefore Christ says: [[Matt 10:28|fear him that can destroy both soul and body in hell|Eum timete qui potestatem habet corpus et animam perdere in gehennam]].

paras.t: Et pondus ejus, id est majestatem Dei, ferre non potui, nisi misericorditer ageret mecum: ideo aliis fui misericors: et nisi Deo me per timorem humiliter inclinarem: ideo quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. Pondus quoque Dei ferre non possumus, quoniam magnitudine sua et perfectione sua immensa infinite excedit et superat nos, nec ad ejus contemplationem sufficimus. In ejus etiam dilectione et gustu deficimus, juxta illud in Psalmo: Quia inflammatum est cor meum et renes mei commutati sunt, et ego ad nihilum redactus sum. Defecit caro mea et cor meum. Itemque: Defecit in salutare tuum anima mea. Quoniam ergo timor Dei retrahit a peccato, Deum jugiter timeamus, quam terribilia sint ejus judicia, quam intolerabilia quæ infligit inferni supplicia, perpendentes: quam item malum sit eum offendere, eum amittere, ab eo æternaliter separari. Sicque illud Isaiæ implere conemur: Dominum exercituum sanctificate: ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester; et quod ait Apostolus: Cum metu et timore ac tremore vestram operamini salutem. Hinc monet Psalmista: Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore.
paras.en: [[31:23|and his weight|Et pondus ejus]], that is, God's majesty, [[31:23|I was unable to bear|ferre non potui]], unless he dealt mercifully with me: therefore I was merciful to others; and unless I bowed myself humbly before God through fear: therefore I [[31:23|feared God as waves swelling over me|quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]]. We too cannot bear the weight of God, since by his greatness and his immense perfection he infinitely exceeds and surpasses us, and we are not equal to contemplating him. In loving and tasting him also we faint, according to that verse in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:21|For my heart hath been inflamed, and my reins have been changed|Quia inflammatum est cor meum et renes mei commutati sunt]], [[Ps 72:22|And I am brought to nothing|et ego ad nihilum redactus sum]]. [[Ps 72:26|my flesh and my heart hath fainted away|Defecit caro mea et cor meum]]. And likewise: [[Ps 118:81|My soul hath fainted after thy salvation|Defecit in salutare tuum anima mea]]. Since, then, the fear of God draws us back from sin, let us fear God continually, pondering how terrible are his judgements, how unbearable the torments of hell which he inflicts, and again how evil it is to offend him, to lose him, to be separated from him for ever. And so let us strive to fulfil that saying of Isaias: [[Is 8:13|Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself: and let him be your fear, and let him be your dread|Dominum exercituum sanctificate: ipse pavor vester, et ipse terror vester]]; and what the Apostle says: [[Phil 2:12|with fear and trembling work out your salvation|Cum metu et timore ac tremore vestram operamini salutem]]. Hence the Psalmist admonishes: [[Ps 2:11|Serve ye the Lord with fear: and rejoice unto him with trembling|Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore]].

paras.t: Si, pro non, putavi aurum robur meum: id est, in auro fortitudinem meam non posui, sed in Deo. A pretiosiori autem metallo (secundum Albertum) omnes designat divitias: quia, secundum Philosophum, quinto Ethicorum, Omnia hoc mensurantur metallo, in quo multi robur suum constituunt, in quantum est fidejussor necessitatis futuræ, et pretium redimens ab eadem. Job autem in Creatore robur suum constituit, juxta illud in Psalmo: Mihi autem adhærere Deo bonum est. Et iterum: Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea. Itemque: Fortitudinem meam ad te custodiam. Hinc in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Qui diligit aurum, non justificatur. Et rursus: Beatus dives qui post aurum non abiit. Et obrizo dixi, Fiducia mea es: id est, in auro rudi, videlicet in sua puritate manenti, quod pretiosissimum est juxta præhabita: in eo, inquam, spem meam non collocavi, sed in Deo beatitudinis meæ: quemadmodum ait Apostolus, Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe, non altum sapere, nec sperare in incerto divitiarum, sed in Deo vivo.
paras.en: [[31:24|If|Si]] (put for *not*) [[31:24|I have thought gold my strength|putavi aurum robur meum]]: that is, I did not place my strength in gold, but in God. By the most precious metal (according to Albert) he means all riches; for, according to the Philosopher in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, all things are measured by this metal [that is, by money], in which many set their strength, inasmuch as it is a surety against future need and a price that ransoms from it. But Job set his strength in the Creator, according to that verse in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:28|But it is good for me to adhere to my God|Mihi autem adhærere Deo bonum est]]. And again: [[Ps 17:2|I will love thee, O Lord, my strength|Diligam te, Domine, fortitudo mea]]. And likewise: [[Ps 58:10|I will keep my strength to thee|Fortitudinem meam ad te custodiam]]. Hence it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 31:5|He that loveth gold, shall not be justified|Qui diligit aurum, non justificatur]]. And again: [[Ecclus 31:8|Blessed is the rich man|Beatus dives]] [[Ecclus 31:8|that hath not gone after gold|qui post aurum non abiit]]. [[31:24|and have said to fine gold: My confidence|Et obrizo dixi, Fiducia mea]] art thou: that is, in unwrought gold, namely gold that remains in its purity, which is the most precious, as was said earlier[[Job 28:15||]] [the margin reads Job xxvii, 13 or the like; Job 28:15–16 speak of fine gold and the most precious things]: in it, I say, I did not place my hope, but in God, my beatitude; as the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 6:17|Charge the rich of this world not to be highminded nor to trust in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God|Divitibus hujus sæculi præcipe, non altum sapere, nec sperare in incerto divitiarum, sed in Deo vivo]].

paras.t: Si lætatus sum super divitiis meis multis: id est, inordinate de eis gloriatus non sum, quia nec eas immoderanter amavi, nec in eis confisus sum, sed ordinate usus sum eis, tanquam instrumentis et mediis ad beatitudinem veram. Scriptum est enim in Ecclesiastico: Nihil iniquius quam amare pecuniam: hic enim animam suam habet venalem. Et in Psalmo: Super eum (scilicet impium et avarum) ridebunt justi, et dicent: Ecce homo qui non posuit Deum adjutorem suum, sed speravit in multitudine divitiarum suarum. De hujusmodi divite, terrena cœlestibus, creaturam Creatori præferente, ait in Evangelio Christus: Possibilius est camelum per foramen acus transire, quam divitem intrare in regnum cœlorum. Et quia plurima reperit manus mea: id est, de hoc quod multa possedi, inordinate lætatus non sum, nec in illis superflue occupor: implens illud Psalmographi, Divitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere. Itaque in affectu et usu divitiarum inordinatus non fuit. Quum enim corporalia bona ad spiritualia finaliter ordinentur, in tantum possunt ordinate quæri ac diligi, in quantum necessaria vel utilia sunt ad spiritualia bona acquirenda, atque ad sustentaculum vitæ, quatenus Deus ultimate possideatur. Hinc fertur: Qui confidit in divitiis suis, corruet.
paras.en: [[31:25|If I have rejoiced over my great riches|Si lætatus sum super divitiis meis multis]]: that is, I did not glory in them inordinately, for I neither loved them immoderately nor trusted in them, but used them in due order, as instruments and means to true beatitude. For it is written in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:10|There is not a more wicked thing than to love money: for such a one setteth even his own soul to sale|Nihil iniquius quam amare pecuniam: hic enim animam suam habet venalem]]. And in the Psalm: The just [[Ps 51:8|shall laugh at him|Super eum]] (namely at the wicked and covetous man) [[Ps 51:8|and say|ridebunt justi, et dicent]]: [[Ps 51:9|Behold the man that made not God his helper: But trusted in the abundance of his riches|Ecce homo qui non posuit Deum adjutorem suum, sed speravit in multitudine divitiarum suarum]]. Of such a rich man, who prefers earthly things to heavenly and the creature to the Creator, Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 19:24|It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven|Possibilius est camelum per foramen acus transire, quam divitem intrare in regnum cœlorum]]. [[31:25|and because my hand had gotten much|Et quia plurima reperit manus mea]]: that is, I did not rejoice inordinately in having possessed many things, nor am I taken up with them beyond need, fulfilling that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 61:11|if riches abound, set not your heart upon them|Divitiæ si affluant, nolite cor apponere]]. So he was not disordered in his affection for riches or in his use of them. For since bodily goods are ordered, as to their end, to spiritual ones, they can be sought and loved in due order so far as they are necessary or useful for acquiring spiritual goods and for the support of life, so that God may be possessed in the end. Hence it is said: [[Prov 11:28|He that trusteth in his riches shall fall|Qui confidit in divitiis suis, corruet]].

paras.t: Si, pro non, vidi solem quum fulgeret hominibus, non interpositis nubibus, et lunam incedentem clare, et lætatum est in abscondito cor meum: id est, intus lætatus sum in his creaturis lætitia fruitionis, quasi in diis et cultu latriæ dignis; et osculatus sum manum meam ore meo, in honorem solis et lunæ, quasi eorum cultui devote intentus: quæ res, scilicet deosculatio manus hujusmodi, et abscondita perfruitionis creaturæ lætitia, seu luminarium cœli cultura, est iniquitas maxima, quum sit idololatria et superstitio vitiosa, qua creaturæ impenditur quod soli Creatori debetur, et negatio contra Deum altissimum. Adoratio namque et fruitiva lætitia ac latriæ cultus, soli altissimo Deo debentur: quæ quum creaturis exhibentur, ipso facto Deus altissimus denegatur. His verbis fatetur se luminaria cœli non adorasse, nec idololatram exstitisse. Suis enim temporibus gentiles communiter luminaria cœli et stellas tanquam deos colebant: quorum insaniam frequenter imitabantur Judæi, ut patet in libris Regum. Porro quidam idololatrarum solem colebant, ut ducem fortunæ in potentatu, fama et gloria; lunam vero, ut ducem in sanitate et prosperitate terrena, sicut in Jeremia habetur, quod mulieres Judæorum placentas fecerunt reginæ cœli, videlicet lunæ. Contra quod scriptum est in Deuteronomio: Ne oculis elevatis ad cœlum videas solem et lunam et omnia astra cœli, et errore deceptus adores ea, et colas quæ creavit Dominus Deus in ministerium cunctis gentibus quæ sub cœlo sunt. Unde Jeremias loquitur: A signis cœli, inquiens, nolite metuere, quæ timent gentes: quia leges populorum vanæ sunt.
paras.en: [[31:26|If|Si]] (put for *not*) [[31:26|I beheld the sun when it shined|vidi solem quum fulgeret]] on men, with no clouds between, [[31:26|and the moon going in brightness|et lunam incedentem clare]], [[31:27|And my heart in secret hath rejoiced|et lætatum est in abscondito cor meum]]: that is, I rejoiced inwardly in these creatures with the joy of fruition [that is, the delight of resting in a thing as one's final good, which is due to God alone], as though they were gods and worthy of the worship of latria [that is, the worship owed to God alone]; [[31:27|and I have kissed my hand with my mouth|et osculatus sum manum meam ore meo]], in honour of the sun and moon, as though devoutly intent on their worship: which thing, namely such kissing of the hand, and the hidden joy of enjoying a creature, or the worship of the lights of heaven, [[31:28|is a very great iniquity|est iniquitas maxima]], since it is idolatry and a vicious superstition, by which there is paid to the creature what is owed to the Creator alone, [[31:28|and a denial against the most high God|et negatio contra Deum altissimum]]. For adoration, the joy of fruition and the worship of latria are owed to the most high God alone: and when they are shown to creatures, by that very fact the most high God is denied. By these words he declares that he did not adore the lights of heaven, nor was an idolater. For in his times the gentiles commonly worshipped the lights of heaven and the stars as gods: whose madness the Jews often imitated, as is plain in the books of Kings[[4 Kings 21:3||]]. Further, some idolaters worshipped the sun as the guide of fortune in power, fame and glory[[4 Kings 23:5||]] [the margin note here is hard to read; 4 Kings 23:5 and 11 tell of the worship of the sun and moon], and the moon as the guide in health and earthly prosperity: as is found in Jeremias, that the women of the Jews made cakes to the queen of heaven, that is, the moon[[Jer 7:18||]]. Against which it is written in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 4:19|Lest perhaps lifting up thy eyes to heaven, thou see the sun and the moon, and all the stars of heaven, and being deceived by error thou adore and serve them, which the Lord thy God created for the service of all the nations, that are under heaven|Ne oculis elevatis ad cœlum videas solem et lunam et omnia astra cœli, et errore deceptus adores ea, et colas quæ creavit Dominus Deus in ministerium cunctis gentibus quæ sub cœlo sunt]]. Whence Jeremias speaks, saying: [[Jer 10:2|be not afraid of the signs of heaven, which the heathens fear|A signis cœli, inquiens, nolite metuere, quæ timent gentes]]: [[Jer 10:3|For the laws of the people are vain|quia leges populorum vanæ sunt]].

paras.t: Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui me oderat: id est, de adversitate seu morte hostium meorum non exsultavi, quia eos non odi. Imo personas dilexi, peccata odivi: ideo naturæ condolui. Et exsultavi, quod invenisset eum malum: id est, de hoc gloriatus non sum, quod malum culpæ seu pœnæ incurrit. Imo potius dolui inde, quemadmodum David Saulem deplanxit. In hoc ostenditur Job fuisse vir evangelicæ conversationis, implens quod præcipit Christus: Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos. Hinc Proverbiorum libro dicitur: Qui in ruina lætatur alterius, non erit impunitus. Rursusque Proverbiorum vicesimo quarto Salomon docet: Ne dicas, Quomodo fecit mihi, sic faciam ei. Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas, et in ruina illius ne exsultet cor tuum. Hoc est quod ait Apostolus: Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum. Unde fatetur Psalmista: Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis. Ecclesiasticus quoque optime dicit: Memento novissimorum tuorum, et desine inimicari; et ne irascaris proximo tuo, et abstine te a lite. Sed et in Levitico Moyses ait: Non quæras ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum. Porro quod ait lex, Odio habebis inimicum tuum, intelligendum est quantum ad culpam, non quoad naturam illius.
paras.en: [[31:29|If I have been glad at the downfall of him that hated me|Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui me oderat]]: that is, I did not exult over the adversity or death of my enemies, because I did not hate them. Rather, I loved the persons and hated the sins: and so I grieved with their nature. [[31:29|and have rejoiced that evil had found him|Et exsultavi, quod invenisset eum malum]]: that is, I did not glory in this, that he incurred the evil of guilt or of punishment. Rather, I grieved over it, as David lamented Saul[[2 Kings 1:17||]]. In this Job is shown to have been a man of gospel life, fulfilling what Christ commands: [[Matt 5:44|Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you|Diligite inimicos vestros, benefacite his qui oderunt vos]] [a second margin note here cannot be read; perhaps Luke 6:27, where the same words stand]. Hence it is said in the book of Proverbs: [[Prov 17:5|he that rejoiceth at another man's ruin, shall not be unpunished|Qui in ruina lætatur alterius, non erit impunitus]]. And again, in the twenty-fourth of Proverbs, Solomon teaches: [[Prov 24:29|Say not: I will do to him as he hath done to me|Ne dicas, Quomodo fecit mihi, sic faciam ei]]. [[Prov 24:17|When thy enemy shall fall, be not glad, and in his ruin let not thy heart rejoice|Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas, et in ruina illius ne exsultet cor tuum]]. This is what the Apostle says: [[Rom 12:21|Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good|Noli vinci a malo, sed vince in bono malum]]. Whence the Psalmist professes: [[Ps 7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils, let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies|Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis]]. Ecclesiasticus also says excellently: [[Ecclus 28:6|Remember thy last things, and let enmity cease|Memento novissimorum tuorum, et desine inimicari]]; [[Ecclus 28:8|and be not angry with thy neighbour|et ne irascaris proximo tuo]], and [[Ecclus 28:10|refrain from strife|abstine te a lite]]. And Moses too says in Leviticus: [[Lev 19:18|Seek not revenge, nor be mindful of the injury of thy citizens|Non quæras ultionem, nec memor eris injuriæ civium tuorum]]. Further, what the law says, [[Matt 5:43|hate thy enemy|Odio habebis inimicum tuum]], is to be understood of his guilt, not of his nature.

paras.t: Non enim dedi ad peccandum guttur meum: id est, per guttur impia verba non protuli, optando infortunia inimici. Ideo subditur: ut expeterem, id est, malum exigerem seu rogarem, maledicens animam ejus, id est mala imprecans animæ adversarii mei: imo correctionem et salutem ejus veraciter concupivi.
paras.en: [[31:30|For I have not been given my mouth to sin|Non enim dedi ad peccandum guttur meum]] [*guttur*, "throat"]: that is, I did not utter wicked words through my throat, wishing misfortunes on my enemy. Therefore it is added: [[31:30|by wishing|ut expeterem]], that is, demanding or asking for evil, [[31:30|a curse to his soul|maledicens animam ejus]], that is, calling down evils on the soul of my adversary: rather, I truly desired his amendment and salvation.

paras.t: Si non dixerunt, id est, imo locuti sunt, viri tabernaculi mei, id est domestici mei: Quis det de carnibus ejus ut saturemur? Hoc Gregorius et Albertus exponunt, quod viri illi in tantum oderant ipsum Job propter suam justitiam, et quia redarguit culpas eorum, quod de carnibus ejus seu mollioribus quæ habuit, saturari optabant, id est de ejus adversitatibus refici, vel de ejus morte lætari: et tamen hos patienter sustinuit. Thomas vero exponit opposito sensu, quod conversatio et præsentia sancti Job fuit suis domesticis tam grata et placita, quod dixerunt, Quis det de carnibus ejus? id est, quis det ut carne præsens sit nobis dominus noster Job, ut saturemur, id est, ad libitum eum intueamur. Et expositio ista rationabilior mihi videtur. Non enim apparet, quod vir tantæ mansuetudinis, simplicitatis ac innocentiæ domesticis fuerit onerosus: præsertim quia superius dixit, quantum ejus præsentia ab extraneis appetebatur, et quam avidissime verba ejus audierant. Verumtamen, utrique expositioni satisfaciendo, dici forsitan posset, quod inter domesticos ejus et familiares fuerint quidam perversi, quibus propter suas justitias fuerat odiosus: quod autem plures eorum boni fuerunt, certum reor.
paras.en: [[31:31|If|Si]] they [[31:31|have not said|non dixerunt]], that is, nay, they did say, [[31:31|the men of my tabernacle|viri tabernaculi mei]], that is, my household: [[31:31|Who will give us of his flesh that we may be filled?|Quis det de carnibus ejus ut saturemur?]] Gregory and Albert explain this to mean that those men so hated Job for his justice, and because he rebuked their faults, that they longed to be filled with his flesh, or with the softer things he had: that is, to be refreshed by his adversities, or to rejoice at his death; and yet he bore them patiently. But Thomas explains it in the opposite sense: that the company and presence of holy Job was so welcome and pleasing to his household that they said, [[31:31|Who will give us of his flesh|Quis det de carnibus ejus]]? that is, who will grant that our master Job be present to us in the flesh, [[31:31|that we may be filled|ut saturemur]], that is, that we may look upon him as much as we wish. And this explanation seems to me the more reasonable. For it does not appear that a man of such gentleness, simplicity and innocence was burdensome to his household: especially since he said above how much his presence was sought by strangers, and how very eagerly they had heard his words[[Job 29:21||]]. Nevertheless, to do justice to both explanations, it might perhaps be said that among his household and familiars there were some perverse men, to whom he was hateful because of his just deeds; but that most of them were good, I hold for certain.

paras.t: Foris non mansit peregrinus: id est, quemcumque peregrinum mihi occurrentem, vel ad me venientem, caritative suscepi, et in domum meam deduxi, ac bene tractavi: ostium meum viatori patuit, ita quod quilibet viator facilem et securum ad me introitum habuit. Sicque beatus Job, sicut et Abraham, hospitalitati liberalissime deditus fuit, sicut et ceteris misericordiæ actibus. Unde ad Hebræos ait Apostolus: Hospitalitatem nolite oblivisci. Et Petrus: Hospitales invicem sine murmuratione.
paras.en: [[31:32|The stranger did not stay without|Foris non mansit peregrinus]]: that is, every stranger who met me or came to me I received with charity, led into my house and treated well: [[31:32|my door was open to the traveller|ostium meum viatori patuit]], so that any wayfarer had easy and safe entry to me. And so blessed Job, like Abraham too[[Gen 18:2||]], was most generously given to hospitality, as also to the other works of mercy. Whence the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 13:2|hospitality do not forget|Hospitalitatem nolite oblivisci]]. And Peter: [[1 Pet 4:9|Using hospitality one towards another, without murmuring|Hospitales invicem sine murmuratione]].

paras.t: Si abscondi quasi homo peccatum meum: id est, false me excusavi, et culpam meam per hypocrisim palliavi, vel alio modo celavi, quando fuit pandenda et confitenda: sicut homines facere solent ex inordinato et stulto timore, in quibus timor Dei non est; et celavi in sinu, id est in corde meo, iniquitatem meam: id est, nec peccatum commissum in proximum, nec iniquitatem in Deum inordinate abscondi, sed humiliter fassus sum. Unde de homine vitioso non confitenti dictum est: Quum dulce fuerit in ore ejus malum, abscondet illud sub lingua sua: parcet illi, et non derelinquet illud, et celabit in gutture suo. Hanc virtutem beati Job imitemur, quia (ut Salomon ait) Justus in principio accusator est sui. Et Isaias hortatur: Dic tu iniquitates tuas, ut justificeris.
paras.en: [[31:33|If as a man I have hid my sin|Si abscondi quasi homo peccatum meum]]: that is, I did not falsely excuse myself, nor cloak my fault by hypocrisy or hide it in any other way, when it was to be laid open and confessed, as men are wont to do out of a disordered and foolish fear, men in whom there is no fear of God; [[31:33|and have concealed|et celavi]] [[31:33|in my bosom|in sinu]], that is, in my heart, [[31:33|my iniquity|iniquitatem meam]]: that is, I did not wrongly hide either a sin committed against my neighbour or an iniquity against God, but humbly confessed it. Whence it is said of the vicious man who does not confess: [[Job 20:12|For when evil shall be sweet in his mouth, he will hide it under his tongue|Quum dulce fuerit in ore ejus malum, abscondet illud sub lingua sua]]: [[Job 20:13|He will spare it, and not leave it, and will hide it in his throat|parcet illi, et non derelinquet illud, et celabit in gutture suo]]. Let us imitate this virtue of blessed Job, for (as Solomon says) [[Prov 18:17|The just is first accuser of himself|Justus in principio accusator est sui]]. And Isaias exhorts: Tell thou thy iniquities, that thou mayest be justified[[Is 43:26||]] [Denis quotes Is 43:26 in an older Latin form; the Vulgate has "tell if thou hast any thing to justify thyself"; the margin note here cannot be read].

paras.t: Si expavi ad multitudinem nimiam: id est, nullam hominum turbam quantumlibet magnam, inordinato timore sic timui, ut propter eam timore corporalis periculi ab æquitate recederem, aut peccata incurrerem, utpote malens mori quam Deum offendere. Peccatum enim est fugibilitatis immensæ, eo quod Deus sit honorabilitatis amabilitatisque infinitæ. Ideo nullo modo debet quis ad peccata induci. Sic et Psalmista testatur: Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me. Itemque: Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea: quem timebo? Si consistant adversum me castra, non timebit cor meum. Isaias quoque dicit: Quis tu ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis qui quasi fœnum arescet? Propter nullius ergo timorem a Dei timore est recedendum, quemadmodum scriptum est: Time Deum, præter eum vero ne timueris alienum. Et despectio propinquorum terruit me: id est, a propinquis et proximis non ita timui sperni, ut ex hoc viam veritatis et æquitatis relinquerem. Beati enim qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam. Hoc sancti martyres maxime impleverunt, quibus et Christus ait: Trademini autem a parentibus, et fratribus, et cognatis, et amicis. Sed jam multi sunt qui potius volunt multa illicita operari, quam ab hominibus despici, et præsertim quam velint consanguineos suos offendere, aut despici ab eisdem: in quibus timor carnalis et sæcularis præponderat divino timori. Et non magis tacui: id est, contumeliosa illorum verba patienter silenterque passus sum: juxta illud Psalmi, Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consisteret peccator adversum me. Hinc in Proverbiis habetur: Gloria viri, iniqua prætergredi. Et sequenti ibi capitulo: Honor est homini qui separat se a contentionibus. Et in Ecclesiastico: Non litiges cum homine potente, et cum homine linguato. Nec egressus sum ostium, ad invadendum injuriantes mihi, sicut impetuosi et præsumptuose audaces facere solent, periculis incaute se exponentes.
paras.en: [[31:34|If I have been afraid at a very great multitude|Si expavi ad multitudinem nimiam]]: that is, I did not so fear any crowd of men, however great, with disordered fear, as to depart from equity on its account for fear of bodily danger, or to fall into sins; being one who would rather die than offend God. For sin is to be shunned beyond measure, since God is infinitely worthy of honour and of love. Therefore no one ought in any way to be led into sin. So the Psalmist too testifies: [[Ps 3:7|I will not fear thousands of the people surrounding me|Non timebo millia populi circumdantis me]]. And likewise: [[Ps 26:1|The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?|Dominus illuminatio mea et salus mea: quem timebo?]] [[Ps 26:3|If armies in camp should stand together against me, my heart shall not fear|Si consistant adversum me castra, non timebit cor meum]]. Isaias also says: [[Is 51:12|who art thou, that thou shouldst be afraid of a mortal man, and of the son of man, who shall wither away like grass?|Quis tu ut timeas ab homine mortali, et a filio hominis qui quasi fœnum arescet?]] For fear of no one, then, must we depart from the fear of God, as it is written: Fear God, but besides him fear no other[[4 Kings 17:35||]][[4 Kings 17:36||]] [the margin gives 4 Kings 17:35–36, where Israel is told to fear the Lord and not strange gods; Denis's words are nearest the Vulgate of Prov 7:1, "Son, honour the Lord ... and besides him fear no other"]. [[31:34|and the contempt of kinsmen hath terrified me|Et despectio propinquorum terruit me]]: that is, I did not so fear being scorned by my kinsmen and neighbours as to leave on that account the way of truth and equity. For [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati enim qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]]. This the holy martyrs fulfilled above all, to whom Christ also says: [[Luke 21:16|you shall be betrayed by your parents and brethren and kinsmen and friends|Trademini autem a parentibus, et fratribus, et cognatis, et amicis]]. But now there are many who would rather do many unlawful things than be despised by men, and above all than offend their kinsfolk or be despised by them: in whom carnal and worldly fear outweighs the fear of God. [[31:34|and have not rather held my peace|Et non magis tacui]]: that is, I bore their insulting words patiently and in silence, according to that verse of the Psalm: [[Ps 38:2|I have set a guard to my mouth, when the sinner stood against me|Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consisteret peccator adversum me]]. Hence we find in Proverbs: The glory of a man [[Prov 19:11|is to pass over wrongs|iniqua prætergredi]]. And in the next chapter there: [[Prov 20:3|It is an honour for a man to separate himself from quarrels|Honor est homini qui separat se a contentionibus]]. And in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 8:1|Strive not with a powerful man|Non litiges cum homine potente]], and [[Ecclus 8:4|with a man that is full of tongue|cum homine linguato]]. [[31:34|and not gone out of the door|Nec egressus sum ostium]], to attack those who wronged me, as the impetuous and the presumptuously bold are wont to do, heedlessly exposing themselves to dangers.

paras.t: Consequenter Job videns sibi a multis non credi, seque contemni, ad divinum se refert judicium, sicut et supra aliquoties jam fecit. Quis mihi tribuat adjutorem? id est, cupio me juvari, ut veritas pateat: vel, Auditorem, ut aliqui textus habent, id est, qui rationes, quibus veritatem defendo, advertat; ut desiderium meum Omnipotens audiat, id est, ad effectum perducat declarando per suam sententiam quis verum dicat, ego vel contradictores mei: et librum scribat ipse qui judicat, id est, Deus justus et infallibilis judex in scriptis redigi faciat, quidquid boni et mali commisi, ne veritati amplius derogetur. Ut in humero portem illum, et circumdem illum quasi coronam mihi, id est, ubique eum circumferam, omnibusque præsentem quidquid in eo conscriptum exstiterit, quatenus omnes qualis sim, noscant. Hoc totum ait beatus Job, ad ostendendum securitatem et innocentiam conscientiæ suæ, quodque nil cupiat, nisi ut veritas causæ ipsum concernentis, universis pandatur. Unde in Joanne legitur: Qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem, ut manifestentur opera ejus, quia in Deo sunt facta.
paras.en: Next, Job, seeing that many did not believe him and that he was despised, refers himself to the judgement of God, as he has already done several times above. [[31:35|Who would grant me|Quis mihi tribuat]] a helper? that is, I long to be helped, so that the truth may be made plain; or [[31:35|a hearing|Auditorem]] [*auditorem*, "a hearer": the reading of the Vulgate, which the Douay-Rheims follows; Denis's text has *adjutorem*, "a helper"], as some texts have, that is, one who would attend to the reasons by which I defend the truth; [[31:35|that the Almighty may hear my desire|ut desiderium meum Omnipotens audiat]], that is, bring it to effect, declaring by his sentence who speaks the truth, I or my gainsayers: [[31:35|and that he himself that judgeth would write a book|et librum scribat ipse qui judicat]], that is, that God, the just and unerring judge, would have set down in writing whatever good and evil I have done, so that the truth may no longer be disparaged. [[31:36|That I may carry it on my shoulder, and put it about me as a crown?|Ut in humero portem illum, et circumdem illum quasi coronam mihi]] that is, that I may carry it about everywhere, and present to all whatever stands written in it, so that all may know what kind of man I am. Blessed Job says all this to show the security and innocence of his conscience, and that he desires nothing but that the truth of the cause concerning him be laid open to all. Whence we read in John: [[John 3:21|But he that doth truth cometh to the light, that his works may be made manifest: because they are done in God|Qui facit veritatem, venit ad lucem, ut manifestentur opera ejus, quia in Deo sunt facta]].

paras.t: Per singulos gradus meos corporales et spirituales, videlicet pedum ac virtutum mearum processus et actus, pronuntiabo illum, loquendo et vera esse testando, quæ Deus in libro illo conscripserit, cujus sententiæ contradicere nolo: et quasi principi offeram eum, id est, hunc offeram Deo principi summo, contentus gratumque habens ut mecum procedat juxta ea quæ ipse de me in libro asseruit. Hæc autem litteraliter de libro conscientiæ propriæ sumi non valent, quia ex illo alteri in hac vita veritas non monstratur. Quis enim scit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus hominis? juxta Apostolum.
paras.en: [[31:37|At every step of mine|Per singulos gradus meos]], bodily and spiritual, namely the movements and acts of my feet and of my virtues, [[31:37|I would pronounce it|pronuntiabo illum]], by declaring and testifying that what God has written in that book is true, whose sentence I will not gainsay: [[31:37|and offer it as to a prince|et quasi principi offeram eum]], that is, I would offer it to God, the supreme prince, content and well pleased that he should proceed with me according to what he himself has set down about me in the book. These words cannot, according to the letter, be taken of the book of one's own conscience, since from that book the truth is not shown to another in this life. [[1 Cor 2:11|For what man knoweth the things of a man, but the spirit of a man|Quis enim scit quid agatur in homine, nisi spiritus hominis?]]? as the Apostle says.

paras.t: Si adversum me terra mea clamat, et cum ipsa sulci ejus deflent. Terra et sulci ejus, materialiter contra possessorem suum clamant et plorant, quando possessor vitiose se habet circa terræ culturam, operarios terræ nimis gravando, aut non debite præmiando, ita quod justam habent rationem clamandi cum fletu adversus dominum terræ, qui mercedem dignam eis non tribuit: quod vitium in beato Job locum non habuit. Juxta istam metaphoram ait Psalmista: Valles abundabunt frumento; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent.
paras.en: [[31:38|If my land cry against me|Si adversum me terra mea clamat]], [[31:38|and with it the furrows thereof mourn|et cum ipsa sulci ejus deflent]]. The land and its furrows, in the material sense, cry and weep against their owner when the owner behaves wrongly in the tilling of the land, burdening the workers of the land too heavily or not rewarding them as he should, so that they have just cause to cry with weeping against the lord of the land, who does not give them a fitting wage: which vice had no place in blessed Job. In keeping with this metaphor the Psalmist says: [[Ps 64:14|the vales shall abound with corn: they shall shout, yea they shall sing a hymn|Valles abundabunt frumento; clamabunt, etenim hymnum dicent]].

paras.t: Unde expositorie subdit: Si fructus ejus comedi absque pecunia: id est, laboratoribus, qui terræ nascentia aptaverunt ad usum meum atque meorum, metendo, molendo, pinsendo, seu aliter cooperando, debitam pro labore pecuniam non solvi; et animam agricolarum ejus afflixi, eis injuriam aliquam irrogando, aut solutionem diu differendo. Pro frumento, quod seminatum præstolor multiplicatum mihi nasci, oriatur mihi tribulus, id est herba inutilis ac spinosa: et pro hordeo, spina. Justum est enim ut qui aliena retinet, propria perdat. Et verbum istud alludit ei, quod in Genesi dictum est homini: Quum operatus fueris terram, non dabit tibi fructus suos; sed spinas et tribulos germinabit tibi.
paras.en: Whence, by way of explanation, he adds: [[31:39|If I have eaten the fruits thereof without money|Si fructus ejus comedi absque pecunia]]: that is, if I did not pay the wage due for their labour to the workers who made the produce of the land fit for the use of me and mine, by reaping, grinding, baking or helping in some other way; [[31:39|and have afflicted|afflixi]] the soul of [[31:39|the tillers thereof|agricolarum ejus]], by doing them some wrong or by long putting off their payment. [[31:40|Instead of wheat|Pro frumento]], which, once sown, I wait to see spring up for me multiplied, [[31:40|let thistles grow up to me|oriatur mihi tribulus]], that is, a useless and thorny plant: [[31:40|and thorns instead of barley|et pro hordeo, spina]]. For it is just that he who keeps back what belongs to others should lose his own. And this saying alludes to what was said to man in Genesis: [[Gen 4:12|When thou shalt till it, it shall not yield to thee its fruit|Quum operatus fueris terram, non dabit tibi fructus suos]]; [[Gen 3:18|Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to thee|spinas et tribulos germinabit tibi]].

paras.t: Præterea, spiritualiter terra contra dominum suum clamat, dum subditi contra prælatum aut principem suum juste conqueruntur, quia debitum prælaturæ et præsidentiæ eis non exhibet. Sulci vero terræ, sunt homines virtuosi virtutibus culti: qui, juxta Joelem, corda sciderunt pœnitentiæ vomere; qui superiorum negligentiam injustitiamque deplorant, imo et boni communis atque animarum deflent pericula et jacturam. Talis autem Job non fuit. Porro fructus terræ absque pecunia edere, est de bonis Ecclesiæ sustentari, nec tamen prædicationis talentum subditis impertiri, sed debitum officii non implere. Quod quam impium sit, quis non advertat? Animam demum agricolarum terræ affligere, est vicarios substitutosque principes seu prælatos injuste vexare. Postremo, quod ait, Pro frumento oriatur mihi tribulus, ita spiritualizatur: Si præfacta mala commisi, pro bonis gloriæ quæ justis donantur, mala mihi damnationis pro mercede præstentur.
paras.en: Moreover, in the spiritual sense, the land cries out against its lord when subjects justly complain against their prelate or prince, because he does not render them what his prelacy and office of presiding owe them. The furrows of the land are virtuous men, tilled by the virtues: who, according to Joel, have rent their hearts[[Joel 2:13||]] with the ploughshare of penance; who lament the negligence and injustice of their superiors, and indeed mourn the dangers and the loss to the common good and to souls. But such a lord Job was not. Further, to eat the fruits of the land without money is to be maintained from the goods of the Church, and yet not impart the talent of preaching to one's subjects, but leave the duty of one's office unfulfilled. Who does not see how impious that is? Lastly, to afflict the soul of the tillers of the land is unjustly to harass the vicars and the deputy princes or prelates beneath one. Finally, what he says, [[31:40|Let thistles grow up to me instead of wheat|Pro frumento oriatur mihi tribulus]], is taken spiritually thus: if I have committed the evils aforesaid, then instead of the goods of glory which are given to the just, let the evils of damnation be given me for my reward.

32.title: Elucidatio capituli tricesimi secundi: Omiserunt autem tres viri isti respondere Job.
32.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-second chapter: So these three men ceased to answer Job

paras.t: Tribus amicis beati Job a sua disputatione et replicatione cessantibus, et assertionibus ipsius Job cedentibus, quartus disputator insurgit, videlicet Eliu, qui (secundum Thomam) acutioribus rationibus utitur contra Job, quam priores, magisque ad veritatem accedit. Unde nec Job ei respondet, quamvis in aliquo a veritate declinet, et verba Job sinistre interpretetur. Quomodo autem intelligendum sit dictum hoc Thomæ, ex dictis Alberti patescit, dicentis: Sententiæ tres præmissæ, antiquiores dicuntur: quia ex communibus sunt et generalibus, quæ in inventione scientiarum et artium prima fuerunt, secundum Philosophum in fine Elenchorum: quæ communia posteriores coarctaverunt atque auxerunt, et ad propositum determinaverunt. Talia autem communia fuerunt, quæ dixerunt tres viri: et quoniam Eliu iste determinat et coaptat talia communia principia ad propositum, magisque arguit ex particularibus, quod fuit (secundum Philosophum) studium posteriorum, idcirco sententia ista dicitur junior atque posterior. Non enim alia dicit quam primi tres: sed quia priorum studia coarctavit, et per adjuncta multiplicavit, et ex his probabilius arguit: hinc sententia ejus junior perhibetur, quam divinitus accepisse se asserit. In rhetoricis quippe disputationibus, quæ (secundum Boetium) sunt involutæ adjunctis, prima et generaliora principia frequenter sunt falsa: particularia autem et coarctata, efficaciora sunt ad persuadendum: quæ tamen posteriora sunt secundum artis inventionem.
paras.en: Now that the three friends of blessed Job are ceasing from their disputation and rejoinder, and yielding to the assertions of Job himself, a fourth disputant rises up, namely Eliu, who (according to Thomas) uses sharper reasons against Job than those before him, and comes closer to the truth. Hence Job does not answer him either, although he departs from the truth in some point and takes Job's words in a bad sense. How this saying of Thomas is to be understood is plain from the words of Albert, who says: The three opinions set out before are called the older, because they are drawn from common and general things, which came first in the discovery of the sciences and arts, according to the Philosopher at the end of the Elenchi [Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations]; and these common things later men narrowed down, enlarged, and applied to the matter in hand. Now such common things were what the three men said: and since this Eliu applies and fits such common principles to the matter in hand, and argues more from particulars, which (according to the Philosopher) was the pursuit of later men, therefore his opinion is called younger and later. For he does not say other things than the first three: but because he narrowed down what they had worked at, multiplied it by attendant circumstances [adjuncta, a term of rhetoric: the particular circumstances of a case], and argued more probably from these, his opinion is called younger; and he asserts that he received it from God. For in rhetorical disputations, which (according to Boethius) are wrapped up in attendant circumstances, the first and more general principles are often false, while particular and narrowed ones are more effective for persuading; yet these come later in the order in which the art was discovered.

paras.t: Præterea, secundum Gregorium, verba Eliu tanto graviori circumspectione pensanda sunt, quanto per juventutis audaciam ferventiore spiritu proferuntur. Postremo, quam sublimia sint quæ dicit, constat ex eo quod Dominus ait de eo: Quis est iste involvens sententias sermonibus imperitis? Alta etenim dixit; sed in modo loquendi excessit, debitam non observans modestiam, sicut in processu patebit.
paras.en: Moreover, according to Gregory, the words of Eliu are to be weighed with all the graver circumspection as they are uttered with a more fervent spirit, through the boldness of youth. Lastly, how lofty are the things he says is clear from what the Lord says of him: [[Job 38:2|Who is this that wrappeth up sentences in unskilful words?|Quis est iste involvens sententias sermonibus imperitis?]] [Denis, with Gregory, takes these words of the Lord as spoken of Eliu]. For he said lofty things; but he went too far in his manner of speaking, not keeping due modesty, as will appear as we go on.

paras.t: Itaque dicitur: Omiserunt autem tres viri isti respondere Job, eo quod justus sibi videretur, sicut et fuit. Bonæ enim conscientiæ fuit, et Dei auxilio, non propriis viribus, justum se censuit; atque hoc tot verbis monstravit, quod amici ejus ei consensisse creduntur. Et iratus indignatusque est Eliu filius Barachel, qui forte fuit proximus pater ejus, Buzites, id est de progenie Buz, qui, sicut in Genesi legitur, fuit secundogenitus filius Nachor fratris Abrahæ, ut quidam exponunt; de cognatione Ram. Secundum Albertum, Abraham primo vocatus est Ram, id est excelsus, postea dictus est Abram, id est pater excelsus, postremo dictus est Abraham, id est pater multarum gentium. Quum autem primo habitaret in Chaldæa, non dicebatur nisi Ram. Hoc alibi non legi. Itaque, secundum Albertum, Eliu fuit de cognatione Abrahæ per Esau: quod præinducto verbo non consonat.
paras.en: Thus it is said: [[32:1|So these three men ceased to answer Job|Omiserunt autem tres viri isti respondere Job]], [[32:1|because he seemed just to himself|eo quod justus sibi videretur]], as indeed he was. For he was of a good conscience, and it was by God's help, not by his own strength, that he judged himself just; and he showed this with so many words that his friends are believed to have agreed with him. And Eliu [[32:2|was angry and was moved to indignation|Et iratus indignatusque est]], [[32:2|the son of Barachel|filius Barachel]] (who was perhaps his father in the nearest degree), [[32:2|the Buzite|Buzites]], that is, of the stock of Buz, who, as we read in Genesis, was the second son of Nachor[[Gen 22:21||]], the brother of Abraham, as some explain; [[32:2|of the kindred of Ram|de cognatione Ram]]. According to Albert, Abraham was first called Ram, that is, exalted; afterwards he was called Abram, that is, exalted father; lastly he was called Abraham, that is, father of many nations. And when he first lived in Chaldea he was called only Ram. This I have not read elsewhere. So, according to Albert, Eliu was of the kindred of Abraham through Esau: which does not agree with the word given before [that is, Buzite, which makes him a descendant of Nachor's son Buz].

paras.t: Iratus est autem contra Job, eo quod justum se diceret coram Deo, id est in veritate et secundum infallibile judicium Dei, non tamen comparatione ipsius. Superius enim Job dixit: Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar. Et iterum: Viam ejus custodivi, et non declinavi ex ea. Rursusque: Neque reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea. Hæc etenim dicens, videbatur præsumptuosus, et agere contra illud Ecclesiastici: Non te justifices ante Deum, quoniam cognitor cordis ipse est. Verum hæc ira Eliu, quamvis sibi videbatur justa, seu ira per zelum, utpote ex amore Dei ac veritatis procedens, tamen non fuit secundum scientiam, id est discreta: imo et ex errore processit, quia non recte intellexit verba beati Job. Denique, non semper nec universaliter exstat illicitum, ut homo justum se dicat coram Deo, secundum expositionem prætactam, quum et Ezechias alloquens Deum: Memento, inquit, quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et corde perfecto. Atque Psalmista: Custodi animam meam, quoniam sanctus sum. Quod autem in Ecclesiastico scriptum est, tantumdem convincit, quod homo non debet se passim et sine grandi necessitate seu rationabili causa justificare coram Deo.
paras.en: Now [[32:2|he was angry against Job|Iratus est autem contra Job]], [[32:2|because he said he was just before God|eo quod justum se diceret coram Deo]], that is, in truth and according to the infallible judgment of God, though not in comparison with God. For earlier Job said: [[Job 13:18|If I shall be judged, I know that I shall be found just|Si fuero judicatus, scio quod justus inveniar]]. And again: [[Job 23:11|I have kept his way, and have not declined from it|Viam ejus custodivi, et non declinavi ex ea]]. And again: [[Job 27:6|my heart doth not reprehend me in all my life|Neque reprehendit me cor meum in omni vita mea]]. For in saying these things he seemed presumptuous, and to act against that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 7:5|Justify not thyself before God, for he knoweth the heart|Non te justifices ante Deum, quoniam cognitor cordis ipse est]]. But this anger of Eliu, although it seemed just to him, or an anger of zeal, as proceeding from love of God and of the truth, was nevertheless not according to knowledge, that is, discerning; indeed it even proceeded from error, because he did not rightly understand the words of blessed Job. Moreover, it is not always nor universally unlawful for a man to call himself just before God, in the sense touched on above, since Ezechias too, addressing God: [[4 Kings 20:3|remember|Memento]], he says, [[4 Kings 20:3|how I have walked before thee in truth, and with a perfect heart|quomodo ambulaverim coram te in veritate et corde perfecto]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 85:2|Preserve my soul, for I am holy|Custodi animam meam, quoniam sanctus sum]]. And what is written in Ecclesiasticus proves only this much: that a man ought not to justify himself before God at every turn, and without great necessity or a reasonable cause.

paras.t: Porro adversus amicos ejus indignatus est, eo quod non invenissent responsionem rationabilem argumentorum Job, quibus se justum probavit, illosque reprobavit; sed tantummodo condemnassent Job, id est, verbis multis eum reprobassent, non rationibus idoneis dicta sua firmantes.
paras.en: [[32:3|And he was angry with his friends|Porro adversus amicos ejus indignatus est]], [[32:3|because they had not found a reasonable answer|eo quod non invenissent responsionem rationabilem]] to the arguments of Job, by which he proved himself just and refuted them, [[32:3|but only had condemned Job|sed tantummodo condemnassent Job]], that is, had refuted him with many words, without confirming what they said by fitting reasons.

paras.t: Igitur Eliu exspectavit Job loquentem, id est, verba ejus non interrupit, et tamdiu conticuit, quousque speravit aliquem trium amicorum Job locuturum aut responsurum, eo quod seniores essent qui loquebantur, videlicet Eliphaz, Baldad et Sophar. Ideo cessit eis propter eorum ætatem, juxta illud: Adolescens, loquere in causa tua vix quum necesse fuerit. Si bis interrogatus fueris, habeat caput responsum tuum; et ubi sunt senes, non multum loquaris. In Levitico quoque scribitur: Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis. Quum autem vidisset oculo interiori, et id ipsum etiam exteriori oculo perpendisset, quod respondere non possent beato Job, iratus est vehementer: quia putavit quod ex superatione et taciturnitate illorum Deo derogaretur, veritas deperiret, et Job in suis obduraretur erroribus. Respondensque Eliu filius Barachel, Buzites, dixit.
paras.en: [[32:4|So Eliu waited while Job was speaking|Igitur Eliu exspectavit Job loquentem]], that is, he did not interrupt his words, and kept silent until he hoped that one of Job's three friends would speak or answer, [[32:4|because they were his elders that were speaking|eo quod seniores essent qui loquebantur]], namely Eliphaz, Baldad and Sophar. So he gave way to them on account of their age, according to that word: [[Ecclus 32:10|Young man, scarcely speak in thy own cause|Adolescens, loquere in causa tua vix]] when there is need. [[Ecclus 32:11|If thou be asked twice, let thy answer be short|Si bis interrogatus fueris, habeat caput responsum tuum]] [literally, let thy answer have a head, that is, be summed up in a few words]; [[Ecclus 32:13|and when the ancients are present, speak not much|et ubi sunt senes, non multum loquaris]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xxxii, 10, 11; this last clause is verse 13].
