In Leviticus too it is written: [[Lev 19:32|Rise up before the hoary head, and honour the person of the aged man|Coram cano capite consurge, et honora personam senis]]. [[32:5|But when he saw|Quum autem vidisset]] with the inner eye, and had weighed that very thing with the outward eye as well, [[32:5|that the three were not able to answer|quod respondere non possent]] blessed Job, [[32:5|he was exceedingly angry|iratus est vehementer]]: because he thought that through their defeat and silence God was being disparaged, the truth was perishing, and Job was being hardened in his errors. [[32:6|Then Eliu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered, and said|Respondensque Eliu filius Barachel, Buzites, dixit]].

paras.t: Ex hoc quod omnia ista tam determinate et circumstantionaliter describuntur, certissime liquet, quod historia libri hujus sit de re veraciter gesta, non de quodam conficto vel tantum parabola.
paras.en: From the fact that all these things are described so definitely and with all their circumstances, it is most certainly clear that the history of this book is about a thing that really happened, not about something made up, or a mere parable.

paras.t: Junior sum tempore, non tamen scientia aut eloquentia minor, saltem loquendo de nuda atque informi veritatis notitia; vos autem, amici Job, antiquiores: idcirco demisso, id est reverenter inclinato, capite, veritus sum, id est timui, vobis indicare meam sententiam, ne loquacitatis et præsumptionis arguerer. Allegat Albertus Ciceronem, dicentem quod Socrates in juventute sua septem annis siluit, antequam aliquid loqueretur respondendo.
paras.en: [[32:6|I am younger in days|Junior sum tempore]], yet not less in knowledge or eloquence, at least when speaking of a bare and unformed knowledge of the truth [informis, unformed: the scholastic term for knowledge or faith not yet given its form by charity]; [[32:6|and you|vos autem]], friends of Job, [[32:6|are more ancient|antiquiores]]: [[32:6|therefore hanging down|idcirco demisso]], that is, reverently bowed, [[32:6|my head|capite]], [[32:6|I was afraid|veritus sum]], that is, I feared, [[32:6|to shew you my opinion|vobis indicare meam sententiam]], lest I should be charged with talkativeness and presumption. Albert cites Cicero, who says that Socrates in his youth kept silence for seven years before he said anything in answer.

paras.t: Sperabam enim, quod ætas prolixior loqueretur, id est, quod vos senes rationabilius responsuri essetis, et annorum multitudo doceret sapientiam, id est, vos qui tot annis vixistis, et multa experti estis, ostenderetis errorem et insipientiam Job, et quid vere tenendum est in materia disputationis præsentis. Unde superius dictum est: In antiquis est sapientia, et in multo tempore prudentia. In Proverbiorum quoque libro fertur: Dignitas senum canities. Quod intelligitur de canitie mentis: de qua Sapiens asserit, Cani sunt sensus hominis, et ætas senectutis vita immaculata. Ad insinuandum quoque quam detestabilis sit insipientia in antiquis, scripsit Ecclesiasticus: Tres species odivit anima mea, et aggravor valde animæ illorum: pauperem superbum, divitem mendacem, et senem fatuum et insensatum.
paras.en: [[32:7|For I hoped that greater age would speak|Sperabam enim, quod ætas prolixior loqueretur]], that is, that you elders would answer more reasonably, [[32:7|and that a multitude of years would teach wisdom|et annorum multitudo doceret sapientiam]], that is, that you who have lived so many years and have experienced much would show up the error and folly of Job, and what is truly to be held in the matter of the present disputation. Hence it was said above: [[Job 12:12|In the ancient is wisdom, and in length of days prudence|In antiquis est sapientia, et in multo tempore prudentia]]. In the book of Proverbs too it is said: [[Prov 20:29|the dignity of old men, their grey hairs|Dignitas senum canities]]. This is understood of greyness of mind, of which the Wise man declares: [[Wis 4:8|the understanding of a man is grey hairs|Cani sunt sensus hominis]], and [[Wis 4:9|a spotless life is old age|ætas senectutis vita immaculata]]. And to suggest how detestable folly is in the old, Ecclesiasticus wrote: [[Ecclus 25:3|Three sorts my soul hateth, and I am greatly grieved at their life|Tres species odivit anima mea, et aggravor valde animæ illorum]]: [[Ecclus 25:4|A poor man that is proud: a rich man that is a liar: an old man that is a fool, and doting|pauperem superbum, divitem mendacem, et senem fatuum et insensatum]].

paras.t: Sed, ut video, experimentaliter ex superatione atque silentio amicorum Job, spiritus est in hominibus. Hoc quidam exponunt de Spiritu Dei seu Spiritu Sancto, qui est in eo quem per gratiam suam inhabitat et illustrat. Potest tamen (ut reor) aptius interpretari de anima hominis, quæ est spiritus rationalis: tanquam dicat, Omnibus hominibus est commune, spiritum seu animam rationalem habere, sed non omnibus commune est sapientiam possidere. Hinc subditur: Et inspiratio, id est interna illuminatio, Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam, id est certam veritatis notitiam, a qua ratio naturalis desuper non adjuta, multipliciter deficit. Hinc Daniel inducit: Deus dat sapientiam sapientibus, et prudentiam intelligentibus disciplinam. Et Ecclesiasticus: Omnis sapientia a Domino Deo est. Salvator quoque ait: Quum venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem. Deus autem quandoque per se ipsum immediate edocet mentem humanam, quandoque per angelum. Hinc Sapiens orat: Mitte, Domine, sapientiam de cœlis sanctis tuis, et a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit et mecum laboret, ut sciam quid acceptum sit coram te omni tempore. Porro juxta S. Gregorium his verbis Eliu ruit ad arrogantiam, reputans se aliis sapientiorem. Quatuor enim (secundum Gregorium) sunt species superborum: Prima, eorum qui bonum a se ipsis habere se arbitrantur; secunda, eorum qui illud propriis meritis suis attribuunt; tertia, eorum qui se jactant habere quod non habent; quarta, eorum qui despectis ceteris, singulariter appetunt videri habere quod habent.
paras.en: [[32:8|But, as I see|Sed, ut video]] by experience from the defeat and silence of Job's friends, [[32:8|there is a spirit in men|spiritus est in hominibus]]. Some explain this of the Spirit of God, or the Holy Spirit, who is in the one whom He indwells and enlightens by His grace. Yet (as I think) it can more fittingly be interpreted of the soul of man, which is a rational spirit: as if he said, It is common to all men to have a spirit or rational soul, but it is not common to all to possess wisdom. Hence it is added: [[32:8|and the inspiration|Et inspiratio]], that is, the inward illumination, [[32:8|of the Almighty giveth understanding|Omnipotentis dat intelligentiam]], that is, a sure knowledge of the truth, of which natural reason, unaided from above, falls short in many ways. Hence Daniel brings in: God [[Dan 2:21|giveth wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to them that have understanding|dat sapientiam sapientibus, et prudentiam intelligentibus disciplinam]] [Denis has prudentiam, prudence, where the Vulgate has scientiam, knowledge]. And Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 1:1|All wisdom is from the Lord God|Omnis sapientia a Domino Deo est]]. The Saviour too says: [[John 16:13|when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth|Quum venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem]]. Now God sometimes teaches the human mind immediately by Himself, sometimes through an angel. Hence the Wise man prays: [[Wis 9:10|Send|Mitte]], O Lord, wisdom [[Wis 9:10|out of thy holy heaven, and from the throne of thy majesty, that she may be with me, and may labour with me, that I may know what is acceptable with thee|de cœlis sanctis tuis, et a sede magnitudinis tuæ, ut mecum sit et mecum laboret, ut sciam quid acceptum sit coram te]] at all times [the Vulgate has Mitte illam, Send her, and apud te, with thee, without at all times]. Moreover, according to St Gregory, with these words Eliu falls headlong into arrogance, reckoning himself wiser than others. For (according to Gregory) there are four kinds of the proud: the first, of those who think they have good from themselves; the second, of those who attribute it to their own merits; the third, of those who boast of having what they have not; the fourth, of those who, despising the rest, desire to be seen to have singularly what they have.

paras.t: Non sunt longævi, id est antiqui, sapientes, cognoscendo divina, nec senes intelligunt judicium, id est rectam veramque censuram actuum humanorum. Hoc ad litteram dicit contra Job, et præsertim contra ejus amicos, quod consenserint verbis Job derogantibus justitiæ ac providentiæ Dei, secundum Eliu æstimationem, et quod crediderint ipsum Job esse justum.
paras.en: [[32:9|They that are aged|Non sunt longævi]], that is, the old, [[32:9|are not the wise men|sapientes]] in knowing divine things, [[32:9|neither do the ancients understand judgment|nec senes intelligunt judicium]], that is, the right and true assessment of human acts. He says this literally against Job, and especially against his friends, for having agreed with Job's words, which (in Eliu's estimation) disparaged the justice and providence of God, and for having believed Job himself to be just.

paras.t: Ideo dicam digna auditu. Audite me auribus mentis et corporis; ostendam vobis etiam ego meam sapientiam. In quibus verbis notatur hic Eliu de immoderata sui reputatione et suæ scientiæ præsumptione.
paras.en: [[32:10|Therefore I will speak|Ideo dicam]] things worth hearing. [[32:10|Hearken to me|Audite me]] with the ears of mind and body; [[32:10|I also will shew you my wisdom|ostendam vobis etiam ego meam sapientiam]]. In these words this Eliu is taxed with an immoderate opinion of himself and presumption on his own knowledge.

paras.t: Exspectavi enim sermones vestros, audivi prudentiam vestram, donec disceptaretis, id est, pariter disputaretis, sermonibus; et donec putabam vos aliquid dicere, quod efficax esset ad ostendendum propositum, considerabam vestra verba, et quis vestrum rationabilius loqueretur: ideo decet ut nunc me audire dignemini. Sed, ut video, non est aliquis vestrum, qui arguere possit Job, id est dicta ejus improbare, et respondere ex vobis, id est ex sensu vel numero vestro, sermonibus ejus, quibus se excusat atque justificat, vosque accusat.
paras.en: [[32:11|For I have waited for your words|Exspectavi enim sermones vestros]], [[32:11|I have given ear to your wisdom|audivi prudentiam vestram]], [[32:11|as long as you were disputing|donec disceptaretis]] [the margin notes the reading disceptaremini, that of the Vulgate], that is, were disputing with one another, [[32:11|in words|sermonibus]]; [[32:12|and as long as I thought you said some thing|et donec putabam vos aliquid dicere]] that would be effective for proving your point, [[32:12|I considered|considerabam]] your words, and which of you spoke more reasonably: so it is fitting that you should now deign to hear me. But, [[32:12|as I see|ut video]], [[32:12|there is none of you that can convince Job|non est aliquis vestrum, qui arguere possit Job]], that is, disprove what he says, [[32:12|and answer|et respondere]] from among you, that is, from your understanding or your number, [[32:12|his words|sermonibus ejus]], by which he excuses and justifies himself and accuses you.

paras.t: Itaque, Ostendam vobis scientiam meam, ne forte vos, amici Job, dicatis: Invenimus sapientiam, id est, vere et sapienter argumentati sumus adversus Job, dicendo: Deus projecit eum, non homo: id est, per hoc sufficienter probavimus ipsum Job esse injustum, quoniam Deus eum in hanc adversitatem projecit, qui errare non potest: et non homo, qui frequenter errat in judicando ac puniendo. Ex hoc enim potissime arguerunt, quod Job esset pro suis peccatis percussus, quia a Deo plagatus, qui est justus et infallibilis judex, non inferens pœnam nisi pro culpa. Sed (ut patuit) istud argumentum non exstat sufficiens, quoniam falsum est quod Deus nullum puniat in hac vita, nisi pro suis peccatis. Hinc Eliu intendit per efficaciora argumenta intentum probare.
paras.en: So: I [[32:17|will shew my knowledge|Ostendam vobis scientiam meam]] to you [Denis takes up v. 10 again, in the words of v. 17], [[32:13|Lest you|ne forte vos]], friends of Job, [[32:13|should say|dicatis]]: [[32:13|We have found wisdom|Invenimus sapientiam]], that is, we argued truly and wisely against Job in saying: [[32:13|God hath cast him down, not man|Deus projecit eum, non homo]]: that is, by this we sufficiently proved Job himself to be unjust, since God, who cannot err, has cast him into this adversity, and not man, who often errs in judging and punishing. For it was above all from this that they argued that Job had been struck for his sins: because he was smitten by God, who is a just and infallible judge, and inflicts punishment only for guilt. But (as has been shown) this argument is not sufficient, since it is false that God punishes no one in this life except for his own sins. Hence Eliu means to prove his point by more effective arguments.

paras.t: Nihil locutus est mihi: id est, in hac disputatione non ad me, sed ad vos verba sua direxit; nec mihi injuriam intulit, ut putetis me ex ira et passione irrationabili provocatum ad impugnandum verba ipsius; et ego non secundum vestros sermones respondebo illi, id est, non tam invalidis utar argumentis, ut vos, sed subtilius arguam. Aliqui autem affirmant quod Eliu ideo dicit hoc, quia ponebat animam hominis immortalem, cujus oppositum senserunt amici Job. Verum, ut frequenter ostensum est, amici Job non senserunt oppositum hujus.
paras.en: [[32:14|He hath spoken nothing to me|Nihil locutus est mihi]]: that is, in this disputation he has directed his words not to me but to you; nor has he done me any injury, so that you might think me provoked by anger and unreasoning passion to attack his words; [[32:14|and I will not answer him according to your words|et ego non secundum vestros sermones respondebo illi]], that is, I will not use such feeble arguments as you, but will argue more subtly. Some, however, affirm that Eliu says this because he held the soul of man to be immortal, the opposite of which Job's friends held. But, as has often been shown, Job's friends did not hold the opposite of this.

paras.t: Extimuerunt, nec responderunt ultra: id est, amici Job ita ex verbis ejus perterriti sunt, quod sibi ultra respondere ausi non erant, putantes quod esset veraciter justus, et quod ipsi male egissent eum sic objurgando; abstuleruntque a se eloquium, id est, sibi ipsis imposuerunt silentium.
paras.en: [[32:15|They were afraid, and answered no more|Extimuerunt, nec responderunt ultra]]: that is, Job's friends were so terrified by his words that they no longer dared to answer him, thinking that he was truly just, and that they themselves had done wrong in rebuking him so; [[32:15|and they left off speaking|abstuleruntque a se eloquium]], that is, they imposed silence on themselves.

paras.t: Quoniam igitur exspectavi, deferendo senioribus, nec loquendo quousque loqui cessarent: secundum illud Ecclesiastici, Audi tacens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi bona gratia; itemque, Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus, lascivus autem et imprudens non servabunt tempus; et non sunt locuti, id est, isti tres viri post ultimam sermocinationem Job ultra non responderunt; steterunt, advertendo quæ protulit Job, nec responderunt ultra; respondebo et ego partem meam, id est tantumdem ut spectat ad me, et ostendam vobis scientiam meam. Hoc semel jam dixit, et rursus illud nunc repetit: quia, etsi zelo æquitatis fuit utcumque succensus, tamen, quoniam juvenis imperfectusque fuit, vanitas se miscebat, et ostentare se concupivit. Imperfecti nempe et passionati, quamvis aliquando bonum concipiant, et ex bono fonte quid inchoent, multiplex tamen se miscet in processu defectus.
paras.en: [[32:16|Therefore because I have waited|Quoniam igitur exspectavi]], deferring to my elders, and not speaking until they had ceased to speak, according to that word of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 32:9|Hear in silence, and for thy reverence good grace shall come to thee|Audi tacens, et pro reverentia accedet tibi bona gratia]]; and again: [[Ecclus 20:7|A wise man will hold his peace till he see opportunity: but a babbler, and a fool, will regard no time|Homo sapiens tacebit usque ad tempus, lascivus autem et imprudens non servabunt tempus]]; [[32:16|and they have not spoken|et non sunt locuti]], that is, these three men answered no more after Job's last discourse; [[32:16|they stood|steterunt]], attending to what Job brought forth, [[32:16|and answered no more|nec responderunt ultra]]: [[32:17|I also will answer my part|respondebo et ego partem meam]], that is, as much as falls to me, [[32:17|and will shew my knowledge|et ostendam vobis scientiam meam]]. He has said this once already, and now repeats it again: because, though he was in some way kindled with zeal for equity, yet, since he was young and imperfect, vanity mingled itself in, and he desired to show himself off. For the imperfect and those ruled by their passions, even if at times they conceive something good and begin something from a good source, yet manifold defect mingles itself in as they go on.

paras.t: Plenus sum sermonibus mentalibus, id est, ad loquendum multa concepi, et ad loquendum rhetorice pronus sum, tanquam eminenter facundus et doctus. Sed revera vitio loquacitatis subjacuit. Contra quod ait Scriptura: Est odibilis qui procax est ad loquendum. Et coarctat me spiritus uteri mei. Uteri nomine, mens seu intellectus exprimitur, quo verbum internum concipitur, sicut in utero corporeo proles. Spiritus autem uteri, est vel voluntas ad actum intellectus impellens, vel ipsa anima, cujus vis est ipse intellectus: qui spiritus coarctavit, id est, constrinxit et incitavit seu impulit, ipsum Eliu ad loquendum, partim ex vanitate, et partim ex impatientia. Interdum vero justi ad loquendum impelluntur ex Dei et proximi caritate, ad Dei honorem et proximorum salutem, prout in Actis de Paulo narratur, quod incitabatur spiritus ejus in semetipso, videns idololatriæ deditam civitatem Atheniensem.
paras.en: [[32:18|I am full of matter to speak of|Plenus sum sermonibus]], words of the mind, that is, I have conceived many things to say, and I am inclined to speak with rhetoric, as one eminently eloquent and learned. But in truth he was subject to the vice of talkativeness, against which Scripture says: [[Ecclus 20:5|there is another that is hateful, that is bold in speech|Est odibilis qui procax est ad loquendum]]. And [[32:18|the spirit of my bowels straiteneth me|coarctat me spiritus uteri mei]]. By the name of womb [uterus, which the Douay-Rheims renders bowels] is meant the mind or intellect, in which the inner word [that is, the concept, which the mind forms within before it speaks] is conceived, as offspring in the bodily womb. And the spirit of the womb is either the will, which impels the intellect to its act, or the soul itself, whose power the intellect is: and this spirit straitened, that is, constrained and incited or impelled, Eliu himself to speak, partly from vanity and partly from impatience. Sometimes, however, the just are impelled to speak by the love of God and neighbour, for the honour of God and the salvation of their neighbours, as is told in the Acts of Paul at Athens, that [[Acts 17:16|his spirit was stirred within him, seeing the city wholly given to idolatry|incitabatur spiritus ejus in semetipso, videns idololatriæ deditam civitatem]].

paras.t: En venter meus quasi mustum absque spiraculo: id est, intellectus meus ita conatur in verba oris erumpere, sicut mustum carens spiraculo seu foramine, per quod vapor ex musto ascendens erumpat, conatur vaporem suum emittere; quod lagunculas novas disrumpit, id est vasa in quibus est, quæ nisi aperturam habeant, per quam vapor ascendens emanet, solent disrumpi et frangi. Multiplicatur enim vapor interior musti, egredi quærens. Unde in Evangelio loquitur Christus: Nemo mittit vinum novum in utres veteres; alioqui rumpuntur utres, et vinum effunditur. Hoc ipsum et justi aliquando patiuntur ex purissimo zelo veri et æqui, quemadmodum asserit Jeremias: Factus sum quasi vir ebrius, et quasi homo madidus vino, a facie Domini, et a facie verborum sanctorum ejus. Unde de Apostolis ferventissime in die Pentecostes loquentibus, scelerati dixerunt: Quia musto pleni sunt isti.
paras.en: [[32:19|Behold, my belly is as new wine which wanteth vent|En venter meus quasi mustum absque spiraculo]]: that is, my intellect strives to burst out into the words of the mouth just as new wine that lacks a vent or hole, through which the vapour rising from the wine may break out, strives to give off its vapour; [[32:19|which bursteth the new vessels|quod lagunculas novas disrumpit]], that is, the vessels it is in, which, unless they have an opening through which the rising vapour may escape, commonly burst and break. For the vapour within new wine multiplies, seeking to get out. Hence Christ says in the Gospel: [[Mark 2:22|no man putteth new wine into old bottles|Nemo mittit vinum novum in utres veteres]]; [[Matt 9:17|Otherwise the bottles break, and the wine runneth out|alioqui rumpuntur utres, et vinum effunditur]] [the margin gives Matt. ix, 17; Denis's opening words, Nemo mittit, are those of Mark 2:22 and Luke 5:37]. The just too sometimes suffer this very thing from a most pure zeal for truth and equity, as Jeremias declares: [[Jer 23:9|I am become as a drunken man, and as a man full of wine, at the presence of the Lord, and at the presence of his holy words|Factus sum quasi vir ebrius, et quasi homo madidus vino, a facie Domini, et a facie verborum sanctorum ejus]]. Hence of the Apostles, speaking most fervently on the day of Pentecost, the wicked said: [[Acts 2:13|These men are full of new wine|Quia musto pleni sunt isti]].

paras.t: Loquar, et respirabo paululum, id est, loquendo anxietatem et æstuantem cordis fervorem ad loquendum pro Deo, aliqualiter temperabo, consolabor, et requiescere faciam. Aperiam labia mea, quasi ex deliberatione sublimia prolaturus, et respondebo. Etenim, quo diutius tacuit, quum ea quæ sibi displicuerunt, et Deo atque justitiæ obviare tanquam blasphemiæ videbantur; eo ardentius desiderium respondendi succrevit in eo. Sic et Eliphaz ad Job dixit: Conceptum sermonem tenere quis poterit?
paras.en: [[32:20|I will speak and take breath a little|Loquar, et respirabo paululum]], that is, by speaking I will in some measure temper, soothe and bring to rest the anxiety and the seething fervour of my heart to speak for God. [[32:20|I will open my lips|Aperiam labia mea]], as one about to bring forth lofty things after deliberation, [[32:20|and will answer|et respondebo]]. For the longer he kept silent, while the things that displeased him seemed to oppose God and justice like blasphemies, the more ardently the desire to answer grew in him. So too Eliphaz said to Job: [[Job 4:2|who can withhold the words he hath conceived?|Conceptum sermonem tenere quis poterit]]

paras.t: Non accipiam personam viri, id est, intuitu hominis a veritate et justitia non recedam. Ille equidem, secundum Thomam, in respondendo personam hominis accipit, qui veritatem relinquit, ut homini deferat sive complaceat. In quo verbo Eliu ostendit se Deum imitari: de quo in Paralipomenon Actuumque libris scriptum est, quod non sit personarum acceptor. Et Deum homini non æquabo, quum Deus sit infinite, et per consequens, incomparabiliter melior atque perfectior homine, imo et toto universo: quod etiam Eliu ideo ait, quia, secundum suam æstimationem, Job immoderanter comparavit se Deo. Nam infra ait ad Job: Numquid tibi justa videtur cogitatio tua, ut diceres, Justior Deo sum?
paras.en: [[32:21|I will not accept the person of man|Non accipiam personam viri]], that is, I will not depart from truth and justice out of regard for a man. For, according to Thomas, he accepts a man's person in answering who forsakes the truth in order to defer to or please a man. In this word Eliu shows that he imitates God, of whom it is written in the books of Paralipomenon [2 Par 19:7] and of the Acts that [[Acts 10:34|God is not a respecter of persons|non sit personarum acceptor]]. And [[32:21|I will not level God with man|Deum homini non æquabo]]: since God is infinitely, and consequently incomparably, better and more perfect than man, indeed than the whole universe. Eliu says this too because, in his estimation, Job had compared himself with God beyond measure. For further on he says to Job: [[Job 35:2|Doth thy thought seem right to thee, that thou shouldst say: I am more just than God?|Numquid tibi justa videtur cogitatio tua, ut diceres, Justior Deo sum?]]

paras.t: Cur autem tam juste loqui intendat, adjicit: Nescio enim quamdiu subsistam, id est, diem et horam mortis ignoro; et si post modicum tollat me factor meus, id est, ignoro an Creator meus cito auferet me de hac vita. Vel sensus est: Nescio an post breve tempus vel longum adducet me ad suum tribunal. Ideo sic agere debeo, quasi quotidie moriturus, quia tempus pœnitendi mihi dandum esse non novi: unde pro modico dubiæ atque corruptibilis vitæ, a veritate et æquitate nequaquam recedere debeo. Sic et Christus hortatur: Videte, vigilate, et orate; nescitis enim quando Dominus veniat: sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu, an mane.
paras.en: And why he means to speak so justly, he adds: [[32:22|For I know not how long I shall continue|Nescio enim quamdiu subsistam]], that is, I do not know the day and hour of death; [[32:22|and whether after a while my Maker may take me away|et si post modicum tollat me factor meus]], that is, I do not know whether my Creator will soon take me from this life. Or the sense is: I do not know whether after a short time or a long one He will bring me before His tribunal. Therefore I ought so to act as one who is to die any day, because I do not know that time for repentance will be given me: and so, for the sake of a short, uncertain and corruptible life, I ought by no means to depart from truth and equity. So too Christ exhorts: [[Mark 13:33|Take ye heed, watch and pray. For ye know not|Videte, vigilate, et orate; nescitis enim]] [[Mark 13:35|when the lord of the house cometh, at even, or at midnight, or at the cock crowing, or in the morning|quando Dominus veniat: sero, an media nocte, an galli cantu, an mane]].

paras.t: Denique Eliu (ut moris est inaniter sapientium, et in propriis oculis virtuosorum) verbis jactantiæ sapientiæ verba commiscet, ut sapiens judicetur, et rationabiliter loqui monstretur. Sed in talibus hominibus passiones et vitia actui rationis se intus permiscent, atque ad reprehensibilia verba inducunt.
paras.en: Lastly, Eliu (as is the way of those who are wise in vain, and virtuous in their own eyes) mingles words of wisdom with words of boasting, so as to be judged wise and to be seen to speak reasonably. But in such men passions and vices mingle themselves inwardly with the act of reason, and lead them on to blameworthy words.

33.title: Explanatio capituli tricesimi tertii: Audi ergo, Job, eloquia mea.
33.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-third chapter: Hear therefore, O Job, my speeches

paras.t: Inito suæ disputationis proœmio, Eliu nunc disputationem ipsam adversus Job inchoat; et partim ira ac impatientia, partimque præsumptione et elatione cæcatus, modestiam in loquendo non servat. Audi ergo, Job, eloquia mea, id est evidentia verba, quasi extra seu aperte ac lucide pronuntianda; et omnes sermones meos ausculta. Quasi dicat: Omnia quæ effabor, advertentia sunt condigna. Ecce aperui os meum: loquatur lingua mea in faucibus meis, id est, intra fauces ad formationem verborum movebitur: lingua quippe continuatur ad cor; idcirco præmeditata, articulata, litterataque profert. Numquid parvus fuit in oculis suis, qui hoc magnum atque notabile reputavit, quod aperuisset os suum, idque pronuntiavit, quod lingua sua in faucibus suis mox loqueretur? Non utique parvi sapientiæ aut modici ponderis se putavit, qui proprios actus sic extulit.
paras.en: Having finished the preamble of his disputation, Eliu now begins the disputation itself against Job; and, blinded partly by anger and impatience, partly by presumption and pride, he does not keep modesty in speaking. [[33:1|Hear therefore, O Job, my speeches|Audi ergo, Job, eloquia mea]], that is, plain words, to be uttered as it were outwardly, that is, openly and clearly [the Latin *eloquia*, “speeches”, is taken as words spoken *out*, from *e-loqui*]; [[33:1|and hearken to all my words|et omnes sermones meos ausculta]]. As if to say: All that I shall utter is well worthy of attention. [[33:2|Behold now I have opened my mouth|Ecce aperui os meum]], [[33:2|let my tongue speak within my jaws|loquatur lingua mea in faucibus meis]], that is, it shall be moved within the jaws to form words [a margin note beside this line is unreadable in the scan]: for the tongue is joined to the heart; therefore it brings forth things premeditated, articulate and lettered. Was he little in his own eyes, who counted it a great and notable thing that he had opened his mouth, and who announced that his tongue would presently speak within his jaws? Surely he did not think himself of little wisdom or slight weight, who so extolled his own acts.

paras.t: Simplici corde omnes sermones mei, id est, verba mea ex sincera intentione pendent, ita quod nihil intendo nisi veritatis defensionem, ad Dei honorem et aliorum ædificationem; nec loquar ad calumniandum, nilque calliditatis vel duplicitatis in me reperietur, neque in verbis meis sonabit. Verumtamen, juxta præhabita, istud ita non fuit: quia non tantum ex zelo veritatis motus est loqui, sed insuper ex gloria vana, utpote excellentiam sapientiæ et eloquentiæ suæ cupiens demonstrare, indeque reputari. Et sententiam labia mea loquentur puram, id est, sensus altos ac sapientiales sine admixtione falsitatis pronuntiabo. Quod rursus penitus verum non est: quamvis enim multa vera sententiosaque proferat, falsa tamen ex eis conclusit adversus Job, et multa crimina ei mendose imposuit.
paras.en: [[33:3|My words are from my upright heart|Simplici corde omnes sermones mei]], that is, my words hang upon a sincere intention, so that I intend nothing but the defence of the truth, for the honour of God and the edification of others; nor shall I speak to slander, and no craft or doubleness shall be found in me, nor shall it sound in my words. And yet, as was said before, this was not so: for he was moved to speak not only by zeal for the truth but also by vainglory, desiring as he did to display the excellence of his wisdom and eloquence, and to be esteemed for it. [[33:3|and my lips shall speak a pure sentence|Et sententiam labia mea loquentur puram]], that is, I shall utter lofty and wise meanings without admixture of falsehood. This again is not wholly true: for although he brings forth many true and weighty sayings, yet from them he drew false conclusions against Job, and laid many crimes upon him untruly.

paras.t: Spiritus Dei fecit me: ideo dignum et justum est, ut me verbis divinæ majestati derogativis opponam. Quemadmodum enim totum quod sumus et habemus, a Deo suscepimus; ita omne id in ejus honorem expendere reverenter debemus, ut ait Hilarius. Porro, per Spiritum Dei, intelligi potest Spiritus Sanctus, vel intellectus seu voluntas divina, seu Deus absolute, qui spiritus est. Et spiraculum Omnipotentis vivificavit me. In Genesi ait Scriptura: Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ, et inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitæ, et factus est homo in animam viventem. Ubi per spiraculum, intelligitur spiritus seu anima rationalis, corpus vivificans vita naturæ, imo dans homini vitam vegetativam, sensitivam, secundum locum motivam, et intellectivam. Et ita hic accipi potest spiraculum: quod dicitur spiraculum Omnipotentis, quia ab ipso procedit, creatur, infunditur, imo quodammodo insufflatur. Hinc in Scripturis veteris Testamenti, anima flatus vocatur, ut quum per Isaiam Dominus ait: Spiritus a facie mea egredietur, et flatus ego faciam. Daniel quoque propheta Balthasar regi loquens: Deum, inquit, qui habet flatum tuum in manu sua, non honorasti. Insuper, per spiraculum, intelligi potest ipsa inspiratio Dei per gratiam illustrantem: qua vivificat mentem ad vitam sapientialem, seu interiorem sapientiæ actum, qui animæ vita est, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Sapientia vitam filiis suis inspirat. Christus etiam in Evangelio: Justificata est, ait, sapientia ab omnibus filiis suis.
paras.en: [[33:4|The spirit of God made me|Spiritus Dei fecit me]]: therefore it is fitting and just that I should set myself against words that detract from the divine majesty. For as we have received from God all that we are and have, so we ought reverently to spend all of it for his honour, as Hilary says. Now by the Spirit of God may be understood the Holy Ghost, or the divine intellect or will, or God taken absolutely, who is a spirit. [[33:4|and the breath of the Almighty gave me life|Et spiraculum Omnipotentis vivificavit me]]. In Genesis the Scripture says: [[Gen 2:7|the Lord God formed man of the slime of the earth: and breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul|Formavit Deus hominem de limo terræ, et inspiravit in faciem ejus spiraculum vitæ, et factus est homo in animam viventem]]. There by the *breath* is understood the spirit or rational soul, which quickens the body with the life of nature, nay, which gives man vegetative, sensitive, locomotive and intellective life. And so *breath* may be taken here: and it is called the breath of the Almighty because it proceeds from him, is created and infused by him, nay, is in a manner breathed in by him. Hence in the Scriptures of the Old Testament the soul is called a *breath*, as when the Lord says by Isaias: [[Is 57:16|the spirit shall go forth from my face, and breathings I will make|Spiritus a facie mea egredietur, et flatus ego faciam]] [*flatus*, “breath”, which the Douay-Rheims renders “breathings”]. And the prophet Daniel, speaking to king Balthasar: [[Dan 5:23|the God|Deum]], he says, [[Dan 5:23|who hath thy breath in his hand|qui habet flatum tuum in manu sua]], [[Dan 5:23|thou hast not glorified|non honorasti]]. Further, by the *breath* may be understood the very inspiration of God through enlightening grace, by which he quickens the mind to the life of wisdom, that is, to the inward act of wisdom, which is the life of the soul, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 4:12|Wisdom inspireth life into her children|Sapientia vitam filiis suis inspirat]]. Christ too in the Gospel: [[Luke 7:35|wisdom is justified|Justificata est]], he says, [[Luke 7:35|by all her children|sapientia ab omnibus filiis suis]] [the margin gives Matth. xi, 19; Denis's wording, “by all her children”, is that of Luke 7:35].

paras.t: Si potes, responde mihi, et adversus faciem meam consiste, id est, argumentationibus meis satisfac et resiste, si vales: quasi dicat, Paratus sum morem gerere tibi, tuamque responsionem suscipere. Sed hoc verbum rursus superbiam videtur prætendere. Quid enim est dicere, Si potes, etc., nisi, Scio quia non poteris mihi respondere atque resistere?
paras.en: [[33:5|If thou canst, answer me|Si potes, responde mihi]], [[33:5|and stand up against my face|et adversus faciem meam consiste]], that is, satisfy and withstand my arguments, if thou art able: as if to say, I am ready to humour thee and to receive thy answer. But this word again seems to betray pride. For what is it to say, [[33:5|If thou canst|Si potes]], etc., but, I know that thou wilt not be able to answer and withstand me?

paras.t: Ecce, me sicut te fecit Deus: juxta illud Malachiæ, Numquid non Deus unus creavit nos? Etenim, quantum ad animam, immediate a Deo sumus creati. Substantia vero corporis, a Deo originaliter condita est, sed per causas secundas formatur et organizatur, atque a propriis parentibus propagatur. Sed opus naturæ est principaliter opus primæ causæ, etiam juxta philosophos. Et de eodem luto ego quoque formatus sum. Quamvis corpus humanum ex quatuor elementis mixtum dicatur, nihilo minus de limo terræ primus parens formatus describitur, quia in hominis corpore dominatur terra præ ceteris elementis. De eodem ergo luto in specie, non eodem in numero, Job Eliuque formati fuerunt: quoniam utriusque materia, ejusdem est rationis: et quantum ad primam hominis formationem, omnes de luto seu terræ limo formati asserimur, quia videlicet is ita formatus est, in quo omnes quodammodo eramus et continebamur, tanquam in originali quodam principio. Unde et omnes in ipso peccavimus, secundum Apostolum. Præterea, per lutum apte designatur materia corporis nostri propinqua, videlicet semen jam coagulatum in utero matris, atque per hoc luto assimilatum. Unde et supra Job ait ad Deum: Memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me. Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me, et sicut caseum me coagulasti? Hinc per Jeremiam Dominus loquitur: Sicut lutum in manu figuli, ita et vos in manu mea. Hæc Eliu introduxit, ut ex consideratione paris conditionis, Job sumat respondendi fiduciam, vel ne Job despiceret disputare cum Eliu, eo quod minor esset.
paras.en: [[33:6|Behold God hath made me as well as thee|Ecce, me sicut te fecit Deus]]: according to that of Malachias, [[Mal 2:10|hath not one God created us?|Numquid non Deus unus creavit nos?]] For as to the soul we are created by God immediately. The substance of the body was indeed made by God in the beginning, but it is formed and organized through second causes, and propagated by one's own parents. But the work of nature is chiefly the work of the first cause, even according to the philosophers. [[33:6|and of the same clay I also was formed|Et de eodem luto ego quoque formatus sum]]. Although the human body is said to be mixed of the four elements, nevertheless the first parent is described as formed of the slime of the earth[[Gen 2:7||]], because in man's body earth prevails over the other elements. Job and Eliu, then, were formed of the same clay in kind, not the same in number, since the matter of both is of the same nature; and as to the first forming of man, we are all said to be formed of clay, that is, of the slime of the earth [Denis uses *lutum*, “clay”, and *limus*, “slime”, as one], because he was so formed in whom we all in a manner were and were contained, as in an original principle. Hence too we all sinned in him, according to the Apostle[[Rom 5:12||]]. Moreover, by *clay* is fitly signified the proximate matter of our body, namely the seed already curdled in the mother's womb, and by this made like clay. Hence Job said above to God: [[Job 10:9|Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay|Memento, quæso, quod sicut lutum feceris me]]. [[Job 10:10|Hast thou not milked me as milk, and curdled me like cheese?|Nonne sicut lac mulsisti me, et sicut caseum me coagulasti?]] Hence the Lord speaks by Jeremias: [[Jer 18:6|as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand|Sicut lutum in manu figuli, ita et vos in manu mea]]. Eliu brought this in so that from the thought of their equal condition Job might take confidence to answer, or so that Job might not disdain to dispute with Eliu because he was younger.

paras.t: Verumtamen miraculum meum, id est sapientia mea mihi desuper mirabiliter data: in qua ita præfulgeo, quod quasi miraculum videatur quod ego qui juvenis sum, in tantum seniores in sapientia vinco, quum tamen de luto sim sicut et illi; non te terreat; et eloquentia mea non sit tibi gravis, id est, non erubescas, quod ego junior te, ita te in eloquentia supero. Aliquibus enim molestum est, quod alius eis invenitur perfectior. Communiter quoque minus periti, et minus facundi, terreri solent coram sapientiore et eloquentiore. Itaque consolatur et admonet sanctum Job, ne immoderanter gravetur audiendo suæ positionis reprobationem per verba et argumenta rhetorica. Siquidem tanto solet alicui alterius eloquentia esse molestior, quanto per illam sua assertio apparentius confutatur. Denique, secundum Gregorium, arrogantibus proprium est, ut antequam aliquid dicunt, mira se dicturos existiment, et locutionem suam mirando præveniant: quia [vel] in acutis sensibus ipsa elatio quanta fatuitas sit, ignorant. Hinc Paulus Hebræos sublimiter exhortatus, subjunxit: Rogo autem vos, fratres, ut sufferatis verbum solatii; etenim perpaucis scripsi vobis. Eliu autem quædam inania protulit, et quasi consolando subjungit: Miraculum meum non te terreat, et eloquentia mea non sit tibi gravis. Ille dicta sua, verbum solatii: hic vero eloquentiam et miraculum vocat.
paras.en: [[33:7|But yet let not my wonder|Verumtamen miraculum meum]], that is, my wisdom wondrously given me from above, in which I so shine forth that it seems a kind of wonder that I, who am young, so far surpass my elders in wisdom, though I am of clay as they are, [[33:7|terrify thee|non te terreat]]; [[33:7|and let not my eloquence be burdensome to thee|et eloquentia mea non sit tibi gravis]], that is, do not be ashamed that I, younger than thou, so surpass thee in eloquence. For to some it is irksome that another is found more perfect than they. Commonly too the less skilled and less fluent are wont to be daunted before one wiser and more eloquent. So he comforts and admonishes holy Job not to be burdened beyond measure at hearing his position refuted by rhetorical words and arguments. For another's eloquence is the more irksome to a man, the more plainly his own assertion is confuted by it. Lastly, according to Gregory, it is proper to the arrogant to think, before they say anything, that they are going to say wonderful things, and to forestall their own speech with wonder: for they do not know, even in keen minds, what folly pride itself is. Hence Paul, after exhorting the Hebrews in lofty terms, added: [[Heb 13:22|And I beseech you, brethren, that you suffer this word of consolation. For I have written to you in a few words|Rogo autem vos, fratres, ut sufferatis verbum solatii; etenim perpaucis scripsi vobis]]. But Eliu brought forth some empty things, and adds as if to console: [[33:7|let not my wonder terrify thee|Miraculum meum non te terreat]], [[33:7|and let not my eloquence be burdensome to thee|et eloquentia mea non sit tibi gravis]]. The one calls his sayings a word of consolation; this one calls his eloquence and a wonder.

paras.t: Dixisti ergo in auribus meis, et vocem verborum tuorum audivi. Dupliciter dicitur aliquid alteri dici in auribus ejus. Primo, quia occulte ei quid dicitur, ore loquentis applicato auribus audientis. Secundo, quia sic dicitur, quod verba pertingunt usque ad aures perceptionemque audientis: et ita intelligit Eliu. Mundus sum ego, et absque delicto: immaculatus, et non est iniquitas in me. Hoc formaliter Job non dixit; et quamvis quædam similia protulit, non tamen ad sensum quem Eliu inde elicit et intendit. Denique moris est quorumdam animo fervidorum, dum quid sibi displicens audiunt, illud repetendo exaggerare, aliisque verbis durius iterare. Passiones equidem ratione non refrenatæ, faciunt a medio virtutis ac veritatis recedere. Imponit autem Eliu ipsi Job, quod verba hæc dixerit, quia jam frequenter et diffuse suas recitavit justitias, atque justum se esse probavit, nec meruisse flagella sibi illata. Nam inter cetera affirmavit: Vestigia ejus, scilicet Dei, secutus est pes meus; viam ejus custodivi, et non declinavi ex ea. Itemque: Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum. Et rursus: Hæc passus sum absque iniquitate manus meæ, quum haberem mundas ad Deum preces.
paras.en: [[33:8|Now thou hast said in my hearing|Dixisti ergo in auribus meis]], [[33:8|and I have heard the voice of thy words|et vocem verborum tuorum audivi]]. A thing is said to be spoken to another *in his ears* [that is, in his hearing] in two ways. First, because it is told him secretly, the speaker's mouth put to the hearer's ears. Secondly, because it is so spoken that the words reach the ears and perception of the hearer: and so Eliu means it. [[33:9|I am clean, and without sin: I am unspotted, and there is no iniquity in me|Mundus sum ego, et absque delicto: immaculatus, et non est iniquitas in me]]. Job did not say this in so many words; and although he brought forth some like things, it was not in the sense that Eliu draws from them and intends. Moreover, it is the way of some hot-tempered men, when they hear something displeasing to them, to exaggerate it in repeating it and to restate it more harshly in other words. For passions not curbed by reason make men depart from the mean of virtue and of truth. Eliu charges Job with having said these words because he had already often and at length recounted his own just deeds, and maintained that he was just and had not deserved the scourges laid upon him. For among other things he affirmed: [[Job 23:11|My foot hath followed his steps|Vestigia ejus, scilicet Dei, secutus est pes meus]] (that is, God's steps); [[Job 23:11|I have kept his way, and have not declined from it|viam ejus custodivi, et non declinavi ex ea]]. And again: [[Job 31:23|I have always feared God as waves swelling over me|Semper quasi tumentes super me fluctus timui Deum]]. And once more: [[Job 16:18|These things have I suffered without the iniquity of my hand, when I offered pure prayers to God|Hæc passus sum absque iniquitate manus meæ, quum haberem mundas ad Deum preces]].

paras.t: Insuper, quamvis verba inducta soleant accipi pro eodem, tamen hic possunt distingui hoc modo: Mundus sum corde a cogitationibus et affectionibus inordinatis, et absque delicto, id est sine culpa omissionis, immaculatus corpore a vitiis carnis, et non est iniquitas commissionis ac operum seu injustitiæ contra Deum aut proximum, in me. Et hoc Eliu accepit, quasi Job dicere voluisset, quod nulli unquam peccato etiam veniali subjacuit, quum tamen Job hujus oppositum fassus sit, dicens: Peccavi: quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum? Et denuo: Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti, sed parce peccatis meis. Non itaque a venialibus prorsus asseruit se immunem.
paras.en: Further, although the words brought in are usually taken to mean the same, here they may be distinguished thus: [[33:9|I am clean|Mundus sum]] in heart from disordered thoughts and affections, [[33:9|and without sin|et absque delicto]], that is, without the fault of omission; [[33:9|I am unspotted|immaculatus]] in body from the vices of the flesh, [[33:9|and there is no iniquity|et non est iniquitas]] of commission, of deeds, or of injustice against God or neighbour, [[33:9|in me|in me]]. And Eliu took this as though Job had meant to say that he was never subject to any sin, even venial, whereas Job confessed the opposite, saying: [[Job 7:20|I have sinned: what shall I do to thee, O keeper of men?|Peccavi: quid faciam tibi, o custos hominum?]] And again: [[Job 14:16|Thou indeed hast numbered my steps, but spare my sins|Tu quidem gressus meos dinumerasti, sed parce peccatis meis]]. So he did not assert that he was wholly free from venial sins.

paras.t: Quia querelas in me reperit: id est, ita se circa me habuit, sicut qui de alio conqueritur, et ei mala imponit, quum ille sit innocens. Albertus autem exponit sic: Quia querelas, etc., id est, occasiones inveniendi querelas adversus me molitus est. Ideo arbitratus est me inimicum sibi. Hoc sumit ex eo quod Job supra dixit, alloquens atque interrogans Deum: Quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata? scelera mea et delicta ostende mihi. Cur faciem tuam abscondis, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum? Sed, ut ex dictis in expositione verborum istorum claruit, sanctus Job ad talem sensum non protulit verba hæc, ad qualem Eliu ea retorquet. Non enim Deus insidiatur homini tanquam malevolus, ut capiat vel circumveniat eum. Imo potius occasiones miserendi exquirit.
paras.en: [[33:10|Because he hath found complaints against me|Quia querelas in me reperit]]: that is, he has so dealt with me as one who complains of another and lays evils upon him, though the other is innocent. But Albert expounds it thus: [[33:10|Because he hath found complaints|Quia querelas]], etc., that is, he has contrived occasions of finding complaints against me. [[33:10|therefore he hath counted me for his enemy|Ideo arbitratus est me inimicum sibi]]. He takes this from what Job said above, addressing and questioning God: [[Job 13:23|How many are my iniquities and sins? make me know my crimes and offenses|Quantas habeo iniquitates et peccata? scelera mea et delicta ostende mihi]]. [[Job 13:24|Why hidest thou thy face, and thinkest me thy enemy?|Cur faciem tuam abscondis, et arbitraris me inimicum tuum?]] But, as was made clear from what was said in expounding those words, holy Job did not bring forth these words in such a sense as Eliu twists them to. For God does not lie in wait for man like one ill-disposed, to catch or ensnare him. Rather he seeks out occasions of showing mercy.

paras.t: Posuit in nervo pedes meos, ut me quasi captum teneret; et custodivit, id est, ad puniendum observavit, omnes semitas meas, ut occasiones contra me reperiret. Verba hæc jamdudum scripta atque exposita sunt, atque ex dictis ibidem patescit, quod secundum hunc intellectum beatus Job verba non protulit ista.
paras.en: [[33:11|He hath put my feet in the stocks|Posuit in nervo pedes meos]], to hold me as it were a captive; [[33:11|he hath observed|et custodivit]], that is, watched in order to punish, [[33:11|all my paths|omnes semitas meas]], to find occasions against me. These words were written and expounded long ago[[Job 13:27||]] [the margin's reference is unclear; the words are at Job 13:27], and it is plain from what was said there that blessed Job did not utter these words in this sense.

paras.t: Hoc est ergo in quo non es justificatus: id est, quamvis in nullo alio excessisses, quam in verbis his Deo sic derogantibus, clarum esset quod graviter offendisses: quod verum est, si Job tam male sensisset de Deo, aut sensum hunc prætendisset. Præterea, juxta Gregorium, mens arrogantium, dictorum suorum sensum non penetrat, quia interno gustu privatur, et in exteriores favores quos amat, relabitur. Vera autem scientia afficit, non extollit: et quos impleverit, non superbientes efficit, sed calentes.
paras.en: [[33:12|Now this is the thing in which thou art not justified|Hoc est ergo in quo non es justificatus]]: that is, though thou hadst gone too far in nothing else than in these words so detracting from God, it would be clear that thou hadst grievously offended: which is true, if Job had thought so ill of God, or had put forward this meaning. Moreover, according to Gregory, the mind of the arrogant does not penetrate the sense of its own sayings, because it is deprived of the inward taste, and slips back into the outward favours it loves. But true knowledge moves, it does not puff up: and those whom it has filled it makes not proud but fervent.

paras.t: Respondebo tibi, quia major sit Deus homine, id est sapientior, justior, perfectior. Hoc præmittit Eliu, ad innuendum quod Job non debuit conqueri de dispositione Dei circa se, nec asserere se injuste percussum, sed divinæ mentis judicium sensui suo præferre, tacere et contentari; item, ad insinuandum quod Job præsumptuose locutus sit, Disputare cum Deo cupio, quasi Deo esset tam par, quod idoneus esset disputare cum Deo; itemque, ad comprobandum quod Deus melius scit defectus et vitia hominis, quam ipsemet homo, et ideo homo se ipsum nimis justificare non debeat.
paras.en: [[33:12|I will answer thee, that God is greater than man|Respondebo tibi, quia major sit Deus homine]], that is, wiser, juster, more perfect. Eliu puts this first to hint that Job ought not to have complained of God's ordering of his affairs, nor asserted that he was struck unjustly, but should have preferred the judgment of the divine mind to his own sense, held his peace and been content; also, to suggest that Job spoke presumptuously in saying [[Job 13:3|I desire to reason with God|Disputare cum Deo cupio]], as though he were so much God's equal as to be fit to dispute with God; and also, to prove that God knows man's defects and vices better than man himself, and that therefore man ought not to justify himself overmuch.

paras.t: Adversus eum contendis, id est, Deo litigiose imponis, quod non ad omnia responderit tibi, id est, justitiis tuis non reddiderit vicem seu præmium singulatim; vel, Non ad omnia responderit tibi, id est, omnia dubia et quæsita quæ ei proposuisti de causis flagellationis tuæ atque similibus, tibi non solverit. Hoc ideo dicit, quia superius dixerat Job: Responde mihi, quantas habeo iniquitates, etc. Rursusque: Voca me, et ego respondebo tibi: aut certe loquar, et tu responde mihi.
paras.en: [[33:13|Dost thou strive against him|Adversus eum contendis]], that is, dost thou litigiously charge God [[33:13|because he hath not answered thee to all|quod non ad omnia responderit tibi]], that is, has not repaid thy just deeds one by one with their return or reward; or, [[33:13|hath not answered thee to all|Non ad omnia responderit tibi]], that is, has not resolved for thee all the doubts and questions which thou didst put to him about the causes of thy scourging and the like. He says this because Job had said above: [[Job 13:22|do thou answer me|Responde mihi]], [[Job 13:23|How many are my iniquities|quantas habeo iniquitates]], etc. And again: [[Job 13:22|Call me, and I will answer thee: or else I will speak, and do thou answer me|Voca me, et ego respondebo tibi: aut certe loquar, et tu responde mihi]].

paras.t: Consequenter innuit, cur Job ista dicere non debebat. Semel loquitur Deus, et secundo idipsum non repetit. Hoc tripliciter explanatur. Primo sic: Semel in Scripturis et verbis Sanctorum aperuit Deus modum sui regiminis, et cur hominem puniat seu flagellet: ideo secundo id non resumit, unicuique seorsum et singulariter respondendo ad singula, cur eum ita et ita in hoc et in hoc flagellaverit. Propterea tu, Job, irrationabiliter quæris tibi divinitus ad singula responderi. Hinc ait Gregorius: In Scripturis nobis in eo quod specialiter patimur, omnibus communiter respondetur: ibi vita præcedentium fit forma sequentium. Sic exponit Gregorius.
paras.en: Next he hints why Job ought not to have said these things. [[33:14|God speaketh once|Semel loquitur Deus]], [[33:14|and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time|et secundo idipsum non repetit]]. This is explained in three ways. First thus: Once, in the Scriptures and the words of the Saints, God has made known the manner of his government, and why he punishes or scourges man; therefore he does not take it up a second time, answering each man separately and singly on each point, why he has scourged him in this way and that, in this thing and that. Therefore thou, Job, unreasonably askest that God should answer thee on each point. Hence Gregory says: In the Scriptures, in what we each suffer in particular, an answer is given to us all in common: there the life of those who went before becomes the pattern of those who follow. So Gregory expounds it.

paras.t: Thomas exponit sic: Semel loquitur Deus, id est sua locutione causali ad extra, qua omnia facit, juxta illud, Ipse dixit et facta sunt. Semel animabus rationalibus impressit naturale lumen rationis, per quod inter verum et falsum, bonum et malum discernere, veritatem quoque et causam suorum eventuum inquirere, invenire, seu discere queunt. Ideo opus non est, ut Deus singulis seorsum respondeat. Hoc autem lumen naturale Deus non repetit, quoniam semel inditum animæ, in ea jugiter manet. Estque quasi quædam impressio lucis divinæ in anima: per quod videri potest, quid agendum, omittendum, quid bonum, quid malum. Hinc quum in Psalmo dixisset Psalmista, Multi dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona? statim addit, Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine, etc. Porro Albertus exponit sic: Semel loquitur Deus, id est, uno modo admonet in communi flagellando; et secundo id ipsum non repetit, ut scilicet per singula peccata admoneat eum.
paras.en: Thomas expounds it thus: [[33:14|God speaketh once|Semel loquitur Deus]], that is, by his causal speech outward, by which he makes all things, according to that saying, [[Ps 148:5|he spoke, and they were made|Ipse dixit et facta sunt]]. Once he imprinted on rational souls the natural light of reason, by which they can discern between true and false, good and evil, and also seek, find or learn the truth and the cause of what befalls them. So there is no need for God to answer each one separately. And this natural light God does not repeat, since once put into the soul it abides in it continually. And it is as it were an imprint of the divine light in the soul, by which it can be seen what is to be done and left undone, what is good and what evil. Hence, when the Psalmist had said in the Psalm, [[Ps 4:6|many say, Who sheweth us good things?|Multi dicunt, Quis ostendit nobis bona?]] he at once adds, [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]], etc. Again, Albert expounds it thus: [[33:14|God speaketh once|Semel loquitur Deus]], that is, he admonishes in one way, in common, by scourging; [[33:14|and repeateth not the selfsame thing the second time|et secundo id ipsum non repetit]], that is, so as to admonish him for each sin singly.

paras.t: Per somnium in visione nocturna, quando irruit sopor super homines, et dormiunt in lectulo; tunc aperit aures virorum, et erudiens eos instruit disciplina. Verbum hoc concordat et correspondet ei quod supra Eliphaz ait: In horrore visionis nocturnæ, quando solet sopor occupare homines, pavor tenuit me et tremor, et omnia ossa mea perterrita sunt. Stetit quidam, cujus non agnoscebam vultum, imago coram oculis meis, et vocem quasi auræ lenis audivi, etc. Unde multa quæ circa hujus loci explanationem possent induci, illo in loco inducta sunt et requirenda ibidem, ne sine necessitate multiplicatio fiat verborum.
paras.en: [[33:15|By a dream in a vision by night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, and they are sleeping in their beds|Per somnium in visione nocturna, quando irruit sopor super homines, et dormiunt in lectulo]]; [[33:16|Then he openeth the ears of men, and teaching instructeth them in what they are to learn|tunc aperit aures virorum, et erudiens eos instruit disciplina]]. This word agrees and corresponds with what Eliphaz said above: [[Job 4:13|In the horror of a vision by night, when deep sleep is wont to hold men|In horrore visionis nocturnæ, quando solet sopor occupare homines]], [[Job 4:14|Fear seized upon me, and trembling, and all my bones were affrighted|pavor tenuit me et tremor, et omnia ossa mea perterrita sunt]]. [[Job 4:16|There stood one whose countenance I knew not, an image before my eyes, and I heard the voice, as it were, of a gentle wind|Stetit quidam, cujus non agnoscebam vultum, imago coram oculis meis, et vocem quasi auræ lenis audivi]], etc. So the many things that could be brought in for the explanation of this place were brought in at that place and are to be sought there, lest words be multiplied without need.

paras.t: Nempe (ut ibi patuit) in somno exterioribus sensibus ab occupatione, tumultu et strepitu operationum suarum cessantibus, anima ad susceptionem revelationum aptatur; estque capacior infusionis specierum occulta signantium atque cœlestium impressionum, quo minus circa alia occupatur sive distrahitur. Ideo Eliu asserit, quod per somnium, id est tempore somni, in visione imaginaria seu intellectuali, seu ex utraque commixta, nocturna, id est, quæ fit in nocte, sopore seu gravi somno in homines irruente; tunc Deus per se, vel ministerium angelorum, aperit interiores aures virorum, videlicet imaginativam et intellectivam, quibus interiora verba percipiuntur, proferuntur, noscuntur, sicut in libro de Trinitate Augustinus deducit: virorum (inquam) virtute virentium, scilicet virtuosorum, quamvis interdum ex speciali dispensatione et ratione seu consilio Dei etiam vitiosis id fiat, ut patet in Balaam: quem S. Hieronymus et alii multi putant fuisse hunc Eliu. Et erudiens eos instructione interna, instruit eos disciplina, id est cognitione seu eruditione agendorum, videlicet pertinente ad mores: imo etiam frequenter cognitione speculativa et notitia futurorum penitus contingentium. Hic tamen potissime loquitur de instructione morali. Nam subditur:
paras.en: For (as was shown there) in sleep, when the outward senses cease from the business, tumult and din of their workings, the soul is fitted to receive revelations; and it is the more open to the infusion of images that signify hidden things, and of heavenly impressions, the less it is busied or distracted about other things. Therefore Eliu asserts that [[33:15|by a dream|per somnium]], that is, in the time of sleep, [[33:15|in a vision|in visione]] imaginary or intellectual, or mixed of both, [[33:15|by night|nocturna]], that is, one that comes in the night, when slumber or heavy sleep falls upon men, then God, by himself or through the ministry of angels, [[33:16|openeth|aperit]] the inner [[33:16|ears of men|aures virorum]], namely the imaginative and the intellective, by which inward words are perceived, uttered and known, as Augustine sets out in the book On the Trinity: of men (I say) flourishing in virtue, that is, of virtuous men [the Latin plays on *viri*, “men”, *virtus*, “virtue”, and *virere*, “to flourish”]; although sometimes by a special dispensation and reason or counsel of God it happens to the wicked too, as is plain in Balaam[[Num 22:5||]] [the margin note here is unreadable; Balaam's story is told in Num 22–24], whom St Jerome and many others think to have been this Eliu. [[33:16|and teaching|Et erudiens eos]] them by inward instruction, [[33:16|instructeth them in what they are to learn|instruit eos disciplina]], that is, in the knowledge or teaching of what is to be done, namely what pertains to morals; nay, often also in speculative knowledge and the knowledge of future things that are wholly contingent. Here, however, he speaks chiefly of moral instruction. For there follows:

paras.t: Ut avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit, id est peccatis commissis, et liberet eum de superbia, id est, ad humilitatem perducat, ad quam homo tanto perfectius profundiusque perducitur, quanto desuper clarius illustratur. Specialiter quoque, postquam communiter dixit, Avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit, expressit superbiam: primo, quia superbia omnium origo, caput atque regina est vitiorum; secundo, ut insinuaret ipsum Job potissime excæcatum, quod scilicet nimis justus et sapiens esset in oculis suis, ideoque putaret se absque suis percussum demeritis, nec acquiesceret rationibus oppositum hujus probantibus.
paras.en: [[33:17|That he may withdraw a man from the things he is doing|Ut avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit]] [Denis reads *fecit*, "he has done", where the Vulgate has *facit*, "he is doing"], that is, from the sins he has committed, [[33:17|and may deliver him from pride|et liberet eum de superbia]], that is, may bring him to humility, to which a man is brought the more perfectly and the more deeply, the more clearly he is enlightened from above. And after speaking in general terms, [[33:17|withdraw a man from the things he is doing|Avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit]], he named pride in particular: first, because pride is the origin, the head and the queen of all vices[[Ecclus 10:15||]]; secondly, to hint that Job himself was chiefly blinded by it, in that he was too just and wise in his own eyes, and therefore thought he had been struck without any deserving of his own, and would not yield to the reasons that proved the contrary.

paras.t: Eruens animam ejus de corruptione, id est læsione et languore peccati, quod vulnus est animi. Unde et in Sapientiæ libro habetur: Incorruptio facit esse proximum Deo. De peccatoribus quoque ait Psalmista: Corrupti sunt, et abominabiles facti sunt in iniquitatibus. Et vitam illius corporalem ac temporalem liberans a pœnis præsentibus, ut non transeat in gladium, id est in occisionem; vel, Vitam animæ ejus, ne transeat in gladium, id est, ne incidat in divini judicii districtionem, pœnam ac damnationem. Unde superius ait Job: Ultor iniquitatum gladius est.
paras.en: [[33:18|Rescuing his soul from corruption|Eruens animam ejus de corruptione]], that is, from the hurt and sickness of sin, which is a wound of the soul. Hence in the book of Wisdom too we read: [[Wis 6:20|incorruption bringeth near to God|Incorruptio facit esse proximum Deo]]. And of sinners the Psalmist says: [[Ps 52:2|They are corrupted, and become abominable in iniquities|Corrupti sunt, et abominabiles facti sunt in iniquitatibus]]. Delivering also [[33:18|his life|vitam illius]], his bodily and temporal life, from present punishments, [[33:18|from passing to the sword|ut non transeat in gladium]], that is, to being slain; or, the life of his soul, lest it pass to the sword, that is, lest it fall into the strictness of the divine judgement, into punishment and damnation. Hence Job said above: [[Job 19:29|the sword is the revenger of iniquities|Ultor iniquitatum gladius est]].

paras.t: Porro, secundum Albertum, ad hanc eruditionem supernam reducitur omnis instructio quæ fit per vehementem a sensibilibus abstractionem homini per oraculum vel per visionem revelationis, sive fiat per signa cœli, sive per angelos, sive per inspirationem immediatam a Deo: et vix est homo qui non aliquo horum modorum admoneatur de futuris, ut dicit Tullius in libro de Divinatione et natura deorum. Ideo quoque Eliu ait, Ut avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit, quia peccatoribus terribilia somnia solent occurrere. Alluditque ei quod supra dixit Job Deo: Terrebis me per somnia. Per quod ipse Eliu pungit Job: quasi dicat, Ideo terruit te per somnia, ut recederes a tua malitia. Item hoc ait, ut innuat quod Deus per somnium ei satis respondit, immittendo ei visiones horribiles.
paras.en: Further, according to Albert, to this heavenly teaching is reduced all the instruction that is given to a man, through a strong withdrawal from the things of sense, by an oracle or by a vision of revelation, whether it come through signs in the heavens, or through angels, or through inspiration immediately from God; and there is scarcely a man who is not warned of things to come in one of these ways, as Tully says in the book On Divination and the Nature of the Gods [Cicero's *De divinatione* and *De natura deorum* are two separate works]. And so Eliu says, [[33:17|That he may withdraw a man from the things he is doing|Ut avertat hominem ab his quæ fecit]], because terrible dreams are wont to come to sinners. And he alludes to what Job said to God above: [[Job 7:14|Thou wilt frighten me with dreams|Terrebis me per somnia]]. By this Eliu stings Job, as if to say: This is why he frightened thee with dreams, that thou mightest turn back from thy malice. He also says it to hint that God had answered him well enough by a dream, by sending him horrible visions.

paras.t: Circa præhabita scribit multa pulchra Gregorius. Nam super illud, Per somnium, etc., ait: Quid est quod per somnium locutio nobis divinitatis innotescit, nisi quod Dei secreta non cognoscimus, si in terrenis desideriis vigilemus? Si ergo interna contemplari volumus, ab implicatione externa dormiamus. Vox Dei quasi per somnium auditur, quando tranquilla mente ab hujus sæculi actione quiescitur, et ipso mentis silentio divina præcepta pensantur.
paras.en: On what has gone before, Gregory writes many fine things. On the words [[33:15|By a dream|Per somnium]], etc., he says: What does it mean that the speech of the Godhead becomes known to us by a dream, but that we do not come to know the secrets of God if we keep awake in earthly desires? If then we wish to contemplate the things within, let us sleep to entanglement in the things without. The voice of God is heard as if in a dream when, with a tranquil mind, one rests from the business of this world, and in the very silence of the mind the divine precepts are weighed.

paras.t: Denique, super illud, Erudiens eos instruit disciplina, testatur: Consideranti et sese per pœnitentiam laceranti, quasi quædam plagæ percussionis sunt lamenta compunctionis. Hinc Salomon loquitur: Livor vulneris absterget mala, et plagæ in secretioribus ventris. Per livorem quippe vulneris, disciplinam insinuat corporeæ percussionis; plagæ vero in secretioribus ventris, sunt interna mentis vulnera, quæ per compunctionem fiunt. Quæ duo inter se differunt, quoniam plagæ percussionum dolent, lamenta compunctionum sapiunt; illæ affligentes cruciant, ista reficiunt dum affligunt; per illas in afflictione mœror est, per hæc in mœrore lætitia.
paras.en: Then, on the words [[33:16|teaching instructeth them in what they are to learn|Erudiens eos instruit disciplina]] [*disciplina*, "instruction", also means "chastisement", and Gregory takes it so], he declares: To one who considers himself and tears himself by penance, the laments of compunction are like stripes of a scourging. Hence Solomon says: [[Prov 20:30|The blueness of a wound shall wipe away evils: and stripes in the more inward parts of the belly|Livor vulneris absterget mala, et plagæ in secretioribus ventris]]. By the blueness of the wound he signifies the chastisement of bodily scourging; but the stripes in the more inward parts of the belly are the inward wounds of the mind, which are made by compunction. These two differ from each other, for the stripes of scourging give pain, the laments of compunction give savour; the former torment as they afflict, the latter refresh even while they afflict; through the former there is sorrow in affliction, through the latter joy in sorrow.

paras.t: Quatuor quippe sunt qualitates, quibus viri justi anima in compunctione vehementer afficitur: prima, dum malorum seu vitiorum suorum reminiscitur, considerans ubi fuit; secunda, dum judiciorum Dei sententiam metuens, et secum quærens, cogitat ubi erit; tertia, dum mala vitæ præsentis solerter attendens, metuens, considerat ubi est; quarta, dum bona supernæ patriæ contemplatur: quæ quia necdum adipiscitur, lugens conspicit ubi non est. Insuper, præsentis vitæ mala sicut sunt, conspicere nequit: quia bona æternæ patriæ per contemplationis gustum non attigit. Unde aliquando mens devota ad quamdam inusitatam dulcedinem interni saporis admittitur, et raptim aliquo modo ardenti spiritu afflata, renovatur: tantoque magis inhiat, quanto magis quod amet, degustat; atque ad hoc intrare appetit, quod sibi dulciter sapere intrinsecus sentit: quia videlicet hujus dulcedinis amore sibi coram se viluit, et postquam hanc utcumque percipere potuit, quid sine illa dudum fuerat, invenit. Cui inhærere conatur, sed ab ejus fortitudine, sua adhuc infirmitate repellitur; nec potest mentis oculum in id, quod intra se raptim conspexerat, figere, quia ipso vetustatis suæ usu deorsum compellitur ire. Inter hæc anhelat, æstuat, super se ire conatur; sed ad familiares tenebras suas, victa fatigatione, relabitur.
paras.en: For there are four states by which the soul of a just man is strongly moved in compunction: the first, when it remembers its evils or vices, considering where it has been; the second, when, fearing the sentence of God's judgements and searching within itself, it thinks where it will be; the third, when, carefully weighing the evils of the present life and fearing them, it considers where it is; the fourth, when it contemplates the good things of the heavenly fatherland, and because it does not yet obtain them, it beholds with grief where it is not. Moreover, the mind cannot see the evils of the present life as they are, because it has not reached the good things of the eternal fatherland through the taste of contemplation. Hence the devout mind is sometimes admitted to a certain unwonted sweetness of inward savour, and, breathed upon in some manner suddenly by the ardent Spirit, it is renewed; and it longs the more, the more it tastes what it may love; and it desires to enter into that which it feels to be sweet to it within: because, through love of this sweetness, it has grown worthless in its own sight, and after it has been able in some way to perceive this sweetness, it finds out what it had long been without it. It strives to cling to it, but is driven back from its strength by its own weakness still; nor can it fix the eye of the mind on what it had suddenly glimpsed within itself, because by the very habit of its old state it is forced to go downwards. Amid all this it pants, it burns, it strives to rise above itself; but, overcome by weariness, it falls back into its own familiar darkness.

paras.t: Consequenter ponitur tertius modus locutionis seu responsionis divinæ. Increpat quoque Deus peccatorem, per dolorem, id est infirmitatem, in lectulo, quo jacet ægrotus, et omnia ossa ejus marcescere facit: id est, tam graviter eum affligit interdum, ut robur corporis attenuetur, caro consumatur, ossa siccentur.
paras.en: Next is set down the third manner of God's speaking or answering. [[33:19|He rebuketh also|Increpat quoque]], God rebukes the sinner, [[33:19|by sorrow|per dolorem]], that is, by sickness, [[33:19|in the bed|in lectulo]] in which he lies sick, [[33:19|and he maketh all his bones to wither|et omnia ossa ejus marcescere facit]]: that is, he sometimes afflicts him so heavily that the strength of the body is worn down, the flesh is consumed, the bones are dried up.

paras.t: Asserit autem Albertus, quod verba Eliu non sunt nisi determinationes et expressiones clariores verborum trium amicorum: et primo exprimit verba Eliphaz. Ideo contra Job loquens, incipit sicut Eliphaz incepit supra, dicens: In horrore visionis nocturnæ. Similiter, quod nunc Eliu ait, Increpat quoque, etc., superius ita locutus est Eliphaz: Increpationem Domini ne reprobes, quia ipse vulnerat et medetur, etc.
paras.en: Albert asserts, moreover, that the words of Eliu are nothing but determinations and clearer expressions of the words of the three friends; and first he expresses the words of Eliphaz. So, speaking against Job, he begins as Eliphaz began above, saying: [[Job 4:13|In the horror of a vision by night|In horrore visionis nocturnæ]]. Likewise, where Eliu now says, [[33:19|He rebuketh also|Increpat quoque]], etc., Eliphaz spoke thus above: [[Job 5:17|refuse not, therefore, the chastising of the Lord|Increpationem Domini ne reprobes]], [[Job 5:18|For he woundeth, and cureth|quia ipse vulnerat et medetur]], etc.

paras.t: Abominabilis ei fit in vita sua panis: id est, præ magnitudine infirmitatis, cibaria vertuntur ei in nauseam; et animæ illius cibus ante desiderabilis: id est, durante languore, anima ægri cibos detestatur, quos tempore sanitatis dulces et concupiscibiles reputavit. Infirmitas namque per adustam choleram inficit gustum, seu palatum et linguam. Ideo infirmis omnia videntur amara, turbaturque appetitus et cadit.
paras.en: [[33:20|Bread becometh abominable to him in his life|Abominabilis ei fit in vita sua panis]]: that is, because of the greatness of his sickness, food turns to loathing in him; [[33:20|and to his soul the meat which before he desired|et animæ illius cibus ante desiderabilis]]: that is, while the sickness lasts, the sick man's soul loathes the foods which in time of health he held sweet and desirable. For sickness, through burnt choler [that is, bile overheated, in the medicine of the day], infects the taste, that is, the palate and the tongue. That is why everything seems bitter to the sick, and the appetite is upset and fails.

paras.t: Tabescet caro ejus, id est, in tabem putredinemque vertetur, durante languore; et ossa quæ tecta fuerant pelle et carnibus, nudabuntur eisdem in toto aut parte, ita quod sola pelle apparebunt operta, carne consumpta.
paras.en: [[33:21|His flesh shall be consumed away|Tabescet caro ejus]], that is, shall turn to wasting and rottenness while the sickness lasts; [[33:21|and his bones that were covered|et ossa quæ tecta fuerant]] with skin and flesh [[33:21|shall be made bare|nudabuntur]] of them, wholly or in part, so that they will appear covered with skin alone, the flesh being consumed.

paras.t: Appropinquabit corruptioni, id est morti, anima, id est vita sensitiva animalis, illius peccatoris, divinitus ita plagati. Sic anima sumitur in Genesi, dum Ruben fratribus suis ait de Joseph: Non interficiamus animam ejus. Et in Jeremia Johanan loquitur Godoliæ de Ismaele: Ne veniat et interficiat animam tuam. Et vita illius præfata, appropinquabit mortiferis, id est signis et causis mortis.
paras.en: [[33:22|His soul|anima]], that is, the sensitive, animal life of that sinner so stricken by God, [[33:22|hath drawn near to corruption|Appropinquabit corruptioni]], that is, to death. *Soul* is taken in this way in Genesis, when Ruben says to his brothers about Joseph: [[Gen 37:22|Do not take away his life|Non interficiamus animam ejus]] [the Latin has *animam*, "his soul"]; and in Jeremias, where Johanan says to Godolias about Ismahel: [[Jer 40:15|lest he kill thee|Ne veniat et interficiat animam tuam]] [Latin *animam tuam*, "thy soul"; Denis's words are "lest he come and kill thee"]. And [[33:22|his life|vita illius]], the life just spoken of, shall draw near [[33:22|to the destroyers|mortiferis]] [*mortiferis*, "deadly things"], that is, to the signs and causes of death.

paras.t: Si fuerit pro eo angelus loquens unum de similibus his quæ dicta sunt, id est, quod æger per somnii terrorem vel inspirationem, aut infirmitatem correptus, instructus et emendatus sit. Aliqui legunt, Si fuerit pro eo angelus loquens, unus de millibus, id est unus de numero millium angelorum: secundum illud Danielis, Millia millium ministrabant ei. Ut annuntiet hominis æquitatem, id est, Deo præsentet et offerat justitiam ægri et peccatoris, ad quam per pœnitentiam conversus, et per aliquod prædictorum adductus est, ita quod inspirationi divinæ acquievit, vel vexatione intellectum accepit.
paras.en: [[33:23|If there shall be an angel speaking for him|Si fuerit pro eo angelus loquens]] one thing like those that have been said [Denis's text reads *unum de similibus his*, "one of things like these", for the Vulgate's *unus de millibus*, "one among thousands"], that is, that the sick man, chastened by the terror of a dream, or by inspiration, or by sickness, has been instructed and amended. Some read: [[33:23|If there shall be an angel speaking for him, one among thousands|Si fuerit pro eo angelus loquens, unus de millibus]], that is, one of the number of the thousands of angels, according to that saying of Daniel: [[Dan 7:10|thousands of thousands ministered to him|Millia millium ministrabant ei]]. He speaks [[33:23|to declare man's uprightness|Ut annuntiet hominis æquitatem]], that is, to present and offer to God the justice of the sick man and sinner, to which he has turned by penance, and to which he has been brought by one of the things spoken of, so that he has yielded to the divine inspiration, or has received understanding through vexation.

paras.t: Miserebitur ejus Deus, qui non continet in ira sua misericordias suas, et post tempestatem tranquillitatem largitur; et dicet angelo: Libera eum ab infirmitate, ut non descendat in corruptionem, id est, ne moriatur. Inveni in quo ei propitier: id est, quia mihi obtulisti æquitatem pœnitentiæ ejus, et quod corporaliter tam dure afflictus est, idque æquanimiter tulit; hinc habeo rationem propitiandi ei etiam in corporis curatione. In quo pietas Dei ostenditur, qui tam pronus est indulgere ac subvenire, et quasi occasionem quærit ad propitiandum.
