paras.en: [[33:24|He shall have mercy on him|Miserebitur ejus]], that is, God, who does not shut up his mercies in his anger[[Ps 76:10||]], and after the storm grants a calm[[Tob 3:22||]] [the margin's reference here is illegible in the scan; the words recall Tob 3:22 and Ps 76:10]; [[33:24|and shall say|et dicet]] to the angel: [[33:24|Deliver him|Libera eum]] from sickness, [[33:24|that he may not go down to corruption|ut non descendat in corruptionem]], that is, that he may not die. [[33:24|I have found wherein I may be merciful to him|Inveni in quo ei propitier]]: that is, since thou hast offered me the uprightness of his penance, and since he has been so hard afflicted in body and has borne it with an even mind, I have from this a reason to be merciful to him in healing his body as well. In this is shown the loving-kindness of God, who is so ready to forgive and to help, and as it were seeks an occasion to be merciful.

paras.t: Consumpta est caro ejus a suppliciis pro suis peccatis sibi inflictis; revertatur ad dies adolescentiæ suæ, id est ad talem dispositionem in sanitate ac prosperitate, in quali fuit tempore adolescentiæ suæ, prout quarto Regum legitur caro Naaman restituta sicut caro pueri parvuli.
paras.en: [[33:25|His flesh is consumed with punishments|Consumpta est caro ejus a suppliciis]] inflicted on him for his sins; [[33:25|let him return to the days of his youth|revertatur ad dies adolescentiæ suæ]], that is, to such a state of health and prosperity as he was in at the time of his youth, as we read in the fourth book of Kings of Naaman, that [[4 Kings 5:14|his flesh was restored, like the flesh of a little child|caro Naaman restituta sicut caro pueri parvuli]].

paras.t: Deprecabitur Deum æger sic castigatus, et placabilis ei erit, mentem ejus virtutibus decorando, et corpus sanando, vel in sanitate conservando. Et videbit faciem ejus, id est piam et gratiosam præsentiam ejus, seu ipsum præsentem per fidem et divinæ virtutis effectum, in jubilo, id est in excessivo et maximo gaudio. In patria autem videbit faciem Dei clare per speciem in jubilo consummato. Et reddet homini justitiam suam, id est secundum justitiam suam seu juxta actus et merita suæ justitiæ: quia propter pœnitentiam suam sanat eum in corpore, justificatque in mente. Juxta hunc modum loquendi sæpe ait Dominus in Prophetis: Reddam vobis iniquitates vestras in caput vestrum; vel simile aliquid. Vel, Reddet homini justitiam suam, id est, virtutes et gratiam, quas peccando perdidit homo, Deus per pœnitentiam illius restituet illi. Virtus autem et justitia nostra, est Dei, ut dantis, et nostra, ut recipientis.
paras.en: [[33:26|He shall pray to God|Deprecabitur Deum]], the sick man thus chastised, [[33:26|and he will be gracious to him|et placabilis ei erit]], adorning his mind with virtues and healing his body, or keeping it in health; [[33:26|and he shall see his face|Et videbit faciem ejus]], that is, his loving and gracious presence, or God himself present through faith and through the working of the divine power, [[33:26|with joy|in jubilo]], that is, in surpassing and very great gladness. But in the fatherland he will see the face of God clearly, by sight, in joy made perfect. And [[33:26|he will render to man his justice|reddet homini justitiam suam]], that is, according to his justice, or according to the acts and merits of his justice: since because of his penance God heals him in body and justifies him in mind. In this manner of speaking the Lord often says in the Prophets: I will render your iniquities upon your own head[[Joel 3:4||]] [most of the margin's references here are illegible in the scan; one reads Joel iii; compare Joel 3:4 and 3:7, Ezech 9:10 and 22:31], or something like it. Or, [[33:26|he will render to man his justice|Reddet homini justitiam suam]], that is, the virtues and grace which man lost by sinning, God will give back to him through his penance. Now our virtue and justice is God's, as the giver's, and ours, as the receiver's.

paras.t: Respiciet homines, id est, recognoscet ac intuebitur eos lætus, de sua sanatione exsultans; et dicet: Peccavi, et vere deliqui: id est, peccata sua, tam commissionis quam omissionis, humiliter confitebitur, seque pro eis percussum testabitur. Hoc etenim facit, quia jam Deus cor ejus illuminat, ideo se ipsum humiliat et accusat. Et ut eram dignus, non recepi, id est, citra condignum castigatus sum, et misericorditer actum est mihi: quia æterna, quam merui, pœna mihi in temporalem, parvam et brevem commutata est pœnam: ideo gratias ago.
paras.en: [[33:27|He shall look upon men|Respiciet homines]], that is, he will know them again and look on them gladly, rejoicing at his healing; [[33:27|and shall say|et dicet]]: [[33:27|I have sinned, and indeed I have offended|Peccavi, et vere deliqui]]: that is, he will humbly confess his sins, of commission as well as of omission, and will bear witness that he was struck for them. He does this because God now enlightens his heart; therefore he humbles and accuses himself. And [[33:27|I have not received what I have deserved|ut eram dignus, non recepi]], that is, I have been chastised less than I deserved, and I have been dealt with mercifully: for the eternal punishment I deserved has been changed for me into a temporal one, small and short: therefore I give thanks.

paras.t: Verba ista notanda et imitanda sunt nobis indesinenter, ut in adversis non murmuremus; sed quæ, quanta et qualia commiserimus peccata pensantes, nunquam putemus nos in vita hac condigne puniri: imo omne quod patimur, patientissime toleremus, velutque nihilum ponderemus respectu vitiorum nostrorum, atque intuitu infernalium quæ meruimus tormentorum, implentes illud Judith: Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur; sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini (quasi servi qui corripimur) ad emendationem, et non ad perditionem nostram, evenisse credamus. Hinc superius dictum est: Multo minora exigeris, quam meretur iniquitas tua.
paras.en: These words are to be marked and followed by us without ceasing, so that in adversity we do not murmur; but weighing what sins, how great and of what kind, we have committed, let us never think ourselves punished in this life as we deserve: rather, let us bear most patiently all that we suffer, and count it as nothing in comparison with our vices, and in view of the torments of hell which we have deserved, fulfilling that saying of Judith: [[Jdt 8:26|let us not revenge ourselves for these things which we suffer|Non ulciscamur nos pro his quæ patimur]]. [[Jdt 8:27|But esteeming these very punishments to be less than our sins deserve, let us believe that these scourges of the Lord, with which like servants we are chastised, have happened for our amendment, and not for our destruction|sed reputantes peccatis nostris hæc ipsa supplicia minora esse, flagella Domini (quasi servi qui corripimur) ad emendationem, et non ad perditionem nostram, evenisse credamus]]. Hence it was said above: [[Job 11:6|he exacteth much less of thee, than thy iniquity deserveth|Multo minora exigeris, quam meretur iniquitas tua]].

paras.t: Liberavit enim animam suam, id est, Deus animam rei percussi flagellando et gratiam infundendo a morte peccati salvavit. Vel ipsemet reus, per pœnitentiam liberavit animam per modum causæ meritoriæ, sicut Ezechieli Dominus loquitur: Tu animam tuam liberasti. Ne pergeret in interitum, id est, ne in æternum periret: quemadmodum pater erudit et flagellat filium suum, ne a judice condemnetur; sed vivens lucem videret, id est, vivendo per gratiam ad lumen gloriæ perducatur, et Deum qui vera lux est intueatur; vivens quoque in sæculo isto vita naturæ, videret lumen solare et prospera hujus vitæ, juxta illud in Ecclesiaste: Dulce lumen, et delectabile oculis videre solem.
paras.en: [[33:28|He hath delivered his soul|Liberavit enim animam suam]], that is, God, by scourging the guilty man he struck and by pouring in grace, has saved his soul from the death of sin. Or the guilty man himself, by penance, has delivered his soul as a meritorious cause, as the Lord says to Ezechiel: [[Ezech 3:19|thou hast delivered thy soul|Tu animam tuam liberasti]][[Ezech 3:21||]][[Ezech 33:9||]]. He delivered it [[33:28|from going into destruction|Ne pergeret in interitum]], that is, lest he perish for ever: just as a father teaches and beats his son so that he may not be condemned by the judge; [[33:28|that it may live and see the light|sed vivens lucem videret]], that is, that living by grace he may be brought to the light of glory, and may behold God, who is the true light; and also that, living in this world the life of nature, he may see the light of the sun and the good things of this life, according to that saying in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 11:7|The light is sweet, and it is delightful for the eyes to see the sun|Dulce lumen, et delectabile oculis videre solem]].

paras.t: Ecce hæc omnia, id est præscriptas jam admonitiones et correptiones per visionem nocturnam et infirmitatis immissionem, per angelicam subventionem et illuminationem secretam, ut homo redeat a peccatis ad gratiam, operatur Deus tribus vicibus per singulos. Verbum hoc intricatum est satis, multisque fuit erroris occasio, ita ut dicerent hominem non posse pœnitere post tertiam recidivationem: cujus erroris assertor (ut Lyra hic recitat) fuit et quidam Rabbi Salomon, excæcatorum Judæorum excæcatus magister. Novatus quoque hæreticus, Romanæ Ecclesiæ olim diaconus, dixit sacramentum Pœnitentiæ iterari non posse, allegans illud Apostoli ad Hebræos: Impossibile est eos qui semel sunt illuminati, et gustaverunt donum cæleste, et prolapsi sunt, renovari rursus ad pœnitentiam; et quod primo Regum habetur: Si peccaverit vir in virum, placari ei potest Deus; si autem in Deum peccaverit, quis orabit pro eo? Istam difficultatem Thomas in Summa contra gentiles rite determinat. Apostolus enim de renovatione ad pœnitentiam per sacramentum Baptismi, quod non iteratur, locutus est loco præfato, quamvis verba ejus aliis modis possint exponi. In verbis quoque libri Regum inductis, non impossibilitas absoluta, sed difficultas magna exprimitur.
paras.en: [[33:29|Behold, all these things|Ecce hæc omnia]], that is, the warnings and chastisements described above, by a vision in the night and the sending of sickness, by the help of an angel and secret enlightenment, so that man may come back from sin to grace, [[33:29|God worketh three times within every one|operatur Deus tribus vicibus per singulos]]. This saying is intricate enough, and has been an occasion of error for many, so that some said a man cannot repent after the third relapse: an error asserted (as Lyra relates here) by a certain Rabbi Salomon too, the blinded teacher of the blinded Jews. Novatus the heretic also, once a deacon of the Roman Church, said that the sacrament of Penance cannot be repeated, alleging that saying of the Apostle to the Hebrews: [[Heb 6:4|For it is impossible for those who were once illuminated, have tasted also the heavenly gift|Impossibile est eos qui semel sunt illuminati, et gustaverunt donum cæleste]], [[Heb 6:6|And are fallen away: to be renewed again to penance|et prolapsi sunt, renovari rursus ad pœnitentiam]]; and what we have in the first book of Kings: [[1 Kings 2:25|If one man shall sin against another, God may be appeased in his behalf: but if a man shall sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?|Si peccaverit vir in virum, placari ei potest Deus; si autem in Deum peccaverit, quis orabit pro eo?]] Thomas settles this difficulty rightly in the Summa against the Gentiles. For the Apostle, in the place cited, spoke of renewal to penance through the sacrament of Baptism, which is not repeated, though his words can be explained in other ways too. And in the words quoted from the book of Kings, not an absolute impossibility but a great difficulty is expressed.

paras.t: Porro quod jam Eliu ait, Deum omnia hæc tribus vicibus operari per singulos, nequaquam superficialiter verificatur. Multi enim fuerunt, quos Deus per horribiles visiones somniales et per infirmitates corporales non monuit. Oportet ergo ut distributio hic notata, sit accommoda, et intelligatur de his, quos Deus præfatis visitat modis et vicibus: juxta quem modum loquendi fertur in Psalmo, Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt. Per trinarium vero seu per tres vices, insinuatur numerus indeterminatus. Et convenienter hoc loco per trinarium indeterminatus numerus denotatur, quia nunc agitur de judicio quo Deus judicat actus humanos: in quibus sententiam præcedit trina monitio. Interdum equidem per millenarium, quandoque per denarium, aliquando per septenarium, nunc autem per trinarium indeterminatus exprimitur numerus. Denique non sequitur: Deus agit hæc tribus vicibus, ergo non pluribus. Postremo, quum tota hæc vita, sit peregrinatio quædam et via ad aliam vitam, quamdiu durat hæc via, durat et status atque facultas merendi ac demerendi: ad quod ex utroque Testamento plura ac certissima possent testimonia introduci.
paras.en: Further, what Eliu now says, that God works all these things three times within every one, is by no means true on the surface. For there have been many whom God did not warn by horrible visions in dreams and by bodily sicknesses. The distribution marked here must therefore be an accommodated one [a term of logic: the universal "every one" is to be taken of a fitting class, not of every man without exception], and be understood of those whom God visits in the ways and times spoken of: in the manner of speaking used in the Psalm, [[Ps 144:14|The Lord lifteth up all that fall|Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt]]. By the number three, or the three times, an indefinite number is signified. And fittingly in this place an indefinite number is denoted by three, since the subject now is the judgement by which God judges human acts: in which three warnings go before the sentence [as in the Church's courts, where three canonical warnings precede a sentence]. Sometimes, indeed, an indefinite number is expressed by a thousand, sometimes by ten, sometimes by seven, but here by three. Finally, it does not follow: God does these things three times, therefore not more. Lastly, since the whole of this life is a kind of pilgrimage and a way to another life, as long as this way lasts, so long lasts the state and power of meriting and demeriting; to which many and most certain testimonies could be brought from both Testaments.

paras.t: Ut revocet animas eorum a corruptione, id est peccato, quod mentis corruptio est, et illuminet luce viventium, id est lumine gratiæ in præsenti, et lumine gloriæ in futuro, juxta illud in Psalmo: Placeam coram Deo in lumine viventium. Qui enim Deo fruuntur, præ ceteris creaturis propriissime vivere asseruntur. Virtuosi etiam viatores, quoniam fonti vitæ per caritatem et cetera gratiarum charismata juncti sunt, vivere proprie perhibentur: in quibus multiplex lux invenitur, videlicet gratia gratum faciens, dona Spiritus Sancti, inter quæ donum sapientiæ splendidius micat; ceteræ quoque virtutes, fructus ac beatitudines frequenter lumina appellantur: quibus omnibus anima intus coram Deo pulchriformiter clarificatur.
paras.en: [[33:30|That he may withdraw their souls from corruption|Ut revocet animas eorum a corruptione]], that is, from sin, which is the corruption of the mind, [[33:30|and enlighten them with the light of the living|et illuminet luce viventium]], that is, with the light of grace in the present and the light of glory in the future, according to that saying in the Psalm: [[Ps 55:13|that I may please in the sight of God, in the light of the living|Placeam coram Deo in lumine viventium]]. For those who enjoy God are said to live most properly of all creatures. Virtuous wayfarers too [that is, those still on the way in this life, as against the blessed in heaven], since they are joined to the fountain of life by charity and the other gifts of grace, are rightly said to live: in them a manifold light is found, namely sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God], the gifts of the Holy Ghost, among which the gift of wisdom shines most brightly; and the other virtues, fruits and beatitudes are also often called lights: by all of which the soul is inwardly made bright and beautiful before God.

paras.t: Deinceps admonet Eliu sanctum Job, non parum animose atque frontose. Attende, Job, et audi me; et tace dum ego loquor, ne tanti tamque sapientis viri verba interrumpere audeas. Si autem habes quod loquaris, responde mihi. Loquere, quia paratus sum, et facile mihi erit satisfacere tibi. Volo enim te apparere justum: id est, non ex invidia increpo te, quia justitiam tibi nunc faveo; et quantum in me est, vellem quod posses te vere justum probare. Quod si non habes, quod mihi respondeas, et quo te justum ostendas, audi me; tace, tanquam discipulus et convictus, et docebo te sapientiam, ut ea quæ Dei sunt, vere intelligas, atque per illa de te ipso discretius judices.
paras.en: Next Eliu admonishes holy Job, with no little spirit and boldness [*frontose*, literally "with a bold forehead"]: [[33:31|Attend, Job, and hearken to me|Attende, Job, et audi me]]; [[33:31|and hold thy peace, whilst I speak|et tace dum ego loquor]], and do not dare to interrupt the words of so great and so wise a man. [[33:32|But if thou hast any thing to say|Si autem habes quod loquaris]], [[33:32|answer me|responde mihi]]: [[33:32|speak|Loquere]], for I am ready, and it will be easy for me to satisfy thee; [[33:32|for I would have thee to appear just|Volo enim te apparere justum]]: that is, I do not rebuke thee out of envy, for I now favour thy justice; and as far as in me lies, I would that thou couldst prove thyself truly just. [[33:33|And if thou have not|Quod si non habes]] anything to answer me, or to show thyself just by, [[33:33|hear me|audi me]]; [[33:33|hold thy peace|tace]] like a disciple, and one convicted, [[33:33|and I will teach thee wisdom|et docebo te sapientiam]], so that thou mayest truly understand the things of God, and by them judge of thyself with more discernment.

34.title: Expositio capituli tricesimi quarti: Pronuntians quoque Eliu.
34.title_en: Exposition of the thirty-fourth chapter: And Eliu continued his discourse

paras.t: Pronuntians quoque Eliu, etiam hæc verba locutus est. In eo quod dicitur Pronuntians, datur intelligi quod cum grandi auctoritate, audacia atque facundia loquebatur, ceteros quasi minus sapientes, infra se reputans constitutos. Audite, sapientes in divinis, verba mea, et eruditi in moralibus et rebus humanis ac naturalibus, auscultate me. Quasi dicat: Talia loquar, quæ non nisi a sapientibus et eruditis queunt intelligi: quemadmodum ait Apostolus, Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos. In quibus etiam verbis Eliu de se ipso non mediocriter magnifice sentit, utpote in sapientia et doctrina se innuens eminentem, sapientiumque et eruditorum advertentia dignum.
paras.en: [[34:1|And Eliu continued his discourse, and said|Pronuntians quoque Eliu, etiam hæc verba locutus est]]. In that it says *Pronuntians* [literally, "pronouncing" or "declaring"; the Douay-Rheims renders it "continued his discourse"], it is given to understand that he spoke with great authority, boldness and eloquence, reckoning the others as less wise and placed beneath him. [[34:2|Hear ye, wise men|Audite, sapientes]] in divine things, [[34:2|my words|verba mea]], [[34:2|and ye learned|et eruditi]] in moral things and in human and natural matters, [[34:2|hearken to me|auscultate me]]. As if to say: I shall speak such things as cannot be understood except by the wise and learned; as the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 2:6|we speak wisdom among the perfect|Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos]]. In these words, too, Eliu thinks no little and very grandly of himself, hinting that he is eminent in wisdom and learning, and worthy of the attention of the wise and the learned.

paras.t: Auris enim verba probat, id est, percipit et judicat cujus sint soni; et guttur escas gustu dijudicat. Guttur enim per nervum gustativum usque ad ipsum protensum, escarum sapores percipit, atque dijudicat quales sint: quod facit gustu, id est per sensum gustus, cujus objectum est sapor; vigetque gustus in nervo gustativo, et fundatur in eo. Hoc Eliu ait, ad innuendum quod sicut exteriorum sensuum est de propriis objectis bene judicare, sic sapientium et eruditorum de intelligibilibus, præsertim sublimibus ac divinis, qualia ipse Eliu intendit proponere: ita quod sicut auris non noscit aut percipit escas, nec guttur verba, ita nec stultus sententiam sapientis. Hoc ipsum et Job superius ait: Nonne auris verba dijudicat, et fauces comedentis, saporem? Porro sensus seu potentiæ animæ dicuntur operari seu agere tanquam a quo agens: quia per eas suppositum, quod est homo, agit, qui agit tanquam quod agens. Quemadmodum enim esse, ita agere et pati proprie sunt suppositorum, secundum Philosophum.
paras.en: [[34:3|For the ear trieth words|Auris enim verba probat]], that is, perceives and judges of what sound they are; [[34:3|and the mouth discerneth meats by the taste|et guttur escas gustu dijudicat]]. For the throat [*guttur*, which the Douay-Rheims renders "mouth"], by the nerve of taste that stretches as far as it, perceives the savours of meats and judges what they are like: this it does by the taste, that is, by the sense of taste, whose object is savour; and taste thrives in the nerve of taste and is grounded in it. Eliu says this to hint that, as it belongs to the outward senses to judge well of their proper objects, so it belongs to the wise and learned to judge of things of the understanding, above all of lofty and divine things, such as Eliu himself means to set forth; so that, as the ear does not know or perceive meats, nor the throat words, so neither does the fool perceive the meaning of the wise man. Job too said this very thing above: [[Job 12:11|Doth not the ear discern words, and the palate of him that eateth, the taste?|Nonne auris verba dijudicat, et fauces comedentis, saporem?]] Further, the senses or powers of the soul are said to work or act as that by which one acts [*a quo agens*]: for through them the subject, that is, the man, acts; and he acts as that which acts [*quod agens*; that is, the senses are the means of acting, the man is the one who acts]. For just as being, so acting and being acted upon belong properly to subjects [*supposita*, that is, complete individual beings], according to the Philosopher.

paras.t: Judicium eligamus nobis: id est, falsitate et præcipitatione animi spretis ac evitatis, verum amplectamur judicium, discrete agendo, rite considerando; sicque quid verius sit, dictum Job an meum, idonee judicemus. Tale judicium quilibet nostrum eligere debet in his, quæ ipsum concernunt, et ad ipsius judicium pertinent, Christo dicente: Nolite judicare secundum faciem, sed justum judicium judicate. Unde Apostolus ait: Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur. Et inter nos videamus oculo intellectuali, id est, vivaciter perpendamus, quid sit melius, id est verius et justius de materia disputationis præsentis. Ideo enim datus est homini intellectus, ut verum a falso, bonum a malo, appetendum a fugiendo discernat ac segreget. Quod agere quam sit placitum Deo, ipse testatur per Jeremiam; Si separaveris, inquiens, pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris.
paras.en: [[34:4|Let us choose to us judgment|Judicium eligamus nobis]]: that is, scorning and shunning falsehood and rashness of mind, let us embrace true judgment, acting with discretion and weighing things duly; and so let us judge fitly which is the truer, the saying of Job or mine. Such judgment each of us ought to choose in the things that concern him and belong to his judgment, as Christ says: [[John 7:24|Judge not according to the appearance: but judge just judgment.|Nolite judicare secundum faciem, sed justum judicium judicate]] Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:31|if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged|Si nos ipsos dijudicaremus, non utique judicaremur]]. [[34:4|And let us see among ourselves|Et inter nos videamus]] with the eye of the understanding, that is, let us weigh keenly, [[34:4|what is the best|quid sit melius]], that is, what is truer and juster on the matter of the present dispute. For understanding was given to man for this, that he may discern and set apart the true from the false, the good from the evil, what is to be sought from what is to be shunned. How pleasing it is to God to do this, he himself bears witness through Jeremias, saying: If [[Jer 15:19|thou wilt separate|Si separaveris]], he says, [[Jer 15:19|the precious from the vile, thou shalt be as my mouth|pretiosum a vili, quasi os meum eris]].

paras.t: Consequenter aggreditur ipsum Job. Quia dixit Job: Justus sum. Hoc utique dixit: Si judicatus, inquit, fuero, scio quod justus inveniar. Et Deus subvertit judicium meum, id est, perverse atque injuste me judicavit, videlicet contra ordinem juris, infligendo mihi pœnam absque meo demerito. Verbum istud sanctus Job non dixit formaliter, sed simile aliquid, quod Eliu cepit ad sensum istum. Superius enim Job dixit: Saltem nunc intelligite, quia Deus non æquo judicio afflixerit me, et flagellis suis me cinxerit. Judicium autem non æquum, videtur esse iniquum. Et iterum dixit: Vivit Deus qui abstulit judicium meum. Sed, sicut expositum est, talia Job non dixit, intendens quod absolute iniquo judicio esset divinitus judicatus, sed quod judicium quo judicatus fuit, non esset æquum, loquendo de æquitate humani judicii, quo unicuique datur secundum quod meruit.
paras.en: Next he attacks Job himself. [[34:5|For Job hath said: I am just|Quia dixit Job: Justus sum]]. This indeed he said: [[Job 13:18|If I shall be judged|Si judicatus]], he says, [[Job 13:18|I know that I shall be found just|fuero, scio quod justus inveniar]]. [[34:5|And God hath overthrown my judgment|Et Deus subvertit judicium meum]], that is, has judged me perversely and unjustly, against the order of law, by inflicting punishment on me without any fault of mine. Holy Job did not say this in so many words, but something like it, which Eliu took in this sense. For above Job said: [[Job 19:6|At least now understand, that God hath not afflicted me with an equal judgment, and compassed me with his scourges.|Saltem nunc intelligite, quia Deus non æquo judicio afflixerit me, et flagellis suis me cinxerit]] And a judgment that is not equal seems to be unjust. And again he said: [[Job 27:2|As God liveth, who hath taken away my judgment|Vivit Deus qui abstulit judicium meum]]. But, as has been explained, Job did not say such things meaning that he had been judged by God with a judgment simply unjust, but that the judgment with which he was judged was not equal, speaking of the equity of human judgment, by which each is given according to what he has deserved.

paras.t: In judicando enim me, mendacium est, id est, error et falsitas fuit in judicio, quo Deus me judicavit, et pœnis istis exposuit. Hoc Job nequaquam asseruit; sed Eliu hoc ipsi mendose imponit, quia videbatur sibi sequi ex verbis Job. Consequens quippe in antecedente quodammodo dicitur, scilicet virtualiter atque implicite. Violenta sagitta mea: id est, pœna mihi a Deo inflicta, non per justitiam, sed per violentiam seu tyrannidem Dei mihi inflicta est. Hoc rursus Job non dixit directe, imo nec æquivalenter. Eliu tamen hoc ipsi imponit, quia supra Job locutus est Deo: Sto, et non respicis me; mutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in duritia manus tuæ adversaris mihi. Quod quomodo intelligendum sit, in superioribus jam patuit. Iterum ait Job: Iratus est contra me furor Domini, et sic me habuit quasi hostem suum. Absque ullo peccato, id est, nullam habui culpam, ut paterer ista. Verum est quod Job testatus est se absque peccato suo esse percussum; nam dixit: Non peccavi, et in amaritudinibus moratur oculus meus. Tamen non dixit se absolute esse absque omni peccato: imo oppositum fassus est, deprecans Deum, Parce peccatis meis. Unde dicere voluit, quod licet aliquoties venialiter peccavit, non tamen tam graviter, ut tanta adversa meruerit, præsertim quia et pro venialibus quotidie satisfecit. Eliu autem sequitur eos, qui alio repetunt sermone, et quædam adjiciunt: quod impium est et plurimorum origo malorum. Propter quod in Proverbiis scribitur: Qui alio sermone repetit, separat fœderatos.
paras.en: [[34:6|For in judging me there is a lie|In judicando enim me, mendacium est]], that is, there was error and falsehood in the judgment by which God judged me and exposed me to these punishments. Job never asserted this; but Eliu falsely lays it on him, because it seemed to him to follow from Job's words. For the consequent is in a way said in the antecedent, that is, virtually and implicitly. [[34:6|My arrow is violent|Violenta sagitta mea]]: that is, the punishment inflicted on me by God has been inflicted on me not by justice, but by the violence or tyranny of God. Again Job did not say this directly, nor even in equivalent words. Yet Eliu lays it on him, because above Job spoke to God: [[Job 30:20|I stand up, and thou dost not regard me|Sto, et non respicis me]]; [[Job 30:21|Thou art changed to be cruel toward me, and in the hardness of thy hand thou art against me.|mutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in duritia manus tuæ adversaris mihi]] How this is to be understood has already been made plain above. Again Job says: [[Job 19:11|His wrath is kindled against me, and he hath counted me as his enemy.|Iratus est contra me furor Domini, et sic me habuit quasi hostem suum]] [Denis reads *furor Domini*, "the wrath of the Lord"]. [[34:6|Without any sin|Absque ullo peccato]], that is, I had no fault, that I should suffer these things. It is true that Job testified that he had been struck without sin of his own; for he said: [[Job 17:2|I have not sinned, and my eye abideth in bitterness.|Non peccavi, et in amaritudinibus moratur oculus meus]] Yet he did not say that he was simply without any sin at all; rather he confessed the opposite, praying God: [[Job 14:16|spare my sins|Parce peccatis meis]]. So he meant that, though he sometimes sinned venially, it was not so grievously as to deserve such great adversities, all the more since he made satisfaction daily even for venial sins. But Eliu follows those who repeat a thing in other words and add something to it: which is wicked and the origin of very many evils. For this reason it is written in Proverbs: [[Prov 17:9|he that repeateth it again, separateth friends|Qui alio sermone repetit, separat fœderatos]].

paras.t: Ex præinductis præmissis Eliu infert, loquens ad adsistentes: Quis est vir ut est Job? id est, nullus invenitur ei similis in malitia, quia sacrilegus est et blasphemus. Juxta quem modum tertio Regum, de Achab rege Israel scribitur: Igitur non fuit alter talis ut Achab, qui venundatus est ut faceret malum in conspectu Domini. Qui bibit, id est, quasi poculum intra se sumit, subsannationem, id est peccata subsannanda, seu divini derisionem judicii, quasi aquam, id est abundanter et absque mensura ac freno; qui graditur, id est, conversando communicat, cum operantibus iniquitatem, et ambulat ad infernum cum viris impiis, ita quod affectu, verbo et opere eis conformis est.
paras.en: From the premises brought forward, Eliu draws his conclusion, speaking to those standing by: [[34:7|What man is there like Job|Quis est vir ut est Job]]? that is, none is found like him in malice, for he is sacrilegious and a blasphemer. In the same way it is written in the third book of Kings of Achab king of Israel: [[3 Kings 21:25|there was not such another as Achab, who was sold to do evil in the sight of the Lord|non fuit alter talis ut Achab, qui venundatus est ut faceret malum in conspectu Domini]]. [[34:7|Who drinketh up|Qui bibit]], that is, takes into himself like a draught, [[34:7|scorning|subsannationem]], that is, sins that deserve scorn, or the mockery of God's judgment, [[34:7|like water|quasi aquam]], that is, abundantly and without measure or bridle; [[34:8|Who goeth in company|qui graditur]], that is, shares by his way of life, [[34:8|with them that work iniquity|cum operantibus iniquitatem]], [[34:8|and walketh|et ambulat]] to hell [[34:8|with wicked men|cum viris impiis]], in that he is like them in affection, word and deed.

paras.t: Dixit enim: Non placebit vir Deo, etiamsi cucurrerit cum eo, id est, quamvis ferventer atque alacriter fuerit voluntatem Dei secutus, et obedierit ei. Ire autem cum Deo, est bene agendo ei in omnibus consentire, seu ejus voluntati se conformare, quemadmodum in Genesi legitur Enoch ambulasse cum Deo. Qui autem hoc ipsum ferventer peregerit, non solum vadit, sed insuper currit cum Deo. Porro, hæc verba beatus Job non dixit, sed Eliu ea illi imponit: quia hinc inde quædam asseruit, ex quibus hæc sequi ipsi Eliu videbantur. Siquidem supra ait Job: Innocentem et impium ipse (videlicet Deus) consumit. Et iterum: Si flagellat, occidat semel, et non de pœnis innocentium rideat. Rursusque: Si lotus fuero quasi aquis nivis, et fulserint velut mundissimæ manus meæ, tamen sordibus intinges me. Denique Job multipliciter probavit se justum, sicque cucurrisse cum Deo; et tamen dixit ad eum, Arbitraris me inimicum tuum. Ex quibus Eliu intulit, quod Job dixerit se innocentem, et Deo nihilominus displicentem. Verum (ut patuit) inducta hæc verba Job, non ita sunt intelligenda, ut Eliu interpretatur.
paras.en: [[34:9|For he hath said: Man shall not please God, although he run with him|Dixit enim: Non placebit vir Deo, etiamsi cucurrerit cum eo]], that is, although he has followed God's will fervently and eagerly, and obeyed him. Now to go with God is, by doing well, to agree with him in all things, or to conform oneself to his will, as we read in Genesis that Enoch walked with God[[Gen 5:22||]]. And he who does this fervently not only goes but runs with God. But blessed Job did not say these words; Eliu lays them on him, because here and there he asserted certain things from which these seemed to Eliu to follow. For above Job says: [[Job 9:22|both the innocent and the wicked he|Innocentem et impium ipse]] (that is, God) [[Job 9:22|consumeth|consumit]]. And again: [[Job 9:23|If he scourge, let him kill at once, and not laugh at the pains of the innocent.|Si flagellat, occidat semel, et non de pœnis innocentium rideat]] And again: [[Job 9:30|If I be washed, as it were, with snow waters, and my hands shall shine ever so clean:|Si lotus fuero quasi aquis nivis, et fulserint velut mundissimæ manus meæ]] [[Job 9:31|yet thou shalt plunge me in filth|tamen sordibus intinges me]]. Lastly, Job proved in many ways that he was just, and so had run with God; and yet he said to him: [[Job 13:24|thinkest me thy enemy?|Arbitraris me inimicum tuum]] From these Eliu inferred that Job had said he was innocent and yet displeasing to God. But (as has been shown) these words of Job brought forward are not to be understood as Eliu interprets them.

paras.t: Ideo, viri cordati, id est magnanimes, fortes et intelligentes, audite me, quia tales verborum meorum capaces sunt, nec alii digni sunt me audire, ut Job vitiis passionibusque repletus, et ideo incorrigibilis manens. Sic Eliu sensit. Insipientes autem et vitiosi dicuntur non habere cor, juxta illud Jeremiæ: Audi, popule stulte, qui non habes cor. Osee quoque ait: Ephraim quasi columba seducta, non habens cor. In Proverbiis quoque legitur: Qui despicit amicum suum, indigens corde est. In quibus verbis, cor pro intellectu seu ratione accipitur. Similiter formidolosi dicuntur non habere cor, quia in eis ratio passioni timoris statim succumbit.
paras.en: [[34:10|Therefore, ye men of understanding|Ideo, viri cordati]] [*cordati*, literally "men with heart"], that is, great-souled, strong and intelligent, [[34:10|hear me|audite me]], because such men can take in my words, and others are not worthy to hear me, such as Job, full of vices and passions and so remaining incorrigible. So Eliu thought. Now the foolish and vicious are said not to have a heart, according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 5:21|Hear, O foolish people, and without understanding|Audi, popule stulte, qui non habes cor]] [literally, "who hast no heart"]. Osee too says: [[Osee 7:11|Ephraim|Ephraim]] [[Osee 7:11|as a dove that is decoyed, not having a heart|quasi columba seducta, non habens cor]]. In Proverbs too we read: [[Prov 11:12|He that despiseth his friend, is mean of heart|Qui despicit amicum suum, indigens corde est]] [literally, "is lacking in heart"]. In these words *heart* is taken for the understanding or reason. Likewise the fearful are said not to have a heart, because in them reason at once gives way to the passion of fear.

paras.t: Absit a Deo impietas mentis, et ab Omnipotente iniquitas operis. Hoc est quod ait Psalmista: Quoniam rectus Dominus Deus noster, et non est iniquitas in eo. Etenim Deus sublimis et benedictus naturaliter bonus est, essentialiter sanctus, pure et infinite, substantialiterque perfectus, universæ bonitatis, sanctitatis atque justitiæ mensura, causa et ratio.
paras.en: [[34:10|far from God be wickedness|Absit a Deo impietas]] of mind, [[34:10|and iniquity from the Almighty|et ab Omnipotente iniquitas]] of deed. This is what the Psalmist says: [[Ps 91:16|That the Lord our God is righteous, and there is no iniquity in him|Quoniam rectus Dominus Deus noster, et non est iniquitas in eo]]. For God, most high and blessed, is good by nature, holy by essence, purely and infinitely and substantially perfect, the measure, cause and reason of all goodness, holiness and justice.

paras.t: Opus enim hominis reddet ei, id est, secundum exigentiam et meritum actionis seu vitæ hominis reddet ei, infligendo adversa, tribuendove prospera: et juxta vias singulorum restituet eis, id est secundum affectiones et studia, quibus bene vel male egerunt. Sed quoniam virtus et vitium, meritum et demeritum, magis in interioribus quam exterioribus actibus constituuntur, ipsumque præmium essentiale in patria interiori atque elicito actui caritatis correspondet: certum est quod in verbis Eliu atque similibus Scripturæ locis, per opus non solum exterior operatio designetur, sed quælibet actio hominis. Juxta quem modum Christus loquitur Judæis: Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum quem misit ille. Denique, quamvis verba hic Eliu vera sint, et multis locis Scripturæ conformia, tamen secundum sensum quem Eliu hic intendit, non semper veritatem sortiuntur. Ideo namque hic verba inducit, ut probet quod Deus non puniat quemquam in vita hac, nisi pro suis peccatis: quod jam supra frequenter patuit falsum.
paras.en: [[34:11|For he will render to a man his work|Opus enim hominis reddet ei]], that is, he will render to him according to the demand and desert of the man's action or life, by inflicting adversity or granting prosperity: [[34:11|and according to the ways of every one he will reward them|et juxta vias singulorum restituet eis]], that is, according to the affections and pursuits by which they have done well or ill. But since virtue and vice, merit and demerit, consist more in inward than in outward acts, and the essential reward itself in the fatherland [that is, in heaven] answers to the inward and elicited act of charity [an *elicited* act is one that a power itself puts forth, as distinct from one it commands another power to do], it is certain that in the words of Eliu and in like places of Scripture, by *work* is meant not only outward working but any action of man. In this way Christ says to the Jews: [[John 6:29|This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he hath sent|Hoc est opus Dei, ut credatis in eum quem misit ille]]. Lastly, though Eliu's words here are true and agree with many places of Scripture, yet in the sense which Eliu intends here they do not always hold true. For he brings in these words to prove that God punishes no one in this life except for his sins: which has often been shown above to be false.

paras.t: Vere enim Deus non condemnabit frustra, id est sine ratione idonea, puta peccato, ut Eliu sensit: quod verum est, si ad finalem atque æternam condemnationem referatur; si vero intelligatur ut Eliu intendebat, quod Deus neminem in hac vita objicit seu exponit adversis et plagis, nisi pro suis peccatis, stare non valet. Nec huic verbo secundum quod verum est, obviat quod supra Dominus ait ad Satan: Tu commovisti me adversus eum, ut affligerem eum frustra. Absolute enim loquendo, Deus nullum frustra affligit. Quomodo tamen dicat se frustra sanctum Job afflixisse, in expositione secundi capituli requiratur. Nec Omnipotens subvertet judicium. Justus enim Dominus et justitias dilexit. Hinc Baldad disseruit: Numquid Deus supplantat judicium, et Omnipotens subvertit quod justum est?
paras.en: [[34:12|For in very deed God will not condemn without cause|Vere enim Deus non condemnabit frustra]], that is, without fitting reason, namely sin, as Eliu thought: which is true if it is referred to the final and eternal condemnation; but if it is understood as Eliu meant it, that God casts or exposes no one in this life to adversities and blows except for his own sins, it cannot stand. Nor, taking this saying in its true sense, does it conflict with what the Lord said above to Satan: [[Job 2:3|thou hast moved me against him, that I should afflict him without cause|Tu commovisti me adversus eum, ut affligerem eum frustra]]. For, speaking absolutely, God afflicts no one without cause. How he can nevertheless say that he afflicted holy Job without cause is to be looked for in the exposition of the second chapter[[Job 2:3||]]. [[34:12|Neither will the Almighty pervert judgment|Nec Omnipotens subvertet judicium]]. [[Ps 10:8|For the Lord is just, and hath loved justice|Justus enim Dominus et justitias dilexit]]. Hence Baldad argued: [[Job 8:3|Doth God pervert judgment, or doth the Almighty overthrow that which is just?|Numquid Deus supplantat judicium, et Omnipotens subvertit quod justum est?]]

paras.t: Quem constituit alium super terram? id est, nullum alium præfecit terræ in principem, sed ipse omnium terrenorum provisor, judex et Dominus est. Aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est? id est, alium non ordinavit mundi rectorem, sed ipse qui condidit omnia, regit. Sed his obviare videtur, quod ipsemet Christus ex parte naturæ assumptæ protestatur: Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. Hinc, secundum doctores, anima Christi prælata et dominans facta est omni creaturæ, humanitatique Christi subjecta sunt omnia. Denique inferiora reguntur per superiora, sicut corpora cœlestia a suis motoribus, et terrena seu mixta et elementa, ab orbibus, planetis, et stellis. Unde, secundum Philosophum, oportet hunc mundum contiguum esse lationibus superiorum, ut tota ejus virtus inde gubernetur. Imo superius dictum est: Terra data est in manus impii. Sed omnium horum atque similium una solutio est, quod scilicet Deus nullum constituit regem et principem, provisorem ac judicem terræ aut orbis alium, quam se tanquam principalem et propria auctoritate, voluntate et lege agentem: sed hoc modo solus Deus præsidet universis. Alii vero quos sibi in quibusdam agendis substituit, sunt ministri ipsius, et velut instrumentales ac secundarii præsidentes, quibus desuper lex certa præfigitur, quam nisi sequantur, a summo Principe punientur. Sicque intelligenda sunt, quæ hic scribit Gregorius: Per se mundum regit, qui per se hunc condidit. Unde Eliu verba ista induxit, ad demonstrandum quod mundus bene regatur, nec actus hominum injuste desuper judicentur: quia omnipotens Deus, si per se ipsum regere non negligit quod creavit, quod bene creavit utique bene regit; et qui necdum facta creavit ut essent, quæ jam fecit non deserit. Hinc non licet ad alium appellare, ut quum Deus sit mensura et regula universæ æquitatis ac veritatis, eo ipso quo ipse aliquid agit, sequitur quod sit rectum et bonum, justum et verum. Unde judicia Dei aliquando occulta sunt, nunquam injusta.
paras.en: [[34:13|What other hath he appointed over the earth?|Quem constituit alium super terram?]] that is, he has set no other over the earth as its prince, but he himself is the provider, judge and Lord of all earthly things. [[34:13|Or whom hath he set over the world which he made?|Aut quem posuit super orbem quem fabricatus est?]] that is, he has appointed no other ruler of the world, but he who made all things rules them himself. But against this seems to stand what Christ himself declares in respect of the nature he assumed: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]. Hence, according to the doctors, the soul of Christ was set over and made lord of every creature, and all things are subject to the humanity of Christ. Further, lower things are ruled by higher, as the heavenly bodies by their movers, and earthly things, whether mixed bodies or elements, by the spheres, the planets and the stars. Hence, according to the Philosopher, this world must be contiguous with the motions of the higher bodies, so that all its power may be governed from there. Indeed it was said above: [[Job 9:24|The earth is given into the hand of the wicked|Terra data est in manus impii]]. But there is one solution to all these and the like: namely that God has appointed no other king and prince, provider and judge of the earth or of the world, than himself, as acting principally and by his own authority, will and law; in this way God alone presides over all things. Those others whom he puts in his place in certain things to be done are his ministers, and as it were instrumental and secondary presidents, for whom a fixed law is laid down from above; unless they follow it, they will be punished by the supreme Prince. And so is to be understood what Gregory writes here: He rules the world by himself who made it by himself. Hence Eliu brought in these words to show that the world is well ruled, and that the acts of men are not unjustly judged from above: for if almighty God does not neglect to rule by himself what he created, what he created well he surely rules well; and he who created things not yet made, that they might be, does not forsake what he has already made. Hence there is no appealing to another, since God is the measure and rule of all equity and truth, so that by the very fact that he does a thing, it follows that it is right and good, just and true. Hence the judgments of God are sometimes hidden, never unjust.

paras.t: Si direxerit ad eum cor suum, id est, si homo mentem suam ad Deum converterit, seu ad susceptionem gratiæ ejus aptaverit, faciendo quod in se est, juxta illud Threnorum: Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum. Itemque in Osee: Convertere ad Dominum Deum tuum, quoniam corruisti in iniquitate tua. In Proverbiis quoque scriptum est: Hominis est animum præparare. Et denuo ibidem: Cor hominis disponit viam suam, sed Dei est dirigere gressus ejus. Spiritum illius, id est mentem seu animam, et flatum, id est desiderium, quod flatui comparatur, quum sit quædam adspiratio ad desideratum; vel per flatum designatur anima, quantum ad vires suas inferiores; ad se trahet, id est, Deus gratiose sibi conjunget, et per caritatem in se transformabit ac vertet; et quod homo per se ipsum non valet, Deus efficiet et complebit. Ideo monet Apostolus: Accedamus cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ ejus. Et Psalmista: Accedite, inquit, ad eum, et illuminamini, et facies vestræ non confundentur. Ecclesiasticus quoque inducit: Quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum? Hinc per Jeremiam Dominus loquitur: Quis est iste qui applicet cor suum, ut appropinquet mihi? Præterea, curvatur cor, quum appetit ima; rectificatur vero, quum ad Deum dirigitur: et quo homo se ad divinam illuminationem ac inflammationem magis disponit, pœnitendo, orando, adspirando, seu aliis virtuosis exercitiis se parando; eo Deus eum gratiosius abundantiusque implebit, illustrabit, accendet.
paras.en: [[34:14|If he turn his heart to him|Si direxerit ad eum cor suum]], that is, if a man turns his mind to God, or makes it fit to receive his grace, by doing what is in him [that is, doing all he can of his own part], according to that of Lamentations: [[Lam 3:40|Let us search our ways, and seek, and return to the Lord|Scrutemur vias nostras, et quæramus, et revertamur ad Dominum]]. And likewise in Osee: [[Osee 14:2|Return|Convertere]] [[Osee 14:2|to the Lord thy God: for thou hast fallen down by thy iniquity|ad Dominum Deum tuum, quoniam corruisti in iniquitate tua]]. In Proverbs too it is written: [[Prov 16:1|It is the part of man to prepare the soul|Hominis est animum præparare]]. And again in the same place: [[Prov 16:9|The heart of man disposeth his way: but the Lord must direct his steps.|Cor hominis disponit viam suam, sed Dei est dirigere gressus ejus]] [[34:14|His spirit|Spiritum illius]], that is, the mind or soul, [[34:14|and breath|et flatum]], that is, desire, which is likened to breath, since it is a kind of breathing towards the thing desired; or by *breath* the soul is meant as to its lower powers; [[34:14|he shall draw|ad se trahet]] to himself, that is, God will graciously join it to himself, and by charity will transform and turn it into himself; and what man cannot do by himself, God will bring about and fulfil. Therefore the Apostle advises: [[Heb 4:16|Let us go|Accedamus]] [[Heb 4:16|with confidence to the throne of grace|cum fiducia ad thronum gratiæ ejus]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 33:6|Come ye to him|Accedite]], he says, [[Ps 33:6|and be enlightened: and your faces shall not be confounded|ad eum, et illuminamini, et facies vestræ non confundentur]]. Ecclesiasticus too brings in: [[Ecclus 2:12|who hath called upon him, and he despised him?|Quis invocavit illum, et despexit eum?]] Hence the Lord speaks through Jeremias: [[Jer 30:21|who is this that setteth his heart to approach to me|Quis est iste qui applicet cor suum, ut appropinquet mihi]]? Further, the heart is bent when it desires low things, and is made straight when it is directed to God: and the more a man disposes himself for divine enlightenment and kindling, by repenting, praying, aspiring, or preparing himself by other virtuous exercises, the more graciously and abundantly will God fill, enlighten and kindle him.

paras.t: Deficiet omnis caro simul, id est, Deo spiritum hominis ad se trahente, caro deficiet, et omnis carnalis affectio exstinguetur, corporaleque robur debilitabitur, juxta illud in Psalmo: Defecit caro mea et cor meum, Deus cordis mei. Quo enim anima in divina plus transformatur ac rapitur, eo pars sensitiva et corpus in suis actibus amplius remittuntur ac debilitantur. Et homo in cinerem revertetur, id est, cinerem et pulverem se esse humiliter recognoscet: quia quo altius contemplando erigitur, eo propriam infirmitatem clarius intuetur. Denique comparatione divinæ potestatis spiritum hominis ad se trahentis, omnis virtus humana occumbit et deficit, ipseque homo per mortem in cinerem redit. Quemadmodum etiam Eliphaz dixit: Qui habitant domos luteas, consumentur velut a tinea.
paras.en: [[34:15|All flesh shall perish together|Deficiet omnis caro simul]], that is, as God draws the spirit of man to himself, the flesh will fail, and every carnal affection will be quenched, and bodily strength weakened, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 72:26|my flesh and my heart hath fainted away: thou art the God of my heart|Defecit caro mea et cor meum, Deus cordis mei]]. For the more the soul is transformed into divine things and rapt into them, the more the sensitive part and the body are slackened and weakened in their acts. [[34:15|And man shall return into ashes|Et homo in cinerem revertetur]], that is, he will humbly acknowledge that he is ashes and dust: for the higher he is raised in contemplation, the more clearly he sees his own weakness. Lastly, in comparison with the divine power that draws the spirit of man to itself, all human strength sinks and fails, and man himself returns to ashes by death. As Eliphaz too said: [[Job 4:19|they that dwell in houses of clay|Qui habitant domos luteas]], [[Job 4:19|be consumed as with the moth|consumentur velut a tinea]].

paras.t: Præterea, quidam exponunt hæc aliter. Si direxerit ad eum cor suum, id est, si Deus ad aliquem voluntatem suam direxerit ad eum destruendum, spiritum illius et flatum ad se trahet, id est, ab esse in corpore tollet, atque deficere faciet, ita quod caro prorsus corrumpetur, homoque morietur. Expositio ista videtur inepta, idcirco pertranseo.
paras.en: Besides, some expound these words otherwise. [[34:14|If he turn his heart to him|Si direxerit ad eum cor suum]], that is, if God directs his will towards someone to destroy him, [[34:14|he shall draw his spirit and breath unto himself|spiritum illius et flatum ad se trahet]], that is, he will take it away from being in the body and make it fail, so that the flesh will utterly perish and the man will die. This exposition seems unfitting, and so I pass it over.

paras.t: Si ergo habes intellectum, id est intellectualem capacitatem ad ea quæ dico, o Job, audi quod dicitur, et ausculta vocem eloquii mei a me. In quibus verbis clarescit, quod Eliu rursus a sua superbia tactus sit, et de altitudine eloquentiæ atque scientiæ suæ inaniter elevatus. Hinc ait Gregorius: Habent hoc proprium arrogantes, ut quum acutum quid sentiunt, inde mox ad vitium elationis erumpant, sensusque omnium in sui comparatione despiciant, et se in suo judicio aliorum meritis anteponant: quia dum minora incaute negligunt, ad majora perniciose prorumpunt.
paras.en: [[34:16|If then thou hast understanding|Si ergo habes intellectum]], that is, the capacity of understanding for what I say, O Job, [[34:16|hear what is said, and hearken to the voice of my words|audi quod dicitur, et ausculta vocem eloquii mei]] from me. In these words it becomes clear that Eliu was again touched by his pride, and vainly puffed up over the height of his eloquence and knowledge. Hence Gregory says: The arrogant have this peculiar to them, that when they perceive something keen, they at once break out from it into the vice of self-exaltation, despise everyone's understanding in comparison with their own, and in their own judgment set themselves above the merits of others: for while they heedlessly neglect lesser things, they rush ruinously into greater.

paras.t: Numquid qui non amat judicium, sanari potest? Hoc dupliciter potest exponi. Primo, quod qui judicium discretionis quo inter bonum et malum, inter verum et falsum discernitur, non diligit, a vitiis non curatur. Talis enim est indiscretus, rationis judicio non acquiescens. Secundo, quod qui judicium Dei non amat, sed reprobat, in anima non sanatur. Per quod Eliu notat Job, quod nec anima nec corpore possit sanari, quia divino judicio se opponat, et informationi humanæ acquiescere spernat. Itaque debet homo rectæ rationis amare judicium, examinare et increpare se ipsum, aliorum recto judicio stare, in proprio sensu pertinax non manere. Et quomodo tu eum qui justus est, scilicet Deum, in tantum condemnas, ut dicas eum subvertisse judicium tuum, teque mendaciter judicasse? Quod rursum Eliu erronee imponit beato Job.
paras.en: [[34:17|Can he be healed that loveth not judgment?|Numquid qui non amat judicium, sanari potest?]] This can be expounded in two ways. First, that he who does not love the judgment of discretion, by which good is told from evil and true from false, is not cured of his vices. For such a man is without discretion, not resting in the judgment of reason. Secondly, that he who does not love the judgment of God but rejects it is not healed in his soul. By this Eliu censures Job, as one who can be healed neither in soul nor in body, because he sets himself against God's judgment and scorns to rest in human instruction. And so a man ought to love the judgment of right reason, examine and rebuke himself, abide by the right judgment of others, and not remain stubborn in his own opinion. [[34:17|And how dost thou|Et quomodo tu]] [[34:17|so far condemn|in tantum condemnas]] [[34:17|him that is just|eum qui justus est]], namely God, as to say that he has overthrown thy judgment and judged thee falsely? This again Eliu wrongly lays on blessed Job.

paras.t: Qui dicit regi: Apostata, id est, impios reges Deus vocat apostatas, id est a Deo atque justitia apostatantes, ita quod Deus potestati aut personæ non defert contra justitiam, sed reges deponit, occidit, condemnat, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus. Qui vocat duces, impios, dum impii sunt, ita quod Deus neminem timet, nullique cedit in derogationem veritatis. Dicit autem Gregorius: Unusquisque rector superbus, toties ad culpam apostasiæ labitur, quoties præesse hominibus delectatur. Sub quo enim sit, non considerat. Unde necesse est ut qui aliis præest, quæ exempla subditis præbeat, solerter attendat, et tantis se sciat vivere, quantis præest.
paras.en: [[34:18|Who saith to the king: Thou art an apostate|Qui dicit regi: Apostata]], that is, God calls wicked kings apostates, that is, men who fall away from God and from justice; so that God does not defer to power or person against justice, but deposes, slays and condemns kings, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus]]. [[34:18|Who calleth rulers ungodly|Qui vocat duces, impios]], while they are ungodly, so that God fears no one and yields to no one to the detriment of truth. And Gregory says: Every proud ruler falls into the guilt of apostasy as often as he delights in being over men. For he does not consider under whom he himself is. Hence it is needful that he who is over others should carefully attend to what examples he gives his subjects, and know that he lives for as many as he is set over.

paras.t: Qui non accipit personas principum, id est, contra justitiam eis non defert propter dignitatem principatus eorum. Unde in Numerorum libro jussit omnes principes Israel suspendi in patibulis. Et Sapiens habet: Potentes potenter tormenta patientur; et: Fortioribus fortior instat cruciatus. Nec cognovit tyrannum, id est, eum non approbavit, nec causam ejus justificavit, dum disceptaret contra pauperem, id est, judicio contra eum injuste contenderet. Imo judicium sine misericordia facit his, qui non faciunt misericordiam, præsertim pauperibus. His autem similia et majora locutus est Job, dicens: Balteum regum Deus dissolvit, et præcingit fune renes eorum; ducit sacerdotes inglorios, et optimates supplantat. Multaque alia loquitur ibi, ex quorum prolixa elucidatione illic inducta, ista clarius patent. Opus enim manuum ejus sunt universi, id est, creaturæ Dei sunt parvi et magni, juxta illud in libro Sapientiæ: Pusillum et magnum fecit Dominus, et æqualiter ei cura est de omnibus.
paras.en: [[34:19|Who accepteth not the persons of princes|Qui non accipit personas principum]], that is, does not defer to them against justice on account of the dignity of their rule. Hence in the book of Numbers he commanded all the princes of Israel to be hanged on gibbets[[Num 25:4||]]. And the Wise Man has: [[Wis 6:7|the mighty shall be mightily tormented|Potentes potenter tormenta patientur]]; and: [[Wis 6:9|a greater punishment is ready for the more mighty|Fortioribus fortior instat cruciatus]]. [[34:19|Nor hath regarded the tyrant|Nec cognovit tyrannum]], that is, has not approved him nor justified his cause, [[34:19|when he contended against the poor man|dum disceptaret contra pauperem]], that is, strove unjustly against him at law. Rather he executes [[Jas 2:13|judgment without mercy|judicium sine misericordia]] on those who do not show mercy, above all to the poor. Things like these, and greater, Job spoke, saying: [[Job 12:18|He looseth the belt of kings, and girdeth their loins with a cord|Balteum regum Deus dissolvit, et præcingit fune renes eorum]]; [[Job 12:19|He leadeth away priests without glory, and overthroweth nobles|ducit sacerdotes inglorios, et optimates supplantat]]. And he says many other things there, from the long explanation of which given in that place these things are made plainer. [[34:19|For all are the work of his hands|Opus enim manuum ejus sunt universi]], that is, small and great are God's creatures, according to that in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 6:8|he made the little and the great, and he hath equally care of all|Pusillum et magnum fecit Dominus, et æqualiter ei cura est de omnibus]].

paras.t: Subito morientur, id est, justo Dei judicio repente et improvise de vita tollentur præsidentes iniqui, secundum illud Psalmi: Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitatem suam. Et in media nocte curvabuntur populi, id est, divina virtute humiliabuntur et dejicientur; et pertransibunt, id est, de vita ista ad aliam atque ignotam regionem transibunt. Potestque per mediam noctem, tempus illud nocturnum intelligi, vel quæcumque grandis adversitas et tempestas, vel ignorantia, ac vitiositas mentis. Hinc Isaias asserit: Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum. Est autem et curvatio seu curvitas bona, qua quis propriam parvitatem perpendens, deprimit semetipsum, humiliter de se sentiens, seque in cunctis spernens et vilipendens. Unde Baruch inducit: Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva, dat tibi gloriam Domino. Per Isaiam quoque Deus promittit Ecclesiæ: Venient ad te curvi filii eorum qui detrahebant tibi.
paras.en: [[34:20|They shall suddenly die|Subito morientur]]: that is, by the just judgment of God wicked rulers shall be taken from life all at once and unforeseen, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 72:19|How are they brought to desolation? they have suddenly ceased to be: they have perished by reason of their iniquity|Quomodo facti sunt in desolationem? Subito defecerunt, perierunt propter iniquitatem suam]]. [[34:20|and the people shall be troubled at midnight|Et in media nocte curvabuntur populi]] [Denis reads *curvabuntur*, "shall be bowed down", where the Vulgate has *turbabuntur*, "shall be troubled"; his gloss follows his own reading], that is, they shall be humbled and cast down by the power of God; [[34:20|and they shall pass|et pertransibunt]], that is, they shall pass from this life to another and unknown region. And by *midnight* may be understood that time of the night itself, or any great adversity and storm, or ignorance and viciousness of mind. Hence Isaias declares: [[Is 2:17|the loftiness of men shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be humbled|Incurvabitur sublimitas hominum, et humiliabitur altitudo virorum]]. But there is also a good bowing, or bentness, by which a man, weighing his own littleness, presses himself down, thinking humbly of himself, and scorning and holding himself cheap in all things. Whence Baruch brings in: [[Bar 2:18|the soul that is sorrowful for the greatness of evil she hath done, and goeth bowed down|Anima quæ tristis est super magnitudine mali, et incedit curva]], [[Bar 2:18|giveth glory|dat tibi gloriam]] to thee the Lord. Through Isaias too God promises the Church: [[Is 60:14|the children of them that afflict thee, shall come bowing down to thee|Venient ad te curvi filii eorum]], [[Is 60:14|that slandered thee|qui detrahebant tibi]] [Denis joins two clauses of the verse: "the children of them that slandered thee shall come bowing down to thee"].

paras.t: Et auferent violentum absque manu, id est, tyranni et violenti ab adversariis suis tollentur ac perimentur, quoniam contra tales frequenter excitatur seditio subditorum, vel occulte interficiuntur. Ideo subditur, Absque manu, id est insidiose, non potestative. Gregorius vero exponit, quod divina judicia auferunt violentum, absque manu, id est invisibiliter, sicut in Daniele de Antichristo seu Antiocho scribitur, quia sine manu conteretur.
paras.en: [[34:20|and take away the violent without hand|Et auferent violentum absque manu]]: that is, tyrants and violent men shall be taken away and slain by their adversaries, since a rising of their subjects is often stirred up against such men; or they are slain in secret. Therefore it is added, [[34:20|without hand|Absque manu]], that is, by stealth, not by open power. But Gregory explains that the divine judgments take away the violent man [[34:20|without hand|absque manu]], that is, invisibly, as it is written in Daniel of Antichrist, or of Antiochus, that he [[Dan 8:25|shall be broken without hand|sine manu conteretur]] [the margin's chapter is unread ("Dan. 35"); the words are Dan 8:25].

paras.t: Oculi enim ejus, scilicet Dei, sunt super vias hominum, id est, actus hominum intuentur; et omnes gressus eorum considerat. Non sunt tenebræ, et non est umbra mortis, id est, in Deo non sunt tenebræ ignorantiæ aut oblivio, quæ est velut umbra mortis. Similiter nec extra Deum sunt hujusmodi tenebræ, talisve umbra mortis, ut abscondantur ibi, id est in eis seu per eas, qui operantur iniquitatem, id est, peccatores lateant Deum. Nil enim occultare potest creaturam a Creatore. Istis, quia sæpissime dicta sunt, immorandum non reor. Deum omnia intueri, pensare et judicare, ideo tam frequenter profert Scriptura, ut hominibus timorem Dei, custodiam cordis, emendationem vitæ incutiat. Unde in Ecclesiastico legitur: Oculi Domini multo lucidiores sole, in omni loco contemplantur bonos et malos. In Jeremia quoque Dominus protestatur: Oculi mei super omnes vias eorum; non sunt abscondita ab oculis meis.
paras.en: [[34:21|For his eyes|Oculi enim ejus]], namely God's, [[34:21|are upon the ways of men|sunt super vias hominum]], that is, they behold the acts of men; [[34:21|and he considereth all their steps|et omnes gressus eorum considerat]]. [[34:22|There is no darkness, and there is no shadow of death|Non sunt tenebræ, et non est umbra mortis]]: that is, in God there is no darkness of ignorance, nor forgetfulness, which is as it were a shadow of death. Likewise outside God there is no such darkness, or such shadow of death, [[34:22|where they may be hid|ut abscondantur ibi]], that is, in it or by it, [[34:22|who work iniquity|qui operantur iniquitatem]]: that is, that sinners may lie hidden from God. For nothing can hide a creature from the Creator. On these things, since they have been said very often, I do not think we need dwell. Scripture says so often that God beholds, weighs and judges all things in order to strike into men the fear of God, the guarding of the heart and the amendment of life. Whence we read in Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 23:28|the eyes of the Lord are far brighter than the sun|Oculi Domini multo lucidiores sole]], [[Prov 15:3|in every place behold the good and the evil|in omni loco contemplantur bonos et malos]] [Denis joins Ecclus 23:28 with Prov 15:3, and the margin gives both]. In Jeremias too the Lord declares: [[Jer 16:17|my eyes are upon all their ways|Oculi mei super omnes vias eorum]]; [[Jer 16:17|they are not hid|non sunt abscondita]] from my eyes [the margin's reference is unread; the words are Jer 16:17].

paras.t: Neque enim ultra in hominis potestate est, ut veniat ad eum in judicium. Jam de violento asseruit, quod auferetur absque manu; et causam adjecit, quoniam oculi Dei sunt super omnes vias hominum: ideo pro peccatis debitas pœnas infligit. Quibus verbum istud subjunxit: Neque enim, etc. Unde ad litteram, de violento loqui videtur, vel de iniquo ac reprobo: ut sit sensus, quod ultra, scilicet postquam de vita sublatus est, et a Deo in suis iniquitatibus deprehensus, seu definitiva sententia condemnatus, non est in ejus potestate ut veniat rursus ad Deum in judicium disceptationis seu examinationis: quia non amplius ad judicium istud habet reduci, præsertim loquendo de particulari judicio. Gregorius vero exponit de judicio discretionis seu propriæ discussionis, quo homo in vita hac examinat judicatque se ipsum salubriter, atque per hoc venit ad Deum, ejusque gratiam, reprobando et castigando se ipsum. Post mortem autem non est in hominis potestate venire ad Deum, in seu per tale judicium, quia post mortem non est status merendi. Potest etiam ita exponi, quod ex quo Deus omnium habet notitiam, hinc post mortem [non] est in hominis alicujus potestate venire ad Deum in judicium, quia, velit nolit, ad divinum judicium trahitur, dicente Apostolo: Omnes nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi.
paras.en: [[34:23|For it is no longer in the power of man to enter into judgment with God|Neque enim ultra in hominis potestate est, ut veniat ad eum in judicium]]. He had said of the violent man that he would be taken away without hand, and had added the cause: that the eyes of God are upon all the ways of men, and therefore he inflicts the penalties due for sins. To these words he joined this: [[34:23|For it is|Neque enim]], etc. Hence, literally, he seems to speak of the violent man, or of the wicked and reprobate, so that the sense is this: [[34:23|no longer|ultra]], namely after he has been taken from life and caught by God in his iniquities, or condemned by a final sentence, it is not in his power to come again to God for a judgment of hearing or examination, because he is no more to be brought back to that judgment; this is said above all of the particular judgment. But Gregory explains it of the judgment of discernment, that is, of one's own self-examination, by which a man in this life examines and judges himself to his salvation, and by this comes to God and to his grace, by reproving and chastising himself. But after death it is not in man's power to come to God in or through such a judgment, because after death there is no state of meriting. It may also be explained thus: since God has knowledge of all things, after death it is not in any man's power whether he comes to God for judgment [the *non*, "not", is printed in brackets, as the editor's addition], because, willing or not, he is dragged to the divine judgment, as the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:10|we must all be manifested before the judgment seat of Christ|Omnes nos manifestari oportet ante tribunal Christi]] [the margin's reference is unread; the words are 2 Cor 5:10].

paras.t: Conteret multos et innumerabiles, et stare faciet alios pro eis, id est, Deus innumerabiles homines in sæculo isto sæpe occidet propter eorum peccata, quibus alios succedere faciet. Quod etiam spiritualiter facit, dum plurimos justo judicio gratia privat et perire permittit: aliis vero in illorum succedentibus locum, vitam naturæ et gratiæ confert. Hoc est quod supra dixit Job: Qui multiplicat gentes, et perdit eas, et subversas in integrum restituit.
paras.en: [[34:24|He shall break in pieces many and innumerable, and shall make others to stand in their stead|Conteret multos et innumerabiles, et stare faciet alios pro eis]]: that is, God often slays innumerable men in this world for their sins, and makes others succeed them. This he also does spiritually, when by just judgment he deprives very many of grace and lets them perish, but gives the life of nature and of grace to others who succeed in their place. This is what Job said above: [[Job 12:23|He multiplieth nations, and destroyeth them, and restoreth them again after they were overthrown|Qui multiplicat gentes, et perdit eas, et subversas in integrum restituit]] [the margin's reference is hard to read; the words are Job 12:23].

paras.t: Novit enim opera eorum, vitiosa, notitia simplicis cognitionis, non approbationis, quemadmodum in Amos fatetur: Cognovi multa scelera vestra. Et idcirco inducet noctem, id est æternæ lucis privationem, juxta illud in Isaia: Tollatur impius ne videat gloriam Dei. In præsenti quoque nox, hoc est caligo peccati et ignorantiæ, seu privatio gratiæ, eis inducitur. Unde ait Apostolus: Non sumus noctis neque tenebrarum. Et conterentur, id est, corporaliter morientur, spiritualiterque peribunt. Hoc loco scribit S. Gregorius: Omne peccatum, quod tamen citius pœnitendo non tergitur, aut peccatum est et causa peccati, aut peccatum et pœna peccati. Peccatum namque quod pœnitentia non diluit, ipso suo pondere mox ad aliud trahit. Unde fit, ut non solum peccatum sit, sed peccatum et causa peccati. Sed peccatum quod ex peccato oritur, non jam peccatum tantummodo, sed peccatum et pœna est peccati: quia justo judicio Deus omnipotens cor peccantis obnubilat, ut præcedentis peccati merito, etiam in alia cadat. Hinc de quibusdam scribit ad Romanos primo Apostolus: Quum cognovissent Deum non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt. Propter quod tradidit illos Deus in reprobum sensum, ut contumeliis afficiant corpora sua in se ipsis. In Psalmo quoque dicitur Deo: Appone iniquitatem super iniquitatem eorum.
paras.en: [[34:25|For he knoweth their works|Novit enim opera eorum]], their vicious works, with a knowledge of simple cognizance, not of approval [the schoolmen distinguish God's knowledge of simple cognizance, by which he knows evil as well as good, from his knowledge of approval, by which he approves only the good], as he avows in Amos: [[Amos 5:12|I know your manifold crimes|Cognovi multa scelera vestra]]. [[34:25|and therefore he shall bring night on them|Et idcirco inducet noctem]], that is, the privation of eternal light, according to that in Isaias: Let the wicked be taken away, lest he see the glory of God[[Is 26:10||]] [Denis quotes the old reading of Is 26:10, from the Septuagint; the Vulgate has "he shall not see the glory of the Lord"]. In the present life too night, that is, the darkness of sin and of ignorance, or the privation of grace, is brought upon them. Whence the Apostle says: [[1 Thess 5:5|we are not of the night nor of darkness|Non sumus noctis neque tenebrarum]]. [[34:25|and they shall be destroyed|Et conterentur]], that is, they shall die in body and perish in spirit. On this place St Gregory writes: "Every sin that is not quickly wiped away by repentance is either sin and the cause of sin, or sin and the punishment of sin. For the sin which repentance does not wash away soon drags to another by its own weight; whence it comes about that it is not only sin, but sin and the cause of sin. But the sin which springs from sin is no longer sin only, but sin and the punishment of sin: because almighty God by just judgment clouds the heart of the sinner, so that by the desert of the sin that went before he falls into others also." Hence the Apostle writes of certain men, in the first chapter to the Romans: [[Rom 1:21|when they knew God, they have not glorified him as God or given thanks|Quum cognovissent Deum non sicut Deum glorificaverunt, aut gratias egerunt]]. [[Rom 1:24|Wherefore, God gave them up|Propter quod tradidit illos Deus]] [[Rom 1:28|to a reprobate sense|in reprobum sensum]], [[Rom 1:24|to dishonour their own bodies among themselves|ut contumeliis afficiant corpora sua in se ipsis]] [Denis joins Rom 1:24 with words of Rom 1:28]. In the Psalm too it is said to God: [[Ps 68:28|Add thou iniquity upon their iniquity|Appone iniquitatem super iniquitatem eorum]].

paras.t: Quasi impios percussit eos in loco videntium: id est, præfatos innumerabiles homines malos Deus contrivit atque plagavit in sæculo isto, quod est viventium atque videntium mansio, ita quod coram aliis eos percussit, sicut decuit percuti impios, vel sicut alios infideles sacrilegosque percussit. Sicque, Quasi, notare potest tam similitudinem quam veritatem. Ideo demum percutit Deus iniquos in loco videntium seu in conspectibus aliorum, ut illorum exemplo alii terreantur et emendentur. Hinc Albertus allegat Ptolemæum in Almagesti dicentem: Qui ad alios non corrigitur, alii corrigentur ad ipsum.
paras.en: [[34:26|He hath struck them, as being wicked, in open sight|Quasi impios percussit eos in loco videntium]] [literally "in the place of them that see"; Denis's gloss follows the Latin]: that is, God crushed and smote the innumerable wicked men spoken of in this world, which is the dwelling of the living and the seeing, so that he struck them before others, as it was fitting that the wicked be struck, or as he struck other unbelievers and sacrilegious men. And so *as* [*quasi*] can mark a likeness as well as the truth. God strikes the wicked in the place of them that see, that is, in the sight of others, so that by their example others may be frightened and amend. Hence Albert cites Ptolemy in the Almagest, saying: "He who is not corrected by others, others will be corrected by him."

paras.t: Qui quasi de industria recesserunt ab eo: id est, a Deo, et a luce justitiæ aversi sunt mente ex studio atque proposito vitioso: et peccaverunt non ex infirmitate, vel ignorantia pura, sed ex habitu pravo, ex certa malitia, ex deliberatione iniqua, excogitantes quasi industriose vias et media perpetrandi iniqua: quales sunt, qui concupiscentias suas conceptasque malitias studiose ad effectum perducere moliuntur, et præcepta Creatoris sui scienter transgrediuntur, atque in rebus creatis, caducis et vanis, carnalibus seu terrenis finem sibi constituunt, amorem defigunt, delectationem exquirunt, talia summo, immenso, ac incommutabili bono impiissime et insipientissime præferentes. De quibus loquitur Jeremias: Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt. Isti sunt qui lætantur quum malefecerint: quibus competit illud Psalmi: Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso; non est timor ante oculos ejus. Et omnes vias ejus intelligere noluerunt, id est, divina præcepta, consilia, testimonia, documenta cognoscere contempserunt. Vel si eas nude atque informiter sciverunt, aut scire optarunt ex vanitate ad commodum sui, non tamen eas scire voluerunt notitia formata et efficaci, de qua in prima sua epistola ait Joannes: Qui dicit se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est. Horum ignorantia inexcusabilis est, gravans et affectata, quemadmodum Judæorum: de quibus ait Salvator: Si non venissem et locutus eis fuissem, peccatum non haberent: nunc autem excusationem non habent. Cujus causam subjungens: Viderunt, inquit, et oderunt me et Patrem meum gratis. Horum ergo sequuntur malitiam, qui veritatis odiunt instructorem.
paras.en: [[34:27|Who as it were on purpose have revolted from him|Qui quasi de industria recesserunt ab eo]]: that is, they turned away in mind from God and from the light of justice through vicious zeal and purpose; and they sinned, not from weakness or pure ignorance, but from a depraved habit, from certain malice [that is, malice that knows what it does: sin committed with full knowledge and will, not from passion or ignorance], from wicked deliberation, devising, as it were of set purpose, ways and means of doing wicked things. Such are those who strive with zeal to bring their desires and the malice they have conceived to effect, and knowingly transgress the precepts of their Creator, and in created things, perishable and vain, carnal or earthly, set their end, fix their love and seek their delight, most impiously and most foolishly preferring such things to the highest, immense and unchangeable good. Of these Jeremias speaks: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil, but to do good they have no knowledge|Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt]]. These are they [[Prov 2:14|who are glad when they have done evil|qui lætantur quum malefecerint]], to whom that of the Psalm applies: [[Ps 35:2|The unjust hath said within himself, that he would sin: there is no fear of God before his eyes|Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso; non est timor ante oculos ejus]]. [[34:27|and would not understand all his ways|Et omnes vias ejus intelligere noluerunt]], that is, they scorned to know the divine precepts, counsels, testimonies and teachings.
