Or if they knew them barely and in an unformed way, or wished to know them out of vanity for their own advantage, yet they would not know them with a formed and effective knowledge [*formata*: knowledge given its form by charity and issuing in deeds, as against a bare or "unformed" knowledge], of which John says in his first epistle: [[1 John 2:4|He who saith that he knoweth him and keepeth not his commandments is a liar|Qui dicit se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est]]. The ignorance of these men is inexcusable, aggravating and affected [that is, chosen on purpose, which makes the sin heavier rather than excusing it], like that of the Jews, of whom the Saviour says: [[John 15:22|If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin: but now they have no excuse|Si non venissem et locutus eis fuissem, peccatum non haberent: nunc autem excusationem non habent]]. Adding the cause of this: [[John 15:24|they have both seen|Viderunt]], he says, [[John 15:24|and hated both me and my Father|et oderunt me et Patrem meum]] [[John 15:25|without cause|gratis]]. Those, then, follow their malice who hate the teacher of the truth.

paras.t: De hac materia dicta sunt plura in superioribus; ubi etiam verbum istud sententialiter continetur, quum dicitur: Qui dixerunt Deo: Recede a nobis, scientiam viarum tuarum nolumus. Sed occurrit hic dubitatio una, quæ solet quosdam movere, quomodo scilicet aliquis peccet ex certa scientia atque malitia, seu ex deliberatione, et velut industria, quum tamen secundum beatissimum principem theologorum, divinum Dionysium, nullus respiciens ad malum, operetur, et juxta Philosophum, omnis malus sit ignorans. Secundum quem, etiam objectum appetitus, est bonum, ita ut malum (secundum quod tale) appeti nequeat. Et respondendum, quod nullus appetit aut efficit malum culpæ, in quantum est malum, sed in quantum est apparens bonum. Nisi enim videretur aliquo modo bonum, videlicet ad aliquid utile et delectabile, nullatenus appeteretur, nec fieret. Propter quod Salomon loquitur: Omnis viri via, recta sibi videtur. In quantum ergo peccator judicat aliquo modo bonum, quod vere est malum, errat atque ignorans vocatur. Hinc, secundum Philosophum, notitiam veri quam homo in generali sinceriter habet, passio seu malitia in particulari obtenebrat, ita quod caret scientia actuali formata, quæ dicitur practica et boni efficaciter approbativa. Itaque peccat quis ex deliberatione et certa scientia, quia quod agit, novit esse illicitum, et tamen id facere decrevit, loquendo de informi et nuda notitia; nihilo minus caret formata et actuali notitia sive scientia. Illa quoque informis notitia in particulari facto, ignorantiæ et errori alicui permiscetur, ut dictum est.
paras.en: Much has been said on this matter above, where this saying is also found in substance, when it is said: [[Job 21:14|Who have said to God: Depart from us, we desire not the knowledge of thy ways|Qui dixerunt Deo: Recede a nobis, scientiam viarum tuarum nolumus]]. But here a doubt arises which is wont to trouble some: how, namely, anyone can sin from certain knowledge and malice, or from deliberation and as it were of set purpose, since according to the most blessed prince of theologians, the divine Dionysius, no one acts with his eye on evil, and according to the Philosopher every wicked man is ignorant; and according to him, too, the object of the appetite is the good, so that evil (as such) cannot be desired. The answer is that no one desires or does the evil of fault [*malum culpae*, evil as sin, as against the evil of punishment] in so far as it is evil, but in so far as it is an apparent good. For unless it seemed good in some way, namely useful or delightful for something, it would never be desired or done. For which reason Solomon says: [[Prov 21:2|Every way of a man seemeth right to himself|Omnis viri via, recta sibi videtur]]. In so far, then, as the sinner judges that to be in some way good which is truly evil, he errs and is called ignorant. Hence, according to the Philosopher, passion or malice darkens in the particular case the knowledge of the truth which a man sincerely holds in general, so that he lacks the actual, formed knowledge which is called practical and which effectively approves the good. And so a man sins from deliberation and certain knowledge because he knows that what he does is unlawful and yet has resolved to do it (speaking of an unformed and bare knowledge); none the less he lacks formed and actual knowledge, or science. And that unformed knowledge, in the particular deed, is mixed with some ignorance and error, as has been said.

paras.t: Sic ergo perversi quasi de industria recesserunt a Deo, ejusque vias intelligere noluerunt, ut pervenire facerent ad eum clamorem, id est querelam, fletum, orationem, egeni, quem impie oppresserunt, et audiret Deus, id est, per effectum et exauditionem cognoscere se monstraret, vocem pauperum ab impiis afflictorum. Itaque, Ut, concomitanter, non causaliter, hic tenetur. Ex hoc enim quod perversi se tam impie habuerunt, consequitur quod Deus magis attendit seu audit vel vindicat eos qui opprimuntur ab illis. Unde in Genesi ait ad Cain: Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me. Et in Exodo: Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me: quia videlicet ab Ægyptiis opprimebantur crudeliter.
paras.en: So, then, the perverse [[34:27|as it were on purpose have revolted|quasi de industria recesserunt]] from God and would not understand his ways, [[34:28|So that they caused|ut pervenire facerent]] [[34:28|the cry|clamorem]] (that is, the complaint, the weeping, the prayer) [[34:28|of the needy|egeni]], whom they wickedly oppressed, [[34:28|to come to him|ad eum]], [[34:28|and he heard|et audiret]], that is, God, showing by effect and by granting their prayer that he knew it, [[34:28|the voice of the poor|vocem pauperum]] afflicted by the wicked. And so *ut*, "so that", is taken here of what follows along with it, not of a cause [that is, it marks a consequence, not a purpose]. For from the fact that the perverse behaved so wickedly, it follows that God attends more to, or hears, or avenges, those who are oppressed by them. Whence in Genesis he says to Cain: [[Gen 4:10|the voice of thy brother's blood crieth to me|Vox sanguinis fratris tui clamat ad me]]. And in Exodus: [[Ex 3:9|the cry of the children of Israel is come unto me|Clamor filiorum Israel venit ad me]]: because, that is, they were cruelly oppressed by the Egyptians.

paras.t: Ipso enim concedente pacem, quis est qui condemnet? Id est, si Deus dederit alicui pacem pectoris in præsenti, vel pacem æternitatis in futuro, quam potissime dat pauperibus et oppressis, nullus poterit electum hunc Dei damnare; quod si Deus concesserit pacem temporis, nullus poterit temporaliter perturbare, Deo resistere, ejus propositum opusque impedire. Sic et Apostolus ait: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Ex quo absconderit vultum suum, id est, gratiam contemplationis atque præsentiæ suæ gratiosam serenitatem abstraxerit: quod etiam bonis aliquando dispensative quodammodo facit; quis est qui contempletur eum? Nullus plane, quia ad contemplationem summæ et incomprehensibilis veritatis, ad intuendam pulchritudinem Dei, ad delectandum in eo sinceriter, requiruntur gratia gratum faciens, caritas, donumque sapientiæ. Et super gentem et super omnes homines, id est, tam in qualibet gente, quam in tota hominum multitudine seu in hominibus singulis, istud dictum locum et veritatem sortitur, quod scilicet Deo pacem donante, non est qui damnet; et si vultum suum absconderit, non est qui hominem consoletur. Hoc patet (secundum Gregorium) in gentilitate conversa, et in Synagoga relicta. Nullus ergo suis viribus gratiam contemplationis adscribat.
paras.en: [[34:29|For when he granteth peace, who is there that can condemn|Ipso enim concedente pacem, quis est qui condemnet]]? That is, if God has given anyone peace of heart in the present, or the peace of eternity in the future, which he gives above all to the poor and the oppressed, no one will be able to condemn this chosen one of God; and if God has granted peace in time, no one will be able to disturb it in time, to resist God, or to hinder his purpose and his work. So too the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:31|If God be for us, who is against us|Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos]]? [[34:29|When he hideth his countenance|Ex quo absconderit vultum suum]], that is, when he has withdrawn the grace of contemplation and the gracious serenity of his presence (which in a manner he does at times even to the good, by way of dispensation), [[34:29|who is there that can behold him|quis est qui contempletur eum]]? No one at all; for the contemplation of the highest and incomprehensible truth, for gazing on the beauty of God and delighting in him sincerely, there are required sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God], charity, and the gift of wisdom. [[34:29|whether it regard nations, or all men|Et super gentem et super omnes homines]] [Denis reads *gentem*, "nation", where the Vulgate has *gentes*], that is, this saying finds its place and its truth as well in any nation as in the whole multitude of mankind, or in men one by one: namely that when God gives peace there is none to condemn, and if he hides his face there is none to console man. This is seen (according to Gregory) in the Gentiles converted and in the Synagogue forsaken. Let no one, then, ascribe the grace of contemplation to his own powers.

paras.t: Qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi. Deus indignos, insufficientes, inidoneosque prælatos seu principes aliis præficere dicitur permissive magis quam effective, nisi forte in quantum per impios præsidentes corrigit et emendat vitia subditorum, electos purgans subjectos per rectores iniquos. Hinc per Isaiam ait: Dabo pueros principes eorum, et effeminati dominabuntur eis. Atque in Osee: Dabo tibi regem in furore meo, et principes in indignatione mea. Hoc ergo propter populi fit peccata. Denique, quod interim particulariter agitur, in fine sæculi generalissime durissimeque complebitur, quando propter Judæorum totiusque mundi excessus, homo peccati, filius perditionis Antichristus, mundi monarchiam suscipiet. De quo Judæis locutus est Christus: Ego veni in nomine Patris mei, et non accepistis me. Si alius venerit in nomine suo, illum accipietis. De quo ad Thessalonicenses scribit Apostolus: Mittet illis Deus operationem erroris, ut credant mendacio, eo quod caritatem veritatis non receperunt.
paras.en: [[34:30|Who maketh a man that is a hypocrite to reign for the sins of the people|Qui regnare facit hominem hypocritam propter peccata populi]]. God is said to set unworthy, inadequate and unfit prelates or princes over others by permitting it rather than by bringing it about, except perhaps in so far as through wicked rulers he corrects and amends the vices of their subjects, purging the elect among the subjects through wicked rulers. Hence he says through Isaias: [[Is 3:4|I will give children to be their princes, and the effeminate shall rule over them|Dabo pueros principes eorum, et effeminati dominabuntur eis]]. And in Osee: [[Osee 13:11|I will give thee a king in my wrath|Dabo tibi regem in furore meo]], and princes [[Osee 13:11|in my indignation|in indignatione mea]] [the Vulgate has "and will take him away in my indignation"; Denis reads *et principes*, "and princes"]. This, then, comes about for the sins of the people. Lastly, what is done meanwhile in particular cases will be fulfilled most generally and most harshly at the end of the world, when for the excesses of the Jews and of the whole world the man of sin, the son of perdition, Antichrist, will take up the monarchy of the world. Of him Christ spoke to the Jews: [[John 5:43|I am come in the name of my Father, and you receive me not: if another shall come in his own name, him you will receive|Ego veni in nomine Patris mei, et non accepistis me. Si alius venerit in nomine suo, illum accipietis]]. Of him the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: [[2 Thess 2:10|God shall send them the operation of error, to believe lying|Mittet illis Deus operationem erroris, ut credant mendacio]], [[2 Thess 2:10|because they receive not the love of the truth|eo quod caritatem veritatis non receperunt]] [in the Vulgate *Mittet illis* begins verse 11; the Douay-Rheims prints all these words in verse 10].

paras.t: Hinc ait Gregorius: Nullus qui injustum rectorem patitur, illum immoderanter accuset, quoniam sui fuit meriti, perversi rectoris subjacere ditioni: culpam ergo proprii magis accuset operis, quam injustitiam gubernantis. Sic quoque secundum merita subditorum, tribuuntur personæ regentium, ut sæpe qui videntur boni, accepto mox regimine permutentur, sicut de Saule primo Regum habetur. Iterum sic pro qualitatibus subditorum aliquando disponuntur acta regentium, ut sæpe pro malo gregis, delinquat etiam vita boni pastoris, ut patet de David in numeratione populi: cujus culpam ideo populus luit. Sed quia ipse David culpa in hoc ipso non caruit, nam voluntarie superbiens fuit, hinc et ipse punitus est: quia intimo dolore atque ingenti timore angelum intuendo, et populi sui plagam cernendo, fuit prostratus. Sed quia rectores habent judicem suum, magna cautela est subditorum, non temere judicare vitam regentium, sed propriam infirmitatem incessanter pensare. Sæpe etenim quia de nobis ipsis fortia credimus, prælatos nostros districte judicamus. Quo enim nos ipsos minus cognoscimus, eo illos quos reprehendere nitimur, plus videmus. Hæc atque similia multa, pulchra ac valde utilia, circa hunc locum scribit Gregorius de his, quæ præsidentes subditosque concernunt, et quomodo quilibet eorum de se ipso humiliter æstimare et ad alium habere se debeat: quæ in Gregorio requirantur.
paras.en: Hence Gregory says: Let no one who suffers an unjust ruler accuse him immoderately, since it was by his own desert that he became subject to the sway of a perverse ruler; let him therefore accuse the fault of his own doing rather than the injustice of the one who governs. So too the persons of rulers are allotted according to the deserts of their subjects, so that often those who seem good are changed as soon as they have received the rule, as is told of Saul in the first book of Kings[[1 Kings 15:17||]] [the margin's reference is unread; 1 Kings 15:17, where Samuel recalls that Saul was once little in his own eyes, is a likely place]. Again, the acts of rulers are sometimes so ordered according to the qualities of their subjects that often, for the evil of the flock, even the life of a good shepherd goes astray, as is plain of David in the numbering of the people[[2 Kings 24:1||]], whose fault the people therefore paid for[[2 Kings 24:15||]]. But because David himself was not without fault in this very thing (for he was wilfully proud), he too was punished: for he was laid low with inward grief and great fear on seeing the angel and beholding the plague of his people[[2 Kings 24:17||]] [the margin's references in this passage are mostly unread; the story is 2 Kings 24]. But because rulers have their own judge, it is a great caution for subjects not to judge rashly the life of those who rule, but to weigh their own weakness unceasingly. For often, because we think ourselves strong, we judge our superiors severely; for the less we know ourselves, the more we see in those whom we try to find fault with. These and many like things, beautiful and very useful, Gregory writes on this place, about what concerns rulers and subjects, and how each of them ought to think humbly of himself and bear himself towards the other: let them be sought in Gregory.

paras.t: Postremo, Eliu ideo verbum istud induxit, ut insinuaret ipsum Job fuisse hypocritam, et propter populi sui peccata, divina permissione regnasse.
paras.en: Lastly, Eliu brought in this saying to hint that Job himself had been a hypocrite, and had reigned by God's permission for the sins of his people.

paras.t: Consequenter alloquitur sanctum Job. Quia ergo locutus sum, probando intentum, ad Deum, id est ad ipsius honorem, atque finaliter propter eum, ad quem etiam aliquando direxi sermonem, te quoque non prohibeo loqui. Disputantium enim est, se invicem audire. Si erravi, tu doce me. Condisputantes etenim dociles esse debent, non pertinaces. Ideo si unus alio quid melius novit, alter acquiescere debet. Nec propter victoriam aut laudem inanem, sed propter veritatis notitiam et virtutis profectum disputatio fieri debet ex caritate. Si iniquitatem locutus sum, id est verba iniqua, ultra non addam: quia peccatis præteritis non sunt nova addenda, sed de illis dolendum, et de futuris cavendum, secundum illud Ecclesiastici: Fili, peccasti? ne adjicias iterum, sed et de præteritis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur, et quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata. Præterea (juxta Gregorium) consuetudo arrogantium est, tunc auditores de verborum suorum errore inquirere, quum se noverint non errasse, sed fortia quædam dixisse, ut de ipsa inquisitione laudentur: qui tamen de errore argui aspernantur, dum errasse noscuntur.
paras.en: Next he addresses holy Job. [[34:31|Seeing then I have spoken|Quia ergo locutus sum]], in proving my point, [[34:31|of God|ad Deum]] [literally "to God"], that is, for his honour, and with him for my end, to whom also I have at times directed my speech, [[34:31|I will not hinder thee|te quoque non prohibeo]] from speaking. For it belongs to disputants to hear one another. [[34:32|If I have erred, teach thou me|Si erravi, tu doce me]]. For those who dispute together ought to be teachable, not stubborn; so if one knows something better than the other, the other ought to give way. And a disputation ought to be held out of charity, not for victory or empty praise, but for the knowledge of the truth and progress in virtue. [[34:32|if I have spoken iniquity|Si iniquitatem locutus sum]], that is, wicked words, [[34:32|I will add no more|ultra non addam]]: because new sins are not to be added to past ones, but one must grieve for those and beware of those to come, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 21:1|My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more: but for thy former sins also pray that they may be forgiven thee|Fili, peccasti? ne adjicias iterum, sed et de præteritis deprecare, ut tibi dimittantur]], and [[Ecclus 21:2|Flee from sins as from the face of a serpent|quasi a facie colubri fuge peccata]]. Moreover (according to Gregory) it is the custom of the arrogant to ask their hearers about the error of their words when they know that they have not erred but have said something forceful, so that they may be praised for the very asking; and yet they scorn to be reproved for error when they are known to have erred.

paras.t: Numquid a te Deus expetit eam? id est, si loquendo iniquitatem incurri, hanc Deus exquiret a me, non a te: quoniam ego pro ea rationem dare et pœnam perpeti exigar, non tu; quia displicuit tibi iniquitas mea vel sermo meus. Ideo pro meo peccato non punieris: sicut frequenter unus fit particeps culpæ alterius per consensum ad illam. Quasi dicat: Non debes de verborum meorum prosecutione turbari, quia si in his excedo, egomet puniar. Unusquisque enim, teste Apostolo, pro se ipso rationem reddet. Ad quod insuper aliam rationem adducit: Tu enim cœpisti loqui, id est, occasionem huic disputationi dedisti, dicendo, Pereat dies in qua natus sum, etc., et non ego. Hoc etiam Eliu ait, quoniam culpabiliores esse solent qui in contentionibus inchoant, quam qui respondent. Quod si quid melius nosti, loquere: quod dicit, non putando quod Job aliquid melius ipso sciret, sed ut eum magis confunderet. Imo ad ostendendum insipientiam sancti Job, superbe mox subdit:
paras.en: [[34:33|Doth God require it of thee|Numquid a te Deus expetit eam]]? That is, if in speaking I have fallen into iniquity, God will require it of me, not of thee: since I, not thou, shall be made to give account for it and suffer the penalty; [[34:33|because it hath displeased thee|quia displicuit tibi]], my iniquity or my speech. Therefore thou wilt not be punished for my sin, in the way that one often becomes a sharer in another's fault by consenting to it. As if he said: Thou oughtest not to be troubled at my going on with my words, because if I go too far in them, I myself shall be punished. For [[Rom 14:12|every one|Unusquisque]], as the Apostle witnesses, [[Rom 14:12|shall render account to God for himself|pro se ipso rationem reddet]]. To this he adds a further reason: [[34:33|for thou begannest to speak|Tu enim cœpisti loqui]], that is, thou gavest occasion to this disputation by saying, [[Job 3:3|Let the day perish wherein I was born|Pereat dies in qua natus sum]], etc., [[34:33|and not I|et non ego]]. Eliu says this too because those who start quarrels are usually more to blame than those who answer. [[34:33|but if thou know any thing better, speak|Quod si quid melius nosti, loquere]]: this he says, not thinking that Job knew anything better than himself, but to confound him the more. Indeed, to show the folly of holy Job, he proudly goes on at once:

paras.t: Viri intelligentes loquantur mihi, quia tales dumtaxat digni et apti sunt mecum conferre et disputare; et vir sapiens audiat me, quia talis solum capax est sententiæ verborum meorum. Quasi dicat: Iste Job propter passiones et vitia sua, indignus est me alloqui et audire. Hinc subditur: Job autem stulte locutus est: quum tamen jam dictum sit, In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis, nec stultum quid contra Deum locutus est. Et verba illius non sonant disciplinam, id est, non indicant eum moralem, reformatum et disciplinatum, nec continent veram doctrinam: imo ostendunt, quod sit penitus vitiosus. Siquidem minus dicit, et magis significat. In quibus verbis rursus Eliu præsumptionem suam arrogantiamque demonstrat. Verumtamen consequenter zelum Dei habere se simulat.
paras.en: [[34:34|Let men of understanding speak to me|Viri intelligentes loquantur mihi]], since only such are worthy and fit to confer and dispute with me; [[34:34|and let a wise man hearken to me|et vir sapiens audiat me]], since only such a one can take in the meaning of my words. As if he said: This Job, because of his passions and vices, is unworthy to speak with me and to hear me. Hence it is added: [[34:35|But Job hath spoken foolishly|Job autem stulte locutus est]]: though it has already been said: [[Job 1:22|In all these things Job sinned not by his lips, nor spoke he any foolish thing against God|In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis, nec stultum quid contra Deum locutus est]][[Job 2:10||]] [the margin gives Job 1:22, and with it what seems to be ii, 10: Job 2:10 repeats the first words]. [[34:35|and his words sound not discipline|Et verba illius non sonant disciplinam]], that is, they do not show him to be moral, reformed and disciplined, nor do they contain true doctrine; rather they show that he is wholly vicious. For he says less and means more [that is, the phrase is an understatement]. In these words Eliu again shows his presumption and arrogance. Yet next he feigns to have zeal for God.

paras.t: Pater mi, id est, o Deus creator, ratione conditionis et gubernationis Pater, probetur Job usque in finem, id est, usque ad mortem adversitatibus exerceatur, quousque ab errore cessaverit, et veritas tua ei per flagella ista probetur, quia per rationem instrui dedignatur. Ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis, hoc est, non cesses impium istum percutere, quia non emendatur verberibus, qui tantæ est impietatis, quasi homagium fecerit ipsi peccato. Unde Antichristum Apostolus hominem peccati appellat.
paras.en: [[34:36|My father|Pater mi]], that is, O God the Creator, Father by reason of creation and governance, [[34:36|let Job be tried even to the end|probetur Job usque in finem]], that is, let him be exercised with adversities until death, until he ceases from his error, and let thy truth be proved to him through these scourges, since he disdains to be taught by reason. [[34:36|cease not from the man of iniquity|Ne desinas ab homine iniquitatis]], that is, cease not to strike this wicked man, for he is not amended by blows, being of such impiety as though he had done homage to sin itself [Denis takes "man of iniquity" as one who has made himself sin's vassal: *homagium* is the homage a vassal does to his lord]. Whence the Apostle calls Antichrist [[2 Thess 2:3|the man of sin|hominem peccati]].

paras.t: Qui addidit super peccata sua alia multa et magna, blasphemiam: quæ est impositio falsi criminis in Deum, a quo se perhibet injuste judicatum et cæsum. Inter nos interim constringatur, id est, pœnis coarctetur, et flagellis cingatur, ut se libere movere non queat; et tunc, id est ita constrictus, ad judicium ultionis, videlicet pœnas condebitas divino judicio infligendas, provocet sermonibus suis blasphematoriis Deum, id est, causam pœnarum harum Deo ministret: non quod quietissimus et invariabilis Deus nostris vitiis aut modo aliquo provocetur; sed quoniam ob nostra peccata tales nobis pœnas infligit, quasi per hæc provocatus exsisteret. In tantum enim hoc est, ut etiam ira et furor ei ob similitudinem operis adscribantur. Porro quod ait, Provocet sermonibus suis Deum, non imprecative seu optative, sed ironice dixit. Quasi dicat, Obstinatus et incorrigibilis est, ideo peccet et agat quod vult: quemadmodum in Apocalypsi dicitur, Qui in sordibus est, sordescat adhuc.
paras.en: [[34:37|Because he addeth|Qui addidit]] [[34:37|upon his sins|super peccata sua]] many other great ones, [[34:37|blasphemy|blasphemiam]] [Denis reads *Qui addidit*, "who hath added", where the Vulgate has *quia addit*]: that is, the imputing of a false charge to God, by whom he declares he has been unjustly judged and struck. [[34:37|let him be tied fast in the mean time amongst us|Inter nos interim constringatur]], that is, let him be hemmed in with penalties and girt about with scourges, so that he cannot move freely; [[34:37|and then|et tunc]], that is, thus bound, [[34:37|let him provoke God|provocet]] [[34:37|to judgment|ad judicium]] of vengeance (namely to the penalties that are due to be inflicted by the divine judgment) [[34:37|with his speeches|sermonibus suis]], his blasphemous ones: that is, let him furnish God with the cause of these penalties. Not that God, who is utterly at rest and unchangeable, is provoked by our vices or in any way at all; but because for our sins he inflicts such penalties on us, as though he were provoked by them. So far is this so that even anger and fury are ascribed to him because of the likeness of the work. Further, when he says, [[34:37|let him provoke God|Provocet]] [[34:37|with his speeches|sermonibus suis]], he said it not as an imprecation or a wish, but ironically. As if he said: He is obstinate and incorrigible, so let him sin and do what he will; as it is said in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 22:11|he that is filthy, let him be filthy still|Qui in sordibus est, sordescat adhuc]].

35.title: Elucidatio litteralis capituli tricesimi quinti: Igitur Eliu hæc rursum locutus est
35.title_en: Literal explanation of the thirty-fifth chapter: Moreover Eliu spoke these words

paras.t: Igitur Eliu hæc rursum locutus est. Eliu multis argumentationibus usus est, et vicissim intento concluso, paulisper conticuit, dans locum respondendi beato Job. Quo silente, Eliu arbitrans eum, vel ex ignorantia, vel ex indignatione tacere, disputationem suam resumpsit, ipsumque Job acriter impugnavit, quia se victum non fatebatur, nec culpabilem affirmabat.
paras.en: [[35:1|Moreover Eliu spoke these words|Igitur Eliu hæc rursum locutus est]]. Eliu had used many arguments, and, having in his turn brought what he intended to a conclusion, fell silent for a little, giving blessed Job room to answer. When Job kept silent, Eliu, thinking that he was silent either from ignorance or from indignation, took up his disputation again and attacked Job sharply, because he would not admit himself beaten, nor declare himself guilty.

paras.t: Numquid æqua tibi videtur tua cogitatio, ut diceres, illam verbis prodendo, Justior Deo sum? Dixisti enim: Non tibi, o Deus, placet quod bonum est, id est vita seu actio virtuosa. Verba ista beatus Job non deprompsit formaliter, imo nec virtualiter; sed Eliu asserit eum ista dixisse, quia sequebantur ex præhabitis verbis Job, secundum quod ea Eliu intellexit. Siquidem superius ait Job: Quis mihi tribuat, ut veniam usque ad solium ejus (scilicet Dei)? Ponam coram eo judicium. Nolo multa fortitudine contendat mecum, nec magnitudinis suæ mole me premat. Proponat æquitatem contra me, et perveniat ad victoriam judicium meum. Ex quo sequi videtur, quod secundum sincerum processum justitiæ, Job in causa judiciali contra Deum prævaluisset, sicque senserit Deo esse se justiorem. Sed ad quem sensum verba illa protulerit, ibidem expositum est. Quod autem Job dixerit Deo, Non tibi placet quod justum est, Eliu sumpsit ex eo, quod Job superius dixit: Si fuero justus, non levabo caput, videlicet quasi non habeam spem placendi Deo per hoc.
paras.en: [[35:2|Doth thy thought seem right to thee, that thou shouldst say|Numquid æqua tibi videtur tua cogitatio, ut diceres]], by uttering it in words, [[35:2|I am more just than God|Justior Deo sum]]? [[35:3|For thou saidst: That which is right doth not please thee|Dixisti enim: Non tibi, o Deus, placet quod bonum est]] [Denis reads *Non tibi, o Deus, placet quod bonum est*, “that which is good doth not please thee, O God”], that is, a virtuous life or action. Blessed Job did not utter these words formally, nor even virtually [that is, neither in so many words nor by plain implication]; but Eliu asserts that he said them, because they followed from Job's earlier words, as Eliu understood them. For earlier Job said: [[Job 23:3|Who will grant me that|Quis mihi tribuat, ut]] I might [[Job 23:3|come even to his throne|veniam usque ad solium ejus]] (that is, God's)? [[Job 23:4|I would set judgment before him|Ponam coram eo judicium]]. [[Job 23:6|I would not that he should contend with me with much strength, nor overwhelm me with the weight of his greatness.|Nolo multa fortitudine contendat mecum, nec magnitudinis suæ mole me premat]] [[Job 23:7|Let him propose equity against me, and let my judgment come to victory.|Proponat æquitatem contra me, et perveniat ad victoriam judicium meum]] From which it seems to follow that, by an honest process of justice, Job would have prevailed in a lawsuit against God, and so that he thought himself more just than God. But in what sense he uttered those words has been explained in that place. And that Job said to God, [[35:3|That which is right doth not please thee|Non tibi placet quod justum est]], Eliu took from what Job said earlier: [[Job 10:15|if just, I shall not lift up my head|Si fuero justus, non levabo caput]]; as if, that is, he had no hope of pleasing God by it.

paras.t: Vel dixisti Deo: Quid, id est aliquid, tibi, o Deus, proderit, si ego peccavero. Vel legendum est hoc interrogative, eritque sensus: O Deus, quid proderit tibi, si ego peccavero? tanquam dicat: Placet tibi ut peccem, quasi hoc tibi prosit: et tamen quid tibi hoc potest prodesse? Sic itaque Eliu imponit beato Job errorem illorum qui dixerunt Deo nostram iniquitatem placere, quasi sibi ad aliqua utilem, ut scilicet ipse ex ea justior appareret, eamque ulciscendo, suam declararet justitiam: ad quod aliqui allegaverunt illud Psalmisti, Tibi soli peccavi, ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris. Contra quorum errorem Apostolus ad Romanos tertio disputat, inter reliqua dicens: Si Dei veritas in meo mendacio abundavit in gloriam ipsius, quid adhuc ego tanquam peccator judicor? Præterea, verbum istud Eliu imponit beato Job, quia superius dixit Deo: Cur mundum me esse non pateris?
paras.en: Or thou saidst to God: [[35:3|what|Quid]], that is, something, [[35:3|will it profit thee if I sin|tibi, o Deus, proderit, si ego peccavero]], O God [taken so, *Quid* asks nothing: “something will profit thee, O God, if I sin”]. Or this is to be read as a question, and the sense will be: O God, [[35:3|what will it profit thee if I sin?|quid proderit tibi, si ego peccavero?]] as though he were saying: It pleases thee that I sin, as if this were of profit to thee; and yet what profit can this be to thee? So Eliu lays on blessed Job the error of those who said that our iniquity pleases God, as being useful to him for something: namely, that he himself might appear more just by it, and by punishing it might show forth his justice. For this some alleged that saying of the Psalmist: [[Ps 50:6|To thee only have I sinned|Tibi soli peccavi]], [[Ps 50:6|that thou mayst be justified in thy words, and mayst overcome when thou art judged|ut justificeris in sermonibus tuis, et vincas quum judicaris]]. Against their error the Apostle disputes in the third chapter to the Romans, saying among other things: [[Rom 3:7|if the truth of God hath more abounded through my lie, unto his glory, why am I also yet judged as a sinner?|Si Dei veritas in meo mendacio abundavit in gloriam ipsius, quid adhuc ego tanquam peccator judicor?]] Moreover, Eliu lays this word on blessed Job because earlier he said to God: [[Job 10:14|why dost thou not suffer me to be clean|Cur mundum me esse non pateris]]?

paras.t: Itaque ego respondebo sermonibus tuis, quibus te justum probasti, ostendendo quod falsi sint; et amicis tuis tecum, id est tribus viris istis, qui a te convicti et tibi nunc consentientes, pariter tecum sunt reprobandi.
paras.en: [[35:4|Therefore I will answer thy words|Itaque ego respondebo sermonibus tuis]], by which thou hast proved thyself just, showing that they are false; [[35:4|and thy friends with thee|et amicis tuis tecum]], that is, these three men, who, having been overcome by thee and now agreeing with thee, are to be refuted together with thee.

paras.t: Suspice cœlum, id est orbes cœlestes et stellas, seu cives supernos, et intuere naturam, cursum, dignitatem, actionem et perfectionem omnium horum; et contemplare æthera quod altior te sit: id est, ex consideratione creaturarum istarum Dei altissimi, perpendere potes, quod Deus sit justior, altior, perfectior, sanctior, sapientior quam tu; sitque extra sphæram et ordinem activorum et passivorum, ita quod malum in eum cadere nullatenus possit. Invisibilia etenim Dei (secundum Apostolum) ex creatura mundi cognoscuntur. Et in libro Sapientiæ scriptum est: A magnitudine speciei et creaturæ, poterit creator horum cognoscibiliter videri. Unde et ab Isaia admonemur: Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc. Omnia equidem condidit Deus omnipotens perfectionaliter infinitus, ut sua in eis reluceret perfectio, atque ex creaturarum ordinisque earum consideratione, ipse a rationali creatura honoraretur. Propter quod in Proverbiis dicitur: Universa propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus. Ecclesiastes quoque ait: Fecit Deus opera sua ut timeatur. Denique, quamvis omne creatum finitum sit: omnia etenim in numero, mensura, et pondere Deus creavit; nihilominus ex creaturarum speculatione cognoscitur Creator esse immensus, hoc est infinitæ perfectionis in potestate, bonitate et sapientia. Ideo Eliu admonet ipsum Job ad cœli et ætheris seu aeris intuitionem. Quasi dicat: Si illa, o Job, rite consideras, cognoscis quod Deus sit te justior et absolute perfectior infinite. Ideo ei nec obesse vales, neque prodesse. Hinc subditur:
paras.en: [[35:5|Look up to heaven|Suspice cœlum]], that is, the heavenly spheres and the stars, or the citizens on high, [[35:5|and see|et intuere]] the nature, course, dignity, action and perfection of all these; [[35:5|and behold the sky, that it is higher than thee|et contemplare æthera quod altior te sit]]: that is, from the consideration of these creatures of the most high God thou canst weigh that God is more just, higher, more perfect, holier and wiser than thou; and that he is outside the sphere and order of things that act and are acted upon, so that evil can in no way fall upon him. For [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things|Invisibilia]] of God (according to the Apostle) are known [[Rom 1:20|from the creation of the world|ex creatura mundi]]. And in the book of Wisdom it is written: [[Wis 13:5|by the greatness of the beauty, and of the creature, the creator of them may be seen, so as to be known thereby|A magnitudine speciei et creaturæ, poterit creator horum cognoscibiliter videri]]. Hence we are also admonished by Isaias: [[Is 40:26|Lift up your eyes on high, and see who hath created these things|Levate in excelsum oculos vestros, et videte quis creavit hæc]]. Almighty God, infinite in perfection, made all things so that his perfection might shine out in them, and that from the consideration of creatures and of their order he might be honoured by the rational creature. For which reason it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 16:4|The Lord hath made all things for himself|Universa propter se ipsum operatus est Dominus]]. Ecclesiastes also says: [[Eccles 3:14|God hath made that he may be feared|Fecit Deus opera sua ut timeatur]] [the margin gives Eccle. iii, 11; the words are from 3:14, where Denis has *Fecit Deus opera sua ut timeatur*, “God made his works that he may be feared”]. Lastly, although everything created is finite (for God created all things in number, measure and weight[[Wis 11:21||]]), nevertheless from the contemplation of creatures the Creator is known to be immeasurable, that is, of infinite perfection in power, goodness and wisdom. Therefore Eliu urges Job to look at the heaven and the sky, or air. As though he were saying: If thou considerest these things rightly, O Job, thou knowest that God is more just than thou, and absolutely and infinitely more perfect. Therefore thou canst neither harm him nor profit him. Hence it is added:

paras.t: Si peccaveris, quid ei nocebis, qui invariabilis impassibilisque consistit? Et si multiplicatæ fuerint iniquitates tuæ, quid facies contra eum, id est in nocumentum ipsius seu minorationem perfectionis et beatitudinis ejus? Quamvis enim Deus in Scripturis frequenter perhibeat se ex hominum peccatis ad iracundiam provocari; imo in Isaia testatur: Laboravi sustinens. Et rursus: Præbuisti mihi laborem in iniquitatibus tuis. Itemque in Genesi de Deo asseritur, quod videns iniquitatem hominum, tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus, dixit: Pœnitet me fecisse hominem. Et per Malachiam loquitur: Si configet homo Deum, quia vos configitis me? Quamvis (inquam) ista atque similia in Scriptura veritatis contenta sint, non tamen ita dicuntur, quasi divina mens infinitæ tranquillitatis et gloriæ suæ internæ usquam sustineat detrimentum; sed propter similitudinem operis ejus ad extra, talia asseruntur. Ideo in Jeremia legitur: Numquid me ad iracundiam provocant? dicit Dominus; nonne semetipsos in confusione vultus sui?
paras.en: [[35:6|If thou sin, what shalt thou hurt him|Si peccaveris, quid ei nocebis]], who abides unchangeable and impassible? [[35:6|and if thy iniquities be multiplied, what shalt thou do against him?|Et si multiplicatæ fuerint iniquitates tuæ, quid facies contra eum]] that is, to his harm, or to the lessening of his perfection and beatitude? For God in the Scriptures often declares that he is provoked to anger by men's sins; indeed he testifies in Isaias: [[Is 1:14|I am weary of bearing them|Laboravi sustinens]]; and again: [[Is 43:24|thou hast wearied me with thy iniquities|Præbuisti mihi laborem in iniquitatibus tuis]]. Likewise it is said of God in Genesis that, seeing the iniquity of men[[Gen 6:5||]], [[Gen 6:6|being touched inwardly with sorrow of heart|tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus]], he said: [[Gen 6:7|it repenteth me that I have made|Pœnitet me fecisse]] man. And he speaks by Malachias: [[Mal 3:8|Shall a man afflict God, for you afflict me|Si configet homo Deum, quia vos configitis me]]? [Denis has *configet*, “shall pierce”, where the Vulgate has *affliget*.] Yet although (I say) these and similar things are contained in the Scripture of truth, they are not said as though the divine mind, of infinite tranquillity and inward glory, ever suffered loss; but such things are asserted because of the likeness of his outward working. Therefore we read in Jeremias: [[Jer 7:19|Do they provoke me to anger, saith the Lord? is it not themselves, to the confusion of their own countenance?|Numquid me ad iracundiam provocant? dicit Dominus; nonne semetipsos in confusione vultus sui?]]

paras.t: Porro, si juste egeris, quid donabis ei, aut quid de manu tua accipiet? id est, perfectioni ejus nihil adjicies, nec aliquid quo perficiatur, a te sumet. De quo ait Psalmographus: Dixi Domino: Deus meus es tu, quoniam bonorum meorum non eges.
paras.en: [[35:7|And if thou do justly, what shalt thou give him, or what shall he receive of thy hand?|Porro, si juste egeris, quid donabis ei, aut quid de manu tua accipiet?]] that is, thou wilt add nothing to his perfection, nor will he take from thee anything by which he might be perfected. Of which the Psalmographer says: [[Ps 15:2|I have said to the Lord, thou art my God, for thou hast no need of my goods.|Dixi Domino: Deus meus es tu, quoniam bonorum meorum non eges]]

paras.t: Nec obstat quod in Jeremia scriptum est: Date gloriam Domino Deo vestro, antequam contenebrescat; et in Apocalypsi: Regnavit Dominus Deus noster omnipotens: gaudeamus et exsultemus, et demus gloriam ei. Talia quippe dicuntur, non quod demus Deo quod ipse non habet, aut quo caret vel indiget; sed quia quod tenemur, vel ab ipso accepimus, ei exsolvimus, quemadmodum primo Paralipomenon David loquitur Deo: Quis ego et quis populus tuus, ut possimus tibi ista promittere? Tua enim sunt omnia, et quæ de manu tua accepimus, dedimus tibi.
paras.en: Nor does it stand in the way that it is written in Jeremias: [[Jer 13:16|Give ye glory to the Lord your God, before it be dark|Date gloriam Domino Deo vestro, antequam contenebrescat]]; and in the Apocalypse: [[Apoc 19:6|the Lord our God, the Almighty, hath reigned|Regnavit Dominus Deus noster omnipotens]]: [[Apoc 19:7|Let us be glad and rejoice and give glory to him|gaudeamus et exsultemus, et demus gloriam ei]]. For such things are said, not because we give God what he does not have, or what he lacks or needs, but because we pay him what we owe, or what we have received from him; as David speaks to God in the first book of Paralipomenon: [[1 Par 29:14|Who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to promise thee|Quis ego et quis populus tuus, ut possimus tibi ista promittere?]]? [Denis has *populus tuus*, “thy people”.] [[1 Par 29:14|all things are thine: and we have given thee what we received of thy hand|Tua enim sunt omnia, et quæ de manu tua accepimus, dedimus tibi]].

paras.t: Homini qui similis tui est, nocebit impietas tua. Culpa unius, alteri non nocet nocumento culpæ, ita quod propter peccatum unius, alter reddatur culpabilis culpa personali et propria, cui pœna sensus debeatur, nisi alter ex peccato alterius inducatur ad culpam, personaliter peccans per impatientiam, iram, consensum, aut simili modo. Sed peccatum uniuscujusque in proprium redundat auctorem. Propter quod Ecclesiasticus ait: Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam; et facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur. Ecclesiastes quoque: Qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber. Quomodo ergo impietas unius nociva est alteri? Et respondendum, quod impietas, id est impia et crudelis seu vitiosa actio unius, nociva est alteri directe nocumento pœnæ seu damno pœnali, inferendo damnum in persona, substantia, fama, aut sobole, ut patet de homicidio, oblocutione et furto. Interdum etiam et quasi indirecte, culpa unius nocet alteri nocumento culpabili, in quantum est sibi occasio delinquendi. Immediate tamen alter non incidit culpam personalem, nisi per propriam voluntatem, secundum Augustinum, dicentem quod peccatum adeo est voluntarium, quod si non esset voluntarium, non esset peccatum.
paras.en: [[35:8|Thy wickedness may hurt a man that is like thee|Homini qui similis tui est, nocebit impietas tua]]. The fault of one does not harm another with the harm of guilt, in such a way that because of one man's sin another is made guilty with a personal guilt of his own, to which the pain of sense is due [that is, positive punishment by suffering, as distinct from the pain of loss], unless the other is led into fault by the other's sin, sinning personally through impatience, anger, consent, or in some like manner. But each one's sin redounds upon its own author. For which reason Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 27:29|He that diggeth a pit, shall fall into it|Qui fodit foveam, incidet in eam]]; [[Ecclus 27:30|A mischievous counsel shall be rolled back upon the author|facienti nequissimum consilium, super ipsum devolvetur]]. Ecclesiastes also: [[Eccles 10:8|he that breaketh a hedge, a serpent shall bite him|Qui dissipat sepem, mordebit eum coluber]]. How then is one man's wickedness harmful to another? The answer must be that wickedness, that is, the wicked and cruel or vicious action of one, is harmful to another directly with the harm of punishment, or penal loss, by inflicting loss in person, substance, good name or offspring, as is plain in murder, slander and theft. Sometimes also, and as it were indirectly, the fault of one harms another with a harm of guilt, inasmuch as it is an occasion of sinning for him. Yet the other does not fall into personal guilt immediately, except through his own will, according to Augustine, who says that sin is so far voluntary that if it were not voluntary it would not be sin.

paras.t: Et filium hominis adjuvabit justitia tua. Virtus enim et perfectio unius alteri, imo et multis prodest, bonum exemplum præstando, veniam et gratiam impetrando, ad cautelam providam inducendo, ab erroribus corrigendo, ad veritatis notitiam perducendo. Ideo Jacobus monet: Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini: multum enim valet deprecatio justi assidua. Et in Ecclesiastico scriptum est: Videte quia non solum mihi laboravi, sed omnibus exquirentibus sapientiam. Denique, quomodo impietas unius noceat alteri, atque justitia unius alium juvet, præcipue constat ex eo quod ad Romanos ait Apostolus de Adam et Christo: Sicut per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per unius hominis obedientiam justi constituentur multi. Postremo, hoc loco, inter hominem et filium hominis, non oportet differentiam realem inducere. Siquidem in toto hoc libro rhetorice scripto, eadem res atque sententia sub aliis verbis frequenter exprimitur.
paras.en: [[35:8|and thy justice may help the son of man|Et filium hominis adjuvabit justitia tua]]. For the virtue and perfection of one profits another, and indeed many: by giving a good example, by obtaining pardon and grace, by leading to prudent caution, by correcting from errors, by bringing to the knowledge of the truth. Therefore James admonishes: [[Jas 5:16|pray one for another, that you may be saved. For the continual prayer of a just man availeth much|Orate pro invicem, ut salvemini: multum enim valet deprecatio justi assidua]]. And in Ecclesiasticus it is written: [[Ecclus 24:47|See ye that I have not laboured myself only, but for all that seek out|Videte quia non solum mihi laboravi, sed omnibus exquirentibus]] wisdom [Denis has *sapientiam*, “wisdom”, where the Vulgate has *veritatem*, “the truth”]. Lastly, how the wickedness of one harms another, and the justice of one helps another, appears above all from what the Apostle says to the Romans of Adam and Christ: [[Rom 5:19|as by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so also by the obedience of one, many shall be made just|Sicut per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per unius hominis obedientiam justi constituentur multi]]. Finally, no real difference should be drawn in this place between *man* and *son of man*: for in this whole book, which is written rhetorically, the same thing and the same thought are often expressed in other words.

paras.t: Insuper, quæ induxit, consequenter et explanat. Propter multitudinem calumniatorum clamabunt, id est, calumniam patientes dolorose vociferabuntur, et a Deo vel ab homine auxilium postulabunt propter injuriam et violentiam eis a calumniatoribus factam: sicut filii Israel clamaverunt ad Dominum in Ægypto, propter multitudinem Ægyptiorum calumniantium eos. Talis autem clamor venit interdum ex zelo justitiæ, prout in Evangelio ait Salvator: Deus non faciet vindictam electorum suorum, clamantium ad se die ac nocte? tanquam dicat, Imo utique faciet. Nam subjecit, Dico vobis, quia cito faciet vindictam illorum.
paras.en: Further, he goes on to explain what he has brought in. [[35:9|By reason of the multitude of oppressors they shall cry out|Propter multitudinem calumniatorum clamabunt]] [*calumniatores*: those who wrong others by false charges, extortion and violence], that is, those who suffer oppression will cry aloud in their pain, and will ask help of God or of man because of the injury and violence done to them by the oppressors: as the children of Israel cried to the Lord in Egypt[[Ex 2:23||]] because of the multitude of the Egyptians who oppressed them [the margin gives Exod. ii]. Now such a cry comes at times from zeal for justice, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: [[Luke 18:7|will not God revenge his elect who cry to him day and night?|Deus non faciet vindictam electorum suorum, clamantium ad se die ac nocte?]] as though he were saying: Indeed he certainly will. For he added: [[Luke 18:8|I say to you that he will quickly revenge them|Dico vobis, quia cito faciet vindictam illorum]].

paras.t: Juxta hanc expositionem, quod dicitur, Calumniatorum, active accipitur. Potest quoque sumi passive, eritque sensus: Propter multitudinem calumniatorum, id est injuriam violentiamque passorum, clamabunt calumniatores, quando pro suis peccatis debita sustinebunt tormenta. Prima tamen expositio sequentibus amplius consonat. Nam sequitur: et ejulabunt propter vim brachii tyrannorum, id est, impotentiores et inopes flebunt propter oppressionem et contumeliam eis a tyrannis et duris illatam.
paras.en: In this exposition the word [[35:9|oppressors|Calumniatorum]] is taken actively. It can also be taken passively [so that *calumniatorum* means “of the oppressed”], and the sense will be: [[35:9|By reason of the multitude of oppressors|Propter multitudinem calumniatorum]], that is, of those who have suffered injury and violence, the oppressors [[35:9|shall cry out|clamabunt]], when they suffer the torments due for their sins. But the first exposition agrees better with what follows. For there follows: [[35:9|and shall wail for the violence of the arm of tyrants|et ejulabunt propter vim brachii tyrannorum]], that is, the weaker and the needy will weep because of the oppression and insult brought upon them by tyrants and hard men.

paras.t: Quod spiritualiter sumi potest. Quemadmodum enim quidam corporalia damna inferunt, persuadendo aut opprimendo: sic quidam spiritualiter nocent ad vitia inducendo, blandiendo aut perterrendo. Unde, secundum Augustinum, duplicem aciem mundus producit adversus Dei electos seu martyres. Nam blanditur ut fallat, terret ut vincat.
paras.en: This can be taken spiritually. For as some inflict bodily harm, by persuading or by oppressing, so some do harm spiritually, leading into vices by flattering or by terrifying. Hence, according to Augustine, the world draws up a double battle-line against God's elect, or martyrs: for it flatters in order to deceive, and terrifies in order to conquer.

paras.t: Et non dicit: Ubi est Deus qui fecit me? Hoc quidam singulariter trahunt ad Job, ita quod Eliu dicere voluit, quod Job contradicendo divinæ justitiæ, et in adversis cedendo impatientiæ, non attendit divinæ majestatis præsentiam, nec pensavit Deum esse suum factorem et omnium justissimum conditorem.
paras.en: [[35:10|And he hath not said: Where is God, who made me|Et non dicit: Ubi est Deus qui fecit me]]? Some refer this to Job in particular, so that Eliu meant that Job, by contradicting the divine justice and by giving way to impatience in adversity, did not attend to the presence of the divine majesty, nor consider that God is his Maker and the most just Founder of all things.

paras.t: Insuper, indeterminate accipi potest, quod quicumque in adversis deficiens, non dicit verbo seu facto, Ubi est Deus qui fecit me? id est, in ipso non sperat, et ejus adsistentiam non perpendit, neque præsentiam intuetur. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Quisquis adversitatum tribulatione frangitur, a quo factus sit, minime contemplatur. Nam Deus, qui quod non erat, fecit, factum sine gubernatione non deserit; et qui benigne hominem condidit, nequaquam cruciari injuste eum permittit. Nunquam ergo injuste nos tribulari putemus.
paras.en: Moreover, it can be taken of anyone: whoever fails in adversity does not say, by word or deed, [[35:10|Where is God, who made me|Ubi est Deus qui fecit me]]? that is, he does not hope in him, and does not weigh his help, nor look to his presence. Hence Gregory says: Whoever is broken by the tribulation of adversities gives little thought to him by whom he was made. For God, who made what was not, does not forsake what he has made without governing it; and he who in his kindness made man by no means allows him to be tormented unjustly. Let us never think, then, that we are afflicted unjustly.

paras.t: Qui dedit carmina in nocte, id est cantica jucunda seu consolationem in adversitate: quia per gratiam suam dat Deus electis adversa cum gaudio ferre, prout Jacobus monet: Omne gaudium existimate, fratres, quum in diversas tentationes incideritis. Et Paulus ait: Spe gaudentes, in tribulatione patientes. Christus quoque hortatur: Gaudete in illa hora, et exsultate. Hinc dicit Gregorius: Carmen in nocte, est lætitia in tribulatione: quia etsi pressuris temporalitatis affligimur, spe æternorum gaudemus. In quibus verbis Eliu notat Job, quod in tribulationibus suis non debuit sic tristari.
paras.en: [[35:10|who hath given songs in the night|Qui dedit carmina in nocte]], that is, joyful songs, or consolation in adversity: for by his grace God grants the elect to bear adversity with joy, as James admonishes: [[Jas 1:2|count it all joy|Omne gaudium existimate]], brethren, [[Jas 1:2|when you shall fall into divers temptations|quum in diversas tentationes incideritis]]. And Paul says: [[Rom 12:12|Rejoicing in hope. Patient in tribulation|Spe gaudentes, in tribulatione patientes]]. Christ also exhorts: [[Luke 6:23|Be glad|Gaudete]] in that hour, [[Luke 6:23|and rejoice|et exsultate]]. Hence Gregory says: A song in the night is gladness in tribulation: for though we are afflicted by the pressures of this passing time, we rejoice in the hope of eternal things. In these words Eliu reproves Job, because in his tribulations he ought not to have been so sad.

paras.t: Vel sic: Qui dedit carmina, id est psalmos et spiritualia cantica ac revelationes per modum carminum scriptas; in nocte, id est in sæculo et caligine ignorantiæ vitæ hujus.
paras.en: Or thus: [[35:10|who hath given songs|Qui dedit carmina]], that is, psalms and spiritual canticles, and revelations written in the manner of songs; [[35:10|in the night|in nocte]], that is, in this world and in the darkness of the ignorance of this life.

paras.t: Vel, ad litteram, In nocte, quando revelationes divinæ communius fiunt, exterioribus (ut dictum est) sensibus quietatis. Talia carmina in libro Justorum poterant contineri, de quo Scriptura canonica facit aliquando mentionem. Unde Albertus: In nocte, inquit, ignorantiæ hujus prima carmina de Deo fuerunt, illud Catonis allegans: Si Deus est animus, nobis ut carmina dicunt.
paras.en: Or, according to the letter, [[35:10|in the night|In nocte]]: when divine revelations most commonly come, the outward senses (as has been said) being at rest. Such songs could have been contained in the book of the Just, of which the canonical Scripture sometimes makes mention[[Jos 10:13||]][[2 Kings 1:18||]]. Hence Albert says: In the night of this ignorance, he says, the first songs were about God; and he cites that line of Cato: If God is a spirit, as the songs tell us [the opening line of the *Distichs* ascribed to Cato; *carmina* there means “poems”, the same word as the “songs” of the verse].

paras.t: Qui docet nos super jumenta terræ, et super volucres cœli erudit nos. Illa enim sunt irrationalis naturæ, in quibus nec intellectus, nec ratio est, sed sola sensitiva cognitio. Hominibus autem contulit intellectum, quo inter verum et falsum, bonum et malum discernunt, a particularibus abstrahunt, immaterialia, insensibilia et divina cognoscunt, studendo proficiunt, unum ex alio considerant et concludunt. Insuper, Deus homines erudivit per legem scriptam et evangelicam, per illuminationem angelicam, per instructionem divinam; unum quoque hominem per alium multipliciter erudit: quod per Apostolos præcipue fecit, quemadmodum Paulus testatur, Corripientes, inquiens, omnem hominem, et docentes omnem hominem in omni sapientia.
paras.en: [[35:11|Who teacheth us more than the beasts of the earth, and instructeth us more than the fowls of the air|Qui docet nos super jumenta terræ, et super volucres cœli erudit nos]] [*super*, which the Douay-Rheims gives as “more than”, also means “above”: Denis uses both senses below]. For those are of an irrational nature, in which there is neither understanding nor reason, but only the knowledge of the senses. But to men he has given understanding, by which they distinguish between true and false, good and evil, abstract from particulars, know things immaterial, beyond the senses, and divine, make progress by study, and consider and conclude one thing from another. Moreover, God has taught men through the written law and the law of the Gospel, through the enlightenment of angels, through divine instruction; and he also teaches one man through another in many ways, which he did above all through the Apostles, as Paul testifies: [[Col 1:28|admonishing|Corripientes]], he says, [[Col 1:28|every man and teaching every man in all wisdom|omnem hominem, et docentes omnem hominem in omni sapientia]].

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per jumenta terræ, designantur homines carnalibus vitiis dediti; per volucres cœli, notantur superbi et curiosi: qui divinarum illustrationum capaces non sunt. Unde super illos, seu plus quam illos, Deus instruit virtuosos ac spirituales, quorum unum Eliu esse se sensit. Postremo, dispositioni animæ rationalis, qua inferioribus formis per rationem præfulget, etiam corporis dispositio correspondet. Non enim ut cetera animalia, habet homo corpus et vultum prona in terram, sed elevata ad cœlum, ut ex hoc perpendat se propter cœlestium ac divinorum contemplationem plasmatum, sicque terrenis et carnalibus spretis, ad superna feratur. Hinc Ovidius ait: Os homini sublime dedit, cœlumque tueri Jussit, et erectos ad sidera tollere vultus.
paras.en: Spiritually, by [[35:11|the beasts of the earth|jumenta terræ]] are signified men given to carnal vices; by [[35:11|the fowls of the air|volucres cœli]] are meant the proud and the curious, who are not capable of divine enlightenment. Hence God instructs the virtuous and spiritual above them, or more than them; and Eliu felt himself to be one of these. Lastly, the disposition of the body also answers to the disposition of the rational soul, by which, through reason, it outshines the lower forms. For man does not have his body and face bent down to the earth, like the other animals, but raised up towards heaven, so that from this he may weigh that he was formed for the contemplation of heavenly and divine things, and so, despising earthly and carnal things, may be borne towards the things above. Hence Ovid says: He gave man a lofty face, and bade him look upon the heavens and lift his countenance erect towards the stars.

paras.t: Ibi, videlicet in tribulatione, secundum Gregorium; vel, Ibi, id est, quia eruditioni qua Deus homines erudivit, non acquieverunt; clamabunt vitiosi atque feroces dignis plagis percussi, et non exaudiet eos Deus, propter superbiam malorum, id est propter eorum arrogantiam in qua manserunt, ac divinis præceptis fuerunt rebelles: ita quod non pœnituerunt veraciter, nec ex amore Dei, sed ex privato amore ac servili timore procedit clamor oratioque ipsorum. Unde in Proverbiis Dominus de talibus protestatur: Tunc (scilicet in adversitatis necessitatisque tempore) clamabunt, et non exaudiam; mane consurgent, et non invenient me, eo quod exosam habuerint disciplinam, et timorem Domini non susceperint. Et Psalmista fatetur: Clamaverunt, nec erat qui salvos faceret; ad Dominum, nec exaudivit eos. Itaque, qui desuper cupit audiri, nequaquam remaneat in affectu peccati, nec in voluntate peccandi; sed ex corde pœniteat et emendet, atque ad Deum mentaliter amorose conversus, ac justitiam zelans, preces fiducialiter fundat indesinenter. Hinc in Isaia Dominus loquitur: Si quæritis, quærite; convertimini et venite: hoc est, si me quæritis, vere et ex corde me quærite.
paras.en: [[35:12|There|Ibi]], namely in tribulation, according to Gregory; or, [[35:12|There|Ibi]], that is, because they did not rest content with the instruction with which God instructed men: there [[35:12|shall they cry|clamabunt]], namely the vicious and fierce, struck with the blows they deserve, [[35:12|and he will not hear|et non exaudiet]] them, that is, God will not, [[35:12|because of the pride of evil men|propter superbiam malorum]], that is, because of their arrogance, in which they persisted and were rebels against the divine commands: so that they did not truly repent, and their cry and prayer proceeds not from the love of God but from private love and servile fear. Hence in Proverbs the Lord declares of such men: [[Prov 1:28|Then|Tunc]] (that is, in the time of adversity and need) they shall cry [Denis has *clamabunt* where the Vulgate has *invocabunt me*], [[Prov 1:28|and I will not hear: they shall rise in the morning, and shall not find me|et non exaudiam; mane consurgent, et non invenient me]], [[Prov 1:29|Because they have hated instruction, and received not the fear of the Lord|eo quod exosam habuerint disciplinam, et timorem Domini non susceperint]]. And the Psalmist declares: [[Ps 17:42|They cried, but there was none to save them, to the Lord: but he heard them not.|Clamaverunt, nec erat qui salvos faceret; ad Dominum, nec exaudivit eos]] Therefore whoever desires to be heard from on high, let him by no means remain in the affection for sin, nor in the will to sin; but let him repent from the heart and amend, and, turned to God in mind and with love, and zealous for justice, let him pour out his prayers with confidence and without ceasing. Hence in Isaias the Lord says: [[Is 21:12|if you seek, seek: return, come|Si quæritis, quærite; convertimini et venite]]: that is, if you seek me, seek me truly and from the heart.

paras.t: Non enim frustra audiet Deus. Superius dixit, quod calumniam patientes seu injuriati, clamabunt et ejulabunt: quorum Deus audit clamorem. Deinde subjecit, quod Deus vitiosos et oppressores aliorum non audiet: cujus rationem assignans, nunc ait, Non enim frustra audiet Deus. Itaque sensus est, quod Deus non frustra audiet clamorem, precem et gemitum afflictorum; sed pie atque salubriter eos exaudiet: quorum clamorem frustra audiret, si et oppressores eorum in suis precibus exaudiret, præsertim quia (ut dictum est) oppressi, ex zelo justitiæ orant Deum, ut adversariorum suorum impietatem ac ferociam debite ulciscatur. Et Omnipotens causas singulorum intuebitur, id est, actus, negotia, necessitates, vota, preces et studia omnium considerabit, imo indesinenter considerat, ut omnia juste judicet et disponat. Circa quod scribit Gregorius: Nemo qui tardius exauditur, credat quod a superna cura negligitur. Sæpe enim quod impleri velociter petimus, ex ipsa tarditate melius prosperatur.
paras.en: [[35:13|God therefore will not hear in vain|Non enim frustra audiet Deus]] [Denis reads *enim*, “for”, where the Vulgate has *ergo*, “therefore”, and takes the words as giving a reason]. He said above that those who suffer oppression or are wronged will cry and wail, and God hears their cry. Then he added that God will not hear the vicious and the oppressors of others; and, giving the reason for this, he now says, [[35:13|God therefore will not hear in vain|Non enim frustra audiet Deus]]. So the sense is that God will not hear in vain the cry, prayer and groaning of the afflicted, but will hear them graciously and for their salvation; whereas he would hear their cry in vain if he also heard their oppressors in their prayers, especially since (as has been said) the oppressed pray to God, out of zeal for justice, that he may duly avenge the wickedness and ferocity of their adversaries. [[35:13|and the Almighty will look into the causes of every one|Et Omnipotens causas singulorum intuebitur]], that is, he will consider, and indeed unceasingly considers, the acts, dealings, needs, vows, prayers and pursuits of all, so as to judge and order all things justly. On which Gregory writes: Let no one who is heard more slowly believe that he is neglected by the care on high. For often what we ask to be fulfilled quickly prospers the better for the very delay.

paras.t: Etiam quum, o Job, dixeris, Non considerat, id est, Deus hominum acta non pensat, nec judicat; judicare coram illo, id est, coram Deo judica per rectam rationem te ipsum, omnia tua discutiendo, et invenies quod Deus providentiam actuum habeat humanorum, et quod per tuos excessus justo ejus judicio sis percussus. Vel, Judicare coram illo, id est, ab eo utique judicaberis, et per damnationis tuæ experientiam scies, quod Deus cuncta consideret. Ideo subditur: et exspecta eum. Quasi dicat, Tempore suo videbis quantum erraveris: juxta illud Machabæorum, Sustine, et videbis qualiter te Deus torquebit.
paras.en: [[35:14|Yea, when thou shalt say: He considereth not|Etiam quum, o Job, dixeris, Non considerat]] [Denis adds *o Job*: “Yea, when thou, O Job, shalt say”], that is, God does not weigh or judge the acts of men: [[35:14|be judged before him|judicare coram illo]], that is, before God judge thyself by right reason, examining all thy doings, and thou wilt find that God has providence over human acts, and that thou hast been struck by his just judgment for thy excesses. Or, [[35:14|be judged before him|Judicare coram illo]], that is, thou shalt surely be judged by him, and through the experience of thy damnation thou shalt know that God considers all things [Denis takes *judicare* first as a command, “judge (thyself)”, then as a future, “thou shalt be judged”]. Therefore it is added: [[35:14|and expect him|et exspecta eum]]. As though he were saying: In his own time thou shalt see how far thou hast erred; according to that saying of the Machabees: [[2 Mach 7:17|stay patiently|Sustine]], [[2 Mach 7:17|and thou shalt see|et videbis]] [[2 Mach 7:17|in what manner he will torment thee|qualiter te Deus torquebit]].

paras.t: Nunc enim non infert furorem suum, id est, in hac vita Deus peccatores longanimiter tolerat, et pœnitentiam eorum patienter exspectat. Flagella quoque quæ hic infert, ex misericordia prodeunt, et ad correctionem hominum communiter ordinantur: quoniam pœnæ vitæ præsentis medicinales dicuntur, tanquam ad correctionem patientium ordinatæ; quamvis interdum contingat oppositum in quibusdam, quos Deus in vita hac horribiliter plagat, et æternaliter insuper damnat, ut in Pharaone et suis, in Dathan et Abiron innotescit. Nec ulciscitur scelus valde, id est, peccata hominum in sæculo isto non vindicat secundum rigorem suæ justitiæ, nec multum districte, sed citra condignum et pie nunc punit et admonet per adversa, juxta illud Sapientis: Misereris omnium, Domine, quoniam omnia potes, et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam. Hæc autem Eliu introducit contra ea quæ superius Job induxit, in quibus asseruit se ultra quam meruit flagellatum, et quod contra eum furor Dei esset iratus. Præterea, juxta Gregorium, Deus diu nunc impios tolerat, quoniam æternaliter damnat; et furorem suum nunc inferre dissimulat, quia effundendum sine fine in posterum servat. Eant ergo nunc reprobi, et voluptatum suarum desideria inulta iniquitate consumment: atque eo temporalia flagella non sentiant, quo supplicia eos æterna exspectant.
paras.en: [[35:15|For he doth not now bring on his fury|Nunc enim non infert furorem suum]], that is, in this life God bears with sinners long-sufferingly, and waits patiently for their repentance. The scourges too which he brings on here proceed from mercy and are commonly ordained for the correction of men: for the pains of the present life are called medicinal, as being ordained for the correction of those who suffer them; although at times the opposite happens in some, whom God strikes horribly in this life and damns eternally besides, as is shown in Pharao and his men[[Ex 14:28||]], and in Dathan and Abiron[[Num 16:32||]] [the margin here is hard to read: it seems to give Exod. xiv and Num. xvi, with the verses unclear]. [[35:15|neither doth he revenge wickedness exceedingly|Nec ulciscitur scelus valde]], that is, he does not punish men's sins in this world according to the rigour of his justice, nor very strictly, but now punishes and admonishes through adversity mercifully and short of what is deserved, according to that saying of the Wise man: [[Wis 11:24|thou hast mercy upon all|Misereris omnium]], O Lord, [[Wis 11:24|because thou canst do all things, and overlookest the sins of men for the sake of repentance|quoniam omnia potes, et dissimulas peccata hominum propter pœnitentiam]]. Now Eliu brings this in against what Job alleged above, where he asserted that he had been scourged beyond what he deserved, and that the fury of God was angered against him. Moreover, according to Gregory, God now bears long with the wicked because he damns them eternally; and he forbears now to bring on his fury, because he keeps it to be poured out without end hereafter. Let the reprobate go on now, then, and fulfil the desires of their pleasures with unpunished iniquity; and let them feel no temporal scourges, for the very reason that eternal torments await them.

paras.t: Ex præinductis concludit: Ergo Job frustra aperit os suum, quia quod loquendo intendit ostendere, non potest firmis rationibus comprobare. Sed oppositum jam probavi. Et absque scientia verba multiplicat, id est, indiscrete et insipienter est garrulus, quemadmodum in Ecclesiaste legitur: Stultus verba multiplicat. Porro, secundum Gregorium, proprium arrogantium esse solet, ut pauca credant, quæ ipsi multa dixerint, et multa credant, quæ ipsis pauca dicuntur. Quia enim sua semper dicere volunt, aliena audire non possunt; vim se pati existimant, si ea quæ immoderate sentiunt, immoderatius non effundant.
paras.en: From what he has brought in before, he concludes: [[35:16|Therefore Job openeth his mouth in vain|Ergo Job frustra aperit os suum]], because what he intends to show by speaking he cannot prove by firm reasons. But I have now proved the opposite. [[35:16|and multiplieth words without knowledge|Et absque scientia verba multiplicat]], that is, he chatters without discretion and foolishly, as we read in Ecclesiastes: [[Eccles 10:14|A fool multiplieth words|Stultus verba multiplicat]]. Further, according to Gregory, it is commonly the mark of the arrogant to think few the many things they have said themselves, and to think many the few things said to them. For because they always want to say their own things, they cannot listen to those of others; they think they suffer violence if they do not pour out still more immoderately what they immoderately think.

36.title: Elucidatio capituli tricesimi sexti: Addens quoque Eliu.
36.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-sixth chapter: Eliu also proceeded

paras.t: Addens quoque Eliu, hæc etiam locutus est. Tacente beato Job, Eliu positionem suam multipliciter confirmare curavit, et nunc in isto capitulo aliis rationibus probat idem, quod superius jam probavit. Sustine me paululum, id est, patienter me audi paulisper, quia succincte loquar, et indicabo tibi quod verum est, et quod scire te convenit. Adhuc enim habeo quod pro Deo loquar, id est, alias intueor rationes ad defendendum justitiam Dei, cui tu derogas, dum te ipsum præsumptuose justificas. Repetam scientiam meam a principio, id est, ea quæ ab exordio hujus disputationis locutus sum de ista materia, nunc de novo plenius prosequar, eademque cum clariori probatione resumam; et operatorem, id est Deum creatorem, meum probabo justum. Vere enim absque mendacio sermones mei. Veruntamen Eliu iste nonnunquam false conclusit, et ex veris præmissis contra Job inania intulit. Et perfecta scientia probabitur tibi: id est, probabo tibi, quod scientia mea quam de Deo et ejus providentia, æquitate, judicio habeo et propono, sit integraliter vera, et in genere suo perfecta, videlicet quantum spectat ad viatorem meumque statum. Perfectum quippe pluribus dicitur modis.
paras.en: [[36:1|Eliu also proceeded, and said|Addens quoque Eliu, hæc etiam locutus est]]. Blessed Job keeping silent, Eliu took care to confirm his position in many ways, and now in this chapter he proves by other arguments the same thing that he proved above. [[36:2|Suffer me a little|Sustine me paululum]], that is, hear me patiently for a little while, for I shall speak briefly, [[36:2|and I will shew thee|et indicabo tibi]] what is true and what it befits thee to know. [[36:2|for I have yet somewhat to speak in God's behalf|Adhuc enim habeo quod pro Deo loquar]], that is, I see other arguments for defending the justice of God, which thou disparagest while thou presumptuously justifiest thyself. [[36:3|I will repeat my knowledge from the beginning|Repetam scientiam meam a principio]], that is, what I have said on this matter from the start of this disputation I shall now pursue afresh and more fully, and take up the same things again with clearer proof; [[36:3|and I will prove my Maker just|et operatorem, id est Deum creatorem, meum probabo justum]]: my Maker, that is, God the Creator. [[36:4|For indeed my words are without a lie|Vere enim absque mendacio sermones mei]]. Yet this Eliu sometimes drew false conclusions, and from true premises inferred empty things against Job. [[36:4|and perfect knowledge shall be proved to thee|Et perfecta scientia probabitur tibi]]: that is, I shall prove to thee that the knowledge which I hold and set forth concerning God and his providence, equity and judgment is wholly true, and perfect in its kind, namely as far as concerns a wayfarer [that is, a man still on the way in this life, not yet in the homeland of heaven] and my state. For "perfect" is said in many ways.

paras.t: Consequenter probat rectitudinem divini judicii. Deus potentes non abjicit, id est, ea ratione qua potentes sunt, eos non detestatur, nec odit, repellit aut damnat, quum et ipse sit potens, imo omnipotens. Non enim odit aut abjicit eos ob id, vel per id, in quo ei assimilantur: quoniam similitudo per se est causa dilectionis, secundum illud Ecclesiastici, Omne animal diligit simile sibi. Quum ergo potentes per potentiam Deo assimilentur, a quo illam etiam sortiuntur, prout ad Romanos legitur, Non est potestas nisi a Deo; constat quod ratione potentiæ eos non abjicit, sed quia abutuntur potentia: qua si bene utantur, eos acceptat, ut Samsonem, David, Judam Machabæum. Simili modo divites non abjicit, quum et ipse sit dives. Porro quod Sapiens habet, Potentes potenter tormenta patientur, et, Fortioribus fortior instat cruciatus, de potentibus et fortibus sua potentia abutentibus dictum est: quemadmodum et quod loquitur Christus, Possibilius est camelum intrare per foramen acus, quam divitem intrare in regnum cælorum.
paras.en: Next he proves the rightness of the divine judgment. [[36:5|God doth not cast away the mighty|Deus potentes non abjicit]], that is, he does not detest, hate, repel or condemn them by reason of their being mighty, [[36:5|whereas he himself also is mighty|quum et ipse sit potens]], nay almighty. For he does not hate or cast them away on account of, or through, that in which they are made like him; since likeness is of itself a cause of love, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 13:19|Every beast loveth its like|Omne animal diligit simile sibi]]. Since, then, the mighty are made like God through their might, which they also receive from him, as we read in Romans: [[Rom 13:1|there is no power but from God|Non est potestas nisi a Deo]]; it is plain that he does not cast them away by reason of their might, but because they abuse their might: if they use it well, he accepts them, as he did Samson, David and Judas Machabeus. In like manner he does not cast away the rich, since he himself also is rich. Moreover what the Wise Man has, [[Wis 6:7|the mighty shall be mightily tormented|Potentes potenter tormenta patientur]], and, [[Wis 6:9|a greater punishment is ready for the more mighty|Fortioribus fortior instat cruciatus]], was said of the mighty and strong who abuse their might; as was also what Christ says: [[Matt 19:24|It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle, than for a rich man to enter into the kingdom of heaven|Possibilius est camelum intrare per foramen acus, quam divitem intrare in regnum cælorum]].

paras.t: Sed non salvat impios impœnitentes: id est, si potentes abjicit et condemnat, hoc est propter impietatem eorum: in quo notat, quod Job qui tempore sanctitatis potentissimus fuit, propter sua sit abjectus et cæsus peccata. Sed argumentum istud nihil concludit. Quamvis enim Deus potentes justos non abjiciat, spiritualia dona eis tollendo aut damnationem infligendo; tamen quantum ad temporalem tribulationem et exteriorum bonorum privationem, eos aliquando abjicit seu quasi relinquit, propter majorem eorum profectum, et ob alias causas frequenter expressas. Et judicium pauperibus tribuit. Deus enim est pauperum specialis adjutor et judex in bonum eorum, juxta illud Psalmi: Tibi derelictus est pauper. Et item: Judicabit pauperes populi, et salvos faciet filios pauperum. Injuriam etiam pauperum singulariter vindicat.
paras.en: [[36:6|But he saveth not the wicked|Sed non salvat impios]] who are impenitent: that is, if he casts away and condemns the mighty, it is because of their wickedness. By this Eliu implies that Job, who in the time of his holiness was most mighty, was cast away and struck down for his sins. But this argument concludes nothing. For although God does not cast away the just among the mighty by taking spiritual gifts from them or inflicting damnation on them, yet as regards temporal tribulation and the loss of outward goods he sometimes casts them away, or as it were forsakes them, for their greater progress and for other causes often stated. [[36:6|and he giveth judgment to the poor|Et judicium pauperibus tribuit]]. For God is the special helper of the poor, and judge in their favour, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 9:35|To thee is the poor man left|Tibi derelictus est pauper]]. And again: [[Ps 71:4|He shall judge the poor of the people, and he shall save the children of the poor|Judicabit pauperes populi, et salvos faciet filios pauperum]]. He also avenges in a singular way the wrong done to the poor.

paras.t: Non aufert a justo oculos suos, id est, pietatis suæ respectum non subtrahit justis, imo per complacentiam respicit eos, et gratiose conservat ac diligit, etiam dum eos adversitatibus tribulationibusque exponit, juxta illud Psalmi: Cum ipso sum in tribulatione.
