Et reges in solio, id est throno regali, collocat in perpetuum, id est per omne tempus vitæ eorum, si potestate sua bene utantur, quemadmodum in Proverbiis inducitur: Rex qui judicat in veritate pauperes, thronus ejus in æternum firmabitur. Potestque perpetuatio ista ad successores regum referri, dummodo et successores hujusmodi justitiam patrum suorum sectentur. Et illi eriguntur potestate regali, vel elatione superbiæ. Et si fuerint in catenis, id est, propter suam iniquitatem et pompam humilientur et captiventur, catenisque constringantur, et vinciantur funibus paupertatis, id est, quibusdam penuriis velut funibus aggraventur, videlicet fame, siti, nuditate et frigore, indicabit eis opera eorum et scelera eorum: id est, per illa adversa Deus reducet eos ad vitiorum suorum considerationem, ita quod ex pœnis considerabunt proprias culpas, prout in Isaia habetur: Tantummodo sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui. Quia violenti fuerunt. Potentes enim, præcipue reges, multoties potestate utuntur pro lege justitiæ, nec voluntatem dirigunt ratione, dicentes verbo vel facto: Hoc volo, sic jubeo; sit pro ratione voluntas. Animosi sunt enim, et animositas rationem ineffabiliter cæcat. Hoc modo reduxit Manassen regem ad pœnitentiam, ut secundo Paralipomenon fertur.
paras.en: [[36:7|He will not take away his eyes from the just|Non aufert a justo oculos suos]], that is, he does not withdraw the regard of his kindness from the just; nay, he looks on them with good pleasure, and graciously keeps and loves them, even while he exposes them to adversities and tribulations, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation|Cum ipso sum in tribulatione]]. [[36:7|and he placeth kings on the throne|Et reges in solio]], that is, on the royal throne, [[36:7|for ever|collocat in perpetuum]], that is, through the whole time of their life, if they use their power well, as is brought forward in Proverbs: [[Prov 29:14|The king that judgeth the poor in truth, his throne shall be established for ever.|Rex qui judicat in veritate pauperes, thronus ejus in æternum firmabitur.]] And this perpetuity can also be referred to the successors of kings, provided that such successors too follow the justice of their fathers. [[36:7|and they are exalted|Et illi eriguntur]] by royal power, or by the elation of pride. [[36:8|And if they shall be in chains|Et si fuerint in catenis]], that is, if for their iniquity and pomp they are humbled and taken captive and bound fast with chains, [[36:8|and be bound with the cords of poverty|et vinciantur funibus paupertatis]], that is, are weighed down by certain wants as by cords, namely hunger, thirst, nakedness and cold, [[36:9|He shall shew them their works, and their wicked deeds|indicabit eis opera eorum et scelera eorum]]: that is, through those adversities God will bring them back to the consideration of their vices, so that from their punishments they will consider their own faults, as is had in Isaias: [[Is 28:19|vexation alone shall make you understand what you hear|Tantummodo sola vexatio dabit intellectum auditui]] [the margin's numerals are misprinted or misread; the words are those of Is 28:19]. [[36:9|because they have been violent|Quia violenti fuerunt]]. For the mighty, especially kings, often use their power in place of the law of justice, and do not direct their will by reason, saying in word or deed: "This I will, thus I command; let my will stand in place of reason" [a line of Juvenal, Satires 6, 223]. For they are headstrong, and headstrong passion blinds reason beyond telling. In this way God brought King Manasses back to penance, as is told in the second book of Paralipomenon[[2 Par 33:12||]] [the margin reads 2 Par. xxxiii, with verse numbers hard to read; the story is told in 2 Par 33:11–16].

paras.t: Revelabit quoque aurem eorum, id est, interiorem illorum aurem docebit, ut corripiat, id est, de peccatis eos increpet et emendet; et loquetur, per verba interna seu verbera exhortando, ut revertantur ab iniquitate, id est, vere pœniteant. Si audierint, id est, divinæ exhortationi et increpationi consenserint, et observaverint, id est, opere compleverint quæ Deus eis injungit; complebunt dies suos in bono, id est, liberabuntur a captivitate, et ad prosperitatem pristinam reducentur, et annos suos in gloria, id est regia dignitate atque lætitia. Si autem non audierint, id est, obstinati permanserint, transibunt per gladium, id est, gladio percutientur, et consumentur in stultitia, id est, in suo errore et malitia morientur. Apteque ait, In stultitia, quia nec verberibus et adversis corrigi velle, stultissimum est. De talibus Jeremias asserit: Domine, percussisti eos, et non doluerunt; attrivisti eos, et renuerunt accipere disciplinam. In Isaia quoque: Populus non est reversus ad percutientem se, et Dominum exercituum non exquisierunt.
paras.en: [[36:10|He also shall open their ear|Revelabit quoque aurem eorum]], that is, he will teach their inner ear, [[36:10|to correct them|ut corripiat]], that is, to rebuke them for their sins and amend them; [[36:10|and shall speak|et loquetur]], exhorting them by inward words or by blows [*verba* … *verbera*, "words" … "lashes": a play on the Latin], [[36:10|that they may return from iniquity|ut revertantur ab iniquitate]], that is, may truly repent. [[36:11|If they shall hear|Si audierint]], that is, consent to God's exhortation and rebuke, [[36:11|and observe|et observaverint]], that is, fulfil in deed what God enjoins on them, [[36:11|they shall accomplish their days in good|complebunt dies suos in bono]], that is, they will be freed from captivity and brought back to their former prosperity, [[36:11|and their years in glory|et annos suos in gloria]], that is, in royal dignity and gladness. [[36:12|But if they hear not|Si autem non audierint]], that is, if they remain obstinate, [[36:12|they shall pass by the sword|transibunt per gladium]], that is, will be struck with the sword, [[36:12|and shall be consumed in folly|et consumentur in stultitia]], that is, will die in their error and malice. And he aptly says [[36:12|in folly|In stultitia]], for to be unwilling to be corrected even by blows and adversities is the height of folly. Of such Jeremias declares: [[Jer 5:3|O Lord|Domine]], [[Jer 5:3|thou hast struck them, and they have not grieved: thou hast bruised them, and they have refused to receive correction|percussisti eos, et non doluerunt; attrivisti eos, et renuerunt accipere disciplinam]]. And in Isaias: [[Is 9:13|the people are not returned to him who hath struck them, and have not sought after the Lord of hosts|Populus non est reversus ad percutientem se, et Dominum exercituum non exquisierunt]].

paras.t: Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei. Simulatores dicuntur, qui aliud intus sunt, et aliud foris confingunt: sicut hypocritæ et sophistæ, qui virtuosos se simulant desiderio laudis humanæ seu commodi temporalis, quemadmodum de Pharisæis loquitur Christus, quod devorabant domos viduarum sub prætextu prolixæ orationis. Callidi vero vocantur homines astuti, vel potius versuti et nequam, qui ingenio suo male utuntur, subtiliter excogitando media vitiosa obtinendi seu adimplendi intentum: ut quidam ambitiosi, qui per fictam humilitatem conantur sortiri prælationem. Quibus illud Ecclesiastici competit: Est qui nequiter se humiliat, et interiora ejus plena sunt dolo. Hi ergo iram Dei contra se provocant, quia gravissime peccant: tantoque gravius, quanto industriosius et magis scienter, quanto etiam eorum peccata magis directe contrariantur simplicitati, veritati et æquitati divinæ. Hinc simulata æquitas non est æquitas, sed duplex iniquitas, quia et iniquitas est et simulatio. Simulatores autem et callidi a sinceritate et simplicitate mentis divinæ præsertim recedunt, suntque duplices animo, sequentes Scribas et Pharisæos, quibus in Evangelio loquitur Christus: Væ vobis, qui similes estis sepulcris dealbatis, quæ a foris parent hominibus speciosa, intus vero plena sunt ossibus mortuorum et omni spurcitia. Sic et vos quidem a foris paretis hominibus justi; intus vero pleni estis hypocrisi et iniquitate. Hinc in Proverbiis dicitur: Vir versutus odiosus est. Tantam ergo impietatem vitemus, atque in omnibus coram Deo sinceriter ambulemus, scientes quod ipse indesinenter cordium nostrorum inspector et judex est. Porro, verbum hoc Eliu protulit, ad innuendum quod Job non vere exstiterat justus, sed simulator et callidus, ideoque a Deo percussus sit.
paras.en: [[36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores et callidi provocant iram Dei]] [*provocant*, "provoke"; the Douay-Rheims text here reads "prove"]. Those are called *dissemblers* who are one thing within and feign another without: like hypocrites and sophists, who make a show of virtue from desire of human praise or of temporal advantage, as Christ says of the Pharisees that they devoured the houses of widows under pretence of long prayer[[Luke 20:47||]] [the margin gives Luke, without a verse; Denis's wording is closest to Mark 12:40]. But those are called *crafty* who are cunning, or rather wily and wicked, who make bad use of their wit, subtly devising vicious means of gaining or fulfilling their purpose: like certain ambitious men who try to obtain a prelacy through feigned humility. To them that of Ecclesiasticus applies: [[Ecclus 19:23|There is one that humbleth himself wickedly, and his interior is full of deceit|Est qui nequiter se humiliat, et interiora ejus plena sunt dolo]]. These, then, provoke the wrath of God against themselves, because they sin most grievously: and the more grievously, the more industriously and knowingly they sin, and the more directly their sins are opposed to the divine simplicity, truth and equity. Hence feigned equity is not equity but double iniquity, for it is both iniquity and pretence. And dissemblers and crafty men depart above all from the sincerity and simplicity of the divine mind, and are double-minded, following the Scribes and Pharisees, to whom Christ says in the Gospel: [[Matt 23:27|Woe to you|Væ vobis]], [[Matt 23:27|you are like to whited sepulchres, which outwardly appear to men beautiful but within are full of dead men's bones and of all filthiness|qui similes estis sepulcris dealbatis, quæ a foris parent hominibus speciosa, intus vero plena sunt ossibus mortuorum et omni spurcitia]]. [[Matt 23:28|So you also outwardly indeed appear to men just: but inwardly you are full of hypocrisy and iniquity.|Sic et vos quidem a foris paretis hominibus justi; intus vero pleni estis hypocrisi et iniquitate]] Hence it is said in Proverbs: [[Prov 14:17|the crafty man is hateful|Vir versutus odiosus est]]. Let us therefore shun so great an impiety, and walk sincerely before God in all things, knowing that he is unceasingly the searcher and judge of our hearts. Now Eliu brought out this saying to hint that Job had not truly been just, but a dissembler and crafty, and had therefore been struck by God.

paras.t: Neque clamabunt, id est, Deum non invocabunt vere ex corde, quum vincti fuerint, id est adversitatibus seu vinculis aggravati: quoniam tales raro aut nunquam convertuntur vere ad Deum, secundum Thomam. Et, ut ait Gregorius, quo plus ab hominibus se justos reputari gaudent et appetunt, eo difficilius etiam in adversis suam malitiam confitentur. Si autem aliquando graviter coarctantur, iniquos se vix superficie tenus confitentur, quia interna sua detegere veraci confessione confunduntur.
paras.en: [[36:13|neither shall they cry|Neque clamabunt]], that is, they will not call upon God truly from the heart, [[36:13|when they are bound|quum vincti fuerint]], that is, weighed down by adversities or bonds: since such men seldom or never truly turn to God, according to Thomas. And, as Gregory says, the more they rejoice and long to be thought just by men, the harder it is for them to confess their malice even in adversity. And if at times they are sorely pressed, they barely confess themselves wicked on the surface, because they are ashamed to lay bare what is within them by a truthful confession.

paras.t: Morietur in tempestate anima eorum. Duplici morte moritur anima, scilicet morte peccati in præsenti, et morte pœnæ seu æternæ miseriæ in futuro. De prima morte dicitur in Sapientiæ libro: Os quod mentitur, occidit animam. De secunda, in Apocalypsi: Pars impiorum erit in stagno ardenti igni et sulfure, quod est mors secunda. Simulatorum ergo callidorumque anima in vita hac moritur morte culpæ, in tempestate, id est multiplici strepitu tentationum, impetu passionum, inquietudine vitiorum, quibus succumbunt; deinde moritur in inferno, in vario impetu gehennalium tormentorum. Tales equidem in vita hac innumerabilibus vitiis implicantur. Et vita eorum inter effeminatos reputabitur, id est, effeminatis comparabuntur. Quemadmodum enim effeminati feruntur, qui ad femineam mollitiem sunt deducti, omni peccato et concupiscentiæ succumbentes, ut molles et habituati in vitiis carnis et spiritus: sic illi cunctis flagitiis enerviter cedunt, et rationis fortitudinem viliter deserunt, sicque pusillanimibus ac timidis conformantur, quia quærunt latere. Magnanimus vero quærit sinceriter apparere, ut dicitur septimo Ethicorum. Detestabile igitur atque ignobile prorsus est genus simulatorum ac callidorum, qui et dæmonibus et effeminatis sunt comparandi.
paras.en: [[36:14|Their soul shall die in a storm|Morietur in tempestate anima eorum]]. The soul dies a twofold death: the death of sin in the present, and the death of punishment, or of eternal misery, in the life to come. Of the first death it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os quod mentitur, occidit animam]]. Of the second, in the Apocalypse, of the wicked: [[Apoc 21:8|they shall have their portion in the pool burning with fire and brimstone, which is the second death|Pars impiorum erit in stagno ardenti igni et sulfure, quod est mors secunda]] [Denis has "the portion of the wicked shall be in the pool…"]. So the soul of dissemblers and crafty men dies in this life the death of guilt, [[36:14|in a storm|in tempestate]], that is, in the manifold din of temptations, the onset of passions, the restlessness of vices, to which they give way; and afterwards it dies in hell, under the varied onset of the torments of Gehenna. Such men are indeed entangled in this life in countless vices. [[36:14|and their life among the effeminate|Et vita eorum inter effeminatos]] shall be reckoned, that is, they will be likened to the effeminate. For as those are called effeminate who have been brought down to womanish softness, giving way to every sin and lust, as soft men grown habituated to the vices of the flesh and of the spirit: so these yield feebly to all wickedness and basely forsake the strength of reason, and so are made like the fainthearted and timid, because they seek to lie hidden. But the magnanimous man seeks to appear sincerely as he is, as is said in the seventh book of the Ethics [Aristotle; the passage on the magnanimous man is in book 4 of the Nicomachean Ethics]. Utterly detestable and base, then, is the race of dissemblers and crafty men, who are to be likened both to demons and to the effeminate.

paras.t: Eripiet pauperem de angustia sua. Pauperibus misereri Deus singulariter est paratus, si clament ad eum, et spiritu pauperes sint seu humiles: quos etsi aliquando in præsenti permittat vel diu vel usque ad mortem a visibilibus seu invisibilibus hostibus infestari, tamen in morte eripit eos de omni hujus vitæ angustia; et si purgandum nil habeant, deducit eos mox ad gaudia sempiterna. Hinc Isaias inducit: Domine Deus, confitebor tibi, quia factus es fortitudo pauperi et egeno in tribulatione sua. Jeremias quoque: Cantate Domino, quia liberavit animam pauperis de manu malorum. Et revelabit in tribulatione animam ejus, id est, tempore tribulationis, seu per ipsam tribulationem, illuminabit atque erudiet mentem ipsius. Quo enim quis gravius tribulatur, magisque spernitur, tanto Deus gratiosius solet adesse et adest, si ejus auxilium imploretur: imo ex sua miseratione immensa nonnunquam prævenit tales, corda eorum gratiose tangendo et convertendo. Tunc quoque consolationes occultas infundit, ad contemplationem cælestis præmii animam elevat, ita ut in adversis velut in omnibus divitiis glorietur, utpote tribulationis profectum experiens, et Christo libenter cruciformiter se conformans.
paras.en: [[36:15|He shall deliver the poor out of his distress|Eripiet pauperem de angustia sua]]. God is singularly ready to have mercy on the poor, if they cry to him and are poor in spirit, that is, humble: and though he sometimes allows them in this present life to be harassed, for a long while or even until death, by visible or invisible enemies, yet at death he delivers them from all the distress of this life; and if they have nothing to be purged, he leads them at once to everlasting joys. Hence Isaias brings in: O Lord God, I will give praise to thee [these opening words recall Is 25:1], [[Is 25:4|Because thou hast been a strength to the poor|quia factus es fortitudo pauperi]], and [[Is 25:4|to the needy in his distress|egeno in tribulatione sua]]. And Jeremias: [[Jer 20:13|Sing ye to the Lord|Cantate Domino]], [[Jer 20:13|because he hath delivered the soul of the poor out of the hand of the wicked|quia liberavit animam pauperis de manu malorum]]. [[36:15|and shall open his ear in affliction|Et revelabit in tribulatione animam ejus]] [Denis reads *animam*, "soul", where the Vulgate has *aurem*, "ear"; hence his gloss "mind"], that is, in the time of tribulation, or through the tribulation itself, he will enlighten and instruct his mind. For the more grievously anyone is afflicted and the more he is despised, the more graciously God is wont to be at hand, and is at hand, if his help is implored: nay, out of his boundless mercy he sometimes goes before such men, graciously touching and converting their hearts. Then too he pours in hidden consolations, and lifts up the soul to the contemplation of the heavenly reward, so that it glories in adversities as in all riches, as one who experiences the profit of tribulation and gladly conforms himself to Christ in the form of the cross.

paras.t: Igitur salvabit te Deus, si pœnitueris conversusque fueris, de ore angusto, id est ab arcta et dira tribulatione, quæ te quodammodo devoravit: juxta illud Jeremiæ, Absorbuit me quasi draco. Vel, Os angustum, nominat Satanæ, qui Job percussit, ferocitatem. Salvabit te, inquam, latissime, id est abundantissime, reducendo te ad maximam prosperitatem. Vel quod ait, Latissime, refertur ad Os angustum, ut os dicatur angustum latissime, quoniam tribulatio una est velut parvus introitus ad multiplicem calamitatem, quia ex uno malo homo incidit plura. Et non habente fundamentum subter se, id est prædicto ore angusto: quod dicitur absque fundamento, quoniam tribulatio impiorum hic inchoatur, et in futuro continuatur, nunquam vero finitur. Quemadmodum autem pelagus dicitur infinitum et sine fundo, non quia simpliciter careat fundo et fine, sed quia a nobis investigari fundus ejus non valet; sic mala quæ incidit homo paulatim ex aliqua prima sua tribulatione, nequeunt numerari, dum quis in mala pœnæ seu culpæ, continue atque quotidie profundius mergitur. Ideo, os istud dicitur sine fundamento et fundo, præsertim quum stabili basi non innitatur. Juxta hunc modum […]rum dicitur absque fundo et termino. Propterea Habacuc habet: Vir superbus quasi infernus dilatat animam suam; et ipse quasi mors, et non implebitur. In Proverbiis quoque legitur: Infernus et perditio non replebuntur; similiter oculi hominum insatiabiles. Rursusque Salomon loquitur: Venter impiorum insatiabilis. De inferni vero immensa quadam voragine scriptum est in Isaia: Dilatavit infernus animam suam, et aperuit os suum absque ullo termino.
paras.en: [[36:16|Therefore he shall set thee|Igitur salvabit te]] (God shall, if thou repent and be converted) [[36:16|out of the narrow mouth|de ore angusto]], that is, from the strait and dire tribulation which has in a manner devoured thee; according to that of Jeremias: [[Jer 51:34|he hath swallowed me up like a dragon|Absorbuit me quasi draco]]. Or by [[36:16|the narrow mouth|Os angustum]] he means the ferocity of Satan, who struck Job. He shall set thee, I say, [[36:16|at large|latissime]], that is, most abundantly, bringing thee back to the greatest prosperity. Or the word *latissime* ["most broadly", which the Douay-Rheims renders "at large"] is referred to *the narrow mouth*, so that the mouth is called narrow yet most broad, since one tribulation is like a small entrance to manifold calamity, for from one evil a man falls into many. [[36:16|and which hath no foundation under it|Et non habente fundamentum subter se]], that is, the aforesaid narrow mouth: it is said to be without foundation because the tribulation of the wicked begins here and continues in the life to come, but never ends. And as the sea is called infinite and bottomless, not because it simply lacks bottom and end, but because its bottom cannot be searched out by us; so the evils into which a man falls little by little from some first tribulation of his cannot be numbered, while he sinks continually and daily deeper into the evils of punishment or of guilt. Therefore that mouth is said to be without foundation and bottom, especially since it rests on no stable base. In this way […] is said to be without bottom or limit. Therefore Habacuc has: The proud man [[Hab 2:5|hath enlarged his desire like hell: and is himself like death, and he is never satisfied|quasi infernus dilatat animam suam; et ipse quasi mors, et non implebitur]] [Denis's wording, "dilatat animam suam", differs a little from the Vulgate's "dilatavit quasi infernus animam suam"]. In Proverbs too we read: [[Prov 27:20|Hell and destruction are never filled: so the eyes of men are never satisfied.|Infernus et perditio non replebuntur; similiter oculi hominum insatiabiles]] And again Solomon says: [[Prov 13:25|the belly of the wicked is never to be filled|Venter impiorum insatiabilis]]. And of a certain boundless abyss of hell it is written in Isaias: [[Is 5:14|hell enlarged her soul, and opened her mouth without any bounds|Dilatavit infernus animam suam, et aperuit os suum absque ullo termino]].

paras.t: Requies autem mensæ tuæ, id est quieta tua in mensa refectio, erit plena pinguedine, id est abundantia alimentorum, ita quod victualibus abundabis, reddita tibi pristina prosperitate. Spiritualiter vero, requies mensæ viri justi, id est tranquilla cordis sui refectio in contemplatione et gustu delectationeque divinorum, repletur pinguedine, id est uberrimis charismatibus gratiarum, exuberantia consolationum, profectu virtutum. Propter quod orat Propheta: Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea. Ad hanc mensam per pœnitentiam et quotidianam compunctionem pertingitur, dum omnis carnalis delectatio spernitur, et mundi vanitates vilipenduntur.
paras.en: [[36:16|and the rest of thy table|Requies autem mensæ tuæ]], that is, thy quiet refreshment at table, [[36:16|shall be full of fatness|erit plena pinguedine]], that is, of abundance of food, so that thou shalt abound in victuals, thy former prosperity being restored to thee. But spiritually, the rest of the table of the just man, that is, the tranquil refreshment of his heart in the contemplation, taste and delight of divine things, is filled with fatness, that is, with the richest gifts of graces, overflowing consolations and progress in virtues. Wherefore the Prophet prays: [[Ps 62:6|Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness|Sicut adipe et pinguedine repleatur anima mea]]. To this table one attains through penance and daily compunction, while all carnal delight is spurned and the vanities of the world are held cheap.

paras.t: Causa tua, quæ fuit inter Deum judicem et te, id est actio seu conversatio tua qua judicari meruisti, quasi impii judicata est: id est, propter causæ tuæ demerita a Deo plagatus es, ut impii solent, et sicut causa iniqui solita est judicari: quasi dicat, Non quia potens, sed quia iniquus fuisti, sic es judicatus a Deo. Unde, secundum intentionem Eliu, Quasi, dicit hic veritatem, non similitudinem tantum. Causam judiciumque recipies: id est, si vere pœnitueris, restituet tibi Deus causam bonam de cætero, et pium tibi judicium faciet: ut pœnitentibus fieri solet, qui divino judicio ad bona peccando perdita reducuntur, quemadmodum per Ezechielem Dominus protestatur: Si impius egerit pœnitentiam, omnium iniquitatum ejus […]. Et Psalmista loquitur Deo: Quoniam fecisti judicium meum et causam meam. Ita exponit Albertus.
paras.en: [[36:17|Thy cause|Causa tua]], which was between God the judge and thee, that is, thy action or conduct for which thou didst deserve to be judged, [[36:17|hath been judged as that of the wicked|quasi impii judicata est]]: that is, for the demerits of thy cause thou hast been stricken by God, as the wicked are wont to be, and as the cause of an unjust man is wont to be judged; as if he should say: Not because thou wast powerful, but because thou wast unjust, hast thou been so judged by God. Hence, according to Eliu's meaning, the word [[36:17|as|Quasi]] here states the truth, not a mere likeness. [[36:17|cause and judgment thou shalt recover|Causam judiciumque recipies]]: that is, if thou truly repent, God will give thee back a good cause from now on, and will pass a kindly judgment on thee: as is wont to happen to penitents, who by God's judgment are brought back to the good things they lost by sinning, as the Lord declares through Ezechiel: [[Ezech 18:21|if the wicked do penance|Si impius egerit pœnitentiam]], [[Ezech 18:22|all his iniquities|omnium iniquitatum ejus]] […]. And the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 9:5|For thou hast maintained my judgment and my cause|Quoniam fecisti judicium meum et causam meam]]. So Albertus expounds it.

paras.t: Thomas vero exponit: Causam judiciumque recipies, id est, causa et judicium tibi reddentur, seu auctoritatem et potestatem judicandi quas dudum habebas, recipies, ut aliorum possis causas discernere, et judicare de eis.
paras.en: But Thomas expounds it: [[36:17|cause and judgment thou shalt recover|Causam judiciumque recipies]], that is, cause and judgment will be given back to thee; or, thou shalt recover the authority and power of judging which thou hadst before, so that thou mayest decide the causes of others and judge them.

paras.t: Spiritualiter ita exponitur, ut cuilibet justo conveniat. Causa […] quasi impii judicata est, quia videlicet eorum justa vita et actio a malis hominibus reprobatur, persecutionibusque impeditur: a Deo quoque in vita hac affliguntur quasi impii essent. Sed causam judiciumque recipient, quia in futuro cum Christo judicabunt, et judiciariæ potestatis erigentur honore. Sicque versiculus iste maxime competit Christo, qui quum esset Sanctus sanctorum, inter sceleratos est reputatus, et sua humiliatione, dijudicatione ac passione judiciariam potestatem promeruit, et vivorum ac mortuorum constitutus est judex.
paras.en: Spiritually it is expounded so as to fit any just man. The cause […] [[36:17|hath been judged as that of the wicked|quasi impii judicata est]], because, that is, the just life and action of such men is rejected by wicked men and hindered by persecutions; and by God too they are afflicted in this life as if they were wicked. But they shall recover cause and judgment, because in the world to come they shall judge with Christ, and be raised to the honour of judicial power. And thus this little verse fits Christ above all, who, though he was the Holy of holies, was reputed among the wicked, and by his humiliation, his being judged and his passion merited judicial power, and was appointed judge of the living and the dead.

paras.t: Consequenter instruit ipsum Job, quomodo habeat se, dum judicandi potestas sibi fuerit in vita hac restituta. Non te ergo superet ira, id est, commotio, fervor seu impetus iræ in te rationem non vincat: secundum illud Ecclesiastæ, Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quia ira in sinu stulti requiescit; ut aliquem opprimas in judicio seu aliquo facto, ut aliqui judices facere solent. Judex quippe debet esse velut animata justitia, ita quod peccatis et passionibus careat, atque in omnibus rationem sequatur, neque alicui injuriam irroget. Ideo Ecclesiasticus dicit: Noli quærere fieri judex, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitates. Nec multitudo donorum inclinet te: id est, avaritiam fuge, ne munera accipiendo, a justitia usquam recedas. Hinc in Deuteronomio Moyses scribit: Non accipies personam nec munera, quia munera excæcant oculos etiam sapientium, et pervertunt verba justorum.
paras.en: Next he instructs Job himself how he should behave when the power of judging has been given back to him in this life. [[36:18|Therefore let not anger overcome thee|Non te ergo superet ira]], that is, let not the stirring, heat or rush of anger in thee overcome reason: according to that word of Ecclesiastes, [[Eccles 7:10|Be not quickly angry: for anger resteth in the bosom of a fool|Ne sis velox ad irascendum, quia ira in sinu stulti requiescit]]; [[36:18|to oppress any man|ut aliquem opprimas]] in judgment or in any deed, as some judges are wont to do. For a judge ought to be as it were justice alive, so as to be free of sins and passions, to follow reason in all things, and to do wrong to no one. Therefore Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 7:6|Seek not to be made a judge, unless thou have strength enough to extirpate iniquities|Noli quærere fieri judex, nisi valeas virtute irrumpere iniquitates]]. [[36:18|neither let multitude of gifts turn thee aside|Nec multitudo donorum inclinet te]]: that is, flee avarice, lest by taking gifts thou depart anywhere from justice. Hence Moses writes in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 16:19|Thou shalt not accept person nor gifts: for gifts blind the eyes of the wise, and change the words of the just|Non accipies personam nec munera, quia munera excæcant oculos etiam sapientium, et pervertunt verba justorum]].

paras.t: Depone magnitudinem tuam, id est cordis tui pompam, absque tribulatione, id est absque hoc quod, seu antequam Deus per adversa te rursus dejiciat; et omnes robustos fortitudine depone per tuam justitiam atque sententiam a sua præsumptione et violentia qua opprimunt alios: hoc est, quantum tibi possibile est, non cedas eis contra justitiam, sicut nonnulli judices potentibus deferunt ex timore. Hinc in Deuteronomio judicibus dicitur: Ita parvum audietis ut magnum; nec accipietis cujusquam personam.
paras.en: [[36:19|Lay down thy greatness|Depone magnitudinem tuam]], that is, the pomp of thy heart, [[36:19|without tribulation|absque tribulatione]], that is, without God casting thee down again by adversity, or before he does so; [[36:19|and all the mighty of strength|et omnes robustos fortitudine]] bring down, by thy justice and sentence, from their presumption and the violence with which they oppress others: that is, as far as thou canst, do not yield to them against justice, as some judges defer to the powerful out of fear. Hence it is said to judges in Deuteronomy: [[Deut 1:17|you shall hear the little as well as the great: neither shall you respect any man's person|Ita parvum audietis ut magnum; nec accipietis cujusquam personam]].

paras.t: Ne protrahas noctem, id est, quieti corporali non immoderanter indulgeas, sed tempestive et mane ad justitiam faciendam consurge; ut ascendant populi pro eis: id est, si noctem protraheres et tardares, contingeret quod populus multus adunaretur atque accederet pro robustis, id est ad laborandum seu pugnandum pro eis contra justitiam; vel, Pro eis, id est ad faciendam querelam tibi contra robustos propter eorum violentiam et offensam.
paras.en: [[36:20|Prolong not the night|Ne protrahas noctem]], that is, do not give thyself immoderately to bodily rest, but rise in good time, in the morning, to do justice; [[36:20|that people may come up for them|ut ascendant populi pro eis]]: that is, if thou wert to prolong the night and delay, it would come about that many people would gather and come up for the mighty, that is, to labour or fight for them against justice; or, [[36:20|for them|Pro eis]], that is, to make complaint to thee against the mighty because of their violence and wrongdoing.

paras.t: Potest et ita exponi: Ne protrahas noctem, id est, statim sine dilatione fac contra robustos justum judicium, ne per tuam dilationem robusti aggregent sibi populos, qui ad eos defendendos ascendant.
paras.en: It can also be expounded thus: [[36:20|Prolong not the night|Ne protrahas noctem]], that is, at once, without delay, give just judgment against the mighty, lest through thy delay the mighty gather peoples to themselves who would come up to defend them.

paras.t: Cave ne declines ad iniquitatem, id est, peracta pœnitentia, non recidives: sicut et Christus in Evangelio ait cuidam: Ecce sanus factus es; jam amplius noli peccare, ne deterius aliquid tibi contingat. Hanc enim cœpisti sequi post miseriam, id est, etiam post afflictionem istam pœnosam tibi a Deo immissam, non pœnituisti, sed justificasti te ipsum in derogationem divinæ justitiæ. Ideo admonendus es, ne tempore prosperitatis ad vitia corruas: juxta illud Proverbiorum, Prosperitas stultorum perdet eos. Facilius etenim atque frequentius peccant homines tempore prosperitatis quam adversitatis.
paras.en: [[36:21|Beware thou turn not aside to iniquity|Cave ne declines ad iniquitatem]], that is, once thy penance is done, do not fall back: as Christ too says to someone in the Gospel: [[John 5:14|Behold thou art made whole: sin no more, lest some worse thing happen to thee|Ecce sanus factus es; jam amplius noli peccare, ne deterius aliquid tibi contingat]]. [[36:21|for this thou hast begun to follow after misery|Hanc enim cœpisti sequi post miseriam]], that is, even after this painful affliction sent upon thee by God thou hast not repented, but hast justified thyself to the disparagement of God's justice. Therefore thou must be warned not to fall into vices in the time of prosperity, according to that word of Proverbs: [[Prov 1:32|the prosperity of fools shall destroy them|Prosperitas stultorum perdet eos]]. For men sin more easily and more often in time of prosperity than in time of adversity.

paras.t: Præterea, quoniam Eliu supra jam imposuit sancto Job quod derogavit divinæ justitiæ, ideo nunc ostendit incomparabilem excellentiam Dei in omni æquitate et sanctitate. Ecce, Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua, id est, propria potestate, non aliunde participata, sublimis est absolute, videlicet celsior cunctis. De quo fertur in Psalmo: Qui dominatur in virtute sua in æternum. Et in Isaia: Hæc dicit Dominus excelsus et sublimis, habitans æternitatem. Circa hoc allegat Albertus Aristotelem, dicentem in libro de Causis: Primum regit res, præterquam commisceatur cum eis. Per quod Albertus insinuare videtur, quod Aristoteles librum de Causis ediderit: quod dici non potest. Nec Albertus, ut arbitror, hoc intendit; sed ideo forsitan sic allegat, quia (ut in commento suo super librum de Causis testatur) quidam Judæus philosophus nomine David, librum illum composuit ex quadam epistola Aristotelis de principio universi esse, quædam adjungens ex dictis Alphorabii et Avicennæ ac Algazelis. Verumtamen magis consentiendum est Thomæ, qui in commento suo super librum de Causis, affirmat præfatum librum ex Elementatione theologica Procli Platonici compilatum: cujus signum est, quod omnia in libro de Causis contenta, in libro Procli habentur, etiam quasi sub eadem forma verborum frequenter.
paras.en: Moreover, since Eliu above has already charged holy Job with disparaging God's justice, he now shows God's incomparable excellence in all equity and holiness. [[36:22|Behold, God is high in his strength|Ecce, Deus excelsus in fortitudine sua]], that is, by his own power, not shared from elsewhere, he is high absolutely, namely loftier than all. Of him it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 65:7|Who by his power ruleth for ever|Qui dominatur in virtute sua in æternum]]. And in Isaias: [[Is 57:15|thus saith the High and the Eminent that inhabiteth eternity|Hæc dicit Dominus excelsus et sublimis, habitans æternitatem]]. On this Albertus cites Aristotle as saying in the Book of Causes [the *Liber de causis*, a short treatise on the First Cause, long ascribed to Aristotle]: The First rules things without being mingled with them. By this Albertus seems to imply that Aristotle wrote the Book of Causes, which cannot be said. Nor, I think, does Albertus mean this; but perhaps he cites it so because (as he testifies in his commentary on the Book of Causes) a certain Jewish philosopher named David composed that book from a certain letter of Aristotle on the principle of the being of the universe, adding some things from the sayings of Alfarabi, Avicenna and Algazel. Yet we should rather agree with Thomas, who in his commentary on the Book of Causes affirms that this book was compiled from the Elements of Theology of Proclus the Platonist: a sign of which is that everything contained in the Book of Causes is found in the book of Proclus, often even in nearly the same form of words.

paras.t: Et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus. Omnis enim legislator creatus, a perfectione sapientiæ atque justitiæ Dei deficit infinite; et quidquid sapientiæ aut justitiæ, perfectionisque habet, ab illo sortitus est. Ideo Deus in Proverbiis disseruit: Per me reges regnant, et legum conditores justa decernunt: per me principes imperant, et potentes decernunt justitiam. De quo legislatore scriptum est in Isaia: Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster; atque in Psalmo: Etenim benedictionem dabit legislator. Denique, Deus est lator legis naturæ, legis scriptæ, et legis evangelicæ. Unde et verba hæc de Unigenito Dei incarnato Jesu Christo legislatore nostro, præcipue exponuntur, cui nec Moyses, nec aliquis legis cujuscumque dator poterit comparari. Nunc enim de similitudine æquiparantiæ, non imitationis, est mentio, sicut et in Isaia, quo habetur: Cui similem fecistis Deum? aut quam imaginem ponetis ei? Præterea lex Christi longe perfectior est omni alia lege: quod in epistola ad Hebræos, quantum ad legem Moysis, probat Apostolus.
paras.en: [[36:22|and none is like him among the lawgivers|Et nullus ei similis in legislatoribus]]. For every created lawgiver falls infinitely short of the perfection of God's wisdom and justice; and whatever wisdom, justice and perfection he has, he has received from him. Therefore God declared in Proverbs: [[Prov 8:15|By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree just things|Per me reges regnant, et legum conditores justa decernunt]]: [[Prov 8:16|By me princes rule, and the mighty decree justice|per me principes imperant, et potentes decernunt justitiam]]. Of this lawgiver it is written in Isaias: [[Is 33:22|the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king|Dominus judex noster, Dominus legifer noster, Dominus rex noster]]; and in the Psalm: [[Ps 83:8|For the lawgiver shall give a blessing|Etenim benedictionem dabit legislator]]. Finally, God is the giver of the law of nature, of the written law and of the law of the Gospel. Hence these words are expounded above all of the only-begotten Son of God incarnate, Jesus Christ our lawgiver, to whom neither Moses nor any giver of any law whatever can be compared. For here the likeness spoken of is one of equality, not of imitation [that is, no lawgiver is God's *equal*, though creatures may *imitate* him], as also in Isaias, where we read: [[Is 40:18|To whom then have you likened God? or what image will you make for him?|Cui similem fecistis Deum? aut quam imaginem ponetis ei?]] Moreover the law of Christ is far more perfect than any other law: which the Apostle proves in the Epistle to the Hebrews as regards the law of Moses[[Heb 10:1||]] [the margin seems to give Hebr. x, 1–18].

paras.t: Quis poterit scrutari vias ejus, id est processus ejus in operando ad extra, seu ejus effectus, quæ sunt viæ seu media ascendendi ad Creatoris notitiam? Opera enim Dei plenarie cognoscere non valemus, videlicet quoad singulas eorum proprietates, actiones, vires et habitudines. Unde in libro Sapientiæ habetur: Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore: quæ autem in cœlo sunt, quis investigabit? Et Ecclesiastes ait: Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone. Apostolus quoque ad Romanos loquitur: Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus! Aut quis ei dicere potest, Operatus es iniquitatem? id est, Deum nullus reprehendere potest, quum ipse sit bonus, sanctus et sapiens per essentiam, mensura et regula prima ac summa universæ bonitatis, sanctitatis ac sapientiæ, ita ut eo ipso quo Deus sic agit aut judicat, bonum et irreprehensibile sit.
paras.en: [[36:23|Who can search out his ways|Quis poterit scrutari vias ejus]], that is, his proceedings in working outside himself, or his effects, which are the ways or means of ascending to the knowledge of the Creator? For we cannot know God's works fully, namely as to each of their properties, actions, powers and relations. Hence it is said in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 9:16|And hardly do we guess aright at things that are upon earth: and with labour do we find the things that are before us. But the things that are in heaven, who shall search out?|Difficile invenimus quæ in terra sunt; et quæ in prospectu sunt, invenimus cum labore: quæ autem in cœlo sunt, quis investigabit?]] [Denis reads *invenimus*, "we find", where the Vulgate has *æstimamus*, "we guess"] And Ecclesiastes says: [[Eccles 1:8|All things are hard: man cannot explain them by word|Cunctæ res difficiles; non potest eas homo explicare sermone]]. The Apostle too says to the Romans: [[Rom 11:33|How incomprehensible are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!|Quam incomprehensibilia sunt judicia ejus, et investigabiles viæ ejus!]] [[36:23|or who can say to him: Thou hast wrought iniquity?|Aut quis ei dicere potest, Operatus es iniquitatem?]] that is, no one can reprehend God, since he is good, holy and wise by his essence, the first and highest measure and rule of all goodness, holiness and wisdom, so that by the very fact that God so acts or judges, it is good and beyond reproach.

paras.t: Memento quod ignores opus ejus. Opus Dei, est totum universum seu mundus, qui, ut in libro de Civitate Dei asserit Augustinus, majus miraculum est omni, quod in eo perpetratur, miraculo. Ideo opus hoc homo in vita hac perfecte cognoscere nequit, scilicet ordinem universi, et naturam differentiamque specificam cujuslibet rei. Potest autem hoc loco, per opus Dei, quodcumque excellens opus ejus intelligi; vel opera ejus pluraliter, quoniam in Scripturis frequenter pro plurali ponitur singulare. De quo, scilicet Deo, vel opere ejus, cecinerunt viri, id est sapientes, qui de Deo et ejus operibus multa metrice conscripserunt.
paras.en: [[36:24|Remember that thou knowest not his work|Memento quod ignores opus ejus]]. The work of God is the whole universe or world, which, as Augustine asserts in the book of the City of God, is a greater miracle than every miracle wrought in it. Therefore man cannot know this work perfectly in this life, namely the order of the universe, and the nature and specific difference of each thing. But here by God's work can be understood any excellent work of his; or his works in the plural, since in the Scriptures the singular is often put for the plural. [[36:24|concerning which|De quo]], that is, concerning God, or his work, [[36:24|men have sung|cecinerunt viri]], that is, wise men, who wrote much in verse about God and his works.

paras.t: Omnes homines vident eum, id est, aliqualem saltem habent de Deo cognitionem, per naturalem rationem, vel famam, seu aliorum providam instructionem, seu per Scripturas, aut per creaturas. Unde, secundum Damascenum, omnibus naturaliter insita est cognitio exsistendi Deum: quod si aliqui fuerunt, vel nunc sunt, qui unum verum et summum Deum esse ignoraverint aut ignorent, tales omnino sunt bestiales, et hominis appellatione indigni. Unde distributio ista intelligenda est pro generibus singulorum, præsertim quoniam infantes et naturaliter stolidi Deum non noscunt, quia nec ratione utuntur. Et unusquisque intuetur procul, id est obscure et imperfecte, quia in hac vita Deum non noscimus, nisi ex suis effectibus, qui a plena Dei repræsentatione deficiunt infinite, quoniam in infinitum imperfectiores sunt Creatore; sed nec ipsos Dei effectus perfecte cognoscere hic valemus. Unde Deum intuemur, quantum ad quia est, et quid non est. Nunc quoque intuemur per fidem, et in exsilio degimus: ideo dicit Apostolus: Dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino; per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem. Et rursus: Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate; tunc autem (scilicet in patria) facie ad faciem; et: Nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc autem cognoscam sicut et cognitus sum.
paras.en: [[36:25|All men see him|Omnes homines vident eum]], that is, they have at least some knowledge of God, through natural reason, or report, or the careful instruction of others, or through the Scriptures, or through creatures. Hence, according to Damascene, the knowledge that God exists is naturally implanted in all: and if there have been, or now are, any who did not or do not know that there is one true and supreme God, such men are wholly brutish and unworthy of the name of man. Hence this universal statement is to be understood of every kind of men [Latin *pro generibus singulorum*, the schoolmen's distinction: "all" taken for some of every kind, not for every single one], especially since infants and those witless by nature do not know God, for they do not use reason. And [[36:25|every one beholdeth afar off|unusquisque intuetur procul]], that is, obscurely and imperfectly, because in this life we know God only from his effects, which fall infinitely short of representing God fully, since they are infinitely less perfect than the Creator; and not even God's effects themselves can we know perfectly here. Hence we behold of God that he is, and what he is not [that is, not what he is]. Now too we behold him through faith, and live in exile: therefore the Apostle says: [[2 Cor 5:6|while we are in the body we are absent from the Lord|Dum sumus in corpore, peregrinamur a Domino]]; [[2 Cor 5:7|For we walk by faith and not by sight|per fidem enim ambulamus, non per speciem]]. And again: [[1 Cor 13:12|We see now through a glass in a dark manner|Videmus nunc per speculum in ænigmate]]: [[1 Cor 13:12|but then|tunc autem]] (that is, in our homeland) [[1 Cor 13:12|face to face|facie ad faciem]]; and: [[1 Cor 13:12|Now I know in part: but then I shall know even as I am known|Nunc cognosco ex parte, tunc autem cognoscam sicut et cognitus sum]].

paras.t: Ecce, Deus magnus, non quantitate seu mole, sed omnipotentia, beatitudine, perfectione et gloria substantialiter infinitus, juxta illud in Psalmo: Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis. Vincens scientiam nostram: quia majoris scientiæ est quam nos incomparabiliter, et sua scibilitate, cognoscibilitate et actualitate nostram capacitatem atque scientiam transcendit et superat infinite. Propter quod ait Philosophus, quod sicut se habet oculus noctuæ ad lumen solis, ita intellectus noster ad manifestissima naturæ, id est ad cognitionem substantiarum separatarum, potissime Dei: quæ ex sua natura sunt maxime cognoscibiles, quia plurimum habent de formalitate et actualitate, quæ est ratio cognoscibilitatis: propter quod res dicitur tantum habere de cognoscibilitate, quantum habet de actualitate. Unde quod talia non cognoscimus, ex nostra est imperfectione. Ideo, Deo Psalmista fatetur: Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me; confortata est, et non potero ad eam. Et Apostolus ait: O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei! Itemque Psalmista: Magnus Dominus et magna virtus ejus, et sapientiæ ejus non est numerus.
paras.en: [[36:26|Behold, God is great|Ecce, Deus magnus]], not in quantity or bulk, but infinite in his substance by omnipotence, beatitude, perfection and glory, according to that word in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:3|Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised: and of his greatness there is no end|Magnus Dominus et laudabilis nimis, et magnitudinis ejus non est finis]]. [[36:26|exceeding our knowledge|Vincens scientiam nostram]]: because he is of incomparably greater knowledge than we, and by his knowability, intelligibility and actuality he transcends and surpasses our capacity and knowledge infinitely. For this reason the Philosopher says that as the eye of the owl is to the light of the sun, so is our intellect to the things most manifest in nature, that is, to the knowledge of separated substances [that is, purely spiritual beings, wholly free of matter], and above all of God: which of their nature are most knowable, because they have most of form and actuality, which is the ground of knowability; for which reason a thing is said to have as much knowability as it has actuality. Hence that we do not know such things comes from our own imperfection. Therefore the Psalmist confesses to God: [[Ps 138:6|Thy knowledge is become wonderful to me: it is high, and I cannot reach to it|Mirabilis facta est scientia tua ex me; confortata est, et non potero ad eam]]. And the Apostle says: [[Rom 11:33|O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and of the knowledge of God!|O altitudo divitiarum sapientiæ et scientiæ Dei!]] And again the Psalmist: [[Ps 146:5|Great is our Lord, and great is his power: and of his wisdom there is no number|Magnus Dominus et magna virtus ejus, et sapientiæ ejus non est numerus]].

paras.t: Numerus annorum ejus inæstimabilis, id est, innumerabilibus infinitisque annis, si fuissent aut sint, Deus consistit: non quod tempus cadat in ipsum, tanquam sui esse mensura; sed quia æternitas competit ei, tanquam mensura sui invariabilis esse, quæ omne tempus ambit et comprehendit. Propter quod ait Psalmista: Tu autem idem ipse es, et anni tui non deficient. De quo Daniel ait: Antiquus dierum sedit. Et in Exodo dicitur: Dominus regnabit in æternum et ultra.
paras.en: [[36:26|the number of his years is inestimable|Numerus annorum ejus inæstimabilis]], that is, God abides through countless and infinite years, if such there had been or are: not that time falls upon him as the measure of his being; but because eternity belongs to him, as the measure of his unchanging being, which embraces and comprehends all time. For this reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 101:28|But thou art always the selfsame, and thy years shall not fail|Tu autem idem ipse es, et anni tui non deficient]]. Of him Daniel says: [[Dan 7:9|the ancient of days sat|Antiquus dierum sedit]]. And in Exodus it is said: [[Ex 15:18|The Lord shall reign for ever and ever|Dominus regnabit in æternum et ultra]].

paras.t: Consequenter excellentiam Dei per opera ejus declarat, Qui aufert stillas pluviæ, id est, stillicidia pluviæ in aere aliquando non producit, nec terræ infundit: sicut ad preces Eliæ tribus annis et mensibus sex non pluit. Unde in Jeremia scriptum est: Quod factum est verbum Domini ad Jeremiam de sermonibus siccitatis. Et effundit imbres ad instar gurgitum, id est, quum sibi placuerit, dat pluviam copiosam. Porro Gregorius legit: Qui aufert stellas pluviæ. Quod exponitur de stellis, quarum est pluviam suo influxu causare, sicut sunt stellæ Hyades et Pleiades: quas Deus aufert, quantum ad hoc quod, eo volente, pluviam non producant vel non appareant.
paras.en: Next he declares God's excellence through his works: [[36:27|He lifteth up the drops of rain|Qui aufert stillas pluviæ]] [Latin *aufert*, "takes away"], that is, at times he does not produce the drops of rain in the air, nor pour them upon the earth: as at the prayers of Elias it did not rain for three years and six months[[Jas 5:17||]]. Hence it is written in Jeremias: [[Jer 14:1|The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words of the drought|Quod factum est verbum Domini ad Jeremiam de sermonibus siccitatis]]. [[36:27|and poureth out showers like floods|Et effundit imbres ad instar gurgitum]], that is, when it pleases him, he gives abundant rain. But Gregory reads: Who takes away the *stars* of rain [*stellas*, "stars", for *stillas*, "drops"]. This is expounded of the stars whose part it is to cause rain by their influence, such as the stars Hyades and Pleiades: these God takes away in that, by his will, they do not produce rain or do not appear.

paras.t: Qui imbres de nubibus fluunt, quia exinde descendunt dum nubes resolvuntur in aquas: non tamen semper tanta pluvia simul actualiter in nubibus continetur, sed vapores nubium successive in pluvias condensantur. Quæ prætexunt cuncta desuper. Nubes enim sic extenduntur, quod cœlum visui nostro operiunt, et terram totam cui superextenduntur, humectant. Propter quod ait Psalmographus: Qui operit cœlum nubibus, et parat terræ pluviam.
paras.en: [[36:28|Which flow from the clouds|Qui imbres de nubibus fluunt]], because they come down from there when the clouds are resolved into waters: yet so much rain is not always actually held in the clouds at once, but the vapours of the clouds are condensed into rain by degrees. [[36:28|that cover all above|Quæ prætexunt cuncta desuper]]. For the clouds are so spread out that they cover the sky from our sight, and moisten the whole earth over which they are spread. For this reason the Psalmist says: [[Ps 146:8|Who covereth the heaven with clouds, and prepareth rain for the earth|Qui operit cœlum nubibus, et parat terræ pluviam]].

paras.t: Si voluerit extendere nubes quasi tentorium suum, id est sic eas augere in aere, ut totum hemisphærium cœli nostro visui tegant, sicque instar cœli atque tentorii videantur extensæ: et fulgurare lumine suo desuper, id est de nubibus emittere micantia fulgura: quæ sunt lumina quædam a Deo principaliter procedentia, sicut a prima causa, cujus opus est omne opus naturæ et intelligentiæ; cardines quoque maris operiet, id est littora maris, quæ infra nubes contineri videntur aut etiam continentur: sed et aqua nubium ad littora quædam maris pertingere potest.
paras.en: [[36:29|If he will spread out clouds as his tent|Si voluerit extendere nubes quasi tentorium suum]], that is, so increase them in the air that they cover the whole hemisphere of the sky from our sight, and so seem stretched out like a sky and a tent: [[36:30|And lighten with his light from above|et fulgurare lumine suo desuper]], that is, send forth flashing lightnings from the clouds: which are lights proceeding from God principally, as from the first cause, whose work is every work of nature and of intelligence; [[36:30|he shall cover also the ends of the sea|cardines quoque maris operiet]] [*cardines*, literally "hinges"], that is, the shores of the sea, which seem to be held beneath the clouds, or even are: indeed the water of the clouds can reach to certain shores of the sea.

paras.t: Per hæc enim judicat populos multos, id est, per impressiones istas pluviales, inter gentes judicialiter ac juste discernit, quibusdam pluvias misericorditer concedendo, aliis subtrahendo, juxta illud Amos: Plui super unam civitatem, et super aliam non plui. Et dat escas multis mortalibus: quia per pluvias terram fecundat, ut fructus, quibus homines sustententur, producat, secundum quod Isaias ait: Descendit imber de cœlo, et infundit terram, et dat semen serenti et panem comedenti.
paras.en: [[36:31|For by these he judgeth people|Per hæc enim judicat populos multos]] [Denis reads "many peoples"], that is, by these rainy impressions [*impressiones*, the schoolmen's word for the phenomena of the air] he distinguishes between the nations judicially and justly, granting rains to some in mercy and withdrawing them from others, according to that word of Amos: [[Amos 4:7|I caused it to rain upon on city, and caused it not to rain upon another city|Plui super unam civitatem, et super aliam non plui]]. [[36:31|and giveth food to many mortals|Et dat escas multis mortalibus]]: because by rains he makes the earth fruitful, so that it brings forth fruits by which men are sustained, as Isaias says: [[Is 55:10|the rain and the snow come down from heaven|Descendit imber de cœlo]], [[Is 55:10|and water it|et infundit terram]], [[Is 55:10|and give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater|et dat semen serenti et panem comedenti]] [Denis gives the verse in short: "the rain cometh down from heaven, and watereth the earth, and giveth seed…"].

37.title: Declaratio capituli tricesimi septimi: In manibus abscondit lucem.
37.title_en: Explanation of the thirty-seventh chapter: In his hands he hideth the light

paras.t: Quidam incipiunt capitulum tricesimum septimum in his verbis; aliqui vero in verbis paulo post subditis, scilicet, Super hoc expavit. Convenientius tamen hoc loco inchoari videtur, quia hic specialis sensus exordium habet, et quod subditur, Super hoc, etc., est determinatio, explanatio et prosecutio sensus verbi istius. In manibus abscondit lucem, et præcipit ei ut rursus adveniat. Annuntiat de ea amico suo, quod possessio ejus sit, et ad eam possit ascendere. Hucusque intelligentia condependet. Est autem verbum istud sublime atque subtile: in cujus expositione adsit illuminatio Spiritus Sancti.
paras.en: Some begin the thirty-seventh chapter with these words; others with the words set down a little after, namely, [[37:1|At this my heart trembleth|Super hoc expavit]]. Yet it seems more fitting to begin it at this place, because here a particular sense has its beginning, and what follows, [[37:1|At this|Super hoc]], etc., is the determination, explanation and continuation of the sense of this saying. [[Job 36:32|In his hands he hideth the light, and commandeth it to come again|In manibus abscondit lucem, et præcipit ei ut rursus adveniat]]. [In the Vulgate these words and the next close chapter 36; Denis begins chapter 37 with them.] [[Job 36:33|He sheweth his friend concerning it, that it is his possession, and that he may come up to it|Annuntiat de ea amico suo, quod possessio ejus sit, et ad eam possit ascendere]]. Up to this point the meaning hangs together. Now this saying is lofty and subtle: may the illumination of the Holy Ghost be present at its exposition.

paras.t: Itaque, planissime procedendo, manus incorporei ac supersimplicissimi Dei, sunt sapientia et potentia, justitia et clementia, itemque voluntas ipsius. Hæc enim præcipue sunt principia operationis divinæ ad extra. In his manibus Deus sublimis et benedictus lucem abscondit: quia tam lucem gratiæ et dona ad ipsam spectantia, quam lumen gloriæ in sua habet et continet potestate, ad omnipotentis sui arbitrium lumen gratiæ occultans et pandens, retinens et effundens, auferens atque restituens. Ideo dicitur, Præcipit ei, scilicet lumini gratiæ, ut rursus adveniat: quia ad ejus imperium, lumen gratiæ indignis reprobisque absconsum, seu peccanti ablatum, vel etiam virtuoso dispensative suspensum quoad aliquem luminis hujus actum, rursum advenit, oritur atque infunditur pœnitenti, sive ostenditur fervide diligenti. In qua re, infusione aut iterata ostensione, annuntiat Deus per allocutionem internam, per spei bonæ immissionem, per angelicam inspirationem, per testimonia Scripturarum, per os hominum vicariorum et ministrorum suorum: annuntiat, inquam, amico, id est suo electo atque dilecto, utpote homini virtuoso, quod lux ista possessio ejus sit, id est, lumen gratiæ stabiliter valeat velut bonum quoddam hereditarium in vita hac possidere, et ad ipsum hoc lumen, etiam quum deest, aut actualiter non monstratur neque infulget, queat ascendere, atque per ipsum ad lumen gloriæ possit pertingere: ita ut non solum lux creata sit ejus possessio, sed per eam luci divinæ æternæ, fontanæ ac infinitæ possit uniri, infigi, immergi, ut Deus sit ejus possessio, suæ fruitionis objectum, suæ felicitatis dator ac terminus.
paras.en: Therefore, to proceed most plainly: the hands of the incorporeal and supremely simple God are his wisdom and power, his justice and clemency, and likewise his will. For these above all are the principles of the divine working ad extra [that is, of God's works outside himself, in creatures]. In these hands God, lofty and blessed, [[Job 36:32|hideth the light|lucem abscondit]]: because he has and holds in his power both the light of grace, with the gifts that belong to it, and the light of glory, hiding and disclosing the light of grace at the pleasure of his almighty will, withholding and pouring it out, taking it away and restoring it. Therefore it is said, [[Job 36:32|And commandeth it|Præcipit ei]], namely the light of grace, [[Job 36:32|to come again|ut rursus adveniat]]: because at his command the light of grace, hidden from the unworthy and the reprobate, or taken away from the sinner, or even withheld by dispensation from the virtuous man as regards some act of this light, comes again, rises and is poured into the penitent, or is shown to him who loves fervently. And in this matter, in the infusion or the renewed showing, God makes it known by inward speech, by sending good hope, by angelic inspiration, by the testimonies of the Scriptures, by the mouth of men who are his vicars and ministers: he, I say, [[Job 36:33|sheweth his friend|annuntiat, inquam, amico]], that is, his chosen and beloved, as being a virtuous man, [[Job 36:33|that it is his possession|quod lux ista possessio ejus sit]], that is, that he may steadfastly possess the light of grace in this life as a kind of inherited good, and that to this very light, even when it is absent, or is not actually shown nor shines in, [[Job 36:33|he may come up|queat ascendere]], and through it may attain to the light of glory: so that not only created light may be his possession, but through it he may be united to the divine, eternal, fontal and infinite light, fixed and plunged in it, so that God may be his possession, the object of his enjoyment, the giver and the end of his happiness.

paras.t: Hæc est una et facilis verborum interpretatio horum: quæ dante ac illustrante Spiritu Sancto, longe subtilius ac multo profundius possunt exponi, prout perfectis dumtaxat conveniunt. Etenim Deus gloriosus et felix, naturaliter, pure ac penitus infinite pius, dulcis ac supermunificentissimus, tanquam superessentialis immensaque bonitas ac superardentissima caritas, qui omnia operatur secundum consilium voluntatis suæ, id est sapienter ac libere (juxta Apostolum ad Ephesios), quos vult illuminat, sicut vult, quando vult, quantum vult, et quoties vult. Denique infusæ lucis radium, splendorem, augmentum, sive essentiam, ad libitum suspendit, retrahit, tollit, sapienter et juste omnia agens. Insuper, quos vult, obtenebratos et gratia destitutos relinquit, quemadmodum in Exodo Moysi ait: Miserebor cui voluero, et clemens ero in quem mihi placuerit.
paras.en: This is one easy interpretation of these words, which, as the Holy Ghost gives and enlightens, can be expounded far more subtly and much more deeply, as they befit the perfect only. For God, glorious and happy, by nature, purely and wholly, infinitely kind, sweet and supremely bountiful, as being superessential and immense goodness and supremely ardent charity, [[Eph 1:11|who worketh all things according to the counsel of his will|qui omnia operatur secundum consilium voluntatis suæ]], that is, wisely and freely (according to the Apostle to the Ephesians), enlightens whom he will, as he will, when he will, as much as he will, and as often as he will. Again, the ray of the infused light, its splendour, its increase, or its very being, he suspends, withdraws and takes away at his pleasure, doing all things wisely and justly. Moreover, whom he will he leaves darkened and destitute of grace, as he says to Moses in Exodus: [[Ex 33:19|I will have mercy on whom I will, and I will be merciful to whom it shall please me|Miserebor cui voluero, et clemens ero in quem mihi placuerit]].

paras.t: Hic itaque Deus supersanctus et superliberrimus, cujus vivere est amare, amantes se amat, sibi conformatis se applicat, transformatis in ipsum se monstrat. Quumque sui amatoris mentem viderit per privati amoris meram atque purissimam evulsionem, a se prorsus aversam, Deoque plene, pure et integre conversive unitam, intentam et inhiantem, toto zelo Dei honorem et gloriam in omnibus fervide cupientem, omniumque conversionem ac salutem cordialiter ac efficaciter appetentem, ac per hoc in ipsum sincerissimum omnis boni honesti affectum mutatam: quum, inquam, talem viderit eam, complacentiam magnam habet in ea, eamque velut amicam et sponsam apprehendit, stringit, amplectitur, et de bonis suis liberalissime ei communicat. Et ecce in momento, in ictu oculi, in instanti, magnitudinis suæ mole sic vincit, sic occupat, sicque non violenter aut pœnaliter, sed caritative atque suaviter opprimit eam, ut ipsa defluat, deficiatque a se ipsa; et victa amore, stupens præ admiratione ejus quam intuetur superclaræ caliginis, præ lucis quam cernit deliciosissima ac amœnissima serenitate, nesciat de se ipsa. Siquidem instantanee inflammatur tam vehementer, ostendente se ei dilecto, ut prorsus succumbat, vires et sensus corporales amittat. Tunc Deus omnipotens et excelsus lucem theoricæ contemplationis, claritatem doni sapientiæ decorativam ac perfectivam, excitativam et elevativam, quam lucem absconsam habet in manibus, menti propalat, per lucem hanc erigens apicem mentis ad increatæ lucis fulgidissimam contemplationem: quæ a principe theologorum magno Dionysio appellatur mystica theologia; estque caliginis intuitio, et secretissima mentis cum Deo locutio, divinæ supersplendidissimæ ac invisibilis lucis amorosa inspectio, dum mens in increatæ lucis abysso demergitur, in immensi amoris igne comburitur, in supervastissimæ ac superplanissimæ solitudinis impermeabili immensaque amplitudine tutissime errat ac feliciter deviat, perdens se ipsam, nesciens ubi vel quomodo.
paras.en: This God, then, supremely holy and supremely free, whose life is to love, loves those who love him, applies himself to those conformed to him, and shows himself to those transformed into him. And when he sees the mind of one who loves him turned wholly away from itself through the sheer and most pure uprooting of private love [that is, love of self for one's own sake], and fully, purely and wholly united to God by turning to him, intent upon him and longing for him, fervently desiring with all zeal the honour and glory of God in all things, and seeking heartily and effectually the conversion and salvation of all, and through this changed into the most sincere love of every honest good: when, I say, he sees it to be such, he takes great pleasure in it, and seizes it as a friend and spouse, clasps and embraces it, and shares his goods with it most liberally. And behold, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, in an instant, he so overcomes it by the weight of his greatness, so takes possession of it, and so overwhelms it, not violently or painfully but lovingly and sweetly, that it flows away and fails from itself; and, overcome by love, stunned with wonder at the more than bright darkness [the dark cloud of Dionysius, dark from excess of light] on which it gazes, and at the most delightful and lovely serenity of the light that it beholds, it knows nothing of itself. For it is set on fire in an instant so vehemently, as the Beloved shows himself to it, that it gives way altogether and loses its bodily strength and senses. Then God, almighty and most high, discloses to the mind the light of theoric contemplation [that is, of pure contemplation; theorica, from the Greek theoria], the brightness of the gift of wisdom, which adorns and perfects, rouses and lifts up: the light which he holds hidden in his hands; through this light he raises the summit of the mind to the most resplendent contemplation of the uncreated light, which the prince of theologians, the great Dionysius, calls mystical theology; and it is a gazing into the darkness, and the most secret converse of the mind with God, the loving beholding of the divine, supremely resplendent and invisible light, while the mind is plunged into the abyss of the uncreated light, is burnt up in the fire of immense love, and in the trackless and immense breadth of a solitude supremely vast and supremely level wanders most safely and happily strays, losing itself, knowing not where or how.

paras.t: Verum in hac intuitione mens, ut in pluribus, non diu defigitur; sed Deus adorandus, sanctus ac sapiens, lucem quam menti ostendit, superfudit et propalavit, rursus retrahit et abscondit in manibus, atque post paucum horulæ spatium denuo præcipit ei, ut menti oriatur sive adveniat majori vicissim cum claritate quam ante; qua luce menti micante, iterum intus splendescit, ignescit, alteratur, miratur, opprimitur, deficit. Tuncque Deus immensæ amœnitatis annuntiat de ea, hoc est de luce ista, quam paulo ante abscondit in manibus, nuncque menti propalat: annuntiat, inquam, dilecto, id est puro ac fervido divinitatis amatori, quod possessio ejus sit, eo quod ipse cuncta mundana, caduca, præsentia, carnalia, exteriora contempserit, et ad eam Deo suffragante possit ascendere, ita ut quotidie crescens in ea, tandem incessabiliter luci fontali, Deo suavi, creatori æterno, beatifice stet intentus, fruitive immersus, amative absorptus.
paras.en: Yet in this gazing the mind, for the most part, is not held fixed for long; but God, adorable, holy and wise, withdraws again and hides in his hands the light which he showed, poured over and disclosed to the mind, and after the space of a short hour once more [[Job 36:32|commandeth it|præcipit ei]] to rise upon the mind or [[Job 36:32|to come again|adveniat]], in its turn with greater brightness than before; and as this light flashes upon the mind, it again grows bright within, takes fire, is changed, wonders, is overwhelmed, and faints. And then God of immense delight [[Job 36:33|sheweth his friend concerning it|annuntiat de ea]], that is, concerning this light, which a little before he hid in his hands and now discloses to the mind: he sheweth, I say, to the beloved, that is, to the pure and fervent lover of the Godhead, [[Job 36:33|that it is his possession|quod possessio ejus sit]], because he has despised all things worldly, perishable, present, carnal and outward, [[Job 36:33|and that he may come up to it|et ad eam Deo suffragante possit ascendere]] with God's help, so that growing in it daily, he may at last stand unceasingly intent upon the fontal light, the sweet God, the eternal Creator, in beatitude, plunged in him in enjoyment, absorbed in him in love.

paras.t: Porro lux ista, quam Deus superamabilis, infiniteque bonus, ita abscondit in manibus, proprie ac subtilissime de ea loquendo, non est, ut dicitur, realiter idem quod lumen gratiæ (id est ipsa gratia gratificans, quæ lumen quoddam est), nec caritas, nec donum sapientiæ, nec proprius atque elicitus actus ipsius, nec aliquid habituale et fixum in anima, sicut nec prophetia; sed actualis quidam fulgor lucis divinæ, vultui mentis creatæ instantanee desuper incidens, superque fulgens, ineffabiliter eam clarificans et perlustrans, ita quod sicut in patria lumen gloriæ disponit ad beatificam visionem, ita lux ista elevat, actuat atque clarificat ad præfatam contemplationem, mysticam intuitionem, huicque vitæ possibilem altissimam perfectionem: in qua tamen multi varii ac diversi sunt gradus, secundum quod unus Sanctorum alio sanctior fuisse non dubitatur, quamvis omnes in gradu perfectionis exstitisse ferantur. Nec istud mirum putetur, quum juxta concordem doctorum doctrinam, in omni actu meritorio, præter habitualem caritatem et gratiam, requiratur actualis motio Spiritus Sancti animam excitantis, quæ a quibusdam vibratio nuncupatur, estque infulsio quædam summæ lucis in mente.
paras.en: Further, this light which God, supremely lovable and infinitely good, thus hides in his hands is not, speaking of it properly and most subtly, really the same, as is said, as the light of grace (that is, sanctifying grace itself [gratia gratificans: the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God], which is a kind of light), nor charity, nor the gift of wisdom, nor its proper and elicited act [that is, the act that issues from that gift itself], nor anything habitual and fixed in the soul, just as prophecy is not either; but a certain actual flash of the divine light, falling instantly from above upon the face of the created mind and shining over it, ineffably brightening and illumining it, so that, as in the fatherland [that is, in heaven] the light of glory disposes the mind for the beatific vision, so this light raises, actuates and brightens it for the contemplation spoken of, the mystical gazing, and the highest perfection possible in this life: in which, however, there are many various and different degrees, according as one of the Saints is held without doubt to have been holier than another, although all are said to have stood in the state of perfection. Nor let this be thought strange, since according to the concordant teaching of the doctors, in every meritorious act, besides habitual charity and grace, there is required an actual motion of the Holy Ghost stirring the soul, which some call a vibration, and which is a certain shining-in of the highest light upon the mind.

paras.t: Postremo, de præinducta materia sanctus Pater noster, dulcis devotissimusque Bernardus, Dei amicus, juxta experientiam suam sublimem, convenientissime loquitur ad Fratres de Monte Dei, inter cetera dicens: Quidquid hic de visione et cognitione Dei fidelibus impertitur, speculum est et ænigma, tantum distans a futura visione et cognitione, quantum fides distat a veritate et tempus ab æternitate, nisi quum aliquando fit, quod de Deo legitur in libro Job: Qui abscondit lucem in manibus, etc. Electo enim et dilecto Dei, aliquando lumen quoddam vultus Dei ostenditur, sicut lumen clausum in manibus, quodque patet et latet ad tenentis arbitrium, ut per hoc quod quasi in transcursu vel in puncto videre permittitur, inardescat animus ad possessionem plenam luminis æterni et hereditatem plenæ visionis Dei: cui ut innotescat aliquatenus id quod ei deest, nonnunquam quasi pertransiens gratia perstringit sensum amantis, et eripit eum sibi, et rapit in diem qui est a tumultu rerum ad gaudia silentii, et pro modulo suo ad momentum et punctum id ipsum ostendens ei videndum sicuti est. Interim etiam efficit ipsum in id ipsum, ut sit et ipse pro modulo suo, sicut illud est. Ubi quum didicerit quid intersit inter mundum et immundum, sibi redditur, et remittitur ad mundandum cor, ut si aliquando rursus admittatur, sit purior ad videndum, et stabilior ad fruendum. Nusquam enim melius se deprehendit modus humanæ imperfectionis, quam in lumine vultus Dei, ubi vicissim in osculo et amplexu Patris et Filii, mediam quodammodo se invenit mens sincera.
paras.en: Lastly, on the matter brought forward, our holy Father, the sweet and most devout Bernard, friend of God, speaks most fittingly from his own lofty experience to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu [the "Golden Epistle", then ascribed to Bernard, now to William of Saint-Thierry], saying among other things: Whatever is imparted here to the faithful of the vision and knowledge of God is a glass and a riddle, as far from the vision and knowledge to come as faith is from truth and time from eternity, except when that sometimes comes about which is read of God in the book of Job: [[Job 36:32|In his hands he hideth the light|Qui abscondit lucem in manibus]], etc. For to the chosen and beloved of God there is sometimes shown a certain light of the face of God, like a light shut in the hands, which is uncovered and hidden at the will of him who holds it, so that through what it is allowed to see as if in passing or for a point of time, the soul may burn for the full possession of the eternal light and the inheritance of the full vision of God: and that it may come to know in some measure what it lacks, grace sometimes, as if passing by, touches the sense of the lover, snatches him from himself, and carries him off into a day that is apart from the tumult of things, to the joys of silence, and in its small measure, for a moment and an instant, shows him that very thing to be seen as it is. Meanwhile it also makes him into that very thing, so that he too is, in his small measure, as that is. And there, when he has learned what difference there is between clean and unclean, he is given back to himself and sent back to cleanse his heart, so that if he is ever admitted again, he may be purer for seeing and steadier for enjoying. For nowhere does the measure of human imperfection better show itself than in the light of the face of God, where, in the mutual kiss and embrace of the Father and the Son, the sincere mind finds itself in some manner in the middle.

paras.t: Ad hanc perfectionem nemo pertingit, nisi per sui ipsius plenariam mortificationem, per omnium mundanorum integerrimam aspernationem, per veram profundissimam humilitatem. Et o quam multi hujus serenissimæ humilitatis naturam et actus aut nesciunt, aut non advertunt, qui tamen se vere humiles putant! Sed nullus vere et pure se humilem arbitretur, qui timet nesciri, qui appetit apparere, qui amat præesse, qui alium sibi similem aut se majorem esse vel fieri aut apparere veretur. Itaque vitam nostram in vera, serenissimæ ac securissimæ humilitatis virtute fundemus, omnem mundanum, carnalem, vanum et stultum affectum funditus exstirpemus.
paras.en: No one attains to this perfection except through the full mortification of himself, through the most entire contempt of all worldly things, and through true and most profound humility. And oh, how many either do not know or do not heed the nature and the acts of this most serene humility, who nevertheless think themselves truly humble! But let no one think himself truly and purely humble who fears to be unknown, who longs to be seen, who loves to be over others, who fears that another may be, or become, or appear his equal or his superior. Let us therefore found our life on the true virtue of most serene and most secure humility, and root out utterly every worldly, carnal, vain and foolish affection.

paras.t: Hæc, Deo præstante, de hujus præclari subtilisque verbi interpretatione prolata sint, quatenus sic conversari conemur, quod ad gustum verborum istorum, experientiamque dictorum nunc viriliter consurgamus.
paras.en: Let this much, by God's gift, be set forth on the interpretation of this noble and subtle saying, so that we may strive so to live that we may now rise up manfully to the taste of these words and the experience of what has been said.

paras.t: Denique Albertus, quod dictum est, In manibus, exponit ut sit una dictio dativi casus, per immanes intelligendo crudeles, qui metas rationis et æquitatis transcendunt: quibus propter eorum peccata, lux gratiæ et veritatis absconditur. Quam expositionem etiam Gregorius tangit. Thomas vero exponit hunc passum de luce corporali solis atque stellarum, quæ divina virtute aliquando nubibus occultatur. Sed hoc ordini litteræ consonum non videtur. Siquidem de ipsa hac luce sub eodem contextu mox subditur, Annuntiat de ea dilecto, quod possessio ejus sit: ex quo clarissime patet, de ea luce fieri mentionem, quæ virtuosis debetur: lux autem solis, bonis et malis communis est, quemadmodum Christus testatur, quod Pater solem suum facit oriri super bonos et malos. Insuper, de luce solis non annuntiat Deus dilecto, quod ad eam possit ascendere: neque ob hanc annuntiationem Eliu subderet, Super hoc expavit cor meum, etc.
