paras.en: Albert, again, expounds what is said, [[Job 36:32|In his hands|In manibus]], as one word in the dative case [immanibus, "from the savage"], understanding by the savage the cruel, who pass beyond the bounds of reason and equity: from whom, because of their sins, the light of grace and truth is hidden. Gregory too touches on this exposition. Thomas, for his part, expounds this passage of the bodily light of the sun and stars, which by divine power is sometimes hidden by the clouds. But this does not seem to agree with the order of the letter. For of this very light it is added straightway in the same context, [[Job 36:33|He sheweth his friend concerning it, that it is his possession|Annuntiat de ea dilecto, quod possessio ejus sit]] [Denis reads dilecto, "his beloved", for amico suo, "his friend"]: from which it is very clear that mention is made of the light which is due to the virtuous; but the light of the sun is common to good and bad, as Christ testifies, that the Father [[Matt 5:45|maketh his sun to rise upon the good, and bad|solem suum facit oriri super bonos et malos]]. Moreover, of the light of the sun God does not show his beloved [[Job 36:33|that he may come up to it|quod ad eam possit ascendere]]: nor because of such a showing would Eliu add, [[37:1|At this my heart trembleth|Super hoc expavit cor meum]], etc.

paras.t: Super hoc, id est de his jam dictis mirabilibus Dei effectibus, et de benignitate Dei ad homines electos, et quod homo tam fragilis, ad tam sublimem possessionem lucis deificæ queat ascendere, expavit cor meum, pavore admirationis ac reverentiæ: aut certe pavore timoris, formidando ne lucis hujus possessione privetur. Proprie tamen, pavor hic pro ecstasi sumitur, sicut in Psalmo, quo dicitur secundum antiquam translationem: Ego dixi in pavore meo, Projectus sum a facie oculorum tuorum. Ubi Hieronymus transtulit: Ego autem dixi in excessu mentis meæ. Sicut enim in excessu seu ecstasi, sic et in pavore animus a se alienatur. Qui autem prædicta profunde considerat, in excessum mentis mox elevatur, Deique gratiosissimam omnipotentiam ac superpiissimam caritatem intensissime admiratur, quod ita se habet ad hominem, eum videlicet qui ex se ipso tam vilis ac fragilis est, atque ad omne malum proclivis, tam supernaturaliter ac intime sibi applicat et conjungit.
paras.en: [[37:1|At this|Super hoc]], that is, at these wonderful works of God just spoken of, and at God's kindness towards chosen men, and that man, so frail, can come up to so lofty a possession of the deifying light, [[37:1|my heart trembleth|expavit cor meum]], with the dread of wonder and reverence: or else with the dread of fear, fearing lest it be deprived of the possession of this light. Properly, however, this dread is taken for ecstasy, as in the Psalm, where it is said according to the old translation: I said in my dread, [[Ps 30:23|I am cast away from before thy eyes|Projectus sum a facie oculorum tuorum]]. Where Jerome translated: [[Ps 30:23|But I said in the excess of my mind|Ego autem dixi in excessu mentis meæ]]. For as in excess [that is, ecstasy, the mind's going out of itself] or ecstasy, so too in dread the mind is estranged from itself. And whoever considers deeply what has been said is soon lifted up into excess of mind, and wonders most intensely at the most gracious omnipotence and the supremely loving charity of God, in that he so bears himself towards man, that is, towards one who of himself is so vile and frail, and prone to every evil, as to apply him and join him to himself so supernaturally and so intimately.

paras.t: Et emotum est de loco suo, id est, relictis terrenis et infimis, in quibus ante quievit per complacentiam et amorem, sola cœlestia expetivit post hanc supernam illustrationem. Etenim divina suavitate gustata, et superna luce taliter contemplata, vilescunt menti carnalia et caduca, jamque in cœlestibus demoratur: quia ut Christus fatetur, Ubi est thesaurus tuus, ibi est et cor tuum. Augustinus quoque disseruit: Ubi amor, ibi oculus. Porro, secundum Albertum, expavescit cor et movetur secundum systolen in consideratione altorum; naturaleque est, quod quando cor a magnitudine considerata resilit in se ipsum, paulatim redeat considerare illud magnum: et hoc vocat, Motum de loco suo, quando paulatim cor resumit vires, et inquirit de alto quod consideravit. Ex quibus verbis elicitur, quod istud etiam de corde, prout est quid corporale, quodammodo possit intelligi, ut scilicet ex magnitudine pavoris et admirationis in mente, facta sit redundantia pavoris in partem sensitivam et cor corporale, ita quod corporaliter sit concussum et motum secundum systolen, ut tangit Albertus. Cujus tamen verba satis obscura sunt. Cordi namque, cui competit secundum systolen moveri, non competit contemplari divina, considerareque alta.
paras.en: [[37:1|and is moved out of its place|Et emotum est de loco suo]], that is, leaving the earthly and lowest things in which it rested before through complacency and love, it has sought heavenly things alone after this enlightening from on high. For when the divine sweetness has been tasted and the heavenly light so contemplated, carnal and perishable things grow cheap to the mind, and it now dwells in heavenly things: because, as Christ declares, [[Matt 6:21|where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also|Ubi est thesaurus tuus, ibi est et cor tuum]]. Augustine too has said: Where love is, there is the eye. Further, according to Albert, the heart takes fright and is moved by systole [that is, by contraction] in considering lofty things; and it is natural that when the heart springs back into itself from the greatness it has considered, it should little by little come back to consider that great thing: and this he calls [[37:1|moved out of its place|Motum de loco suo]], when the heart little by little takes up its strength again and inquires into the lofty thing it considered. From these words it is gathered that this can in some way be understood also of the heart as a bodily thing: namely that from the greatness of dread and wonder in the mind, the dread has overflowed into the sensitive part and the bodily heart, so that it is bodily shaken and moved by systole, as Albert touches on. His words, however, are rather obscure. For the heart, to which it belongs to be moved by systole, does not have it in its power to contemplate divine things and consider lofty ones.

paras.t: Præinducto autem Eliu verbo consonat illud Habacuc, secundum translationem Septuaginta interpretum: Domine, consideravi opera tua, et expavi.
paras.en: And with these words of Eliu agrees that saying of Habacuc according to the translation of the Seventy interpreters: O Lord, I have considered thy works, and was afraid[[Hab 3:2||]] [this is the Septuagint reading; the Vulgate has I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid].

paras.t: Audiet homo, vel cor meum: de quo statim prædixit, Expavit cor meum; auditionem, id est divinam instructionem seu allocutionem, qua dilecto lucem præfatam propalat, in terrore vocis ejus, id est cum timore reverentiali, quo vocem instructionis divinæ suscipiet, timens ne ad Deum indecenter se habeat. Vel, In terrore vocis ejus, id est cum exteriori voce terribili seu tubali, quia frequenter per exteriores sonos horribiles, fiunt revelationes divinæ: quemadmodum in Exodo scribitur, quod in datione legis primo cœperunt audiri tonitrua. Ezechiel quoque primo sui libri capitulo, et in Apocalypsi Joannes testantur sonum se audisse, quasi sonum castrorum et aquarum multarum seu tonitrui magni, in revelationibus sibi factis. Per talia enim exteriora realiter vel imaginarie facta, manuducitur homo in reverentiam Dei. Hinc Thomas affirmat: Sicut per visionem lucis corporalis, homo reducitur in cognitionem et exspectationem cujusdam altioris spiritualisque lucis; ita per auditum corporalium sonorum divina virtute formatorum, homo manuducitur ad audiendam spiritualem Dei doctrinam. Idcirco Joannes ait, quod Christo Patrem orante, Pater, clarifica Filium tuum, venit vox de cœlo: quam audiens turba, dixit tonitruum factum esse; alii dicebant, Angelus ei locutus est.
paras.en: Man shall hear [Denis reads Audiet, "shall hear", where the Vulgate has Audite, "hear ye"], or my heart shall hear, of which he has just said, [[37:1|my heart trembleth|Expavit cor meum]]; shall hear the hearing [auditionem: in the Douay-Rheims "Hear ye attentively"], that is, the divine instruction or address by which he discloses to the beloved the light spoken of, in [[37:2|the terror of his voice|terrore vocis ejus]], that is, with the reverential fear with which he will receive the voice of the divine instruction, fearing lest he bear himself unbecomingly towards God. Or, in [[37:2|the terror of his voice|terrore vocis ejus]], that is, with a terrible outward voice, like a trumpet's, because divine revelations are often made through dreadful outward sounds: as it is written in Exodus that at the giving of the law first [[Ex 19:16|thunders began to be heard|cœperunt audiri tonitrua]]. Ezechiel too in the first chapter of his book[[Ezech 1:24||]], and John in the Apocalypse[[Apoc 1:15||]][[Apoc 14:2||]], testify that they heard a sound, as the sound of an army and of many waters, or of great thunder, in the revelations made to them. For by such outward things, done really or in the imagination, man is led by the hand into reverence for God. Hence Thomas affirms: As by the sight of bodily light man is led back to the knowledge and expectation of a certain higher and spiritual light, so by the hearing of bodily sounds formed by divine power man is led by the hand to hear the spiritual teaching of God. Therefore John says that when Christ prayed to the Father, Father, [[John 17:1|Glorify thy Son|clarifica Filium tuum]] [these are the words of John 17:1; at John 12:28 Christ prays, Father, glorify thy name], [[John 12:28|A voice therefore came from heaven|venit vox de cœlo]]: [[John 12:29|The multitude therefore that stood and heard said that it thundered|quam audiens turba, dixit tonitruum factum esse]]; [[John 12:29|Others said: An angel spoke to him|alii dicebant, Angelus ei locutus est]].

paras.t: Et sonum de ore illius procedentem. Hoc, secundum Thomam, expositorie additur, ut sit explanatio verbi præcedentis, videlicet quod homo audiet in terrore, ut dictum est, sonum de ore Dei manantem, id est doctrinam sapientiæ Dei ex divino intellectu exortam, quam infundendo Deus loquitur menti. Vel sonus iste spiritualis, est interna concussio qua Deus animam suo movet concutitque timore. Hinc ait Gregorius: Sonus de Dei ore, est vis timoris de superna irruens adspiratione. De hujusmodi sono Sponsa in Canticis: Sonet, inquit, vox tua in auribus meis.
paras.en: [[37:2|and the sound that cometh out of his mouth|Et sonum de ore illius procedentem]]. This, according to Thomas, is added by way of exposition, to explain the preceding words: namely that man shall hear in terror, as was said, the sound flowing from the mouth of God, that is, the teaching of God's wisdom springing from the divine intellect, which God speaks to the mind by pouring it in. Or this spiritual sound is an inward shaking by which God moves the soul and shakes it with his fear. Hence Gregory says: The sound from the mouth of God is the force of fear rushing in from the inspiration on high. Of such a sound the Spouse says in the Canticle: [[Cant 2:14|let thy voice sound in my ears|Sonet, inquit, vox tua in auribus meis]].

paras.t: Super omnes cœlos ipse considerat: id est, Deus omnibus præsidens cœlis et altior eis, omnium superiorum providentiam habet, motus et actus cœlorum disponit, per quos et inferioribus influit. Sic Albertus et Thomas litteram legunt. Porro Gregorius legit: Subter omnes cœlos, etc., ut sit sensus, quod Deus etiam inferiora sub cœlo contenta ordinat, cognoscit, gubernat, quamvis per causas secundas providentiam in talibus exsequatur. Et lumen illius super omnes terminos terræ. Lumen Dei potest intelligi, claritas sapientiæ ejus, quæ est super omnes terminos terræ, quoniam omnia quæ in terra sunt, intuetur. Est quoque lux divina super omnes terminos terræ, quia sublimior est atque præstantior omni luce terrena. Insuper lumen istud Dei intelligi potest, lumen quod per luminaria cœli, solem, lunam et stellas, super omnia climata terræ expandit et spargit. Rursus lumen hoc Dei est doctrina legis divinæ, quam cunctis terræ habitatoribus communicavit.
paras.en: Over all the heavens [[37:3|he beholdeth|ipse considerat]] [Denis reads Super, "over", where the Vulgate has Subter, "under"; Gregory's reading follows]: that is, God, presiding over all the heavens and higher than they, has providence over all things above, and disposes the motions and acts of the heavens, through which he also flows into things below. So Albert and Thomas read the letter. But Gregory reads: [[37:3|under all the heavens|Subter omnes cœlos]], etc., so that the sense is that God also orders, knows and governs the lower things contained under heaven, although he carries out his providence in such things through second causes. [[37:3|and his light is upon the ends of the earth|Et lumen illius super omnes terminos terræ]] [Denis reads over all the ends]. The light of God can be understood as the brightness of his wisdom, which is over all the ends of the earth, since it beholds all things that are on the earth. The divine light is also over all the ends of the earth because it is loftier and more excellent than every earthly light. Moreover, this light of God can be understood as the light which he spreads and scatters over all the climes of the earth through the lights of heaven, the sun, the moon and the stars. Again, this light of God is the teaching of the divine law, which he has communicated to all the dwellers on earth.

paras.t: Post eum rugiet sonitus: id est, imperium, influentiam seu effectum Dei consequetur quicumque sonitus magnus a Deo imperatus, sicut tonitruum, aliique fragores, et venti, et motus obedientium divino imperio creaturarum. In hominibus vero, post Dei illuminationem, consurgit rugitus lamentationis pro propriis culpis, et sonitus laudis divinæ pro ejus bonitate ac donis. Tonabit voce magnitudinis suæ, id est voce a sua majestate causata, suamque excellentiam condecente. Per quam vocem quidam intelligunt tonitruum; alii, spiritualem vocem, quæ est infusa doctrina sapientiæ Dei illam donantis. Denique, juxta Gregorium, tonat Deus voce magnitudinis suæ, quum nobis majestatem suam insinuat, et quam magnus sit ipse in cœlestibus pandit. Sicque, tonare Dei, est menti ad intra magnifice loqui, magnaliaque monstrare. Et non investigabitur, quum audita fuerit vox ejus: id est, ipsi quibus Deus ad intra loquitur, quos item illuminat, verba sapientiæ sibi infusa perfecte penetrare non poterunt, nec sensum verborum plenarie capient. Vel sensus est, quod mens humana Deum tonantem investigare perfecte non queat, etiam quum vocem ejus perceperit: quia ex suis creaturis Creator plene cognosci non valet, quum sit omnibus infinite sublimior, nec potestatem ejus effectus adæquat. Tonitruum quoque et aliæ impressiones quæ fiunt in aere, quamvis quantum ad causas naturales et proximas valeant investigari, tamen quoad causas primas et altissimas rationes ob quas Deus talia facit, perfecte ac particulariter investigari a nobis non possunt, secundum Albertum.
paras.en: [[37:4|After it a noise shall roar|Post eum rugiet sonitus]]: that is, upon the command, influence or effect of God there follows whatever great noise God commands, such as thunder and other crashes, and winds, and the motions of creatures obeying the divine command. In men, however, after God's illumination there rises up the roaring of lamentation for their own faults, and the sound of the divine praise for his goodness and gifts. [[37:4|he shall thunder with the voice of his majesty|Tonabit voce magnitudinis suæ]], that is, with a voice caused by his majesty and befitting his excellence. By this voice some understand thunder; others a spiritual voice, which is the infused teaching of the wisdom of God who gives it. Again, according to Gregory, God thunders with the voice of his majesty [*magnitudinis*, literally "of his greatness"] when he makes his majesty known to us and discloses how great he is in heavenly things. And so for God to thunder is to speak magnificently to the mind within, and to show it great things. [[37:4|and shall not be found out, when his voice shall be heard|Et non investigabitur, quum audita fuerit vox ejus]]: that is, those to whom God speaks within, whom he likewise enlightens, will not be able to penetrate perfectly the words of wisdom infused into them, nor grasp the full sense of the words. Or the sense is that the human mind cannot perfectly search out God when he thunders, even when it has perceived his voice: for the Creator cannot be fully known from his creatures, since he is infinitely higher than all things, and no effect is equal to his power. Thunder too, and the other impressions [that is, the phenomena of the air, the *impressiones* of medieval meteorology] that take place in the air, though they can be searched out as to their natural and proximate causes, yet as to the first causes and the highest reasons for which God does such things, they cannot be searched out by us perfectly and in detail, according to Albert.

paras.t: Tonabit Deus voce sua: sicut expositum est; mirabiliter, id est ex alta et incomprehensibili ratione sapientiæ suæ, et taliter ut homines admirentur, propter eminentiam divini effectus, cujus rationes et causas perscrutari non queunt. Qui facit magna et inscrutabilia. Hoc supra habitum est atque expositum. Opera quippe Dei, in se ipsis sunt magna et nobis imperscrutabilia; et sicut Deus est incomparabilis sapientiæ ac potentiæ operator, sic incomparabilia et præclarissima sunt opera ejus, prout etiam Plato in primo Timæi insinuat.
paras.en: [[37:5|God shall thunder|Tonabit Deus]] [[37:5|with his voice|voce sua]]: as has been explained; [[37:5|wonderfully|mirabiliter]], that is, by the deep and incomprehensible reason of his wisdom, and in such a way that men wonder, because of the eminence of the divine effect, whose reasons and causes they cannot search out. [[37:5|he that doth great and unsearchable things|Qui facit magna et inscrutabilia]]. This was treated and explained above[[Job 5:9||]]. For the works of God are great in themselves and unsearchable to us; and as God is a worker of incomparable wisdom and power, so his works are incomparable and most excellent, as Plato too intimates in the first book of the Timaeus.

paras.t: Qui præcipit nivi ut descendat in terram: quia ad Dei ordinationem ac jussionem nix generatur in aere, labiturque deorsum, secundum illud Ecclesiastici: Imperio suo acceleravit nivem. Et in Psalmo: Qui dat nivem sicut lanam. Opera autem naturæ tam particularis quam universalis, Deo principaliter adscribuntur, ad ostendendum perfectissimam cognitionem ac providentiam ejus: quod etiam in libro isto potissime agitur. Et hiemis pluviis. Pluviæ hiemis appellantur, quia tunc magis abundant, solis cessante calore, qui in æstate vapores frequenter consumit et nubes dispergit. His pluviis præcipit Deus ut producantur et ruant in terram. Et imbribus fortitudinis suæ, id est pluviis cum impetu et copia descendentibus: qui dicuntur imbres fortitudinis Dei, quia ab ea proveniunt, eamque ostendunt, quibus præcipit Deus generari in aere et venire.
paras.en: [[37:6|He commandeth the snow to go down upon the earth|Qui præcipit nivi ut descendat in terram]]: for at God's ordering and bidding snow is generated in the air and glides downward, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:14|By his commandment he maketh the snow to fall apace|Imperio suo acceleravit nivem]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 147:5|Who giveth snow like wool|Qui dat nivem sicut lanam]]. Now the works of nature, both particular and universal, are ascribed principally to God, to show his most perfect knowledge and providence: which is also the chief business of this book. [[37:6|and the winter rain|Et hiemis pluviis]] [in the Latin the rains too are governed by "commandeth": God gives his command to the winter rains]. They are called winter rains because they are more abundant then, when the heat of the sun fails, which in summer often consumes the vapours and scatters the clouds. These rains God commands to be produced and to rush down upon the earth. [[37:6|and the shower of his strength|Et imbribus fortitudinis suæ]], that is, rains coming down with force and in plenty: these are called showers of God's strength because they come from it and show it; and God commands them to be generated in the air and to come.

paras.t: Qui in manu, id est operativa potentia, omnium hominum signat, id est, disponit, ingenerat, imprimit, aptat quid quo tempore facere debeant. Talem enim operativam virtutem dedit hominibus, ut secundum varietates temporum dispositionumque ejus ac aeris, ad diversas operationes sit magis disposita: quia ad alios actus aptus est homo in die, et ad alios nocte; ad alios in æstate, ad alios hieme; ad alios tempore siccitatis et serenitatis, atque ad alios tempore pluviositatis et tempestatis. Hinc subditur, ut noverint singuli opera sua, id est, quibus operibus intendere debeant diversis temporibus. Iterum, manus seu vis ista operativa, specialiter accipi potest ratio practica: in qua Deus signat, id est, vim discretivam inter bonum et malum constituit, ut noverint singuli opera sua, an sint virtuosa vel vitiosa: quod homo per naturalem rationem in pluribus cognoscere potest et noscit. Nam et conscientia atque secundum multos synderesis, a Deo rationi sunt inditæ. Talis autem ingeniatio sive signatio, etiam brutis a divina providentia quodammodo est impressa. Deus enim tanquam auctor naturæ et institutor ordinis universi, singulis de necessariis providit, et unicuique naturalem contulit inclinationem ad ea quæ suæ naturæ conveniunt. Unde irrationalia naturali moventur instinctu ad opera connaturalia sibi. Itaque, secundum Damascenum, potius aguntur quam agant. Hinc subditur:
paras.en: [[37:7|He sealeth up the hand|Qui in manu]], that is, in the operative power, [[37:7|of all men|omnium hominum signat]] [Denis's Latin reads "who sets a seal (or mark) in the hand of all men"]: that is, he disposes, implants, imprints and fits what they ought to do at what time. For he gave men such an operative power that it is more disposed to different operations according to the varieties of the seasons, of its own dispositions and of the air: for man is fit for some acts by day and for others at night; for some in summer, for others in winter; for some in time of drought and fair weather, and for others in time of rain and storm. Hence it is added, [[37:7|that every one may know his works|ut noverint singuli opera sua]], that is, to what works they ought to apply themselves at different times. Again, by this hand or operative power can be taken especially the practical reason: in which God seals, that is, establishes a power of discerning between good and evil, [[37:7|that every one may know his works|ut noverint singuli opera sua]], whether they be virtuous or vicious: which man can know in most things by natural reason, and does know. For conscience, and also, according to many, synderesis [that is, the natural habit of the first principles of moral action, the spark of conscience], have been put into the reason by God. And such an implanting or sealing has in a manner been impressed by divine providence even on the brutes. For God, as author of nature and founder of the order of the universe, has provided each thing with what it needs, and has given each a natural inclination to the things that suit its nature. Hence irrational things are moved by natural instinct to works connatural to them. And so, according to Damascene, they are acted upon rather than act. Hence it is added:

paras.t: Ingredietur bestia latibulum suum, et in antro suo morabitur. Certis enim temporibus bestiæ intrant suas speluncas, et manent in eis brevius sive diutius, secundum diversas naturarum suarum dispositiones. Hinc in Psalmo dicitur Deo: Posuisti tenebras, et facta est nox; in ipsa pertransibunt omnes bestiæ silvæ. Ortus est sol, et congregati sunt; et in cubilibus suis collocabuntur. Et apud Jeremiam Dominus loquitur: Milvus in cœlo cognovit tempus suum; turtur, et hirundo, et ciconia custodierunt tempus adventus sui. Denique, secundum Albertum, tempore frigido, quando generatur phlegma, ingreditur suum latibulum quælibet bestia frigidæ complexionis, frigidi et viscosi nutrimenti, spissæ pellis, parvi caloris digestivi, ut serpens, rana, ciconia, hirundo, glis, coturnix, et quædam alia. Hæc enim viscosos contrahunt humores circa locum digestionis, et nisi ad tempus jaceant et dormiant, scilicet tempore generationis phlegmatis, ut in hieme, calor digestivus in eis suffocaretur et moreretur. In somno enim calor confortatur, et humor viscosus subtiliatur, ut membra possit nutrire.
paras.en: [[37:8|Then the beast shall go into his covert, and shall abide in his den|Ingredietur bestia latibulum suum, et in antro suo morabitur]]. For at certain seasons beasts go into their caves and stay in them a shorter or a longer while, according to the different dispositions of their natures. Hence it is said to God in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:20|Thou hast appointed darkness, and it is night: in it shall all the beasts of the woods go about|Posuisti tenebras, et facta est nox; in ipsa pertransibunt omnes bestiæ silvæ]]. [[Ps 103:22|The sun ariseth, and they are gathered together: and they shall lie down in their dens|Ortus est sol, et congregati sunt; et in cubilibus suis collocabuntur]]. And in Jeremias the Lord says: [[Jer 8:7|The kite in the air hath known her time: the turtle, and the swallow, and the stork have observed the time of their coming|Milvus in cœlo cognovit tempus suum; turtur, et hirundo, et ciconia custodierunt tempus adventus sui]]. Again, according to Albert, in the cold season, when phlegm is generated, every beast of cold complexion, of cold and viscous nourishment, of thick skin and of little digestive heat goes into its covert, such as the serpent, the frog, the stork, the swallow, the dormouse, the quail and certain others. For these gather viscous humours about the place of digestion, and unless they lie up and sleep for a time, that is, in the time when phlegm is generated, as in winter, the digestive heat in them would be stifled and die. For in sleep the heat is strengthened and the viscous humour is made thin, so that it can nourish the limbs.

paras.t: Ab interioribus, id est a polo antarctico nobis semper occulto, interiori atque depresso, et a locis quæ sunt versus polum hunc, egreditur tempestas: quia ab illis locis veniunt nubes tempestuosæ et motu involutionis flantes. Meridionales quoque venti inde flantes, videlicet a parte quæ est versus polum antarcticum, tempestates pluviasque producunt; et ab arcturo, id est a parte plagaque terræ quæ est versus polum arcticum seu septentrionalem et aquilonarem, egreditur frigus. Venti quippe septentrionales producunt frigus in aere. Propter quod Ecclesiasticus dicit: Frigidus ventus Aquilo flavit, et gelavit crystallus ab aqua. Arcturus autem proprie dicitur constellatio, quæ movetur circa polum arcticum, et dicitur Ursa major, ut superius plenius dictum est super illud Job: Qui facit Arcturum, et Oriona, et interiora austri. Et ex illa parte procedit Aquilo, qui causat frigus propter remotionem solis ab illa plaga cœli.
paras.en: [[37:9|Out of the inner parts|Ab interioribus]], that is, from the antarctic pole, always hidden from us, inner and sunk below, and from the places that lie towards this pole, [[37:9|shall a tempest come|egreditur tempestas]]: for from those places come stormy clouds, blowing with a whirling motion. The southern winds too, blowing from there, that is, from the quarter that lies towards the antarctic pole, bring storms and rains; and [[37:9|out of the north|ab arcturo]] [the Vulgate has *ab Arcturo*, "from Arcturus"], that is, from the quarter and region of the earth that lies towards the arctic pole, the northern or aquilonian, there goes forth [[37:9|cold|frigus]]. For the northern winds produce cold in the air. Wherefore Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 43:22|The cold north wind bloweth, and the water is congealed into crystal|Frigidus ventus Aquilo flavit, et gelavit crystallus ab aqua]]. Now Arcturus properly means the constellation that moves about the arctic pole and is called the Great Bear, as was said more fully above on that verse of Job: [[Job 9:9|Who maketh Arcturus, and Orion|Qui facit Arcturum, et Oriona]], [[Job 9:9|and the inner parts of the south|et interiora austri]]. And from that quarter comes the north wind [*Aquilo*], which causes cold because the sun is far from that region of the sky.

paras.t: Flante Deo concrescit gelu: id est, ad Dei imperium flante vento boreali seu septentrionali, congelatio oritur et augetur, juxta illud Ecclesiastici: Gelu sicut salem Dominus fundet super terram; et rursum latissime funduntur aquæ: id est, flante vento australi, fit degelatio, et aquæ gelu constrictæ laxantur, et undique diffunduntur, ac pluviæ producuntur latissime distillantes. Auster equidem conducit aquas, aperit terram, et evocat eam, germinareque facit. Hinc ait Psalmista: Flabit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ.
paras.en: [[37:10|When God bloweth there cometh frost|Flante Deo concrescit gelu]]: that is, when at God's command the boreal or northern wind blows, freezing arises and increases, according to that of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:21|He shall pour frost as salt upon the earth|Gelu sicut salem Dominus fundet super terram]] [Denis's wording adds "the Lord"]; [[37:10|and again the waters are poured out abundantly|et rursum latissime funduntur aquæ]]: that is, when the south wind blows, a thaw comes, and the waters bound by frost are loosed and poured out on every side, and rains are produced that fall far and wide. For the south wind brings the waters together, opens the earth, calls it forth and makes it bud. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 147:7|his wind shall blow, and the waters shall run|Flabit spiritus ejus, et fluent aquæ]] [the margin gives Ps. cxlvii, 18, the Hebrew numbering; in the Vulgate it is Ps 147:7].

paras.t: Frumentum desiderat nubes. Nubes enim frumento sunt necessariæ, tam ut melius crescat, quam ut umbra nubium protegatur contra solis ardorem ne desiccetur. Mystice, frumentum, id est electi et boni desiderant nubes, id est doctorum irrigationes doctrinales, consolationesque spirituales, ut magis fructificent, nec æstu tentationum urantur. Et nubes spargunt lumen suum, id est, lumen quod a sole ceterisque plane[…] terræ diffundunt, non solum ad aliqualem terræ clarificationem, sed ad ejus fecundationem. Virtute enim lucis illius, nubium aqua descendens in terram, eam fe[…] nubes elevantur a terra, virtutes stellarum per lumen influuntur eis, et beneficio illarum virtutum fiunt fecundativæ: ideoque circa terram moventur. Aqua enim, quum sit frigida et humida, de se virtutem germinativam non habet, sed a stellis eam sortitur.
paras.en: [[37:11|Corn desireth clouds|Frumentum desiderat nubes]]. For clouds are necessary to the corn, both that it may grow better and that it may be protected by the shade of the clouds against the heat of the sun, lest it dry up. Mystically, the corn, that is, the elect and the good, desire clouds, that is, the doctrinal waterings of teachers and spiritual consolations, so that they may bear more fruit and not be scorched by the heat of temptations. [[37:11|and the clouds spread their light|Et nubes spargunt lumen suum]], that is, the light which from the sun and the other plane[…] they spread over the earth, not only for some brightening of the earth but for its fecundation. For by the virtue of that light the water of the clouds, coming down upon the earth, fe[…] the clouds are raised from the earth, the virtues of the stars flow into them through light, and by the benefit of those virtues they become fecundating [that is, able to make the earth fruitful]: and therefore they move about the earth. For water, being cold and moist, has no power of making things sprout of itself, but receives it from the stars.

paras.t: Quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum, id est, super omnia terræ climata successive impulsu ventorum feruntur, ut lumen suum et vim germinativam undique influant, quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit, id est, imperium Dei ferri voluerit: secundum cujus dispositionem providentialem, nunc hic, nunc ibi nubes discurrunt et pluunt. Nam et Deo ordinante, ventorum impulsum sequuntur. Venti autem communiter gyrum facere solent sequendo motum solis. In mane namque communiter flant venti orientales, postea meridionales, de vespere autem occidentales. Ad omne quod præcipit illis super faciem orbis terrarum: id est, quidquid Deus per nubes fieri voluerit in superficie terræ, in hoc statim Creatori obediunt, cujus in ditione cuncta sunt posita. Unde etiam per nubes diversi descendunt effectus in terram, videlicet grando, nix, pluvia, fulgura atque tonitrua. Sive in una tribu. Quandoque enim nubes deveniunt solum ad unam familiam sive provinciam aut etiam urbem. Sive in terra sua, id est in terra ex qua seu ex cujus aquis vapores nubium sunt accepti. Interdum enim manent in tali terra, dum non impelluntur a fortibus ventis. Sive in quocumque loco misericordiæ suæ, id est omni loco cui misericordiæ suæ effectum voluerit impertiri, jusserit eas inveniri, id est apparere et conspici a desiderantibus eas. Ex grandi etenim Dei procedit clementia, quod de pluviis provideat regionibus temporibus […] quibus sunt pluviæ rariores.
paras.en: [[37:12|Which go round about|Quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum]] [Denis's Latin has "which go round about all things"], that is, they are borne one after another by the drive of the winds over all the regions of the earth, so as to pour their light and their power of making things sprout everywhere, [[37:12|whithersoever the will of him that governeth them shall lead them|quocumque eas voluntas gubernantis duxerit]], that is, wherever God's command wills them to be borne: by whose providential disposition the clouds run about and rain now here, now there. For by God's ordering they follow the drive of the winds. And the winds commonly go round in a circle, following the motion of the sun: for in the morning east winds commonly blow, afterwards south winds, and in the evening west winds. [[37:12|to whatsoever he shall command them upon the face of the whole earth|Ad omne quod præcipit illis super faciem orbis terrarum]]: that is, whatever God wills to be done through the clouds on the surface of the earth, in that they at once obey the Creator, in whose power all things are set. Hence too various effects come down upon the earth through the clouds, namely hail, snow, rain, lightning and thunder. [[37:13|Whether in one tribe|Sive in una tribu]]. For sometimes the clouds come only to one family or province, or even a city. [[37:13|or in his own land|Sive in terra sua]], that is, in the land from which, or from whose waters, the vapours of the clouds were taken. For sometimes they stay in such a land, while they are not driven by strong winds. [[37:13|or in what place soever of his mercy|Sive in quocumque loco misericordiæ suæ]], that is, in every place to which he wills to impart the effect of his mercy, [[37:13|he shall command them to be found|jusserit eas inveniri]], that is, to appear and be seen by those who long for them. For it comes from God's great clemency that he provides rains for regions at the times […] in which rains are rarer.

paras.t: Præterea, spiritualiter nubes, id est doctores, prædicatores et boni prælati, atque idonei admonitores, instar nubium per con[…]vati, sapientia splendidi, virtute boniflui, spargunt lumen suum, dum per sapientiam et scientiam sibi concessas, aliorum corda illuminant: quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum, quia ubique inveniuntur hujusmodi illuminatores, ubicumque Spiritus Sanctus eos adduxerit. Interdum enim divinitus prohibentur alicubi seu aliquibus prædicare, quemadmodum in Actis legitur: Vetati sunt (Paulus et sui) a Spiritu Sancto loqui verbum Dei; Et non permisit eos Spiritus Jesu. Ezechieli quoque Dominus ait: Linguam tuam adhærere faciam palato tuo, et eris mutus, nec quasi vir objurgans, quia domus exasperans est. Itaque, in quocumque loco et populo misericordiæ suæ præceperit Deus prædicatores tales esse et loqui, ibi et illic fluenta pluunt doctrinæ.
paras.en: Moreover, spiritually the clouds, that is, teachers, preachers and good prelates, and fit admonishers, like clouds through con[…], shining in wisdom, flowing with good in virtue, [[37:11|spread their light|spargunt lumen suum]], when by the wisdom and knowledge granted them they enlighten the hearts of others: [[37:12|Which go round about|quæ lustrant cuncta per circuitum]], for illuminators of this kind are found everywhere, wherever the Holy Ghost has brought them. For sometimes they are forbidden by God to preach in some place or to some people, as we read in the Acts: [[Acts 16:6|they were forbidden|Vetati sunt]] (Paul and his companions) [[Acts 16:6|by the Holy Ghost to preach the word|a Spiritu Sancto loqui verbum Dei]]; [[Acts 16:7|and the Spirit of Jesus suffered them not|Et non permisit eos Spiritus Jesu]]. To Ezechiel also the Lord says: [[Ezech 3:26|I will make thy tongue stick fast to the roof of thy mouth, and thou shalt be dumb, and not as a man that reproveth: because they are a provoking house|Linguam tuam adhærere faciam palato tuo, et eris mutus, nec quasi vir objurgans, quia domus exasperans est]]. And so, in whatever place and people [[37:13|of his mercy|misericordiæ suæ]] God has commanded such preachers to be and to speak, there and in that place the streams of doctrine rain down.

paras.t: Ausculta hæc, Job, quia sublimia sunt, et advertentia digna, utpote in quibus sapientia atque potentia Dei evidenter patescunt. Sta, id est, rursum mente te erige, recteque vivendo ad contemplationem te præpara; et considera mirabilia Dei quæ dixi et dicam: quæ quamvis sint naturalia, nihilo minus mirabilia appellantur, in quantum ab hominibus plene comprehendi non valent.
paras.en: [[37:14|Hearken to these things, Job|Ausculta hæc, Job]], for they are lofty and worthy of attention, since in them the wisdom and power of God are plainly disclosed. [[37:14|Stand|Sta]], that is, raise thyself up again in mind, and by living rightly prepare thyself for contemplation; [[37:14|and consider the wondrous works of God|et considera mirabilia Dei]] which I have spoken of and will speak of: which, though they are natural, are nonetheless called wondrous inasmuch as they cannot be fully comprehended by men.

paras.t: Numquid scis quando præcepit Deus pluviis, ut ostenderent lucem nubium ejus? id est, quo tempore jussit a principio et inde frequenter pluvias in terram descendere, quatenus per earum casum nubibus rarefactis, lux nubium appareret, quam a luminaribus cœli suscipiunt, nec apparet quamdiu nubes sunt densæ et grossæ. Numquid nosti semitas nubium, id est motus et processus earum, quomodo et ex qua causa ad diversas partes propellantur ex impulsu ventorum; magnas et perfectas scientias? id est in quarum rerum cognitione consistunt scientiæ magnæ atque perfectæ, secundum quod ista referuntur non solum ad causas suas naturales et proximas, sed insuper ad causas primas et summas, videlicet ad rationes sapientiæ Dei, quas in vita hac comprehendere non valemus, cur scilicet Deus cuncta hæc taliter instituerit. Porro, secundum Thomam, nubium cognitio, est principium cognoscendi omnes aeris permutationes, utpote ventos, pluvias, nives, grandines, tonitrua, atque similia. Ideo pluraliter dicit, Magnas et perfectas scientias: magnas, propter hoc quod hujusmodi impressiones in sublimi corpore fiunt; perfectas autem, quoniam nubium scientia comprehendit omnem notitiam et scientiam prædictarum impressionum atque effectuum, qui ex eis consequuntur in inferioribus istis.
paras.en: [[37:15|Dost thou know when God commanded the rains, to shew his light of his clouds?|Numquid scis quando præcepit Deus pluviis, ut ostenderent lucem nubium ejus?]] That is, at what time he commanded, from the beginning and often since, rains to come down upon the earth, so that, the clouds being thinned by their fall, the light of the clouds might appear, which they receive from the lights of heaven, and which does not appear so long as the clouds are dense and thick. [[37:16|Knowest thou the great paths of the clouds|Numquid nosti semitas nubium]], that is, their motions and progress, how and from what cause they are driven to different parts by the drive of the winds; [[37:16|and the perfect knowledges?|magnas et perfectas scientias?]] [Denis takes *magnas*, "great", which the Douay-Rheims joins to "paths", with *scientias*: "great and perfect knowledges"] That is, the things in the knowledge of which great and perfect sciences consist, in so far as they are referred not only to their natural and proximate causes, but also to the first and highest causes, namely to the reasons of God's wisdom, which we cannot comprehend in this life: why, that is, God has ordered all these things so. Further, according to Thomas, the knowledge of the clouds is the principle for knowing all the changes of the air, such as winds, rains, snows, hails, thunders and the like. Therefore he says in the plural, great [[37:16|and the perfect knowledges|et perfectas scientias]]: great, because impressions of this kind take place in a lofty body; and perfect, because the science of the clouds comprehends all the knowledge and science of the aforesaid impressions and of the effects that follow from them in these lower things.

paras.t: Nonne vestimenta tua calida sunt, quum perflata fuerit terra Austro? Ventus enim australis ex calidis regionibus venit, et calidus est, aeremque et vestes ac corpora calefacit: qui ventus quasi ab imo veniens, vapores congregando condensat, quos ventus Aquilo magis dispergit. Spiritualiter, Auster est Spiritus Sanctus, seu fervida inspiratio ejus. Vestimenta autem animæ, sunt virtutes et dona Spiritus Sancti, quæ cum Spiritu Sancto afflantur, excitantur et actuantur, fervescunt et potissime agunt.
paras.en: [[37:17|Are not thy garments hot, when the south wind blows upon the earth?|Nonne vestimenta tua calida sunt, quum perflata fuerit terra Austro?]] For the south wind comes from hot regions and is hot, and warms the air, clothes and bodies: and this wind, coming as it were from below, condenses the vapours by gathering them, which the north wind rather scatters. Spiritually, the south wind is the Holy Ghost, or his fervent inspiration. And the garments of the soul are the virtues and gifts of the Holy Ghost, which, when they are breathed upon by the Holy Ghost, are stirred up and brought into act, grow warm and work most powerfully.

paras.t: Tu forsitan cum eo fabricatus es cœlos. Hoc ironice ait, tanquam dicat: In tantum te erigis, quasi cooperator Dei fuisses in creatione cœlorum, quum tamen aeriarum impressionum scientiam non attingas. Qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt: id est, corpora cœlestia nec divisibilia nec pertransibilia sunt, ut aer et aqua, ac cetera mollia; sed tam firma et indivisibilia sunt, quasi fusa essent ex ære, quod non cedit tangenti. Quo verbo redarguuntur, dicentes corpora cœlestia esse divisibilia, ita quod stellæ transirent per cœlos dividendo eosdem sicut avis per aerem, et piscis per aquam. Cujus etiam opinionis fuerunt Plato in primo Timæi, et Ptolemæus, qui secundum Hieronymum, in dogma Platonis cadere videbatur. Qui insuper asserebant orbes cœlestes non moveri aut circumferri, sed planetas et stellas per illos meare choreamque ducere. Spiritualiter, cœli sunt angelici spiritus, quorum natura firma ac stabilis est, atque per gratiam sic confirmata in bono, ut æri merito comparetur. Similiter homines virtuosi, propter roborationem mentis in gratia et virtute, æri assimilantur. Solus autem Deus est institutor et actor naturæ ac gratiæ.
paras.en: [[37:18|Thou perhaps hast made the heavens with him|Tu forsitan cum eo fabricatus es cœlos]]. This he says ironically, as if to say: Thou raisest thyself so high, as if thou hadst been God's fellow worker in the creation of the heavens, though thou dost not attain to the knowledge of the impressions of the air. [[37:18|which are most strong, as if they were of molten brass|Qui solidissimi quasi ære fusi sunt]]: that is, the heavenly bodies are neither divisible nor passable, as air and water and other soft things are; but they are as firm and indivisible as if they were cast of brass, which does not yield to the touch. By this word those are refuted who say that the heavenly bodies are divisible, so that the stars would pass through the heavens, dividing them as a bird does the air and a fish the water. Of this opinion too were Plato, in the first book of the Timaeus, and Ptolemy, who according to Jerome seemed to fall into Plato's teaching. They further asserted that the heavenly spheres are not moved or carried round, but that the planets and stars travel through them and lead their dance. Spiritually, the heavens are the angelic spirits, whose nature is firm and stable, and by grace so confirmed in good that it is rightly compared to brass. Likewise virtuous men are likened to brass because of the strengthening of their minds in grace and virtue. But God alone is the founder and doer of nature and of grace.

paras.t: Insuper irrisorie subdit: Ostende nobis quid dicamus ei: id est, quum tantæ te sapientiæ reputes, ut disputare cum Deo velis, doce nos qualiter nos quoque Deo respondere possimus, vel quomodo dignum aliquid ei seu in laude ejus dicamus, qui major omni est laude. Nos quippe involvimur tenebris, id est, ignorantiis variis implicamur, ideo instructione hac tua egemus, quum putes te tenebris non involvi. Quamvis autem Eliu hoc ironice dicat, nihilo minus verum est quod omnes nos in sæculo isto variis errorum, vitiorum et ignorantiarum tenebris offuscamur, et ea quæ scimus, minima sunt respectu eorum quæ ignoramus. Demum, quæ scimus, non tam plene ac limpide scimus, ut res ipsa cognoscibilis exstat. Idcirco scriptum est: Cogitationes mortalium timidæ, et incertæ providentiæ nostræ; corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitantem. Hinc dicit Albertus: Ex reverberatione incircumscriptæ lucis, oculus nostri intellectus involvitur tenebris, sicut corporeus oculus inspiciens lucem in rota solis. Quod significatur in Exodo, ubi Moyses dicitur ingressus ad Dominum in caliginem: quæ caligo fuit reverberatio intellectus Moysis ab incircumscripta luce præsentis Dei.
paras.en: Further he adds mockingly: [[37:19|Shew us what we may say to him|Ostende nobis quid dicamus ei]]: that is, since thou thinkest thyself of such wisdom that thou wouldst dispute with God, teach us how we too may answer God, or how we may say something worthy to him or in his praise, who is greater than all praise. [[37:19|or we are wrapped up in darkness|Nos quippe involvimur tenebris]] [the Latin *quippe* means "for": "for we are wrapped up in darkness"], that is, we are entangled in various ignorances; therefore we need this instruction of thine, since thou thinkest thou art not wrapped in darkness. Now although Eliu says this ironically, it is nonetheless true that all of us in this world are darkened by various darknesses of errors, vices and ignorances, and the things we know are very small compared with those we do not know. Moreover, what we know we do not know as fully and clearly as the thing itself is knowable. Therefore it is written: [[Wis 9:14|For the thoughts of mortal men are fearful, and our counsels uncertain|Cogitationes mortalium timidæ, et incertæ providentiæ nostræ]]; [[Wis 9:15|For the corruptible body is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the mind that museth upon many things|corpus enim quod corrumpitur, aggravat animam, et deprimit terrena inhabitatio sensum multa cogitantem]]. Hence Albert says: From the dazzling [*reverberatio*, the beating back of the eye by a light too strong for it] of the uncircumscribed light the eye of our understanding is wrapped in darkness, as the bodily eye is when it looks at the light in the disc of the sun. This is signified in Exodus, where Moses is said to have gone in to the Lord into the dark cloud[[Ex 20:21||]]: which dark cloud was the dazzling of Moses' understanding by the uncircumscribed light of God present.

paras.t: Quis narrabit ei quæ loquor? quasi dicat: Quum ipse omnia sciat, nil ei quasi ignoranti potest narrari. Vel sensus est, quod sicut ista quæ dixit, nullus hic perfecte intelligit, ita nec Deo potest narrare. Etiam si locutus fuerit homo, id est, si de Deo et ejus operibus mirabilibus loqui immoderanter præsumpserit, devorabitur, id est, magnitudine materiæ prorsus vincetur, ita quod velut quadam voragine tenebrarum ac profunditatis absorbebitur, juxta illud Proverbiorum: Sicut qui mel comedit multum, non est ei bonum; sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria. Imperscrutabilem enim, incomprehensibilem et immensum præsumptuose scrutari, maxima est stultitia. Potest quoque sic legi: Etiam si locutus fuerit ipse Deus homini, homo devorabitur, id est, parvitatem suam cognoscet, et respectu Dei quasi nihil se esse conspiciet, neque tam sublimem rem capere poterit, juxta illud Deuteronomii: Quid est omnis caro, ut audiat vocem Dei viventis? In Exodo quoque filii Israel loquuntur ad Moysen: Loquere tu nobis, et audiemus; non loquatur nobis Dominus, ne moriamur. Similiter in Joanne ait Salvator discipulis: Multa habeo vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare modo.
paras.en: [[37:20|Who shall tell him the things I speak?|Quis narrabit ei quæ loquor?]] As if to say: since he knows all things, nothing can be told him as though he were ignorant. Or the sense is that, as no one here perfectly understands these things he has said, so neither can he tell them to God. [[37:20|even if a man shall speak|Etiam si locutus fuerit homo]], that is, if he presumes to speak without measure of God and of his wonderful works, [[37:20|he shall be swallowed up|devorabitur]], that is, he will be utterly overcome by the greatness of the matter, so that he will be swallowed up as by a kind of whirlpool of darkness and depth, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 25:27|As it is not good for a man to eat much honey, so he that is a searcher of majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory|Sicut qui mel comedit multum, non est ei bonum; sic qui perscrutator est majestatis, opprimetur a gloria]]. For to search presumptuously into the unsearchable, incomprehensible and immense is the greatest folly. It can also be read thus: Even if God himself shall have spoken to man, man [[37:20|shall be swallowed up|devorabitur]], that is, he will know his littleness and see himself as nothing in respect of God, and will not be able to grasp so lofty a thing, according to that of Deuteronomy: [[Deut 5:26|What is all flesh, that it should hear the voice of the living God|Quid est omnis caro, ut audiat vocem Dei viventis?]]? In Exodus too the children of Israel say to Moses: [[Ex 20:19|Speak thou to us, and we will hear: let not the Lord speak to us, lest we die|Loquere tu nobis, et audiemus; non loquatur nobis Dominus, ne moriamur]]. Likewise in John the Saviour says to the disciples: [[John 16:12|I have yet many things to say to you: but you cannot bear them now|Multa habeo vobis dicere, sed non potestis portare modo]].

paras.t: At nunc non vident lucem, id est, homines in hac vita lucem veritatis clare non intuentur, nec Deum qui prima lux est, per speciem contemplantur. Nunc vero vident eum per suos effectus, postea eum clare visuri. Subito aer cogetur in nubes: id est, vapor elevatus in aere, constringetur in formam ac spissitudinem nubis, ex quo aer ingrossatur, ac tenebrosus efficitur. Et ventus transiens, id est volitans, fugabit eas, id est, ad diversa loca impellet, quo Deus eas pluere jusserit: quod ventus Aquilo potissime facit, juxta illud Proverbiorum, Ventus Aquilo dissipat pluvias.
paras.en: [[37:21|But now they see not the light|At nunc non vident lucem]], that is, men in this life do not clearly behold the light of truth, nor contemplate God, who is the first light, by sight [*per speciem*, that is, face to face, as opposed to knowing him through his effects]. Now indeed they see him through his effects; afterwards they will see him clearly. [[37:21|the air on a sudden shall be thickened into clouds|Subito aer cogetur in nubes]]: that is, vapour raised into the air will be drawn together into the form and thickness of a cloud, by which the air is thickened and made dark. [[37:21|and the wind shall pass|Et ventus transiens]], that is, flying, [[37:21|and drive them away|fugabit eas]], that is, will drive them to different places, wherever God has bidden them rain: which the north wind does most of all, according to that of Proverbs: [[Prov 25:23|The north wind driveth away rain|Ventus Aquilo dissipat pluvias]].

paras.t: Ab aquilone aurum venit. In septentrionalibus namque regionibus multum de auro invenitur, quoniam ibi calore propter circumstans aeris frigus recurrente ad interiora viscera terræ, efficacius ibi operatur ad auri generationem. Hinc ait Albertus: Aurum inter metalla melioris est digestionis ac commixtionis. Ad hoc autem exigitur, ut frigus extrinsecum circumstans, ad interiora viscerum terræ reprimat calorem mineralem, ut fortis sit ad digerendum metalli materiam. Ideo in aquilone ubi frigus circumstat, melius aurum generatur. Hæc est etiam causa, quare in arenulis fluviorum frigidorum sæpe generatur aurum. Frigus enim aquæ, calorem repellit in profundum, ut melius digerat materiam, et faciat puriorem. Unde in Genesi habetur, quod Phison, qui est fluvius turbidus, circuit omnem regionem terræ Hevilath, quæ est ad aquilonem, ubi nascitur aurum; et aurum terræ illius optimum est. Hæc Albertus. Verumtamen, per Hevilath, intelligitur India, quæ videtur esse in oriente posita magis quam ad aquilonem. Denique, in libro de Proprietatibus rerum, fertur quod in montibus Saxoniæ, qui sunt versus aquilonem, omnia fere metalla fodiuntur præter stannum. Spiritualiter, aquilo terram gentilitatis designat: ex qua aurum venit, id est Ecclesia ex gentibus electa atque collecta.
paras.en: [[37:22|Cold cometh out of the north|Ab aquilone aurum venit]] [Challoner's Douay-Rheims has "Cold" here; the Vulgate, which Denis expounds, has *aurum*: "Gold cometh out of the north"]. For in the northern regions much gold is found, because there the heat, driven back into the inner bowels of the earth by the cold of the surrounding air, works more effectively towards the generation of gold. Hence Albert says: Gold is, among metals, of better digestion and mixture. And for this it is required that the cold surrounding it from outside should press the mineral heat back into the inner bowels of the earth, so that it may be strong to digest the matter of the metal. Therefore in the north, where cold surrounds, better gold is generated. This is also the reason why gold is often generated in the sands of cold rivers. For the cold of the water drives the heat back into the depth, so that it may digest the matter better and make it purer. Hence we have in Genesis that Phison, which is a turbid river, [[Gen 2:11|compasseth all the land of Hevilath|circuit omnem regionem terræ Hevilath]], which is towards the north, [[Gen 2:11|where gold groweth|ubi nascitur aurum]]; [[Gen 2:12|And the gold of that land is very good|et aurum terræ illius optimum est]]. Thus far Albert. Yet by Hevilath is understood India, which seems to lie in the east rather than to the north. Again, in the book On the Properties of Things it is reported that in the mountains of Saxony, which lie towards the north, almost all metals are mined except tin. Spiritually, the north signifies the land of the heathen: from which gold comes, that is, the Church chosen and gathered from the gentiles.

paras.t: Et a Deo formidolosa laudatio venit, id est, ex gratia Dei confertur, quod Deum reverenter ac timorate laudemus: cui cum timore cultum et laudem debemus impendere, juxta illud Psalmi, Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore. Non enim digni et idonei sumus ad laudem ipsius, nisi quantum ipse misericorditer tribuit et acceptat; nec scimus an digni simus amore, ideo formidare debemus ne laus nostra sibi displiceat, dicatque de nobis: Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me; et quod rursus ait Scriptura: Peccatori autem dixit Deus, Quare tu enarras justitias meas?
paras.en: [[37:22|and to God praise with fear|Et a Deo formidolosa laudatio venit]] [Denis reads *a Deo*, "from God", where the Vulgate has *ad Deum*, "to God": in his reading, "and from God cometh fearful praise"], that is, it is bestowed by the grace of God that we praise God reverently and with fear: to whom we owe worship and praise with fear, according to that of the Psalm: [[Ps 2:11|Serve ye the Lord with fear: and rejoice unto him with trembling|Servite Domino in timore, et exsultate ei cum tremore]]. For we are not worthy and fit to praise him except so far as he mercifully grants and accepts it; nor do we know whether we be worthy of love[[Eccles 9:1||]], and therefore we ought to fear lest our praise displease him and he say of us: [[Matt 15:8|This people honoureth me with their lips: but their heart is far from me|Populus hic labiis me honorat, cor autem eorum longe est a me]]; and what Scripture says again: [[Ps 49:16|But to the sinner God hath said: Why dost thou declare my justices|Peccatori autem dixit Deus, Quare tu enarras justitias meas?]]?

paras.t: Digne eum invenire non possumus, id est, ex creaturis eum cognoscere non valemus secundum dignitatem, perfectionem et excellentiam qua in se ipso subsistit: imo a perfecta repræsentatione divinæ essentiæ, omnes creaturæ deficiunt infinite, quemadmodum in infinitum imperfectiores sunt Deo. Ideo, in Elementatione theologica Procli Platonici, et in libro de Causis habetur, quod primum seu prima causa, superior est omni narratione. Ecclesiasticus quoque: Quis, inquit, vidit eum et enarrabit? et quis magnificabit eum sicut est ab initio? Magnus fortitudine: quia omnipotens, et ei idem est esse, fortemque esse, ita quod sua infinita essentia est sua infinita potentia. Ideo omnia sunt ei non solum non impossibilia aut difficilia, imo cuncta sunt ei æque facilia, nec potest in tot, quin possit in infinities plura. Et judicio. Justa namque et incomprehensibilia sunt ejus judicia. Et justitia ejus enarrari non potest: quia etiam est ipsemet Deus justus, cujus non minor est justitia, quam clementia atque essentia. Unde et pro uno peccato mortali pœnam infligit æternam.
paras.en: [[37:23|We cannot find him worthily|Digne eum invenire non possumus]], that is, we cannot know him from creatures according to the dignity, perfection and excellence in which he subsists in himself: rather all creatures fall infinitely short of a perfect representation of the divine essence, just as they are infinitely more imperfect than God. Therefore in the Theological Elements of Proclus the Platonist, and in the Book of Causes, it is held that the first, or the first cause, is above all telling. Ecclesiasticus too: [[Ecclus 43:35|Who|Quis]], he says, [[Ecclus 43:35|shall see him, and declare him? and who shall magnify him as he is from the beginning?|vidit eum et enarrabit? et quis magnificabit eum sicut est ab initio?]] [[37:23|he is great in strength|Magnus fortitudine]]: for he is almighty, and for him to be and to be strong are the same, so that his infinite essence is his infinite power. Therefore all things are to him not only not impossible or difficult, but all are equally easy to him; nor can he do so many things that he could not do infinitely more. [[37:23|and in judgment|Et judicio]]. For his judgments are just and incomprehensible. [[37:23|and in justice, and he is ineffable|Et justitia ejus enarrari non potest]] [Denis reads "and his justice cannot be told"]: for it is God himself, the just one, whose justice is no less than his clemency and his essence. Hence for one mortal sin he inflicts eternal punishment.

paras.t: Ideo timebunt eum viri, qui vere digni sint nomine viri, tanquam virtute virentes, animique vigore viriles: quorum est non servili, sed filiali vel saltem initiali timore Deum timere, qui effeminatis et fatuis, utpote intimoratis, loquitur per Jeremiam: Audi, popule stulte, qui non habes cor, me non timebis, qui posui arenam terminum mari? Quum enim laus sit virtutis, secundum Philosophum, is cujus virtus propter suam excellentiam perfecte non noscitur, cum timore laudatur. Et non audebunt contemplari, id est, Deum per contemplationem adspicere non præsument, quasi valentes comprehendere eum, aut per speciem in vita hac cernere, seu perfecte cognoscere; omnes qui sibi videntur sapientes, id est, qui vere sunt sapientes in sæculo isto. Quo enim fuerint sapientiores, eo Dei incomparabilem excellentiam ac propriæ mentis imbecillitatem clarius noscunt, discretiusque perpendunt. Idcirco non ingerunt se ad impossibilia peragenda, sed honorem dant Deo. Unde et Plato ait in primo Timæi: Genitorem opificemque universi tam difficile invenire, quam inventum impossibile digne profari. Perfectissima quoque contemplatio, qua Deum in vita hac contemplari valemus, est per abnegationem: per quam etiam in mystica theologia mens Deo intendit, prout divinus Dionysius docet.
paras.en: [[37:24|Therefore men shall fear him|Ideo timebunt eum viri]]: men who are truly worthy of the name of men [*viri*], as flourishing in virtue [*virtute virentes*] and manly [*viriles*] in vigour of soul; whose part it is to fear God not with servile fear but with filial, or at least initial, fear [that is, the fear of beginners, between servile and filial, which still fears punishment but already loves God]. To the effeminate and foolish, as being without fear, he speaks by Jeremias: [[Jer 5:21|Hear, O foolish people, and without understanding|Audi, popule stulte, qui non habes cor]] [Denis's Latin has "who hast no heart"], [[Jer 5:22|Will not you then fear me|me non timebis]], [[Jer 5:22|I have set the sand a bound for the sea|qui posui arenam terminum mari]]? For since praise belongs to virtue, according to the Philosopher, he whose virtue is not perfectly known because of its excellence is praised with fear. [[37:24|shall not dare to behold him|Et non audebunt contemplari]], that is, they will not presume to gaze upon God by contemplation as though able to comprehend him, or to see him by sight in this life, or to know him perfectly: [[37:24|all that seem to themselves to be wise|omnes qui sibi videntur sapientes]], that is, those who are truly wise in this world. For the wiser they are, the more clearly they know, and the more discerningly they weigh, God's incomparable excellence and the weakness of their own mind. Therefore they do not thrust themselves into doing the impossible, but give honour to God. Hence Plato too says in the first book of the Timaeus: To find the begetter and maker of the universe is as hard as, once he is found, it is impossible to speak of him worthily. The most perfect contemplation too by which we can contemplate God in this life is by negation: by which, in mystical theology also, the mind tends to God, as the divine Dionysius teaches.

paras.t: Itaque Eliu, ad confutandum præsumptionem quam sancto Job imposuit, sermonem suum in conclusione incomparabilis excellentiæ Dei finivit. Et in disputatione præfata quæ inter Job ejusque fuit amicos, Eliu personam determinantis assumpsit, nunc ipsum Job, nunc ejus amicos redarguens: in quo etiam per præsumptionem excessit.
paras.en: And so Eliu, to confute the presumption he laid upon holy Job, ended his discourse with a conclusion on the incomparable excellence of God. And in the aforesaid disputation between Job and his friends, Eliu took on the part of one who determines [that is, of the master who settles a disputed question at its close, as in the schools], reproving now Job himself, now his friends: in which he too went too far through presumption.

paras.t: Porro, secundum Thomam, Job non respondet ipsi Eliu: quia in principalibus magis secum concordat, quam alii tres amici, vel quam cum aliis tribus amicis. Secundo, quia ex juvenili quadam præsumptione more contentiosorum aliqua verba imposuit Job, quæ non dixit, vel quæ aliter dixit, et multa opprobria effudit in eum: ideo, ut a contentionibus abstineret, maluit non respondere, secundum illud Apostoli: Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium.
paras.en: Further, according to Thomas, Job does not answer Eliu himself: because in the principal points Eliu agrees with him more than the other three friends do, or more than with the other three friends. Secondly, because out of a certain youthful presumption, in the manner of contentious men, he laid upon Job some words which he did not say, or which he said otherwise, and poured out many reproaches upon him: therefore, to abstain from contentions, Job preferred not to answer, according to that of the Apostle: [[2 Tim 2:14|Contend not in words: for it is to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers|Noli verbis contendere; ad nihil enim utile est, nisi ad subversionem audientium]].

paras.t: Quoniam in disputatione præhabita de providentia Dei et modo regiminis actuum humanorum, varia fuit dissensio tam inter Job et ejus amicos, quam inter Eliu et Job et ejus amicos præfatos; ipseque Eliu quæstionem determinare usurpavit, nec potuit: ideo Dominus eam determinat. Respondens autem Dominus Job de turbine, dixit. Circa hæc scribit Gregorius: Utrum per se ipsum, an per angelum ei sit locutus, ambigitur. Potuerunt quippe per angelum commotiones aeris fieri, et per eum verba sequentia pronuntiari. Rursusque potuit exterius angelus in turbine aerem excutere, et tamen per semetipsum Dominus vim suæ sententiæ cordi Job sine verbis insonare. Thomas quoque ait, quia ad litteram intelligi potest, vocem formatam fuisse miraculose in aere cum quadam aeris turbatione, sicut in monte Sinai legitur factum, vel sicut ad Christum vox facta est, quando nonnulli dixerunt tonitruum factum esse, ut Joannes scribit. Aliqui vero dicunt, quod vox ista processit divina virtute, seu angelico ministerio, quasi de nubis densitate. Albertus vero se faciliter expediens, per turbinem intelligit disputationis hujus conflictum. Sicque de turbine, quasi de causa materiali, non quasi de loco, Dominus dicitur respondisse.
paras.en: Since in the foregoing disputation on the providence of God and the manner of his governing human acts there was disagreement of many kinds, both between Job and his friends and between Eliu and Job and the friends already named, and Eliu took it upon himself to settle the question and could not, the Lord therefore settles it. [[38:1|Then the Lord answered Job out of a whirlwind, and said|Respondens autem Dominus Job de turbine, dixit]]. On this Gregory writes: Whether he spoke to him by himself or through an angel is doubtful. For the stirrings of the air could have been made by an angel, and the words that follow uttered through him. Or again, an angel could have stirred up the air outwardly in the whirlwind, while the Lord by himself made the force of his sentence sound in Job's heart without words. Thomas too says that it can be understood according to the letter that a voice was formed miraculously in the air, with a certain disturbance of the air, as we read was done on Mount Sinai[[Ex 19:16||]], or as when a voice came to Christ, and some said that it had thundered, as John writes[[John 12:29||]]. Others say that this voice came forth by divine power, or by the ministry of an angel, as it were out of the thickness of a cloud. Albert, getting out of the matter easily, understands by the whirlwind the conflict of this disputation; and so the Lord is said to have answered out of the whirlwind as out of a material cause, not as out of a place.

paras.t: Quis est iste involvens sententias sermonibus imperitis? Quibus verbis Dominus increpat ipsum Eliu, quod quamvis sententias, id est sensus sublimes et veraces, locutus sit, tamen per verba indiscreta, præsumptuosa et frivola fecit hoc, aliqua quoque falsa invective contra Job dixit. Unde Dominus quasi despective ac reprobative sic sciscitatur, Quis est iste? quasi dicat, Non decet eum sic loqui: quemadmodum per Jeremiam Dominus sciscitatur, Quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo? Porro, secundum Thomam, ideo dicitur Eliu locutus sermonibus imperitis, quoniam omnis inordinatio ex defectu rationis procedere dicitur. Secundum Albertum vero, hoc dicitur, quia conjugatio inutilis est, dum probationes non tenent, nec ad formam syllogisticam reducuntur.
paras.en: [[38:2|Who is this that wrappeth up sentences in unskilful words?|Quis est iste involvens sententias sermonibus imperitis?]] With these words the Lord rebukes Eliu himself, because, though he uttered sentences, that is, lofty and true meanings, he did so in words that were indiscreet, presumptuous and frivolous, and he also said some false things against Job by way of invective. Hence the Lord asks, as if in contempt and reproof, [[38:2|Who is this|Quis est iste?]]? as if to say: It does not become him to speak so; just as the Lord asks through Jeremias, [[Jer 49:19|who is that shepherd that can withstand my countenance?|Quis est iste pastor qui resistat vultui meo?]] [the same words stand in Jer 50:44]. Further, according to Thomas, Eliu is said to have spoken in unskilful words because all disorder is said to proceed from a defect of reason. According to Albert, it is said because the combination is useless [*conjugatio*, the joining of premisses in an argument], since the proofs do not hold and are not reduced to the form of a syllogism.

paras.t: Accinge sicut vir lumbos tuos, id est, viriliter præpara te ad audiendum quæ dicam, et ad respondendum, si vales. Unde per hunc modum loquendi, Dominus quasi metaphorice admonet eum ad audiendum: quia qui corporaliter aliquid sunt acturi, lumbos solent præcingere, sicut et Christus in Cœna linteo se præcinxit. Specialiter vero exprimit lumbos, quia sunt loca delectationum carnalium, ad innuendum quod sensualitas necessario sit refrenanda volenti illuminationem sortiri divinam et revelationem cœlestem. Ideo Ephesios hortatur Apostolus: State succincti lumbos vestros in veritate. Et Christus in Evangelio ait: Sint lumbi vestri præcincti. Isaias quoque inducit: Quem docebit Dominus scientiam? ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere.
paras.en: [[38:3|Gird up thy loins like a man|Accinge sicut vir lumbos tuos]], that is, prepare thyself manfully to hear what I shall say, and to answer, if thou canst. By this manner of speaking, then, the Lord as it were metaphorically admonishes him to listen: for those who are about to do some bodily work are wont to gird their loins, as Christ too girded himself with a towel at the Supper[[John 13:4||]]. He names the loins in particular because they are the seat of carnal pleasures, to hint that sensuality must needs be reined in by one who wishes to receive divine illumination and heavenly revelation. Therefore the Apostle exhorts the Ephesians: [[Eph 6:14|Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth|State succincti lumbos vestros in veritate]]. And Christ says in the Gospel: [[Luke 12:35|Let your loins be girt|Sint lumbi vestri præcincti]]. Isaias too brings in: [[Is 28:9|Whom shall he teach knowledge?|Quem docebit Dominus scientiam?]] [[Is 28:9|them that are weaned from the milk, that are drawn away from the breasts|ablactatos a lacte, avulsos ab ubere]]

paras.t: Interrogabo te, et responde mihi. S. Thomas, et Albertus, ac alii eos sequentes, affirmant beatum Job de providentia Dei vere sensisse, tamen in modo loquendi excessisse, ita quod ex inordinato suo modo loquendi adsistentes fuerant scandalizati, quia secundum superficiem quorumdam verborum suorum videbatur eis de se ipso nimis alte sentire, atque divinæ excellentiæ ac justitiæ derogare. Unde infra Job confitetur: Insipienter locutus sum, et quæ ultra modum excederent scientiam meam. Hinc, secundum doctores hos, Dominus in hac parte redarguit Job de inordinatione hac ipsa: et primo, quia Job supra dixit: Disputare cum Deo cupio. Et rursus: Voca me, et ego respondebo tibi: aut certe loquar, et tu responde mihi. Quibus verbis dedit Deo quasi optionem duorum, ut scilicet teneret partem vel opponentis, vel respondentis: quæ verba prima facie videbantur male sonare, quamvis Job non male intenderet. Quia tamen alios scandalizavit et perturbavit, Dominus eum pie nunc increpat, partemque elegit opponentis, multa per modum interrogationis ac argumentationis proponens Job, ad ostendendam incomparabilem eminentiam sapientiæ suæ, propter quam Job debuit moderatius loqui, nec eatenus conqueri, quamvis in verbis suis mortaliter non excessit. Porro Gregorius omnino nititur approbare, beatum Job non excessisse in verbis, præsertim quum supra scriptum sit: In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis, nec stultum quid contra Deum locutus est. Et infra Dominus ait ad Eliphaz: Non estis rectum locuti coram me, sicut servus meus Job. Dominus quoque insultando Satanæ dixit, postquam Job in rebus et sobole fuit plagatus, quod adhuc innocentiam retineret. Vult ergo Gregorius, quod Deus non increpat sanctum Job propter excessum in verbis, sed ne de perfectionis atque victoriæ suæ magnitudine inaniter gloriaretur et superbiret. Verum, quid inter hæc magis tenendum sit, et quomodo prætactæ positiones valeant concordare, quantum Dominus dederit, infra dicetur.
paras.en: [[38:3|I will ask thee, and answer thou me|Interrogabo te, et responde mihi]]. St Thomas and Albert, and others who follow them, affirm that blessed Job thought truly about the providence of God, yet went too far in his manner of speaking, so that those present had been scandalized by his disordered manner of speaking: for, going by the surface of some of his words, he seemed to them to think too highly of himself and to detract from the excellence and justice of God. Hence below Job confesses: [[Job 42:3|I have spoken unwisely, and things that above measure exceeded my knowledge|Insipienter locutus sum, et quæ ultra modum excederent scientiam meam]]. Hence, according to these doctors, the Lord in this part reproves Job for this very disorder: and first, because Job said above: [[Job 13:3|I desire to reason with God|Disputare cum Deo cupio]]. And again: [[Job 13:22|Call me, and I will answer thee: or else I will speak, and do thou answer me|Voca me, et ego respondebo tibi: aut certe loquar, et tu responde mihi]]. By these words he gave God, as it were, the choice between two things, namely that he should take the part either of the one who objects or of the one who answers [the parts of opponent and respondent in a scholastic disputation]; and these words at first sight seemed to sound ill, although Job did not mean ill. Yet because he scandalized and troubled others, the Lord now kindly rebukes him, and has chosen the part of the opponent, putting many things to Job by way of question and argument, to show the incomparable eminence of his wisdom, on account of which Job ought to have spoken more moderately and not have complained so far, although in his words he did not go beyond bounds mortally [that is, so far as to commit mortal sin]. Gregory, on the other hand, strives in every way to prove that blessed Job did not go too far in his words, especially since it is written above: [[Job 1:22|In all these things Job sinned not by his lips, nor spoke he any foolish thing against God|In omnibus his non peccavit Job labiis suis, nec stultum quid contra Deum locutus est]][[Job 2:10||]] [the margin seems to give Job 2:10 as well, where the first words recur]. And below the Lord says to Eliphaz: [[Job 42:7|you have not spoken the thing that is right before me, as my servant Job hath|Non estis rectum locuti coram me, sicut servus meus Job]]. The Lord too, taunting Satan, said, after Job had been stricken in his goods and his offspring, that he still kept his innocence[[Job 2:3||]]. Gregory holds, then, that God does not rebuke holy Job for excess in his words, but lest he should glory vainly and grow proud of the greatness of his perfection and of his victory. But which of these is rather to be held, and how the positions touched on can be brought into agreement, will be told below, so far as the Lord shall grant.

paras.t: Itaque Dominus excellentiam suam manifestare orditur ex productione, dispositione et proprietatibus terræ, quæ est infimum elementorum, et magis hominibus cognitum. Ubi eras quando ponebam fundamenta terræ, id est, elementum terræ et singulas ejus partes produxi et situavi in debito loco in medio universi? quasi dicat: Tunc nondum eras; quo constat, quod duratione et causalitate præcedo te, nec tuo consilio egui in creatione dispositioneque mundi. Hinc in Isaiæ libro habetur: Ego sum Dominus faciens omnia, extendens cœlos solus, stabiliens terram, et nullus mecum. De quo Proverbiorum liber asserit: Appendebat fundamenta terræ. Porro quod ait, Fundamenta terræ, intransitive legendum est, ut sit sensus: Ponebam terram pro aliorum fundamento elementorum. Elementa namque quæ proprio non terminantur termino, ut aer et aqua, fundantur et terminantur ad eam. Indica mihi, non quasi ignoranti, sed, Indica mihi, id est, ostende te scire, si vales, si habes intelligentiam ejus quod quæro.
paras.en: And so the Lord begins to show forth his excellence from the production, disposition and properties of the earth, which is the lowest of the elements and the better known to men. [[38:4|Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?|Ubi eras quando ponebam fundamenta terræ]] that is, when I brought forth the element of earth and each of its parts and set them in their due place in the middle of the universe? as if to say: Then thou wast not yet; whence it is plain that I go before thee in duration and in causality, and needed not thy counsel in the creation and disposition of the world. Hence we have in the book of Isaias: [[Is 44:24|I am the Lord, that make all things, that alone stretch out the heavens, that established the earth, and there is none with me|Ego sum Dominus faciens omnia, extendens cœlos solus, stabiliens terram, et nullus mecum]]. Of which the book of Proverbs declares: [[Prov 8:29|he balanced the foundations of the earth|Appendebat fundamenta terræ]]. Further, where he says, [[38:4|the foundations of the earth|Fundamenta terræ]], it is to be read intransitively [that is, the earth itself is the foundation, not something laid beneath it], so that the sense is: I laid the earth as the foundation of the other elements. For the elements that are not bounded by a boundary of their own, as air and water, are founded upon it and bounded by it. [[38:4|tell me|Indica mihi]], not as to one who does not know; but, [[38:4|tell me|Indica mihi]], that is, show that thou knowest, if thou canst, [[38:4|if thou hast understanding|si habes intelligentiam]] of what I ask.

paras.t: Quis posuit mensuras ejus, si nosti? id est, quis dedit et determinavit ei certas has suas dimensiones quas habet? quæ non sunt ei determinatæ ex necessitate, vel ex sua natura, quoniam major quantitas non repugnaret; sed ex ordinatione sapientiæ ac providentiæ Dei, qua omnia in numero, mensura et pondere fecit.
