Potest et ita exponi: Quis posuit mensuras, id est proportiones ejus ad alia elementa in grossitudine seu densitate et subtilitate, secundum quod ex uno pugillo terræ fiunt decem pugilli aquæ; ex uno quoque pugillo aquæ, decem aeris: ita quod locus aquæ decuplus est ad locum terræ. Vel demum, Quis tetendit super eam lineam? id est, certum ei situm in universis partibus assignavit, ejusque partes distinxit? juxta illud Actuum: Definiens terminos habitationis eorum. Dicit autem Albertus, quod terra est minimum corporum simplicium, præter lunam atque Mercurium.
paras.en: [[38:5|Who hath laid the measures thereof, if thou knowest|Quis posuit mensuras ejus, si nosti?]]? that is, who gave it and fixed for it these definite dimensions of its own that it has? These were not fixed for it of necessity or by its own nature, since a greater size would not be repugnant to it, but by the ordinance of the wisdom and providence of God, by which he made all things [[Wis 11:21|in measure, and number, and weight|in numero, mensura et pondere]] [Denis has the words in the order *number, measure and weight*]. It can also be expounded thus: [[38:5|Who hath laid the measures|Quis posuit mensuras]], that is, its proportions to the other elements in grossness, or density, and in subtlety, according as from one handful of earth are made ten handfuls of water, and from one handful of water ten of air; so that the place of water is tenfold the place of earth. Or finally, [[38:5|who hath stretched the line upon it?|Quis tetendit super eam lineam?]] that is, who assigned it a definite site among all the parts of the world, and marked out its parts? according to that of the Acts: [[Acts 17:26|determining|Definiens]] [[Acts 17:26|the limits of their habitation|terminos habitationis eorum]]. Albert says, moreover, that the earth is the smallest of the simple bodies, except the moon and Mercury.

paras.t: Super quo bases illius solidatæ sunt? Basis dicitur fundamentum. Bases ergo terræ sunt fundamenta ipsius: quæ aliquando nominantur interiores partes terræ, quibus aliæ videntur inniti. Vel basis terræ est centrum mundi; sicque, bases terræ possent dici partes centro viciniores. Quibus verbis Dominus insinuare videtur, quod nihil sit sub terra eam sustentans, quum tamen sit corpus gravissimum: sed divina virtute manet in medio fixa, Sapientia increata id ordinante, ut omnes partes terræ naturaliter inclinentur ad centrum. Hinc ait Psalmista: Qui fundasti terram super stabilitatem suam: non inclinabitur in sæculum sæculi. Aut quis demisit lapidem angularem ejus? id est, quis de alta potestate deorsum misit id terræ, quod in ea se habet per modum lapidis angularis, quod est centrum terræ, secundum Thomam, vel pars centro propinquior, cui aliæ partes annectuntur et aggregantur, atque ibidem stabiliuntur, quemadmodum ad lapidem angularem alii lapides congregantur, et per eum sibi cohærent atque firmantur, ipseque lapis angularis ad se et ad parietes ædificium firmat ac tenet.
paras.en: [[38:6|Upon what are its bases grounded?|Super quo bases illius solidatæ sunt?]] A base is called a foundation. The bases of the earth, then, are its foundations: by which are sometimes meant the inner parts of the earth, on which the others seem to rest. Or the base of the earth is the centre of the world; and so the bases of the earth could be called the parts nearer the centre. By these words the Lord seems to hint that there is nothing under the earth to hold it up, though it is a most heavy body: but by divine power it stays fixed in the middle, uncreated Wisdom so ordering it that all the parts of the earth naturally incline to the centre. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 103:5|Who hast founded the earth upon its own bases: it shall not be moved for ever and ever|Qui fundasti terram super stabilitatem suam: non inclinabitur in sæculum sæculi]] [the Latin reads *upon its own stability: it shall not incline for ever*, which is the point Denis takes from it]. [[38:6|or who laid the corner stone thereof|Aut quis demisit lapidem angularem ejus]]? that is, who from his high power sent down that part of the earth which stands in it as a corner stone: which is the centre of the earth, according to Thomas, or the part nearest the centre, to which the other parts are joined and gathered and are made steady there; as other stones are gathered to a corner stone and through it hold together and are made firm, and the corner stone itself, binding them to itself and to the walls, makes the building firm and holds it together.

paras.t: Præterea, circa hæc quæri potest, quod quæstiones istæ non videntur fuisse difficiles. Quis enim ignorat, quod Deus posuit terræ mensuras, eique situm et distinctionem contribuit, et centrum in ipsa constituit? Et respondendum, quod Dominus non intendebat hoc solum inquirere, quis hæc fecit, sed originalem horum rationem, et cur per divinam providentiam ista sint instituta, consistant, qualiterque peracta: quorum utique scientia intellectum excedit humanum.
paras.en: Further, it may be objected on this point that these questions do not seem to have been difficult. For who does not know that God laid the measures of the earth, gave it its site and the distinction of its parts, and set the centre in it? And the answer is that the Lord did not mean only to ask who made these things, but what is their first reason, and why by divine providence they were established and stand as they do, and how they were brought about: and the knowledge of these things certainly exceeds the human understanding.

paras.t: Cum me laudarent simul astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei? id est, quando terram ita constitui, tunc me astra matutina laudabant, mihique jubilabant omnes filii Dei. Ex quo loco quidam arguere sunt conati, quod spirituales creaturæ, videlicet angeli, ante mundum sensibilem sint creatæ. Sed hoc ex his verbis non sequitur. Quamvis enim simul tempore creata sint, cœlum et angeli ac terra, nihilominus distinctio elementorum secuta est, secundum unam litteræ Genesis expositionem.
paras.en: [[38:7|When the morning stars praised me together, and all the sons of God made a joyful melody?|Cum me laudarent simul astra matutina, et jubilarent omnes filii Dei?]] that is, when I so established the earth, then the morning stars were praising me, and all the sons of God were making a joyful melody to me. From this place some have tried to argue that the spiritual creatures, namely the angels, were created before the world of sense. But this does not follow from these words. For though heaven and the angels and the earth were created together in time, the distinction of the elements nonetheless came after, according to one exposition of the letter of Genesis.

paras.t: Porro, si quis dicat, sicut et Thomas dicit, per astra matutina intelligi stellas corporeas, quæ quarto die factæ leguntur: unde astra matutina vocantur, quasi de novo tunc facta, prout apud nos astra matutina dicuntur, quæ in principio diei apparent; nihilominus astra ista dicuntur tunc Deum laudasse, quia circa hoc tempus Deum laudare cœperunt; vel quia simul cum cœlo stellato substantialiter facta sunt, quamvis dicantur quarta die producta, videlicet quoad distinctionem sive ornatum, ut quidam exponunt. Denique, si per astra intelligantur hæc sidera, tunc verbum hoc dupliciter accipi potest. Primo, quod astra ista laudant Deum occasionaliter et materialiter, quoniam suo decore, motu, influxu ac ceteris ad ea spectantibus præbent omni menti creatæ occasionem materiamque laudandi proprium Creatorem: juxta quem modum etiam inanimata, mixta et irrationalia Deum laudare, superexaltare et benedicere asseruntur. Secundo, quod laudant Deum formaliter, cognitive et proprie, secundum opinionem dicentium corpora cœlestia animata. Unde Rabbi Moyses in libro Ducis neutrorum affirmat, quod non sunt inanimata, ut insipientes putant, sed vivunt atque intelligunt, et Creatori suo sublimem laudem decantant. De qua re plura dici hic possent, quæ potius transilienda censentur, præsertim quum opinio illa displiceat multis: quæ tamen, secundum Thomam in Summa contra gentiles, fidei non repugnat.
paras.en: Further, suppose one says, as Thomas also says, that by the [[38:7|morning stars|astra matutina]] are understood the bodily stars, which we read were made on the fourth day, and that they are called morning stars as being then newly made, as among us those are called morning stars which appear at the beginning of the day: these stars are nonetheless said to have praised God then, because about that time they began to praise God; or because they were made in their substance together with the starry heaven, though they are said to have been brought forth on the fourth day, namely as to their distinction or adornment, as some expound. Lastly, if by the stars these heavenly bodies are understood, then this word can be taken in two ways. First, that these stars praise God occasionally and materially [that is, by giving others the occasion and the matter for praise, not by praising him themselves], since by their beauty, motion, influence and the other things that belong to them they afford every created mind occasion and matter for praising its own Creator: in which way even inanimate things, mixed bodies [that is, bodies compounded of the elements] and irrational creatures are said to praise God, to exalt him above all and to bless him[[Dan 3:57||]] [the margin note here is hard to read; it seems to point to Dan. iii, the song of the three children]. Second, that they praise God formally, knowingly and properly, according to the opinion of those who say that the heavenly bodies are animate [that is, living, with souls of their own]. Hence Rabbi Moyses, in the book *Dux neutrorum* [that is, Maimonides's *Guide of the Perplexed*], affirms that they are not inanimate, as the ignorant think, but live and understand, and sing a sublime praise to their Creator. More could be said here on this matter, but it seems better passed over, especially since that opinion displeases many: though according to Thomas in the *Summa contra Gentiles* it is not repugnant to the faith.

paras.t: Aliqui vero per astra matutina intelligunt angelos sanctos ac splendidos, eos præsertim qui de inferioribus choris sunt, et quorum est corpora movere cœlestia. Per filios autem Dei, intelligunt angelos ordinum superiorum, quorum est adsistere Deo: qui et excellentius laudant Deum: idcirco ei jubilasse dicuntur. Quod autem angeli appellentur filii Dei, in exordio libri hujus scriptum est: Quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino, etc.
paras.en: Others understand by the [[38:7|morning stars|astra matutina]] the holy and shining angels, especially those who are of the lower choirs, and whose office it is to move the heavenly bodies. By the [[38:7|sons of God|filios autem Dei]] they understand the angels of the higher orders, whose office it is to stand before God; and these praise God more excellently, and for that reason are said to have made a joyful melody to him. That the angels are called sons of God is written at the beginning of this book: [[Job 1:6|when the sons of God came to stand before the Lord|Quum venissent filii Dei ut adsisterent coram Domino]], etc.

paras.t: Consequenter Deus eminentiam sapientiæ atque potentiæ suæ ostendit in dispositione maris, præsertim Oceani. Quis conclusit ostiis, id est certis terminis seu littoribus, mare, quando erumpebat, id est abundanter et fortiter exsurgebat, quasi de vulva procedens, id est sicut fetus qui de utero matris tempore suo quasi impetuose erumpit, ita quod retineri non valet? Vel, Quasi de vulva procedens, id est ex secreto providentiæ seu dispositionis divinæ, aut certe de loco in quo primum fuit creatum et situm, quando, secundum quosdam Sanctorum, totam terram operuit et alte in aere erigebatur, deinde Deo jubente ad unum locum redactum est, prout in Genesi habetur: Dixit Deus, Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Et in Psalmo: Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris, ponens in thesauris abyssos. In Proverbiis quoque: Certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos.
paras.en: Next God shows the eminence of his wisdom and power in the disposition of the sea, especially of the Ocean. [[38:8|Who shut up|Quis conclusit]] [[38:8|with doors|ostiis]], that is, with definite bounds or shores, [[38:8|the sea|mare]], [[38:8|when it broke forth|quando erumpebat]], that is, rose up abundantly and strongly, [[38:8|as issuing out of the womb|quasi de vulva procedens]], that is, like a child that in its time bursts forth from its mother's womb as if with violence, so that it cannot be held back? Or, [[38:8|as issuing out of the womb|Quasi de vulva procedens]], that is, from the secret of divine providence or disposition; or else from the place in which it was first created and set, when, according to some of the Saints, it covered the whole earth and rose high into the air, and afterwards at God's command was brought back into one place, as we have in Genesis: [[Gen 1:9|God also said; Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Dixit Deus, Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. And in the Psalm: [[Ps 32:7|Gathering together the waters of the sea, as in a vessel; laying up the depths in storehouses|Congregans sicut in utre aquas maris, ponens in thesauris abyssos]]. In Proverbs too: [[Prov 8:27|with a certain law, and compass, he enclosed the depths|Certa lege et gyro vallabat abyssos]].

paras.t: Cum ponerem nubem vestimentum ejus, id est, nubibus illud circumdarem, sicut homo circumdatur vestimento. Nubes enim ex vaporibus de mari elevatis maxime generantur. Ideo circa mare magis abundant: circa quod etiam nubilosus aer remansit, dum aquæ congregabantur ad locum unum. Et caligine illud quasi pannis infantiæ obvolverem, id est, operirem seu tegerem. Quum enim nubes ibi abundent, nebulosusque aer et quidam vapores nondum elevati in altum, constat quod frequenter sit ibi caligo: et videtur ei alludere, quod scriptum est in Genesi: Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi.
paras.en: [[38:9|When I made a cloud the garment thereof|Cum ponerem nubem vestimentum ejus]], that is, when I surrounded it with clouds, as a man is surrounded with a garment. For clouds are generated chiefly from vapours raised from the sea. Therefore they are more abundant about the sea; and about it a cloudy air also remained while the waters were being gathered into one place. [[38:9|and wrapped it in a mist as in swaddling bands?|Et caligine illud quasi pannis infantiæ obvolverem]] that is, covered or concealed it. For since clouds abound there, and a misty air and certain vapours not yet raised on high, it is plain that there is often a mist there: and what is written in Genesis seems to allude to this: [[Gen 1:2|darkness was upon the face of the deep|Tenebræ erant super faciem abyssi]].

paras.t: Circumdedi illud terminis meis, id est littoribus, ripis seu finibus a sapientia mea præordinatis, videlicet quousque effluat et refluat; et posui vectem, id est obstacula procedendi, et ostia, id est clausuras vel etiam aperturas, per quas de Oceano egrediuntur particularia maria et flumina. Et dixi, id est, præcepto meo institui: Usque huc venies, id est, usque ad terminos istos a me præstitutos extrema tua pertingent, et ex his locis te per maria et flumina præfata diffundes, et non procedes amplius, ne terram operias; et hic, scilicet ad ripas has, confringes tumentes fluctus tuos, id est undas cum impetu abundanti fluentes, et ex fundo fortiter exsurgentes: quæ ad littora rejiciuntur.
paras.en: [[38:10|I set my bounds around it|Circumdedi illud terminis meis]], that is, shores, banks or limits fore-ordained by my wisdom, namely how far it should flow out and flow back; [[38:10|and made it bars|et posui vectem]], that is, hindrances to its going further, [[38:10|and doors|et ostia]], that is, closures, or else openings through which the particular seas and the rivers go out from the Ocean. [[38:11|And I said|Et dixi]], that is, I established by my command: [[38:11|Hitherto thou shalt come|Usque huc venies]], that is, thy outer edges shall reach as far as these bounds appointed by me, and from these places thou shalt spread thyself through the seas and rivers aforesaid, [[38:11|and shalt go no further|et non procedes amplius]], lest thou cover the earth; [[38:11|and here|et hic]], namely at these shores, [[38:11|thou shalt break thy swelling waves|confringes tumentes fluctus tuos]], that is, the waves that flow with abundant force and rise strongly from the bottom, and are thrown back upon the shores.

paras.t: Circa prædicta de dispositione maris, asserit Thomas: Videtur naturalis ordo elementorum requirere, ut aqua ex omni parte circumdaret terram, sicut aer ex omni parte circumdat aquam; sed divina dispositione factum est, ad generationem hominum et animalium ac plantarum, ut aliqua pars terræ discooperta remaneret ab aquis, Deo sua virtute aquas maris sub certis limitibus retinente. Sed contra id quis potest objicere, quia secundum hoc dispositio ista mundi et elementorum non est naturalis, sed miraculosa et supernaturalis, quum tamen Augustinus super Genesim dicat, quod in prima rerum institutione ac ordinatione non quæritur, quid Deus potuit, sed quid rerum conveniebat naturis. Et respondendum, quod terra et aqua dupliciter attenduntur. Primo, secundum proprias naturas quibus comparantur ad invicem: et sic naturaliter competeret terræ, tanquam graviori, esse omnino sub aqua. Secundo, per comparationem ad ordinem universi, et quoad finem suæ creationis: sicque convenit eis naturaliter dispositio ista quam habent, quia ad hoc facta sunt, ut homini et ceteris animalibus deserviant: quod esse non valet, nisi pars terræ sit sicca. Unde, secundum philosophos, in generatione mixtorum, ignis naturaliter descendit, non per respectum ad propriam naturam secundum se, sed per comparationem ejus ad ordinem universi, qui exigit quamlibet naturam peragere id propter quod facta est. Hinc fertur in Psalmo: Terminum posuisti quem non transgredientur, scilicet aquæ: neque convertentur operire terram. Et in Jeremiæ libro Dominus contestatur: Posui arenam terminum mari, præceptum sempiternum quod non præteribit: intumescent fluctus ejus, et non transibunt illud.
paras.en: On what has been said of the disposition of the sea, Thomas asserts: The natural order of the elements seems to require that water should surround the earth on every side, as air surrounds water on every side; but by divine disposition it has come about, for the generation of men and animals and plants, that some part of the earth should remain uncovered by the waters, God by his power holding the waters of the sea within definite limits. But against this one may object that by this account the disposition of the world and of the elements is not natural but miraculous and supernatural; whereas Augustine, on Genesis, says that in the first institution and ordering of things we do not ask what God could do, but what befitted the natures of things. And the answer is that earth and water are considered in two ways. First, according to their own natures, by which they are compared with each other: and so it would naturally befit the earth, as the heavier, to be wholly under the water. Second, by comparison with the order of the universe, and as to the end of their creation: and so the disposition they have befits them naturally, since they were made for this, to serve man and the other animals; which cannot be unless part of the earth is dry. Hence, according to the philosophers, in the generation of mixed bodies fire naturally descends, not with respect to its own nature in itself, but by comparison with the order of the universe, which requires every nature to carry out that for which it was made. Hence it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:9|Thou hast set a bound which they shall not pass over|Terminum posuisti quem non transgredientur]], namely the waters, [[Ps 103:9|neither shall they return to cover the earth|neque convertentur operire terram]]. And in the book of Jeremias the Lord solemnly declares: [[Jer 5:22|I have set the sand a bound for the sea, an everlasting ordinance, which it shall not pass over|Posui arenam terminum mari, præceptum sempiternum quod non præteribit]]: [[Jer 5:22|they shall swell, and shall not pass over it|intumescent fluctus ejus, et non transibunt illud]].

paras.t: Numquid post ortum tuum, id est postquam natus es, qui ante nativitatem tuam nil facere potuisti, præcepisti diluculo, ut tempore suo exsurgeret, et noctem diei continuaret, vel ut aliquid ageret ad tuam jussionem, et ostendisti auroræ locum suum, ubi primo lux solis incipit apparere? hoc est, ista in tua potestate non sunt, nec ordinare potuisti temporum varietates, cursum et ordinem, et ubi aurora inchoaretur. Præterea, secundum Thomam, claritas diluculi sive auroræ diversificatur secundum diversas partes elevationis signorum quæ sol perambulat. Dum enim fuerit in signo velocis ascensionis, in quo cito oritur, parum durat aurora; quando autem sol est in signo tardæ ascensionis, diutius durat: estque determinata mensura loci ex quo ibi exsistente sole, incipit claritas diluculi.
paras.en: [[38:12|Didst thou since thy birth|Numquid post ortum tuum]], that is, after thou wast born, who before thy birth couldst do nothing, [[38:12|command the morning|præcepisti diluculo]], that it should rise in its time and join the night to the day, or that it should do anything at thy bidding, [[38:12|and shew the dawning of the day its place?|et ostendisti auroræ locum suum]] namely the place where the light of the sun first begins to appear? That is to say: these things are not in thy power, nor couldst thou order the changes of the seasons, their course and order, and where the dawn should begin. Further, according to Thomas, the brightness of the morning or dawn varies according to the different parts of the rising of the signs through which the sun passes. For when the sun is in a sign of swift ascension [that is, a sign of the zodiac that rises quickly above the horizon], in which it rises quickly, the dawn lasts a short time; but when the sun is in a sign of slow ascension, it lasts longer: and there is a fixed measure of the place from which, when the sun is there, the brightness of the morning begins.

paras.t: Hæc omnia Deus commemorat ad declarandam excellentiam suam in omni perfectione, sapientia et virtute: ita ut si Job respondisset ad quæstiones prætactas, Tu, o Domine, mare ostiis conclusisti: Dominus mox intulisset: Ergo tanta est eminentia mea, quod mecum disputare aut contendere nequis.
paras.en: All these things God recalls to make known his excellence in every perfection, wisdom and power: so that if Job had answered the questions touched on, Thou, O Lord, didst shut up the sea with doors, the Lord would at once have inferred: Then so great is my eminence that thou canst not dispute or contend with me.

paras.t: Numquid tenuisti concutiens extrema terræ? Hoc quidam exponunt de terræ motu, tanquam dicat: Numquid extrema terræ potes tua virtute seu manibus apprehendere et tenere atque concutere, ut terræ motus causetur? in quo non tota terra movetur, sed aliquæ ejus extremitates, exterioresve partes. Alii ita exponunt: Numquid tenuisti concutiens extrema terræ, id est homines ab extremo seu fine terræ usque ad extremum, concutiendo eos per mutuam impugnationem? Hinc de Deo in Psalmo cantatur: Qui respicit terram, et facit eam tremere. Et rursus: In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ. Itemque Ecclesiasticus: Ecce cœlum et cœli cœlorum, abyssus et universa terra, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, in conspectu Dei commovebuntur, montes simul et colles, et fundamenta terræ: et quum conspexerit ea Deus, tremore concutientur. Et excussisti impios ex ea? id est, peccatores impœnitentes per terræ motum vel alias plagas auferre a terra et vita præsenti, non tuæ sed meæ est potestatis.
paras.en: [[38:13|didst thou hold the extremities of the earth shaking them|Numquid tenuisti concutiens extrema terræ]]? Some expound this of an earthquake, as if he said: Canst thou by thy power or with thy hands seize and hold and shake the extremities of the earth, so that an earthquake is caused? in which not the whole earth is moved, but some of its extremities or outer parts. Others expound it thus: [[38:13|didst thou hold the extremities of the earth shaking them|Numquid tenuisti concutiens extrema terræ]], that is, men from one end or border of the earth to the other, shaking them by their warring on one another? Hence it is sung of God in the Psalm: [[Ps 103:32|He looketh upon the earth, and maketh it tremble|Qui respicit terram, et facit eam tremere]]. And again: [[Ps 94:4|in his hand are all the ends of the earth|In manu ejus sunt omnes fines terræ]]. And Ecclesiasticus likewise: [[Ecclus 16:18|Behold the heaven, and the heavens of heavens, the deep, and all the earth, and the things that are in them, shall be moved in his sight|Ecce cœlum et cœli cœlorum, abyssus et universa terra, et omnia quæ in eis sunt, in conspectu Dei commovebuntur]], [[Ecclus 16:19|The mountains also, and the hills, and the foundations of the earth: when God shall look upon them, they shall be shaken with trembling|montes simul et colles, et fundamenta terræ: et quum conspexerit ea Deus, tremore concutientur]]. [[38:13|and hast thou shaken the ungodly out of it?|Et excussisti impios ex ea?]] that is, to take impenitent sinners away from the earth and from the present life by an earthquake or by other plagues is not in thy power but in mine.

paras.t: Restituetur ut lutum signaculum: id est, impiis de terra ablatis, signaculum, id est homo ad Dei imaginem factus, reparabitur, ita quod loco interfectorum impiorum alii Deo disponente succedent, sicut lutum, id est copiose, quemadmodum lutum abundat, vel, sicut lutum divisum faciliter reintegratur. Hinc superius Eliu dixit de Deo: Conteret multos et innumerabiles, et stare faciet alios pro eis. Et stabit sicut vestimentum, id est, ad tempus subsistet, et continuo atque paulatim consumetur, ut vestes paulatim a tinea. Unde supra Job dixit: Qui quasi putredo consumendus sum, et quasi vestimentum quod comeditur a tinea.
paras.en: [[38:14|The seal shall be restored as clay|Restituetur ut lutum signaculum]]: that is, when the ungodly have been taken from the earth, the seal, that is, man made to the image of God, shall be restored, so that in the place of the ungodly who have been slain others shall succeed by God's disposing, as clay, that is, abundantly, as clay abounds; or, as clay that has been divided is easily made whole again. Hence Eliu said of God above: [[Job 34:24|He shall break in pieces many and innumerable, and shall make others to stand in their stead|Conteret multos et innumerabiles, et stare faciet alios pro eis]]. [[38:14|and shall stand as a garment|Et stabit sicut vestimentum]], that is, shall last for a time, and be consumed continually and little by little, as clothes are little by little by the moth. Hence Job said above: [[Job 13:28|Who am to be consumed as rottenness, and as a garment that is motheaten|Qui quasi putredo consumendus sum, et quasi vestimentum quod comeditur a tinea]].

paras.t: Auferetur ab impiis lux sua, id est vita, prosperitas, gloria temporalis, per mortem in terræ motu, aut in alia Dei plaga: et brachium excelsum confringetur, id est, tyrannica virtus seu robur violentorum et superborum, vel iniqua dominatio, divinitus destruetur atque damnabitur, quemadmodum in Ecclesiastico Sapientia ait: Superborum et sublimium colla propria virtute calcavi. Et in eodem volumine legitur: Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus. Zacharias quoque de impio pastore asserit: Brachium ejus ariditate siccabitur. Sed et Isaias fert: Contrivit Dominus baculum impiorum, virgam dominantium. Hinc primo Machabæorum habetur: A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quia gloria ejus stercus et vermis: hodie extollitur, et cras non invenitur, quia conversus est in terram suam, et cogitatio ejus periit.
paras.en: [[38:15|From the wicked their light shall be taken away|Auferetur ab impiis lux sua]], that is, life, prosperity, temporal glory, through death in an earthquake or in some other plague of God; [[38:15|and the high arm shall be broken|et brachium excelsum confringetur]], that is, the tyrannical strength or might of the violent and the proud, or wicked dominion, shall be destroyed and condemned by God; as Wisdom says in Ecclesiasticus: The necks of the proud and the lofty I have trodden down by my own power[[Ecclus 24:11||]] [Denis's wording differs from the Vulgate, which has *the hearts of all the high and low*; the margin note beside it cannot be read]. And in the same book we read: [[Ecclus 10:17|God hath overturned the thrones of proud princes|Sedes ducum superborum destruxit Deus]]. Zacharias too declares of the wicked shepherd: [[Zach 11:17|his arm shall quite wither away|Brachium ejus ariditate siccabitur]]. And Isaias says: [[Is 14:5|The Lord hath broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of the rulers|Contrivit Dominus baculum impiorum, virgam dominantium]]. Hence we have in the first book of Machabees: [[1 Mach 2:62|fear not the words of a sinful man, for his glory is dung and worms|A verbis peccatoris ne timueritis, quia gloria ejus stercus et vermis]]: [[1 Mach 2:63|Today he is lifted up, and tomorrow he shall not be found, because he is returned into his earth and his thought is come to nothing|hodie extollitur, et cras non invenitur, quia conversus est in terram suam, et cogitatio ejus periit]].

paras.t: Numquid ingressus es profundum maris Oceani, ad videndum varias piscium species et cetera quæ latent ibidem? et in novissimis, id est extremis seu remotissimis et ultimis ac profundissimis locis abyssi, id est maris jam dicti, deambulasti, videlicet super fundum ipsius, ubi nullus hominum unquam devenit, nec quomodo terra illa disposita sit, conspexit?
paras.en: [[38:16|Hast thou entered into the depths of the sea|Numquid ingressus es profundum maris]] of the Ocean, to see the various kinds of fish and the other things that lie hidden there? and [[38:16|in the lowest parts|in novissimis]], that is, in the outermost or most remote, the last and deepest places, [[38:16|of the deep|abyssi]], that is, of the sea just named, hast thou [[38:16|walked|deambulasti]], namely upon its bottom, where no man ever came, nor saw how that ground is laid out?

paras.t: Numquid apertæ sunt tibi portæ mortis, id est portæ inferni? Vel, Portæ mortis dicuntur causæ corruptionis mixtorum, potissime hominis, per quas est ad mortem ingressus: quas sigillatim, distincte, perfecte et plene homo non noscit: quia nonnunquam causa corruptionis ex supernorum influxu procedit, interdum est ex causa interiori valde occulta, aliquando ex causa supernaturali, dum homines pro suis peccatis divinitus occiduntur. Et ostia tenebrosa vidisti? Ostia tenebrosa idem dicuntur quod portæ mortis. Vel ostia ista sunt varii modi quibus homines vadunt et corruunt in infernum. Pluribus autem modis homines decipiuntur ac pereunt, quam aliquis valeat determinare.
paras.en: [[38:17|Have the gates of death been opened to thee|Numquid apertæ sunt tibi portæ mortis]], that is, the gates of hell? Or, [[38:17|the gates of death|Portæ mortis]] are the name given to the causes of the corruption of mixed bodies, above all of man, through which is the way in to death: and these man does not know one by one, distinctly, perfectly and fully; for sometimes the cause of corruption proceeds from the influence of the heavenly bodies, sometimes it is from a very hidden cause within, sometimes from a supernatural cause, when men are slain by God for their sins. [[38:17|and hast thou seen the darksome doors?|Et ostia tenebrosa vidisti?]] The [[38:17|darksome doors|Ostia tenebrosa]] are said to be the same as the [[38:17|gates of death|portæ mortis]]. Or these doors are the various ways by which men go and fall headlong into hell. And men are deceived and perish in more ways than anyone could determine.

paras.t: Numquid considerasti latitudinem terræ? id est, latitudinem terræ certitudinaliter non agnoscis. Accipitur autem latitudo terræ, a parte australi seu meridiana, in aquilonem seu septentrionem: quæ latitudo (ut dicitur) tota pertransiri non potest, quoniam torrida zona intermedia, impertransibilis est, propter excessum caloris, ut dicunt. Circa hoc asserit Thomas: Longitudo terræ, secundum astrologos, sumitur secundum processum ab oriente in occidentem: latitudo autem, a meridie in aquilonem: quia in qualibet re major dimensio dicitur longitudo, et minor dimensio, latitudo. Est autem experimento probatum, quod dimensio terræ, a nobis habitatæ, major est ab oriente in occidentem, quam a meridie in aquilonem. Ideo latitudo terræ, a meridie ad aquilonem attenditur.
paras.en: [[38:18|Hast thou considered the breadth of the earth?|Numquid considerasti latitudinem terræ?]] That is, thou dost not know the breadth of the earth with certainty. Now the breadth of the earth is taken from the southern or meridional part to the north or septentrion; and this breadth (so it is said) cannot be crossed in its whole extent, since the torrid zone lying between is impassable because of the excess of heat, as they say. On this Thomas asserts: The length of the earth, according to the astronomers [astrologi: in Denis's day the word covers what we call astronomers], is taken along the course from east to west, and the breadth from south to north; for in any thing the greater dimension is called the length and the lesser the breadth. Now it has been proved by experience that the dimension of the earth inhabited by us is greater from east to west than from south to north. Therefore the breadth of the earth is reckoned from south to north.

paras.t: Indica mihi, si nosti omnia, ita ut cum Deo valeas disputare, in qua via habitet lux. Lux corporum cœlestium in eis dicitur habitare, secundum quod manet in eis, hoc est in luminaribus cœli. Itaque, quærere in qua via habitet lux, est investigare per quæ itinera seu quibus modis atque processibus luminaria moveantur: quod hominibus est incertum, ut patet ex diversitate opinionum eorum, circa hoc ipsum quibusdam affirmantibus, ea moveri per epicyclos atque excentricos, aliis per diversarum motum sphærarum. Porro, secundum Albertum, habitatio lucis, est relatio, id est iterata motio seu reditio, solis ad terram, videlicet nostri horizontis. Vias autem ascensionum descensionumque solis, explicare determinate quis poterit? Et tenebrarum quis locus sit. Quemadmodum lux terræ habitabilis ex luminarium motu causatur, prout in hemisphærio superiori moventur: sic tenebræ sunt ex recessu eorum, prout in inferiori moventur hemisphærio: quod eamdem habet difficultatem, quantum ad vias et modos motuum luminarium cœli. Non autem perfecte mensurari potest locus alicujus corporis, nisi via per quam ambulat cognoscatur. Quoniam ergo via motus luminarium certitudinaliter a nobis cognosci non potest, nec viam tenebrarum cognoscere possumus, puta exordium loci in quo ex solis luminariumque recessu, caligo noctis incipit.
paras.en: [[38:18|tell me, if thou knowest all things|Indica mihi, si nosti omnia]], so that thou art able to dispute with God: [[38:19|Where is the way where light dwelleth|in qua via habitet lux]]. The light of the heavenly bodies is said to dwell in them, inasmuch as it abides in them, that is, in the luminaries of heaven. So to ask by what way the light dwells is to inquire by what paths, or in what manners and courses, the luminaries are moved: and this is uncertain to men, as is plain from the diversity of their opinions on this very point, some affirming that they are moved by epicycles and eccentrics, others by the motion of diverse spheres. Further, according to Albert, the dwelling of the light is its being brought back [relatio], that is, the repeated motion or return of the sun to the earth, namely to our horizon. But who will be able to set out with certainty the ways of the sun's risings and settings? [[38:19|and where is the place of darkness|Et tenebrarum quis locus sit]]. Just as the light of the habitable earth is caused by the motion of the luminaries as they move in the upper hemisphere, so darkness comes of their withdrawal as they move in the lower hemisphere: and this has the same difficulty, as regards the ways and manners of the motions of the luminaries of heaven. Now the place of a body cannot be perfectly measured unless the way by which it travels be known. Since, then, the way of the motion of the luminaries cannot be known by us with certainty, neither can we know the way of the darkness, for instance the beginning of the place in which the gloom of night begins from the withdrawal of the sun and the luminaries.

paras.t: Ut ducas unumquodque, id est tam lucem quam tenebras, ad terminos suos, id est usque ad ea ad quæ valent pertingere, deducendo lucem et caliginem usque ad extrema ad quæ attingere queunt. Quasi dicat: Hoc nequaquam tuæ est potestatis, sed Dei, qui (ut in Genesi habetur) divisit lucem a tenebris. Et intelligas semitas domus ejus, videlicet lucis: cujus domus est luminare cœleste, quod est velut vas luminis, utpote sol, qui per varia incedit itinera, secundum quod motus habet diversos: quas semitas distincte et certe homo in hoc sæculo non agnoscit, ut dictum est.
paras.en: [[38:20|That thou mayst bring every thing|Ut ducas unumquodque]], that is, both light and darkness, [[38:20|to its own bounds|ad terminos suos]], that is, as far as the things they are able to reach, leading out the light and the gloom to the furthest limits they can attain. As if he said: This is in no way in thy power, but in God's, who (as we read in Genesis) [[Gen 1:4|divided the light from the darkness|divisit lucem a tenebris]]. [[38:20|and understand the paths of the house thereof|Et intelligas semitas domus ejus]], namely of the light: whose house is a heavenly luminary, which is as it were a vessel of light, for instance the sun, which goes along various paths according as it has diverse motions; and these paths man in this world does not know distinctly and certainly, as has been said.

paras.t: Sciebas tunc, id est in exordio quando ego ista ita disposui, quod nasciturus esses? et numerum dierum tuorum noveras? id est, quamdiu in vita subsisteres? Non utique, quoniam necdum eras: scire autem præsupponit esse. Sed ego hoc præscivi: ideo me scientia comparari non vales.
paras.en: [[38:21|Didst thou know then|Sciebas tunc]], that is, at the beginning, when I disposed these things so, [[38:21|that thou shouldst be born|quod nasciturus esses]]? [[38:21|and didst thou know the number of thy days|et numerum dierum tuorum noveras]]? that is, how long thou wouldst continue in life? Surely not, since thou wast not yet: and knowing presupposes being. But I foreknew this: therefore thou canst not be compared with me in knowledge.

paras.t: Numquid ingressus es, per considerationem acutam et claram, thesauros nivis, id est virtutem per quam, et materiam ex qua generatur? Divina enim potestate omnes hujusmodi impressiones principaliter fiunt, et ex vaporibus seu exhalationibus materialiter producuntur, aut thesauros grandinis adspexisti, puta virtutem effectivam et materiam grandinis? Hæc autem perfecte ac particulariter scire, est super hominem, maxime dum supernaturaliter producuntur in ultionem iniquitatis pravorum, secundum quod subditur: Quæ præparavi in tempus hostis, id est pro tempore quo hostes et adversarios decrevi affligere: sicut in Exodo legitur, quod grando horribilis cecidit in terra Ægypti. In diem pugnæ et belli, id est præliorum, sive intestinorum, sive extrinsecus inductorum.
paras.en: [[38:22|Hast thou entered|Numquid ingressus es]], by keen and clear consideration, [[38:22|into the storehouses of the snow|thesauros nivis]], that is, the power by which and the matter from which it is generated? For all impressions of this kind [impressiones: in the old natural philosophy, the phenomena formed in the air, such as snow, hail, rain and thunder] come about principally by the divine power, and are produced materially from vapours or exhalations; [[38:22|or hast thou beheld the treasures of the hail|aut thesauros grandinis adspexisti]], that is, the effective power and the matter of the hail? Now to know these things perfectly and in particular is above man, especially when they are produced supernaturally to punish the iniquity of the wicked, according to what follows: [[38:23|Which I have prepared for the time of the enemy|Quæ præparavi in tempus hostis]], that is, for the time in which I have decided to afflict enemies and adversaries; as we read in Exodus that a horrible hail fell in the land of Egypt[[Ex 9:23||]] [the margin gives Exod. ix, its verse number unread; the hail on Egypt is told at Ex 9:23–25]. [[38:23|against the day of battle and war|In diem pugnæ et belli]], that is, of battles, whether civil or brought in from without.

paras.t: Insuper dic, Per quam viam spargitur, id est diffunditur, lux luminarium cœli, præcipue solis, per terram? per quam etiam viam dividitur æstus super terram, id est calor qui in terra consequitur diffusionem lucis solaris? tanquam dicat: Modum causalitatis et diffusionis istorum perfecte non capis, quomodo scilicet lux, vel in instanti, vel in tempore imperceptibili, per totum hemisphærium diffundatur, et in diversis terris diversus calor diversimode generetur. Denique, notanter asserit lucem spargi, caloremque dividi, quoniam serenitate aeris exsistente, lux solis ad omnes æqualiter indifferenterque venit, ita quod sensibiliter claritatis intensio non diversificatur, sicut diversificatur caloris intensio seu augmentum. Præterea hæc duo conjungit, secundum Albertum, quoniam æstus sequitur lucem, et modus æstus modum lucis. Ubi enim lux spargitur ad angulum rectum, ibi reflectitur angulus in se ipsum, et fit intensior calor. Ubi vero ad angulum acutum, fit minor æstus: ubi autem ad angulum hebetem seu expansum, æstus fit minimus: sicque semper secundum modum anguli ad quem reflectitur lux, fit etiam modus caloris. Unde Ecclesiasticus dicit: In meridiano sol exurit terram, et in conspectu ardoris ejus quis poterit sustinere?
paras.en: Moreover, tell me: [[38:24|By what way is the light spread|Per quam viam spargitur]], that is, diffused (the light of the luminaries of heaven, especially of the sun) over the earth? by what way, too, is [[38:24|heat divided upon the earth|dividitur æstus super terram]], that is, the warmth that follows in the earth on the spreading of the sun's light? As if he said: Thou dost not fully grasp the manner in which these things are caused and spread: how, that is, light is spread over the whole hemisphere either in an instant or in an imperceptible time, and how in diverse lands diverse heat is generated in diverse ways. Further, he says pointedly that the light is spread and the heat divided, since when the air is clear the sun's light comes to all equally and without difference, so that the intensity of brightness is not perceptibly varied, as the intensity or increase of heat is varied. Moreover, according to Albert, he joins these two because heat follows light, and the manner of the heat the manner of the light. For where the light falls at a right angle, there the angle is reflected back on itself, and the heat becomes more intense; where at an acute angle, the heat is less; and where at an obtuse or open angle, the heat is least: and so the manner of the heat always follows the manner of the angle at which the light is reflected. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: [[Ecclus 43:3|At noon he burneth the earth|In meridiano sol exurit terram]], [[Ecclus 43:3|and who can abide his burning heat?|et in conspectu ardoris ejus quis poterit sustinere?]]

paras.t: Quis dedit vehementissimo imbri, id est pluviæ, quæ cum maxima vehementia cadit, cursum, id est tam impetuosum ac celerem motum? et viam sonantis tonitrui? id est, quis dedit tonitruo sonoro suum processum, ita quod sonat, non quasi res in uno permanens loco, sed quasi procedens de loco ad locum? quis, inquam, hæc dedit, nisi ego qui cuncta disposui, sicque institui, ut pluvia validis ventis impulsa et agitata, vel ex nube aquosissima decidens, cum tanta vehementia cadat, atque tonitruum taliter sonet? Ut plueret super terram absque homine, id est absque hominis cooperatione sive industria; vel, Super terram absque homine, id est quæ ab hominibus non habitatur, videlicet in deserto, ubi nullus mortalium commoratur hominum, quamvis habitent ibi bruta, ut imber præfatus impleret inviam et desolatam, id est terram incultam, non deambulatam nec habitatam, et produceret terra hujusmodi sic irrigata, herbas virentes. Itaque sapienter Deus instituit, ut nubes per ventos impellantur ad talia loca, quæ aliter irrigari et fecundari non possunt: quum enim sint sicca, vapores pluviales ex eis non elevantur, sed aliunde adducuntur.
paras.en: [[38:25|Who gave|Quis dedit]] [[38:25|to violent showers|vehementissimo imbri]], that is, to rain that falls with the greatest violence, [[38:25|a course|cursum]], that is, so impetuous and swift a motion? [[38:25|or a way for noisy thunder|et viam sonantis tonitrui]]? that is, who gave the sounding thunder its progress, so that it sounds not like a thing staying in one place but like one going on from place to place? Who, I say, gave these things, if not I who disposed all things, and so ordained that rain driven and tossed by strong winds, or falling from a cloud full of water, should fall with such violence, and that thunder should sound in such a way? [[38:26|That it should rain on the earth without man|Ut plueret super terram absque homine]], that is, without the co-operation or industry of man; or, [[38:26|on the earth without man|Super terram absque homine]], that is, earth not inhabited by men, namely [[38:26|in the wilderness|in deserto]], [[38:26|where no mortal dwelleth|ubi nullus mortalium commoratur]] among men, though brute beasts live there; so that the said shower [[38:27|should fill the desert and desolate land|impleret inviam et desolatam]], that is, untilled land, not walked over nor inhabited, [[38:27|and should bring forth|et produceret]], the land being so watered, [[38:27|green grass|herbas virentes]]. So God has wisely ordained that the clouds be driven by the winds to such places, which could not otherwise be watered and made fruitful: for since they are dry, rainy vapours do not rise from them, but are brought from elsewhere.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, vehementissimus imber, est efficacissima et ardentissima evangelicæ legis doctrina: cui per Apostolos Deus contulit cursum, quorum prædicatio fuit sonans tonitruum. Nam et in Evangelio Christus Petrum, Jacobum et Joannem, Filios appellat tonitrui. Itaque per Apostolos Deus hunc imbrem diffudit in deserto et invia desolataque via, id est per gentilitatem, olim a Deo relictam, nullaque Sancti Spiritus consolatione refectam, in qua nullus mortalium, id est hominum vere rationaliter viventium, morabatur, ut gentiles conversi producerent herbas virentes, id est opera virtuosa.
paras.en: Spiritually, the [[38:25|violent showers|vehementissimus imber]] are the most effective and most ardent teaching of the law of the Gospel, to which God gave a [[38:25|course|cursum]] through the Apostles, whose preaching was [[38:25|noisy thunder|sonans tonitruum]]. For in the Gospel too Christ calls Peter, James and John [[Mark 3:17|The sons of thunder|Filios appellat tonitrui]] [in Mark the name is given to James and John only]. So through the Apostles God poured out this shower [[38:26|in the wilderness|in deserto]] and on the [[38:27|desert and desolate|invia desolataque]] way, that is, through the Gentile world, once forsaken by God and refreshed by no consolation of the Holy Ghost, in which [[38:26|no mortal|nullus mortalium]], that is, no man living truly according to reason, dwelt; so that the converted Gentiles might bring forth [[38:27|green grass|herbas virentes]], that is, virtuous works.

paras.t: Quis est pluviæ pater? vel quis genuit stillas roris? De cujus utero egressa est glacies? et gelu de cœlo quis genuit? Hæc omnia loquitur Deus ad insinuandum, quod ipse horum prima et principalis est causa, et quod hi ejus effectus perfecte investigari non valent, quoad omnes causas eorum, sicut lucidius dictum est. Porro variis modis dicitur Deus alicujus pater et genitor. Pluviæ vero et roris pater seu genitor vocatur, secundum latam patris acceptionem, prout omne principium productivum dicitur pater ejus quod causat. Per uterum vero de quo egreditur glacies, intelligi potest, vel causa glaciei materialis, vel locus quo generatur, vel virtus divina quæ est prima vis productiva. Gelu quoque de cœlo, id est cœlesti virtute, producitur. Dicit enim Albertus, quod lumen Saturni causa sit gelicidii. Sunt tamen et aliæ causæ ipsius.
paras.en: [[38:28|Who is the father of rain|Quis est pluviæ pater]]? [[38:28|or who begot the drops of dew|vel quis genuit stillas roris]]? [[38:29|Out of whose womb came the ice|De cujus utero egressa est glacies]]? [[38:29|and the frost from heaven who hath gendered it|et gelu de cœlo quis genuit]]? God says all these things to suggest that he himself is their first and principal cause, and that these effects of his cannot be perfectly searched out as to all their causes, as has been said more clearly. Now God is said in various ways to be the father and begetter of something. He is called the father or begetter of rain and dew according to a broad taking of the word father, inasmuch as every productive principle is called the father of what it causes. By the womb out of which the ice comes may be understood either the material cause of ice, or the place in which it is generated, or the divine power, which is the first productive force. The [[38:29|frost|Gelu]] too is produced [[38:29|from heaven|de cœlo]], that is, by a heavenly power: for Albert says that the light of Saturn is a cause of frost. Yet there are other causes of it too.

paras.t: Præterea, secundum Thomam, causa glaciei est frigus, quæ est qualitas feminina. Feminæ enim communiter sunt frigidiores viris. Pluviarum autem et roris causa, calor est, resolvens nec permittens congelari vaporem. Calor autem est qualitas masculina. Ideoque signanter circa generationem glaciei, utitur nomine uteri spectantis ad matrem; circa generationem vero roris et pluviæ, utitur nomine patris.
paras.en: Further, according to Thomas, the cause of ice is cold, which is a feminine quality, for women are commonly colder than men. But the cause of rains and of dew is heat, which dissolves the vapour and does not allow it to freeze; and heat is a masculine quality. And so, pointedly, in speaking of the generation of ice he uses the word womb, which belongs to a mother, but in speaking of the generation of dew and rain he uses the word father.

paras.t: Ex frigore demum duplex glacies generatur. Una in aere: quod pertinet ad pruinam de cœlo cadentem. Ad quod referri potest, quod dictum est, Gelu de cœlo quis genuit? Quod idcirco attribuit patri, quoniam non apparet tanta vis frigoris in pruina, sicut in glacie ulteriori ac grossiori. Mirum quoque apparet, quod in elemento raro, calido et humido, puta in aere, glacies sic formatur. Alia vero est glacies quæ in inferioribus generatur aquis: in qua frigoris vis major apparet. Unde subjungitur:
paras.en: Lastly, cold generates ice of two kinds. One is in the air, and this belongs to the hoar frost falling from heaven; to it may be referred what was said, [[38:29|the frost from heaven who hath gendered it|Gelu de cœlo quis genuit]]? He attributes this to the father [genuit, begot, is a father's word] because so great a force of cold does not appear in hoar frost as in ice that is more advanced and thicker. It seems wonderful too that ice should be formed in this way in an element that is rare, hot and moist, namely in the air. The other is the ice that is generated in the waters below, in which a greater force of cold appears. Hence there follows:

paras.t: In similitudinem lapidis aquæ durantur, id est, per intensum frigus sic constringuntur, ut instar saxi duræ reddantur: quod quidam de crystallo exponunt. Nam et Philosophus ait: Ex aqua generatur crystallus, remoto totaliter calido. Cui illud Ecclesiastici consonat: Frigidus ventus Aquilo flavit, et gelavit crystallus ab aqua. Circa hæc scribit Lyra: Omnia ista hic posita sunt ad ostendendum, quod non sunt ad plenum naturali ratione investigabilia hæc opera Dei. Licet enim philosophi de causis istorum aliqua dixerunt in generali, hoc tamen fuit obscure et imperfecte. Nec unquam fuit dictum ab aliquo perfecte in speciali et declaratum, quomodo res tam mollis et fluida possit in tantum solidari: et si aliquis esset qui non vidisset, nullo modo crederet dicenti, sicut de motu ferri a magnete. Et quoniam causa talium determinata ignoratur, dicitur quod habent hoc a tota specie, id est a proprietate speciem consequente: sed quæ sit illa proprietas determinata, nullus dicit. Et superficies abyssi constringitur. In frigidissimis enim terris, sicut in partibus aquilonaribus, interdum superficies Oceani congelatur, potissime circa ripas: non tamen irrumpere potest frigus aeris usque ad maris profundum.
paras.en: [[38:30|The waters are hardened like a stone|In similitudinem lapidis aquæ durantur]], that is, they are so bound together by intense cold that they are made hard like rock: which some expound of crystal. For the Philosopher too says: Crystal is generated from water when the hot is wholly removed. With this agrees that saying of Ecclesiasticus: [[Ecclus 43:22|The cold north wind bloweth, and the water is congealed into crystal|Frigidus ventus Aquilo flavit, et gelavit crystallus ab aqua]]. On these things Lyra writes: All these things are set down here to show that these works of God cannot be fully searched out by natural reason. For though the philosophers said some things about their causes in general, this was done obscurely and imperfectly. Nor has anyone ever said perfectly and in particular, and made clear, how so soft and fluid a thing can be made so solid: and if there were anyone who had not seen it, he would in no way believe one who told him of it, as with the motion of iron by the magnet. And since the determinate cause of such things is not known, they are said to have this from the whole species [that is, from their specific form as a whole, not from any one quality that can be named], that is, from a property that follows on the species; but what that determinate property is, no one says. [[38:30|and the surface of the deep is congealed|Et superficies abyssi constringitur]]. For in the coldest lands, as in the northern parts, the surface of the Ocean is sometimes frozen, especially near the shores; yet the cold of the air cannot break through to the depth of the sea.

paras.t: Numquid conjungere valebis micantes stellas Pleiades? Stellæ Pleiades alio nomine dicuntur Septistellium: suntque stellæ pluviales, habentes dominium quoddam super aquas, sicut et luna. Unde, secundum Albertum, habent virtutem movendi, elevandique humidum, et ea quæ ex humido generantur vapore. Hæ stellæ dicuntur micantes, quia etsi parvæ videantur, tamen claræ ac splendentes apparent: una tamen non evidenter et clare apparet. Quæ conjungi non valent, quamvis propinquæ sibi invicem sint: semper enim in eodem permanent situ atque in eadem ad invicem vicinitate, ab invicemque distantia, sicut et ceteræ stellæ fixæ. Ex quo sumpserunt quidam philosophi occasionem dicendi, quod astra octavæ sphæræ sint fixa in ea velut clavus in navi, et quod sphæra illa movetur, stellæque ejus motu ipsius. Plato tamen et Ptolemæus, his non obstantibus, posuerunt, stellas non esse sic fixas, sed proprio motu moveri, sphæra non mota.
paras.en: [[38:31|Shalt thou be able to join together the shining stars the Pleiades|Numquid conjungere valebis micantes stellas Pleiades]]? The stars of the Pleiades are called by another name the Septistellium [the Seven Stars]; and they are rainy stars, having a certain dominion over the waters, as the moon has too. Hence, according to Albert, they have the power of moving and raising up moisture, and the things that are generated from moist vapour. These stars are called shining because, though they seem small, yet they appear bright and splendid; one of them, however, does not appear plainly and clearly. They cannot be joined together, though they are close to one another; for they always remain in the same position and in the same nearness to one another and distance from one another, as do the other fixed stars as well. From this some philosophers took occasion to say that the stars of the eighth sphere are fixed in it like a nail in a ship, and that that sphere is moved, and its stars by its motion. Yet Plato and Ptolemy, notwithstanding this, held that the stars are not so fixed, but are moved by a motion of their own, the sphere not being moved.

paras.t: Aut gyrum Arcturi poteris dissipare? id est circuitum Ursæ majoris? in qua septem sunt stellæ, quæ nobis semper apparent, et moventur circa polum septentrionalem seu arcticum: quarum gyrum vel circumvolutionem homo dissipare aut impedire non valet, sed Deus qui omnium est creator. Denique septem sunt stellæ in Arcturo seu Ursa majori, quemadmodum in Ursa minori; sed in majori sunt stellæ majores et clariores. Quatuor quoque stellæ sunt in capite et tres in cauda. Quas Dominus nominat, quoniam sunt principium frigoris congelantis ea quæ ex humido fiunt vapore, secundum Albertum. De quibus plenius dictum est in expositione illius, Qui facit Arcturum, etc.
paras.en: [[38:31|or canst thou stop the turning about of Arcturus|Aut gyrum Arcturi poteris dissipare]]? that is, the circuit of the Great Bear? in which there are seven stars that always appear to us and are moved about the northern or arctic pole: and their turning or revolving man cannot stop or hinder, but God, who is the creator of all things. Now there are seven stars in Arcturus or the Great Bear, as in the Little Bear; but in the greater the stars are larger and brighter. Four stars, too, are in the head and three in the tail. The Lord names these because they are the source of the cold that freezes the things which come from moist vapour, according to Albert. Of these more has been said in the exposition of that verse, [[Job 9:9|Who maketh Arcturus|Qui facit Arcturum]], etc.

paras.t: Numquid producis Luciferum in tempore suo? id est, tuæ potestatis non est planetam illum tempore suo ortui deputato super horizontem tuum adducere, ejusque motum disponere. Et Vesperum super filios terræ consurgere facis? id est, planetam sic dictum non potes facere oriri terrigenis. Secundum Thomam, planeta Venus quandoque oritur ante solem, et tunc dicitur Lucifer: quandoque occidit post solem, et tunc Vesperus appellatur. Porro planetæ qui semper tardioris sunt motus quam sol, incipiunt mane apparere ante solis ortum, eo quod sol proprio motu quo movetur ab occidente in orientem deserit eas, atque pertransit ad ortum: quemadmodum patet in Saturno, Jove et Marte. Luna autem quæ habet velociorem motum quam sol, incipit apparere in sero, quasi deserens solem, et præcedens ipsum versus orientem. Venus vero et Mercurius quandoque incipiunt apparere de mane, quandoque de sero; sed de Mercurio, quia raro videtur et parvæ est quantitatis, non est tam manifestum, sicut de Venere, de quo manifestum est quod aliquando habet velociorem motum quam sol, et aliquando tardiorem. Itaque, secundum Thomam, Lucifer et Vesperus sunt idem planeta, diversa sortitus vocabula, prout diversis temporibus oritur et apparet. Porro, secundum Albertum, Lucifer semper est Venus vel Mercurius, qui habent tempus suum indicandi lucem de mane, quando secundum ordinem singulorum sunt post solem duodecim gradibus vel amplius. Tunc enim de mane ante solem emergunt. Vesperus quoque, secundum Albertum, est stella vespertina, quæ est etiam semper Venus vel Mercurius, quoniam illæ duæ stellæ perfectam distantiam a sole non habent, et sole occidente, post eum emergunt de sub radiis ejus quandoque secundum ordinem singulorum.
paras.en: [[38:32|Canst thou bring forth the day star in its time|Numquid producis Luciferum in tempore suo]]? that is, it is not in thy power to bring that planet up above thy horizon at its own time, the time appointed for its rising, and to order its motion. [[38:32|and make the evening star to rise upon the children of the earth|Et Vesperum super filios terræ consurgere facis]]? that is, thou canst not make the planet so called rise for the children of the earth. According to Thomas, the planet Venus sometimes rises before the sun, and then it is called Lucifer [that is, light-bearer: the day star]; sometimes it sets after the sun, and then it is called Vesperus [the evening star]. Further, the planets that are always of slower motion than the sun begin to appear in the morning before sunrise, because the sun, by its own motion by which it moves from west to east, leaves them behind and passes on towards the rising: as is plain in Saturn, Jupiter and Mars. But the moon, which has a swifter motion than the sun, begins to appear in the evening, as though leaving the sun behind and going before it towards the east. Venus and Mercury sometimes begin to appear in the morning, sometimes in the evening; but of Mercury, since it is seldom seen and is of small size, this is not so manifest as of Venus, of which it is manifest that it sometimes has a swifter motion than the sun and sometimes a slower. So, according to Thomas, Lucifer and Vesperus are the same planet, which has received different names according as it rises and appears at different times. Further, according to Albert, Lucifer is always Venus or Mercury, which have their time for heralding the light in the morning when, each in its own order, they are twelve degrees or more behind the sun; for then they come up in the morning before the sun. Vesperus too, according to Albert, is the evening star, which is also always Venus or Mercury, since those two stars have no full distance from the sun, and when the sun sets they come out after it from under its rays, at times, each in its own order.

paras.t: Numquid nosti ordinem cœli, id est ordinem situs et motus cœlestium corporum, vel proportionem, habitudinem, influentiam eorum ad inferiora, vel cœlestium orbium mutuam coordinationem? et pones rationem ejus in terra, id est, rationem seu causam præfati ordinis cœlestium corporum expones hominibus, scilicet propter quas causas sic instituta et coordinata sint ista? quod humanum transcendit ingenium.
paras.en: [[38:33|Dost thou know the order of heaven|Numquid nosti ordinem cœli]], that is, the order of the position and motion of the heavenly bodies, or their proportion, relation and influence on the things below, or the mutual co-ordination of the heavenly orbs? [[38:33|and canst thou set down the reason thereof on the earth|et pones rationem ejus in terra]], that is, wilt thou set out to men the reason or cause of the said order of the heavenly bodies, namely for what causes these things were so established and co-ordinated? And this surpasses human wit.

paras.t: Spiritualiter, per ordinem cœli, angelicorum spirituum hierarchica designatur distinctio: quæ ab hominibus determinate non scitur, quum divinus Dionysius angelicorum spirituum distinctiones assignet in generali, videlicet quantum ad distinctiones novem chororum.
paras.en: Spiritually, by [[38:33|the order of heaven|ordinem cœli]] is signified the hierarchical distinction of the angelic spirits, which is not known by men determinately, since the divine Dionysius assigns the distinctions of the angelic spirits in general, namely as to the distinctions of the nine choirs.

paras.t: Numquid elevabis in nebula vocem tuam? id est, numquid nebulæ jubebis, ut ad tuum præceptum ascendat, vel tonitruum generetur in ea, et tibi ad nutum obediat? et impetus aquarum operiet te? id est, in tua virtute non est, ut aqua pluvialis copiose descendat, ita ut te valeat operire. Numquid mittes fulgura, et ibunt; et revertentia dicent tibi, Adsumus? id est, tuæ potentiæ non est emittere fulgura, ita quod ad tuam dispositionem discurrant, teque præcipiente revertantur, et dicant tibi verbo vel facto, Ecce adsumus, id est, reversa sumus secundum quod imperasti.
paras.en: [[38:34|Canst thou lift up thy voice to the clouds|Numquid elevabis in nebula vocem tuam]]? that is, wilt thou command the cloud to rise at thy bidding, or thunder to be generated in it, and obey thee at a nod? [[38:34|that an abundance of waters may cover thee|et impetus aquarum operiet te]]? that is, it is not in thy power that the rain-water should come down in abundance so as to be able to cover thee. [[38:35|Canst thou send lightnings, and will they go|Numquid mittes fulgura, et ibunt]]; [[38:35|and will they return and say to thee: Here we are|et revertentia dicent tibi, Adsumus]]? that is, it is not of thy power to send forth lightnings so that they run about at thy disposal, and return at thy command, and say to thee by word or deed, Behold, here we are, that is, we have come back as thou didst command.

paras.t: Quis posuit in visceribus hominis, id est intimis ac secretissimis animæ viribus, scilicet intellectu speculativo et practico, sapientiam? Multipliciter enim Deus intellectibus hominum sapientiam indidit, utpote habitus cognoscitivos principiorum, tam in agibilibus quam in practicis; naturaleque lumen rationis, per quod naturalem sapientiam invenit homo. Insuper, per se ipsum, per angelicas mentes, per homines sanctos ac eminentes ceteros illustravit. Ipsosque homines ceteris illuminatiores, videlicet Apostolos et Prophetas ac sanctos doctores Deus multipliciter atque multiplici sapientia et scientia decoravit. Hinc Ecclesiasticus scripsit: Deus de terra creavit hominem. Creavit eis scientiam spiritus, sensu implevit corda illorum: dedit illis cor.
paras.en: [[38:36|Who hath put|Quis posuit]] [[38:36|in the heart of man|in visceribus hominis]] [the Latin says in the bowels of man], that is, in the inmost and most secret powers of the soul, namely the speculative and the practical intellect, [[38:36|wisdom|sapientiam]]? For God has put wisdom into the intellects of men in many ways: such as the habits by which first principles are known, both in matters of action and in practical ones [so printed; one would expect in speculative ones]; and the natural light of reason, by which man finds natural wisdom. Moreover he has enlightened them by himself, by the angelic minds, and by holy and eminent men. And those men more enlightened than the rest, namely the Apostles and Prophets and the holy doctors, God has adorned in many ways and with manifold wisdom and knowledge. Hence Ecclesiasticus wrote: [[Ecclus 17:1|God created man of the earth|Deus de terra creavit hominem]]. [[Ecclus 17:6|He created in them the science of the spirit, he fired their heart with wisdom|Creavit eis scientiam spiritus, sensu implevit corda illorum]]: [[Ecclus 17:5|he gave them|dedit illis]] [[Ecclus 17:5|a heart|cor]] [the margin gives Ecclus. xvii; Denis joins 17:1 and 17:6 and ends with words from 17:5].

paras.t: Vel quis dedit gallo intelligentiam, id est naturalem æstimationem, qua per modum intelligentis in aliquibus agit, determinatis horis die ac nocte cantando, quasi proportiones cœlestium cognosceret motuum, distinctionemque horarum noctis atque diei? Unde, secundum Albertum, intelligentiam vocat æstimationem, quam habet gallus de horis distinguendis ad immutationem solis ab angulis cœli in mane, meridie, vespere, media nocte. Et etiam ad immutationem auræ per dispositionem factam in aere cantat; et quædam alia animalia, quæ circa regimen suæ vitæ non sollicitantur, ideo facile deprehendunt impressiones factas in corporibus suis, vel a motu cœli, vel a dispositione aeris, et secundum illas moventur. Hinc, secundum Damascenum, aguntur magis quam agunt: quia non libere, sed secundum naturalem agunt instinctum.
paras.en: [[38:36|or who gave the cock understanding|Vel quis dedit gallo intelligentiam]], that is, a natural estimation [æstimatio: the instinctive judgment by which animals sense what is useful or harmful to them], by which it acts in some things after the manner of one who understands, crowing at fixed hours of day and night as though it knew the proportions of the heavenly motions and the division of the hours of night and day? Hence, according to Albert, he calls understanding the estimation the cock has for telling the hours by the change of the sun from the angles of heaven [the four cardinal points of the sky in astronomy], at morning, noon, evening and midnight. And it crows also at a change of the air, through a disposition brought about in the air; and so do certain other animals, which are not anxious about the ordering of their life and therefore readily catch the impressions made on their bodies, either by the motion of heaven or by the disposition of the air, and are moved according to them. Hence, according to Damascene, they are acted upon rather than act: for they act not freely but according to natural instinct.

paras.t: Quis enarrabit cœlorum rationem, id est causam, proportionem et ordinem cœlestium corporum, et cur ita disposita sint in magnitudine, multitudine, propinquitate, distantia, motu et influentia, cur tot stellæ in firmamento, quæ ratio diversitatis earum in mole, situ, luce ac proprietatibus aliis? Hæc atque similia ab homine investigari non accidit. Et concentum cœli quis dormire faciet? Per concentum cœli, intelligit cœlorum atque cœlestium motuum proportionatam cohabitudinem, et velut harmonicam quamdam convenientiam, quam creatura eis auferre non potest. Præterea advertendum quod Pythagoras et ejus sequaces, prout secundo de Cœlo refert Philosophus, posuerunt ex contactu seu motu cœlestium corporum harmonicum sonum causari: quæ sonorum consonantia, secundum eos, concentus potest vocari, qui cœlestia corpora posuerunt animata. Quam dicebant a nobis sensibiliter non percipi, quoniam ab exordio nativitatis nostræ cœpimus eam percipere, et indesinenter quasi connata est ejus perceptio ac continuata auribus nostris: sicque ex nimia assuefactione non discernimus eam, sicut qui diu sedet in fœtido loco, tandem fœtorem non percipit. Sed hanc opinionem Aristoteles reprobat. Idcirco concentus hic metaphorice dicitur convenientia præinducta.
paras.en: [[38:37|Who can declare the order of the heavens|Quis enarrabit cœlorum rationem]], that is, the cause, proportion and order of the heavenly bodies, and why they are so disposed in size, number, nearness, distance, motion and influence, why there are so many stars in the firmament, what is the reason of their diversity in mass, position, light and other properties? It does not fall to man to search out these and like things. [[38:37|or who can make the harmony of heaven to sleep|Et concentum cœli quis dormire faciet]]? By the harmony of heaven he means the proportioned relation of the heavens and of the heavenly motions to one another, and as it were a kind of harmonious agreement, which no creature can take from them. Note further that Pythagoras and his followers, as the Philosopher relates in the second book On the Heavens, held that a harmonious sound is caused by the contact or motion of the heavenly bodies; and this consonance of sounds, according to them (who held the heavenly bodies to be animate), can be called a harmony [concentus: a singing together]. They said that it is not perceived by our senses because we began to perceive it from the beginning of our birth, and its perception is unceasing, inborn as it were and continuous in our ears; and so from too great familiarity we do not discern it, as one who sits long in a fetid place in the end does not perceive the stench. But Aristotle rejects this opinion. Therefore harmony is said here metaphorically of the agreement established from the beginning.

paras.t: Præfata autem positio sapientiæ in visceribus hominis, concentusque cœli, ab initio fundationis terræ fuit vel circiter. Hinc subditur: Quando fundabatur pulvis in terra, id est, pulveres terræ firmiter locabantur in infimo loco ubi est terra; et glebæ compingebantur, id est, partes terræ pariter jungebantur per humorem eas simul tenentem et continuantem, ne terra ob suam siccitatem in pulverem resolvatur. Denique, juxta Albertum, loquitur secundum dispositionem primi mixti atque confusi, in quo elementa commixta fuerunt, et in quo per modum pulveris terra vaporabiliter ferebatur in humido. Hinc dicitur, Et glebæ compingebantur, residente scilicet pulvere in fundo, juxta illud Genesis: Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida. Istud procedit secundum unam expositionem litteræ Genesis. Glebæ autem compinguntur dupliciter. Uno modo ad locum: sicque distinguitur terra ab aliis elementis. Alio modo ad complexionem: sicque complexio quæ magis appropinquat ad cœlum seu ad cœlestem æqualitatem, meliorem in apprehendendo et appetendo sortitur dispositionem et animam, ut sexto de Animalibus asserit Avicenna. Itaque bona complexio non parvum est Dei donum.
paras.en: Now the said putting of wisdom [[38:36|in the heart of man|in visceribus hominis]], and [[38:37|the harmony of heaven|concentusque cœli]], was from the beginning of the founding of the earth, or about then. Hence there follows: [[38:38|When was the dust poured on the earth|Quando fundabatur pulvis in terra]] [Denis reads fundabatur, was founded, where the Vulgate has fundebatur, was poured], that is, when the dusts of the earth were firmly set in the lowest place, where the earth is; [[38:38|and the clods fastened together|et glebæ compingebantur]], that is, the parts of the earth were joined together by the moisture that holds them together and keeps them continuous, lest the earth by its dryness should fall apart into dust. Further, according to Albert, he speaks of the state of the first mixed and confused matter, in which the elements were mingled together, and in which the earth was borne like dust, as a vapour, in the moist. Hence it is said, [[38:38|and the clods fastened together|Et glebæ compingebantur]], the dust, that is, settling at the bottom, according to that of Genesis: [[Gen 1:9|Let the waters that are under the heaven, be gathered together into one place: and let the dry land appear|Congregentur aquæ quæ sub cœlo sunt, in locum unum, et appareat arida]]. This goes according to one exposition of the letter of Genesis. Now the clods are fastened together in two ways. In one way as to place: and so the earth is distinguished from the other elements. In another way as to complexion [complexio: the blend of the qualities hot, cold, moist and dry in a body]: and so the complexion that comes nearer to heaven, or to the heavenly evenness, receives a better disposition and soul for apprehending and desiring, as Avicenna asserts in the sixth book On Animals. So a good complexion is no small gift of God.

paras.t: Numquid capies leænæ prædam, id est sufficienter ei de alimento poteris providere, et animam, id est animalitatem seu animalem appetitum ac vitam, catulorum ejus implebis necessariis nutrimentis? quasi dicat, Non poteris. Divina tamen providentia sufficientiam sibi ac catulis suis procurant leænæ, quamvis sint multum voraces. Potius quoque leænam exprimit quam leonem, quoniam propter curam et educationem catulorum, ipsa avidior est ad prædam. Quando cubant in antris, id est in speluncis manent nutritioni catulorum vacantes, et in specubus, id est cavernis, insidiantur, id est, animalia transeuntia observant ad rapiendum ac devorandum: secundum illud Psalmi, Insidiatur quasi leo in spelunca sua.
paras.en: [[38:39|Wilt thou take the prey for the lioness|Numquid capies leænæ prædam]], that is, wilt thou be able to provide her with food enough, [[38:39|and satisfy the appetite|et animam]], that is, the animal nature, or animal appetite and life, [[38:39|of her whelps|catulorum ejus implebis]] with the nourishment they need? As if he said: Thou wilt not be able. Yet by divine providence lionesses procure enough for themselves and their whelps, though they are very voracious. And he names the lioness rather than the lion because, on account of her care for the whelps and their rearing, she is the greedier for prey. [[38:40|When they couch in the dens|Quando cubant in antris]], that is, they stay in caves, giving themselves to nourishing their whelps, and [[38:40|in holes|in specubus]], that is, in caverns, [[38:40|lie in wait|insidiantur]], that is, they watch for passing animals to seize and devour them: according to that of the Psalm, [[Ps 9:30|He lieth in wait|Insidiatur]] [[Ps 9:30|like a lion in his den|quasi leo in spelunca sua]].

paras.t: Quis præparat corvo escam suam, id est, de alimentis providet corvis, nisi principaliter Deus? quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum, id est, naturali desiderio appetunt necessaria vitæ, quæ principaliter sortiuntur a Deo. Clamant quoque ad Deum, non quasi ejus habentes notitiam, sed quasi tristem sonitum emittentes, qui a Deo attenditur, ita quod providet eis. Quælibet etenim res naturalis per hoc ipsum quod naturali desiderio appetit aliquod bonum, quodammodo interpretative seu æquivalenter clamat ad Deum, velut ab ipso illud intendens accipere, qui omnium est actor bonorum. Sicque fertur in Psalmo: Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine, et tu das escam illorum in tempore opportuno. Et rursus: Omnia a te exspectant, ut des illis escam in tempore.
paras.en: [[38:41|Who provideth food for the raven|Quis præparat corvo escam suam]], that is, who provides food for ravens, if not principally God? [[38:41|when her young ones cry to God|quando pulli ejus clamant ad Deum]], that is, they desire with natural desire the necessaries of life, which they receive principally from God. They cry to God, too, not as having knowledge of him, but as uttering a mournful sound, which God attends to, so that he provides for them. For every natural thing, by the very fact that it desires some good with natural desire, in some way cries to God interpretatively or equivalently [that is, its desire amounts to a cry, though it is not one in form], as though intending to receive that good from him who is the author of all goods. And so it is said in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:15|The eyes of all hope in thee, O Lord: and thou givest them meat in due season|Oculi omnium in te sperant, Domine, et tu das escam illorum in tempore opportuno]]. And again: [[Ps 103:27|All expect of thee that thou give them food in season|Omnia a te exspectant, ut des illis escam in tempore]].

paras.t: Vagantes, eo quod non habeant cibos. Pullis corvorum, pro tempore quo a matribus suis non aluntur, ut dicitur, scilicet infra septem primos dies, non competit vagari seu hinc inde volare. Ideo quidam legunt, Vagientes, scilicet suo modo quasi plorantes ex famis angustia. Vel, Vagantes, id est visu hinc inde distracti ac prospicientes, quia nutrimentum non habent. Dicitur enim (ut recitat et Thomas), quod corvus pullos suos natos videns plumis albos, non pascit eos donec cernat eos nigrescere, ita quod septem diebus eos non alit, sed a Deo sustentantur per inditam eis naturalem virtutem. Alii autem affirmant, quod Deo ordinante, quidam vermiculi volitant circa ora eorum, quos attrahunt, sicque aluntur. Insuper, secundum Albertum, nominat corvum magis quam cetera bruta, quia voracior et cibi avidior est: cujus signum est, quia, ut in Genesi habetur, emissus ex arca, requievit in cadavere.
paras.en: [[38:41|wandering about, because they have no meat|Vagantes, eo quod non habeant cibos]]. It does not suit the young of ravens to wander or fly about here and there in the time when they are not fed by their mothers, as is said, namely within the first seven days. Therefore some read Vagientes [wailing, for Vagantes, wandering], that is, as it were weeping in their own way from the distress of hunger. Or, Vagantes, that is, with their sight drawn this way and that, looking about, because they have no food. For it is said (as Thomas too relates) that the raven, seeing its newly hatched young white with down, does not feed them until it sees them turning black, so that for seven days it does not nourish them, but they are sustained by God through a natural power put into them. Others affirm that by God's ordering certain little worms fly about their mouths, which they draw in, and so they are fed. Moreover, according to Albert, he names the raven rather than the other brute beasts because it is more voracious and greedier for food: a sign of which is that, as we read in Genesis, when it was sent out of the ark it rested on a carcass[[Gen 8:7||]] [the margin note is unread; the raven is sent out of the ark at Gen 8:7, and the carcass comes from the traditional gloss, not from the text].

paras.t: Postremo, ex his clare ostenditur falsitas opinantium, quod Deus irrationalium animalium providentiam et distinctam cognitionem non habeat. Nam et Psalmista testatur: Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum. Christus quoque in Evangelio errorem hunc destruens, ait: Nonne quinque passeres veneunt dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo? Et iterum asserit: Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea, scilicet volatilia cœli. Nec obstat illud Apostoli: Numquid de bobus cura est Deo? Hoc siquidem dicit ad innuendum, quod rationalium creaturarum cura et providentia, speciali altiorique modo convenit Deo.
paras.en: Lastly, from these things is clearly shown the falsehood of those who think that God has no providence over irrational animals and no distinct knowledge of them. For the Psalmist too bears witness: [[Ps 146:9|Who giveth to beasts their food: and to the young ravens that call upon him|Qui dat jumentis escam ipsorum, et pullis corvorum invocantibus eum]]. Christ too, overthrowing this error in the Gospel, says: [[Luke 12:6|Are not five sparrows sold for two farthings, and not one of them is forgotten before God?|Nonne quinque passeres veneunt dipondio, et unus ex illis non est in oblivione coram Deo?]] And again he asserts: [[Matt 6:26|your heavenly Father feedeth them|Pater vester cœlestis pascit ea]], namely the birds of the air. Nor does that saying of the Apostle stand in the way: [[1 Cor 9:9|Doth God take care for oxen?|Numquid de bobus cura est Deo?]] For he says this to suggest that the care and providence of rational creatures belongs to God in a special and higher way.
